. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Aṅguttaranikāye

The Aṅguttara Nikāya

Dukanipāta-ṭīkā

Subcommentary on the Book of the Twos

1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

1. The First Fifty

1. Kammakāraṇavaggo

1. The Chapter on Instruments of Torture

1. Vajjasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Vajja Sutta

1. Dukanipātassa [M 2.0001][V 2.0001] paṭhame pahārasādhanatthanti daṇḍappahārassa sukhasiddhi-atthaṃ. Kañjito nibbattaṃ kañjiyaṃ, āranālaṃ, yaṃ bilaṅgantipi vuccati, taṃ yattha siñcati, sā kañjiyaukkhalikā bilaṅgathālikā, taṃsadisaṃ kāraṇaṃ bilaṅgathālikaṃ. Sīsakaṭāhaṃ uppāṭetvāti ayoguḷappavesappamāṇaṃ chiddaṃ katvā. Saṅkhamuṇḍakammakāraṇanti saṅkhaṃ viya muṇḍakaraṇaṃ kammakāraṇaṃ. Rāhumukhakammakāraṇanti rāhumukhagatasūriyasadisakammakāraṇaṃ.

1. In the first of the Book of the Twos, the phrase 'for the purpose of accomplishing a strike' means for the purpose of easily achieving a blow with a stick. Kañjiyaṃ is what is produced from fermented rice-gruel, that is, sour gruel, which is also called bilaṅga. The vessel into which it is poured is a kañjiyaukkhalikā or bilaṅgathālikā (a sour gruel pot). An instrument of torture similar to that is the bilaṅgathālikaṃ. 'Having torn open the skull-pan' means having made a hole the size for an iron ball to enter. The saṅkhamuṇḍaka instrument of torture is one that shaves the head like a conch shell. The rāhumukha instrument of torture is one that makes one resemble the sun that has entered Rāhu's mouth.

Jotimālikanti [V 2.0002] jotimālavantaṃ kammakāraṇaṃ. Hatthapajjotikanti hatthassa pajjotanakammakāraṇaṃ. Erakavattakammakāraṇanti erakavattasadise sarīrato cammavatte uppāṭanakammakāraṇaṃ. Cīrakavāsikakammakāraṇanti sarīrato uppāṭitavattacīrakehi nivāsāpanakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā yathā gīvato paṭṭhāya vaddhe kantitvā kaṭiyaṃ ṭhapenti, evaṃ gopphakato paṭṭhāya kantitvāpi kaṭiyameva ṭhapenti. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana [M 2.0002] “kaṭito paṭṭhāya kantitvā gopphakesu ṭhapentī”ti vuttaṃ. Eṇeyyakakammakāraṇanti eṇimigasadisakammakāraṇaṃ. Ayavalayāni datvāti ayavalayāni paṭimuñcitvā. Ayasūlāni koṭṭentīti kapparajaṇṇukakoṭīsu ayasūlāni pavesenti. Tanti taṃ tathākatakammakāraṇaṃ sattaṃ.

'The jotimālikā' means an instrument of torture involving a garland of flames. 'The hatthapajjotikā' means an instrument of torture that makes the hands into a torch. 'The erakavattaka instrument of torture' means one that tears strips of skin from the body in the manner of a reed mat. 'The cīrakavāsika instrument of torture' means one that makes a person wear strips of bark torn from their own body. When doing this, just as they cut strips from the neck downwards and place them at the waist, so too they cut from the ankles upwards and place them at the waist. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'They cut from the waist downwards and place them at the ankles.' 'The eṇeyyaka instrument of torture' means one that makes a person resemble an antelope. 'Having given iron rings' means having fastened on iron rings. 'They hammer in iron spikes' means they drive iron spikes into the tips of the elbows and knees. 'That' refers to that being who is subjected to such an instrument of torture.

Baḷisamaṃsikanti balisehi maṃsuppāṭanakammakāraṇaṃ. Kahāpaṇikanti kahāpaṇamattaso chindanakammakāraṇaṃ. Koṭṭentīti chindanti. Khārāpatacchikanti tacchetvā khārāpasiñcanakammakāraṇaṃ. Palighaparivattikanti palighassa viya parivattanakammakāraṇaṃ. Ekābaddhaṃ karonti ayasūlassa koṭṭanena. Palālapīṭhakanti palālapīṭhassa viya sarīrassa saṃvellanakammakāraṇaṃ. Kāraṇikāti ghātanakārakā. Palālavaṭṭiṃ viya katvāti yathā palālapīṭhaṃ karontā palālaṃ vaṭṭiṃ katvā saṃvellanavasena puna veṭhenti, evaṃ karontīti attho. Chātakasunakhehīti khuddakehi koleyyakasunakhehi. Te hi balavantā javayogā sūrā ca honti. Sahassabhaṇḍikanti sahassatthavikaṃ.

'The baḷisamaṃsika' means an instrument of torture for tearing out flesh with fishhooks. 'The kahāpaṇika' means an instrument of torture for cutting off pieces the size of a coin. 'They strike' means they cut. 'The khārāpatacchika' means an instrument of torture involving scraping the body and sprinkling it with a caustic substance. 'The palighaparivattika' means an instrument of torture involving turning one around like a door-bar. They make the person a single fixture by hammering with an iron stake. 'The palālapīṭhaka' means an instrument of torture involving rolling up the body like a straw mat. 'Executioners' means the killers. 'Having made it like a straw roll' means: just as those making a straw mat make a roll of straw and then wrap it again by rolling, so they do this; this is the meaning. 'By hungry dogs' means by small, well-bred dogs. For they are strong, swift, and fierce. 'A thousand-fold penalty' means a purse of a thousand.

Yāhanti yaṃ ahaṃ. Yanti ca kāraṇavacanaṃ. Tenāha “yena aha”nti. Chinnamūlaketi taṇhāmūlassa ucchinnattā sañchinnamūlake.

'Yāhaṃ' means 'which I.' And 'yena' is a word indicating cause. Therefore it is said, 'by which I.' 'With root cut off' means, because the root of craving is severed, 'with root completely cut off.'

Vajjasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vajja Sutta is finished.

2. Padhānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Padhāna Sutta

2. Dutiye ubhatobyūḷhasaṅgāmappavesanasadisanti yuddhatthāya ubhatorāsikatacaturaṅginisenāmajjhappavesanasadisaṃ. Dānañca yuddhañca samānamāhūti ettha kathaṃ panīdamubhayaṃ samānaṃ? Jīvitavināsabhīruko hi yujjhituṃ na sakkoti, bhogakkhayabhīruko dānaṃ dātuṃ na sakkoti. “Jīvitañca rakkhissāmi, yujjhissāmī”ti hi vadanto na yujjhati, jīvite pana ālayaṃ vissajjetvā “hatthapādādicchedo vā hotu maraṇaṃ vā, gaṇhissāmetaṃ issariya”nti ussahantova yujjhati[V 2.0003]. “Bhoge ca rakkhissāmi, dānañca dassāmī”ti vadantopi na dadāti, bhogesu pana ālayaṃ pissajjetvā “mahādānaṃ dassāmī”ti ussahantova deti. Evaṃ [M 2.0003] dānañca yuddhañca samaṃ hoti. Kiñca bhiyyo – appāpi santā bahuke jinanti, yathā ca yuddhe appakāpi vīrapurisā bahuke bhīrupurise jinanti, evaṃ saddhādisampanno appakampi dānaṃ dadanto bahuvidhaṃ lobhadosaissāmacchariyadiṭṭhivicikicchādibhedaṃ tappaṭipakkhaṃ abhibhavati, bahuñca dānavipākaṃ adhigacchati. Evampi dānañca yuddhañca samānaṃ. Tenāha “appampi ce saddahāno dadāti, teneva so hoti sukhī paratthā”ti.

2. In the second, 'like entering a battle drawn up on both sides' means like entering the middle of a four-limbed army amassed on both sides for battle. As to 'they say giving and battle are the same': how are these two the same? One who is afraid of losing his life cannot fight; one who is afraid of the destruction of his wealth cannot give a gift. One who says, 'I will protect my life and I will fight,' does not fight; only one who abandons longing for life and exerts himself, thinking, 'Let my hands and feet be cut off or let there be death, I will seize this sovereignty!' truly fights. Similarly, one who says, 'I will protect my wealth and I will give a gift,' does not give; only one who abandons longing for his wealth and exerts himself, thinking, 'I will give a great gift!' truly gives. Thus giving and battle are the same. Furthermore, regarding 'though few, they conquer many': just as in battle a few heroes conquer many cowards, so one endowed with faith and other virtues, though giving only a little, overcomes his various opponents—greed, hatred, envy, stinginess, wrong views, doubt, and so on—and he attains the great fruit of giving. In this way, too, giving and battle are the same. Therefore it is said: 'If, having faith, one gives even a little, by that alone one becomes happy in the next world.'

Agārassa hitaṃ kasigorakkhādi agāriyaṃ, taṃ natthi etthāti anagāriyaṃ, pabbajjāti āha “agārassa…pe… anagāriyaṃ pabbajja”nti. Sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggatthāyāti ettha cattāro upadhī – kāmupadhi, khandhupadhi, kilesupadhi, abhisaṅkhārupadhīti. Kāmāpi hi “yaṃ pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ kāmānaṃ assādo”ti (a. ni. 9.34) evaṃ vuttassa sukhassa, tadassādanimittassa vā dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato upadhīyati ettha sukhanti iminā vacanatthena “upadhī”ti vuccanti. Khandhāpi khandhamūlakassa dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, kilesāpi apāyadukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, abhisaṅkhārāpi bhavadukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato “upadhī”ti vuccanti. Sabbesaṃ upadhīnaṃ paṭinissaggo pahānaṃ etthāti sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggaṃ, nibbānaṃ. Tenāha “sabbesaṃ khandhūpadhi…pe… nibbānassa atthāyā”ti.

What is beneficial for the household, such as agriculture and cattle-herding, is the household life (agāriyaṃ). That which is not this is the homeless life (anagāriyaṃ), that is, the going forth (pabbajjā). Thus it is said: 'beneficial for the household… the homeless life, the going forth.' Regarding 'for the sake of relinquishing all acquisitions': Here there are four acquisitions: the acquisition of sensual pleasures, the acquisition of the aggregates, the acquisition of the defilements, and the acquisition of volitional formations. Sensual pleasures are called 'acquisitions' (upadhi) with the meaning 'pleasure is placed upon this' (upadhīyati), because they are the basis for the pleasure spoken of thus: 'Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on the five cords of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification in sensual pleasures' (AN 9.34), or because they are the basis for the suffering that is the sign of that gratification. The aggregates, too, are called 'acquisitions' because they are the basis for suffering rooted in the aggregates. The defilements are called 'acquisitions' because they are the basis for the suffering of the plane of misery. Volitional formations are called 'acquisitions' because they are the basis for the suffering of existence. The relinquishing of all acquisitions is their abandonment; this is the 'relinquishing of all acquisitions,' Nibbāna. Therefore it is said: 'for the sake of Nibbāna, which is the relinquishing of all acquisitions such as the aggregates....'

Padhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Padhāna Sutta is finished.

3. Tapanīyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Tapanīya Sutta

3. Tatiye tapanīyāti ettha kattuatthe anīya-saddoti āha “tapantīti tapanīyā”ti. Tapantīti vibādhenti, viheṭhentīti attho. Tapanaṃ vā dukkhaṃ, diṭṭhe ceva dhamme abhisamparāyañca tassa uppādanena ceva anubalappadānena ca hitāti tapanīyā. Atha vā tapanti tenāti tapanaṃ, anutāpo, vippaṭisāroti attho. Tassa hetubhāvato hitāti tapanīyā. Anusocatīti vippaṭisārī hutvā katākataṃ anugamma socati. Socanañhi katattā ca hoti akatattā ca. Tathā ceva pāḷiyaṃ vibhattaṃ. Nandayakkhādīnaṃ vatthūni pākaṭānīti tāni [V 2.0004] adassetvā [M 2.0004] dvebhātikavatthuṃ dassento “te kirā”ti ādimāha. Tattha teti dve bhātaro. Puna kiṃ maggasīti puna kiṃ icchasi.

3. In the third, regarding 'tapanīyā', the word 'anīya' is in the sense of agent; thus it is said, 'they torment, therefore they are tormenting' (tapantīti tapanīyā). 'They torment' means they afflict, they harass. Or, torment (tapanaṃ) is suffering. They are 'tormenting' (tapanīyā) because they are conducive to producing and strengthening that suffering both in the present life and in the life to come. Alternatively, 'one torments by means of it, thus it is torment' (tapanti tenāti tapanaṃ); the meaning is remorse, regret. Because they are a cause of that, they are 'tormenting' (tapanīyā). 'He grieves afterward' (anusocati) means that, having become regretful, he grieves in consequence of what was done and what was not done. For grief arises from what has been done and from what has not been done. Thus it is analyzed in the Pāli. Since the stories of the yakkha Nanda and others are well-known, without relating them, he introduces the story of the two brothers, beginning with the words, 'It is said that they...' (te kirā). Therein, 'they' (te) means the two brothers. 'What more do you seek?' (puna kiṃ maggasi) means 'What more do you want?'

Tapanīyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Tapanīya Sutta is finished.

5. Upaññātasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Upaññāta Sutta

5. Pañcame imañhi dhammadvayanti kusalesu dhammesu asantuṭṭhitā, padhānasmiṃ anosakkanasaṅkhātaṃ dhammadvayaṃ. Imināti “asantuṭṭhitā kusalesu dhammesū”ti vacanena. Imaṃ dīpetīti “yāva so uppajjati, na tāvāhaṃ santuṭṭho ahosi”nti etaṃ pariyantaṃ katvā vakkhamānatthaṃ dīpeti. Padhānasminti vīriyārambhe. Imamatthanti “padhānasmiñcā”tiādinā vuttamatthaṃ. Vīriyappavāhe vattamāne antarā eva paṭigamanaṃ nivattanaṃ paṭivānaṃ, tadassa atthīti paṭivānī, na paṭivānī appaṭivānī, tassa bhāvo appaṭivānitā, anosakkanāti āha “appaṭivānitāti appaṭikkamanā anosakkanā”ti. Tattha anosakkanāti appaṭinivatti.

5. In the fifth, this pair of states means the pair of states called discontent with wholesome states and not shrinking back in striving. By this means by the words 'discontent with wholesome states.' He clarifies this, that is, he clarifies the meaning to be explained by setting a limit with the statement: 'So long as that had not arisen, I was not content.' In striving means in the arousal of energy. This meaning is the meaning stated in the passage beginning 'and in striving.' When the stream of energy is flowing, turning back in the middle is regression (paṭivāna). One who has this is one who regresses (paṭivānī); one who does not regress is an appaṭivānī. The state of being such is non-regression (appaṭivānitā), which is not shrinking back. Thus he says: 'Non-regression means not turning back, not shrinking back.' Therein, not shrinking back means not retreating.

Āgamanīyapaṭipadāti samathavipassanāsaṅkhātā pubbabhāgapaṭipatti. Sā hi āgacchanti visesamadhigacchanti etāya, āgacchati vā visesādhigamo etāyāti āgamanīyā, sā eva paṭipajjitabbato paṭipadāti āgamanīyapaṭipadā. Appaṭivānapadhānanti osakkanārahitappadhānaṃ, antarā anosakkitvā katavīriyanti attho.

The path leading to arrival is the preliminary-part practice consisting of serenity and insight. For by means of it one arrives at and attains distinction, or by means of it the attainment of distinction arrives; thus it is 'leading to arrival.' Because it is to be practiced, it is a 'path.' Hence it is 'the path leading to arrival.' Effort without regression means effort devoid of shrinking back; the meaning is energy exerted without shrinking back in the middle.

Upaññātasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Upaññāta Sutta is finished.

6. Saṃyojanasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Saṃyojana Sutta

6. Chaṭṭhe saṃyojanānaṃ hitā paccayabhāvenāti saṃyojaniyā, tebhūmakā dhammā. Tenāha “dasannaṃ saṃyojanāna”ntiādi. Saṃyojaniye dhamme assādato anupassati sīlenāti assādānupassī, tassa bhāvo assādānupassitā. Nibbidānupassitāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ukkaṇṭhanavasenāti saṃyojaniyesu tebhūmakadhammesu nibbindanavasena. Jananaṃ jāti, khandhānaṃ pātubhāvoti āha “jātiyāti khandhanibbattito”ti, khandhānaṃ tattha tattha bhave aparāparaṃ nibbattitoti attho. Khandhaparipāko [M 2.0005] ekabhavapariyāpannānaṃ khandhānaṃ purāṇabhāvo. Ekabhavapariyāpannajīvitindriyappabandhavicchedavasena [V 2.0005] khandhānaṃ bhedo idha maraṇanti āha “maraṇenāti khandhabhedato”ti. Antonijjhānaṃ cittasantāpo. Paridevo nāma ñātibyasanādīhi phuṭṭhassa vācāvippalāpo. So ca sokasamuṭṭhānoti āha “tannissitalālappitalakkhaṇehi paridevehī”ti. Lālappitaṃ vācāvippalāpo, so ca atthato saddoyeva.

6. In the sixth: They are conducive to the fetters by being their condition, thus they are things pertaining to the fetters (saṃyojaniyā); these are phenomena of the three planes. Hence he says: 'of the ten fetters,' and so on. One who habitually contemplates gratification in things pertaining to the fetters is one who contemplates gratification; the state of being such is contemplation of gratification. The same method applies also to contemplation of disenchantment. By way of agitation means by way of becoming disenchanted with the phenomena of the three planes that pertain to the fetters. Generation is birth, the manifestation of the aggregates. Thus he says: 'By birth means from the production of the aggregates.' The meaning is the successive production of the aggregates in this or that existence. The maturing of the aggregates is the aging of the aggregates comprised within a single existence. The breakup of the aggregates by way of the cutting off of the continuity of the life faculty comprised within a single existence is here 'death.' Thus he says: 'By death means from the breakup of the aggregates.' Inner burning is mental torment. Lamentation is the verbal raving of one who is afflicted by such things as the loss of relatives. And it arises from sorrow. Thus he says: 'by lamentations having the characteristic of wailing that is dependent on that.' Wailing is verbal raving, and in essence it is just sound.

Dukkhanti idha kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ adhippetanti āha “kāyapaṭipīḷanadukkhehī”ti. Manovighātadomanassehīti manaso vighātakarehi domanassehi. Byāpādasampayogena manaso vihananarasañhi domanassaṃ. Bhuso āyāso upāyāso yathā “bhusamādānaṃ upādāna”nti, so ca atthato ñātibyasanādīhi phuṭṭhassa adhimattacetodukkhappabhāvito dosoyeva. Kāyacittānañhi āyāsanavasena dosasseva pavattiākāro upāyāsoti vuccati saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpanno. Taṃ cuddasahi akusalacetasikehi añño eko cetasikadhammoti eke. Yaṃ visādoti ca vadanti.

Pain: here bodily pain is intended. Thus he says: 'by pains of bodily affliction.' By mental distress and displeasure means by displeasure that causes mental distress. For displeasure has the characteristic of striking the mind through its association with ill will. Intense trouble is distress (upāyāso), just as 'intense taking is clinging' (upādāna). And in essence this is just hatred, produced by the excessive mental pain of one afflicted by such things as the loss of relatives. For the mode of occurrence of hatred by way of the trouble of body and mind is called 'distress,' which is included in the aggregate of formations. Some say that it is a single mental factor different from the fourteen unwholesome mental factors. And they call it 'dejection.'

Saṃyojanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṃyojana Sutta is finished.

7. Kaṇhasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Kaṇha Sutta

7. Sattame yathā “kaṇhā gāvī”tiādīsu kāḷavaṇṇena samannāgatā “kaṇhā”ti vuccati, na evaṃ kāḷavaṇṇatāya dhammā “kaṇhā”ti vuccanti, atha kho kaṇhābhijātinibbattihetuto appabhassarabhāvakaraṇato vā “kaṇhā”ti vuccantīti dassento “na kāḷavaṇṇatāyā”tiādimāha. Kaṇhatāyāti kaṇhābhijātitāya. Kaṇhābhijātīti ca apāyā vuccanti manussesu ca dobhaggiyaṃ. Sarasenāti sabhāvena. Na hirīyati na lajjatīti ahiriko, puggalo, cittaṃ, taṃ sampayuttadhammasamudāyo vā. Tassa bhāvo ahirikkanti vattabbe ekassa ka-kārassa lopaṃ katvā ahirikanti vuttanti āha “ahirikanti ahirikabhāvo”ti. Na ottappatīti anottāpī, puggalo, yathāvuttadhammasamudāyo vā, tassa bhāvo anottappanti āha “anottāpibhāvo”ti.

7. In the seventh, just as in such phrases as 'a black cow,' what possesses a black color is called 'black.' However, phenomena are not called 'black' because of their black color. Rather, to show that they are called 'black' because they are a cause for rebirth in a dark destiny or because they produce a state of non-radiance, the text says 'not because of black color,' etc. 'By blackness' means by a dark destiny. And 'dark destiny' refers to the planes of misery and, among humans, misfortune. 'By its essence' means by its intrinsic nature. 'He is not ashamed, he does not feel shame': this defines a shameless person (ahiriko), or a shameless mind, or the collection of associated phenomena. Its state is shamelessness (ahirikkaṃ), but with the elision of one letter 'k' it is stated as ahirikaṃ. Thus he says: 'Ahirikaṃ is the state of shamelessness.' 'He does not have moral dread': this defines a person without moral dread (anottāpī), or the aforementioned collection of phenomena. Its state is lack of moral dread (anottappaṃ). Thus he says: 'the state of being without moral dread.'

Kaṇhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kaṇha Sutta is finished.

8. Sukkasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sukka Sutta

8. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0006] “sukkaṃ vattha”ntiādīsu viya na vaṇṇasukkatāya dhammānaṃ sukkatā, atha kho [V 2.0006] sukkābhijātihetuto pabhassarabhāvakaraṇato cāti dassento “na vaṇṇasukkatāyā”tiādimāha. Sukkatāyāti sukkābhijātitāya. Hirī pāpadhamme gūthaṃ viya passantī jigucchatīti āha “pāpato jigucchanalakkhaṇā hirī”ti. Ottappaṃ te uṇhaṃ viya passantaṃ tato bhāyatīti vuttaṃ “bhāyanalakkhaṇaṃ otappa”nti. Idañca hirottappaṃ aññamaññavippayogī pāpato vimukhabhūtañca, tasmā nesaṃ idaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ – ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā hirī, bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ. Attādhipati hirī, lokādhipati otappaṃ. Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā hirī, bhayasabhāvasaṇṭhitaṃ ottappaṃ. Sappatissavalakkhaṇā hirī, vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappanti.

8. In the eighth, just as in such phrases as 'a white cloth,' the whiteness of phenomena is not due to whiteness of color, but rather because it is a cause for a bright destiny and produces a radiant state. To show this, he says, 'not because of whiteness of color,' etc. 'By whiteness' means by a bright destiny. Moral shame (hirī) is disgusted by evil as one is disgusted by filth; thus it is said: 'Moral shame has the characteristic of disgust at evil.' Moral dread (ottappa) fears evil as one fears something hot; thus it is said: 'Moral dread has the characteristic of fear.' And this moral shame and moral dread are inseparable from each other and are averse to evil. Therefore, this is their distinction: Moral shame arises internally; moral dread arises externally. Moral shame has the self as sovereign; moral dread has the world as sovereign. Moral shame is established in the nature of modesty; moral dread is established in the nature of fear. Moral shame has the characteristic of respect; moral dread has the characteristic of seeing danger and being fearful of wrongdoing.

Tattha ajjhattasamuṭṭhānaṃ hiriṃ catūhi kāraṇehi samuṭṭhāpeti jātiṃ paccavekkhitvā, vayaṃ, sūrabhāvaṃ, bāhusaccaṃ paccavekkhitvā. Kathaṃ? “Pāpakaraṇaṃ nāmetaṃ na jātisampannānaṃ kammaṃ, hīnajaccānaṃ kevaṭṭādīnaṃ kammaṃ, mādisassa jātisampannassa idaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ tāva jātiṃ paccavekkhitvā pāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā “pāpakaraṇaṃ nāmetaṃ daharehi kattabbaṃ kammaṃ, mādisassa vaye ṭhitassa idaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ vayaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā “pāpakaraṇaṃ nāmetaṃ dubbalajātikānaṃ kammaṃ, mādisassa sūrabhāvasampannassa idaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ sūrabhāvaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā “pāpakammaṃ nāmetaṃ andhabālānaṃ kammaṃ, na paṇḍitānaṃ, mādisassa paṇḍitassa bahussutassa idaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ bāhusaccaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ ajjhattasamuṭṭhānaṃ hiriṃ catūhi kāraṇehi samuṭṭhāpeti, samuṭṭhāpento ca hiriṃ nissāya pāpakammaṃ na karoti.

Therein, one arouses internally arisen moral shame for four reasons: by reflecting on one's birth, age, heroism, and great learning. How so? 'To do an evil deed is not the action of the well-born; it is the action of those of low birth, such as fishermen. It is not proper for one like me, who is well-born, to do this.' Thus, by reflecting on one's birth, one refrains from evil and arouses moral shame. Similarly: 'To do an evil deed is the action of the young. It is not proper for one like me, who is advanced in age, to do this.' Thus, by reflecting on one's age, one refrains from evil and arouses moral shame. Likewise: 'To do an evil deed is the action of the weak. It is not proper for one like me, who is endowed with heroism, to do this.' Thus, by reflecting on one's heroism, one refrains from evil and arouses moral shame. Similarly: 'To do an evil deed is the action of the blind and foolish, not of the wise. It is not proper for one like me, who is wise and learned, to do this.' Thus, by reflecting on one's great learning, one refrains from evil and arouses moral shame. In this way, one arouses internally arisen moral shame for these four reasons. And having aroused moral shame, relying on it, one does not commit evil deeds.

Kathaṃ bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ? “Sace tvaṃ pāpakammaṃ karissasi, catūsu parisāsu garahappatto bhavissasi, tato taṃ sīlavanto sabrahmacārī vivajjissantī”ti paccavekkhitvā bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ nissāya pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Evaṃ bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ.

How is moral dread externally arisen? Reflecting, 'If you do an evil deed, you will incur blame in the four assemblies, and then the virtuous among your spiritual companions will shun you,' one relies on externally arisen moral dread and does not commit an evil deed. Thus is moral dread externally arisen.

Kathaṃ [M 2.0007] attādhipati hirī? Idhekacco kulaputto attānaṃ adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā “mādisassa saddhāpabbajitassa bahussutassa dhutadharassa na yuttaṃ pāpakammaṃ kātu”nti pāpaṃ na karoti. Evaṃ attādhipati hirī. Tenāha bhagavā “so attānaṃyeva adhipatiṃ karitvā akusalaṃ pajahati, kusalaṃ bhāveti, sāvajjaṃ pajahati, anavajjaṃ bhāveti, suddhaṃ attānaṃ pariharatī”ti (a. ni. 3.40).

How does moral shame have the self as sovereign? Here, a certain clansman, having made the self his sovereign and chief, reflects: 'It is not proper for one like me—who has gone forth in faith, is learned, and observes the ascetic practices—to do an evil deed.' Thus he does not do evil. In this way moral shame has the self as sovereign. For this reason the Blessed One has said: 'Having made the self his sovereign, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; he maintains himself in purity' (AN 3.40).

Kathaṃ [V 2.0007] lokādhipati ottappaṃ? Idhekacco kulaputto lokaṃ adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā “sace kho tvaṃ pāpakammaṃ kareyyāsi, sabrahmacārino tāva taṃ jānissanti, mahiddhikā mahānubhāvā loke ca samaṇabrāhmaṇā devatā ca, tasmā te na yuttaṃ pāpaṃ kātu”nti pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Yathāha – “mahā kho panāyaṃ lokasannivāso, mahantasmiṃ kho pana lokasannivāse santi samaṇabrāhmaṇā iddhimanto dibbacakkhukā paracittaviduno. Te dūratopi passanti, āsannāpi na dissanti, cetasāpi cittaṃ jānanti, tepi maṃ evaṃ jānissanti ‘passatha, bho, imaṃ kulaputtaṃ, saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito samāno vokiṇṇo viharati pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehī’ti. Santi devatā iddhimantiniyo dibbacakkhukā paracittaviduniyo, tā dūratopi passanti, āsannāpi na dissanti, cetasāpi cittaṃ jānanti, tāpi maṃ jānissanti ‘passatha, bho, imaṃ kulaputtaṃ, saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito samāno vokiṇṇo viharati pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehī’ti…pe… so lokaṃyeva adhipatiṃ karitvā akusalaṃ…pe… pariharatī”ti. Evaṃ lokādhipati ottappaṃ.

How does moral dread have the world as sovereign? Here, a certain clansman, having made the world his sovereign and chief, reflects: 'If you were to do an evil deed, your spiritual companions would know it, and so would the ascetics and brahmins in the world who are powerful and mighty, and the deities too. Therefore it is not proper for you to do evil.' Thus he does not commit an evil deed. As it is said: 'This world-assemblage is vast. And in this vast world-assemblage there are ascetics and brahmins who possess psychic power, the divine eye, and who know the minds of others. They see from afar, yet are not seen when near; they know the mind with their own mind. They will know me thus: “Look, sirs, at this clansman! Though he went forth from the home life into homelessness in faith, he dwells intermingled with evil, unwholesome states.” There are also deities who possess psychic power, the divine eye, and who know the minds of others. They see from afar... They too will know me thus: “Look, sirs, at this clansman... who dwells intermingled with evil, unwholesome states.” ... So, having made the world his sovereign, he abandons the unwholesome ... and maintains himself in purity.' Thus moral dread has the world as sovereign.

Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitāti ettha lajjāti lajjanākāro, tena sabhāvena saṇṭhitā hirī. Bhayanti apāyabhayaṃ, tena sabhāvena saṇṭhitaṃ ottappaṃ. Tadubhayaṃ pāpaparivajjane pākaṭaṃ hoti. Tattha yathā dvīsu ayoguḷesu eko sītalo bhaveyya gūthamakkhito, eko uṇho āditto. Tesu yathā sītalaṃ gūthamakkhitattā jigucchanto viññujātiko na gaṇhāti, itaraṃ ḍāhabhayena. Evaṃ paṇḍito lajjāya jigucchanto pāpaṃ na karoti, ottappena apāyabhayabhīto pāpaṃ na karoti, evaṃ lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā hirī, bhayasabhāvasaṇṭhitaṃ ottappaṃ.

Regarding 'established in the nature of modesty': herein 'modesty' (lajjā) is the state of being ashamed; moral shame (hirī) is established by that nature. 'Fear' (bhaya) is the fear of the planes of misery; moral dread (ottappa) is established by that nature. Both become manifest in the avoidance of evil. It is as if there were two iron balls, one cold and smeared with excrement, the other hot and blazing. A sensible person would not take hold of the cold one because, being smeared with excrement, it is disgusting; and he would not take hold of the other for fear of being burned. Similarly, a wise person, being disgusted with evil through his sense of modesty, does not commit evil; and being fearful of the planes of misery through his moral dread, he does not commit evil. Thus moral shame is established in the nature of modesty, and moral dread is established in the nature of fear.

Kathaṃ [M 2.0008] sappatissavalakkhaṇā hirī, vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ? Ekacco hi jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇā, satthumahattapaccavekkhaṇā, dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇā, sabrahmacārimahattapaccavekkhaṇāti evaṃ catūhi kāraṇehi tattha gāravena sappatissavalakkhaṇaṃ hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā pāpaṃ na karoti. Ekacco attānuvādabhayaṃ, parānuvādabhayaṃ, daṇḍabhayaṃ, duggatibhayanti evaṃ catūhi kāraṇehi vajjato bhāyanto vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Ettha ca ajjhattasamuṭṭhānāditā hirottappānaṃ tattha tattha pākaṭabhāvena vuttā, na pana nesaṃ kadāci aññamaññavippayogo. Na hi lajjanaṃ nibbhayaṃ, pāpabhayaṃ vā alajjanaṃ atthīti. Evamettha vitthārato atthavaṇṇanā veditabbā.

How does moral shame (hirī) have the characteristic of respect, and moral dread (ottappa) the characteristic of seeing danger and being fearful of what is blameworthy? One person, by reflecting on the greatness of his birth, the greatness of the Teacher, the greatness of his heritage, and the greatness of his spiritual companions—for these four reasons, out of reverence, arouses moral shame characterized by respect and does not commit evil. Another person, fearing self-reproach, fearing the reproach of others, fearing punishment, and fearing a bad destination—for these four reasons, being fearful of what is blameworthy, establishes moral dread characterized by seeing danger and being fearful, and does not commit evil deeds. Herein, the internal arising and so on of moral shame and moral dread have been spoken of in terms of their prominent manifestation in various contexts, but there is never any separation between them. For there is no modesty without fear, nor is there fear of evil without modesty. Thus the detailed explanation of the meaning should be understood here.

Sukkasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sukka Sutta is finished.

9. Cariyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Cariya Sutta

9. Navame [V 2.0008] lokanti sattalokaṃ. Sandhārentīti ācārasandhāraṇavasena dhārenti. Ṭhapentīti mariyādāyaṃ ṭhapenti. Rakkhantīti ācārasandhāraṇena mariyādāyaṃ ṭhapetvā rakkhanti. Garucittīkāravasena na paññāyethāti garuṃ katvā citte karaṇavasena na paññāyetha, ayamācāro na labbheyya. Mātucchāti vāti ettha iti-saddo ādyattho. Tena mātulānīti vā ācariyabhariyāti vā garūnaṃ dārāti vāti ime saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha mātu bhaginī mātucchā. Mātulabhariyā mātulānī. Garūnaṃ dārā mahāpitucūḷapitujeṭṭhabhātuādīnaṃ garuṭṭhāniyānaṃ bhariyā. Yathā ajeḷakātiādīsu ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yathā ajeḷakādayo tiracchānā hirottapparahitā mātāti saññaṃ akatvā bhinnamariyādā sabbattha sambhedena vattanti, evamayaṃ manussaloko yadi lokapāladhammā na bhaveyyuṃ, sabbattha sambhedena vatteyya. Yasmā panime lokapālakadhammā lokaṃ pālenti, tasmā natthi sambhedoti.

9. In the ninth (sutta): 'the world' means the world of beings. 'They uphold' means they uphold by way of maintaining proper conduct. 'They establish' means they establish a boundary. 'They protect' means they protect by maintaining proper conduct and establishing a boundary. 'It would not be discerned' means: because of making it a weighty matter and bearing it in mind with respect, it would not be discerned; this improper conduct would not be found. In 'or a maternal aunt,' the particle iti has the sense of 'and so on.' By this, it includes 'or the wife of a maternal uncle,' 'or a teacher's wife,' or 'the wives of respected persons.' Therein, a mother's sister is a 'maternal aunt' (mātucchā). The wife of a maternal uncle is a mātulānī. The wives of respected persons are the wives of those in a position of respect, such as a father's elder brother, a younger paternal uncle, an elder brother, and so on. As in 'like goats and sheep,' this is the meaning in brief: just as animals such as goats and sheep, being devoid of shame and fear of wrongdoing, without having the perception 'this is my mother,' break the boundaries and behave with promiscuity everywhere, so too this human world, if the dhammas that guard the world did not exist, would behave with promiscuity everywhere. But since these dhammas that guard the world protect the world, therefore there is no such promiscuity.

Cariyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cariya Sutta is concluded.

10. Vassūpanāyikasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Vassūpanāyika Sutta

10. Dasame [M 2.0009] apaññattāti ananuññātā, avihitā vā. Vasseti vassārattaṃ sandhāya vadati, utuvasseti hemantaṃ sandhāya. Ekindriyaṃ jīvaṃ viheṭhentāti rukkhalatādīsu jīvasaññitāya evamāhaṃsu. Ekindriyanti ca kāyindriyaṃ atthīti maññamānā vadanti. Saṅghātaṃ āpādentāti vināsaṃ āpādentā. Saṃkasāyissantīti appossukkā nibaddhavāsaṃ vasissanti. Aparajjugatāya āsāḷhiyā upagantabbāti ettha aparajju gatāya assāti aparajjugatā, tassā aparajjugatāya atikkantāya, aparasmiṃ divaseti attho, tasmā āsāḷhipuṇṇamāya anantare pāṭipadadivase upagantabbāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Māsagatāya āsāḷhiyā upagantabbāti māso gatāya assāti māsagatā, tassā māsagatāya atikkantāya, māse paripuṇṇeti attho. Tasmā āsāḷhipuṇṇamato parāya puṇṇamāya anantare pāṭipadadivase upagantabbāti attho daṭṭhabbo.

10. In the tenth (sutta): 'Not laid down' means not allowed, or not prescribed. 'Rains' refers to the rainy season; 'seasonal rains' refers to the winter season. 'Harming a one-facultied living being': they said this because of their perception of life in trees, vines, and so on. And 'one-facultied' they say, thinking that the body faculty exists. 'They bring about destruction' means they cause ruin. 'They will become stained' means they will dwell in a fixed residence without concern. 'One should enter on the day after Āsāḷhī has passed': here, aparajjugatā is when the next day has come for it. The meaning is 'on the following day.' Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: one should enter the rains retreat on the first day of the lunar fortnight immediately following the full moon of Āsāḷhī. 'One should enter when a month has passed since Āsāḷhī': māsagatā is when a month has passed for it. The meaning is 'when the month is complete.' Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: one should enter the rains retreat on the first day of the lunar fortnight immediately following the full moon that is a month after the Āsāḷhī full moon.

Vassūpanāyikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vassūpanāyika Sutta is concluded.

Kammakāraṇavaggavaṇṇanāya līnatthappakāsanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Concealed Meaning in the Commentary on the Kammakāraṇa Vagga is concluded.

2. Adhikaraṇavaggavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Adhikaraṇa Vagga

11. Dutiyavaggassa [V 2.0009] paṭhame appaṭisaṅkhāne na kampatīti paṭisaṅkhānabalaṃ, upaparikkhanapaññāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Vīriyasīsena satta bojjhaṅge bhāventassa uppannaṃ balaṃ bhāvanābalaṃ. Vīriyupatthambhena hi kusalabhāvanā balavatī thirā uppajjati, tathā uppannā balavatī kusalabhāvanā balavanto satta bojjhaṅgātipi vuccanti. Atthato vīriyasambojjhaṅgasīsena satta bojjhaṅgā honti. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “tattha katamaṃ bhāvanābalaṃ? Yā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ āsevanā bhāvanā bahulīkammaṃ, idaṃ vuccati bhāvanābalaṃ. Sattapi bojjhaṅgā bhāvanābala”nti (dha. sa. 1361).

11. In the first (sutta) of the second chapter: 'He does not waver through non-reflection'—this is the power of reflection; this is a designation for the wisdom of thorough investigation. The power that arises for one who develops the seven factors of enlightenment with energy as the head is the power of development. For through the support of energy, the development of wholesome states arises powerful and firm; the powerful development of wholesome states that has so arisen, as well as the seven factors of enlightenment, are also called powerful. In terms of meaning, the seven factors of enlightenment have the factor of enlightenment of energy as their head. And this has been said: 'Therein, what is the power of development? The cultivation, development, and repeated practice of wholesome states: this is called the power of development. The seven factors of enlightenment are also the power of development' (Dhs 1361).

Akampiyaṭṭhenāti paṭipakkhehi akampanīyaṭṭhena. Durabhibhavanaṭṭhenāti durabhibhavanīyaṭṭhena. Anajjhomaddanaṭṭhenāti adhibhavitvā anavamaddanaṭṭhena. Etānīti [M 2.0010] etāni yathāvuttāni dvepi balāni. Etadaggaṃ nāgatanti “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, dvinnaṃ balānaṃ yadidaṃ bhāvanābala”nti evamettha etadaggaṃ nāgatanti attho.

'In the sense of being unshakable' means in the sense of being unshakable by opposing forces. 'In the sense of being hard to overcome' means in the sense of being difficult to overcome. 'In the sense of not being crushed' means in the sense of not being trampled down after being overcome. 'These' means these two powers as stated. 'This is the chief' means: 'Bhikkhus, this is the chief of two powers, namely, the power of development'—this is the meaning here.

12. Dutiye vivekaṃ nissitanti vivekanissitaṃ, yathā vā vivekavasena pavattaṃ jhānaṃ “vivekaja”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ vivekavasena pavatto satisambojjhaṅgo “vivekanissito”ti daṭṭhabbo. Nissayaṭṭho ca vipassanāmaggānaṃ vasena maggaphalānaṃ veditabbo, asatipi vā pubbāparabhāve “paṭiccasamuppādo”ti ettha paccayena samuppādanaṃ viya avinābhāvidhammabyāpārā nissayanabhāvanā sambhavantīti. “Tadaṅgasamucchedanissaraṇavivekanissita”nti vatvā paṭippassaddhivivekanissitassa avacanaṃ “satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvetī”tiādinā idha bhāvetabbānaṃ sambojjhaṅgānaṃ vuttattā. Bhāvitabojjhaṅgassa hi sacchikātabbā balabojjhaṅgā, tesaṃ kiccaṃ paṭippassaddhiviveko. Ajjhāsayatoti “nibbānaṃ sacchikarissāmī”ti pavattaajjhāsayato. Yadipi hi vipassanākkhaṇe saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ, saṅkhāresu pana ādīnavaṃ disvā tappaṭipakkhe nibbāne ninnatāya ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissito hoti uṇhābhibhūtassa puggalassa sītaninnacittatā viya.

12. In the second (sutta): 'Based on seclusion' means dependent on seclusion. Just as the jhānic absorption that proceeds by way of seclusion is called 'born of seclusion,' so the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness that proceeds by way of seclusion should be understood as 'based on seclusion.' The meaning of 'basis' should be understood in terms of the path and fruit by way of the insight-paths. Or, even when there is no before-and-after sequence, the state of being a basis is possible through the operation of inseparably related phenomena, just as in 'dependent origination' there is origination by way of a condition. Having said 'based on the seclusion of substitution, of eradication, and of escape,' the non-mention of being 'based on the seclusion of tranquility' is because the factors of enlightenment to be developed here have been stated by 'develops the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness,' etc. For one who has developed the factors of enlightenment, the powerful factors of enlightenment are to be realized, and their function is the seclusion of tranquility. As to 'by disposition': it is from the disposition that proceeds as 'I will realize Nibbāna.' Although at the moment of insight the mind has formations as its object, still, having seen the danger in formations, because of the disposition of inclining towards Nibbāna, which is their opposite, one is 'based on the seclusion of escape,' like the mind of a person overcome by heat inclining to coolness.

“Pañcavidhavivekanissitampīti eke”ti vatvā tattha yathāvuttavivekattayato aññaṃ vivekadvayaṃ [V 2.0010] uddharitvā dassetuṃ “te hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha jhānakkhaṇe tāva kiccato vikkhambhanavivekanissitaṃ, vipassanākkhaṇe ajjhāsayato paṭippassaddhivivekanissitaṃ bhāvetīti vattabbaṃ “evāhaṃ anuttaraṃ vimokkhaṃ upasampajja viharissāmī”ti tattha ninnajjhāsayatāya. Tenāha “tasmā tesaṃ matenā”tiādi. Heṭṭhā kasiṇajjhānaggahaṇena āruppānampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tasmā “etesaṃ jhānāna”nti imināpi tesaṃ saṅgaho veditabbo. Yasmā pahānavinayo viya virāganirodhāpi idhādhippetavivekena atthato nibbisiṭṭhā, tasmā vuttaṃ “esa nayo virāganissitantiādīsū”ti. Tenāha “vivekatthā eva hi virāgādayo”ti.

Having said, 'Some say, "It is also based on the fivefold seclusion,"' the words 'for they...' and so on are stated to extract and show the other two kinds of seclusion apart from the three kinds already mentioned. Therein, it should be said that at the moment of jhāna one develops what is 'based on the seclusion of suppression' in terms of function, and at the moment of insight one develops what is 'based on the seclusion of tranquility' in terms of disposition, because of the disposition that inclines towards it thus: 'Thus I will attain and dwell in the unsurpassed deliverance.' Hence it is said, 'Therefore, according to their opinion,' and so on. Below, by the inclusion of the kasiṇa jhānas, the inclusion of the formless attainments should also be understood; therefore, by 'of these jhānas,' their inclusion should also be understood. Because, like the discipline of abandoning, dispassion and cessation are also in meaning not different from the seclusion intended here, it is said, 'This is the method in "based on dispassion," etc.' Hence it is said: 'For dispassion and so on are indeed for the sake of seclusion.'

Vossagga-saddo pariccāgattho pakkhandanattho cāti vossaggassa duvidhatā vuttā. Vossajjanañhi pahānaṃ vissaṭṭhabhāvena nirodhanapakkhandanampi ca[M 2.0011]. Tasmā vipassanākkhaṇe tadaṅgavasena maggakkhaṇe samucchedavasena paṭipakkhassa pahānaṃ vossaggo, tathā vipassanākkhaṇe tanninnabhāvena, maggakkhaṇe ārammaṇakaraṇena vissaṭṭhasabhāvatā vossaggoti veditabbaṃ. Tenevāha “tattha pariccāgavossaggo”tiādi. Ayaṃ satisambojjhaṅgoti ayaṃ missakavasena vutto satisambojjhaṅgo. Yathāvuttena pakārenāti tadaṅgappahānasamucchedappahānappakārena tanninnatadārammaṇappakārena ca. Pubbe vossaggavacanasseva atthassa vuttattā āha “sakalena vacanenā”ti. Pariṇamantanti vipassanākkhaṇe tadaṅgatanninnappakārena pariṇamantaṃ. Pariṇatanti maggakkhaṇe samucchedatadārammaṇappakārena pariṇataṃ. Pariṇāmo nāma idha paripākoti āha “paripaccantaṃ paripakkañcā”ti. Paripāko ca āsevanalābhena laddhasāmatthiyassa kilese pariccajituṃ nibbānaṃ pakkhandituṃ tikkhavisadabhāvo. Tenāha “ayañhī”tiādi. Esa nayoti yvāyaṃ nayo “vivekanissita”ntiādinā satisambojjhaṅge vutto, sesesu dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādīsupi eseva nayo, evaṃ tattha netabbanti attho.

The word `vossagga` has the meaning of relinquishment and the meaning of leaping forward; thus the twofold nature of `vossagga` is stated. For relinquishing (vossajjana) is both abandoning by way of letting go and also leaping forward into cessation. Therefore, `vossagga` is the abandoning of opposing states by way of substitution at the moment of insight, and by way of eradication at the moment of the path. Similarly, `vossagga` should be understood as the state of having let go by way of inclining towards it at the moment of insight, and by way of making it the object at the moment of the path. For that reason it is said: 'Therein, relinquishment as abandoning,' etc. 'This factor of enlightenment of mindfulness' means this factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is spoken of in a mixed way. 'By the mode as stated' means by the mode of abandoning by substitution and abandoning by eradication, and by the mode of inclining towards it and making it the object. Because the meaning of the word `vossagga` has already been stated before, it says 'by the entire phrase.' 'Maturing' means maturing at the moment of insight by the mode of substitution and inclining towards it. 'Matured' means matured at the moment of the path by the mode of eradication and making it the object. Transformation (pariṇāmo) here is maturation (paripāko); thus it says 'maturing and matured.' And maturation is the sharp and clear state of one who has gained the capacity through the acquisition of practice to relinquish the defilements and leap forward into Nibbāna. Hence it says, 'For this...,' etc. 'This is the method' means: that method which was stated in regard to the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness beginning with 'based on seclusion,' that same method should be applied also to the remaining factors of enlightenment such as investigation-of-dharmas. This is the meaning.

“Vivekanissita”ntiādīsu labbhamānamatthaṃ sāmaññato dassetvā idāni idhādhippetamatthaṃ dassento “idha panā”tiādimāha. Tattha sabbasaṅkhatehīti sabbehi paccayasamuppannadhammehi. Sabbesanti saṅkhatadhammānaṃ. Vivekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvāti nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ vivekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā. Tañca khoti tadeva satisambojjhaṅgaṃ.

Having first shown in a general way the meaning obtained in 'based on seclusion,' etc., now, showing the meaning intended here, he says, 'But here...,' etc. Therein, 'from all conditioned things' means from all phenomena that have arisen from conditions. 'Of all' means of conditioned phenomena. 'Having made seclusion the object' means having made the seclusion called Nibbāna the object. 'And that indeed' means that same factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.

13. Tatiye cittekaggatthāyāti cittasamādhānatthāya, diṭṭhadhamme sukhavihārāyāti attho. Cittekaggatāsīsena hi diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāro vutto. Sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavānaṃ vasena hetaṃ vuttaṃ. Te hi samāpajjitvā “ekaggacittā sukhaṃ divasaṃ viharissāmā”ti icceva kasiṇaparikammaṃ [V 2.0011] katvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattenti. Vipassanāpādakatthāyātiādīsu pana sekkhaputhujjanā “samāpattito vuṭṭhāya samāhitena cittena vipassāmā”ti nibbattentā vipassanāpādakatthāya bhāventi.

13. 'For the purpose of one-pointedness of mind' means for the purpose of concentration of mind; the meaning is 'for a pleasant abiding in this very life.' For the pleasant abiding in this very life is spoken of with one-pointedness of mind as its head. This is said with reference to dry-insight practitioners and arahants whose taints are destroyed. For they, having entered upon an attainment, think, 'With a one-pointed mind, we will abide pleasantly for the day,' and thus, having done the preliminary work on a kasiṇa, they generate the eight attainments. But in such cases as 'for the purpose of a basis for insight,' trainees and worldlings generate them thinking, 'Having emerged from the attainment, we will practice insight with a concentrated mind,' and thus they develop it for the purpose of a basis for insight.

Ye pana aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā samāpattito vuṭṭhāya “ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.238; ma. ni. 1.147; saṃ. ni. 2.70; 5.834, 842) vuttanayā [M 2.0012] abhiññāyo patthentā nibbattenti, te abhiññāpādakatthāya bhāventi. Ye aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā “sattāhaṃ acittā hutvā diṭṭheva dhamme nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ patvā sukhaṃ viharissāmā”ti nibbattenti, te nirodhapādakatthāya bhāventi. Ye pana aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā “aparihīnajjhānā brahmaloke uppajjissāmā”ti nibbattenti, te bhavavisesatthāya bhāventi.

Those who, having generated the eight attainments, enter the jhāna that is the basis for the direct knowledges, and, on emerging from that attainment, aspiring to the direct knowledges in the way stated, 'Having been one, he becomes many…,' generate them—they develop them for the purpose of a basis for the direct knowledges. Those who, having generated the eight attainments, enter the attainment of cessation and think, 'Having been without mind for seven days, we will attain cessation, Nibbāna, in this very life and abide happily'—they develop them for the purpose of a basis for cessation. And those who, having generated the eight attainments, think, 'Without having fallen away from the jhānas, we will be reborn in the Brahma-world'—they develop them for the purpose of a superior state of existence.

Yuttaṃ tāva cittekaggatāya bhavavisesatthatā viya vipassanāpādakatthatāpi catukkajjhānasādhāraṇāti tesaṃ vasena “cattāri jhānānī”ti vacanaṃ, abhiññāpādakatthatā pana nirodhapādakatthatā ca catutthasseva jhānassa āveṇikā, sā kathaṃ catukkajjhānasādhāraṇā vuttāti? Paramparādhiṭṭhānabhāvato. Padaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānampi hi padaṭṭhānanti vuccati kāraṇakāraṇanti yathā “tiṇehi bhattaṃ siddha”nti.

It is proper, first, that being a basis for insight is common to the four jhānas, just as are the purposes of one-pointedness of mind and a superior state of existence, and that on account of these the expression 'the four jhānas' is used. But being a basis for the direct knowledges and a basis for cessation are exclusive to the fourth jhāna. How, then, are they said to be common to the four jhānas? Because they are established indirectly. For the basis of a basis is also called a basis, and the cause of a cause is also called a cause, as when it is said, 'The rice is cooked with grass.'

14. Catutthe sasakassa uppatanaṃ viya hotīti pathavijigucchanasasakassa uppatanaṃ viya hoti. Tatthāyaṃ atthasallāpikā upamā – pathavī kira sasakaṃ āha – “he sasakā”ti. Sasako āha – “ko eso”ti. Kasmā mameva upari sabbairiyāpathe kappento uccārapassāvaṃ karonto maṃ na jānāsīti? Suṭṭhu tayā ahaṃ diṭṭho, mayā akkantaṭṭhānañhi aṅgulaggehi phuṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ viya hoti, vissaṭṭhaudakaṃ appamattakaṃ, karīsaṃ kaṭakaphalamattaṃ, hatthiassādīhi pana akkantaṭṭhānampi mahantaṃ, passāvopi nesaṃ ghaṭamatto, uccāropi pacchimatto hoti, alaṃ mayhaṃ tayāti uppatitvā aññasmiṃ ṭhāne patito. Tato naṃ pathavī āha – “aho dūraṃ gatopi nanu mayhaṃyeva upari patitosī”ti? So puna taṃ jigucchanto uppatitvā aññattha patito. Evaṃ vassasahassampi uppatitvā uppatitvā patamāno sasako neva pathaviyā antaṃ pāpuṇituṃ sakkoti. Na koṭinti na pubbakoṭiṃ. Itaresanti vipañcitaññuneyyapadaparamānaṃ.

14. In the fourth, 'it is like the leaping of a hare' means it is like the leaping of a hare disgusted with the earth. Here is a simile illustrating the meaning: The earth, it is said, said to a hare, 'Hey, hare!' The hare said, 'Who is that?' 'Why, when you spend all your time in every posture upon me, making excrement and urine, do you not know me?' 'You have observed me well. The place I tread on is like a place touched by the tips of my toes; the water I release is a tiny amount, my dung the size of a clearing-nut fruit. But the place trodden by elephants, horses, and so on is large; their urine is a potful, and their dung is a basketful. Enough of you for me!' So saying, it leaped up and landed in another place. Then the earth said to it, 'Ah, though you have gone far, have you not landed right on me?' Disgusted with it again, the hare leaped up and landed elsewhere. In this way, even if the hare were to leap and leap for a thousand years, it would never be able to reach the end of the earth. 'Not its end' means not its beginning-point. 'The others' refers to those for whom the highest is a term to be inferred by one who understands what has been elaborated.

15. Pañcame [V 2.0012] samathehi adhikarīyati vūpasammatīti adhikaraṇaṃ, aṭṭhārasa bhedakaravatthūni nissāya uppanno vivādoyeva vivādādhikaraṇaṃ. “Idha bhikkhū bhikkhuṃ anuvadanti sīlavipattiyā vā”tiādinā (cūḷava. 215) catasso [M 2.0013] vipattiyo nissāya uppanno anuvādoyeva anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ. Pañcapi āpattikkhandhā āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. “Sattapi āpattikkhandhā āpattādhikaraṇa”nti (cūḷava. 215) vacanato āpattiyeva āpattādhikaraṇaṃ. “Yā saṅghassa kiccayatā karaṇīyatā apalokanakammaṃ ñattikammaṃ ñattidutiyakammaṃ ñatticatutthakamma”nti (cūḷava. 215) evamāgataṃ catubbidhaṃ saṅghakiccaṃ kiccādhikaraṇanti veditabbaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva.

15. In the fifth, an issue (adhikaraṇa) is so called because it is dealt with and settled by means of settlements. A dispute that has arisen based on the eighteen grounds for quarrels is a dispute-issue. An accusation that has arisen based on the four kinds of failure, as in 'Here, bhikkhus accuse a bhikkhu of a failure in virtue…,' is an accusation-issue. The five groups of offenses are an offense-issue. According to the statement, 'The seven groups of offenses are an offense-issue,' an offense itself is an offense-issue. The fourfold formal act of the Sangha that has come down as, 'Whatever duty of the Sangha there is, whatever is to be done: an act of information, an act by motion, an act by motion and one announcement, an act by motion and three announcements,' should be understood as a duties-issue. The rest here is plain.

16. Chaṭṭhe apākaṭanāmoti “selo, kūṭadanto”tiādinā anabhiññāto. Yena vā kāraṇenāti hetumhi idaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Hetuattho hi kiriyākāraṇaṃ, na karaṇaṃ viya kiriyattho, tasmā nānappakāraguṇavisesādhigamatthā idha upasaṅkamanakiriyāti “annena vasati, ajjhenena vasatī”tiādīsu viya hetuatthamevetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ yuttaṃ, na karaṇatthaṃ tassa ayujjamānattāti vuttaṃ “yena vā kāraṇenā”ti. Avibhāgato satataṃ pavattitaniratisayasāduvipulāmatarasasaddhammaphalatāya sāduphalaniccaphalitamahārukkhena bhagavā upamito. Sāduphalūpabhogādhippāyaggahaṇeneva hi rukkhassa sāduphalatā gahitāti. Upasaṅkamīti upasaṅkanto. Sampattakāmatāya hi kiñci ṭhānaṃ gacchanto taṃtaṃpadesātikkamanena upasaṅkami, upasaṅkantoti ca vattabbataṃ labhati. Tenāha “gatoti vuttaṃ hotī”ti, upagatoti attho. Upasaṅkamitvāti pubbakālakiriyāniddesoti āha “upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpana”nti. Tatoti yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patto “upasaṅkamī”ti vutto, tato upagataṭṭhānato.

16. Sixth, 'not well-known by name' means not known by such names as Sela or Kūṭadanta. 'By which reason': this is the instrumental case in the sense of cause. For the meaning of cause is the reason for an action, not, like the instrument, the meaning of the action itself. Therefore, since the action of approaching here is for the purpose of attaining various special qualities, this instrumental case has the meaning of cause, as in such phrases as 'he lives by food' and 'he lives by study.' It is not used in the sense of instrument, as that would be unsuitable. Hence it is said, 'by which reason.' The Blessed One is compared to a great tree always bearing sweet fruit because he produces without distinction the fruit of the good Dhamma, which is constantly available, unsurpassed, sweet, abundant, and has the taste of the deathless. For the tree's quality of having sweet fruit is grasped just by grasping the intention to enjoy its sweet fruit. 'He approached' means one who has approached. For when someone goes to a place out of a desire to reach it, by passing beyond one region after another, he approaches and can be said to have approached. Hence it is said, 'this means "gone,"' the meaning being 'arrived.' 'Having approached' is a description of a prior action; thus it is said, 'it indicates the completion of the act of approaching.' 'From there' means from the place he has reached, about which it is said 'he approached'; that is, from the place he has arrived at.

Yathā khamanīyādīni pucchantoti yathā bhagavā “kacci te, brāhmaṇa, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīya”ntiādinā khamanīyādīni pucchanto tena brāhmaṇena saddhiṃ samappavattamodo ahosi pubbabhāsitāya, evaṃ sopi brāhmaṇo tadanukaraṇena bhagavatā saddhiṃ samappavattamodo ahosīti yojanā. Taṃ pana samappavattamodataṃ upamāya dassetuṃ “sītodakaṃ viyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sammoditanti saṃsanditaṃ. Ekībhāvanti sammodanakiriyāya samānataṃ. Khamanīyanti “idaṃ catucakkaṃ navadvāraṃ sarīrayantaṃ dukkhabahulatāya sabhāvato dussahaṃ, kacci khamituṃ sakkuṇeyya”nti [M 2.0014] pucchati. Yāpanīyanti āhārādippaṭibaddhavuttikaṃ cirappabandhasaṅkhātāya yāpanāya kacci yāpetuṃ sakkuṇeyyaṃ. Sīsarogādiābādhābhāvena kacci appābādhaṃ. Dukkhajīvikābhāvena kacci appātaṅkaṃ. Taṃtaṃkiccakaraṇe uṭṭhānasukhatāya kacci lahuṭṭhānaṃ. Tadanurūpabalayogato kacci balaṃ[V 2.0013]. Sukhavihārasambhavena kacci phāsuvihāro atthīti sabbattha kacci-saddaṃ yojetvā attho veditabbo.

The construction is: Just as the Blessed One, by asking about his well-being and so on, saying, 'I hope you are keeping well, brahmin, I hope you are getting by,' exchanged courtesies with that brahmin because of his previous friendly talk, so too that brahmin, imitating him, exchanged courtesies with the Blessed One. To illustrate that exchange of courtesies with a simile, it is said, 'like cool water,' and so on. Here, 'exchanged greetings' means corresponded. 'Oneness' means similarity through the act of exchanging greetings. 'Keeping well': he asks, 'This body-machine with its four wheels and nine doors is by nature hard to bear because of its great suffering; I hope you are able to bear it.' 'Getting by': he asks, 'This life, which is dependent on food and so on, I hope you are able to maintain it for a long time.' 'Free from illness': free from headaches and other ailments. 'Free from affliction': free from a difficult livelihood. 'Lightness of body': ease in rising for various duties. 'Strength': strength appropriate to that. 'Comfortable abiding': the possibility of a comfortable abiding. In all cases, the word 'kacci' (I hope) should be connected and the meaning understood.

Balappattā pīti pītiyeva. Taruṇapīti pāmojjaṃ. Sammodaṃ janeti karotīti sammodanīkaṃ, tadeva sammodanīyaṃ. Sammoditabbato sammodanīyanti imaṃ pana atthaṃ dassetuṃ “sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato”ti āha. Saritabbabhāvatoti anussaritabbabhāvato. “Saraṇīya”nti vattabbe dīghaṃ katvā “sāraṇīya”nti vuttaṃ. Suyyamānasukhatoti āpāthagatamadhurataṃ āha, anussariyamānasukhatoti vimaddaramaṇīyataṃ. Byañjanaparisuddhatāyāti sabhāvaniruttibhāvena tassā kathāya vacanacāturiyamāha. Atthaparisuddhatāyāti atthassa nirupakkilesataṃ. Anekehi pariyāyehīti anekehi kāraṇehi.

Rapture that has gained strength is simply rapture. Tender rapture is gladness. It generates and creates gladness, thus it is 'gladdening' (sammodanīka); that itself is 'to be gladdened by' (sammodanīya). To show this meaning, 'sammodanīya because it is fit to be gladdened by,' he said, 'because of its fitness to be gladdened by.' 'Because it is fit to be remembered' means because it is fit to be recollected. When 'saraṇīya' should be said, it is made long and 'sāraṇīya' is said. 'The happiness of being heard' refers to the sweetness that comes within range of the ear. 'The happiness of being recollected' refers to its delightfulness when pondered. 'By purity of phrasing' refers to the verbal dexterity of that talk through its natural expression. 'By purity of meaning' refers to the undefiled nature of the meaning. 'In many ways' means for many reasons.

Atidūraaccāsannappaṭikkhepena nātidūraṃ naccāsannaṃ nāma gahitaṃ, taṃ pana avakaṃsato ubhinnaṃ pasāritahatthāsaṅghaṭṭanena daṭṭhabbaṃ. Gīvaṃ pasāretvāti gīvaṃ parivaṭṭanavasena pasāretvā.

'Not too far, not too near' is taken by way of rejecting what is too far and too near. This, however, should be understood by the non-touching of the outstretched hands of both from a lowered position. 'Having extended the neck' means having extended the neck by way of turning it.

Etadavocāti etaṃ “ko nu kho, bhante, hetū”tiādipucchāvacanaṃ avoca. Teneva “etadavocā”ti padaṃ uddharitvā duvidhā hi pucchātiādinā pucchāvibhāgaṃ dasseti. Tattha agāre niyutto agāriko, tassa pucchā agārikapucchā. Agārikato añño anagāriko pabbajjūpagato, tassa pucchā anagārikapucchā. Kiñcāpi aññattha “janako hetu, paggāhako paccayo. Asādhāraṇo hetu, sādhāraṇo paccayo. Sabhāgo hetu, asabhāgo paccayo. Pubbakāliko hetu, sahapavatto paccayo”tiādinā hetupaccayā vibhajja vuccanti. Idha pana “cattāro kho, bhikkhave, mahābhūtā hetu cattāro mahābhūtā paccayo rūpakkhandhassa paññāpanāyā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.86) viya hetupaccayasaddā samānatthāti dassento “ubhayampetaṃ kāraṇavevacanamevā”ti āha. Visamacariyāti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso.

He said this: this refers to the statement containing the question, 'What, venerable sir, is the cause?' and so on. For that reason, having cited the word 'etadavocā,' he shows the twofold division of questions. Therein, one engaged in household life is a householder, and his question is a householder's question. One other than a householder is the homeless one who has gone forth, and his question is a homeless one's question. Although elsewhere cause and condition are distinguished and explained thus: 'The generator is the cause, the supporter is the condition; the uncommon is the cause, the common is the condition; the similar is the cause, the dissimilar is the condition; the prior is the cause, the simultaneous is the condition,' and so on, here, however, as in passages like, 'Bhikkhus, the four great elements are the cause, the four great elements are the condition for the manifestation of the form aggregate' (MN 3.86), he shows that the words 'cause' and 'condition' are synonymous when he says: 'Both these are merely synonyms for reason.' The term 'visamacariyā' is a designation as a neuter abstract noun.

Abhikkantāti [M 2.0015] atikkantā, vigatāti atthoti āha “khaye dissatī”ti. Tathā hi “nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo”ti upari vuttaṃ. Abhikkantataroti ativiya kantataro manoramo, tādiso ca sundaro bhaddako nāma hotīti āha “sundare dissatī”ti. Koti devanāgayakkhagandhabbādīsu ko katamo? Meti mama. Pādānīti pāde. Iddhiyāti imāya evarūpāya deviddhiyā. Yasasāti iminā edisena parivārena paricchedena ca. Jalanti vijjotamāno. Abhikkantenāti ativiya kantena kamanīyena abhirūpena. Vaṇṇenāti chavivaṇṇena [V 2.0014] sarīravaṇṇanibhāya. Sabbā obhāsayaṃ disāti dasa disā pabhāsento, cando viya sūriyo viya ca ekobhāsaṃ ekālokaṃ karontoti gāthāya attho. Abhirūpeti uḷārarūpe sampannarūpe.

'Abhikkantā' means surpassed, gone past; therefore it is said, 'it is seen in the sense of passing away.' For it is said above: 'The first watch has passed.' 'Abhikkantataro' means exceedingly lovely, more charming; and such a one is called beautiful, excellent. Therefore it is said, 'it is seen in the sense of beauty.' 'Ko' means: which one among the devas, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so on? 'Me' means my. 'Pādāni' means at the feet. 'Iddhiyā' means by this very kind of divine psychic power. 'Yasasā' means by such a retinue and glory. 'Jalanti' means shining brightly. 'Abhikkantena' means by an exceedingly lovely, delightful, and beautiful form. 'Vaṇṇena' means by complexion, by the radiance of the body's appearance. 'Illuminating all directions' means illuminating the ten directions, making a single radiance, a single light, like the moon and the sun—this is the meaning of the verse. 'Abhirūpe' means in a splendid and perfect form.

“Coro, coro; sappo, sappo”tiādīsu bhaye āmeḍitaṃ. “Vijjha, vijjha; pahara, paharā”tiādīsu kodhe. “Sādhu, sādhū”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 327.saṃ. ni. 2.127; 3.35; 5.1085) pasaṃsāyaṃ. “Gaccha, gaccha; lunāhi, lunāhī”tiādīsu turite. “Āgaccha, āgacchā”tiādīsu kotūhale. “Buddho, buddhoti cintento”tiādīsu (bu. vaṃ. 2.44) acchare. “Abhikkamathāyasmanto, abhikkamathāyasmanto”tiādīsu hāse. “Kahaṃ ekaputtaka, kahaṃ ekaputtakā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.353; saṃ. ni. 2.63) soke. “Aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”ntiādīsu (udā. 20; dī. ni. 3.305; cūḷava. 332) pasāde. Ca-saddo avuttasamuccayatto. Tena garahāasammānādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tattha “pāpo, pāpo”tiādīsu garahāyaṃ. “Abhirūpaka, abhirūpakā”tiādīsu asammāne daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Repetition occurs in fear, as in 'Thief, thief; snake, snake'; in anger, as in 'Shoot, shoot; strike, strike'; in praise, as in 'Good, good'; in haste, as in 'Go, go; cut, cut'; in curiosity, as in 'Come, come'; in wonder, as in 'The Buddha, the Buddha, thinking'; in laughter, as in 'Come forward, venerable sirs, come forward, venerable sirs'; in sorrow, as in 'Where is my only son, where is my only son?'; and in serene confidence, as in 'Ah, happiness, ah, happiness.' The particle 'ca' serves to include what has not been stated. By it, the inclusion of censure, disrespect, and so on should be understood. Therein, 'Wicked, wicked,' and so on is in censure; 'Handsome one, handsome one,' and so on should be seen in disrespect.

Nayidaṃ āmeḍitavasena dvikkhattuṃ vuttaṃ, atha kho atthadvayavasenāti dassento “atha vā”tiādimāha. “Abhikkanta”nti vacanaṃ apekkhitvā napuṃsakavasena vuttaṃ, taṃ pana bhagavato vacanaṃ dhammassa desanāti katvā tathā vuttaṃ “bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanā”ti. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Dosanāsanatoti rāgādikilesavidhamanato. Guṇādhigamanatoti sīlādiguṇānaṃ sampāpanato. Ye guṇe desanā adhigameti, tesu padhānabhūte tāva dassetuṃ “saddhājananato paññājananato”ti vuttaṃ. Saddhāpamukhā hi lokiyā guṇā, paññāpamukhā lokuttarā[M 2.0016].

This was not said twice by way of repetition, but rather on account of a twofold meaning; to show this, he said, 'or else,' and so on. The word 'abhikkanta' (excellent) was stated in the neuter gender with reference to the utterance. But since that utterance of the Blessed One is a teaching of the Dhamma, it was spoken of thus: 'the Dhamma teaching of Master Gotama.' The same principle applies to the second term. 'By the dispelling of faults' means by the destruction of defilements such as lust. 'By the attainment of virtues' means by the acquisition of qualities such as virtue. To indicate the primary qualities among those which the teaching leads one to attain, it is first said, 'by the generation of faith, by the generation of wisdom.' For worldly qualities are headed by faith, while supramundane qualities are headed by wisdom.

Sīlādiatthasampattiyā sātthato, sabhāvaniruttisampattiyā sabyañjanato. Suviññeyyasaddappayogatāya uttānapadato, saṇhasukhumabhāvena duviññeyyatthatāya gambhīratthato. Siniddhamudumadhurasaddappayogatāya kaṇṇasukhato, vipulavisuddhapemanīyatthatāya hadayaṅgamato. Mānātimānavidhamanena anattukkaṃsanato, thambhasārambhanimmaddanena aparavambhanato. Hitādhippāyappavattiyā paresaṃ rāgapariḷāhādivūpasamanena karuṇāsītalato, kilesandhakāravidhamanena paññāvadātato. Karavīkarutamañjutāya āpātharamaṇīyato, pubbāparāviruddhasuvisuddhatthatāya vimaddakkhamato. Āpātharamaṇīyatāya evaṃ suyyamānasukhato, vimaddakkhamatāya hitajjhāsayappavattitatāya ca vīmaṃsiyamānahitato[V 2.0015]. Evamādīhīti ādi-saddena saṃsāracakkanivattanato, saddhammacakkappavattanato, micchāvādavigamanato, sammāvādapatiṭṭhāpanato, akusalamūlasamuddharaṇato, kusalamūlasaṃropanato, apāyadvārapidhānato, saggamokkhadvāravivaraṇato, pariyuṭṭhānavūpasamanato, anusayasamugghātanatoti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

It is meaningful (sāttha) because of its accomplishment in meaning, such as virtue. It is well-phrased (sabyañjana) because of its accomplishment in natural expression. Its phrasing is plain (uttānapada) because of its use of easily intelligible words. Its meaning is profound (gambhīrattha) because its meaning is difficult to understand owing to its subtle and refined nature. It is pleasing to the ear (kaṇṇasukha) because of its use of smooth, soft, and sweet sounds. It is heart-captivating (hadayaṅgama) because its meaning is abundant, pure, and lovely. It does not exalt oneself (anattukkaṃsana) because it dispels conceit and arrogance. It does not disparage others (aparavambhana) because it crushes stubbornness and contention. It is cool with compassion (karuṇāsītala) because it proceeds from a beneficial intention and calms the fever of passion and the like in others. It is radiant with wisdom (paññāvadāta) because it dispels the darkness of defilements. It is delightful at first hearing (āpātharamaṇīya) because of a loveliness like the call of the Karavīka bird. It withstands scrutiny (vimaddakkhama) because its meaning is thoroughly pure and without contradiction between earlier and later parts. Because it is delightful at first hearing, it is pleasant to listen to. Because it withstands scrutiny and proceeds from a beneficial intention, it is beneficial when examined. By 'and so on,' the inclusion of the following should be understood: turning back the wheel of saṃsāra, setting in motion the wheel of the good Dhamma, dispelling wrong view, establishing right view, uprooting unwholesome roots, implanting wholesome roots, closing the doors to the planes of misery, opening the doors to heaven and liberation, calming obsessions, and eradicating the underlying tendencies.

Adhomukhaṭṭhapitanti kenaci adhomukhaṃ ṭhapitaṃ. Heṭṭhāmukhajātanti sabhāveneva heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ. Uparimukhanti uddhaṃmukhaṃ. Ugghāṭeyyāti vivaṭaṃ kareyya. Hatthe gahetvāti “puratthābhimukho uttarābhimukho vā gacchā”tiādīni avatvā hatthe gahetvā “nissandehaṃ esa maggo, evaṃ gaccheyyā”ti vadeyya. Kāḷapakkhacātuddasīti kāḷapakkhe cātuddasī.

'Placed face down' means placed face down by someone. 'Born face down' means born face down by its very nature. 'Face up' means facing upward. 'One would uncover' means one would make it open. 'Having taken by the hand' means that without saying, 'Go facing east or go facing north,' and so on, having taken one by the hand, one would say: 'This is the path without a doubt; go this way.' 'The fourteenth of the dark fortnight' means the fourteenth day in the dark fortnight.

Nikkujjitaṃ ādheyyassa anādhārabhūtaṃ bhājanaṃ ādhārabhāvāpādanavasena ukkujjeyya. Heṭṭhāmukhajātatāya saddhammavimukhaṃ, adhomukhaṭhapitatāya asaddhamme patitanti evaṃ padadvayaṃ yathārahaṃ yojetabbaṃ, na yathāsaṅkhyaṃ. Kāmaṃ kāmacchandādayopi paṭicchādakā nīvaraṇabhāvato, micchādiṭṭhi pana savisesaṃ paṭicchādikā satte micchābhinivesanavasenāti āha “micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchanna”nti. Tenāha bhagavā “micchādiṭṭhiparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, vajjaṃ vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 1.310). Sabbo apāyagāmimaggo kummaggo “kucchito maggo”ti katvā. Sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ ujupaṭipakkhatāya micchādiṭṭhiādayo aṭṭha micchattadhammā micchāmaggo. Teneva hi tadubhayappaṭipakkhataṃ sandhāya “saggamokkhamaggaṃ āvikarontenā”ti vuttaṃ. Sappiādisannissayo padīpo [M 2.0017] na tathā ujjalo, yathā telasannissayoti telapajjotaggahaṇaṃ. Etehi pariyāyehīti etehi nikkujjitukkujjanappaṭicchannavivaraṇādiupamopamitabbākārehi.

One would turn upright an overturned vessel, which is not a receptacle for its contents, so as to make it a receptacle. Because of being born face down, one is turned away from the good Dhamma; because of being placed face down, one has fallen into the bad Dhamma. Thus these two phrases should be connected as is appropriate, not in numerical order. Granted, sensual desire and so on also conceal because they are hindrances, but wrong view in particular conceals beings by way of wrong adherence; thus it is said: 'concealed by the thicket of wrong view.' Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, I say that wrong view is the ultimate fault' (AN 1.310). Every path leading to the planes of misery is a wrong path (kummagga), since it is a 'despised path.' Because they are the direct opposites of right view and so on, the eight wrong states beginning with wrong view constitute the wrong path. For that very reason, with reference to the opposition between these two, it is said: 'by one who makes manifest the path to heaven and liberation.' A lamp dependent on ghee and so on is not as bright as one dependent on oil; hence, an oil lamp is taken as the example. 'By these methods' means by these modes of analogy, such as overturning and righting, concealing and revealing, and so on, and what is to be compared to them.

Pasannakāranti pasannehi kātabbaṃ sakkāraṃ. Saraṇanti paṭisaraṇaṃ. Tenāha “parāyaṇa”nti. Parāyaṇabhāvo ca anatthanisedhanena atthasampaṭipādanena ca hotīti āha “aghassa, tātā, hitassa ca vidhātā”ti. Aghassāti dukkhatoti vadanti, pāpatoti pana attho yutto. Nissakke cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Ettha ca nāyaṃ gami-saddo nī-saddādayo viya dvikammako, tasmā yathā “ajaṃ gāmaṃ netī”ti vuccati, evaṃ “bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti vattuṃ na sakkā. “Saraṇanti gacchāmī”ti pana vattabbaṃ. Iti-saddo cettha luttaniddiṭṭho. Tassa cāyamattho – gamanañca tadadhippāyena bhajanaṃ jānanaṃ vāti dassento “iti iminā adhippāyenā”tiādimāha. Tattha bhajāmītiādīsu purimassa purimassa pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ atthavacanaṃ. Bhajanaṃ vā saraṇādhippāyena upasaṅkamanaṃ. Sevanaṃ santikāvacaratā. Payirupāsanaṃ vattappaṭivattakaraṇena upaṭṭhānanti [V 2.0016] evaṃ sabbathāpi anaññasaraṇataṃyeva dīpeti. “Gacchāmī”ti padassa bujjhāmīti ayamattho kathaṃ labbhatīti āha “yesaṃ hī”tiādi.

'The act of the confident' means the honor that should be shown by those with confidence. 'Refuge' means a resort. Therefore he said 'final resort.' The state of being a final resort comes about by warding off what is harmful and providing what is beneficial; thus he said: 'the remover of harm, dear one, and the provider of benefit.' 'Of harm' (aghassa): some say this means 'of suffering,' but the meaning 'of evil' is more suitable. And this is a genitive of relation. Here, the verb 'gami' (to go) is not a transitive verb taking two objects like 'nī' (to lead). Therefore, just as one says, 'He leads the goat to the village,' it is not possible to say, 'I go the Blessed One as refuge' (bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi). Rather, one should say, 'I go to it as refuge' (saraṇanti gacchāmi). Here the word 'iti' is indicated as elided. And this is its meaning: to show that one goes, or resorts, or knows with that intention, he says, 'with this intention,' and so on. Therein, in 'I resort' (bhajāmi) and so on, each subsequent word explains the meaning of the one preceding it. 'Resorting' (bhajana) is approaching with the intention of taking refuge. 'Associating' (sevana) is dwelling in his presence. 'Attending' (payirupāsana) is waiting upon him by performing one's duties and services. Thus in every way it indicates having no other refuge. How is the meaning 'I understand' (bujjhāmi) obtained for the word 'I go' (gacchāmi)? He explains this beginning with the phrase, 'For those...'

Adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodheti padadvayenapi phalaṭṭhā eva dassitā, na maggaṭṭhāti te dassento “yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne cā”ti āha. Nanu ca kalyāṇaputhujjanopi yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjatīti vuccatīti? Kiñcāpi vuccati, nippariyāyena pana maggaṭṭhā eva tathā vattabbā, na itare sammattaniyāmokkamanābhāvato. Tathā hi te eva vuttā “apāyesu apatamāne dhāretī”ti. Sammattaniyāmokkamanena hi apāyavinimuttisambhavo. Akkhāyatīti ettha iti-saddo ādyattho, pakārattho vā. Tena “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (itivu. 90; a. ni. 4.34) suttapadaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, “vitthāro”ti vā iminā. Ettha ca ariyamaggo niyyānikatāya, nibbānaṃ tassa tadatthasiddhihetutāyāti ubhayameva nippariyāyena dhammoti vutto. Nibbānañhi ārammaṇapaccayabhūtaṃ labhitvā ariyamaggo tadatthasiddhiyā saṃvattati, tathāpi yasmā ariyaphalānaṃ “tāya saddhāya avūpasantāyā”tiādivacanato maggena [M 2.0018] samucchinnānaṃ kilesānaṃ paṭippassaddhippahānakiccatāya niyyānānuguṇatāya niyyānapariyosānatāya ca. Pariyattidhammassa pana niyyānikadhammasamadhigamahetutāyāti iminā pariyāyena vuttanayena dhammabhāvo labbhati eva. Svāyamattho pāṭhāruḷho evāti dassento “na kevala”ntiādimāha.

By the two phrases 'in the attained path' and 'in realized cessation,' those in the state of fruition are indicated, not those on the path. To show this, he says, 'and for one practicing as instructed.' But is it not also said that a virtuous worldling practices as instructed? Although it is said, in the primary sense only those on the path should be described thus, not others, because they have not entered the fixed course of rightness. For it is they who are described thus: 'It keeps one from falling into the planes of misery.' For liberation from the planes of misery is possible only by entering the fixed course of rightness. Here the word 'iti' has the sense of 'beginning' or 'manner.' Thus it includes the sutta passage, 'Bhikkhus, whatever phenomena there are, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the chief among them' (Itivuttaka 90; AN 4.34), or this is indicated by 'in detail.' Here, the Noble Path is called 'Dhamma' in the primary sense because it leads out, and Nibbāna is called 'Dhamma' because it is the cause for achieving that goal. For the Noble Path, having obtained Nibbāna as its object-condition, leads to the attainment of that goal. So too, for the noble fruitions, this is because of such statements as 'by that faith not being calmed,' and because of their function of abandoning by tranquillization the defilements cut off by the path, and because they are conducive to leading out and are the culmination of leading out. The Dhamma of the scriptures, however, obtains the status of 'Dhamma' in a secondary sense, by the method stated, because it is the cause for the full realization of the Dhamma that leads out. To show that this meaning is established in the text itself, he says, 'not only,' and so on.

Kāmarāgo bhavarāgoti evamādibhedo sabbopi rāgo virajjati pahīyati etenāti rāgavirāgoti maggo kathito. Ejāsaṅkhātāya taṇhāya antonijjhānalakkhaṇassa sokassa ca taduppattiyaṃ sabbaso parikkhīṇattā anejamasokanti phalaṃ kathitaṃ. Appaṭikūlanti avirodhadīpanato kenaci aviruddhaṃ, iṭṭhaṃ paṇītanti vā attho. Paguṇarūpena pavattitattā, pakaṭṭhaguṇavibhāvanato vā paguṇaṃ. Sabbadhammakkhandhā kathitāti yojanā.

'Lust for sensual pleasures, lust for existence'—all such kinds of lust fade away and are abandoned by means of this; thus the path is called 'dispassion for lust.' Because craving, known as agitation, and sorrow, characterized by inner torment, are utterly exhausted in their arising, the fruition is called 'unagitated and sorrowless.' 'Not repulsive' indicates non-opposition, meaning not conflicting with anything; or it means 'desirable and sublime.' 'Proficient' because it proceeds in a proficient manner, or because it manifests excellent qualities. 'All aggregates of the Dhamma have been spoken of'—this is the connection.

Diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātenāti “yāyaṃ diṭṭhi ariyā niyyānikā niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya, tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhisāmaññagato viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.324, 357; ma. ni. 1.492; 3.54; a. ni. 6.12; pari. 274) evaṃ [V 2.0017] vuttāya diṭṭhiyā, “yāni tāni sīlāni akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni bhujissāni viññuppasatthāni aparāmaṭṭhāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni, tathārūpehi sīlehi sīlasāmaññagato viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.324; ma. ni. 1.492; 3.54; a. ni. 6.12; pari. 274) ca evaṃ vuttānaṃ sīlānañca saṃhatabhāvena, diṭṭhisīlasāmaññenāti attho. Saṃhatoti ghaṭito, sametoti attho. Ariyapuggalā hi yattha katthaci dūre ṭhitāpi attano guṇasāmaggiyā saṃhatā eva. Aṭṭha ca puggala dhammadasā teti te purisayugavasena cattāropi puggalavasena aṭṭheva ariyadhammassa paccakkhadassāvitāya dhammadasā. Tīṇi vatthūni saraṇanti gamanena tikkhattuṃ gamanena ca tīṇi saraṇagamanāni. Paṭivedesīti attano hadayagataṃ vācāya pavedesi.

'By the conjunction of view and virtue' means: by the view spoken of thus, 'He dwells having come to communion in view with such a view as is noble, leading out, which leads one who acts upon it to the complete destruction of suffering'; and by the virtues spoken of thus, 'He dwells having come to communion in virtue with such virtues as are unbroken, flawless, unblemished, unblotched, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, and conducive to concentration.' The meaning is: by the state of being conjoined, that is, by communion in view and virtue. 'Conjoined' means fitted together, united.
