For noble persons, though they may be standing far apart anywhere, are indeed conjoined by the harmony of their qualities. And the eight persons are seers of the Dhamma: they are four in terms of pairs of persons, and eight in terms of individual persons; they are seers of the Dhamma because they see the noble Dhamma directly. The three objects are a refuge. By the act of going, and by the threefold going, there are three goings for refuge. 'He made known' means he proclaimed by speech what was in his heart.

Saraṇagamanassa visayappabhedaphalasaṃkilesabhedānaṃ viya kattuvibhāvanā tattha kosallāya hotīti saraṇagamanesu atthakosallatthaṃ “saraṇaṃ, saraṇagamanaṃ, yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchati, saraṇagamanappabhedo, saraṇagamanaphalaṃ, saṃkileso, bhedoti ayaṃ vidhi veditabbo”ti [M 2.0019] vuttaṃ tena vinā saraṇagamanasseva asambhavato. Kasmā panettha vodānaṃ na gahitaṃ, nanu vodānavibhāvanāpi tattha kosallāya hotīti? Saccametaṃ, taṃ pana saṃkilesaggahaṇena atthato dīpitaṃ hotīti na gahitaṃ. Yāni hi nesaṃ saṃkilesakāraṇāni aññāṇādīni, tesaṃ sabbena sabbaṃ anuppannānaṃ anuppādanena, uppannānañca pahānena vodānaṃ hotīti.

An analysis of the agent, like an analysis of the going for refuge in terms of its object, varieties, fruit, defilement, and breach, is for the sake of skillfulness in this matter. Therefore, for the sake of skill in the meaning of the goings for refuge, it is said: 'Refuge, the going for refuge, one who goes for refuge, the varieties of going for refuge, the fruit of going for refuge, defilement, and breach—this method should be understood,' because without this, the going for refuge itself is impossible. Why is purification not included here? Is not the analysis of purification also for the sake of skillfulness in this matter? This is true, but it is not included because it is indicated in meaning by the inclusion of defilement. For purification occurs by not allowing the unarisen causes of their defilement, such as ignorance, to arise at all, and by abandoning those that have arisen.

Hiṃsatthassa dhātusaddassa vasenetaṃ padaṃ daṭṭhabbanti “hiṃsatīti saraṇa”nti vatvā taṃ pana hiṃsanaṃ kesaṃ, kathaṃ, kassa vāti codanaṃ sodhento “saraṇagatāna”ntiādimāha. Tattha bhayanti vaṭṭabhayaṃ. Santāsanti cittutrāsaṃ. Teneva cetasikadukkhassa gahitattā dukkhanti kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ. Duggatiparikilesanti duggatipariyāpannaṃ sabbampi dukkhaṃ. Tayidaṃ sabbaṃ parato phalakathāya āvi bhavissati. Etanti saraṇanti padaṃ. Evaṃ avisesato saraṇasaddassa padatthaṃ dassetvā idāni visesato dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Hite pavattanenāti “sampannasīlā, bhikkhave, viharathā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.64, 69) atthe niyojanena. Ahitā nivattanenāti “pāṇātipātassa kho pāpako vipāko abhisamparāya”ntiādinā ādīnavadassanādimukhena anatthato nivattanena. Bhayaṃ hiṃsatīti hitāhitesu appavattippavattihetukaṃ byasanaṃ appavattikaraṇena vināseti buddho. Bhavakantārā uttāraṇena maggasaṅkhāto dhammo. Itaro assāsadānena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsatīti yojanā. Kārānanti dānavasena pūjāvasena ca upanītānaṃ sakkārānaṃ. Vipulaphalappaṭilābhakaraṇena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsati saṅgho anuttaradakkhiṇeyyabhāvatoti adhippāyo. Imināpi pariyāyenāti imināpi vibhajitvā vuttena kāraṇena.

This word should be understood in accordance with the verbal root 'hiṃs,' meaning 'to harm.' Thus it is said, 'It harms, therefore it is a refuge (saraṇa).' Resolving the objection, 'Whose harming is this, how, and for whom?' he says, 'of those who have gone for refuge,' and so on. Here, 'fear' (bhaya) is the fear of the round of existence. 'Terror' (santāsa) is mental dread. Since mental suffering is included by that very word, 'suffering' (dukkha) here is bodily suffering. 'The defilement of a bad destination' (duggatiparikilesa) is all the suffering included in a bad destination. All this will become clear below in the discussion of the fruit. 'This' means the word 'refuge.' Having thus explained the meaning of the word 'refuge' generally, to now explain it specifically, 'or alternatively,' etc., is said. 'By promoting what is beneficial' means by enjoining what is good with such words as, 'Bhikkhus, dwell endowed with virtue' (MN 1:33, 46). 'By turning away from what is unbeneficial' means by turning them away from what is disadvantageous by such means as showing the danger with such words as, 'The killing of living beings has a bad result in the life to come.' The Buddha 'harms fear'—he destroys the calamity caused by engaging in what is unbeneficial and not engaging in what is beneficial by preventing its occurrence. The Dhamma, designated as the path, does so by leading them across the wilderness of existence. The other, the Saṅgha, 'harms the fear' of beings by giving them assurance—this is the connection. 'Of honors' means of the respectful offerings brought by way of gifts and veneration. The Saṅgha harms the fear of beings by causing them to obtain abundant fruit, because it is an unsurpassed field of merit—this is the intention. 'By this method too' means by this reason stated analytically.

“Sammāsambuddho [V 2.0018] bhagavā, svākkhāto dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅgho”ti evaṃ pavatto tattha ratanattaye pasādo tappasādo, tadeva rattanattayaṃ garu etassāti taggaru, tabbhāvo taggarutā, tappasādo ca taggarutā ca tappasādataggarutā. Tāhi tappasādataggarutāhi. Vidhutadiṭṭhivicikicchāsammohaassaddhiyāditāya vihatakileso. Tadeva ratanattayaṃ parāyaṇaṃ gati tāṇaṃ leṇanti evaṃ pavattiyā tapparāyaṇatākārappavatto cittuppādo [M 2.0020] saraṇagamanaṃ saraṇanti gacchati etenāti. Taṃsamaṅgīti tena yathāvuttacittuppādena samannāgato. Evaṃ upetīti evaṃ bhajati sevati payirupāsati, evaṃ vā jānāti bujjhatīti evamattho veditabbo.

'The Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Saṅgha is practicing the good way'—confidence in the Three Jewels that proceeds in this way is 'that confidence.' That same Three Jewels is revered by this one, thus 'one who holds it in reverence'; the state of that is 'reverence.' 'That confidence' and 'that reverence' are 'confidence-and-reverence.' Through that confidence-and-reverence. One whose defilements are struck down because wrong view, doubt, delusion, faithlessness, and so on, have been shaken off. A thought-process that proceeds in the manner of having that same Three Jewels as the final resort, the goal, the protection, and the shelter is the 'going for refuge,' because one 'goes' to 'refuge' by means of it. 'Endowed with that' means endowed with that aforesaid thought-process. 'Thus he approaches' means he thus resorts to, serves, and attends upon it; or, he thus knows and understands—this is the meaning to be understood.

Ettha ca pasādaggahaṇena lokiyasaraṇagamanamāha. Tañhi pasādappadhānaṃ. Garutāgahaṇena lokuttaraṃ. Ariyā hi ratanattayaguṇābhiññatāya pāsāṇacchattaṃ piya garuṃ katvā passanti, tasmā tappasādena vikkhambhanavasena vihatakileso, taggarutāya samucchedavasenāti yojetabbaṃ agāravakaraṇahetūnaṃ samucchindanato. Tapparāyaṇatā panettha taggatikatāti tāya catubbidhampi vakkhamānaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Avisesena vā pasādagarutā jotitāti pasādaggahaṇena aveccappasādassa itarassa ca gahaṇaṃ, tathā garutāgahaṇenāti ubhayenapi ubhayaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ yojetabbaṃ.

Here, by the inclusion of confidence, he speaks of the worldly going for refuge, for that is based primarily on confidence. By the inclusion of reverence, he speaks of the supramundane. For the noble ones, having directly known the qualities of the Three Jewels, regard even a stone parasol as dear and venerable. Therefore, it should be connected thus: defilements are struck down through that confidence by way of suppression, and through that reverence by way of eradication, because the causes for disrespect have been cut off. Here, 'having that as the final resort' is 'having that as one's goal.' By this, it should be seen, all four kinds of going for refuge to be described are included. Or, confidence and reverence are indicated without distinction. Thus, by the inclusion of confidence, both confirmed confidence and the other kind are included; likewise by the inclusion of reverence. Thus by both, both goings for refuge should be connected.

Maggakkhaṇe ijjhatīti yojanā. Nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvāti etena atthato catusaccādhigamo eva lokuttarasaraṇagamananti dasseti. Tattha hi nibbānadhammo sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena, maggadhammo bhāvanābhisamayavasena paṭivijjhiyamānoyeva saraṇagamanattaṃ sādheti, buddhaguṇā pana sāvakagocarabhūtā pariññābhisamayavasena, tathā ariyasaṅghaguṇā. Tenāha “kiccato sakalepi ratanattaye ijjhatī”ti. Ijjhantañca saheva ijjhati, na lokiyaṃ viya paṭipāṭiyā asammohappaṭivedhena paṭividdhattāti adhippāyo. Ye pana vadanti “na saraṇagamanaṃ nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvā pavattati, maggassa adhigatattā pana adhigatameva hoti ekaccānaṃ tevijjādīnaṃ lokiyavijjādayo viyā”ti, tesaṃ lokiyameva saraṇagamanaṃ siyā, na lokuttaraṃ, tañca ayuttaṃ duvidhassapi icchitabbattā.

“It succeeds at the moment of the path”: this is the connection. “Having Nibbāna as its object”: by this it is shown that in terms of meaning, the attainment of the Four Truths is itself the supramundane going for refuge. For there, the state of Nibbāna, being penetrated by way of the full understanding of realization, and the state of the path, being penetrated by way of the full understanding of development, alone accomplish the state of going for refuge. But the qualities of the Buddha, which are the domain of disciples, are penetrated by way of the full understanding of comprehension, as are the qualities of the noble Saṅgha. Therefore it is said: “In function, it succeeds in the entire Triple Gem.” And it succeeds simultaneously, not sequentially like a mundane attainment, because it is penetrated through the penetration of non-delusion—this is the intention. But those who say, “The going for refuge does not proceed with Nibbāna as its object; rather, since the path has been attained, it is already attained for some, just as the threefold knowledge and other mundane knowledges are”—for them, the going for refuge would be only mundane, not supramundane. And that is improper, since both kinds are to be desired.

Tanti lokiyasaraṇagamanaṃ. Saddhāpaṭilābho “sammāsambuddho bhagavā”tiādinā. Saddhāmūlikāti yathāvuttasaddhāpubbaṅgamā. Sammādiṭṭhi buddhasubuddhataṃ, dhammasudhammataṃ, saṅghasuppaṭipattiñca lokiyāvabodhavaseneva sammā ñāyena dassanato. Saddhāmūlikā ca sammādiṭṭhīti etena saddhūpanissayā yathāvuttalakkhaṇā paññā lokiyasaraṇagamananti dasseti. Tenāha [V 2.0019] “diṭṭhijukammanti vuccatī”ti. Diṭṭhiyeva attano paccayehi uju karīyatīti katvā[M 2.0021], diṭṭhi vā uju karīyati etenāti diṭṭhijukammaṃ, tathāpavatto cittuppādo. Evañca katvā “tapparāyaṇatākārappavatto cittuppādo”ti idañca vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti, saddhāpubbaṅgamasammādiṭṭhiggahaṇaṃ pana cittuppādassa tappadhānatāyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saddhāpaṭilābhoti iminā mātādīhi ussāhitadārakādīnaṃ viya ñāṇavippayuttaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ dasseti, sammādiṭṭhīti iminā ñāṇasampayuttaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ.

That is the mundane going for refuge. “The acquisition of faith” is through such phrases as “the Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One.” “Rooted in faith” means having the aforesaid faith as its forerunner. “Right view” is the right understanding of the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma's well-proclaimed nature, and the Saṅgha's good practice, by way of mundane comprehension in the correct manner. By this—that is, by the terms “rooted in faith” and “right view”—it is shown that wisdom, having the aforesaid characteristics and supported by faith, is the mundane going for refuge. Hence it is said, “It is called the straightening of view.” Because view itself is straightened by its own conditions, or view is straightened by this, it is the straightening of view, a mental state that has occurred in such a way. And thus the statement “a mental state that has occurred in the mode of being devoted to that” is established. But the inclusion of right view preceded by faith should be understood as due to the predominance of that in the mental state. “The acquisition of faith”: by this is shown the going for refuge dissociated from knowledge, like that of children encouraged by their mothers and others. “Right view”: by this is shown the going for refuge associated with knowledge.

Tayidaṃ lokiyaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ. Attā sanniyyātīyati appīyati pariccajīyati etenāti attasanniyyātanaṃ, yathāvuttaṃ diṭṭhijukammaṃ. Taṃ ratanattayaṃ parāyaṇaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ etassāti tapparāyaṇo, puggalo cittuppādo vā, tassa bhāvo tapparāyaṇatā, yathāvuttaṃ diṭṭhijukammameva. Saraṇanti adhippāyena sissabhāvaṃ antevāsikabhāvaṃ upagacchati etenāti sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ. Saraṇagamanādhippāyeneva paṇipatati etenāti paṇipāto. Sabbattha yathāvuttadiṭṭhijukammavaseneva attho veditabbo. Attapariccajananti saṃsāradukkhanissaraṇatthaṃ attano atthabhāvassa pariccajanaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Buddhādīnaṃyevāti avadhāraṇaṃ attasanniyyātanādīsupi tattha tattha vattabbaṃ. Evañhi tadaññanivattanaṃ kataṃ hoti.

This is the mundane going for refuge. “Self-surrender” (attasanniyyātana) is so called because by this one surrenders, dedicates, and relinquishes oneself; it is the aforesaid straightening of view. One who is “devoted to that” (tapparāyaṇo) is one for whom that Triple Gem is the final destination and refuge, whether a person or a mental state. The state of being devoted to that is devotion to that (tapparāyaṇatā), which is the aforesaid straightening of view itself. “Entering into discipleship” (sissabhāvūpagamana) is so called because by this, with the intention of going for refuge, one undertakes the state of a pupil, the state of an apprentice. “Prostration” (paṇipāto) is so called because by this one bows down with the very intention of going for refuge. In all cases the meaning should be understood by way of the aforesaid straightening of view. “Self-relinquishment” is the relinquishing of one's own existence for the sake of release from the suffering of saṃsāra. This is the method in the remaining cases as well. The exclusive particle in “to the Buddha and others alone” should be stated in each case of self-surrender and the others. For in this way, the turning away from others is effected.

Evaṃ attasanniyyātanādīni ekena pakārena dassetvā idāni aparehipi pakārehi dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tena pariyāyantarehipi attasanniyyātanaṃ katameva hoti atthassa abhinnattāti dasseti. Āḷavakādīnanti ādi-saddena sātāgirihemavatādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Nanu cete āḷavakādayo maggeneva āgatasaraṇagamanā, kathaṃ tesaṃ tapparāyaṇatāsaraṇagamanaṃ vuttanti? Maggenāgatasaraṇagamanehipi “so ahaṃ vicarissāmi…pe… sudhammataṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 194). Te mayaṃ vicarissāma, gāmā gāmaṃ nagā nagaṃ…pe… sudhammata”nti (su. ni. 182) ca tehi tapparāyaṇatākārassa paveditattā tathā vuttaṃ.

Having thus shown self-surrender and so forth in one way, the passage beginning “Moreover…” is now introduced to show them in other ways. This shows that by alternative expressions self-surrender is indeed accomplished, since the meaning is not different. In “Āḷavaka and others,” by the word “others” the inclusion of Sātāgiri, Hemavata, and others should be understood. But did not these, Āḷavaka and others, arrive at the going for refuge by the path itself? How then is their going for refuge as devotion to that stated? Even though they had arrived at the going for refuge by the path, it is stated thus because the mode of their devotion to that was declared by them in the words: “So I shall wander… for the sake of the well-proclaimed Dhamma” (SN 1.246; Snp 194), and “We shall wander from village to village, from mountain to mountain… for the sake of the well-proclaimed Dhamma” (Snp 182).

So panesa ñāti…pe… vasenāti ettha ñātivasena, bhayavasena, ācariyavasena, dakkhiṇeyyavasenāti paccekaṃ “vasenā”ti padaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tattha ñātivasenāti ñātibhāvavasena. Evaṃ sesesupi[M 2.0022]. Dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātenāti dakkhiṇeyyatāhetukena paṇipatanenāti attho. Itarehīti ñātibhāvādivasappavattehi tīhi paṇipātehi. Itarehītiādinā saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “tasmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vandatīti paṇipātassa lakkhaṇavacanaṃ[V 2.0020]. Evarūpanti diṭṭhadhammikaṃ sandhāya vadati. Samparāyikañhi niyyānikaṃ vā aniyyānikaṃ vā anusāsaniṃ paccāsīsanto dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātameva karotīti adhippāyo. Saraṇagamanappabhedoti saraṇagamanavibhāgo.

In the passage “This one… by way of kinsmen… etc.,” the word “by way of” should be connected with each term: “by way of kinsmen,” “by way of fear,” “by way of a teacher,” “by way of one worthy of offerings.” Herein, “by way of kinsmen” means by way of the state of being a kinsman. So too for the rest. “By prostration to one worthy of offerings” means by prostration on account of his being worthy of offerings. “By the others” means by the three prostrations that occur by way of the state of being a kinsman and so on. To show in detail the meaning stated concisely by “by the others, etc.,” the passage beginning “Therefore…” is stated. “He pays homage” is a statement of the characteristic of prostration. “Of such a kind” is said with reference to the present life. For one who hopes for instruction concerning the future life, whether it leads to release or not, performs only the prostration to one worthy of offerings—this is the intention. “The distinction in going for refuge” means the classification of going for refuge.

Ariyamaggo eva lokuttaraṃ saraṇagamananti āha “cattāri sāmaññaphalāni vipākaphala”nti. Sabbadukkhakkhayoti sakalassa vaṭṭadukkhassa anuppādanirodho. Etanti “cattāri ariyasaccāni, sammappaññāya passatī”ti (dha. pa. 190) evaṃ vuttaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ dassanaṃ.

To show that the noble path itself is the supramundane going for refuge, he says: “the four fruits of recluseship are the resultant fruit.” “The destruction of all suffering” is the non-arising and cessation of the entire suffering of the round of rebirth. “This” is the seeing of the noble truths stated thus: “He sees the four noble truths with perfect wisdom” (Dhp 190).

Niccato anupagamanādivasenāti niccanti aggahaṇādivasena. Aṭṭhānanti hetuppaṭikkhepo. Anavakāsoti paccayappaṭikkhepo. Ubhayenapi kāraṇameva paṭikkhipati. Yanti yena kāraṇena. Diṭṭhisampannoti maggadiṭṭhiyā samannāgato sotāpanno. Kañci saṅkhāranti catubhūmakesu saṅkhatasaṅkhāresu ekasaṅkhārampi. Niccato upagaccheyyāti niccoti gaṇheyya. Sukhato upagaccheyyāti “ekantasukhī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā”ti (dī. ni. 1.76, 79) evaṃ attadiṭṭhivasena sukhato gāhaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Diṭṭhivippayuttacittena pana ariyasāvako pariḷāhavūpasamanatthaṃ mattahatthiparitāsito viya cokkhabrāhmaṇo ukkārabhūmiṃ kañci saṅkhāraṃ sukhato upagacchati. Attavāre kasiṇādipaññattisaṅgahatthaṃ “saṅkhāra”nti avatvā “kañci dhamma”nti vuttaṃ. Imesupi ṭhānesu catubhūmakavaseneva paricchedo veditabbo tebhūmakavaseneva vā. Yaṃ yañhi puthujjano gāhavasena gaṇhāti, tato tato ariyasāvako gāhaṃ viniveṭheti.

“By way of not taking them as permanent, etc.” means by way of not grasping them as permanent, etc. “It is impossible” is a rejection of the cause. “There is no opportunity” is a rejection of the condition. By both, the reason is rejected. The word “that” (yaṃ) means “for which reason.” “One endowed with view” is a stream-enterer endowed with the view of the path. “Any formation” means even a single formation among the conditioned formations pertaining to the four planes. “He would take it as permanent” means he would grasp it as permanent. “He would take it as pleasant”: this is said with reference to the grasping of something as pleasant by way of a self-view, such as “the self is exclusively happy and healthy after death” (DN 1.76, 79). But a noble disciple, with a mind dissociated from wrong view, for the sake of allaying a feverish distress, might take some formation as pleasant, like the brahmin Cokkha who, terrified by a maddened elephant, took to a refuse heap. In the section on the self, in order to include concepts such as the kasiṇas, “any phenomenon” is said instead of “any formation.” In these instances too, the delimitation should be understood by way of the four planes or by way of the three planes. For from whatever a worldling grasps by way of grasping, from that a noble disciple disentangles the grasping.

Mātarantiādīsu janikā mātā, janako pitā, manussabhūto khīṇāsavo arahāti adhippeto. Kiṃ pana ariyasāvako aññaṃ jīvitā voropeyyāti? Etampi aṭṭhānaṃ, puthujjanabhāvassa pana mahāsāvajjabhāvadassanatthaṃ ariyabhāvassa ca phaladassanatthaṃ evaṃ vuttaṃ. Paduṭṭhacittoti vadhakacittena paduṭṭhacitto. Lohitaṃ uppādeyyāti jīvamānakasarīre [M 2.0023] khuddakamakkhikāya pivanamattampi lohitaṃ uppādeyya. Saṅghaṃ bhindeyyāti samānasaṃvāsakaṃ samānasīmāyaṃ ṭhitaṃ saṅghaṃ “kammena uddesena voharanto anussāvanena salākaggāhenā”ti (pari. 458) evaṃ vuttehi pañcahi kāraṇehi bhindeyya. Aññaṃ satthāranti aññaṃ titthakaraṃ “ayaṃ me satthā”ti evaṃ gaṇheyyāti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti attho.

In “mother,” etc., the mother is the one who gives birth, the father is the one who begets, and an arahant is intended as a human being whose taints are destroyed. But would a noble disciple deprive another of life? This too is impossible. However, it is stated thus to show the great blameworthiness of the state of a worldling and to show the fruit of the noble state. “With a malevolent mind” means with a mind corrupted by a murderous thought. “Would cause blood to flow” means he would cause to flow from a living body even a drop of blood sufficient for a tiny fly to drink. “Would cause a schism in the Sangha” means he would split a Sangha dwelling in communion and established within the same boundary by the five causes stated as: “by a formal act, by a designation, by a transaction, by a proclamation, or by taking up tickets” (Pari 458). “Another teacher” means he would take another sectarian teacher, thinking, “This is my teacher.” The meaning is that this is impossible.

Na te [V 2.0021] gamissanti apāyanti te buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatā tannimittaṃ apāyaṃ na gamissanti, devakāyaṃ pana paripūressantīti attho. Dasahi ṭhānehīti dasahi kāraṇehi. Adhigaṇhantīti adhibhavanti.

“They will not go to a plane of misery”: the meaning is that those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha will not go to a plane of misery on account of that; rather, they will fill the host of devas. “On ten grounds” means by ten reasons. “They acquire” means they overpower.

Velāmasuttādivasenāti ettha “karīsassa catutthabhāgappamāṇānaṃ caturāsītisahassasaṅkhānaṃ suvaṇṇapātirūpiyapātikaṃsapātīnaṃ yathākkamaṃ rūpiyasuvaṇṇahiraññapūrānaṃ sabbālaṅkārappaṭimaṇḍitānaṃ caturāsītiyā hatthisahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā assasahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā rathasahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā dhenusahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā kaññāsahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā pallaṅkasahassānaṃ, caturāsītiyā vatthakoṭisahassānaṃ, aparimāṇassa ca khajjabhojjādibhedassa āhārassa pariccajanavasena sattamāsādhikāni satta saṃvaccharāni nirantaraṃ pavattavelāmamahādānato ekassa sotāpannassa dinnadānaṃ mahapphalataraṃ. Tato sataṃ sotāpannānaṃ dinnadānato ekassa sakadāgāmino, tato ekassa anāgāmino, tato ekassa arahato, tato ekassa paccekabuddhassa, tato sammāsambuddhassa, tato buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa dinnadānaṃ mahapphalataraṃ, tato cātuddisaṃ saṅghaṃ uddissa vihārakaraṇaṃ, tato saraṇagamanaṃ mahapphalatara”nti imamatthaṃ pakāsentassa velāmasuttassa (a. ni. 9.20) vasena. Vuttañhetaṃ “yaṃ, gahapati, velāmo brāhmaṇo dānaṃ adāsi mahādānaṃ, yo ekaṃ diṭṭhisampannaṃ bhojeyya, idaṃ tato mahapphalatara”ntiādi (a. ni. 9.20). Velāmasuttādīti ādi-saddena aggappasādasuttādīnaṃ (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

By way of the Velāma Sutta, etc.: Herein, more fruitful than the great gift of Velāma—which consisted of giving away, continuously for seven years and seven months, eighty-four thousand gold, silver, and bronze bowls, each the size of a quarter of a karīsa, filled respectively with silver, gold, and bullion; eighty-four thousand elephants adorned with all their ornaments; eighty-four thousand horses; eighty-four thousand chariots; eighty-four thousand milk-cows; eighty-four thousand maidens; eighty-four thousand couches; eighty-four thousand crores of cloth; and an immeasurable amount of various kinds of food, solid and soft—is a gift given to a single stream-enterer. More fruitful than a gift to a hundred stream-enterers is a gift to a single once-returner; than that to a hundred once-returners, a gift to a single non-returner; than that to a hundred non-returners, a gift to a single arahant; than that to a hundred arahants, a gift to a single paccekabuddha; than that to a hundred paccekabuddhas, a gift to a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. More fruitful than a gift to a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is a gift to the Sangha with the Buddha at its head. More fruitful than that is building a monastery for the Sangha of the four quarters. And more fruitful than that is going for refuge. This meaning is shown by way of the Velāma Sutta (AN 9.20), which clarifies this matter. For it is said: “Householder, whatever great gift the brahmin Velāma gave, if one were to feed a single person accomplished in view, this would be more fruitful than that,” and so on (AN 9.20). By “Velāma Sutta, etc.,” the word “etc.” should be understood as including suttas such as the Aggappasāda Sutta (AN 4.34; Itiv 90).

Aññāṇaṃ vatthuttayassa guṇānaṃ ajānanaṃ tattha sammoho, “buddho nu kho, na nu kho”tiādinā vicikicchā saṃsayo. Micchāñāṇaṃ tassa guṇānaṃ aguṇabhāvaparikappanena viparītaggāho. Ādi-saddena anādarāgāravādīnaṃ [M 2.0024] saṅgaho. Na mahājutikanti na ujjalaṃ, aparisuddhaṃ apariyodātanti attho. Na mahāvipphāranti anuḷāraṃ. Sāvajjoti diṭṭhitaṇhādivasena sadoso. Lokiyaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ sikkhāsamādānaṃ viya aggahitakālaparicchedaṃ jīvitapariyantameva hoti, tasmā tassa khandhabhedena bhedoti āha “anavajjo kālakiriyāyā”ti. Soti anavajjo saraṇagamanabhedo. Satipi anavajjatte iṭṭhaphalopi na hotīti āha “aphalo”ti. Kasmā? Avipākattā. Na hi taṃ akusalanti.

Ignorance is not knowing the qualities of the Three Jewels. Delusion therein is doubt and uncertainty, such as, “Is he the Buddha or not?” Wrong knowledge is perverse grasping, conceiving of those qualities as faults. By the word “etc.” is included disrespect, irreverence, and so on. Not greatly luminous means not bright, impure, not pristine. Not greatly expansive means not sublime. Faulty means defective on account of views, craving, and so on. Mundane going for refuge, not having a specified time limit, lasts only for the extent of one’s life, like the undertaking of the training rules. Therefore, since it is broken with the breakup of the aggregates, it is said to be “unblameworthy at the time of death.” That is the unblameworthy breaking of the going for refuge. Although it is unblameworthy, it does not have the desired fruit; hence it is said to be “fruitless.” Why? Because it is without result. For it is not unwholesome.

Ko upāsakoti sarūpapucchā, tasmā “kiṃlakkhaṇo upāsako”ti vuttaṃ hoti. Kasmāti hetupucchā. Tena kena pavattinimittena upāsakasaddo tasmiṃ puggale niruḷhoti dasseti[V 2.0022]. Tenāha “kasmā upāsakoti vuccatī”ti. Saddassa abhidheyyo pavattinimittaṃ tadatthassa tabbhāvakāraṇaṃ. Kimassa sīlanti kīdisaṃ assa upāsakassa sīlaṃ, kittakena sīlenāyaṃ sīlasampanno nāma hotīti attho. Ko ājīvoti ko assa sammāājīvo? So pana micchājīvassa parivajjanena hotīti sopi vibhajīyatīti. Kā vipattīti kā sīlassa, ājīvassa vā vipatti. Anantarassa hi vidhi vā paṭisedho vāti. Kā sampatīti etthāpi eseva nayo.

“What is a lay follower?” is a question about the definition; therefore, it means, “What is the characteristic of a lay follower?” “Why?” is a question about the reason. This shows by what ground of application the term “lay follower” is used for that person. Therefore it is said: “Why is one called a lay follower?” The ground for the application of a word is its denotation, the reason for that meaning’s existence. “What is his virtue?” means what kind of virtue does this lay follower have, and with how much virtue is he called accomplished in virtue? “What is his livelihood?” means what is his right livelihood? Since that comes about by avoiding wrong livelihood, that too is analyzed. “What is the failure?” means what is the failure in regard to virtue or livelihood? For what immediately follows is either an injunction or a prohibition. “What is the success?” Here too, the same method applies.

Yo kocīti khattiyādīsu yo koci. Tena saraṇagamanamevettha kāraṇaṃ, na jātiādivisesoti dasseti. Upāsanatoti teneva saraṇagamanena tattha ca sakkaccakiriyāya ādaragāravabahumānādiyogena payirupāsanato. Veramaṇiyoti veraṃ vuccati pāṇātipātādidussīlyaṃ, tassa maṇanato hananato vināsanato veramaṇiyo, pañca viratiyo viratippadhānattā tassa sīlassa. Tenevāha “paṭivirato hotī”ti.

“Whoever” means whoever among khattiyas and others. This shows that the going for refuge itself is the reason here, not distinctions of birth and so on. “Because of attending upon”: one is an upāsaka because one attends upon the Three Jewels by that very going for refuge, and by acting respectfully, with application of esteem, reverence, and high regard. “Abstinence” (veramaṇī): “enmity” (vera) refers to immoral conduct such as the destruction of life. “Abstinence” is so called because it crushes (maṇana), strikes, and destroys that. The five abstinences constitute that virtue, since for that virtue, abstinence is primary. Therefore it is said, “he abstains.”

Micchāvaṇijjāti na sammāvaṇijjā ayuttavaṇijjā asāruppavaṇijjā. Pahāyāti akaraṇeneva pajahitvā. Dhammenāti dhammato anapetena. Tena aññampi adhammikaṃ jīvikaṃ paṭikkhipati. Samenāti avisamena. Tena kāyavisamādiduccaritaṃ vajjetvā kāyasamādinā sucaritena ājīvaṃ dasseti. Satthavaṇijjāti āyudhabhaṇḍaṃ katvā vā kāretvā vā yathākataṃ [M 2.0025] vā paṭilabhitvā tassa vikkayo. Sattavaṇijjāti manussavikkayo. Maṃsavaṇijjāti sūnakārādayo viya migasūkarādike posetvā maṃsaṃ sampādetvā vikkayo. Majjavaṇijjāti yaṃ kiñci majjaṃ yojetvā tassa vikkayo. Visavaṇijjāti visaṃ yojetvā visaṃ gahetvā vā tassa vikkayo. Tattha satthavaṇijjā paroparodhanimittatāya akaraṇīyā vuttā. Sattavaṇijjā abhujissabhāvakaraṇato, maṃsavisavaṇijjā vadhahetuto, majjavaṇijjā pamādaṭṭhānato.

“Wrong trade” means trade that is not right, improper trade, unsuitable trade. “Having abandoned” means having given it up by not doing it. “Righteously” means in accordance with the Dhamma, not deviating from it. By this, he rejects any other unrighteous livelihood. “Evenly” means without crookedness. By this, having avoided bodily misconduct and other evil conduct consisting of crookedness, he shows a livelihood of good conduct consisting of bodily uprightness. “Trade in weapons” is the selling of instruments of weaponry after making them, having them made, or acquiring them ready-made. “Trade in living beings” is the selling of human beings. “Trade in meat” is raising deer, pigs, and other such animals, like a butcher, and then preparing and selling the meat. “Trade in intoxicants” is preparing and selling any kind of intoxicant. “Trade in poisons” is preparing poison, or acquiring it, and then selling it. Among these, trade in weapons is said to be something that should not be done as it is a cause for harming others. Trade in living beings, because it makes others unfree. Trade in meat and poisons, because they are a cause of slaughter. Trade in intoxicants, because it is a basis for heedlessness.

Tassevāti pañcaveramaṇilakkhaṇassa sīlassa ceva pañcamicchāvaṇijjālakkhaṇassa ājīvassa ca. Vipattīti bhedo pakopo ca. Yāyāti yāya paṭipattiyā. Caṇḍāloti upāsakacaṇḍālo. Malanti upāsakamalaṃ. Paṭikuṭṭhoti upāsakanihīno. Buddhādīsu kammakammaphalesu ca saddhāvipariyāyo assaddhiyaṃ micchādhimokkho, yathāvuttena assaddhiyena samannāgato assaddho. Yathāvuttasīlavipattiājīvavipattivasena dussīlo. “Iminā diṭṭhādinā idaṃ nāma maṅgalaṃ hotī”ti – evaṃ bālajanaparikappitakotūhalasaṅkhātena diṭṭhasutamutamaṅgalena samannāgato kotūhalamaṅgaliko. Maṅgalaṃ paccetīti diṭṭhamaṅgalādibhedaṃ maṅgalameva pattiyāyati. No kammanti [V 2.0023] kammassakataṃ no pattiyāyati. Ito bahiddhāti ito sabbaññubuddhasāsanato bahiddhā bāhirakasamaye. Dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesatīti duppaṭipannaṃ dakkhiṇārahasaññī gavesati. Pubbakāraṃ karotīti dānamānanādikaṃ kusalakiriyaṃ paṭhamataraṃ karoti. Ettha ca dakkhiṇeyyapariyesanapubbakāre ekaṃ katvā pañca dhammā veditabbā.

“Of that very same” refers to that very virtue characterized by the five abstinences and that livelihood characterized by the five kinds of wrong trade. “Failure” means a breach and corruption. “By which” means by which practice. “Outcaste” means an outcaste among lay followers. “Stain” means a stain on a lay follower. “Despised” means a base lay follower. Lack of faith is the perversion of faith concerning the Buddha and so on, and concerning kamma and its fruit; it is wrong conviction. One endowed with such lack of faith is “faithless.” One is “immoral” on account of the aforesaid failure in virtue and failure in livelihood. One is “addicted to superstitious signs” who is endowed with auspicious signs seen, heard, or cognized, which are reckoned as superstitions fabricated by foolish people, as in the thought: “By this or that sight, etc., such and such is an auspicious sign.” “He trusts in signs” means he believes only in signs, such as things seen. “Not in kamma” means he does not believe in the ownership of kamma. “Outside of this” means outside of this dispensation of the Omniscient Buddha, in an external creed. “He seeks one worthy of gifts” means, perceiving one of wrong practice as worthy of gifts, he seeks him out. “He gives precedence to him” means he performs wholesome actions such as giving and honoring for him first. Here, five things are to be understood, taking the seeking of one worthy of gifts and the giving of precedence as one.

Vipattiyaṃ vuttavipariyāyena sampatti veditabbā. Ayaṃ pana viseso – catunnampi parisānaṃ ratijananaṭṭhena upāsakova ratanaṃ upāsakaratanaṃ. Guṇasobhākittisaddasugandhatāhi upāsakova padumaṃ upāsakapadumaṃ. Tathā upāsakapuṇḍarīko.

Success should be understood as the opposite of what was stated concerning failure. This, however, is the distinction: a lay follower is a “jewel,” a jewel among lay followers, in the sense of generating delight for the four assemblies. A lay follower is a “lotus,” a lotus among lay followers, because of the splendor of his virtues and the fragrance of the sound of his fame. Similarly, he is a “white lotus” among lay followers.

Ādimhīti ādiatthe. Koṭiyanti pariyantakoṭiyaṃ. Vihāraggenāti ovarakakoṭṭhāsena, “imasmiṃ gabbhe vasantānaṃ idaṃ nāma phalaṃ pāpuṇātī”tiādīnā taṃ taṃ vasanaṭṭhānakoṭṭhāsenāti attho. Ajjatanti ajja icceva attho.

“In the beginning” means in the sense of “beginning.” “At the end” means at the final limit. “By a portion of the monastery” means by a portion of an inner chamber; the meaning is by a particular portion of a dwelling place, as in: “May those dwelling in this chamber attain such and such a fruit.” “Today” (ajjatana) simply means today (ajja).

Pāṇehi [M 2.0026] upetanti iminā tassa saraṇagamanassa āpāṇakoṭikataṃ dassento “yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattatī”tiādīni vatvā puna jīvitenapi taṃ vatthuttayaṃ paṭipūjento saraṇagamanaṃ rakkhāmīti uppannaṃ tassa brāhmaṇassa adhippāyaṃ vibhāvento “ahañhī”tiādimāha. Pāṇehi upetanti hi yāva me pāṇā dharanti, tāva saraṇaṃ upetaṃ. Upento ca na vācāmattena na ekavāraṃ cittuppādamattena, atha kho pāṇānaṃ pariccajanavasenapi yāvajīvaṃ upetanti evamettha attho veditabbo.

By “endowed with my life-breath,” he shows that his going for refuge is for the duration of his life. Having said, “As long as my life lasts,” etc., and then, honoring the Three Jewels even with his life, he reveals the intention that arose in that brahmin, “I will protect the refuge,” by saying, “For I…,” etc. “Endowed with my life-breath” means: “As long as my life-breath lasts, so long have I gone for refuge.” And one goes for refuge not by mere speech, not by a single arising of thought, but rather one goes for refuge for life, even to the point of giving up one's life-breath. Thus the meaning should be understood here.

17-19. Sattame jāṇussoṇīti netaṃ tassa mātāpitūhi kataṃ nāmaṃ, apica kho ṭhānantarappaṭilābhaladdhanti dassento āha “jāṇussoṇīti ṭhānantaraṃ kirā”tiādi. Ekaṃ ṭhānantaranti ekaṃ purohitaṭṭhānaṃ. Uṇhīsaādikakudhabhaṇḍehi saddhiṃ laddhaṃ tathā cassa raññā dinnanti vadanti. Tenāha “rañño santike ca laddhajāṇussoṇisakkārattā”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Aṭṭhamanavamesu natthi vattabbaṃ.

17–19. In the seventh sutta: The name “Jāṇussoṇi” was not one given by his parents, but rather one acquired on gaining a high position. Showing this, the text says: “Jāṇussoṇi, it is said, is a high position,” etc. “A high position” means the position of a royal chaplain. It is said that he received it together with the royal insignia such as the turban, and that it was given by the king. Hence it is said: “because of the honor of Jāṇussoṇi having been received from the king.” The rest here is clear. There is nothing to be said on the eighth and ninth.

20-21. Dasame dunnikkhittanti duṭṭhu nikkhittaṃ padapaccābhaṭṭhaṃ katvā manasi ṭhapitaṃ. Pajjati ñāyati attho etenāti padaṃ, atthaṃ byañjayati pakāsetīti byañjanaṃ, padameva. Tenevāha “uppaṭipāṭiyā…pe… byañjananti vuccatī”ti. Padasamudāyabyatirekena visuṃ pāḷi nāma [V 2.0024] natthīti āha “ubhayametaṃ pāḷiyāva nāma”nti. Pakaṭṭhānañhi vacanappabandhānaṃ āḷiyeva pāḷīti vuccati. Sesamettha ekādasamañca uttānatthameva.

20-21. In the tenth, dunnikkhitta means badly placed—placed in the mind with the words disarranged. Pada is that by which the meaning is known or understood; byañjana is that which expresses or reveals the meaning—it is the word itself. Therefore it is said: “In reverse order... it is called byañjana.” Since there is no separate Pāḷi apart from a collection of words, it is said: “Both of these are names for the Pāḷi.” For a series of excellent verbal compositions is indeed called “Pāḷi.” The rest here, and the eleventh, are clear in meaning.

Adhikaraṇavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Adhikaraṇavagga is concluded.

3. Bālavaggavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Chapter on the Fool

22-24. Tatiyassa paṭhamadutiyatatiyāni uttānatthāneva.

22-24. The first, second, and third of the third are clear in meaning.

25. Catutthe netabboti aññato āharitvā bodhetabbo, ñāpetabboti attho.

25. In the fourth, netabbo means he should be brought from elsewhere and made to understand; the meaning is ñāpetabbo.

27. Chaṭṭhe no cepi paṭicchādetvā karontīti pāṇātipātādīni karonto sacepi appaṭicchādetvā karonti. Paṭicchannamevāti viññūhi garahitabbabhāvato [M 2.0027] paṭicchādanārahattā paṭicchannamevāti vuccati. Avīciādayo padesavisesā tatthūpapannā sattā ca nirayaggahaṇena gahitāti āha “nirayoti sahokāsakā khandhā”ti. Tiracchānayoni nāma visuṃ padesaviseso natthīti āha “tiracchānayoniyaṃ khandhāva labbhantī”ti.

27. In the sixth, the phrase even if they do not do it concealingly means: even if one commits acts such as killing living beings without concealing them. It is concealed indeed is said because it is to be censured by the wise and thus deserves to be concealed. The particular places such as Avīci and the beings reborn there are included by the term 'hell'; thus he said: 'Hell means the aggregates together with their location.' There is no separate particular place called the animal realm; thus he said: 'In the animal realm only the aggregates are found.'

31. Dasame attho phalaṃ tadadhīnavuttitāya vaso etassāti atthavaso, hetūti āha “atthavaseti kāraṇānī”ti. Araññavanapatthānīti araññalakkhaṇappattāni vanapatthāni. Vanapattha-saddo hi saṇḍabhūte rukkhasamūhepi vattatīti araññaggahaṇaṃ. Vanīyati vivekakāmehi bhajīyati, vanute vā te attasampattiyā vasanatthāya yācanto viya hotīti vanaṃ, patiṭṭhahanti ettha vivekakāmā yathādhippetavisesādhigamenāti patthaṃ, vanesu patthaṃ gahanaṭṭhāne senāsanaṃ vanapatthaṃ. Kiñcāpīti anujānanasambhāvanatthe nipāto. Kiṃ anujānāti? Nippariyāyato araññabhāvaṃ gāmato bahi araññanti. Tenāha “nippariyāyenā”tiādi. Kiṃ sambhāveti? Āraññakaṅganipphādakattaṃ. Yañhi āraññakaṅganipphādakaṃ, taṃ visesato araññanti vattabbanti. Tenāha “yaṃ taṃ pañcadhanusatika”ntiādi. Nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlāti indakhīlato bahi nikkhamitvā, tato bahi paṭṭhāyāti attho. Bahi indakhīlāti vā yattha dve tīṇi indakhīlāni, [V 2.0025] tattha bahiddhā indakhīlato paṭṭhāya. Yattha taṃ natthi, tadarahaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāyāti vadanti. Gāmantanti gāmasamīpaṃ. Anupacāraṭṭhānanti niccakiccavasena na upacaritabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Tenāha “yattha na kasīyati na vapīyatī”ti.

31. In the tenth, atthavaso: attha is the fruit; vasa is mastery over it due to dependence on it. The cause, he said, is: 'Atthavasa means reasons.' Araññavanapatthāni refers to forest tracts that have the characteristic of a wilderness. The term vanapattha also applies to a dense grove of trees; hence the inclusion of arañña. A forest (vana) is so called because it is frequented by those who desire seclusion, or because it, as it were, begs them to dwell there for the sake of their own attainment. Pattha is a place where those who desire seclusion become established to attain the special qualities they wish for. Thus, vanapattha refers to a lodging in a remote place in the woods. Kiñcāpi is a particle indicating concession and possibility. What does it concede? The state of being a wilderness in the direct sense: 'a wilderness is outside a village.' Therefore he said: 'Without circumlocution,' etc. What does it make possible? The accomplishment of the forest-dweller's ascetic practice. For whatever accomplishes the forest-dweller's practice, that in particular should be called a 'wilderness.' Therefore he said: 'That which is five hundred bow-lengths,' etc. Having gone out beyond the city post means departing beyond the city post and starting from outside it. Alternatively, beyond the city post refers to a place where there are two or three city posts, starting from beyond the outermost one. Where these are absent, they say it begins from a place suitable for one. Gāmanta means the vicinity of a village. Anupacāraṭṭhāna is a place not to be frequented for one's daily duties. Therefore he said: 'where it is not plowed or sown.'

Attano ca diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāranti etena satthā attano vivekābhiratiṃ pakāseti. Tattha diṭṭhadhammo nāma ayaṃ paccakkho attabhāvo, sukhavihāro nāma catunnaṃ iriyāpathavihārānaṃ phāsutā. Ekakassa hi araññe antamaso uccāravassāvakiccaṃ upādāya sabbe iriyāpathā phāsukā honti, tasmā diṭṭhadhamme sukhavihāraṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāranti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

And by the phrase for my own pleasant dwelling in the here and now, the Teacher reveals his own delight in seclusion. Herein, the here and now means this present state of existence, and a pleasant dwelling means the comfort of the four postures. For one who is alone in the wilderness, all postures are comfortable, even down to the need to urinate and defecate. Therefore, a pleasant dwelling in the here and now is diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra; or the meaning here should be understood in this way.

Pacchimañca janataṃ anukampamānoti kathaṃ araññavāsena pacchimā janatā anukampitā hoti? Saddhāpabbajitā hi kulaputtā bhagavato araññavāsaṃ [M 2.0028] disvā “bhagavāpi nāma araññasenāsanāni na muñcati, yassa nevatthi pariññātabbaṃ na pahātabbaṃ na bhāvetabbaṃ na sacchikātabbaṃ, kimaṅgaṃ pana maya”nti cintetvā tattha vasitabbameva maññissanti, evaṃ khippameva dukkhassantakarā bhavissanti. Evaṃ pacchimā janatā anukampitā hoti. Etamatthaṃ dassento āha “pacchime mama sāvake anukampanto”ti.

And out of compassion for the future generation: How is the future generation shown compassion by dwelling in the wilderness? Clansmen who have gone forth in faith, on seeing the Blessed One’s dwelling in the wilderness, will think: 'The Blessed One himself does not abandon forest lodgings—he for whom there is nothing left to fully understand, nothing to abandon, nothing to develop, and nothing to realize—so what to speak of us?' They will resolve to dwell there, and thus quickly make an end of suffering. In this way, compassion is shown to the future generation. To show this meaning, he said: 'out of compassion for my future disciples.'

32. Ekādasame vijjaṃ bhajantīti vijjābhāgiyā, vijjābhāge vijjākoṭṭhāse vattantītipi vijjābhāgiyā. Padaṃ pacchindatīti maggacittassa patiṭṭhaṃ upacchindati, maggacittaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ na detīti attho. Ubbaṭṭetvāti samucchedavasena samūlaṃ uddharitvā. Aṭṭhasu ṭhānesūti buddhādīsu aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu. Rāgassa khayavirāgenāti rāgassa khayasaṅkhātena virāgena, rāgassa anuppattidhammatāpādanenāti vuttaṃ hoti.

32. In the eleventh, vijjābhāgiyā means they partake of knowledge; they are also vijjābhāgiyā because they exist in the share of knowledge, the portion of knowledge. It cuts off the footing means it severs the support of the path-consciousness; that is, it does not allow the path-consciousness to be established. Having uprooted means having pulled it up completely by the root, by way of eradication. In eight instances refers to the eight instances beginning with the Buddha. Through the destruction and fading away of lust means through the fading away reckoned as the destruction of lust; this is said to mean bringing about the non-arising nature of lust.

Bālavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Fool is concluded.

4. Samacittavaggavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Chapter on the Even-Minded

33. Catutthassa [V 2.0026] paṭhame bhavanti ettha patiṭṭhahantīti bhūmi, asappurisānaṃ bhūmi asappurisabhūmi. Sappurisabhūmiyampi eseva nayo. Kataṃ na jānātīti akataññū, asamatthasamāsoyaṃ gamakattā “asūriyapassā”tiādīsu viya. Tenāha “kataṃ na jānātī”ti. Akatavedīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Pākaṭaṃ katvā na jānātīti “idañcidañca mayhaṃ iminā kata”nti saṅghamajjhagaṇamajjhādīsu pākaṭaṃ katvā na jānāti, na pakāsetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Upaññātanti thomanāvasena upagantvā ñātaṃ. Tenāha “vaṇṇita”ntiādi.

33. In the first of the fourth: Bhūmi (ground) is so called because they exist (bhavanti) here, they are established (patiṭṭhahanti) here. The ground of inferior persons is asappurisabhūmi. The same method applies to sappurisabhūmi. Akataññū (ungrateful) is one who does not know what has been done. This is an incapable compound (asamatthasamāsa), like 'those who do not see the sun' and so on, which is acceptable because it conveys the meaning. Therefore it is said: 'he does not know what has been done.' The same method applies here to akatavedī (unappreciative). He does not know it even when it has been made public means that he does not acknowledge or declare, 'This and that was done for me by this person,' even when it has been made public in the midst of the Sangha, a group, etc.; that is to say, he does not make it known. Upaññātaṃ means known by approaching by way of praise. Therefore it is said: 'praised' (vaṇṇitaṃ), and so on.

34. Dutiye vassasataparimāṇamāyu assāti vassasatāyuko, vassasatāyukatañca vassasatāyukakāle jātasseva hoti, nāññassāti āha “vassasatāyukakāle jāto”ti. Vassasataṃ jīvati sīlenāti vassasatajīvī. Vassasatanti ca accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ. Tenāha “sakalaṃ vassasataṃ jīvanto”ti. Mātāpitūnaṃ mātāva bahūpakāratarāti tassāyeva padhānabhāvena paṭikātabbattā dakkhiṇaṃ aṃsakūṭaṃ vadanti. Hadayalohitaṃ pāyetvāti khīraṃ sandhāya [M 2.0029] vadati. Lohitañhi khīrabhāvena pariṇāmaṃ gacchati. Tyāssāti te assa. Sesamettha uttānameva.

34. In the second: Vassasatāyuko is one whose lifespan has the measure of a hundred years. And having a hundred-year lifespan occurs only for one born in an age of a hundred-year lifespan, not for another; therefore it is said: 'born in an age of a hundred-year lifespan.' Vassasatajīvī is one who lives for a hundred years by means of virtue. And 'a hundred years' is a usage in the sense of continuous duration. Therefore it is said: 'living for the entire hundred years.' Among mother and father, the mother is of much greater help; therefore, because she is pre-eminent in respect of the obligation to be repaid, they speak of the right shoulder. Having given him her heart's blood to drink is said in reference to milk, for blood undergoes transformation into the state of milk. Tyāssa means te assa. The rest here is clear.

35. Tatiye tenupasaṅkamīti ettha yenādhippāyena so brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkami, taṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ “so hi brāhmaṇo”tiādimāha. Virajjhanapañhanti yaṃ pañhaṃ puṭṭho virajjhitvā kathesi, aviparītaṃ katvā sampādetuṃ na sakkoti, tādisaṃ pañhanti attho. Ubhatokoṭikaṃ pañhanti ubhohi koṭīhi yuttaṃ pañhaṃ. “Kiṃvādī bhavaṃ gotamo”ti hi puṭṭho “kiriyavādimhī”ti vā vadeyya “akiriyavādimhī”ti vā, tasmā imassa pañhassa vissajjane “kiriyavādimhī”ti ekā koṭi, “akiriyavādimhī”ti dutiyāti koṭidvayayutto ayaṃ pañho. Uggilitunti dve koṭiyo mocetvā kathetuṃ asakkonto bahi nīharituṃ atthato apanetuṃ na sakkhissati. Dve koṭiyo mocento hi taṃ bahi nīharati nāma. Niggilitunti pucchāya dosaṃ datvā hāretuṃ asakkonto pavesetuṃ na sakkhissati. Tattha dosaṃ datvā hārento hi gilitvā viya adassanaṃ gamento paveseti nāma. Kiṃladdhikoti kiṃddiṭṭhiko. Vadanti etenāti vādo, diṭṭhi. Ko vādo etassāti kiṃvādī. Kimakkhāyīti kimabhidhāyī, kīdisī dhammakathā. Tenāha “kiṃ nāma…pe… pucchatī”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

35. In the third, regarding then he approached him: to show clearly the intention with which that brahmin approached the Blessed One, the text says, 'For that brahmin…,' and so on. A question of evasion: this means a question of such a kind that, when asked, one speaks evasively, unable to answer it without contradiction. A question with two horns: a question connected with two horns, or extremes. For when asked, 'What does the good Gotama advocate?' he might say either, 'I am an advocate of action,' or 'I am an advocate of inaction.' Therefore, in answering this question, 'I am an advocate of action' is one horn, and 'I am an advocate of inaction' is the second. Thus this question has two horns. To disgorge: unable to speak by releasing the two horns, he will not be able to get it out, that is, to remove it in meaning. For one who releases the two horns is said to get it out. To swallow: unable to refute it by pointing out a flaw in the question, he will not be able to make it enter. For one who refutes it by pointing out a flaw is said to make it enter, that is, to make it disappear as if by swallowing it. Of what doctrine?: of what view? Vāda (doctrine) is that by which they speak; it means view. Kiṃvādī (what does he advocate?) means 'what is his doctrine?' Kimakkhāyī (what does he proclaim?) means 'what does he state?,' 'what kind of Dhamma talk?' Therefore it is said: 'What indeed… (etc.) … he asks.' The rest here is clear.

36. Catutthe [V 2.0027] dakkhiṇaṃ arahantīti dakkhiṇeyyā. Āhunaṃ vuccati dānaṃ, taṃ arahantīti āhuneyyā.

36. In the fourth: They are worthy of a donation, thus they are dakkhiṇeyyā, worthy of donations. An offering is called āhunaṃ; they are worthy of that, thus they are āhuneyyā, worthy of offerings.

37. Pañcame kathamayaṃ migāramātā nāma jātāti āha “sā hī”tiādi. Sabbajeṭṭhakassa puttassāti attano puttesu sabbapaṭhamaṃ jātassa puttassa. Ayyakaseṭṭhinova samānanāmakattāti migāraseṭṭhinā eva sadisanāmakattā. Tassā kira sabbajeṭṭhassa puttassa nāmaggahaṇadivase ayyakassa migāraseṭṭhisseva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Anibaddhavāso hutvāti ekasmiṃyeva vihāre nibaddhavāso ahutvā. Dhuvaparibhogānīti niyataparibhogāni. Nanu bhagavā kadāci cārikampi pakkamati, kathaṃ tāni senāsanāni dhuvaparibhogena paribhuñjīti āha “utuvassaṃ cārikaṃ caritvāpī”tiādi. Tattha utuvassanti hemantagimhe sandhāya vadati. Maggaṃ ṭhapetvāti therassa āgamanamaggaṃ ṭhapetvā. Uṇhavalāhakāti uṇhautuno [M 2.0030] paccayabhūtameghamālāsamuṭṭhāpakā devaputtā. Tesaṃ kira tathācittuppādasamakālameva yathicchitaṃ ṭhānaṃ uṇhaṃ pharamānā, valāhakamālā nātibahalā ito cito nabhaṃ chādentī vidhāvati. Esa nayo sītavalāhakavassavalāhakāsu. Abbhavalāhakā pana devatā sītuṇhavassehi vinā kevalaṃ abbhapaṭalasseva samuṭṭhāpakā veditabbā. Kevalaṃ vā vātasseva, teneva devatā vātavalāhakā.

37. In the fifth: As to how she came to be named Migāramātā, the text says, 'For she…,' and so on. Of her eldest son means of the son born first among her own sons. Because he had the same name as her grandfather, the banker means because he had a name similar to that of Migāra the banker. It is said that on the naming day of her eldest son, they gave him the name of his grandfather, Migāra the banker. Not having a fixed residence means not having a fixed residence in a single monastery. Dhuvaparibhogāni means things for regular use. But does the Blessed One not sometimes set out on tour? How then did he use those lodgings with regular use? It is explained: 'Even after wandering on tour for the season…,' and so on. Here, utuvassaṃ is said in reference to winter and summer. Setting aside the path means setting aside the path for the elder's arrival. Uṇhavalāhakā are devas who produce garlands of clouds that are a condition for heat. It is said that at the very moment such a thought arises for them, a not-very-thick garland of clouds, spreading heat to a desired place, rushes about here and there, covering the sky. This is the method for the cold-cloud and rain-cloud devas. The abbhavalāhakā devas, however, should be understood as those who produce only a layer of clouds, without cold, heat, or rain. Or simply of the wind alone; hence those devas are called vātavalāhakā, wind-cloud devas.

Ettha ca yaṃ vassāne ca sisire ca abbhaṃ uppajjati, taṃ utusamuṭṭhānaṃ pākatikameva. Yaṃ pana abbhamhiyeva atiabbhaṃ sattāhampi candasūriye chādetvā ekandhakāraṃ karoti, yañca cittavesākhamāsesu abbhaṃ, taṃ devatānubhāvena uppannaṃ abbhanti veditabbaṃ. Yo ca tasmiṃ tasmiṃ utumhi uttaradakkhiṇādipakativāto hoti, ayaṃ utusamuṭṭhāno. Vātepi vanarukkhakkhandhādippadālano ativāto nāma atthi. Ayañceva, yo ca aññopi akālavāto, ayañca devatānubhāvena nibbatto. Yaṃ gimhāne uṇhaṃ, taṃ utusamuṭṭhānikaṃ pākatimeva. Yaṃ pana uṇhepi atiuṇhaṃ sītakāle ca uppannaṃ uṇhaṃ, taṃ devatānubhāvena nibbattaṃ. Yaṃ vassāne ca hemante ca sītaṃ hoti, taṃ utusamuṭṭhānameva. Yaṃ pana sītepi atisītaṃ, gimhe ca uppannaṃ sītaṃ, taṃ devatānubhāvena nibbattaṃ. Yaṃ vassike cattāro māse vassaṃ, taṃ utusamuṭṭhānameva, yaṃ pana vasseyeva ativassaṃ, yañca cittavesākhamāsesu vassaṃ, taṃ devatānubhāvena nibbattaṃ.

Here, the clouds that arise during the rainy season and the cool season are natural, arisen from the season. But the excessive clouds that, even when there are clouds, cover the sun and moon for seven days creating total darkness, and the clouds in the months of Citta and Vesākha—these should be understood as clouds that have arisen through the power of devas. The natural wind from the north, south, and so on, that occurs in its respective season is arisen from the season. But among winds there is also a great wind that splits forest trees, trunks, and so on. This, and any other unseasonal wind, is produced through the power of devas. The heat in the hot season is natural, arisen from the season. But the excessive heat even in the hot season, and the heat that arises in the cold season—this is produced through the power of devas. The cold that occurs in the rainy season and the winter is arisen from the season. But the excessive cold even in the cold season, and the cold that arises in the hot season—this is produced through the power of devas. The rain during the four months of the rainy season is arisen from the season. But the excessive rain even in the rainy season, and the rain in the months of Citta and Vesākha—this is produced through the power of devas.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – eko kira vassavalāhakadevaputto tagarakūṭavāsikhīṇāsavattherassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Thero – “kosi tva”nti pucchi. Ahaṃ, bhante, vassavalāhako devaputtoti[V 2.0028]. Tumhākaṃ kira cittena devo vassatīti? Āma, bhanteti. Passitukāmā mayanti. Temissatha, bhanteti. Meghasīsaṃ vā gajjitaṃ vā na paññāyati, kathaṃ temissāmāti? Bhante, amhākaṃ cittena devo vassati, tumhe paṇṇasālaṃ pavisathāti. Sādhu devaputtāti pāde dhovitvā paṇṇasālaṃ pāvisi. Devaputto tasmiṃ pavisanteyeva ekaṃ gītaṃ gāyitvā hatthaṃ ukkhipi, samantā tiyojanaṭṭhānaṃ ekameghaṃ ahosi. Thero aḍḍhatinto paṇṇasālaṃ paviṭṭhoti.

Here is the story: A certain rain-cloud deva, it is said, went to the Elder Tagarakūṭavāsī, an arahant, paid homage, and stood to one side. The elder asked, 'Who are you?' 'Venerable sir, I am a rain-cloud deva.' 'Is it true that it rains by your thought?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'We wish to see.' 'You will get wet, venerable sir.' 'But neither the top of a cloud nor thunder is seen; how will we get wet?' 'Venerable sir, it rains by our thought. Please enter your leaf-hut.' 'Very well, deva.' After washing his feet, he entered the leaf-hut. Just as he was entering, the deva sang a song and raised his hand, and a single cloud formed over an area of three yojanas all around. The elder entered the leaf-hut half-wet.

Kāmaṃ [M 2.0031] heṭṭhā vuttāpi devatā cātumahārājikāva, tā pana tena tena visesena vatvā idāni tadaññe paṭhamabhūmike kāmāvacaradeve sāmaññato gaṇhanto “cātumahārājikā”ti āha. Dhataraṭṭhavirūḷhakavirūpakkhakuverasaṅkhātā cattāro mahārājāno etesanti cātumahārājikā, te sinerussa pabbatassa vemajjhe honti. Tesu pabbataṭṭhakāpi atthi ākāsaṭṭhakāpi. Tesaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ pattā. Khiḍḍāpadosikā manopadosikā candimā devaputto sūriyo devaputtoti ete sabbepi cātumahārājikadevalokaṭṭhā eva.

Although the devas mentioned before are Cātumahārājikā, having spoken of them with their specific distinctions, the text now includes other sense-sphere devas of the first plane under the general term 'Cātumahārājikā.' The Cātumahārājikā are so called because for them there are the four great kings named Dhataraṭṭha, Virūḷhaka, Virūpakkha, and Kuvera. They are in the middle of Mount Sineru. Among them, some dwell on the mountain and some dwell in the air. Their domain extends to the Cakkavāḷa mountain range. The Khiḍḍāpadosikā, the Manopadosikā, the deva Candimā, the moon, and the deva Suriya, the sun—all these dwell in the world of the Cātumahārājikā devas.

Tāvatiṃsāti tāvatiṃsānaṃ devānaṃ nāmaṃ, tepi atthi pabbataṭṭhakā, atthi ākāsaṭṭhakā, tesaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ pattā. Tathā yāmādīnaṃ. Ekadevalokepi hi devānaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ appattā nāma natthi. Tattha maghena māṇavena saddhiṃ macalagāme kālaṃ katvā tettiṃsa sahapuññakārino ettha nibbattāti taṃ sahacāritaṃ ṭhānaṃ tettiṃsaṃ, tadeva tāvatiṃsaṃ, taṃ nivāso etesanti tāvatiṃsāti vadanti. Yasmā pana sesacakkavāḷesupi chakāmāvacaradevalokā atthi. Vuttampi cetaṃ “sahassaṃ cātumahārājikānaṃ sahassaṃ tāvatiṃsāna”nti (a. ni. 3.81). Tasmā nāmapaṇṇattiyevesā tassa devalokassāti veditabbā. Dukkhato yātā apayātāti yāmā. Attano sirisampattiyā tusaṃ itā gatāti tusitā. Nimmāne rati etesanti nimmānaratino. Vasavattī devatāti paranimmitavasavattino devā. Paranimmitesu bhogesu vasaṃ vattentīti paranimmitavasavattino.

Tāvatiṃsa is the name of the Tāvatiṃsa devas. They too dwell on the mountain and in the air; their domain extends to the Cakkavāḷa mountain range. The same is true for the Yāma devas and others. For in any single deva world, there is no domain of devas that does not reach the Cakkavāḷa mountain range. Because Magha the youth, together with thirty-three co-doers of merit, passed away in the village of Macala and were reborn there, that place where they lived together is called Tettiṃsa, which is Tāvatiṃsa. They are called Tāvatiṃsā because it is their residence. However, since in other world-systems too there are the six sense-sphere deva worlds—as it is said: 'A thousand Cātumahārājikā, a thousand Tāvatiṃsā'—this should be understood as merely the designation of that deva world. They have gone, departed from suffering, thus they are the Yāmā. They have gone to satisfaction with their own glorious fortune, thus they are the Tusitā. Delight in creations is theirs, thus they are the Nimmānaratino. The devas who exercise power are the Paranimmitavasavattino devas; they exercise power over pleasures created by others, thus they are the Paranimmitavasavattino.

Brūhito parivuddho tehi tehi jhānādīhi visiṭṭhehi guṇehīti brahmā. Vaṇṇavantatāya ceva dīghāyukatāya ca brahmapārisajjādīhi mahanto brahmāti mahābrahmā. Tassa parisāyaṃ bhavā paricārikāti brahmapārisajjā. Tasseva purohitaṭṭhāne ṭhitāti brahmapurohitā. Ābhassarehi parittā ābhā etesanti parittābhā. Appamāṇā ābhā etesanti appamāṇābhā. Dīpikāya acci viya etesaṃ sarīrato ābhā chijjitvā chijjitvā patantī viya sarati vissaratīti ābhassarā, yathāvuttappabhāya ābhāsanasīlā vā ābhassarā. Subhāti sobhanā pabhā. Subhāti hi [V 2.0029] ekagghanā niccalā sarīrābhā vuccati[M 2.0032], sā parittā subhā etesanti parittasubhā. Appamāṇā subhā etesanti appamāṇasubhā. Subhena okiṇṇā vikiṇṇā, subhena sarīrappabhāvaṇṇena ekagghanā suvaṇṇamañjūsāya ṭhapitasampajjalitakañcanapiṇḍasassirikāti subhakiṇṇā. Tattha sobhanāya pabhāya kiṇṇā subhākiṇṇāti vattabbe bhā-saddassa rassattaṃ antima ṇa-kārassa ha-kārañca katvā “subhakiṇhā”ti vuttaṃ. Vipulaphalā vehapphalā. Vipulaphalāti ca vipulasantasukhavaṇṇādiphalā. Appakena kālena attano ṭhānaṃ na vijahantīti avihā. Kenaci na tapanīyāti atappā. Akicchena sukhena passitabbā manuññarūpatāyāti sudassā. Suparisuddhadassanatāya sammā passanti sīlenāti sudassī. Ukkaṭṭhasampattīhi yogato natthi etesaṃ kaniṭṭhā sampattīti akaniṭṭhā.

A brahmā is so called because he is augmented and developed by those distinguished qualities such as jhāna. He is called a Mahābrahmā because he is great in beauty and long life, and because he is greater than the gods of Brahmā's Retinue and others. Those in his assembly as attendants are the gods of Brahmā's Retinue (Brahmapārisajjā). Those who stand in the position of his ministers are the Brahmā's Ministers (Brahmapurohitā). Those whose radiance is limited are the gods of Limited Radiance (Parittābhā). Those whose radiance is immeasurable are the gods of Immeasurable Radiance (Appamāṇābhā). They are called the gods of Streaming Radiance (Ābhassarā) because their radiance, like the flame of a lamp, seems to break off and stream from their bodies; or because they are by nature radiant with the aforesaid luster. 'Glory' (subhā) means beautiful radiance. For 'glory' refers to a consolidated, unmoving bodily radiance; those whose glory is limited are the gods of Limited Glory (Parittasubhā). Those whose glory is immeasurable are the gods of Immeasurable Glory (Appamāṇasubhā). They are called the gods of Refulgent Glory (Subhakiṇṇā) because they are strewn and pervaded with glory, and their bodily radiance is consolidated, like a blazing golden ingot placed in a golden casket. Here, though it should be said 'subhākiṇṇā,' meaning 'strewn with splendid glory,' the syllable 'bhā' is shortened and the final 'ṇa' is changed to 'ha,' thus it is said 'subhakiṇhā.' The gods of Great Fruit (Vehapphalā) have abundant fruit. 'Abundant fruit' means the fruit of great peace, happiness, beauty, and so on. They are called the Avihā (the Non-falling) because they do not fall away from their place. They are called the Atappā (the Untroubled) because they are not vexed by anything. They are called the Sudassā (the Clearly Visible) because they are easily and happily seen due to their pleasing appearance. They are called the Sudassī (the Clear-Sighted) because they see rightly due to their perfectly pure vision. They are called the Akaniṭṭhā (the Peerless) because, on account of their connection with the highest attainments, there is no lesser attainment for them.

Kāyasakkhīhīti nāmakāyena desanāya sampaṭicchanavasena sakkhibhūtehi. Halāhalanti kolāhalaṃ. Mahaggatacittenāti catutthajjhānapādakena abhiññācittena.

By 'bodily witness' is meant those who have become witnesses by way of accepting the teaching with the mental body. 'Halāhala' means a great noise. By 'with an exalted mind' is meant with a mind of direct knowledge that has the fourth jhāna as its basis.

Nanu ca “ajjhattanti kāmabhavo, bahiddhāti rūpārūpabhavo”ti ca ayuttametaṃ? Yasmiñhi bhave sattā bahutaraṃ kālaṃ vasanti, so nesaṃ ajjhattaṃ. Yasmiñca appataraṃ kālaṃ vasanti, so nesaṃ bahiddhāti vattuṃ yuttaṃ. Rūpārūpabhave ca sattā cirataraṃ vasanti, appataraṃ kāmabhave, tasmā “ajjhattanti kāmabhavo, bahiddhāti rūpārūpabhavo”ti kasmā vuttanti āha “kiñcāpī”tiādi. Catutthameva koṭṭhāsanti vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyisaṅkhātaṃ catutthaṃ asaṅkhyeyyakappaṃ. Itaresūti saṃvaṭṭasaṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyivivaṭṭasaṅkhātesu tīsu asaṅkhyeyyakappesu. Ālayoti saṅgo. Patthanāti “kathaṃ nāma tatrūpapannā bhavissāmā”ti abhipatthanā. Abhilāsoti tatrūpapajjitukāmatā. Tasmātiādinā yathāvuttamatthaṃ nigameti.

But is it not improper to say: 'The internal is the plane of sensual desire, the external is the plane of form and formlessness'? For it would be proper to say that whichever plane beings dwell in for a longer time is internal to them, and whichever they dwell in for a shorter time is external to them. Beings dwell longer in the planes of form and formlessness, and a shorter time in the plane of sensual desire. Therefore, why is it said: 'The internal is the plane of sensual desire, the external is the plane of form and formlessness'? To this, he replies with 'Even so...' and so on. 'The fourth part alone' refers to the fourth incalculable aeon, called the aeon of expansion-duration. 'In the others' refers to the three incalculable aeons designated as the aeon of contraction, the aeon of contraction-duration, and the aeon of expansion. 'Resort' (ālayo) means clinging. 'Aspiration' (patthanā) is the longing, 'How might we be reborn there?' 'Yearning' (abhilāso) is the wish to be reborn there. With 'Therefore...' and so on, he concludes the meaning as stated.

Etthāyaṃ adhippāyo – kassacipi kilesassa avikkhambhitattā kenacipi pakārena vikkhambhanamattenapi avimutto kāmabhavo ajjhattaggahaṇassa attānaṃ adhikicca uddissa pavattaggāhassa visesapaccayoti ajjhattaṃ nāma. Tattha bandhanaṃ ajjhattasaṃyojanaṃ, tena saṃyutto ajjhattasaṃyojano. Tabbipariyāyato bahiddhāsaṃyojanoti.

Here, this is the intended meaning: Because no defilement whatsoever has been suppressed, and one is not liberated even by mere suppression in any way, the plane of sensual existence is a specific condition for internal grasping—a grasping that proceeds by taking oneself as its object—and thus it is called 'internal.' The fetter in regard to that is an internal fetter. One yoked by that is 'one with an internal fetter.' Conversely, one has an external fetter.

Chandarāgavaseneva [M 2.0033] ajjhattasaṃyojanaṃ bahiddhāsaṃyojanañca puggalaṃ dassetvā idāni orambhāgiyauddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanavasenapi dassetuṃ “orambhāgiyāni vā”tiādimāha. Oraṃ vuccati kāmadhātu, paṭisandhiyā paccayabhāvena taṃ oraṃ bhajantīti orambhāgiyāni. Tattha ca kammunā [V 2.0030] vipākaṃ sattena ca dukkhaṃ saṃyojentīti saṃyojanāni, sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsakāmarāgapaṭighā. Uddhaṃ vuccati rūpārūpadhātu, vuttanayenetaṃ uddhaṃ bhajantīti uddhambhāgiyāni, saṃyojanāni. Rūparāgārūparāgamānuddhaccāvijjā. Atha vā orambhāgo vuccati kāmadhātu rūpārūpabhavato heṭṭhābhūtattā, tatrūpapattiyā paccayabhāvato orambhāgassa hitānīti orambhāgiyāni yathā “vacchāyogo duhako”ti. Uddhambhāgo nāma mahaggatabhāvo, tassa hitāni uddhambhāgiyāni. Pādesu baddhapāsāṇo viya pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni heṭṭhā ākaḍḍhamānākārāni honti. Hatthehi gahitarukkhasākhā viya pañcuddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni upari ākaḍḍhamānākārāni. Yesañhi sakkāyadiṭṭhiādīni appahīnāni, te bhavaggepi nibbatte etāni ākaḍḍhitvā kāmabhaveyeva pātenti, tasmā etāni pañca gacchantaṃ vārenti, gataṃ puna ānenti. Rūparāgādīni pañca gacchantaṃ na vārenti, āgantuṃ pana na denti.

Having shown a person in terms of internal and external fetters by way of sensual desire, now, to show this in terms of the lower and higher fetters, he says: 'Or the lower fetters...' and so on. 'The lower shore' (oraṃ) is said to be the sense-sphere. Since they partake of that 'lower shore' by being a condition for rebirth there, they are 'partaking of the lower shore' (orambhāgiyāni). And there, they are fetters because they bind the result by means of kamma and the being by means of suffering—namely, identity view, doubt, clinging to rules and observances, sensual desire, and ill will. 'The higher shore' (uddhaṃ) is said to be the form and formless spheres. In the way described, those that partake of this 'higher shore' are the higher fetters: desire for form, desire for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. Alternatively, the 'lower part' (orambhāgo) is said to be the sense-sphere because it is situated beneath the planes of form and formlessness; being a condition for arising there, the lower fetters are conducive to that lower part, just as 'a yoke for a calf is for the milker.' The 'higher part' (uddhambhāgo) is the exalted state; what is conducive to that are the higher fetters. Like a stone tied to the feet, the five lower fetters are of a nature to drag one downwards. Like tree branches grasped by the hands, the five higher fetters are of a nature to pull one upwards. For those whose identity view and other fetters are unabandoned, even if they are reborn at the peak of existence, these fetters drag them down and make them fall into the sense-sphere. Thus, these five prevent one from going on, and bring back one who has gone. The five higher fetters—desire for form and so on—do not prevent one from going on, but they do not allow one to return.

Asamucchinnesu orambhāgiyasaṃyojanesu laddhapaccayesu uddhambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni agaṇanūpagāni hontīti labbhamānānampi puthujjanānaṃ vasena avibhajitvā ariyānaṃ yogavasena vibhajitukāmo “ubhayampi ceta”ntiādimāha. Tattha vaṭṭanissitamahājanassāti puthujjane sandhāya vadati. Dvedhā paricchinnoti kāmasugatirūpārūpabhavavasena dvīhi pakārehi paricchinno.

When the lower fetters are unextirpated and have obtained their conditions, the higher fetters do not come into account. Wishing to make a division according to the practice of noble ones—not according to ordinary people, in whom they are also found—he says, 'both of these,' and so on. Here, 'for the great populace dependent on the round' is said in reference to ordinary people. 'Divided in two' means divided in two ways: as the sensual happy destinations and the form and formless planes.

Vacchakasālopamaṃ uttānatthameva. Opammasaṃsandane pana kassaci kilesassa avikkhambhitattā, kathañcipi avimutto kāmabhavo ajjhattaggahaṇassa visesapaccayattā, imesaṃ sattānaṃ abbhantaraṭṭhena anto nāma. Rūpārūpabhavo tabbipariyāyato bahi nāma. Tathā hi yassa orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni appahīnāni, so ajjhattasaṃyojano vutto. Yassa tāni pahīnāni, so bahiddhāsaṃyojano. Tasmā anto asamucchinnabandhanatāya bahi ca pavattamānabhavaṅgasantānatāya antobaddho bahisayito [M 2.0034] nāma. Nirantarappavattabhavaṅgasantānavasena hi sayitavohāro. Kāmaṃ nesaṃ bahibandhanampi asamucchinnaṃ, antobandhanassa pana mūlatāya evaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenāha “saṃyojanaṃ pana tesaṃ kāmāvacarūpanibaddhamevā”ti. Iminā nayena sesattayepi attho veditabbo.

The simile of the calf-shed is clear in meaning. However, in connecting the simile: because no defilement has been suppressed, and because the plane of sensual existence, from which one is in no way liberated, is a specific condition for internal grasping, for these beings 'inside' (anto) refers to what is internal. The form and formless planes, conversely, are called 'outside' (bahi). Thus, one whose lower fetters are unabandoned is said to be 'one with an internal fetter.' One for whom they are abandoned is 'one with an external fetter.' Therefore, because the internal bond is unextirpated and because the stream of the life-continuum flows externally, one is called 'bound inside, lying outside.' The term 'lying' is used because of the uninterrupted flow of the stream of the life-continuum. Granted, their external bond is also unextirpated, but it is stated thus because the internal bond is the root. Hence he says: 'But their fetter is bound only to the sensual sphere and the form sphere.' The meaning of the remaining three cases should be understood in this way.

Ettāvatā ca kirāti kira-saddo arucisaṃsūcanattho. Tenettha ācariyavādassa attano aruccanabhāvaṃ dīpeti. “Sīlavā”ti anāmaṭṭhavisesasāmaññato sīlasaṅkhepena gahitaṃ, tañca catubbidhanti ācariyatthero “catupārisuddhisīlaṃ uddisitvā”ti āha. Tatthāti catupārisuddhisīlesu. Jeṭṭhakasīlanti padhānasīlaṃ. Ubhayatthāti uddesaniddesesu, niddese viya uddesepi [V 2.0031] pātimokkhasaṃvarova therena vutto “sīlavā”ti vuttattāti adhippāyo. Sīlaggahaṇañhi pāḷiyaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvaravaseneva āgataṃ. Tenāha “pātimokkhasaṃvaroyevā”tiādi. Tattha avadhāraṇena itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ ekadesena pātimokkhantogadhabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Tathā hi anolokiyolokane ājīvahetu ca sikkhāpadavītikkame gilānapaccayassa apaccavekkhitaparibhoge ca āpatti vihitāti. Tīṇīti indriyasaṃvarasīlādīni. Sīlanti vuttaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthīti sīlapariyāyena tesaṃ katthaci sutte gahitaṭṭhānaṃ nāma kiṃ atthi yathā “pātimokkhasaṃvaro”ti? Ācariyassa sammukhatāya appaṭikkhipanto upacārena pucchanto viya vadati. Tenāha “ananujānanto”ti. Chadvārarakkhāmattakamevāti tassa sallahukabhāvamāha cittādhiṭṭhānabhāvamattena paṭipākatikabhāvāpattito. Itaradvayepi eseva nayo. Paccayuppattimattakanti phalena hetuṃ dasseti. Uppādanahetukā hi paccayānaṃ uppatti. Idamatthanti idaṃ payojanaṃ imassa paccayassa paribhuñjaneti adhippāyo. Nippariyāyenāti iminā indriyasaṃvarādīni tīṇi padhānassa sīlassa paripālanavasena pavattiyā pariyāyasīlāni nāmāti dasseti. Idāni pātimokkhasaṃvarasseva padhānabhāvaṃ byatirekato anvayato ca upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yassā”tiādimāha. Tattha so pātimokkhasaṃvaro. Sesāni indriyasaṃvarādīni.

At this point, the word kira is used to indicate disapproval. Here, it reveals the teacher’s own dissatisfaction with the view. The phrase ‘one who is virtuous’ is taken as a summary of virtue, as a general term without touching on specifics. The elder teacher states that this is fourfold, having declared the ‘fourfold purification virtue.’ Here, among the fourfold purification virtues, the principal virtue is the chief virtue. ‘In both places’ means in both the summary statement and the detailed exposition. The intention is that just as in the exposition, in the summary statement too, the elder has spoken only of the Pātimokkha restraint, since it is said ‘one who is virtuous.’ For in the Pāli canon, the term ‘virtue’ is used in the sense of the Pātimokkha restraint. Hence he says, ‘It is solely the Pātimokkha restraint,’ and so on. Here, by the emphatic particle, he indicates that the other three are partially included within the Pātimokkha. For an offense is prescribed for looking at what should not be looked at, for transgressing a training rule for the sake of livelihood, and for using requisites for the sick without reflection. The ‘three’ are the virtue of sense restraint and so on. ‘Is there a place where virtue is mentioned?’—that is, is there any place in a sutta where these are taken up by the term ‘virtue,’ as in ‘Pātimokkha restraint’? Not rejecting this in the teacher’s presence, he speaks as if asking figuratively. Hence he says, ‘not approving.’ ‘Merely the guarding of the six doors’—this indicates its lightness, because it becomes natural merely through mental resolve. The same method applies to the other two. ‘Merely the arising of requisites’—this shows the cause by its result, for the arising of requisites is caused by their production. ‘This is the purpose’—the intention is, this is the purpose of using this requisite. ‘Directly’—by this he shows that the three, such as sense restraint, are called figurative virtues because they function by way of protecting the principal virtue. Now, to clarify the principal nature of the Pātimokkha restraint both by negative and positive concomitance and by a simile, he says, ‘of which,’ etc. Here, ‘that’ is the Pātimokkha restraint. The ‘remaining’ are sense restraint and so on.

Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti [M 2.0035] yo hi naṃ pāti rakkhati, taṃ mokkheti moceti āpāyikādīhi dukkhehīti pātimokkhanti laddhanāmena sikkhāpadasīlena pihitakāyavacīdvāro. So pana yasmā evaṃbhūto tena samannāgato nāma hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “pātīmokkhasaṃvarena samannāgato”ti.

‘Restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha’ means one whose doors of body and speech are closed by the virtue of the training rules. This has acquired the name Pātimokkha because it liberates and frees him who guards and protects it from the sufferings of the states of woe, etc. Since he has become like this, he is endowed with it; therefore it is said, ‘endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha.’

Aparo nayo – kilesānaṃ balavabhāvato, pāpakiriyāya ca sukarabhāvato, puññakiriyāya ca dukkarabhāvato bahukkhattuṃ apāyesu patanasīloti pātī, puthujjano. Aniccatāya vā bhavādīsu kammavegakkhitto ghaṭiyantaṃ viya anavaṭṭhānena paribbhamanato gamanato gamanasīloti pātī, maraṇavasena tamhi tamhi sattanikāye attabhāvassa pātanasīlo vā pātī, sattasantāno, cittameva vā. Taṃ pātiṃ saṃsāradukkhato mokkhetīti pātimokkhaṃ. Cittassa hi vimokkhena satto vimuttoti vuccati. Vuttañhi “cittavodānā visujjhantī”ti, “anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimutta”nti (mahāva. 28) ca.

Another method: Because of the strength of the defilements, the ease of doing evil deeds, and the difficulty of doing meritorious deeds, the worldling is prone to falling into the states of woe many times; hence he is a pātī. Or, because of impermanence, being hurled by the force of kamma into the various kinds of existence, wandering and moving about without stability like a pot on a water-wheel, he is prone to going; hence he is a pātī. Or, by way of death, the continuum of a being, or just the mind, is prone to causing the fall of an individual existence in this or that class of beings; hence it is a pātī. That which liberates this pātī from the suffering of saṃsāra is the Pātimokkha. For it is through the liberation of the mind that a being is said to be liberated. For it is said: ‘Through the cleansing of the mind they are purified,’ and ‘The mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging’ (cf. Mv I.6.47).

Atha vā avijjādinā hetunā saṃsāre patati gacchati pavattatīti pāti, “avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarata”nti [V 2.0032] (saṃ. ni. 2.124) hi vuttaṃ, tassa pātino sattassa taṇhādisaṃkilesattayato mokkho etenāti pātimokkho. “Kaṇṭhekāḷo”tiādīnaṃ viyassa samāsasiddhi veditabbā.

Or, because of causes such as ignorance, one falls, goes, and proceeds in saṃsāra; hence one is a pāti. For it is said: ‘For beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, transmigrating and wandering on…’ (SN 15:3). For such a being who falls, liberation from the threefold defilements of craving and so on is by means of this; hence Pātimokkha. The formation of the compound should be understood as in such cases as kaṇṭhekāḷo and so on.

Atha vā pāteti vinipāteti dukkheti pāti, cittaṃ. Vuttañhi –

Or else, that which causes to fall, brings to ruin, and causes suffering is a pāti; this is the mind. For it is said:

“Cittena nīyate loko, cittena parikassatī”ti; (Saṃ. ni. 1.62);

“By mind the world is led, by mind is dragged about.” (SN 1:62)

Tassa pātino mokkho etenāti pātimokkho. Patati vā etena apāyadukkhe saṃsāradukkhe cāti pāti, taṇhādisaṃkileso. Vuttañhi –

Liberation for that pāti is by means of this; hence Pātimokkha. Or, one falls by means of this into the suffering of the states of woe and the suffering of saṃsāra; that by which one falls is a pāti, i.e., the defilement of craving and so on. For it is said:

“Taṇhā janehi purisaṃ, (saṃ. ni. 1.56-57) taṇhādutiyo puriso”ti (itivu. 15, 105; a. ni. 4.9) ca ādi;

“Craving gives birth to a person,” (SN 1:38) and “A person has craving as his companion” (Iti 109; AN 4:10), and so on.

Tato pātito mokkhoti pātimokkho.

Liberation from that which causes one to fall is the Pātimokkha.
