Atha [M 2.0036] vā patati etthāti pāti, cha ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni. Vuttañhi –

Or, one falls in this; hence this is a pāti: the six internal and external sense bases. For it is said:

“Chasu loko samuppanno, chasu kubbati santhava”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.70; su. ni. 171);

“In the six the world has arisen; in the six it enters into intimacy.” (SN 1:41)

Tato chaajjhattikabāhirāyatanasaṅkhātato pātito mokkhoti pātimokkho.

Liberation from that pāti designated as the six internal and external sense bases is the Pātimokkha.

Atha vā pāto vinipāto assa atthīti pātī, saṃsāro. Tato mokkhoti pātimokkho.

Or, that which has falling and ruin is a pātī; this is saṃsāra. Liberation from that is the Pātimokkha.

Atha vā sabbalokādhipatibhāvato dhammissaro bhagavā “patī”ti vuccati, muccati etenāti mokkho, patino mokkho patimokkho tena paññattattāti, patimokkho eva pātimokkho. Sabbaguṇānaṃ vā mūlabhāvato uttamaṭṭhena pati ca so yathāvuttaṭṭhena mokkho cāti patimokkho, patimokkho eva pātimokkho. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “pātimokkhanti ādimetaṃ mukhametaṃ pamukhameta”nti (mahāva. 135) vitthāro.

Or, because he is the sovereign of all worlds and the lord of the Dhamma, the Blessed One is called pati (lord). That by which one is freed is mokkho (liberation). The lord's liberation is patimokkha; because it was laid down by him, patimokkha becomes pātimokkha. Or, because it is the root of all virtues, it is the lord (pati) in the supreme sense, and it is liberation (mokkho) in the sense already stated; hence patimokkha, and patimokkha becomes pātimokkha. For so it is said: ‘The Pātimokkha is the beginning, it is the head, it is the chief’ (cf. Mv II.13.8). This is the detailed explanation.

Atha [V 2.0033] vā pa-iti pakāre, atīti accantatthe nipāto, tasmā pakārehi accantaṃ mokkhetīti pātimokkho. Idañhi sīlaṃ sayaṃ tadaṅgavasena, samādhisahitaṃ paññāsahitañca vikkhambhanavasena, samucchedavasena ca accantaṃ mokkheti mocetīti pātimokkho. Pati pati mokkhoti vā patimokkho, tamhā tamhā vītikkamadosato paccekaṃ mokkhoti attho. Patimokkho eva pātimokkho. Mokkho vā nibbānaṃ, tassa mokkhassa patibimbabhūtoti patimokkho. Sīlasaṃvaro hi sūriyassa aruṇuggamanaṃ viya nibbānassa udayabhūto tappaṭibhāgo viya yathārahaṃ kilesanibbāpanato patimokkhaṃ, patimokkhaṃyeva pātimokkhaṃ.

Or, pa is in the sense of ‘in various ways’; ati is a particle in the sense of ‘exceedingly’; therefore, because it exceedingly liberates in various ways, it is the Pātimokkha. For this virtue, by itself, liberates by way of substitution of opposites; together with concentration, by way of suppression; and together with wisdom, by way of eradication. Because it exceedingly liberates and frees, it is the Pātimokkha. Or, pati pati mokkho is patimokkha; the meaning is liberation from each particular fault of transgression. Patimokkha becomes pātimokkha. Or, mokkho is Nibbāna, and this is a reflection of that liberation; hence patimokkha. For the restraint of virtue is like the sunrise for the sun; it is the arising of Nibbāna, its counterpart, so to speak, since it appropriately extinguishes the defilements; hence patimokkha, and patimokkha becomes pātimokkha.

Atha vā mokkhaṃ pati vattati, mokkhābhimukhanti vā patimokkhaṃ, patimokkhameva pātimokkhanti evamettha pātimokkhasaddassa attho veditabbo.

Or it is called patimokkha because it proceeds towards liberation, or because it faces liberation. Patimokkha becomes pātimokkha. Thus the meaning of the word Pātimokkha is to be understood.

Ācāragocarasampannoti kāyikavācasikaavītikkamasaṅkhātena ācārena, navesiyādigocaratādisaṅkhātena gocarena sampanno, sampannaācāragocaroti [M 2.0037] attho. Appamattakesūti parittakesu anāpattigamanīyesu. “Dukkaṭadubbhāsitamattesū”ti apare. Vajjesūti gārayhesu. Te pana ekantato akusalasabhāvā hontīti āha “akusaladhammesū”ti. Bhayadassīti bhayato dassanasīlo, paramāṇumattampi vajjaṃ sineruppamāṇaṃ viya katvā bhāyanasīlo. Sammā ādiyitvāti sammadeva sakkaccaṃ sabbasova ādiyitvā. Sikkhāpadesūti niddhāraṇe bhummanti samudāyato avayavaniddhāraṇaṃ dassento “sikkhāpadesu taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyitvā sikkhatī”ti atthamāha, sikkhāpadameva hi samādātabbaṃ sikkhitabbañcāti adhippāyo. Yaṃ kiñci sikkhāpadesūti sikkhākoṭṭhāsesu mūlapaññattianupaññattisabbatthapaññattipadesapaññattiādibhedaṃ yaṃ kiñci sikkhitabbaṃ. Yaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ pūretabbaṃ sīlaṃ, taṃ pana dvāravasena duvidhamevāti āha “kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā”ti. Imasmiṃ atthavikappe sikkhāpadesūti ādhāre bhummaṃ sikkhābhāgesu kassaci visuṃ aggahaṇato. Tenāha “taṃ sabba”nti.

‘Endowed with good conduct and resort’ means endowed with conduct, designated as non-transgression by body and speech, and with resort, designated as a suitable alms-round area and so on. The meaning is: one whose conduct and resort are perfected. ‘In minor matters’ means in trivial matters that do not constitute an offense. Others say it means in mere offenses of wrong-doing and wrong speech. ‘In faults’ means in blameworthy things. To show that these are exclusively of an unwholesome nature, he says, ‘in unwholesome states.’ ‘Seeing danger’ means one who is accustomed to seeing danger, one who is accustomed to being afraid, regarding even a minute fault as being the size of Mount Sineru. ‘Having undertaken them correctly’ means having undertaken them rightly, carefully, and in all respects. ‘In the training rules’: this is the locative of specification. To show the specification of a part from the whole, he states the meaning as: ‘having undertaken this or that training rule among the training rules, one trains.’ The intention is that it is the training rule itself that is to be undertaken and trained in. ‘Whatever in the training rules’: whatever is to be trained in among the divisions of the training, which are distinguished as root-formulations, sub-formulations, universal formulations, specific-area formulations, and so on. The virtue that is to be practiced and fulfilled is just twofold by way of the doors; hence he says, ‘bodily or verbal.’ In this alternative meaning, ‘in the training rules’ is the locative of location, because among the parts of the training none is taken up separately. Hence he says, ‘all that.’

Aññataraṃ devaghaṭanti aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ. Āgāmī hotīti paṭisandhivasena āgamanasīlo hoti. Āgantāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Iminā aṅgenāti iminā kāraṇena.

‘One group of devas’ means a certain class of devas. ‘He is a comer’ means he is one who is accustomed to coming by way of rebirth-linking. ‘A comer’: here too the same method applies. ‘By this factor’ means by this reason.

Sukkhavipassako yebhuyyena catudhātuvavatthānamukhena kammaṭṭhānābhinivesī hotīti āha “sukkhavipassakassa dhātukammaṭṭhānikabhikkhuno”ti. Vuttamevatthaṃ sampiṇḍetvā nigamento “paṭhamena aṅgenā”tiādimāha.

A bare-insight practitioner is for the most part intent on his meditation subject by way of the determination of the four elements; thus he says, ‘for a bhikkhu who is a bare-insight practitioner devoted to the elements as his meditation subject.’ Summarizing the meaning just stated, in conclusion he says, ‘by the first factor,’ and so on.

Cittassa [V 2.0034] sukhumabhāvo idha sukhamattabhāvamāpannena daṭṭhabboti āha “sabbāpi hi tā”tiādi. Tantivasenāti kevalaṃ tantiṭṭhapanavasena, na pana therassa kassaci maggassa vā phalassa vā uppādanatthāya, nāpi sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ yojanatthāyāti adhippāyo.

Here, the subtlety of the mind should be seen as its having attained a state of mere happiness; thus he says: ‘For all those,’ etc. ‘By means of the textual line’ means merely for the sake of establishing the textual line, not for the purpose of producing any path or fruit for some elder, nor for the purpose of engaging one in right practice—this is the intention.

38. Chaṭṭhe mahākaccānoti gihikāle ujjenirañño purohitaputto abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko suvaṇṇavaṇṇo ca. Varaṇā nāma rukkho, tassa avidūre bhavattā nagarampi varaṇasaddena vuccatīti āha “varaṇā nāma ekaṃ nagara”nti. Dvandapadassa paccekaṃ abhisambandho hotīti [M 2.0038] hetusaddaṃ paccekaṃ yojetvā dassento “kāmarāgābhinivesahetū”tiādimāha. Hetusaddena sambandhe sati yo attho sambhavati, taṃ dassetuṃ “idaṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādimāha. Tattha kāmarāgena abhiniviṭṭhattāti etena kāmarāgābhinivesahetūti imassa atthaṃ dīpeti, tathā vinibaddhattātiādīhi kāmarāgavinibaddhahetūtiādīnaṃ. Tato mukhoti tadabhimukho. Mānanti āḷhakādimānabhaṇḍaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva.

38. In the sixth: Mahākaccāna, during his household life, was the son of the chaplain of the king of Ujjeni, handsome, good-looking, inspiring, and of golden complexion. Varaṇā is the name of a tree; because it was not far from it, the city too is called by the word Varaṇā. Thus he says: ‘Varaṇā is the name of a city.’ Showing that each member of a compound has a separate connection, he connects the word ‘cause’ to each separately and says: ‘because of obsession with sensual lust,’ etc. To show the meaning that is possible when there is a connection with the word ‘cause,’ he says: ‘This is what is said,’ etc. Herein, by ‘because one is obsessed with sensual lust,’ he explains the meaning of ‘because of obsession with sensual lust’; similarly, by ‘because one is bound,’ etc., he explains the meaning of ‘because of being bound by sensual lust,’ etc. ‘Facing it’ (tato mukho) means facing towards that. ‘Measure’ (mānaṃ) means a measuring vessel such as an āḷhaka. The rest here is plain.

39. Sattame madhurāyanti uttaramadhurāyaṃ. Gundāvaneti kaṇhagundāvane, kāḷapippalivaneti attho. Jarājiṇṇeti jarāya jiṇṇe, na byādhiādīnaṃ vasena jiṇṇasadise nāpi akālikena jarāya abhibhūte. Vayovuddheti jiṇṇattā eva cassa vayovuddhippattiyā vuddhena sīlādivuddhiyā. Jātimahallaketi jātiyā mahantatāya cirarattatāya mahallake, na bhogaparivārādīhīti attho. Addhagateti ettha addha-saddo dīghakālavācīti āha “dīghakāladdhānaṃ atikkante”ti. Vayoti purimapadalopenāyaṃ niddesoti āha “pacchimavaya”nti, vassasatassa tatiyakoṭṭhāsasaṅkhātaṃ pacchimavayaṃ anuppatteti attho.

39. In the seventh: ‘In Madhurā’ means in Northern Madhurā. ‘In Gundāvana’ means in the Dark Gundā Grove; the meaning is, in the Kāḷapippali Grove. ‘Broken down by old age’ (jarājiṇṇe) means broken down by old age, not like one broken down by illness and so on, nor overwhelmed by premature old age. ‘Advanced in years’ (vayovuddhe): advanced on account of being old, and also advanced in years and in virtue, etc. ‘An elder by birth’ (jātimahallake) means an elder because of his great age, because of its long duration, not because of wealth, retinue, etc.—this is the meaning. ‘Gone on in the journey of life’ (addhagate): here the word addha signifies a long time; thus he says: ‘having traversed a long stretch of time.’ ‘Age’ (vayo): this is a designation by omission of the preceding word; thus he says: ‘the last age.’ The meaning is: he has reached the last age, reckoned as the third portion of a hundred years.

Bhavati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti bhūmi, kāraṇanti āha “yena kāraṇenā”tiādi. Paripakkoti pariṇato, vuddhibhāvaṃ pattoti attho. Moghajiṇṇoti anto thirakaraṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhāvena tucchajiṇṇo nāma. Bāladārakopi daharoti vuccatīti tato visesanatthaṃ “yuvā”ti vuttaṃ. Atikkantapaṭhamavayā eva sattā sabhāvena palitasirā hontīti paṭhamavaye ṭhitabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “susukāḷakeso”ti vuttaṃ. Bhadrenāti laddhakena. Ekacco hi daharopi samāno kāṇo vā hoti kuṇiādīnaṃ vā aññataro, so na bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato nāma hoti. Yo pana abhirūpo hoti dassanīyo pāsādiko sabbasampattisampanno yaṃ yadeva alaṅkāraparihāraṃ icchati, tena tena alaṅkato devaputto viya carati, ayaṃ bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato nāma hoti. Tenevāha “yena yobbanena samannāgato”tiādi.

‘Ground’ (bhūmi) is so called because fruit exists in it, its occurrence being dependent on that; it is a cause. Thus he says: ‘by which cause,’ etc. ‘Ripened’ (paripakko) means mature; the meaning is, it has reached a state of growth. ‘Aged in vain’ (moghajiṇṇo) means one who is aged emptily because of the absence of qualities that make for inner stability. Since even a young boy is called ‘young’ (daharo), to distinguish from that, ‘a youth’ (yuvā) is said. Since beings who have passed the first stage of life naturally have gray hair, to show that he is in the first stage of life, it is said ‘with very black hair.’ ‘With the bloom’ (bhadrena) means with what is auspiciously obtained. For a certain person, though young, might be one-eyed or crippled, or have some other such defect; he is not said to be endowed with the bloom of youth. But one who is handsome, good-looking, inspiring, endowed with every accomplishment, who goes about adorned like a son of the gods with whatever ornament or attire he desires—this one is said to be endowed with the bloom of youth. Therefore he says: ‘endowed with which youth,’ etc.

Yamhi [V 2.0035] saccañca dhammo cāti yamhi puggale soḷasahākārehi paṭividdhattā catubbidhaṃ saccaṃ, ñāṇena sacchikatattā navavidhalokuttaradhammo ca atthi. Ahiṃsāti [M 2.0039] desanāmattametaṃ, yamhi pana catubbidhāpi appamaññābhāvanā atthīti attho. Saṃyamo damoti sīlañceva indriyasaṃvaro ca. Vantamaloti maggañāṇena nīhaṭamalo. Dhīroti dhitisampanno. Theroti so imehi thirabhāvakāraṇehi samannāgatattā theroti pavuccatīti attho.

‘In whom there are truth and Dhamma’: in which person there is the fourfold truth, because it has been penetrated in sixteen aspects, and the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, because it has been realized by knowledge. ‘Harmlessness’ (ahiṃsā): this is just a heading for the teaching; the meaning is that in him there is also the development of the four immeasurables. ‘Restraint and taming’ (saṃyamo damo) means virtue and restraint of the sense faculties. ‘One who has vomited stains’ (vantamalo) means one whose stains have been expelled by the knowledge of the path. ‘Steadfast’ (dhīro) means endowed with fortitude. ‘An elder’ (thero): because he is endowed with these causes of steadfastness, he is called an elder—this is the meaning.

40. Aṭṭhame “corā balavanto hontī”ti padaṃ uddharitvā yehi kāraṇehi te balavanto honti, tesaṃ sabbhāvaṃ dassento “pakkhasampannā”tiādimāha. Tattha nivāsaṭṭhānasampannatā giriduggādisabbhāvato. Atiyātunti anto yātuṃ, gantuṃ pavisitunti attho. Taṃ pana antopavisanaṃ kenaci kāraṇena bahigatassa hotīti āha “bahiddhā janapadacārikaṃ caritvā”tiādi. Niyyātunti bahi nikkhamituṃ. Tañca bahinikkhamanaṃ bahiddhākaraṇīye sati sambhavatīti āha “corā janapadaṃ vilumpantī”tiādi. Anusaññātunti anusañcarituṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva.

40. In the eighth, having cited the phrase ‘thieves become powerful,’ he shows the existence of the reasons why they become powerful, saying: ‘endowed with a faction,’ etc. Therein, ‘endowed with a dwelling place’ is because of the existence of mountain fastnesses and the like. ‘To enter’ (atiyātuṃ) means to go inside, to enter. But that entering inside happens for one who has gone outside for some reason; thus he says: ‘having wandered on tour in the countryside,’ etc. ‘To go out’ (niyyātuṃ) means to exit outside. And that exiting happens when there is business to be done outside; thus he says: ‘thieves plunder the country,’ etc. ‘To patrol’ (anusaññātuṃ) means to move about. The rest here is plain.

41. Navame micchāpaṭipattādhikaraṇahetūti ettha adhi-saddo anatthakoti āha “micchāpaṭipattiyā karaṇahetū”ti. Na ārādhakoti na sampādako na paripūrako. Ñāyati paṭivijjhanavasena nibbānaṃ gacchatīti ñāyo, so eva taṃsamaṅginaṃ vaṭṭadukkhapātato dhāraṇaṭṭhena dhammoti ñāyo dhammo, ariyamaggo. So panettha saha vipassanāya adhippetoti āha “sahavipassanakaṃ magga”nti. Ārādhanaṃ nāma saṃsiddhi, sā pana yasmā sampādanena paripūraṇena icchitā, tasmā vuttaṃ “sampādetuṃ pūretu”nti.

41. In the ninth: In the phrase 'a cause which is an occasion for wrong practice' (micchāpaṭipattādhikaraṇahetu), here the word adhi is redundant; thus he says: 'a cause for wrong practice.' 'He does not accomplish' (na ārādhako) means he is not one who achieves, not one who fulfills. The method (ñāyo) is so called because one goes to Nibbāna by means of it through penetration. That itself is the Dhamma because it supports one endowed with it from falling into the suffering of the round; thus it is the right method, the Dhamma (ñāyo dhammo), the noble path. Here it is intended along with insight; thus he says: 'the path together with insight.' 'Accomplishment' (ārādhanaṃ) is success. Since this is wished for by way of achieving and fulfilling, it is therefore said: 'to achieve, to fulfill.'

42. Dasame duggahitehīti atthato byañjanato ca duṭṭhu gahitehi, ūnādhikaviparītapadapaccābhaṭṭhādivasena vilometvā gahitehīti attho. Uppaṭipāṭiyā gahitehīti idaṃ pana nidassanamattaṃ duggahassa ūnādhikādivasenapi sambhavato. Tenevāha “attano duggahitasuttantānaṃyeva atthañca pāḷiñca uttaritaraṃ katvā dassentī”ti.

42. In the tenth: 'By what is badly grasped' (duggahitehi) means badly grasped in both meaning and phrasing; the meaning is, grasped in a distorted way by means of omission, addition, wrong words, contrary meaning, etc. 'Grasped in the wrong order' (uppaṭipāṭiyā gahitehi) is just an illustration, since bad grasping is also possible by way of omission, addition, etc. Therefore he says: 'They present the meaning and the Pāli text of the suttas they have badly grasped as something superior.'

Samacittavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Samacitta Chapter is concluded.

5. Parisavaggavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Chapter on the Assembly

43. Pañcamassa [V 2.0036] paṭhame uddhaccena samannāgatāti akappiye kappiyasaññitāya, kappiye akappiyasaññitāya, avajje vajjasaññitāya, vajje avajjasaññitāya [M 2.0040] uddhaccappakatikā. Ye hi vinaye apakataññuno saṃkilesavodāniyesu dhammesu na kusalā sakiñcanakārino vippaṭisārabahulā, tesaṃ anuppannañca uddhaccaṃ uppajjati, uppannañca bhiyyobhāvaṃ vepullaṃ āpajjati. Sārābhāvena tucchattā naḷo viyāti naḷo, mānoti āha “unnaḷāti uggatanaḷā”ti. Tenāha “uṭṭhitatucchamānā”ti. Māno hi seyyassa seyyoti sadisoti ca pavattiyā visesato tuccho. Cāpallenāti capalabhāvena, taṇhāloluppenāti attho. Mukhakharāti mukhena pharusā, pharusavādinoti attho.

43. In the first of the fifth, the phrase 'possessed of restlessness' means being of a restless nature on account of perceiving the unsuitable as suitable, the suitable as unsuitable, the blameless as blameworthy, and the blameworthy as blameless. For in those who are ungrateful in regard to the Vinaya, who are unskilled in the dhammas that defile and the dhammas that cleanse, who act with impediments, and who are full of remorse, unarisen restlessness arises, and arisen restlessness increases and expands. Like a reed (naḷo viya): because it is hollow due to an absence of substance, it is a naḷa. Regarding pride (māno), it is said: ‘unnaḷā’ means ‘a raised reed.’ Therefore it is said: ‘with arisen, hollow pride.’ For pride is especially hollow in its occurrence as ‘better than the better’ or ‘equal to the equal.’ By fickleness (cāpallena) means by the state of being fickle; the meaning is with craving and greed. Harsh in speech (mukhakharā) means harsh with the mouth; the meaning is speaking harshly.

Vikiṇṇavācāti vissaṭavacanā samphappalāpitāya apariyantavacanā. Tenāha “asaṃyatavacanā”tiādi. Vissaṭṭhasatinoti sativirahitā. Paccayavekallena vijjamānāyapi satiyā satikiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya evaṃ vuttā. Na sampajānantīti asampajānā, taṃyoganivattiyaṃ cāyaṃ akāro “ahetukā dhammā (dha. sa. dukamātikā 2), abhikkhuko āvāso”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 76) viyāti āha “nippaññā”ti, paññārahitāti attho. Pāḷiyaṃ vibbhantacittāti ubbhantacittā. Samādhivirahena laddhokāsena uddhaccena tesaṃ samādhivirahānaṃ cittaṃ nānārammaṇesu paribbhamati vanamakkaṭo viya vanasākhāsu. Pākatindriyāti saṃvarābhāvena gihikāle viya vivaṭaindriyā. Tenāha “pakatiyā ṭhitehī”tiādi. Vivaṭehīti asaṃvutehi.

Of scattered speech means of released speech, of frivolous talk, of limitless speech. Hence it is said: ‘of unrestrained speech,’ and so on. Of lapsed mindfulness means devoid of mindfulness. It is said thus because of the inability to perform the function of mindfulness, even when mindfulness is present, due to a deficiency of conditions. Not clearly comprehending means without clear comprehension. This prefix ‘a-’ serves to negate the connection, as in such cases as ‘rootless dhammas’ and ‘a residence without a bhikkhu’; hence it is said, ‘without wisdom,’ the meaning being devoid of wisdom. In the Pāḷi, with mind distraught means with mind bewildered. Because of the lack of concentration, restlessness finds its opportunity, and the minds of those who lack concentration wander among various objects like a forest monkey among the forest branches. With faculties in their natural state means with faculties uncovered as in the time of a householder, due to the absence of restraint. Hence it is said: ‘standing in their natural state,’ and so on. Uncovered means unrestrained.

44. Dutiye bhaṇḍanaṃ vuccati kalahassa pubbabhāgoti kalahassa hetubhūtā paribhāsā taṃsadisī ca aniṭṭhakiriyā bhaṇḍanaṃ nāma. Kalahajātāti hatthaparāmāsādivasena matthakappatto kalaho jāto etesanti kalahajātāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Viruddhavādanti “ayaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo”tiādinā viruddhavādabhūtaṃ vivādaṃ. Mukhasannissitatāya vācā idha “mukha”nti adhippetāti āha “dubbhāsitā vācā mukhasattiyoti vuccantī”ti. Catubbidhampi saṅghakammaṃ sīmāparicchinnehi pakatattehi bhikkhūhi ekato kattabbattā ekakammaṃ nāma. Pañcavidhopi pātimokkhuddeso ekato uddisitabbattā ekuddeso nāma. Paññattaṃ pana sikkhāpadaṃ sabbehipi lajjīpuggalehi samaṃ sikkhitabbabhāvato samasikkhatā nāma[M 2.0041]. Pāḷiyaṃ khīrodakībhūtāti yathā khīrañca [V 2.0037] udakañca aññamaññaṃ saṃsandati, visuṃ na hoti, ekattaṃ viya upeti. Satipi hi ubhayesaṃ kalāpānaṃ paramatthato bhede pacurajanehi pana duviññeyyanānattaṃ khīrodakaṃ samoditaṃ accantameva saṃsaṭṭhaṃ viya hutvā tiṭṭhati, evaṃ sāmaggivasena ekattūpagatacittuppādā viyāti khīrodakībhūtāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Mettācakkhūhīti mettācittaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā olokanacakkhūhi. Tāni hi piyabhāvadīpanato “piyacakkhūnī”ti vuccanti.

44. In the second, quarreling is said to be the preliminary stage of conflict. Verbal abuse, which is the cause of conflict, and similar disagreeable actions are what is called quarreling. Having conflict arisen: conflict that has reached its peak by way of seizing by the hand, etc., has arisen for them, thus they are ‘those for whom conflict has arisen.’ This is how the meaning should be understood here. Opposing speech means a dispute that has become opposing speech by way of such statements as, ‘This is the Dhamma, this is not the Dhamma.’ Because speech is dependent on the mouth, ‘mouth’ is intended here; thus it is said: ‘Ill-spoken speech is called a mouth-spear.’ The fourfold formal act of the Saṅgha is called a single act because it must be performed together by bhikkhus with normal standing within a defined boundary. The fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha is called a single recitation because it must be recited together. But the laid-down training rule is called equal training because it must be trained in equally by all conscientious persons. In the Pāḷi, become like milk and water: just as milk and water blend with each other, are not separate, and approach a state of oneness. For although in the ultimate sense there is a difference between the material groups of both, for the many folk the difference is hard to discern, and the mixed milk and water stand as if completely blended. So too, through harmony, they are as if their arisings of mind have attained oneness. This is how the meaning of become like milk and water should be understood here. With eyes of loving-kindness means with eyes that look after having established a mind of loving-kindness. For because they show a state of endearment, they are called ‘dear eyes.’

45. Tatiye aggavatīti ettha agga-saddo uttamapariyāyo, tena visiṭṭhassa puggalassa, visiṭṭhāya vā paṭipattiyā gahaṇaṃ idhādhippetanti āha “aggavatīti uttamapuggalavatī”tiādi. Avigatataṇhatāya taṃ taṃ parikkhārajātaṃ bahuṃ lanti ādiyantīti bahulā, bahulā eva bāhulikā yathā “venayiko”ti (a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 8; ma. ni. 1.246). Te pana yasmā paccayabahubhāvāya yuttappayuttā nāma honti, tasmā āha “cīvarādibāhullāya paṭipannā”ti. Sikkhāya ādaragāravābhāvato sithilaṃ adaḷhaṃ gaṇhantīti sāthalikāti vuttaṃ. Sithilanti ca bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, sithilasaddena vā samānatthassa sāthalasaddassa vasena sāthalikāti padasiddhi veditabbā. Avagamanaṭṭhenāti adhogamanaṭṭhena, orambhāgiyabhāvenāti attho. Upadhiviveketi sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggatāya upadhivivitte. Oropitadhurāti ujjhitussāhā. Duvidhampi vīriyanti kāyikaṃ cetasikañca vīriyaṃ.

45. In the third, regarding possessing the highest: here the word ‘agga’ is a synonym for ‘supreme.’ By this, the taking of a distinguished person or a distinguished practice is intended here. Thus it is said: ‘possessing the highest’ means ‘possessing a supreme person,’ and so on. Because their craving has not departed, they take up many kinds of requisites, thus they are abundant (bahulā). Those who are abundant (bahulā) are themselves given to abundance (bāhulikā), as in the case of venayiko (a specialist in the Vinaya). But since they are devoted to an abundance of requisites, therefore it is said: ‘entered upon abundance in robes, etc.’ Because they have no care and respect for the training, they grasp it loosely, not firmly, thus they are called lax (sāthalikā). And loosely (sithilaṃ) is an abstract neuter expression; or the formation of the word sāthalikā should be understood by way of the word sāthala, which has the same meaning as the word sithila. In the sense of going down means in the sense of descending; the meaning is in the state of pertaining to the lower shore. In seclusion from the substrates means secluded through the relinquishment of all substrates of existence. Having laid down the burden means having given up striving. Both kinds of energy are meant: bodily and mental energy.

46. Catutthe idaṃ dukkhanti dukkhassa ariyasaccassa paccakkhato aggahitabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Ettakameva dukkhanti tassa paricchijja aggahitabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Ito uddhaṃ dukkhaṃ natthīti anavasesetvā aggahitabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Yathāsabhāvato nappajānantīti sarasalakkhaṇappaṭivedhena asammohato nappaṭivijjhanti. Asammohapaṭivedho ca yathā tasmiṃ ñāṇe pavatte paccā dukkhassa rūpādiparicchede sammoho na hoti, tathā pavatti. Accantakkhayoti accantakkhayanimittaṃ nibbānaṃ. Asamuppattīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Yaṃ nibbānaṃ maggassa ārammaṇapaccayaṭṭhena kāraṇabhūtaṃ āgamma tadubhayampi nirujjhati, taṃ tesaṃ asamuppatti nibbānaṃ dukkhanirodhoti vuccati.

46. In the fourth, ‘this is suffering’ is said to show the state of not having grasped the noble truth of suffering directly. ‘Only this much is suffering’ is said to show the state of not having grasped it by delimiting it. ‘Beyond this there is no suffering’ is said to show the state of not having grasped it without remainder. They do not understand it according to its true nature means they do not penetrate it without delusion by penetrating its individual and general characteristics. And the penetration without delusion occurs in such a way that when that knowledge is proceeding, there is afterwards no delusion in the delimitation of suffering as form, etc. Utter destruction means Nibbāna, the sign of utter destruction. Non-arising: here too the same method applies. Having approached that Nibbāna which is the cause for the path by way of being its object-condition, both suffering and its origin cease. That non-arising, Nibbāna, is called for them the cessation of suffering.

47. Pañcame [M 2.0042] visesanassa paranipātena “parisākasaṭo”ti vuttanti āha “kasaṭaparisā”tiādi. “Kasaṭaparisā”ti hi vattabbe “parisākasaṭo”ti vuttaṃ. Parisāmaṇḍoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sesamettha uttānameva.

47. In the fifth, it is said parisākasaṭo by the post-posing of the qualifier; thus it says kasaṭaparisā, and so on. For when kasaṭaparisā (a refuse-assembly) should have been said, parisākasaṭo (an assembly-refuse) is said. Here too, in the case of parisāmaṇḍo, the same method applies. The rest here is plain in meaning.

48. Chaṭṭhe [V 2.0038] gambhīrāti agādhā dukkhogāḷhā. Pāḷivasenāti iminā yo dhammapaṭisambhidāya visayo gambhīrabhāvo, tamāha. Dhammappaṭivedhassa hi dukkarabhāvato dhammassa pāḷiyā dukkhogāḷhatāya gambhīrabhāvo. “Pāḷivasena gambhīrā”ti vatvā “sallasuttasadisā”ti vuttaṃ tassa “animittamanaññāta”ntiādinā (su. ni. 579) pāḷivasena gambhīratāya labbhanato. Tathā hi tattha tā gāthā duviññeyyarūpā tiṭṭhanti. Duviññeyyañhi ñāṇena dukkhogāḷhanti katvā “gambhīra”nti vuccati. Pubbāparampettha kāsañci gāthānaṃ duviññeyyatāya dukkhogāḷhameva, tasmā taṃ “pāḷivasena gambhīrā”ti vuttaṃ. Imināva nayena “atthavasena gambhīrā”ti etthāpi attho veditabbo. Mahāvedallasuttassa (ma. ni. 1.449 ādayo) atthavasena gambhīratā suviññeyyāva. Lokaṃ uttaratīti lokuttaro, navavidho appamāṇadhammo. So atthabhūto etesaṃ atthīti lokuttarā. Tenāha “lokuttaraatthadīpakā”ti.

48. In the sixth, 'profound' means unfathomable, difficult to penetrate. 'By way of the text': by this he speaks of that profundity which is the domain of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. For because the penetration of the Dhamma is difficult to do, the Dhamma is profound by way of the text's being difficult to penetrate. Having said 'profound by way of the text,' it is said to be 'like the Salla Sutta' because its profundity by way of the text is obtained from the passage beginning with ‘signless, unknown…’. For there those verses stand in a form that is difficult to understand. For what is difficult to understand with knowledge is called ‘profound’ because it is difficult to penetrate. Here, the beginning and end of some verses are indeed difficult to penetrate because they are difficult to understand; therefore it is said to be 'profound by way of the text.' By this same method, the meaning should be understood here too in the case of 'profound by way of the meaning.' The profundity by way of meaning of the Mahāvedalla Sutta is very easy to understand. It crosses beyond the world, thus it is supramundane: the ninefold immeasurable Dhamma. That which has become the meaning exists for them, thus they are supramundane. Therefore it is said: 'illuminating the supramundane meaning.'

Sattasuññaṃ dhammamattamevāti sattena attanā suññaṃ kevalaṃ dhammamattameva. Uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbanti liṅgavacanavipallāsena vuttanti āha “uggahetabbe ca pariyāpuṇitabbe cā”ti. Kavino kammaṃ kavitā. Yaṃ panassa kammaṃ, taṃ tena katanti vuccatīti āha “kavitāti kavīhi katā”ti. Itaranti kāveyyāti padaṃ, kābyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Kābyanti ca kavinā vuttanti attho. Tenāha “tasseva vevacana”nti. Vicitraakkharāti vicittākārakkharā viññāpanīyā. Sāsanato bahibhūtāti na sāsanāvacarā. Tesaṃ sāvakehīti buddhānaṃ sāvakāti apaññātānaṃ yesaṃ kesañci sāvakehi. Na ceva aññamaññaṃ paṭipucchantīti ye vācenti, ye ca suṇanti, te aññamaññaṃ atthādiṃ nappaṭipucchanti, kevalaṃ vācanasavanamatteneva parituṭṭhā honti. Cārikaṃ na vicarantīti asukasmiṃ ṭhāne atthādiṃ jānantā atthīti pucchanatthāya cārikaṃ na gacchanti tādisassa puggalassa abhāvato tassa ca pubbāparavirodhato. Kathaṃ ropetabbanti kena pakārena nikkhipitabbaṃ. Attho nāma sabhāvato anusandhito sambandhato [M 2.0043] pubbāparato ādipariyosānato ca ñāto sammāñāto hotīti āha “ko attho”tiādi. Anuttānīkatanti akkharasannivesādinā anuttānīkataṃ. Kaṅkhāyāti saṃsayassa.

'Empty of a being, merely the Dhamma' (sattasuññaṃ dhammamattameva) means empty of a being and a self, merely the Dhamma. 'It should be learned and mastered' (uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ) is said with a reversal of phrasing, as stated: 'in what should be learned and in what should be mastered.' The work of a poet is poetry (kavitā). Whatever his work is, it is said to be done by him—thus it is said: 'Poetry is made by poets.' The other word is kāveyya, meaning kābya. And kābya means 'spoken by a poet.' Therefore, it is said: 'That is its synonym.' 'With varied syllables' (vicitraakkharā) means syllables of diverse forms that are expressive. 'Outside the Dispensation' (sāsanato bahibhūtā) means not within the scope of the Teaching. 'By their disciples' (tesaṃ sāvakehi) means by the disciples of some unknown persons, who are not disciples of the Buddhas. 'And they do not question one another' (na ceva aññamaññaṃ paṭipucchanti) means those who recite and those who listen do not question each other about the meaning and so on, being satisfied merely with the act of reciting and hearing. 'They do not wander about' (cārikaṃ na vicaranti) means they do not go wandering to ask if there is anyone in a certain place who knows the meaning and so on, due to the absence of such a person and because of its internal contradictions. 'How should it be planted?' (kathaṃ ropetabbaṃ) means in what manner should it be established? Meaning is known, rightly known, by its nature, through its sequence, through its context, from beginning to end—thus it is said: 'What is the meaning?' and so on. 'Not made clear' (anuttānīkataṃ) means not clarified by the arrangement of syllables and so on. 'Of doubt' (kaṅkhāya) means of uncertainty.

49. Sattame kilesehī āmasitabbato āmisaṃ, cattāro paccayā. Tadeva garu garukātabbaṃ etesaṃ, na dhammoti āmisagarū. Tenāha “lokuttaradhammaṃ lāmakato gahetvā ṭhitaparisā”ti. Ubhato bhāgato vimuttoti ubhatobhāgavimutto. Dvīhi bhāgehi dve vāre vimutto. Paññāya vimuttoti samathasannissayena vinā aggamaggapaññāya vimutto. Tenāha “sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavo”ti[V 2.0039]. Kāyenāti nāmakāyena. Jhānaphassaṃ phusitvāti aṭṭhasamāpattisaññitaṃ jhānaphassaṃ adhigamavasena phusitvā. Pacchā nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ yathā ālocitaṃ nāmakāyena sacchikarotīti kāyasakkhī. Na tu vimutto ekaccānaṃ āsavānaṃ aparikkhīṇattā. Diṭṭhantaṃ pattoti diṭṭhassa anto anantaro kālo diṭṭhanto, dassanasaṅkhātassa sotāpattimaggañāṇassa anantaraṃ pattoti attho. Paṭhamaphalato paṭṭhāya hi yāva aggamaggā diṭṭhippatto. Tenāha “ime dvepi chasu ṭhānesu labbhantī”ti.

49. In the seventh section, the four requisites are called 'āmisa' because they are to be touched by defilements. That very thing is weighty and should be regarded as weighty for them, but not the Dhamma—thus, they are 'āmisa-garū' (those who revere material things). Hence it is said, 'the assembly that stands holding the supramundane Dhamma in low esteem.' 'Liberated in both ways' (ubhatobhāgavimutto). Liberated in two parts, twice. 'Liberated by wisdom' (paññāvimutto) means liberated by the wisdom of the highest path without relying on serenity. Hence it is said, 'a dry-insight meditator whose taints are destroyed.' 'By the body' (kāyena) means by the mental body. 'Having touched jhāna-contact' (jhānaphassaṃ phusitvā) means having touched by way of attainment the jhāna-contact associated with the eight attainments. Later, he realizes with the mental body cessation, Nibbāna, as contemplated—thus, he is a 'body-witness' (kāyasakkhī). But he is not liberated, due to the non-destruction of some taints. 'One who has reached the end of vision' (diṭṭhantaṃ patto) means having attained immediately after the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, which is called 'seeing.' Indeed, from the first fruit up to the highest path, one is a 'diṭṭhippatta' (one who has attained the view). Hence it is said, 'these two are obtainable in six instances.'

Saddahanto vimuttoti etena sabbathā avimuttassa saddhāmattena vimuttabhāvadassanena saddhāvimuttassa sekkhabhāvameva vibhāveti. Saddhāvimuttoti vā saddhāya avimuttoti attho. Chasu ṭhānesūti paṭhamaphalato paṭṭhāya chasu ṭhānesu. Dhammaṃ anussaratīti paṭhamamaggapaññāsaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ anussarati. Saddhaṃ anussaratīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ubhopi hete sotāpattimaggaṭṭhāyeva. Imaṃ kasmā gaṇhantīti evaṃ ekantapāsaṃsesu ariyesu gayhamānesu imaṃ ekantaninditaṃ lāmakaṃ dussīlaṃ kasmā gaṇhanti. Sabbesu sabbatā sadisesu labbhamānopi viseso na paññāyati, visabhāge pana sati eva paññāyati paṭabhāvena viya cittapaṭassāti āha “ekaccesu panā”tiādi. Ganthitāti avabaddhā. Mucchitāti mucchaṃ sammohaṃ āpannā. Chandarāgaapakaḍḍhanāyāti chandarāgassa apanayanatthaṃ. Nissaraṇapaññāyāti tato nissaraṇāvahāya paññāya virahitā.

By this phrase, 'believing, one is liberated' (saddahanto vimutto), it clarifies that the faith-liberated one (saddhāvimutta) is a trainee, by showing a state of liberation through mere faith for one who is in no way fully liberated. Or, 'faith-liberated' (saddhāvimutto) means 'not liberated by faith.' 'In six instances' (chasu ṭhānesu) means in six instances starting from the first fruit. 'He recollects the Dhamma' (dhammaṃ anussarati) means he recollects the Dhamma, namely, the wisdom associated with the first path. 'He recollects faith' (saddhaṃ anussarati)—here too, the same principle applies. Both of these pertain to the stage of the stream-entry path. 'Why do they take this one?' (imaṃ kasmā gaṇhanti) means when noble ones who are entirely praiseworthy are being considered, why do they take this utterly blameworthy, inferior, immoral one? Among those who are similar in every way, a distinction, though present, is not apparent; but when there is dissimilarity, it becomes apparent, just as the canvas is the basis for a painting. Thus it is said, 'but in some cases,' etc. 'Bound' (ganthitā) means fettered. 'Stupefied' (mucchitā) means having fallen into delusion and confusion. 'For the removal of desire and lust' (chandarāgaapakaḍḍhanāya) means for the purpose of removing desire and lust. 'Devoid of the wisdom of escape' (nissaraṇapaññāya) means lacking the wisdom that brings about escape from it.

Paññādhurenāti [M 2.0044] vipassanābhinivesena. Abhiniviṭṭhoti vipassanāmaggaṃ otiṇṇo. Tasmiṃ khaṇeti sotāpattimaggakkhaṇe. Dhammānusārī nāma paññāsaṅkhātena dhammena ariyamaggasotassa anussaraṇato. Kāyasakkhī nāma nāmakāyena sacchikātabbassa nibbānassa sacchikaraṇato. Vikkhambhanasamucchedānaṃ vasena dvikkhattuṃ. Arūpajjhānehi rūpakāyato, aggamaggena sesakāyatoti dvīhi bhāgehi nissakkavacanañcetaṃ. Diṭṭhantaṃ patto, diṭṭhattā vā pattoti diṭṭhippatto. Tattha diṭṭhantaṃ pattoti dassanasaṅkhātassa sotāpattimaggañāṇassa anantaraṃ pattoti attho. Diṭṭhattāti catusaccadassanasaṅkhātāya paññāya nirodhassa diṭṭhattā. Jhānaphassarahitāya sātisayāya paññāya eva vimuttoti paññāvimutto. Sesaṃ vuttanayattā suviññeyyameva.

'By the foremost of wisdom' (paññādhurena) means through dedication to insight. 'Dedicated' (abhiniviṭṭho) means having entered the path of insight. 'At that moment' (tasmiṃ khaṇe) means at the moment of the stream-entry path. One is called a 'Dhamma-follower' (dhammānusārī) because of following the stream of the noble path by means of the Dhamma known as wisdom. One is called a 'body-witness' (kāyasakkhī) because of realizing with the mental body Nibbāna, which is to be so realized. Twice, by way of suppression and eradication. This is an expression of renunciation in two parts: from the form-body by means of the formless attainments, and from the remaining body by means of the highest path. A 'diṭṭhippatta' (one who has attained the view) is so called because he is 'one who has reached the end of vision' (diṭṭhantaṃ patto), or 'one who has reached due to seeing' (diṭṭhattā patto). Here, 'one who has reached the end of vision' means having attained immediately after the knowledge of the stream-entry path, which is called seeing. 'Due to seeing' means because of having seen cessation through the wisdom designated as the vision of the four truths. A 'paññāvimutta' is one liberated by extraordinary wisdom alone, a wisdom devoid of jhāna-contact. The rest should be easily understood according to the method already stated.

50. Aṭṭhame na samāti visamā. Kāyakammādīnaṃ visamattā tato eva tattha pakkhalanaṃ sulabhanti āha “sapakkhalanaṭṭhenā”ti. Nippakkhalanaṭṭhenāti pakkhalanābhāvena. Uddhammānīti dhammato apetāni. Ubbinayānīti etthāpi eseva nayo.

50. In the eighth section, 'not uniform' (na samā) means uneven. Because of the unevenness of bodily actions and so on, slipping there is easy; therefore, it is said, 'in the sense of slipping.' 'In the sense of not slipping' means by the absence of slipping. 'Deviated from the Dhamma' (uddhammāni) means gone away from the Dhamma. 'Deviated from the Vinaya' (ubbinayāni)—here too, the same method applies.

51. Navame [V 2.0040] adhammikāti adhamme niyuttā. Tenāha “niddhammā”ti, dhammarahitāti attho.

51. In the ninth section, 'unrighteous' (adhammikā) means engaged in unrighteousness. Hence it is said 'devoid of Dhamma' (niddhammā), meaning lacking in Dhamma.

52. Dasame gaṇhantīti pavattenti. Na ceva aññamaññaṃ saññāpentīti mūlato paṭṭhāya taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ yathā vūpasammati, evaṃ aññamaññaṃ itarītare na sammā jānāpenti. Saññāpanatthaṃ sannipāte sati tattha yuttapattakaraṇena saññattiyā bhavitabbaṃ, te pana saññāpanatthaṃ na sannipatanti. Na pekkhāpentīti taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ mūlato paṭṭhāya aññamaññaṃ na pekkhāpenti. Asaññattiyeva attanā gahitapakkhassa balaṃ etesanti asaññattibalā. Na tathā mantentīti sandiṭṭhiparāmāsiādhānaggāhiduppaṭinissaggibhāvena tathā na mantenti. Tenāha “thāmasā”tiādi. Uttānatthoyeva kaṇhapakkhe vuttappaṭipakkhena gahetabbattā.

52. In the tenth section, 'they take' means 'they keep it going.' 'And they do not inform each other' means that from the very beginning, they do not properly inform one another how that dispute might be settled so that it subsides. When there is an assembly for the purpose of informing, there should be a formal motion by one who is fit to act, but they do not assemble for the purpose of informing. 'They do not make each other see' means that from the very beginning, they do not make each other see concerning that dispute. Their strength is the side they have taken without a formal motion, thus they are 'strong due to lack of a formal motion.' 'They do not consult in that way' means they do not consult in that way, due to holding firmly to their own views, insisting on them, being difficult to dislodge, and being unwilling to relinquish them. Therefore, it is said: 'with force,' etc. The meaning is straightforward, as it is to be understood as the opposite of what was said in the dark section.

Parisavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Parisavagga is concluded.

Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The First Fifty is completed.

2. Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

2. The Second Fifty

(6) 1. Puggalavaggavaṇṇanā

(6) 1. Commentary on the Chapter on Individuals

53. Dutiyapaṇṇāsakassa [M 2.0045][V 2.0041] paṭhame hitaggahaṇena mettā vuttā hoti, na karuṇā, anukampāgahaṇena pana karuṇāti cakkavattinā saddhiṃ gahitattā “lokānukampāyā”ti na vuttaṃ. Nippariyāyato lokānukampā nāma sammāsambuddhādhīnāti. Dveti manussadevasampattivasena dve sampattiyo. Tā dve, nibbānasampatti cāti tisso.

53. In the first sutta of the Second Fifty, loving-kindness is meant by the adoption of 'welfare,' not compassion; but by the adoption of 'compassion,' compassion is meant. Since it is taken together with the wheel-turning monarch, the phrase 'for the world's compassion' was not stated. Unconditionally, compassion for the world is dependent on the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones. 'Two' means the two accomplishments, that is, human and divine accomplishment. These two, together with the accomplishment of Nibbāna, make three.

54. Dutiye bahuso loke na ciṇṇā na pavattā manussāti āciṇṇamanussā. Kadācideva hi nesaṃ loke nibbatti abhūtapubbā bhūtāti abbhutamanussā.

54. In the second sutta: 'Uncommon humans' are humans not often met with nor prevalent in the world. And they are 'marvelous humans' because their arising in the world is rare, something that has not occurred before.

55. Tatiye dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu anutāpaṃ karoti tassa ekabuddhakhettabhāvato.

55. In the third sutta: He illumines the ten thousand world-systems because that constitutes a single Buddha-field.

56. Catutthe thūpassa yuttāti dhātuyo pakkhipitvā thūpakaraṇassa yuttā.

56. In the fourth sutta: 'Worthy of a stupa' means worthy of the construction of a stupa after the relics have been enshrined.

57. Pañcame attano ānubhāvenāti sayambhuñāṇena. Buddhāti buddhavanto.

57. In the fifth sutta: 'By his own power' means by self-originated knowledge. 'Buddhas' means those possessing enlightenment.

58. Chaṭṭhe pahīnattā na bhāyatīti attasinehābhāvato na bhāyati. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiggahaṇañcettha nidassanamattaṃ, attasinehassa paṭighassa tadekaṭṭhasammohassa ca vasena bhāyanaṃ hotīti tesampi pahīnattā na bhāyati, aññathā sotāpannādīnaṃ abhayena bhavitabbaṃ siyā. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā balavattāti ettha ahaṃkārasammohanatādīnampi balavattāti vattabbaṃ.

58. In the sixth sutta: 'He does not fear because of its abandonment' means he does not fear due to the absence of affection for self. The mention of identity view here is merely an illustration. Fearing arises from affection for self, aversion, and the delusion that has the same foundation; since these too are abandoned, he does not fear. Otherwise, stream-enterers and others would also have to be fearless. Where it says 'because of the strength of identity view,' it should be stated as 'because of the strength of the delusion of I-making and so on.'

59. Sattame assājānīyoti likhanti, usabhājānīyoti pana pāṭhoti.

59. In the seventh sutta: They write 'a thoroughbred horse,' but the reading is 'a thoroughbred bull.'

61. Navame tatthāti antarāpaṇe. Ekoti dvīsu kinnaresu eko. Ambilikāphalañca addasāti ānetvā sambandho. Ambilikāphalanti tintiṇīphalanti [M 2.0046] vadanti, caturambilanti apare. Dve attheti pāḷiyaṃ vutte dve atthe.

61. In the ninth sutta: 'There' means in the marketplace. 'One' means one of two kinnaras. The phrase 'and he saw an ambilika fruit' should be supplied and connected. As for 'ambilika fruit,' some say it is tamarind fruit; others say the four sour fruits. 'Two meanings' refers to the two meanings stated in the Pāli text.

62. Dasame [V 2.0042] yathāāraddhe kicce vattamāne antarā eva paṭigamanaṃ paṭivānaṃ, natthi etassa paṭivānanti appaṭivāno. Tattha asaṃkocappatto. Tenāha “anukkaṇṭhito”tiādi.

62. In the tenth sutta: Turning back is returning in the middle of a task that has been undertaken. One for whom there is no turning back is 'one who does not turn back.' Therein, he has attained a state of not shrinking back. Hence it is said: 'unafflicted with longing,' etc.

63. Ekādasame sannivāsanti sahavāsaṃ. Yathā asappurisā saha vasantā aññamaññaṃ agāravena anādariyaṃ karonti, tappaṭikkhepena sappurisānaṃ sagāravappaṭipattidassanaparamidaṃ suttaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

63. In the eleventh sutta: 'Living together' means co-residence. Just as inferior persons, while living together, treat one another with disrespect and disregard, this sutta should be seen as intended to show, by way of contrast, the respectful conduct of superior persons.

64. Dvādasame dvīsupi pakkhesūti vivādāpannānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dvīsupi pakkhesu. Saṃsaramānāti pavattamānā. Diṭṭhipaḷāsoti diṭṭhisannissayo paḷāso yugaggāho. Āghātentoti āhananto bādhento. Anabhirādhanavasenāti yassa uppajjati, tassa tadaññesañca atthassa anabhirādhanavasena. Sabbampetanti vacīsaṃsāroti sabbampetaṃ. Attano citte parisāya ca citteti ānetvā sambandho.

64. In the twelfth sutta: 'In both factions' means in both factions of the bhikkhus engaged in a dispute. 'Wandering on' means proceeding. 'The overgrowth of views' means the overgrowth that is dependence on views, a contentious grasp. 'By vexing' means striking, harming. 'By way of not accomplishing' means in the sense of not accomplishing the welfare of oneself, for whom it arises, and of others. 'All this' means all this is verbal wandering. The connection is made by supplying 'in one's own mind and in the mind of the assembly.'

Puggalavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Individuals is finished.

(7) 2. Sukhavaggavaṇṇanā

(7) 2. Commentary on the Chapter on Happiness

65. Dutiyassa paṭhame sabbakāmanipphattimūlakaṃ sukhanti anavasesaupabhogaparibhogavatthunipphattihetukaṃ kāmasukhaṃ. Pabbajjāmūlakaṃ sukhanti pabbajjāhetukaṃ pavivekasukhaṃ.

65. In the first sutta of the second vagga: 'Happiness rooted in the fulfillment of all desires' means sensual pleasure, which is caused by the production of objects for complete use and enjoyment. 'Happiness rooted in renunciation' means the happiness of seclusion, which is caused by renunciation.

66. Dutiye kāmeti pañca kāmaguṇe, sabbepi vā tebhūmake dhamme. Vuttañhetaṃ “sabbepi tebhūmakā dhammā kamanīyaṭṭhena kāmā”ti (mahāni. 1). Nekkhammaṃ vuccati pabbajjā gharabandhanato nikkhantattā. Nibbānameva vā –

66. In the second sutta: 'Sensual pleasures' means the five cords of sensual pleasure, or all phenomena of the three planes. For it has been said: 'All phenomena of the three planes are "sensual pleasures" in the sense of being desirable' (Mahāni. 1). 'Renunciation' is so called because it is a going out from the bondage of the home. Or it is Nibbāna itself—

“Pabbajjā paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, nibbānañca vipassanā;

Sabbepi kusalā dhammā, nekkhammanti pavuccare”ti. (itivu. aṭṭha. 109) –

'The going forth, the first jhāna, Nibbāna, and insight; all wholesome states are called "renunciation."' (It-a 109)

Hi vuttaṃ.

For so it has been said.

67. Tatiye [M 2.0047][V 2.0043] upadhī vuccanti pañcupādānakkhandhā, tannissitaṃ sukhaṃ upadhisukhaṃ. Tappaṭipakkhato nirupadhisukhaṃ lokuttarasukhaṃ.

67. In the third sutta: The five aggregates subject to clinging are called 'acquisitions.' Happiness dependent on them is happiness based on acquisitions. In contrast, happiness without acquisitions is supramundane happiness.

68. Catutthe vaṭṭapariyāpannaṃ sukhaṃ vaṭṭasukhaṃ. Nibbānārammaṇaṃ sukhaṃ vivaṭṭasukhaṃ.

68. In the fourth sutta: Happiness included in the round of existence is happiness of the round. Happiness that has Nibbāna as its object is happiness that transcends the round.

69. Pañcame saṃkilesanti saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ. Tenāha “vaṭṭagāmisukha”nti. Vivaṭṭasukhanti maggaphalasahagataṃ sukhaṃ.

69. In the fifth sutta: 'Defiling' means defiled. Hence it is said, 'happiness that leads to the round.' 'Happiness that transcends the round' is the happiness associated with the path and its fruition.

70. Chaṭṭhe ariyānameva sukhaṃ ariyasukhaṃ, ariyañca taṃ sukhañcātipi ariyasukhaṃ. Anariyānameva sukhaṃ anariyasukhaṃ. Anariyañca taṃ sukhañcātipi anariyasukhaṃ.

70. In the sixth sutta: 'Noble happiness' is the happiness of the noble ones; or it is 'noble happiness' because it is both noble and happiness. 'Ignoble happiness' is the happiness of the ignoble ones; or it is 'ignoble happiness' because it is both ignoble and happiness.

71. Sattame tanti cetasikasukhaṃ.

71. In the seventh sutta: 'That' means mental happiness.

72. Aṭṭhame saha pītiyā vattatīti sappītikaṃ, pītisahagataṃ sukhaṃ. Sabhāvato virāgato ca natthi etassa pītīti nippītikaṃ sukhaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ panettha jhānasukhameva uddhaṭaṃ, tathā ca “lokiyasappītikasukhato lokiyanippītikasukhaṃ agga”nti vuttaṃ. Lokiyanippītikampi hi aggaṃ labbhatevāti bhūmantaraṃ bhinditvā aggabhāvo veditabbo.

72. In the eighth sutta: It is 'with rapture' because it occurs together with rapture; it is happiness accompanied by rapture. Because by its nature and through dispassion there is no rapture in it, it is happiness 'without rapture.' Here in the commentary, only the happiness of jhāna is cited, and so it is said: 'Worldly happiness without rapture is superior to worldly happiness with rapture.' Since worldly happiness without rapture is indeed obtained as superior, its superiority should be understood as due to breaking through to another plane.

73. Navame sātasabhāvameva sukhaṃ sātasukhaṃ, na upekkhāsukhaṃ viya asātasabhāvaṃ. Kāmañcettha kāyaviññāṇasahagatampi sātasukhameva, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “tīsu jhānesu sukha”nteva vuttaṃ.

73. In the ninth sutta: Pleasant happiness is happiness that is pleasant by nature, not of an unpleasant nature like the happiness of equanimity. And here, even happiness accompanied by body-consciousness is pleasant happiness, but in the commentary it is simply stated as 'happiness in the three jhānas.'

74. Dasame samādhisampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ samādhisukhaṃ. Na samādhisampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ asamādhisukhaṃ.

74. In the tenth sutta: Happiness associated with concentration is happiness of concentration. Happiness not associated with concentration is happiness without concentration.

75. Ekādasame suttantakathā esāti “sappītikaṃ jhānadvaya”nti vuttaṃ.

75. In the eleventh sutta: Because this is a Suttanta-style explanation, it is said, 'the pair of jhānas accompanied by rapture.'

77. Terasame rūpajjhānaṃ rūpaṃ uttarapadalopena, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ etassāti rūpārammaṇaṃ. Catutthajjhānaggahaṇaṃ pana yadassa paṭiyogī, tena samānayogakkhamadassanaparaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci rūpanti yaṃ kiñci ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ. Tappaṭikkhepena arūpaṃ veditabbaṃ.

77. In the thirteenth sutta: 'Form-jhāna' becomes 'form' by elision of the latter word. Because form is its object, it is 'having form as object.' The inclusion of the fourth jhāna, however, is for the purpose of showing its counterpart, which has a similar application and suitability. 'Whatever form' means any form that has the characteristic of being afflicted. In contrast to this, the formless should be understood.

Sukhavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Happiness is finished.

(8) 3. Sanimittavaggavaṇṇanā

(8) 3. The Commentary on the Section with a Sign

78-79. Tatiyassa [M 2.0048][V 2.0044] paṭhame nimīyati ettha phalaṃ avasesapaccayehi pakkhipīyati viyāti nimittaṃ, kāraṇanti āha “sanimittāti sakāraṇā”ti. Dutiyādīsūti dutiyasuttādīsu. Eseva nayoti iminā nidānādipadānampi kāraṇapariyāyameva dīpeti. Nidadāti phalanti nidānaṃ, hinoti phalaṃ patiṭṭhāti etenāti hetu, saṅkharoti phalanti saṅkhāro, paṭicca etasmā phalaṃ etīti paccayo, ruppati niruppati phalaṃ etthāti rūpanti evaṃ nidānādipadānampi hetupariyāyatā veditabbā.

78-79. In the first of the third, a sign (nimitta) is so called because the fruit is determined here, as if placed within by the remaining conditions; it means a cause, thus he said: ‘“With a sign” means with a cause.’ In the second and following suttas, this is the method. By this same method, he shows that even terms such as source are just synonyms for cause. It lays down (nidadāti) the fruit, thus it is a source (nidāna). The fruit proceeds and is established by this, thus it is a cause (hetu). It constructs (saṅkharoti) the fruit, thus it is a formation (saṅkhāra). Dependent on this the fruit comes to be, thus it is a condition (paccayo). The fruit is afflicted (ruppati) or ceases here, thus it is form (rūpa). In this way, terms such as source should be understood as synonyms for cause.

84. Sattame paccayabhūtāyāti sahajātādipaccayabhūtāya.

84. In the seventh: by being a condition means by being a condition such as co-nascence and so on.

87. Dasame samecca sambhuyya paccayehi katoti saṅkhato, saṅkhato dhammo ārammaṇaṃ etesanti saṅkhatārammaṇā. Maggakkhaṇe na honti nāma pahīyantīti katvā. Nāhesunti ettha “vuccantī”ti ajjhāharitabbaṃ. Yāva arahattā desanā desitā taṃtaṃsuttapariyosāne “na hontī”ti vuttattā.

87. In the tenth: made by conditions coming together and combining means conditioned (saṅkhata). Conditioned phenomena are their object, thus they have conditioned phenomena as their object. They do not exist at the moment of the path because they are being abandoned. In regard to 'they were not,' the words ‘they are said’ should be supplied. For in the teaching taught all the way up to arahantship, it is said at the conclusion of the respective suttas, ‘they do not exist.’

Sanimittavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section with a Sign is finished.

(9) 4. Dhammavaggavaṇṇanā

(9) 4. The Commentary on the Dhamma Section

88. Catutthassa paṭhame phalasamādhīti catūsupi ariyaphalesu samādhi. Tathā phalapaññā veditabbā.

88. In the first of the fourth: concentration in the fruit means concentration in the four noble fruits. Similarly, wisdom in the fruit should be understood.

89. Dutiye sampayuttadhamme pariggaṇhātīti paggāho. Na vikkhipatīti avikkhepo.

89. In the second: exertion (paggāho) is so called because it takes up associated states. Non-distraction (avikkhepo) is so called because it does not scatter the mind.

90. Tatiye namanaṭṭhena nāmaṃ. Ruppanaṭṭhena rūpaṃ. Sammasanacārassa adhippetattā “cattāro arūpakkhandhā”tveva vuttaṃ. Tenāha “dhamma-koṭṭhāsaparicchedañāṇaṃ nāma kathita”nti.

90. In the third: name (nāma) is so called in the sense of bending; form (rūpa) is so called in the sense of being afflicted. Because the practice of comprehension is intended, it is simply stated as ‘the four formless aggregates.’ Therefore he said: ‘Knowledge that defines the divisions of phenomena is called name.’

91. Catutthe [V 2.0045] vijānanaṭṭhena vijjā. Vimuccanaṭṭhena vimutti.

91. In the fourth: true knowledge (vijjā) is so called in the sense of discerning; liberation (vimutti) is so called in the sense of being liberated.

92. Pañcame [M 2.0049] bhavo nāma sassataṃ sadā bhāvato, sassatavasena uppajjanadiṭṭhi bhavadiṭṭhi. Vibhavo nāma ucchedo vināsanaṭṭhena, vibhavavasena uppajjanadiṭṭhi vibhavadiṭṭhi. Uttānatthāneva heṭṭhā vuttanayattā.

92. In the fifth: existence (bhava) means eternal, from its always existing; the view that arises in terms of eternalism is the view of existence. Non-existence (vibhava) means annihilation, in the sense of destruction; the view that arises in terms of annihilationism is the view of non-existence. The meaning is plain because of the method stated above.

95. Aṭṭhame dukkhaṃ vaco etasmiṃ vippaṭikūlagāhimhi vipaccanīkasāte anādare puggaleti dubbaco, tassa kammaṃ dovacassaṃ, tassa dubbacassa puggalassa anādariyavasena pavattā cetanā. Tassa bhāvo dovacassatā. Tassa bhāvoti ca tassa yathāvuttassa dovacassassa atthibhāvo, atthato dovacassameva. Vitthārato panesā “tattha katamā dovacassatā? Sahadhammike vuccamāne dovacassāya”nti abhidhamme āgatā. Sā atthato saṅkhārakkhandho hoti. Catunnaṃ vā khandhānaṃ etenākārena pavattānaṃ etaṃ adhivacananti vadanti.

95. In the eighth: a person who is difficult to speak to (dukkhaṃ vaco)—one who is contrary, hostile, and disrespectful—is a person difficult to admonish (dubbaco). His action is difficulty of admonition (dovacassaṃ). The volition that proceeds by way of disrespect in such a person who is difficult to admonish is the quality of being difficult to admonish (dovacassatā). The state of that means the existence of the aforesaid difficulty of admonition; in meaning, it is just difficulty of admonition. In detail, this is found in the Abhidhamma: ‘Therein, what is the quality of being difficult to admonish? When one is addressed in accordance with the Dhamma, one’s being difficult to admonish….’ In meaning, it is the aggregate of formations. Or, they say, it is a designation for the four aggregates proceeding in this manner.

Pāpayogato pāpā assaddhādayo puggalā etassa mittāti pāpamitto, tassa bhāvo pāpamittatā. Vitthārato panesā “tattha katamā pāpamittatā? Ye te puggalā assaddhā dussīlā appassutā maccharino duppaññā. Yā tesaṃ sevanā nisevanā saṃsevanā bhajanā sambhajanā bhatti sambhatti taṃsampavaṅkatā”ti (dha. sa. 1333) evaṃ āgatā. Sāpi atthato dovacassatā viya daṭṭhabbā. Yāya hi cetanāya puggalo pāpasampavaṅko nāma hoti, sā cetanā cattāropi vā arūpino khandhā tadākārappavattā pāpamittatā.

Because of association with evil, evil persons—those who are faithless and so on—are his friends; thus he is an evil friend. The state of that is evil friendship. In detail, this is found thus: ‘Therein, what is evil friendship? It is the frequenting, cultivating, consorting with, devotion to, close devotion to, fondness for, close fondness for, and inclining towards those persons who are faithless, unvirtuous, with little learning, stingy, and unwise.’ This too, in meaning, should be seen like the quality of being difficult to admonish. For the volition by which a person is called ‘inclined towards evil’—that volition, or the four formless aggregates proceeding in that manner—is evil friendship.

96. Navame sukhaṃ vaco etasmiṃ padakkhiṇagāhimhi anulomasāte sādare puggaleti subbacotiādinā, kalyāṇā saddhādayo puggalā etassa mittāti kalyāṇamittotiādinā vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo.

96. In the ninth, the meaning should be understood in the opposite way to what was said above, beginning with: a person who is easy to speak to (sukhaṃ vaco)—one who is receptive, compliant, and respectful—is a person easy to admonish (subbaco); and: good persons—those who are faithful and so on—are his friends, thus he is a good friend (kalyāṇamitta).

97. Dasame pathavīdhātuādayo sukhadhātukāmadhātuādayo ca etāsveva antogadhāti etāsu kosalle dassite tāsupi kosallaṃ dassitameva hotīti “aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo”ti vuttaṃ. Dhātūti jānananti iminā aṭṭhārasannaṃ dhātūnaṃ sabhāvaparicchedikā savanadhāraṇasammasanappaṭivedhapaññā vuttā. Tattha dhātūnaṃ savanadhāraṇapaññā sutamayā, itarā bhāvanāmayā. Tatthāpi sammasanapaññā lokiyā[M 2.0050]. Vipassanā hi sā, itarā lokuttarā. Lakkhaṇādivasena aniccādivasena ca manasikaraṇaṃ manasikāro, tattha kosallaṃ manasikārakusalatā. Aṭṭhārasannaṃyeva [V 2.0046] dhātūnaṃ sammasanappaṭivedhapaccavekkhaṇapaññā manasikārakusalatā, sā ādimajjhapariyosānavasena tidhā bhinnā. Tathā hi sammasanapaññā tassā ādi, paṭivedhapaññā majjhe, paccavekkhaṇapaññā pariyosānaṃ.

97. In the tenth: since the earth element and so on, and the pleasure element, the element of sensual desire, and so on, are included within these, when skill in these is shown, skill in those is also shown. Therefore it is said, ‘the eighteen elements.’ By knowing the elements is meant the wisdom that defines the specific nature of the eighteen elements, comprising wisdom from hearing, retaining, comprehending, and penetrating. Therein, the wisdom of hearing and retaining concerning the elements is based on learning; the other is based on mental development. Therein, too, the wisdom of comprehension is mundane, for it is insight; the other is supramundane. Attention (manasikāra) is attending by way of characteristics, etc., and by way of impermanence, etc. Skill in that is skill in attention. Skill in attention is the wisdom of comprehending, penetrating, and reviewing the eighteen elements, and it is threefold as beginning, middle, and end. For the wisdom of comprehension is its beginning, the wisdom of penetration is the middle, and the wisdom of reviewing is the end.

98. Ekādasame āpattiyova āpattikkhandhā. Tā pana antarāpattīnaṃ aggahaṇena pañca, tāsaṃ gahaṇena satta hontīti āha “pañcannañca sattannañca āpattikkhandhāna”nti. Jānananti “imā āpattiyo, ettakā āpattiyo, evañca tāsaṃ āpajjanaṃ hotī”ti jānanaṃ. Evaṃ tippakārena jānanapaññā hi āpattikusalatā nāma. Āpattito vuṭṭhāpanappayogatāya kammabhūtā vācā kammavācā, tathābhūtā anussāvanavācā. “Imāya kammavācāya ito āpattito vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, hontañca paṭhame, tatiye vā anussāvane yya-kāraṃ patte, ‘saṃvarissāmī’ti vā pade pariyosite hotī”ti evaṃ taṃ taṃ āpattīhi vuṭṭhānaparicchedajānanapaññā āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā. Vuṭṭhānanti ca yathāpannāya āpattiyā yathā tathā anantarāyatāpādanaṃ. Evaṃ vuṭṭhānaggahaṇeneva desanāyapi saṅgaho siddho hoti.

98. In the eleventh: the offenses themselves are the aggregates of offenses. But they are five when the intermediate offenses are not included, and seven when they are included. Thus he said, ‘of the five and seven aggregates of offenses.’ Knowing means knowing: ‘These are the offenses; this many are the offenses; and this is how one falls into them.’ Wisdom that knows in this threefold way is called skill in offenses. A formal act of speech (kammavācā) is speech that has become a formal act for the purpose of rehabilitation from an offense; such is a speech of announcement. Skill in rehabilitation from offenses is the wisdom that knows how to define the rehabilitation from the respective offenses, thus: ‘By this formal act of speech, rehabilitation from this offense occurs; and it occurs either at the first or third announcement when the ya-kāra is reached, or when the words “I will restrain myself” are concluded.’ And rehabilitation means bringing about non-obstruction in whatever way is proper for the offense one has fallen into. Thus, by taking up rehabilitation, the inclusion of confession is also established.

Dhammavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dhamma Section is finished.

(10) 5. Bālavaggavaṇṇanā

(10) 5. Commentary on the Chapter of the Foolish.

99. Pañcamassa paṭhame anāgataṃ bhāraṃ vahatīti attano asampattaṃ bhāraṃ vahati. Atherova samāno therehi vahitabbaṃ bījanaggāhadhammajjhesanādibhāraṃ vahatīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 159-160) pana yasmā sammajjanādinavavidhaṃ pubbakiccaṃ āṇatteneva kātabbaṃ, pātimokkhañca āṇatteneva uddisitabbaṃ, tasmā taṃ sabbaṃ vinā āṇattiyā karonto anāgataṃ bhāraṃ vahati nāmāti dassetuṃ “sammajjanī padīpo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yañhi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, uposathāgāraṃ sammajjitu”ntiādinā nayena pāḷiyaṃ āgataṃ. Aṭṭhakathāsu ca –

99. In the first of the fifth, "he carries a future burden" means he carries a burden that has not yet come to him. Though not an elder, he carries the burden that should be carried by elders, such as the burden of receiving seeds and studying the Dhamma—this is the meaning to be understood here. In the commentary (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 159-160), however, because the nine kinds of preliminary duties such as sweeping must be done only when instructed, and the Pātimokkha must be recited only when instructed, therefore, to show that one who does all this without instruction is said to "carry a future burden," the words "the broom, the lamp," and so on, are stated. For it is found in the Pāli canon in the manner of such passages as, "I allow, monks, the sweeping of the Uposatha hall," and in the commentaries—

“Sammajjanī [M 2.0051][V 2.0047] padīpo ca, udakaṃ āsanena ca;

Uposathassa etāni, ‘pubbakaraṇa’nti vuccati.

"The broom and the lamp, water and a seat; these are called the 'preliminary preparations' for the Uposatha.

“Chandapārisuddhiutukkhānaṃ, bhikkhugaṇanā ca ovādo;

Uposathassa etāni, ‘pubbakicca’nti vuccatī”ti. (mahāva. aṭṭha 168) –

"Consent, purity, announcement of the season, the counting of monks, and the exhortation; these are called the 'preliminary duties' for the Uposatha." (Mahāvagga Aṭṭha 168) –

Evaṃ dvīhi nāmehi navavidhaṃ pubbakiccaṃ dassitaṃ, taṃ akatvā uposathaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Tasmā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, therena bhikkhunā navaṃ bhikkhuṃ āṇāpetu”nti vacanato therena āṇattena agilānena bhikkhunā uposathāgāraṃ sammajjitabbaṃ, pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhapetabbaṃ, āsanaṃ paññāpetabbaṃ, padīpo kātabbo, akaronto dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati.

Thus, the ninefold preliminary duty has been shown under two names. It is not proper to perform the Uposatha without having done this. Therefore, according to the statement, "I allow, monks, a senior monk to instruct a junior monk," a non-sick monk, having been instructed by a senior, should sweep the Uposatha hall, set out drinking water and water for use, arrange the seats, and light the lamp. One who does not do so commits an offense of wrong-doing.

Therenapi patirūpaṃ ñatvā āṇāpetabbaṃ, āṇāpentenapi yaṃ kiñci kammaṃ karonto vā sadā kālameva eko vā bhāranittharaṇako vā sarabhāṇakadhammakathikādīsu vā aññataro na uposathāgārasammajjanatthaṃ āṇāpetabbo, avasesā pana vārena āṇāpetabbā. Sace āṇatto sammajjaniṃ tāvakālikampi na labhati, sākhābhaṅgaṃ kappiyaṃ kāretvā sammajjitabbaṃ, tampi alabhantassa laddhakappiyaṃ hoti. Padīpakaraṇepi vuttanayeneva āṇāpetabbo, āṇāpentena ca “amukasmiṃ nāma okāse telaṃ vā kapallikā vā atthi, taṃ gahetvā karohī”ti vattabbo. Sace telādīni natthi, pariyesitabbāni. Pariyesitvā alabhantassa laddhakappiyaṃ hoti. Api ca kapāle aggi jāletabbo. Āsanapaññāpanāṇattiyampi vuttanayeneva āṇāpetabbo, āṇattena ca sace uposathāgāre āsanāni natthi, saṅghikāvāsato āharitvā paññāpetvā puna āharitabbāni, āsanesu asati kaṭasārakepi taṭṭikāyopi paññāpetuṃ vaṭṭati, tāsupi asati sākhābhaṅgāni kappiyaṃ kāretvā paññāpetabbāni. Kappiyakārakaṃ alabhantassa laddhakappiyaṃ hoti.

A senior monk, too, should give instructions after knowing what is appropriate. When giving instructions, a monk who is always engaged in some task, or is alone, or is completing a heavy duty, or is one among the chanters, Dhamma-speakers, and so on, should not be instructed to sweep the Uposatha hall. The remaining monks, however, should be instructed in turn. If the instructed monk cannot obtain a broom even for temporary use, he should have a tree branch made allowable and sweep with it. If he cannot obtain even that, it is considered allowable for one who does not obtain it. For preparing the lamp, instructions should be given in the same way as stated. The one giving instructions should say: "In such-and-such a place there is oil or a lamp-dish; take it and prepare it." If there is no oil and so on, they should be sought. If they are not obtained after searching, it is considered allowable for one who does not obtain them. Moreover, a fire may be lit in a potsherd. For the instruction to arrange the seats, instructions should also be given in the same way as stated. If there are no seats in the Uposatha hall, the instructed monk should bring them from the Sangha's lodgings, arrange them, and then return them. If there are no seats, it is permissible to arrange reed mats or wickerwork mats. If even these are unavailable, tree branches should be made allowable and arranged. If one cannot find a person to make them allowable, it is considered allowable for one who does not obtain one.

Chandapārisuddhīti ettha uposathakaraṇatthaṃ sannipatite saṅghe bahi uposathaṃ katvā āgatena sannipātaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā kāyasāmaggiṃ adentena chando dātabbo. Yopi gilāno vā kiccappasuto vā, tena pārisuddhiṃ dentena chando dātabbo. Kathaṃ dātabbo? Ekassa bhikkhuno [M 2.0052] santike “chandaṃ dammi, chandaṃ me hara, chandaṃ me ārocehī”ti ayamattho kāyena vā vācāya vā ubhayena vā viññāpetabbo. Evaṃ dinno hoti chando. Akatūposathena pana gilānena vā kiccappasutena vā pārisuddhi [V 2.0048] dātabbā. Kathaṃ dātabbā? Ekassa bhikkhuno santike “pārisuddhiṃ dammi, pārisuddhiṃ me hara, pārisuddhiṃ me ārocehī”ti ayamattho kāyena vā vācāya vā ubhayena vā viññāpetabbo. Evaṃ dinnā hoti pārisuddhi. Taṃ pana dentena chandopi dātabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, tadahuposathe pārisuddhiṃ dentena chandampi dātuṃ, santi saṅghassa karaṇīya”nti. Tattha pārisuddhidānaṃ saṅghassapi attanopi uposathakaraṇaṃ sampādeti, na avasesaṃ saṅghakiccaṃ. Chandadānaṃ saṅghasseva uposathakaraṇañca sesakiccañca sampādeti, attano pana uposatho akatoyeva hoti, tasmā pārisuddhiṃ dentena chandopi dātabbo.

Regarding 'Consent and Purity': Here, when the Sangha has gathered to perform the Uposatha, a monk who has performed the Uposatha elsewhere and then comes to the assembly place without joining the physical communion should give his consent. Also, one who is sick or occupied with some business should give his consent when giving his purity. How is consent to be given? The meaning, "I give my consent; carry my consent; announce my consent for me," should be communicated to a certain monk by body, speech, or both. Thus consent is given. But purity should be given by one who has not performed the Uposatha because he is sick or occupied with some business. How is purity to be given? The meaning, "I give my purity; carry my purity; announce my purity for me," should be communicated to a certain monk by body, speech, or both. Thus purity is given. However, one giving purity should also give consent. For this was said by the Blessed One: "I allow, monks, on the Uposatha day, for one giving purity to give consent as well, for the Sangha has business to attend to." Here, giving purity accomplishes the Uposatha observance for both the Sangha and for oneself, but not the remaining business of the Sangha. Giving consent accomplishes the Sangha’s Uposatha observance and its other business, but one’s own Uposatha remains unperformed. Therefore, one giving purity should also give consent.

Utukkhānanti “hemantādīnaṃ utūnaṃ ettakaṃ atikkantaṃ, ettakaṃ avasiṭṭha”nti evaṃ utūnaṃ ācikkhanaṃ. Bhikkhugaṇanāti “ettakā bhikkhū uposathagge sannipatitā”ti bhikkhūnaṃ gaṇanā. Idampi ubhayaṃ katvāva uposatho kātabbo. Ovādoti bhikkhunovādo. Na hi bhikkhūnīhi yācitaṃ ovādaṃ anārocetvā uposathaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhuniyo hi “sve uposatho”ti āgantvā “ayaṃ uposatho cātuddaso, pannaraso”ti pucchitvā puna uposathadivase āgantvā “bhikkhunisaṅgho, ayya, bhikkhusaṅghassa pāde vandati, ovādūpasaṅkamanañca yācati, labhatu kira, ayya, bhikkhunisaṅgho ovādūpasaṅkamana”nti evaṃ ovādaṃ yācanti. Taṃ ṭhapetvā bālagilānagamiye añño sacepi āraññako hoti, appaṭiggahetuṃ na labhati, tasmā yena so paṭiggahito, tena bhikkhunā uposathagge pātimokkhuddesako bhikkhu evaṃ vattabbo “bhikkhunisaṅgho, bhante, bhikkhusaṅghassa pāde vandati, ovādūpasaṅkamanañca yācati, labhatu kira, bhante, bhikkhunisaṅgho ovādūpasaṅkamana”nti.

"'Announcement of the season' is the declaration of the seasons, thus: 'This much of the winter and other seasons has passed; this much remains.' 'Counting of the monks' is the counting of the monks, thus: 'This many monks have gathered in the Uposatha hall.' The Uposatha should be performed only after doing both of these. 'Exhortation' is the exhortation to the bhikkhunīs. It is not proper to perform the Uposatha without announcing the exhortation that has been requested by the bhikkhunīs. For the bhikkhunīs come on the day before the Uposatha and ask, "Is this Uposatha the fourteenth or the fifteenth?" Then, on the Uposatha day, they come again and request the exhortation, saying: "Venerable sirs, the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs pays homage at the feet of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and requests the exhortation and an opportunity to approach. May the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs, venerable sirs, receive the exhortation and an opportunity to approach." Except for a foolish, sick, or travelling monk, no other monk, even if he is a forest-dweller, is allowed to refuse to accept this request. Therefore, the monk who has accepted it should say this to the monk reciting the Pātimokkha in the Uposatha hall: "Venerable sir, the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs pays homage at the feet of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and requests the exhortation and an opportunity to approach. May the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs, venerable sir, receive the exhortation and an opportunity to approach."

Pātimokkhuddesakena vattabbaṃ – “atthi koci bhikkhu bhikkhunovādako sammato”ti. Sace hoti koci bhikkhu bhikkhunovādako sammato, tato tena so vattabbo – “itthannāmako bhikkhu [M 2.0053] bhikkhunovādako sammato, taṃ bhikkhunisaṅgho upasaṅkamatū”ti. Sace natthi, tato tena pucchitabbaṃ – “ko āyasmā ussahati bhikkhuniyo ovaditu”nti. Sace koci ussahati, sopi ca aṭṭhahi aṅgehi samannāgato, taṃ tattheva sammannitvā ovādappaṭiggāhako vattabbo – “itthannāmo bhikkhu bhikkhunovādako sammato, taṃ bhikkhunisaṅgho upasaṅkamatū”ti. Sace pana na koci ussahati, pātimokkhuddesakena vattabbaṃ – “natthi koci bhikkhu bhikkhunovādako sammato, pāsādikena bhikkhunisaṅgho sampādetū”ti. Ettāvatā hi sikkhattayasaṅgahitaṃ sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ ārocitaṃ hoti. Tena bhikkhunā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā pāṭipade bhikkhunīnaṃ ārocetabbaṃ. Pātimokkhampi “na, bhikkhave, anajjhiṭṭhena pātimokkhaṃ uddisitabbaṃ, yo uddiseyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti vacanato anāṇattena na uddisitabbaṃ. “Therādheyyaṃ pātimokkha”nti hi vacanato saṅghatthero vā pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyya[V 2.0049], “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, yo tattha bhikkhu byatto paṭibalo, tassādheyyaṃ pātimokkha”nti vacanato navakataro vā therena āṇatto. Dutiyādīni uttānatthāneva.

The Pātimokkha-reciter should say: 'Is there any monk appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs?' If there is a monk appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs, then the receiver of the exhortation should be informed: 'The monk named so-and-so is appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs; let the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs approach him.' If there is none, then the reciter should ask: 'Which venerable one is able to exhort the bhikkhunīs?' If someone is able, and he is endowed with the eight qualities, he should be appointed right there, and the receiver of the exhortation should be informed: 'The monk named so-and-so is appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs; let the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs approach him.' But if no one is able, the Pātimokkha-reciter should say: 'There is no monk appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs. Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs proceed with inspiring confidence.' By this much, the entire teaching comprised in the three trainings has been announced. That monk should accept this with 'Sādhu' and announce it to the bhikkhunīs on the following day. The Pātimokkha, too, should not be recited without authorization, according to the text: 'Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited by one who has not been requested. Whoever should recite it commits an offense of wrong-doing.' For according to the text, 'The Pātimokkha is the responsibility of the elder,' the elder of the Saṅgha should recite the Pātimokkha, or a more junior monk authorized by the elder, according to the text: 'I allow, monks, that the Pātimokkha be the responsibility of whichever monk there is who is accomplished and capable.' The second and following points have an obvious meaning.

109. Ekādasame na kukkuccāyitabbaṃ kukkuccāyatīti na kukkuccāyituṃ yuttakaṃ kukkuccāyati. Sūkaramaṃsaṃ labhitvā “acchamaṃsa”nti kukkuccāyati, “sūkaramaṃsa”nti jānantopi “acchamaṃsa”nti kukkuccāyati, na paribhuñjatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ migamaṃsaṃ “dīpimaṃsa”nti, kāle santeyeva “kālo natthī”ti, appavāretvā “pavāritomhī”ti, patte rajasmiṃ apatiteyeva “patita”nti, attānaṃ uddissa macchamaṃse akateyeva “maṃ uddissa kata”nti kukkuccāyati. Kukkuccāyitabbaṃ na kukkuccāyatīti kukkuccāyituṃ yuttaṃ na kukkuccāyati. Acchamaṃsaṃ labhitvā “sūkaramaṃsa”nti na kukkuccāyati, “acchamaṃsa”nti jānantopi “sūkaramaṃsa”nti na kukkuccāyati, madditvā vītikkamatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ dīpimaṃsaṃ migamaṃsanti…pe… attānaṃ uddissa macchamaṃse kate “maṃ uddissa kata”nti na kukkuccāyatīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “na kukkuccāyitabbanti saṅghabhogassa apaṭṭhapanaṃ avicāraṇaṃ na kukkuccāyitabbaṃ nāma, taṃ kukkuccāyati. Kukkuccāyitabbanti tasseva paṭṭhapanaṃ vicāraṇaṃ, taṃ na kukkuccāyatī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Tattha [M 2.0054] saṅghabhogassāti saṅghassa catupaccayaparibhogatthāya dinnakhettavatthutaḷākādikassa, tato uppannadhaññahiraññādikassa ca saṅghassa bhogassa. Apaṭṭhapananti asaṃvidahanaṃ. Tenāha “avicāraṇa”nti. Tassevāti yathāvuttasseva saṅghabhogassa.

109. In the eleventh section, 'one is scrupulous about what one should not be scrupulous about' means one is scrupulous about what is not proper to be scrupulous about. For example, having obtained pork, one is scrupulous, thinking, 'This is bear meat.' Even knowing it is pork, one is scrupulous, thinking, 'This is bear meat,' and thus does not consume it—this is what is meant. Similarly, one is scrupulous about deer meat, thinking it is leopard meat; when it is the proper time, thinking, 'It is not the time'; without having been formally satisfied, thinking, 'I have been formally satisfied'; when dust has not fallen into the bowl, thinking, 'It has fallen'; when fish and meat have not been prepared specifically for oneself, thinking, 'It was prepared for me.' Conversely, 'one is not scrupulous about what one should be scrupulous about' means one is not scrupulous about what is proper to be scrupulous about. For example, having obtained bear meat, one is not scrupulous, thinking it is pork. Even knowing it is bear meat, one is not scrupulous, thinking it is pork, and thus transgresses by consuming it—this is what is meant. Similarly, one is not scrupulous about leopard meat, thinking it is deer meat… and so on… and when fish and meat have been prepared specifically for oneself, one is not scrupulous that it was prepared for oneself. In this way, the meaning should be understood here.
