In the commentary, however, it is said: 'What one should not be scrupulous about refers to not allocating or managing the Saṅgha's property—this is called 'what should not be scrupulous about,' yet one is scrupulous over it. What one should be scrupulous about refers to allocating and managing that very property, yet one is not scrupulous over it'—only this much is said. Therein, 'the Saṅgha's property' refers to fields, lands, ponds, and so on, given for the Saṅgha's use of the four requisites, as well as grain, gold, and so on, produced from them—the property of the Saṅgha. 'Not allocating' means not administering. Hence it is said, 'not managing.' 'That very' refers to the aforementioned Saṅgha's property.

Bālavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter of Fools is concluded.

Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Second Fifty is completed.

3. Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

3. The Third Fifty

(11) 1. Āsāduppajahavaggavaṇṇanā

(11) 1. Explanation of the Chapter on Hopes Difficult to Abandon

119. Tatiyapaṇṇāsakassa [V 2.0050][M 2.0055] paṭhame dukkhena pajahitabbāti duppajahā. Duccajātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Dvinnaṃ āsānaṃ duccajabhāvo kathaṃ jānitabboti paṭhamaṃ tāva lābhāsāya duccajabhāvaṃ vibhāveti “lābhāsāyā”tiādinā. Ubhatobyūḷhanti yuddhatthāya ubhato sannipatitaṃ. Pakkhandantīti anuppavisanti. Jīvitāsāya duppajahattātiādinā jīvitāsāya duccajabhāvaṃ vibhāveti.

119. In the first of the Third Fifty, duppajahā means 'to be abandoned with difficulty'. The same principle applies to duccajāti and so on. How is the difficulty of abandoning the two hopes to be understood? First, he explains the difficulty of abandoning the hope for gain with 'the hope for gain,' and so on. Ubhatobyūḷhaṃ means 'assembled on both sides for battle'. Pakkhandanti means 'they enter'. With 'hard to abandon the hope for life,' and so on, he explains the difficulty of abandoning the hope for life.

120. Dutiye dullabhāti na sulabhā. Iṇaṃ demīti saññaṃ karotīti evaṃ saññaṃ karonto viya hotīti attho. Ettha ca “pubbakārīti paṭhamaṃ upakārassa kārako. Kataññū katavedīti tena kataṃ ñatvā pacchā kārako. Tesu pubbakārī ‘iṇaṃ demī’ti saññaṃ karoti, pacchā kārako ‘iṇaṃ jīrāpemī’ti saññaṃ karotī”ti ettakameva idha vuttaṃ. Puggalapaṇṇattisaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (pu. pa. aṭṭha. 83) pana –

120. In the second discourse, dullabha means 'not easy to find'. The meaning is that one acts as if making the perception, 'I am giving a loan.' Here, it is said: 'A prior benefactor is one who first does a favor. A grateful and thankful person is one who later acts, knowing what was done. Among these, the prior benefactor makes the perception, 'I am giving a loan,' while the later actor makes the perception, 'I am repaying a loan.'' Only this much is stated here. However, in the commentary to the Puggalapaññatti (Pu. Pa. Aṭṭha. 83), it is said:

“Pubbakārīti paṭhamameva kārako. Katavedīti kataṃ vedeti, viditaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti. Te agāriyānagāriyehi dīpetabbā. Agārikesu hi mātāpitaro pubbakārino nāma, puttadhītaro pana mātāpitaro paṭijaggantā abhivādanādīni tesaṃ kurumānā katavedino nāma. Anagāriyesu ācariyupajjhāyā pubbakārino nāma, antevāsikasaddhivihārikā ācariyupajjhāye paṭijaggantā abhivādanādīni ca tesaṃ kurumānā katavedino nāma. Tesaṃ āvibhāvatthāya upajjhāyaposakasoṇattherādīnaṃ vatthūni kathetabbāni.

'A prior benefactor is one who does a service first. A grateful one (katavedī) makes known what has been done, makes it known, makes it evident. They should be made known by both householders and the homeless. Among householders, parents are called prior benefactors; while sons and daughters, attending to their parents and performing acts like salutation for them, are called grateful ones. Among the homeless, teachers and preceptors are called prior benefactors; while pupils and co-residents, attending to their teachers and preceptors and performing acts like salutation for them, are called grateful ones. To illustrate this, stories should be told of those like the Elder Soṇa, who supported his preceptor.'

“Aparo nayo – parena akateyeva upakāre attani kataṃ upakāraṃ anapekkhitvā kārako pubbakārī, seyyathāpi mātāpitaro ceva ācariyupajjhāyā ca. So dullabho sattānaṃ taṇhābhibhūtattā. Parena katassa upakārassa anurūpappavattiṃ [M 2.0056] attani [V 2.0051] kataṃ upakāraṃ upakārato jānanto vediyanto kataññukatavedī seyyathāpi mātāpituācariyupajjhāyesu sammāpaṭipanno. Sopi dullabho sattānaṃ avijjābhibhūtattā. Apica akāraṇavacchalo pubbakārī, sakāraṇavacchalo kataññukatavedī. ‘Karissati me’ti evamādikāraṇanirapekkhakiriyo pubbakārī, ‘karissati me’ti evamādikāraṇasāpekkhakiriyo kataññukatavedī. Tamojotiparāyaṇo pubbakārī, jotijotiparāyaṇo kataññukatavedī. Desetā pubbakārī, paṭipajjitā kataññukatavedī. Sadevake loke arahaṃ sammāsambuddho pubbakārī, ariyasāvako kataññukatavedī”ti vuttaṃ.

'Another way: Even without a prior act of kindness from another, one who acts without expecting a kindness done to oneself is a prior benefactor, just as parents and teachers and preceptors are. Such a being is rare among beings because they are overwhelmed by craving. One whose conduct is appropriate to a kindness done by another, knowing and experiencing the kindness done to oneself as a kindness, is grateful and appreciative, just as one who behaves properly towards parents, teachers, and preceptors. Such a being is also rare among beings because they are overwhelmed by ignorance. Furthermore, one who is affectionate without cause is a prior benefactor, while one who is affectionate with cause is grateful and appreciative. One whose action is without regard to a reason such as, 'They will do for me,' is a prior benefactor; one whose action is with regard to a reason such as, 'They will do for me,' is grateful and appreciative. One who is inclined toward darkness becoming light is a prior benefactor; one who is inclined toward light becoming more light is grateful and appreciative. The teacher is a prior benefactor; the practitioner is grateful and appreciative. In the world with its devas, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha, is a prior benefactor, while the noble disciple is grateful and appreciative.' Thus it was said.

Tattha kāraṇena vinā pavattahitacitto akāraṇavacchalo. Anāgatamhi payojanaṃ apekkhamāno “karissati me”tiādinā cittena paṭhamaṃ gahitaṃ tādisaṃ kataṃ upādāya kataññū eva nāma hoti, na pubbakārīti adhippāyena “karissati meti evamādikāraṇasāpekkhakiriyo kataññukatavedī”ti vuttaṃ. Tamojotiparāyaṇo puññaphalāni anupajīvanto eva puññāni karotīti “pubbakārī”ti vutto. Puññaphalaṃ upajīvanto hi kataññupakkhe tiṭṭhati.

Herein, one whose mind is inclined toward the welfare of others without a reason is 'affectionate without cause.' One who, anticipating a future benefit with a mind such as, 'He will do for me,' is called 'grateful' only in reliance on such a deed previously received, and not 'a prior benefactor.' It is with this meaning that it was said: 'One whose action depends on a reason such as, "He will do for me," is grateful and appreciative.' One who is 'inclined toward darkness becoming light' is called a 'prior benefactor' because he performs meritorious deeds without subsisting on their fruits. For one who subsists on the fruits of merit stands on the side of the grateful.

121. Tatiye tittoti suhito pariyosito niṭṭhitakiccatāya nirussukko. Guṇapāripūriyā hi paripuṇṇo yāvadattho idha titto vutto. Tappetāti aññesampi tittikaro. Paccekabuddho ca tathāgatasāvako ca khīṇāsavo tittoti ettha paccekabuddho navalokuttaradhammehi sayaṃ titto paripuṇṇo, aññaṃ pana tappetuṃ na sakkoti. Tassa hi dhammakathāya abhisamayo na hoti, sāvakānaṃ pana dhammakathāya aparimāṇānaṃ devamanussānaṃ abhisamayo hoti. Evaṃ santepi yasmā te dhammaṃ desentā na attano vacanaṃ katvā kathenti, buddhānaṃ vacanaṃ katvā kathenti, sotuṃ nisinnaparisāpi – “ayaṃ bhikkhu na attanā paṭividdhaṃ dhammaṃ kathetī”ti cittīkāraṃ karoti. Iti so cittīkāro buddhānaṃyeva hoti. Evaṃ tattha sammāsambuddhova tappetā nāma. Yathā hi “asukassa nāma idañcidañca dethā”ti raññā āṇatte [M 2.0057] kiñcāpi ānetvā denti, atha kho rājāva tattha dāyako. Yehipi laddhaṃ hoti, te “raññā amhākaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ dinnaṃ, issariyavibhavo dinno”tveva gaṇhanti, na “rājapurisehī”ti evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ.

121. In the third discourse, titto means satisfied, fulfilled, free from anxiety due to completed duties. Here, titto refers to one who is complete through the fullness of virtues and has attained their goal. Tappetā means one who also brings contentment to others. A Paccekabuddha and a disciple of the Tathāgata, both with cankers destroyed, are called 'content.' In this context, a Paccekabuddha is self-satisfied and complete in the nine supramundane states but cannot bring contentment to others. For through his teaching of the Dhamma, there is no realization, whereas through the disciples' teaching, immeasurable devas and humans attain realization. Even so, since when they teach the Dhamma they do not speak their own words but speak the words of the Buddhas, the assembly seated to listen also pays respect, thinking, 'This monk does not teach a Dhamma he has penetrated by himself.' Thus, that respect is for the Buddhas alone. Therefore, in that context, only the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha is called 'one who brings contentment.' Just as when a king orders, 'Give this and that to so-and-so,' even though others bring and give it, the king is the true giver. Those who receive it consider, 'The king has given us this position, this lordly wealth,' not 'the king’s men.' This matter should be understood in this way.

122. Catutthe duttappayāti atappayā, na sakkā kenaci tappetuṃ. Yo hi upaṭṭhākakulaṃ vā ñātikulaṃ vā nissāya vasamāno cīvare jiṇṇe tehi dinnaṃ cīvaraṃ nikkhipati, na paribhuñjati[V 2.0052]. Punappunaṃ dinnampi gahetvā nikkhipateva. Yo ca teneva nayena laddhaṃ laddhaṃ vissajjeti, parassa deti, punappunaṃ laddhampi tatheva karoti. Ime dve puggalā sakaṭehipi paccaye upanentena tappetuṃ na sakkāti duttappayā.

122. In the fourth discourse, duttappayā means those who are impossible to satisfy, who cannot be satisfied by anyone. For instance, one who lives dependent on a supporting family or relatives, when their robes become worn out, stores away the robes given by them without using them. Even when repeatedly given robes, they just take them and store them away. Another, in the same way, gives away whatever is received, offering it to others, and continues doing so even when receiving repeatedly. These two persons cannot be satisfied even if requisites are brought by cartloads—thus, they are called 'hard to satisfy.'

123. Pañcame na vissajjetīti attano akatvā parassa na deti, atireke pana sati na nikkhipati, parassa deti. Tenevāha “sabbaṃyeva paresaṃ na detī”tiādi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “yo bhikkhu upaṭṭhākakulā vā ñātikulā vā jiṇṇacīvaro sāṭakaṃ labhitvā cīvaraṃ katvā paribhuñjati na nikkhipati, aggaḷaṃ datvā pārupantopi punapi diyyamāne sahasā nappaṭiggaṇhāti. Yo ca laddhaṃ laddhaṃ attanā paribhuñjati, paresaṃ na deti. Ime dvepi sukhena sakkā tappetunti sutappayā”ti.

123. In the fifth discourse, 'he does not relinquish' means he does not give to another without making it for his own use; but if there is a surplus, he does not store it away, but gives it to another. Hence it is said, 'He does not give absolutely everything to others,' and so on. This means: 'A monk whose robe is worn out, having obtained a garment from a supporting family or relatives, makes it into a robe, uses it, and does not store it away. Even while wearing it fastened, if offered another, he does not readily accept it. And there is one who uses whatever he obtains for himself and does not give it to others. Both of these can be easily contented—thus they are easily contented.'

124-127. Chaṭṭhasattamādīni uttānatthāneva.

124-127. The sixth, seventh, and so on, are clear in meaning in themselves.

Āsāduppajahavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Āsāduppajaha Vagga is concluded.

(12) 2. Āyācanavaggavaṇṇanā

(12) 2. Commentary on the Āyācana Vagga

131. Saddho bhikkhūti saddhāya samannāgato bhikkhu. Yo bhikkhu sāriputtamoggallānehi sadisabhāvaṃ pattheti, so yehi guṇehi sāriputtamoggallānā etadagge ṭhapitā, te guṇe attano abhikaṅkheyyāti āha “yādiso sāriputtatthero paññāyā”tiādi. Ito uttari patthento micchā pattheyyāti sāriputtamoggallānānaṃ ye paññādayo guṇā upalabbhanti, tato uttari patthento micchā pattheyya. Aggasāvakaguṇaparamā hi sāvakaguṇamariyādā. Tesaṃ sāvakaguṇānaṃ [M 2.0058] yadidaṃ aggasāvakaguṇā, na tato paraṃ sāvakaguṇā nāma atthi. Tenevāha “yaṃ natthi, tassa patthitattā”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

131. 'A faithful monk' (saddho bhikkhu) means a monk endowed with faith. A monk who aspires to a state similar to that of Sāriputta and Moggallāna should desire for himself those very qualities for which Sāriputta and Moggallāna were established in the foremost position. Hence it is said, 'Such as the Elder Sāriputta in wisdom,' and so on. To aspire for something beyond this would be a wrong aspiration. For if one aspires for something beyond the qualities of wisdom and so on that are found in Sāriputta and Moggallāna, one would be aspiring wrongly. Indeed, the qualities of the chief disciples are the ultimate limit of a disciple's qualities. Among those disciple qualities, the qualities of the chief disciples are supreme; there are no disciple qualities higher than that. Therefore, it is said, 'Because one aspires for what does not exist.' The rest here is clear in itself.

135. Pañcame yassa guṇā khatā upahatā ca, so khato upahato nāma hotīti āha “guṇānaṃ khatattā”tiādi. Khatattāti chinnattā. Upahatattāti naṭṭhattā. Tenāha “chinnaguṇaṃ naṭṭhaguṇanti [V 2.0053] attho”ti. Apuññassa pasavo nāma atthato paṭilābhoti āha “pasavatīti paṭilabhatī”ti, attano santāne uppādetīti attho. Ananupavisitvāti ñāṇena anogāhetvā. Sesamettha chaṭṭhādīni ca suviññeyyāneva.

135. In the fifth discourse, one whose qualities are 'broken' (khatā) and 'destroyed' (upahatā) is called 'broken and destroyed.' Hence it is said, 'Because his qualities are broken,' and so on. 'Broken' (khatattā) means severed (chinnattā). 'Destroyed' (upahatattā) means lost (naṭṭhattā). Therefore, it is said, 'The meaning is having severed qualities, having lost qualities.' 'The production of demerit' (apuññassa pasavo) means, in essence, acquisition. Hence it is said, 'Produces (pasavati) means acquires (paṭilabhati),' that is, it means he produces it in his own continuum. 'Without having penetrated' (ananupavisitvā) means not having entered with knowledge (ñāṇena anogāhetvā). The rest here, including the sixth and so on, are easily understood.

Āyācanavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Āyācana Vagga is concluded.

(13) 3. Dānavaggavaṇṇanā

(13) 3. Commentary on the Dāna Vagga

142. Tatiyassa paṭhame dīyatīti dānaṃ, deyyadhammassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Dīyati anenāti vā dānaṃ, pariccāgacetanāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayaṃ duvidhopi attho idhādhippetoti āha “diyyanakavasena dānānī”tiādi. Tattha diyyanakavasenāti dātabbavasena. Amatapattipaṭipadanti amatappattihetubhūtaṃ sammāpaṭipadaṃ.

142. In the first of the third chapter, 'what is given' (dīyati) is a gift (dāna); this is a designation for the object to be given (deyyadhamma). Or, 'that by which one gives' (dīyati anena) is a gift (dāna); this is a designation for the intention to relinquish (pariccāgacetanā). That both these meanings are intended here is stated thus: 'gifts in terms of what is to be given' (diyyanakavasena dānāni), and so on. There, 'in terms of what is to be given' means in terms of what ought to be given. 'The path to attaining the Deathless' (amatapattipaṭipadā) means the right practice that is the cause for attaining the Deathless.

143-151. Dutiyādīni ca suviññeyyāneva.

143-151. The second and following are also easily understood.

Dānavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dāna Vagga is concluded.

(14) 4. Santhāravaggavaṇṇanā

(14) 4. Commentary on the Santhāra Vagga

152. Catutthassa paṭhame āmisassa ca dhammassa ca alābhena attano parassa ca antare sambhavantassa chiddassa vivarassa bhedassa santharaṇaṃ pidahanaṃ saṅgaṇhanaṃ santhāro. Ayañhi lokasannivāso alabbhamānena āmisena dhammena cāti dvīhi chiddo. Tassa taṃ chiddaṃ yathā na paññāyati[M 2.0059], evaṃ pīṭhassa viya paccattharaṇena āmisena dhammena ca santharaṇaṃ saṅgaṇhanaṃ santhāroti vuccati. Ettha ca āmisena saṅgaho āmisasanthāro nāma. Taṃ karontena mātāpitūnaṃ bhikkhugatikassa [V 2.0054] veyyāvaccakarassa rañño corānañca aggaṃ aggahetvāpi dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Āmasitvā dinnehi rājāno ca corā ca anatthampi karonti, jīvitakkhayampi pāpenti. Anāmasitvā dinnena attamanā honti, coranāgavatthuādīni cettha vatthūni kathetabbāni. Tāni samantapāsādikāya vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. 185) vitthāritāni. Sakkaccaṃ uddesadānaṃ pāḷivaṇṇanā dhammakathākathananti evaṃ dhammena saṅgaho dhammasanthāro nāma.

152. In the first of the fourth chapter, a 'spreading' (santhāra) is the covering (santharaṇa), closing (pidahana), and mending (saṅgaṇhana) of the gap (chidda), opening (vivara), or fissure (bheda) that arises between oneself and others due to the lack of both material things (āmisa) and the Dhamma. For this worldly cohabitation is flawed by two things: the non-receipt of material things and of the Dhamma. The act of covering (santharaṇa) and mending (saṅgaṇhana) of this gap with material things and the Dhamma, so that it does not appear, like spreading a cover over a seat, is called a 'spreading' (santhāra). Here, helping with material things is called a 'material spreading' (āmisasanthāra). One who practices this may properly give to parents, visiting monks, those doing service, kings, and thieves, even without taking the best portion for oneself. If given after taking a portion, kings and thieves may cause harm or even take life. But if given without taking a portion, they are pleased. Stories like that of the thief Nāga and others should be told here. These are elaborated in the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya (Pārā. 185). Respectful recitation, Pāli exposition, and Dhamma teaching—this kind of helping through the Dhamma is called 'Dhamma spreading' (dhammasanthāra).

153-163. Dutiyādīni uttānatthāneva.

153-163. The second and following are clear in meaning in themselves.

Santhāravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Santhāra Vagga is concluded.

(15) 5. Samāpattivaggavaṇṇanā

(15) 5. Commentary on the Samāpatti Vagga

164. Pañcamassa paṭhame “ito pubbe parikammaṃ pavattaṃ, ito paraṃ bhavaṅgaṃ majjhe samāpattī”ti evaṃ saha parikammena appanāparicchedappajānanā paññā samāpattikusalatā. Vuṭṭhāne kusalabhāvo vuṭṭhānakusalatā. Pageva vuṭṭhānaparicchedakañāṇanti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

164. In the first of the fifth chapter, 'skill in attainment' (samāpattikusalatā) is the wisdom (paññā) that understands the delimitation of absorption (appanāpariccheda) along with its preparatory work (parikamma), as in: 'before this, preparatory work occurred; after this, the life-continuum; in between, the attainment.' 'Skill in emerging' (vuṭṭhānakusalatā) is the state of being skilled in emerging. The meaning here should be understood precisely as the knowledge that discerns the emerging.

165. Dutiye ujuno bhāvo ajjavaṃ, ajimhatā akuṭilatā avaṅkatāti attho. Abhidhammepi (dha. sa. 1346) vuttaṃ – “tattha katamo ajjavo? Yā ajjavatā ajimhatā akuṭilatā avaṅkatā, ayaṃ vuccati ajjavo”ti. Anajjavañca ajjavappaṭikkhepena veditabbaṃ. Gomuttavaṅkatā, candalekhāvaṅkatā, naṅgalakoṭivaṅkatāti hi tayo anajjavā. Ekacco hi bhikkhu paṭhamavaye majjhima-pacchimavaye ca ekavīsatiyā anesanāsu chasu ca agocaresu carati, ayaṃ gomuttavaṅkatā nāma, ādito paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā paṭipattiyā vaṅkabhāvato. Eko paṭhamavaye pacchimavaye ca catupārisuddhisīlaṃ pūreti, lajjī kukkuccako sikkhākāmo hoti, majjhimavaye purimasadiso, ayaṃ candalekhāvaṅkatā nāma, paṭipattiyā majjhaṭṭhāne [M 2.0060] vaṅkabhāvāpattito. Eko paṭhamavayepi majjhimavayepi catupārisuddhisīlaṃ pūreti, lajjī kukkuccako sikkhākāmo hoti, pacchimavaye purimasadiso, ayaṃ naṅgalakoṭivaṅkatā nāma, pariyosāne vaṅkabhāvāpattito. Eko sabbampetaṃ vaṅkataṃ pahāya tīsu vayesu [V 2.0055] pesalo lajjī kukkuccako sikkhākāmo hoti, tassa yo so ujubhāvo, idaṃ ajjavaṃ nāma, sabbattha ujubhāvasiddhito.

165. In the second [case], 'uprightness' (ajjava) is the state of being straight (ujuno bhāvo), meaning non-deviousness (ajimhatā), non-crookedness (akuṭilatā), and non-bending (avaṅkatā). As stated in the Abhidhamma (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1346): 'Here, what is uprightness (ajjavo)? That which is uprightness (ajjavatā), non-deviousness (ajimhatā), non-crookedness (akuṭilatā), non-bending (avaṅkatā)—this is called uprightness (ajjavo).' And 'non-uprightness' (anajjava) should be understood as the opposite of uprightness. Indeed, there are three types of non-uprightness: the crookedness of a cow's urine (gomuttavaṅkatā), the crookedness of a crescent moon (candalekhāvaṅkatā), and the crookedness of a plow's tip (naṅgalakoṭivaṅkatā). For instance, a certain monk in his early, middle, and later years engages in the twenty-one unsuitable pursuits and the six unsuitable places; this is called the crookedness of a cow's urine, because his conduct is crooked from beginning to end. Another monk fulfills the fourfold purity of moral conduct in his early and later years, being conscientious, scrupulous, and eager in training, but in his middle years, he is like the former [type of monk]; this is called the crookedness of a crescent moon, because his conduct becomes crooked in the middle. Yet another monk fulfills the fourfold purity of moral conduct in his early and middle years, being conscientious, scrupulous, and eager in training, but in his later years, he is like the former [type of monk]; this is called the crookedness of a plow's tip, because his conduct becomes crooked at the end. But one who abandons all such crookedness and remains amiable (pesalo), conscientious (lajjī), scrupulous (kukkuccako), and eager in training (sikkhākāmo) throughout all three stages of life—his state of being straight (ujubhāvo) is called uprightness (ajjava), as he achieves straightness in all respects.

Maddavanti ettha “lajjava”ntipi paṭhanti. Evaṃ panettha attho – “tattha katamo lajjavo? Yo hirīyati hirīyitabbena hirīyati pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpattiyā, ayaṃ vuccati lajjavo”ti evaṃ vutto lajjibhāvo lajjavaṃ nāma. Idaṃ panettha nibbacanaṃ – lajjatīti lajjo, hirimā, tassa bhāvo lajjavaṃ, hirīti attho. Lajjā etassa atthīti lajjī yathā “mālī māyī”ti, tassa bhāvo lajjibhāvo, sā eva lajjā.

Here, some read 'maddava' as 'lajjava'. The meaning here is as follows: 'Here, what is modesty (lajjavo)? One who feels ashamed (hirīyati) of what should be ashamed, who feels ashamed of the arising of evil, unwholesome states—this is called modesty (lajjavo).' Thus, the state of being modest (lajjibhāvo) is called modesty (lajjava). Here is the derivation: 'One who feels ashamed (lajjati) is modest (lajjo), conscientious (hirimā); his state is modesty (lajjava),' meaning a sense of shame (hirī). 'One who possesses shame (lajjā) is modest (lajjī),' just as 'one who wears a garland is mālī,' 'one who deceives is māyī.' His state is modesty (lajjibhāvo); that itself is shame (lajjā).

166. Tatiye adhivāsanakhantīti ettha adhivāsanaṃ vuccati khamanaṃ. Tañhi paresaṃ dukkaṭaṃ duruttañca paṭivirodhākaraṇena attano upari āropetvā vāsanato “adhivāsana”nti vuccati. Adhivāsanalakkhaṇā khanti adhivāsanakhanti. Sucisīlatā soraccaṃ. Sā hi sobhanakammaratatā. Suṭṭhu vā pāpato oratabhāvo viratatāti āha “suratabhāvo”ti. Teneva abhidhammepi (dha. sa. 1349) –

166. In the third [case], regarding 'patient endurance' (adhivāsanakhanti), 'endurance' (adhivāsana) is called 'bearing' (khamana). Indeed, because one bears others' misdeeds and harsh speech without opposition, accepting them upon oneself, it is called 'endurance' (adhivāsana). Forbearance with the characteristic of endurance is patient endurance (adhivāsanakhanti). 'Gentleness' (soracca) is purity of moral conduct (sucisīlatā). For it is delighting in beautiful actions. Or, because of thoroughly turning away from evil, being abstinent (viratatā), it is called 'the state of being well-behaved' (suratabhāvo). Therefore, in the Abhidhamma also (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1349)—

“Tattha katamaṃ soraccaṃ? Yo kāyiko avītikkamo vācasiko avītikkamo kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo, idaṃ vuccati soraccaṃ, sabbopi sīlasaṃvaro soracca”nti – āgato.

'Here, what is gentleness (soraccaṃ)? That which is non-transgression by body, non-transgression by speech, non-transgression by both body and speech—this is called gentleness (soraccaṃ). All restraint in morality (sīlasaṃvaro) is gentleness (soraccaṃ).' Thus it is stated.

167. Catutthe sakhilo vuccati saṇhavāco, tassa bhāvo sākhalyaṃ, saṇhavācatā. Tenāha “saṇhavācāvasena sammodamānabhāvo”ti. Saṇhavācāvasena hi sammodamānassa puggalassa bhāvo nāma saṇhavācatā. Teneva abhidhamme (dha. sa. 1350) –

167. In the fourth [case], 'amiable' (sakhilo) is called 'gentle-spoken' (saṇhavāco); its state is 'amiability' (sākhalya), which is gentle speech (saṇhavācatā). Hence it is said, 'the state of being friendly through gentle speech' (saṇhavācāvasena sammodamānabhāvo). Indeed, the state of a person who is friendly through gentle speech is called gentle speech (saṇhavācatā). Therefore, in the Abhidhamma (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1350)—

“Tattha katamaṃ sākhalyaṃ? Yā sā vācā aṇḍakā kakkasā parakaṭukā parābhisajjanī kodhasāmantā asamādhisaṃvattanikā, tathārūpiṃ [M 2.0061] vācaṃ pahāya yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā pemanīyā hadayaṅgamā porī bahujanakantā bahujanamanāpā, tathārūpiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti, yā tattha saṇhavācatā sakhilavācatā apharusavācatā, idaṃ vuccati sākhalya”nti vuttaṃ.

'Here, what is amiability (sākhalyaṃ)? That speech which is harsh (aṇḍakā), rough (kakkasā), bitter to others (parakaṭukā), abusive to others (parābhisajjanī), bordering on anger (kodhasāmantā), unconducive to concentration (asamādhisaṃvattanikā)—having abandoned such speech, one speaks words that are smooth (nelā), pleasing to the ear (kaṇṇasukhā), endearing (pemanīyā), penetrating the heart (hadayaṅgamā), civil (porī), liked by many (bahujanakantā), pleasing to many (bahujanamanāpā). That gentle speech (saṇhavācatā), amiable speech (sakhilavācatā), non-harsh speech (apharusavācatā) therein—this is called amiability (sākhalyaṃ).' Thus it is stated.

Tattha aṇḍakāti sadose savaṇe rukkhe niyyāsapiṇḍo, ahicchattādīni vā uṭṭhitāni aṇḍakānīti [V 2.0056] vadanti, pheggurukkhassa pana kuthitassa aṇḍāni viya uṭṭhitā cuṇṇapiṇḍiyo vā gaṇṭhiyo vā aṇḍakā. Idha pana byāpajjanakakkasādisabhāvato kaṇṭakappaṭibhāgena vācā aṇḍakāti vuttā. Padumanāḷaṃ viya sotaṃ ghaṃsayamānā pavisantī kakkasā daṭṭhabbā. Kodhena nibbattā tassa parivārabhūtā kodhasāmantā. Pure saṃvaddhanārī porī. Sā viya sukumārā mudukā vācā porī viyāti porī. Saṇhavācatātiādinā taṃ vācaṃ pavattamānaṃ dasseti.

Here, 'harsh' (aṇḍakā) refers to a lump of gum on a diseased, oozing tree, or they say that aṇḍakā are things like mushrooms that have sprung up, or lumps of powder or knots that have sprung up like the 'eggs' of a rotten tree with no heartwood. But here, speech is called 'harsh' (aṇḍakā) because of its harmful, rough nature, or because it is like a thorn. 'Rough' (kakkasā) should be seen as speech that grates, entering the ear like a lotus stalk. 'Bordering on anger' (kodhasāmantā) means speech born of anger, being its attendant. 'Civil' (porī) is a woman brought up in a city. Speech that is delicate and soft like her is called 'civil' (porī). 'Gentle speech' (saṇhavācatā) and so on describe the way such speech occurs.

168. Pañcame “avihiṃsāti karuṇāpubbabhāgo”ti ettakameva idha vuttaṃ, dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya saṅgītisuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.304) pana “avihiṃsāti karuṇāpi karuṇāpubbabhāgopī”ti vuttaṃ. Abhidhammepi (vibha. 182) “tattha katamā avihiṃsā? Yā sattesu karuṇā karuṇāyanā karuṇāyitattaṃ karuṇācetovimutti, ayaṃ vuccati avihiṃsā”ti āgataṃ. Etthāpi hi yā kāci karuṇā “karuṇā”ti vuttā, karuṇācetovimutti pana appanāppattāva.

168. In the fifth, it is stated here only that 'non-harming is a precursor to compassion.' However, in the Dīghanikāya commentary’s explanation of the Saṅgīti Sutta (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.304), it is stated: 'Non-harming is compassion or its precursor.' In the Abhidhamma (Vibh. 182) as well, it appears: 'Here, what is non-harming? That which is compassion for beings, the act of being compassionate, the state of being compassionate, liberation of mind through compassion—this is called non-harming.' Here too, any kind of compassion is called 'compassion,' but liberation of mind through compassion refers only to that which has attained absorption.

Sucisaddato bhāve yakāraṃ ikārassa ca ukārādesaṃ katvā ayaṃ niddesoti āha “socabyaṃ sucibhāvo”ti. Ettha ca socabyanti sīlavasena sucibhāvoti vuttaṃ. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya saṅgītisuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.304) pana “soceyyanti mettāya ca mettāpubbabhāgassa ca vasena sucibhāvo”ti vuttaṃ. Teneva abhidhammepi “tattha katamaṃ socabyaṃ? Yā sattesu metti mettāyanā mettāyitattaṃ mettācetovimutti, idaṃ vuccati socabya”nti niddeso kato. Etthāpi hi “mettī”tiādinā yā kāci mettā vuttā, mettācetovimutti pana appanāppattāva.

Having derived the term from the word 'suci' by applying the suffix 'ya' in the sense of 'state' and substituting 'u' for 'i', this directive is given: 'Socabyaṃ is the state of purity (sucibhāvo).' Here, 'socabyaṃ' is stated to be purity by way of virtue. In the Dīghanikāya commentary’s explanation of the Saṅgīti Sutta (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.304), however, it is stated: 'Soceyyaṃ means purity by way of loving-kindness and its precursor.' Therefore, in the Abhidhamma, it is explained: 'Here, what is socabyaṃ? That which is loving-kindness towards beings, the act of being loving, the state of being loving, liberation of mind through loving-kindness—this is called socabyaṃ.' Here too, whatever loving-kindness is spoken of by 'mettī' and so on, 'mettācetovimutti' refers only to that which has attained absorption.

169-171. Chaṭṭhasattamaaṭṭhamāni [M 2.0062] heṭṭhā vuttanayāneva.

169-171. The sixth, seventh, and eighth are just as explained above.

172. Navame kāmaṃ sampayuttadhammesu thirabhāvopi balaṭṭho eva, paṭipakkhehi pana akampanīyataṃ sātisayaṃ balaṭṭhoti vuttaṃ “muṭṭhassacce akampanenā”tiādi.

172. In the ninth, although steadfastness in concomitant states is indeed in the sense of strength, unshakability by opposing factors is called strength in a pre-eminent sense, as stated: 'by being unshaken by forgetfulness,' and so on.

173. Dasame paccanīkadhammasamanato samatho, samādhīti āha “samathoti cittekaggatā”ti. Aniccādinā vividhenākārena dassanato passanato vipassanā, paññāti āha “saṅkhārapariggāhakañāṇa”nti.

173. In the tenth, tranquility (samatho) is from the calming of opposing states; it is concentration (samādhi), and it is said: 'tranquility is one-pointedness of mind.' Insight (vipassanā) is from seeing in various ways, such as impermanence; it is wisdom (paññā), and it is said: 'knowledge that comprehends formations.'

174. Ekādasame [V 2.0057] dussīlyanti samādinnassa sīlassa bhedakaro vītikkamo. Diṭṭhivipattīti “atthi dinna”ntiādinayappavattāya sammādiṭṭhiyā dūsikā micchādiṭṭhīti āha “diṭṭhivipattīti micchādiṭṭhī”ti.

174. In the eleventh, 'moral depravity' (dussīlya) is the transgression that breaks the virtue that has been undertaken. 'Corruption of view' (diṭṭhivipatti) is the wrong view that corrupts the right view which proceeds by way of 'there is what is given' and so on; thus it is said: 'Corruption of view is wrong view.'

175. Dvādasame sīlasampadāti sabbabhāgato tassa anūnatāpatti paripuṇṇabhāvo sīlasampadā. Paripūraṇattho hettha sampadāsaddo. Tenevāha “paripuṇṇasīlatā”ti. Diṭṭhisampadāti atthikadiṭṭhiādisammādiṭṭhipāripūribhāvena pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Tañca kammassakatāsammādiṭṭhiādivasena pañcavidhaṃ hotīti āha “tena kammassakatā”ti.

175. In the twelfth, 'perfection of virtue' (sīlasampadā) is the attainment of non-deficiency in every respect, its state of being full. Here, the word 'sampadā' has the meaning of fulfillment. Therefore it is said, 'complete virtue' (paripuṇṇasīlatā). 'Perfection of view' (diṭṭhisampadā) is knowledge occurring through the fulfillment of right view, such as the view that there is (fruit of) giving and so on. And that is fivefold by way of right view regarding ownership of kamma and so on; thus it is said: 'by that, ownership of kamma...'

176. Terasame sīlavisuddhīti visuddhiṃ pāpetuṃ samatthaṃ sīlaṃ, cittavisuddhiādiuparivisuddhiyā paccayo bhavituṃ samatthaṃ visuddhasīlanti vuttaṃ hoti. Suvisuddhameva hi sīlaṃ tassā padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tenāha “sīlavisuddhīhi visuddhisampāpakaṃ sīla”nti. Etthāpi visuddhisampāpakanti cittavisuddhiādiuparivisuddhiyā sampāpakanti attho daṭṭhabbo. Abhidhamme (dha. sa. 1372) panāyaṃ “tattha katamā sīlavisuddhi? Kāyiko avītikkamo vācasiko avītikkamo kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo, ayaṃ vuccati sīlavisuddhī”ti evaṃ vibhattā.

176. In the thirteenth, 'purification of virtue' means virtue capable of leading to purification; that is to say, purified virtue capable of being a condition for higher purifications such as purification of mind. Truly purified virtue is indeed its basis. Hence it is said: 'Purification of virtue is virtue that brings about purification.' Here too, 'bringing about purification' should be understood as bringing about higher purifications such as purification of mind. In the Abhidhamma (Dhs. 1372), this is analyzed as: 'Herein, what is purification of virtue? Non-transgression in body, non-transgression in speech, non-transgression in both body and speech—this is called purification of virtue.'

Diṭṭhivisuddhīti visuddhiṃ pāpetuṃ samatthaṃ dassanañāṇaṃ dassanavisuddhi, paramatthavisuddhiṃ nibbānañca pāpetuṃ upanetuṃ samatthaṃ kammassakatañāṇādi sammādassananti attho. Tenāha “visuddhisampāpikā…pe… pañcavidhāpi vā sammādiṭṭhī”ti. Etthāpi visuddhisampāpikāti ñāṇadassanavisuddhiyā dassananibbānasaṅkhātāya [M 2.0063] paramatthavisuddhiyā ca sampāpikāti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Abhidhamme (dha. sa. 1373) panāyaṃ “tattha katamā diṭṭhivisuddhi? Kammassakatañāṇaṃ, saccānulomikaṃ ñāṇaṃ, maggassa maggasamaṅgissa ñāṇaṃ, phalasamaṅgissa ñāṇa”nti evaṃ vuttaṃ.

Purification of view means the knowledge of seeing capable of leading to purification, which is purification of vision; and it means right seeing, such as the knowledge of ownership of kamma, capable of leading to and bringing near the ultimate purification, Nibbāna. Hence it is said: 'that which brings about purification... or the fivefold right view.' Here too, 'that which brings about purification' should be understood as bringing about the purification of knowledge and vision, and the ultimate purification reckoned as the vision of Nibbāna. In the Abhidhamma (Dhs. 1373), it is stated: 'Herein, what is purification of view? The knowledge of ownership of kamma, the knowledge conforming to the truths, the knowledge of one endowed with the path, the knowledge of one endowed with the fruition.'

Ettha ca idaṃ akusalakammaṃ no sakaṃ, idaṃ pana kammaṃ sakanti evaṃ byatirekato anvayato ca kammassakatajānanañāṇaṃ kammassakatañāṇaṃ. Tividhaduccaritañhi attanā katampi parena katampi no sakakammaṃ nāma hoti atthabhañjanato, sucaritaṃ sakakammaṃ nāma atthajananato. Vipassanāñāṇaṃ pana vacīsaccañca anulometi, paramatthasaccañca na vilometīti saccānulomikañāṇanti vuttaṃ. Vipassanāñāṇañhi lakkhaṇāni paṭivijjhanatthaṃ ārambhakāle [V 2.0058] “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti pavattaṃ vacīsaccañca anulometi, tatheva paṭivijjhanato paramatthasaccaṃ nibbānañca na vilometi na virādheti ekanteneva sampāpanato.

Here, the knowledge that discerns ownership of kamma by way of exclusion and inclusion—knowing 'this unwholesome kamma is not one's own, but this wholesome kamma is one's own'—is called the knowledge of ownership of kamma. For threefold misconduct, whether done by oneself or by others, is not called one's own kamma because it destroys welfare; but good conduct is called one's own kamma because it generates welfare. The knowledge of insight, moreover, accords with verbal truth and does not contradict ultimate truth; thus it is called knowledge in conformity with the truths. For insight knowledge, at the initial stage, in order to penetrate the characteristics, accords with the verbal truth which proceeds as 'impermanent, suffering, non-self.' Similarly, by penetrating thus, it does not contradict or deviate from ultimate truth, Nibbāna, but leads to it exclusively.

177. Cuddasame diṭṭhivisuddhīti paṭhamamaggasammādiṭṭhi vuttā. Yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānanti taṃsampayuttameva vīriyaṃ. Teneva dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.304) “diṭṭhivisuddhīti ñāṇadassanaṃ kathitaṃ. Yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānanti taṃsampayuttameva vīriya”nti vuttaṃ. Ettha hi ñāṇadassananti ñāṇabhūtaṃ dassanaṃ. Tena dassanamaggaṃ vadati. Taṃsampayuttameva vīriyanti paṭhamamaggasampayuttavīriyamāha. Apica diṭṭhivisuddhīti sabbāpi maggasammādiṭṭhi. Yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānanti taṃsampayuttameva vīriyaṃ. Teneva dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “apica purimapadena catumaggañāṇaṃ, pacchimapadena taṃsampayuttaṃ vīriya”nti vuttaṃ.

177. In the fourteenth, 'purification of view' is said to be the right view of the first path. And 'the striving of one who sees accordingly' refers to the energy associated with it. Therefore, in the Dīghanikāya commentary (D. N. A. 3.304), it is said: 'Purification of view is called knowledge and vision. And the striving of one who sees accordingly is the energy associated with it.' Here, 'knowledge and vision' means vision that is knowledge. Thus, it speaks of the path of vision. 'The energy associated with it' refers to the energy associated with the first path. Furthermore, 'purification of view' is all the right view of the paths. 'The striving of one who sees accordingly' is the energy associated with it. Hence, in the Dīghanikāya commentary, it is said: 'Moreover, the first expression refers to the knowledge of the four paths, and the latter expression refers to the energy associated with them.'

Atha vā diṭṭhīvisuddhīti kammassakatañāṇādisaṅkhātā sabbāpi sammādiṭṭhi vuttā. Yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānanti yo cetasiko vīriyārambho…pe… sammāvāyāmoti. Ayameva pāḷiyā sameti. Abhidhamme hi “diṭṭhivisuddhi kho panāti yā paññā pajānanā…pe… amoho dhammavicayo sammādiṭṭhi. Yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānanti yo cetasiko vīriyārambho…pe… sammāvāyāmo”ti evamayaṃ duko vibhatto. Teneva abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1374) “yā paññā pajānanātiādīhi heṭṭhā vuttāni kammassakatañāṇādīneva cattāri ñāṇāni vibhattāni. ‘Yo cetasiko vīriyārambho’tiādīhi [M 2.0064] padehi niddiṭṭhaṃ vīriyaṃ gahitaṃ paññāya lokiyaṭṭhāne lokiyaṃ, lokuttaraṭṭhāne lokuttara”nti vuttaṃ.

Alternatively, 'purification of view' is said to be all right view, which is reckoned as the knowledge of ownership of kamma and so on. And 'the striving of one who sees accordingly' refers to 'the mental exertion of energy... up to... right effort.' This accords with the Pāli. In the Abhidhamma, this pair is analyzed thus: 'Purification of view is that wisdom, understanding... up to... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view. The striving of one who sees accordingly is the mental exertion of energy... up to... right effort.' Accordingly, in the Abhidhamma commentary (Dhs. A. 1374), it is said: 'By 'that wisdom, understanding' and so on, the four knowledges stated previously, such as the knowledge of ownership of kamma, are analyzed. By the terms 'the mental exertion of energy' and so on, the energy indicated is taken as mundane in the mundane sphere of wisdom, and supramundane in the supramundane sphere.'

Idhāpi visuddhisampāpikā catumaggasammādiṭṭhi, pañcavidhāpi vā sammādiṭṭhi diṭṭhivisuddhīti adhippāyena “diṭṭhivisuddhīti visuddhisampāpikā sammādiṭṭhiyevā”ti vuttaṃ. Heṭṭhimamaggasampayuttaṃ vīriyanti idaṃ pana “yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānanti paṭhamamaggasampayuttaṃ vīriyanti vutta”nti adhippāyena vadati. Ettha ca taṃtaṃbhāṇakānaṃ matabhedenāyaṃ vaṇṇanābhedoti na aṭṭhakathāvacanānaṃ aññamaññavirodho saṅkitabbo. Atha yathādiṭṭhissa ca padhānanti heṭṭhimamaggasampayuttameva vīriyaṃ kasmā vuttanti āha “tañhi tassā diṭṭhiyā anurūpattā”tiādi. Tattha tassā diṭṭhiyāti heṭṭhimamaggasampayuttāya diṭṭhiyā. Yathādiṭṭhissāti anurūpadiṭṭhissa kalyāṇadiṭṭhissa nibbattitappakāradiṭṭhissa vā nibbattetabbapadhānānurūpadiṭṭhissa yathādiṭṭhippavattakiriyassa vāti evampettha atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇayanti.

Here too, with the intention that purification of view is the right view of the four paths that brings about purification, or the fivefold right view, it is said: 'Purification of view is indeed the right view that brings about purification.' But this, 'the energy associated with the lower path,' is said with the intention that 'the striving of one who sees accordingly' refers to what was stated as 'the energy associated with the first path.' Here, this difference in explanation is due to differences in opinion among the respective reciters, so a contradiction among the commentarial statements should not be suspected. Then, why is 'the striving of one who sees accordingly' said to be the energy associated with the lower path? He says, 'because it is suitable to that view,' etc. There, 'to that view' means to the view associated with the lower path. 'Of one who sees accordingly' (yathādiṭṭhissa) is explained thus: of one whose view is suitable, of one whose view is wholesome, of one whose view is of a kind that has been produced, of one whose view is suitable to the striving to be produced, or of one whose action proceeds according to how he sees. Thus they explain the meaning here.

178. Pannarasame [V 2.0059] samattaṃ tussanaṃ titti santuṭṭhi, natthi etassa santuṭṭhīti asantuṭṭhi, asantuṭṭhissa bhāvo asantuṭṭhitā. Yā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya asantuṭṭhassa bhiyyokamyatā, tassā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tāya hi samaṅgibhūto puggalo sīlaṃ pūretvā jhānaṃ uppādeti, jhānaṃ labhitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhati, āraddhavipassako arahattaṃ aggahetvā antarā vosānaṃ nāpajjati, “alamettāvatā katamettāvatā”ti saṅkocaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Tenāha “aññatra arahattamaggā kusalesu dhammesu asantuṭṭhibhāvo”ti. Tatra aññatra arahattamaggāti arahattamaggasampattaṃ vināti attho. “Appaṭivānitā ca padhānasmi”nti idaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthamevāti na vibhattaṃ.

178. In the fifteenth, contentment (santuṭṭhi) is completeness, satisfaction, and fulfillment. One for whom there is no contentment is discontent (asantuṭṭhi); the state of being discontent is discontentedness (asantuṭṭhitā). This term is a designation for the desire for more on the part of one who is discontented in the cultivation of wholesome qualities. For a person endowed with this, having perfected virtue, gives rise to jhāna; having attained jhāna, he undertakes insight meditation; having begun insight, he does not reach cessation midway without grasping arahantship, not shrinking back with the thought, 'This much is enough, this much has been done.' Therefore, it is said, 'The state of discontent in wholesome qualities, apart from the path of arahantship.' Here, 'apart from the path of arahantship' means 'without the attainment of the path of arahantship.' 'And unretreating in exertion' is not analyzed, as its meaning is clear from what was stated earlier and is thus self-evident.

179. Soḷasame muṭṭhā naṭṭhā sati etassāti muṭṭhassati, tassa bhāvo muṭṭhassaccanti āha “muṭṭhassaccanti muṭṭhassatibhāvo”ti. Muṭṭhassatibhāvoti ca satippaṭipakkho dhammo, na satiyā abhāvamattaṃ. Asampajaññanti “tattha katamaṃ asampajaññaṃ? Yaṃ aññāṇaṃ adassanaṃ…pe… avijjālaṅghī moho akusalamūla”nti (dha. sa. 1357) evaṃ vuttā avijjāyeva. Tathā hi vijjāpaṭipakkho avijjā vijjāya pahātabbato, evaṃ sampajaññappaṭipakkho asampajaññaṃ[M 2.0065]. Yasmā pana sampajaññappaṭipakkhe sati tassa vasena ñāṇassa abhāvo hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “aññāṇabhāvo”ti.

179. In the sixteenth, `muṭṭhassati` means one whose mindfulness is lost or destroyed, and its state is `muṭṭhassacca`. Thus, it is said, '`Muṭṭhassacca` is the state of lost mindfulness.' The state of lost mindfulness is a quality opposed to mindfulness, not merely the absence of mindfulness. 'Lack of clear comprehension' (asampajañña) is indeed ignorance (avijjā), as stated: 'Herein, what is lack of clear comprehension? It is unknowing, not seeing... the overstepping of ignorance, delusion, the unwholesome root' (Dhs. 1357). For just as ignorance is the opposite of knowledge and is to be abandoned by knowledge, so too is lack of clear comprehension the opposite of clear comprehension. And because, when there is this opposite of clear comprehension, there is an absence of knowledge on account of it, it is therefore called 'the state of unknowing.'

180. Sattarasame apilāpanalakkhaṇā satīti udake lābu viya yena cittaṃ ārammaṇe pilavitvā viya tiṭṭhati, na ogāhati, taṃ pilāpanaṃ. Na pilāpanaṃ apilāpanaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ sabhāvo etissāti apilāpanalakkhaṇā.

180. In the seventeenth, mindfulness has the characteristic of non-floating. That state wherein the mind stands as if floating on the object and does not plunge into it, like a gourd on water, is 'floating.' 'Non-floating' is the absence of floating. That this is its characteristic, its intrinsic nature, is why mindfulness is said to have the characteristic of non-floating.

Samāpattivaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Samāpatti section is concluded.

Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The third set of fifty is concluded.

1. Kodhapeyyālaṃ

1. The Section on Anger

181. Ito paresu kodhavaggādīsu upanandhanalakkhaṇoti kujjhanavasena “akkocchi maṃ avadhi [V 2.0060] ma”ntiādinā (dha. pa. 3, 4) cittapariyonandhanalakkhaṇo. Pubbakālikaṃ kodhaṃ upanayhati bandhati, kujjhanākāraṃ pabandhati ghaṭeti. Āghātavatthunā cittaṃ bandhantī viya hotīti aparakālo kodho upanāho. Suṭṭhu kataṃ kāraṇaṃ upakāro sukatakāraṇaṃ, tassa pubbakāritālakkhaṇassa guṇassa makkhanaṃ udakapuñchaniyā viya sarīrānugatassa udakassa puñchanaṃ vināsanaṃ lakkhaṇametassāti sukatakaraṇamakkhanalakkhaṇo. Tathā hi so paresaṃ guṇānaṃ makkhanaṭṭhena makkhoti vuccati. Bahussutepi puggale ajjhotthariṃsu, “īdisassa ca bahussutassa aniyatā gahitā, tava ca mama ca ko viseso”tiādinā nayena uppajjamāno yugaggāhī palāsoti āha “yugaggāhalakkhaṇo palāso”ti. Tattha yugaggāho nāma samadhuraggāho, asamampi attanā samaṃ katvā gaṇhanaṃ. Palāsatīti palāso, paresaṃ guṇe ḍaṃsitvā dantehi viya chinditvā attano guṇehi same karotīti attho.

181. Hereafter, in the sections on anger and so forth, the characteristic of resentment is the characteristic of the mind's entanglement through anger, as in, 'He abused me, he struck me,' and so on (Dhammapada 3, 4). One harbors and binds past anger; one arranges and fabricates an appearance of anger. Subsequent anger is called resentment because it is as if the mind is bound by an object of ill will. A well-done deed, a helpful action, is a 'good deed'; its characteristic is the effacement of the virtue characterized by having been done well in the past, like wiping away water clinging to the body with a cloth. Thus, it is characterized by the effacement of good deeds. Indeed, it is called disparagement (makkha) because of its wiping away the virtues of others. Even a learned person might be overwhelmed. Arising in the manner of, 'Such a learned person has grasped uncertain things; what is the difference between you and me?' and so on, is competitiveness (palāsa), which grasps at the yoke. Thus it is said, 'competitiveness has the characteristic of grasping at the yoke.' Here, 'grasping at the yoke' means grasping at equality, making even the unequal equal to oneself. It is called competitiveness (palāsa) because it competes; the meaning is that after biting at the virtues of others as if with teeth and cutting them down, it makes them equal to one's own virtues.

Usūyanalakkhaṇāti paresaṃ sakkārādīni khiyyanalakkhaṇā. Maccherassa bhāvo macchariyaṃ. Tañca āvāsamacchariyādivasena pañcavidhanti āha “pañcamaccherabhāvo macchariya”nti. Maccharāyanalakkhaṇanti attano sampattiyā [M 2.0066] parehi sādhāraṇabhāve asahanalakkhaṇaṃ. Katappaṭicchādanalakkhaṇāti katapāpappaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā. Kerāṭikabhāvena uppajjamānaṃ sāṭheyyanti āha “kerāṭikalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyya”nti. Aññathā attano pavedanapuggalo kerāṭiko nekatikavāṇijoti vadanti. Kerāṭiko hi puggalo ānandamaccho viya hoti.

The characteristic of envy is being displeased with the honors and so on of others. The state of being miserly is stinginess. And it is fivefold in terms of stinginess regarding dwellings, etc., as stated: 'The state of being miserly is fivefold stinginess.' The characteristic of stinginess is the inability to bear one's own possessions being shared with others. The characteristic of concealment is concealing one's wrongdoings. Deceit arises from the nature of being a cheat, as stated: 'Deceit has the characteristic of cheating.' A person who presents himself otherwise is a cheat, a deceitful merchant, so they say. For a deceitful person is like the Ānanda fish.

187. Yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ nirayeti yathā ābhataṃ kañci āharitvā ṭhapito, evaṃ attano kammunā nikkhitto niraye ṭhapitoyevāti attho.

187. As one is brought, so one is cast into hell—just as someone is brought and placed, so one is cast down by one's own deeds and placed in hell—this is the meaning.

2. Akusalapeyyālaṃ

2. The Section on the Unwholesome

191-200. Dukkhassa vaḍḍhi etesanti dukkhavaḍḍhikā. Ye hi dukkhaṃ vaḍḍhenti, punappunaṃ uppādenti, dukkhassa vaḍḍhi tesaṃ atthīti evaṃ vuttaṃ. Sukhavaḍḍhikāti etthāpi eseva nayo.

191-200. They are 'increasers of suffering' because for them there is an increase of suffering. For those who increase suffering, who repeatedly produce it, for them there is an increase of suffering—thus it is said. The same method applies here also to 'increasers of happiness.'

3. Vinayapeyyālaṃ

3. The Section on Discipline

201. Atthavaseti [V 2.0061] vuddhivisese ānisaṃsavisese. Tesaṃ pana sikkhāpadapaññattikāraṇattā āha “dve kāraṇāni sandhāyā”ti. Atthoyeva vā atthavaso, dve atthe dve kāraṇānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā attho phalaṃ tadadhīnavuttitāya vaso etassāti atthavaso, kāraṇanti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yathā “anabhijjhā dhammapada”nti vutte anabhijjhā eko dhammakoṭṭhāsoti attho hoti. Evamidhāpi sikkhāpadanti sikkhākoṭṭhāso sikkhāya eko padesoti ayamettha attho daṭṭhabboti āha “sikkhāpadaṃ paññattanti sikkhākoṭṭhāso ṭhapito”ti.

201. The term 'atthavasa' refers to a special growth, a special advantage. And because these are the reasons for the formulation of the training rules, he says, 'having considered two reasons.' Or 'atthavasa' is simply the purpose itself; it is said that there are two purposes, two reasons. Alternatively, 'attha' is the result, and 'vasa' is that which has its existence dependent on that; thus 'atthavasa'. The meaning here should be understood as 'reason.' Just as when it is said 'non-covetousness is a Dhamma-item,' the meaning is that non-covetousness is one section of Dhamma. Similarly here, when 'sikkhāpada' is said, the meaning to be understood here is that it is a section of training, one part of the training. Therefore, he says: 'A training rule is formulated' means 'a section of the training is established.'

Saṅghasuṭṭhu nāma saṅghassa suṭṭhubhāvo “suṭṭhu devā”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 39) āgataṭṭhāne viya “suṭṭhu, bhante”ti vacanasampaṭicchanabhāvo. Tenāha “saṅghasuṭṭhutāyāti saṅghassa suṭṭhubhāvāyā”tiādi. Dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyāti dummaṅkū nāma dussīlapuggalā. Ye maṅkutaṃ āpādiyamānāpi dukkhena āpajjanti, vītikkamaṃ karontā vā katvā vā [M 2.0067] na lajjanti, tesaṃ niggahatthāya. Te hi sikkhāpade asati “kiṃ tumhehi diṭṭhaṃ, kiṃ sutaṃ, kiṃ amhehi kataṃ, katarasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ katamaṃ āpattiṃ ropetvā amhe niggaṇhathā”ti saṅghaṃ viheṭhessanti, sikkhāpade pana sati tesaṃ saṅgho sikkhāpadaṃ dassetvā dhammena vinayena satthusāsanena niggahessati. Tena vuttaṃ “dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggahāyā”ti.

The term 'Saṅghasuṭṭhu' refers to the excellence of the Saṅgha, as in the phrase 'Well done, gods' (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 39) where it occurs, or the acceptance of words like 'Well done, venerable sir.' Therefore, he says, 'for the well-being of the Saṅgha' means 'for the excellence of the Saṅgha,' and so on. For the restraint of unruly individuals: 'unruly' refers to individuals of bad conduct. Those who are difficult to make ashamed, and who do not feel shame for transgressing or having transgressed—it is for their restraint. For if there were no training rule, they would trouble the Saṅgha, saying, 'What have you seen? What have you heard? What have we done? On what grounds and for what offense do you accuse us and restrain us?' But when there is a training rule, the Saṅgha will show them the training rule and restrain them righteously, in accordance with the Dhamma, the Discipline, and the Teacher’s instruction. Therefore, it is said, 'for the restraint of unruly individuals.'

Pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāyāti pesalānaṃ piyasīlānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihāratthāya. Piyasīlā hi bhikkhū kattabbākattabbaṃ sāvajjānavajjaṃ velaṃ mariyādaṃ ajānantā sikkhattayapāripūriyā ghaṭamānā kilamanti, ubbāḷhā honti, kattabbākattabbaṃ pana sāvajjānavajjaṃ velaṃ mariyādañca ñatvā sikkhattayapāripūriyā ghaṭentā na kilamanti, na ubbāḷhā honti. Tena tesaṃ sikkhāpadappaññāpanā phāsuvihārāya saṃvattati. Yo vā dummaṅkūnaṃ puggalānaṃ niggaho, sveva etesaṃ phāsuvihāro. Dussīlapuggale nissāya hi uposatho na tiṭṭhati, pavāraṇā na tiṭṭhati, saṅghakammāni nappavattanti, sāmaggī na hoti, bhikkhū anekaggā uddesaparipucchākammaṭṭhānādīni anuyuñjituṃ na sakkonti. Dussīlesu pana niggahitesu sabbopi ayaṃ upaddavo na hoti, tato pesalā bhikkhū phāsu viharanti. Evaṃ “pesalānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ phāsuvihārāyā”ti ettha dvidhā attho veditabbo.

For the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved monks: this is for the sake of comfortable dwelling for well-behaved, virtuously amiable monks. For virtuously amiable monks, not knowing what should and should not be done, what is blameworthy and blameless, the proper time and limits, become weary and distressed when striving for the fulfillment of the threefold training. But knowing what should and should not be done, what is blameworthy and blameless, the proper time and limits, they do not become weary or distressed when striving for the fulfillment of the threefold training. Therefore, the laying down of training rules leads to their comfortable dwelling. Or, the disciplining of unruly individuals itself is their comfortable dwelling. For on account of immoral persons, the Uposatha does not take place, the Pavāraṇā does not take place, Saṅgha acts are not carried out, there is no harmony, and the monks, being divided, cannot devote themselves to recitation, questioning, meditation subjects, and so on. But when the immoral are disciplined, all these troubles do not arise, and thus the well-behaved monks dwell comfortably. In this way, the phrase 'for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved monks' should be understood in two ways.

“Na [V 2.0062] vo ahaṃ, cunda, diṭṭhadhammikānaṃyeva āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya dhammaṃ desemī”ti (dī. ni. 3.182) ettha vivādamūlabhūtā kilesā āsavāti āgatā.

In the passage, 'I do not teach the Dhamma, Cunda, merely for the restraint of the taints pertaining to this present life' (D.N. 3.182), the defilements that are the root of disputes are what is meant by 'taints'.

“Yena devūpapatyassa, gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo;

Yakkhattaṃ yena gaccheyyaṃ, manussattañca abbaje;

Te mayhaṃ āsavā khīṇā, viddhastā vinaḷīkatā”ti. (a. ni. 4.36) –

'By which I might be reborn as a god, or as a gandhabba or a bird; by which I might reach the state of a yakkha, or attain a human existence—those taints of mine are destroyed, vanquished, and uprooted.' (A.N. 4.36)

Ettha tebhūmakaṃ kammaṃ avasesā ca akusalā dhammā. Idha pana parūpavādavippaṭisāravadhabandhanādayo ceva apāyadukkhabhūtā ca nānappakārā upaddavā āsavāti āha – “diṭṭhadhamme imasmiṃyeva attabhāve vītikkamapaccayā paṭiladdhabbāna”ntiādi. Yadi hi bhagavā sikkhāpadaṃ na paññāpeyya, tato asaddhammappaṭisevanaadinnādānapāṇātipātādihetu ye uppajjeyyuṃ parūpavādādayo diṭṭhadhammikā nānappakārā anatthā, ye ca tannimittameva [M 2.0068] nirayādīsu nibbattassa paññavidhabandhanakammakāraṇādivasena mahādukkhānubhavanappakārā anatthā, te sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ “diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāyā”ti. Diṭṭhadhammo vuccati paccakkho attabhāvo, tattha bhavā diṭṭhadhammikā. Samparetabbato pecca gantabbato samparāyo, paraloko, tattha bhavā samparāyikā.

Here, kamma pertaining to the three planes and the remaining unwholesome states are included. However, in this context, slander from others, regret, execution, imprisonment, and various kinds of troubles that are the suffering of the lower realms are called 'āsavas,' because he said they 'are to be obtained in this very life, in this very existence, due to transgression,' and so on. For if the Blessed One had not laid down the training rules, then due to causes such as engaging in false teachings, stealing, and killing living beings, various harms in this life such as slander from others and the like would arise. And with regard to those various kinds of harms—such as experiencing great suffering in hell and other realms by way of the five kinds of binding, forced labor, and so on, which arise precisely because of that—it is said: 'for the restraint of the taints pertaining to this life, and for the warding off of the taints pertaining to the next life.' The present existence is called 'diṭṭhadhamma' because it is directly perceived; those arising therein are 'diṭṭhadhammika.' 'Samparāya' means the other world, because one is to go there after death; those arising therein are 'samparāyika.'

Akusalaverānanti pāṇātipātādipañcaduccaritānaṃ. Tāni verakāraṇattā “verānī”ti vuccanti, puggalesu pana uppajjamānāni verāni. Te eva vā dukkhadhammāti heṭṭhā vuttā vadhabandhanādayo. Tesaṃ pakkhupacchedanatthāyāti tesaṃ pāpicchānaṃ pakkhupacchedāya gaṇabhojanasadisaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ. Paṇḍitamanussānanti lokiyaparikkhakajanānaṃ. Te hi sikkhāpadapaññattiyā sati sikkhāpadapaññattiṃ ñatvā vā yathāpaññattaṃ paṭipajjamāne bhikkhū disvā vā – “yāni vata loke mahājanassa rajjanadussanamuyhanaṭṭhānāni, tehi ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā ārakā viharanti, dukkaraṃ vata karonti, bhāriyaṃ vata karontī”ti pasādaṃ āpajjanti vinayapiṭake potthakaṃ disvā micchādiṭṭhikatavedibrāhmaṇo viya. Uparūparipasādabhāvāyāti bhiyyo bhiyyo pasāduppādanatthaṃ. Yepi hi sāsane pasannā kulaputtā, tepi sikkhāpadapaññattiṃ vā ñatvā yathāpaññattaṃ paṭipajjamāne bhikkhū vā disvā “aho, ayyā, dukkarakārino, ye yāvajīvaṃ ekabhattaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vinayasaṃvaraṃ anupālentī”ti bhiyyo bhiyyo pasīdanti.

Unwholesome hostilities: this refers to the five kinds of misconduct, such as killing living beings. Because they are the cause of enmity, they are called 'hostilities'; they are the enmities that arise in individuals. Or they are indeed the states of suffering, such as execution and imprisonment, mentioned below. For the purpose of cutting off their faction: this means for cutting off the faction of those with evil desires; thus, a training rule similar to the one on group meals is laid down. Wise people: this refers to discerning worldly individuals. For when a training rule is laid down, they, either knowing of the laying down of the training rule or seeing monks practicing accordingly, think: 'Indeed, these Sakyan ascetics dwell far from the things in the world that are occasions for the masses to lust, hate, and be deluded. Truly, they do what is hard to do; they do what is difficult to do.' They gain confidence, just like the brahmin Vedī of wrong view upon seeing a book of the Vinaya Piṭaka. For the sake of ever-increasing confidence: this means for the purpose of repeatedly arousing confidence. For even those noble sons already confident in the Dispensation, upon knowing of the laying down of the training rule or seeing monks practicing accordingly, think: 'Ah, the venerables are doers of the difficult—they who maintain for life the single meal, the holy life, and the restraint of the Vinaya!' And so, they become ever more confident.

Saddhammassa [V 2.0063] ciraṭṭhitatthanti pariyattisaddhammo, paṭipattisaddhammo, adhigamasaddhammoti tividhassapi saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ. Tattha piṭakattayasaṅgahitaṃ sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ pariyattisaddhammo nāma. Terasa dhutaguṇā, cuddasa khandhakavattāni, dveasīti mahāvattāni, sīlasamādhivipassanāti ayaṃ paṭipattisaddhammo nāma. Cattāro ariyamaggā cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni nibbānañcāti ayaṃ adhigamasaddhammo nāma. So sabbo yasmā sikkhāpadapaññattiyā sati bhikkhū sikkhāpadañca tassa vibhaṅgañca tadatthajotanatthaṃ aññañca buddhavacanaṃ pariyāpuṇanti, yathāpaññattañca paṭipajjamānā paṭipattiṃ pūretvā paṭipattiyā adhigantabbaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ adhigacchanti, tasmā sikkhāpadapaññattiyā ciraṭṭhitiko hoti.

For the long-lasting of the True Dhamma: this means for the long-lasting of the three kinds of True Dhamma—the Dhamma of learning, the Dhamma of practice, and the Dhamma of attainment. Herein, all the Buddha's words contained in the three Piṭakas are called the Dhamma of learning. The thirteen ascetic practices, the fourteen duties from the Khandhakas, the eighty-two major duties, and morality, concentration, and insight—this is called the Dhamma of practice. The four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—this is called the Dhamma of attainment. Since, when the training rules are laid down, the monks learn the training rule, its analysis, and other words of the Buddha to illuminate its meaning, and by practicing as laid down, they fulfill the practice and attain the supramundane Dhamma that is to be attained through practice, therefore, through the laying down of the training rules, it becomes long-lasting.

Pañcavidhassapi [M 2.0069] vinayassāti tadaṅgavinayādivasena pañcappakārassa vinayassa. Vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 39) pana sikkhāpadapaññattiyā sati saṃvaravinayo ca pahānavinayo ca samathavinayo ca paññattivinayo cāti catubbidhopi vinayo anuggahito hoti upatthambhito supatthambhito. Tena vuttaṃ “vinayānuggahāyā”ti. Tattha saṃvaravinayoti sīlasaṃvaro, satisaṃvaro, ñāṇasaṃvaro, khantisaṃvaro, vīriyasaṃvaroti pañcavidhopi saṃvaro yathāsakaṃ saṃvaritabbānaṃ vinetabbānañca kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ saṃvaraṇato saṃvaro, vinayanato vinayoti vuccati. Pahānavinayoti tadaṅgappahānaṃ, vikkhambhanappahānaṃ, samucchedappahānaṃ, paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ, nissaraṇappahānanti pañcavidhampi pahānaṃ yasmā cāgaṭṭhena pahānaṃ, vinayanaṭṭhena vinayo, tasmā pahānavinayoti vuccati. Samathavinayoti satta adhikaraṇasamathā. Paññattivinayoti sikkhāpadameva. Sikkhāpadapaññattiyā hi vijjamānāya eva sikkhāpadasambhavato sikkhāpadasaṅkhāto paññattivinayoti sikkhāpadapaññattiyā anuggahito hoti.

Of the fivefold discipline: this refers to the five kinds of discipline by way of the discipline by substitution and so on. However, in the Vinaya Commentary (Pārā. Aṭṭha. 39), when a training rule is laid down, all four types of discipline—the discipline of restraint, the discipline of abandoning, the discipline of settling, and the discipline of regulation—are supported, upheld, and well-established. Therefore, it is said, 'for the support of the discipline.' Herein, the discipline of restraint refers to five kinds of restraint: moral restraint, mindfulness restraint, wisdom restraint, patience restraint, and effort restraint. It is called restraint (saṃvara) because it restrains (saṃvaraṇato) bodily misconduct and other things that should be restrained and disciplined, and it is called discipline (vinaya) because it disciplines (vinayanato) them. The discipline of abandoning refers to the five kinds of abandoning: abandoning by substitution, abandoning by suppression, abandoning by eradication, abandoning by calming, and abandoning by escape. Because abandoning has the meaning of relinquishment and discipline has the meaning of training, it is called the discipline of abandoning. The discipline of settling refers to the seven methods for settling legal issues. The discipline of regulation refers to the training rule itself. For it is only through the existence of the laying down of a training rule that a training rule itself can exist. Therefore, the discipline of regulation, known as the training rule, is supported by the laying down of the training rule.

202-230. Bhikkhūnaṃ pañcāti nidānapārājikasaṅghādisesāniyatavitthāruddesavasena pañca bhikkhūnaṃ uddesā. Bhikkhunīnaṃ cattāroti bhikkhūnaṃ vuttesu aniyatuddesaṃ ṭhapetvā avasesā cattāro.

202-230. For monks, there are five recitations: by way of the recitation of the Introduction, the Pārājikas, the Saṅghādisesas, the Aniyatas, and the detailed section. For nuns, there are four: among those mentioned for monks, setting aside the recitation of the Aniyatas, the remaining four.

Ehibhikkhūpasampadāti “ehi bhikkhū”ti vacanamattena paññattaupasampadā. Bhagavā hi ehibhikkhubhāvāya upanissayasampannaṃ puggalaṃ disvā rattapaṃsukūlantarato suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ dakkhiṇahatthaṃ nīharitvā brahmaghosaṃ nicchārento “ehi bhikkhu, cara brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyā”ti vadati. Tassa saheva bhagavato vacanena gihiliṅgaṃ antaradhāyati, pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca ruhati, bhaṇḍu kāsāvavasano hoti – ekaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā ekaṃ aṃse ṭhapetvā vāmaaṃsakūṭe āsattanīluppalavaṇṇamattikāpatto.

The 'Come, bhikkhu' ordination is the ordination prescribed merely by the words 'Come, bhikkhu.' For the Blessed One, seeing a person endowed with the supporting conditions for the 'Come, bhikkhu' state, extends his golden-hued right hand from within his red rag-robe and, uttering a voice like Brahmā's, says, 'Come, bhikkhu, live the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.' Simultaneously with the Blessed One's words, the householder's marks disappear, and both the going forth and the higher ordination are established. He becomes shaven-headed, clad in ochre robes—wearing one, wrapping another, and placing one over his shoulder—with an earthenware bowl the color of a blue lotus attached to his left shoulder.

“Ticīvarañca [V 2.0064] patto ca, vāsi sūci ca bandhanaṃ;

Parissāvanena aṭṭhete, yuttayogassa bhikkhuno”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.215; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.294; 2.349; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.198; pārā. aṭṭha. 45 padabhājanīyavaṇṇanā; apa. aṭṭha. 1.avidūrenidānakathā; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 27.avidūrenidānakathā; jā. aṭṭha. 1.avidūrenidānakathā; mahāni. aṭṭha. 206) –

"The three robes and the bowl, a razor, a needle, and a belt; with a water-strainer—these eight are for a monk devoted to the practice."

Evaṃ [M 2.0070] vuttehi aṭṭhahi parikkhārehi sarīre paṭimukkehiyeva vassasatikatthero viya iriyāpathasampanno buddhācariyako buddhupajjhāyako sammāsambuddhaṃ vandamānoyeva tiṭṭhati.

Thus, with these eight requisites just mentioned as if fastened to his body, he stands like an elder of a hundred years, endowed with perfect deportment, having the Buddha as his teacher and the Buddha as his preceptor, venerating the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Saraṇagamanūpasampadāti “buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”tiādinā nayena tikkhattuṃ vācaṃ bhinditvā vuttehi tīhi saraṇagamanehi anuññātaupasampadā. Ovādūpasampadāti ovādappaṭiggahaṇaupasampadā. Sā ca “tasmātiha te, kassapa, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘tibbaṃ me hirottappaṃ, paccupaṭṭhitaṃ bhavissati theresu navesu majjhimesū’ti. Evañhi te, kassapa, sikkhitabbaṃ. Tasmātiha te, kassapa, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘yaṃ kiñci dhammaṃ suṇissāmi kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ aṭṭhiṃ katvā manasi karitvā sabbacetasā samannāharitvā ohitasoto dhammaṃ suṇissāmī’ti, evañhi te, kassapa, sikkhitabbaṃ. Tasmātiha te, kassapa, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘sātasahagatā ca me kāyagatāsati na vijahissatī’ti, evañhi te, kassapa, sikkhitabba”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) iminā ovādappaṭiggahaṇena mahākassapattherassa anuññātaupasampadā.

Ordination by going for refuge is the full ordination granted through the threefold going for refuge by uttering the words three times, in the manner of "I go to the Buddha for refuge," and so forth. Ordination by exhortation is the full ordination of receiving instruction. And that is the full ordination granted to the Venerable Mahākassapa through receiving this instruction: "Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘Keen shame and fear of wrongdoing will be present in me toward seniors, juniors, and those of middle standing.’ Thus, Kassapa, you should train. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘Whatever Dhamma connected with the wholesome I hear, I will attend to all of it, taking it to heart, applying my whole mind, and listening to the Dhamma with an attentive ear.’ Thus, Kassapa, you should train. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: ‘Mindfulness of the body accompanied by pleasure will not be abandoned by me.’ Thus, Kassapa, you should train." (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.154).

Pañhabyākaraṇūpasampadā nāma sopākassa anuññātaupasampadā. Bhagavā kira pubbārāme anucaṅkamantaṃ sopākasāmaṇeraṃ “uddhumātakasaññāti vā, sopāka, rūpasaññāti vā ime dhammā nānatthā nānābyañjanā, udāhu ekatthā byañjanameva nāna”nti dasa asubhanissite pañhe pucchi. So byākāsi. Bhagavā tassa sādhukāraṃ datvā “kativassosi, tvaṃ sopākā”ti pucchi. Sattavassohaṃ bhagavāti. Sopāka, tvaṃ mama sabbaññutaññāṇena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā pañhe byākāsīti āraddhacitto upasampadaṃ anujāni. Ayaṃ pañhabyākaraṇūpasampadā.

Ordination by answering questions is the full ordination granted to Sopāka. It is said that the Blessed One, while walking back and forth in the Eastern Park, asked the novice Sopāka ten questions based on the perception of foulness, such as: "Sopāka, are these things—the perception of a bloated corpse or the perception of form—of different meaning and different expression, or of the same meaning but merely different in expression?" He answered them. The Blessed One gave him approval and asked, "How old are you, Sopāka?" "Seven years old, Blessed One." "Sopāka, you have answered these questions by comparing them with my omniscience." Being pleased in mind, he granted him full ordination. This is the ordination by answering questions.

Ñatticatutthaupasampadā nāma bhikkhūnaṃ etarahi upasampadā. Garudhammūpasampadāti garudhammappaṭiggahaṇena upasampadā. Sā ca mahāpajāpatiyā aṭṭhagarudhammappaṭiggahaṇena anuññātā[V 2.0065]. Ubhatosaṅghe upasampadā nāma bhikkhuniyā bhikkhunisaṅghato ñatticatutthena, bhikkhusaṅghato ñatticatutthenāti imehi dvīhi kammehi anuññātā aṭṭhavācikūpasampadā. Dūtena upasampadā nāma aḍḍhakāsiyā gaṇikāya anuññātā upasampadā.

The ordination by a motion and three announcements is the present full ordination for monks. Ordination by the weighty rules is the full ordination by accepting the weighty rules. And that was permitted for Mahāpajāpatī by accepting the eight weighty rules. Ordination in both Sanghas is the full ordination of a nun by a motion and three announcements from the community of nuns, and by a motion and three announcements from the community of monks—thus, the full ordination by eight utterances permitted by these two procedures. Ordination by a messenger is the full ordination permitted for the courtesan Aḍḍhakāsī.

Ñattikammaṃ [M 2.0071] nava ṭhānāni gacchatīti katamāni nava ṭhānāni gacchati? Osāraṇaṃ, nissāraṇaṃ, uposatho, pavāraṇā, sammuti, dānaṃ, paṭiggahaṃ, paccukkaḍḍhanaṃ, kammalakkhaṇaññeva navamanti evaṃ vuttāni nava ṭhānāni gacchati. Tattha “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, itthannāmo itthannāmassa āyasmato upasampadāpekkho, anusiṭṭho so mayā, yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, itthannāmo āgaccheyya, āgacchāhīti vattabbo”ti (mahāva. 126) evaṃ upasampadāpekkhassa osāraṇā osāraṇā nāma.

The act of announcement applies to nine instances. What are these nine instances to which it applies? Introduction, expulsion, the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, appointment, giving, acceptance, withdrawal, and the characteristic of the act itself as the ninth—thus are the nine instances to which it applies. Herein, "Venerable sirs, may the Sangha hear me. This person named so-and-so is seeking full ordination from the venerable so-and-so. He has been instructed by me. If the Sangha is ready, this person named so-and-so should come. He should be told, 'Come.'" (Mahāvagga 126) Thus, the introduction for one seeking full ordination is called introduction.

“Suṇantu me, āyasmantā, ayaṃ itthannāmo bhikkhu dhammakathiko, imassa neva suttaṃ āgacchati, no suttavibhaṅgo, so atthaṃ asallakkhetvā byañjanacchāyāya atthaṃ paṭibāhati. Yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, itthannāmaṃ bhikkhuṃ vuṭṭhāpetvā avasesā imaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vūpasameyyāmā”ti evaṃ ubbāhikavinicchaye dhammakathikassa bhikkhuno nissāraṇā nissāraṇā nāma.

"Venerable sirs, listen to me. This monk, named so-and-so, is a Dhamma speaker, but neither the Sutta nor the Sutta-analysis comes to him. Without reflecting on the meaning, he rejects the meaning by the shadow of the letter. When it seems fit to the venerable ones, having expelled the monk so-and-so, let us, the rest, settle this issue." Thus, in the judicial procedure of arbitration, the expulsion of the Dhamma-speaking monk is called expulsion.

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, ajjuposatho pannaraso. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho uposathaṃ kareyyā”ti evaṃ uposathakammavasena ṭhapitā ñatti uposatho nāma.

"Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. Today is the fifteenth, the Uposatha day. If the Sangha is ready, the Sangha should perform the Uposatha." Thus, the motion established by way of the Uposatha procedure is called the Uposatha.

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, ajja pavāraṇā pannarasī. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho pavāreyyā”ti evaṃ pavāraṇākammavasena ṭhapitā ñatti pavāraṇā nāma.

"Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. Today is the fifteenth day, the Pavāraṇā. If the Sangha is ready, let the Sangha hold the Pavāraṇā." Thus, the motion established through the procedure of the Pavāraṇā act is called Pavāraṇā.

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, itthannāmo itthannāmassa āyasmato upasampadāpekkho. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ itthannāmaṃ anusāseyya”nti, “yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, itthannāmo itthannāmaṃ anusāseyyā”ti, “yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ itthannāmaṃ antarāyike dhamme puccheyya”nti, “yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, itthannāmo itthannāmaṃ antarāyike dhamme puccheyyā”ti, “yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ itthannāmaṃ vinayaṃ puccheyya”nti, “yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, itthannāmo itthannāmaṃ vinayaṃ puccheyyā”ti, “yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ itthannāmena vinayaṃ puṭṭho [V 2.0066] vissajjeyya”nti, “yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, itthannāmo itthannāmena vinayaṃ puṭṭho [M 2.0072] vissajjeyyā”ti evaṃ attānaṃ vā paraṃ vā sammannituṃ ṭhapitā ñatti sammuti nāma.

"Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. So-and-so is seeking full ordination from Venerable So-and-so. If the Sangha is ready, I shall instruct So-and-so." "If the Sangha is ready, So-and-so shall instruct So-and-so." "If the Sangha is ready, I shall question So-and-so about the obstructive conditions." "If the Sangha is ready, So-and-so shall question So-and-so about the obstructive conditions." "If the Sangha is ready, I shall question So-and-so about the Discipline." "If the Sangha is ready, So-and-so shall question So-and-so about the Discipline." "If the Sangha is ready, I shall answer, having been questioned about the Discipline by So-and-so." "If the Sangha is ready, So-and-so shall answer, having been questioned about the Discipline by So-and-so." Thus, the motion that is established to appoint oneself or another is called appointment.

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, idaṃ cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa bhikkhuno nissaggiyaṃ saṅghassa nissaṭṭhaṃ. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho imaṃ cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa bhikkhuno dadeyyā”ti, “yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, āyasmantā imaṃ cīvaraṃ itthannāmassa bhikkhuno dadeyyu”nti evaṃ nissaṭṭhacīvarapattādīnaṃ dānaṃ dānaṃ nāma.

"Venerable sirs, may the Sangha hear me. This robe, belonging to the monk named so-and-so, is to be forfeited and has been relinquished to the Sangha. If it seems fit to the Sangha, may the Sangha give this robe to the monk named so-and-so." "When it seems fit to the venerable ones, may the venerable ones give this robe to the monk named so-and-so." Thus, the giving of relinquished robes, bowls, and so forth, is called giving.

“Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, ayaṃ itthannāmo bhikkhu āpattiṃ sarati vivarati uttāniṃ karoti deseti. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ itthannāmassa bhikkhuno āpattiṃ paṭiggaṇheyya”nti, “yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, ahaṃ itthannāmassa bhikkhuno āpatiṃ paṭiggaṇheyya”nti, tena vattabbo “passasī”ti? Āma passāmīti. “Āyatiṃ saṃvareyyāsī”ti evaṃ āpattippaṭiggaho paṭiggaho nāma.

"Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. This monk, named so-and-so, remembers, reveals, uncovers, and declares an offense. If it seems right to the Sangha, I will accept the offense of the monk, named so-and-so." "When it seems right to the venerable ones, I will accept the offense of the monk, named so-and-so." He should then be asked, "Do you see it?" "Yes, I see it." "In the future, you should exercise restraint." Thus, the acceptance of an offense is called acceptance.

“Suṇantu me, āyasmantā āvāsikā, yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, idāni uposathaṃ kareyyāma, pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyyāma, āgame kāle pavāreyyāmā”ti, te ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhū bhaṇḍanakārakā kalahakārakā saṅghe adhikaraṇakārakā taṃ kālaṃ anuvaseyyuṃ, āvāsikena bhikkhunā byattena paṭibalena āvāsikā bhikkhū ñāpetabbā “suṇantu me, āyasmantā āvāsikā, yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, idāni uposathaṃ kareyyāma, pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyyāma, āgame juṇhe pavāreyyāmā”ti evaṃ katā pavāraṇā paccukkaḍḍhanā nāma.

"Listen to me, venerable resident monks. When it seems appropriate to you, let us now perform the Uposatha, recite the Pātimokkha, and hold the Pavāraṇā at the coming time." If, monks, those monks who are quarrelsome, makers of disputes, and creators of issues in the Sangha should continue to dwell for that time, then a resident monk who is competent and capable should inform the resident monks: "Listen to me, venerable resident monks. When it seems appropriate to you, let us now perform the Uposatha, recite the Pātimokkha, and hold the Pavāraṇā in the coming bright fortnight." The Pavāraṇā thus made is called a withdrawal.

Sabbeheva ekajjhaṃ sannipatitabbaṃ, sannipatitvā byattena bhikkhunā paṭibalena saṅgho ñāpetabbo “suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho, amhākaṃ bhaṇḍanajātānaṃ kalahajātānaṃ vivādāpannānaṃ viharataṃ bahu assāmaṇakaṃ ajjhāciṇṇaṃ bhāsitaparikkantaṃ. Sace mayaṃ imāhi āpattīhi aññamaññaṃ kāressāma, siyāpi taṃ adhikaraṇaṃ kakkhaḷattāya vāḷattāya bhedāya saṃvatteyya. Yadi saṅghassa pattakallaṃ, saṅgho imaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ tiṇavatthārakena vūpasameyya ṭhapetvā thullavajjaṃ, ṭhapetvā gihipaṭisaṃyutta”nti evaṃ tiṇavatthārakasamathe katā sabbapaṭhamā sabbasaṅgāhikañatti kammalakkhaṇaṃ nāma.

All should gather together in one place. Having gathered, the Sangha should be informed by a competent and capable bhikkhu: 'Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. While we were living having fallen into disputes, quarrels, and contentions, much unmonastic conduct has been habitually practiced, much improper speech has been uttered. If we were to make each other answerable for these offenses, this matter might lead to harshness, ferocity, and schism. If it is ready for the Sangha, may the Sangha settle this matter by covering it over with grass, excluding grave offenses, excluding those connected with laypeople.' Thus, the very first, all-inclusive motion made in the settlement by covering over with grass is called the characteristic of the act.

Ñattidutiyaṃ [M 2.0073] kammaṃ satta ṭhānāni gacchatīti katamāni satta ṭhānāni gacchati? Osāraṇaṃ[V 2.0067], nissāraṇaṃ, sammuti, dānaṃ, uddharaṇaṃ, desanaṃ, kammalakkhaṇaññeva sattamanti evaṃ vuttāni satta ṭhānāni gacchati. Tattha vaḍḍhassa licchavino pattanikkujjanavasena khandhake vuttā nissāraṇā, tasseva pataukkujjanavasena vuttā osāraṇā ca veditabbā.
