Sīmāsammuti ticīvarena avippavāsasammuti santhatasammuti bhattuddesakasenāsanaggāhāpakabhaṇḍāgārika- cīvarappaṭiggāhaka-cīvarabhājaka-yāgubhājaka-phalabhājaka-khajjabhājaka-appamattakavissajjaka- sāṭiyaggāhāpaka-pattaggāhāpaka-ārāmikapesaka-sāmaṇerapesakasammutīti etāsaṃ sammutīnaṃ vasena sammuti veditabbā. Kaṭhinacīvaradānamatakacīvaradānavasena dānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kaṭhinuddhāraṇavasena uddhāro veditabbo. Kuṭivatthuvihāravatthudesanāvasena desanā veditabbā. Yā pana tiṇavatthārakasamathe sabbasaṅgāhikañattiñca ekekasmiṃ pakkhe ekekaṃ ñattiñcāti tissopi ñattiyo ṭhapetvā puna ekasmiṃ pakkhe ekā, ekasmiṃ pakkhe ekāti dvepi ñattidutiyakammavācā vuttā. Tāsaṃ vasena kammalakkhaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

An act with a motion and one proclamation goes to seven instances. What are these seven instances it goes to? Reinstatement, expulsion, appointment, giving, removal, declaration, and the characteristic of the act itself as the seventh. Thus, these are the seven instances it goes to. Herein, the expulsion of the Licchavi Vaḍḍha by overturning the bowl, as stated in the Khandhaka, should be understood as expulsion; and the reinstatement by turning the bowl upright should be understood as reinstatement. Appointment should be understood by means of the appointment regarding boundaries, the appointment regarding non-separation from the three robes, the appointment regarding bedding, the appointment of the meal distributor, the appointment of the lodging assigner, the appointment of the storeroom keeper, the appointment of the robe receiver, the appointment of the robe distributor, the appointment of the gruel distributor, the appointment of the fruit distributor, the appointment of the sweetmeat distributor, the appointment of the distributor of minor requisites, the appointment of the robe-cloth receiver, the appointment of the bowl receiver, the appointment of the monastery attendant assigner, and the appointment of the novice assigner. Giving should be understood by means of the giving of the Kaṭhina robe and the giving of the robe for the deceased. Removal should be understood by means of the removal of the Kaṭhina. Declaration should be understood by means of the declaration of the hut site and the monastery site. As for the all-inclusive motion in the settlement by covering over with grass, and one motion in each faction—thus, excluding these three motions—again, one in one faction and one in the other faction—thus, two acts with a motion and one proclamation are stated. By means of these, the characteristic of the act should be understood.

Ñatticatutthakammaṃ satta ṭhānāni gacchatīti katamāni satta ṭhānāni gacchati? Osāraṇaṃ, nissāraṇaṃ, sammuti, dānaṃ, niggahaṃ, samanubhāsanaṃ, kammalakkhaṇaññeva sattamanti evaṃ vuttāni satta ṭhānāni gacchati. Tattha tajjanīyakammādīnaṃ sattannaṃ kammānaṃ vasena nissāraṇā, tesaṃyeva ca kammānaṃ paṭippassambhanavasena osāraṇā veditabbā. Bhikkhunovādakasammutivasena sammuti veditabbā. Parivāsadānamānattadānavasena dānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Mūlāyapaṭikassanakammavasena niggaho veditabbo. Ukkhittānuvattakā, aṭṭha yāvatatiyakā, ariṭṭho, caṇḍakāḷī ca imete yāvatatiyakāti imāsaṃ ekādasannaṃ samanubhāsanānaṃ vasena samanubhāsanā veditabbā. Upasampadakammaabbhānakammavasena kammalakkhaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

An act with a motion and three proclamations goes to seven instances. What are these seven instances it goes to? Reinstatement, expulsion, appointment, giving, censure, admonition, and the characteristic of the act itself as the seventh. Thus, these are the seven instances it goes to. Herein, expulsion should be understood by means of the seven acts beginning with the act of censure; and reinstatement should be understood by means of the revocation of those same acts. Appointment should be understood by means of the appointment of a bhikkhunī instructor. Giving should be understood by means of the giving of probation (parivāsa) and the giving of penance (mānatta). Censure should be understood by means of the act of sending back to the beginning. Admonition should be understood by means of these eleven admonitions: those who follow a suspended bhikkhu, the eight up to the third time, Ariṭṭha, and Caṇḍakāḷī—these are the ones up to the third time. The characteristic of the act should be understood by means of the act of higher ordination (upasampadā) and the act of rehabilitation (abbhāna).

Dhammasammukhatātiādīsu yena dhammena, yena vinayena, yena satthusāsanena saṅgho kammaṃ karoti, ayaṃ dhammasammukhatā, vinayasammukhatā, satthusāsanasammukhatā. Tattha dhammoti bhūtavatthu. Vinayoti codanā ceva sāraṇā ca. Satthusāsanaṃ nāma ñattisampadā ceva anusāvanasampadā ca. Yāvatikā bhikkhū kammappattā, te āgatā honti, chandārahānaṃ [M 2.0074] chando āhaṭo hoti, sammukhībhūtā nappaṭikkosanti, ayaṃ saṅghasammukhatā. Yassa saṅgho kammaṃ karoti, tassa sammukhībhāvo puggalasammukhatā. Sesamettha vuttanayattā uttānatthameva.

In 'the presence of the Dhamma' and so forth: that Dhamma, that Vinaya, that Teacher’s instruction by which the Sangha performs an act—this is the presence of the Dhamma, the presence of the Vinaya, the presence of the Teacher’s instruction. Herein, 'Dhamma' means the actual matter. 'Vinaya' means both accusation and reminding. 'Teacher’s instruction' means the accomplishment of the motion and the accomplishment of the proclamation. As many bhikkhus as are qualified for the act have come, the consent of those from whom consent is required has been brought, and those present do not object—this is the presence of the Sangha. The presence of the person for whom the Sangha performs the act is the presence of the individual. The rest here is plain in meaning, being explained in the aforementioned way.

Iti manorathapūraṇiyā aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus the Manorathapūraṇī, the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

Dukanipātavaṇṇanāya anuttānatthadīpanā samattā.

The explanation of profound meanings in the Commentary on the Book of Twos is complete.

. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Aṅguttaranikāye

In the Aṅguttara Nikāya

Tikanipāta-ṭīkā

The Subcommentary on the Book of the Threes

1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

1. The First Fifty

1. Bālavaggo

1. The Chapter on the Fool

1. Bhayasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on Fear

1. Tikanipātassa [M 2.0075][V 2.0069] paṭhame bhayanti bhīti cetaso byadhoti āha “cittutrāso”ti. Upaddavoti antarāyo. Tassa pana vikkhepakāraṇattā vuttaṃ “anekaggatākāro”ti. Upasaggoti upasajjanaṃ, devatopapīḷādinā appaṭikāravighātāpatti. Sā pana yasmā paṭikārābhāvena vihaññamānassa kiñci kātuṃ asamatthassa osīdanakāraṇaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “tattha tattha lagganākāro”ti. Yathāvutte divase anāgacchantesūti vañcetvā āgantuṃ niyamitadivase anāgacchantesu. Dvāre aggiṃ datvāti bahi anikkhamanatthāya dvāre aggiṃ datvā.

1. In the first [sutta] of the Tikanipāta, regarding ‘bhayanti’ (they fear), it is said: ‘Fear is the agitation of the mind,’ hence it is called ‘cittutrāso’ (mental terror). Upaddava means danger. And because it is a cause of distraction, it is stated as ‘the state of non-one-pointedness.’ Upasagga means affliction, an unavoidable obstruction due to oppression by deities, etc. And since it is a cause of dejection for one who is afflicted and unable to do anything due to the lack of remedy, it is therefore said to be ‘the state of clinging here and there.’ ‘Yathāvutte divase anāgacchantesu’ means those who, having deceived, do not come on the appointed day. ‘Dvāre aggiṃ datvā’ means setting fire to the door in order to prevent exit.

Naḷehi [V 2.0070] channapaṭicchannāti naḷehi tiṇacchadanasaṅkhepena upari chādetvā tehiyeva dārukuṭikaniyāmena paritopi chāditā. Eseva nayoti iminā tiṇehi channataṃ sesasambhārānaṃ rukkhamayatañca atidisati.

‘Thatched with reeds, covered with reeds’ means covered above with reeds in the manner of grass thatching, and also covered all around with them in the manner of a wooden hut. ‘Eseva nayo’ (This is the method) means that by this, it is further indicated that it was thatched with grass and that the remaining materials were made of wood.

Vidhavaputteti antabhāvopalakkhaṇaṃ. Te hi nippitikā avinītā asaṃyatā yaṃ kiñci kārino. Sesamettha uttānameva.

‘Widow’s son’ is a characteristic indicating an inferior state. For they are fatherless, undisciplined, unrestrained, doing whatever they please. The rest here is clear.

Bhayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Bhayasutta is finished.

2. Lakkhaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Lakkhaṇa Sutta

2. Dutiye lakkhīyati bālo ayanti ñāyati etenāti lakkhaṇaṃ, kammaṃ lakkhaṇametassāti kammalakkhaṇoti āha “kāyadvārādipavattaṃ kamma”ntiādi. Apadīyanti dosā etena rakkhīyanti, lūyanti chijjanti vāti apadānaṃ, sattānaṃ sammā, micchā vā pavattappayogo. Tena sobhatīti apadānasobhanī[M 2.0076]. Tenāha “paññā nāmā”tiādi. Attano caritenevāti attano cariyāya eva. Sesamettha uttānameva.

2. In the second [sutta], by this, ‘this is a fool’ is marked, is known—thus it is a characteristic (lakkhaṇaṃ). Action is his characteristic, thus he is ‘action-characteristic’ (kammalakkhaṇa), as it is said: ‘Action that occurs through the body-door, etc.’ By this, faults are warded off (apadīyanti), protected (rakkhīyanti), or cut off (lūyanti), destroyed (chijjanti)—thus it is called ‘apadāna.’ It is the application of conduct towards beings, whether right or wrong. By that, it shines (sobhatīti)—thus it is called apadānasobhanī. Hence it is said: ‘It is called wisdom (paññā),’ etc. ‘By one’s own conduct’ (attano cariteneva) means by one’s own behavior alone (attano cariyāya eva). The rest here is clear.

Lakkhaṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Lakkhaṇa Sutta is finished.

3-4. Cintīsuttādivaṇṇanā

3–4. Commentary on the Cintī Sutta and Others

3-4. Tatiye etehīti duccintitacintitādīhi. Etena lakkhaṇasaddassa saraṇatthatamāha. Tānevāti lakkhaṇāni eva. Assāti bālassa. Bālo ayanti nimīyati sañjānīyati etehīti bālanimittāni. Apadānaṃ vuccati, vikhyātaṃ kammaṃ, duccintitacintitādīni ca bāle vikhyātāni asādhāraṇabhāvena. Tasmā “bālassa apadānānī”ti. Abhijjhādīhi duṭṭhaṃ dūsitaṃ cintitaṃ duccintitaṃ, taṃ cintetīti duccintitacintī. Lobhādīhi duṭṭhaṃ bhāsitaṃ musāvādādiṃ bhāsatīti dubbhāsitabhāsī. Tesaṃyeva vasena kattabbato dukkaṭakammaṃ pāṇātipātādiṃ karotīti dukkaṭakammakārī. Tenāha “cintayanto”tiādi. Vuttānusārenāti “bālo aya”ntiādinā vuttassa atthavacanassa “paṇḍito ayanti etehi lakkhīyatī”tiādinā anussaraṇena. Manosucaritādīnaṃ vasenāti “cintayanto anabhijjhābyāpādasammādassanavasena [V 2.0071] sucintitameva cintetī”tiādinā manosucaritādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sucaritānaṃ vasena yojetabbāni. Catutthaṃ vuttanayattā uttānatthameva.

3-4. In the third sutta, ‘by these’ refers to ill-conceived thoughts and so forth. By this, it states that the word ‘characteristic’ has the meaning of that by which one recognizes. ‘Those very ones’ means the characteristics themselves. ‘Of the fool’ refers to the fool. ‘This is a fool’ is inferred, is understood by these—thus, the signs of a fool. Apadāna is said to be a renowned deed, a notorious action; and ill-conceived thoughts and so forth are notorious in a fool due to their particular nature. Therefore, it says ‘the apadānas of a fool.’ ‘Ill-conceived’ (duccintitaṃ) is a thought corrupted and defiled by covetousness and so forth. One who thinks that is an ‘ill-thinker’ (duccintitacintī). Speech corrupted by greed and so forth, such as false speech—one who speaks that is a ‘wrong speaker’ (dubbhāsitabhāsī). Because of those very things, one who does wrong actions (dukkaṭakammaṃ) like killing living beings and so forth, is a ‘wrongdoer’ (dukkaṭakammakārī). Hence it is said, ‘thinking,’ and so forth. ‘According to what has been said’ (vuttānusārena) means by recollecting the meaning stated by ‘this is a fool,’ and so forth, and by ‘the wise one is marked by these,’ and so forth. ‘According to the good conduct of mind, and so forth’ (manosucaritādīnaṃ vasena) means it should be connected according to the three kinds of good conduct—of mind, and so forth—as stated by ‘thinking, one thinks only well with non-covetousness, non-ill-will, and right view,’ and so forth. The fourth sutta is easily understood, because of the method stated before.

Cintīsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Cintī Sutta and others is concluded.

5-10. Ayonisosuttādivaṇṇanā

5-10. Commentary on the Ayoniso Sutta and others

5-10. Pañcame kati nu kho anussatiṭṭhānānītiādi chakke āvi bhavissatīti. Evaṃ cintitanti ayoniso cintitaṃ. Apañhameva pañhanti kathesīti apañhameva pañho ayanti maññamāno vissajjesi. Dasavidhaṃ byañjanabuddhiṃ aparihāpetvāti –

5-10. In the fifth sutta, the passage beginning ‘how many objects of recollection are there?’ will become clear in the sixth sutta. ‘Thus he thought’ means he thought unwisely. ‘He spoke of a non-question as a question’ means he answered, considering what was not a question to be a question. ‘Without abandoning the tenfold verbal proficiency’ means:

“Sithilaṃ [M 2.0077] dhanitañca dīgharassaṃ, garukaṃ lahukañca niggahītaṃ;

Sambandhaṃ vavatthitaṃ vimuttaṃ, dasadhā byañjanabuddhiyā pabhedo”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.190; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.291; pari. aṭṭha. 485; vi. saṅga. aṭṭha. 252) –

“Lax and tense, long and short, heavy and light, and nasalized; connected, separated, and released—these are the tenfold distinctions in the understanding of consonants.”

Evaṃ vuttaṃ dasavidhaṃ byañjanabuddhiṃ aparihāpetvā.

Thus, without neglecting the tenfold understanding of consonants as stated.

Tattha ṭhānakaraṇāni sithilāni katvā uccāretabbaṃ akkharaṃ sithilaṃ, tāniyeva dhanitāni asithilāni katvā uccāretabbaṃ akkharaṃ dhanitaṃ. Dvimattakālaṃ dīghaṃ, ekamattakālaṃ rassaṃ. Garukanti dīghameva, yaṃ vā “āyasmato buddharakkhitattherassā”ti saṃyogaparaṃ katvā vuccati, lahukanti rassameva, yaṃ vā “āyasmato buddharakkhitatherassā”ti evaṃ visaṃyogaparaṃ katvā vuccati. Niggahītanti yaṃ karaṇāni niggahetvā avissajjetvā avivaṭena mukhena sānunāsikaṃ katvā vattabbaṃ. Sambandhanti yaṃ parapadena sambandhitvā “tuṇhassā”ti vuccati. Vavatthitanti yaṃ parapadena asambandhaṃ katvā vicchinditvā “tuṇhī assā”ti vuccati. Vimuttanti yaṃ karaṇāni aniggahetvā vissajjetvā vivaṭena mukhena sānunāsikaṃ akatvā vuccati. Dasadhā byañjanabuddhiyā pabhedoti evaṃ sithilādivasena byañjanabuddhiyā akkharuppādakacittassa dasappakārena pabhedo. Sabbāni hi akkharāni cittasamuṭṭhānāni yathādhippetatthabyañjanato byañjanāni ca.

Herein, a letter that should be pronounced by making the articulatory organs lax is ‘lax’; a letter that should be pronounced by making those same organs tense and not lax is ‘tense.’ A long vowel has a duration of two mātrās, and a short vowel has a duration of one mātrā. ‘Heavy’ (garukaṃ) refers to what is long, or what is uttered with a conjunct consonant following, such as in ‘āyasmato buddharakkhitattherassā.’ ‘Light’ (lahukaṃ) refers to what is short, or what is uttered with a single consonant following, such as in ‘āyasmato buddharakkhitatherassā.’ ‘Nasalized’ (niggahītaṃ) refers to what should be uttered by restraining the articulatory organs, without releasing them, with a closed mouth, and making it nasal. ‘Connected’ (sambandhaṃ) refers to what is connected with the following word and is uttered as ‘tuṇhassā.’ ‘Separated’ (vavatthitaṃ) refers to what is made unconnected with the following word and is uttered having separated it, as ‘tuṇhī assā.’ ‘Released’ (vimuttaṃ) refers to what is uttered by not restraining the articulatory organs, releasing them, with an open mouth, and without making it nasal. ‘Tenfold distinctions in the understanding of consonants’ means that there is a tenfold distinction of the understanding of consonants—the mind that produces the letters—based on laxness and so forth. Indeed, all letters arise from the mind, and they are consonants because they express the intended meaning.

“Aṭṭhānaṃ [V 2.0072] kho etaṃ, āvuso sāriputtā”tiādi pañcake āvi bhavissati. “Kati nu kho, ānanda, anussatiṭṭhānānī”tiādi pana chakke āvi bhavissati. Chaṭṭhādīsu natthi vattabbaṃ.

The passage beginning ‘It is impossible, friend Sāriputta,’ will become clear in the group of five suttas. The passage beginning ‘How many, Ānanda, are the bases of recollection?’ will become clear in the group of six suttas. There is nothing further to say about the sixth group and those following.

Ayonisosuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ayoniso Sutta and others is concluded.

Bālavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter of the Fool is concluded.

2. Rathakāravaggo

2. The Chapter on the Chariot-Maker

1. Ñātasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Ñāta Sutta

11. Dutiyassa paṭhame ñātoyeva paññātoti āha “ñāto paññāto”ti. Kassa ananulomiketi āha “sāsanassā”ti, sāsanassa ananulomike appatirūpeti attho. Idāni ananulomikasaddassa nibbacanaṃ dassento “na anulometīti ananulomika”nti āha[M 2.0078]. Sāsanassāti vā sāsananti attho. Sāsanaṃ na anulometīti ananulomikanti evamettha sambandho daṭṭhabbo. Sabhāgavisabhāganti liṅgato sabhāgavisabhāgaṃ. “Viyapuggale”ti āhāti liṅgasabhāgehi avisesetvā āha. Ummādaṃ pāpuṇīti so kira sīlaṃ adhiṭṭhāya pihitadvāragabbhe sayanapiṭṭhe nisīditvā bhariyaṃ ārabbha mettaṃ bhāvento mettāmukhena uppannena rāgena andhīkato bhariyāya santikaṃ gantukāmo dvāraṃ asallakkhetvā bhittiṃ bhinditvāpi nikkhamitukāmatāya bhittiṃ paharanto sabbarattiṃ bhittiyuddhamakāsi. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

11. In the second sutta, regarding the first word, he said, 'it is known and understood,' meaning 'ñāto paññāto.' To what is it uncongenial? He said, 'to the Teaching,' meaning it is uncongenial and unbefitting to the Teaching. Now, showing the derivation of the word 'uncongenial,' he said, 'because it does not accord, it is uncongenial.' Or, 'to the Teaching' means 'the Teaching.' It does not accord with the Teaching, hence it is uncongenial—thus the connection here should be seen. 'Similar and dissimilar' refers to similarity and dissimilarity in gender. He said 'regarding individuals' without differentiating by gender similarity. He reached madness: it is said that he, having undertaken the precepts, sat on a couch in a chamber with a closed door and, directing loving-kindness towards his wife, was blinded by lust that arose through the opening of loving-kindness. Desiring to go to his wife, without noticing the door, and wanting to exit even by breaking through the wall, he struck the wall and fought with it all night. The rest here is easily understood.

Ñātasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ñāta Sutta is concluded.

2. Sāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Sāraṇīya Sutta

12. Dutiye catupārisuddhisīlampi pabbajjānissitamevāti iminā pabbajjūpagatasamanantarameva catupārisuddhisīlampi samādinnameva hotīti dasseti. Maggasannissitāneva hontīti [V 2.0073] maggādhigamatthāya paṭipajjitabbattā kasiṇaparikammādīni maggasannissitāneva honti, tasmā maggaggahaṇeneva tesampi gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, tehi vinā maggādhigamassa asambhavatoti adhippāyo.

12. In the second sutta, the fourfold purification of virtue is also dependent on the going forth—this shows that immediately upon going forth, the fourfold purification of virtue is also undertaken. 'They are dependent on the path alone'—because they must be practiced for the attainment of the path, preliminary practices such as the kasiṇa exercises are also dependent on the path alone. Therefore, by grasping the path alone, their inclusion should be understood, for without them, the attainment of the path is impossible—this is the intended meaning.

Aggamaggādhigamena asammohappaṭivedhassa sikhāpattattā maggadhammesu viya phaladhammesupi sātisayo asammohoti “sayaṃ abhiññā”ti vuttaṃ, sāmaṃ jānitvāti attho. Tathā jānanā panassa sacchikaraṇaṃ attapaccakkhakiriyāti “sacchikatvā”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “attanāva abhivisiṭṭhāya paññāya paccakkhaṃ katvā”ti. Tathā sacchikiriyā cassa attani paṭilābhoti “upasampajjā”ti vuttanti āha “paṭilabhitvā”ti.

Because the attainment of the highest path is the pinnacle of the penetration of non-delusion, just as in the path-states, so too in the fruit-states, non-delusion is supreme—thus it is said, 'by direct knowledge,' meaning knowing by oneself. Moreover, that knowing is realization, the act of personal verification—thus it is said, 'having realized.' Therefore, he says, 'having personally verified with distinguished wisdom.' And that realization is an attainment in oneself; thus, of the phrase 'having entered upon and abided in,' he says it means 'having attained.'

Sāraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sāraṇīya Sutta is concluded.

3. Āsaṃsasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Āsaṃsa Sutta

13. Tatiye santoti ettha santa-saddo “dīghaṃ santassa yojana”ntiādīsu (dha. pa. 60) kilantabhāve āgato. “Ayañca vitakko, ayañca vicāro [M 2.0079] santo honti samitā”tiādīsu (vibha. 576) niruddhabhāve. “Adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo, gambhīro duddaso duranubodho santo paṇīto”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.67; ma. ni. 1.281; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7-8) santañāṇagocaratāyaṃ. “Upasantassa sadā satimato”tiādīsu (udā. 27) kilesavūpasame. “Santo have sabbhi pavedayantī”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 151) sādhūsu. “Pañcime, bhikkhave, mahācorā santo saṃvijjamānā”tiādīsu (pārā. 195) atthibhāve. Idhāpi atthibhāveyevāti āha “santoti atthi upalabbhantī”ti. Tattha atthīti lokasaṅketavasena saṃvijjanti. Atthibhāvo hettha puggalasambandhena vuttattā lokasamaññāvaseneva veditabbo, na paramatthavasena. Atthīti cetaṃ nipātapadaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.110) viya.

13. In the third sutta, the word 'santa' is used in the sense of weariness, as in 'long is the league for the weary' (Dhp. 60). In phrases like 'this thought and this reflection are calmed and quieted' (Vibh. 576), it denotes cessation. In passages such as 'This Dhamma I have attained is profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, excellent' (DN 2.67; MN 1.281; SN 1.172; Mahāva. 7-8), it refers to being the domain of peaceful knowledge. In 'for one who is always mindful and tranquil' (Ud. 27), it signifies the pacification of defilements. In 'the good indeed proclaim' (Dhp. 151), it pertains to the good. In 'Monks, these five great thieves exist, are found' (Pārā. 195), it indicates existence. Here too, it is used in the sense of existence, as stated: 'santa means "they exist, they are found."' In this context, 'they exist' means they are found according to worldly convention. Since existence here is spoken of in relation to individuals, it should be understood according to worldly convention alone, not according to ultimate truth. And this word 'atthi' should be seen as an indeclinable particle, as in 'there are hairs in this body' (MN 1.110).

Saṃvijjamānāti upalabbhamānā. Yañhi saṃvijjati, taṃ upalabbhati. Tenāha “saṃvijjamānāti tasseva vevacana”nti. Anāsoti patthanārahito. Tenāha “apatthano”ti. Āsaṃsati patthetīti āsaṃso. Veṇuvettādivilīvehi suppādibhājanakārakā vilīvakārakā. Migamacchādīnaṃ nisādanato nesādā, māgavikamacchabandhādayo. Rathesu cammena nahanakaraṇato rathakārā[V 2.0074], dhammakārā. Puiti karīsassa nāmaṃ, taṃ kusenti apanentīti pukkusā, pupphacchaḍḍakā.

'Saṃvijjamānā' means 'being found.' For what exists is found. Therefore, it is said: 'saṃvijjamānā is a synonym for that.' 'Anāso' means 'without aspiration.' Therefore, it is said: 'apatthano' (without desire). 'Āsaṃso' is one who craves or desires. 'Vilīvakārakā' are those who make containers like winnowing baskets from bamboo and cane splints. 'Nesādā' are hunters, so called from their trapping of deer, fish, and so on; they are hunters, fishermen, and the like. 'Rathakārā' are chariot-makers, so called because they bind chariots with leather; they are also called 'dhammakārā' (leather-workers). 'Puti' is a name for excrement; those who remove it ('kusenti') are 'pukkusā,' also called 'pupphacchaḍḍakā' (refuse-collectors).

Dubbaṇṇoti virūpo. Okoṭimakoti ārohābhāvena heṭṭhimako, rassakāyoti attho. Tenāha “lakuṇḍako”ti. Laku viya ghaṭikā viya ḍeti pavattatīti hi lakuṇḍako, rasso. Kaṇati nimīlatīti kāṇo. Taṃ panassa nimīlanaṃ ekena akkhinā dvīhipi cāti āha “ekakkhikāṇo vā ubhayakkhikāṇo vā”ti. Kuṇanaṃ kuṇo, hatthavekallaṃ. Taṃ etassa atthīti kuṇī. Khañjo vuccati pādavikalo. Heṭṭhimakāyasaṅkhāto sarīrassa pakkho padeso hato assāti pakkhahato. Tenāha “pīṭhasappī”ti. Padīpe padīpane etabbaṃ netabbanti padīpeyyaṃ, telādiupakaraṇaṃ.

'Dubbaṇṇa' means ugly. 'Okoṭimako' means one who is short due to a lack of height; the meaning is 'one with a short body.' Therefore, it is said: 'lakuṇḍako' (a dwarf). A 'lakuṇḍako' is so called because one moves or proceeds (ḍeti) like a 'laku' or a small pot; it means short. 'Kāṇo' is one who squints or closes the eyes. This closing of the eyes may occur in one eye or both, hence it is said: 'one-eyed or blind in both eyes.' 'Kuṇanaṃ' is 'kuṇo,' a defect of the hand. One who has this is called 'kuṇī.' 'Khañjo' refers to one who is defective in the foot. 'Pakkhahato' means one whose side, a region of the lower body, is afflicted. Therefore, it is said: 'pīṭhasappī' (one who crawls on a stool). 'Padīpeyyaṃ' refers to what should be brought or led for lighting a lamp, i.e., the requisites for lighting, such as oil.

Āsaṃ na karotīti rajjābhiseke kaniṭṭho patthanaṃ na karoti jeṭṭhe sati kaniṭṭhassa anadhikārattā. Abhisekaṃ arahatīti abhisekāraho, na abhisekāraho kāṇakuṇiādidosasamannāgato.

'Āsaṃ na karoti' means one who does not have an aspiration; the younger brother does not aspire to royal consecration when the elder is present, due to the younger's lack of entitlement. 'Abhisekāraho' means one worthy of consecration; one who possesses defects such as being one-eyed or crippled in the hand is not worthy of consecration.

Sīlassa [M 2.0080] duṭṭhu nāma natthi, tasmā abhāvattho idha du-saddoti āha “nissīlo”ti. “Pāpaṃ pāpena sukara”ntiādīsu (udā. 48; cūḷava. 343) viya pāpa-saddo nihīnapariyāyoti āha “lāmakadhammo”ti. Sīlavipattiyā vā dussīlo. Diṭṭhivipattiyā pāpadhammo. Kāyavācāsaṃvarabhedena vā dussīlo, manosaṃvarabhedena, satisaṃvarādibhedena vā pāpadhammo. Asuddhappayogatāya dussīlo, asuddhāsayatāya pāpadhammo. Kusalasīlavirahena dussīlo, akusalasīlasamannāgamena pāpadhammo. Asucīhīti aparisuddhehi. Saṅkāhi saritabbasamācāroti “imassa maññe idaṃ kamma”nti evaṃ parehi saṅkāya saritabbasamācāro. Tenāha “kiñcidevā”tiādi. Attanāyeva vā saṅkāhi saritabbasamācāroti etenapi kammasādhanataṃyeva saṅkassarasaddassa dasseti. Attano saṅkāya paresaṃ samācārakiriyaṃ sarati āsaṅkati vidhāvatītipi saṅkassarasamācāroti evamettha kattusādhanatāpi daṭṭhabbā. Tassa hi dve tayo jane kathente disvā “mama dosaṃ maññe kathentī”ti tesaṃ samācāraṃ saṅkāya sarati dhāvati.

There is no such thing as 'bad virtue,' therefore the prefix 'du-' here has the sense of absence, hence it says 'nissīlo' (without virtue). As in such passages as 'Evil is easily done by the evil' (Ud. 48; Cūḷava. 343), the word 'pāpa' (evil) is a synonym for 'inferior,' hence it says 'lāmakadhammo' (of base qualities). One is 'dussīlo' (of bad virtue) due to a failure in virtue; one is 'pāpadhammo' (of evil qualities) due to a failure in view. Or, one is 'dussīlo' due to a breach of bodily and verbal restraint; one is 'pāpadhammo' due to a breach of mental restraint, or a breach of restraint in mindfulness and so on. One is 'dussīlo' due to impure application; one is 'pāpadhammo' due to impure inclination. One is 'dussīlo' due to the absence of wholesome virtue; one is 'pāpadhammo' due to the possession of unwholesome virtue. 'Asucīhi' (by the impure) means by the unpurified. 'Saṅkāhi saritabbasamācāro' means one whose conduct is to be recalled with suspicion by others, who think, 'I suppose this is his deed.' Hence it says 'whatever,' etc. Alternatively, 'one whose conduct is to be recalled with suspicion by oneself' also shows that the word 'saṅkassara' is formed with a passive sense. The active sense should also be understood here, as in 'saṅkassarasamācāro,' meaning one who, out of suspicion of himself, recalls, suspects, or runs after the conduct of others. For when he sees two or three people talking, he recalls or runs after their conduct with the suspicion, 'I suppose they are talking about my fault.'

Evaṃpaṭiññoti salākaggahaṇādīsu “kittakā vihāre samaṇā”ti gaṇanāya āraddhāya “ahampi samaṇo, ahampi samaṇo”ti paṭiññaṃ datvā salākaggahaṇādīni karotīti samaṇo ahanti [V 2.0075] evaṃsamaṇappaṭiñño. Sumbhakapattadhareti mattikāpattadhare. Pūtinā kammenāti saṃkiliṭṭhakammena, nigguṇatāya vā guṇasāravirahitattā antopūti. Kasambukacavaro jāto sañjāto assāti kasambujātoti āha “sañjātarāgādikacavaro”ti. Atha vā kasambu vuccati tintakuṇapakasaṭaṃ udakaṃ, imasmiñca sāsane dussīlo nāma jigucchanīyattā tintakuṇapaudakasadiso, tasmā kasambu viya jātoti kasambujāto. Lokuttaradhammaupanissayassa natthitāyāti yattha patiṭṭhitena sakkā bhaveyya arahattaṃ laddhuṃ, tassā patiṭṭhāya bhinnattā vuttaṃ. Mahāsīlasmiṃ paripūrakāritāyāti yattha patiṭṭhitena sakkā bhaveyya arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ, tasmiṃ paripūrakāritāya.

'Evaṃpaṭiñño' (one who acknowledges thus): in matters like the taking of voting tickets, when the count has begun with the question, 'How many monks are in the monastery?', he gives the acknowledgement, 'I too am a monk, I too am a monk,' and then performs the act of taking a ticket, etc. Thus he is one who acknowledges, 'I am a monk.' 'Sumbhakapattadhare' means one who bears a clay bowl. 'Pūtinā kammena' (with a foul deed) means with a defiled deed; or, due to being without virtue, or devoid of the essence of virtue, one is inwardly rotten. 'Kasambujāto' (born of scum) means one in whom the refuse of lust and so on has arisen, hence it says 'sañjātarāgādikacavaro' (one in whom the refuse of lust, etc., has arisen). Alternatively, 'kasambu' refers to putrid, stagnant water, and in this Dispensation, an immoral person is like putrid, stagnant water because he is disgusting; therefore, he is 'kasambujāto,' born as if from scum. 'Lokuttaradhammaupanissayassa natthitāya' (because there is no basis for supramundane states): this is said because the foundation upon which one could be established to attain arahantship has been broken. 'Mahāsīlasmiṃ paripūrakāritāya' (because of being a fulfiller of the great virtue): because of being a fulfiller of that upon which one could be established to attain arahantship.

Āsaṃsasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Āsaṃsa Sutta is concluded.

4. Cakkavattisuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Cakkavatti Sutta

14. Catutthe [M 2.0081] catūhi saṅgahavatthūhīti dānapiyavacanaatthacariyāsamānattatāsaṅkhātehi catūhi saṅgahakāraṇehi. Cakkaṃ vattetīti āṇācakkaṃ pavatteti. Cakkanti vā idha ratanacakkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayañhi cakkasaddo sampattiyaṃ, lakkhaṇe, rathaṅge, iriyāpathe, dāne, ratanadhammakhuracakkādīsu ca dissati. “Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, cakkāni, yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussāna”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.31) hi sampattiyaṃ dissati. “Pādatalesu cakkāni jātānī”ti (dī. ni. 2.35; 3.204) ettha lakkhaṇe. “Cakkaṃva vahato pada”nti (dha. pa. 1) ettha rathaṅge. “Catucakkaṃ navadvāra”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.29) ettha iriyāpathe. “Dadaṃ bhuñja mā ca pamādo, cakkaṃ vattaya sabbapāṇina”nti (jā. 1.7.149) ettha dāne. “Dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosī”ti (dī. ni. 2.243) ettha ratanacakke. “Mayā pavattitaṃ cakka”nti (su. ni. 562) ettha dhammacakke. “Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake”ti (jā. 1.5.103) ettha khuracakke. “Khurapariyantena cakkenā”ti (dī. ni. 1.166) ettha paharaṇacakke. “Asanivicakka”nti (dī. ni. 3.61) ettha asanimaṇḍale. Idha panāyaṃ ratanacakke daṭṭhabbo.

14. In the fourth sutta, 'catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi' means by the four bases of sympathy, which are the four causes of sympathy designated as giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. 'Cakkaṃ vatteti' (he turns the wheel) means he sets in motion the wheel of command. Or, 'cakka' here should be understood as the wheel-treasure. Indeed, this word 'cakka' is seen in the sense of accomplishment, a mark, a chariot-wheel, a posture, giving, the wheel-treasure, the Dhamma-wheel, the razor-wheel, and so on. For instance, in 'These four wheels, monks, possessed of which gods and humans...' (AN 4.31), it is seen in the sense of accomplishment. In 'Wheels appeared on the soles of his feet' (DN 2.35; 3.204), it is in the sense of a mark. In 'like the wheel following the foot of the ox' (Dhp. 1), it is in the sense of a chariot-wheel. In 'four-wheeled, nine-doored' (SN 1.29), it is in the sense of a posture. In 'Give, enjoy, and be not heedless; turn the wheel for all beings' (Jā. 1.7.149), it is in the sense of giving. In 'the divine wheel-treasure appeared' (DN 2.243), it is in the sense of the wheel-treasure. In 'the wheel set in motion by me' (SNip. 562), it is in the sense of the Dhamma-wheel. In 'a wheel spins on the head of a man smitten by desire' (Jā. 1.5.103), it is in the sense of a razor-wheel. In 'with a wheel having a razor edge' (DN 1.166), it is in the sense of a weapon-wheel. In 'asanivicakka' (DN 3.61), it is in the sense of a thunderbolt-disc. Here, however, it should be understood as the wheel-treasure.

Kittāvatā panāyaṃ cakkavattī nāma hoti? Ekaṅguladvaṅgulamattampi cakkaratanaṃ ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā pavattati. Sabbacakkavattīnañhi nisinnāsanato uṭṭhahitvā cakkaratanasamīpaṃ gantvā hatthisoṇḍasadisapanāḷiṃ suvaṇṇabhiṅgāraṃ ukkhipitvā udakena abbhukkiritvā “abhivijinātu [V 2.0076] bhavaṃ cakkaratana”nti vacanasamanantarameva vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā cakkaratanaṃ pavattatīti. Yassa pavattisamakālameva, so rājā cakkavattī nāma hoti.

And to what extent is one called a wheel-turning monarch? The wheel-treasure rises up into the sky even by a finger's breadth or two fingers' breadth and proceeds onwards. For all wheel-turning monarchs, having risen from their seat and approached the wheel-treasure, lift up a golden pitcher with a spout like an elephant's trunk, sprinkle water with it, and say, "May the venerable wheel-treasure conquer." Immediately after these words, the wheel-treasure rises into the sky and proceeds onwards. At the very moment it begins to proceed, that king is called a wheel-turning monarch.

Dhammoti dasakusalakammapathadhammo, dasavidhaṃ vā cakkavattivattaṃ. Dasavidhe vā kusaladhamme agarahite vā rājadhamme niyuttoti dhammiko. Tena ca dhammena sakalalokaṃ rañjetīti dhammarājā. Dhammena vā laddharajjattā dhammarājā. Cakkavattīhi dhammena ñāyena rajjaṃ adhigacchati, na adhammena. Dasavidhena cakkavattivattenāti dasappabhedena cakkavattīnaṃ vattena.

The Dhamma is the ten paths of wholesome action, or the tenfold duty of a wheel-turning monarch. One who is devoted to the ten kinds of wholesome qualities or the unblamed royal virtues is righteous. Because he delights the whole world by that Dhamma, he is a righteous king. Or, because he has obtained kingship through Dhamma, he is a righteous king. Wheel-turning monarchs attain kingship through Dhamma and justice, not through unrighteousness. By 'the tenfold duty of a wheel-turning monarch' is meant the ten kinds of duties of wheel-turning monarchs.

Kiṃ [M 2.0082] pana taṃ dasavidhaṃ cakkavattivattanti? Vuccate –

But what is that tenfold duty of a wheel-turning monarch? It is said:

“Katamaṃ pana taṃ, deva, ariyaṃ cakkavattivattanti? Tena hi tvaṃ, tāta, dhammaṃyeva nissāya dhammaṃ sakkaronto dhammaṃ garuṃ karonto dhammaṃ mānento dhammaṃ pūjento dhammaṃ apacāyamāno dhammaddhajo dhammaketu dhammādhipateyyo dhammikaṃ rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ saṃvidahassu antojanasmiṃ balakāyasmiṃ khattiyesu anuyantesu brāhmaṇagahapatikesu negamajānapadesu samaṇabrāhmaṇesu migapakkhīsu. Mā ca te, tāta, vijite adhammakāro pavattittha. Ye ca te, tāta, vijite adhanā assu, tesañca dhanamanuppadeyyāsi. Ye ca te, tāta, vijite samaṇabrāhmaṇā madappamādā paṭiviratā khantisoracce niviṭṭhā ekamattānaṃ damenti, ekamattānaṃ samenti, ekamattānaṃ parinibbāpenti. Te kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paripuccheyyāsi pariggaṇheyyāsi – ‘kiṃ, bhante, kusalaṃ kiṃ akusalaṃ, kiṃ sāvajjaṃ kiṃ anavajjaṃ, kiṃ sevitabbaṃ kiṃ na sevitabbaṃ, kiṃ me kariyamānaṃ dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya assa, kiṃ vā pana me kariyamānaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya assā’ti. Tesaṃ sutvā yaṃ akusalaṃ, taṃ abhinivajjeyyāsi, yaṃ kusalaṃ, taṃ samādāya vatteyyāsi. Idaṃ kho, tāta, taṃ ariyaṃ cakkavattivatta”nti –

"But what, Your Majesty, is that noble duty of a wheel-turning monarch?" "It is this, dear one: you should rely on the Dhamma, respect the Dhamma, revere the Dhamma, esteem the Dhamma, venerate the Dhamma, and pay homage to the Dhamma. With the Dhamma as your banner, the Dhamma as your standard, the Dhamma as your sovereign, establish righteous protection, shelter, and security for your household, your troops, the nobles, the vassals, the brahmins and householders, the town and country people, the ascetics and brahmins, and even the beasts and birds. Let no unrighteousness prevail in your realm, dear one. And to those in your realm who are without wealth, provide them with wealth. And those ascetics and brahmins in your realm who are rid of intoxication and negligence, who are established in patience and gentleness, who train themselves, calm themselves, and attain final extinguishment—approach them from time to time, question them, and consult them: ‘Venerable sirs, what is skillful and what is unskillful? What is blameworthy and what is blameless? What should be practiced and what should not? What actions, when performed by me, will lead to my harm and suffering for a long time? And what actions, when performed by me, will lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time?’ Having heard them, you should avoid what is unskillful and undertake and practice what is skillful. This, dear one, is the noble duty of a wheel-turning monarch."

Evaṃ cakkavattisutte (dī. ni. 3.84) āgatanayena antojanasmiṃ balakāye ekaṃ, khattiyesu ekaṃ, anuyantesu ekaṃ, brāhmaṇagahapatikesu ekaṃ, negamajānapadesu ekaṃ, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu ekaṃ, migapakkhīsu ekaṃ, adhammakārappaṭikkhepo ekaṃ, adhanānaṃ dhanānuppadānaṃ ekaṃ, samaṇabrāhmaṇe upasaṅkamitvā pañhapucchanaṃ ekanti evamevaṃ taṃ cakkavattivattaṃ dasavidhaṃ hoti. Gahapatike pana pakkhijāte ca visuṃ katvā gaṇhantassa dvādasavidhaṃ hoti.

Thus, in the Cakkavattisutta (Dī. Ni. 3.84), according to the method described, the duty of a wheel-turning monarch is tenfold: one regarding the inner circle and the armed forces; one regarding the nobles; one regarding the vassals; one regarding brahmins and householders; one regarding town and country dwellers; one regarding ascetics and brahmins; one regarding beasts and birds; one regarding the prevention of unrighteous behavior; one regarding providing wealth to the destitute; and one regarding approaching ascetics and brahmins to ask questions. However, for one who counts householders and birds separately, it becomes twelvefold.

Aññathā [V 2.0077] vattituṃ adento so dhammo adhiṭṭhānaṃ etassāti tadadhiṭṭhānaṃ. Tena tadadhiṭṭhānena cetasā. Sakkarontoti ādarakiriyāvasena karonto. Tenāha “yathā”tiādi. Garuṃ karontoti pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garukaraṇavasena garuṃ karonto. Tenevāha [M 2.0083] “tasmiṃ gāravuppattiyā”ti. Dhammādhipatibhūtāgatabhāvenāti iminā yathāvuttadhammassa jeṭṭhakabhāvena purimataraṃ attabhāvesu sakkaccaṃ samupacitabhāvaṃ dasseti. Dhammavaseneva ca sabbakiriyānaṃ karaṇenāti etena ṭhānanisajjādīsu yathāvuttadhammaninnapoṇapabbhārabhāvaṃ dasseti. Assāti rakkhāvaraṇaguttiyā. Paraṃ rakkhantoti aññaṃ diṭṭhadhammikādianatthato rakkhanto. Teneva pararakkhasādhanena khantiādiguṇena attānaṃ tato eva rakkhati. Mettacittatāti mettacittatāya. Nivāsanapārupanagehādīni sītuṇhādippaṭibāhanena āvaraṇaṃ.

That Dhamma, not allowing it to be otherwise, is its foundation—thus, it is called 'tadadhiṭṭhāna' (that foundation). With that foundation in mind, one honors it—acting by way of reverence. Hence it is said, "as follows." Respecting it—respecting it in the manner of holding a stone parasol—thus, one respects it. Therefore, it is said, "due to the arising of respect for it." By having the Dhamma as the chief support in past and future existences—this indicates that the Dhamma mentioned earlier has been carefully accumulated in previous existences due to its preeminence. And because all actions are performed solely through the Dhamma—this shows the inclination and leaning towards that Dhamma in matters of standing, sitting, etc., as previously described. The word 'assāti' (it should be) refers to protection, shelter, and security. "Protecting others"—guarding others from harm, such as visible, present losses, and other disadvantages. By that very means of protecting others—through qualities like patience and so on—one protects oneself from that very thing. Mettacittatā means the state of having a mind of loving-kindness. Dwellings, garments, houses, and so forth, are a shelter for warding off cold, heat, and the like.

Antojanasminti abbhantarabhūte puttadārādijane. Sīlasaṃvare patiṭṭhāpentoti iminā rakkhaṃ dasseti. Vatthagandhamālādīni cassa dadamānoti iminā āvaraṇaṃ, itarena guttiṃ. Sampadānenapīti pi-saddena sīlasaṃvaresu patiṭṭhāpanādīnaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Esa nayo paresupi pi-saddaggahaṇe. Nigamo nivāso etesanti negamā. Evaṃ jānapadāti āha “tathā nigamavāsino”tiādinā.

`Antojanasmiṃ` means among the people of the inner circle, such as children and wives. By establishing them in moral restraint, he shows protection. By giving them clothing, perfumes, garlands, and so forth, he provides shelter, and by other means, security. The particle 'pi' in 'sampadānenapi' (also by giving) includes establishing in moral restraint and the like. This is the method for understanding the particle 'pi' in other instances as well. `Negamā` are those for whom a market town (`nigama`) is their dwelling. Similarly for `jānapadā` (country-dwellers); hence it is said, 'so too, town-dwellers,' and so forth.

Rakkhāvaraṇaguttiyā kāyakammādīsu saṃvidahanaṃ ṭhapanaṃ nāma tadupadesoyevāti vuttaṃ “kathetvā”ti. Etesūti pāḷiyaṃ vuttesu samaṇādīsu. Paṭivattetuṃ na sakkā khīṇānaṃ kilesānaṃ puna anuppajjanato. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

The establishing (saṃvidahanaṃ) or setting up (ṭhapanaṃ) of protection, shelter, and security in bodily actions and so forth, is simply that instruction, as stated by 'having spoken'. ‘Among these’ means among the ascetics and others mentioned in the Pāli text. It is impossible to turn back to defilements because the defilements, once destroyed, do not arise again. The rest here is easily understood.

Cakkavattisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Cakkavatti Sutta is completed.

5. Sacetanasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Sañcetanā Sutta

15. Pañcame isayo patanti sannipatanti etthāti isipatananti āha “buddhapaccekabuddhasaṅkhātāna”ntiādi. Sabbūpakaraṇāni sajjetvāti sabbāni rukkhassa chedanatacchanādisādhanāni upakaraṇāni raññā āṇattadivaseyeva sajjetvā. Nānā karīyati etenāti nānākaraṇaṃ, nānābhāvoti āha “nānatta”nti. Nesanti saralopenāyaṃ niddesoti āha “na esa”nti. Tathā atthesanti etthāpīti āha “atthi esa”nti. Pavattanatthaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ abhisaṅkhāro, tassa gati vegasā pavatti. Taṃ sandhāyāha “payogassa gamana”nti.

15. In the fifth section, it is called 'Isipatana' because sages fall and congregate there. This refers to 'those designated as Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas,' and so on. 'Having prepared all the tools' means having prepared all the implements for cutting, carving, and other such tasks for the tree, by the king’s command on that very day. 'Nānākaraṇa' (diversification) is that by which something is done in various ways; 'nānatta' (diversity) means a state of difference. 'Nesanti' is a designation by vowel elision, meaning 'na esa' (this is not). Similarly, `atthesanti` here also means `atthi esa` (this exists). 'Abhisaṅkhāra' (volitional formation) is the act of preparing for the purpose of causing something to occur; its movement is a swift progression. Referring to that, it is said, 'the movement of application.'

Sagaṇḍāti [M 2.0084][V 2.0078] khuddānukhuddakagaṇḍā. Tenāha “uṇṇatoṇataṭṭhānayuttā”ti. Sakasāvāti sakasaṭā. Tenāha “pūtisārenā”tiādi. Evaṃ guṇapatanena patitāti yathā taṃ cakkaṃ nābhiaranemīnaṃ sadosatāya na patiṭṭhāsi, evamekacce puggalā kāyavaṅkādivasena sadosatāya guṇapatanena patitā sakaṭṭhāne na tiṭṭhanti. Ettha ca pharusavācādayopi apāyagamanīyā sotāpattimaggeneva pahīyantīti daṭṭhabbā.

`Sagaṇḍā` means with minor and insignificant defects. Hence it is said, 'uṇṇatoṇataṭṭhānayuttā' (connected with high and low places). `Sakasāvāti` means `sakasaṭā` (with faults). Hence it is said, 'with rotten heartwood' (pūtisārenā), and so on. Thus, having fallen through the decline of virtues—just as a wheel, due to defects in its hub, spokes, and rim, does not stand firm, so too some individuals, due to bodily crookedness and other defects, having fallen through the decline of virtues, do not remain in their proper place. And here, harsh speech and other such faults, which lead to the realms of loss, should be seen as abandoned only by the path of stream-entry.

Sacetanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sañcetanā Sutta is concluded.

6. Apaṇṇakasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta

16. Chaṭṭhe virajjhanakiriyā nāma pacchā samādātabbatāya apaṇṇakappayogasamādānā viya hoti, avirajjhanakiriyā pana pacchā asamādātabbatāya anūnāti taṃsamaṅgipuggalo apaṇṇako, tassa bhāvo apaṇṇakatāti āha “apaṇṇakapaṭipadanti aviraddhapaṭipada”ntiādi. Yasmā sā adhippetatthasādhanena ekaṃsikā vaṭṭato niyyānāvahā, tattha ca yuttiyuttā asārāpagatā aviruddhatāya apaccanīkā anulomikā anudhammabhūtā ca, tasmā vuttaṃ “ekaṃsapaṭipada”ntiādi. Na takkaggāhena vā nayaggāhena vāti takkaggāhena vā paṭipanno na hoti nayaggāhena vā apaṇṇakapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno. Tattha takkaggāhena vāti ācariyaṃ alabhitvā “evaṃ me sugati, nibbānaṃ vā bhavissatī”ti attano takkaggahaṇamattena. Nayaggāhenāti paccakkhato adisvā nayato anumānato gahaṇena. Evaṃ gahetvā paṭipannoti takkamattena, nayaggāhena vā paṭipanno. Paṇḍitasatthavāho viya sampattīhi na parihāyatīti yojanā.

16. In the sixth section, the act of straying is like undertaking the unerring practice because it is to be undertaken later. The act of not straying, however, is not to be undertaken later, as it is complete. A person endowed with that is 'apaṇṇaka'; his state is 'apaṇṇakatā.' Thus it is said: 'The unerring path is the un-straying path,' and so on. Because that path, by accomplishing the intended purpose, is certain—leading out of the round of existence—and is also agreeable to reason, free from the worthless, uncontradicted, unopposed, compliant, and in accordance with the Dhamma, it is said: 'The certain path,' and so on. One who undertakes a path by grasping at logic or by grasping at method has not undertaken the unerring path. Here, 'by grasping at logic' means without having a teacher, thinking, 'Thus, I will attain a good destination or Nibbāna,' based solely on one's own grasping at logic. 'By grasping at method' means grasping through inference, from reasoning, without seeing directly. One who has undertaken a path having grasped in such a way has undertaken it by mere logic or by grasping at method. The connection is that, like a wise caravan leader, he does not fall away from his attainments.

Yaṃ sandhāya vuttanti parihānañca aparihānañca sandhāya jātake (jā. 1.1.1) vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha gāthāya atthayojanā – apaṇṇakaṃ ṭhānaṃ aviraddhakāraṇaṃ niyyānikakāraṇaṃ eke bodhisattappamukhā paṇḍitamanussā gaṇhiṃsu. Ye pana te bālasatthavāhaputtappamukhā takkikā āhu, te dutiyaṃ sāparādhaṃ [M 2.0085] anekaṃsikaṃ ṭhānaṃ aniyyānikaṃ kāraṇaṃ aggahesuṃ, te kaṇhapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā. Tattha sukkapaṭipadā aparihānipaṭipadā, kaṇhapaṭipadā parihānipaṭipadā, tasmā ye sukkapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā, te aparihīnā sotthibhāvaṃ pattā. Ye pana kaṇhapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā, te parihīnā anayabyasanaṃ āpannāti imamatthaṃ bhagavā anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatino vatvā uttari idamāha “etadaññāya medhāvī, taṃ gaṇhe yadapaṇṇaka”nti.

With reference to what was this said? It was said in the Jātaka with reference to decline and non-decline. Here, this is the explanation of the meaning of the verse: Some wise people, with the Bodhisatta as their chief, took up the unerring position, the cause of not straying, the cause of liberation. But those others, the logicians headed by the son of the foolish caravan leader, took up the second position, the one with fault, the uncertain position, the cause of not leading to liberation; they undertook the dark path. Therein, the bright path is the path of non-decline, and the dark path is the path of decline. Therefore, those who undertook the bright path, not having declined, attained well-being. But those who undertook the dark path, having declined, encountered misfortune and ruin. Having spoken this meaning to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, the Blessed One further said, 'Knowing this, the intelligent one should take up that which is unerring.'

Tattha [V 2.0079] etadaññāya medhāvīti medhāti laddhanāmāya visuddhāya uttamāya paññāya samannāgato kulaputto etaṃ apaṇṇakaṃ ṭhānaṃ dutiyañcāti dvīsu atakkaggāhatakkaggāhasaṅkhātesu ṭhānesu guṇadosaṃ vuddhihāniṃ atthānatthaṃ ñatvāti attho. Taṃ gaṇhe yadapaṇṇakanti yaṃ apaṇṇakaṃ ekaṃsikaṃ sukkapaṭipadāaparihāniyapaṭipadāsaṅkhātaṃ niyyānikakāraṇaṃ, tadeva gaṇheyya. Kasmā? Ekaṃsikādibhāvatoyeva. Itaraṃ pana na gaṇheyya. Kasmā? Anekaṃsikādibhāvatoyeva.

Here, 'the wise one, knowing this' means a son of good family endowed with that pure and supreme wisdom called 'medhā,' having known this. The meaning is: having known the benefits and faults, growth and decline, the beneficial and the unbeneficial in the two positions—this unerring position and the second one—designated as 'not grasping by logic' and 'grasping by logic.' 'One should grasp that which is unerring' means: one should grasp only that which is unerring, certain, designated as the bright path, the path of non-decline, the cause of liberation. Why? Because it is certain, and so on. But one should not grasp the other. Why? Because it is not certain, and so on.

Yavanti tāya sattā amissitāpi samānajātitāya missitā viya hontīti yoni. Sā pana atthato aṇḍādiuppattiṭṭhānavisiṭṭho khandhānaṃ bhāgaso pavattivisesoti āha “khandhakoṭṭhāso yoni nāmā”ti. Kāraṇaṃ yoni nāma, yonīti taṃ taṃ phalaṃ anupacitañāṇasambhārehi duravagādhabhedatāya missitaṃ viya hotīti. Yato ekattanayena so evāyanti bālānaṃ micchāgāho. Passāvamaggo yoni nāma yavanti tāya sattā yonisambandhena missitā hontīti. Paggahitā anuṭṭhānena, punappunaṃ āsevanāya paripuṇṇā.

It is a 'yoni' because by it beings, though unmixed, appear as if mixed on account of being of the same species. In terms of meaning, however, it is a particular mode of the aggregates' partial arising, distinguished as a place of origin such as from an egg, thus it is said: 'The section of aggregates is called "yoni."' Cause is called 'yoni'; this is because by it this or that result appears as if mixed, due to the difficulty of penetrating its distinction for those who have not accumulated the provisions of knowledge. Whence, through a sense of unity, comes the wrong grasping of fools that 'this is that very one.' The urinary passage is called 'yoni' because by it beings are mixed through connection with the womb. Upheld by non-exertion, and perfected by repeated cultivation.

“Cakkhutopī”tiādimhi pana cakkhuviññāṇādivīthīsu tadanugatamanoviññāṇavīthīsu ca kiñcāpi kusalādīnaṃ pavatti atthi, kāmāsavādayo eva pana vaṇato yūsaṃ viya paggharanakaasucibhāvena sandanti, tasmā te eva “āsavā”ti vuccanti. Tattha hi paggharanakaasucimhi āsavasaddo niruḷhoti. Dhammato yāva gotrabhūti tato paraṃ maggaphalesu appavattanato vuttaṃ. Ete hi ārammaṇakaraṇavasena dhamme gacchantā tato paraṃ na gacchanti. Nanu tato paraṃ bhavaṅgādīnipi gacchantīti ce? Na, tesampi pubbe ālambitesu lokiyadhammesu [M 2.0086] sāsavabhāvena antogadhattā tato paratābhāvato. Ettha ca gotrabhuvacanena gotrabhuvodānaphalasamāpattipurecārikaparikammāni vuttānīti veditabbāni. Paṭhamamaggapurecārikameva vā gotrabhu avadhinidassanabhāvena gahitaṃ, tato paraṃ pana maggaphalasamānatāya aññesu maggesu maggavīthiyaṃ samāpattivīthīyaṃ nirodhānantarañca pavattamānesu phalesu nibbāne ca āsavānaṃ pavatti nivāritāti veditabbaṃ. Savantīti gacchanti, ārammaṇakaraṇavasena pavattantīti attho. Avadhiattho ā-kāro, avadhi ca mariyādābhividhibhedato duvidho. Tattha mariyādaṃ kiriyaṃ bahi katvā pavattati yathā “āpāṭalīputtaṃ vuṭṭho devo”ti. Abhividhi pana kiriyaṃ byāpetvā pavattati yathā “ābhavaggaṃ bhagavato yaso pavattatī”ti. Abhividhiattho cāyamā-kāro idha gahitoti vuttaṃ “antokaraṇattho”ti.

In the phrase 'beginning with the eye,' etc., although there is the occurrence of wholesome and other states in the cognitive processes of eye-consciousness and so on, and in the subsequent mind-consciousness processes that follow them, the taints such as sensual desire flow like juice from a wound due to their oozing, impure nature. Therefore, they alone are called 'taints' (āsavā). For here the word 'āsava' is established in the sense of an oozing impurity. In terms of phenomena, they flow up to the change-of-lineage moment; this is stated because beyond that they do not occur in the paths and fruits. For these, while proceeding among phenomena by way of taking them as object, do not proceed beyond that. If it is asked, 'Do they not proceed beyond that into life-continuum, etc.?' No, because even those states, having previously taken mundane phenomena as object, are included in the tainted state, and thus there is no going beyond. And here, by the word 'gotrabhū' should be understood the preliminary works that precede change-of-lineage, purification, and fruition attainment. Alternatively, only the change-of-lineage moment preceding the first path is taken as illustrative of the limit. Beyond that, in the same way, in the other paths, in the path process, in the attainment process, and in the fruition states arising immediately after cessation, as well as in Nibbāna, the occurrence of taints is understood to be prevented. 'They flow' (savanti) means they proceed; that is, they occur by way of taking an object. The prefix 'ā-' has the sense of a limit (avadhi), and 'limit' is of two kinds: by way of delimitation (mariyādā) and extension (abhividhi). Therein, delimitation operates by excluding the action, as in 'the rain fell up to Pāṭaliputta.' Extension, however, operates by encompassing the action, as in 'the glory of the Blessed One extends up to the highest existence.' And here this prefix 'ā-' is taken in the sense of extension, hence it is said to have the sense of 'inclusion.'

Madirādayoti [V 2.0080] ādi-saddena sindhavakādambarikāpotikādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Cirapārivāsiyaṭṭho ciraparivuṭṭhatā purāṇabhāvo. Avijjā nāhosītiādīti ettha ādi-saddena “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati bhavataṇhāyā”ti (a. ni. 10.62) idaṃ suttaṃ saṅgahitaṃ. Avijjāsavabhavāsavānaṃ ciraparivuṭṭhatāya dassitāya tabbhāvabhāvino kāmāsavassa ciraparivuṭṭhatā dassitāva hoti. Aññesu ca yathāvutte dhamme okāsañca ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattamānesu mānādīsu vijjamānesu attattaniyādiggāhavasena abhibyāpanaṃ madakaraṇavasena āsavasadisatā ca etesaṃyeva, na aññesanti etesveva āsavasaddo niruḷhoti daṭṭhabbo. Āyataṃ anādikālikattā. Pasavantīti phalanti. Na hi kiñci saṃsāradukkhaṃ atthi, yaṃ āsavehi vinā uppajjeyya. Purimāni cetthāti etesu catūsu atthavikappesu purimāni tīṇi. Yatthāti yesu suttābhidhammappadesesu. Tattha yujjanti kilesesuyeva yathāvuttassa atthattayassa sambhavato. Pacchimaṃ kammepīti pacchimaṃ “āyataṃ vā saṃsāradukkhaṃ savanti pasavantī”ti vuttanibbacanaṃ kammepi yujjati dukkhappasavanassa kilesakammasādhāraṇattā.

'Madirādayo' (intoxicants, etc.)—by the word 'ādi,' the inclusion of terms like 'sindhavaka,' 'kādambarika,' 'āpotika,' and others should be understood. 'Cirapārivāsiyaṭṭho' (the meaning of long-standing) is long-establishedness, an ancient state. 'Avijjā nāhosītiādi' (Ignorance was not, etc.)—here, by the word 'ādi,' the sutta 'Monks, a first point of craving for existence is not discerned' (AN 10.62) is included. When the long-establishedness of the taints of ignorance and existence is shown, the long-establishedness of the taint of sensual desire, which has its being in that state, is also shown. And when other things such as conceit exist, which arise having made the aforementioned phenomena their opportunity and object, the pervasion by way of grasping at self and what is mine, and the similarity to intoxicants by way of causing intoxication, belong only to these, not to others. Thus, it should be understood that the word 'āsava' is established only in these. 'Long-lasting' (āyataṃ) means because it is from beginningless time. 'They bring forth' (pasavanti) means they bear fruit. For there is no suffering in saṃsāra that could arise without the taints. 'And the former here' means the first three among these four alternative meanings. 'Where' means in those passages of the Suttas and Abhidhamma. There, they apply only to the defilements, because of the possibility of the three meanings mentioned. 'The last also in kamma' means the last definition given—'or they flow and bring forth the long-lasting suffering of saṃsāra'—also applies to kamma, since the bringing forth of suffering is common to both defilements and kamma.

Diṭṭhadhammā vuccanti paccakkhabhūtā khandhā, diṭṭhadhamme bhavā diṭṭhadhammikā. Vivādamūlabhūtāti vivādassa mūlakāraṇabhūtā kodhūpanāhamakkhapalāsaissāmacchariyamāyāsāṭheyyathambhasārambhamānātimānā. Yena devūpapatyassāti [M 2.0087] yena kammakilesappakārena āsavena devesu upapatti nibbatti assa mayhanti sambandho. Gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo ākāsacārī assanti vibhattiṃ vipariṇāmetvā yojetabbaṃ. Ettha ca yakkhagandhabbavinimuttā sabbā devatā devaggahaṇena gahitā. Naḷo vuccati mūlaṃ, tasmā vinaḷīkatāti vigatanaḷā vigatamūlā katāti attho. Avasesā ca akusalā dhammāti akusalakammato avasesā akusalā dhammā āsavāti āgatāti sambandho.

The seen phenomena are called the directly experienced aggregates; 'diṭṭhadhammikā' refers to those existing in the seen phenomena. 'The root of disputes' refers to the root causes of disputes, such as anger, hostility, depreciation, malice, jealousy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, rivalry, conceit, and excessive pride. 'By which one might be reborn among the devas' means: 'by which kind of action, defilement, or taint rebirth among the devas might occur for me'—this is the connection. 'A gandhabba or a bird, a sky-roamer, might be'—the inflection should be altered and applied here. And here, all deities, except yakkhas and gandhabbas, are included under the term 'deva.' 'Naḷa' is called a root; therefore, 'vinaḷīkatā' means 'made devoid of reeds, made devoid of roots'—this is the meaning. And 'the remaining unwholesome phenomena' means the unwholesome phenomena apart from unwholesome action are understood as the taints; this is the connection.

Paṭighātāyāti paṭisedhanāya. Parūpavāda…pe… upaddavāti idaṃ yadi bhagavā sikkhāpadaṃ na paññāpeyya, tato asaddhammappaṭisevanaadinnādānapāṇātipātādihetu ye uppajjeyyuṃ parūpavādādayo diṭṭhadhammikā nānappakārā anatthā, ye ca tannimittameva nirayādīsu nibbattassa pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇādivasena mahādukkhānubhavādippakārā anatthā, te sandhāya vuttaṃ.

'For warding off' means for preventing. 'Slander...and so on...trouble'—this is said with reference to the various kinds of disadvantages in this very life that would arise, such as slander and so on, due to indulgence in false doctrines and causes such as taking what is not given, killing living beings, etc., if the Blessed One had not laid down the training rule; and also with reference to the various kinds of disadvantages, such as the experience of great suffering for one reborn in hells and so on, arising from that very cause, by way of the five kinds of bondage, karmic causes, and so forth.

Te [V 2.0081] paneteti ete kāmarāgādikilesatebhūmakakammaparūpavādādiuppaddavappakārā āsavā. Yatthāti yasmiṃ vinayādipāḷippadese. Yathāti yena duvidhādippakārena avasesesu ca suttantesu tidhā āgatāti sambandho. Nirayaṃ gamentīti nirayagāminiyā. Chakkanipāteti chakkanipāte āhuneyyasutte (a. ni. 6.58). Tattha hi āsavā chadhā āgatā.

These, indeed, are the taints, namely: the defilements such as sensual desire; the kamma of the three realms; the slander of others; and various kinds of troubles. 'Where' refers to which passage of the Vinaya or other texts. 'How' refers to in what twofold manner, etc.; and in the remaining discourses they appear classified in three ways; this is the connection. 'Leads to hell' means by means of that which leads to hell. 'In the Book of Sixes' refers to the Book of Sixes, in the Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings (Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.58). There, indeed, the taints appear classified in six ways.

Sarasabhedoti khaṇikanirodho. Khīṇākāroti accantāya khīṇatā. Āsavā khīyanti pahīyanti etenāti āsavakkhayo, maggo. Āsavānaṃ khayante uppajjanato āsavakkhayo, phalaṃ. Āsavakkhayena pattabbato āsavā khīyanti etthāti āsavakkhayo, nibbānaṃ. Visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.557-560) vitthārito, tasmā tattha, taṃ saṃvaṇṇanāya ca vuttanayena veditabbo.

'Sarasabheda' means momentary cessation. 'Khīṇākāra' means utter destruction. 'Āsavakkhaya' (destruction of taints) is the path, because the taints are exhausted and abandoned by it. 'Āsavakkhaya' is the fruit, because it arises at the exhaustion of the taints. 'Āsavakkhaya' is Nibbāna, because the taints are exhausted in it, and it is to be attained by the destruction of taints. It is elaborated in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhimagga 2.557-560); therefore, it should be understood there and by the method stated in its explanation.

Tathāti iminā visuddhimagge vitthāritataṃ upasaṃharati. Kusalappavattiṃ āvaranti nivārentīti āvaraṇīyā. Purimappavattivasenāti niddokkamanato pubbe kammaṭṭhānassa pavattivasena. Ṭhapetvāti hatthagataṃ kiñci ṭhapento viya kammaṭṭhānaṃ satisampajaññavasena ṭhapetvā kammaṭṭhānameva manasikaronto niddaṃ okkamati, jhānasamāpanno viya yathāparicchinneneva kālena [M 2.0088] pabujjhamāno kammaṭṭhānaṃ ṭhapitaṭṭhāne gaṇhantoyeva pabujjhati nāma. Tena vuttaṃ “tasmā…pe… nāma hotī”ti. Mūlakammaṭṭhāneti ādito paṭṭhāya parihariyamānakammaṭṭhāne. Pariggahakammaṭṭhānavasenāti sayanaṃ upagacchantena pariggahamānakammaṭṭhānamanasikāravasena. So pana dhātumanasikāravasena icchitabboti dassetuṃ “ayaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Thus'—with this he summarizes its detailed exposition in the Visuddhimagga. 'Āvaraṇīyā' means they obstruct and hinder the occurrence of wholesome states. 'Purimappavattivasena' means by way of the occurrence of the meditation subject before going to sleep. 'Having established' means, like one establishing something held in the hand, so too, having established the meditation subject by way of mindfulness and clear comprehension, one goes to sleep while attending to the meditation subject itself, and, like one absorbed in jhāna, awakening at just the appointed time, one awakens indeed while taking up the meditation subject in the place where it was established. Therefore it was said, 'Therefore...it is called.' 'Mūlakammaṭṭhāna' means the meditation subject being cultivated from the beginning. 'Pariggahakammaṭṭhānavasena' means by way of attending to the meditation subject taken up by one approaching sleep. But to show that that should be desired by way of attending to the elements, it was said, 'For this...' and so on.

Apaṇṇakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Sutta is concluded.

7. Attabyābādhasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Attabyābādha Sutta

17. Sattame byābādhanaṃ dukkhāpananti āha “attabyābādhāyāti attadukkhāyā”ti. Maggaphalacittuppādāpi kāyasucaritādisaṅgaho evāti āha “avāritānevā”ti.

17. In the seventh discourse, 'tormenting is causing suffering' is said, meaning, 'for tormenting oneself' is 'for one's own suffering.' Even the arising of path and fruition consciousness is included within good bodily conduct and so forth, thus it is said: 'indeed unrestrained.'

Attabyābādhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Attabyābādha Sutta is concluded.

8. Devalokasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Devaloka Sutta

18. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0082] itīti padasandhibyañjanasiliṭṭhatāti purimapadānaṃ pacchimapadehi atthato sahitatāya byañjanānaṃ vākyānaṃ siliṭṭhatāya dīpane nipāto.

18. In the eighth discourse, 'iti' is a particle that indicates the connection of words and the elegance of expression, due to the cohesion in meaning between the preceding and following words, and the elegance of the phrasing in the sentences.

Devalokasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Devaloka Sutta is concluded.

9. Paṭhamapāpaṇikasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Shopkeeper

19. Navame ugghāṭetvāti āsanadvārañceva bhaṇḍapasibbake ca vivaritvā. Nādhiṭṭhātīti taṃtaṃkayavikkaye attanā voyogaṃ nāpajjati. Divākāleti majjhanhikasamaye. Assāmiko hoti tīsupi kālesu laddhabbalābhassa alabhanato. Apativātābādhaṃ rattiṭṭhānaṃ. Chāyudakasampannaṃ divāṭṭhānaṃ. Vipassanāpi vaṭṭati vipassanākammikoyeva. Tenapi hi navadhā indriyānaṃ tikkhattaṃ āpādentena samādhinimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ, vipassanānimittaṃ samāhitākārasallakkhaṇāya.

19. In the ninth discourse, 'having opened' means opening both the shop door and the containers of goods. 'Does not apply himself' means not engaging personally in this and that buying and selling. 'During the day' refers to midday. 'Ownerless' means not obtaining the gain that should be obtained at any of the three times. 'Sheltered from the wind and free from disease' is the place for staying at night. 'Shaded and with water' is the place for staying during the day. Even insight meditation is suitable, because he is one who practices insight. By that too, having developed the faculties ninefold three times, one should grasp the sign of concentration, and the sign of insight by discerning the characteristics of the state of concentration.

Paṭhamapāpaṇikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on the Shopkeeper is concluded.

10. Dutiyapāpaṇikasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Shopkeeper Sutta

20. Dasame [M 2.0089] visiṭṭhadhuroti visiṭṭhadhurasampaggāho vīriyasampanno. Ñāṇavīriyāyattā hi atthasiddhiyo. Tenāha “uttamadhuro”tiādi. Vikkāyikabhaṇḍanti vikkayetabbabhaṇḍaṃ. Nikkhittadhanenāti nidahitvā ṭhapitadhanavasena. Vaḷañjanakavasenāti divase divase dānūpabhogavasena vaḷañjitabbadhanavasena. Upabhogaparibhogabhaṇḍenāti upabhogaparibhogūpakaraṇena. Nipatantīti nipātenti, attano dhanaggahena nipātavuttike karonti. Tenāha “nimantentī”ti.

20. In the tenth, 'one with outstanding responsibilities' means possessing outstanding responsibilities and being endowed with effort. Indeed, success in undertakings depends on wisdom and effort. Therefore, it is said, 'the supreme responsibility,' etc. 'Merchandise for sale' means merchandise to be sold. 'With wealth deposited' means in the manner of wealth deposited and kept. 'By way of daily usage' means in the manner of wealth to be spent day by day for giving and consumption. 'With goods for consumption and use' means with equipment for consumption and use. 'They fall upon' means they cause to fall, making them have a fallen livelihood by seizing their wealth. Therefore, it is said, 'they invite.'

Ñāṇathāmenāti ñāṇassa thirabhāvena. Ñāṇaparakkamenāti ñāṇasahitena vīriyena. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthabhedañhi yena sutena ijjhati, taṃ sutaṃ nāma. Ukkaṭṭhaniddesena dassento “ekanikāya…pe… bahussutā”ti āha. Āgatoti suppavattibhāvena svāgato. Tenāha “paguṇo pavattito”ti. Abhidhamme āgatā kusalādikkhandhādibhedabhinnā dhammā suttantapiṭakepi otarantīti “dhammadharāti suttantapiṭakadharā”icceva vuttaṃ. Na hi ābhidhammikabhāvena [V 2.0083] vinā nippariyāyato suttantapiṭakaññutā sambhavati. Dvemātikādharāti bhikkhubhikkhunimātikāvasena dvemātikādharāti vadanti, “vinayābhidhammamātikādharā”ti yuttaṃ. Paripucchatīti sabbabhāgena pucchitabbaṃ pucchati. Tenāha “atthānatthaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ pucchatī”ti. Pariggaṇhātīti vicāreti.

'By the strength of wisdom' means by the firmness of wisdom. 'By the exertion of wisdom' means by effort accompanied by wisdom. For the distinction of benefits pertaining to this life, to future lives, and to the ultimate goal is achieved by what is learned; that is called learning. Showing this through an excellent explanation, it is said, 'of one Nikāya... learned.' 'Learned' means well-learned due to fluency. Hence, it is said, 'familiar through practice.' 'One who retains the Dhamma' means one who retains the Sutta Piṭaka, because the various categories of wholesome states, etc., defined in the Abhidhamma, also appear in the Sutta Piṭaka. For without being skilled in the Abhidhamma method, a thorough understanding of the Sutta Piṭaka is not possible. 'One who retains the two matrices' means they say one who retains the two matrices with reference to bhikkhus and bhikkhunis; it is appropriate to say, 'one who retains the matrices of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma.' 'Questions thoroughly' means asking about everything that needs to be asked. Hence, it is said, 'asks about meaning and non-meaning, cause and non-cause.' 'Examines' means investigates.

Na evaṃ attho daṭṭhabboti evaṃ desanānukkamena attho na gahetabbo. Añño hi desanākkamo veneyyajjhāsayavasena pavattanato, añño paṭipattikkamo. Heṭṭhimena vā paricchedoti sīlasamādhipaññāsaṅkhātesu tīsu bhāgesu katthaci heṭṭhimanayena desanāya paricchedaṃ veditabbaṃ sīlena, katthaci uparimena bhāgena paññāya, katthaci dvīhipi bhāgehi sīlapaññāvasena. Idha pana sutte uparimena bhāgena paricchedo veditabboti vatvā taṃ dassento “tasmā”tiādimāha. Yasmā vā bhagavā veneyyajjhāsayavasena paṭhamaṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ dassento arahattaṃ pavedetvā “tayidaṃ arahattaṃ imāya āraddhavīriyatāya hotī”ti dassento vīriyārambhaṃ pavedetvā “svāyaṃ vīriyārambho iminā kalyāṇamittasannissayena [M 2.0090] bhavatī”ti dassento nissayasampattiṃ pavedeti heṭṭhā dassitanidassanānurūpanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The meaning should not be seen in this way; that is, the meaning should not be grasped according to the sequence of the teaching. For the sequence of the teaching is one thing, as it proceeds according to the inclination of those to be trained, while the sequence of practice is another. Or, by the lower section: it should be understood that in the three sections designated as virtue, concentration, and wisdom, in some instances the definition should be known by the lower method, that is, by virtue, in some instances by the higher section, that is, by wisdom, and in some instances by both sections, that is, by virtue and wisdom. Here in this discourse, however, having said that the definition should be known by the higher section, he shows this by saying, 'Therefore,' etc. Or, it should be seen as corresponding to the illustration shown below, because the Blessed One, in accordance with the inclination of those to be trained, first shows the good friend, then declares arahantship; then, showing that 'this arahantship comes about through this initiated energy,' he declares the undertaking of energy; then, showing that 'this undertaking of energy comes about through this reliance on a good friend,' he declares the attainment of reliance.

Dutiyapāpaṇikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Shopkeeper is concluded.

Rathakāravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Chariot-Maker is concluded.

3. Puggalavaggo

3. The Chapter on Persons

1. Samiddhasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Discourse with Samiddha

21. Tatiyassa paṭhame ruccatīti kāyasakkhiādīsu puggalesu ativiya sundaratarapaṇītatarabhāvena te cittassa abhiruciuppādako katamoti pucchati. Saddhindriyaṃ dhuraṃ ahosi saddhādhuraṃ maggavuṭṭhānanti katvā, sesindriyāni pana kathanti āha “sesānī”tiādi. Paṭividdhamaggovāti tīhipi therehi attano attano paṭividdhaarahattamaggo eva kathito, tasmā na [V 2.0084] sukaraṃ ekaṃsena byākātuṃ “ayaṃ…pe… paṇītataro cā”ti. Bhummantareneva kathesi “tīsupi puggalesu aggamaggaṭṭhova paṇītataro”ti.

21. In the first discourse of the third section, regarding the word 'ruccati' (he is pleased), he asks: 'Among the persons such as the body-witness, which one produces delight for his mind by their exceedingly beautiful and sublime nature?' Taking it that the faculty of faith was the leader—the leadership of faith being the emergence from the path—he then asks about the remaining faculties, saying, 'the remaining,' etc. 'By the penetrated path' means that each of the three elders spoke only of their own respectively penetrated path to arahantship. Therefore, it is not easy to declare definitively, 'this one... is more sublime.' He spoke as if on the same level: 'Among all three persons, the one established in the highest path is indeed the most sublime.'

Samiddhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse with Samiddha is concluded.

2. Gilānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Discourse on the Sick Person

22. Dutiye hitānīti bhabyāni. Vuddhikarānīti ārogyādivuddhikarāni. Anucchavikanti upaṭṭhānakiriyāya anurūpaṃ. Vātāpamārarogenāti vātarogena ca apamārarogena ca, vātanidānena vā apamārarogena. Niṭṭhappattagilānoti “iminā rogena na cirasseva marissatī”ti niṭṭhaṃ patto gilāno. Khipitakaṃ nāma vamathurogo. Kacchūti thullakacchuābādho. Tiṇapupphakajaro visamavātasamphassajarogo. Yesanti yesaṃ rogānaṃ. Paṭijagganenāti paṭikāramattena. Phāsukanti byādhivūpasamanena sarīrassa phāsubhāvo. Byādhinidānasamuṭṭhānajānanena paṇḍito, paṭikārakiriyāya yuttakāritāya dakkho, uṭṭhānavīriyasampattiyā analaso.

22. In the second, 'beneficial' (hitāni) means suitable (bhabyāni). 'Promoting growth' (vuddhikarāni) means promoting growth in health and the like. 'Suitable' (anucchavikaṃ) means suitable for the act of attending. 'By wind disease and epilepsy' (vātāpamārarogena) means by wind disease and by epilepsy, or by epilepsy that is caused by wind. 'A patient who has reached the final stage' (niṭṭhappattagilāno) is a patient who has reached the end, with the prognosis that 'he will die from this disease before long.' 'Khipitaka' is a vomiting disease. 'Scabies' (kacchu) is a severe scabies affliction. 'Grass-and-flower fever' (tiṇapupphakajaro) is a fever-disease from contact with irregular winds. 'Of which' (yesaṃ) means of which diseases. 'By attending' (paṭijagganena) means by mere treatment. 'Comfort' (phāsukaṃ) means the body's comfort due to the subsiding of the illness. He is wise (paṇḍito) in knowing the causes and arising of diseases, skilled (dakkho) in properly applying remedies, and tireless (analaso) through the possession of energetic effort.

Padaparamo [M 2.0091] puggalo kathito sammattaniyāmokkamanassa ayoggabhāvato. Alabhantova tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ savanāya okkamati niyāmaṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattaṃ paccekabodhiṃ. Yanti, yato. Ovādaṃ labhitvāti ābhisamācārikavattaṃ ovādamattaṃ. Ettakopi hi tassa hitāvahoti. Tannissitovāti vipañcitaññunissitova hoti. Punappunaṃ desetabbova sammattaniyāmokkamanassa yoggabhāvato.

The person who is at most concerned with the letter is said to be incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness, due to his lack of aptitude. Another, even without obtaining the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata for hearing, enters the fixed course in wholesome qualities, rightness, and attains individual enlightenment. 'They go' (yanti), means 'from where' (yato). 'Having received advice' refers to mere advice concerning proper conduct. Even this much is beneficial for him. 'Dependent on that' means he is dependent on one who understands after a detailed explanation. He should be taught again and again, since he is capable of entering the fixed course of rightness.

Gilānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Sick Person is concluded.

3. Saṅkhārasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Discourse on Formations

23. Tatiye vividhehi ākārehi ābādhanato byābādhova byābajjhaṃ, kāyikaṃ cetasikañca dukkhaṃ. Saha byābajjhena vattatīti sabyābajjhaṃ. Tenāha “sadukkha”nti. Cetanārāsinti pubbacetanādirāsiṃ. Cetanaṃ punappunaṃ pavattento “rāsiṃ karoti piṇḍaṃ karotī”ti ca vutto. Sadukkhanti nirantaradukkhaṃ. Tenāha “sābādhaṃ nirassāda”nti. Atthīti ujukaṃ dukkhavedanā [V 2.0085] natthīti avattabbattā vuttaṃ. Aniṭṭhasabhāvattā aniṭṭhārammaṇattā ca dukkhapakkhikāva sā daṭṭhabbā. Na hi akusalavipākā iṭṭhā nāma atthī, kusalavipākā pana upekkhāvedanā tattha appāvasarā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana nirayassa dukkhabahulattā dukkhassa ca tattha balavatāya sā abbohārikaṭṭhāne ṭhitāti vuttaṃ. Upamaṃ katvā āhaṭo viseso viya sāmaññassa yathā ayopiṇḍirohino viya rūpānanti. Paṭibhāgaupamāti paṭibimbaupamā.

23. In the third, because it afflicts in various ways, affliction itself is that which is afflicted, namely, bodily and mental suffering. Because it occurs with affliction, it is 'with affliction' (sabyābajjha). Therefore, it is said, 'with suffering' (sadukkha). 'Accumulation of volition' (cetanārāsi) means a mass of past volitions and so on. Because volition arises repeatedly, it is said to 'form a heap, a mass.' 'With suffering' (sadukkha) means continuous suffering. Therefore, it is said, 'afflicted, devoid of delight.' The word 'is' is used because it cannot be said that there is directly no feeling of suffering. Because of its undesirable nature and having an undesirable object, it should be seen as belonging to the side of suffering. For there are no desirable results of unwholesome actions, and as for the neutral feeling resulting from wholesome actions, there is little opportunity for it there. In the commentary, however, it is said that because hell is abundant with suffering and suffering is very intense there, that feeling stands in a place beyond practical consideration. A specific point is brought by way of a simile for a general one, as in: 'forms are like the rust on an iron ball.' 'A counterpart simile' (paṭibhāgaupamā) means a simile of a reflection.

Te aggahetvāti heṭṭhimabrahmaloke aggahetvā. Vomissakasukhadukkhanti vimissakasukhadukkhaṃ pītimissakabhāvato. Kammanti pāpakammaṃ. Kammasīsena phalaṃ vadati. Kāmañcettha “abyābajjhaṃ lokaṃ upapajjatī”ti āgataṃ, “abyābajjhā phassā phusantī”ti pana vacanena lokuttaraphassāpi saṅgayhantīti “tīṇi sucaritāni lokiyalokuttaramissakāni kathitānī”ti vuttaṃ.

Not having taken them (as the highest), i.e., not having taken them in the lower brahma-worlds. 'Mixed pleasure and pain' (vomissakasukhadukkhaṃ) means mixed pleasure and pain due to being mixed with joy. 'Kamma' means evil kamma. He speaks of the fruit under the heading of kamma. And here, although it is stated, 'he is reborn in a world free from affliction,' yet by the statement, 'they experience contacts free from affliction,' supramundane contacts are also included. Thus, it is said: 'Three kinds of good conduct—mundane, supramundane, and mixed—are spoken of.'

Saṅkhārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Formations is concluded.

4. Bahukārasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Discourse on Great Help

24. Catutthe [M 2.0092] avassayaṃ gatoti vaṭṭadukkhaparimuttiyā avassayo mayhanti saraṇagamanakkamena upagato hoti. Satantikanti sapariyattidhammaṃ. Aggahitasaraṇapubbassāti aggahitapubbasaraṇassa. Akatābhinivesassa vasena vuttanti tasmiṃ attabhāve na kato saraṇagamanābhiniveso yenāti akatābhiniveso, tassa vasena vuttaṃ. Kāmaṃ pubbepi saraṇadāyako ācariyo vutto, pabbajjādāyakopi saraṇadāyakova. Pubbe pana upāsakabhāvāpādakavasena saraṇadāyako adhippeto. Idaṃ pana gahitapabbajjassa saraṇagamanaṃ. Pabbajā hi savisesaṃ saraṇagamananti pabbajjādāyako puna vutto. Eteti pabbajjādāyakādayo. Duvidhena paricchinnāti lokiyadhammasampāpako lokuttaradhammasampāpakoti dvippakārena paricchinnā, katābhinivesaakatābhinivesavasena vā. Uparīti paṭhamamaggato upari. Neva sakkotīti ācariyena katassa upakārassa mahānubhāvattā tassa patikāraṃ nāma kātuṃ na sakkoti.

24.
