In the fourth, 'gone for refuge' (avassayaṃ gato) means that by the procedure of going for refuge, one has approached that which is a refuge for oneself for liberation from the suffering of the cycle of rebirths. 'With the text' (satantikaṃ) means the Dhamma together with the scriptures. 'Of one who has not previously gone for refuge' (aggahitasaraṇapubbassa) is a gloss for aggahitapubbasaraṇassa. 'It is said by way of one who has not made a commitment' (akatābhinivesassa vasena vuttaṃ) means it is said by way of one by whom no commitment to going for refuge has been made in that existence. Although previously the teacher who gives the refuges was mentioned, the one who gives the ordination is also a giver of the refuges. However, earlier, the giver of the refuges was intended in the sense of one who brings about the state of a lay follower. This, however, is the going for refuge of one who has taken ordination. For ordination is a special kind of going for refuge, and thus the ordination-giver is mentioned again. 'These' (ete) refers to the ordination-giver and others. 'Distinguished in two ways' (duvidhena paricchinnā) means distinguished in two types: as one who brings about worldly Dhamma and one who brings about supramundane Dhamma, or by way of one who has made a commitment and one who has not. 'Above' (upari) means above the first path. 'He is not able' (neva sakkoti) means that due to the great power of the help rendered by the teacher, he is not able to make any repayment for it.

Bahukārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Great Help is concluded.

5. Vajirūpamasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Discourse with the Simile of the Diamond

25. Pañcame [V 2.0086] aruiti purāṇaṃ duṭṭhavaṇaṃ vuccati. Ka-kāro padasandhikaroti arukūpamaṃ cittaṃ etassāti arukūpamacitto appamattakassapi dukkhassa asahanato. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Ittarakālobhāsenāti parittameva kālo ñāṇobhāsavirahena. Lagatīti kodhāsaṅgavasena kuppanto puggalo sammukhā, “kiṃ vadasī”tiādinā parammukhā ca upanayhanavasena lagati, na taṇhāsaṅgavasena. Kuppatīti kujjhati. Byāpajjatīti vipannacitto hoti. Thaddhabhāvaṃ āpajjati īsakampi muduttābhāvato. Duṭṭhārukoti maṃsalohitānaṃ duṭṭhabhāvena pakatibhāvaṃ jahitvā ṭhito duṭṭhavaṇo. “Duṭṭhārutā”tipi paṭhanti, tatthāpi tākāro padasandhikaro.

25. In the fifth, 'aru' is said to be an old, festering wound. The letter 'ka' makes a word connection. 'Arukūpamacitta' (one whose mind is like a festering wound) is so called because he cannot endure even a slight suffering. The same principle applies to the remaining two words. 'Ittarakālobhāsena' means for only a short time, due to the absence of the radiance of knowledge. 'Lagati' (clings) means a person who becomes angry clings by way of attachment to anger, face-to-face with words like, 'What are you saying?' and so on, and behind his back by way of resentment, but not by way of attachment to craving. 'Kuppati' (becomes angry) means he becomes angry. 'Byāpajjati' (becomes corrupt) means his mind becomes corrupt. He becomes stiff, lacking even a little softness. 'Duṭṭhāruka' means a festering wound that has abandoned its natural state due to the corruption of flesh and blood. Some read it as 'duṭṭhārutā,' where the letter 'tā' also makes a word connection.

Tassāti duṭṭhārukassa. Savananti asucivisandanaṃ. Uddhumātassa viyāti kodhena uddhaṃ uddhaṃ dhumātakassa viya kodhūpāyāsassa avissajjanato. Caṇḍikatassāti [M 2.0093] kupitassa. Ettha ca kiñcāpi heṭṭhimamaggavajjhāpi kilesā tehi anuppattidhammataṃ āpāditattā samucchinnā, tathāpi tasmiṃ santāne aggamaggassa anuppannattā tattha appahīnāpi kilesā atthevāti katvā tesaṃ ñāṇānaṃ vijjūpamatā vuttā, na tehi maggehi pahīnānaṃ kilesānaṃ atthibhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Tassa' (of that) means of the festering wound. 'Savana' (oozing) refers to the flow of impurity. 'Uddhumātassa viya' (like one swollen) is like one puffed up with anger, due to the non-release of anger and distress. 'Caṇḍikatassa' (of the wrathful one) means of the angry one. Here, although the defilements to be abandoned by the lower paths have been eradicated, having been rendered incapable of arising by those paths, still, since the highest path has not yet arisen in that continuum, it is said that those knowledges are like lightning on the grounds that defilements not yet abandoned still exist there. It should be understood that this is not due to the existence of defilements abandoned by those paths.

Vajirūpamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vajirūpama Sutta is concluded.

6. Sevitabbasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sevitabba Sutta

26. Chaṭṭhe upasaṅkamitabboti kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitabbo. Allīyitabboti chāyāya viya vinā bhāvanāya nillīyitabbo. Punappunaṃ upāsitabboti abhiṇhaso upanisīditabbo. Anuddayāti mettāpubbabhāgo. Upasaṅkamituṃ vaṭṭatīti “etassa sīlena abhivuddhi bhavissatī”ti upakāratthaṃ upasevanādi vaṭṭati.

26. In the sixth, 'upasaṅkamitabbo' means one should approach from time to time. 'Allīyitabbo' means one should adhere to him without separation, like a shadow. 'Punappunaṃ upāsitabbo' means one should sit nearby repeatedly. 'Anuddayā' means having loving-kindness as a preliminary part. 'Upasaṅkamituṃ vaṭṭati' means it is fitting to approach, thinking, 'Growth will occur for this one due to his virtue,' for the sake of benefit; associating with him and so on is fitting.

Na paṭihaññissatīti “apehi, kiṃ etenā”ti paṭikkhepābhāvato piyasīlattā na paṭihaññissati. Phāsu bhavissatīti dvīsu hi sīlavantesu ekena sīlassa vaṇṇe kathite itaro anumodati. Tena tesaṃ kathā phāsu ceva hoti pavattinī ca. Ekasmiṃ pana dussīle sati dussīlassa sīlakathā dukkathā, neva sīlakathā hoti, na phāsu hoti, na pavattinī. Dussīlassa hi sīlakathā aphāsu bhavissati. Sīlakathāya vuttamatthaṃ samādhipaññākathāsupi atidisati [V 2.0087] “samādhipaññākathāsupi eseva nayo”ti. Dve hi samādhilābhino samādhikathaṃ sappaññā ca paññākathaṃ kathentā rattiṃ vā divasaṃ vā atikkamantampi na jānanti.

'Na paṭihaññissati' means he will not be rejected with words like, 'Go away, what use is this?'—due to the absence of rejection and his pleasing virtue. 'Phāsu bhavissati' means when, between two virtuous people, one speaks in praise of virtue, the other approves. Thus, their conversation is both pleasant and progressive. But if one is unvirtuous, for the unvirtuous person a discussion of virtue is painful talk; it is not a discussion of virtue, it is not pleasant, and it is not progressive. For an unvirtuous person, a discussion of virtue will be unpleasant. The meaning stated regarding the discussion of virtue is also applied to discussions of concentration and wisdom: 'The same principle applies to discussions of concentration and wisdom.' For two who have attained concentration, when discussing concentration, and the wise, when discussing wisdom, do not know even when the night or day passes.

Tattha tattha paññāya anuggahessāmīti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ anuggahetabbe paññāya sodhetabbe vaḍḍhetabbe ca adhikasīlaṃ nissāya uppannapaññāya anuggahessāmīti attho. Tañca anuggaṇhanaṃ sīlassa asappāyānupakāradhamme vajjetvā tappaṭipakkhasevanena hotīti āha “sīlassa asappāye”tiādi. Sīlassa asappāyānupakāradhammā nāma anācārāgocarādayo, tappaṭipakkhato upakāradhammā veditabbā. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ [M 2.0094] ṭhāneti taṃtaṃsikkhākoṭṭhāsapadaṭṭhāne. Anuggaṇhāti nāmāti abhinnaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ katvā anuggaṇhāti nāma. Khāraparissāvaneti rajakānaṃ ūsakhārādikhāraparissāvanapaṭe. Hāyatīti sīlādinā parihāyati. Seṭṭhaṃ puggalanti sīlādiguṇehi seṭṭhaṃ uttaritaraṃ uttamaṃ puggalaṃ.

'In each instance, I will support with wisdom'—this means that in each case where something should be supported, purified, and increased with wisdom, one should rely on higher virtue and support with the wisdom that arises. And that support is done by avoiding qualities that are uncongenial and unhelpful to virtue and cultivating their opposites, as stated: 'uncongenial to virtue,' and so forth. Qualities uncongenial and unhelpful to virtue are misconduct, improper pastures, and the like; their opposites should be understood as helpful qualities. 'In each instance' refers to the specific portions and bases of the training. 'Supports' means to support by making it unbroken and uncorrupted. 'Filtering with lye' refers to the cloth of washermen for filtering lye, such as saline lye. 'Declines' means one declines in virtue and other qualities. 'The best person' refers to a person who is best, superior, and supreme through qualities such as virtue.

Sevitabbasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sevitabba Sutta is concluded.

7. Jigucchitabbasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Jigucchitabba Sutta

27. Sattame abbhuggacchatīti ettha abhi-saddāpekkhāya “na”nti sāmiatthe upayogavacananti āha “assā”ti “taṃ kho pana bhavanta”ntiādīsu viya. Pāpako kittisaddoti lāmakabhāvena kathetabbasaddo. Gūthakūpo viya dussīlyanti etena dussīlassa gūthasadisattameva dasseti. Vacananti aniṭṭhavacanaṃ. Purimanayenevāti “gūthakūpo viya dussīlya”ntiādinā pubbe vuttanayena. Sucimittoti sīlācārasuddhiyā sucimitto. Saha ayanti pavattantīti sahāyāti āha “sahagāmino”ti.

27. In the seventh, regarding 'abbhuggacchati': here, with reference to the prefix 'abhi-', the word 'naṃ' is a usage in the sense of possession; therefore, he says 'assā,' as in phrases like 'taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ,' and so forth. 'Pāpako kittisaddo' means a sound that is spoken of as base. 'Gūthakūpo viya dussīlyaṃ' (immorality is like a cesspool)—by this is shown that an immoral person is indeed comparable to filth. 'Vacanaṃ' means unpleasant speech. 'In the same way as before' means in the way previously stated with phrases like 'immorality is like a cesspool,' and so forth. 'Sucimitto' means a friend who is pure due to purity of virtue and conduct. Because 'they go and proceed together' (saha ayanti pavattanti), they are 'companions' (sahāyā); thus he says 'those who go together' (sahagāmino).

Jigucchitabbasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Jigucchitabba Sutta is concluded.

8. Gūthabhāṇīsuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Gūthabhāṇī Sutta

28. Aṭṭhame gūthabhāṇīti gūthasadisavacanattā gūthabhāṇī. Yathā hi gūthaṃ nāma mahājanassa aniṭṭhaṃ hoti, evameva imassa puggalassa vacanaṃ devamanussānaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ hoti. Duggandhakathanti kilesāsucisaṃkiliṭṭhatāya gūthaṃ viya duggandhavāyanakathaṃ. Pupphabhāṇīti supupphasadisavacanattā pupphabhāṇī[V 2.0088]. Yathā hi phullāni vassikāni vā adhimuttikāni vā mahājanassa iṭṭhāni kantāni honti, evameva imassa puggalassa vacanaṃ devamanussānaṃ iṭṭhaṃ hoti kantaṃ. Pupphāni viyāti campakasumanādisugandhapupphāni viya. Sugandhakathanti sucigandhavāyanakathaṃ kilesaduggandhābhāvato. Madhubhāṇīti ettha “mudubhāṇī”tipi paṭhanti. Ubhayatthāpi hi madhuravacanoti attho. Yathā hi [M 2.0095] catumadhuraṃ nāma madhuraṃ paṇītaṃ, evameva imassa puggalassa vacanaṃ devamanussānaṃ madhuraṃ hoti. Madhurakathanti kaṇṇasukhatāya pemanīyatāya ca saddato atthato ca madhurasabhāvakathaṃ. Attahetu vāti attano vā hatthapādādicchedanaharaṇahetu. Parahetu vāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tenāha “attano vā”tiādi.

28. In the eighth, 'gūthabhāṇī' (foul-mouthed) is so called because his speech is like filth. Just as filth is unpleasant to the multitude, so too is the speech of this person unpleasant to gods and humans. 'Duggandhakathā' (foul-smelling talk) refers to talk that emits a foul odor like filth, due to being tainted with the impurity of defilements. 'Pupphabhāṇī' (flower-like speaker) is so called because his speech is like a beautiful flower. Just as fully bloomed jasmine or adhimuttaka flowers are pleasing and delightful to the multitude, so too is the speech of this person pleasing and delightful to gods and humans. 'Like flowers' means like fragrant blossoms such as campaka and sumana flowers. 'Sugandhakathā' (sweet-smelling talk) is talk that emits a pure fragrance, due to the absence of the foul odor of defilements. 'Madhubhāṇī' (honeyed speaker)—here, some also read 'mudubhāṇī' (gentle speaker). In both cases, the meaning is one who speaks sweetly. Just as the 'four sweets' are sweet and excellent, so too is the speech of this person sweet to gods and humans. 'Madhurakathā' (honeyed talk) refers to talk of a sweet nature in sound and meaning, due to being pleasant to the ear and endearing. 'For one’s own sake' means for the sake of the cutting off or taking away of one’s own hands, feet, and so forth. 'For another’s sake' follows the same principle. Hence he says, 'for one’s own sake,' and so forth.

“Nelaṅgoti kho, bhante, sīlānametaṃ adhivacana”nti sutte (saṃ. ni. 4.347) āgatattā vuttaṃ “ettha vuttasīlaṃ viyā”ti. Pūreti guṇānaṃ pāripūriyaṃ. Sukumārāti apharusatāya mudukā komalā. Purassāti ettha pura-saddo tannivāsivācako daṭṭhabbo “gāmo āgato”tiādīsu viya. Tenāha “nagaravāsīna”nti. Manaṃ appāyati vaḍḍhetīti manāpā. Tenāha “cittavuddhikarā”ti.

'Nelaṅgo (spotless), venerable sir, is a term for virtue,' as stated in the Sutta (Saṃ. Ni. 4.347), hence it is said, 'like the virtue mentioned here.' 'Pūreti' (fulfills) means the completion, the fullness of virtues. 'Sukumārā' (gentle) means soft and tender due to being uncoarse. 'Purassa': here, the word 'pura' should be understood as referring to its residents, just as in examples such as 'the village has come.' Hence, he says, 'for town-dwellers.' 'Manaṃ appāyati vaḍḍheti' (pleases and increases the mind)—thus it is 'manāpā' (pleasing). Therefore, he says, 'cittavuddhikarā' (mind-enhancing).

Gūthabhāṇīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Gūthabhāṇī Sutta is concluded.

9. Andhasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Andha Sutta

29. Navame andhotiādīsu pāḷipadesu paṭhamo diṭṭhadhammikabhogasaṃharaṇapaññācakkhuno ca samparāyikatthasādhanapaññācakkhuno ca abhāvā “andho”ti vuccati dutiyopi, tatiyo pana dvinnampi bhāvā “dvicakkhū”ti vuccati. Paññācakkhūti āyakosallabhūtā paññācakkhu. Tenāha “phātiṃ kareyyā”ti. Adhamuttameti adhame ceva uttame ca. Paṭipakkhavasenāti paṭipakkhassa atthitāvasena. Sukkasappaṭibhāgāti sukkadhammehi pahāyakehi sappaṭibhāgāti jāneyya. Kaṇhasappaṭibhāgāti kaṇhadhammehi pahātabbehi sappaṭibhāgāti jāneyya.

29. In the ninth, regarding the terms 'blind,' and so on, in the Pāli passages: the first is called 'blind' because of the absence of both the eye of wisdom for gathering wealth in this life and the eye of wisdom for securing benefits in the next life; the second is also called 'blind.' The third, however, possessing both, is called 'two-eyed.' 'The eye of wisdom' is the eye of wisdom that is skill in gain. Hence it is said, 'he would bring about prosperity.' 'Lowest and highest' means in the lowest and in the highest. 'By way of opposition' means by way of the existence of the opposite. 'Analogous to the bright' means one should understand it as analogous to bright qualities, which are abandoning. 'Analogous to the dark' means one should understand it as analogous to dark qualities, which are to be abandoned.

Tathājātikāti yādisehi saputtadāraparijanasañātimittabandhavaggaṃ attānaṃ sukheti pīṇeti, tādisā bhogāpi na santi. Puññāni ca na karotīti samaṇabrāhmaṇakapaṇaddhikayācakānaṃ santappanavasena puññāni na karoti. Ubhayatthāti ubhayasmiṃ loke, ubhayasmiṃ vā attheti viggahoti dassento “idhaloke”tiādimāha. Ubhayenāti vuttamatthaṃ [V 2.0089] yojetvā dassetuṃ “katha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmiṃ ṭhāneti yasmiṃyeva [M 2.0096] ṭhāne. Na socatīti sokahetūnaṃ tattha abhāvato na socati.

'Of such a kind' means: he does not have possessions of the kind by which he could make himself, together with his sons, wife, retinue, kinsmen, friends, and relatives, happy and content. 'And does not perform meritorious deeds' means: he does not perform meritorious deeds by way of satisfying ascetics, brahmins, the poor, travellers, and beggars. 'In both respects' means in both worlds, or 'in both meanings' is the analysis; showing this, he says 'in this world,' and so on. To connect and show the stated meaning, 'how?' and so on, is said. 'In whatever place' means in that very place. 'Does not grieve' means he does not grieve because the causes for sorrow are absent there.

Andhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Andha Sutta is concluded.

10. Avakujjasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Avakujja Sutta

30. Dasame avakujjapaññoti nikkujjapañño. Tenāha “adhomukhapañño”ti. Pubbapaṭṭhapanāti paṭhamārambho. Sanniṭṭhānanti kathāpariyosānaṃ. Appanāti desanāya niṭṭhāpanaṃ. Aneke vā anusandhiyoti yojetabbaṃ. Samādhi vātiādīsu lokuttaradhammā paramatthato sāsananti tadatthopādakasamādhi tassa ādīti vutto, tadāsannattā vipassanā, tassa mūlabhāvena ekadesattā maggo.

30. In the tenth, 'downward wisdom' means inverted wisdom. Therefore it is said, 'downward-facing wisdom.' 'Initial establishment' means the first beginning. 'Conclusion' means the end of the discourse. 'Application' means the completion of the teaching. 'Or many connections' should be connected. Regarding 'concentration, or,' and so on: the supramundane states are the teaching in the ultimate sense. Therefore, the concentration that produces that goal is said to be its beginning; due to its proximity, insight is mentioned; and because it is the root-part, the path is mentioned.

Sāsanassa pāripūrisuddhiyo nāma satthārā desitaniyāmeneva siddhā, tā panettha kathentassa vasena gahetabbāti dassetuṃ “anūnaṃ katvā desentī”ti, “niggaṇṭhiṃ katvā desentī”ti ca vuttaṃ. Tattha nijjaṭanti niggumbaṃ anākulaṃ. Niggaṇṭhinti gaṇṭhiṭṭhānarahitaṃ suviññeyyaṃ katvā.

The purities of the teaching’s fulfillment are accomplished only by the Teacher’s definitive instruction. Thus, to show that they should be understood in the way the speaker here explains, it is said, 'teaching without deficiency' and 'teaching without knots.' There, 'unentangled' means without thickets, without confusion. 'Without knots' means making it easily understandable by removing places for knots.

Ākiṇṇānīti ākiritvā saṃkiritvā ṭhapitānīti attho. Tenāha “pakkhittānī”ti. Ucchaṅgo viya ucchaṅgapañño puggalo daṭṭhabboti ucchaṅgasadisapaññatāya ucchaṅgapañño. Evaṃ paññā viya puggalopi ucchaṅgo viya hoti, tasmiṃ dhammānaṃ aciraṭṭhānatoti adhippāyena vuttaṃ. Yathā ca ucchaṅgasadisā paññā, evaṃ nikkujjakumbhasadisā paññā evāti daṭṭhabbā.

'Ākiṇṇāni' means scattered about, strewn around, placed in disarray. Therefore, it is said, 'thrown in.' A person with 'lap-wisdom' is so called because his wisdom is similar to a lap. Thus, just as the wisdom is like a lap, so too the person is like a lap; this is said with the intention that teachings do not remain long with him. And just as wisdom is like a lap, so it should be understood that wisdom is also like an overturned pot.

Saṃvidahanapaññāyāti “evaṃ kate idaṃ nāma bhavissatī”ti evaṃ taṃtaṃatthakiccaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ samatthatāya vicāraṇapaññāya rahito. Seyyoti seṭṭho pāsaṃso. Pubbabhāgapaṭipadanti cittavisuddhiādikaṃ ariyamaggassa adhigamāya pubbabhāgapaṭipattiṃ.

'Lacking planning wisdom' means he is devoid of the reflective wisdom capable of arranging various tasks and purposes, thinking, 'If this is done, such and such will result.' 'Excellent' means superior, praiseworthy. 'Preliminary practice' refers to the purification of mind and so on, the preliminary practice for attaining the noble path.

Avakujjasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Avakujja Sutta is concluded.

Puggalavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Individuals is concluded.

4. Devadūtavaggo

4. The Chapter on the Divine Messengers

1. Sabrahmakasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sabrahmaka Sutta

31. Catutthassa [M 2.0097][V 2.0090] paṭhame sabrahmakānīti saseṭṭhakāni. Yesanti yesaṃ kulānaṃ. Puttānanti puttehi. Pūjitasaddayogena hi idaṃ karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Tenāti āhārādinā. Paṭijaggitā gopitāti yathākālaṃ tassa tassa dātabbassa dānena veyyāvaccassa ca karaṇena paṭijaggitā ceva uppannānatthappaharaṇena gopitā ca honti. Tesanti mātāpitūnaṃ. Brahmādibhāvasādhanatthanti tesaṃ guṇānaṃ atthitāya loke brahmā nāma vuccati, ācariyo nāma vuccati, āhuneyyo nāma vuccati, te mātāpitūnaṃ puttakaṃ paṭilabhantīti dassanavasena nesaṃ brahmādibhāvasādhanatthaṃ “bahukārā”ti, vatvā taṃ tesaṃ bahukārataṃ nānākārato dassetuṃ “āpādakā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Mātāpitaro hi puttānaṃ jīvitassa āpādakā, sarīrassa posakā, ācārasamācārānaṃ sikkhāpakā sakalassapi imassa lokassa dassetāro. Tenāha “puttānaṃ hī”tiādi. Iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ tāva te dassentu, aniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ kathanti? Tampi dassetabbameva vajjanīyabhāvajānāpanatthaṃ.

31. In the fourth section, the first, 'sabrahmakāni' means 'with those who are superior.' 'Yesaṃ' means of which families. 'Puttānaṃ' means 'by sons,' for in connection with the word 'honored,' this is a genitive used in the sense of the instrumental. 'Tena' means by food and so on. 'Cared for and protected' means they are cared for by providing what should be given at the proper time and by performing services, and they are protected by warding off any harm that has arisen. 'Tesaṃ' refers to parents. To establish their status as Brahma and so on, it is said 'greatly beneficial.' This is because, due to their virtues, they are called 'Brahma,' 'teacher,' and 'worthy of offerings' in the world. To show their great benefit in various ways after having said 'greatly beneficial,' it is said 'givers of life,' and so on. For parents are the givers of life to their children, nurturers of their bodies, instructors in conduct and behavior, and revealers of this entire world. Therefore, it is said, 'for the children,' and so on. They show what is a desirable object. But what about an undesirable object? That too must be shown, for the purpose of making known what should be avoided.

Avijahitā hontīti tāsaṃ bhāvanāya brahmānaṃ brahmaloke uppannattā avijahitā honti bhāvanā. Lobhanīyavayasmiṃ paṭhamayobbane ativiya mudubhāvappattadassanatthaṃ satavihataggahaṇaṃ. Pāṭiyekkanti visuṃ. Iminā kāraṇenāti iminā yathāvuttena puttesu pavattitehi atikkamena mettādisamuppattisaṅkhātena kāraṇena.

'They are not abandoned' means the meditative cultivations are not abandoned, because through their cultivation, one is born as a Brahma in the Brahma world. The phrase 'a hundred times beaten' is used to show the attainment of extreme tenderness in the first stage of youth, which is delightful. 'Separately' means individually. 'By this reason' means by this reason as stated: by the surpassing love directed towards their children, designated as the arising of loving-kindness and so on.

Tharusippanti asisattikuntakalāpādiāyudhasippaṃ. Muddāgaṇanāti aṅgulisaṃkocanādinā hatthamuddāya gaṇanā. Ādisaddena pāṇādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Pacchācariyā nāma mātāpitūnaṃ santike uggahitagahaṭṭhavattasseva puggalassa yathāsakaṃ hatthācariyādīnaṃ sippaggāhāpananti katvā sabbapaṭhamaṃ ācariyā nāmāti yojetabbaṃ. Ānīya hutaṃ āhutaṃ. Pakārehi hutaṃ pāhutaṃ. Abhisaṅkhatanti tasseva vevacanaṃ.

'The art of the sword' refers to the skill of weapons such as swords, spears, lances, quivers, and so on. 'Counting by gestures' refers to calculation using hand gestures, such as by contracting the fingers. The word 'and so on' includes living beings and so on. 'Later teachers' are those who, after a person has learned the householder's duties from his parents, cause him to take up a craft from a craft-teacher, and so on, according to his ability; therefore, it should be understood that parents are called 'teachers first of all.' 'Āhuta' is an offering that is brought. 'Pāhuta' is an offering made with various preparations. 'Abhisaṅkhata' is a synonym for that very thing.

Namo kareyyāti sāyaṃ pātaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “idaṃ mayhaṃ uttamapuññakkhetta”nti namakkāraṃ kareyya. Tāya naṃ pāricariyāyāti ettha nanti nipātamattaṃ, yathāvuttaparicaraṇenāti attho[V 2.0091]. Atha vā pāricariyāyāti [M 2.0098] bharaṇakiccakaraṇakulavaṃsappatiṭṭhānāpanādinā pañcavidhaupaṭṭhānena. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'One should pay homage' means: in the evening and morning, one should go to attend upon them and pay homage, thinking, 'This is my supreme field of merit.' 'By that service to them'—here, 'naṃ' is merely a particle; the meaning is 'by the service as described.' Alternatively, 'by service' means through the fivefold attendance: providing sustenance, performing duties, establishing the family lineage, and so on. For this has been said—

“Pañcahi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi puttena puratthimā disā mātāpitaro paccupaṭṭhātabbā – ‘bhato nesaṃ bharissāmi, kiccaṃ nesaṃ karissāmi, kulavaṃsaṃ ṭhapessāmi, dāyajjaṃ paṭipajjāmi, atha vā pana petānaṃ kālakatānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ anuppadassāmī’ti. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi puttena puratthimā disā mātāpitaro paccupaṭṭhitā pañcahi ṭhānehi puttaṃ anukampanti, pāpā nivārenti, kalyāṇe nivesenti, sippaṃ sikkhāpenti, patirūpena dārena saṃyojenti, samaye dāyajjaṃ niyyādentī”ti (dī. ni. 3.267).

'In five ways, son of a householder, should a child attend to his parents as the eastern direction: “Having been supported by them, I will support them in return; I will perform their duties; I will maintain the family lineage; I will be worthy of the inheritance; furthermore, I will give an offering on behalf of departed ancestors.” When parents are attended to by their child in these five ways, son of a householder, they show compassion to their child in five ways: they restrain him from evil; they encourage him in what is good; they train him in a skill; they arrange a suitable marriage for him; and in due time, they hand over his inheritance to him.' (DN 31)

Apica yo mātāpitaro tīsu vatthūsu abhippasanne katvā sīlesu vā patiṭṭhāpetvā pabbajjāya vā niyojetvā upaṭṭhahati, ayaṃ mātāpitūpaṭṭhākānaṃ aggoti veditabbo. Sā panāyaṃ pāricariyā puttassa ubhayalokahitasukhāvahāti taṃ dassetuṃ “idheva naṃ pasaṃsanti, pecca sagge pamodatī”ti vuttaṃ. Pasaṃsantīti “ayaṃ puggalo matteyyo petteyyo saggasaṃvattaniyaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūretī”ti idheva naṃ pasaṃsanti. Āmodati ādito paṭṭhāya modappattiyā. Pamodati nānappakāramodasampavattiyā.

Furthermore, one who serves their parents by making them deeply confident in the three jewels, or by establishing them in virtue, or by encouraging them to go forth, should be recognized as the foremost among those who serve their parents. This service brings happiness and benefit to the child in both this world and the next, as it is said: 'Here they praise him, and after death, he rejoices in heaven.' They praise him here, saying: 'This person is respectful to mother and father, fulfilling the practice leading to heaven.' He rejoices (āmodati) from the beginning by attaining joy. He delights (pamodati) in the arising of manifold joy.

Sabrahmakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sabrahmaka Sutta is concluded.

2. Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta

32. Dutiye tathājātikoti tathāsabhāvo. Cittekaggatālābhoti cittekaggatāya adhigamo. Rūpameva kilesuppattiyā kāraṇabhāvato rūpanimittaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Sassatādinimittanti sassatucchedabhāvanimittaṃ. Puggalanimittanti puggalābhinivesananimittaṃ. Dhammanimittanti dhammārammaṇasaṅkhātaṃ nimittaṃ. “Siyā nu kho, bhante”ti therena puṭṭho bhagavā “siyā”ti avoca lokuttarasamādhippaṭilābhaṃ sandhāya. So hi nibbānaṃ santaṃ paṇītanti ca passati. Tenāha “idhānandā”tiādi.

32. In the second, 'of such a nature' means 'of such a characteristic.' 'Attainment of one-pointedness of mind' means the acquisition of one-pointedness of mind. The sign of form (rūpanimitta) is so called because form itself is the cause for the arising of defilements. This method applies to the rest as well. 'The sign of eternalism, etc.' means the sign of the state of eternalism and annihilation. 'The sign of a person' means the sign of clinging to a person. 'The sign of phenomena' means the sign reckoned as the object of phenomena. When asked by the elder, 'Could it be, venerable sir?' the Blessed One replied, 'It could be,' referring to the attainment of supramundane concentration. For he sees Nibbāna as peaceful and sublime. Therefore, he said, 'Here, Ānanda,' etc.

Nibbānaṃ [M 2.0099] santanti samāpattiṃ appetvāti nibbānaṃ santanti ābhujitvā phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā[V 2.0092]. Divasampītiādinā asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā accantasantapaṇītādibhāvaṃ dasseti. Aṭṭhavidheti “santaṃ paṇītaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho nibbāna”nti evaṃ aṭṭhavidhe ābhogasaññite samannāhāre. Niddhāraṇe cetaṃ bhummaṃ. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne…pe… labbhantevāti “idhānanda, bhikkhuno evaṃ hotī”ti āgate imasmiṃ suttappadese ekopi ābhogasamannāhāro cepi sabbe aṭṭhapi ābhogasamannāhārā labbhanteva samannāharataṃ atthāvahattā.

'Nibbāna is peaceful' means: having reflected 'Nibbāna is peaceful,' one enters the fruition attainment. By the phrase 'even for a day,' etc., it shows the utterly peaceful, sublime, and other qualities of the unconditioned element. 'In the eightfold': this refers to the eightfold reflection designated as reviewing, namely: 'peaceful, sublime, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' This is a locative of determination. 'In this place... they are indeed obtained' means: in this passage of the sutta where it says, 'Here, Ānanda, it occurs to a bhikkhu thus...', whether it is one reflection or all eight reflections, they are indeed obtained by those who reflect, because it is beneficial.

Ñāṇena jānitvāti vipassanāñāṇasahitena maggañāṇena jānitvā. Parāni ca oparāni ca cakkhādīni āyatanāni. Santatāyāti paṭippassaddhitāya. Kāyaduccaritādidhūmavirahitoti kāyaduccaritādi eva santāpanaṭṭhena dhūmo, tena virahito. Anīghoti apāpo. Jātijarāgahaṇeneva byādhimaraṇampi gahitamevāti tabbhāvabhāvatoti vuttaṃ.

'Having known with knowledge' means having known with the path knowledge accompanied by insight knowledge. 'Superior and inferior' refers to the sense bases such as the eye, both superior and inferior. 'Through continuity' means through tranquillisation. 'Free from the smoke of misconduct by body, etc.' means free from that which is smoke in the sense of tormenting, namely misconduct by body, etc. 'Without anguish' means without evil. By the taking up of birth and old age, sickness and death are also taken up; thus it is said, 'because they are of that same nature.'

Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta is concluded.

3. Sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta

33. Tatiye, “sāriputta, mayā saṃkhittena desitaṃ dhammaṃ tādisenapi na sukaraṃ viññātu”nti iminā adhippāyeneva vadanto therassa ñāṇaṃ sabbamatikkamaṃ. Aññātāro ca dullabhāti hi iminā sāmaññavacanena sāriputtattherampi antogadhaṃ katvā dassento tenapi attano desanāya duppaṭividdhabhāvaṃ dasseti.

33. In the third, when he speaks with the intention, 'Sāriputta, the Dhamma taught in brief by me is not easy to understand even by one such as you,' this shows that his teaching surpasses all the elder's knowledge. And by the general statement, 'Those who understand are rare,' he includes even the Elder Sāriputta, thereby showing the difficult-to-penetrate nature of his own teaching.

Sammāti hetunā kāraṇena. Tenāha “upāyenā”tiādi. Mānābhisamayāti mānassa dassanābhisamayā. Pahānābhisamayoti ca dassanābhisamayoti ca pariññābhisamayo vutto. Arahattamaggo hi pariññākiccasiddhiyā kiccavasena mānaṃ passati, asammohappaṭivedhavasenāti vuttaṃ hoti, ayamassa dassanābhisamayo. Tena diṭṭho pana pahānābhisamayo ca. Dassanābhisamayena hi pariññābhisamayameva pahīyati. Diṭṭhavisena diṭṭhasattānaṃ jīvitaṃ viya ayamassa pahānābhisamayo[M 2.0100]. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana pahānābhisamayassa dassanābhisamayanānantariyakattā “pahānābhisamayena”icceva vuttaṃ. Pahānābhisamaye hi gahite dassanābhisamayo gahitova hoti.

'Rightly' (sammā) means by a cause, by a reason. Hence it is said, 'by a method,' etc. 'Penetration of conceit' means the penetration of conceit by seeing. Both 'penetration by abandoning' and 'penetration by seeing' are called 'penetration by full understanding.' For the path of arahantship, by accomplishing the function of full understanding, sees conceit by way of its function; that is to say, by means of penetrating non-delusion. This is its penetration by seeing. And by that seeing, there is also penetration by abandoning. For through penetration by seeing, that which is to be fully understood is abandoned. This penetration of abandoning is like the life of beings seen by a snake with sight-poison. However, in the commentary, because the penetration of abandoning immediately follows the penetration of seeing, it is simply stated as 'through the penetration of abandoning.' For when the penetration of abandoning is grasped, the penetration of seeing is also grasped.

Antamakāsi [V 2.0093] dukkhassāti arahattamaggena mānassa pahīnattā ye ime “kāyabandhanassa anto jīrati (cūḷava. 278), haritantaṃ vā”ti (ma. ni. 1.304) evaṃ vuttaantimamariyādanto ca “antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.80; itivu. 91) evaṃ vuttalāmakanto ca “sakkāyo eko anto”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.103) evaṃ vuttakoṭṭhāsanto ca “esevanto dukkhassa sapaccayasaṅkhayā”ti evaṃ vuttakoṭṭhāsanto cāti cattāro antā, tesu sabbasseva vaṭṭadukkhassa aduṃ catutthakoṭisaṅkhātaṃ antamakāsi, paricchedaṃ parivaṭumaṃ akāsi, antimasamudayamattāvasesaṃ dukkhamakāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “vaṭṭadukkhassa antamakāsī”ti.

'He made an end of suffering': Since conceit is abandoned by the path of arahantship, this refers to the four kinds of 'end': (1) the end as an ultimate boundary, as in 'the end of the bodily bond decays' and 'the green end'; (2) the end as something inferior, as in 'this, bhikkhus, is the lowest of livelihoods'; (3) the end as a portion, as in 'the personal identity is one end'; and (4) the end as a portion, as in 'this is the end of suffering with the exhaustion of its cause.' Of these, he made an end—that which is reckoned as the fourth portion—of all the suffering of the cycle. He made a termination, a limitation. That is to say, he made suffering have only its final existence remaining. Therefore, it is said, 'he made an end of the suffering of the cycle.'

Nanu ca “pahāna”nti imassa niddese nibbānaṃ āgataṃ? Idha paṭippassaddhippahānasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaphalaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā niddesenāyaṃ vaṇṇanā virujjhatīti āha “niddese panā”tiādi. Tattha tāni padāni āgatānīti tasmiṃ niddese “pahānaṃ vūpasamaṃ paṭinissagga”ntiādīni (cūḷani. 75 udayamāṇavapucchāniddeso) padāni āgatāni.

But surely, in the explanation of 'abandonment,' does Nibbāna not come up? Here, the fruit of arahantship, known as abandonment by tranquilisation, is stated. Therefore, this commentary contradicts that explanation. Thus, it is said, 'but in the explanation,' etc. There, those terms have come; in that explanation, the terms 'abandonment, cessation, relinquishment,' and so on have come.

Dhammatakkapurejavanti iminā tasmiṃ catutthajjhānavimokkhe ṭhatvā jhānaṅgāni vipassitvā adhigataṃ arahattavimokkhaṃ vadati. Arahattavimokkhassa hi maggasampayuttasammāsaṅkappasaṅkhāto dhammatakko purejavo hoti.

By 'preceded by righteous thought,' he speaks of the liberation of arahantship, which is attained by abiding in the liberation of the fourth jhāna and seeing its factors with insight. For in the liberation of arahantship, righteous thought—reckoned as right intention associated with the path—is the forerunner.

Sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta is concluded.

4. Nidānasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Nidāna Sutta

34. Catutthe piṇḍakaraṇatthāyāti āyūhanavasena rāsikaraṇatthāya. Abhinnānīti ekadesenapi akhaṇḍitāni. Bhinnakālato paṭṭhāya hi bījaṃ bījakiccāya na upakappati. Apūtīnīti udakatemanena pūtibhāvaṃ na upagatāni. Pūtibījañhi bījatthāya na upakappati. Tenāha “pūtibhāvena abījattaṃ appattānī”ti. Na vātena na ca ātapena hatānīti [M 2.0101] vātena ca ātapena ca na hatāni, nirojataṃ na pāpitāni. Nirojañhi kasaṭabījaṃ bījatthāya na upakappati. Sārādānīti taṇḍulasārassa ādānato sārādāni. Nissārañhi bījaṃ bījatthāya na upakappati. Tenāha “gahitasārānī”ti, patiṭṭhitasārānīti attho. Sannicayabhāvena sukhaṃ sayitānīti cattāro māse koṭṭhapakkhittaniyāmeneva sukhasayitāni.

34. In the fourth, 'for the purpose of making a heap' means for the purpose of accumulating by way of effort. 'Unbroken' means not broken even in a single part. For from the time it is broken, a seed is no longer suitable for its function as a seed. 'Unspoiled' means not having become putrid through moisture. For a putrid seed is not suitable for its purpose as a seed. Thus it is said, 'not having reached the state of being a non-seed through putrefaction.' 'Not destroyed by wind or heat' means not destroyed by wind and heat, not rendered sapless. For a sapless, worthless seed is not suitable for its purpose as a seed. 'Possessing essence' means they possess essence because they have taken up the essence of the rice grain. For a seed without essence is not suitable for its purpose as a seed. Thus it is said, 'having taken up the essence,' which means 'with essence established.' 'Lying comfortably in storage' means lying comfortably for four months, in the same way as those regularly placed in a granary.

Kammavibhattīti [V 2.0094] kammavibhāgo. Diṭṭhadhammo vuccati paccakkhabhūto paccuppanno attabhāvo, tattha veditabbaphalaṃ kammaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ. Paccupannabhavato anantaraṃ veditabbaphalaṃ kammaṃ upapajjavedanīyaṃ. Aparapariyāyavedanīyanti diṭṭhadhammānantarabhavato aññasmiṃ attabhāvapariyāye attabhāvaparivatte veditabbaphalaṃ kammaṃ. Paṭipakkhehi anabhibhūtatāya paccayavisesena paṭiladdhavisesatāya ca balavabhāvappattā tādisassa pubbābhisaṅkhārassa vasena sātisayā hutvā pavattā paṭhamajavanacetanā tasmiṃyeva attabhāve phaladāyinī diṭṭhadhammavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Sā hi vuttākārena balavatī javanasantāne guṇavisesayuttesu upakārānupakāravasappavattiyā āsevanālābhena appavipākatāya ca paṭhamajavanacetanā itaradvayaṃ viya pavattasantānuparamāpekkhaṃ okāsalābhāpekkhañca kammaṃ na hotīti idheva pupphamattaṃ viya pavattivipākamattaṃ phalaṃ deti. Tathā asakkontanti kammassa vipākadānaṃ nāma upadhippayogādipaccayantarasamavāyeneva hotīti tadabhāvato tasmiṃyeva attabhāve vipākaṃ dātuṃ asakkontaṃ. Ahosikammanti ahosi eva kammaṃ, na tassa vipāko ahosi atthi bhavissati cāti evaṃ veditabbaṃ kammaṃ.

The analysis of kamma is the classification of kamma. The present life is called the directly experienced, present existence; the kamma whose fruit is to be experienced therein is kamma to be experienced in the present life. The kamma whose fruit is to be experienced immediately after the present existence is kamma to be experienced in the next life. 'Kamma to be experienced in a subsequent life' refers to kamma whose fruit is to be experienced in another turn of existence, in a different cycle of existence, other than the one immediately following the present life. The first javana-volition—which, by way of such a prior accumulation, has become pre-eminent, having attained a powerful state by not being overcome by opposing factors and by acquiring special conditions—gives its fruit in that very same existence; this is called kamma to be experienced in the present life. For it, being powerful in the manner described, occurring in a javana-continuum endowed with special qualities, proceeding by way of helpful and unhelpful circumstances, having gained repetition, and being of quick result, is not, unlike the other two, a kamma that awaits the cessation of the ongoing process and the gaining of an opportunity. Thus, it gives its fruit right here, a mere result in the course of life, like a mere flower. Similarly, 'unable' means that the giving of a kamma's fruit occurs only through the conjunction of other conditions such as the application of substrata; due to the absence of these, it is unable to give its fruit in that very same existence. 'Kamma that has become defunct' means the kamma has indeed been, but its fruit has not been, is not, and will not be; thus this kamma should be understood.

Atthasādhikāti dānādipāṇātipātādiatthassa nipphādikā. Kā pana sāti āha “sattamajavanacetanā”ti. Sā hi sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā vuttanayena paṭiladdhavisesā purimajavanacetanāhi laddhāsevanā ca samānā anantarattabhāve vipākadāyinī upapajjavedanīyakammaṃ nāma. Purimaupamāyayevāti migaluddakopamāyayeva.

'Accomplishing the purpose' means that which brings about the purpose of acts such as giving, etc., or killing living beings, etc. But what is that? It is said, 'the seventh javana-volition.' For that is the concluding volition, which, having attained distinction in the way described and having gained repetition from the preceding javana-volitions, gives fruit in the immediately following existence and is called kamma to be experienced in the next life. 'Just as in the previous simile' means, indeed, like the simile of the deer hunter.

Sati saṃsārappavattiyāti iminā asati saṃsārappavattiyaṃ ahosikammapakkhe tiṭṭhati vipaccanokāsassa abhāvatoti dīpeti. Yaṃ garukanti [M 2.0102] yaṃ akusalaṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ, kusalañca mahānubhāvaṃ kammaṃ. Kusalaṃ vā hi hotu akusalaṃ vā, yaṃ garukaṃ mātughātādikammaṃ vā mahaggatakammaṃ vā, tadeva paṭhamaṃ vipaccati. Tenāha “kusalākusalesu panā”tiādi. Yaṃ bahulanti yaṃ bahulaṃ abhiṇhaso kataṃ samāsevitaṃ. Tenāha “kusalākusalesu pana yaṃ bahulaṃ hotī”tiādi. Yadāsannaṃ nāma maraṇakāle anussaritaṃ kammaṃ, āsannakāle kate pana vattabbameva natthīti āha “yaṃ pana kusalākusalesu āsannamaraṇe”tiādi. Anussaritunti paribyattabhāvena anussarituṃ.

By 'when there is the continuation of saṃsāra,' it is shown that if there is no continuation of saṃsāra, it falls into the category of defunct kamma due to the absence of an opportunity for ripening. What is weighty is unwholesome kamma of great fault or wholesome kamma of great power. For whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, whatever is weighty kamma—such as matricide and so on, or kamma pertaining to the sublime sphere—that ripens first. Hence it is said, 'But among wholesome and unwholesome kammas…' and so on. What is habitual is that which is frequently performed and cultivated. Hence it is said, 'But among wholesome and unwholesome kammas, what is frequently done…' and so on. What is proximate is the kamma recollected at the time of death; as for what was done near the time of death, there is nothing to be said. Hence it is stated, 'But among wholesome and unwholesome kammas, at the approach of death…' and so on. 'Recollected' means to recollect it as being manifest.

Tesaṃ abhāveti tesaṃ yaṃgarukādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ kammānaṃ abhāve. Yattha katthaci vipākaṃ detīti paṭisandhijanakavasena vipākaṃ deti. Paṭisandhijanakavasena hi garukādikammacatukkaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha garukaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ vipaccati, garuke asati bahulīkataṃ, tasmiṃ asati yadāsannaṃ[V 2.0095], tasmiṃ asati “kaṭattā vā panā”ti vuttaṃ purimajātīsu katakammaṃ vipaccati. Bahulāsannapubbakatesu ca balābalaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Pāpato pāpantaraṃ kalyāṇañca, kalyāṇato kalyāṇantaraṃ pāpañca bahulīkataṃ. Tato mahatova pubbakatādi appañca bahulānussaraṇena vippaṭisārādijananato, paṭipakkhassa aparipuṇṇatāya āraddhavipākassa kammassa kammasesassa vā aparapariyāyavedanīyassa aparikkhīṇatāya santatiyā pariṇāmavisesatoti tehi tehi kāraṇehi āyūhitaphalaṃ paṭhamaṃ vipaccati. Mahānāradakassapajātake (jā. 2.22.1153 ādayo) videharañño senāpati alāto, bījako dāso, rājakaññā rucā ca ettha nidassanaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ bhagavatā –

In the absence of these, that is, in the absence of the three kammas beginning with the weighty. 'It gives its fruit somewhere or other' means it gives its fruit by way of generating rebirth-linking. For the fourfold kamma beginning with the weighty is spoken of with regard to generating rebirth-linking. Among these, the weighty kamma ripens first. In the absence of the weighty, the habitual ripens. In the absence of that, the proximate ripens. In the absence of that, the kamma done in previous lives, referred to as 'or because it was done,' ripens. And among the habitual, proximate, and previously done, their relative strength should be understood. From an evil action, another evil or a good action is made habitual; from a good action, another good or an evil action is made habitual. Then, the accumulated fruit ripens first for these various reasons: because a great previously done action is rendered minor by frequent recollection that generates remorse, etc.; because of the incompleteness of an opposing factor; because of the non-exhaustion of a kamma whose result has begun or of the remainder of a kamma to be experienced in a subsequent life; because of a special transformation in the continuum. In the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka (Jā. 2.22.1153ff), Alāta the general of King Videha, Bījaka the slave, and the princess Rucā are examples here. For thus it was spoken by the Blessed One—

“Tatrānanda, yvāyaṃ puggalo idha pāṇātipātī…pe… micchādiṭṭhi. Kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati, pubbe vāssa taṃ kataṃ hoti pāpakammaṃ dukkhavedanīyaṃ, pacchā vāssa taṃ kataṃ hoti pāpakammaṃ dukkhavedanīyaṃ, maraṇakāle vāssa hoti micchādiṭṭhi samattā samādinnā, tena so kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti –

“Here, Ānanda, a certain person is one who destroys life… holds wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of downfall, in hell. Either they have previously done an evil kamma that is to be experienced as painful, or they have later done an evil kamma that is to be experienced as painful, or at the time of death they have adopted and undertaken wrong view. Because of that, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of downfall, in hell.”

Ādi[M 2.0103]. Sabbaṃ mahākammavibhaṅgasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 3.303) vitthāretabbaṃ. Kiṃ bahunā. Yaṃ taṃ tathāgatassa mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇaṃ, tassevāyaṃ visayo, yadidaṃ tassa tassa kammassa tena tena kāraṇena pubbāparavipākatā samatthīyati.

And so on. The entire Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta (MN 136) should be elaborated. What more is there to say? That which is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the great analysis of kamma—this is its domain, namely, that for each and every kamma, for this or that reason, its ripening sooner or later is established.

Idāni janakādikammacatukkaṃ vibhajanto “janakaṃ nāmā”tiādimāha. Pavattiṃ na janetīti pavattivipākaṃ na janeti. Paṭhamanaye janakakammassa paṭisandhivipākamattasseva vuttattā tassa pavattivipākadāyakattampi anujānanto “aparo nayo”tiādimāha. Tattha paṭisandhidānādivasena vipākasantānassa nibbattakaṃ janakaṃ. Sukhadukkhasantānassa nāmarūpappabandhassa vā cirataraṃ pavattihetubhūtaṃ upatthambhakaṃ. Tenāha “sukhadukkhaṃ upatthambheti, addhānaṃ pavattetī”ti. Upapīḷakaṃ sukhadukkhappabandhe pavattamāne saṇikaṃ saṇikaṃ hāpeti. Tenāha “sukhadukkhaṃ pīḷeti bādheti, addhānaṃ pavattituṃ na detī”ti.

Now, analyzing the tetrad of kamma beginning with generative kamma, he says, “Generative kamma is so-called,” and so on. It does not generate the process—meaning, it does not generate the result in the course of existence. In the first method, since only the rebirth-linking result of generative kamma is mentioned, acknowledging also its ability to give results in the course of existence, he says, “Another method is as follows,” and so on. Herein, generative kamma is that which produces the continuum of results beginning with rebirth-linking. Supportive kamma is the cause of the long continuation of the continuum of pleasure and pain or of the stream of name and form. Hence it is said, “It supports pleasure and pain, it prolongs the duration.” Obstructive kamma gradually weakens the stream of pleasure and pain as it unfolds. Hence it is said, “It oppresses and harasses pleasure and pain, not allowing the duration to continue.”

Vātakāḷako mahallako core ghātetuṃ na sakkotīti so kira mahallakakāle ekappahārena sīsaṃ chindituṃ na sakkoti, dve tayo vāre paharanto manusse kilameti, tasmā te evamāhaṃsu. Anulomikaṃ khantiṃ paṭilabhitvāti sotāpattimaggassa orato anulomikaṃ khantiṃ labhitvā[V 2.0096]. Taruṇavacchāya gāviyā madditvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpitoti ekā kira yakkhinī dhenuvesena āgantvā ure paharitvā māresi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Nagare bhavo nāgariyo.

'The old man, weak as a withered tree, cannot kill the thief' means that, it is said, in his old age he could not cut off a head with a single blow; striking two or three times, he wearied the men, so they spoke thus. 'Having obtained conforming patience' means having obtained conforming patience just prior to the path of stream-entry. 'Having been crushed by a cow with a young calf and brought to the end of its life'—it is said that a certain yakkhiṇī came in the guise of a cow, struck him on the chest, and killed him; this was said in reference to that. 'One who is from the city' is a citizen (nāgariyo).

Ghātetvāti upacchinditvā. Kammassa upacchindanaṃ nāma tassa vipākappaṭibāhanamevāti āha “tassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā”ti. Tañca attano vipākuppattiyā okāsakaraṇanti vuttaṃ “attano vipākassa okāsaṃ karotī”ti. Vipaccanāya katokāsaṃ kammaṃ vipakkammeva nāma hotīti āha “evaṃ pana kammena kate okāse taṃ vipākaṃ uppannaṃ nāma vuccatī”ti. Upapīḷakaṃ aññassa vipākaṃ upacchindati, na sayaṃ attano vipākaṃ deti. Upaghātakaṃ pana dubbalakammaṃ upacchinditvā attano vipākaṃ uppādetīti ayametesaṃ viseso. Kiñci bahvābādhatādipaccayūpasannipātena vipākassa vibādhakaṃ upapīḷakaṃ, tathā vipākasseva upacchedakaṃ. Upaghātakakammaṃ pana upaghātetvā attano vipākassa okāsakaraṇena vipaccane [M 2.0104] sati janakameva siyā. Janakādibhāvo nāma vipākaṃ pati icchitabbo, na kammaṃ patīti vipākasseva upaghātakatā yuttā viya dissati, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ.

‘Having destroyed’ means ‘having cut off.’ The cutting off of kamma means the very obstruction of its result, as it is said: ‘having obstructed its result.’ And that is said to be the making of an opportunity for the arising of one’s own result, as it is said: ‘it makes an opportunity for its own result.’ Kamma for which an opportunity has been made to ripen is called ‘ripened kamma,’ as it is said: ‘but when an opportunity is thus made by kamma, that result is said to have arisen.’ Oppressive kamma cuts off another’s result but does not itself give its own result. Destructive kamma, however, having cut off a weak kamma, produces its own result—this is the distinction between them. Something that obstructs a result due to the convergence of conditions such as severe affliction is oppressive kamma; likewise, that which cuts off the result itself. Destructive kamma, however, by destroying and making an opportunity for its own result, may indeed be generative when ripening occurs. The nature of being generative and so forth should be understood in relation to the result, not in relation to the kamma. Thus, it seems that destructiveness is properly spoken of only in relation to the result—this should be investigated.

Aparo nayo – yasmiṃ kamme kate paṭisandhiyaṃ pavatte ca vipākakaṭattārūpānaṃ uppatti hoti, taṃ janakaṃ. Yasmiṃ pana kate aññena janitassa iṭṭhassa vā aniṭṭhassa vā phalassa vibādhakavicchedakapaccayānuppattiyā upabrūhanapaccayuppattiyā janakasāmatthiyānurūpaṃ parisuddhiciratarappabandhā hoti, taṃ upatthambhakaṃ. Janakena nibbattitaṃ kusalaphalaṃ vā akusalaphalaṃ vā yena paccanīkabhūtena rogadhātuvisamatādinimittatāya vibādhayati, taṃ upapīḷakaṃ. Yena pana kammunā janakasāmatthiyavasena ciratarappabandhārahampi samānaṃ phalaṃ vicchedakapaccayuppattiyā upahaññati vicchijjati, taṃ upaghātakanti ayamettha sāro.

Another method: The kamma which, when performed, gives rise to resultant mental aggregates and kamma-born matter at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence—that is generative kamma. But that kamma is supportive which, when performed, ensures that the desirable or undesirable fruit generated by another kamma has a pure and long-lasting continuity, in accordance with the generative kamma's capacity, by preventing the arising of obstructing and cutting-off conditions and by the arising of strengthening conditions. The wholesome or unwholesome result produced by generative kamma is obstructed by an opposing kamma, which, through factors such as disease and the imbalance of elements, causes affliction—that is oppressive kamma. And the kamma by which a result, though capable of a long-lasting continuity according to the generative kamma's potential, is instead harmed and cut off by the arising of disruptive conditions—that is destructive kamma. This is the essence here.

Tattha keci dutiyassa kusalabhāvaṃ itthattamāgatassa appābādhadīghāyukatāsaṃvattanavasena, pacchimānaṃ dvinnaṃ akusalabhāvaṃ bahvābādhaappāyukatāsaṃvattanavasena vaṇṇenti. Tathā ca vuttaṃ majjhimanikāye cūḷakammavibhaṅgasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.290) –

Therein, some describe the wholesome nature of the second kamma, which has come to be in such a state, as conducive to good health and long life, and the unwholesome nature of the last two as conducive to much sickness and short life. And thus it is said in the commentary to the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya:

“Cattāri hi kammāni – upapīḷakaṃ, upacchedakaṃ, janakaṃ, upatthambhakanti. Balavakammena hi nibbattaṃ pavatte upapīḷakaṃ āgantvā atthato evaṃ vadati nāma ‘sacāhaṃ paṭhamataraṃ jāneyyaṃ, na te idha nibbattituṃ dadeyyaṃ, catūsuyeva taṃ apāyesu nibbattāpeyyaṃ. Hotu, tvaṃ yattha katthaci nibbatta, ahaṃ upapīḷakakammaṃ nāma taṃ pīḷetvā [V 2.0097] nirojaṃ niyūsaṃ kasaṭaṃ karissāmī’ti. Tato paṭṭhāya taṃ tādisaṃ karoti. Kiṃ karoti? Parissayaṃ upaneti, bhoge vināseti.

“There are indeed four kinds of kamma: oppressive, destructive, generative, and supportive. For when the result produced by a strong kamma is occurring, the oppressive kamma comes and speaks thus in essence, as it were: ‘If I had known sooner, I would not have allowed you to arise here. I would have made you arise in the four woeful states. Very well, wherever you have arisen, I, called oppressive kamma, will torment you, making you without health, without vitality, and worthless.’ From then on, it does just that. What does it do? It brings hardship and destroys possessions.

“Tattha dārakassa mātukucchiyaṃ nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya mātu assādo vā sukhaṃ vā na hoti, mātāpitūnaṃ pīḷāva uppajjati. Evaṃ parissayaṃ upaneti. Dārakassa pana mātukucchimhi nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya gehe bhogā udakaṃ patvā loṇaṃ viya rājādīnaṃ vasena nassanti, kumbhadohanadhenuyo [M 2.0105] khīraṃ na denti, sūratā goṇā caṇḍā honti, kāṇā honti, khañjā honti, gomaṇḍale rogo patati, dāsādayo vacanaṃ na karonti, vāpitaṃ sassaṃ na jāyati, gehagataṃ gehe, araññagataṃ araññe nassati, anupubbena ghāsacchādanamattaṃ dullabhaṃ hoti, gabbhaparihāro na hoti, vijātakāle mātu thaññaṃ chijjati, dārako parihāraṃ alabhanto pīḷito nirojo niyūso kasaṭo hoti. Idaṃ upapīḷakakammaṃ nāma.

“Therein, from the time the child has arisen in the mother’s womb, the mother experiences no enjoyment or comfort, and only affliction arises for the parents. Thus, it brings hardship. Moreover, from the time the child has arisen in the mother’s womb, the household’s wealth diminishes like salt that has reached water, due to kings and the like. Milk cows give no milk; valiant oxen become fierce, blind, or lame; disease falls upon the herd of cattle; servants do not obey orders; sown crops do not grow; goods kept in the house perish in the house, and those kept in the forest perish in the forest. Gradually, even basic food and clothing become scarce; proper care during pregnancy is lacking; and at the time of birth the mother’s milk ceases. The child, not receiving care, becomes afflicted, without health, without vitality, and worthless. This is called oppressive kamma.”

“Dīghāyukakammena pana nibbattassa upacchedakakammaṃ āgantvā āyuṃ chindati. Yathā hi puriso aṭṭhusabhagamanaṃ katvā saraṃ khipeyya, tamañño dhanuto muttamattaṃ muggarena paharitvā tattheva pāteyya, evaṃ dīghāyukakammena nibbattassa upacchedakakammaṃ āyuṃ chindati. Kiṃ karoti? Corānaṃ aṭaviṃ paveseti, vāḷamacchodakaṃ otāreti, aññataraṃ vā pana saparissayaṭhānaṃ upaneti. Idaṃ upacchedakakammaṃ nāma. ‘Upaghātaka’ntipi etasseva nāmaṃ. Paṭisandhinibbattakaṃ pana kammaṃ janakakammaṃ nāma. Appabhogakulādīsu nibbattassa bhogasampadādikaraṇena upatthambhakakammaṃ upatthambhakakammaṃ nāma.

“However, for one born as a result of long-life kamma, destructive kamma arrives and cuts off their lifespan. Just as a man might shoot an arrow a distance of eight usabhas, and another might strike it with a hammer just as it is released from the bow and make it fall right there—so too, destructive kamma cuts short the life of one born as a result of long-life kamma. What does it do? It sends them into a forest of thieves, makes them go down into water with fierce fish, or brings them to some other perilous place. This is called destructive kamma. ‘Upaghātaka’ kamma is also its name. Kamma that produces rebirth-linking is called generative kamma. For one born into a family lacking possessions, kamma that supports them by bringing wealth and so on is called supportive kamma.

“Parittakammenapi nibbattaṃ etaṃ pavatte pāṇātipātādiviratikammaṃ āgantvā atthato evaṃ vadati nāma ‘sacāhaṃ paṭhamataraṃ jāneyyaṃ, na te idha nibbattituṃ dadeyyaṃ, devalokeyeva taṃ nibbattāpeyyaṃ, hotu, tvaṃ yattha katthaci nibbatta, ahaṃ upatthambhakakammaṃ nāma upatthambhaṃ te karissāmī’ti upatthambhaṃ karoti. Kiṃ karoti? Parissayaṃ nāseti, bhoge uppādeti.

“For one born from even a minor kamma, when this kamma of abstaining from killing living beings and so on occurs, it comes and speaks thus in essence: ‘If I had known sooner, I would not have allowed you to be born here. I would have caused you to be born in the heavenly world itself. Very well, wherever you have been born, I, called supportive kamma, will give you support.’ And it gives support. What does it do? It eliminates dangers and generates wealth.

“Tattha dārakassa mātukucchiyaṃ nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya mātāpitūnaṃ sukhameva sātameva hoti. Yepi pakatiyā manussāmanussaparissayā honti, te sabbe apagacchanti[V 2.0098]. Evaṃ parissayaṃ nāseti. Dārakassa pana mātukucchimhi nibbattakālato paṭṭhāya gehe bhogānaṃ pamāṇaṃ na hoti, nidhikumbhiyo puratopi pacchatopi gehaṃ parivaṭṭamānā pavisanti. Mātāpitaro [M 2.0106] parehi ṭhapitadhanassapi sammukhībhāvaṃ gacchanti, dhenuyo bahukhīrā honti, goṇā sukhasīlā honti, vappaṭṭhāne sassāni sampajjanti, vaḍḍhiyā vā sampayuttaṃ, tāvakālikaṃ vā dinnaṃ dhanaṃ acoditā sayameva āharitvā denti, dāsādayo subbacā honti, kammantā na parihāyanti, dārako gabbhato paṭṭhāya parihāraṃ labhati, komārikavejjā sannihitāva honti. Gahapatikule jāto seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ, amaccakulādīsu jāto senāpatiṭṭhānādīni labhati. Evaṃ bhoge uppādeti. So aparissayo sabhogo ciraṃ jīvati. Idaṃ upatthambhakakammaṃ nāma. Imesu catūsu purimāni dve akusalāneva, janakaṃ kusalampi akusalampi, upatthambhakaṃ kusalamevā”ti.

“Therein, from the time the child has arisen in the mother’s womb, the parents experience only happiness and ease. Even those dangers that normally come from humans and non-humans all depart. Thus, it removes dangers. Moreover, from the time the child has arisen in the mother’s womb, the measure of wealth in the household becomes limitless. Treasure pots enter the house, circling it from the front and the back. The parents gain access to wealth deposited even by others; cows yield abundant milk; bulls become docile; crops flourish in the fields; wealth connected with interest or given for a time is brought back and handed over of its own accord without being asked for; servants and others become obedient; work does not decline; the child receives care from the womb itself; and pediatric physicians are always present. If born in a householder’s family, he attains the position of a chief merchant; if born in a minister’s family or the like, he attains positions such as army commander. Thus, it generates wealth. He lives long, free from danger and endowed with riches. This is called supportive kamma. Among these four, the first two are only unwholesome, the generative can be either wholesome or unwholesome, and the supportive is solely wholesome.”

Ettha vibādhūpaghātā nāma kusalavipākamhi na yuttāti adhippāyena “dve akusalānevā”ti vuttaṃ. Devadattādīnaṃ pana nāgādīnaṃ ito anuppadinnayāpanakapetānañca narakādīsu akusalavipākūpatthambhanūpapīḷanūpaghātakāni santīti catunnampi kusalākusalabhāvo na virujjhati. Evañca katvā yā bahūsu ānantariyesu katesu ekena gahitappaṭisandhikassa itaresaṃ tassa anubalappadāyitā vuttā, sāpi samatthitā hoti.

Here, the phrase ‘the two are unwholesome’ is stated with the intention that obstruction and harm are not fitting in connection with wholesome results. However, for Devadatta and others, as well as for nāgas and for departed spirits who are sustained by what is not given from here, there exist in hell and other realms supportive, oppressive, and destructive unwholesome results. Thus, even in the case of these four, the nature of wholesome and unwholesome is not contradicted. And having done so, the statement that, among the many ānantarika deeds, the one that effects rebirth supports the others—this too is established.

Suttantapariyāyena ekādasa kammāni vibhajitvā idāni abhidhammapariyāpannaṃ dassento “atthekaccāni pāpakāni kammasamādānānī”tiādinā vibhaṅgapāḷiṃ (vibha. 810) dasseti. Tattha gatisampattipaṭibāḷhānīti gatisampattiyā paṭibāhitāni nivāritāni paṭisedhitāni. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Tattha ca gatisampattīti sampannagati devaloko ca manussaloko ca. Gativipattīti vipannagati cattāro apāyā. Upadhisampattīti attabhāvasamiddhi. Upadhivipattīti hīnaattabhāvatā. Kālasampattīti surājasumanussakālasaṅkhāto sampannakālo. Kālavipattīti durājadummanussakālasaṅkhāto vipannakālo. Payogasampattīti sammāpayogo. Payogavipattīti micchāpayogo.

Now, having classified the eleven kinds of kamma according to the Suttanta method, it now shows what is included in the Abhidhamma method by citing the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi (Vibh. 810), beginning with ‘There are some evil actions undertaken.’ Herein, ‘hindered by accomplishment of destiny’ means obstructed, prevented, or opposed by accomplishment of destiny. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Herein, accomplishment of destiny (gatisampatti) refers to accomplished destinies, the deva world and the human world. Failure of destiny (gativipatti) refers to failed destinies, the four woeful planes. Accomplishment of basis (upadhisampatti) means success in one’s own being. Failure of basis (upadhivipatti) means inferiority of one’s own being. Accomplishment of time (kālasampatti) refers to accomplished time, reckoned as the time of good kings and virtuous people. Failure of time (kālavipatti) refers to failed time, reckoned as the time of wicked kings and immoral people. Accomplishment of endeavor (payogasampatti) means right endeavor. Failure of endeavor (payogavipatti) means wrong endeavor.

Idāni [M 2.0107] yathāvuttapāḷiyā atthaṃ dassento “tatthā”tiādimāha. Tattha aniṭṭhārammaṇānubhavanārahe kamme vijjamāneyevāti iminā aniṭṭhārammaṇānubhavananimmittakassa pāpakammassa sabbhāvaṃ dasseti. Taṃ kammanti taṃ pāpakaṃ kammaṃ. Ekaccassa hi aniṭṭhārammaṇānubhavananimittaṃ [V 2.0099] bahupāpakammaṃ vijjamānampi gativipattiyaṃ ṭhitasseva vipaccati. Yadi pana so ekena kalyāṇakammena gatisampattiyaṃ devesu vā manussesu vā nibbatteyya, tādise ṭhāne akusalassa vāro natthi, ekantaṃ kusalassevāti taṃ kammaṃ gatisampattipaṭibāḷhaṃ na vipaccati. Patibāhitaṃ hutvāti bādhitaṃ hutvā. Attabhāvasamiddhiyanti sarīrasampattiyaṃ. Kiliṭṭhakammassāti hatthimeṇḍaassabandhakagopālakādikammassa. Palāyitabbayuttakāleti hatthiādipaccatthikasamāgamakāle. Lañjaṃ detīti evaṃ me bādhataṃ paresaṃ vase na hotīti deti. Corikayuttakāleti pakkhabalādīnaṃ labbhamānakāle. Antarakappeti pariyosānappatte antarakappe.

Now, explaining the meaning of the aforementioned Pāli text, he begins with 'here.' Here, the phrase 'when there exists kamma fit to experience undesirable objects' indicates the existence of unwholesome kamma that is the cause of experiencing undesirable objects. That kamma—that unwholesome kamma. For some, though much unwholesome kamma exists that is the cause of experiencing undesirable objects, it ripens only when one is in an unfortunate destination. However, if that person were to be reborn in a fortunate destination among devas or humans due to some wholesome kamma, in such a case, there is no opportunity for the unwholesome; it is entirely the wholesome. Thus, that kamma, being hindered by a fortunate destination, does not ripen. 'Being hindered' means being obstructed. 'Perfection of one’s being' refers to bodily well-being. 'Defiled kamma' refers to the kamma of elephant-drivers, shepherds, horse-trainers, cattle-herders, and so on. 'Time for flight' refers to the time of encountering enemies like elephants. 'He gives a bribe' means he gives it thinking, 'May I not be oppressed thus and fall into the power of others.' 'Time for thievery' refers to the time when opportunities for theft, such as obtaining the strength of a faction, arise. 'He shortens the intermediate aeon' means he shortens it when the intermediate aeon is nearing its end.

Abhidhammanayena soḷasa kammāni vibhajitvā paṭisambhidāmaggapariyāyena (paṭi. ma. 1.234-235) dvādasa kammāni vibhajitvā dassetuṃ “aparānipī”tiādimāha. Tattha atītabhavesu katassa kammassa atītabhavesuyeva vipakkavipākaṃ gahetvā “ahosi kammaṃ ahosi kammavipāko”ti vuttanti āha “yaṃ kammaṃ atīte āyūhita”ntiādi. Vipākavāranti vipaccanāvasaraṃ vipākavāraṃ. “Vipākavāraṃ labhatī”ti iminā vuttamevatthaṃ “paṭisandhiṃ janesī”tiādinā vibhāveti. Tattha paṭisandhiṃ janesīti iminā ca paṭisandhidāyakassa kammassa pavattivipākadāyitāpi vuttā hoti. Pavattivipākasseva pana dāyakaṃ rūpajanakasīsena vadati. Tasseva atītassa kammassa diṭṭhadhammavedanīyassa upapajjavedanīyassa ca paccayavekallena atītabhavesuyeva avipakkavipākañca, atīteyeva parinibbutassa diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaupapajjavedanīyaaparapariyāyavedanīyassa kammassa avipakkavipākañca gahetvā “ahosi kammaṃ nāhosi kammavipāko”tipi vuttanti āha “yaṃ pana vipākavāraṃ na labhī”tiādi.

Now, to show the sixteen kinds of kamma analyzed by the Abhidhamma method, and the twelve kinds of kamma analyzed by the exposition of the Path of Discrimination (Paṭis. Ma. 1.234-235), he begins with 'furthermore,' and so on. Therein, taking the result of kamma done in past existences that ripened in those very past existences, it is said, 'There was kamma; there was the result of kamma.' This is stated as, 'That kamma which was accumulated in the past,' and so on. 'Vipākavāra' means the turn for ripening, the opportunity for ripening. The meaning conveyed by 'attains the turn for ripening' is further explained by 'generated rebirth-linking,' and so on. Here, by 'generated rebirth-linking,' it is also stated that the kamma that gives rebirth-linking also gives rise to results during the course of existence. However, it speaks of the giver of results during existence by way of the generator of material form. Taking the unripened result of that same past kamma—which was to be experienced in that very life or in the next—due to the lack of conditions in past existences, and taking the unripened result of kamma—which was to be experienced in that very life, the next life, or in subsequent existences—for one who attained final Nibbāna in the past, it is also said, 'There was kamma, but there was no result of kamma.' This is stated as, 'But that which did not obtain the turn for ripening,' and so on.

Atītasseva kammassa avipakkavipākassa paccuppannabhave paccayasampattiyā vipaccamānaṃ vipākaṃ gahetvā “ahosi kammaṃ atthi kammavipāko”ti vuttanti āha “yaṃ pana atīte āyūhita”ntiādimāha. Atītasseva kammassa [M 2.0108] atikkantavipākakālassa ca paccuppannabhave parinibbāyantassa ca avipaccamānavipākaṃ gahetvā “ahosi kammaṃ natthi kammavipāko”ti vuttanti āha “aladdhavipākavāra”ntiādi. Atītasseva kammassa vipākārahassa avipakkavipākassa anāgatabhave paccayasampattiyā vipaccitabbaṃ vipākaṃ gahetvā “ahosi kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko”ti vuttanti dassento “yaṃ pana atīte āyūhita”ntiādimāha. Atītasseva kammassa atikkantavipākakālassa ca anāgatabhave parinibbāyitabbassa avipaccitabbavipākañca gahetvā “ahosi kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko”ti [V 2.0100] vuttanti āha “yaṃ anāgate vipākavāraṃ na labhissatī”tiādi. Evaṃ tāva atītakammaṃ atītapaccuppannānāgatavipākāvipākavasena chadhā dassitaṃ.

Taking the result of past kamma whose result did not ripen, which is ripening in the present existence due to the completeness of conditions, it is said, 'There was kamma; there is the result of kamma.' This is stated by 'But that which was accumulated in the past,' and so on. Taking the unripened result of past kamma whose time for ripening has passed, and for one who is attaining final Nibbāna in the present existence, it is said, 'There was kamma; there is no result of kamma.' This is stated by 'The turn for ripening was not obtained,' and so on. Showing that it is said, 'There was kamma; there will be the result of kamma,' taking the result of past kamma that is fit for ripening but whose result did not ripen, which is to ripen in a future existence due to the completeness of conditions, he says, 'But that which was accumulated in the past,' and so on. Taking the unripened result of past kamma whose time for ripening has passed, and for one who will attain final Nibbāna in a future existence, it is said, 'There was kamma; there will be no result of kamma.' This is stated by 'But that which will not obtain the turn for ripening in the future,' and so on. Thus, past kamma has been shown in six ways by way of its results and non-ripening in the past, present, and future.

Idāni paccuppannabhave katassa diṭṭhadhammavedanīyassa idheva vipaccamānaṃ vipākaṃ gahetvā “atthi kammaṃ atthi kammavipāko”ti vuttanti dassento “yaṃ pana etarahi āyūhita”ntiādimāha. Yaṃ pana etarahi vipākavāraṃ na labhatītiādinā tasseva paccuppannassa kammassa paccayavekallena idha avipaccamānañca diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyantassa idha avipaccamānañca vipākaṃ gahetvā “atthi kammaṃ natthi kammavipāko”ti vuttanti dasseti. Paccuppannasseva kammassa upapajjavedanīyassa aparapariyāyavedanīyassa ca anāgatabhave vipaccitabbavipākaṃ gahetvā “atthi kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko”ti vuttanti āha “yaṃ pana etarahi āyūhitaṃ anāgate vipākavāraṃ labhissatī”tiādi. Paccuppannasseva kammassa upapajjavedanīyassa paccayavekallena anāgatabhave avipaccitabbañca anāgatabhave parinibbāyitabbassa aparapariyāyavedanīyassa avipaccitabbañca vipākaṃ gahetvā “atthi kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko”ti vuttanti āha “yaṃ pana vipākavāraṃ na labhissatī”tiādi.

Now, showing that it is said, 'There is kamma; there is the result of kamma,' taking the ripening result here itself of the kamma done in the present existence, which is to be experienced in this very life, he says, 'But that which is now accumulated,' and so on. By 'But that which does not obtain the turn for ripening now,' and so on, he shows that it is said, 'There is kamma; there is no result of kamma,' taking the unripened result here itself for that same present kamma due to the lack of conditions, and taking the unripened result here itself for one who is attaining final Nibbāna in this very life. He says, 'But that which is now accumulated will obtain the turn for ripening in the future,' and so on, showing that it is said, 'There is kamma; there will be the result of kamma,' taking the result of that same present kamma, which is to be experienced upon rebirth or in subsequent existences, that is to ripen in a future existence. He says, 'But that which will not obtain the turn for ripening,' and so on, showing that it is said, 'There is kamma; there will be no result of kamma,' taking the result of that same present kamma, which is to be experienced upon rebirth, that will not ripen in a future existence due to the lack of conditions, and taking the result of kamma to be experienced in subsequent existences that will not ripen for one who will attain final Nibbāna in a future existence.

Evañca paccuppannakammaṃ paccuppannānāgatavipākāvipākavasena catudhā dassetvā idāni anāgatabhave katassa kammassa anāgate vipaccitabbavipākaṃ gahetvā “bhavissati kammaṃ bhavissati kammavipāko”ti vuttanti dassento “yaṃ panānāgate āyūhissatī”tiādimāha. Tasseva anāgatassa kammassa paccayavekallena avipaccitabbañca anāgatabhave parinibbāyitabbassa avipaccitabbañca vipākaṃ gahetvā “bhavissati kammaṃ na bhavissati kammavipāko”ti vuttanti āha “yaṃ pana vipākavāraṃ na labhissatī”tiādi[M 2.0109]. Evaṃ anāgatakammaṃ anāgatavipākāvipākavasena dvidhā dassitaṃ. Evantiādinā yathāvuttadvādasakammāni nigameti.

Having thus shown present kamma as fourfold by way of present and future results and non-ripening, now, showing that it is said, 'There will be kamma; there will be the result of kamma,' taking the result of kamma done in a future existence that is to ripen in the future, he says, 'But that which one will accumulate in the future,' and so on. Taking the result of that same future kamma that is not to be ripened due to a deficiency of conditions, and the result that is not to be ripened for one who is to attain final Nibbāna in a future existence, he says, 'But that which will not obtain the turn for ripening,' and so on, showing that it is said, 'There will be kamma; there will be no result of kamma.' Thus, future kamma is shown as twofold by way of future results and non-ripening. By 'Thus,' and so on, he concludes the twelve kinds of kamma as stated.

Idāni sabbesu yathāvuttappabhedesu kammesu yāni abhidhammanayena vibhattāni soḷasa kammāni, yāni ca paṭisambhidāmaggapariyāyena vibhattāni dvādasa kammāni, tāni sabbāni suttantikapariyāyena vibhattesu ekādasavidhesuyeva kammesu antogadhāni, tāni ca diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaupapajjavedanīyaaparapariyāyavedanīyesu tīsuyeva antogadhānīti dassento “iti imāni cevā”tiādimāha. Tattha attano ṭhānā osakkitvāti attano yathāvuttadvādasasoḷasappabhedasaṅkhātaṭṭhānato parihāpetvā, taṃ taṃ pabhedaṃ hitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekādasa kammāniyeva [V 2.0101] bhavantīti taṃsabhāvānaṃyeva kammānaṃ dvādasadhā soḷasadhā ca vibhajitvā vuttattā evamāha. Yasmā ekādasadhā vuttakammāni diṭṭhadhammavedanīyāni vā siyuṃ upapajjavedanīyāni vā aparapariyāyavedanīyāni vā, tasmā vuttaṃ “tīṇiyeva kammāni hontī”ti.

Now, showing that among all the types of kamma as previously explained, the sixteen kammas classified according to the Abhidhamma method, and the twelve kammas classified according to the Paṭisambhidāmagga method—all these are included within the eleven types of kammas classified according to the Suttanta method, and they are included within just three types: those to be experienced in this life, those to be experienced in the next life, and those to be experienced in subsequent existences—he begins with 'Thus, these indeed,' and so on. Here, 'having fallen away from their own position' means having abandoned their own position, which is reckoned as the twelve or sixteen divisions as previously stated; that is to say, having abandoned that particular division. He says, 'There are only eleven kammas,' because these kammas, being of that nature, are spoken of as divided into twelve or sixteen parts. Since the kammas explained as elevenfold may be either to be experienced in this life, to be experienced in the next life, or to be experienced in subsequent existences, therefore it is said, 'There are only three kammas.'

Tesaṃ saṅkamanaṃ natthīti tesaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādīnaṃ saṅkamanaṃ natthi, saṅkamanaṃ upapajjavedanīyādibhāvāpatti. Tenāha “yathāṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhantī”ti, attano diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādiṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhantīti attho. Diṭṭhadhammavedanīyameva hi paṭhamajavanacetanā, upapajjavedanīyameva sattamajavanacetanā, majjhe pañca aparapariyāyavedanīyamevāti natthi tesaṃ aññamaññaṃ saṅgaho, tasmā attano attano diṭṭhadhammavedanīyādisabhāveyeva tiṭṭhanti. Teneva bhagavatā – “diṭṭhe vā dhamme, upapajja vā, apare vā pariyāye”ti tayo vikappā dassitā. Tenevāha “diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ kamma”ntiādi. Tattha “diṭṭhe vā dhamme”ti satthā na vadeyyāti asati niyāme na vadeyya. Yasmā pana tesaṃ saṅkamanaṃ natthi, niyatasabhāvā hi tāni, tasmā satthā “diṭṭhe vā dhamme”tiādimavoca.

For them, there is no transition: that is, for the kamma to be experienced in this very life, and so on, there is no transition. Transition means becoming kamma to be experienced upon rebirth, and so forth. Therefore, it is said, 'They remain just where they are,' meaning they remain in their own state of being kamma to be experienced in this very life, and so on. For the first javana consciousness is indeed to be experienced in this very life, the seventh javana consciousness is indeed to be experienced upon rebirth, and the five in between are indeed to be experienced in subsequent existences. There is no mutual intermingling among them. Therefore, they remain in their own inherent nature of being kamma to be experienced in this very life, and so on. For this very reason, the Blessed One has shown three alternatives: 'either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent existence.' For the same reason, it is said, 'kamma to be experienced in this very life,' and so on. Here, the Teacher would not say, 'either in this very life,' and so on, if there were no fixed rule. But since there is no transition for them—for they are of a determined nature—therefore, the Teacher spoke thus: 'either in this very life,' and so on.

Sukkapakkheti “alobho nidānaṃ kammānaṃ samudayāyā”tiādinā āgate kusalapakkhe. Niruddheti ariyamaggādhigamena anuppādanirodhena niruddhe. Tālavatthu viya katanti yathā tāle chinne ṭhitaṭṭhāne kiñci na hoti, evaṃ kamme pahīne kiñci na hotīti attho. Tālavatthūti vā matthakacchinno tālo vutto pattaphalamakulasūciādīnaṃ abhāvato. Tato eva so aviruḷhidhammo. Evaṃ pahīnakammo sattasantāno. Tenāha [M 2.0110] “matthakacchinnatālo viyā”ti. Anuabhāvaṃ kataṃ pacchato dhammappavattiyā abhāvato. Tenāha “yathā”tiādi. Appavattikatakālo viyāti bījānaṃ sabbaso appavattiyā katakālo viya. Chinnamūlakānanti kilesamūlassa sabbaso chinnattā chinnamūlakānaṃ. Kilesā hi khandhānaṃ mūlāni.

'In the wholesome side' refers to the wholesome side mentioned in the passage beginning, 'Non-greed is the cause for the arising of kamma,' and so on. 'Ceased' means ceased through the attainment of the Noble Path, by the cessation of non-arising. 'Made like a palm-stump' means that just as when a palm tree is cut, nothing remains in its place, so too, when kamma is abandoned, nothing remains—this is the meaning. Or, 'palm-stump' refers to a palm-tree cut at the crown, because leaves, fruits, sprouts, and so on, are absent. For that very reason it is incapable of growing again. Similarly, the continuum of a being whose kamma has been abandoned is like this. Therefore, it is said, 'like a palm tree cut at its crown.' 'Made non-existent' means there is no subsequent arising of phenomena due to its absence. Therefore, it is said, 'just as,' and so on. 'Like a time made for non-occurrence' means like a time made for the complete non-occurrence of seeds. 'With roots cut off' means that the root of defilements has been entirely severed. For defilements are indeed the roots of the aggregates.

Vedanīyanti veditabbaṃ. Aññaṃ vatthu natthīti aññaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ natthi. Sugatisaññitāpi heṭṭhimantena saṅkhāradukkhato anapagatattā duggatiyo evāti vuttaṃ “sabbā duggatiyo”ti, evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Lobho etassa kāraṇabhūto atthīti lobhaṃ, lobhanimittaṃ kammaṃ. Tathā dosanti etthāpi. Tenāha “lobhadosasīsena lobhajañca dosajañca kammameva niddiṭṭha”nti. Vaṭṭavivaṭṭanti vaṭṭañca vivaṭṭañca.

'To be experienced' means it should be experienced. 'There is no other thing' means there is no other basis. Even what is considered a good destination, being at the lower end, is not free from the suffering of formations; hence it is called 'all bad destinations.'
