Kevalīti kevalavā, pāripūrimāti attho. Tenāha “paripuṇṇabhāvena yutto”ti. Etaṃ kevalīti padaṃ. Abhiññāpāranti abhijānassa pāraṃ. Pariyantaṃ gatattā pāragū. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Khettavinicchayasavanenāti [M 2.0130] “imehi sīlādiguṇasampannā sadevake loke puññassa khettaṃ, tadañño na khetta”nti evaṃ khettavinicchayasavanena rahitā.

'Kevalī' (the perfect one) means one who is whole; the meaning is 'complete.' Therefore, it is said, 'endowed with a state of completeness.' This is the term 'kevalī.' 'Abhiññāpāraṃ' means the further shore of direct knowledge. 'Pāragū' (gone beyond) means having reached the limit. This is the method for the remaining terms as well. 'Lacking the hearing that determines the field' means being without hearing the determination that 'these endowed with virtues such as morality are the field of merit in the world with its gods, and another is not the field.'

Vacchagottasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vacchagotta Sutta is concluded.

8. Tikaṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Tikaṇṇa Sutta

59. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0120] durāsadāti durupasaṅkamanā. Garahā muccissatīti mayi evaṃ kathente samaṇo gotamo kiñci kathessati, evaṃ me vacanamattampi na laddhanti ayaṃ garahā muccissatīti. Paṇḍitāti paṇḍiccena samannāgatā. Dhīrāti dhitisampannā. Byattāti paravādamaddanasamatthena veyyattiyena samannāgatā. Bahussutāti bāhusaccavanto. Vādinoti vādimaggakusalā. Sammatāti bahuno janassa sādhusammatā. Paṇḍitādiākāraparicchedanti tesaṃ tevijjānaṃ paṇḍitākārādiākāraparicchedaṃ. Ākārasaddo kāraṇapariyāyo, paricchedasaddo parimāṇatthoti āha “ettakena kāraṇenā”ti.

59. In the eighth, 'difficult to approach' means difficult to visit. 'He will escape censure' means: 'While I am speaking thus, the ascetic Gotama will say something, and in this way, the opportunity for even a mere utterance from me will not be obtained; thus this censure will be escaped.' 'Wise' means endowed with wisdom. 'Steadfast' means possessed of steadfastness. 'Eloquent' means endowed with an eloquence capable of subduing the arguments of others. 'Learned' means possessing great learning. 'Speakers' means skilled in the way of debate. 'Esteemed' means well-regarded by many people. 'The determination of the characteristics of the wise, etc.' refers to the determination of the characteristics, such as the characteristic of being wise, of those possessing the three knowledges. The word 'characteristic' here is a synonym for 'reason'; and 'determination' has the meaning of 'measure.' Thus it is said, 'by so much reason.'

Yathāti yenākārena, yena kāraṇenāti attho. Tenāha “yathāti kāraṇavacana”nti. “Dvīhipi pakkhehī”ti vatvā te pakkhe sarūpato dassento “mātito ca pitito cā”ti āha. Tesaṃ pakkhānaṃ vasenassa sujātataṃ dassetuṃ “yassa mātā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Janakajanikābhāvena vināpi loke mātāpitusamaññā dissati, idha pana sā orasaputtavaseneva icchitāti dassetuṃ “saṃsuddhagahaṇiko”ti vuttaṃ. Gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti dhāretīti gahaṇī, gabbhāsayasaññito mātukucchippadeso. Yathābhuttassa āhārassa vipācanavasena gaṇhanato achaḍḍanato gahaṇī, kammajatejodhātu.

'As to how' means 'by which manner, by which cause.' Therefore, it is said: ''As to how' is a term denoting cause.' Having stated 'by both sides,' he then explains those sides in their own nature by saying 'from the mother's side and from the father's side.' To show his good birth by means of these sides, 'whose mother,' etc., is stated. Even without the actual relationship of begetter and birth-giver, the designations of mother and father are seen in the world. Here, however, it is intended in the sense of a legitimate child; to show this, the phrase 'of pure conception' is used. 'Gahaṇī' is that which takes and holds the embryo—the part of the mother's belly known as the womb. It is also 'gahaṇī'—the fire element born of kamma—from taking and not discarding the consumed food by means of digestion.

Pitā ca mātā ca pitaro, pitūnaṃ pitaro pitāmahā, tesaṃ yugo pitāmahayugo, tasmā “yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā pitāmahadvandā”ti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana dvandaṃ aggahetvā “yuganti āyuppamāṇaṃ vuccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Yuga-saddassa ca atthakathā dassitā “pitāmahoyeva [M 2.0131] pitāmahayuga”nti. Pubbapurisāti purisaggahaṇañcettha ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evañhi “mātito”ti pāḷivacanaṃ samatthitaṃ hoti. Akkhittoti akkhepo. Anavakkhittoti saddhathālipākādīsu anavakkhitto na chaḍḍito. Jātivādenāti hetumhi karaṇavacananti dassetuṃ “kena kāraṇenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ettha ca “ubhato…pe… pitāmahayugā”ti etena brāhmaṇassa yonidosābhāvo dassito saṃsuddhagahaṇikatākittanato. “Akkhitto”ti iminā kiriyāparādhābhāvo. Saṃsuddhajātikāpi hi sattā kiriyāparādhena khepaṃ pāpuṇanti. “Anupakkuṭṭho”ti iminā ayuttasaṃsaggābhāvo. Ayuttasaṃsaggañhi paṭicca sattā suddhajātikā kiriyāparādharahitāpi akkosaṃ labhanti.

Father and mother are parents; the parents of the parents are grandfathers; their generation is a grandfather-generation. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'up to the seventh grandfather-generation' means 'grandfather-pairs.' In the commentary, however, without taking it as a pair, it is said: 'A 'yuga' refers to a lifespan.' And the commentary's meaning of the word 'yuga' is shown as 'the grandfather himself is the grandfather-yuga.' The term 'pubbapurisā' (ancient men) here should be understood as the mention of men done by way of a superior designation. For thus, the Pāli expression 'from the mother's side' is justified. 'Akkhitto' means censured. 'Anavakkhitto' means not censured, not rejected in matters like faith, ritual cooking, and so on. 'By birth-accusation'—to show that this is the instrumental case in the sense of reason, 'by what reason' and so on is stated. Here, by 'on both sides... up to the seventh grandfather-generation,' the absence of a flaw in the brahmin's origin is shown, because of the declaration of his pure conception. By 'not censured' (Anakkhitto), the absence of misconduct is indicated. For even beings of pure birth may face censure due to misconduct. By 'not reviled' (anupakkuṭṭho), the absence of improper association is indicated. For due to improper association, beings of pure birth, even if free from misconduct, may receive abuse.

Tanti [V 2.0121] garahāvacanaṃ. Mante parivattetīti vede sajjhāyati, pariyāpuṇātīti attho. Mante dhāretīti yathāadhīte mante asammuṭṭhe katvā hadaye ṭhapeti.

'Tanti' is a term of reproach. 'Recites the mantras' means he studies the Vedas; the meaning is he masters them. 'Retains the mantras' means, having learned the mantras without forgetting, he fixes them in his heart.

Oṭṭhapahatakaraṇavasenāti atthāvadhāraṇavasena. Sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānanti ettha vacanīyavācakabhāvena atthaṃ saddañca khaṇḍati bhindati vibhajja dassetīti nikhaṇḍu, so eva idha kha-kārassa gha-kāraṃ katvā “nighaṇḍū”ti vutto. Kiṭati gameti kiriyādivibhāgaṃ, taṃ vā anavasesapariyādānato gamento pūretīti keṭubhaṃ. Vevacanappakāsakanti pariyāyasaddadīpakaṃ, ekekassa atthassa anekapariyāyavacanavibhāvakanti attho. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ anekesampi atthānaṃ ekasaddavacanīyatāvibhāvanavasenapi tassa ganthassa pavattattā. Vacībhedādilakkhaṇā kiriyā kappīyati vikappīyati etenāti kiriyākappo, so pana vaṇṇapadasambandhapadatthādivibhāgato bahukappoti āha “kiriyākappavikappo”ti. Idañca mūlakiriyākappaganthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. So hi mahāvisayo satasahassaparimāṇo namācariyādippakaraṇaṃ. Ṭhānakaraṇādivibhāgato nibbacanavibhāgato ca akkharā pabhedīyanti etehīti akkharappabhedā, sikkhāniruttiyo. Etesanti catunnaṃ vedānaṃ.

'By means of the Oṭṭhapahatakaraṇa method' means by way of determining the meaning. Regarding 'Sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ': here, that which, through the relationship of the signified and the signifier, analyzes, breaks down, and distinctly shows meaning and words, is called 'nikhaṇḍu'; and here, by changing the 'kha' sound to 'gha,' it is called 'nighaṇḍu.' 'Keṭubha' is that which makes known the division of verbs, etc., or that which fulfills by completely comprehending it without remainder. 'A revealer of synonyms' means an illuminator of synonymous words; the meaning is that which elucidates the various synonymous expressions for a single meaning. This is merely an example, since that text also proceeds by way of elucidating how many meanings can be expressed by a single word. 'Kiriyākappo' is that by which action, characterized by divisions of speech etc., is arranged and modified. But because it has many arrangements, based on divisions of sound, word, connection, word-meaning, etc., it is said, 'kiriyākappavikappo.' And this is said with reference to the root 'Kiriyākappagantha' text. For that is a vast subject, amounting to a hundred thousand, the treatise of Namācariya and other teachers. 'Akkharappabhedā' are those texts by which letters are differentiated based on the division of place of articulation, articulator, etc., and on the division of pronunciation—these are the sikkhā and nirutti. 'Etesaṃ' refers to 'of the four Vedas.'

Padanti [M 2.0132] catubbidhaṃ, pañcavidhaṃ vā padaṃ, taṃ padaṃ kāyatīti padako, teyeva vā vede padaso kāyatīti padako. Tadavasesanti vuttāvasesaṃ vākyaṃ. Ettāvatā saddabyākaraṇaṃ vatvā puna “byākaraṇa”nti atthabyākaraṇamāha. Taṃ taṃ saddaṃ tadatthañca byākaroti byācikkhati etenāti byākaraṇaṃ, saddasatthaṃ. Āyatiṃ hitaṃ tena loko na yatati na īhatīti lokāyataṃ. Tañhi ganthaṃ nissāya sattā puññakiriyāya cittampi na uppādenti.

'Pada' (word) is said to be fourfold or fivefold; one who recites those words is a reciter. Or, one who recites the words of the Vedas by segment is a reciter. 'Tadavasesaṃ' (what remains after that) is the remainder of the speech mentioned. Having thus explained word-grammar, he then speaks of the explanation of meaning as 'byākaraṇa.' It explains and clarifies each word and its meaning—this is the science of words. 'Lokāyataṃ' (materialism) is that by which the world does not strive or exert itself for future welfare. For, relying on such texts, beings do not even arouse their minds toward meritorious deeds.

Asīti mahāsāvakāti aññāsikoṇḍañño, vappo, bhaddiyo, mahānāmo, assaji, nāḷako, yaso, vimalo, subāhu, puṇṇaji, gavampati, uruvelakassapo, nadīkassapo, gayākassapo, sāriputto, mahāmoggallāno, mahākassapo, mahākaccāno, mahākoṭṭhiko, mahākappino, mahācundo, anuruddho, kaṅkhārevato, ānando, nandako, bhagu, nandiyo, kimilo, bhaddiyo, rāhulo, sīvali, upāli, dabbo, upaseno, khadiravaniyarevato, puṇṇo mantāniputto, puṇṇo sunāparantako, soṇo kuṭikaṇṇo, soṇo koḷiviso, rādho, subhūti, aṅgulimālo, vakkali, kāḷudāyī, mahāudāyī, pilindavaccho, sobhito, kumārakassapo, raṭṭhapālo, vaṅgīso, sabhiyo, selo, upavāṇo, meghiyo, sāgato, nāgito, lakuṇḍakabhaddiyo, piṇḍolo bhāradvājo, mahāpanthako, cūḷapanthako, bākulo, kuṇḍadhāno, dārucīriyo, yasojo, ajito[V 2.0122], tissametteyyo, puṇṇako, mettagu, dhotako, upasīvo, nando, hemako, todeyyo, kappo, jatukaṇṇī, bhadrāvudho, udayo, posalo, mogharājā, piṅgiyoti ete asīti mahāsāvakā nāma.

The eighty great disciples are: Aññāsikoṇḍañña, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahānāma, Assaji, Nāḷaka, Yasa, Vimala, Subāhu, Puṇṇaji, Gavampati, Uruvelakassapa, Nadīkassapa, Gayākassapa, Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, Mahākaccāna, Mahākoṭṭhika, Mahākappina, Mahācunda, Anuruddha, Kaṅkhārevata, Ānanda, Nandaka, Bhagu, Nandiya, Kimila, Bhaddiya, Rāhula, Sīvali, Upāli, Dabba, Upasena, Khadiravaniyarevata, Puṇṇa Mantāniputta, Puṇṇa Sunāparantaka, Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa, Soṇa Koḷivisa, Rādha, Subhūti, Aṅgulimāla, Vakkali, Kāḷudāyī, Mahāudāyī, Pilindavaccha, Sobhita, Kumārakassapa, Raṭṭhapāla, Vaṅgīsa, Sabhiya, Sela, Upavāṇa, Meghiya, Sāgata, Nāgita, Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya, Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, Mahāpanthaka, Cūḷapanthaka, Bākula, Kuṇḍadhāna, Dārucīriya, Yasoja, Ajita, Tissametteyya, Puṇṇaka, Mettagu, Dhotaka, Upasīva, Nanda, Hemaka, Todeyya, Kappa, Jatukaṇṇī, Bhadrāvudha, Udaya, Posala, Mogharājā, and Piṅgiya—these are the names of the eighty great disciples.

Kasmā panete eva therā “mahāsāvakā”ti vuccantīti? Abhinīhārassa mahantabhāvato. Tathā hi dve aggasāvakāpi mahāsāvakesu antogadhā. Te hi sāvakapāramiñāṇassa matthakappattiyā sāvakesu aggadhammādhigamena aggaṭṭhāne ṭhitāpi abhinīhāramahantatāsāmaññena “mahāsāvakā”tipi vuccanti, itare pana pakatisāvakehi sātisayaṃ mahābhinīhārā. Tathā hi te padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle katapaṇidhānā, tato eva sātisayaṃ abhiññāsamāpattīsu vasino pabhinnappaṭisambhidā ca. Kāmaṃ sabbepi arahanto sīlavisuddhiādike sampādetvā catūsu [M 2.0133] satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacittā satta bojjhaṅge yathābhūtaṃ bhāvetvā maggappaṭipāṭiyā anavasesato kilese khepetvā aggaphale patiṭṭhahanti, tathāpi yathā saddhāvimuttato diṭṭhippattassa, paññāvimuttato ca ubhatobhāgavimuttassa pubbabhāgabhāvanāvisesasiddho maggabhāvanāviseso, evaṃ abhinīhāramahantattapubbayogamahantattā hi sasantāne sātisayassa guṇavisesassa nipphāditattā sīlādīhi guṇehi mahantā sāvakāti mahāsāvakā. Tesuyeva pana ye bodhipakkhiyadhammesu pāmokkhabhāvena dhurabhūtānaṃ sammādiṭṭhisaṅkappādīnaṃ sātisayaṃ kiccānubhāvanipphattiyā kāraṇabhūtāya tajjābhinīhārābhinīhaṭāya sakkaccaṃ nirantaraṃ cirakālasambhāvitāya sammāpaṭipattiyā yathākkamaṃ paññāya samādhismiñca ukkaṭṭhapāramippattiyā savisesaṃ sabbaguṇehi aggabhāve ṭhitā, te sāriputtamoggallānā. Itare aṭṭhasattati therā sāvakapāramiyā matthake sabbasāvakānaṃ aggabhāvena aṭṭhitattā “mahāsāvakā”icceva vuccanti. Pakatisāvakā pana abhinīhāramahantattābhāvato pubbayogamahantattābhāvato ca “satthusāvakā”icceva vuccanti. Te pana aggasāvakā viya mahāsāvakā viya ca na parimitā, atha kho anekasatā anekasahassā.

But why are these elders called "great disciples"? Because of the greatness of their aspiration. Indeed, even the two chief disciples are included among the great disciples. Though they stand in the highest position among disciples due to their attainment of the pinnacle of a disciple's perfection-knowledge and their attainment of the foremost Dhamma among disciples, they are still called "great disciples" by virtue of the commonality of the greatness of their aspiration. The others, however, greatly surpass ordinary disciples in aspiration. For these elders made their resolutions in the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, and from then on, they were masterful in the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and possessed of unhindered analytical insights. Indeed, though all arahants accomplish purification of virtue and so forth, establish their minds well in the four foundations of mindfulness, develop the seven factors of enlightenment according to reality, and eradicate all defilements without remainder through the progression of the path to be established in the supreme fruit, still, just as the path-development achieved through special prior development differs for one liberated by faith, for one attained to view, for one liberated by wisdom, and for one liberated both ways, so too, due to the greatness of their aspiration and the greatness of their prior practice, having produced a surpassing quality in their own continuum, they are great disciples, great in qualities such as virtue and so on. Among these, those who, by means of right practice—which was undertaken with care, continuously, and cultivated for a long time, brought forth by the aspiration for that which is the cause for the manifestation of the surpassing efficacy of the functions of right view, right intention, and so forth, which are pre-eminent and carry the burden among the factors of enlightenment—attained supreme perfection in wisdom and in concentration respectively, and stand pre-eminent in all qualities, are Sāriputta and Moggallāna. The other seventy-eight elders, not standing at the pinnacle of a disciple's perfection, in the foremost position among all disciples, are simply called "great disciples." Ordinary disciples, however, lacking the greatness of aspiration and the greatness of prior practice, are simply called "disciples of the Teacher." However, unlike the chief disciples and great disciples, they are not limited in number, but are many hundreds and thousands.

Vayatīti vayo, ādimajjhapariyosānesu katthaci aparikilamanto avitthāyanto te ganthe santāneti paṇetīti attho. Dve paṭisedhā pakatiṃ gamentīti dassetuṃ “avayo na hotī”ti vatvā tattha avayaṃ dassetuṃ “avayo nāma…pe… na sakkotī”ti vuttaṃ.

Vigor (vayo) is so called because one exerts oneself (vayati); the meaning is that one continues and sets forth those texts without tiring or becoming diffuse anywhere in the beginning, middle, or end. To show that two negations affirm the original meaning, it is said, 'It is not without vigor.' To explain 'without vigor' in that context, it is stated, 'Without vigor means... one is not able.'

Idhāti imasmiṃ sutte. Etanti “vivicceva kāmehī”tiādivacanaṃ. Tatiyavijjādhigamāya paṭipattikkamo visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.70) sātisayaṃ vitthārito, tathā [V 2.0123] idha avattukāmatāya bhayabheravasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 1.34 ādayo) viya saṅkhepato ca vattukāmatāya “dvinnaṃ vijjāna”micceva vuttaṃ.

Here, means in this discourse. This refers to the statement beginning with "secluded from sensual pleasures." The order of practice for attaining the third knowledge is explained with surpassing detail in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 1.70). Similarly, here, because there is no intention to elaborate, and because it is intended to be stated concisely, as in the Bhayabheravasutta and others (MN 4), it is simply said 'of the two knowledges.'

Vijjāti pubbenivāsappaṭicchādakassa mohakkhandhassa vijjanaṭṭhenapi vijjā. Moho paṭicchādakaṭṭhena tamoti vuccati tamo viyāti katvā. Kātabbato karaṇaṃ, obhāsova karaṇaṃ obhāsakaraṇaṃ, attano paccayehi obhāsabhāvena nibbattetabbaṭṭhenāti attho. Ayaṃ atthoti [M 2.0134] ayameva adhippetattho. Pasaṃsāvacananti tasseva atthassa thomanāvacanaṃ paṭipakkhavidhamanapavattivisesānaṃ bodhanato. Yojanāti pasaṃsāvasena vuttapadānaṃ atthadassanavasena vuttapadassa ca yojanā. Avijjā vihatāti etena vijjanaṭṭhena vijjāti ayampi attho dīpitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasmā vijjā uppannāti etena vijjāpaṭipakkhā avijjā, paṭipakkhatā cassā pahātabbabhāvena vijjāya ca pahāyakabhāvenāti dasseti. Itarasmimpi padadvayeti “tamo vihato, āloko uppanno”ti padadvayepi. Eseva nayoti yathāvuttayojanaṃ atidisati. Tatthāyaṃ yojanā – evaṃ adhigatavijjassa tamo vihato viddhasto. Kasmā? Yasmā āloko uppanno ñāṇāloko pātubhūtoti. Pesitattassāti yathādhippetatthasiddhippattiṃ vissaṭṭhacittassa, paṭhamavijjādhigamāya pesitacittassāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Knowledge (vijjā) is so called because of its characteristic of dispelling the mass of delusion that conceals past lives. Delusion is called 'darkness' (tamo) due to its characteristic of concealing, just as if it were darkness. It is a 'making' because it is to be made; a making of light is 'light-making'; the meaning is that it is to be produced as the state of light by its own conditions. This meaning—this itself is the intended meaning. 'Pasaṃsāvacana' (a praising expression) is a speech in praise of that very meaning, because it makes known the special processes of dispelling the opposition. 'Yojanā' (connection) is the connection between the words spoken in praise and the word spoken to show the meaning. By 'ignorance is dispelled,' it should be seen that this meaning is also shown: 'knowledge' in the sense of dispelling. By 'because knowledge has arisen,' it shows that ignorance is the opposite of knowledge, and its opposition consists in its being what is to be abandoned, and in knowledge being what abandons. In the other pair of terms also—in the pair of terms 'darkness is dispelled, light has arisen.' The same method applies, extending the connection as explained above. Here is the connection: For one who has thus attained knowledge, darkness is dispelled, destroyed. Why? Because the light has arisen, the light of knowledge has become manifest. 'Pesitattassa' means of one whose mind is released for the attainment of the intended purpose; that is to say, of one whose mind is directed towards the attainment of the first knowledge.

Vipassanāpādakanti iminā tassa jhānacittassa nibbedhabhāgiyatamāha. Vipassanā tividhā vipassakapuggalabhedena. Mahābodhisattānañhi paccekabodhisattānañca vipassanā cintāmayañāṇasaṃvaḍḍhitattā sayambhuñāṇabhūtā, itaresaṃ sutamayañāṇasaṃvaḍḍhitattā paropadesasambhūtā. Sā “ṭhapetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ avasesarūpārūpajjhānānaṃ aññatarato vuṭṭhāyā”tiādinā anekadhā arūpamukhavasena catudhātuvavatthāne vuttānaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ dhātupariggahamukhānaṃ aññataramukhavasena ca anekadhāva visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.306) nānānayato vibhāvitā. Mahābodhisattānaṃ pana catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassamukhena pabhedagamanato nānānayaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇasannissayassa ariyamaggañāṇassa adhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ pubbabhāgañāṇagabbhaṃ gaṇhāpentaṃ paripākaṃ gacchantaṃ paramagambhīraṃ saṇhasukhumataraṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ hoti, yaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu “mahāvajirañāṇa”nti vuccati. Yassa ca pavattivibhāgena catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassappabhedassa pādakabhāvena samāpajjiyamānā catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhā devasikaṃ satthu vaḷañjanakasamāpattiyo vuccanti, svāyaṃ buddhānaṃ vipassanācāro paramatthamañjūsāyaṃ visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.144) dassito, atthikehi tato gahetabboti. Idha pana sāvakānaṃ vipassanācāraṃ sandhāya “vipassanāpādaka”nti vuttaṃ.

By 'the foundation of insight,' he indicates that this jhāna-mind possesses the quality of leading to penetration. Insight is threefold, classified according to the types of individuals who develop it. For the Great Bodhisattas and the Solitary Buddhas, insight arises from wisdom cultivated through reflective thought, being self-originated knowledge. For others, it arises from wisdom cultivated through learning, being dependent on the instruction of others. This is explained in various ways in the Visuddhimagga (1.306), starting with 'having emerged from any of the remaining form and formless jhānas except the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,' and in various ways through any of the approaches to the comprehension of those elements mentioned in the analysis of the four elements by way of the formless door. For the Great Bodhisattas, however, insight unfolds through twenty-four koṭi hundred thousand methods, serving as the preliminary knowledge-womb that matures into the foundation of the noble path-knowledge, the basis of omniscient knowledge. This insight is supremely profound, exceedingly subtle, and unique—not shared by others. In the commentaries, it is called the 'Great Diamond Knowledge.' Moreover, the twenty-four koṭi hundred thousand attainments, which are entered upon as the basis for the twenty-four koṭi hundred thousand divisions of this knowledge according to its mode of arising, are called the 'Teacher’s Daily Customary Attainments.' This practice of insight for the Buddhas is shown in the Paramatthamañjūsā, the sub-commentary on the Visuddhimagga (Mahāṭīkā 1.144), and should be understood from there by those who seek it. Here, however, the term 'foundation of insight' is used with reference to the practice of insight for disciples.

Kāmaṃ [M 2.0135][V 2.0124] heṭṭhimamaggañāṇānipi āsavānaṃ khepanañāṇāni eva, anavasesato pana tesaṃ khepanaṃ aggamaggañāṇenevāti āha “arahattamaggañāṇatthāyā”ti. Āsavavināsanatoti āsavānaṃ nissesaṃ samucchindanato. Āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ āsavakkhayañāṇanti dassento “tatra cetaṃ ñāṇa”nti vatvā “khaye”ti ādhāre bhummaṃ, na visayeti dassento “tattha pariyāpannattā”ti āha. Abhinīharatīti abhimukhaṃ nīharati, yathā maggābhisamayo hoti, savanaṃ tadabhimukhaṃ pavatteti. Idaṃ dukkhanti dukkhassa ariyasaccassa tadā bhikkhunā paccakkhato gahitabhāvadassanaṃ. Ettakaṃ dukkhanti tassa paricchijja gahitabhāvadassanaṃ. Na ito bhiyyoti tassa anavasesato gahitabhāvadassanaṃ. Tenāha “sabbampi dukkhasacca”ntiādi. Sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhenāti sabhāvasaṅkhātassa lakkhaṇassa asammohato paṭivijjhanena. Asammohapaṭivedhoti ca yathā tasmiṃ ñāṇe pavatte pacchā dukkhasaccassa sarūpādiparicchede sammoho na hoti, tathā pavatti. Tenevāha “yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti. Dukkhaṃ samudeti etasmāti dukkhasamudayo. Yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvāti yaṃ nibbānaṃ maggassa ārammaṇapaccayaṭṭhena kāraṇabhūtaṃ āgamma. Patvāti ca tadubhayavato puggalassa pavattiyāti katvā vuttaṃ. Patvāti vā pāpuṇanahetu. Appavattinti appavattinimittaṃ. Te vā na pavattanti etthāti appavatti, nibbānaṃ. Tassāti dukkhanirodhassa. Sampāpakanti sacchikiriyāvasena sammadeva pāpakaṃ.

Indeed, even the lower path knowledges are knowledges that destroy the taints, but their complete destruction is only achieved by the knowledge of the supreme path. Hence it is said, 'for the sake of the knowledge of the path to arahantship.' By 'the destruction of the taints' is meant their complete eradication. To show that 'knowledge of the destruction of the taints' means 'knowledge in the destruction of the taints,' he says 'and this knowledge is in that,' and to show that 'in destruction' is a locative of basis, not of object, he says 'because it is included therein.' 'Directs' means turns towards; just as the breakthrough to the path occurs, he directs his attention towards it. 'This is suffering' refers to the monk's direct grasp of the truth of suffering at that time. 'This much is suffering' shows the grasp of it as delimited. 'Not more than this' shows the complete grasp of it. Therefore, it is said, 'all is the truth of suffering,' and so on. 'By penetrating the characteristic of essence' means by unconfusedly penetrating the characteristic understood as intrinsic nature. And 'penetration without delusion' means that when that knowledge arises, later, there is no delusion in distinguishing the truth of suffering by its nature and so forth; thus it proceeds. Thus, it is said, 'he understands as it really is.' 'Suffering arises from this' is the origin of suffering. 'Having reached that state' means having reached Nibbāna, which is the cause for the path by way of being its object-condition. And 'having reached' is said with reference to the proceeding of the individual who possesses both (the path and its fruit). Alternatively, 'having reached' means the cause of attainment. 'Non-occurrence' means the sign of non-occurrence. 'Those do not occur here' means non-occurrence, that is, Nibbāna. 'Of that' refers to the cessation of suffering. 'Sampāpaka' means 'that which rightly causes to attain' by way of realization.

Kilesavasenāti āsavasaṅkhātakilesavasena. Yasmā āsavānaṃ dukkhasaccapariyāyo tappariyāpannattā sesasaccānañca taṃsamudayādipariyāyo atthi, tasmā vuttaṃ “pariyāyato”ti. Dassento saccānīti yojanā. Āsavānañcettha gahaṇaṃ “āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyā”ti āraddhattā. Tathā hi “kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccatī”tiādinā āsavavimuttisīseneva sabbakilesavimutti vuttā. “Idaṃ dukkhanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”tiādinā missakamaggo idha kathitoti “saha vipassanāya koṭippattaṃ maggaṃ kathesī”ti vuttaṃ. Jānato passatoti iminā pariññāsacchikiriyābhāvanābhisamayā vuttā. Vimuccatīti iminā pahānābhisamayo vuttoti āha “iminā maggakkhaṇaṃ dassetī”ti. Jānato [M 2.0136] passatoti vā hetuniddeso. Yaṃ jānanahetu kāmāsavāpi cittaṃ vimuccatīti yojanā. Dhammānañhi samānakālikānampi paccayapaccayuppannatā sahajātakoṭiyā labbhati. Bhavāsavaggahaṇeneva ettha bhavarāgassa viya bhavadiṭṭhiyāpi samavarodhoti diṭṭhāsavassapi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

By way of defilements, i.e., by way of the defilements reckoned as taints. Because the taints have the aspect of the truth of suffering by being included in it, and the other truths have the aspect of its origin and so forth, therefore it is said 'by way of aspect.' The construction is: 'showing the truths.' The mention of the taints here is because it begins with 'for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.' Indeed, with the phrase 'the mind is freed even from the taint of sensual desire' and so forth, liberation from all defilements is stated under the heading of liberation from the taints. The mixed path is discussed here with phrases like 'he understands as it really is, "This is suffering"' and so forth, hence it is said, 'He taught the path that reaches its culmination together with insight.' By 'for one who knows and sees' are stated the penetrations of full understanding, realization, and development. By 'is freed' is stated the penetration of abandonment, hence it is said, 'This shows the moment of the path.' Alternatively, 'for one who knows and sees' is an explanation of the cause. The construction is: because of knowing, the mind is freed even from the taint of sensual desire. For even among phenomena that are simultaneous, the relationship of cause and effect is obtained by way of co-nascence. Here, by the inclusion of the taint of existence, the inclusion of the view of existence is also accomplished, just like with craving for existence. Thus, the inclusion of the taint of views should also be understood.

Khīṇā jātītiādīhi padehi. Tassāti paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa. Bhūminti pavattiṭṭhānaṃ. Yenādhippāyena “katamā panassā”tiādinā codanā katā, taṃ vivaranto “na tāvassā”tiādimāha[V 2.0125]. Tattha na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā maggabhāvanāyāti adhippāyo. Tattha kāraṇamāha “pubbeva khīṇattā”ti. Na anāgatā assa jāti khīṇāti yojanā. Na anāgatāti ca anāgatabhāvasāmaññaṃ gahetvā lesena codeti. Tenāha “anāgate vāyāmābhāvato”ti. Anāgataviseso panettha adhippeto, tassa khepane vāyāmo labbhateva. Tenāha “yā pana maggassā”tiādi. Ekacatupañcavokārabhavesūti bhavattayaggahaṇaṃ vuttanayena anavasesato jātiyā khīṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tanti yathāvuttaṃ jātiṃ. Soti khīṇāsavo bhikkhu.

With the phrases 'destroyed is birth' and so forth. 'His' refers to the knowledge of reviewing. 'Ground' means the place of occurrence. Explaining the intention behind the objection raised with 'but what is his?' and so forth, he says 'not yet is his' and so forth. Here, the meaning is that his past birth is not yet destroyed by the development of the path. The reason for that is stated: 'because it was already destroyed.' The construction is: his future birth is not destroyed. 'Not future' subtly objects by taking the general characteristic of the future. Hence he says, 'due to the absence of effort regarding the future.' A specific aspect of the future is intended here, for effort can indeed be made regarding its elimination. Therefore, he says, 'but that which is of the path' and so forth. By 'in one-, four-, or five-constituent realms of existence' is stated the inclusion of the three realms of existence, in the manner explained, to show the complete destruction of birth. 'That' refers to birth as explained. 'He' is the monk whose taints are destroyed.

Brahmacariyavāso nāma idha maggabrahmacariyassa nibbattanamevāti āha “parivuttha”nti. Sammādiṭṭhiyā catūsu saccesu pariññādikiccasādhanavasena pavattamānāya sammāsaṅkappādīnampi dukkhasacce pariññābhisamayānuguṇā pavatti, itaresu ca saccesu nesaṃ pahānābhisamayādivasena pavatti pākaṭā eva. Tena vuttaṃ “catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanābhisamayavasenā”ti. Puthujjanakalyāṇakādayoti ādi-saddena sattasekhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

The living of the holy life here means simply the accomplishment of the holy life of the path, hence he says 'has been lived.' When right view functions by way of accomplishing the task of full understanding and so forth in the four truths, then the functioning of right intention and so forth is in accordance with the penetration of full understanding of the truth of suffering; and their functioning in relation to the other truths—by way of the penetration of abandonment and so forth—is quite evident. Therefore, it was said, 'in the four truths by the four paths, by way of the penetrations of full understanding, abandonment, realization, and development.' 'Virtuous ordinary persons and so forth'—the word 'and so forth' includes the seven trainees.

Itthattāyāti ime pakārā itthaṃ, tabbhāvo itthattaṃ, tadatthanti vuttaṃ hoti. Te pana pakārā ariyamaggabyāpārabhūtā pariññādayo idhādhippetāti āha “evaṃsoḷasavidhakiccabhāvāyā”ti. Te hi maggaṃ paccavekkhato maggānubhāvena pākaṭā hutvā upaṭṭhahanti, pariññādīsu ca pahānameva padhānaṃ tadatthattā itaresanti āha “kilesakkhayāya vā”ti. Pahīnakilesapaccavekkhaṇavasena vā etaṃ vuttaṃ. Dutiyavikappe itthattāyāti nissakke sampadānavacananti āha “itthabhāvato”ti[M 2.0137]. Aparanti anāgataṃ. Ime pana carimakattabhāvasaṅkhātā pañcakkhandhā. Pariññātā tiṭṭhantīti etena tesaṃ appatiṭṭhataṃ dasseti. Apariññāmūlakā hi patiṭṭhā. Yathāha “kabaḷīkāre ce, bhikkhave, āhāre atthi rāgo, atthi nandī, atthi taṇhā, patiṭṭhitaṃ tattha viññāṇaṃ viruḷha”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.64; kathā. 296; mahāni. 7). Tenevāha – “chinnamūlakā rukkhā viyā”tiādi.

'Itthattāya' means 'these modes are thus,' their state is 'thusness,' and it is said to be for that purpose. Those modes, however, are intended here as the functions of the Noble Path, such as full understanding and so forth, hence he says, 'for this sixteenfold mode of functioning.' For when one reviews the path, they become evident through the power of the path and present themselves; and among full understanding and so forth, abandonment is indeed primary, the others being for that purpose. Hence he says, 'or for the destruction of defilements.' Or this is said with reference to reviewing the abandoned defilements. In the second alternative, 'itthattāya' is a dative expression in the sense of accomplishment, hence he says, 'from the state of being thus.' 'Aparaṃ' means the future. These, however, are the five aggregates designated as the final state of being. By 'they stand fully understood' is shown their non-establishment. For establishment has its roots in non-full-understanding. As he says: 'Bhikkhus, if there is lust, delight, or craving for nutriment, consciousness becomes established there and grows,' and so forth (Saṃ. Ni. 2.64; Kathā. 296; Mahāni. 7). Therefore, he says: 'Like trees with roots cut off,' and so forth.

Yassāti puthujjanassa. Tassa hi sīlaṃ kadāci vaḍḍhati, kadāci hāyati. Sekkhāpi pana sīlesu paripūrakārinova, asekkhesu vattabbameva natthi. Tenāha “khīṇāsavassā”tiādi. Vasippattanti vasībhāvappattaṃ. Suṭṭhu samāhitanti aggaphalasamādhinā sammadeva samāhitaṃ. Dhitisampannanti aggaphaladhitiyā samannāgataṃ. Maccuṃ jahitvā ṭhitanti āyatiṃ punabbhavābhāvato vuttaṃ. Kathaṃ punabbhavābhāvoti āha “sabbe pāpadhamme pajahitvā ṭhita”nti. Sabbassapi ñeyyadhammassa catusaccantogadhattā vuttaṃ “buddhanti catusaccabuddha”nti. Buddhasāvakāti sāvakabuddhā namassanti, [V 2.0126] pageva itarā pajā. Itarā hi pajā sāvakepi namassanti. Iti ettakena ṭhānena sammāsambuddhassa vasena gāthānaṃ atthaṃ vatvā idāni sāvakassapi vasena atthaṃ yojetvā dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sāvakopi gotamo mukhanibbattena sampattena sambandhena, yato sabbepi ariyasāvakā bhagavato orasaputtāti vuccantīti.

'Whose' refers to the ordinary person. For their virtue sometimes increases, sometimes decreases. But the trainees are indeed fulfillers of the virtues, and nothing need be said of those beyond training. Hence he says, 'of one whose taints are destroyed' and so forth. 'Mastery attained' means having attained mastery. 'Well concentrated' means properly concentrated with the supreme fruition concentration. 'Endowed with resolution' means possessing the supreme fruition resolution. 'Having abandoned death, he stands' is said with reference to the non-arising of future becoming. How is there non-arising of future becoming? He says, 'having abandoned all evil qualities, he stands.' Because all knowable phenomena are encompassed by the four truths, it is said, 'a Buddha is one who has awakened to the four truths.' 'Disciples of the Buddha' means that the disciple-Buddhas pay homage, let alone other people. For other people pay homage even to disciples. Thus, having explained the meaning of the verses in terms of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One to this extent, now to show the meaning in terms of the disciple, 'or else' and so forth is said. A disciple, too, is a Gotama by the connection of being born from the mouth, by attainment, and by relationship, since all noble disciples are called the Blessed One's legitimate sons.

Nivussatīti nivāso, nivuttho khandhasantānoti āha “nivutthakkhandhaparampara”nti. Aveti, avedīti pāṭhadvayenapi pubbenivāsañāṇassa kiccasiddhiṃyeva dasseti. Ekattakāyaekattasaññibhāvasāmaññato vehapphalāpi ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchantīti “cha kāmāvacare, nava brahmaloke”icceva vuttaṃ. Itare pana apacurabhāvato na vuttā. Ekaccānaṃ avisayabhāvato ca avacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Jāti khīyati etenāti jātikkhayo, arahattanti āha “arahattaṃ patto”ti. “Abhiññāyā”ti vattabbe yakāralopena “abhiññā”ti niddeso katoti āha “jānitvā”ti. Kiccavosānenāti catūhi maggehi kattabbassa soḷasavidhassa kiccassa pariyosānena. Vositoti pariyosito, niṭṭhitoti attho. Moneyyena samannāgatoti kāyamoneyyādīhi samannāgato. Lapitaṃ [M 2.0138] lapatīti lapitalāpano. Attapaccakkhato ñatvāti iminā tesaṃ vijjānaṃ paṭiladdhabhāvaṃ dīpeti.

'Nivussati' means dwelling; 'the succession of aggregates has been dwelt in,' hence he says, 'the succession of aggregates in which one has dwelt.' 'Knows, has known'—both readings show the accomplishment of the function of the knowledge of past abodes. Due to the commonality of being of one body and one perception, even the Vehapphala deities are included here. Hence it is said, 'six in the sensual realm, nine in the Brahma world.' Others, however, are not mentioned due to their scarcity. And it should be understood that they are not mentioned because they are beyond the scope of certain individuals. 'Destruction of birth' means that by this, birth is destroyed; he says that arahantship is meant, 'has attained arahantship.' Where 'abhiññāya' should be said, the explanation is given as 'abhiññā' by dropping the 'ya,' hence he says, 'having known.' By 'completion of the task' is meant the conclusion of the sixteenfold task to be done by the four paths. 'Accomplished' means concluded, finished—this is the meaning. 'Endowed with sagacity' means possessing bodily sagacity and so forth. 'Speaks what is spoken' means one who speaks what is spoken. By 'having known for oneself by direct experience' is shown the acquisition of those knowledges.

Tikaṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Tikaṇṇa Sutta is concluded.

9. Jāṇussoṇisuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Sutta

60. Navame deyyadhammassetaṃ nāmanti yāgaṃ karontena dātabbadeyyadhammaṃ sandhāya vadati tadaññassa pāḷiyaṃ deyyadhammaggahaṇeneva gahitattā. Matakabhattanti matake uddissa dātabbabhattaṃ, pitupiṇḍanti vuttaṃ hoti. Varapurisānanti visiṭṭhapurisānaṃ, uttamapurisānanti attho. Sabbametaṃ dānanti yathāvuttabhedaṃ yaññasaddhādidānaṃ.

60. In the ninth, the phrase 'This is the name of a gift-item' refers to the gift-item to be given by one performing a sacrifice, because other items are already included in the Pāli text by the very use of the term 'deyyadhamma.' 'Food for the dead' means food to be given in dedication to the deceased; it is said to be an 'ancestral offering.' 'Of excellent men' means of distinguished men, that is, of the best of men. 'All this is a gift' means the kinds of gifts mentioned, such as sacrifices, faith, and so forth.

Jāṇussoṇisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Sutta is concluded.

10. Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta

61. Dasame jiṇṇānaṃ hatthisālādīnaṃ paṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ puna pākatikakaraṇaṃ jiṇṇapaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ[V 2.0127], tassa kārako jiṇṇapaṭisaṅkharaṇakārako. Bāhirasamayeti satthusāsanato bāhire aññatitthiyasamaye. Sabbacatukkenātiādīsu sabbesu dvipadacatuppadādibhedesu pāṇesu ekekasmiṃ cattāro cattāro pāṇe vadhitvā yajitabbaṃ yaññaṃ sabbacatukkaṃ nāma. Sesesupi iminā nayena attho veditabbo. Yassa vā tassa vāti nissakke sāmivacananti āha “yasmā vā tasmā vā”ti. Evamassāyanti ettha assūti nipātamattanti āha “evaṃ santepi aya”nti.

61. In the tenth, 'restoration of old things' means the restoration of old elephant halls and so forth, that is, making them functional again; the one who does this is called 'the restorer of old things.' 'In an external system' means outside the Teacher's dispensation, in the system of other sectarians. In 'by the all-fourfold,' etc., a sacrifice called 'all-fourfold' is one to be performed by killing four beings in each category among all beings, such as two-footed and four-footed. The meaning in the rest should be understood in this way. The genitive expression 'yassa vā tassa vā' ('of whomever or of whatever') is used here with an ablative sense, hence he says 'yasmā vā tasmā vā' ('from whom or from what'). In 'Evamassāyaṃ,' the word 'assu' is merely a particle, hence he says 'evaṃ sante pi ayaṃ' ('even so, this...').

Vaḍḍhentoti paṭṭhapento. Maggabrahmacariyassa ogadhaṃ mūlaṃ patiṭṭhābhūtaṃ brahmacariyogadhaṃ. Tenāha “arahattamaggasaṅkhātassā”tiādi. Ukkaṭṭhaniddesena cettha arahattamaggasseva gahaṇaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Uttamaṃ patiṭṭhābhūtaṃ ārammaṇūpanissayabhāvena.

'Vaḍḍhento' means establishing. 'Immersion in the holy life' means the immersion, root, and foundation of the holy life of the path. Hence it is said, 'of that designated as the path of Arahantship,' and so forth. Here, it should be seen that only the path to arahantship is taken by way of this supreme specification. It is the supreme foundation by way of being an objective support-condition.

Appehi veyyāvaccakarādīhi attho etissāti appaṭṭhā ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā. Tenāha “yattha bahū”tiādi. Yatthāti yassaṃ paṭipadāyaṃ[M 2.0139]. Appo samārambho etassāti appasamārambho. Pāsaṃsāti pasaṃsārahā. Etaṃ yeva kathāpessāmīti eteneva brāhmaṇena kathāpessāmi.

'Appaṭṭhā' (having little purpose) means that its purpose is with few attendants and so forth, by changing the letter 'ttha' to 'ṭṭha.' Hence he says, 'where many,' and so forth. 'Where' means in which course of practice. 'Appasamārambho' (having little undertaking) means that its undertaking is little. 'Pāsaṃsā' means worthy of praise. 'I will have him speak only about this' means: I will have this very brahmin speak.

Soppenāti niddāya. Pamādenāti jāgariyādīsu ananuyuñjanato sativippavāsalakkhaṇena pamādena. Paccanīkapaṭiharaṇavasenāti paṭipakkhāpanayanavasena. Tathā hi bhagavato ca sāsanassa ca paṭipakkhā titthiyā, tesaṃ haraṇato paṭihāriyaṃ. Te hi diṭṭhiharaṇavasena diṭṭhippakāsane asamatthabhāvena ca iddhiādesanānusāsanīhi haritā apanītā hontīti. “Paṭī”ti vā ayaṃ saddo “pacchā”ti etassa atthaṃ bodheti “tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhasmiṃ, añño āgañchi brāhmaṇo”tiādīsu (su. ni. 985; cūḷani. vatthugāthā 4) viya, tasmā samāhite citte vigatūpakkilese katakiccena pacchā haritabbaṃ pavattetabbanti paṭihāriyaṃ, attano vā upakkilesesu catutthajjhānamaggehi haritesu pacchāharaṇaṃ paṭihāriyaṃ, iddhiādesanānusāsaniyo ca vigatūpakkilesena katakiccena ca sattahitatthaṃ puna pavattetabbā, haritesu ca attano upakkilesesu parasattānaṃ upakkilesaharaṇāni hontīti paṭihāriyāni bhavanti, paṭihāriyameva pāṭihāriyaṃ. Paṭihāriye vā iddhiādesanānusāsanisamudāye bhavaṃ ekekaṃ pāṭihāriyanti vuccati. Paṭihāriyaṃ vā catutthajjhānaṃ maggo ca paṭipakkhaharaṇato, tattha jātaṃ nimittabhūte, tato vā āgatanti pāṭihāriyaṃ.

'By dozing' means by sleepiness. 'Through negligence' refers to negligence characterized by the absence of mindfulness, due to not engaging in wakefulness and other duties. 'By way of warding off opposition' means by way of removing adversaries. For indeed, the adversaries of the Blessed One and his teaching are the sectarians, and their removal constitutes a miracle. They are removed and dispelled by psychic power, teaching, and instruction, by way of removing their wrong views and by their inability to proclaim their own views. The word 'paṭi' also conveys the meaning of 'after,' as in the phrase, 'After he had entered, another brahmin arrived' (Sn 985; Cūḷani. Vatthugāthā 4). Therefore, a miracle (paṭihāriya) is what should be brought about afterward—when the mind is concentrated, free from defilements, and has accomplished its task. Alternatively, a miracle (paṭihāriya) is the subsequent removal of one’s own defilements by the fourth jhāna and the path. Psychic power, teaching, and instruction should be brought about again for the welfare of beings by one who is free from defilements and has fulfilled his purpose. And when one’s own defilements are removed, the removal of the defilements of other beings becomes a miracle. Thus, 'paṭihāriya' is indeed 'pāṭihāriya.' Or, each single phenomenon existing in the aggregate of psychic power, teaching, and instruction, is called a miracle (pāṭihāriya). Or, the fourth jhāna and the path are 'paṭihāriya' because they remove opposition; what arises from that, being a sign, or what comes from that, is called a miracle (pāṭihāriya).

Āgatanimittenāti āgatākārasallakkhaṇavasena. Esa nayo sesesupi. Eko rājāti dakkhiṇamadhurādhipati [V 2.0128] eko paṇḍurājā. Evampi te manoti iminā ākārena tava mano pavattoti attho. Tena pakārena pavattoti āha “somanassito vā”tiādi. Sāmaññajotanā visese avatiṭṭhatīti adhippāyenevaṃ vuttaṃ. “Evaṃ tava mano”ti idañca manaso somanassitatādimattadassanaṃ, na pana yena so somanassito vā domanassito vā, taṃdassanaṃ. Somanassaggahaṇena cettha tadekaṭṭhā rāgādayo saddhādayo ca dassitā honti, domanassaggahaṇena dosādayo. Dutiyanti “itthampi te mano”ti padaṃ. Itipīti ettha iti-saddo nidassanattho “atthīti [M 2.0140] kho, kaccāna, ayameko anto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.15; 3.90) viya. Tenāha “imañca imañca atthaṃ cintayamāna”nti. Pi-saddo vuttatthasampiṇḍanattho.

'By the sign of what has come' means by way of observing the characteristics of what has appeared. This is the method for the rest as well. 'One king' refers to Paṇḍurājā, the ruler of Dakkhiṇamadhurā. 'Even so is your mind'—the meaning is that your mind is operating in this way. To show that it operates in that manner, he says 'joyful or...' and so on. It is said thus with the intention that a general indication settles on the specific. 'Thus is your mind'—this shows merely the joyfulness, etc., of the mind, but not a showing of that by which it is joyful or sorrowful. Here, by the taking up of joyfulness, lust and similar states which share the same basis are indicated, as well as faith and similar states. By the taking up of sorrow, hatred and similar states are indicated. 'Secondly' means the phrase 'in this way also is your mind'. Here, in 'itipī', the word 'iti' serves as an illustration, as in passages like, 'This, Kaccāna, is one extreme' (SN 2.15; 3.90). Hence it is said, 'contemplating this and that meaning.' The particle 'pi' serves to summarize what has been stated.

Kathentānaṃ sutvāti kathentānaṃ saddaṃ sutvā. Tassa vasenāti tassa vitakkitassa vasena. Aṭṭakārakenāti vinicchayakārakena.

'Having heard those speaking' means having heard the sound of those speaking. 'By means of that' means by means of that which was thought. 'By the one who decides' is the meaning of Aṭṭakārakena.

Na ariyānanti ariyānaṃ maggaphalacittaṃ na jānātīti attho. Tañhi tena anadhigatattā cetopariyañāṇenapi na sakkā viññātuṃ, aññaṃ pana cittaṃ jānātiyeva. Heṭṭhimo uparimassa cittaṃ na jānātītiādīnipi maggaphalacittameva sandhāya vuttānīti veditabbāni. Sotāpannādayopi hi attanā adhigatameva maggaphalaṃ parehi uppāditaṃ sammā cetopariyañāṇena jānituṃ sakkonti, na attanā anadhigataṃ. Sabbepi ariyā attano phalaṃ samāpajjanti adhigatattāti dassento “etesu cā”tiādimāha. Yadi ariyā attanā adhigataphalaṃ samāpajjanti, uparimāpi heṭṭhimaṃ phalaṃ samāpajjanti adhigatattā lokiyasamāpattiyo viyāti kassaci āsaṅkā siyā, tannivattanatthamāha “uparimo heṭṭhimaṃ na samāpajjatī”ti.

'Not of the noble ones' means that one does not know the path and fruition consciousness of the noble ones. For that, because it has not been attained by oneself, cannot be known even with the knowledge of others' minds. However, one can indeed know other types of consciousness. Statements like 'the lower does not know the mind of the higher' should be understood as referring specifically to path and fruition consciousness. For even stream-enterers and others are able to know, through correct knowledge of others' minds, the path and fruition produced by others—but only that which they themselves have attained, not that which they have not attained. To show that all noble ones attain their own fruition because they have attained it, the text states, 'and in these...' and so on. If someone should have the doubt that 'since noble ones attain the fruition they have attained, the higher ones might also attain the lower fruition, since they have attained it, just as with mundane attainments'—to dispel this, it is said, 'the higher does not attain the lower.'

Uparimoti sakadāgāmiādiariyapuggalo. Heṭṭhimanti sotāpattiphalādiṃ. Na samāpajjatīti satipi adhigatatte na samāpajjati. Kasmāti ce? Kāraṇamāha “tesañhī”tiādi, tesaṃ sakadāgāmiādīnaṃ heṭṭhimā heṭṭhimā phalasamāpatti tesu tesuyeva heṭṭhimesu ariyapuggalesu pavattati, na uparimesūti attho. Iminā heṭṭhimaṃ phalacittaṃ uparimassa na uppajjatīti dasseti. Kasmāti ce? Puggalantarabhāvūpagamanena paṭippassaddhattā. Etena uparimo ariyo heṭṭhimaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati attanā adhigatattā yathā taṃ lokiyasamāpattinti evaṃ pavatto hetu byabhicāritoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi lokiyajjhānesu puggalantarabhāvūpagamanaṃ nāma atthi visesābhāvato, idha pana asamugghāṭitakammakilesanirodhanena puthujjanehi [V 2.0129] viya sotāpannassa sotāpannādīhi sakadāgāmiādīnaṃ puggalantarabhāvūpagamanaṃ atthi. Yato heṭṭhimā heṭṭhimā phaladhammā uparūparimaggadhammehi nivattitā paṭipakkhehi viya abhibhūtā appavattidhammataṃyeva āpannā. Teneva vuttaṃ “paṭippassaddhattā”ti.

'The higher one' refers to the noble individual such as the once-returner and others. 'The lower' refers to the fruition of stream-entry and so on. 'He does not attain it' means that even though it has been attained, he does not attain it. If asked why, the reason is stated: 'For them,' etc. For those once-returners and others, the lower and lower fruition attainments occur only in those very lower noble individuals, not in the higher ones—this is the meaning. By this, it is shown that the lower fruition consciousness does not arise for the higher one. If asked why, it is because it has subsided due to the attainment of the state of another person. Through this, it should be understood that the reason thus advanced—that the higher noble one attains the lower fruition attainment because he has realized it himself, just as with mundane attainments—is fallacious. For in the case of mundane jhānas, there is no such thing as the attainment of the state of another person, due to the absence of distinction. Here, however, for the stream-enterer in relation to ordinary people, and for the once-returner and others in relation to the stream-enterer and others, there is the attainment of the state of another person through the cessation of kamma and defilements not previously uprooted. Since the lower and lower fruition states are turned back by the higher and higher path states, as if overcome by adversaries, they have attained a state of non-occurrence. Therefore, it is said, 'because of having subsided.'

Apica [M 2.0141] kusalakiriyappavatti nāma aññā, vipākappavatti ca aññāti anantaraphalattā ca lokuttarakusalānaṃ heṭṭhimato uparimo bhavantaragato viya hoti. Taṃtaṃphalavaseneva hi ariyānaṃ sotāpannādināmalābho. Te sace aññaphalasamaṅginopi honti, sotāpannādināmampi tesaṃ avavatthitaṃ siyā. Tassa tassa vā ariyassa taṃ taṃ phalaṃ sadisanti katvā na uparimassa heṭṭhimaphalasamaṅgitāya lesopi sambhavati, kuto tassā samāpajjananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Heṭṭhimā ca sotāpannādayo uparimaṃ sakadāgāmiphalādiṃ na samāpajjanti anadhigatattā. Na hi anadhigataṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjituṃ sakkā, tasmā sabbepi ariyā attanoyeva phalaṃ samāpajjantīti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

Moreover, the occurrence of wholesome and functional actions is one thing, and the occurrence of their result is another. And due to the immediately subsequent fruition of supramundane wholesome actions, it is as if the higher one has gone to another existence from the lower one. Indeed, the noble ones gain names such as stream-enterer and so on only by way of their respective fruits. If they were also endowed with another fruit, their designation as stream-enterer and so on would be unfixed. Or, considering that for each noble one the respective fruit is suitable, even the slightest possibility of a higher one being endowed with a lower fruit does not exist; how much less its actual attainment! And lower ones, stream-enterers and the like, do not attain the higher fruit, such as that of the once-returner, because they have not attained it. For it is not possible to attain an attainment that has not been attained. Therefore, the conclusion to be reached here is that all noble ones attain only their own fruit.

Pavattentāti pavattakā hutvā, pavattanavasenāti attho. Evanti yathānusiṭṭhāya anusāsaniyā vidhivasena paṭisedhavasena ca pavattitākāraparāmasanaṃ. Sā ca sammāvitakkā nāma micchāvitakkānañca pavattiākāradassanavasena pavattati. Tattha ānisaṃsassa ādīnavassa ca vibhāvanatthaṃ aniccasaññameva, na niccasaññanti attho. Paṭiyoginivattanatthañhi eva-kāraggahaṇaṃ. Idhāpi evasaddaggahaṇassa attho payojanañca vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Idaṃ-gahaṇepi eseva nayo. Pañcakāmaguṇarāganti nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ tadaññarāgassa dosādīnañca pahānassa icchitattā tappahānassa ca tadaññarāgādikhepassa upāyabhāvato. Tathā vuttaṃ duṭṭhalohitavimocanassa pubbaduṭṭhamaṃsakhepanūpāyatā viya. Lokuttaradhammamevāti avadhāraṇaṃ paṭikkhepabhāvato sāvajjadhammanivattanaparaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tassa adhigamūpāyānisaṃsabhūtānaṃ tadaññesaṃ anavajjadhammānaṃ nānantariyabhāvato.

'Pavattentāti' means: having become originators, by way of originating. 'Evanti' refers to the consideration of the manner of occurrence according to the instructed guidance, both by way of injunction and prohibition. And that right thought occurs by way of seeing the manner of occurrence of wrong thoughts. Therein, for the purpose of clarifying the benefit and the danger, the meaning is 'only the perception of impermanence,' not 'the perception of permanence.' Indeed, the inclusion of the particle 'eva' is for the purpose of negating the opposite. Here too, the meaning and purpose of including the word 'eva' should be understood in the same way as stated. The same principle applies to the inclusion of 'idaṃ'. The phrase 'lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure' should be seen as a mere indication, because the abandonment of other lust, hatred, and so on, is desired, and because its abandonment is the means for dispelling that other lust and so on. Thus it is said: just as the expelling of previously corrupted flesh is the means for releasing bad blood. The phrase 'only the supramundane states' is an emphasis which, due to its nature of rejection, should be seen as concerned with turning away from blameworthy states, because those other blameless states, which are the means for and benefits of its attainment, are not excluded.

Cintāmaṇikavijjāsarikkhakatanti iminā “cintāmaṇī”ti evaṃ laddhanāmā loke ekā vijjā atthi, yāya paresaṃ cittaṃ vijānantīti dīpeti. “Tassā kira vijjāya sādhako puggalo tādise desakāle mantaṃ parijappitvā yassa cittaṃ jānitukāmo, tassa diṭṭhahatthādivisesasañjānanamukhena cittācāraṃ anuminanto kathetī”ti keci. Apare “vācaṃ niccharāpetvā tattha akkharasallakkhaṇavasenā”ti vadanti.

By the phrase 'made similar to the Cintāmaṇi knowledge,' it is shown that there is a certain knowledge in the world that has obtained the name 'Cintāmaṇī,' by which they know the minds of others. Some say: 'It is said that a practitioner of this knowledge, having recited the mantra at a suitable time and place, wishing to know someone's mind, infers the conduct of their mind by means of recognizing specific visible signs such as their hands, and then speaks.' Others say: 'Having caused speech to be emitted, by way of observing the characteristics of the syllables therein.'

Idañca [M 2.0142][V 2.0130] pana sabbanti “bhavaṃ gotamo anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhotī”tiādinayappavattaṃ sabbampi.

And by 'all this' is meant all that which proceeds in the manner of 'The venerable Gotama experiences various kinds of psychic power,' and so forth.

Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta is concluded.

Brāhmaṇavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Vagga is concluded.

(7) 2. Mahāvaggo

(7) 2. The Great Section

1. Titthāyatanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Titthāyatanasutta.

62. Dutiyassa paṭhame titthaṃ nāma dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo tabbinimuttassa kassaci diṭṭhivipphanditassa abhāvato. Ettha hi sattā taranti uppilavanti ummujjanimujjaṃ karonti, tasmā “tittha”nti vuccati. Pāragamanasaṅkhātañhi taraṇaṃ diṭṭhigatikānaṃ natthi, tattheva aparāparaṃ nimujjanummujjanavasena pilavanameva tesaṃ taraṇaṃ nāma. Uppādakāti pūraṇakassapādayo. Titthe jātā titthiyā, yathāvuttaṃ vā diṭṭhigatasaṅkhātaṃ titthaṃ etesaṃ atthīti titthikā, titthikā eva titthiyā. Manorameti sāduphalabharitatāya abhayadisatāya ca manorame. Imesuyeva tīsu ṭhānesūti yathāvuttesu titthāyatanesu.

62. In the first [sutta] of the second [vagga], 'tittha' means the sixty-two views, because for one who is liberated from them, there is no agitation of views whatsoever. For here beings cross, float up, and make immersions and emergences; therefore it is called a 'ford' (tittha). For those whose destination is a view, there is no crossing over in the sense of going to the far shore; their crossing, so-called, is merely floating again and again by way of immersing and emerging right there. 'Originators' means Pūraṇa Kassapa and the others. Those born in a 'tittha' are 'titthiyas'; or, as it is said, because they have a 'tittha' in the sense of a set of views, they are 'titthikas'; 'titthikas' are the same as 'titthiyas'. 'Pleasing to the mind' means: pleasing because of being laden with sweet fruit and because it is a place of safety. 'In just these three positions' means in the aforementioned sectarian grounds.

Yo yathā jānāti, tassa tathā vuccatīti iminā puggalajjhāsayavasena tathā vuttanti dasseti. Puggala-saddo ca tissannampi pakatīnaṃ sādhāraṇo, tasmā purisaggahaṇena tato visesanaṃ yathā “aṭṭha purisapuggalā”ti. Paṭisaṃviditaṃ karotīti kevalaṃ jānanavasena viditaṃ karoti. Anubhavati vāti vipākalakkhaṇappattaṃ anubhavati. Pubbekatahetūti antogadhāvadhāraṇaṃ padanti āha “pubbekatakammapaccayenevā”ti. Imināti “sabbaṃ taṃ pubbekatahetū”ti iminā vacanena. Kammavedananti kusalākusalakammasahajaṃ vedanaṃ. Kiriyavedananti “neva kusalākusalā na ca kammavipākā”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ kiriyacittasahajaṃ vedanaṃ. Na kevalañca te kammakiriyavedanā eva paṭikkhipanti, atha kho sāsane loke ca pākaṭe vātābādhādiroge ca paṭikkhipanti evāti dassetuṃ “ye vā ime”tiādimāha. Tattha pittasamuṭṭhānāti pittavikārādhikasambhūtā[V 2.0131]. Anantaradvayepi eseva nayo. Sannipātikāti pittādīnaṃ tiṇṇampi [M 2.0143] vikārānaṃ sannipātato jātā. Utupariṇāmajāti sītādiutuno vipariṇāmato visamaparivuttito jātā. Visamaparihārajāti asappāyāhārayogapaṭisevanavasena kāyassa visamaṃ pariharaṇato jātā. Opakkamikāti upakkamato nibbattā. Kammavipākajāti kammassa vipākabhūtakkhandhato jātā. Virodhipaccayasamuṭṭhānā dhātūnaṃ vikārāvatthā, tappaccayā vā dukkhā vedanā ābādhanaṭṭhena ābādho, so eva rujjanaṭṭhena rogo. Tattha “yo yāpyalakkhaṇo, so rogo, itaro ābādho”ti vadanti. Sabbesañca nesaṃ taṃtaṃdhātūnaṃ visamaṃ āsannakāraṇaṃ, na tathā itarāni. Tatthāpi ca pakopāvatthā dhātuyo āsannakāraṇaṃ, na tathā parapaccayāvatthāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aṭṭhamaṃyeva kammavipākajaṃ ābādhaṃ sampaṭicchanti “sabbaṃ taṃ pubbekatahetū”ti vipallāsaggāhena. “Pubbe”ti purātanasseva kammassa gahitattā upapajjavedanīyampi te paṭikkhipantīti vuttaṃ “dve paṭibāhitvā”ti. Sampaṭicchantīti anujānanti.

By 'As one knows, so it is spoken to them,' it is shown that it is spoken thus according to the individual's disposition. The word 'individual' (puggala) is common to all three natures, hence the specification by 'person' (purisa), as in 'eight kinds of persons.' 'Makes it known' means makes it known simply by way of knowing. 'Or experiences' means experiences that which has reached the characteristic of a result. The phrase 'due to past deeds' is a term with an implicit emphasis; thus it is said: 'solely due to past kamma as a condition.' By 'this' is meant by this statement: 'all that is due to past deeds.' 'Feeling associated with kamma' means feeling concomitant with wholesome and unwholesome kamma. 'Functional feeling' means feeling concomitant with functional consciousness, which is described as 'neither wholesome nor unwholesome, nor a result of kamma.' And not only do they reject those feelings associated with kamma and functional feelings, but they also reject ailments such as those caused by wind, etc., which are well-known in the Dispensation and in the world. To show this, it is said, 'or these,' and so on. Therein, 'arisen from bile' means arisen predominantly from a disorder of bile. The same method applies to the next two. 'Arisen from a combination' means arisen from the combination of the disorders of the three—bile, and so on. 'Arisen from a change of season' means arisen from a change or irregular transformation of the seasons, such as cold, etc. 'Arisen from irregular care' means arisen from irregular maintenance of the body by partaking of unsuitable food and regimen. 'Arisen from assault' means produced from an attack. 'Arisen from the result of kamma' means arisen from the aggregates that are the result of kamma. The state of disorder of the elements arises from opposing conditions, or the painful feeling conditioned by that is an 'ailment' in the sense of afflicting; that itself is a 'disease' in the sense of causing pain. Therein, some say: 'That which has the characteristic of being manageable is a disease; the other is an ailment.' For all of these, the imbalance of their respective elements is the immediate cause, not the others. And there too, it should be understood that the elements in a state of agitation are the immediate cause, not those in a state conditioned by others. They accept only the eighth kind of ailment, that which arises from the result of kamma, due to grasping the perversion, 'all that is due to past deeds.' Because by 'in the past' only old kamma is taken, they also reject feeling to be experienced in the next life; thus it is said, 'having rejected two.' 'They accept' means they approve.

Attanā katamūlakenāti sāhatthikakammahetu. Āṇattimūlakenāti parassa āṇāpanavasena katakammahetu. Imāti tisso vedanā. Sabbe paṭibāhantīti sabbe roge paṭisedhenti sabbesampi tesaṃ ekena issareneva nimmitattā tabbhāvībhāvāsambhavato. Esa nayo sesesupi. Sabbaṃ paṭibāhantīti hetupaccayapaṭisedhanato sabbaṃ nisedhenti.

'With what is done by oneself as the root' means: due to an action performed by one's own hand. 'With command as the root' means: due to an action performed by way of commanding another. 'These' refers to these three feelings. 'They reject all' means they deny all diseases, because all of them have been created by a single lord, and thus their arising and ceasing is impossible. This is the principle in the remaining cases as well. 'They reject all' means they deny everything by rejecting cause and condition.

Mātikaṃ nikkhipitvāti tiṇṇampi vedānaṃ asārabhāvadassanatthaṃ uddesaṃ katvā. Tanti taṃ mātikaṃ. Vibhajitvā dassetunti dosadassanavaseneva vibhāgato dassetuṃ. Laddhipatiṭṭhāpanatthanti attano laddhiyā paṭijānāpanatthaṃ. Laddhito laddhiṃ saṅkamantīti mūlaladdhito aññaladdhiṃ upagacchanti paṭijānanti. Pubbekatahetuyeva paṭisaṃvedetīti kammavedanampi vipākavedanaṃ katvā vadanti. Diṭṭhigatikā hi byāmūḷhacittā kammantaravipākantarādīni āloḷenti, asaṅkarato saññāpetuṃ na sakkonti. Yathā ca akusalakamme, evaṃ kusalakammepīti dassetuṃ “evaṃ pāṇātipātā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha evanti yathā pubbekatahetu eva pāṇātipātino nāma honti, na idāni sayaṃkatakāraṇā, evaṃ pāṇātipātā viramaṇampi pubbekatahetu evāti vicāriyamāno pubbekatavādo akiriyavādo eva sampajjati.

'Having laid down the matrix' means: having set forth a summary for the purpose of showing the essencelessness of the three feelings. 'That' refers to that matrix. 'To show after analyzing' means to show by way of division, by means of showing the faults. 'For the purpose of establishing a doctrine' means for the purpose of making others profess one's own doctrine. 'They pass from doctrine to doctrine' means they go from their original doctrine to another doctrine and profess it. 'One experiences solely due to past deeds' means they speak of even feeling associated with kamma as a resultant feeling. For those whose destination is a view, with their minds bewildered, mix up different kammas, different results, and so on, and are unable to explain them without confusion. And to show that as it is with unwholesome kamma, so it is with wholesome kamma, it is said, 'Thus, from killing living beings,' and so on. Therein, 'thus' means: just as there are killers of living beings solely due to a past cause, not due to a cause made by themselves now, so too the abstinence from killing living beings is solely due to a past cause. When examined, the doctrine of past deeds becomes a doctrine of non-action.

Kattukamyatāchando [M 2.0144] na taṇhāchando. Kattukamyatāti kātumicchā. Paccattapurisakāroti tena tena purisena kattabbakiccaṃ na hoti pubbekatahetu eva sijjhanato. Ubhayampi taṃ esa na labbhatīti kattabbakaraṇaṃ sucaritapūraṇaṃ, akattabbaakaraṇaṃ duccaritaviratīti idaṃ ubhayampi esa [V 2.0132] na labhati. Samaṇāpi hi pubbekatakāraṇāyeva hontīti pubbekatakāraṇāyeva samaṇāpi honti, na idāni saṃvarasamādānādinā. Assamaṇāpi pubbekatakāraṇāyevāti pubbekatakāraṇāyeva assamaṇāpi honti, na saṃvarabhedena.

The desire to act is a desire for action, not the desire that is craving. 'The desire for action' means the wish to do. 'Personal exertion' means there is no duty to be done by any particular individual, as it is accomplished solely due to past actions. 'Both of these are unattainable by this' means that this person does not attain both: the fulfillment of good conduct by doing what should be done, and the abstention from bad conduct by not doing what should not be done. For ascetics become so solely due to past actions, not through present restraint, undertaking of vows, and so on. Likewise, non-ascetics become so solely due to past actions, not through breaking restraint.

Yathā pubbekatavāde chandavāyāmānaṃ asambhavato paccattapurisakārānaṃ abhāvo, evaṃ issaranimmānavādepi issareneva sabbassa nimmitabhāvānujānanatoti vuttaṃ “pubbekatavāde vuttanayeneva veditabbo”ti. Esa nayo ahetukavādepīti āha “tathā ahetukavādepī”ti.

Just as in the doctrine of past deeds there is an absence of personal effort due to the impossibility of desire and striving, so too in the doctrine of a creator's fashioning, because of the acceptance that everything is fashioned by a creator alone, it is said, 'It should be understood in the same way as stated in the doctrine of past deeds.' This same method applies to the doctrine of no-cause as well; thus it is said, 'Similarly, in the doctrine of no-cause.'

Imesantiādinā imesaṃ titthāyatanānaṃ tucchāsāratāya thusakoṭṭanena kuṇḍakamattassapi alābho viya paramatthalesassapi abhāvo, tathā khajjopanakobhāsato tejaso phuliṅgamattassapi abhāvo viya andhaveṇikassapi maggassa appaṭilābho viya saddamattaṃ nissāya micchābhāgena vipallatthatāya daddarajātake (jā. 1.2.43-43) sasakasadisatā ca vibhāvitā hoti. Sārabhāvanti sīlasārādisampattiyā sārasabbhāvaṃ. Niyyānikabhāvanti ekanteneva vaṭṭato niyyānāvahabhāvaṃ. Aniggahitoti na niggahetabbo. Tenāha “niggahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyo”ti. Asaṃkiliṭṭhoti saṃkilesavirahito. Tenāha “nikkileso”tiādi. Anupavajjoti dhammato na upavaditabbo. Appaṭikuṭṭho nāma appaṭisedhanaṃ vā siyā anakkosanaṃ vāti tadubhayaṃ dassento “appaṭibāhito anupakkuṭṭho”ti āha.

By 'By this...' and so on, the emptiness and worthlessness of these heretical tenets is shown: just as from pounding husks not even a bit of bran is obtained, so there is an absence of even a trace of ultimate reality; and just as from a firefly's glow not even a spark of fire is obtained, or as a line of blind men fails to find a path, so too, as in the Daddara Jātaka (Jā. 1.2.43-43), their similarity to a hare is made clear, due to their perversion through wrong understanding by relying on mere sound. 'Essential nature' means the existence of an essence through the attainment of the essence of virtue and so on. 'The liberating quality' means the state of leading entirely away from the cycle of existence. 'Not to be refuted' means it is not to be refuted; therefore, it is said, 'incapable of being refuted.' 'Untainted' means free from defilement; therefore, it is said, 'stainless,' and so on. 'Unblameable' means not to be reproached according to the Dhamma. 'Unrebuked' may mean either 'not to be rejected' or 'not to be reviled.' Showing both, it is said, 'unobstructed, unreviled.'

Tassa dhammassāti “ayaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave”tiādinā uddhaṭassa dhammassa. Pañhaṃ pucchitvāti kathetukamyatāvasena pañhaṃ pucchitvā. Yathāpaṭipāṭiyāti mātikāya yathānikkhittappaṭipāṭiyā. Dhātuyoti sabhāvadhāraṇaṭṭhena dhātuyo. Tā pana yasmā taṇhādiṭṭhikappanāparikappitaattasubhasukhasassatādipakatiādidhuvādijīvādikāyādikā viya [M 2.0145] na icchāsabhāvā diṭṭhiādirahitehi vimuccamānaudumbarapupphādilokavohāravatthūni viya ca vācāvatthumattā, atha kho saccaparamatthabhūtāti āha “sabhāvā”ti, saccasabhāvāti attho. Attano sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti hi dhātuyo. Nijjīvanissattabhāvappakāsakoti bāhiraparikappitajīvābhāvappakāsako lokiyamahājanasaṃkappitasattābhāvappakāsako ca. Ākaraṭṭhenāti uppajjanaṭṭhānabhāvena. Uppattiṭṭhānampi hi ākaro āyatananti vuccati yathā “kambojo assānaṃ āyatana”nti. Manopavicārāti taṃ taṃ ārammaṇaṃ upecca manaso vividhacaraṇākāro. Kehi katthāti āha “vitakkavicārapādehī”tiādi. Aṭṭhārasasu ṭhānesūti cha somanassaṭṭhāniyāni[V 2.0133], cha domanassaṭṭhāniyāni, cha upekkhāṭṭhāniyānīti evaṃ aṭṭhārasasu ṭhānesu.

'Of that teaching' refers to the teaching extracted beginning with 'Now, monks,' and so on. 'Having asked a question' means having posed a question out of a desire to speak. 'In order' means according to the sequence laid out in the matrix. 'Elements' means elements in the sense of sustaining their intrinsic nature. Now, since these are not of an arbitrary nature—like the self, beauty, pleasure, permanence, and so on, imagined by craving, views, and conceptual proliferation—nor are they merely objects of speech—like worldly conventional things such as the udumbara flower, which are devoid of views and so on—but rather are ultimately true in their intrinsic nature, therefore it is said, 'by their intrinsic nature,' meaning they are true in essence. For elements are so called because they sustain their own intrinsic nature. 'Revealing the state of being lifeless and devoid of a being' means disclosing the absence of an externally fabricated life-principle and the absence of a being as conceived by worldly people. 'As a source' means as a place of arising. For a place of arising is also called a source or a base, just as it is said, 'Kamboja is the source of horses.' 'Mental exploration' refers to the mind’s diverse modes of engagement when approaching various objects. 'By what, where?' it is said, 'by the foot of thought and examination,' and so on. 'In eighteen instances' means in six instances that are bases for joy, six instances that are bases for displeasure, and six instances that are bases for equanimity—thus in eighteen instances.

Patiṭṭhādhātūti sesabhūtattayassa ceva sabbūpādārūpānañca patiṭṭhāsabhāvā dhātu. Iminā nayena ābandhanadhātūtiādīsupi attho veditabbo. Apica kakkhaḷabhāvasiddho sahajātadhammānaṃ ādhārabhāvo patiṭṭhābhāvo. Dravabhāvasiddhaṃ sampiṇḍanaṃ ābandhanaṃ. Uṇhabhāvasiddhaṃ mudutāpakkatāvahaṃ paripācanaṃ. Thaddhabhāvāvahaṃ uddhumātanaṃ vitthambhanaṃ. Rūpavivitto rūpapariyanto ākāsoti yesaṃ so paricchedo, tehi so asamphuṭṭhovāti vuttaṃ “ākāsadhātūti asamphuṭṭhadhātū”ti. Sañjānanavidhurā ārammaṇūpaladdhi vijānanadhātu. Vitthāratopi kathetuṃ vaṭṭati saṅkhepantogadhattā vitthārassa. Saṅkhepato kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati kathetabbassa atthassa anavasesapariyādānābhāvato. Tenāha “vitthāratova vaṭṭatī”ti. Ubhayathāti saṅkhepato vitthārato ca.

'The supporting element' is the element that has the nature of a foundation for the remaining three great elements and all derived material phenomena. In this way, the meaning should be understood also in the cases of the binding element, and so forth. Moreover, the state of being a support is the state of being a basis for co-arisen phenomena, established by the characteristic of hardness. Binding is cohesion, established by the characteristic of fluidity. Ripening, which brings about softness and maturity, is established by the characteristic of heat. Stiffening is swelling, which brings about a state of rigidity. Space is that which is delimited by 'distinct from form, the boundary of form'; because it is untouched by those forms, it is said, 'The space element is the uncontacted element.' The consciousness element is the apprehension of an object, which is devoid of perceiving. It is suitable to explain in detail because the extensive contains the brief. It is not suitable to explain briefly because of the inability to completely encompass the meaning to be conveyed without remainder. Therefore, it is said, 'Only a detailed explanation is suitable.' 'Both ways' means both briefly and in detail.

Anipphannāpi ākāsadhātu bhūtāni upādāya gahetabbatāmattena “upādārūpa”nteva vuccati. Diṭṭhānevāti sallakkhetabbāni upādārūpabhāvasāmaññato. Tena sahajātā vedanā vedanākkhandho samudāye pavattavohārassa avayavepi dissanato yathā “vatthekadese daḍḍhe vatthaṃ daḍḍha”nti. “Phasso ca cetanā ca saṅkhārakkhandho”ti vuttaṃ mahābhūmakattā tesaṃ tappadhānattā ca saṅkhārakkhandhassa. Arūpakkhandhā nāmaṃ ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ namanato nāmādhīnaggahaṇato ca. Rūpakkhandho rūpaṃ paribyattaṃ ruppanaṭṭhena. Paccayanti nissayabhūtaṃ paccayaṃ. Vibhāgena dvācattālīsa. Ekāsīti [M 2.0146] cittāni “sammasanacāroya”nti katvā. Anukkamena paṭipajjamānoti evaṃ kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiyaṃ ṭhito uparimena tissannaṃ visuddhīnaṃ sampādanavasena visuddhibhāvanaṃ ussukkāpento.

Even though it is unproduced, the space element is called 'derived form' merely because it is to be grasped in dependence on the great elements. 'In the visible bases' means they should be discerned by the common characteristic of being derived form. Feeling, which is co-nascent with it, is the feeling aggregate, because a convention applied to a whole is also seen applied to a part, just as when one part of a cloth is burned, it is said, 'the cloth is burned.' It is said, 'Contact and volition are the formation aggregate,' because they are universal mental factors and because they are predominant in the formation aggregate. The formless aggregates are 'name' because they bend towards an object and because their apprehension is dependent on a name. The form aggregate is form, which is manifest through its characteristic of being afflicted. 'Condition' means a supporting condition. By analysis, there are forty-two. Having considered the eighty-one types of consciousness as 'this is the range of comprehension.' 'Proceeding gradually' means one who, being established in the purification by overcoming doubt, strives to cultivate purification by way of accomplishing the three higher purifications.

Phassāyatananti phassassa uppattiṭṭhānaṃ. Suvaṇṇādīnanti suvaṇṇamaṇivajirādīnaṃ. Ākiṇṇaṃ viya hutvā uppajjanti etthāti ākaro. Yathā cakkhu vipākaphassassa visesapaccayo, na tathā itaresanti katvā vuttaṃ “dve cakkhuviññāṇānī”tiādi. Esa nayo sesavāresupi. Dvattiṃsāya vipākaphassesu dvipañcaviññāṇasahagataphasse ṭhapetvā sesā dvāvīsati vipākaphassā veditabbā. Diṭṭhameva hoti tena samānayogakkhamattā. “Saṅkhepato tāvā”ti saṅkhepakathaṃ ārabhitvāpi vitthārakathāpettha vuttanayattā suviññeyyāvāti vuttaṃ “heṭṭhā…pe… veditabba”nti.

'The base of contact' means the place of arising for contact. 'Of gold, etc.' means of gold, gems, diamonds, and so on. It is a 'mine' (ākaro) because things arise in it as if scattered. Because the eye is a specific condition for resultant contact in a way that the others are not, it is said, 'two eye-consciousnesses,' and so on. This method applies in the remaining instances as well. Among the thirty-two resultant contacts, having excluded the ten contacts associated with the two sets of five-sense consciousness, the remaining twenty-two resultant contacts should be understood. It is just what is seen, merely by its suitability for a similar application. 'In brief, for now'—even though a brief explanation was begun, because the detailed explanation here is easy to understand due to the stated method, it is said, 'below... should be understood.'

Somanassassa [V 2.0134] uppattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ somanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ. Tenāha “somanassassa kāraṇabhūta”nti. Upavicaratīti upecca pavattati. Sabhāvato saṅkappato ca somanassādiuppattihetukā somanassaṭṭhāniyāditāti āha “iṭṭhaṃ vā hotū”tiādi. Catutthaṃ diṭṭhameva hoti tadavinābhāvato.

A base of joy is that which is the place of arising for joy. Therefore, it is said, 'that which is the cause of joy.' 'It explores' means it approaches and proceeds. Because they are causes for the arising of joy and so on, both by their nature and by intention, they are called bases of joy and so on; therefore, it is said, 'may it be agreeable,' and so on. The fourth is just what is seen, due to its inseparability from that.

Ariyasaccānīti purimapade uttarapadalopenāyaṃ niddesoti āha “ariyabhāvakarānī”tiādi. Visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.531) pakāsitaṃ, tasmā na idha pakāsetabbanti adhippāyo. Sukhāvabodhanatthanti desiyamānāya vaṭṭakathāya sukhena avabodhanatthaṃ. Tenāha “yassa hī”tiādi. Dvādasapadanti avijjādīhi padehi dvādasapadaṃ. Paccayavaṭṭanti paccayappabandhaṃ. Kathetukāmo hoti paccayākāramukhena saccāni dassetukāmatāya. Gabbhāvakkantivaṭṭanti gabbhokkantimukhena vipākavaṭṭaṃ dasseti “gabbhassāvakkanti hotī”tiādinā. Tasmā panettha gabbhāvakkantivaseneva vaṭṭaṃ dassitanti āha “gabbhāvakkantivaṭṭasmiṃ hī”tiādi. Gabbhāvakkantivaṭṭasminti mātukucchimhi nibbattanavasena pavattadhammappabandhe. Dassiteti desanāvasena dassite. Purimā dve yoniyo itarāhi oḷārikatāya [M 2.0147] paribyattatarāti vuttaṃ “gabbhāvakkanti…pe… avabodhetumpī”ti.

Ariyasaccāni, 'the noble truths'—this exposition is given by the elision of the latter word in the former compound, hence it is said, 'producing the noble state,' and so on. It is explained in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 16.87), therefore it need not be explained here—this is the intention. Sukhāvabodhanatthaṃ, 'for the purpose of easy comprehension,' means for the sake of easy understanding of the discourse on the cycle of existence being taught. Therefore, it is said, 'for whom,' and so on. Dvādasapadaṃ, 'twelve terms,' means the twelve terms beginning with ignorance, and so on. Paccayavaṭṭaṃ, 'the cycle of conditions,' means the sequence of conditions. He wishes to explain, desiring to show the truths by way of the mode of conditions. Gabbhāvakkantivaṭṭaṃ, 'the cycle of entering the womb,' means he shows the resultant cycle through the process of entering the womb, as stated: 'there is descent into the womb,' and so on. Therefore, here the cycle is shown only by way of entering the womb, hence it is said, 'for in the cycle of entering the womb,' and so on. Gabbhāvakkantivaṭṭasmiṃ, 'in the cycle of entering the womb,' means in the sequence of phenomena occurring through birth in the mother’s womb. Dassite, 'shown,' means shown by way of teaching. The first two modes of generation are more manifest than the others due to being grosser, hence it is said, 'entering the womb... to comprehend as well.'

Paccayamattanti channaṃ dhātūnaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ paccayabhāvamattaṃ, na tehi bhāgaso nipphādiyamānaṃ paccayavisesaṃ “kuto panetaṃ channaṃ dhātūna”nti avibhāgena vuttattā. Tenāha “idaṃ vuttaṃ hotī”tiādi.
