Na mātu na pitu tāsaṃ dhātūnaṃ imassa sattassa bāhirabhāvato. Gabbhassāti ettha gabbhati attabhāvabhāvena vattatīti gabbho, kalalādiavattho dhammappabandho. Tannissitattā pana sattasantāno gabbhoti vutto yathā mañcanissitā “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti. Tannissayabhāvato mātukucchi gabbhoti vuccati “gabbhe vasati māṇavo”tiādīsu (jā. 1.15.363). Gabbho viyāti vā gabbho. Yathā hi nivāsaṭṭhānatāya sattānaṃ ovarako “gabbho”ti vuccati, evaṃ gabbhaseyyakānaṃ sattānaṃ yāva abhijāti nivāsaṭṭhānatāya mātukucchi “gabbho”ti vuccati. Idha pana paṭhamaṃ vuttaattheneva gabbhoti veditabbo. Tenāha “gabbho ca nāmā”tiādi.

Paccayamattaṃ, 'the mere conditionality,' is common to the six elements, being just the state of a condition, not a particular condition produced by them in parts—'how then is this for the six elements?'—because it is spoken of without distinction. Therefore it is said, 'this is what is meant,' and so on. It is neither of the mother nor of the father, as those elements are external to this being. Gabbhassa, 'of the womb'—here gabbha, 'womb,' means that which proceeds as the state of individual existence; the sequence of phenomena in the state beginning with the kalala. Dependent on that, the continuum of a being is called 'gabbha,' just as those dependent on a couch are said to 'make the couch cry out.' Due to being a basis for that, the mother's womb is called 'gabbha,' as in 'the young man dwells in the womb,' and so on (Jā. 1.15.363). Or, 'gabbha' is like a 'gabbha' (chamber). Just as a dwelling place for beings is called a 'gabbha' (chamber), so too, for beings lying in the womb until birth, the mother's womb is called 'gabbha' as their dwelling place. Here, however, 'gabbha' should be understood in the sense first stated. Therefore it is said, 'and what is called a gabbha,' and so on.

Niratiatthena nirayo ca so yathāvuttena atthena gabbho cāti nirayagabbho. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Ayaṃ pana viseso – devamanujādayo viya uddhaṃ dīghā ahutvā tiriyaṃ añcitā dīghāti tiracchānā. Te eva khandhakoṭṭhāsabhāvena yoni ca so vuttanayena gabbho cāti [V 2.0135] tiracchānayonigabbho. Pakaṭṭhato sukhato apetaṃ apagamo petabhāvo, taṃ pattānaṃ visayoti pettivisayo, petayoni. Manassa ussannatāya sūrabhāvādiguṇehi upacitamānasatāya ukkaṭṭhaguṇacittatāya manussā. Dibbanti kāmaguṇādīhi kīḷanti laḷanti jotantīti devā. Gabbhasaddo vuttanayo eva. Nānappakāroti yathāvuttena tadanantarabhedena ca nānappakārako. Manussagabbho adhippeto supākaṭatāya paccakkhabhāvato. Okkanti mātukucchiṃ okkamitvā viya uppatitvāti katvā. Nibbattanaṃ nibbatti. Pātubhāvo uppattippakāsako ca.

Hell (niraya) is so called because it is devoid of delight (nirati-attha), and 'gabbha' (womb) is so called in the sense explained; hence, 'nirayagabbha'. This method applies to the remaining terms as well. Here, however, is the distinction: unlike gods and humans, who are vertically long, animals (tiracchānā) are so called because they are long while moving horizontally. That very realm (yoni), by its nature of being a portion of the aggregates, and the womb (gabbha) in the way explained, is 'tiracchānayonigabbha'. The 'pettivisaya' (realm of ghosts) is so called because the state of ghosts (petabhāva) is a departure from prominent happiness; it is the sphere attained by them; hence, 'pettivisaya', 'petayoni'. Humans (manussā) are so called because of the prominence of their minds, their minds being endowed with qualities such as courage, and their minds possessing outstanding qualities. Gods (devā) are so called because they play, delight, and shine with sensual pleasures and so on. The term 'gabbha' (womb) is explained in the same way. 'Of various kinds' (nānappakāro) means of various kinds in the way previously described and by subsequent distinctions. The human womb (manussagabbho) is intended due to its being very clear and directly perceptible. ‘Descent’ (okkanti) is so called because it is an arising as if by descending into the mother’s womb. 'Birth' (nibbattanaṃ) is 'nibbatti'. 'Manifestation' (pātubhāvo) is also that which proclaims arising.

Sannipāto nāma avekallajātihīnavekalleti dassetuṃ “idha mātāpitaro”tiādi vuttaṃ. Idhāti imasmiṃ sattaloke. Sannipatitāti [M 2.0148] samodhānabhāvato sannipatitā samāgatā saṃsiliṭṭhā. Utunīti utumatī sañjātapupphā. Idañca utusamayaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na lokasamaññākarajassa lagganadivasamattaṃ. Mātugāmassa hi yasmiṃ gabbhāsahasaññite okāse dārako nibbattati, tattha mahatī lohitapīḷakā saṇṭhahitvā aggahitapubbā eva bhijjitvā paggharati, vatthu suddhaṃ hoti paggharitalohitattā anāmayattā ca. Visuddhe vatthumhi mātāpitūsu ekavāraṃ sannipatitesu yāva satta divasāni khettameva hoti. Suddhaṃ vatthu nahānato parampi katipayāni divasāni gabbhasaṇṭhahanatāya khettameva hoti parittassa lohitalesassa vijjamānattā. Tasmiṃ samaye hatthaggāhaveṇiggāhādinā aṅgaparāmasanenapi dārako nibbattatiyeva. Itthisantānepi hi sattapi dhātū labbhanteva. Tathā hi pārikāya nābhiparāmasanena sāmassa bodhisattassa, diṭṭhamaṅgalikāya nābhiparāmasanena (jā. aṭṭha. 4.15.mātaṅgajātakavaṇṇanā; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.65) maṇḍabyassa nibbatti ahosi. Gandhanato uppannagatiyā nimittūpaṭṭhānena sūcanato dīpanato gandhoti laddhanāmena bhavagāmikammunā abbati pavattatīti gandhabbo, tattha uppajjamānakasatto. Paccupaṭṭhito hotīti na mātāpitūnaṃ sannipātaṃ olokayamāno samīpe ṭhito paccupaṭṭhito nāma hoti, kammayantayantito pana eko satto tasmiṃ okāse nibbattanako hotīti ayamettha adhippāyo. Tadā hi tatrūpagasatto tatrūpapattiāvahantakammasaṅkhātena pellakayantena tathatthāya pellito upanīto viya hoti.

The term 'confluence' (sannipāta) is used to show the suitability for birth and the absence of defects, as indicated by the phrase 'here, the mother and father,' and so on. 'Here' (idha) means in this world of beings. 'Have come together' (sannipatitā) means they have assembled, united, and joined due to their state of coming together. 'Utunī' means a woman in her fertile period, having menstruated. This is stated with reference to the fertile season, not merely the day of conception as commonly understood in the world. For a woman, in the place designated as the 'womb-receptacle' (gabbhāsaya), where a child is born, a large blood clot forms, and having never been held before, it bursts and flows out. The site becomes pure due to the flowing out of the blood and its freedom from disease. When the site is purified and the parents have come together once, it remains a fertile field for up to seven days. Even after bathing, the pure site remains a fertile field for conception for several days, as a small trace of blood is still present. During that time, a child may be conceived even through the touching of limbs, such as taking the hand or grasping the braid. Indeed, even in the female line, the seven elements can be obtained. For example, the Bodhisatta Sāma was conceived through the touching of the navel of the Pārikā woman. Similarly, Maṇḍavya was born through the touching of the navel of the Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā woman (Jā. Aṭṭha. 4.15, Mātaṅgajātaka-vaṇṇanā; MA. 2.310). 'Gandhabba' is a being about to be born there, who goes and proceeds, impelled by kamma that leads to a future existence; it gets the name 'gandha' from indicating, from the appearance of a sign of a destination that has arisen, from suggesting, from illuminating. 'Is present' (paccupaṭṭhito hoti) does not mean that the being is standing nearby, observing the parents' union. Rather, the meaning here is that, impelled by the mechanism of kamma, a being is to be born in that place. At that time, a being fit for that place is, as it were, propelled and brought there for that purpose by the propelling mechanism known as the kamma that brings about rebirth there.

Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti ettha viññāṇassa paccayabhāvena gahitattā “tayo arūpino khandhā”ti vuttaṃ. Idha pana viññāṇaṃ paccayabhāvena aggahetvā gabbhokkantiyā eva paccayabhāvena gahitattā “viññāṇakkhandhampi pakkhipitvā”ti vuttaṃ. Idha pana manussagabbhassa okkantiyā adhippetattā “gabbhaseyyakānaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe”ti vuttaṃ.

In the statement 'With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises,' because consciousness is taken as a condition, it is said, 'the three immaterial aggregates.' Here, however, since consciousness is not taken as the condition, but the descent into the womb itself is taken as the condition, it is said, 'including the consciousness aggregate.' Here, however, because the descent into a human womb is intended, it is said, 'at the moment of rebirth-linking for those lying in the womb'.

Taṇhāya [V 2.0136] samudayasaccabhāvena gahitattā “ṭhapetvā taṇha”nti vuttaṃ. Tasseva pabhāvikāti tasseva yathāvuttassa dukkhasaccassa uppādikā. Dukkhanirodhoti [M 2.0149] ettha dukkhaggahaṇena taṇhāpi gahitāti āha “tesaṃ dvinnampi…pe… dukkhanirodho”ti. Avisesena hi tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ idha dukkhanti adhippetaṃ. Atha vā dukkhassa anuppattinirodho tabbhāvikāya taṇhāya anuppattinirodhena vinā na hotīti vuttaṃ “tesaṃ dvinnampi…pe… dukkhanirodho”ti. Anuppattinirodhoti ca anuppattinirodhanimittaṃ nibbānaṃ dasseti.

Because craving is taken as the truth of origination, it is said, 'except for craving.' Its producer (pabhāvikā) means it is the producer of that same truth of suffering as described. Regarding 'the cessation of suffering' (dukkhanirodho), here, by the term 'suffering,' craving is also included, hence it is said, 'of both of these... the cessation of suffering.' For, without distinction, the cycle of the three planes is intended here as suffering. Alternatively, the non-arising cessation of suffering does not occur without the non-arising cessation of craving, which produces it; hence it is said, 'of both of these... the cessation of suffering.' And 'non-arising cessation' (anuppattinirodho) indicates Nibbāna, the condition for non-arising cessation.

“Tattha vuttanayeneva veditabba”nti vatvā ubhayattha pāḷiyā pavattiākārabhedaṃ dassetuṃ “ayaṃ pana viseso”ti āha. Tatthāti visaddhimagge. Idhāti imasmiṃ sutte. Avijjāya tvevāti avijjāya tu eva. Asesavirāganirodhāti ettha accantameva saṅkhāre virajjati etenāti virāgo, maggo, tasmā virāgasaṅkhātena maggena asesanirodhā asesetvā nirodhā samucchindanāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Having said, 'There, it should be understood according to the method already stated,' he then said, 'But this is the distinction,' to show the difference in the way the Pāli text occurs in both places. 'There' (tattha) means in the Visuddhimagga. 'Here' (idha) means in this Sutta. 'Of ignorance, indeed' (avijjāya tveva) means 'of ignorance, truly' (avijjāya tu eva). Regarding 'complete cessation through dispassion' (asesavirāganirodha), here, 'dispassion' (virāga) is that by which one becomes utterly dispassionate towards formations; it is the path. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: by means of the path, which is called dispassion, there is complete cessation, a cessation without remainder, an utter cutting off.

Sakalassāti anavasesassa. Kevalassāti vā suddhassa, paraparikappitasattajīvādivirahitassāti attho. Khīṇākāropi vuccati “nirujjhanaṃ nirodho”ti iminā atthena. Arahattampi nirodhoti vuccati nirodhante uppannattā. Nibbānampi nirodhoti vuccati avijjādīnaṃ nirodhassa nimittabhāvato avijjādayo nirujjhanti etthāti nirodhoti katvā. Khīṇākāradassanavasenāti avijjādīnaṃ anuppattinirodhena nirujjhanākāradassanavasena. Nibbānameva sandhāya, na pana arahattanti adhippāyo. Sabhāvadhammānaṃ niggaho nāma yathāvuttadhammaparicchedato ūnādhikabhāvappakāsanena attasabhāvavibhāvaneneva hotīti āha “niggaṇhanto hī”tiādi.

'Of all' (sakalassa) means without remainder. 'Of the whole' (kevalassa) means either pure, or devoid of beings, life, etc., imagined by others—this is the meaning. Even the state of destruction (khīṇākāra) is called 'cessation' (nirodha) with this meaning: 'ceasing is cessation' (nirujjhanaṃ nirodho). Arahantship is also called cessation because it arises at the end of cessation. Nibbāna is also called cessation because it is the ground for the cessation of ignorance and so on, in the sense that 'ignorance and so on cease here.' 'By seeing the state of destruction' (khīṇākāradassanavasena) means by seeing the mode of ceasing through the non-arising cessation of ignorance and so on. This refers to Nibbāna itself, not to Arahantship—this is the intention. The restraint of intrinsic phenomena occurs by revealing a state of deficiency or excess in relation to the definition of phenomena as stated, and by distinguishing their own intrinsic nature; hence he said, 'for one restraining,' etc.

Titthāyatanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Titthāyatana Sutta is finished.

2. Bhayasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Bhaya Sutta

63. Dutiye parittātuṃ samatthabhāvenāti uppannabhayato rakkhituṃ samatthabhāvena. Natthi ettha mātāputtaṃ aññamaññaṃ tāyituṃ samatthanti amātāputtāni, tāniyeva amātāputtikāni. Tenāha “natthi etthā”tiādi. Yanti bhummatthe upayogavacananti āha “yasmiṃ samaye”ti. Mātāpi puttaṃ passituṃ na labhati, parittātuṃ na samatthanti adhippāyo[M 2.0150]. Puttopi mātaranti etthāpi eseva nayo. Cittutrāsoyeva bhayaṃ cittutrāsabhayaṃ. Iminā ottappabhayādiṃ nivatteti. Aṭaviggahaṇena aṭavivāsino [V 2.0137] vuttā “sabbo gāmo āgato”tiādīsu viyāti āha “aṭavīti cettha aṭavivāsino corā veditabbā”ti. Eteti aṭavivāsino corā. Etaṃ vuttanti “aṭavisaṅkopo”ti idaṃ vuttaṃ. Ṭhānagamanādiiriyāpathacakkasamaṅgino iriyāpathacakkasamāruḷhā nāma hontīti āha “iriyāpathacakkampi vaṭṭatī”ti. Iriyāpathoyeva pavattanaṭṭhena cakkanti iriyāpathacakkaṃ.

63. In the second case, 'by the ability to protect' means by the ability to guard from fear that has arisen. 'Here, a mother and son are not able to protect each other' means they are without mother and son, truly motherless and sonless. Hence he said, 'There is not here,' etc. 'The word yanti is a locative expression,' means he said 'at which time.' The meaning is that the mother is not able to see her son, nor is she able to protect him. The same method applies to 'the son, too, the mother.' Fear is simply terror of the mind (cittutrāsa); hence 'fear which is terror of the mind' (cittutrāsabhayaṃ). By this, he excludes fear such as moral dread. By the term 'forest,' forest-dwellers are meant, as in such phrases as 'the whole village has come'; hence he said, 'And here, by "forest," forest-dwelling robbers are to be understood.' 'These' (ete) means these forest-dwelling robbers. 'This is said' means the phrase 'a disturbance in the forest' (aṭavisaṅkopo) is said. 'Those endowed with the wheel of postures such as standing, going, etc., are called "mounted on the wheel of postures"'; hence he said, 'The wheel of postures also turns.' A posture itself is a 'wheel' in the sense of proceeding; hence 'wheel of postures' (iriyāpathacakkaṃ).

Pariyāyantīti parito tena tena disābhāgena gacchanti. Tenāha “ito cito ca gacchantī”ti. Mātupemena gantuṃ avisahitvā attano santikaṃ āgacchantaṃ. Attasinehassa balavabhāvato mātarampi anapekkhitvā “attānaṃyeva rakkhissāmī”ti gacchantaṃ. Ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nilīnanti vuttanayeneva gantvā ekasmiṃ kheme padese nisinnaṃ. Kulle vātiādīsu kūlaṃ paratīraṃ vahati pāpetīhi kullo, taraṇatthāya veḷunaḷādīhi kalāpaṃ katvā baddho. Pattharitvā baddho pana uḷumpo, cāṭiādi mattikābhājanaṃ. Vuyhamānanti udakoghena adhosotaṃ nīyamānaṃ.

'They wander about' (pariyāyanti) means they go around in this or that direction. Hence he said, 'they go here and there.' 'Coming to his own mother,' unable to bear leaving due to his love for her. 'Going,' disregarding even his mother due to the strength of his self-love, thinking, 'I will protect myself.' 'Hidden in one place' means having gone in the way described and sat down in a safe place. Regarding 'on a raft' (kulle) and so on: a 'raft' (kullo) is so called because it carries or conveys one to the far shore (kūlaṃ); it is a bundle of reeds, bamboo, or the like, bound together for the purpose of crossing. A float (uḷumpo), however, is something spread out and bound. A pot (cāṭi) is an earthenware vessel. 'Being swept away' (vuyhamānaṃ) means being carried downstream by a flood of water.

Yathāvuttāni tīṇi bhayāni samātāputtikāniyeva assutavato puthujjanassa vasena amātāputtikāni dassitānīti āha “evaṃ pariyāyato amātāputtikāni bhayāni dassetvā”ti.

The three fears already mentioned, although they are indeed related to mother and son, are shown as unrelated to mother and son with respect to an uninstructed ordinary person. Thus he said: 'Having thus, by way of explanation, shown the fears as unrelated to mother and son...'

Bhayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhaya Sutta is finished.

3. Venāgapurasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Venāgapura Sutta

64. Tatiye evaṃnāmake janapadeti yattha nāmaggahaṇena kosalasaddassa ruḷhīsaddataṃ dasseti. Tathā hi kosalā nāma jānapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado ruḷhīsaddena “kosalā”ti vuccati. Akkharacintakā hi īdisesu ṭhānesu yutte viya saliṅgavacanāni (pāṇini 1.2.51) icchanti. Ayamettha ruḷhī yathā aññatthāpi “kurūsu viharati, aṅgesu viharatī”ti ca. Tabbisesane pana janapadasadde jātisadde ekavacanameva [M 2.0151] yathā “kosalesu janapade”ti. Cārikanti caraṇaṃ. Caraṇaṃ vā cāro, so eva cārikā. Tayidaṃ maggagamanaṃ idhādhippetaṃ, na cuṇṇikagamanamattanti āha “addhānagamanaṃ gacchanto”ti. Taṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ “cārikā ca nāmesā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha dūrepīti dūrepi nātidūrepi. Sahasā gamananti sīghagamanaṃ. Mahākassapapaccuggamanādīsūti ādi-saddena āḷavakādīnaṃ atthāya gamanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Bhagavā hi mahākassapattheraṃ paccuggacchanto muhuttena tigāvutamaggamagamāsi. Āḷavakassatthāya [V 2.0138] tiṃsayojanaṃ, tathā aṅgulimālassa, pukkusātissa pana pañcacattālīsayojanaṃ, mahākappinassa vīsayojanasataṃ, dhaniyassatthāya satta yojanasatāni, dhammasenāpatino saddhivihārikassa vanavāsissa tissasāmaṇerassa tigāvutādhikaṃ vīsayojanasataṃ agamāsi. Imaṃ sandhāyāti imaṃ aturitacārikaṃ sandhāya.

64. In the third case, regarding 'in the country of that name,' by the mention of the name he shows that the word 'Kosala' is a conventional term. For the people and princes of the country are called 'the Kosalas' (Kosalā), and even the single country where they live is called 'Kosala' by conventional usage. Grammarians, in such cases, desire words of corresponding gender and number, as if they were adjectives (cf. Pāṇini 1.2.51). This is the conventional usage here, just as elsewhere in 'he dwells among the Kurus' and 'he dwells among the Aṅgas.' But when the word for country (janapada) or people (jāti) is used to specify it, it is in the singular, as in 'in the country of the Kosalas' (kosalesu janapade). 'Wandering' (cārikaṃ) means journeying (caraṇaṃ). Journeying is 'cāra,' and that itself is 'cārikā.' Here, this is intended as travel along a road, not just a short walk; hence he said, 'going on a long journey.' To show this with its divisions, the passage beginning 'And this wandering' was stated. Therein, 'even far' means far, but not too far. 'Swift travel' means rapid travel. Regarding 'in going to meet Mahākassapa, etc.,' with the word 'etc.' he includes travel for the sake of Āḷavaka and others. For the Blessed One, when going to meet the Elder Mahākassapa, traveled a three-gāvuta road in a moment. For Āḷavaka he traveled thirty leagues, likewise for Aṅgulimāla; for Pukkusāti, forty-five leagues; for Mahākappina, one hundred and twenty leagues; for Dhaniya, seven hundred leagues; and for the novice Tissa, the forest-dwelling co-resident of the General of the Dhamma, he traveled one hundred and twenty leagues plus three gāvutas. 'Referring to this' means referring to this unhurried wandering.

Upalabhiṃsūti ettha savanavasena upalabhiṃsūti imamatthaṃ dassento “sotadvāra…pe… jāniṃsū”ti āha. Sabbampi vākyaṃ avadhāraṇaphalattā antogadhāvadhāraṇanti āha “padapūraṇamatte vā nipāto”ti. Avadhāraṇatthenāti pana iminā iṭṭhatthatovadhāraṇatthaṃ kho-saddaggahaṇanti dasseti. Assosīti padaṃ kho-sadde gahite tena phullitamaṇḍitavibhūsitaṃ viya hontaṃ pūritaṃ nāma hoti, tena ca purimapacchimapadāni saṃsiliṭṭhāni nāma honti, na tasmiṃ aggahiteti āha “padapūraṇena byañjanasiliṭṭhatāmattamevā”ti. Mattasaddo visesanivattiattho. Tenassa anatthantaradīpanatā dassitā hoti, evasaddena pana byañjanasiliṭṭhatāya ekantikatā.

Regarding 'they learned' (upalabhiṃsū), showing that this means 'they learned by way of hearing,' he said, 'through the ear-door... they knew.' Because the entire sentence has the effect of emphasis, the emphasis is contained within it; thus he says, 'Or, the particle is merely a line-filler.' But by 'with the meaning of emphasis,' he shows that the particle 'kho' is taken for the purpose of emphasizing the desired meaning. When the particle 'kho' is included, the word 'he heard' (assosi) becomes as if blossomed, adorned, and beautified; it is called 'filled.' And by that, the preceding and following words are called 'well-connected.' If it is not included, he says, 'by the word-filler there is merely smoothness of phrasing.' The word 'merely' (matta) has the meaning of excluding qualification. By this is shown its non-elucidation of any other meaning. But by the word 'eva' (in 'mattamevā'), the definiteness of the smoothness of phrasing is shown.

Samitapāpattāti accantaṃ anavasesato savāsanaṃ samitapāpattā. Evañhi bāhirakavītarāgasekkhāsekkhapāpasamanato bhagavato pāpasamanaṃ visesitaṃ hoti. Tenassa yathābhūtaguṇādhigatametaṃ nāmaṃ yadidaṃ samaṇoti dīpeti. Anekatthattā nipātānaṃ idha anussavattho adhippetoti āha “khalūti anussavatthe nipāto”ti. Ālapanamattanti piyālāpavacanamattaṃ. Piyasamudāhārā hete “bho”ti vā “āvuso”ti vā “devānaṃ piyā”ti vā. Gottavasenāti ettha gaṃ tāyatīti gottaṃ. Gotamoti hi pavattamānaṃ vacanaṃ buddhiñca tāyati ekaṃsikavisayatāya rakkhatīti gottaṃ. Yathā hi buddhi ārammaṇabhūtena atthena [M 2.0152] vinā na vattati, tathā abhidhānaṃ abhidheyyabhūtena, tasmā so gottasaṅkhāto attho tāni tāyati rakkhatīti vuccati. Ko pana soti? Aññakulaparamparāsādhāraṇaṃ tassa kulassa ādipurisasamudāgataṃ taṃkulapariyāpannasādhāraṇaṃ sāmaññarūpanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca samaṇoti iminā parikkhakajanehi bhagavato bahumatabhāvo dassito samitapāpatākittanato. Gotamoti iminā lokiyajanehi uccākulasambhūtatā dīpitā tena uditoditavipulakhattiyakulavibhāvanato. Sabbakhattiyānañhi ādibhūtamahāsammatamahārājato paṭṭhāya asambhinnaṃ uḷāratamaṃ sakyarājakulaṃ.

‘Samitapāpattā’ means having evil completely and entirely stilled, without remainder, along with its latent tendencies. Thus, the Blessed One’s stilling of evil is distinguished from the stilling of evil by external passionless ones, trainees, and perfected ones. Therefore, this name, ‘samaṇa,’ rightly declares His attainment of true qualities, illuminating Him as a true ascetic. Because particles have multiple meanings, here the meaning of hearsay is intended, as stated: ‘khalū’ is a particle used in the sense of hearsay. ‘Ālapanamattanti’ refers merely to a term of address. These are affectionate forms of address, such as ‘bho,’ ‘āvuso,’ or ‘devānaṃ piyā.’ ‘Gottavasenāti’: Here, ‘gotta’ means that which protects the earth. For the term ‘Gotama’ is a designation that, as it continues, protects the intellect and preserves it by being the unique object. Just as the intellect cannot function without an object as its basis, so too a name depends on what it signifies. Hence, this meaning, designated as ‘gotta,’ is said to protect and preserve those things. But what is it? It should be understood as the common form particular to that family, originating from the first ancestor of that family and shared by those included in that family. Here, the term ‘samaṇa’ demonstrates the Blessed One’s high esteem among the examining people due to the proclamation of His stilling of evil. ‘Gotama’ reveals His noble birth to worldly people, highlighting His arising from the eminent and extensive Khattiya lineage. For among all Khattiyas, the Sakyan royal family, unbroken and most eminent, has its origin from the great King Mahāsammata, the first monarch.

Kenaci pārijuññenāti ñātipārijuññabhogapārijuññādinā kenacipi pārijuññena parihāniyā anabhibhūto anajjhotthaṭo. Tathā hi tassa kulassa na kiñci pārijuññaṃ lokanāthassa abhijātiyaṃ, atha kho vaḍḍhiyeva. Abhinikkhamane ca tatopi samiddhatamabhāvo loke [V 2.0139] pākaṭo paññātoti. Sakyakulā pabbajitoti idaṃ vacanaṃ bhagavato saddhāpabbajitabhāvadīpanaṃ vuttaṃ mahantaṃ ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ mahantañca bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya pabbajitabhāvasiddhito.

‘By any kind of loss’ means not being overwhelmed or oppressed by any loss due to any deprivation whatsoever, be it the loss of relatives, wealth, or anything else. Indeed, for him, there was no deprivation whatsoever to that clan in the lineage of the Lord of the World; rather, there was only growth. Moreover, at his renunciation, the unsurpassed state of their prosperity became evident and known in the world. ‘Having gone forth from the Sakyan clan’—this statement is said to reveal the Blessed One's going forth out of faith, signifying the accomplishment of his renunciation by abandoning a vast circle of relatives and an immense accumulation of wealth.

Itthambhūtākhyānattheti itthaṃ evaṃpakāro bhūto jātoti evaṃ kathanatthe. Upayogavacananti “abbhuggato”ti ettha abhi-saddo itthambhūtākhyānatthajotako, tena yogato “taṃ kho pana bhavanta”nti idaṃ sāmiatthe upayogavacanaṃ. Tenāha “tassa kho pana bhoto gotamassāti attho”ti. Kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgatoti kalyāṇehi guṇehi yutto, tannissito tabbisayatāyāti adhippāyo. Seṭṭhoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Kittetabbato kitti, sā eva saddanīyato saddoti āha “kittisaddoti kittiyevā”ti. Abhitthavanavasena pavatto saddo thutighoso. Sadevakaṃ lokaṃ ajjhottharitvā uggatoti anaññasādhāraṇe guṇe ārabbha pavattattā sadevakaṃ lokaṃ ajjhottharitvā abhibhavitvā uggato.

‘Itthambhūtākhyānattheti’ means ‘in the sense of stating what has become thus,’ that is, ‘itthaṃ’ (thus), ‘evaṃpakāro’ (of such a kind), ‘bhūto’ (become), ‘jāto’ (arisen), thus ‘in the sense of speaking in this manner.’ ‘Upayogavacananti’ refers to the usage of words; as in ‘abbhuggato’ (arisen), where the prefix ‘abhi-’ signifies the meaning of ‘itthambhūta,’ by connection with that, ‘taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ’ (that venerable one) is a word used in the sense of mastery. Hence it is said, ‘tassa kho pana bhoto gotamassāti attho’ (this is the meaning of ‘that venerable Gotama’). ‘Kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgatoti’ means endowed with excellent qualities, dependent on them, with the intention of being their sphere. ‘Seṭṭhoti’ (the best) follows the same principle here. ‘Kitti’ (fame) is so-called because it is to be proclaimed, and that very fame is called ‘sadda’ (sound) because it is to be sounded out; hence it is said, ‘kittisaddoti kittiyevā’ (the sound of fame is indeed fame). The sound arises in the manner of praise, a voice of acclaim. Having pervaded the world with its gods, it has arisen—because it arises in connection with unparalleled qualities, it has overcome and arisen, pervading the world with its gods.

So bhagavāti yo so samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbakilese bhañjitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho devānaṃ atidevo [M 2.0153] sakkānaṃ atisakko brahmānaṃ atibrahmā lokanātho bhāgyavantatādīhi kāraṇehi sadevake loke “bhagavā”ti patthaṭakittisaddo, so bhagavā. “Bhagavā”ti ca idaṃ satthu nāmakittanaṃ. Tenāha āyasmā dhammasenāpati “bhagavāti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kata”ntiādi (mahāni. 84). Parato pana bhagavāti guṇakittanaṃ. Yathā kammaṭṭhānikena “araha”ntiādīsu navasu ṭhānesu paccekaṃ iti-saddaṃ yojetvā buddhaguṇā anussariyanti, evaṃ buddhaguṇasaṃkittanenapīti dassento “itipi arahaṃ itipi sammāsambuddho…pe… itipi bhagavā”ti āha. “Itipetaṃ bhūtaṃ itipetaṃ taccha”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.6) viya idha itisaddo āsannapaccakkhakaraṇattho, pi-saddo sampiṇḍanattho, tena ca tesaṃ guṇānaṃ bahubhāvo dīpito, tāni ca saṃkittentena viññunā cittassa sammukhībhūtāneva katvā saṃkittetabbānīti dassento “iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenāti vuttaṃ hotī”ti āha. Evaṃ nirūpetvā kittento yo kitteti, tassa bhagavati ativiya abhippasādo hoti.

He, the Blessed One, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, destroyed all defilements, and awakened to unsurpassed perfect self-awakening, is the supreme god of gods, the supreme Sakka of Sakkas, the supreme Brahmā of Brahmās, the lord of the world—for such reasons, in the world with its deities, the well-known title “Blessed One” is proclaimed. “Blessed One” is indeed the designation of the Teacher. Therefore, the Venerable General of the Dhamma said, “‘Blessed One’—this name was not given by his mother,” and so on (Mahāni. 84). Further, “Blessed One” is a recitation of qualities. Just as a meditator recollects the Buddha’s qualities by connecting ‘iti’ to each of the nine designations such as ‘Arahant,’ so too, showing that by a brief recitation of the Buddha's qualities, it is said: “He is indeed an Arahant, he is indeed Perfectly Self-Enlightened… he is indeed the Blessed One.” Here, the word ‘iti’ has the meaning of making something immediately present, as in phrases like “Indeed, this is true, indeed this is factual” (Dī. Ni. 1.6), while the particle ‘pi’ has the meaning of collecting, thereby indicating the multiplicity of these qualities. Thus, showing that the wise one, when reciting them, should do so by making them present to the mind, he says, “it is said by this and that reason.” In this way, one who thus defines and recites has profound confidence in the Blessed One.

Ārakattāti suvidūrattā. Arīnanti kilesārīnaṃ. Arānanti saṃsāracakkassa arānaṃ. Hatattāti viddhaṃsitattā. Paccayādīnanti cīvarādipaccayānañceva pūjāvisesānañca. Tatoti visuddhimaggato (visuddhi. 1.125-127). Yathā ca visuddhimaggato, evaṃ taṃsaṃvaṇṇanātopi nesaṃ vitthāro gahetabbo.

‘Ārakattā’ means because of being very far away. ‘Arīnaṃ’ refers to enemies, namely the defilement-enemies. ‘Arānaṃ’ means the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra. ‘Hatattā’ signifies being destroyed. ‘Paccayādīnaṃ’ includes requisites such as robes, as well as special offerings. ‘Tato’ refers to the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 1.125-127). And just as it is explained in the Visuddhimagga, so too should their detailed explanation be understood from its commentary.

Imaṃ [V 2.0140] lokanti nayidaṃ mahājanassa sammukhamattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, atha kho anavasesaṃ pariyādāyāti dassetuṃ “sadevaka”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tenāha “idāni vattabbaṃ nidassetī”ti. Pajātattāti yathāsakaṃ kammakilesehi nibbattattā. Pañcakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ pārisesanayena itaresaṃ padantarena gahitattā. Sadevakanti ca avayavena viggaho samudāyo samāsattho. Chaṭṭhakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ paccāsattinayena. Tattha hi so jāto tannivāsī ca. Sabrahmakavacanena brahmakāyikādibrahmaggahaṇanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Paccatthikasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇanti nidassanamattametaṃ apaccatthikānaṃ samitabāhitapāpānañca samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇavacanena gahitattā. Kāmaṃ “sadevaka”ntiādivisesanānaṃ vasena sattavisayo lokasaddoti viññāyati tulyayogavisayattā [M 2.0154] tesaṃ, “salomako sapakkhako”tiādīsu pana atulyayogepi ayaṃ samāso labbhatīti byabhicāradassanato pajāgahaṇanti āha “pajāvacanena sattalokaggahaṇa”nti.

‘This world’ is not spoken merely in reference to what is directly visible to the masses, but to indicate the entirety without omission; hence the phrase ‘including the devas’ and so on is stated. Therefore, it is said, “Now, what should be stated is shown.” ‘Because of being born’ means being produced according to one's own actions and defilements. The inclusion of the five sense-sphere deva groups is by way of the remainder, since others are included by another term. ‘Including the devas’ is a collective term where a breakdown into its components conveys a comprehensive meaning. The inclusion of the sixth sense-sphere deva group is by way of proximity, for he was born and dwelt there. The phrase ‘including the Brahmās’ refers to the Brahmā-world deities and so on; here too, the same principle applies. The inclusion of ‘hostile ascetics and brahmins’ is merely illustrative, for even non-hostile ascetics and brahmins, who have calmed and banished evil, are included under the term ‘ascetics and brahmins.’ Indeed, through such qualifiers as ‘including the devas’ and so on, the term ‘world’ is understood to refer to the realm of beings, due to the similarity in scope of these qualifiers; however, in phrases like ‘with hair and feathers,’ this collective usage is found even where the connection is dissimilar; thus, from the observation of deviation, the inclusion of beings is explained by the phrase ‘the term ‘beings’ encompasses the world of beings.’

Arūpino sattā attano āneñjavihārena viharantā dibbantīti devāti imaṃ nibbacanaṃ labhantīti āha “sadevakaggahaṇena arūpāvacaraloko gahito”ti. Tenāha “ākāsānañcāyatanūpagānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyata”nti (a. ni. 3.117). Samārakaggahaṇena chakāmāvacaradevaloko gahito tassa savisesaṃ mārassa vase vattanato. Sabrahmakaggahaṇena rūpībrahmaloko gahito arūpībrahmalokassa gahitattā. Catuparisavasenāti khattiyādicatuparisavasena. Itarā pana catasso parisā samārakādiggahaṇena gahitā evāti. Avasesasattaloko nāgagaruḷādibhedo. Tīhākārehīti devamārabrahmasahitatāsaṅkhātehi tīhi pakārehi. Tīsu padesūti “sadevaka”ntiādīsu tīsu padesu. Tena tenākārenāti sadevakattādinā tena tena pakārena. Tedhātukameva pariyādinnanti porāṇā āhūti yojanā.

Formless beings, dwelling with their imperturbable abiding, are said to 'sport'; thus they obtain the designation 'deva'. Hence it is said, “By the inclusion of ‘with its devas,’ the formless-sphere world is included.” Therefore, it is stated, “for the sake of companionship with the devas who have attained the base of infinite space.” (A. Ni. 3.117) By the inclusion of ‘with its Māra,’ the world of the six sense-sphere devas is included, because it is especially under the sway of Māra. By the inclusion of ‘with its Brahmās,’ the form-sphere Brahmā world is included, as the formless Brahmā world has already been included. ‘By means of the four assemblies’ refers to the four assemblies of nobles and so on. But the other four assemblies are indeed included by the inclusion of ‘with its Māra’ and so on. The remaining world of beings is of various kinds, such as nāgas and garuḷas. ‘By three aspects’ refers to the three modes reckoned as the inclusion of devas, Māra, and Brahmās. ‘In the three terms’ refers to the three terms ‘with its devas’ and so on. ‘In each respective way’ means according to each respective mode, such as being ‘with its devas.’ The ancients said that the three-realmed world itself is completely encompassed; this is the connection.

Abhiññāti yakāralopenāyaṃ niddeso, abhijānitvāti ayamettha atthoti āha “abhiññāya adhikena ñāṇena ñatvā”ti. Anumānādipaṭikkhepoti anumānaatthāpattiādippaṭikkhepo ekappamāṇattā. Sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇacāratāya hi sabbapaccakkhā buddhā bhagavanto.

‘Abhiññā’—this is an explanation with the elision of the letter ‘ya’; the meaning here is ‘having directly known.’ Thus it is said: ‘“by direct knowledge” means having known with superior knowledge.’ The rejection of inference and so on is the rejection of inference, presumption, and the like, because of having a single standard. For the Blessed Buddhas directly perceive all things, due to the unimpeded range of their knowledge everywhere.

Anuttaraṃ vivekasukhanti phalasamāpattisukhaṃ. Tena vimissāpi kadāci bhagavato dhammadesanā hotīti “hitvāpī”ti pi-saddaggahaṇaṃ. Bhagavā hi dhammaṃ desento yasmiṃ khaṇe parisā sādhukāraṃ vā deti, yathāsutaṃ vā dhammaṃ paccavekkhati, taṃ khaṇaṃ pubbabhāgena paricchinditvā phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, yathāparicchedañca samāpattito vuṭṭhāya ṭhitaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya [V 2.0141] dhammaṃ deseti. Appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā desentoti ugghaṭitaññussa vasena appaṃ vā, vipañcitaññussa neyyassa vā vasena bahuṃ vā desento. Dhammassa kalyāṇatā ca niyyānikatā ca sabbaso anavajjabhāvenevāti āha “anavajjameva katvā”ti.

‘The unsurpassed bliss of seclusion’ is the bliss of the attainment of fruition. Because the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma is sometimes mixed with that, the particle ‘pi’ is included in ‘hitvāpi’. For when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, at the moment when the assembly gives a cry of approval or reflects on the Dhamma as they have heard it, he marks off that moment with a preliminary part, enters the attainment of fruition, and then, having emerged from the attainment according to the demarcation, teaches the Dhamma, beginning from the point where he left off. ‘Teaching little or much’ means teaching a little for one of quick understanding, or teaching much for one of expansive understanding or one who is to be led. He teaches, having made the Dhamma entirely blameless, because its goodness and its quality of leading out are entirely due to its blameless nature. Thus it is said, “having made it entirely blameless.”

Desakāyattena [M 2.0155] āṇādividhinā atisajjanaṃ pabodhanaṃ desanāti sā pariyattidhammavasena veditabbāti āha “desanāya tāva cātuppadikagāthāyapī”tiādi. Nidānanigamānipi satthu desanāya anuvidhānato tadantogadhāni evāti āha “nidānaṃ ādi, idamavocāti pariyosāna”nti.

Teaching (desanā) is the instigation and awakening by means of command and so on, which is dependent on the teacher; it is to be understood as the scriptural Dhamma. Thus it is said: “Of the teaching, in the first place, even a four-lined verse…” and so on. Because the introduction and conclusion also conform to the Teacher's teaching, they are included within it. Thus it is said: “The introduction is the beginning; ‘Thus he spoke’ is the conclusion.”

Sāsitabbapuggalagatena yathāparādhādisāsitabbabhāvena anusāsanaṃ tadaṅgavinayādivasena vinayanaṃ sāsananti taṃ paṭipattidhammavasena veditabbanti āha “sīlasamādhivipassanā”tiādi. Kusalānanti anavajjadhammānaṃ sīlasamathavipassanānaṃ sīladiṭṭhīnañca ādibhāvo taṃmūlikattā uttarimanussadhammānaṃ. Ariyamaggassa antadvayavigamena majjhimāpaṭipadābhāvo viya sammāpaṭipattiyā ārabbha nibbattīnaṃ vemajjhatāpi majjhabhāvoti vuttaṃ “atthi, bhikkhave…pe… majjhimaṃ nāmā”ti. Phalaṃ pariyosānaṃ nāma saupādisesatāvasena. Nibbānaṃ pariyosānaṃ nāma anupādisesatāvasena. Idāni tesaṃ dvinnampi sāsanassa pariyosānataṃ āgamena dassetuṃ “tasmātiha tva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. “Sātthaṃ sabyañjana”ntiādivacanato dhammadesanāya ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ adhippetanti āha “idha…pe… adhippeta”nti. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe kathāvadhisaddappabandho gāthāvasena suttavasena ca vavatthito pariyattidhammo, so idha desanāti vutto, tassa pana attho visesato sīlādi evāti āha “bhagavā hi dhammaṃ desento…pe… dassetī”ti. Tattha sīlaṃ dassetvāti sīlaggahaṇena sasambhāraṃ sīlaṃ gahitaṃ, tathā maggaggahaṇena sasambhāro maggoti tadubhayavasena anavasesato pariyattiatthaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati. Tenāti sīlādidassanena. Atthavasena hi idha desanāya ādikalyāṇādibhāvo adhippeto. Kathikasaṇṭhitīti kathikassa saṇṭhānaṃ kathanavasena samavaṭṭhānaṃ.

Instruction (anusāsanaṃ) is instructing a person who is to be instructed according to their faults and the nature of what needs to be taught. Discipline (vinayanaṃ) is training by way of its components, etc. This is the Teaching (sāsanaṃ), and it should be understood as the Dhamma of practice, as stated: ‘virtue, concentration, insight,’ and so on. ‘Of wholesome qualities’ refers to the beginning of blameless states—virtue, tranquility, insight, and right view—because they are the root of the higher human states. Just as the Noble Path is the Middle Way by avoiding the two extremes, so too the centeredness of things that arise beginning with right practice is the middle state, as stated: ‘There is, monks… called the middle.’ The culmination called ‘fruit’ is in the sense of the state with residue remaining. The culmination called ‘Nibbāna’ is in the sense of the state with no residue remaining. Now, to show through scripture that both of these are the culmination of the Teaching, it is said: ‘Therefore, you…’ and so on. From the statement ‘with meaning and phrasing,’ the beginning, middle, and end of the Dhamma teaching are intended, as stated: ‘Here… is intended.’ In each and every meaning, the composition of words limited to the discourse, established by way of verses and suttas, is the scriptural Dhamma; that is here called ‘teaching’ (desanā). But its meaning is specifically virtue and so on, as stated: ‘For the Blessed One, while teaching the Dhamma… shows.’ Therein, ‘having shown virtue’—by the term ‘virtue,’ virtue with its requisites is included; similarly, by the term ‘path,’ the path with its requisites is included. Thus, by means of both, the meaning of the scriptures is completely encompassed without remainder. ‘Therefore’ means by showing virtue and so on. For here, the quality of being good in the beginning, etc., of the teaching is intended in the sense of the meaning. ‘The speaker's stability’ (kathikasaṇṭhiti) is the speaker’s firm standing, the firm establishment by way of speaking.

Na so sātthaṃ deseti niyyānatthavirahato tassā desanāya. Ekabyañjanādiyuttā vāti sithilādibhedesu byañjanesu ekappakāreneva dvippakāreneva vā byañjanena yuttā damiḷabhāsā viya. Vivaṭakaraṇatāya oṭṭhe aphusāpetvā uccāretabbato sabbaniroṭṭhabyañjanā vā kirātabhāsā viya. Sabbasseva vissajjanīyayuttatāya sabbavissaṭṭhabyañjanā [M 2.0156] vā yavanabhāsā viya. Sabbasseva sānusāratāya [V 2.0142] sabbaniggahitabyañjanā vā pārasikādimilakkhabhāsā viya. Sabbāpesā byañjanekadesavaseneva pavattiyā aparipuṇṇabyañjanāti katvā “abyañjanā”ti vuttā.

He does not teach with meaning, as his teaching is devoid of the meaning of deliverance. Or, it is endowed with one type of consonant, etc.—meaning that among consonants of various kinds, such as lax and so on, it is endowed with only one or two types of consonants, like the Tamil language. Or, because it must be pronounced without touching the lips due to its open articulation, it is entirely composed of non-labial consonants, like the Kirāta language. Or, because it is entirely connected with the vissajjanīya (aspirate), it is entirely composed of released consonants, like the Yavana language. Or, because it is entirely nasalized, it is entirely composed of nasalized consonants, like the Persian and other barbarian languages. Because all these proceed by way of only a portion of the consonants, being incomplete in consonants, they are called ‘without phrasing’ (abyañjanā).

Ṭhānakaraṇāni sithilāni katvā uccāretabbaṃ akkharaṃ pañcasu vaggesu paṭhamatatiyanti evamādi sithilaṃ. Tāni asithilāni katvā uccāretabbaṃ akkharaṃ vaggesu dutiyacatutthanti evamādi dhanitaṃ. Dvimattakālaṃ dīghaṃ. Ekamattakālaṃ rassaṃ. Tadeva lahukaṃ lahukameva. Saṃyogaparaṃ dīghañca garukaṃ. Ṭhānakaraṇāni niggahetvā uccāretabbaṃ niggahitaṃ. Parena sambandhaṃ katvā uccāretabbaṃ sambandhaṃ. Tathā na sambandhaṃ vavatthitaṃ. Ṭhānakaraṇāni vissaṭṭhāni katvā uccāretabbaṃ vimuttaṃ. Dasadhā byañjanabuddhiyā pabhedoti evaṃ sithilādivasena byañjanabuddhiyā akkharuppādakacittassa dasappakārena pabhedo. Sabbāni hi akkharāni cittasamuṭṭhānāni yathādhippetatthabyañjanato byañjanāni ca.

A letter to be pronounced by making the places and organs of articulation lax—such as the first and third letters in the five classes—is sithila (lax). A letter to be pronounced by making those same organs non-lax—such as the second and fourth letters in the classes—is dhanita (aspirated). A sound of two moras' duration is long. A sound of one mora's duration is short. That same short vowel is light. A long vowel and a vowel followed by a conjunct consonant are heavy. A sound to be pronounced by restraining the places and organs of articulation is niggahita (nasalized). A sound to be pronounced by connecting it with the following is sambandha (connected). Similarly, one not connected is vavatthita (separated). A sound to be pronounced by releasing the places and organs of articulation is vimutta (released). The classification of the cognition of phrasing is tenfold: thus, the mind that produces letters is classified in ten ways by means of the cognition of phrasing, based on laxness and so on. For all letters originate from the mind, and they are also ‘expressions’ (byañjanāni) because they express the intended meaning.

Amakkhetvāti amilecchetvā, avināsetvā, ahāpetvāti attho. Bhagavā yamatthaṃ ñāpetuṃ ekagāthaṃ ekavākyampi deseti, tamatthaṃ tāya desanāya parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanāya eva desetīti āha “paripuṇṇabyañjanameva katvā dhammaṃ desetī”ti. Idha kevalasaddo anavasesavācako, na avomissatādivācakoti āha “sakalādhivacana”nti. Paripuṇṇanti sabbaso puṇṇaṃ. Taṃ pana kiñci ūnaṃ vā adhikaṃ vā na hotīti “anūnādhikavacana”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha yadatthaṃ desitaṃ, tassa sādhakattā anūnatā veditabbā, tabbidhurassa pana asādhakattā anadhikatā. Sakalanti sabbabhāgavantaṃ. Paripuṇṇamevāti sabbaso paripuṇṇameva. Tenāha “ekadesanāpi aparipuṇṇā natthī”ti. Aparisuddhā desanā nāma hoti taṇhāsaṃkilesattā. Lokāmisaṃ cīvarādayo paccayā, tattha agadhitacittatāya lokāmisanirapekkho. Hitapharaṇenāti hitūpasaṃharaṇena. Mettābhāvanāya muduhadayoti mettābhāvanāya karuṇāya vā muduhadayo. Ullumpanasabhāvasaṇṭhitenāti sakalasaṃkilesato vaṭṭadukkhato ca uddharaṇākārāvaṭṭhitena cittena, karuṇādhippāyenāti attho. Tasmāti yasmā [M 2.0157] sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ idha brahmacariyanti adhippetaṃ, tasmā. Brahmacariyanti iminā samānādhikaraṇāni sabbapadāni yojetvā atthaṃ dassento “so dhammaṃ deseti…pe… pakāsetīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo”ti āha.

‘Not disparaging’ (amakkhetvā) means not soiling, not destroying, not diminishing—this is the meaning. The Blessed One, in order to make known a meaning, teaches even a single verse or a single statement, and he teaches that meaning by that very teaching with perfectly rounded phrases and syllables. Thus it is said, ‘He teaches the Dhamma, having made the phrases fully complete.’ Here, the word ‘only’ (kevala) signifies a totality without remainder, not indicating mixture or the like. Thus it is said, ‘a term denoting the whole.’ ‘Fully complete’ (paripuṇṇa) means complete in every way. But it has nothing deficient or excessive. Thus it is said, ‘a term without deficiency or excess.’ Therein, its lack of deficiency is to be understood from its effectiveness for the purpose for which it was taught, while its lack of excess is to be understood from its ineffectiveness for anything other than that. ‘Whole’ (sakala) means possessing all parts. ‘Fully complete’ (paripuṇṇa) means fully complete in every way. Therefore, it is said, ‘Even a single teaching is not incomplete.’ An impure teaching is so called because of the defilement of craving. Worldly enticements are requisites such as robes; being without greed for them, he is independent of worldly enticements. ‘By suffusing with benefit’ (hitapharaṇena) means by bringing about benefit. ‘With a soft heart’ (muduhadayo) means with a heart softened by the development of loving-kindness or compassion. ‘Established in the nature of uplifting’ (ullumpanasabhāvasaṇṭhitena) means with a mind established in the aspect of lifting up from all defilements and from the suffering of the round, with an intention of compassion—this is the meaning. ‘Therefore’ (tasmā): because the entire teaching, which encompasses the threefold training, is here intended as the holy life, therefore. Connecting all the terms that have the same referent with ‘the holy life’ (brahmacariya), showing the meaning, he says, ‘He teaches the Dhamma… he proclaims it’—thus the meaning here should be understood.

Sundaranti bhaddakaṃ. Bhaddakatā ca passantassa hitasukhāvahabhāvena veditabbāti āha “atthāvahaṃ sukhāvaha”nti. Tattha atthāvahanti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthasaṃhitahitāvahaṃ. Sukhāvahanti yathāvuttatividhasukhāvahaṃ. Tathānurūpānanti tādisānaṃ. Yādisehi pana guṇehi bhagavā [V 2.0143] samannāgato, tehi catuppamāṇikassa lokassa sabbathāpi accantappasādanīyo tesaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvattāti dassento “yathārūpo”tiādimāha. Tattha yathābhūta…pe… arahatanti iminā dhammappamāṇalūkhappamāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ bhagavato pasādāvahatā dassitā, itarena itaresaṃ. Dassanamattampi sādhu hotīti ettha kosiyavatthu kathetabbaṃ. Ubhatopakkhikāti micchādiṭṭhisammādiṭṭhivasena ubhayapakkhikā. Kerāṭikāti saṭhā.

‘Beautiful’ (sundara) means auspicious (bhaddaka). And auspiciousness should be understood as bringing benefit and happiness to one who sees it. Thus he says, ‘bringing benefit, bringing happiness.’ Here, ‘bringing benefit’ (atthāvaha) means bringing welfare that is beneficial and related to the ultimate goal both in this life and the next. ‘Bringing happiness’ (sukhāvaha) means bringing the threefold happiness as previously stated. ‘Similarly appropriate’ (tathānurūpānaṃ) refers to those who are like that. Showing that the Blessed One, with the virtues with which he is endowed, is altogether exceedingly pleasing in every way to the world of the four types of persons, because of their true nature, he says, ‘of such form,’ and so on. Here, by ‘as He truly is’… up to ‘the Arahant,’ the Blessed One’s inspiring of faith in beings who measure by the Dhamma or by a rough measure is shown; by the other, he inspires the others. Regarding ‘Even the mere sight is good,’ here the story of Kosiyavatthu should be told. ‘Belonging to both sides’ (ubhatopakkhikā) refers to those who hold wrong views and right views, being of both sides. ‘Deceitful’ (kerāṭikā) means fraudulent.

Anekatthattā nipātānaṃ yāvañcidanti nipātasamudāyo adhimattappamāṇaparicchedaṃ dīpetīti āha “adhimattappamāṇaparicchedavacanameta”nti. Adhimattavippasannānīti adhikappamāṇena vippasannāni. Vippasannānīti ca pakatiākāraṃ atikkamitvā vippasannānīti attho. Nanu ca cakkhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ manoviññeyyattā kathaṃ tena tesaṃ vippasannatā viññāyatīti āha “tassa hī”tiādi. Tassāti brāhmaṇassa. Tesanti cakkhādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ. Evampi manindriyena patiṭṭhitokāsassa adiṭṭhattā kathaṃ manindriyassa vippasannatā tena viññāyatīti āha “yasmā panā”tiādi. Nayaggāhapaññā hesā tassa brāhmaṇassa. Mane vippasanneyeva hoti pasannacittasamuṭṭhitarūpasampadāhi eva cakkhādīnaṃ patiṭṭhitokāsassa pasannatāsambhavato.

Because particles have multiple meanings, the particle combination ‘yāvañcid’ indicates an extreme measure or limit. Thus he says, ‘this is a term denoting an extreme measure or limit.’ ‘Extremely clear’ (adhimattavippasannāni) means excessively clear. And ‘clear’ (vippasannāni) implies surpassing their natural state in clarity—this is the meaning. But since the faculties like the eye are knowable by the mind, how is their clarity known by it? He explains thus: ‘For this one…’ and so on. ‘This one’ (tassa) refers to the brahmin. ‘Them’ (tesaṃ) refers to the five faculties beginning with the eye. Even so, since the established space of the mind faculty is unseen, how is the clarity of the mind faculty known by him? He explains thus: ‘But because…’ and so on. That brahmin possesses wisdom that grasps the method. For the clarity of the established space of the eye and other faculties is possible only when the mind is clear, due to the perfection of form that arises from a clear mind.

Jambonadasuvaṇṇaṃ rattavaṇṇameva hotīti āha “surattavaṇṇassā”ti. Jambonadasuvaṇṇassa ghaṭikāti jambonadasuvaṇṇapiṇḍaṃ. Iminā nekkhanti nekkhappamāṇajambonadasuvaṇṇena kataṃ akatabhaṇḍaṃ vuttanti dasseti. Nekkhanti vā atirekapañcasuvaṇṇena katapilandhanaṃ katabhaṇḍaṃ vuttaṃ. Tañhi ghaṭṭanamajjanakkhamaṃ hotīti. Suvaṇṇanti ca pañcadharaṇassa [M 2.0158] samaññā, tasmā pañcavīsatidharaṇahiraññavicitaṃ ābharaṇaṃ idha nekkhanti adhippetaṃ. Jambonadanti mahājambusākhāya pavattanadiyaṃ nibbattaṃ. Taṃ kira ratanaṃ rattaṃ. Suvaṇṇākāre mahājambuphalarase vā pathaviyaṃ paviṭṭhe suvaṇṇaṅkurā uṭṭhahanti, tena suvaṇṇena katapilandhanantipi attho. Suparikammakatanti suṭṭhu kataparikammaṃ. Sampahaṭṭhanti sammā pahaṭṭhaṃ ghaṭṭanādivasena sukataparikammaṃ. Tenāha “suvaṇṇakāra…pe… suparimajjitanti attho”ti.

Jambonada gold is indeed of a red color. Thus he says, ‘of a red hue’ (surattavaṇṇassa). ‘A lump of jambonada gold’ (ghaṭikā jambonadasuvaṇṇassa) refers to a mass of jambonada gold. By this, it is shown that ‘nekkha’ refers to unfashioned articles made from jambonada gold measured by the nekkha standard. Alternatively, ‘nekkha’ is said to refer to fashioned ornaments made with an excess of five gold coins. For they are durable against rubbing and polishing. And ‘suvaṇṇa’ is a general designation for five dharanas. Therefore, an ornament adorned with twenty-five dharanas of gold is here intended as the nekkha. ‘Jambonada’ refers to gold originating in the river flowing from the branches of the great Jambu tree. It is said that this gem is red. In a gold mine, or when the juice of the great Jambu fruit enters the earth, golden sprouts arise; it also means an ornament made from that gold. ‘Well-prepared’ (suparikammakata) means thoroughly worked. ‘Properly polished’ (sampahaṭṭha) means well-finished by rubbing and other processes. Therefore, he says: ‘Well-crafted by goldsmiths… thoroughly polished’—this is the meaning.

Vāḷarūpānīti āharimāni vāḷarūpāni. “Akappiyarūpākulo akappiyamañco pallaṅkoti sārasamāse. Ratanacitranti bhitticchedādivasena ratanacitraṃ. Rukkhatūlalatātūlapoṭakitūlānaṃ vasena tiṇṇaṃ tūlānaṃ. Uddalomiyaṃ kecīti sārasamāsācariyā uttaravihārino ca. Tathā ekantalomiyaṃ. Koseyyakaṭṭissamayanti koseyyakasaṭamayaṃ. Ajinacammehīti [V 2.0144] ajinamigacammehi. Tāni kira cammāni sukhumatarāni. Tasmā dupaṭṭatipaṭṭāni katvā sibbanti. Tena vuttaṃ “ajinappaveṇī”tiādi.

‘Forms of wild animals’ (vāḷarūpāni) refers to artificial forms of wild animals. ‘Unsuitable forms, unsuitable beds, couches’—this is in the Sārasamāsa. ‘Jeweled designs’ (ratanacitta) refers to jeweled designs made by cutting walls, etc. There are three types of cotton: tree cotton, creeper cotton, and seed-pod cotton. Regarding ‘uddalomiya,’ some—that is, the teachers of the Sārasamāsa and the monks of the Uttaravihāra—(hold this view). Similarly, regarding ‘ekantalomiya’. ‘Koseyya-kaṭṭissa’ refers to a covering made of Koseyya silk cloth. ‘With antelope hides’ (ajinacammehi) means with hides of antelope deer. It is said that these hides are very fine. Therefore, they are made into double or triple layers and sewn together. Hence, it is said: ‘ajinappaveṇī,’ and so on.

Nikāmalābhīti yathicchitalābhī. Tenāha “icchiticchitalābhī”ti. Vipulalābhīti uḷāralābhī. Kasiranti hi parittaṃ vuccati, tappaṭikkhepena akasiraṃ uḷāraṃ. Tenāha “mahantalābhī”tiādi.

‘He obtains at will’ (nikāmalābhī) means he obtains as he wishes. Therefore, it is said, ‘he obtains whatever he desires.’ ‘He obtains abundantly’ (vipulalābhī) means he obtains generously. For ‘scanty’ (kasira) refers to what is little, and by rejecting that, ‘not scanty’ (akasira) means generous. Therefore, it is said, ‘he obtains greatly,’ and so on.

Laddhā ca na kappantīti sāmaññena paṭisiddhattā sabbathā na kappatīti kassaci āsaṅkā siyā, tannivattanatthaṃ “kiñci kiñci kappatī”tiādimāha. Tattha suddhakoseyyanti ratanaparisibbanarahitaṃ. Ettha ca “suddhakoseyyaṃ pana vaṭṭatī”ti vinaye (mahāva. aṭṭha. 254) vuttattā idhāpi ettakameva vuttaṃ. Dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.15) pana “ṭhapetvā tūlikaṃ sabbāneva gonakādīni ratanaparisibbitāni na vaṭṭantī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha “ṭhapetvā tūlika”nti etena ratanasibbanarahitāpī tūlikā na vaṭṭatīti dīpeti. Vacanatoti etena vinaye (cūḷava. 297) vuttabhāvaṃ dasseti. Ekena vidhānenāti yathāvuttameva vidhānaṃ sandhāya vadati. Yadi evaṃ kasmā bhagavatā “laddhā ca na kappantī”ti sāmaññena paṭisedho katoti āha “akappiyaṃ pana upādāyā”tiādi.

‘Having been obtained, they are not allowable’ (laddhā ca na kappanti): because it is prohibited generally, someone might suspect that it is not allowable in any way. To dispel that doubt, he said, ‘some things are allowable,’ and so on. Herein, ‘pure silk’ (suddhakoseyya) means without jeweled embroidery. And here, because in the Vinaya (Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā 254) it is said, ‘pure silk is allowable,’ only this much is stated here. However, in the Dīghanikāya Aṭṭhakathā (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.15), it is said, ‘except for a cotton mattress, all other materials like wool blankets, etc., adorned with jewels, are not allowable.’ Herein, by ‘except for a cotton mattress,’ it is indicated that even a cotton mattress without jeweled embroidery is not allowable. By ‘the statement’ (vacanato), this shows that it is stated in the Vinaya (Cūḷavagga 297). ‘By one method’ (ekena vidhānena): this speaks referring to the method as previously described. If so, why did the Blessed One make a general prohibition with ‘having been obtained, they are not allowable’? He said, ‘but with reference to what is unallowable,’ and so on.

Pallaṅkanti ettha pari-saddo samantatoti etasmiṃ atthe vattati, tasmā vāmūruṃ dakkhiṇūruñca samaṃ ṭhapetvā ubho pāde aññamaññasambandhe katvā [M 2.0159] nisajjā pallaṅkanti āha “samantato ūrubaddhāsana”nti. Ūrūnaṃ bandhanavasena nisajjā. Pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvāti ca yathā pallaṅkavasena nisajjā hoti, evaṃ ubho pāde ābhuje samiñjite katvāti attho. Taṃ pana ubhinnaṃ pādānaṃ tathā sambandhatākaraṇanti āha “bandhitvā”ti. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyāti uparimaṃ sarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭake koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādetvā. Evañhi nisinnassa cammamaṃsanhārūni na paṇamanti. Athassa yā tesaṃ paṇamanapaccayā khaṇe khaṇe vedanā uppajjeyyuṃ, tā na uppajjanti. Tāsu anuppajjamānāsu cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ na paripatati, vuddhiṃ phātiṃ gacchati. Tenāha “aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭake”tiādi. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ ṭhapetvāti uparimaṃ kāyaṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Heṭṭhimakāyassa hi anujukaṭṭhapanaṃ nisajjāvacaneneva bodhitanti. Ujuṃ kāyanti ettha kāya-saddo uparimakāyavisayo.

Here, in 'pallaṅka' (cross-legged), the prefix 'pari-' is used in the sense of 'all around.' Therefore, it is said, 'seated with the thighs bound all around,' meaning a sitting posture where, having placed the left and right thighs evenly, both feet are made to be mutually connected. It is a sitting by way of binding the thighs. And 'having folded the legs cross-legged' means that, just as the sitting is in the cross-legged posture, so one has bent and drawn in both feet. The making of such a connection of both feet is what is meant by 'having bound.' 'Setting the body upright' means placing the upper body straight, aligning the eighteen spinal vertebrae tip to tip. For one seated thus, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not sag. And whatever pains might arise moment by moment due to their sagging do not arise. When these do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject does not fall away, and it grows and flourishes. Hence it is said, 'the eighteen spinal vertebrae,' and so on. 'Setting the body upright' means placing the upper body straight; or this may be the reading. For the fact that the lower body is not held straight is understood simply by the word 'sitting.' Here, the word 'body' in 'upright body' refers to the upper body.

Parimukhanti [V 2.0145] ettha pari-saddo abhisaddena samānatthoti āha “kammaṭṭhānābhimukha”nti, bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇato nivāretvā kammaṭṭhānaṃyeva purakkhatvāti attho. Ettha yathā “vanantaññeva pavisāmī”tiādinā bhāvanānurūpaṃ senāsanaṃ dassitaṃ, evaṃ “nisīdāmī”ti iminā alīnānuddhaccapakkhiyo santo iriyāpatho dassito, “pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā”ti iminā nisajjāya daḷhabhāvo, “parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti iminā ārammaṇapariggahūpāyo. Pariggahitaniyyānanti sabbathā gahitāsammosaṃ pariccattasammosaṃ satiṃ katvā, paramasatinepakkaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti attho. Parīti pariggahaṭṭho “pariṇāyikā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 16.20) viya. Mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho “suññatavimokkha”ntiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 1.209-210) viya. Paṭipakkhato niggamanaṭṭho hi niyyānaṭṭho.

Here, in 'parimukhaṃ', the prefix 'pari-' is synonymous with the word 'abhi-,' as it is said, 'facing the meditation subject.' The meaning is that, having averted the mind from external, diverse objects, one places the meditation subject right in front. Here, just as by 'I will enter the forest...' a dwelling suitable for meditation is shown, so by 'I sit down,' a posture that is on the side of being neither sluggish nor agitated is shown; by 'having folded the legs cross-legged,' the firmness of the sitting posture; and by 'establishing mindfulness in front,' the method of grasping the object. 'Thoroughly grasped as a way of release' means having made mindfulness one where forgetfulness is grasped and abandoned, establishing supreme mindfulness and discernment. 'Pari-' has the meaning of 'grasping,' as in 'pariṇāyikā' (leading) and so on (Dhs. 16, 20). 'Mukha' has the meaning of 'release,' as in 'suññatavimokkha' (emptiness liberation) and so on (Paṭis.M. i.209–210). For the meaning of 'release' is the meaning of 'departing from what is opposed'.

Cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānāni dibbabhāvāvahattā dibbavihārā nāma hontīti tadāsannappavattacaṅkamopi tadupacārato dibbo nāma hotīti āha “cattāri hi rūpajjhānānī”tiādi. Samāpajjitvā caṅkamantassāti idañca caṅkamantassa antarantarā samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāya caṅkamanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Na hi samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā avuṭṭhitena sakkā caṅkamituṃ. Samāpattito vuṭṭhāya caṅkamantassapi caṅkamoti idaṃ pana samāpattito vuṭṭhahitvā antarantarā samāpajjitvā caṅkamantassa vasena vuttaṃ. Dvīsu vihāresūti [M 2.0160] brahmavihāre, ariyavihāre ca. Mettājhānādayo hitūpasaṃhārādivasena pavattiyā brahmabhūtā seṭṭhabhūtā vihārāti brahmavihārā. Anaññasādhāraṇattā pana ariyānaṃ vihārāti ariyavihārā, catassopi phalasamāpattiyo. Idha pana arahattaphalasamāpattiyeva āgatā.

The four fine-material jhānas are called divine abodes because they bring about a divine state. Therefore, even walking meditation practiced in their vicinity is called 'divine' by extension, as it is said, 'Indeed, the four fine-material jhānas…' and so on. 'Of one who walks after attaining'—this is said with reference to one who walks by entering into attainment from time to time and emerging again and again. For it is not possible to walk having entered attainment without emerging from it. And this 'walking' of one who walks after emerging from attainment is spoken of in the sense of one who, having emerged from attainment, walks while entering it from time to time. 'Among the two abodes' refers to the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) and the noble abodes (ariyavihāra). The jhānas of loving-kindness and so on are called divine abodes because, in their proceeding by way of bringing benefit, they have become sublime and excellent abodes. And because they are not common to others, the four fruition attainments are the abodes of the noble ones, thus they are called noble abodes. Here, however, only the attainment of the fruition of arahantship is intended.

Paccavekkhaṇāya phalasamāpatti kathitā samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhitassa paccavekkhaṇāsambhavato. Caṅkamādayoti phalasamāpattiṃ samāpannassapi samāpattito vuṭṭhitassapi caṅkamaṭṭhānanisajjādayo. Ariyacaṅkamādayo honti na pana paccavekkhantassāti adhippāyo.

Fruition attainment is spoken of for the purpose of reviewing, because reviewing is possible for one who has emerged after attaining it. 'Walking and so on' means walking, standing, sitting, and so on, both for one who has attained fruition attainment and for one who has emerged from the attainment. The intention is that these are noble walks and so on, but this is not so for one who is reviewing.

Venāgapurasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Venāgapura Sutta is concluded.

4. Sarabhasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Sarabha Sutta

65. Catutthe gijjhā ettha santīti gijjhaṃ, kūṭaṃ. Taṃ etassāti gijjhakūṭo. Gijjho viyāti vā gijjhaṃ, kūṭaṃ. Taṃ etassāti gijjhakūṭo, pabbato. Tasmiṃ gijjhakūṭe. Tenāha “gijjhā [V 2.0146] vā”tiādi. Acirapakkantoti ettha na desantarapakkamanaṃ adhippetaṃ, atha kho sāsanapakkamananti dassento “imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvā”tiādimāha, teneva hi “imassā dhammavinayā”ti vuttaṃ. Labbhatīti lābho, catunnaṃ paccayānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sakkaccaṃ kātabbo dātabboti sakkāro. Paccayā eva hi paṇītapaṇītā sundarasundarā abhisaṅkharitvā katā sakkārāti vuccanti. Sakkāroti vā sundarakāro, parehi attano gāravakiriyā pupphādīhi vā pūjā. Lābho ca sakkāro ca lābhasakkārā, te naṭṭhā pahīnā etesanti naṭṭhalābhasakkārā.

65. In the fourth [sutta]: 'Vultures are here (gijjhā ettha santi),' thus it is 'gijjhaṃ'; 'kūṭaṃ' is peak. 'It has this,' thus it is Gijjhakūṭo. Or, 'like a vulture (gijjho viya),' thus it is 'gijjhaṃ'; 'kūṭaṃ' is peak. 'It has this,' thus it is Gijjhakūṭo, the mountain. On that Gijjhakūṭa (Vulture's Peak). Hence it is said, 'vultures or…' and so on. Here, 'not long departed' (acirapakkanto) is not intended as departure to another country, but rather, showing that it is departure from the Dispensation, he said, 'having gone forth in this Dispensation…' and so on. For that very reason it was said, 'from this Dhamma and Vinaya.' 'It is received (labbhati),' thus it is 'gain' (lābho); this is a designation for the four requisites. 'To be done respectfully (sakkaccaṃ kātabbo),' thus it is 'honor' (sakkāro). For the requisites themselves, when they are prepared and made to be fine and excellent, are called 'honor.' Or, 'sakkāro' means good treatment, the act of reverence by others toward oneself, or worship with flowers and so on. 'Gain and honor' are 'lābhasakkārā.' 'They are lost (naṭṭhā) and abandoned (pahīnā) for them (etesanti),' thus they are 'naṭṭhalābhasakkārā' (those for whom gain and honor are lost).

Mahālābhasakkāro uppajjīti tadā kira bhagavato mahālābhasakkāro uppajji yathā taṃ cattāro asaṅkheyye pūritadānapāramisañcayassa. Sabbadisāsu hi yamakamahāmegho vuṭṭhahitvā mahogho viya sabbapāramiyo “ekasmiṃ attabhāve vipākaṃ dassāmā”ti sampiṇḍitā viya lābhasakkāramahoghaṃ nibbattayiṃsu. Tato tato annapānayānavatthamālāgandhavilepanādihatthā khattiyabrāhmaṇādayo āgantvā “kahaṃ buddho[M 2.0161], kahaṃ bhagavā, kahaṃ devadevo narāsabho purisasīho”ti bhagavantaṃ pariyesanti, sakaṭasatehipi paccaye āharitvā okāsaṃ alabhamānā samantā gāvutappamāṇampi sakaṭadhurena sakaṭadhuraṃ āhacca tiṭṭhanti ceva anubandhanti ca andhakavindabrāhmaṇo viya. Yathā ca bhagavato, evaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassapi. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Great gain and honor arose—so it is said, at that time great gain and honor arose for the Blessed One, as is befitting for one whose accumulation of the perfection of giving was fulfilled over four incalculable aeons. For from all directions, all the perfections, like a great flood from a pair of great clouds that had arisen, as if compressed together saying, 'We will give our result in a single existence,' produced a great flood of gain and honor. From here and there, nobles, brahmins, and others came with food, drink, vehicles, clothes, garlands, perfumes, and ointments in their hands, searching for the Blessed One, asking, 'Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the god of gods, the bull among men, the lion of men?' Bringing requisites even in hundreds of carts, unable to find an opportunity, they stood all around for the extent of a gāvuta, cart-yoke touching cart-yoke, and they both stood waiting and followed after him, like the brahmin Andhakavinda. And as it was for the Blessed One, so also for the community of monks. And this has been said:

“Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hoti garukato mānito pūjito apacito lābhī cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghopi sakkato hoti…pe… parikkhārāna”nti (udā. 38).

'At that time the Blessed One was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed, a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. The community of monks was also honored… a recipient of… requisites.'

Tathā –

Likewise:

“Yāvatā kho pana, cunda, etarahi saṅgho vā gaṇo vā loke uppanno, nāhaṃ, cunda, aññaṃ ekaṃ saṅghampi samanupassāmi evaṃlābhaggayasaggappattaṃ yatharivāyaṃ, cunda, bhikkhusaṅgho”ti (dī. ni. 3.176).

'Cunda, of all the communities or groups that have presently arisen in the world, I do not see, Cunda, even one other community that has reached such a pinnacle of gain and fame as this community of monks.'

Svāyaṃ bhagavato ca saṅghassa ca uppanno lābhasakkāro ekato hutvā dvinnaṃ mahānadīnaṃ udakaṃ viya appameyyo ahosi, bhagavato pana bhikkhusaṅghassa ca uppanno lābhasakkāro dhammassapi [V 2.0147] uppannoyeva. Dhammadharānañhi kato sakkāro dhammassa kato nāma hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ mahālābhasakkāro uppajjī”ti.

This gain and honor that arose for the Blessed One and the Sangha, having come together, became immeasurable, like the water of two great rivers. Moreover, the gain and honor that arose for the Blessed One and the community of monks also arose for the Dhamma. For honor done to those who uphold the Dhamma is indeed honor done to the Dhamma. Therefore it was said, 'Great gain and honor arose for the Three Jewels.'

Vuttamatthaṃ pāḷiyā nidassento “yathāhā”tiādimāha. Tattha sakkatoti sakkārappatto. Yassa hi cattāro paccaye sakkatvā suabhisaṅkhate paṇītapaṇīte upaneti, so sakkato. Garukatoti garubhāvahetūnaṃ uttamaguṇānaṃ matthakappattiyā anaññasādhāraṇena garukārena sabbadevamanussehi pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garukato. Yasmiñhi garubhāvaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā paccaye denti, so garukato. Mānitoti sammāpaṭipattiyā mānito manena piyāyito. Tāya hi viññūnaṃ manāpatā. Pūjitoti mānanādipūjāya ceva catupaccayapūjāya ca pūjito. Yassa hi sabbametaṃ pūjanañca karonti, so pūjito. Apacitoti nīcavuttikaraṇena apacito. Satthārañhi disvā manussā hatthikkhandhādīhi otaranti, maggaṃ denti, aṃsakūṭato sāṭakaṃ apanenti. Āsanato [M 2.0162] vuṭṭhahanti, vandantīti evaṃ so tehi apacito nāma hoti.

To illustrate the meaning expressed, he begins with 'as it is said' in the Pāli. Here, 'honored' means having attained honor. For one to whom the four requisites are respectfully offered, carefully prepared, and presented as the finest, is honored. 'Revered' means held in the highest esteem by all devas and humans due to possessing supreme qualities, unmatched by others, like a stone parasol. For when offerings are made to one whose greatness is acknowledged, that one is revered. 'Esteemed' means held dear in the mind through right practice. For by that, one is pleasing to the wise. 'Worshipped' means honored both through respect and the offering of the four requisites. For one to whom all such worship is given is worshipped. 'Deferred to' means humbled by service. For upon seeing the Teacher, people descend from elephants, etc., make way, remove their upper garments from their shoulders, rise from their seats, and pay homage—thus is he deferred to by them.

Avaṇṇaṃ pattharitvāti avaṇṇaṃ tattha tattha saṃkittanavasena pattharitvā. Āvaṭṭanimāyanti āvaṭṭetvā gahaṇamāyaṃ. Āvaṭṭeti purimākārato nivatteti attano vase vatteti etāyāti āvaṭṭanī, māyā, taṃ āvaṭṭanimāyaṃ osāretvā parijappetvāti attho. Koṭito paṭṭhāyāti antimakoṭito paṭṭhāya. Thaddhakāyena pharusavācāya tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ avaṇṇakathanaṃ anatthāvahattā visasiñcanasadisā hotīti āha “visaṃ siñcitvā”ti. Aññātoti āñāto. Tenāha “ñāto”tiādi.

“Spreading dispraise” (avaṇṇaṃ pattharitvā) means spreading dispraise here and there by way of recounting. “With a turning-trick” (āvaṭṭanimāyaṃ) means a trick for drawing in by turning around. “It turns around” (āvaṭṭeti) means it turns one back from a former state, brings one under one’s control; this is “turning around” (āvaṭṭanī), a trick (māyā). The meaning is “having applied that turning-trick, having whispered or schemed.” “From the very end” (koṭito paṭṭhāya) means starting from the final extremity. Speaking dispraise of the Three Jewels with a rigid body and harsh speech is harmful, like sprinkling poison; thus he said, “having sprinkled poison.” “Aññāto” means “āñāto” (known). Therefore he said, “ñāto” (known), etc.

Kāyaṅganti kāyameva aṅgaṃ, kāyassa vā aṅgaṃ, sīsādi. Vācaṅganti “hotu, sādhū”ti evamādivācāya avayavaṃ. Ekakenāti asahāyena. Imassa panatthassāti “cariyaṃ caraṇakāle”tiādinā vuttassa. Yato yato garu dhuranti yasmiṃ yasmiṃ ṭhāne dhuraṃ garu bhārikaṃ hoti, aññe balibaddā ukkhipituṃ na sakkonti. Yato gambhīravattanīti vattanti etthāti vattanī, dummaggassetaṃ nāmaṃ, yasmiṃ ṭhāne udakacikkhallamahantatāya vā visamacchinnataṭabhāvena vā maggo gambhīro hotīti attho. Tadāssu kaṇhaṃ yuñjentīti assūti nipātamattaṃ, tadā kaṇhaṃ yuñjentīti attho. Yadā dhurañca garu hoti maggo ca gambhīro, tadā aññe balibadde apanetvā kaṇhameva yuñjentīti vuttaṃ hoti. Svāssu taṃ vahate dhuranti etthapi assūti nipātamattameva, so taṃ dhuraṃ vahatīti attho.

“The body’s limb” (kāyaṅgaṃ) means the body itself is a limb, or a limb of the body, such as the head and so on. “The speech’s limb” (vācaṅgaṃ) refers to a component of speech, like saying “let it be,” “good,” and so forth. “Alone” (ekakena) means without a companion. “But of this meaning” (imassa panatthassa) refers to that which was stated by “when practicing the practice” (cariyaṃ caraṇakāle) and so on. “Wherever the burden is heavy” (yato yato garu dhuraṃ) means in whatever place the burden is heavy and weighty, other oxen cannot lift it. “Where the path is a deep rut” (yato gambhīravattanī)—here, “vattanī” means a rut (vattanti ettha); this is a name for a bad path, meaning where the path is deep due to the vastness of muddy water or the unevenness of broken banks. “Then they yoke the black one” (tadāssu kaṇhaṃ yuñjenti)—here, “assu” is merely a particle; the meaning is “then they yoke the black one.” When the burden is heavy and the path is deep, then, setting aside other oxen, they yoke only the black one—this is what is meant. “Surely it bears that burden” (svāssu taṃ vahate dhuraṃ)—here too, “assu” is merely a particle; the meaning is “it bears that burden.”

Gehavetananti [V 2.0148] gehe nivuṭṭhabhāvahetu dātabbaṃ. Kāḷako nāma nāmenāti añjanavaṇṇo kiresa, tenassa “kāḷako”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Kāḷakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āhāti kāḷako kira ekadivasaṃ cintesi “mayhaṃ mātā duggatā maṃ puttaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā dukkhena poseti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ bhatiṃ katvā imaṃ duggatabhāvato moceyya”nti. So tato paṭṭhāya bhatiṃ upadhārento vicarati. Atha tasmiṃ divase gāmagorūpehi saddhiṃ tattha samīpe carati. Satthavāhaputtopi gosuttavittako, so “atthi nu kho etesaṃ gunnaṃ antare sakaṭāni uttāretuṃ samattho[M 2.0163] usabhājānīyo”ti upadhārayamāno bodhisattaṃ disvā “ayaṃ ājānīyo sakkhissati mayhaṃ sakaṭāni uttāretu”nti aññāsi. Tena taṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha. So aññesaṃ…pe… gehameva agamāsīti tadā kira gāmadārakā “kiṃ nāmetaṃ kāḷakassa gale”ti tassa santikaṃ āgacchanti. So te anubandhitvā dūratova palāpento mātu santikaṃ gato. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

“Household payment” (gehavetanaṃ) means a payment to be given on account of having lived in the household. “Kāḷako nāma nāmena” (named Kāḷaka by name)—it is said he was collyrium-colored, therefore they gave him the name “Kāḷaka.” “Approaching Kāḷaka, he said”—it is said that one day Kāḷaka thought: “My mother is poor and raises me with difficulty, placing me in the position of a son. Why don’t I earn wages and free her from this state of poverty?” From then on, he began wandering, seeking wages. On that day, he was moving about nearby with the village cattle. The caravan leader’s son, who was skilled in the lore of oxen, was observing, thinking, “Is there among these oxen a thoroughbred bull capable of pulling the carts across?” Seeing the Bodhisatta, he knew, “This thoroughbred will be able to pull my carts across.” Therefore, approaching him, he spoke thus. “He went only to the house…”—at that time, it is said, the village boys came near him, asking, “What is this around Kāḷaka’s neck?” Chasing them and making them flee from a distance, he went to his mother. This was said in reference to that.

Sāyanhasamayanti sāyanhakāle. Bhummatthe etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Na hettha accantasaṃyogo sambhavati. Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti ettha tehi tehi saddhivihārikaantevāsikaupāsakaupāsikādisattehi ceva rūpārammaṇādisaṅkhārehi ca paṭinivattetvā apasakkitvā nilīyanaṃ vivecanaṃ kāyacittehi tato vivittatāya paṭisallānaṃ kāyaviveko, cittaviveko ca. Yo tato duvidhavivekato vuṭṭhito bhavaṅgappattiyā sabrahmacārīhi samāgamena ca apeto. So paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito nāma hoti. Ayaṃ pana yasmā paṭisallānānaṃ uttamato phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhāsi, tasmā “phalasamāpattito”ti vuttaṃ. Kāyasakkhino bhavissāmāti nāmakāyena desanāsampaṭicchanavasena sakkhibhūtā bhavissāma. Nanu ca “paññatte āsane nisīdī”ti idaṃ kasmā vuttaṃ. Titthiyā hi bhagavato paṭipakkhā, te kasmā tassa āsanaṃ paññāpentīti āha “tathāgato hī”tiādi.

“In the evening time” (sāyanhasamayaṃ) means at the evening hour. This is a term of practical use in the sense of the locative case. Here, absolute connection is not possible. “Having emerged from seclusion” (paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito)—here, seclusion (paṭisallānaṃ) is the hiding (nilīyanaṃ) and separation (vivecanaṃ) due to being secluded by body and mind from those various co-residents, pupils, laymen, laywomen, and other beings, as well as from form-objects and other formations, having turned back and withdrawn from them. This is bodily seclusion and mental seclusion. One who emerges from this twofold seclusion, being removed from the attainment of bhavaṅga and from association with fellow practitioners, is said to have “emerged from seclusion.” However, since he emerged from the highest of seclusions, namely the attainment of fruition, it is said, “from the attainment of fruition.” “We shall become bodily witnesses” (kāyasakkhino bhavissāma)—we shall become witnesses by way of the mind-body through accepting the teaching. Now, why was it said, “He sat down on the prepared seat”? The sectarians are opponents of the Blessed One, so why would they prepare a seat for him? To this, it is said, “For the Tathāgata,” and so on.

Viggāhikakathanti viggāhasaṃvattanikaṃ sārambhakathaṃ. Āyāceyyāsīti vacībhedaṃ katvā yāceyyāsi. Pattheyyāsīti manasā āsīseyyāsi. Piheyyāsīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Nittejataṃ āpannoti tejahāniyā nittejabhāvaṃ āpanno, nittejabhūtoti attho. Tato eva bhikkhuādayopi sammukhā oloketuṃ asamatthatāya pattakkhandho, patitakkhandhoti attho. Tenāha “onatagīvo”ti. Dassitadhammesūti vuttadhammesu. Vacanamattameva hi tesaṃ, na pana dassanaṃ tādisasseva dhammassa abhāvato. Bhagavato eva vā “ime dhammā anabhisambuddhā”ti parassa vacanavasena dassitadhammesu. Paṭicarissatīti paṭicchādanavase carissati pavattissati, paṭicchādanattho [V 2.0149] eva vā carati-saddo anekatthattā dhātūnanti āha “paṭicchādessatī”ti. Aññena [M 2.0164] vā aññanti pana paṭicchādanākāradassananti āha “aññena vā vacanenā”tiādi.

“Disputative talk” (viggāhikakathaṃ) means talk that leads to disputes, quarrelsome talk. “You would plead” (āyāceyyāsi) means you would plead by making a verbal distinction. “You would desire” (pattheyyāsi) means you would wish for it in your mind. “You would long for” (piheyyāsi) is another term for the same. “He has reached a state of diminished vigor” (nittejataṃ āpanno) means he has attained a condition of lost vigor, has become devoid of vigor—that is the meaning. For that very reason, he had drooping shoulders—meaning fallen shoulders—due to the inability of even the monks and others to look at him directly. Hence it is said, “with neck bent down.” “In the teachings shown” (dassitadhammesu) means in the teachings spoken. For them, it was mere words, not actual seeing, due to the absence of such a teaching. Or, it refers to the teachings shown by way of another’s statement concerning the Blessed One, that “these teachings have not been fully understood.” “He will evade” (paṭicarissati) means he will proceed by way of concealment; the meaning is simply concealment. Alternatively, since the verb “carati” has multiple meanings, it is said, “he will conceal.” Or, “one thing by another” (aññena vā aññaṃ) means showing the manner of concealment—hence it is said, “by one speech or another,” etc.
