Tattha aññaṃ vacananti yaṃ samanuyuñjantena bhagavatā parassa dosavibhāvanaṃ vacanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ tato aññeneva vacanena paṭicchādeti. “Āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti codakena vuttavacanaṃ viya “ko āpanno, kiṃ āpanno, kismiṃ āpanno, kaṃ bhaṇatha, kiṃ bhaṇathā”tiādivacanena aññaṃ āgantukakathaṃ āharanto “tvaṃ itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti puṭṭho “pāṭaliputtaṃ gatomhī”ti vatvā puna “na tava pāṭaliputtagamanaṃ pucchāma, āpattiṃ pucchāmā”ti vutte tato rājagahaṃ gatomhi. Rājagahaṃ vā yāhi brāhmaṇagehaṃ vā, āpattiṃ āpannosīti. “Tattha me sūkaramaṃsaṃ laddha”ntiādīni vadanto viya samanuyuñjakena vuttavacanato aññaṃ āgantukakathaṃ āharanto apanāmessati, vikkhepaṃ gamayissati. Appatītā honti tena atuṭṭhā asomanassikāti apaccayo, domanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Neva attano, na paresaṃ hitaṃ abhirādhayatīti anabhiraddhi, domanassameva. Tenevāha “apaccayena domanassaṃ vutta”nti.

There, 'another statement' refers to when one covers up with a different statement the words spoken by the cross-examiner for the purpose of clarifying another's fault. For example, when the accuser says, 'You have committed an offense,' the other brings up extraneous talk with words like, 'Who has committed an offense? What offense has been committed? In what has it been committed? Of whom do you speak? What do you speak of?' Or, when asked, 'You have committed such-and-such an offense,' one replies, 'I went to Pāṭaliputta.' When told again, 'We are not asking about your going to Pāṭaliputta, we are asking about the offense,' one then says, 'I went to Rājagaha.' [The accuser might say:] 'Go to Rājagaha or to a brahmin's house, you have committed an offense.' Or, like one who, when cross-examined, brings up extraneous talk different from the statement of the cross-examiner—such as saying, 'There I obtained pork,' and so on—thus leading the conversation astray and causing distraction. 'They become displeased' (appatītā honti) means they are dissatisfied, mentally unhappy. This is 'displeasure' (apaccayo), a term for mental distress (domanassa). 'It does not accomplish one's own or others' benefit' (anabhiraddhi) is simply mental distress. Therefore, it is said, 'By displeasure, mental distress is meant.'

Yassa kho pana te atthāya dhammo desitoti ettha dhamma-saddena catusaccadhammo vuttoti āha “yassa maggassa vā phalassa vā atthāyā”ti. Catusaccadhammo hi maggaphalādhigamatthāya desīyati. Na niggacchatīti na pavatteti. Nanti naṃ dhammaṃ. Idāni “yassa kho pana te atthāya dhammo desito”ti ettha dhamma-saddena paṭipattidhammo dassito, na pana catusaccadhammoti adhippāyena atthavikappaṃ dassento “atha vā”tiādimāha. Pañca dhammāti gambhīrañāṇacariyabhūtānaṃ khandhādīnaṃ uggahasavanadhāraṇaparicayayonisomanasikāre sandhāyāha. Takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyāti ettha sammāsaddo ubhayatthāpi yojetabbo “sammā takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyā”ti. Yo hi sammā dhammaṃ paṭipajjati, tasseva sammā dukkhakkhayo hotīti. Yo pana vuttanayena takkaro, tassa niyyānaṃ atthato dhammasseva niyyānanti tappaṭikkhepena “so dhammo…pe… na niyyāti na niggacchatī”ti āha.

“For whose sake the Dhamma was taught” (yassa kho pana te atthāya dhammo desito)—here, by the word “Dhamma,” the Dhamma of the Four Truths is meant, as it is said: “For the sake of which path or fruit.” For the Dhamma of the Four Truths is taught for the attainment of the path and fruit. “It does not lead out” (na niggacchati) means it does not proceed. “Naṃ” refers to that Dhamma. Now, in the phrase “for whose sake the Dhamma was taught,” the word “Dhamma” indicates the Dhamma of practice, not the Dhamma of the Four Truths. With this intention, showing an alternative meaning, it is said “or else,” etc. “Five Dhammas” (pañca dhammā)—this refers to learning, hearing, retaining, familiarity, and wise attention, in connection with the aggregates, etc., which are the sphere of profound knowledge and conduct. “Of one who does it rightly, for the complete destruction of suffering” (takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya)—here the word “rightly” should be applied in both places: “rightly of one who does it, rightly for the complete destruction of suffering.” For one who practices the Dhamma rightly, for them alone does the complete destruction of suffering occur. Moreover, for one who does it in the way described, liberation is, in essence, the liberation of the Dhamma itself. Therefore, rejecting that, it is said: “That Dhamma… does not lead out, does not proceed.”

Yadi tiracchānasīhassa nādo sabbatiracchānaekaccamanussāmanussanādato seṭṭhattā seṭṭhanādo, kimaṅgaṃ pana tathāgatasīhassa nādoti [M 2.0165] āha “sīhanādanti seṭṭhanāda”nti. Yadi vā tiracchānasīhanādassa seṭṭhanādatā nibbhayatāya appaṭisattutāya icchitā, tathāgatasīhanādasseva ayamattho sātisayoti āha “abhītanādaṃ appaṭināda”nti. “Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.129; a. ni. 1.268-271) hi yo attho vutto, tassa bhūtatāya [V 2.0150] ayaṃ nādo seṭṭhanādo nāma hoti uttamanādo. Bhūtattho hi uttamatthoti. Imamatthaṃ pana vadantassa bhagavato aññato bhayaṃ vā āsaṅkā vā natthīti abhītanādo nāma hoti. Abhūtañhi vadato kutoci bhayaṃ vā āsaṅkā vā siyā, evaṃ pana vadantaṃ bhagavantaṃ koci uṭṭhahitvā paṭibāhituṃ samattho nāma natthīti ayaṃ nādo appaṭinādo nāma hoti.

If the roar of a lion among animals is considered the supreme roar because it surpasses the roars of all other animals, some humans, and non-humans, how much more so is the roar of the Tathāgata lion? Thus it is said, "The lion's roar is the supreme roar." Alternatively, if the superiority of a lion's roar among animals is considered to be due to its fearlessness and lack of opposition, then this meaning applies with even greater excellence to the roar of the Tathāgata lion. Hence it is said, "A fearless roar, an unopposed roar." Because the meaning stated in the phrase, "This is impossible, it cannot occur," is true, this roar is called the supreme roar, the highest roar. For the true meaning is the highest meaning. Moreover, when the Blessed One declares this truth, he has no fear or apprehension from any quarter—thus it is called a fearless roar. For one who speaks falsely might have fear or apprehension from somewhere, but no one is capable of rising up to oppose the Blessed One when he speaks thus—therefore, this roar is called an unopposed roar.

Samantato niggaṇhanavasena todanaṃ vijjhanaṃ sannitodakaṃ, sammā vā nitudanti pīḷenti etenāti sannitodakaṃ. Vācāyāti ca paccatte karaṇavacanaṃ. Tenāha “vacanapatodenā”ti. Sañjambharimakaṃsūti samantato sambharitaṃ akaṃsu, sabbe paribbājakā vācātodanehi tudiṃsūti attho. Tenāha “sambharitaṃ…pe… vijjhiṃsū”ti. Siṅgālakaṃyevāti siṅgālameva, “segālakaṃyevā”tipi pāṭho. Tassevāti siṅgālaravasseva. Atha vā bheraṇḍakaṃyevāti bhedaṇḍasakuṇisadisaṃyevāti attho. Bhedaṇḍaṃ nāma eko pakkhī dvimukho, tassa kira saddo ativiya virūpo amanāpo. Tenāha “apica bhinnassaraṃ amanāpasaddaṃ nadatī”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

Goading and piercing from all sides in the manner of restraining is 'sannitodakaṃ'; or, 'they rightly prick (nitudanti) and oppress (pīḷenti) with this,' hence 'sannitodakaṃ.' 'By speech' (vācāya) is the instrumental singular. Therefore, it is said, 'by the goad of speech.' 'They assailed him' (sañjambharimakaṃsu) means they attacked him from all sides; the meaning is that all the wanderers pierced him with verbal goads. Hence, it is said, 'attacked... pierced.' 'Just like a jackal' (siṅgālakaṃyeva) means just a jackal; there is also the reading 'segālakaṃyeva.' 'Of that very one' (tasseva) means of the jackal's cry. Alternatively, 'just like a bheraṇḍaka' means just like a bhedaṇḍa bird. The bhedaṇḍa is a two-headed bird; its sound is said to be exceedingly hideous and unpleasant. Therefore, it is said, 'moreover, it cries with a broken sound, an unpleasant noise.' The rest here is self-explanatory.

Sarabhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sarabha Sutta is finished.

5. Kesamuttisuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Kesamutti Sutta

66. Pañcame kesamuttaṃ nivāso etesanti kesamuttiyāti āha “kesamuttanigamavāsino”ti. Aṭṭhavidhapānakānīti ambapānādiaṭṭhavidhāni pānāni.

66. In the fifth, because their dwelling is at Kesamutta, they are called Kesamuttiyā; thus he said, 'residents of the Kesamutta town.' The eight kinds of drinks: the eight kinds of drinks beginning with mango juice.

“Mā anussavenā”tiādīsu pana eko daharakālato paṭṭhāya evaṃ anussavo atthi, evaṃ cirakālakatāya anussutiyā labbhamānaṃ kathamidaṃ [M 2.0166] aññathā siyā, tasmā bhūtametanti anussavena gaṇhāti, tathā gahaṇaṃ paṭikkhipanto “mā anussavenā”ti āha. Anu anu savanaṃ anussavo. Aparo “amhākaṃ pitupitāmahādivuddhānaṃ upadesaparamparāya idamābhataṃ, evaṃ paramparābhatakathaṃ nāma na aññathā siyā, tasmā bhūtameta”nti gaṇhāti, taṃ paṭikkhipanto “mā paramparāyā”ti āha. Eko kenaci kismiñci vuttamatte “evaṃ kira eta”nti gaṇhāti, taṃ nisedhento “mā itikirāyā”ti āha. Piṭakaṃ gantho sampadīyati etassāti piṭakasampadānaṃ, ganthassa uggaṇhanako. Tena piṭakauggaṇhanakabhāvena ekacco tādisaṃ ganthaṃ paguṇaṃ katvā tena taṃ samentaṃ sameti, tasmā “bhūtameta”nti gaṇhāti, taṃ sandhāyesa paṭikkhepo “mā piṭakasampadānenā”ti, attano uggahaganthasampattiyā mā gaṇhitthāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sametanti saṃgataṃ.

Regarding 'Do not go by oral tradition,' etc.: Here, one, having heard something repeatedly from youth, thinks, 'There has been an oral tradition like this for a long time; how could this, which has been received through long-standing hearsay, be otherwise? Therefore, it is true,' and thus accepts it based on oral tradition. Rejecting such acceptance, it is said, 'Do not go by oral tradition.' 'Oral tradition' (anussavo) is hearing again and again (anu anu savanaṃ). Another accepts something, thinking, 'This has been handed down through the lineage of instruction from our fathers, grandfathers, and other elders. A teaching handed down by tradition cannot be otherwise; therefore, it is true.' Rejecting this, it is said, 'Do not go by tradition.' Someone accepts something merely on the report that 'it is said to be so.' Denying this, it is said, 'Do not go by hearsay.' 'Acquisition of the Piṭaka' (piṭakasampadānaṃ) means one is a learner of the text (ganthassa uggaṇhanako), as the Piṭaka is the text (gantho) that is handed down to him. Because of being a learner of the Piṭaka, a certain person, having mastered such a text, accepts something as true because it is consistent with that text. In reference to this, the rejection is stated: 'Do not go by the authority of a text.' This means, 'Do not accept it based on the accomplishment of having learned a text yourself.' 'Is consistent' (sameti) means it agrees (saṃgataṃ).

Koci [V 2.0151] kañci vitakkento “evameva tena bhavitabba”nti kevalaṃ attano saṅkappavasena “bhūtamida”nti gaṇhāti, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “mā takkahetū”ti. Añño “imāya yuttiyā bhūtamida”nti kevalaṃ anumānato nayaggāhena gaṇhāti, taṃ paṭikkhipanto “mā nayahetū”ti āha. Kassaci “evametaṃ siyā”ti parikappentassa ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ upaṭṭhāti, so “attheta”nti attano parikappitākārena gaṇhāti, taṃ paṭisedhento “mā ākāraparivitakkenā”ti āha. Aparassa cintayato yathāparikappitaṃ kañci atthaṃ “evametaṃ na aññathā”ti abhinivisantassa ekā diṭṭhi uppajjati. Yā yassa taṃ kāraṇaṃ nijjhāyantassa paccakkhaṃ viya nirūpetvā cintentassa khamati. So “attheta”nti diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā gaṇhāti, taṃ sandhāyāha “mā diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā”ti.

When someone speculates about something, thinking, 'It must be so,' and accepts it as true merely based on their own conjecture, it is with reference to this that it is said, 'Do not go by reasoning.' Another, thinking, 'This must be true by this line of reasoning,' accepts it solely through inference, by grasping at a method. Rejecting this, it is said, 'Do not go by a method.' For someone who imagines, 'It might be like this,' a certain reason occurs, and they accept it as true in the form of their own imagining. Refuting this, it is said, 'Do not go by reflection on reasons.' For another person who, while thinking, is certain about a certain meaning as they have conceived it, thinking, 'This is so, not otherwise,' a view arises. Whatever seems acceptable to them while contemplating that reason, scrutinizing it as if it were directly perceived, they accept it as true through the acceptance of a view after scrutiny. Referring to this, it is said, 'Do not go by acceptance of a view after scrutiny.'

Akusalaverassāti pāṇātipātādipañcavidhaṃ veraṃ sandhāya vadati. Kodho nāma cetaso dukkhanti āha “kodhacittassa abhāvenā”ti. Kilesassāti cittaṃ vibādhentassa upatāpentassa uddhaccakukkuccādikilesassa. Sesamettha uttānameva.

Regarding 'unwholesome enmity': this is said with reference to the five kinds of enmity, beginning with the destruction of life. 'Anger is mental suffering,' as it says, 'due to the absence of a mind of anger.' Regarding 'of defilement': of the defilement, such as restlessness and remorse, which harasses and torments the mind. The rest here is self-evident.

Kesamuttisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kesamutti Sutta is finished.

6. Sāḷhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Sāḷha Sutta

67. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0167] pāto asitabbabhojanaṃ pātarāsaṃ, bhuttaṃ pātarāsaṃ etesanti bhuttapātarāsā. Dāsā nāma antojātā vā dhanakkītā vā karamarānītā vā sayaṃ vā dāsabyaṃ upagatā. Bhattavetanabhatā kammakārā nāma.

67. In the sixth, `pātarāsa` is the meal to be eaten in the morning. Those who have eaten the morning meal are `bhuttapātarāsā`. Slaves are those born in the house, bought with wealth, brought as prisoners of war, or who have entered servitude of their own accord. Workers are those supported by food and wages.

Nicchātoti ettha chātaṃ vuccati taṇhā jighacchāhetutāya, sā assa natthīti nicchāto. Tenāha “nittaṇho”ti. Abbhantare santāpakarānaṃ kilesānanti attano santāne darathapariḷāhajananena santāpanakilesānaṃ. Antotāpanakilesānaṃ abhāvā sīto sītalo bhūto jātoti sītibhūto. Tenāha “sītalībhūto”ti. Maggaphalanibbānasukhāni vā paṭisaṃvedetīti sukhappaṭisaṃvedī. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

Here, regarding `nicchāto`: `chāta` is said to be craving, as it is a cause of hunger. He for whom that is not is `nicchāto`. Therefore, it is said, 'without craving.' Regarding 'of the defilements that cause torment within': of the tormenting defilements that generate distress and burning in one's own continuum. Because of the absence of inner tormenting defilements, he has become cool; thus, he is `sītibhūto`. Therefore, it is said, 'become cooled.' Or, 'he experiences the bliss of path, fruition, and Nibbāna'; thus, he is one who experiences bliss. The rest is easily understood.

Sāḷhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sāḷha Sutta is finished.

7. Kathāvatthusuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Kathāvatthu Sutta

68. Sattame [V 2.0152] kathāvatthūnīti kathāya pavattiṭṭhānāni. Yasmā tehi vinā kathā na pavattati, tasmā “kathākāraṇānī”ti vuttaṃ. Atati satati satataṃ gacchati pavattatīti addhā, kāloti āha “atītamaddhānaṃ nāma kālopi vattatī”ti. Dhammappavattimattatāya hi paramatthato avijjamānopi kālo tasseva dhammassa pavattiavatthāvisesaṃ upādāya teneva vohārena atītotiādinā voharīyati, atītādibhedo ca nāmāyaṃ nippariyāyato dhammānaṃyeva hoti, na kālassāti āha “khandhāpi vattantī”ti. Yathāvuttamatthaṃ itaresu dvīsu atidisati “anāgatapaccuppannesupi eseva nayo”ti. Atītamaddhānantiādīsu ca dve pariyāyā suttantapariyāyo, abhidhammapariyāyo ca. Suttantapariyāyena paṭisandhito pubbe atīto addhā nāma, cutito pacchā anāgato addhā nāma, saha cutipaṭisandhīti tadantaraṃ paccuppanno addhā nāma. Abhidhammapariyāyena tīsu khaṇesu uppādato pubbe atīto addhā nāma, uppādato uddhaṃ anāgato addhā [M 2.0168] nāma, khaṇattayaṃ paccuppanno addhā nāma. Tatthāyaṃ suttantadesanāti suttantapariyāyeneva atītādivisayaṃ kathaṃ dassento “atīte kassapo nāmā”tiādimāha.

68. In the seventh, `kathāvatthūni` are the bases for the occurrence of discussion. Since without them discussion does not occur, they are called `kathākāraṇāni` (causes of discussion). `Addhā` is called time because it constantly goes on, flows, and continues. Therefore, it is said, 'The past time is indeed spoken of.' Although time does not ultimately exist, being merely the occurrence of phenomena, it is conventionally spoken of as 'past,' etc., with reference to the specific state of the occurrence of that very phenomenon. And this distinction of past, etc., belongs without qualification to phenomena themselves, not to time. Hence, it is said, 'The aggregates also occur.' The meaning stated above is extended to the other two times: 'The same method applies to the future and the present.' In the phrases 'past time,' etc., there are two modes: the Suttanta mode and the Abhidhamma mode. According to the Suttanta mode, the time before rebirth-linking is called the past, the time after death is called the future, and the interval between, together with death and rebirth-linking, is called the present. According to the Abhidhamma mode, the time before the moment of arising is called the past, the time after the moment of arising is called the future, and the three moments are called the present. Here, this teaching is according to the Suttanta method. Thus, explaining the topic of the past, etc., according to the Suttanta mode, it is said, 'In the past, there was one named Kassapa,' and so on.

Ekaṃseneva byākātabbo vissajjetabboti ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyo. “Cakkhu anicca”nti pañhe uttarapadāvadhāraṇaṃ sandhāya “ekaṃseneva byākātabba”nti vuttaṃ niccatāya lesassapi tattha abhāvato, purimapadāvadhāraṇe pana vibhajjabyākaraṇīyatāya. Tenāha “aniccaṃ nāma cakkhūti puṭṭhena panā”tiādi. Cakkhusote visesatthasāmaññatthānaṃ asādhāraṇabhāvato dvinnaṃ tesaṃ sadisacodanā paṭicchannamukheneva byākaraṇīyā paṭikkhepavasena anuññātavasena ca vissajjitabbatoti āha “yathā cakkhu, tathā sotaṃ…pe… ayaṃ paṭipucchābyākaraṇīyo pañho”ti. Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti jīvasarīrānaṃ anaññatāpañhe yassa yena anaññatā coditā, so eva paramatthato nupalabbhatīti ca jhānattayassa metteyyatākittanasadisoti abyākātabbatāya ṭhapanīyo vutto. Evarūpo hi pañho tidhā avissajjanīyattā byākaraṇaṃ akatvā ṭhapetabbo.

It should be explained in one way, it should be answered; thus it is a question to be answered categorically. Regarding the question, 'Is the eye impermanent?,' the statement 'it should be answered in one way' is said with reference to emphasizing the final word, because there is not even a trace of permanence there. However, with emphasis on the first word, it becomes a question to be answered analytically. Therefore, it is said, 'But when asked, "Is the eye what is impermanent?"...' and so on. Regarding the eye and ear, because their specific and general meanings are not shared, a similar question about the two should be explained by way of a concealed opening, to be answered by way of rejection and by way of permission. Hence, it is said, 'Just as the eye, so is the ear… this is a question that should be answered with a counter-question.' In the question about the non-otherness of the life-principle and the body—'Is the life-principle the same as the body?'—that very thing about which non-otherness is questioned is ultimately not found. And this is similar to the declaration of Metteyya's attainment of the three jhānas; thus it is said it should be set aside as unexplainable. For such a question, being unanswerable in three ways, should be set aside without giving an explanation.

Tiṭṭhati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti ṭhānaṃ, kāraṇanti āha “kāraṇākāraṇe”ti. Yuttena kāraṇenāti anurūpena kāraṇena. Pahotīti niggaṇhituṃ samattho hoti. Sassatavādibhāvameva dīpetīti attanā gahite ucchedavāde dosaṃ disvā attanopi sassatavādibhāvameva [V 2.0153] dīpeti. Puggalavādimhīti iminā vacchakuttiyavādiṃ dasseti. Pañhaṃ pucchantehi paṭipajjitabbā paṭipadā pañhapucchanakānaṃ vattaṃ.

`Ṭhāna` is that on which the result stands, because its occurrence depends on it; it is a cause. Thus he says, 'cause and non-cause.' 'By a proper reason' means by a suitable reason. 'He is able' means he is capable of refuting. 'He reveals only his state as an eternalist' means that, seeing the fault in the annihilationist view he has adopted, he reveals his own state as an eternalist. By 'I am a personalist,' he indicates he is a proponent of the Vacchagottīya school. The practice to be undertaken by those asking questions is the duty of questioners.

Paṭicaratīti paṭicchādanavasena carati pavattati. Paṭicchādanattho eva vā caratisaddo anekatthattā dhātūnanti āha “paṭicchādetī”ti. Aññenaññanti pana paṭicchādanākāradassananti āha “aññena vacanenā”tiādi. Tattha aññena vacanenāti yaṃ codakena cuditakassa dosavibhāvanaṃ vacanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ tato aññena vacanena paṭicchādeti. Yo hi “āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti vutte “ko āpanno, kiṃ āpanno, kismiṃ āpanno, kaṃ bhaṇatha, kiṃ bhaṇathā”ti vadati. “Evarūpaṃ kiñci tayā diṭṭha”nti vutte “na suṇāmī”ti sotaṃ vā upaneti, ayaṃ aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati nāma. “Ko āpanno”tiādinā hi codanaṃ avissajjetvāva vikkhepāpajjanaṃ aññenaññaṃ [M 2.0169] paṭicaraṇaṃ, bahiddhā kathāpanāmanaṃ vissajjetvāti ayametesaṃ viseso. Tenevāha “āgantukakathaṃ otārento”tiādi. Tattha apanāmetīti vikkhepeti. Tatrāti tasmiṃ bahiddhākathāya apanāmane.

`Paṭicarati` means he acts or proceeds by way of concealing. Or, the word `carati` simply has the meaning of concealing, because roots have many meanings; thus it is said, 'he conceals.' But `aññenaññaṃ` (one with another) means showing the manner of concealing; thus it is said, 'with another statement,' and so on. Therein, 'with another statement' means that when the accuser has spoken a statement revealing the fault of the accused, the latter covers it up with a different statement. For example, when told, 'You have committed an offense,' one replies, 'Who has committed it? What was committed? In what was it committed? Whom are you addressing? What are you saying?' Or when told, 'Something like this was seen by you,' one responds, 'I do not hear,' or brings one's ear closer—this is called `aññenaññaṃ paṭicarati`. Indeed, by saying, 'Who has committed it?' and so on, resorting to distraction without having answered the accusation is `aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇaṃ`. Diverting the talk outwards after having answered it—this is the distinction between them. Therefore, it is said, 'introducing talk about a newcomer,' and so on. Therein, 'he diverts' means he distracts. 'Therein' refers to that diverting to external talk.

Upanisīdati phalaṃ etthāti kāraṇaṃ upanisā, upecca nissayatīti vā upanisā, saha upanisāyāti saupanisoti āha “saupanissayo sapaccayo”ti.

The cause is `upanisā` because the result sits near it; or it is `upanisā` because one approaches and relies on it. 'With `upanisā`' is `saupaniso`; thus he says, 'with decisive support, with condition'.

Ohitasototi anaññavihitattā dhammassavanāya apanāmitasoto. Tato eva tadatthaṃ ṭhapitasoto. Kusaladhammanti ariyamaggo adhippetoti āha “ariyamagga”nti.

`Ohitasoto` means one whose ear is applied to hearing the Dhamma, not being directed elsewhere. Therefore, one's ear is established for that purpose. By 'wholesome dhamma,' the noble path is intended; thus it is said, 'the noble path.'

Kathāvatthusuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kathāvatthu Sutta is finished.

8. Aññatitthiyasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Aññatitthiya Sutta

69. Aṭṭhame bhagavā mūlaṃ kāraṇaṃ etesaṃ yāthāvato adhigamāyāti bhagavaṃmūlakā. Tenāha “bhagavantañhi nissāya mayaṃ ime dhamme ājānāma paṭivijjhāmā”ti. Amhākaṃ dhammāti tehi attanā adhigantabbatāya vuttaṃ. Sevitabbāsevitabbānañhi yāthāvato adhigamaññāṇāni adhigacchanakasambandhīni, tāni ca sammāsambuddhamūlakāni anaññavisayattā. Tenāha “pubbe kassapasammāsambuddhenā”tiādi. Ime dhammāti ime ñāṇadhammā. Ājānāmāti abhimukhaṃ paccakkhato jānāma. Paṭivijjhāmāti tasseva vevacanaṃ, adhigacchāmāti attho. Bhagavā netā etesanti [V 2.0154] bhagavaṃnettikā. Netāti sevitabbadhamme veneyyasantānaṃ pāpetā. Vinetāti asevitabbadhamme veneyyasantānato apanetā. Tadaṅgavinayādivasena vā vinetā. Atha vā yathā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso hoti, evaṃ visesato netā. Anunetāti “ime dhammā sevitabbā, ime na sevitabbā”ti ubhayasampāpanāpanayanatthaṃ paññāpetā. Tenāha “yathāsabhāvato”tiādi.

69. In the eighth point, the Blessed One is the root, the cause for the accurate realization of these things; hence, 'rooted in the Blessed One.' Therefore, it is said: 'For we, relying on the Blessed One, understand and penetrate these teachings.' 'Our teachings' refers to that which should be realized by them themselves. The knowledges for the accurate realization of what should and should not be cultivated are connected with the one who attains them, and these are rooted in the Perfectly Enlightened One, as they do not fall within another's domain. Hence, it is said: 'Formerly, by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa...' and so on. 'These teachings' refers to these knowledges as dhammas. 'We understand' means we know directly and manifestly. 'We penetrate' is a synonym for that, meaning 'we attain.' The Blessed One is the leader of these; hence, 'guided by the Blessed One.' 'He guides' means he leads those to be trained to the teachings that should be cultivated. 'He disciplines' means he removes from those to be trained the teachings that should not be cultivated. Or, he disciplines by way of removal by substitution, etc. Alternatively, just as there is the distinction of sufficient noble knowledge and vision, so he leads in a special way. 'He instructs' means he makes known, 'These things should be cultivated, these should not,' for the purpose of both causing attainment and removal. Therefore, it is said, 'according to their true nature,' and so on.

Paṭisaranti [M 2.0170] etthāti paṭisaraṇaṃ, bhagavā paṭisaraṇaṃ etesanti bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Āpāthaṃ upagacchantā hi bhagavā paṭisaraṇaṃ samosaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. Tenāha “catubhūmakadhammā”tiādi. Paṭisarati sabhāvasampaṭivedhavasena paccekaṃ upagacchatīti vā paṭisaraṇaṃ, bhagavā paṭisaraṇaṃ etesanti bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Paṭisarati paṭivijjhatīti vā paṭisaraṇaṃ, tasmā paṭivijjhanavasena bhagavā paṭisaraṇaṃ etesanti bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Tenāha “apicā”tiādi. Paṭivedhavasenāti paṭivijjhitabbatāvasena. Asatipi mukhe atthato evaṃ vadanto viya hotīti āha “phasso āgacchati ahaṃ bhagavā kinnāmo”ti. Phasso ñāṇassa āpāthaṃ āgacchantoyeva hi attano “ahaṃ kinnāmo”ti nāmaṃ pucchanto viya, bhagavā cassa nāmaṃ karonto viya hoti.

A 'resort' (paṭisaraṇa) is that wherein they resort (paṭisaranti); the Blessed One is their resort, hence 'the Blessed One is their resort.' For those who come within his range, the Blessed One is a resort, a place of confluence. Therefore, it is said, 'the dhammas of the four planes,' etc. Or, a 'resort' is so-called because one individually approaches through the thorough penetration of intrinsic nature; the Blessed One is their resort, hence 'the Blessed One is their resort.' Or, a 'resort' is so-called because one penetrates (paṭivijjhati); therefore, the Blessed One is their resort in the sense of penetration, hence 'the Blessed One is their resort.' Therefore, it is said, 'furthermore,' etc. 'Through penetration' means in the sense of what is to be penetrated. Even if not spoken aloud, it is as if one speaks thus in meaning, hence it is said: 'Contact comes, [as if asking,] “O Blessed One, what is my name?”' For when contact comes into the range of knowledge, it is as if contact, asking its own name, says, 'What is my name?' and the Blessed One is as if naming it.

Paṭibhātūti ettha paṭisaddāpekkhāya “bhagavanta”nti upayogavacanaṃ, attho pana sāmivacanavaseneva veditabboti dassento āha “bhagavato”ti. Paṭibhātūti ca bhāgo hotu. Bhagavato hi esa bhāgo, yadidaṃ dhammassa desanā, amhākaṃ pana bhāgo savananti adhippāyo. Evañhi saddalakkhaṇena sameti. Keci pana paṭibhātūti padassa dissatūti atthaṃ vadanti, ñāṇena dissatu, desīyatūti vā attho. Upaṭṭhātūti ñāṇassa paccupatiṭṭhatu. Pāḷiyaṃ ko adhippayāsoti ettha ko adhikappayogoti attho.

Here, in 'paṭibhātu', the word 'bhagavantaṃ' is a term of connection used in expectation of the prefix 'paṭi', but to show that the meaning should be understood in the sense of the genitive case, it says 'bhagavato'. And 'paṭibhātu' means 'let there be a share.' For this is the Blessed One's share, namely the teaching of the Dhamma, while our share is listening—this is the intention. Thus, it accords with the characteristics of the word. Some, however, say the meaning of the word 'paṭibhātu' is 'let it appear,' meaning 'let it appear to wisdom,' or 'let it be taught.' 'Upaṭṭhātu' means 'let it be present to wisdom.' As for the phrase, 'What is the intention in the Pāli?' here the meaning is 'what is the intended application?'

Lokavajjavasenāti lokiyajanehi pakatiyā garahitabbavajjavasena. Vipākavajjavasenāti vipākassa apāyasaṃvattanikavajjavasena. Kathantiādinā ubhayavajjavasenapi appasāvajjatāya visayaṃ dasseti. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

'By way of worldly blame' means by way of blame that is naturally censured by worldly people. 'By way of blame in the result' means by way of blame that leads to the woeful states as its result. By 'how,' and so on, it shows the scope of what is slightly blameworthy with respect to both kinds of blame. The rest here is easy to understand.

Aññatitthiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sutta to Those of Other Sects is concluded.

9. Akusalamūlasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Sutta on Unwholesome Roots

70. Navame lubbhatīti lobho. Dussatīti doso. Muyhatīti moho. Lobhādīni panetāni [V 2.0155] asahajātānaṃ pāṇātipātādīnaṃ kesañci akusalānaṃ upanissayapaccayaṭṭhena, sahajātānaṃ adinnādānādīnaṃ kesañci [M 2.0171] sampayuttā hutvā uppādakaṭṭhena, sayañca akusalānīti sāvajjadukkhavipākaṭṭhenāti āha “akusalānaṃ mūlāni, akusalāni ca tāni mūlānī”ti. Vuttampi cetaṃ “ratto kho, āvuso, rāgena abhibhūto pariyādinnacitto pāṇampi hanatī”tiādi. Yadapīti liṅgavipallāsena vuttanti āha “yopi, bhikkhave, lobho”ti. Tadapīti etthāpi eseva nayoti āha “sopi akusalamūla”nti. Vināpi liṅgavipallāsena atthayojanaṃ dassento “akusalamūlaṃ vā”tiādimāha. Sabbatthāti “yadapi, bhikkhave, doso, tadapi akusalamūla”ntiādīsu. Abhisaṅkharotīti ettha āyūhatīti atthaṃ vatvā tañca āyūhanaṃ paccayasamavāyasiddhito sampiṇḍanaṃ rāsikaraṇaṃ viya hotīti āha “sampiṇḍeti rāsiṃ karotī”ti.

70. In the ninth sutta: because one clings (lubbhati), it is 'greed' (lobha). Because one is corrupted (dussati), it is 'hatred' (dosa). Because one is deluded (muyhati), it is 'delusion' (moha). These—greed, etc.—serve as a supporting condition for some non-co-nascent unwholesome states like killing living beings; being associated, they serve as a producer for some co-nascent unwholesome states like taking what is not given; and they themselves are unwholesome in the sense of being blameworthy and having painful results. Hence it is said: 'They are the roots of the unwholesome, and they are unwholesome roots.' And this is also stated: 'Friends, a person who is impassioned, overcome by passion, with a mind obsessed, may even kill a living being,' etc. Regarding 'yadapi' (whatever), it is said that this is stated with a change of gender, hence it says: 'Whatever greed there is, monks...' (yopi... lobho). Regarding 'tadapi' (that too), it is said that the same method applies here, hence it says: 'That too is an unwholesome root' (sopi akusalamūlaṃ). Showing the application of the meaning even without the change of gender, he says 'or an unwholesome root,' etc. 'In all cases' refers to statements like, 'Whatever hatred there is, monks, that too is an unwholesome root,' etc. Regarding 'abhisaṅkharoti' (constructs), having stated the meaning is 'āyūhati' (strives), and that this striving, being accomplished by a conjunction of conditions, is like a compressing or a heaping up, he says: 'it compresses, it makes a heap.'

Pāḷiyaṃ “vadhenā”tiādīsu vadhenāti māraṇena vā pothanena vā. Vadhasaddo hi hiṃsanattho viheṭhanattho ca hoti. Bandhanenāti addubandhanādinā. Jāniyāti dhanajāniyā, “sataṃ gaṇhatha, sahassaṃ gaṇhathā”ti evaṃ pavattitadaṇḍenāti attho. Garahāyāti pañcasikhamuṇḍakakaraṇaṃ, gomayasiñcanaṃ, gīvāya kuraṇḍakabandhananti evamādīni katvā garahapāpanena. Tattha pañcasikhamuṇḍakakaraṇaṃ nāma kākapakkhakaraṇaṃ. Gomayasiñcanaṃ sīsena kaṇodakāvasecanaṃ. Kuraṇḍakabandhanaṃ gaddulabandhanaṃ.

In the Pāli text, in 'by killing,' etc., 'by killing' means by causing death or by striking. The word 'vadha' (killing) signifies harming and harassing. 'By binding' means by chains and the like. 'By loss' means by loss of wealth, that is, by a penalty imposed by saying, 'Take a hundred, take a thousand.' 'By reproach' means by causing disgrace through acts such as shaving the head to leave five tufts of hair, sprinkling with cow dung, or tying a 'kuraṇḍaka' around the neck. Here, 'shaving the head to leave five tufts of hair' is called 'making crow's wings.' 'Sprinkling with cow dung' is pouring rice-husk water over the head. 'Tying a kuraṇḍaka' is tying with a leather thong.

Kālasmiṃ na vadatīti yuttakāle na vadati, vattabbakālassa pubbe vā pacchā vā ayuttakāle vattā hoti. Abhūtavādīti yaṃ natthi, tassa vattā. Tenāha “bhūtaṃ na vadatī”ti. Atthaṃ na vadatīti kāraṇaṃ na vadati, akāraṇanissitaṃ nipphalaṃ vattā hoti. Dhammaṃ na vadatīti sabhāvaṃ na vadati, asabhāvaṃ vattā ayathāvādīti attho. Vinayaṃ na vadatīti saṃvaravinayaṃ na vadati, na saṃvaravinayappaṭisaṃyuttassa vattā hoti, attano suṇantassa ca na saṃvaravinayāvahassa vattāti attho.

'He does not speak at the right time' means he does not speak at the appropriate time; he is one who speaks at an unsuitable time, either before or after the time to speak. 'He speaks what is not real' means he is a speaker of what does not exist. Therefore, it is said, 'he does not speak what is real.' 'He does not speak what is meaningful' means he does not speak with reason; he is one who speaks what is baseless and fruitless. 'He does not speak in accordance with the Dhamma' means he does not speak of the true nature; he is one who speaks of what is not the true nature, one who does not speak in accordance with reality, that is the meaning. 'He does not speak in accordance with the Vinaya' means he does not speak of the Vinaya of restraint; he is not a speaker of what is connected with the Vinaya of restraint, and his speech does not lead to the Vinaya of restraint for himself or for his listener, that is the meaning.

Atacchanti abhūtatthaṃ. Tenāha “itaraṃ tasseva vevacana”nti. Atha vā abhūtanti asantaṃ avijjamānaṃ. Atacchanti atathākāraṃ.

'Untrue' means having a false meaning. Hence it is said, 'the other is a synonym for that.' Alternatively, 'false' means non-existent, not present. 'Untrue' means not in accordance with how things are.

Puññakammato eti uppajjatīti ayo, vaḍḍhi. Tappaṭikkhepena anayo, avaḍḍhīti āha “anayaṃ āpajjatīti avaḍḍhiṃ āpajjatī”ti. Māluvāsipāṭikā nāma dīghasaṇṭhānaṃ māluvāpakkaṃ[V 2.0156], māluvāphalapoṭṭhalikāti attho[M 2.0172]. Phalitāyāti ātapena sussitvā bhinnāya. Vaṭarukkhādīnaṃ mūleti vaṭarukkhādīnaṃ samīpe. Sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ na sakkontīti kasmā na sakkonti? Bhavanavināsabhayā. Rukkhamūle patitamāluvābījato hi latā uppajjitvā rukkhaṃ abhiruhati. Sā mahāpattā ceva bahupattā ca mahākolirapattasaṇṭhānehi tato ca mahantatarehi sākhāviṭapantarehi pattehi samannāgatā. Atha naṃ rukkhaṃ mūlato paṭṭhāya vinandhamānā sabbaviṭapāni sañchādetvā mahantaṃ bhāraṃ janetvā tiṭṭhati, sā vāte vāyante deve vā vassante oghanaheṭṭhāgatā olambanahetubhūtaṃ ghanabhāvaṃ janetvā tassa rukkhassa sabbasākhaṃ bhijjati, bhūmiyaṃ nipāteti. Tato tasmiṃ rukkhe patiṭṭhitavimānaṃ bhijjati vinassati. Iti tā devatāyo bhavanavināsabhayā sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ na sakkonti. Ettha ca yaṃ sākhaṭṭhakavimānaṃ hoti, taṃ sākhāsu bhijjamānāsu tattha tattheva bhijjitvā sabbasākhāsu bhinnāsu sabbaṃ bhijjati, rukkhaṭṭhakavimānaṃ pana yāva rukkhassa mūlamattampi tiṭṭhati, tāva na nassatīti veditabbaṃ. Tattha tattha palujjitvāti tattha tattha bhijjitvā. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

From meritorious deeds one goes (`eti`) or arises (`uppajjati`), thus it is `ayo`, growth. By its rejection, there is `anayo`, non-growth. Thus it is said: 'One falls into ruin' means 'one attains decline.' The name `Māluvāsipāṭikā` refers to a long-shaped ripe māluvā fruit, meaning a māluvā fruit pod. `Phalitāya` means having split after drying in the sun's heat. 'At the root of banyan and other trees' means near banyan and other trees. Why are they unable to remain in their own state? Because of the fear of the destruction of their dwellings. For from a māluvā seed that has fallen at the foot of a tree, a vine springs up and climbs the tree. It has large leaves and many leaves, endowed with leaves shaped like large kolira leaves, and even larger ones, between its branches and boughs. Then, starting from the root, it entwines the tree, covering all its boughs, and stands creating a great burden. When the wind blows or the rain falls, the vine, having become weighed down and a dense cause for hanging down, breaks all the branches of that tree and causes them to fall to the ground. As a result, the celestial mansion established on that tree shatters and perishes. Thus, those deities, fearing the destruction of their dwellings, are unable to remain in their own state. Herein, a mansion standing on a branch breaks wherever the branches break, and when all the branches are broken, the entire mansion is destroyed. But a mansion standing on the tree itself does not perish as long as even the mere root of the tree remains; this should be understood. 'Breaking apart here and there' means shattering in various places. The rest here is easily understood.

Akusalamūlasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Akusalamūla Sutta is finished.

10. Uposathasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Uposatha Sutta

71. Dasame tadahūti ettha tasmiṃ ahanīti atthoti āha “tasmiṃ ahu uposathe”ti. Upavasanti etthāti uposatho, uposathadivaso. Upavasantīti ca sīlena vā anasanena vā khīrasāyanādividhinā vā upetā hutvā vasantīti attho. Uposathadivase hi sāsanikā sīlena, bāhirakā sabbaso āhārassa abhuñjanena khīrasāyanamadhusāyanādividhinā vā upetā hutvā viharanti. So panesa uposathadivaso aṭṭhamicātuddasipannarasibhedena tividho, tasmā sesadvayanivāraṇatthaṃ “pannarasikauposathadivase”ti vuttaṃ. Vavassaggattheti vacasāyatthe. Divasaddo divāsaddo viya divasapariyāyo, tassa visesanabhāvena vuccamāno divāsaddo savisesena dīpetīti āha “divasassa divā[M 2.0173], majjhanhike kāleti attho”ti. Paṭicchāpetvāti sampaṭicchanaṃ kāretvā. Vipākaphalenāti sadisaphalena. Na mahapphalo hoti manoduccaritadussīlyena upakkiliṭṭhabhāvato. Vipākānisaṃsenāti udrayaphalena. Vipākobhāsenāti paṭipakkhavigamajanitena sabhāvasaṅkhātena vipākobhāsena. Na mahāobhāso aparisuddhabhāvato. Vipākavipphārassāti vipākavepullassa.

71. In the tenth section, regarding 'tadahū,' the meaning is 'on that day'; thus it is said, 'on that Uposatha day.' Because one 'upavasati' (dwells close/observes) on it, it is 'uposatha,' the Uposatha day. And 'upavasanti' means that they dwell having undertaken the practice through virtue, or through fasting, or through methods such as consuming milk-preparations, etc. For on the Uposatha day, those within the Dispensation dwell having undertaken the practice through virtue, while outsiders dwell having undertaken it by entirely abstaining from food or by methods such as consuming milk-preparations, honey-preparations, etc. This Uposatha day is of three kinds, distinguished as the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days. Therefore, to exclude the other two, it is stated as 'the fifteenth-day Uposatha.' Regarding 'vavassaggatthe,' it means 'in the sense of relinquishment by word.' The word 'diva' is a synonym for 'divasa' (day), like the word 'divāsa.' When the word 'divāsa' is stated as a qualifier for it, it clarifies it with a specific distinction. Thus it is said: '`divā` of the day, the meaning is at midday.' Regarding 'paṭicchāpetvā,' it means 'having caused acceptance.' Regarding 'vipākaphalena,' it means 'with a corresponding result.' It is not of great fruit because it is defiled by mental misconduct and immorality. Regarding 'vipākānisaṃsena,' it means 'with the resultant benefit.' Regarding 'vipākobhāsena,' it means 'with the radiance of result,' which is called its intrinsic nature generated by the removal of opposing factors. It is not of great radiance due to its impurity. Regarding 'vipākavipphārassā,' it means 'of the expansion of result.'

Nāhaṃ [V 2.0157] kvacanītiādivacanassa micchābhinivesavasena pavattattā “idaṃ tassa musāvādasmiṃ vadāmī”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ, catukoṭikasuññatādassanavasena pavattaṃ pana ariyadassanamevāti na tattha musāvādo. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Because the statement beginning, “I am not anywhere,” arises due to wrong adherence, it is said in the Pāli, “This I declare to be his false speech.” However, when it arises due to the vision of fourfold emptiness, it is indeed the noble vision; therefore, there is no false speech in that. For it has been said:

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati ‘nāhaṃ kvacani, kassaci kiñcanatasmiṃ, na ca mama kvacani, kismiñci kiñcanatatthī’”tiādi (ma. ni. 3.70).

“Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘I am not anywhere, nor am I anyone's anything; and there is nothing of mine anywhere, in anything whatsoever.’” (MN 3.70)

Ettha hi catukoṭikasuññatā kathitā. Kathaṃ? Ariyo (visuddhi. 2.760; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 3.70) hi nāhaṃ kvacanīti kvaci attānaṃ na passati, kassaci kiñcanatasminti attano attānaṃ kassaci parassa kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ na passati, bhātiṭṭhāne bhātaraṃ, sahāyaṭṭhāne sahāyaṃ, parikkhāraṭṭhāne parikkhāraṃ maññitvā upanetabbaṃ na passatīti attho. Na ca mama kvacanīti ettha mama-saddaṃ tāva ṭhapetvā kvacani parassa ca attānaṃ kvaci na passatīti ayamattho. Idāni mama-saddaṃ āharitvā “mama kismiñci kiñcanatatthī”ti so parassa attānaṃ “mama kismiñci kiñcanabhāvena atthī”ti na passati, attano bhātikaṭṭhāne bhātaraṃ, sahāyaṭṭhāne sahāyaṃ, parikkhāraṭṭhāne parikkhāranti kismiñci ṭhāne parassa attānaṃ iminā kiñcanabhāvena upanetabbaṃ na passatīti attho. Evamayaṃ yasmā neva katthaci attānaṃ passati, na taṃ parassa kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ passati. Na katthaci parassa attānaṃ passati, na parassa attānaṃ attano kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ passati, tasmā ayaṃ suññatā catukoṭikāti veditabbā.

Herein, indeed, the fourfold emptiness is explained. How? A noble one, by reflecting, 'I am not anywhere,' does not see a self anywhere. By reflecting, 'I am not anyone’s anything,' he does not see his own self as something to be brought into the state of being an 'anything' belonging to another; the meaning is that he does not see it as something to be considered and brought into the state of a brother in the place of a brother, a friend in the place of a friend, or a requisite in the place of a requisite. Regarding 'nor is there for me anywhere,' here, having first set aside the word 'mine,' the meaning is this: he does not see another's self anywhere. Now, having brought in the word 'mine,' by reflecting, 'for me... in anything... there is not any thing,' he does not see another's self as 'there is for me in some way as an anything.' The meaning is that he does not see another's self in any place as something to be brought into this state of being an 'anything,' such as a brother in the place of a brother, a friend in the place of a friend, or a requisite in the place of a requisite. Thus, since he neither sees a self anywhere, nor does he see it as something to be brought into the state of being an 'anything' belonging to another; and he neither sees another's self anywhere, nor does he see another's self as something to be brought into the state of being an 'anything' belonging to himself—therefore, this emptiness is to be understood as fourfold.

Yasmā pana micchādiṭṭhikānaṃ yāthāvadassanassa asambhavato yathāvuttacatukoṭikasuññatādassanaṃ na sambhavati, tasmā “natthi mātā, natthi pitā”tiādivacanaṃ [M 2.0174] (dī. ni. 1.171) viya micchāgāhavasena “nāhaṃ kvacanī”tiādi vuttanti yutto cettha musāvādasambhavo. Katthacīti ṭhāne, kāle vā. Atha “nipphalo”ti kasmā vuttaṃ. “Na mahapphalo”ti saddena hi mahapphalābhāvova jotito, na pana sabbathā phalābhāvoti āha “byañjanameva hi ettha sāvasesa”ntiādi. Sesapadesupīti “na mahānisaṃso”tiādīsupi.

However, since for those with wrong views a vision in accordance with reality is impossible, the vision of the aforementioned fourfold emptiness cannot arise. Therefore, just as statements like, “There is no mother, there is no father” (DN 1.55), are uttered based on a wrongly grasped notion, so too is, “I am not anywhere,” etc., uttered in this way, and thus the possibility of false speech is justified here. Regarding 'katthaci' (anywhere), it means in place or in time. But why is it said 'fruitless'? For by the expression 'not greatly fruitful,' only the absence of great fruit is indicated, not the complete absence of fruit. Thus it is said, “Here, indeed, only the expression remains,” and so on. The same applies to the remaining terms, such as 'not of great benefit,' etc.

Aṭṭhahi kāraṇehīti –

By eight reasons:

“Atha [V 2.0158] kho, bhante, sakko devānamindo devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ bhagavato aṭṭha yathābhucce vaṇṇe payirudāhāsi – ‘taṃ kiṃ maññanti, bhonto devā tāvatiṃsā, yāvañca so bhagavā bahujanahitāya paṭipanno bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ, evaṃ bahujanahitāya paṭipannaṃ bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ imināpaṅgena samannāgataṃ satthāraṃ neva atītaṃse samanupassāmi, na panetarahi aññatra tena bhagavatā”ti –

“Then, venerable sir, Sakka, lord of the devas, proclaimed to the Tāvatiṃsa devas the Blessed One's eight true qualities: ‘What do you think, honored devas of Tāvatiṃsa? In that the Blessed One is practicing for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans—I do not see any teacher in the past endowed with this quality who was practicing for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans, nor do I see one now, other than that Blessed One.’”

Ādinā mahāgovindasutte (dī. ni. 2.296) vitthāritehi bahujanahitāya paṭipannādīhi buddhānubhāvadīpakehi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi. Atha “navahi kāraṇehī”ti avatvā “aṭṭhahi kāraṇehī”ti kasmā vuttanti āha “ettha hi…pe… sabbe lokiyalokuttarā buddhaguṇā saṅgahitā”ti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – imasmiṃ sutte “itipi so bhagavā”ti iminā vacanena avisesato sabbepi lokiyalokuttarā buddhaguṇā dīpitā, tasmā tena dīpitaguṇe sandhāya “aṭṭhahi kāraṇehī”ti vuttanti. Arahantiādīhi pāṭiyekkaguṇāva niddiṭṭhāti arahantiādīhi ekekehi padehi ekeke guṇāva niddiṭṭhāti attho.

By the eight reasons, beginning with ‘entered upon the path for the welfare of many,’ which are elaborated in the Mahāgovinda Sutta (Dī. Ni. 2.296) and illuminate the Buddha’s power. Now, why is it said “for eight reasons” and not “for nine reasons”? It is explained: “Here... all worldly and transcendent qualities of the Buddha are included.” This is what is meant: In this sutta, by the phrase “Itipi so Bhagavā,” all worldly and transcendent qualities of the Buddha are illuminated without distinction. Therefore, with reference to those illuminated qualities, it is said “for eight reasons.” By terms such as “arahant,” only individual qualities are indicated; that is, by each term like “arahant,” only a specific quality is indicated.

Sahatantikanti pāḷidhammasahitaṃ. Purimanayeneva yojanā kātabbāti “kiliṭṭhasmiñhi kāye pasādhanaṃ pasādhetvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷamānā na sobhantī”tiādinā nayena yojanā kātabbāti attho.

Regarding “sahatantika,” it means “together with the canonical text.” The explanation should be made in the same way as before—meaning that the interpretation should be made according to the method beginning with “Just as, having adorned a defiled body with ornaments, those sporting at a festival do not shine,” and so forth.

Saṅghassa [M 2.0175] anussaraṇaṃ nāma tassa guṇānussaraṇamevāti āha “aṭṭhannaṃ ariyapuggalānaṃ guṇe anussaratī”ti. Dve tayo vāre gāhāpitaṃ usumanti dve tayo vāre uddhanaṃ āropetvā sedanavasena gāhāpitaṃ usumaṃ. Purimanayeneva yojanā kātabbāti “kiliṭṭhasmiñhi vatthe pasādhanaṃ pasādhetvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷamānā na sobhantī”tiādinā nayena yojanā kātabbā.

The recollection of the Saṅgha is indeed the recollection of its qualities; thus it is said: “One recollects the qualities of the eight noble individuals.” Regarding “heat induced two or three times,” it means the heat induced by placing something on a stove two or three times for the purpose of steaming. The explanation should be made according to the previous method; that is, the interpretation should be made according to the method beginning with “Just as, having adorned a defiled garment with ornaments, those sporting at a festival do not shine,” and so on.

Pahīnakālato paṭṭhāya…pe… viratāvāti etena pahānahetukā idhādhippetā viratīti dasseti. Kammakkhayakarañāṇena hi pāṇātipātadussīlyassa pahīnattā arahanto accantameva tato paṭiviratāti vuccati samucchedavasena pahānaviratīnaṃ adhippetattā. Kiñcāpi pahānaviramaṇānaṃ purimapacchimakālatā natthi, maggadhammānaṃ pana sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ sammāvācādīnañca paccayapaccayuppannabhāve apekkhite sahajātānampi paccayapaccayuppannabhāvena gahaṇaṃ purimapacchimabhāveneva hotīti, gahaṇappavattiākāravasena paccayabhūtesu sammādiṭṭhiādīsu [V 2.0159] pahāyakadhammesu pahānakiriyāya purimakālavohāro, paccayuppannāsu ca viratīsu viramaṇakiriyāya aparakālavohāro ca hotīti pahānaṃ vā samucchedavasena, virati paṭippassaddhivasena yojetabbā.

From the time of abandonment onwards... up to “abstains”—this indicates that the abstention intended here is rooted in abandonment as its cause. For through the knowledge that brings about the destruction of kamma, the unwholesome conduct of killing living beings is abandoned, and thus arahants are said to be entirely abstinent from it, because abstention from what is abandoned is intended by way of eradication. Although there is no prior or subsequent time for abandonment and abstention, when the condition-and-conditioned nature of path factors such as right view and right speech, etc., is considered, even the grasping of co-arisen phenomena as having a condition-and-conditioned nature occurs as if there were a prior and subsequent relationship. Thus, in terms of the manner of the process of grasping, the act of abandoning is spoken of as occurring at a prior time in the abandoning factors that are conditions, such as right view, while the act of abstaining is spoken of as occurring at a subsequent time in the conditioned abstentions. Therefore, abandonment should be construed in terms of eradication, and abstention in terms of tranquilization.

Atha vā pāṇo atipātīyati etenāti pāṇātipāto, pāṇaghātahetubhūto dhammasamūho. Ko pana so? Ahirikānottappadosamohavihiṃsādayo kilesā. Te hi arahanto ariyamaggena pahāya samugghātetvā pāṇātipātadussīlyato accantameva paṭiviratāti vuccanti, kilesesu pahīnesu kilesanimittassa kammassa anuppajjanato. Adinnādānaṃ pahāyātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Viratāvāti avadhāraṇena tassā viratiyā kālādivasena apariyantataṃ dasseti. Yathā hi aññe samādinnaviratikāpi anavaṭṭhitacittatāya lābhajīvitādihetu samādānaṃ bhindanti, na evaṃ arahanto, arahanto pana sabbaso pahīnapāṇātipātattā accantaviratā evāti.

Alternatively, ‘pāṇātipāto’ (killing living beings) is that by which life is destroyed; it is a collection of mental states that are the cause for the destruction of life. And what is that? Shamelessness, lack of moral dread, hatred, delusion, cruelty, and other defilements. For the arahants, having abandoned and eradicated these through the noble path, are said to be entirely abstinent from the unwholesome conduct of killing living beings, since when the defilements are abandoned, the kamma conditioned by them does not arise. The same principle applies to abandoning stealing and so forth. By the emphatic “they abstain,” the boundless nature of that abstention with respect to time and so on is shown. For while others who have undertaken abstention may break their undertaking due to unsteadiness of mind or for the sake of gain or livelihood, this is not the case with arahants; arahants, having entirely abandoned killing living beings, are indeed completely abstinent.

Daṇḍanasaṅkhātassa paraviheṭhanassa ca parivajjanabhāvadīpanatthaṃ daṇḍasatthānaṃ nikkhepavacananti āha “parūpaghātatthāyā”tiādi. Lajjīti ettha vuttalajjāya [M 2.0176] ottappampi vuttamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Na hi pāpajigucchanapāputtāsarahitaṃ, pāpabhayaṃ vā alajjanaṃ atthīti. Dhammagarutāya vā arahantānaṃ dhammassa ca attā dhīnattā attādhipatibhūtā lajjāva vuttā, na pana lokādhipati ottappaṃ. “Dayaṃ mettacittataṃ āpannā”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu dayā-saddo “adayāpanno”tiādīsu karuṇāya pavattatīti? Saccametaṃ, ayaṃ pana dayā-saddo anurakkhaṇatthaṃ antonītaṃ katvā pavattamāno mettāya karuṇāya ca pavattatīti idha mettāya pavattamāno vutto. Mijjati siniyhatīti mettā, mettā etassa atthīti mettaṃ, mettaṃ cittaṃ etassāti mettacitto, tassa bhāvo mettacittatā, mettāicceva attho.

To clarify the state of avoiding the harming of others, which is designated as violence, the statement about laying down rods and weapons is made, beginning with 'for the purpose of harming others.' Here, by the 'shame' (lajjā) that is mentioned, it should be understood that moral dread (ottappa) is also mentioned. For there is no shame without disgust for evil and fear of evil, nor moral dread without fear of evil. Alternatively, due to the arahants' reverence for the Dhamma and the self being subservient to the Dhamma, it is shame, which is governed by the self, that is mentioned, not moral dread, which is governed by the world. Why is it said, 'possessed of compassion (dayā)'? Does not the word 'dayā' usually refer to compassion (karuṇā), as in 'devoid of compassion,' and so forth? That is true, but this word 'dayā,' when used with the sense of protection implicitly included, refers to both loving-kindness and compassion; here, therefore, it is said to refer to loving-kindness. 'Mijjati' means to soften or to be affectionate; thus 'mettā' (loving-kindness). One who has this is 'mettaṃ.' One whose mind is 'mettaṃ' is 'mettacitto' (loving-hearted), and the state of that is 'mettacittatā' (loving-heartedness). The meaning is simply loving-kindness.

Sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampīti etena tassā viratiyā pavattavasena apariyantataṃ dasseti. Pāṇabhūteti pāṇajāte. Anukampakāti karuṇāyanakā, yasmā pana mettā karuṇāya visesapaccayo hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ “tāya eva dayāpannatāyā”ti. Evaṃ yehi dhammehi pāṇātipātā virati sampajjati, tehi lajjāmettākaruṇādhammehi samaṅgibhāvo dassito.

'Compassionate for the welfare of all living beings'—by this, the boundless nature of that abstinence is shown, by way of its application. 'Pāṇabhūta' means the class of living beings. 'Anukampaka' means having compassion; but since loving-kindness is a special condition for compassion, therefore it is said, 'through that very state of being possessed of compassion.' Thus, the state of being endowed with qualities such as shame, loving-kindness, and compassion, by which abstinence from the destruction of life is accomplished, is shown.

Parapariggahitassa ādānanti parasantakassa ādānaṃ. Theno vuccati coro, tassa bhāvo theyyaṃ, kāmañcettha “lajjī dayāpanno”ti na vuttaṃ, adhikāravasena pana atthato vuttamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā hi lajjādayo pāṇātipātappahānassa visesapaccayā, evaṃ adinnādānappahānassapīti[V 2.0160], tasmā sāpi pāḷi ānetvā vattabbā. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Atha vā sucibhūtenāti etena hirottappādīhi samannāgamo, ahirikādīnañca pahānaṃ vuttamevāti “lajjī”tiādi na vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The taking of what is appropriated by another means the taking of what belongs to others. A thief is called a 'thena,' and his state is 'theyya' (theft). Although here it is not said, 'conscientious and compassionate,' it should be understood that the meaning is conveyed by context. Just as shame and so forth are special conditions for abandoning the destruction of life, so too are they for abandoning taking what is not given. Therefore, that passage should also be brought in and stated. This is the method in subsequent instances as well. Alternatively, by 'sucibhūtena' (being pure), it is meant that one is endowed with shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa) and so forth, and the abandonment of shamelessness and so forth is already stated; thus, 'conscientious,' and so forth, are not mentioned, which should be understood.

Aseṭṭhacariyanti aseṭṭhānaṃ hīnānaṃ, aseṭṭhaṃ vā lāmakaṃ cariyaṃ, nihīnavuttiṃ methunanti attho. Brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ ācāranti methunaviratimāha. Ārācārī methunāti etena – “idhekacco na heva kho mātugāmena saddhiṃ dvayaṃdvayasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, apica kho mātugāmassa ucchādanaparimaddananhāpanasambāhanaṃ sādiyati, so taṃ assādeti, taṃ nikāmeti, tena ca vittiṃ āpajjatī”tiādinā (a. ni. 7.50) vuttā sattavidhamethunasaṃyogāpi paṭivirati dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Aseṭṭhacariya' means the conduct of the inferior, the base; or ignoble conduct, that is, low conduct, sexual intercourse. 'Brahmaṃ ācāraṃ' (holy conduct) means the highest conduct, referring to abstinence from sexual intercourse. By 'ārācārī methunā' (one who fares afar from sexual intercourse), it is shown that one abstains even from the seven kinds of sexual connection, as described in the passage: 'Here, someone does not engage in sexual intercourse with a woman, but he does consent to being massaged, rubbed, bathed, or groomed by a woman; he takes pleasure in it, delights in it, and derives satisfaction from it,' and so forth (A. Ni. 7.50). This should be understood.

“Saccato [M 2.0177] thetato”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.19) viya theta-saddo thirapariyāyo, thirabhāvo ca saccavāditāya ṭhitakathattā kathāvasena veditabboti āha “ṭhitakathāti attho”ti. Na ṭhitakathoti yathā haliddirāgādayo anavaṭṭhitasabhāvatāya na ṭhitā, evaṃ na ṭhitā kathā yassa so na ṭhitakathoti haliddirāgādayo yathā kathāya upamā honti, evaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Esa nayo “pāsāṇalekhā viyā”tiādīsupi. Saddhā ayati pavattati etthāti saddhāyā, saddhāyā eva saddhāyikā yathā venayikā. Saddhāya vā ayitabbā saddhāyikā, saddheyyāti attho. Vattabbataṃ āpajjati visaṃvādanatoti adhippāyo.

In phrases like 'saccato thetato' (truly, firmly), and so forth (Ma. Ni. 1.19), the word 'theta' is a synonym for 'firm.' And that firmness, since one is steadfast in speech due to speaking truth, should be understood in the context of speech. Thus, it is said, 'ṭhitakathā means steadfast speech.' 'Na ṭhitakatho' (one whose speech is not steadfast) means one whose speech is not steadfast, just as turmeric stains and so forth are not fixed due to their unstable nature. Just as turmeric stains and so forth serve as an analogy for speech, so should this be construed. This is the method in phrases like 'pāsāṇalekhā viya' (like a line on rock), and so forth. Regarding 'saddhāyikā' (trustworthy): one in whom faith (saddhā) proceeds (ayati) is 'saddhāyikā'; 'saddhāyikā' is formed from 'saddhā' just as 'venayikā' is from 'vinaya'. Alternatively, 'saddhāyikā' means one who should be believed (ayitabbā) with faith (saddhāya); that is, trustworthy (saddheyyā). The intention is that due to deception, one becomes subject to censure.

Ekaṃ bhattaṃ ekabhattaṃ, taṃ etesamatthīti ekabhattikā, ekasmiṃ divase ekavārameva bhuñjanakā. Tayidaṃ rattibhojanenapi siyāti āha “rattūparatā”ti. Evampi sāyanhabhojanenapi siyuṃ ekabhattikāti tadāsaṅkānivattanatthaṃ “viratā vikālabhojanā”ti vuttaṃ. Aruṇuggamanato paṭṭhāya yāva majjhanhikā ayaṃ buddhānaṃ ariyānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo bhojanassa kālo nāma, tadañño vikālo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana dutiyapadena rattibhojanassa paṭikkhittattā aparaṇho “vikālo”ti vutto.

'Ekaṃ bhattaṃ' (one meal) is 'ekabhatta.' Those who have this are 'ekabhattikā,' meaning those who eat only once a day. This could also be so through abstaining from eating at night; therefore, it is said, 'rattūparatā' (abstaining from eating at night). Lest they be 'ekabhattikā' even with an evening meal, to dispel that doubt, it is said, 'viratā vikālabhojanā' (abstaining from untimely food). From the rising of dawn until midday is the time for meals that is habitually practiced by the Buddhas and noble ones; any other time is untimely. However, in the commentary, the afternoon is referred to as 'vikāla' (untimely), because eating at night is prohibited by the second term.

Saṅkhepato “sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”ntiādinayappavattaṃ (dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 183) bhagavato sāsanaṃ sacchandarāgappavattito naccādīnaṃ dassanaṃ na anulometīti āha “sāsanassa ananulomattā”ti. Attanā payojiyamānaṃ parehi payojāpīyamānañca naccaṃ naccabhāvasāmaññato pāḷiyaṃ ekeneva naccasaddena gahitaṃ, tathā gītavāditasaddā cāti āha “naccananaccāpanādivasenā”ti[V 2.0161]. Ādi-saddena gāyanagāyāpanavādanavādāpanāni saṅgaṇhāti. Dassanena cettha savanampi saṅgahitaṃ virūpekasesanayena. Ālocanasabhāvatāya vā pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ savanakiriyāyapi dassanasaṅkhepasabbhāvato dassanāicceva vuttaṃ. Avisūkabhūtassa gītassa savanaṃ kadāci vaṭṭatīti āha “visūkabhūtaṃ dassana”nti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ paramatthajotikāya khuddakapāṭhaṭṭhakathāya “dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ gītaṃ vaṭṭati, gītūpasaṃhito dhammo na vaṭṭatī”ti.

In brief, the Blessed One's teaching, which proceeds according to the method of 'the non-doing of all evil' and so forth (Dī. Ni. 2.90; Dha. Pa. 183), does not allow for the viewing of dancing and the like, which arises from one's own desire and passion. Hence, it is said, 'because it is contrary to the teaching.' Dancing, whether performed by oneself or caused to be performed by others, is included in the Pāli by the single word 'nacca' due to its general nature as dancing; similarly for the words 'gīta' (singing) and 'vādita' (instrumental music). Thus, it is said, 'by way of dancing, causing to dance, and so forth.' The term 'and so forth' includes singing, causing to sing, playing instruments, and causing to play instruments. Here, listening is also included under seeing, following the principle of including dissimilar items under one term. Alternatively, due to the nature of perception, even in the act of hearing by the five consciousnesses, there is the presence of a summary in 'seeing'; therefore, it is simply called 'seeing.' The hearing of music that is not a frivolous show is occasionally permissible. Therefore, it is said, 'seeing that is a frivolous show.' As stated in the Paramatthajotikā, the commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha: 'Singing connected with the Dhamma is allowable, but the Dhamma connected with singing is not.'

Yaṃ [M 2.0178] kiñcīti ganthitaṃ vā aganthitaṃ vā yaṃ kiñci pupphaṃ. Gandhajātanti gandhajātiyaṃ. Tassāpi “yaṃ kiñcī”ti vacanato dhūpitassapi adhūpitassapi yassa kassaci vilepanādi na vaṭṭatīti dasseti. Uccāti uccasaddena samānatthaṃ ekaṃ saddantaraṃ. Seti etthāti sayanaṃ. Uccāsayanaṃ mahāsayanañca samaṇasārupparahitaṃ adhippetanti āha “pamāṇātikkantaṃ akappiyattharaṇa”nti, āsandādiāsanañcettha sayanena saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yasmā pana ādhāre paṭikkhitte tadādhārakiriyā paṭikkhittāva hoti, tasmā “uccāsayanamahāsayanā”icceva vuttaṃ. Atthato pana tadupabhogabhūtanisajjānipajjanehi virati dassitāti daṭṭhabbā. Atha vā “uccāsayanāsanamahāsayanāsanā”ti, etasmiṃ atthe ekasesanayena ayaṃ niddeso kato yathā “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”nti. (Ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1) āsanakiriyāpubbakattā vā sayanakiriyāya sayanaggahaṇeneva āsanampi saṅgahitanti veditabbaṃ.

'Yaṃ kiñci' (whatever) means any flower, whether strung or unstrung. 'Gandhajāti' means of a fragrant kind. By the phrase 'yaṃ kiñci,' it shows that any kind of unguent or the like, whether scented with incense or not, is not allowed. 'Uccā' is another word synonymous with the word 'ucca' (high). One lies (seti) on it (ettha), therefore it is a bed (sayanaṃ). A high bed and a great bed are intended to be unsuitable for an ascetic; thus, it is said, 'an improper spread that exceeds the proper measure.' Here, seats like couches and so forth should be understood as included under 'bed.' Since when the support is prohibited, the act of using that support is also prohibited, it is therefore simply stated, 'high beds and great beds.' But in meaning, abstention from sitting and lying down, which constitute the use of them, is shown, it should be understood. Alternatively, this explanation is given in the sense of 'high seats and great seats' by the principle of ekasesa, just as in 'from name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise.' (Ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1) Or, because the act of sitting precedes the act of lying, by the mention of 'bed,' 'seat' is also included—this should be understood.

“Kīvā”ti ayaṃ nipāto. “Kittaka”nti imassa atthaṃ bodhetīti āha “kīvamahapphaloti kittakaṃ mahapphalo”ti. Sesapadesūti “kīvamahānisaṃso”tiādīsu. Ratta-saddo ratanapariyāyoti āha “pahūtarattaratanānanti pahūtena rattasaṅkhātena ratanena samannāgatāna”nti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “pahūtasattaratanāna”ntipi pāṭho dissati. Bheritalasadisaṃ katvāti bheritalaṃ viya samaṃ katvā. Tato ekaṃ bhāgaṃ na agghatīti yathāvuttaṃ cakkavattirajjaṃ tato soḷasabhāgato ekaṃ bhāgaṃ na agghati. Tato bahutaraṃ hotīti cakkavattirajjasirito bahutaraṃ hoti.

'Kīva' is a particle. It conveys the meaning of 'kittaka' (how much); thus, it is said, 'kīvamahapphalo' (how great the fruit) means 'kittakaṃ mahapphalo' (how much is the great fruit). In the remaining instances, such as 'kīvamahānisaṃso' (how great the benefit), and so forth. The word 'ratta' is a synonym for 'ratana' (jewel); thus, it is said, 'pahūtarattaratanānaṃ' means 'possessed of abundant jewels designated as 'ratta'.' However, in the Pāli text, the reading 'pahūtasattaratanānaṃ' (possessed of the seven abundant jewels) is also found. 'Having made it like a drumhead' means having made it even like a drumhead. 'Then, one part is not worth' means that the aforementioned rule of a wheel-turning monarch is not worth even one-sixteenth part of that. 'It is far greater than that' means it is far greater than the glory of a wheel-turning monarch.

Cātumahārājīkānantiādīsu cātumahārājikā nāma sinerupabbatassa vemajjhe honti, tesu bahū pabbataṭṭhāpi ākāsaṭṭhāpi, tesaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ pattā, khiḍḍāpadosikā, manopadosikā, sītavalāhakā, uṇhavalāhakā, candimā, devaputto, sūriyo, devaputtoti ete sabbe [V 2.0162] cātumahārājikadevalokaṭṭhakā eva. Tettiṃsa janā tattha uppannāti tāvatiṃsā. Apica tāvatiṃsāti tesaṃ devānaṃ nāmamevāti vuttaṃ. Tepi atthi pabbataṭṭhakā, atthi ākāsaṭṭhakā, tesaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ pattā, tathā yāmādīnaṃ. Ekadevalokepi [M 2.0179] hi devānaṃ paramparā cakkavāḷapabbataṃ appattā nāma natthi. Tattha dibbasukhaṃ yātā payātā sampattāti yāmā. Tuṭṭhā pahaṭṭhāti tusitā. Pakatipaṭiyattārammaṇato atirekena ramitukāmakāle yathārucite bhoge nimminitvā nimminitvā ramantīti nimmānarati. Cittācāraṃ ñatvā parehi nimmitesu bhogesu vasaṃ vattentīti paranimmitavasavattī.

Among the Cātumahārājika gods and so forth, the Cātumahārājika are located in the middle of Mount Sineru. Among them, many dwell on mountains and many in the sky. Their range reaches the Cakkavāḷa mountain. The Khiḍḍāpadosikā, Manopadosikā, Sītavalāhakā, Uṇhavalāhakā, the moon-deva, and the sun-deva—all these are indeed dwellers in the Cātumahārājika deva-world. Thirty-three persons were born there, hence Tāvatiṃsa. Moreover, it is said that 'Tāvatiṃsa' is simply the name of those devas. Among them too, some dwell on mountains and some in the sky, and their range reaches the Cakkavāḷa mountain; similarly for the Yāma devas and others. Indeed, in no single deva-world is there a range of devas that does not reach the Cakkavāḷa mountain. There, those who have gone, proceeded, and attained divine pleasure are the Yāmā. Those who are pleased and delighted are the Tusitā. Those who, at a time when they desire to delight in excess of the naturally prepared sense-objects, create and recreate pleasures as they wish, are the Nimmānarati. Those who, knowing the mental dispositions of others, exercise control over the pleasures created by others, are the Paranimmitavasavattī.

Tattha cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ manussagaṇanāya navutivassasatasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ. Tāvatiṃsānaṃ devānaṃ tisso ca vassakoṭiyo saṭṭhi ca vassasatasahassāni. Yāmānaṃ devānaṃ cuddasa ca vassakoṭiyo cattāri ca vassasatasahassāni. Tusitānaṃ devānaṃ sattapaññāsa ca vassakoṭiyo saṭṭhi ca vassasatasahassāni. Nimmānaratīnaṃ devānaṃ dve ca vassakoṭisatāni tisso ca vassakoṭiyo cattāri ca vassasatasahassāni. Paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ devānaṃ nava ca vassakoṭisatāni ekavīsa koṭiyo ca saṭṭhi ca vassasatasahassāni.

Therein, for the Cātumahārājika devas, the measure of their lifespan is nine million years by human reckoning. For the Tāvatiṃsa devas, it is thirty-six million years. For the Yāma devas, it is one hundred and forty-four million years. For the Tusita devas, it is five hundred and seventy-six million years. For the Nimmānarati devas, it is two billion, three hundred and four million years. For the Paranimmitavasavattī devas, it is nine billion, two hundred and sixteen million years.

Muṭṭhihatthapādaketi pādatalato yāva aṭaniyā heṭṭhimanto, tāva muṭṭhiratanappamāṇapādake. Tañca kho majjhimassa purisassa hatthena, yassidāni vaḍḍhakīhatthoti samaññā. Sīlasamādānato paṭṭhāya aññaṃ kiñci akatvā dhammassavanena vā kammaṭṭhānamanasikārena vā vītināmetabbanti āha “taṃ pana upavasantena…pe… vicāretabba”nti.

The term 'muṭṭhihatthapādake' refers to a seat with legs the measure of a 'fist-jewel', that is, from the sole of the foot up to the lower end of the ankle-bone. And that is by the hand of an average man, which is now known as a carpenter's hand. From the undertaking of the precepts onwards, one should pass the time doing nothing else but listening to the Dhamma or attending to a meditation subject. Therefore, it is said: 'But while observing the Uposatha… it should be reflected upon.'

Vācaṃ bhinditvā uposathaṅgāni samādātabbānīti “imañca rattiṃ imañca divasa”nti kālaparicchedaṃ katvā “uposathaṅgavasena aṭṭha sikkhāpadāni samādiyāmī”ti ekato katvā puna paccekaṃ “pāṇātipātā veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi…pe… uccāsayanamahāsayanā veramaṇisikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmī”ti evaṃ vacībhedaṃ katvā yathāpāḷi samādātabbāni. Pāḷiṃ ajānantena pana attano bhāsāya paccekaṃ vā “buddhapaññattaṃ uposathaṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti ekato adhiṭṭhānavasena vā samādātabbāni, aññaṃ alabhantena adhiṭṭhātabbāni. Upāsakasīlañhi attanā samādiyantenapi samādinnaṃ parasantike samādiyantenapi, ekajjhaṃ samādinnampi samādinnameva hoti paccekaṃ samādinnampi. Taṃ pana ekajjhaṃ samādiyato ekāyeva virati ekā cetanā hoti. Sā pana sabbaviraticetanānaṃ kiccakārīti tenapi sabbasikkhāpadāni samādinnāneva. Paccekaṃ samādiyato pana nānāviraticetanāyo yathāsakaṃ kiccavasena uppajjanti[V 2.0163], sabbasamādāne pana [M 2.0180] vacībhedo kātabboyeva. Parūparodhapaṭisaṃyuttā paravihiṃsāsaṃyuttā.

The Uposatha precepts should be undertaken by making separate declarations. Having demarcated the time by saying, 'For this night and this day,' one should undertake them collectively, saying, 'I undertake the eight training rules by way of the Uposatha.' Then, one should undertake them again individually, making separate declarations according to the Pāli text: 'I undertake the training rule of abstaining from taking life… up to… I undertake the training rule of abstaining from high and luxurious beds.' However, one who does not know Pāli should undertake them individually in one's own language, or undertake them collectively by way of a resolution, saying, 'I resolve upon the Uposatha prescribed by the Buddha.' If unable to find another person, one should resolve upon them oneself. For the precepts of a lay follower are properly undertaken whether undertaken by oneself or in the presence of another; they are properly undertaken whether undertaken collectively or individually. For one who undertakes them collectively, however, there is but a single abstinence and a single volition. But that volition performs the function of all the volitions of abstinence; therefore, all the training rules are thereby properly undertaken. For one who undertakes them individually, however, different volitions of abstinence arise according to their respective functions. But in a complete undertaking, the separate declarations must be made. Connected with obstructing others and associated with harming others.

Nanu ca “maṇi”nti vutte veḷuriyampi saṅgahitameva, kimatthaṃ pana veḷuriyanti āha “veḷuriyanti…pe… dassetī”ti. “Maṇi”nti vatvāva “veḷuriya”nti iminā jātimaṇibhāvaṃ dassetīti yojetabbaṃ. Ekavassikaveḷuvaṇṇanti jātito ekavassātikkantaveḷuvaṇṇaṃ. Laddhakanti sundaraṃ. Candappabhā tāragaṇāva sabbeti yathā candappabhāya kalaṃ sabbe tārāgaṇā nānubhavantīti ayamettha atthoti āha “candappabhāti sāmiatthe paccatta”nti.

Surely, when 'jewel' is mentioned, lapis lazuli is also included; why then is 'lapis lazuli' specified? It is said: 'Lapis lazuli… to show.' It should be understood that by saying 'lapis lazuli' after saying 'jewel,' its nature as a genuine jewel is shown. 'Ekavassikaveḷuvaṇṇa' means the color of bamboo that is by nature over one year old. 'Laddhaka' means beautiful. 'Candappabhā tāragaṇāva sabbe' means that just as all the star-clusters do not match even a fraction of the moon's radiance; this is the meaning here. Therefore, it is said: 'Candappabhā' is a possessive compound used in the nominative case.

Uposathasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Uposatha Sutta is completed.

Mahāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Great Division is finished.

(8) 3. Ānandavaggo

(8) 3. The Ānanda Chapter

1. Channasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Channa Sutta

72. Tatiyassa paṭhame channaparibbājakoti na naggaparibbājako. Bāhirakasamayaṃ luñcitvā harantoti bāhirakānaṃ samayaṃ nisedhetvā āpanno.

72. In the first section of the third, “Channa the wanderer” does not refer to a naked ascetic. “Having plundered the custom of outsiders” means having transgressed by rejecting the custom of outsiders.

Paññācakkhussa vibandhanato andhaṃ karotīti andhakaraṇoti āha “yassa rāgo uppajjatī”tiādi. Acakkhukaraṇoti asamatthasamāsoyaṃ “asūriyapassāni mukhānī”tiādīsu viyāti āha “paññācakkhuṃ na karotīti acakkhukaraṇo”ti. Paññānirodhikoti anuppannāya lokiyalokuttarāya paññāya uppajjituṃ na deti, lokiyapaññaṃ pana aṭṭhasamāpattipañcābhiññāvasena uppannampi samucchinditvā khipatīti paññānirodhikoti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Anuppannānuppādauppannaparihāninimittatāya hi paññaṃ nirodhetīti paññānirodhiko. Vihanati vibādhatīti vighāto, dukkhanti āha “dukkhasaṅkhātassa vighātassā”ti. Kilesanibbānanti iminā asaṅkhatanibbānameva vadati. Asaṅkhatañhi nibbānaṃ nāma, taṃ paccakkhaṃ [V 2.0164] kātuṃ na detīti anibbānasaṃvattaniko. Lokuttaramissako kathito pubbabhāgiyassapi ariyamaggassa kathitattā.

Because it obstructs the eye of wisdom, it makes one blind; thus it is called ‘blinding.’ As it is said, ‘for whom lust arises,’ and so on. ‘Not making the eye’ is an incapable compound, like in such phrases as ‘faces that do not see the sun.’ It is said, ‘it does not make the eye of wisdom, thus it is called “not making the eye.”’ ‘Destroyer of wisdom’ means it does not allow unarisen mundane or supramundane wisdom to arise. But even if mundane wisdom has arisen through the eight attainments and the five higher knowledges, it cuts it off and casts it away. Thus, it is called ‘destroyer of wisdom.’ This is how the meaning should be understood here. For it obstructs wisdom by being a cause for the non-arising of the unarisen and the decline of the arisen; thus it is called ‘destroyer of wisdom.’ It injures, it obstructs; thus it is ‘affliction,’ that is, suffering. It is said, ‘of the affliction reckoned as suffering.’ By ‘Nibbāna’ is meant the extinguishing of defilements; by this, it refers only to the unconditioned Nibbāna. For Nibbāna is called the unconditioned, and it does not allow one to realize it directly; thus it is ‘not conducive to Nibbāna.’ It is said to be mixed with the supramundane because the preliminary part of the noble path has also been spoken of.

Channasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Channa Sutta is completed.

2. Ājīvakasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Ājīvaka Sutta

73. Dutiye [M 2.0181] na aññātukāmoti na ājānitukāmoyevāti attho. Tenāha “pariggaṇhanatthaṃ pana āgato”ti, paññāya paricchinditvā upaparikkhitvā gaṇhanatthanti attho. Kāraṇāpadesoti kāraṇaniddeso. Sesamettha uttānameva.

73. In the second [sutta], ‘not wishing to know’ means just not wishing to know. Therefore, it is said, ‘but he came for the purpose of grasping’; the meaning is that he came for the purpose of grasping after discerning and examining with wisdom. ‘Kāraṇāpadeso’ means the pointing out of the reason. The rest here is clear.

Ājīvakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ājīvaka Sutta is completed.

3. Mahānāmasakkasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Mahānāma Sakka Sutta

74. Tatiye gilānassa bhāvo gelaññanti āha “gilānabhāvato”ti. Dīpetīti desanākkameneva paññāpeti. Paṭhamañhi sekhasīlasamādhipaññāyo vatvā pacchā asekhasīlādīni vadanto imamatthaṃ dīpeti.

74. In the third [sutta], the state of being sick is ‘illness’ (gelañña), hence it is said ‘because of the state of being sick.’ ‘He clarifies’ (dīpeti) means he makes known by means of the teaching sequence itself. For first, having spoken of the virtue, concentration, and wisdom of a trainee, and later speaking of the virtue, etc., of one beyond training, he clarifies this meaning.

Mahānāmasakkasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahānāma Sakka Sutta is completed.

4. Nigaṇṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Nigaṇṭha Sutta

75. Catutthe haṃsavaṭṭakacchannenāti haṃsavaṭṭakaparicchannena, haṃsamaṇḍalākārenāti attho. Natthi etassa parisesanti aparisesaṃ. Tenāha “appamattakampi asesetvā”ti. Aparisesadhammajānanato vā aparisesasaṅkhātaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānātīti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Satatanti niccaṃ. Samitanti tasseva vevacananti āha “satataṃ samitanti sabbakālaṃ nirantara”nti. Atha vā niccaṭṭhena satata-saddena abhiṇhappavatti jotitā siyāti “samita”nti vuttaṃ. Tena nirantarappavattiṃ dassetīti āha “sabbakālaṃ nirantara”nti.

75. In the fourth [sutta], ‘enclosed by a circle of geese’ (haṃsavaṭṭakacchannena) means enveloped in the shape of a circle of geese; this is the meaning. ‘There is no remainder of it’ means without remainder. Hence it is said, ‘without leaving even the slightest remainder.’ Or, because he claims knowledge of the Dhamma without remainder, or knowledge and vision reckoned as ‘without remainder,’ this is how the meaning should be understood here. ‘Constant’ (satata) means continuous. ‘Samita’ is a synonym for that; hence it is said, ‘constant, restrained’ (satataṃ samitaṃ) means ‘always uninterrupted.’ Alternatively, by the word ‘satata’ in the sense of ‘continuous,’ frequent occurrence may be indicated; for this reason ‘samita’ is said. By this, it shows uninterrupted occurrence, hence it is said, ‘always uninterrupted.’

Visuddhisampāpanatthāyāti [V 2.0165] rāgādīhi malehi abhijjhāvisamalobhādīhi ca upakkiliṭṭhacittānaṃ sattānaṃ visuddhipāpanatthāya. Samatikkamanatthāyāti sokassa ca paridevassa ca pahānatthāya. Atthaṃ gamanatthāyāti kāyikadukkhassa ca cetasikadomanassassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ atthaṅgamanāya, nirodhāyāti attho. Ñāyati nicchayena kamati nibbānaṃ. Taṃ vā [M 2.0182] ñāyati paṭivijjhati etenāti ñāyo, ariyamaggoti āha “maggassa adhigamanatthāyā”ti. Apaccayanibbānassa sacchikaraṇatthāyāti paccayarahitattā apaccayassa asaṅkhatassa taṇhāvānavirahitattā nibbānanti laddhanāmassa amatassa sacchikiriyāya, attapaccakkhatāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Phusitvā phusitvāti patvā patvā. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.
