‘For the purpose of attaining purity’ means for the sake of bringing about the purity of beings whose minds are defiled by stains such as lust and so forth, and by covetousness, unrighteous greed, and so forth. ‘For the purpose of overcoming’ means for the abandonment of sorrow and lamentation. ‘For the purpose of disappearance’ means for the passing away of both bodily suffering and mental distress; that is, for their cessation. ‘Ñāya’ is so called because one proceeds rightly (ñāyati), that is, one certainly goes to Nibbāna. Or, ‘ñāya’ is that by which Nibbāna is known or penetrated; it is the noble path, hence it is said, ‘for the purpose of realizing the path.’ ‘For the purpose of directly experiencing Nibbāna’ means for the direct realization of the deathless, which has acquired the name Nibbāna because it is unconditioned, being free from conditions, and devoid of the stitching of craving; that is, it is said to be seen for oneself. ‘Having touched, having touched’ means ‘having attained, having attained.’ The rest here is easily understood.

Nigaṇṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nigaṇṭha Sutta is completed.

5. Nivesakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Nivesaka Sutta

76. Pañcame kiccakaraṇīyesu sahabhāvaṭṭhena amā hontīti amaccā. “Ayaṃ ajjhattiko”ti evaṃ jānanti, ñāyanti vāti ñātī. Sassusasurapakkhikāti sassusasurā ca tappakkhiko ca sassusasurapakkhikā. Lohitena sambaddhāti sālohitā. Pitupakkhikā vā ñātī, mātupakkhikā sālohitā. Mātupitupakkhikā vā ñātī, sassusasurapakkhikā sālohitā. Avecca ratanassa guṇe yāthāvato ñatvā pasādo aveccappasādo. So pana yasmā maggenāgatattā kenaci akampanīyo ca appadhaṃsiyo ca hoti, tasmā evaṃ vuttaṃ “acalappasādo”ti. Bhāvaññathattanti sabhāvassa aññathattaṃ.

76. In the fifth [sutta], ‘ministers’ (amaccā) are so called because they are companions (amā) in performing duties. ‘Relatives’ (ñātī) are so called because they know or are known, saying, ‘This is one of us.’ ‘Those on the side of the mother-in-law and father-in-law’ means the mother-in-law and father-in-law and those on their side. ‘Those connected by blood’ (sālohitā) means those connected by blood. Alternatively, relatives on the father’s side are ñātī, and relatives on the mother’s side are sālohitā. Or, relatives on both the mother’s and father’s side are ñātī, and those on the side of the mother-in-law and father-in-law are sālohitā. ‘Unshakable confidence’ (aveccappasādo) is confidence born of having truly known the qualities of the Triple Gem. Since it is attained through the path and is unshakable and indestructible by anything, it is therefore called ‘immovable confidence’ (acalappasādo). ‘Bhāvaññathatta’ means the otherness of a nature.

Vīsatiyā koṭṭhāsesūti kesādimatthaluṅgapariyantesu. Dvādasasu koṭṭhāsesūti pittādimuttapariyantesu. Catūsu koṭṭhāsesūti “yena ca santappati, yena ca jīrīyati, yena ca paridayhati, yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.304) evaṃ vuttesu catūsu koṭṭhāsesu. Chasu koṭṭhāsesūti “uddhaṅgamā vātā, adhogamā vātā, kucchisayā vātā, koṭṭhāsayā vātā, aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātā, assāso passāso”ti (ma. ni. 2.305) evaṃ vuttesu chasu koṭṭhāsesu. Vitthambhanaṃ sesabhūtattayasanthambhitatāpādanaṃ, “upakīḷana”nti eke. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

‘In twenty compartments’ means in those from the hair of the head to the brain. ‘In twelve compartments’ means in those from bile to urine. ‘In four compartments’ means in the four compartments stated thus: ‘by which one is gratified, by which one ages, by which one is consumed, and by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper transformation’ [MN 1.245]. ‘In six compartments’ means in the six compartments stated thus: ‘upward-going winds, downward-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, and in-breath and out-breath’ [MN 2.85]. ‘Supporting’ (vitthambhana) is the causing of the state of being supported by the remaining three elements. Some say it is ‘defiling’ (upakīḷana). The rest is easily understood.

Nivesakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nivesaka Sutta is concluded.

6-7. Paṭhamabhavasuttādivaṇṇanā

6–7. Commentary on the First Discourse on Existence and So Forth

77-78. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0183][V 2.0166] abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇanti kammasahajātaṃ viññāṇaṃ. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva. Sattame natthi vattabbaṃ.

77–78. In the sixth discourse, ‘consciousness connected with formations’ is consciousness co-arisen with kamma. The rest here is easily understood. In the seventh, there is nothing to be said.

Paṭhamabhavasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Discourse on Existence and So Forth is concluded.

8. Sīlabbatasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Discourse on Precepts and Vows

79. Aṭṭhame dukkarakārikānuyogoti dukkarakiriyāya anuyogo. Upaṭṭhānena sāranti upaṭṭhānākārena sāraṃ. “Idaṃ vara”ntiādinā upaṭṭhānākāraṃ vibhāveti. Etthāti etasmiṃ satthārā pucchite pañhe.

79. In the eighth discourse, ‘the practice of austerities’ means the application to difficult practices. ‘Essence in attendance’ means essence in the mode of attendance. He clarifies the mode of attendance with the words, ‘This is best,’ and so forth. ‘Here’ means in this question asked by the Teacher.

Sīlabbatasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Precepts and Vows is concluded.

9. Gandhajātasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Kinds of Scent

80. Navame mūle, mūlassa vā gandho mūlagandhoti āha “mūlavatthuko gandho”ti. Mūlaṃ vatthu etassāti mūlavatthuko. Idāni mūlaṃ gandhayogato gandhoti imamatthaṃ dassento “gandhasampannaṃ vā mūlameva mūlagandho”ti āha. Pacchimoyevettha atthavikappo yuttataroti dassetuṃ “tassa hi gandho”tiādimāha. Vassikapupphādīnanti sumanapupphādīnaṃ.

80. In the ninth discourse, regarding ‘root-scent,’ he says it means ‘a scent with root as its basis,’ or the scent of a root. ‘That which has root as its basis’ is ‘root-based.’ Now, to show the meaning that ‘root’ is called ‘scent’ due to its connection with scent, he says: ‘Or the root itself, endowed with scent, is the root-scent.’ To show that the latter alternative meaning is more suitable here, he says, ‘for its scent,’ and so forth. ‘Of vassikā flowers and so forth’ means of jasmine flowers and so forth.

Gandhajātasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Kinds of Scent is concluded.

10. Cūḷanikāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Cūḷanikā Sutta

81. Dasame aruṇavatisuttantaaṭṭhuppattiyanti “bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā ahosi aruṇavā nāma. Rañño kho pana, bhikkhave, aruṇavato aruṇavatī nāma rājadhānī ahosi. Aruṇavatiṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, rājadhāniṃ sikhī bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho upanissāya vihāsi. Sikhissa [M 2.0184] kho pana, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa abhibhūsambhavaṃ nāma sāvakayugaṃ ahosi aggaṃ bhaddayugaṃ. Atha kho, bhikkhave, sikhī bhagavā arahaṃ [V 2.0167] sammāsambuddho abhibhuṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesī”tiādinā brahmasaṃyutte (saṃ. ni. 1.185) āgatassa aruṇavatisuttantassa aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ. Atippagoti ativiya pago, ativiya pātoti attho, na tāva kulesu bhattaṃ niṭṭhātīti vuttaṃ hoti.

81. In the tenth discourse, ‘in the origin story of the Aruṇavatī Suttanta’ refers to the origin story of the Aruṇavatī Suttanta found in the Brahma Saṃyutta [SN 6.15], which begins: ‘Once, monks, there was a king named Aruṇavā. King Aruṇavā, monks, had a royal capital named Aruṇavatī. The Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, monks, dwelt relying on the royal capital Aruṇavatī. The Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, monks, had a pair of disciples named Abhibhū and Sambhava, a foremost, excellent pair. Then, monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, addressed the monk Abhibhū….’ ‘Too early’ (atippago) means very early in the morning (ativiya pago); the meaning is very early (ativiya pāto). It means that the meal in the households was not yet ready.

Ujjhāyantīti avajhāyanti, heṭṭhā katvā cintenti, lāmakato cintenti. Anekavihitaṃ iddhivikubbanaṃ katvāti “pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā nāgavaṇṇaṃ vā dasseti, supaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ vā dassetī”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 3.13) nayena āgataṃ anekappakāraṃ iddhivikubbanaṃ katvā. Sahassilokadhātunti cakkavāḷasahassaṃ. Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsīti thero kira “kathaṃ desitā kho dhammadesanā sabbesaṃ piyā manāpā”ti cintetvā “sabbepi pāsaṇḍā sabbe devamanussā attano attano samaye purisakāraṃ vaṇṇayanti, vīriyassa avaṇṇavādī nāma natthi, vīriyappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ katvā desessāmi. Evamassa dhammadesanā sabbesaṃ piyā bhavissati manāpā”ti ñatvā tīsu piṭakesu vicinitvā “ārambhatha nikkamathā”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.186) idaṃ gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

‘They complain’ means they despise, they think of them as lowly, they think of them as inferior. ‘Having performed various kinds of psychic transformations’ means having performed many kinds of psychic transformations that are mentioned in the way of the Paṭisambhidāmagga [Ps 2.205]: ‘having abandoned his normal form, he shows the form of a nāga or shows the form of a supaṇṇa,’ and so forth. ‘A thousandfold world-system’ means a thousand world-spheres. ‘He spoke two verses’ means that the elder, it is said, reflected, ‘How should a Dhamma teaching be taught so that it is dear and agreeable to all?’ He knew, ‘All sectarians, all devas and humans, in their own time, praise human effort. There is no one who speaks ill of energy. I will teach in connection with energy. In this way, this Dhamma teaching will be dear and agreeable to all.’ Having searched through the three Piṭakas, he spoke these two verses: ‘Arouse yourselves! Strive on!’ [SN 6.15].

Kiṃ āloko ayanti kassa nu kho ayaṃ ālokoti. Vicinantānanti cintentānaṃ. Sabbeti lokadhātuyaṃ sabbe devā ca manussā ca. Osaṭāya parisāyāti dhammassavanatthaṃ samosaṭāya parimitaparicchinnāya parisāya. Atthopi nesaṃ pākaṭo ahosīti na kevalaṃ te saddameva assosuṃ, atha kho atthopi tesaṃ pakatisavanūpacāre viya pākaṭo ahosi. Tena sahassaṃ lokadhātuṃ viññāpetīti adhippāyo.

‘What is this light?’ means ‘Whose light is this?’ ‘Of those investigating’ means of those reflecting. ‘All’ means all the devas and humans in the world-system. ‘To the assembled gathering’ means to a limited and circumscribed gathering that had assembled for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. ‘The meaning also became clear to them’ means that not only did they hear the sound, but the meaning also became clear to them as if within the range of normal hearing. By this, the intended meaning is, ‘He made a thousandfold world-system understand.’

Pariharantīti sineruṃ dakkhiṇato katvā parivattenti. Virocamānāti attano jutiyā dibbamānā, sobhamānā vā. Tāva sahassadhā lokoti yattako candimasūriyehi obhāsiyamāno lokadhātusaṅkhāto ekeko loko, tattakena pamāṇena sahassadhā loko, iminā cakkavāḷena saddhiṃ cakkavāḷasahassanti attho. Kasmā panesā ānītāti esā cūḷanikā lokadhātu [M 2.0185] kasmā bhagavatā ānītā, desitāti attho. Majjhimikāya lokadhātuyā paricchedadassanatthanti dvisahassilokadhātuyā parimāṇadassanatthaṃ.

‘They circle’ means they revolve, keeping Mount Sineru to their right. ‘Shining’ means glowing with their own radiance, or being resplendent. ‘As far as a thousandfold world’ means a thousandfold world by the measure of each single world, designated as a world-system, that is illuminated by a moon and a sun; the meaning is a thousand world-spheres along with this world-sphere. ‘But why was this brought forth?’ means why was this lesser world-system brought forth, that is, taught, by the Blessed One? ‘To show the extent of the middling world-system’ means to show the measure of the two-thousandfold world-system.

Sahassilokadhātuyā sahassī dvisahassilokadhātu, sā cakkavāḷagaṇanāya dasasatasahassacakkavāḷaparimāṇā. Tenāha “sahassacakkavāḷāni sahassabhāgena gaṇetvā”tiādi. Kampanadevatūpasaṅkamanādinā jātacakkavāḷena saha yogakkhemaṃ ṭhānaṃ jātikkhettaṃ. Tattakāya eva jātikkhettabhāvo [V 2.0168] dhammatāvaseneva veditabbo, “pariggahavasenā”ti keci. Sabbesampi buddhānaṃ evaṃ jātikkhettaṃ tannivāsīnaṃyeva ca devatānaṃ dhammābhisamayoti vadanti. Paṭisandhiggahaṇādīnaṃ sattannaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ nidassanamattaṃ mahābhinīhārādikālepi tassa pakampanassa labbhanato.

The thousandfold of the thousandfold world-system is the two-thousandfold world-system, which in the counting of world-spheres amounts to one million world-spheres. Hence he says, ‘counting a thousand world-spheres by the thousandfold part,’ and so forth. The field of birth is the place of security from the bonds, along with the world-sphere that arises with the trembling, the approach of devas, and so forth. Its being a field of birth to that extent should be understood simply as a natural phenomenon, though some say it is due to appropriation. It is said that for all Buddhas, the field of birth is like this, and the realization of the Dhamma occurs only for the devas dwelling therein. The mention of only the seven events beginning with the grasping of rebirth-linking is merely an illustration, for that trembling is obtainable even at the time of the great aspiration and so forth.

Sahassaṃ sahassadhā katvā gaṇitaṃ majjhimikantiādinā majjhimikāya lokadhātuyā sahassaṃ tisahassilokadhātu, sāyeva ca mahāsahassilokadhātūti dasseti. Saraseneva āṇāpavattanaṃ āṇākkhettaṃ, yaṃ ekajjhaṃ saṃvaṭṭati vivaṭṭati ca. Āṇā pharatīti tannivāsidevatānaṃ sirasā sampaṭicchanena vattati, tañca kho kevalaṃ buddhānubhāveneva, adhippāyavasena ca pana “yāvatā pana ākaṅkheyyā”ti (a. ni. 3.81) vacanato buddhānaṃ avisayo nāma natthi, visayakkhettassa pamāṇaparicchedo nāma natthi. Visamoti sūriyuggamanādīnaṃ visamabhāvato visamo. Tenevāha “ekasmiṃ ṭhāne sūriyo uggato hotī”tiādi. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

By the phrase beginning, ‘A thousand, having been made a thousandfold, is reckoned as the middling one,’ he shows that a thousand times the middling world-system is the three-thousandfold world-system, and that this very one is the great thousandfold world-system. The field of authority is the proceeding of authority by its own nature, which contracts and expands as one. ‘Authority extends’ means it proceeds with the devas dwelling therein accepting it with their heads; and that indeed is solely through the Buddha’s power. And also, by way of intention, from the statement, ‘As far as he might wish…’ [AN 3.80], there is nothing that is not a Buddha’s domain, and there is no limit or boundary to the field of his domain. ‘It is uneven’ means it is uneven because of the unevenness of the sun’s rising and so forth. Therefore he says, ‘in one place the sun has risen,’ and so forth. The rest here is easily understood.

Cūḷanikāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷanikā Sutta is concluded.

Ānandavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ānanda Chapter is concluded.

(9) 4. Samaṇavaggo

(9) 4. The Chapter on Ascetics

1-5. Samaṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–5. Commentary on the Discourses on Ascetics and So Forth

82-86. Catutthassa paṭhame sammā ādānaṃ gahaṇaṃ samādānanti āha “samādānaṃ vuccati gahaṇa”nti. Adhikaṃ visiṭṭhaṃ sīlanti adhisīlaṃ. Lokiyasīlassa [M 2.0186] adhisīlabhāvo pariyāyenāti nippariyāyameva taṃ dassetuṃ “apica sabbampi lokiyasīla”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sikkhitabbatoti āsevitabbato. Pañcapi dasapi vā sīlāni sīlaṃ nāma, pātimokkhasaṃvaro adhisīlaṃ nāma anavasesakāyikacetasikasaṃvarabhāvato maggasīlassa padaṭṭhānabhāvato ca. Aṭṭha samāpattiyo cittaṃ, vipassanāpādakajjhānaṃ adhicittaṃ maggasamādhissa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato. Kammassakatañāṇaṃ paññā, vipassanā adhipaññā maggapaññāya adhiṭṭhānabhāvato. Apica nibbānaṃ [V 2.0169] patthayantena samādinnaṃ pañcasīlaṃ dasasīlampi adhisīlameva nibbānādhigamassa paccayabhāvato. Nibbānaṃ patthayantena samāpannā aṭṭha samāpattiyopi adhicittameva.

82-86. In the first [sutta] of the fourth [section], regarding 'right undertaking' (sammā ādānaṃ), he said that undertaking (samādāna) is grasping (gahaṇa); hence the statement, 'Undertaking is called grasping.' Higher virtue (adhisīla) is virtue that is superior and distinguished. That worldly virtue becomes higher virtue is by way of interpretation; thus, to show it directly, it is said: 'Moreover, all worldly virtue,' and so on. 'Because it should be trained in' means 'because it is to be practiced.' The five or ten precepts are called virtue (sīla), while the restraint of the Pātimokkha is called higher virtue (adhisīla) because it is the state of complete bodily and mental restraint and because it is the foundation for the virtue of the path. The eight attainments are mind (citta), and the jhāna that is a basis for insight is called higher mind (adhicitta) because it is the foundation for the concentration of the path. The knowledge of the ownership of kamma is wisdom (paññā), and insight is higher wisdom (adhipaññā) because it is the foundation for the wisdom of the path. Moreover, for one aspiring to Nibbāna, the five or ten precepts undertaken are indeed higher virtue because they are a condition for attaining Nibbāna. For one aspiring to Nibbāna, even the eight attainments reached are indeed higher mind.

“Kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ, pāpakārī ca pāpakaṃ;

Anubhoti dvayametaṃ, anubandhañhi kāraṇa”nti. –

"The doer of good experiences good,

And the doer of evil, evil;

One experiences both of these,

For the cause indeed has its consequence."

Evaṃ atīte anāgate ca vaṭṭamūlakadukkhasallakkhaṇavasena saṃvegavatthutāya vimuttiākaṅkhāya paccayabhūtā kammassakatapaññāpi adhipaññāti vadanti. Dutiyatatiyacatutthapañcamāni uttānatthāneva.

Thus, the knowledge of the ownership of kamma—which, by way of perceiving the suffering rooted in the cycle in the past and future, becomes a basis for spiritual urgency and a condition for the aspiration for liberation—is also called higher wisdom, they say. The second, third, fourth, and fifth [suttas] are indeed of clear meaning.

Samaṇasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Samaṇa Suttas and others is concluded.

6. Paṭhamasikkhāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the First Discourse on Training

87. Chaṭṭhe samattakārīti anūnena paripūrena ākārena samannāgato. Sikkhāpadānaṃ khuddānukhuddakattaṃ apekkhāsiddhanti āha “tatrāpi saṅghādisesaṃ khuddaka”ntiādi. Aṅguttaramahānikāyavaḷañjanakaācariyāti aṅguttaranikāyaṃ pariharantā ācariyā, aṅguttarabhāṇakāti vuttaṃ hoti. Lokavajjaṃ nāpajjati lokavajjasikkhāpadānaṃ vītikkamasādhakassa kilesagahanassa sabbaso pahīnattā. Paṇṇattivajjameva āpajjati paṇṇattivītikkamaṃ vā ajānatopi āpattisambhavato. Cittena āpajjanto rūpiyappaṭiggahaṇaṃ āpajjatīti upanikkhittasādiyena āpajjati.

87. In the sixth [sutta], 'one who acts completely' (samattakārī) means one endowed with a manner that is not deficient but complete. The minor and lesser nature of the training rules is established by relation, as it is said: 'Even among them, the Saṅghādisesa is minor,' and so on. 'The teachers who use the great Aṅguttara Nikāya' means the teachers who preserve the Aṅguttara Nikāya; this means they are called 'Aṅguttara reciters' (Aṅguttarabhāṇaka). One does not incur worldly blame, because the thicket of defilements that facilitates the transgression of training rules involving worldly blame has been entirely abandoned. One incurs only prescribed blame, as an offense can arise from transgressing a prescription even without knowing it. 'One who incurs an offense with the mind incurs the offense of accepting gold and silver' means one incurs it by consenting to what has been deposited.

Brahmacariyassa ādibhūtāni ādibrahmacariyāni, tāni eva ādibrahmacariyakāni yathā “vinayo eva venayiko”ti āha “maggabrahmacariyassā”tiādi. Cattāri mahāsīlasikkhāpadānīti cattāri pārājikāni sandhāya [M 2.0187] vadati. Paṭipakkhadhammānaṃ anavasesato savanato paggharaṇato soto, ariyamaggoti āha “sotasaṅkhātena maggenā”ti. Vinipāteti virūpaṃ sadukkhaṃ saupāyāsaṃ nipātetīti vinipāto, apāyadukkhe khipanako. Dhammoti sabhāvo. Nāssa vinipāto dhammoti avinipātadhammo, na attānaṃ apāyesu vinipātanasabhāvoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Ye dhammā apāyagamanīyā, tesaṃ pahīnattā. Tenāha “avinipātadhammoti catūsu apāyesu apatanasabhāvo”ti. Tattha apatanasabhāvoti anuppajjanasabhāvo. Sotāpattimagganiyāmena [V 2.0170] niyatoti uparimaggādhigamassa avassaṃbhāvībhāvato niyato. Tenevāha “sambodhiparāyaṇo”ti. Heṭṭhimantato sattamabhavato upari anuppajjanadhammatāya vā niyato. Sambujjhatīti sambodhi, ariyamaggo. So pana paṭhamamaggassa adhigatattā avasiṭṭho ca adhigantabbabhāvena icchitabboti uparimaggattayasaṅkhātā sambodhi paraṃ ayanaṃ parā gati assāti sambodhiparāyaṇo. Tenāha “uparimaggattayasambodhiparāyaṇo”ti.

The fundamentals of the holy life are the initial holy lives (ādibrahmacariya); these are called ādibrahmacariyaka, just as 'discipline' (vinaya) is called 'disciplinary' (venayika). Thus he says, 'of the holy life of the path,' and so on. 'The four great training rules of virtue' refers to the four pārājika offenses. Because it flows (savanato) and streams forth (paggharaṇato), completely washing away opposing states, it is a stream (sota); this is the noble path, as he says: 'by the path called the stream.' A 'downfall' (vinipāta) is so called because it makes one fall (nipāteti) into a deformed, painful, and distressing state; it is that which hurls one into the suffering of the lower realms. 'Dhamma' means nature. 'Not of a nature for downfall' (avinipātadhammo) means he is not of a nature to hurl himself into the lower realms. Why? Because those states that lead to the lower realms have been abandoned. Therefore he said: ''Not of a nature for downfall' means of a nature not to fall into the four lower realms.' Therein, 'of a nature not to fall' means of a nature not to arise [there]. 'Fixed by the principle of the stream-entry path' means he is fixed because the attainment of the higher paths is inevitable. For that reason he said: 'bound for awakening' (sambodhiparāyaṇo). Or, he is fixed by having the nature of not arising above the seventh existence from the lowest. 'Awakening' (sambodhi) is the noble path. Since the first path has been attained, and the remainder is to be attained and is desirable, 'bound for awakening' means that awakening—identified as the three higher paths—is his final goal and ultimate destination. Therefore he said: 'bound for the awakening of the three higher paths.'

Tanubhāvāti pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya ca kadāci karahaci uppattiyā ca tanubhāvena. Tanuttañhi dvīhi kāraṇehi veditabbaṃ adhiccuppattiyā ca pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya ca. Sakadāgāmissa hi vaṭṭānusārimahājanassa viya kilesā abhiṇhaṃ na uppajjanti, kadāci karahaci uppajjanti viraḷākārā hutvā viraḷavāpite khette aṅkurā viya. Uppajjamānāpi ca vaṭṭānusārimahājanasseva maddantā pharantā chādentā andhakāraṃ karontā na uppajjanti, mandamandā uppajjanti tanukākārā hutvā abbhapaṭalamiva makkhikāpattamiva ca. Tattha keci therā bhaṇanti “sakadāgāmissa kilesā kiñcāpi cirena uppajjanti, bahalāva uppajjanti. Tathā hissa puttā ca dhītaro ca dissantī”ti. Etaṃ pana appamāṇaṃ. Puttadhītaro hi aṅgapaccaṅgaparāmasanamattenapi hontīti. Dvīhiyeva kāraṇehissa kilesānaṃ tanuttaṃ veditabbaṃ adhiccuppattiyā ca pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya cāti.

'By their attenuation' (tanubhāva) means by the sluggishness of their manifestation and by their occasional arising, that is, by their attenuated nature. For their attenuation should be understood for two reasons: their chance arising and the sluggishness of their manifestation. For a once-returner, unlike for the great mass of people who follow the cycle of rebirth, defilements do not arise frequently; they arise only occasionally, appearing sparsely like sprouts in a thinly sown field. And even when they do arise, they do not arise crushing, pervading, overshadowing, and creating darkness, as they do for the great mass of people who follow the cycle; rather, they arise very weakly, appearing in an attenuated form, like a patch of cloud or a fly’s wing. In this regard, some elders say: 'Although the defilements of a once-returner arise after a long time, they arise strongly. For this is how sons and daughters are seen to be his.' But this is not a valid measure, for sons and daughters can be conceived merely by the touching of limbs. Therefore, the attenuation of his defilements should be understood for just two reasons: their chance arising and the sluggishness of their manifestation.

Heṭṭhābhāgiyānanti ettha heṭṭhāti mahaggatabhūmito heṭṭhā, kāmabhūmiyanti attho. Tesaṃ paccayabhāvena heṭṭhābhāgassa hitāti heṭṭhābhāgiyā, tesaṃ heṭṭhābhāgiyānaṃ, heṭṭhābhāgassa kāmabhavassa paccayabhāvena gahitānanti attho. Saṃyojenti bandhanti khandhagatibhavādīhi [M 2.0188] khandhagatibhavādayo, kammaṃ vā phalenāti saṃyojanānīti āha “saṃyojanānanti bandhanāna”nti. Asamucchinnarāgādikassa hi etarahi khandhādīnaṃ āyatiṃ khandhādīhi sambandho, samucchinnarāgādikassa pana taṃ natthi, katānampi kammānaṃ asamatthabhāvāpattito rāgādīnaṃ anvayato byatirekato ca saṃyojanaṭṭho siddho. Parikkhayenāti samucchedena.

Regarding 'of those belonging to the lower part' (heṭṭhābhāgiyānaṃ), herein 'lower' means below the exalted planes, that is, the sense-sphere plane. Because they are conditions for the lower part, they are 'belonging to the lower part'; the meaning is that they are taken as conditions for the lower part, for sensual existence. 'They fetter' (saṃyojenti) means they bind; they bind the present aggregates, destinations, and existences to future ones, or they bind kamma to its result. Thus they are 'fetters' (saṃyojanāni); hence he said, 'fetters means bonds.' For one whose lust and so on has not been eradicated, there is a connection of the present aggregates and so on with future aggregates. But for one whose lust and so on has been eradicated, there is no such connection, since even kammas that were done have become incapable of producing a result. Thus, the meaning of 'fetter' is established by the method of presence and absence of lust and so on. 'By the complete destruction' (parikkhayena) means by eradication.

Opapātikoti upapātikayoniko upapatane sādhukārī. Sesayonipaṭikkhepavacanametaṃ. Tena gabbhavāsadukkhābhāvamāha. Tattha parinibbāyīti iminā sesadukkhābhāvaṃ. Tattha parinibbāyitā cassa kāmaloke khandhabījassa apunāgamanavasenevāti dassetuṃ “anāvattidhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Upariyevāti brahmalokeyeva. Anāvattidhammoti tato brahmalokā punappunaṃ paṭisandhivasena na āvattanadhammo. Tenāha “yonigativasena anāgamanadhammo”ti.

'Spontaneously born' (opapātika) means one of spontaneous origin, one who is born spontaneously. This is a statement that excludes the other kinds of birth. By this, he indicates the absence of the suffering of dwelling in a womb. By 'there he attains final Nibbāna' (parinibbāyī), he indicates the absence of remaining suffering. And to show that his attaining final Nibbāna there is precisely by way of the non-return of the seed of the aggregates to the sense-sphere world, it is said, 'of a nature not to return' (anāvattidhammo). 'Only above' means only in the Brahma world. 'Of a nature not to return' means he is not of a nature to return from that Brahma world again and again by way of rebirth-linking. Therefore he said, 'of a nature not to come again by way of birth-origin and destination.'

Padesaṃ [V 2.0171] padesakārī ārādhetīti sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ pāripūriyā ekadesabhūtaṃ heṭṭhimamaggattayaṃ padeso, taṃ karonto padesaṃ ekadesabhūtaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ phalattayameva ārādheti, nipphādetīti attho. Tenāha “padesakārī puggalo nāma sotāpanno”tiādi. Paripūraṃ paripūrakārīti sīlakkhandhādīhi saddhindriyādīhi ca parito pūraṇena paripūrasaṅkhātaṃ arahattamaggaṃ karonto nibbattento paripūraṃ arahattaphalaṃ ārādheti, nipphādetīti attho. Tenāha “paripūrakārī nāma arahā”tiādi.

'One who achieves in part' (padesakārī) accomplishes a part. The 'part' (padesa) refers to the lower three paths, which are a part of the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue and so on. By accomplishing that, one attains just the lower three fruits, which are a part; this is the meaning. Hence it is said, 'The person who achieves in part is a stream-enterer,' and so on. 'One who achieves fully' (paripūrakārī) accomplishes the full. By fulfilling all around with the aggregate of virtue and so on, and the spiritual faculties beginning with faith, one who cultivates and brings into being the path of arahantship, which is called 'fully perfected,' attains the fully perfected fruit of arahantship; this is the meaning. Hence it is said, 'One who achieves fully is an arahant,' and so on.

Paṭhamasikkhāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Training Discourse is concluded.

7-10. Dutiyasikkhāsuttādivaṇṇanā

7–10. Commentary on the Second Training Discourse and so on.

88-91. Sattame kulā kulaṃ gamanakoti kulato kulaṃ gacchanto. Dve vā tayo vā bhaveti devamanussavasena dve vā tayo vā bhave. Missakabhavavasena hetaṃ vuttaṃ. Desanāmattameva cetaṃ “dve vā tīṇi vā”ti. Yāva chaṭṭhabhavā saṃsarantopi kolaṃkolova hoti. Tenevāha “ayañhi dve vā bhave…pe… evamettha vikappo daṭṭhabbo”ti. Uḷārakulavacano vā ettha kulasaddo, kulato kulaṃ gacchatīti [M 2.0189] kolaṃkolo. Sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyato paṭṭhāya hi nīcakule uppatti nāma natthi, mahābhogakulesu eva nibbattatīti attho. Kevalo hi kulasaddo mahākulameva vadati “kulaputto”tiādīsu viya. Ekabījīti ettha khandhabījaṃ nāma kathitaṃ, khandhabījanti ca paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ vuccati. Yassa hi sotāpannassa ekaṃ khandhabījaṃ atthi, ekaṃ bhavaggahaṇaṃ, so ekabījī nāma. Tenāha “ekasseva bhavassa bījaṃ etassa atthīti ekabījī”ti. “Mānusakaṃ bhava”nti idaṃ panettha desanāmattameva, “devabhavaṃ nibbattetī”tipi pana vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva.

88–91. “From family to family” (kulā kulaṃ gamanato) means going from one family to another. “Two or three existences” refers to two or three lives, whether as gods or humans. This is said in the sense of mixed existences. The statement “two or three” is merely a manner of teaching. Even those who wander on to a sixth existence are still a family-to-family transmigrator (kolaṃkolo). Therefore, it is said: “For this one, two existences… and so on… thus the distinction should be seen here.” Or, the word “family” (kula) in this context may refer to a distinguished family, and “going from family to family” (kulato kulaṃ gacchati) means being a family-to-family transmigrator (kolaṃkolo). From the realization of the fruit of stream-entry onward, there is no rebirth in a low family; the meaning is that one is reborn only among families of great wealth. For the word “family” alone signifies a great family, as in instances such as “son of a good family” (kulaputto). “One-seeder” (ekabījī) here refers to what is called “aggregate-seed” (khandhabījaṃ), and “aggregate-seed” means the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ). For a stream-enterer who has one aggregate-seed, one grasping of existence (bhava), is called a “one-seeder.” Therefore, it is said: “This one has the seed for only one existence, thus he is a one-seeder.” “Human existence” (mānusakaṃ bhavaṃ)—this here is merely illustrative, for it is also fitting to say that “he brings about a divine existence” (devabhavaṃ nibbattetī).

Uddhaṃvāhibhāvena uddhamassa taṇhāsotaṃ vaṭṭasotaṃ vāti uddhaṃsoto, uddhaṃ vā gantvā paṭilabhitabbato uddhamassa maggasotanti uddhaṃsoto. Paṭisandhivasena akaniṭṭhabhavaṃ gacchatīti akaniṭṭhagāmī. Yattha katthacīti avihādīsu yattha katthaci. Sappayogenāti vipassanāñāṇābhisaṅkhārasaṅkhātena payogena saha, mahatā vipassanāpayogenāti attho. Upahaccāti etassa upagantvāti attho. Tena vemajjhātikkamo kālakiriyāpagamanañca saṅgahitaṃ hoti, tasmā āyuvemajjhaṃ atikkamitvā parinibbāyanto upahaccaparinibbāyī nāma hotīti āha “yo pana kappasahassāyukesu avihesū”tiādi. So tividho hotīti ñāṇassa tikkhamajjhamudubhāvena tividho hoti. Tenāha “kappasahassāyukesū”tiādi.

One is an 'upward-streamer' (uddhaṃsoto) because, by nature of flowing upward, their stream of craving, or stream of the cycle, flows upward; or, because the path-stream is to be attained by going upward, one is an 'upward-streamer'. One who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm by means of rebirth-linking is called an 'Akaniṭṭha-goer' (akaniṭṭhagāmī). 'Wherever' refers to wherever among the Avihā realms and so on. 'With effort' (sappayogena) means together with the effort designated as the volitional formation of insight-knowledge; the meaning is, with great effort in insight. 'Having approached' (upahacca) means having gone near. By this, the overcoming of the midpoint of the lifespan and the passing away at death are included. Therefore, one who attains final Nibbāna after passing the midpoint of the lifespan is called an 'upahaccaparinibbāyī'. Thus it is said: 'But one among those with a lifespan of a thousand eons in the Avihā realms,' and so on. That one is of three kinds—according to the sharpness, middlingness, or mildness of their knowledge. Therefore it is said: 'Among those with a lifespan of a thousand eons,' and so on.

Saddhādhurena [V 2.0172] abhinivisitvāti “sace saddhāya sakkā nibbattetuṃ, nibbattessāmi lokuttaramagga”nti evaṃ saddhādhuravasena abhinivisitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā. Paññādhurena abhiniviṭṭhoti “sace paññāya sakkā, nibbattessāmi lokuttaramagga”nti evaṃ paññādhuraṃ katvā abhiniviṭṭho. Yathāvuttameva aṭṭhavidhattaṃ kolaṃkolasattakkhattuparamesu atidisanto “tathā kolaṃkolā sattakkhattuparamā cā”ti āha. Vuttanayeneva aṭṭha kolaṃkolā, aṭṭha sattakkhattuparamāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Having resolved with the yoke of faith (saddhādhurena abhinivisitvā): “If it is possible to bring about the supramundane path (lokuttaramagga) through faith, I will bring it about,” thus establishing insight (vipassanaṃ) by resolving by means of the yoke of faith. Having resolved with the yoke of wisdom (paññādhurena abhiniviṭṭho): “If it is possible to bring about the supramundane path through wisdom, I will bring it about,” thus resolving after making wisdom the yoke (paññādhuraṃ). Extending the eightfold nature as stated to those who are “family-to-family transmigrators” (kolaṃkola) and “seven-times-at-most” (sattakkhattuparama), he says, “Thus are the family-to-family transmigrators (kolaṃkolā) and the seven-times-at-most (sattakkhattuparamā).” In the way stated, it is said that there are eight family-to-family transmigrators and eight seven-times-at-most.

Tattha sattakkhattuṃ paramā bhavūpapatti attabhāvaggahaṇaṃ assa, tato paraṃ aṭṭhamaṃ bhavaṃ nādiyatīti sattakkhattuparamo. Bhagavatā gahitanāmavaseneva cetāni ariyāya jātiyā jātānaṃ tesaṃ nāmāni jātāni kumārānaṃ mātāpitūhi gahitanāmāni viya. Ettakañhi ṭhānaṃ gato [M 2.0190] ekabījī nāma hoti, ettakaṃ kolaṃkolo, ettakaṃ sattakkhattuparamoti bhagavatā etesaṃ nāmaṃ gahitaṃ. Niyamato pana ayaṃ ekabījī, ayaṃ kolaṃkolo, ayaṃ sattakkhattuparamoti natthi. Ko pana nesaṃ etaṃ pabhedaṃ niyametīti? Keci tāva therā “pubbahetu niyametī”ti vadanti, keci paṭhamamaggo, keci upari tayo maggā, keci tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanāti.

Therein, one for whom the arising of existence, the grasping of an individual existence, is at most seven times, and who after that does not take up an eighth existence, is a 'seven-times-at-most' (sattakkhattuparamo). These names for them, born into the noble birth, arose by the power of the name-giving by the Blessed One, just like names given by mothers and fathers to born children. For, having reached such a state, one is called a 'one-seeder' (ekabījī); having reached such a state, a 'family-to-family transmigrator' (kolaṃkolo); having reached such a state, a 'seven-times-at-most' (sattakkhattuparamo)—thus a name was given by the Blessed One for these. But as a rule, it is not that 'this one is a one-seeder,' 'this one a family-to-family transmigrator,' 'this one a seven-times-at-most.' Who, then, determines this distinction for them? Some elders say, “A prior cause (pubbahetu) determines it”; some say, the first path (paṭhamamaggo); some, the three higher paths (upari tayo maggā); and some, the insight (vipassanā) of the three paths.

Tattha “pubbahetu niyametī”ti vāde paṭhamamaggassa upanissayo kato nāma hoti, “upari tayo maggā nirupanissayā uppannā”ti vacanaṃ āpajjati. “Paṭhamamaggo niyamehī”ti vāde upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ niratthakatā āpajjati. “Upari tayo maggā niyamentī”ti vāde paṭhamamagge anuppanneyeva upari tayo maggā uppannāti āpajjatīti. “Tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanā niyametī”ti vādo pana yujjati. Sace hi upari tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ vipassanā balavatī hoti, ekabījī nāma hoti, tato mandatarāya kolaṃkolo, tato mandatarāya sattakkhattuparamoti.

Here, in the view that 'a prior cause determines,' a support for the first path is indeed established, but this incurs the assertion that 'the three higher paths arise without support.' In the view that 'the first path determines,' the meaninglessness of the three higher paths is incurred. In the view that 'the three higher paths determine,' it follows that the three higher paths arise even when the first path has not arisen. However, the view that 'the insight of the three paths determines' is valid. For if the insight for the three higher paths is strong, one is called a 'one-seeder'; if it is weaker than that, a 'family-to-family transmigrator'; and if weaker still, a 'seven-times-at-most'.

Ekacco hi sotāpanno vaṭṭajjhāsayo hoti vaṭṭābhirato, punappunaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃyeva carati sandissati. Anāthapiṇḍiko seṭṭhi, visākhā upāsikā, cūḷarathamahārathā devaputtā, anekavaṇṇo devaputto, sakko devarājā, nāgadatto devaputtoti ime hi ettakā janā vaṭṭajjhāsayā vaṭṭābhiratā ādito paṭṭhāya cha devaloke sodhetvā akaniṭṭhe ṭhatvā parinibbāyissanti, ime idha na gahitā. Na kevalañcimeva, yopi manussesuyeva sattakkhattuṃ saṃsaritvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, yopi devaloke nibbatto devesuyeva sattakkhattuṃ aparāparaṃ saṃsaritvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Imepi idha na gahitā, kālena deve, kālena manusse saṃsaritvā [V 2.0173] pana arahattaṃ pāpuṇantova idha gahito, tasmā “sattakkhattuparamo”ti idaṃ idhaṭṭhakavokiṇṇabhavūpapattikasukkhavipassakassa nāmaṃ kathitanti veditabbaṃ.

For some stream-enterers have an inclination for the round and delight in the round; they wander repeatedly in the round itself and are seen there. The merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, the laywoman Visākhā, the devaputtas Cūḷaratha and Mahāratha, the devaputta Anekavaṇṇa, Sakka the king of devas, and the devaputta Nāgadatta—these many people, inclined toward the round and delighting in it from the start, will, after purifying the six deva worlds and abiding in the Akaniṭṭha realm, attain final Nibbāna. These are not included here. Not only these, but also one who attains arahantship after wandering among humans for seven times, and one who, born in a deva world, attains arahantship after wandering successively among devas for seven times—these too are not included here. But one who attains arahantship after wandering at times among devas and at times among humans is included here. Therefore, it should be understood that the term 'seven-times-at-most' (sattakkhattuparamo) is here said to be the name for a dry-insight practitioner whose rebirths are scattered among various existences.

“Sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā”ti (pu. pa. 34) vacanato pañcasu sakadāgāmīsu cattāro vajjetvā ekova gahito. Ekacco hi idha sakadāgāmiphalaṃ patvā idheva parinibbāyati, ekacco idha patvā devaloke parinibbāyati[M 2.0191], ekacco devaloke patvā tattheva parinibbāyati, ekacco devaloke patvā idhūpapajjitvā parinibbāyati. Ime cattāropi idha na gahitā. Yo pana idha patvā devaloke yāvatāyukaṃ vasitvā puna idhūpapajjitvā parinibbāyissati, ayaṃ ekova idha gahitoti veditabbo.

According to the statement, “Having come to this world only once” (sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā) (Pug. 34), among the five types of once-returners, four are excluded and only one is included. For one attains the fruit of once-returning here and attains final Nibbāna right here; another attains it here but attains final Nibbāna in the deva-world; another attains it in the deva-world and attains final Nibbāna right there; another attains it in the deva-world and, after being reborn here, attains final Nibbāna. These four are not included here. But the one who attains it here, lives out the full lifespan in the deva-world, and then, after being reborn here again, attains final Nibbāna—this one alone is to be understood as included here.

Idāni tassa pabhedaṃ dassento “tīsu pana vimokkhesū”tiādimāha. Imassa pana sakadāgāmino ekabījinā saddhiṃ kiṃ nānākaraṇanti? Ekabījissa ekāva paṭisandhi, sakadāgāmissa dve paṭisandhiyo, idaṃ tesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ. Suññatavimokkhena vimuttakhīṇāsavo paṭipadāvasena catubbidho hoti, tathā animittaappaṇihitavimokkhehīti evaṃ dvādasa arahantā hontīti āha “yathā pana sakadāgāmino, tatheva arahanto dvādasa veditabbā”ti. Aṭṭhamanavamadasamāni uttānatthāneva.

Now, showing its divisions, he said what begins with “But among the three liberations.” What is the distinction between this once-returner and the one-seeder? The one-seeder has only one rebirth, while the once-returner has two rebirths—this is their distinction. The one whose taints are destroyed, liberated by the emptiness liberation, is fourfold according to the way of practice; similarly, through the signless and desireless liberations, thus there are twelve arahants. Thus, it is said: “Just as there are once-returners, so too the arahants are to be understood as twelvefold.” The eighth, ninth, and tenth are clear in meaning.

Dutiyasikkhāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Training Sutta, etc., is finished.

11. Saṅkavāsuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Saṅkavāsa Sutta

92. Ekādasame vihārapaṭibaddhanavakammādibhāraṃ harati pavattetīti bhārahāro. Tenevāha “nave āvāse samuṭṭhāpeti, purāṇe paṭijaggatī”ti. Sikkhitabbato sikkhā, pajjitabbato, pajjanti etehīti vā padāni, sikkhāyeva padāni sikkhāpadānīti āha “sikkhāsaṅkhātehi padehī”ti. Dassetīti paccakkhato dasseti, hatthāmalakaṃ viya pākaṭe vibhūte katvā vibhāveti. Gaṇhāpetīti te dhamme manasā anupakkhite diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhe kārento uggaṇhāpeti. Samussāhetīti samādhimhi ussāhaṃ janeti. Paṭiladdhaguṇehīti tāya desanāya tannissayapaccattapurisakārena ca tesaṃ paṭividdhaguṇehi. Vodāpetīti tesaṃ cittasantānaṃ assaddhiyādikilesamalāpagamanena pabhassaraṃ karoti. Saṇhaṃ saṇhaṃ kathetīti ativiya sukhumaṃ katvā katheti.

92. In the eleventh, a 'burden-bearer' (bhārahāro) is one who carries and manages the burden of new works and so on connected with the monastery. Thus it is said: 'He establishes new dwellings and maintains old ones.' 'Training' (sikkhā) is so called because it is to be trained in. 'Terms' (padāni) are so called because one proceeds by them, or they proceed by means of them. 'Training rules' (sikkhāpadāni) are the terms that are themselves the training; thus it is said: 'by terms designated as training.' 'He shows' (dasseti) means he shows directly, making it manifest and clear, illuminating it like a myrobalan fruit on the palm. 'He makes them grasp' (gaṇhāpeti) means he causes them to learn by having those teachings well-considered in the mind and well-penetrated by insight. 'He arouses' (samussāheti) means he generates enthusiasm for concentration. 'By the qualities they have attained' (paṭiladdhaguṇehi) means by the qualities they have penetrated through that teaching and through their own personal effort based on it. 'He purifies' (vodāpeti) means he makes their mental continuum radiant by the removal of the stain of defilements such as lack of faith. 'He speaks gently and subtly' (saṇhaṃ saṇhaṃ katheti) means he speaks making it exceedingly subtle.

Accayanaṃ [V 2.0174] sādhumariyādaṃ madditvā vītikkamanaṃ accayoti āha “aparādho”ti. Acceti atikkamati etenāti vā accayo, vītikkamassa pavattanako akusaladhammo. So eva aparajjhati etenāti aparādho. So hi aparajjhantaṃ purisaṃ adhibhavitvā pavattati. Tenāha “atikkamma [M 2.0192] adhibhavitvā pavatto”ti. Paṭiggaṇhātūti adhivāsanavasena sampaṭicchatūti atthoti āha “khamatū”ti. Sadevakena lokena nissaraṇanti araṇīyato ariyo, tathāgatoti āha “ariyassa vinayeti buddhassa bhagavato sāsane”ti. Puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ karontoti kāmaṃ “vuddhi hesā”ti dhammādhiṭṭhānavasena vākyaṃ āraddhaṃ, tathāpi desanaṃ pana puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ karonto “saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti āhāti yojanā.

A 'transgression' (accaya) is a violation that crushes good custom, hence it is called an 'offense' (aparādho). Or, 'accayo' is that by which one passes beyond or transgresses; it is the unwholesome state that causes violation. It is called 'aparādho' because one offends by it. For it proceeds by overpowering the person who offends. Therefore, it is said: 'It proceeds, having transgressed and overpowered.' 'Let him accept' (paṭiggaṇhātu) means 'let him consent' by way of acquiescence; this is the meaning, hence it is said: 'Let him forgive.' He is noble (ariyo) because he is remote from defilements (araṇīyato); he is the Tathāgata, the liberation from the world with its gods. Thus it is said: 'in the discipline of the noble one,' meaning 'in the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One.' Although the statement 'vuddhi hesā' (this is growth) was begun with the Dhamma as its basis, nevertheless, delivering the teaching by making the individual its foundation, it is said: 'He undertakes restraint.' This is the connection.

Saṅkavāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṅkavāsa Sutta is finished.

Samaṇavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Samaṇa Vagga is finished.

(10) 5. Loṇakapallavaggo

(10) 5. The Chapter on the Lump of Salt

1. Accāyikasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Accāyika Sutta

93. Pañcamassa paṭhame atipātikānīti sīghaṃ pavattetabbāni. Karaṇīyānīti ettha avassake anīyasaddo daṭṭhabboti āha “avassakiccānī”ti. Nikkhantasetaṅkurānīti bījato nikkhantasetaṅkurāni. Sesamettha uttānameva.

93. In the first of the fifth, 'urgent' (atipātikāni) means they should be carried out quickly. In 'to be done' (karaṇīyāni), the suffix 'anīya' should be understood in the sense of 'necessary' (avassaka); thus it is said: 'necessary duties' (avassakiccāni). 'With white shoots emerged' (nikkhantasetaṅkurāni) refers to those with white shoots that have emerged from the seeds. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Accāyikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Accāyika Sutta is finished.

2. Pavivekasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Paviveka Sutta

94. Dutiye sāṇehi vākehi nibbattitāni sāṇāni. Missasāṇāni masāṇāni na bhaṅgāni. Erakatiṇādīnīti ādi-saddena akkamakacikadalivākādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Erakādīhi katāni hi chavāni lāmakāni dussānīti “chavadussānī”ti vattabbataṃ labhanti. Kuṇḍakanti tanutaraṃ [V 2.0175] taṇḍulappakaraṇaṃ. Pañca dussīlyānīti pāṇātipātādīni pañca. Cattāro āsavāti kāmāsavādayo cattāro āsavā. Sīlaggappattoti sīlena, sīlassa vā aggappatto.

94. In the second, 'sāṇāni' are cloths made from hemp fibers or bark. 'Masāṇāni' are mixed hemp cloths, not (pure) hemp. By the word 'etc.' in 'eraka grass, etc.' (erakatiṇādīni), there is the inclusion of akkama, kacikadali bark, and similar materials. Garments made from eraka and other materials are inferior and thus deserve to be called 'wretched garments' (chavadussāni). 'Kuṇḍakaṃ' is very fine rice powder. 'Five kinds of misconduct' (pañca dussīlyāni) are the five beginning with the destruction of life. 'Four taints' (cattāro āsavā) are the four taints beginning with the taint of sensual desire. 'Attained the highest in virtue' (sīlaggappatto) means having attained the highest through virtue, or the highest of virtue.

Pavivekasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Paviveka Sutta is finished.

3. Saradasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sarada Sutta

95. Tatiye [M 2.0193] viddheti dūrībhūte. Dūrabhāvo ca ākāsassa valāhakavigamena hotīti āha “valāhakavigamena dūrībhūte”ti. Teneva hi “viddhe vigatavalāhake”ti vuttaṃ. Nabhaṃ abbhussakkamānoti ākāsaṃ abhilaṅghanto. Iminā taruṇasūriyabhāvo dassito. Nātidūrodite hi ādicce taruṇasūriyasamaññā. Duvidhamevassa saṃyojanaṃ natthīti orambhāgiyauddhambhāgiyavasena duvidhampi saṃyojanaṃ assa paṭhamajjhānalābhino ariyasāvakassa natthi. Kasmā panassa uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanampi natthīti vuttaṃ. Orambhāgiyasaṃyojanānameva hettha pahānaṃ vuttanti āha “itarampī”tiādi, itaraṃ uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanaṃ puna imaṃ lokaṃ paṭisandhivasena ānetuṃ asamatthatāya natthīti vuttanti attho. Jhānalābhino hi sabbepi ariyā brahmalokūpapannā heṭṭhā na uppajjanti, uddhaṃ uddhaṃ uppajjantāpi vehapphalaṃ akaniṭṭhaṃ bhavaggañca patvā na punaññattha jāyanti, tattha tattheva arahattaṃ patvā parinibbāyanti. Tenevāha “imasmiṃ sutte jhānānāgāmī nāma kathito”ti. Jhānavasena hi heṭṭhā na āgacchatīti jhānānāgāmī.

95. In the third, 'cleared' (viddhe) means become distant. The distant state of the sky is due to the removal of clouds; thus it is said: 'become distant by the removal of clouds' (valāhakavigamena dūrībhūte). For this reason, it is also stated: 'cleared, free from clouds' (viddhe vigatavalāhake). 'Ascending the sky' (nabhaṃ abbhussakkamāno) means traversing the sky. By this, the nature of the young sun is shown. For when the sun has not risen too far, it is called the young sun. 'His twofold fetter does not exist' (duvidhamevassa saṃyojanaṃ natthi) means both the lower and higher fetters are absent for the noble disciple who has attained the first jhāna. But why is it said that even his higher fetters do not exist? Because here only the abandoning of the lower fetters is mentioned; thus it is said: 'the other as well' (itarampi), etc. The meaning is that the other, the higher fetter, is said not to exist because it is incapable of bringing him back to this world through rebirth. For all noble ones who attain jhāna and are reborn in the Brahma-world do not arise in lower realms. Even as they arise in higher and higher realms, reaching the Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, and the peak of existence, they are not reborn elsewhere. There, in those very realms, they attain arahantship and attain final Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said: 'In this discourse, the non-returner by jhāna (jhānānāgāmī) is spoken of.' For by means of jhāna, he does not return below—thus, he is a non-returner by jhāna.

Saradasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sarada Sutta is finished.

4. Parisāsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Parisā Sutta

96. Catutthe paccayabāhullikāti cīvarādibāhullāya paṭipannā. Avītataṇhatāya hi taṃ taṃ parikkhārajātaṃ bahuṃ lanti ādiyantīti bahulā, te eva bāhulikā yathā “venayiko”ti (ma. ni. 1.246; a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 8). Te paccayabāhullāya yuttappayuttā hontīti cīvarādibāhullāya paṭipannā nāma honti. Sikkhāya agāravabhāvato sithilaṃ agāḷhaṃ gaṇhantīti sāthalikā. Sithilanti ca bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso. Sithilasaddena samānatthassa sathalasaddassa vasena sāthalikāti padasiddhi veditabbā. Avagamanaṭṭhenāti adhogamanaṭṭhena, orambhāgiyabhāvenāti [V 2.0176] attho. Nikkhittadhurāti oropitadhurā ujjitussāhā. Upadhiviveko nibbānaṃ. Duvidhampi vīriyanti kāyikaṃ cetasikañca vīriyaṃ.

96. In the fourth, 'given to abundance of requisites' means those who are devoted to an abundance of robes and other necessities. For, as their craving is not gone, they take and accept many kinds of requisites, thus they are 'abundant' (bahulā); from this they are called 'given to abundance' (bāhulikā), just as one is called a 'Vinaya expert' (venayiko). They are yoked and engaged in an abundance of requisites, hence they are said to be devoted to an abundance of robes and other necessities. Due to lack of respect for the training, they grasp it loosely and not firmly—thus they are called 'lax' (sāthalikā). 'Loosely' here is an abstract neuter noun. The formation of the word 'lax' (sāthalikā) should be understood from the word 'sathala,' which has a similar meaning to 'sithila.' 'In the sense of going down' means by way of descending, that is, by way of the lower fetters. 'Those who have laid down the yoke' means they have put down the yoke and given up effort. Detachment from the substrates is Nibbāna. The two kinds of effort are bodily and mental effort.

Bhaṇḍanaṃ [M 2.0194] jātaṃ etesanti bhaṇḍanajātā. Visesanassa paranipātavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana visesanassa pubbanipātavaseneva atthaṃ dassento “jātabhaṇḍanā”ti āha. Kalaho jāto etesanti kalahajātāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Kalahassa pubbabhāgoti kalahassa hetubhūtā paṭibhāgā taṃsadisī ca aniṭṭhakiriyā. Hatthaparāmāsādivasenāti kujjhitvā aññamaññassa hatthe gahetvā palapanaacchindanādivasena. “Ayaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo”tiādinā viruddhavādabhūtaṃ vivādaṃ āpannāti vivādapannā. Tenāha “viruddhavādaṃ āpannā”ti. Mukhasannissitatāya vācā idha “mukha”nti adhippetāti āha “pharusā vācā mukhasattiyo”ti.

A quarrel has arisen among them, hence they are called 'quarrel-arisen' (bhaṇḍanajātā). This is stated with the qualifier placed postpositively. However, in the commentary, explaining the meaning with the qualifier placed before, it says 'jātabhaṇḍanā' (arisen-quarrel). Similarly here: a dispute has arisen among them, hence they are called 'dispute-arisen' (kalahajātā). 'The preliminary stage of a dispute' means the cause of a dispute, contributing factors, and similar undesirable actions. 'By means of touching with the hand, etc.' means angrily seizing each other's hands, babbling, snatching, and so on. They have entered into a dispute that has become a contradictory view, saying, 'This is the Dhamma, this is not the Dhamma,' and so forth—hence they are called 'dispute-entangled' (vivādapannā). Therefore, it is said, 'they have engaged in a contradictory view.' Because speech is dependent on the mouth, here 'mouth' is intended; hence it is said, 'harsh speech is verbal daggers' (pharusā vācā mukhasattiyo).

Satipi ubhayesaṃ kalāpānaṃ paramatthato bhede pacurajanehi pana duviññeyyanānattaṃ khīrodakasammoditaṃ accantametaṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ viya hutvā tiṭṭhatīti āha “khīrodakaṃ viya bhūtā”ti. Yathā khīrañca udakañca aññamaññaṃ saṃsandati, visuṃ na hoti, ekattaṃ viya upeti, evaṃ sāmaggivasena ekattūpagatacittuppādāti attho. Mettacittaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā olokanaṃ cakkhūni viya cakkhūni nāmāti āha “upasantehi mettacakkhūhī”ti. Piyabhāvadīpakāni hi cakkhūni piyacakkhūni. Pamuditassa pīti jāyatīti pamodapaccayabalavapītimāha. Pañcavaṇṇā pīti uppajjatīti khuddikādibhedena pañcappakārā pīti uppajjati. Pītimanassāti tāya pītiyā pīṇitamanassa, passaddhiāvahehi uḷārehi pītivegehi tintacittassāti attho. Vigatadarathoti kilesapariḷāhānaṃ dūrībhāvena vūpasantadaratho.

Even though there is an ultimate distinction between the two groups, for the multitude their diversity is difficult to discern, and they stand utterly blended like milk mixed with water. Thus, it is said, 'become like milk and water.' Just as milk and water blend together, are not separate, and seem to become one, so too, the arising of the mind attains unity through concord—this is the meaning. Having established a mind of loving-kindness, one looks with what are indeed eyes; thus it is said, 'with peaceful eyes of loving-kindness.' For eyes that reveal affection are eyes of love. 'Joy arises in one who is joyful'—this refers to the strong joy that has gladness as its condition. 'Five kinds of joy arise'—this means that joy of five types arises, classified as minor and so forth. 'One whose mind is full of joy' means one whose mind is gladdened by that joy, a mind suffused by the sublime waves of joy that bring tranquility—this is the meaning. 'Free from distress' means that because the burning of the defilements has been removed, one's distress is allayed.

Kena udakena dārito pabbatappadesoti katvā āha “kandaro nāmā”tiādi. Udakassa yathāninnaṃ pavattiyā nadinibbattanabhāvena “nadikuñjo”tipi vuccati. Sāvaṭṭā nadiyo padarā. Aṭṭha māseti hemantagimhautuvasena aṭṭha māse. Khuddakā udakavāhiniyo sākhā viyāti sākhā. Khuddakasobbhā kusubbhā okārassa ukāraṃ katvā. Yattha upari unnatappadesato udakaṃ āgantvā tiṭṭhati ceva sandati ca, te [M 2.0195] kusubbhā khuddakaāvāṭā. Khuddakanadiyoti pabbatapādādito nikkhantā khuddakā nadiyo.

'By what water was this mountainous region split?' Having considered this, it was said, 'It is called a `kandara` (ravine),' and so on. Because water flows downwards and rivers are formed from it, it is also called a `nadikuñja` (river-thicket). Rivers with eddies are `padarā` (fissures). 'Eight months' refers to the eight months of the winter and summer seasons. Small watercourses are called `sākhā` (branches) because they are like branches. Small depressions are `kusubbhā`; this is by changing the 'o' to a 'u'. `Kusubbhā` are small hollows where water, having come from a higher place, both stands and flows. 'Small rivers' are the small rivers that issue from the foothills of mountains.

Parisāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Parisā Sutta is finished.

5-7. Paṭhamaājānīyasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-7. The Commentary on the First Ājānīya Sutta, etc.

97-99. Pañcame [V 2.0177] anucchavikoti rañño paribhuñjanayoggo. Hatthapādādiaṅgasamatāyāti hatthapādādiavayavasamatāya, rañño vā senāya aṅgabhūtattā rañño aṅganti vuccati. Ānetvā hunitabbanti āhunaṃ, āhutīti atthato ekanti āha “āhutisaṅkhātaṃ piṇḍapāta”nti. Dūratopi ānetvā sīlavantesu dātabbassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Piṇḍapātanti ca nidassanamattaṃ. Ānetvā hunitabbānañhi cīvarādīnaṃ catunnaṃ paccayānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ āhunanti. Taṃ arahatīti āhuneyyo. Paṭiggahetuṃ yuttoti tassa mahapphalabhāvakaraṇato paṭiggaṇhituṃ anucchaviko.

97-99. In the fifth, `anucchaviko` means suitable for the king's use. `Hatthapādādiaṅgasamatāya` refers to the symmetry of limbs such as hands and feet; or, because they are a component of the king's army, they are called the king's 'limbs'. `Āhunaṃ` is that which should be brought and offered; it is one in meaning with `āhuti`. Therefore it is said, 'almsfood designated as an offering.' This is a term for what should be brought even from afar and given to the virtuous. And 'almsfood' is merely an example, for `āhuna` is a term for the four requisites, such as robes, which should be brought and offered. `Āhuneyyo` is one who is worthy of that offering (`taṃ arahati`). He is suitable to receive it, because his receiving it causes it to be of great fruit.

Pāhunakabhattassāti disavidisato āgatānaṃ piyamanāpānaṃ ñātimittānaṃ atthāya sakkāre paṭiyattassa āgantukabhattassa. Tañhi ṭhapetvā te tathārūpe pāhunake saṅghasseva dātuṃ yuttaṃ, saṅghova taṃ paṭiggahetuṃ yutto. Saṅghasadiso hi pāhunako natthi. Tathā hesa ekasmiṃ buddhantare vītivatte dissati, kadāci asaṅkhyeyyepi kappe vītivatte. Abbokiṇṇañca piyamanāpatādikarehi dhammehi samannāgato. Evaṃ pāhunamassa dātuṃ yuttaṃ, pāhunañca paṭiggahetuṃ yuttoti pāhuneyyo. Ayañhettha adhippāyo “ñātimittā vippavuṭṭhā na cirasseva samāgacchanti, anavaṭṭhitā ca tesu piyamanāpatā, na evamariyasaṅgho, tasmā saṅghova pāhuneyyo”ti.

'Of the meal for guests' means of the guest-meal prepared with honor for the benefit of dear and agreeable relatives and friends who have come from various directions. For, setting aside such guests, it is fitting to give it to the Sangha alone, and the Sangha alone is worthy to receive it. For there is no guest like the Sangha. Such a guest is seen only after a Buddha-interval has passed, and sometimes only after incalculable aeons have passed. And the Sangha is endowed with uninterrupted qualities that make it dear and agreeable. Thus, it is fitting to give a guest-gift to it, and it is fitting to receive a guest-gift; hence, it is called `pāhuneyyo`, worthy of hospitality. Here, this is the intended meaning: 'Relatives and friends who live abroad do not meet again for a long time, and the dearness and agreeableness felt for them is unstable—but it is not so with the noble Sangha. Therefore, the Sangha alone is worthy of hospitality.'

Dakkhanti etāya sattā yathādhippetāhi sampattīhi vaḍḍhantīti dakkhiṇā, paralokaṃ saddahitvā dānaṃ. Taṃ dakkhiṇaṃ arahati, dakkhiṇāya vā hito yasmā mahapphalakaraṇatāya visodhetīti dakkhiṇeyyo.

'Beings grow (`vaḍḍhanti`) with desired attainments by this,' thus it is `dakkhiṇā`; it is a gift given with faith in the next world. One is worthy of that offering (`dakkhiṇā`), or is beneficial for an offering because one purifies it by causing it to be of great fruit; thus one is `dakkhiṇeyyo`.

Puññatthikehi añjali karaṇīyo etthāti añjalikaraṇīyo. Ubho hettha sirasi patiṭṭhāpetvā sabbalokena kayiramānaṃ añjalikammaṃ arahatīti [M 2.0196] vā añjalikaraṇīyo. Tenāha “añjalipaggahaṇassa anucchaviko”ti.

He is one to whom a reverential salutation should be made by those desiring merit; thus, he is `añjalikaraṇīyo`. Or, because he is worthy of the act of reverence performed by the entire world—placing both hands upon the head—he is `añjalikaraṇīyo`. Therefore, it is said: 'Suitable for receiving a reverential salutation.'

Yadipi pāḷiyaṃ “anuttara”nti vuttaṃ, natthi ito uttaraṃ visiṭṭhanti hi anuttaraṃ, samampissa pana natthīti dassento “asadisa”nti āha. Khittaṃ vuttaṃ bījaṃ mahapphalabhāvakaraṇena tāyati rakkhati, khipanti vapanti ettha bījānīti vā khettaṃ, kedārādi, khettaṃ viya khettaṃ, puññānaṃ khettaṃ puññakkhettaṃ. Yathā hi rañño vā amaccassa vā [V 2.0178] sālīnaṃ vā yavānaṃ vā viruhanaṭṭhānaṃ “rañño sālikkhetaṃ yavakkheta”nti vuccati, evaṃ saṅgho sabbalokassa puññānaṃ viruhanaṭṭhānaṃ. Saṅghaṃ nissāya hi lokassa nānappakārahitasukhasaṃvattanikāni puññāni viruhanti, tasmā saṅgho anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Chaṭṭhasattamāni uttānatthāneva.

Although in the Pāli it is said `anuttara` (unsurpassed)—for `anuttara` means that there is nothing superior or more excellent than it—to show that there is nothing even equal to it, it is said `asadisa` (incomparable). A field (`khettaṃ`) is so called because it protects (`tāyati`) a sown seed by causing it to be of great fruit; or, it is a place where they sow (`khipanti`) seeds, like a cultivated plot. A field of merits is `puññakkhettaṃ`. Just as a place where a king's or a minister's rice or barley grows is called 'the king's rice field' or 'barley field,' so the Sangha is the place where the merits of the entire world grow. For, dependent on the Sangha, various kinds of merits that lead to welfare and happiness for the world grow. Therefore, the Sangha is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. The rest is easily understood. The sixth and seventh are clear in meaning.

Paṭhamaājānīyasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Ājānīya Sutta, etc., is finished.

8. Potthakasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Potthaka Sutta.

100. Aṭṭhame navoti navavāyimo. Tenāha “karaṇaṃ upādāya vuccatī”ti. Vākamayavatthanti sāṇādivākasāṭakaṃ. Dubbaṇṇoti vivaṇṇo. Dukkhasamphassoti kharasamphasso. Appaṃ agghatīti appaggho. Atibahuṃ agghanto kahāpaṇagghanako hoti. Paribhogamajjhimoti paribhogakālavasena majjhimo. So hi navabhāvaṃ atikkamitvā jiṇṇabhāvaṃ appatto majjhe paribhogakālepi dubbaṇṇo ca dukkhasamphasso ca appagghoyeva hoti. Atibahuṃ agghanto aḍḍhaṃ agghati, jiṇṇakāle pana aḍḍhamāsakaṃ vā kākaṇikaṃ vā agghati. Ukkhaliparipuñchananti kāḷukkhaliparipuñchanaṃ. Navotipi upasampadāya pañcavassakālato heṭṭhā jātiyā saṭṭhivassopi navoyeva. Dubbaṇṇatāyāti sarīravaṇṇenapi guṇavaṇṇenapi dubbaṇṇatāya. Dussīlassa hi parisamajjhe nittejatāya sarīravaṇṇopi na sampajjati, guṇavaṇṇena vattabbameva natthi. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana sarīravaṇṇena dubbaṇṇatāpi guṇavaṇṇassa abhāvena dubbaṇṇatāyāti vuttaṃ.

100. In the eighth, `nava` (new) means newly woven. Therefore it is said, 'It is so called with reference to its making.' `Vākamayavattha` (cloth made of fiber) means a garment made of hemp fiber and so forth. `Dubbaṇṇa` (of poor color) means `vivaṇṇa` (discolored). `Dukkhasamphassa` (unpleasant to the touch) means `kharasamphasso` (rough to the touch). `Appaggha` (of little value) is so called because `appaṃ agghati` (it is worth little). At most, it is worth a kahāpaṇa. `Paribhogamajjhima` (of medium use) means medium in terms of its period of use. For having passed its new state and not yet reached an old state, even during its middle period of use, it is indeed of poor color, rough to the touch, and of little value. At most, it is worth half a kahāpaṇa, but in its old state, it is worth only half a māsaka or a kākaṇika. `Ukkhaliparipuñchana` (pot-wiper) means a wiper for a black pot. `Nava` (new) also refers to a monk: even if one is sixty years old by birth, if he is within five years of his higher ordination, he is still considered 'new'. `Dubbaṇṇatāya` (by being of poor color) means being of poor color in terms of bodily appearance and in terms of the luster of his virtues. For an immoral person, due to their lack of splendor in the midst of an assembly, even their bodily appearance is not good, and as for the luster of their virtues, there is nothing to be said. However, in the Commentary, it is said that even being of poor color in terms of bodily appearance is due to the absence of the luster of virtue.

Ye kho panassāti ye kho pana tassa upaṭṭhākā vā ñātimittādayo vā etaṃ puggalaṃ sevanti. Tesanti tesaṃ puggalānaṃ cha satthāre sevantānaṃ [M 2.0197] micchādiṭṭhikānaṃ viya. Devadatte sevantānaṃ kokālikādīnaṃ viya ca taṃ sevanaṃ dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya hoti. Majjhimoti pañcavassakālato paṭṭhāya yāva navavassakālā majjhimo nāma. Theroti dasavassato paṭṭhāya thero nāma. Evamāhaṃsūti evaṃ vadanti. Kiṃ nu kho tuyhanti tuyhaṃ bālassa bhaṇitena ko atthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathārūpanti tathājātikaṃ tathāsabhāvaṃ ukkhepanīyakammassa kāraṇabhūtaṃ.

`Ye kho panassa` (But those who...) means those attendants, relatives, friends, and so forth, who associate with that person. `Tesaṃ` (For them) means that for those individuals, just as for those with wrong views who follow the six teachers, and just as for Kokālika and others who followed Devadatta, that association leads to their long-term harm and suffering. `Majjhima` (intermediate) means one is called `majjhima` from the five-year period up to the nine-year period since ordination. `Thera` (elder) means one is called `thera` from ten years onwards. `Evamāhaṃsu` (Thus they said) means 'they say thus.' `Kiṃ nu kho tuyhaṃ` (What indeed is it to you?) means, 'What is the use of what you, a fool, have said?' `Tathārūpaṃ` (such a one) means one of such a kind, of such a nature, who has become the cause for an act of suspension.

Tīhi kappāsaaṃsūhi suttaṃ kantitvā katavatthanti tayo kappāsaaṃsū gahetvā kantitasuttena vāyitaṃ sukhumavatthaṃ, taṃ navavāyimaṃ anagghaṃ hoti, paribhogamajjhimaṃ vīsampi tiṃsampi sahassāni agghati, jiṇṇakāle, aṭṭhapi dasapi sahassāni agghati.

Tīhi kappāsaaṃsūhi suttaṃ kantitvā katavattha (cloth made by spinning thread from three cotton fibers) means fine cloth woven with thread spun by taking three cotton fibers. That newly woven cloth is priceless. When in moderate use, it is worth twenty or thirty thousand, and when old, it is worth eight or ten thousand.

Tesaṃ [V 2.0179] taṃ hotīti tesaṃ sammāsambuddhādayo sevantā viya taṃ sevanaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya hoti. Sammāsambuddhañhi ekaṃ nissāya yāvajjakālā muccanakasattānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi, tathā sāriputtattheramahāmoggallānatthere avasese ca asīti mahāsāvake nissāya saggagatasattānaṃ pamāṇaṃ natthi, yāvajjakālā tesaṃ diṭṭhānugatiṃ paṭipannasattānampi pamāṇaṃ natthiyeva. Ādheyyaṃ gacchatīti tassa mahātherassa taṃ atthanissitaṃ vacanaṃ yathā gandhakaraṇḍake kāsikavatthaṃ ādhātabbataṃ ṭhapetabbataṃ gacchati, evaṃ uttamaṅge sirasmiṃ hadaye ca ādhātabbataṃ ṭhapetabbataṃ gacchati.

Tesaṃ taṃ hoti (For them, that occurs) means that for them, just as for those who associate with the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One and others, that association leads to long-term welfare and happiness. For, relying on the one Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, there is no measure of the beings liberated until the present time. Similarly, relying on the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and the remaining eighty great disciples, there is no measure of the beings who have gone to heaven. And until the present time, there is indeed no measure of the beings who have entered upon their example. Ādheyyaṃ gacchati (it goes to a receptacle) means that statement of the great elder, based on that meaning, goes to being placed and kept on the crown of the head and in the heart, just as a Kāsika cloth is to be placed and kept in a sandalwood box.

Potthakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Potthaka Sutta is finished.

9. Loṇakapallasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Loṇakapalla Sutta

101. Navame yathā yathā kammaṃ karotīti yena yena pakārena pāṇaghātādipāpakammaṃ karoti. Vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvediyatevāti avadhāraṇena kammasiddhiyaṃ tabbipākassa appavatti nāma natthīti dīpeti. Tenevāha “na hi sakkā”tiādi. Evaṃ santanti bhummatthe upayogavacananti āha “evaṃ sante”ti. Abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇanirodhenāti kammaviññāṇassa āyatiṃ anuppattidhammatāpajjanena.

101. In the ninth sutta, yathā yathā kammaṃ karoti (in whatever way one does the deed) means in whatever manner one commits evil deeds such as killing living beings and so forth. Vipākaṃ paṭisaṃvediyateva (one invariably experiences the result) indicates with emphasis that there is no such thing as the non-occurrence of its result once the kamma is accomplished. Therefore it is said, 'For it is impossible,' and so on. Evaṃ santaṃ (thus being) is a locative absolute usage, hence it is said, 'evaṃ sante (thus being).' Abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇanirodhena (by the cessation of volitional consciousness) means by the attainment of the nature of non-arising of kammic consciousness in the future.

“Ayampi [M 2.0198] kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatīto”tiādinā kāyassa asubhāniccādiākāraanupassanā kāyabhāvanāti āha “kāyānupassanāsaṅkhātāya tāya bhāvanāyā”ti. Rāgādīnanti ādi-saddena dosamohānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. “Rāgo kho, āvuso, pamāṇakaraṇo, doso pamāṇakaraṇo, moho pamāṇakaraṇo, te khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṃkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā”ti (ma. ni. 1.459) hi vuttaṃ.

By 'This body too is of such a nature, subject to such conditions, and not exempt from this fate,' and so on, the contemplation of the body's foulness, impermanence, and other aspects is called 'development of the body.' Hence it is said, 'by that development designated as contemplation of the body.' Rāgādīnaṃ (of lust and so on) means that by the term 'and so on,' hatred and delusion should be understood to be included. For it is said: 'Friend, lust is a maker of limits, hatred is a maker of limits, delusion is a maker of limits. These are abandoned by a monk whose taints are destroyed, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.459).

Yathā hi pabbatapāde pūtipaṇṇassa udakaṃ nāma hoti, kāḷavaṇṇaṃ olokentānaṃ byāmasataṃ gambhīraṃ viya khāyati, yaṭṭhiṃ vā rajjuṃ vā gahetvā minantassa piṭṭhipādoddharaṇamattampi na hoti, evameva ekaccassa yāva rāgādayo nuppajjanti, tāva taṃ puggalaṃ sañjānituṃ na sakkā hoti, sotāpanno viya sakadāgāmī viya anāgāmī viya ca khāyati. Yadā panassa rāgādayo uppajjanti, tadā ratto duṭṭho mūḷhoti paññāyati. Iti [V 2.0180] te rāgādayo “ettako aya”nti puggalassa pamāṇaṃ dassentāva uppajjantīti pamāṇakaraṇā nāma vuttā.

Just as at the foot of a mountain there is a pool of water from rotten leaves, dark in color, appearing to be a hundred fathoms deep to those who look at it, yet when one takes a stick or a rope to measure it, there is not even enough water to wet the back of the foot—in the same way, as long as lust and other defilements do not arise in a certain person, it is impossible to recognize him. He may appear like a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner. But when lust and other defilements arise in him, then he is clearly seen as greedy, hateful, or deluded. Thus, these defilements arise showing the measure of a person, as if to say, 'This is how much he is.' Therefore, they are called 'measure-makers.'

Jāpetunti jinadhanaṃ kātuṃ. Soti rājā, mahāmatto vā. Assāti añjaliṃ paggahetvā yācantassa. Sesamettha uttānameva.

`Jāpetuṃ` means to accumulate wealth. `So` means the king or a great minister. `Assa` means to one begging with clasped hands. The rest here is indeed clear.

Loṇakapallasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Loṇakapalla Sutta is finished.

10. Paṃsudhovakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Paṃsudhovaka Sutta

102. Dasame anīhatadosanti anapanītathūlakāḷakaṃ. Anapanītakasāvanti anapagatasukhumakāḷakaṃ. Pahaṭamattanti āhaṭamattaṃ.

102. In the tenth sutta, anīhatadosaṃ (with blemish not removed) means the coarse blackness has not been removed. Anapanītakasāvaṃ (with stain not removed) means the subtle blackness has not been removed. Pahaṭamattaṃ (merely struck) means merely brought.

Dasakusalakammapathavasena uppannaṃ cittaṃ cittameva, vipassanāpādakaaṭṭhasamāpatticittaṃ vipassanācittañca tato cittato adhikaṃ cittanti adhicittanti āha “adhicittanti samathavipassanācitta”nti. Anuyuttassāti anuppannassa uppādanavasena uppannassa paṭibrūhanavasena anu anu yuttassa, tattha yuttappayuttassāti attho. Ettha ca purebhattaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto [M 2.0199] nisīdanaṃ ādāya “asukasmiṃ rukkhamūle vā vanasaṇḍe vā pabbhāre vā samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī”ti nikkhamantopi tattha gantvā hatthehi vā pādehi vā nisajjaṭṭhānato tiṇapaṇṇāni apanentopi adhicittaṃ anuyuttoyeva. Nisīditvā pana hatthapāde dhovitvā mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā bhāvanaṃ anuyuñjanto bhāvanāya appanaṃ appattāyapi adhicittamanuyuttoyeva tadatthenapi taṃsaddavohārato. Cittasampannoti dhammacittassa samannāgatattā sampannacitto. Paṇḍitajātikoti paṇḍitasabhāvo.

The mind arisen through the ten wholesome courses of action is merely mind; but the mind that is the basis for insight, namely the eight attainments, and the mind of insight, is a mind higher than that mind, and thus it is called 'higher mind.' Therefore, it is said: 'Higher mind means the mind of serenity and insight.' Anuyuttassa (of one devoted to it) means one who is repeatedly engaged in bringing forth what has not yet arisen, and in developing what has arisen; this is the meaning of 'engaged and applied' in that context. Here, even one who, having gone for alms in the morning, returned from the alms round after the meal, taken his sitting cloth, and set out thinking, 'I will practice the ascetic's duties at the root of such-and-such a tree, in a forest grove, or in a cave,' or who, having gone there, clears away grass and leaves from his sitting place with hands or feet—such a one is still devoted to the higher mind. Moreover, one who sits down, washes hands and feet, takes up the basic meditation subject, and applies oneself to meditation—even if absorption is not yet attained—is still devoted to the higher mind, by the very meaning of the term and its usage. Cittasampanno (perfect in mind) means one whose mind is perfected by being endowed with a mind of Dhamma. Paṇḍitajātiko (of wise nature) means having the nature of the wise.

Kāme ārabbhāti vatthukāme ārabbha. Kāmarāgasaṅkhātena vā kāmena paṭisaṃyutto vitakko kāmavitakko. Byāpajjati cittaṃ etenāti byāpādo, doso. Vihiṃsanti etāya satte, vihiṃsanaṃ vā tesaṃ etanti vihiṃsā, paresaṃ viheṭhanākārena pavattassa karuṇāpaṭipakkhassa pāpadhammassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ñātake ārabbha uppanno vitakkoti ñātake ārabbha gehassitapemavasena uppanno vitakko. Janapadamārabbha uppanno vitakkoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Aho vata maṃ…pe… uppanno vitakkoti “aho vata maṃ pare na avajāneyyuṃ, na heṭṭhā katvā maññeyyuṃ, pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya [V 2.0181] garuṃ kareyyu”nti evaṃ uppannavitakko. Dasavipassanupakkilesavitakkāti obhāsādidasavipassanupakkilese ārabbha uppannavitakkā.

Kāme ārabbha (based on sensual pleasures) means based on objective sensual pleasures. Or, the thought connected with sensual pleasure, termed as sensual lust, is sensual thought. Byāpādo (ill will) is so called because the mind is harmed (byāpajjati) by this; it is hatred (doso). Vihiṃsā (violence) is so called because they harm (vihiṃsanti) beings with this, or it is the harming of them; this is a designation for the evil quality that opposes compassion, operating in the manner of injuring others. The thought arisen regarding relatives (ñātake ārabbha uppanno vitakko) is the thought arisen based on household affection, regarding relatives. The thought arisen regarding the country (janapadamārabbha uppanno vitakko)—here too, the same method applies. 'Oh, if only...' and so forth—the thought arisen is: 'Oh, if only others would not despise me, would not think little of me, would respect me like a stone parasol.' Such is the arisen thought. The ten insight-corruption thoughts (dasavipassanupakkilesavitakkā) refer to thoughts arisen based on the ten insight-corruptions, such as illumination and so on.

Avasiṭṭhā dhammavitakkā etassāti avasiṭṭhadhammavitakko, vipassanāsamādhi. Na ekaggabhāvappatto na ekaggataṃ patto. Ekaṃ udetīti hi ekodi, paṭipakkhehi anabhibhūtattā aggaṃ seṭṭhaṃ hutvā udetīti attho. Seṭṭhopi hi loke ekoti vuccati, ekasmiṃ ārammaṇe samādhānavasena pavattacittassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ekodissa bhāvo ekodibhāvo, ekaggatāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

Avasiṭṭhadhammavitakko (one with remaining thoughts on the Dhamma) is so called because thoughts on the Dhamma remain for him; this is insight-concentration. Not attained to one-pointedness means not reached one-pointedness. Ekodi is so called because it arises as one (ekaṃ udeti); the meaning is that it arises as the highest and best, being unopposed by counterforces. For even in the world, the best is called 'one.' This is a designation for the mind that operates by concentrating on a single object. The state of being ekodi is ekodibhāva, which is a designation for one-pointedness.

Niyakajjhattanti attasantānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Gocarajjhattanti idha nibbānaṃ adhippetaṃ. Tenāha “ekasmiṃ nibbānagocareyeva tiṭṭhatī”ti. Suṭṭhu nisīdatīti samādhipaṭipakkhe kilese sannisīdento suṭṭhu nisīdati. Ekaggaṃ hotīti abyaggabhāvappattiyā ekaggaṃ hoti. Sammā ādhiyatīti yathā ārammaṇe suṭṭhu appitaṃ hoti, evaṃ sammā sammadeva ādhiyati.

Niyakajjhattaṃ (internal to oneself) is a designation for one's own continuity. Gocarajjhattaṃ (internal to the range)—here, Nibbāna is intended. Therefore, it is said, 'He stands solely in the range of Nibbāna.' Suṭṭhu nisīdati (he sits well) means he sits well by suppressing the defilements opposed to concentration. Ekaggaṃ hoti (he becomes one-pointed) means he becomes one-pointed by attaining a state of non-distraction. Sammā ādhiyati (he is rightly directed) means that just as the mind is well applied to its object, so it is rightly and properly directed.

Abhiññā [M 2.0200] sacchikaraṇīyassāti ettha “abhiññāya sacchikaraṇīyassā”ti vattabbe “abhiññā”ti ya-kāralopena pana puna kālakiriyāniddeso katoti āha “abhijānitvā paccakkhaṃ kātabbassā”ti. Abhiññāya iddhividhādiñāṇena sacchikiriyaṃ iddhividhapaccanubhavanādikaṃ abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyanti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇātīti ettha pana yassa paccakkhaṃ atthi, so sakkhī, sakkhino bhabbatā sakkhibhabbatā, sakkhibhavananti vuttaṃ hoti. Sakkhī ca so bhabbo cāti sakkhibhabbo. Ayañhi iddhividhādīnaṃ bhabbo tattha ca sakkhīti sakkhibhabbo, tassa bhāvo sakkhibhabbatā, taṃ pāpuṇātīti attho.

'To be realized by direct knowledge' (abhiññā sacchikaraṇīyassa)—here, where it should have been said 'to be realized by direct knowledge' (abhiññāya sacchikaraṇīyassa), the letter 'ya' is elided to read 'direct knowledge' (abhiññā), and the specification of the action is given again. Thus, it is said, 'to be done by directly knowing' (abhijānitvā paccakkhaṃ kātabbassa). Or, the realization by direct knowledge (abhiññāya), that is, by the knowledge of psychic powers and so on, of the direct experiencing of psychic powers and the like—this is what is meant by 'to be realized by direct knowledge' (abhiññāsacchikaraṇīya); this is how the meaning should be understood here. 'He attains the state of being a capable witness' (sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti)—here, one who has direct experience is a witness (sakkhī); the state of being capable of being a witness is 'sakkhibhabbatā,' meaning 'becoming a witness' (sakkhibhavana).
