One who is both a witness and capable is a 'sakkhibhabbo.' For he is capable of psychic powers and so on, and is a witness in that regard—thus, 'sakkhibhabbo.' The state of that person is 'sakkhibhabbatā,' and he attains it—this is the meaning.

Abhiññāpādakajjhānādibhedeti ettha abhiññāpādā ca abhiññāpādakajjhānañca abhiññāpādakajjhānāni. Ādi-saddena arahattañca arahattassa vipassanā ca saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Teneva majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.198) –

'In the various kinds, such as the jhānas that are the basis for direct knowledge' (abhiññāpādakajjhānādibhede)—here, 'the jhānas that are the basis for direct knowledge' (abhiññāpādakajjhānāni) refers to the bases for direct knowledge and the jhānas that are the basis for direct knowledge. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), it should be understood that Arahantship and the insight leading to Arahantship are also included. For this reason, in the commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya (M.N. Aṭṭh. 2.198), it is said:

“Sati satiāyataneti sati satikāraṇe. Kiñcettha kāraṇaṃ? Abhiññā vā abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ vā, avasāne pana arahattaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ arahattassa vipassanā vāti veditabba”nti vuttaṃ.

'Mindfulness in the sphere of mindfulness' (sati satiāyatane) means mindfulness in the cause of mindfulness. And what is the cause here? It should be understood that the cause is either direct knowledge or the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, or, in the end, Arahantship or the insight for Arahantship.

Yañhi taṃ tatra tatra sakkhibhabbatāsaṅkhātaṃ iddhividhapaccanubhavanādi, tassa abhiññā kāraṇaṃ[V 2.0182]. Atha iddhividhapaccanubhavanādi abhiññā, evaṃ sati abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Avasāne chaṭṭhābhiññāya pana arahattaṃ, arahattassa vipassanā vā kāraṇaṃ. Arahattañhi “kudāssu nāmāhaṃ tadāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharissāmi, yadariyā etarahi upasampajja viharantī”ti (ma. ni. 1.465; 3.307) anuttaresu vimokkhesu pihaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā abhiññā nibbattentassa kāraṇaṃ. Idañca sādhāraṇaṃ na hoti, sādhāraṇavasena pana arahattassa vipassanā kāraṇaṃ. Imasmiñhi sutte arahattaphalavasena chaṭṭhābhiññā vuttā. Tenevāha “āsavānaṃ khayātiādi cettha phalasamāpattivasena vuttanti veditabba”nti.

For that which is known here and there as the state of being a capable witness, namely, the experiencing of the various kinds of psychic powers and so on, its cause is direct knowledge. Then, if the experiencing of psychic powers and so on is direct knowledge, this being so, the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge is the cause. Finally, for the sixth direct knowledge, the cause is Arahantship, or insight for Arahantship. For Arahantship is the cause for one who generates direct knowledge, having established a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, thinking, 'When, indeed, shall I enter and abide in that sphere in which the noble ones now enter and abide?' (M.N. 1.465; 3.307). And this is not common; but in a general sense, insight is the cause for Arahantship. In this discourse, the sixth direct knowledge is spoken of in terms of the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said: 'it should be understood that “the destruction of the taints,” etc., is spoken of here in terms of the attainment of the fruit.'

Paṃsudhovakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Paṃsudhovaka Sutta is concluded.

11. Nimittasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Nimitta Sutta

103. Ekādasame [M 2.0201] yehi phalaṃ nimīyati, uppajjanaṭṭhāne pakkhipamānaṃ viya hoti, tāni nimittāni. Tenāha “tīṇi kāraṇānī”ti. Kālena kālanti ettha kālenāti bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Kālanti ca upayogavacananti āha “kāle kāle”ti. Manasi kātabbāti citte kātabbā, uppādetabbāti attho. Upalakkhitasamādhānākāro samādhiyeva idha samādhinimittanti āha “ekaggatā hi idha samādhinimittanti vuttā”ti. Ṭhānaṃ taṃ cittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyyāti ettha ṭhānaṃ atthīti vacanaseso. Taṃ bhāvanācittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyya, tassa saṃvattanassa kāraṇaṃ atthīti attho. Taṃ vā manasikaraṇaṃ cittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyya, etassa ṭhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ atthīti attho. Tenāha “kāraṇaṃ vijjatī”tiādi. Ñāṇajavanti saṅkhāresu aniccādivasena pavattamānaṃ paññājavaṃ.

103. In the eleventh sutta: those things by which the fruit is indicated, as if being placed in the place of arising, are signs (nimittāni). Therefore, it is said, 'three causes.' In the phrase 'kālena kālaṃ' (from time to time), 'kālena' is the instrumental case used in the sense of the locative, and 'kālaṃ' is a term of application; hence it is said, 'kāle kāle' (from time to time). 'To be attended to' (manasi kātabbā) means to be done in the mind; the meaning is 'to be produced.' The characteristic of noted collectedness is concentration itself, which is the sign of concentration here; hence it is said, 'for one-pointedness is said to be the sign of concentration here.' In the phrase 'it is a basis that that mind might turn to laziness' (ṭhānaṃ taṃ cittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyya), the words 'there is' (atthi) are the remainder of the statement. The meaning is: that meditation mind might turn to laziness, and there is a cause for its turning. Or, that attention might cause the mind to turn to laziness; there is a basis, a cause for this. Therefore, it is said, 'a cause exists,' etc. 'Swiftness of knowledge' (ñāṇajavaṃ) is the swiftness of wisdom (paññājavaṃ) that proceeds with regard to formations as impermanent, etc.

Yaṃ kiñci suvaṇṇatāpanayoggaaṅgārabhājanaṃ idha “ukkā”ti adhippetanti āha “aṅgārakapalla”nti. Sajjeyyāti yathā tattha pakkhittaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ tappati, evaṃ paṭiyādiyeyya. Ālimpeyyāti ādiyeyya, jaleyyāti attho. Tenāha “tattha aṅgāre…pe… gāhāpeyyā”ti. Mūsāya vā pakkhipeyyāti tattake vā pakkhipeyya. Upadhāretīti sallakkheti.

Whatever charcoal vessel is suitable for heating gold is here intended by 'ukkā'; hence it is said, 'a charcoal pan' (aṅgārakapalla). 'He should prepare' (sajjeyya) means he should prepare it in such a way that gold placed therein is heated. 'He should light' (ālimpeyya) means he should kindle; the meaning is, he should set it ablaze. Therefore, it is said, 'there, having placed coals... he should have it kindled.' 'Or he should place it in a crucible' (mūsāya vā pakkhipeyya) means he should place it in such a vessel. 'He observes' (upadhāreti) means he marks well (sallakkheti).

Nimittasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nimitta Sutta is concluded.

Loṇakapallavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Loṇakapalla Vagga is concluded.

Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Second Fifty is concluded.

3. Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

3. The Third Fifty

(11) 1. Sambodhavaggo

(11) 1. The Chapter on Enlightenment

1-3. Pubbevasambodhasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-3. Commentary on the Pubbevasambodha Sutta and Others

104-106. Tatiyassa [M 2.0202][V 2.0183] paṭhame sambodhito pubbevāti sambodho vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ “sāmaṃ sammā bujjhi etenā”ti katvā, tato pubbeyevāti attho. Tenāha “ariyamaggappattito aparabhāgeyevā”ti. Bodhisattasseva satoti ettha yathā udakato uggantvā ṭhitaṃ paripākagataṃ padumaṃ sūriyarasmisamphassena avassaṃ bujjhissatīti bujjhanakapadumanti vuccati. Evaṃ buddhānaṃ santike byākaraṇassa laddhattā avassaṃ anantarāyena pāramiyo pūretvā bujjhissatīti bujjhanakasattoti bodhisatto. Tenāha “bujjhanakasattasseva…pe… ārabhantasseva sato”ti. Yā vā esā catumaggañāṇasaṅkhātā bodhi, “taṃ bodhiṃ kudāssu nāmāhaṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti patthayamāno paṭipajjatīti bodhiyaṃ satto āsattotipi bodhisatto. Tenāha “sambodhiyā vā sattasseva laggasseva sato”ti.

104-106. In the first sutta of the third paṇṇāsaka: 'Before enlightenment' (sambodhito pubbeva) means even before that which is called enlightenment (sambodho), namely, the knowledge in the four paths, so called because 'by this one awakens rightly by oneself.' Therefore, it is said, 'even in the period before attaining the noble path.' Regarding 'of the Bodhisatta himself being' (bodhisattasseva sato): just as a mature lotus that has risen from the water and is standing ready will certainly blossom upon contact with the sun's rays and is thus called a 'blossoming lotus' (bujjhanakapadumaṃ), so too, because he has received the prediction in the presence of the Buddhas, he will certainly awaken after fulfilling the perfections without obstacle, and is thus a 'being who will awaken' (bujjhanakasatto), a Bodhisatta. Therefore, it is said, 'of the being destined to awaken... of him striving.' Alternatively, there is that enlightenment designated as the knowledge of the four paths; because he practices while aspiring, 'When shall I attain that enlightenment?', he is attached (satto) or clinging (āsatto) to enlightenment (bodhi), thus he is a Bodhisatta. Therefore, it is said, 'or of one who is attached, who is clinging to enlightenment.'

Atha vā bodhīti ñāṇaṃ “bujjhati etenā”ti katvā, bodhimā satto bodhisatto, purimapade uttarapadalopaṃ katvā yathā “ñāṇasatto”ti, ñāṇavā paññavā paṇḍito sattoti attho. Buddhānañhi pādamūle abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya paṇḍitova so satto, na andhabāloti bodhisatto. Evaṃ guṇavato uppannanāmavasena bodhisattasseva sato. Assādīyatīti assādo, sukhaṃ. Tañca sātākāralakkhaṇanti āha “assādoti madhurākāro”ti. Chandarāgo vinīyati ceva pahīyati ca etthāti nibbānaṃ “chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānañcā”ti vuccati. Tenāha “nibbāna”ntiādi. Tattha āgammāti idaṃ yo jano rāgaṃ vineti pajahati ca, tassa ārammaṇakaraṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dutiyatatiyāni uttānatthāneva.

Alternatively, 'bodhi' is knowledge, because 'one awakens by this'; hence, a being possessing awakening (bodhimā satto) is a Bodhisatta, with the elision of the final part of the first word in the compound, as in 'ñāṇasatto,' which means a being with knowledge, a wise, intelligent being. For from the time of his resolve at the feet of the Buddhas, that being is wise, not a blind fool; thus he is a Bodhisatta. Thus it is of the Bodhisatta himself, by way of a name that has arisen for one possessing such qualities. 'Because it is enjoyed, it is gratification' (assādīyatīti assādo); this means pleasure. And it has the characteristic of a pleasant nature; hence it is said, 'gratification is the nature of sweetness.' That wherein desire and lust is both disciplined and abandoned is called Nibbāna, 'the disciplining of desire and lust and the abandoning of desire and lust.' Hence it is said, 'Nibbāna,' etc. Here, the word 'āgamma' (as a basis) is said with reference to its being made an object by the person who disciplines and abandons lust. The second and third suttas are clear in meaning.

Pubbevasambodhasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Pubbevasambodha Sutta and Others is concluded.

4-9. Samaṇabrāhmaṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

4-9. Commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta and Others

107-112. Catutthe [M 2.0203][V 2.0184] sāmaññanti ariyamaggo, tena araṇīyato upagantabbato sāmaññatthaṃ, ariyaphalanti āha “sāmaññatthanti catubbidhaṃ ariyaphala”nti. Brahmaññatthanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tenāha “itaraṃ tasseva vevacana”nti. Ariyamaggasaṅkhātaṃ sāmaññameva vā araṇīyato sāmaññatthanti āha “sāmaññatthena vā cattāro maggā”ti. Pañcamādīni uttānatthāneva.

107-112. In the fourth sutta: 'The state of a recluse' (sāmañña) is the noble path. Because it is free from conflict (araṇīyato) and fit to be approached (upagantabbato), the meaning of 'sāmañña' is the noble fruit; hence it is said, 'the meaning of “sāmañña” is the fourfold noble fruit.' This same method applies to 'the state of a brahmin' (brahmaññattha). Hence it is said, 'the other is a synonym for that very thing.' Or, the state of a recluse, designated as the noble path, is the meaning of 'sāmañña' because it is free from conflict; hence it is said, 'or by the meaning of “sāmañña” is meant the four paths.' The fifth and following suttas are clear in meaning.

Samaṇabrāhmaṇasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta and Others is concluded.

10. Dutiyanidānasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Nidāna Sutta

113. Dasame vivaṭṭagāmikammānanti vivaṭṭūpanissayakammānaṃ. Tadabhinivattetīti ettha taṃ-saddena paccāmasanassa vipākassa parāmāsoti āha “taṃ abhinivattetī”ti, taṃ vipākaṃ abhibhavitvā nivattetīti attho. Idāni na kevalaṃ vipākasseva parāmāso taṃ-saddena, atha kho chandarāgaṭṭhāniyānaṃ dhammānaṃ tabbipākassa ca parāmāso daṭṭhabboti āha “yadā vā tenā”tiādi. Te ceva dhammeti te chandarāgaṭṭhāniye dhamme. Nibbijjhitvā passatīti kilese nibbijjhitvā vibhūtaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā passatīti.

113. Regarding the tenth, 'deeds leading to turning away' (vivaṭṭagāmikammāni) means deeds that are a support for turning away (vivaṭṭūpanissayakammānaṃ). Regarding 'he brings that into being' (tadabhinivatteti), here the word 'that' (taṃ) is a reference to the result being considered. Thus it is said, 'he brings that into being,' meaning having overcome that result, he turns it away. Now, it should be seen that the word 'that' is not merely a reference to the result, but also a reference to the states that are a basis for desire and lust, and to their result, as stated in 'or when by that,' and so on. 'Those very states' (te ceva dhammā) refers to those states that are the basis for desire and lust. 'Having become disenchanted, he sees' (nibbijjhitvā passati) means having become disenchanted with the defilements, he sees, having made it manifest and clear.

Dutiyanidānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Discourse on Causes is concluded.

Sambodhavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Enlightenment is concluded.

(12) 2. Āpāyikavaggo

(12) 2. The Chapter on Those Destined for States of Woe

1. Āpāyikasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on Those Destined for Woe

114. Dutiyassa paṭhame apāyesu nibbattanasīlatāya apāyūpagā āpāyikāti āha “apāyaṃ gacchissantīti āpāyikā”ti. Aññe brahmacārino sunivatthe supārute sumbhakapattadhare gāmanigamarājadhānīsu [V 2.0185] piṇḍāya caritvā jīvikaṃ kappente disvā sayampi tādisena ākārena [M 2.0204] tathāpaṭipajjanato “ahaṃ brahmacārī”ti paṭiññaṃ dento viya hotīti āha “brahmacāripaṭiññoti brahmacāripaṭirūpako”ti. “Ahampi bhikkhū”ti vatvā uposathaṅgādīni pavisanto pana brahmacāripaṭiñño hotiyeva, tathā saṅghikaṃ lābhaṃ gaṇhanto. Tenāha “tesaṃ vā…pe… evaṃpaṭiñño”ti. Akkosatīti “assamaṇosi, samaṇapaṭiññosī”tiādinā akkosati. Paribhāsatīti “so tvaṃ ‘hotu, muṇḍakasamaṇo aha’nti maññasi, idāni te assamaṇabhāvaṃ āropessāmī”tiādinā vadanto paribhāsati.

114. In the first [sutta] of the second [chapter], because of their nature of being reborn in states of woe, those who go to states of woe are called 'āpāyikā.' Thus it is said: 'They will go to a state of woe, hence they are āpāyikā.' Seeing other celibates—well-dressed, well-covered, carrying polished bowls—wandering for alms in villages, towns, and royal capitals to sustain their livelihood, he too, by conducting himself in such a manner, is like one making the claim, 'I am a celibate.' Hence it is said, 'one who claims to be a celibate' (brahmacāripaṭiñño) means 'one who resembles a celibate' (brahmacāripaṭirūpako). Moreover, by saying, 'I too am a bhikkhu,' and undertaking the Uposatha observances and so on, he is indeed one who claims to be a celibate; likewise when accepting a gain belonging to the Sangha. Therefore, it is said, 'of them... or... thus claiming.' 'He abuses' (akkosati) means he insults by saying, 'You are no ascetic, you only claim to be an ascetic,' and so on. 'He harasses' (paribhāsati) means he speaks threateningly, saying, 'You think, "So be it, I am a shaven-headed ascetic," but now I will expose your non-ascetic nature,' and so on.

Kilesakāmopi assādiyamāno vatthukāmantogadhoyeva, kilesakāmavasena ca tesaṃ assādanaṃ siyāti āha “kilesakāmena vatthukāme sevantassā”ti. Kilesakāmenāti karaṇatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Natthi dosoti assādetvā visayaparibhoge natthi ādīnavo, tappaccayā na koci antarāyoti adhippāyo. Pātabbataṃ āpajjatīti paribhuñjanakataṃ upagacchati. Paribhogattho hi ayaṃ pā-saddo, kattusādhano ca tabba-saddo, yathāruci paribhuñjatīti attho. Pivitabbataṃ paribhuñjitabbatanti etthāpi kattuvaseneva attho veditabbo.

Sensual desire as defilement (kilesakāma), when being savored, is included within sensual desire for objects (vatthukāma). And the savoring of them occurs by means of sensual desire as defilement, as stated: 'of one who indulges in sensual objects through sensual desire as defilement.' 'Through sensual desire as defilement' (kilesakāmena) is the instrumental case in the sense of the instrument. 'There is no fault' (natthi doso) means that in savoring and enjoying sense objects there is no danger; the intention is that no obstacle arises on account of that. 'He undertakes a state of consumability' (pātabbataṃ āpajjati) means he undertakes the act of consuming. For this word 'pā-' has the meaning of consuming, and the suffix '-tabba' indicates the agent; the meaning is 'he consumes as he pleases.' Here too, regarding 'what is to be drunk, what is to be enjoyed' (pivitabbataṃ paribhuñjitabbataṃ), the meaning should be understood in terms of the agent.

Āpāyikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on Those Destined for Woe is concluded.

2. Dullabhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Rare

115. Dutiye parena katassa upakārassa anurūpappavatti attani kataṃ upakāraṃ upakārato jānanto vediyanto kataññū katavedīti āha “iminā mayhaṃ kata”ntiādi.

115. In the second [sutta], one who acts in a manner befitting a benefit done by another, knowing and experiencing the benefit done to oneself as a benefit, is called 'grateful and one who acknowledges what has been done' (kataññū katavedī), as when it is said, 'This was done for me,' and so on.

Dullabhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Rare is concluded.

3. Appameyyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on the Immeasurable

116. Tatiye sukhena metabboti yathā parittassa udakassa sukhena pamāṇaṃ gayhati, evameva “uddhato”tiādinā yathāvuttehi aguṇaṅgehi [M 2.0205] samannāgatassa sukhena pamāṇaṃ gayhatīti, sukhena metabbo. Dukkhena metabboti yathā mahāsamuddassa dukkhena pamāṇaṃ gayhati, evameva “anuddhato”tiādinā dassitehi guṇaṅgehi samannāgatassa dukkhena pamāṇaṃ gayhati, “anāgāmī [V 2.0186] nu kho khīṇāsavo nu kho”ti vattabbataṃ gacchati, tenesa dukkhena metabbo. Pametuṃ na sakkotīti yathā ākāsassa na sakkā pamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ, evaṃ khīṇāsavassa, tenesa pametuṃ na sakkāti appameyyo.

116. In the third [sutta], 'to be measured with ease' (sukhena metabbo) means that just as the measure of a small amount of water is easily grasped, so too the measure of one endowed with the aforementioned unwholesome qualities, such as being 'restless' and so on, is easily grasped; thus, 'to be measured with ease.' 'To be measured with difficulty' (dukkhena metabbo) means that just as the measure of the great ocean is grasped with difficulty, so too the measure of one endowed with the wholesome qualities shown by 'not restless' and so on, is grasped with difficulty—such a one approaches the state of being able to be called, 'Is he a non-returner or one whose taints are destroyed?'; thus, 'to be measured with difficulty.' 'Cannot be measured' (pametuṃ na sakkoti) means that just as it is not possible to grasp the measure of space, so too it is not possible to measure one whose taints are destroyed; thus, 'cannot be measured,' meaning 'immeasurable' (appameyyo).

Sārābhāvena tucchattā naḷo viya naḷo, mānoti āha “unnaḷoti uggatanaḷo”ti, uṭṭhitatucchamānoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenāha “tucchamānaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitoti attho”ti. Mano hi seyyassa seyyoti sadisoti ca pavattiyā visesato tuccho. Cāpallenāti capalabhāvena, taṇhāloluppenāti attho. Mukharoti mukhena pharuso, pharusavācoti attho. Vikiṇṇavācoti visaṭavacano samphappalāpitāya apariyantavacano. Tenāha “asaññatavacano”ti, divasampi niratthakavacanaṃ palāpīti vuttaṃ hoti. Cittekaggatārahitoti upacārappanāsamādhirahito caṇḍasote baddhanāvā viya anavaṭṭhitakiriyo. Bhantacittoti anavaṭṭhitacitto paṇṇāruḷhavālamigasadiso. Vivaṭindriyoti saṃvarābhāvena gihikāle viya asaṃvutacakkhādiindriyo.

Pride (māno) is like a reed (naḷo) because it is hollow due to a lack of substance. Thus it is said, 'unnaḷo means a raised reed'; this means 'one whose hollow pride is raised up.' Therefore, it is said, 'the meaning is one who stands having raised up hollow pride.' For the mind, in its tendency to proceed as 'superior' or 'equal,' is especially hollow. 'With fickleness' (cāpallena) means with a fickle nature; the meaning is with craving and greed. 'Harsh' (mukharo) means harsh with the mouth; the meaning is one of harsh speech. 'Scattered speech' (vikiṇṇavāco) means one of disjointed speech; due to idle chatter, one of endless speech. Thus, it is said, 'one of unrestrained speech'; this means one who babbles pointless speech even for a whole day. 'Lacking one-pointedness of mind' (cittekaggatārahito) means devoid of access and absorption concentration, with unsteady actions like a boat tied up in a swift current. 'Wandering mind' (bhantacitto) means an unsteady mind, like a wild animal struck by an arrow. 'Unrestrained faculties' (vivaṭindriyo) means, due to a lack of restraint, one whose faculties such as the eye are unguarded, as in the time of being a householder.

Appameyyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Immeasurable is concluded.

4. Āneñjasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on the Imperturbable

117. Catutthe saha byayati gacchatīti sahabyo, sahapavattanako. Tassa bhāvo sahabyatā, sahapavattīti āha “sahabhāvaṃ upapajjatī”ti. “Yāvatakaṃ tesaṃ devānaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ khepetvā nirayampi gacchatī”tiādivacanato arūpabhavato cutassa apāyūpapatti vuttā viya dissatīti tannivattanatthaṃ bhagavato adhippāyaṃ vivaranto “sandhāyabhāsitamidaṃ vacana”nti dīpeti “nirayādīhi avippamuttattā”tiādinā. Na hi tassa upacārajjhānato balavataraṃ akusalaṃ atthīti. Iminā tato cavantānaṃ upacārajjhānameva paṭisandhijanakaṃ kammanti dīpeti. Adhikaṃ [M 2.0206] payasati payujjati etenāti adhippayāso, savisesaṃ itikattabbakiriyā. Tenāha “adhikappayogo”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

117. In the fourth, 'one who goes along with' is `sahabyo`, a companion in existence. The state of that is `sahabyatā`, co-existence; thus it is said, 'he is reborn into a state of companionship.' From statements like, 'Having exhausted the entire lifespan of those devas, he goes even to hell,' it appears as if rebirth in a state of woe for one who has fallen from a formless existence has been stated. In order to refute that, explaining the Blessed One's intention, he shows that 'this statement was spoken with a specific reference' by means of 'because of not being freed from hell, etc.' For there is no unwholesome kamma of his that is more powerful than the access concentration. By this he shows that for those falling from there, it is the access concentration itself that is the kamma generating rebirth-linking. `Adhippayāso` is that by which one strives or exerts oneself more, a specific action to be done. Therefore it is said, 'additional application.' The rest here is self-evident.

Āneñjasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Imperturbable is concluded.

5. Vipattisampadāsuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on Failure and Success

118. Pañcame [V 2.0187] dinnanti deyyadhammasīsena dānaṃ vuttanti āha “dinnassa phalābhāvaṃ sandhāya vadatī”ti. Dinnaṃ pana annādivatthuṃ kathaṃ paṭikkhipati. Esa nayo “yiṭṭhaṃ huta”nti etthāpi. Mahāyāgoti sabbasādhāraṇaṃ mahādānaṃ. Paheṇakasakkāroti pāhunakānaṃ kātabbasakkāro. Phalanti ānisaṃsaphalaṃ nissandaphalañca. Vipākoti sadisaphalaṃ. Paraloke ṭhitassa ayaṃ loko natthīti paraloke ṭhitassa kammunā laddhabbo ayaṃ loko na hoti. Idhaloke ṭhitassapi paraloko natthīti idhaloke ṭhitassa kammunā laddhabbo paraloko na hoti. Tattha kāraṇamāha “sabbe tattha tattheva ucchijjantī”ti. Ime sattā yattha yattha bhavayonigatiādīsu ṭhitā, tattha tattheva ucchijjanti, dvayavināsena vinassanti.

118. In the fifth, 'what is given' (dinnaṃ) means that giving (dānaṃ) is spoken of as the chief of things to be given. Thus he says, 'he speaks with reference to the non-existence of fruit from what is given.' But how does he reject the given object, such as food? This same method applies here also to 'what is sacrificed, what is offered.' 'Great sacrifice' (mahāyāgo) means a great gift common to all. 'Hospitality' (paheṇakasakkāro) means the honor to be done for guests. 'Fruit' (phalaṃ) means the fruit as benefit and the fruit as outflow. 'Result' (vipāko) means the corresponding fruit. 'For one established in the next world, this world does not exist' means this world, which is to be obtained by the kamma of one established in the next world, does not exist. 'For one established in this world, the next world does not exist' means the next world, which is to be obtained by the kamma of one established in this world, does not exist. There he states the reason: 'all are annihilated right there.' These beings, wherever they are established—in existences, wombs, destinations, etc.—are annihilated right there; they perish with the destruction of the pair.

Phalābhāvavasenāti mātāpitūsu sammāpaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattīnaṃ phalassa abhāvavasena “natthi mātā, natthi pitā”ti vadati, na mātāpitūnaṃ, nāpi tesu sammāpaṭipattimicchāpaṭipattīnaṃ abhāvavasena tesaṃ lokapaccakkhattā. Pubbuḷakassa viya imesaṃ sattānaṃ uppādo nāma kevalo, na ca khanapubbakoti dassanatthaṃ “natthi sattā opapātikā”ti vuttanti āha “cavitvā uppajjanakā sattā nāma natthīti vadatī”ti. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentīti ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ abhivisiṭṭhāya paññāya sayaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā pavedenti, te natthīti sabbaññubuddhānaṃ abhāvaṃ dīpeti.

By way of the absence of result: because of the absence of a result from right and wrong conduct towards parents, he says, 'There is no mother, there is no father.' This is not because of the absence of parents themselves, nor because of the absence of right and wrong conduct towards them, since these are directly perceived in the world. To show that the arising of these beings is merely like that of a bubble, and not preceded by a moment, it is said, 'There are no spontaneously arisen beings,' meaning, he says, 'There are no beings who pass away and are reborn.' 'Those who declare after realizing for themselves through direct knowledge' means those who, having directly perceived this world and the next with superior wisdom, proclaim it. By saying 'they do not exist,' he indicates the absence of omniscient Buddhas.

Vipattisampadāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Vipattisampadā Sutta is concluded.

6-7. Apaṇṇakasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-7. Exposition of the Apaṇṇaka Sutta and so forth

119-120. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0207] chahi talehi samannāgato pāsakoti catūsu passesu cattāri talāni, dvīsu koṭīsu dve talānīti evaṃ chahi talehi samannāgato pāsakakīḷāpasutānaṃ maṇisadiso pāsakaviseso. Sattamaṃ uttānameva.

119-120. In the sixth, a die endowed with six faces: four faces on the four sides, and two faces on the two ends—thus, a special kind of die endowed with six faces, like a gem for those devoted to dice games. The seventh is self-evident.

Apaṇṇakasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Apaṇṇaka Sutta and so forth is concluded.

8. Paṭhamasoceyyasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Exposition of the First Soceyya Sutta

121. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0188] sucibhāvoti kilesāsucivigamena suddhabhāvo asaṃkiliṭṭhabhāvo, atthato kāyasucaritādīni.

121. In the eighth, a state of purity means the state of being pure, unstained, through the removal of the impurity of defilements; in essence, it is good bodily conduct and so forth.

Paṭhamasoceyyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the First Soceyya Sutta is concluded.

9. Dutiyasoceyyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Exposition of the Second Soceyya Sutta

122. Navame samucchedavasena pahīnasabbakāyaduccaritatāya kāye, kāyena vā suci kāyasuci. Tenāha “kāyadvāre”tiādi. Soceyyasampannanti paṭippassaddhakilesattā parisuddhāya soceyyasampattiyā upetaṃ. Ninhātā aggamaggasalilena vikkhālitā pāpā etenāti ninhātapāpako, khīṇāsavo. Tenāha “khīṇāsavova kathito”ti.

122. In the ninth, 'bodily purity' (kāyasuci) means pure in body, or pure by means of the body, because all bodily misconduct has been abandoned by way of eradication. Hence it is said, 'by the door of the body,' and so on. 'Endowed with purity' means endowed with the attainment of purity, which is pure because the defilements are pacified. 'Ninhātapāpaka' means one whose evils are washed away by the water of the supreme path; he is a taint-destroyer. Hence it is said, 'he is declared a taint-destroyer.'

Dutiyasoceyyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Second Soceyya Sutta is concluded.

10. Moneyyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Exposition of the Moneyya Sutta

123. Dasame munino bhāvā moneyyāni, yehi dhammehi ubhayahitamunanato muni nāma hoti, te munibhāvakarā moneyyā paṭipadā dhammā eva vuttā. Munino vā etāni moneyyāni, yathāvuttadhammā eva. Tattha yasmā kāyena akattabbassa akaraṇaṃ, kattabbassa ca karaṇaṃ[M 2.0208], “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.377; ma. ni. 1.110; saṃ. ni. 4.127; khu. pā. 3.dvattiṃsākāra) kāyasaṅkhātassa ārammaṇassa jānanaṃ, kāyassa ca samudayato atthaṅgamato assādato ādīnavato nissaraṇato ca yāthāvato parijānanatā, tathā parijānanavasena pana pavatto vipassanāmaggo, tena ca kāye chandarāgassa pajahanaṃ, kāyasaṅkhāraṃ nirodhetvā pattabbasamāpatti vā, sabbe ete kāyamukhena pavattā moneyyappaṭipadā dhammā kāyamoneyyaṃ nāma. Tasmā tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “katamaṃ kāyamoneyyaṃ? Tividhakāyaduccaritassa pahānaṃ kāyamoneyyaṃ, tividhakāyasucaritampi kāyamoneyya”ntiādinā (mahāni. 14) pāḷi āgatā. Idhāpi teneva pāḷinayena atthaṃ dassento “tividhakāyaduccaritappahānaṃ kāyamoneyyaṃ nāmā”tiādimāha.

123. In the tenth, the states of a sage are sagacities. By those qualities through which one is called a sage, from understanding the welfare of both, those qualities that bring about the state of a sage are indeed called the practices of sagacity. Or, these are the sagacities of a sage, just the qualities as described. Herein, because of refraining from what should not be done with the body and doing what should be done; knowing the object called the body through contemplation such as, 'There are in this body hairs of the head,' and so on; and fully understanding the body as it truly is—its arising, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape; and also the path of insight that proceeds by way of such full understanding, and through it, the abandoning of desire and lust for the body, or the attainment to be reached by ceasing bodily formations—all these qualities of the practice of sagacity that proceed by way of the body are called bodily sagacity. Therefore, to explain this meaning, the Pāli text states: 'What is bodily sagacity? The abandoning of the threefold bodily misconduct is bodily sagacity, and the threefold bodily good conduct is also bodily sagacity,' and so on. Here too, explaining the meaning in the same way, it says: 'The abandoning of the threefold bodily misconduct is called bodily sagacity,' and so forth.

Idāni [V 2.0189] “katamaṃ vacīmoneyyaṃ? Catubbidhavacīduccaritassa pahānaṃ vacīmoneyyaṃ, catubbidhaṃ vacīsucaritaṃ, vācārammaṇe ñāṇaṃ, vācāpariññā, pariññāsahagato maggo, vācāya chandarāgassa pahānaṃ, vacīsaṅkhāranirodho dutiyajjhānasamāpatti vacīmoneyya”nti imāya pāḷiyā vuttamatthaṃ atidīpento “vacīmoneyyepi eseva nayo”tiādimāha. Tattha copanavācañceva saddavācañca ārabbha pavattā paññā vācārammaṇe ñāṇaṃ. Tassā vācāya samudayādito parijānanaṃ vācāpariññā.

Now, greatly clarifying the meaning stated in this Pāli passage—'What is verbal sagacity? The abandoning of the fourfold verbal misconduct is verbal sagacity; the fourfold good verbal conduct, knowledge regarding speech as its object, the full understanding of speech, the path associated with full understanding, the abandoning of desire and lust for speech, the cessation of verbal formations, the attainment of the second jhāna—is verbal sagacity'—he says, 'In verbal sagacity, this is the same method,' and so on. Herein, wisdom that arises concerning both inciting speech and vocalized speech is 'knowledge regarding speech as its object.' The full understanding of that speech, its arising and so forth, is 'the full understanding of speech.'

“Katamaṃ manomoneyyaṃ? Tividhamanoduccaritassa pahānaṃ manomoneyyaṃ, tividhaṃ manosuccaritaṃ, manārammaṇe ñāṇaṃ, manapariññā, pariññāsahagato maggo, manasmiṃ chandarāgassa pahānaṃ, cittasaṅkhāranirodho saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti manomoneyya”nti imāya pāḷiyā āgatanayena atthaṃ vibhāvento “manomoneyyepi imināva nayena atthaṃ ñatvā”tiādimāha. Tattha ca ekāsītividhaṃ lokiyacittaṃ ārabbha pavattañāṇaṃ manārammaṇe ñāṇaṃ. Tassa samudayādito parijānanaṃ manapariññāti ayaṃ viseso.

'What is mental sagacity? The abandoning of the threefold mental misconduct is mental sagacity; the threefold good mental conduct, knowledge regarding mental objects, the full understanding of the mind, the path associated with full understanding, the abandoning of desire and lust for the mind, the cessation of mental formations, the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling—is mental sagacity.' Analyzing the meaning according to the method that has come down in this Pāli passage, he says, 'In mental sagacity too, having known the meaning by this very method,' and so on. And herein, the knowledge that proceeds concerning the eighty-one kinds of worldly consciousness is 'knowledge regarding mental objects.' The full understanding of its arising and so forth is 'the full understanding of the mind'—this is the distinction.

Moneyyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Moneyya Sutta is concluded.

Āpāyikavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Āpāyika Vagga is concluded.

(13) 3. Kusināravaggo

(13) 3. The Kusināra Chapter

1-2. Kusinārasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Exposition of the Kusināra Sutta and so forth

124-125. Tatiyassa [M 2.0209] paṭhame taṇhāgedhena gathitoti taṇhābandhanena baddho. Taṇhāmucchanāyāti taṇhāya vasena mucchāpattiyā. Mucchitoti mucchaṃ mohaṃ pamādaṃ āpanno. Ajjhopannoti adhiopanno. Taṇhāya adhibhavitvā ajjhotthaṭo gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā viya ṭhito. Tenāha “ajjhopannoti taṇhāya gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā pavatto”ti. Anādīnavadassāvīti gathitādibhāvena paribhoge ādīnavamattampi na passati. Nissaraṇapaññoti ayamattho āhāraparibhogeti tattha payojanaparicchedikā “yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23; 2.24; 3.75; saṃ. ni. 4.120; a. ni. 6.58; 8.9) pavattā [V 2.0190] āhārapaṭibaddhachandarāganissaraṇabhūtā paññā assa atthīti nissaraṇapañño. Sesamettha uttānameva. Dutiye natthi vattabbaṃ.

124-125. In the first of the third, 'bound by the greed of craving' means bound by the bond of craving. 'By infatuation with craving' means by falling into infatuation through the power of craving. 'Infatuated' means one who has fallen into infatuation, delusion, and negligence. 'Ajjhopanna' means overwhelmed. Overpowered by craving, submerged, as if having swallowed and completely finished it. Hence it is said, 'Ajjhopanna means one who proceeds as if swallowed and completely finished by craving.' 'Not seeing danger' means that, because of being bound and so forth, one does not see even the slightest danger in enjoyment. 'One with wisdom for escape' means one who possesses the wisdom that is an escape from desire and lust connected with food, a wisdom that delimits the purpose in the partaking of food, and which proceeds according to the text beginning, 'only for the sustenance of this body,' and so on. The rest here is self-evident. In the second, there is nothing to be said.

Kusinārasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Kusināra Sutta and so forth is concluded.

3. Gotamakacetiyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Exposition of the Gotamaka Cetiya Sutta

126. Tatiye sambahulāti pañcasatamattā. Pañcasatā kira brāhmaṇā tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū aparabhāge bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ nekkhamme ca ānisaṃsaṃ passamānā bhagavato santike pabbajitvā na cirasseva sabbaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā pariyattiṃ nissāya mānaṃ uppādesuṃ – “yaṃ yaṃ bhagavā katheti, taṃ taṃ mayaṃ khippameva jānāma. Bhagavā hi itthiliṅgādīni tīṇi liṅgāni, nāmādīni cattāri padāni, paṭhamādayo satta vibhattiyo muñcitvā na kiñci katheti, evaṃ kathite ca amhākaṃ gaṇṭhipadaṃ nāma natthī”ti, te bhagavati agāravā hutvā tato paṭṭhāya bhagavato upaṭṭhānampi dhammassavanampi abhiṇhaṃ na gacchanti. Te sandhāya vuttaṃ “sambahulā kira brāhmaṇapabbajitā…pe… dhammassavanaṃ na gacchantī”ti. Mukhapaṭiññaṃ gahetvāti “saccaṃ kira tumhe, bhikkhave”tiādinā tamatthaṃ paṭipucchitvā “saccaṃ bhagavā”ti tehi bhikkhūhi vuttaṃ paṭivacanaṃ gahetvā. Tañhi attano mukheneva paṭiññātattā “mukhapaṭiññā”ti vuccati.

126. Regarding 'several' in the third instance, it refers to about five hundred. It is said that five hundred brahmins, who were masters of the three Vedas, after hearing the Blessed One's teaching in the latter part of their lives, saw the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation, went forth under the Blessed One, and before long, having learned all the Buddha's words, they became conceited based on their learning, thinking: 'Whatever the Blessed One says, we understand it quickly. The Blessed One speaks using the three genders—masculine, feminine, and neuter—the four word categories—noun, etc.—and the seven declensions—first, etc. He does not say anything more than that. And when he speaks thus, we have no difficulty understanding.' Because of this, they became disrespectful toward the Blessed One, and from then on, they no longer regularly attended upon the Blessed One or listened to the Dhamma. This is what is meant by 'several brahmin renunciates... do not go to listen to the Dhamma.' 'Having taken their verbal acknowledgment' means that the Blessed One questioned them with, 'Is it true, monks?' and so on, thereby taking the reply, 'It is true, Blessed One,' that was spoken by the monks as an acknowledgment. Since they acknowledged it with their own words, it is called 'verbal acknowledgment.'

Neva [M 2.0210] āgataṭṭhānaṃ na gataṭṭhānaṃ addasaṃsu. Kasmā? Aññāṇato. Te kira tassa suttassa atthaṃ na jāniṃsu. Tesañhi tasmiṃ samaye vicitranayaṃ desanāvilāsayuttampi taṃ suttaṃ ghanaputhulena dussapaṭṭena mukhaṃ baddhaṃ katvā purato ṭhapitamanuññabhojanaṃ viya ahosi. Nanu ca bhagavā attanā desitaṃ dhammaṃ pare ñāpetuṃ kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkheyyāni pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaṃ patto, so kasmā yathā te na jānanti, tathā desetīti? Tesaṃ mānabhañjanatthaṃ. Bhagavā hi “abhabbā ime imaṃ mānakhilaṃ anupahacca maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā sacchikātu”nti tesaṃ sutapariyattiṃ nissāya uppannaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā desanākusalo mānabhañjanatthaṃ “sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”ntiādinā mūlapariyāyasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 1.1) abhāsi.

They did not see the place from which they came, nor the place to which they went. Why? Because of ignorance. Indeed, they did not understand the meaning of that discourse. For them at that time, even though that discourse was endowed with the charm of various methods of teaching, it was like a delicious meal placed before them with their mouths bound by a thick, coarse cloth. Surely, the Blessed One, after fulfilling the perfections for four incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons, attained omniscience in order to make known to others the Dhamma he himself had realized. Why then did he teach in a way they did not understand? It was to break their pride. For the Blessed One, knowing that 'these are incapable of realizing the path or the fruit without removing this stake of pride,' being skilled in teaching, created perplexity based on their scriptural learning, and for the purpose of breaking their pride, spoke the Mūlapariyāya Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 1.1), which begins with the words, 'The Root of All Things Discourse'.

Sammāsambuddho [V 2.0191] “mayhaṃ kathā niyyātī”ti mukhasampattameva kathetīti cintayiṃsūti idaṃ aṅguttarabhāṇakānaṃ vaḷañjanakatantinīhārena vuttaṃ. Majjhimabhāṇakā pana evaṃ vadanti – evaṃ mānabhañjanatthaṃ desitañca pana taṃ suttaṃ sutvā te bhikkhū “taṃyeva kira pathaviṃ diṭṭhigatiko sañjānāti, sekhopi arahāpi tathāgatopi abhijānāti, ki nāmidaṃ kathaṃ nāmida”nti cintentā “pubbe mayaṃ bhagavatā kathitaṃ yaṃkiñci khippameva jānāma, idāni panimassa mūlapariyāyassa antaṃ vā koṭiṃ vā na jānāma na passāma, aho buddhā nāma appameyyā atulā”ti uddhatadāṭhā viya sappā nimmadā hutvā buddhūpaṭṭhānañca dhammassavanañca sakkaccaṃ agamaṃsu. Tena samayena dhammasabhāyaṃ sannisinnā bhikkhū “aho buddhānaṃ ānubhāvo, te nāmabrāhmaṇapabbajitā tathā mānamadamattā bhagavatā mūlapariyāyadesanāya nihatamānā katā”ti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Taṃ sutvā bhagavā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi ahaṃ evaṃ ime mānapaggahitasīse carante nihatamāne akāsi”nti vatvā atītaṃ āharanto “bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, aññataro disāpāmokkho brāhmaṇo bārāṇasiyaṃ paṭivasati tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū sanighaṇṭukeṭubhānaṃ sākkharappabhedānaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ padako veyyākaraṇo lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anavayo, so pañcamattāni māṇavakasatāni mante vāceti. Paṇḍitamāṇavakā bahuñca gaṇhanti lahuñca, suṭṭhu ca upadhārentī”tiādinā jātakaṃ kathesi.

According to the traditional method of the Aṅguttara reciters, it is said that they thought: 'The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, thinking, "My discourse is being conveyed," speaks as soon as it comes to his mouth.' However, the Majjhima reciters say this: For the purpose of breaking down pride, that sutta was taught. Having heard it, those monks reflected, 'Indeed, the one with views perceives earth as earth; the trainee, the Arahant, and the Tathāgata also know it thus. What is this? What kind of talk is this?' Pondering thus, they thought, 'Previously, whatever the Blessed One taught, we understood quickly. But now, we neither know nor see the end or limit of this Root Discourse. Ah, indeed, the Buddhas are immeasurable and incomparable!' Like snakes with their fangs removed, they became humble and attentively attended upon the Buddha and listened to the Dhamma. At that time, the monks gathered in the Dhamma hall remarked, 'Ah, the power of the Buddhas! Those brahmin renunciates, so intoxicated with pride, were humbled by the Blessed One’s teaching of the Root Discourse.' Hearing this, the Blessed One said, 'Not only now, monks, but in the past too, I subdued these beings walking around with their heads held high with pride.' Then, recalling the past, He said: 'Once, monks, a brahmin, pre-eminent in a certain region, lived in Bārāṇasī. He was a master of the three Vedas with their Nighaṇṭhu, Keṭubha, Sākkhara, and distinctions of phonology, history as the fifth, skilled in Pada grammar, and unerring in Lokāyata and the marks of a great man. He taught mantras to five hundred young brahmins. Those wise students grasped much, quickly, and retained it well.' Thus, He began the Jātaka.

Taṃ [M 2.0211] sutvā te bhikkhū “pubbepi mayaṃ māneneva upahatā”ti bhiyyosomattāya nihatamānā hutvā attano upakārakammaṭṭhānaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ. Tato bhagavā ekaṃ samayaṃ janapadacārikaṃ caranto vesāliṃ patvā gotamake cetiye viharanto imesaṃ pañcasatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ñāṇaparipākaṃ viditvā idaṃ gotamakasuttaṃ kathesi. Idañca suttaṃ sutvā te pañcasatā bhikkhū tasmiṃyeva āsane saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti.

Hearing that, those monks thought, 'Even before, we were afflicted by conceit,' and with their pride utterly crushed, they became devoted to their own beneficial meditation subject. Then, the Blessed One, while traveling on a tour through the countryside, arrived at Vesālī and stayed at the Gotamaka Shrine. Recognizing the maturity of knowledge in these five hundred monks, he taught them this Gotamaka Sutta. Upon hearing this discourse, those five hundred monks attained arahantship right there on their seats, together with the analytical knowledges.

Abhiññāyāti kusalādibhedaṃ khandhādibhedañca desetabbaṃ dhammaṃ, veneyyānañca āsayānusayacariyādhimuttiādibhedaṃ, tassa ca nesaṃ desetabbappakāraṃ yāthāvato abhijānitvāti attho. Ime pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanānītiādi panettha nidassanamattaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Sappaccayanti sakāraṇaṃ, veneyyānaṃ ajjhāsayena vā pucchāya vā aṭṭhuppattiyā vā sanimittaṃ hetūdāharaṇasahitañcāti attho. Rāgādīnaṃ paṭiharaṇaṃ paṭihāriyaṃ, tadeva pāṭihāriyaṃ, saha pāṭihāriyenāti sappāṭihāriyaṃ. Rāgādippaṭisedhanavaseneva hi satthā dhammaṃ deseti. Tenāha “paccanīkapaṭiharaṇena sappāṭihāriyameva katvā”ti. Apare pana “yathārahaṃ iddhiādesanānusāsanipāṭihāriyasahita”nti [V 2.0192] vadanti anusāsanipāṭihāriyarahitā desanā natthīti katvā. Sesamettha uttānameva.

'Having directly known' means having directly known as they actually are: the Dhamma to be taught, with its distinctions such as wholesome and unwholesome, and the aggregates and so on; the various inclinations, latent tendencies, conduct, and aspirations of those to be taught; and the appropriate way to teach them. Here, 'the five aggregates, twelve sense bases,' and so on are stated merely as a summary list. 'With cause' means with a reason—whether due to the disposition of those to be taught, their questions, arising circumstances, signs, or accompanied by reasons and examples. Warding off lust and so forth is called 'counteraction,' and that itself is a 'miracle.' Thus, with counteraction as a miracle, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma. Therefore it was said, 'Having truly made it a miracle by counteracting the opposing factors.' Others, however, say, 'Accompanied by miracles appropriate to the situation—such as psychic power, telepathy, and instruction.' Because there is no teaching devoid of the miracle of instruction. The rest here is self-explanatory.

Gotamakacetiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Gotamaka Cetiya Sutta is completed.

4. Bharaṇḍukālāmasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Bharaṇḍukālāma Sutta

127. Catutthe āḷārakālāmakāleti āḷārakālāmānaṃ dharamānakāle. Pariññanti pahānapariññaṃ. Sā hi samatikkamo, na itarā. Tenāha “pariññā nāma samatikkamo”ti. Ettha ca paṭhamo satthā rūpāvacarasamāpattilābhī daṭṭhabbo, dutiyo arūpāvacarasamāpattilābhī, tatiyo sammāsambuddho daṭṭhabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ puggalapaññattiyaṃ (pu. pa. 130) –

127. In the fourth, 'at the time of Āḷāra Kālāma' means at the time when Āḷāra Kālāma was alive. 'Full understanding' refers to the full understanding of abandonment. For that is transcendence, not the other kind. Hence it is said, 'Full understanding is indeed transcendence.' Here, the first teacher should be understood as one who attained the form-sphere meditative attainments, the second as one who attained the formless-sphere meditative attainments, and the third as the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. For this is stated in the Puggalapaññatti (Pp. 130):

“Yvāyaṃ [M 2.0212] satthā kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpeti, na rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpeti, na vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpeti, rūpāvacarasamāpattiyā lābhī satthā tena daṭṭhabbo. Yvāyaṃ satthā kāmānañca pariññaṃ paññāpeti, rūpānañca pariññaṃ paññāpeti, na vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpeti, arūpāvacarasamāpattiyā lābhī satthā tena daṭṭhabbo. Yvāyaṃ satthā kāmānañca pariññaṃ paññāpeti, rūpānañca pariññaṃ paññāpeti, vedanānañca pariññaṃ paññāpeti, sammāsambuddho satthā tena daṭṭhabbo”ti.

"The teacher who makes known the full understanding of sensual pleasures, but does not make known the full understanding of forms, nor the full understanding of feelings, should be regarded as a teacher who has attained the form-sphere meditative attainments. The teacher who makes known the full understanding of sensual pleasures and the full understanding of forms, but does not make known the full understanding of feelings, should be regarded as a teacher who has attained the formless-sphere meditative attainments. The teacher who makes known the full understanding of sensual pleasures, the full understanding of forms, and the full understanding of feelings should be regarded as the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Teacher."

Tattha titthiyā samayaṃ jānantā kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpeyyuṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ vadamānā. Rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññāpeyyuṃ arūparāgaṃ vadamānā. Vedanāpariññaṃ paññāpeyyuṃ asaññārāgaṃ vadamānā. Te pana “idaṃ nāma paṭhamajjhānaṃ, ayaṃ rūpabhavo, ayaṃ asaññābhavo”tipi na jānanti. Te paññāpetuṃ asakkontāpi kevalaṃ “paññāpemā”ti vadanti. Tathāgato pana kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ anāgāmimaggena paññāpeti, rūpavedanānaṃ arahattamaggena. Evamettha dve janā bāhirakā, eko sammāsambuddhoti imasmiṃ loke tayo satthāro nāma.

Here, the sectarians, knowing their own doctrines, would declare the full understanding of sensual pleasures while speaking of the first jhāna. They would declare the full understanding of forms while speaking of desire for the formless. They would declare the full understanding of feelings while speaking of desire for the non-percipient. Yet they do not know, "This is indeed the first jhāna, this is the realm of form, this is the realm of the non-percipient." Though unable to declare it, they merely say, "We declare it." The Tathāgata, however, declares the full understanding of sensual pleasures through the path of the non-returner, and the full understanding of forms and feelings through the path of arahantship. Thus, in this matter, there are two kinds of outsiders and one Perfectly Enlightened One—making three teachers in name in this world.

Bharaṇḍukālāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bharaṇḍukālāma Sutta is concluded.

5. Hatthakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Hatthaka Sutta

128. Pañcame [V 2.0193] abhikkantāti atikkantā, vigatāti atthoti āha “khaye dissatī”ti. Teneva hi “nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo”ti anantaraṃ vuttaṃ. Abhikkantataroti ativiya kantataro. Tādiso ca sundaro bhaddako nāma hotīti āha “sundare dissatī”ti. Koti devanāgayakkhagandhabbādīsu ko katamo? Meti mama. Pādānīti pāde. Iddhiyāti imāya evarūpāya deviddhiyā. Yasasāti iminā edisena parivārena paricchedena. Jalanti vijjotamāno. Abhikkantenāti ativiya kantena kamanīyena abhirūpena. Vaṇṇenāti chavivaṇṇena sarīravaṇṇanibhāya. Sabbā obhāsayaṃ disāti dasa disā pabhāsento, cando viya sūriyo viya ca ekobhāsaṃ ekālokaṃ karontoti gāthāya attho. Abhirūpeti uḷārarūpe sampannarūpe. Abbhanumodaneti sampahaṃsane[M 2.0213]. Idha panāti “abhikkantāya rattiyā”ti etasmiṃ pade. Tenāti sundarapariyāyattā. Khaye vā idha abhikkantasaddo daṭṭhabbo, tena “abhikkantāya parikkhīṇāya rattiyā”ti vuttaṃ hoti.

128. In the fifth, 'abhikkantā' means surpassed, gone beyond—thus it is said, 'seen in destruction.' For this reason, it is immediately stated, 'the first watch has passed.' 'Abhikkantataro' means exceedingly delightful. Such a one is indeed beautiful and excellent, thus it is said, 'seen in splendor.' 'Ko ti' refers to which one among gods, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and others? 'Me ti' means 'my.' 'Pādāni ti' means 'feet.' 'Iddhiyā ti' refers to this very divine power. 'Yasasā ti' means with such a retinue and domain. 'Jalanti' means shining brilliantly. 'Abhikkantena ti' means exceedingly delightful, charming, and handsome. 'Vaṇṇena ti' refers to the complexion, the radiance of the body's appearance. 'Sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā' means illuminating the ten directions, making a single radiance, a single light, like the moon or the sun—this is the meaning of the verse. 'Abhirūpe ti' means endowed with magnificent form. 'Abbhanumodane ti' means in rejoicing. Here, however, in the phrase 'abhikkantāya rattiyā,' it is a synonym for 'beautiful.' Or, the word 'abhikkanta' should be understood here in the sense of destruction; for that reason it is said: 'when the night was advanced, when it was spent.'

Rūpāyatanādīsūti ādisaddena akkharādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Suvaṇṇavaṇṇoti suvaṇṇacchavīti ayamettha atthoti āha “chaviya”nti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “kañcanasannibhattaco”ti (ma. ni. 2.399; su. ni. 556). Saññūḷhāti sambandhitā, ganthitāti attho. Vaṇṇāti guṇavaṇṇāti āha “thutiya”nti, thomanāyanti attho. Kulavaggeti khattiyādikulakoṭṭhāse. Tattha “accho vippasanno”tiādinā vaṇṇitabbaṭṭhena vaṇṇo, chavi. Vaṇṇanaṭṭhena abhitthavaṭṭhena vaṇṇo, thuti. Aññamaññaṃ asaṅkarato vaṇṇetabbato ṭhapetabbato vaṇṇo, khattiyādikulavaggo. Vaṇṇīyati ñāpīyati etenāti vaṇṇo, ñāpakakāraṇaṃ. Vaṇṇanato thūlarassādibhāvena upaṭṭhānato vaṇṇo, saṇṭhānaṃ. Mahantaṃ khuddakaṃ majjhimanti vaṇṇetabbato pamitabbato vaṇṇo, pamāṇaṃ. Vaṇṇīyati cakkhunā passīyatīti vaṇṇo, rūpāyatananti evaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe vaṇṇasaddassa pavatti veditabbā. Soti vaṇṇasaddo. Chaviyā daṭṭhabbo rūpāyatane gayhamānassapi chavimukheneva gahetabbato. Chavigatā pana vaṇṇadhātu eva “suvaṇṇavaṇṇo”ti ettha vaṇṇaggahaṇena gahitāti apare.

In 'rūpāyatanādīsu,' by the word 'ādi' (etc.), the inclusion of letters and so on should be understood. 'Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo' means 'golden-skinned'; this is the meaning here, as stated by 'chaviyā' (by the skin). For it is said: 'With skin resembling gold.' 'Saññūḷhā' means connected, bound—this is the meaning. 'Vaṇṇā' refers to quality-vaṇṇa, as stated by 'thutiya' (by praise), meaning commendation. 'Kulavagge' refers to the divisions of clans such as the khattiyas. There, 'vaṇṇa' in the sense of being describable by terms like 'clear and bright' refers to skin, complexion. 'Vaṇṇa' in the sense of description, in the sense of praise, refers to commendation. 'Vaṇṇa' in the sense of being distinguished or established without intermingling with one another refers to the divisions of clans like the khattiyas. 'Vaṇṇa,' as that by which something is made known, is the means of indication. 'Vaṇṇa' in the sense of description, due to its manifestation as coarse, subtle, etc., refers to form, shape. 'Vaṇṇa' in the sense of being measurable as large, small, or medium, refers to measurement. 'Vaṇṇa,' as that which is seen by the eye, is the visual object. Thus, the application of the word 'vaṇṇa' in each of these meanings should be understood. That is the word 'vaṇṇa.' It should be understood as skin, because even when apprehended as a visual object, it is apprehended by means of the skin. Others, however, say that it is the color-element residing in the skin that is grasped by the term 'vaṇṇa' here in 'suvaṇṇavaṇṇo.'

Kevalaparipuṇṇanti ekadesampi asesetvā niravasesatova paripuṇṇanti ayamettha atthoti āha “anavasesatā attho”ti. Kevalakappāti kappa-saddo nipāto padapūraṇamattaṃ, “kevalaṃ”icceva attho. Kevalasaddo ca bahulavācīti āha “yebhuyyatā attho”ti. Keci pana [V 2.0194] “īsakaṃ asamattaṃ kevalaṃ kevalakappa”nti vadanti. Anavasesattho ettha kevalasaddo siyā, anatthantarena pana kappasaddena padavaḍḍhanaṃ kataṃ “kevalā eva kevalakappā”ti. Tathā vā kappanīyattā paññapetabbattā kevalakappā. Abyāmissatā vijātiyena asaṅkaro suddhatā. Anatirekatā taṃparamatā visesābhāvo. Kevalakappanti kevalaṃ [M 2.0214] daḷhaṃ katvāti attho. Kevalaṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ sabbasaṅkhatavivittattā, taṃ etassa adhigataṃ atthīti kevalī, sacchikatanirodho khīṇāsavo.

'Kevalaparipuṇṇa' means entirely perfect, without leaving out even a part, without remainder. This is the meaning here, as stated: 'the meaning is without remainder.' In 'kevalakappa,' the word 'kappa' is a particle, merely filling out the word; the meaning is simply 'kevalaṃ' (entirely). And the word 'kevala' is also a term for 'mostly,' hence it is said: 'the meaning is predominance.' Some, however, say: 'a little, incomplete, entirely, almost entirely.' Here, the word 'kevala' may have the meaning of 'without remainder,' but the word is lengthened by the particle 'kappa' without any other meaning, as in 'kevalā eva kevalakappā.' Alternatively, because it is suitable or declarable, it is 'kevalakappa.' 'Abyāmissatā' means unmixedness, not being blended with a different kind, purity. 'Anatirekatā' means not being surpassed, being the ultimate, the absence of anything superior. 'Kevalakappaṃ' means having made it entirely firm. 'Kevalaṃ' is said of Nibbāna, because it is distinct from all conditioned things. One for whom this is attained is a 'kevalī,' one who has realized cessation, a destroyer of the corruptions.

Kappa-saddo panāyaṃ saupasaggo anupasaggo cāti adhippāyena okappaniyapade labbhamānaṃ okappasaddamattaṃ nidasseti, aññathā kappasaddassa atthuddhāre okappaniyapadaṃ anidassanameva siyā. Samaṇakappehīti vinayasiddhehi samaṇavohārehi. Niccakappanti niccakālaṃ. Paññattīti nāmaṃ. Nāmañhetaṃ tassa āyasmato, yadidaṃ kappoti. Kappitakesamassūti kattariyā cheditakesamassu. Dvaṅgulakappoti majjhanhikavelāya vītikkantāya dvaṅgulatāvikappo. Lesoti apadeso. Anavasesaṃ pharituṃ samatthassa obhāsassa kenaci kāraṇena ekadesapharaṇampi siyā, ayaṃ pana sabbasseva pharatīti dassetuṃ samantattho kappasaddo gahitoti āha “anavasesaṃ samantato”ti.

This word 'kappa,' with the intention that it can be with or without a prefix, illustrates just the word 'okappa' which is found in the word 'okappaniya.' Otherwise, in the explanation of the meaning of the word 'kappa,' the word 'okappaniya' would not be shown. 'Samaṇakappehi' means by monastic conventions established in the Vinaya. 'Niccakappaṃ' means for all time. 'Paññatti' is a name. This is a name for that venerable one, that is, 'Kappa.' 'Kappitakesamassu' means one whose hair and beard are cut with scissors. 'Dvaṅgulakappo' means the suitable time of two finger-breadths after the midday hour has passed. 'Leso' means a pretext. Even though a light capable of pervading completely might, for some reason, pervade only partially, here, to show that this one pervades everything, the word 'kappa' is taken in the sense of 'all around'; therefore it is said, 'without remainder, all around.'

Ābhāya pharitvāti vatthamālālaṅkārasarīrasamuṭṭhitāya ābhāya pharitvā. Devatānañhi sarīrobhāsaṃ dvādasayojanamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ. Tato bhiyyopi pharitvā tiṭṭhati, tathā vatthābharaṇādisamuṭṭhitā pabhā.

'Ābhāya pharitvā' means having pervaded with the radiance arising from the body, garments, garlands, and ornaments. For deities, the radiance of their bodies is a space of twelve yojanas. It stands pervading even beyond that, as does the light arising from clothing, ornaments, and the like.

Hatthakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Hatthaka Sutta is concluded.

6. Kaṭuviyasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Kaṭuviya Sutta

129. Chaṭṭhe gāvīnaṃ kayavikkayavasena yogo etthāti goyogo, kayavikkayaṃ karonto gāvīhi yujjanti etthāti vā goyogo, gāvīnaṃ vikkayaṭṭhānaṃ. Tattha jāto pilakkharukkho goyogapilakkho, tasmiṃ. Samīpatthe cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Tenāha “gāvīnaṃ vikkayaṭṭhāne uṭṭhitapilakkhassa santike”ti. Ritto assādo etassāti rittassādo. Tenāha “jhānasukhābhāvena rittassāda”nti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

129. In the sixth, 'goyogo' is so called because here there is connection ('yogo') by way of buying and selling cattle; or it is 'goyogo' because those who buy and sell contend ('yujjanti') with cattle here; it is a place for selling cattle. The pilakkha tree that has grown there is the 'goyogapilakkha'; 'tasmiṃ' refers to that. And this is a locative case in the sense of proximity. Therefore it is said, “near the pilakkha tree standing in the place for selling cattle.” 'Rittassādo' is so called because its savor is empty ('ritto assādo etassā'). Therefore it is said, “with empty savor due to the absence of the bliss of jhāna.” The rest here is self-evident.

Kaṭuviyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kaṭuviya Sutta is concluded.

8. Dutiyaanuruddhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Second Anuruddha Sutta

131. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0215][V 2.0195] idaṃ te mānasminti ettha mānasminti paccatte bhummavacanaṃ. Idanti ca liṅgavipallāsena napuṃsakaniddeso katoti āha “ayaṃ te navavidhena vaḍḍhitamāno”ti. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

131. In the eighth, regarding 'idaṃ te mānasmiṃ,' here 'mānasmiṃ' is a locative case in the sense of the self. And 'idaṃ' is a neuter designation due to a change of gender, thus it is said, “this is your conceit, increased in nine ways.” The same method applies to the remaining instances.

Dutiyaanuruddhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Anuruddha Sutta is concluded.

9. Paṭicchannasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Paṭicchanna Sutta

132. Navame asādhāraṇasikkhāpadanti bhikkhunīnaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ bhikkhūnaṃyeva paññattasikkhāpadaṃ sādhāraṇasikkhāpadanti bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnañca sādhāraṇaṃ ubhatopaññattisikkhāpadaṃ.

132. In the ninth, an 'unshared training rule' is a training rule laid down only for bhikkhus, not shared with bhikkhunīs. A 'shared training rule' is a training rule shared by both bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, a training rule laid down for both.

Paṭicchannasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Paṭicchanna Sutta is concluded.

10. Lekhasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Lekha Sutta

133. Dasame thiraṭṭhānatoti thiraṭṭhānatova. Pāsāṇe lekhasadisā parāparādhanibbattā kodhalekhā yassa so pāsāṇalekhūpamasamannāgato pāsāṇalekhūpamoti vutto. Evaṃ itarepi. Anusetīti appahīnatāya anuseti. Na khippaṃ lujjatīti na antarā nassati kammaṭṭhāneneva nassanato. Evamevanti evaṃ tassapi puggalassa kodho na antarā punadivase vā aparadivase vā niṭṭhāti, addhaniyo pana hoti, maraṇeneva niṭṭhātīti attho. Kakkhaḷenāti atikakkhaḷena dhammacchedakena thaddhavacanena. Saṃsandatīti ekībhavati. Sammodatīti nirantaro hotīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

133. In the tenth discourse, `thiraṭṭhānatoti` means “firmly established indeed.” He whose anger, born of various offenses, is like a line inscribed on stone, is said to be endowed with the simile of a stone inscription, hence he is called `pāsāṇalekhūpama` (like a stone inscription). Similarly, the others are to be understood. `Anuseti` means it lies dormant because it has not been abandoned. `Na khippaṃ lujjati` means it does not quickly break up—it does not perish in the interim, but only through the meditation subject. Just so, for that person too, anger does not cease in the interim, or the next day or the day after, but it is long-lasting; that is, it ceases only with death—this is the meaning. `Kakkhaḷena` means with exceedingly harsh, virtue-destroying, and obstinate speech. `Saṃsandati` means it unites. `Sammodati` means it becomes uninterrupted—this is the meaning to be understood here.

Atha vā sandhiyatīti ṭhānagamanādīsu kāyakiriyāsu kāyena samodhānaṃ gacchati, tilataṇḍulā viya missībhāvaṃ upetīti attho. Saṃsandatīti cittakiriyāsu cittena samodhānaṃ gacchati, khīrodakaṃ viya ekībhāvaṃ upetīti attho. Sammodatīti uddesaparipucchādīsu vacīkiriyāsu [M 2.0216] vācāya samodhānaṃ gacchati, vippavāsāgatopi piyasahāyako viya piyatarabhāvaṃ upetīti [V 2.0196] attho. Apica kiccakaraṇīyesu tehi saddhiṃ ādītova ekakiriyābhāvaṃ upagacchanto sandhiyati, yāva majjhā pavattanto saṃsandati, yāva pariyosānā anivattanto sammodatīti veditabbo.

Alternatively, `sandhiyati` means it achieves unity with the body in bodily actions such as standing and going, just as sesame seeds and rice grains become mixed—this is the meaning. `Saṃsandati` means it achieves unity with the mind in mental actions, just as milk and water become one—this is the meaning. `Sammodati` means it achieves unity with speech in verbal actions such as recitation and questioning, just as a dear friend who has returned from a separation becomes even dearer—this is the meaning. Furthermore, in performing duties, one initially unites (`sandhiyati`) with them, continues to merge (`saṃsandati`) in the middle, and continues to harmonize (`sammodati`) without turning back until the end—this should be understood.

Lekhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Lekha Sutta is concluded.

Kusināravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kusināra Chapter is concluded.

(14) 4. Yodhājīvavaggo

(14) 4. The Yodhājīva Chapter

1. Yodhājīvasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Yodhājīva Sutta

134. Catutthassa paṭhame yujjhanaṃ yodho, so ājīvo etassāti yodhājīvo. Yuddhamupajīvatīti vā etasmiṃ atthe yodhājīvoti niruttinayena padasiddhi veditabbā. Tenāha “yuddhaṃ upajīvatīti yodhājīvo”ti. Saha…pe… passatīti pubbabhāge vipassanāpaññāya sammasanavasena, maggakkhaṇe abhisamayavasena attapaccakkhena ñāṇena passati.

134. In the first discourse of the fourth chapter, `yujjhanaṃ` (fighting) is a warrior (`yodho`), and `yodhājīvo` (a warrior by profession) means 'whose livelihood is that'. Alternatively, the formation of the word `yodhājīvo` in this sense, 'one who lives by warfare,' should be understood by way of etymological derivation. Therefore it is said, 'one who lives by warfare is a `yodhājīvo`'. `Saha…pe… passati` means that in the preliminary stage, one sees by way of comprehension with insight wisdom, and at the moment of the path, one sees by way of realization with one's own direct knowledge.

Yodhājīvasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Yodhājīva Sutta is concluded.

2. Parisāsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Parisā Sutta

135. Dutiye appaṭipucchitvā vinītāti “taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”tiādinā appaṭipucchitvā kevalaṃ dhammadesanāvaseneva vinītaparisā. Dubbinītaparisāti dukkhena vinītaparisā. Pucchitvā vinītāti “taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave”tiādinā pucchitvā anumatiggahaṇavasena vinītā. Suvinītaparisāti sukhena vinītaparisā. Anumatiggahaṇavasena vinayanañhi na dukkaraṃ hoti.

135. In the second discourse, `appaṭipucchitvā vinītā` means an assembly trained merely through the mode of teaching the Dhamma, without being questioned, such as 'What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?' and so forth. `Dubbinītaparisā` means an assembly that is difficult to train. `Pucchitvā vinītā` means an assembly trained by questioning, such as 'What do you think, bhikkhus?' and so forth, trained through gaining their assent. `Suvinītaparisā` means an assembly that is easy to train. For training through gaining assent is indeed not difficult.

Parisāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Parisā Sutta is concluded.

4. Uppādāsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Uppāda Sutta

137. Catutthe [M 2.0217][V 2.0197] uppādā vā tathāgatānanti tathāgatānaṃ uppādepi veneyyapuggalānaṃ maggaphaluppatti viya saṅkhārānaṃ aniccādisabhāvo na tathāgatuppādāyatto, atha kho tathāgatānaṃ uppādepi anuppādepi hotimevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ṭhitāva sā dhātūti ṭhito eva so aniccasabhāvo byabhicārābhāvato na kadāci saṅkhārā aniccā na hoti. Kāmaṃ asaṅkhatā viya dhātu na nicco so sabhāvo, tathāpi sabbakālikoyevāti adhippāyo.

137. In the fourth discourse, regarding `uppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ` (whether Tathāgatas arise or not), it is said that the nature of impermanence and so forth of conditioned things is not dependent on the arising of Tathāgatas—unlike the arising of path and fruit for trainable individuals. Rather, whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature exists. `Ṭhitāva sā dhātu` (this principle stands firm) means that this nature of impermanence remains steadfast, without variation, for there is never a time when conditioned things are not impermanent. Although this nature is not permanent like the unconditioned element, the intention is that it is always present.

Aparo nayo – ṭhitāva sā dhātūti “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”ti esā dhātu esa sabhāvo tathāgatānaṃ uppādato pubbe uddhañca appaṭivijjhiyamāno na tathāgatehi uppādito, atha kho sabbakālaṃ sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, ṭhitāva sā dhātu, kevalaṃ pana sayambhuñāṇena abhisambujjhanato “ayaṃ dhammo tathāgatena abhisambuddho”ti pavedanato ca tathāgato dhammassāmīti vuccati apubbassa tassa uppādanato. Tena vuttaṃ “ṭhitāva sā dhātū”ti.

Another interpretation: `ṭhitāva sā dhātu` (this principle stands firm) means that this element, this nature, 'all conditioned things are impermanent,' remained unpenetrated before the arising of Tathāgatas and afterwards, and was not produced by Tathāgatas. Rather, at all times, all conditioned things are impermanent; this element stands firm. Yet, because it is fully understood through self-awakened knowledge and proclaimed as 'this Dhamma has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata,' the Tathāgata is called the master of the Dhamma, not because of producing what did not exist before. Therefore it is said, `ṭhitāva sā dhātu`.

Abhisambujjhatīti ñāṇena abhisambujjhati. Abhisametīti ñāṇena abhisamāgacchati. Ācikkhatīti katheti. Desetīti dasseti. Paññāpetīti jānāpeti. Paṭṭhapetīti ñāṇamukhe ṭhapeti. Vivaratīti vivaritvā dasseti. Vibhajatīti vibhāgato dasseti. Uttānīkarotīti pākaṭaṃ karoti.

`Abhisambujjhati` means he fully awakens with knowledge. `Abhisameti` means he comprehends with knowledge. `Ācikkhati` means he tells. `Deseti` means he shows. `Paññāpeti` means he makes known. `Paṭṭhapeti` means he establishes at the forefront of knowledge. `Vivarati` means he reveals and shows. `Vibhajati` means he shows by way of analysis. `Uttānīkaroti` means he makes manifest.

Atha vā abhisambujjhatīti paccakkhakaraṇena abhimukhaṃ bujjhati, yāthāvato paṭivijjhati. Tato eva abhisameti abhimukhaṃ samāgacchati. Ādito kathento ācikkhati, uddisatīti attho. Tameva uddesaṃ pariyosāpento deseti. Yathāuddiṭṭhamatthaṃ nidassanavasena pakārehi ñāpento paññāpeti. Pakārehi etamatthaṃ patiṭṭhapento paṭṭhapeti. Yathāuddiṭṭhaṃ paṭinidassanavasena vivarati vibhajati. Vivaṭaṃ vibhattañca atthaṃ hetūdāharaṇadassanehi pākaṭaṃ karonto uttānīkaroti.

Alternatively, `abhisambujjhati` means he awakens directly by realizing, penetrating it as it truly is. From that, he `abhisameti`, approaching it directly. Speaking from the beginning, he `ācikkhati`—this is the meaning of 'points out.' Completing that pointing out, he `deseti`. Making the meaning as pointed out known through illustrations and various modes, he `paññāpeti`. Establishing that meaning through various modes, he `paṭṭhapeti`. He `vivarati` and `vibhajati` by way of corresponding illustrations as pointed out. Making the revealed and analyzed meaning manifest by showing reasons and examples, he `uttānīkaroti`.

Uppādāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Uppāda Sutta is concluded.

5-10. Kesakambalasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-10. Commentary on the Kesakambala Sutta and others

138-143. Pañcame [M 2.0218][V 2.0198] tantāvutānaṃ vatthānanti idaṃ “yāni kānicī”ti iminā samānādhikaraṇanti āha “paccatte sāmivacana”nti. Vāyitānanti vītānaṃ. Lāmakoti nihīno, makkhali moghapurisoti ettha makkhalīti tassa nāmaṃ. Taṃ kira sakaddamāya bhūmiyā telaghaṭaṃ gahetvā gacchantaṃ, “tāta, mā khalī”ti sāmiko āha. So pamādena khalitvā patitvā sāmikassa bhayena palāyituṃ āraddho. Sāmiko upadhāvitvā naṃ dussakaṇṇe aggahesi, sāṭakaṃ chaḍḍetvā acelako hutvā palāyi. So paṇṇena vā tiṇena vā paṭicchādetumpi ajānanto jātarūpeneva ekaṃ gāmaṃ pāvisi. Manussā taṃ disvā “ayaṃ samaṇo arahā appiccho, natthi iminā sadiso”ti pūvabhattādīni gahetvā upasaṅkamanti. So “mayhaṃ sāṭakaṃ anivatthabhāvena idaṃ uppanna”nti tato paṭṭhāya sāṭakaṃ labhitvāpi na nivāsesi, tadeva ca pabbajjaṃ aggahesi. Tassa santike aññepi aññepīti pañcasatā manussā pabbajiṃsu. Taṃ sandhāyāha “makkhali moghapuriso”ti. Chaṭṭhādīni uttānatthāni eva.

138-143. In the fifth discourse, `tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ` is in apposition with `yāni kānici`. It is said: 'a genitive in the singular.' `Vāyitānaṃ` means `vītānaṃ` (woven). `Lāmako` means `nihīno` (inferior). `Makkhali moghapuriso`—here, `Makkhali` is his name. It is said that while he was walking, holding an oil pot on muddy ground, his master said, “My dear, do not slip (mā khali).” But due to carelessness, he slipped and fell, and out of fear of his master, he began to flee. The master chased him and caught him by the edge of his garment, but he discarded the garment and ran away naked. Not knowing how to cover himself even with leaves or grass, he entered a village just as he was born. People, seeing him, thought, “This ascetic is an arahant, of few wishes—there is none like him,” and brought him cakes, cooked rice, and other food. Thinking, “This has arisen for me because I was not wearing a garment,” from then on, even when he obtained a garment, he did not wear it, and he adopted that very practice as his renunciation. In his presence, five hundred other people also went forth. Referring to this, it is said, `Makkhali moghapuriso` (Makkhali, the worthless man). The sixth discourse and so forth are clear in meaning.

Kesakambalasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kesakambala Sutta and others is concluded.

11-13. Paṭhamamoranivāpasuttādivaṇṇanā

11-13. Commentary on the First Moranivāpa Sutta and others

144-146. Ekādasame akuppadhammatāya khayavayasaṅkhātaṃ antaṃ atītāti accantā, evaṃ aparihāyanasabhāvattā accantā niṭṭhā assāti accantaniṭṭho. Tenāha “antaṃ atikkantaniṭṭho”tiādi. Na hi paṭividdhassa lokuttaradhammassa dassanaṃ kuppanaṃ nāma atthi. Dhuvaniṭṭhoti satataniṭṭho. Accantameva catūhi yogehi khemo etassa atthīti accantayogakkhemī, niccayogakkhemīti attho. Maggabrahmacariyassa vusitattā tassa avihāyanasabhāvattā accantaṃ brahmacārīti accantabrahmacārī, niccabrahmacārīti attho. Pariyosānanti brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ vaṭṭadukkhapariyosānañca[M 2.0219]. Accantaṃ pariyosānamassāti accantapariyosāno. Dvādasamaterasamāni uttānatthāneva.

144-146. In the eleventh, because of his unshakeable nature, he has gone beyond the end, which is designated as destruction and decay—thus, he is ‘accanta’ (ultimate). And because his attainment is of such an unshakeable nature, he is ‘accantaniṭṭho’ (one whose attainment is ultimate). Hence it is said, ‘antaṃ atikkantaniṭṭho’ (one whose attainment has transcended the end), and so forth. For one who has penetrated the supramundane Dhamma, there is no such thing as instability. ‘Dhuvaniṭṭho’ means ‘one of constant attainment.’ ‘Accantayogakkhemī’ means ‘he is utterly secure from the four yogas (bonds)—that is, always secure.’ Because he has lived the holy life of the path and is of an unshakeable nature, he is ‘accantabrahmacārī’ (one whose holy life is ultimate)—that is, always a holy one. ‘Pariyosāna’ means ‘the culmination of the holy life and the end of the round of suffering.’ ‘Accantapariyosāno’ means ‘he whose culmination is ultimate.’ The twelfth and thirteenth are clear in meaning.

Paṭhamamoranivāpasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Moranivāpa Sutta and So Forth is concluded.

Yodhājīvavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Yodhājīva Vagga is concluded.

147-156. Maṅgalavaggo [V 2.0199] uttānatthoyeva.

147-156. The Maṅgala Vagga is clear in meaning.

Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The third set of fifty is concluded.

(16) 6. Acelakavaggavaṇṇanā

(16) 6. Commentary on the Acelaka Vagga

157-163. Ito paresu pana suttapadesu “gāḷhā”ti vuttamatthaṃ vivaranto “kakkhaḷā”ti āha. Kakkhaḷacāro cassā na lūkhasabhāvo. Atha kho taṇhāvasena thiraggahaṇanti āha “lobhavasena thiraggahaṇā”ti. Agāḷhā paṭipadāti vā kāmānaṃ ogāhanaṃ paṭipatti, kāmasukhānuyogoti attho. Nijjhāmā paṭipadāti kāyassa nijjhāpanavasena khepanavasena pavattā paṭipatti, attakilamathānuyogoti attho. Nicceloti nissaṭṭhacelo sabbena sabbaṃ paṭikkhittacelo. Naggiyavatasamādānena naggo. Ṭhitakova uccāraṃ karotītiādi nidassanamattaṃ vamitvā mukhavikkhālanādiācārassapi tena vissaṭṭhattā. Jivhāya hatthaṃ apalekhati avalekhati udakena adhovanato. Dutiyavikappepi eseva nayo. “Ehi, bhadante”ti vutte upagamanasaṅkhāto vidhi ehibhadanto, taṃ caratīti ehibhadantiko, tappaṭikkhepena na ehibhadantiko. Na karoti “samaṇena nāma parassa vacanakarena na bhavitabba”nti adhippāyena.

157-163. Furthermore, in the following sutta passages, explaining the meaning of ‘gāḷhā’ as stated, he says ‘kakkhaḷā’ (rough). Its conduct is rough, but not of a crude nature. Then, regarding the firm grasping due to craving, he says, ‘its firm grasping is due to greed.’ Or, ‘agāḷhā paṭipadā’ means a course of conduct that plunges into sensual pleasures—that is, the pursuit of sensual enjoyment. ‘Nijjhāmā paṭipadā’ means a course of conduct carried out by emaciating and wasting the body—that is, the pursuit of self-mortification. ‘Niccelo’ means without clothes, having completely rejected all garments. He is naked, having undertaken a vow of nudity. The description ‘standing while defecating,’ and so forth, is merely illustrative, for practices such as rinsing the mouth after vomiting have also been abandoned by him. He licks his hand with his tongue, meaning he does not wash it with water. The same method applies to the second alternative. When told, ‘Come, venerable sir,’ the procedure of coming is called ‘ehibhadanto’; one who practices that is ‘ehibhadantiko,’ but by rejecting that, he is ‘na ehibhadantiko.’ He does not do so, with the intention that ‘a recluse should not be one who acts on the words of another.’

Puretaranti taṃ ṭhānaṃ attano upagamanato puretaraṃ. Taṃ kira so “bhikkhunā nāma yadicchakā eva bhikkhā gahetabbā”ti adhippāyena na gaṇhāti. Uddissa kataṃ mama nimittabhāvena bahū khuddakā pāṇā saṅghātaṃ āpāditāti na gaṇhāti. Nimantanaṃ na sādiyati evaṃ tesaṃ vacanaṃ kataṃ bhavissatīti. Kumbhi ādīsupi so sattasaññīti āha “kumbhi-kaḷopiyo”tiādi. Kabaḷantarāyo hotīti uṭṭhitassa dvinnampi kabaḷantarāyo hoti. Gāmasabhāgādivasena saṅgamma kittenti etissāti saṅkitti, yathāsaṃhatataṇḍulādisañcayo. Mānusakānīti veyyāvaccakarā manussā.

‘Puretara’ means that place is earlier than one’s own arrival. It is said that he does not take it with the intention, ‘A monk should take almsfood only as he wishes.’ He does not take it because it was made specially for him, thinking, ‘Many small creatures have been brought to destruction due to me being the cause.’ He does not accept an invitation, thinking, ‘Thus their word will have been kept.’ Regarding pots and so forth, he says that he perceives beings, as in ‘kumbhi-kaḷopiyo’ (pots and jars), and so forth. There is interruption of the morsel—for one who has arisen, there is interruption of both morsels. They gather and praise it in the manner of village assemblies and so forth—this is called ‘saṅkitti,’ like a collection of well-pounded rice and so forth. ‘Mānusakāni’ means human attendants.

Surāpānamevāti [M 2.0220][V 2.0200] majjalakkhaṇappattāya surāya pānameva. Surāgahaṇenevettha merayampi saṅgahitaṃ. Ekāgārameva uñchatīti ekāgāriko. Ekālopeneva vattatīti ekālopiko. Dīyati etāyāti datti, dvattiālopamattaggāhi khuddakaṃ bhikkhādānabhājanaṃ. Tenāha “khuddakapātī”ti. Abhuñjanavasena eko aho etassa atthīti ekāhiko, āhāro, taṃ ekāhikaṃ. So pana atthato ekadivasaṃ laṅghako hotīti āha “ekādivasantarika”nti. Dvāhikantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ekāhaṃ abhuñjitvā ekāhaṃ bhuñjanaṃ ekāhavāro, taṃ ekāhikameva atthato. Dvīhaṃ abhuñjitvā dvīhaṃ bhuñjanaṃ dvīhavāro. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Ukkaṭṭho pana pariyāyabhattabhojaniko dvīhaṃ abhuñjitvā ekāhameva bhuñjati. Sesadvayepi eseva nayo.

‘Surāpānameva’ means the drinking of liquor that has reached the state of intoxication. Here, even fermented liquor is included by the term ‘surā’ (intoxicants). He gleans in only one house—thus, he is an ‘ekāgāriko’ (one-house gleaner). He subsists on only one mouthful—thus, he is an ‘ekālopiko’ (one-mouthful eater). ‘Datti’ means that by which it is given, a small alms bowl, holding just two or three mouthfuls of almsfood. Therefore, it is called ‘khuddakapātī’ (small bowl). Because of not eating, there is one day for him—thus, it is ‘ekāhiko’ (one-day), the food; that is the ‘ekāhikaṃ’ (one-day provision). But, in essence, it means skipping one day—thus, he says, ‘ekādivasantarika’ (having a one-day interval). The same method applies to ‘dvāhikaṃ’ (a two-day provision), and so forth. Eating one day after not eating for one day is a one-day turn (‘ekāhavāro’), which is what ‘ekāhikaṃ’ means in essence. Eating two days after not eating for two days is a two-day turn (‘dvīhavāro’). The same method applies to the remaining two terms. However, the most strict practice is of the one who eats scheduled meals: not eating for two days and eating only for one day. The same method applies to the remaining two.

Micchāvāyāmavaseneva ukkuṭikavatānuyogoti āha “ukkuṭikavīriyamanuyutto”ti. Attakilamathānuyoganti attano kilamathānuyogaṃ, sarīradukkhakāraṇanti attho. Sarīrapariyāyo hi idha attasaddo “attantapo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.413) viya. Dve anteti ubho koṭiyo, ubho lāmakapaṭipattiyoti attho.
