Lāmakampi hi antoti vuccati “antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikānaṃ (saṃ. ni. 3.80; itivu. 61), koṭṭhako anto”ti evamādīsu. Majjhimapaṭipadāya uppathabhāvena amanīyā gantabbā ñātabbāti antā. Tato eva lāmakā.

By means of wrong effort, it is the practice of squatting—thus, he says, ‘one is devoted to the energy of squatting.’ ‘Attakilamathānuyoga’ means devotion to tormenting oneself—that is, causing bodily suffering. Here, the word ‘atta’ (self) is a term for the body, as in ‘attantapo’ (self-mortification) and so forth. ‘Dve anta’ means both ends—that is, both inferior practices. For even the inferior is called an end, as in ‘this, monks, is the lowest of livelihoods,’ ‘the storeroom is an end,’ and so forth. Because they are a wrong path in relation to the middle way, they are undesirable, not to be followed, and not to be known—thus they are ‘ends’ (antā). Therefore, they are inferior.

Acelakavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Acelaka Vagga is concluded.

Peyyālavaggavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Section on Repetitions

164-184. Samanuññoti sammadeva katānuñño. Tenāha “samānajjhāsayo”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

164-184. ‘Samanuñño’ means one who has properly given permission. Therefore, it is said, ‘of similar inclination.’ The remainder here is clear.

Iti manorathapūraṇiyā aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus ends the Manorathapūraṇī, the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

Tikanipātavaṇṇanāya anuttānatthadīpanā samattā.

The Exposition of the Book of the Threes, illuminating the profound meaning, is complete.

. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Aṅguttaranikāye

In the Aṅguttara Nikāya

Catukkanipāta-ṭīkā

The Sub-commentary on the Book of the Fours

1. Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

1. The First Fifty

1. Bhaṇḍagāmavaggo

1. The Chapter on Bhaṇḍagāma

1-2. Anubuddhasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Exposition of the Anubuddha Sutta and So On

1-2. Catukkanipātassa [M 2.0221][V 2.0201] paṭhame anubodho pubbabhāgiyaṃ ñāṇaṃ, paṭivedho anubodhena abhisamayo. Tattha yasmā anubodhapubbako paṭivedho anubodhena vinā na hoti. Anubodho hi ekacco paṭivedhasambaddho, tadubhayābhāvahetukañca vaṭṭe saṃsaraṇaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “ananubodhā…pe… tumhākañcā”ti. Paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena bhavato bhavantarūpagamanaṃ sandhāvanaṃ, aparāparaṃ cavanūpapajjanavasena sañcaraṇaṃ saṃsaraṇanti āha “bhavato”tiādi. Sandhāvitasaṃsaritapadānaṃ kammasādhanataṃ sandhāyāha “mayā ca tumhehi cā”ti paṭhamavikappe. Dutiyavikappe pana bhāvasādhanataṃ hadaye katvā “mamañceva tumhākañcā”ti yathārutavaseneva vuttaṃ[V 2.0202]. Dīgharajjunā baddhasakuṇaṃ viya rajjuhattho puriso desantaraṃ taṇhārajjunā baddhaṃ sattasantānaṃ abhisaṅkhāro bhavantaraṃ neti etāyāti bhavanetti. Tenāha “bhavarajjū”tiādī.

1-2. In the first [discourse of the] Book of the Fours, understanding is preliminary knowledge; penetration is realization, which is an attainment through understanding. Herein, since penetration is preceded by understanding, penetration does not occur without understanding. For understanding is indeed sometimes connected with penetration, and wandering in the round of existence is caused by the absence of both. Therefore, it is said in the Pāli: "Without understanding... and yours." Going from existence to existence by way of rebirth is called "sandhāvana"; wandering from one existence to another by way of passing away and reappearing is called "saṃsaraṇa." Hence, it is said: "from existence" and so on. Reflecting on the fact that the words "sandhāvitasaṃsarita" (run and wandered) are instrumental in the sense of action, it is said: "by me and by you" in the first alternative. In the second alternative, however, bearing in mind that they are instrumental in the sense of state, it is said: "mine and yours," just as it was stated. Just as a bird tied by a long string is led by a man holding the string to another place, so the volitional formation leads the continuum of a being, bound by the string of craving, to another existence—this is called "the conduit of existence." Hence, it is said: "the string of existence" and so on.

Vaṭṭadukkhassa antakaroti sakalavaṭṭadukkhassa sakasantāne parasantāne ca vināsakaro abhāvakaro. Buddhacakkhudhammacakkhudibbacakkhumaṃsacakkhusamantacakkhusaṅkhātehi pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā. Savāsanānaṃ kilesānaṃ samucchinnattā sātisayaṃ kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto. Dutiyaṃ uttānameva.

He is the end-maker of the suffering of the round, the destroyer and abolisher of all the suffering of the round, in his own continuum and in the continuum of others. He is endowed with eyes, having the five eyes known as the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the divine-eye, the flesh-eye, and the all-seeing eye. Because of the complete cutting off of defilements together with their latent tendencies, he is fully extinguished by the unsurpassed final Nibbāna of defilements. The second [discourse] is clear.

Anubuddhasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Anubuddha Sutta and So On is complete.

3-4. Paṭhamakhatasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-4. Exposition of the First Khata Sutta and So On

3-4. Tatiye [M 2.0222] kalinti aparādhaṃ. Vicinātīti ācinoti pasavati. Tena ca kalinā sukhaṃ na paṭilabhatīti tena aparādhena sukhaṃ na vindati. Nindiyappasaṃsāya hi pasaṃsiyanindāya ca samakova vipāko. Pasaṃsiyanindāti ca sampannaguṇaparidhaṃsanavasena pavattiyā mahāsāvajjatāya kaṭukataravipākā. Nindiyappasaṃsā pana kathaṃ tāya samavipākāti ce? Tasmiṃ avijjamānaguṇasamāropanena attano paresañca micchāpaṭipattihetubhāvato pasaṃsiyena tassa sabbhāvakaraṇato ca. Lokepi hi asūraṃ sūrena samaṃ karonto gārayho hoti, pageva duppaṭipannaṃ suppaṭipannena samaṃ karontoti. Sakena dhanenāti attano sāpateyyena. Appamattakova kalīti diṭṭhadhammikattā sappaṭikārattā ca appamattako aparādho. Ayaṃ…pe… mahantataro kali katūpacitattā samparāyikattā appaṭikārattā ca.

3-4. In the third, 'kali' means an offense. 'Vicināti' means one accumulates or produces. And because of that offense, one does not attain happiness—thus, one does not find happiness due to that fault. Indeed, the result of both blameworthy praise and praiseworthy blame is the same. 'Praiseworthy blame' has a more bitter result, for by way of obscuring accomplished virtues, its occurrence is greatly blameworthy. But how is 'blameworthy praise' equal in result to that? Because by falsely ascribing non-existent virtues to that person, it becomes a cause of wrong conduct for oneself and others, and because it makes the blameworthy person appear praiseworthy. For even in the world, one who equates a coward with a hero is worthy of censure—how much more so one who equates one of bad conduct with one of good conduct. 'With his own wealth' means with his own property. 'The offense is slight' means it is a slight offense because it pertains to this present life and is remediable. This... (etc.)... is a far greater offense because it is accumulated and built up, pertains to the next world, and is irremediable.

Nirabbudoti gaṇanāviseso esoti āha “nirabbudagaṇanāyā”ti, satasahassaṃ nirabbudāti attho. Nirabbudaparimāṇaṃ pana vassagaṇanāya evaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yatheva hi sataṃ satasahassānaṃ koṭi hoti, evaṃ sataṃ satasahassānaṃ koṭiyo pakoṭi nāma hoti, sataṃ satasahassānaṃ pakoṭiyo koṭipakoṭi, sataṃ satasahassakoṭipakoṭiyo nahutaṃ, sataṃ satasahassanahutāni ninnahutaṃ, sataṃ satasahassaninnahutāni ekaṃ abbudaṃ, tato vīsatiguṇitaṃ nirabbudaṃ. Yaṃ ariye garahanto nirayaṃ upapajjatīti ariye garahanto yaṃ nirabbudasaṅkhātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati, nirabbudoti ca pāṭiyekko nirayo natthi, avīcimhiyeva pana nirabbudagaṇanāya paccitabbaṭṭhānassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Catutthaṃ uttānameva.

The term 'nirabbuda' is a specific type of counting, hence it is said, 'by the nirabbuda count'; the meaning is 'a hundred thousand is a nirabbuda'. However, the measure of a nirabbuda in terms of years should be understood as follows: Just as a hundred hundred-thousands is a koṭi, so a hundred hundred-thousand koṭis is called a pakoṭi; a hundred hundred-thousand pakoṭis is a koṭipakoṭi; a hundred hundred-thousand koṭipakoṭis is a nahuta; a hundred hundred-thousand nahutas is a ninnahuta; a hundred hundred-thousand ninnahutas is one abbuda; twenty times that is a nirabbuda. 'One who reviles the noble ones is reborn in hell' means that one who reviles the noble ones is reborn in the hell designated as nirabbuda. And there is no separate hell called 'Nirabbuda,' but this is the name for a place in Avīci where one is tormented for a duration measured by the nirabbuda count. The fourth is self-evident.

Paṭhamakhatasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the suttas beginning with the First Khata Sutta is concluded.

5. Anusotasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Anusota Sutta

5. Pañcame [V 2.0203] anusotaṃ gacchatīti saṃsārasotassa anukūlabhāvena gacchati. Paccanīkapaṭipattiyāti saṃsārasotassa paṭikūlavasena pavattanibbidānupassanādipaṭipattiyā[M 2.0223]. Ṭhitasabhāvoti acalappasādādisamannāgamena ṭhitasabhāvo. Anāgāmī hi assaddhiyehi kāmarāgabyāpādehi akampaniyacittatāya tamhā lokā anāvattidhammatāya ca ṭhitasabhāvo nāma. Oghaṃ taritvāti kāmoghādicatubbidhaṃ oghaṃ atikkamitvā. Paratīraṃ gatoti nibbānapāraṃ gato. Brāhmaṇoti bāhitapāpatāya brāhmaṇoti saṅkhaṃ gato khīṇāsavo. Tenāha “seṭṭho niddoso”ti. Pañcaverakammanti pāṇātipātādipañcaduccaritaṃ. Sahāpi dukkhena sahāpi domanassenāti kilesapariyuṭṭhāne sati uppannena dukkhadomanassena saddhimpi. Paripuṇṇanti tissannaṃ sikkhānaṃ ekāyapi anūnaṃ. Parisuddhanti nirupakkilesaṃ. Brahmacariyanti seṭṭhacariyaṃ. Iminā vārena sotāpannasakadāgāmino kathitā. Kiṃ pana te rudantā brahmacariyaṃ carantīti? Āma, kilesarodanena rodantā caranti nāma, sīlasampanno puthujjanabhikkhu ettheva saṅgahito.

5. In the fifth, 'going with the stream' means going along with the flow of the cycle of existence. 'Practicing against the current' means practicing in opposition to the stream of existence through the cultivation of disenchantment, insight, and the like. 'Established in nature' refers to being steadfast in nature due to possessing unwavering serenity and the like. For a non-returner is called 'established in nature' because his mind is unshakable by lack of faith, sensual desire, or ill will, and because of his nature of not returning from that world. 'Having crossed the flood' means having overcome the fourfold flood, beginning with the flood of sensual desire. 'Gone to the far shore' means having reached the far shore of Nibbāna. 'A brahmin' refers to one who, because he has abandoned evil, is reckoned as such—an Arahant whose defilements are destroyed. Hence it is said, 'the best, the faultless one.' 'The fivefold evil conduct' refers to the five kinds of misconduct, starting with killing living beings. 'Even with suffering, even with sorrow' means even together with the suffering and sorrow that arise when defilements are stirred up. 'Complete' means not lacking in even one of the three trainings. 'Purified' means free from defilement. 'The holy life' means the supreme conduct. By this passage, stream-enterers and once-returners are spoken of. But do they practice the holy life while weeping? Yes, they are said to practice while weeping with the weeping of defilements. A virtuous ordinary monk is included here as well.

Cetovimuttinti phalasamādhiṃ. Paññāvimuttinti phalañāṇaṃ. Chahākārehi pāragatoti abhiññāpāragū, pariññāpāragū, bhāvanāpāragū, pahānapāragū, sacchikiriyāpāragū, samāpattipāragūti evaṃ chahi ākārehi sabbadhammānaṃ pāraṃ pariyosānaṃ gato. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

'Liberation of mind' means fruition concentration. 'Liberation by wisdom' means fruition knowledge. 'Gone to the far shore in six ways' means one who has gone to the far shore through direct knowledge, full understanding, development, abandoning, realization, and attainment—thus, in these six ways, one has gone to the far shore, the culmination of all phenomena. The remainder here is easily understood.

Anusotasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Anusota Sutta is concluded.

6. Appassutasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Appassuta Sutta

6. Chaṭṭhe appakaṃ sutaṃ hotīti navaṅgasatthusāsane kiñcideva sutaṃ hoti. Tadeva navaṅgasatthusāsanaṃ dassetuṃ “suttaṃ geyya”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha suttādīni vibhajitvā dassento “ubhatovibhaṅganiddesakkhandhakaparivārā”tiādimāha. Kathaṃ panāyaṃ vibhāgo yujjeyya. Sagāthakañhi suttaṃ geyyaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ. Tadubhayavinimuttañca suttaṃ udānādivisesasaññārahitaṃ natthi, yaṃ suttaṅgaṃ siyā. Maṅgalasuttādīnañca (khu. pā. 5.1 ādayo; su. ni. 261 ādayo) suttaṅgasaṅgaho na siyā gāthābhāvato dhammapadādīnaṃ viya[M 2.0224]. Geyyaṅgasaṅgaho vā siyā sagāthakattā sagāthāvaggassa viya. Tathā ubhatovibhaṅgādīsu sagāthakappadesānanti? Vuccate –

6. In the sixth, 'little has been heard' means that only a little has been heard of the ninefold Dispensation of the Teacher. To show that very ninefold Dispensation of the Teacher, it is said, 'Sutta, Geyya,' etc. There, explaining the divisions of Sutta, etc., it is said, 'the two Vibhaṅgas, the Niddesa, the Khandhakas, and the Parivāra,' etc. But how is this division justified? For a Sutta with verses is a Geyya, and a Sutta without verses is a Veyyākaraṇa. And apart from these two, there is no Sutta devoid of special designations like Udāna, etc., which could be a Sutta-aṅga. Moreover, the inclusion of the Maṅgala Sutta, etc., (Khuddakapāṭha 5.1, etc.; Sutta Nipāta 261, etc.) as a Sutta-aṅga would not be possible because they are verses, like the Dhammapada, etc. Or it could be included as a Geyya-aṅga because it has verses, like the Sagāthāvagga. Similarly, what about the sections with verses in the two Vibhaṅgas, etc.? It is said:

“Suttanti [V 2.0204] sāmaññavidhi, visesavidhayo pare;

Sanimittā niruḷhattā, sahatāññena nāññato”. (netti. aṭṭha. saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā; sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā)

'Sutta' is the general rule; the others are specific rules. They are so called because they have their own marks, are established by convention, or are associated with another, and not otherwise.

Sabbassapi hi buddhavacanassa suttanti ayaṃ sāmaññavidhi. Tenevāha āyasmā mahākaccāno nettiyaṃ (netti. saṅgahavāro) “navavidhasuttantapariyeṭṭhī”ti. Ettakaṃ tassa bhagavato suttāgataṃ suttapariyāpannaṃ (pāci. 655, 1242) sakavāde pañca suttasatānīti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; kathā. aṭṭha. nidānakathā) evamādi ca etassa atthassa sādhakaṃ. Visesavidhayo pare sanimittā tadekadesesu geyyādayo visesavidhayo tena tena nimittena patiṭṭhitā. Tathā hi geyyassa sagāthakattaṃ tabbhāvanimittaṃ. Lokepi hi sasilokaṃ sagāthakaṃ vā cuṇṇiyaganthaṃ “geyya”nti vadanti. Gāthāvirahe pana sati pucchaṃ katvā vissajjanabhāvo veyyākaraṇassa tabbhāvanimittaṃ. Pucchāvissajjanañhi “byākaraṇa”nti vuccati. Byākaraṇameva veyyākaraṇaṃ. Evaṃ sante sagāthakādīnampi pucchaṃ katvā vissajjanavasena pavattānaṃ veyyākaraṇabhāvo āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati geyyādisaññānaṃ anokāsabhāvato, “gāthāvirahe satī”ti visesitattā ca. Tathā hi dhammapadādīsu kevalaṃ gāthābandhesu sagāthakattepi somanassañāṇamayikagāthāyuttesu “vuttaṃ heta”ntiādīvacanasambandhesu abbhutadhammappaṭisaṃyuttesu ca suttavisesesu yathākkamaṃ gāthāudānaitivuttakaabbhutadhammasaññā patiṭṭhitā, tathā satipi gāthābandhabhāve bhagavato atītāsu jātīsu cariyānubhāvappakāsakesu jātakasaññā, satipi pañhavissajjanabhāve sagāthakatte ca kesuci suttantesu vedassa labhāpanato vedallasaññā patiṭṭhitāti evaṃ tena tena sagāthakattādinā nimittena tesu tesu suttavisesesu geyyādisaññā patiṭṭhitāti visesavidhayo suttaṅgato pare geyyādayo. Yaṃ panettha geyyaṅgādinimittarahitaṃ, taṃ suttaṅgaṃ visesasaññāparihārena sāmaññasaññāya pavattanato. Nanu ca sagāthakaṃ suttaṃ geyyaṃ, niggāthakaṃ suttaṃ [M 2.0225] veyyākaraṇanti suttaṅgaṃ na sambhavatīti codanā tadavatthāvāti? Na tadavatthā sodhitattā. Sodhitañhi pubbe “gāthāvirahe sati pucchāvissajjanabhāvo veyyākaraṇassa tabbhāvanimitta”nti.

For indeed, the general rule for all the Buddha's teachings is that they are called 'sutta.' Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāna said in the Netti (Netti, Saṅgahavāro): 'The ninefold investigation of suttas.' This much of the Blessed One’s teachings, included in the suttas (Pāc. 655, 1242), are five hundred suttas in his own school (Dha. Sa. Aṭṭha. Nidānakathā; Kathā. Aṭṭha. Nidānakathā), and so on—this is evidence for this meaning. The other specific classifications, geyya and so on, are established with their characteristics; in certain portions of these teachings, specific classifications like geyya are established by their respective characteristics. For example, the characteristic of geyya is being with verses. Indeed, even in the world, a prose text with verses or stanzas is called 'geyya.' However, when verses are absent, the condition of asking a question and making an explanation is the characteristic of veyyākaraṇa. For a question and its answer is called 'byākaraṇa.' Byākaraṇa itself is veyyākaraṇa. In that case, would the state of veyyākaraṇa apply even to those suttas with verses, etc., that proceed by way of question and answer? No, it does not, because there is no scope for the designations of geyya, etc., and because it is specified as 'when verses are absent.' For instance, in the Dhammapada and other texts consisting solely of verse collections, even though they contain verses, the designations Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, and Abbhutadhamma are established respectively in specific suttas which are connected with verses consisting of joyful knowledge, which begin with 'Thus it was said,' and which are connected with marvelous phenomena. Similarly, even when there is verse composition, in the Jātakas, which express the power of conduct in the Blessed One's past lives, the designation jātaka is established. And even when there is the condition of question and answer, and the presence of verses in some suttas, the designation vedalla is established because of the attainment of knowledge and joy. Thus, in those various sutta classifications, the designations of geyya, etc., are established by their respective characteristics, such as being with verses; these specific classifications, such as geyya and others, are distinct from the Sutta category. But here, that which is devoid of the characteristics of geyya, etc., is the sutta category, operating under the general designation, free from specific designations. Now, is there an objection that a sutta with verses is geyya, and a sutta without verses is veyyākaraṇa, so the sutta category does not apply? That objection does not stand, because it has already been refuted. For it was previously clarified: 'When verses are absent, the condition of asking a question and making an explanation is the characteristic of veyyākaraṇa.'

Yañca vuttaṃ – “gāthābhāvato maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ suttaṅgasaṅgaho na siyā”ti, taṃ na, niruḷhattā. Niruḷho hi maṅgalasuttādīnaṃ suttabhāvo. Na hi tāni dhammapadabuddhavaṃsādayo viya gāthābhāvena paññātāni, atha kho suttabhāveneva, teneva hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “suttanāmaka”nti nāmaggahaṇaṃ [V 2.0205] kataṃ. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “sagāthakattā geyyaṅgasaṅgaho siyā”ti, tadapi natthi, yasmā sahatāññena. Saha gāthāhīti hi sagāthakaṃ. Sahabhāvo nāma atthato aññena hoti, na ca maṅgalasuttādīsu gāthāvinimutto koci suttappadeso atthi, yo “saha gāthāhī”ti vucceyya, na ca samudāyo nāma koci atthi. Yadapi vuttaṃ – “ubhatovibhaṅgādīsu sagāthakappadesānaṃ geyyaṅgasaṅgaho siyā”ti, tadapi na, aññato. Aññā eva hi tā gāthā jātakādipariyāpannattā. Ato na tāhi ubhatovibhaṅgādīnaṃ geyyaṅgabhāvoti. Evaṃ suttādīnaṃ aṅgānaṃ aññamaññaṃ saṅkarābhāvo veditabbo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya sāratthadīpaniyā (sārattha. ṭī. 1.paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā) amhehi pakāsito, icchantehi tatoyeva gahetabbo.

And as to what was said, 'because they consist of verses, the inclusion of suttas like the Maṅgala Sutta under the Suttaṅga category would not be possible,' this is not so, due to their being well-established as such. For the status of the Maṅgala Sutta and others as suttas is well-established. They are not known for being verses, like the Dhammapada, Buddhavaṃsa, and so on, but rather as suttas. For this very reason, in the commentary, the name 'suttanāmaka' (named sutta) was given. As for what was said, 'because they contain verses, they could be included under the Geyyaṅga category,' this is also not the case, because it must be together with something else. For 'sagāthaka' means 'together with verses.' The state of being 'together' is with something else in substance. But in suttas like the Maṅgala Sutta, there is no portion of the sutta apart from the verses that could be called 'together with verses,' nor is there any such composite. As for what was said, 'in texts like the Ubhatovibhaṅga, the portions containing verses could be included under Geyyaṅga,' this is also not the case, because they are from another source. For those verses are indeed different, being included in the Jātakas and so on. Therefore, they do not make the Ubhatovibhaṅga and other texts part of the Geyyaṅga. Thus, it should be understood that there is no intermingling among the categories of Sutta and so on. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation has been set forth by us in the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya, and in the Sāratthadīpanī. Those who wish may learn it from there.

Na atthamaññāya dhammamaññāya dhammānudhammappaṭipanno hotīti aṭṭhakathāñca pāḷiñca jānitvā lokuttaradhammassa anurūpadhammaṃ pubbabhāgappaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno na hotīti evamettha sambandho veditabbo. Tenevāha “na atthamaññāya dhammamaññāyāti aṭṭhakathañca pāḷiñca jānitvā…pe… na paṭipanno hotī”ti.

The phrase 'Not understanding the meaning, not understanding the Dhamma, one does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma' should be understood to be connected thus: it means that having known the commentary and the Pāḷi, one does not become a practitioner of the preliminary practice, the Dhamma that is in conformity with the supramundane Dhamma. Therefore, it is said: 'Not understanding the meaning, not understanding the Dhamma' means that having known the commentary and the Pāḷi... one does not become a practitioner.

Appassutasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Appassuta Sutta is concluded.

7. Sobhanasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Exposition of the Sobhana Sutta

7. Sattame paññāveyyattiyenāti saccasampaṭivedhādipaññāveyyattiyena. Vinayaṃ upetāti tadaṅgādivasena kilesānaṃ vinayaṃ upetā. Vesārajjenāti [M 2.0226] sārajjakarānaṃ diṭṭhivicikicchādipāpadhammānaṃ vigamanato vesārajjena, sārajjarahitenāti attho. Tepiṭakavasena bahu sutaṃ etesanti bahussutā. Tameva pariyattidhammaṃ dhārenti suvaṇṇabhājane pakkhittasīhavasaṃ viya vinassantaṃ akatvā suppaguṇasuppavattibhāvena hadaye ṭhapentīti dhammadharā. Edisā ca attanā sutassa dhammassa ādhārabhūtā nāma hontīti āha “sutadhammānaṃ ādhārabhūtā”ti.

7. In the seventh, 'by the clarity of wisdom' means by the clarity of wisdom that penetrates the truths, and so on. 'Endowed with discipline' means endowed with the discipline for the removal of defilements by way of its constituent parts, and so on. 'With confidence' means with confidence due to the removal of evil states such as wrong views and doubt, which cause timidity; the meaning is 'devoid of timidity.' 'They are well-learned' because they have heard much regarding the Tipiṭaka. 'They bear that very scriptural teaching' means they are bearers of the Dhamma because they establish that teaching in their hearts with excellent practice and proper conduct, not allowing it to perish, like lion's fat placed in a golden vessel. Such ones are indeed receptacles for the Dhamma they have heard, thus it is said: 'they are receptacles for the Dhamma they have heard.'

Sobhanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Sobhana Sutta is concluded.

8. Vesārajjasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Exposition of the Vesārajja Sutta

8. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0206] byāmohavasena saraṇapariyesanaṃ sārajjanaṃ sārado, byāmohabhayaṃ. Vigato sārado etassāti visārado, tassa bhāvo vesārajjaṃ. Taṃ pana ñāṇasampadaṃ, pahānasampadaṃ, desanāvisesasampadaṃ khemañca nissāya pavattaṃ catubbidhapaccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Tenāha “catūsu ṭhānesū”tiādi. Usabhassa idanti āsabhaṃ, seṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ. Sabbaññutapaṭijānanavasena abhimukhaṃ gacchanti, aṭṭha vā parisā upasaṅkamantīti āsabhā, pubbabuddhā. Idaṃ panāti buddhānaṃ ṭhānaṃ sabbaññutameva vadati. Tiṭṭhamānovāti avadantopi tiṭṭhamānova paṭijānāti nāmāti attho. Upagacchatīti anujānāti.

8. In the eighth, the search for refuge through delusion is 'timidity' (sārajjanaṃ); one who is timid (sārado) has the fear of delusion. One who is without timidity is 'confident' (visārado); the state of that is 'confidence' (vesārajjaṃ). That, however, is the fourfold reviewing knowledge that arises relying on the accomplishment of knowledge, the accomplishment of abandonment, the accomplishment of the special teaching, and security. Thus it is said, 'in four places,' and so on. 'That which belongs to a bull' (āsabhaṃ) is the supreme state. 'They go forth' (āsabhā) by way of declaring omniscience, or 'eight assemblies approach them'—these are the former Buddhas. This, indeed, refers to the state of the Buddhas, omniscience itself. 'Though standing' means that even while not speaking, he indeed declares; this is the meaning. 'He accepts' means he approves.

Aṭṭhasu parisāsūti “abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, anekasataṃ khattiyaparisaṃ upasaṅkamitā…pe… brāhmaṇaparisaṃ gahapatiparisaṃ, samaṇaparisaṃ, cātumahārājikaparisaṃ, tāvatiṃsaparisaṃ, māraparisaṃ, brahmaparisaṃ upasaṅkamitā, tatrapi mayā sannisinnapubbañceva sallapitapubbañca sākacchā ca samāpajjitapubbā. Tatra vata maṃ ‘bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā okkamissatī’ti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.151) evaṃ vuttaparisāsu. Abhītanādaṃ nadatīti parato dassitañāṇayogena visārado ahanti abhītanādaṃ nadati. Sīhanādasuttenāti khandhavagge āgatena sīhanādasuttena.

'In the eight assemblies' refers to the assemblies spoken of thus: 'I recall, Sāriputta, having approached many hundreds of assemblies of nobles... assemblies of brahmins, assemblies of householders, assemblies of ascetics, assemblies of the Four Great Kings, assemblies of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, assemblies of Māra, and assemblies of Brahmā. I have sat with them before, conversed with them before, and engaged in discussion with them before. That fear or timidity should overcome me there—this I do not see any cause for, Sāriputta' (MN 12). 'He roars the fearless roar' means, thinking 'I am confident,' he roars the fearless roar through the application of knowledge demonstrated to others. 'By the Lion's Roar Sutta' refers to the Sīhanāda Sutta found in the Khandha Vagga.

“Devamanussānaṃ catucakkaṃ vattatī”ti (a. ni. 4.31) suttasesena sappurisūpanissayādiphalasampattipavatti vuttā, purimasappurisūpanissayādiupanissayā pacchimasappurisūpanissayādisampattipavatti [M 2.0227] vā vuttā. Ādi-saddena tattha ca cakkasaddassa gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vicakkasaṇṭhānā asani eva asanivicakkaṃ. Uracakkādīsūti ādi-saddena āṇāsamūhādīsupi cakkasaddassa pavatti veditabbā. “Saṅghabhedaṃ karissāma cakkabheda”ntiādīsu (pārā. 409; cūḷava. 343) hi āṇā “cakka”nti vuttā. “Devacakkaṃ asuracakka”ntiādīsu samūhoti.

By the remainder of the sutta, 'the four wheels operate for gods and humans' (AN 4.31), the arising of the attainment of results through reliance on good people, etc., is stated; or, the arising of the attainment of later reliance on good people, etc., through the support of earlier reliance on good people, etc., is stated. And there, by the word 'etc.', the inclusion of the word 'wheel' should be understood. The thunderbolt, having a wheel-like shape, is indeed the 'thunderbolt-wheel.' In 'chest-wheel, etc.,' by the word 'etc.', the occurrence of the term 'wheel' should also be understood in relation to commands, groups, etc. For in statements like 'We will cause a schism in the Sangha, a breaking of the wheel' (Pārā. 409; Cūḷava. 343), the command is referred to as the 'wheel.' In phrases like 'the deva-wheel, the asura-wheel,' etc., it denotes a group.

Paṭivedhaniṭṭhattā arahattamaggañāṇaṃ paṭivedhoti “phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Tena paṭiladdhassapi desanāñāṇassa kiccanipphatti parassa bujjhanamattena hotīti “aññāsikoṇḍaññassa sotāpatti…pe… phalakkhaṇe pavattaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Tato paraṃ pana yāva parinibbānā desanāñāṇappavatti tasseva pavattitassa dhammacakkassa ṭhānanti veditabbaṃ.

Because it has penetration as its culmination, the knowledge of the path of arahantship is called 'penetration'; it is said, 'It is named as arisen in the moment of fruition.' Because the accomplishment of the function of the teaching knowledge acquired thereby is achieved merely by another's understanding, it is said, 'For Aññāsikoṇḍañña, stream-entry... is named as occurring in the moment of fruition.' But thereafter, the continuation of teaching knowledge until final Nibbāna should be understood as the basis for that very Dhamma wheel that has been set in motion.

Dassitadhammesūti [V 2.0207] vuttadhammesu. Vacanamattameva hi tesaṃ, na pana dassanaṃ tādisasseva dhammassa abhāvato. Bhagavato eva vā “ime dhammā anabhisambuddho”ti parassa vacanavasena dassitadhammesu. “Dhammapaṭisambhidā”tiādīsu (vibha. 718-721) viya dhamma-saddo hetupariyāyoti āha “sahadhammenāti sahetunā”ti. Hetūti ca upapattisādhanahetu veditabbo, na kārako, sampāpako vā. Nimittanti codanāya kāraṇaṃ. Tattha codako codanaṃ karotīti kāraṇaṃ, dhammo codanaṃ karoti etenāti kāraṇaṃ. Tenāha “puggalopī”tiādi. Khemanti kenaci appaṭibāhiyabhāvena anupaddutaṃ.

'In the shown Dhammas' means in the spoken Dhammas. For them, it is merely speech, not seeing, because of the absence of such a Dhamma. Or, it is in the shown Dhammas by way of another's speech, as in the Blessed One's words, 'These Dhammas were not fully awakened to.' Just as in instances like 'the discrimination of Dhamma,' etc. (Vibh. 718-721), the word 'Dhamma' is a synonym for reason; thus he said, 'with the Dhamma' means 'with reason.' And 'reason' should be understood as the reason for establishing a point, not as the agent or the accomplisher. 'A sign' is the reason for accusation. There, the accuser makes the accusation—that is the reason; the Dhamma makes the accusation by this—that is the reason. Thus he said, 'even a person,' etc. 'Secure' means untroubled, being unassailable by anyone.

Antarāyo etesaṃ atthi, antarāye vā niyuttāti antarāyikā. Evaṃbhūtā pana te yasmā antarāyakarā nāma honti, tasmā āha “antarāyaṃ karontīti antarāyikā”ti. Asañcicca vītikkame nātisāvajjāti katvā vuttaṃ “sañcicca vītikkantā”ti. Satta āpattikkhandhātiādi nidassanamattaṃ itaresampi catunnaṃ “antarāyikā”ti vuttadhammānaṃ tabbhāve byabhicārābhāvato. Idha pana methunadhammo adhippetoti idaṃ aṭṭhuppattivasena vuttaṃ ariṭṭhasikkhāpadaṃ (pāci. 417) viya. Yasmā taṃkhaṇampi kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ disvā virato hoti ce, visesaṃ adhigacchati, na kāmesu āsatto, tasmā vuttaṃ “methuna…pe…antarāyo hotī”ti. Tattha yassa kassacīti na kevalaṃ pabbajitasseva, atha kho [M 2.0228] yassa kassaci. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “methunamanuyuttassa, mussatevāpi sāsana”nti (su. ni. 820).

'An obstacle exists for them, or they are engaged in an obstacle'—thus they are 'obstructive' (antarāyikā). Since they are such, they are called 'obstacle-makers' (antarāyakarā); therefore, he said, 'they create an obstacle, thus they are obstructive.' Having considered that an unintentional transgression is not very blameworthy, it is said, 'intentionally transgressed.' 'The seven groups of offenses, etc.' is merely an illustration; the designation 'obstructive' applies to the other four things as well, because there is no deviation in their nature. Here, however, sexual intercourse is intended—this is said by way of the story of its origin, like the Ariṭṭha training rule (Pāci. 417). Because if, even at that moment, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, one refrains, one attains distinction, not being attached to sensual pleasures, therefore it is said, 'sexual intercourse... is an obstacle.' There, 'for anyone' means not only for one gone forth, but indeed for anyone. Thus it is said, 'For one engaged in sexual intercourse, the teaching is certainly forgotten' (Snp. 820).

Tasmiṃ aniyyānikadhammeti tasmiṃ parehi parikappitaaniyyānikadhammanimittaṃ. Nimittatthe hi idaṃ kammasaṃyoge bhummaṃ.

'In that unleading Dhamma' means with regard to the sign of that unleading Dhamma imagined by others. For this is a locative in connection with action, used in the sense of a sign.

Upanibaddhāti viracitā. Tenāha “abhisaṅkhatā”ti. Puthubhāvanti bahubhāvaṃ. Puthūhi vā sitāti bahūhi samaṇabrāhmaṇehi sitā upanibaddhā.

'Bound to' (Upanibaddhā) means constructed (viracitā). Thus he said, 'fabricated' (abhisaṅkhatā). 'Being many' (Puthubhāvanti) means abundance (bahubhāvaṃ). Or, 'resorted to by many' means resorted to and bound to by many ascetics and brahmins.

Vesārajjasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary to the Vesārajja Sutta is concluded.

9. Taṇhuppādasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Taṇhuppāda Sutta

9. Navame bhavati etena ārogyanti bhavo, gilānapaccayo. Parivuddho bhavo abhavo. Vuddhiattho hi ayamakāro yathā “saṃvarāsaṃvaro, phalāphala”nti ca. Sappinavanītādīnīti ādi-saddena [V 2.0208] telamadhuphāṇitādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Sappinavanītādiggahaṇañcettha nidassanamattaṃ, sabbassapi gilānapaccayassa saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Bhavābhavoti vā khuddako ceva mahanto ca upapattibhavo veditabbo. Tenevāha “sampattibhavesū”tiādi. Bhavoti vā sampatti, abhavoti vipatti. Bhavoti vuddhi, abhavoti hāni. Taṃnimittañca taṇhā uppajjatīti vuttaṃ “bhavābhavahetu vā”ti.

9. In the ninth sutta, 'health (ārogya) comes to be (bhavati) by this'—thus 'becoming' (bhavo), a requisite for the sick. A developed becoming is 'non-becoming' (abhavo). For this 'a' syllable has the meaning of growth, as in 'restraint and non-restraint' (saṃvarāsaṃvaro) and 'fruit and non-fruit' (phalāphala). In 'ghee, fresh butter, and so on,' the word 'and so on' implies the inclusion of oil, honey, molasses, and so forth. And the mention of ghee, fresh butter, and the like here is merely an illustration; the inclusion of all requisites for the sick should be understood. Or, 'becoming and non-becoming' (bhavābhava) should be understood as minor and major rebirth-becoming. Therefore, it was said, 'in fortunate becomings,' and so on. Or, 'becoming' is accomplishment, 'non-becoming' is failure. 'Becoming' is growth, 'non-becoming' is decline. And craving arises on account of that—thus it is said, 'or on account of becoming and non-becoming.'

Taṇhādutiyoti taṇhāsahāyo. Taṇhā hi nirudakakantāre marīcikāya udakasaññā viya pipāsābhibhūtaṃ tasitaṃ sattaṃ assāsadassanavasena sahāyakiccaṃ karontī bhavādīsu anibbinnaṃ katvā paribbhamāpeti. Tathā hi taṃ papātakaṃ acintetvā madhuggaṇhanakaluddakā viya anekādīnavākulesu bhavesu ānisaṃsameva dassentī anatthajāle sā paribbhamāpeti, tasmā taṇhā “purisassa dutiyā”ti vuttā. Nanu ca aññepi kilesādayo bhavanibbattipaccayāti? Saccametaṃ, na pana tathā visesapaccayo, yathā taṇhā. Tathā hi sā kusalehi vinā [M 2.0229] akusalehi, kāmāvacarādikusalehi ca vinā rūpāvacarādikusalehi bhavanibbattiyā visesapaccayo. Yato samudayasaccanti vuccatīti. Itthabhāvaññathābhāvanti itthabhāvo ca aññathābhāvo ca itthabhāvaññathābhāvo, so etassa atthīti itthabhāvaññathābhāvo, saṃsāro, taṃ itthabhāvaññathābhāvaṃ. Tattha itthabhāvo manussattaṃ, aññathābhāvo tato avasiṭṭhasattāvāsā. Itthabhāvo vā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ paccuppanno attabhāvo, aññathābhāvo anāgatattabhāvo. Evarūpo vā aññopi attabhāvo itthabhāvo, na evarūpo aññathābhāvo. Tenevāha “itthabhāvaññathābhāvanti ettha itthabhāvo nāma ayaṃ attabhāvo”tiādi. Saṃsaraṇaṃ saṃsāro.

'Having craving as a second' (taṇhādutiyo) means 'having craving as a companion' (taṇhāsahāyo). For craving, like the perception of water from a mirage in a waterless desert to a thirsty being overcome by thirst, performs the function of a companion by offering the appearance of relief, causing the being to wander without becoming disenchanted with states of existence and so forth. Indeed, without considering the precipice, like honey-gatherers and hunters, it causes one to wander in the net of ruin, showing only the allure in states of existence fraught with many dangers. Therefore, craving is called 'a person's second.' But are there not other defilements and so forth that are also conditions for the production of existence? This is true, yet none is such a special condition as craving. For it is a special condition for the production of existence, which operates through unwholesome states when wholesome states are absent, and through wholesome states of the fine-material sphere and so on when wholesome states of the sense-sphere and so on are absent. Hence, it is called the Truth of the Origin of suffering. 'This state and another state' (itthabhāvaññathābhāva) means 'this state' (itthabhāva) and 'another state' (aññathābhāva), which together form 'this state and another state.' It is called 'this state and another state' because it has this characteristic, namely, saṃsāra; that is, 'this state and another state.' Here, 'this state' refers to human existence, while 'another state' refers to the remaining abodes of beings. Alternatively, 'this state' may mean the present existence of those various beings, and 'another state' may mean a future existence. Or, 'this state' may refer to one particular kind of existence, while 'another state' refers to an existence of a different kind. Thus it is said: 'In "this state and another state," "this state" refers to this present existence,' and so on. Wandering on is saṃsāra.

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccati”. (visuddhi. 2.619; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.95 apasādanāvaṇṇanā; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.60; a. ni. aṭṭha. 2.4.199; dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā; vibha. aṭṭha. 226 saṅkhārapadaniddeso; su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.523; udā. aṭṭha. 39; itivu. aṭṭha. 14);

"The continuity of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, proceeding uninterruptedly, is called saṃsāra."

Tenāha “khandhadhātuāyatanānaṃ paṭipāṭi”nti, khandhadhātuāyatanānaṃ hetuphalabhāvena aparāparappavattinti attho.

Therefore, it was said, 'the continuity of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.' The meaning is the successive occurrence of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases by way of cause and effect.

Evamādīnavaṃ [V 2.0209] ñatvāti ettha etamādīnavaṃ ñatvātipi paṭhanti, etaṃ sakalavaṭṭadukkhassa sambhavaṃ samudayaṃ taṇhaṃ ādīnavaṃ ñatvāti attho. Atha vā evamādīnavaṃ ñatvāti etaṃ yathāvuttaṃ saṃsārānativattanaādīnavaṃ dosaṃ ñatvā. Niggahaṇoti caturūpādānasaṅkhātassa sabbassa gahaṇassa paṭinissajjanena niggahaṇo, khandhaparinibbānena saṅkhārappavattito apagaccheyyāti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

For 'knowing such a danger' (evamādīnavaṃ ñatvā), some here also read 'knowing this danger' (etamādīnavaṃ ñatvā). The meaning is knowing this craving as the danger, the source and origin of all the suffering of the round of existence. Alternatively, 'knowing such a danger' means knowing this fault, as described, of not transcending saṃsāra. 'Restraint' (niggahaṇo) means restraint by relinquishing all grasping, which is reckoned as the four kinds of clinging. Or, the meaning here should be understood as: 'one should depart from the proceeding of formations through the final Nibbāna of the aggregates.'

Taṇhuppādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Taṇhuppāda Sutta is concluded.

10. Yogasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Yoga Sutta.

10. Dasame yojentīti kammaṃ vipākena bhavādiṃ, bhavantarādīhi dukkhena sattaṃ yojenti ghaṭentīti yogā. Kāmanaṭṭhena kāmo ca so yathāvuttenatthena yogo cāti kāmayogo. Bhavayogo nāma bhavarāgoti dassetuṃ “rūpārūpabhavesū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha paṭhamo [M 2.0230] upapattibhavesu rāgo, dutiyo kammabhavesu, tatiyo bhavadiṭṭhisahagato yathā rajjanaṭṭhena rāgo, evaṃ yujjanaṭṭhena yogoti vutto. Catūsu saccesu aññāṇanti idaṃ suttantanayaṃ nissāya vuttaṃ. Suttantasaṃvaṇṇanā hesāti, tadantogadhattā vā pubbantādīnaṃ.

10. In the tenth sutta, 'they bind' (yojenti) means they bind or connect beings to suffering through kamma and its result, through states of existence and so forth, and through other existences and so forth; thus they are called 'bonds' (yogā). 'Sensual bond' (kāmayoga) is so called because it is both 'sensual desire' (kāma) in the sense of desiring, and a 'bond' (yoga) in the sense previously stated. To show that the 'bond of existence' (bhavayoga) is craving for existence, it was said, 'in the realms of form and formlessness,' and so on. Here, the first is craving for rebirth-existence, the second is for kamma-existence, and the third is accompanied by the view of existence—just as 'craving' (rāga) is so called in the sense of delighting, so too 'bond' (yoga) is so called in the sense of binding. 'Ignorance regarding the Four Truths'—this is stated based on the method of the Suttas. For this is a commentary on the Suttas, or because the past and so forth are included within it.

Samudayanti dve samudayā khaṇikasamudayo paccayasamudayo ca. Uppādakkhaṇo khaṇikasamudayo, paccayova paccayasamudayo. Samudayate samudayanaṃ samudayo, samudeti etasmāti samudayoti evaṃ ubhinnaṃ samudayānaṃ saddatthatopi bhedo veditabbo. Paccayasamudayaṃ pajānantopi bhikkhu khaṇikasamudayaṃ pajānāti, khaṇikasamudayaṃ pajānantopi paccayasamudayaṃ pajānāti. Paccayato hi saṅkhārānaṃ udayaṃ passato khaṇato ca nesaṃ udayadassanaṃ sukhaṃ hoti, khaṇato ca nesaṃ udayaṃ passato pageva paccayānaṃ suggahitattā paccayato dassanaṃ sukhena ijjhati. Idha pana khaṇikasamudayaṃ dassento āha “samudayanti uppatti”nti.

There are two kinds of origin (samudaya): momentary origin and causal origin. The moment of arising is momentary origin; conditions themselves are causal origin. 'Origin' (samudaya) is the act of originating (samudayana); 'origin' is that from which something originates (samudeti etasmā). Thus, the distinction between the two kinds of origin should be understood even in terms of their etymology. A bhikkhu who understands causal origin also understands momentary origin, and one who understands momentary origin also understands causal origin. For when one sees the arising of formations from conditions, it is easy to see their arising moment by moment. And when one sees their arising moment by moment, then, because the conditions have been well-grasped, seeing from the perspective of conditions is accomplished with ease. Here, however, while showing momentary origin, he said: 'Origin means arising.'

Atthaṅgamopi duvidho accantatthaṅgamo, bhedatthaṅgamoti. Accantatthaṅgamo appavattinirodho, nibbānanti keci. Bhedatthaṅgamo khaṇikanirodho. Tadubhayaṃ pubbabhāge uggahaparipucchādivasena passato aññataradassanena itaradassanampi siddhameva hoti. Pubbabhāgeyeva ārammaṇavasena khayato vayato sammasanādikāle bhedatthaṅgamaṃ passanto byatirekavasena anussavādito accantatthaṅgamaṃ passati, maggakkhaṇe pana ārammaṇato accantatthaṅgamaṃ passanto asammohato itarampi passati. Idha pana bhedatthaṅgamaṃ dassento āha “atthaṅgamanti bheda”nti. Kāmānaṃ uppattibhedaggahaṇeneva [V 2.0210] cettha yathā kāmānaṃ paṭiccasamuppannatā vibhāvitā, evaṃ kāmavatthunopīti ubhayesampi aniccatā dukkhatā anattatā ca vibhāvitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Madhurabhāvanti iminā kāmasannissitaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ dasseti. “Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ kāmānaṃ assādo”ti (ma. ni. 1.166) hi vuttaṃ. Amadhurabhāvanti iminā pana kāmahetukaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ dasseti.

Cessation (atthaṅgama) is also twofold: absolute cessation and cessation by dissolution. Absolute cessation is the cessation of non-occurrence, which some call Nibbāna. Cessation by dissolution is momentary cessation. For one who sees either of these in the preliminary stage through learning, questioning, and so on, the seeing of the other is also accomplished. Indeed, in the preliminary stage, one who sees cessation by dissolution by way of the object, through contemplation of destruction and vanishing, also sees absolute cessation by way of distinction from what is heard. But at the moment of the path, one who sees absolute cessation regarding the object also sees the other without confusion. Here, however, while showing cessation by dissolution, it is said: 'Cessation means dissolution.' Just as the dependently arisen nature of sensual pleasures is made clear here by grasping their arising and dissolution, so too it should be understood that the impermanence, suffering, and non-self of both sensual pleasures and their objects are thereby made clear. By 'sweet nature' (madhurabhāva), happiness and joy dependent on sensuality are shown. For it is said: 'Whatever happiness and joy, bhikkhus, arises in dependence on these five strands of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification of sensual pleasures' (MN 1.134). By 'unpleasant nature' (amadhurabhāva), however, suffering and sorrow caused by sensuality are shown.

Phassāyatanānanti chadvārikassa phassassa kāraṇabhūtānaṃ cakkhādiāyatanānaṃ. Tenāha “cakkhādīnaṃ cakkhusamphassādikāraṇāna”nti. Punabbhavakaraṇaṃ [M 2.0231] punobhavo uttarapadalopena, mano-saddassa viya ca purimapadassa okārantatā daṭṭhabbā. Punobhavo sīlametesanti ponobhavikā. Atha vā sīlatthena ikasaddena gamitatthattā kiriyāvācakasaddassa adassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ yathā apūpabhakkhanasīlo āpūpiko. Atha vā punabbhavaṃ denti, punabbhavāya saṃvattanti, punappunabbhave nibbattentīti ponobhavikā. “Taddhitā”ti hi bahuvacananiddesā vicittattā vā taddhitānaṃ abhidhānalakkhaṇattā vā “punabbhavaṃ dentī”tiādīsupi atthesu ponobhavikasaddasiddhi daṭṭhabbā.

'The bases of contact' (phassāyatanānaṃ) means the eye and other bases that are the causes of contact at the six doors. Therefore, it was said, 'of the eye and so forth, which are the causes of eye-contact and so forth.' 'Producing rebirth' (punabbhavakaraṇaṃ) is 'rebirth' (punobhavo) with the elision of the latter part; and the initial part should be seen as ending in 'o,' like the word 'mano.' 'Conducive to rebirth' (ponobhavikā) means those whose conduct is rebirth. Alternatively, since the meaning is conveyed by the suffix 'ika' in the sense of 'habit,' the absence of a verbal expression should be noted, as in 'one whose habit is eating cakes is a cake-eater' (āpūpiko). Or, they give rise to rebirth, lead to rebirth, or repeatedly produce rebirth—hence 'conducive to rebirth' (ponobhavikā). For because of the plural designation 'derivatives' (taddhitā), or because of the diversity of derivatives, or because derivatives are characterized by their expressive function, the establishment of the term 'conducive to rebirth' should be understood even in senses like 'they give rise to rebirth,' and so forth.

Visaṃyojenti paṭipannaṃ puggalaṃ kāmayogādito viyojentīti visaṃyogā, asubhajjhānādīni visaṃyojanakāraṇāni. Tenāha “visaṃyogāti visaṃyojanakāraṇānī”tiādi.

'They disjoin' (visaṃyojenti) means they separate the individual who is practicing from the bonds of sensuality and so forth; thus, they are called 'disjunctions' (visaṃyogā). Meditations on foulness and so forth are the causes of disjunction. Therefore, it was said: 'Disjunctions are the causes of disjunction,' and so on.

Yogasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Yoga Sutta is concluded.

Bhaṇḍagāmavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhaṇḍagāma Chapter is concluded.

2. Caravaggo

2. The Chapter on Wandering

1. Carasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Cāra Sutta

11. Dutiyassa paṭhame caratoti gacchantassa, caṅkamantassa vā. Uppajjati kāmavitakko vāti vatthukāmesu avītarāgatāya tādise paccaye kāmapaṭisaṃyutto vā vitakko uppajjati ce[V 2.0211], yadi uppajjati. Byāpādavitakko vā vihiṃsāvitakko vāti āghātavinaye visesena cittassa adamitattā āghātanimitte byāpādapaṭisaṃyutto vā vitakko, leḍḍudaṇḍādīti parahiṃsanavasena vihiṃsāpaṭisaṃyutto vā vitakko uppajjati ceti sambandho. Taṃ ce bhikkhu adhivāsetīti taṃ yathāvuttaṃ kāmavitakkādiṃ yathāpaccayaṃ attano citte uppannaṃ “itipāyaṃ vitakko pāpako, itipi akusalo, itipi sāvajjo, so ca kho attabyābādhāya saṃvattatī”tiādinā nayena paccavekkhaṇāya abhāvato adhivāseti attano cittaṃ āropetvā vāseti. Adhivāsentoyeva ca nappajahati tadaṅgādippahānavasena na paṭinissajjati. Tato eva ca [M 2.0232] na vinodeti attano cittasantānato na nudati na nīharati. Tathā avinodanato na byantīkaroti na vigatantaṃ karoti. Ātāpī pahitatto yathā tesaṃ antopi nāvasissati antamaso bhaṅgamattampi, evaṃ karoti, ayaṃ pana tathā na karotīti attho. Tathābhūto pana na anabhāvaṃ gameti anu anu abhāvaṃ na gameti. Na pajahati ce, na vinodeti ceti itiādinā ce-saddaṃ yojetvā attho veditabbo.

11. In the second sutta, first section: 'while wandering' (carato) means while going or pacing. 'Or a sensual thought arises' means that, due to not being free from lust regarding sensual objects, a thought connected with sensuality arises under such conditions—if it arises. 'Or a thought of ill will or a thought of harming' means that, due to the mind's lack of restraint especially in matters of resentment, a thought connected with ill will arises regarding an object of anger, or a thought connected with harming arises regarding clods, sticks, etc., by way of harming others—this is the connection. 'If that bhikkhu tolerates it' means that, regarding the sensual or other thought as described, which has arisen in his mind according to conditions, he tolerates it because of the absence of reflection in such a way as, 'This thought is evil, this is unwholesome, this is blameworthy, and it leads to self-affliction,' etc. He lets it dwell by allowing it into his mind. And by tolerating it, he does not abandon it; he does not give it up by way of substitution of opposites, etc. And thus he does not dispel it; he does not drive it out or remove it from his mental continuum. By not dispelling it thus, he does not bring it to an end; he does not make it cease. An ardent and resolute person acts in such a way that not even a fragment of them remains, but this one does not act thus—this is the meaning. Being thus, he does not bring it to non-existence; he does not bring it to non-existence bit by bit. The meaning should be understood by connecting the particle 'if' with 'he does not abandon,' 'he does not dispel,' and so on.

Evaṃbhūtoti evaṃ kāmavitakkādīhi pāpavitakkehi samaṅgibhūto. Anātāpīti kilesānaṃ ātāpayikassa vīriyassa abhāvena anātāpī. Pāputrāsalakkhaṇassa ottappassa abhāvena anottāpī. Satataṃ samitaṃ sabbakālaṃ nirantaraṃ. Kusīto hīnavīriyoti kusalehi dhammehi parihāpayitvā akusalapakkhe kucchitaṃ sīdanato kosajjasamannāgamena ca kusīto, sammappadhānavīriyābhāvena hīnavīriyo vīriyavirahitoti vuccati kathīyati. Ṭhitassāti gamanaṃ upacchinditvā tiṭṭhato. Sayanairiyāpathassa visesato kosajjapakkhikattā yathā taṃsamaṅgino bhāvitattā sambhavanti, taṃ dassetuṃ “jāgarassā”ti vuttaṃ.

'Being thus' means being endowed with evil thoughts such as sensual thoughts. 'Without ardor' means lacking the energy that burns up defilements, hence without ardor. 'Without moral dread' means lacking the moral dread which has the characteristic of fear of evil, hence without moral dread. 'Constantly, continuously, always, without interruption.' 'Lazy, of low energy' means he is lazy through association with sloth, sinking into the despicable unwholesome side after having abandoned wholesome states; and he is called 'of low energy' or 'devoid of energy' due to the absence of the energy of right effort. 'Of one standing' means of one who, having stopped moving, is standing still. Because the posture of lying down is particularly on the side of sloth, and as such, it naturally occurs for one endowed with that, to illustrate this, 'while awake' is said.

Sukkapakkhe tañce bhikkhu nādhivāsetīti āraddhavīriyassapi viharato anādimati saṃsāre cirakālabhāvitattā tathārūpapaccayasamāyoge satisammosena vā kāmavitakkādi uppajjati ce, taṃ bhikkhu attano cittaṃ āropetvā na vāseti, abbhantare na vāsetīti attho. Anadhivāsento kiṃ karoti? Pajahati chaḍḍeti. Kiṃ kacavaraṃ viya piṭakenāti? Na, apica kho taṃ vinodeti nudati nīharati. Kiṃ balibaddaṃ viya patodenāti? Na, atha kho byantīkaroti vigatantaṃ karoti, yathā tesaṃ antopi nāvasissati antamaso bhaṅgamattampi, tathā te karoti. Kathaṃ pana te tathā karoti? Anabhāvaṃ gameti anu anu abhāvaṃ gameti, vikkhambhanappahānena yathā suvikkhambhitā honti, tathā ne karotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

On the wholesome side, if a monk does not consent to them—even while dwelling with aroused energy—due to their long cultivation in the beginningless cycle of existence, when such conditions coincide, or due to a lapse of mindfulness, sensual thoughts and the like arise, that monk does not allow them to become established and dwell in his mind—he does not allow them to dwell internally, that is the meaning. Not consenting, what does he do? He abandons, discards them. Like throwing away garbage with a basket? No, rather he dispels, drives them out, removes them. Like driving away an ox with a goad? No, but he eliminates them, makes them vanish, so that not even a trace remains, not even the slightest fragment—thus he deals with them. How does he deal with them in such a way? He leads them to non-existence, repeatedly to non-existence, through abandonment by suppression, so that they are thoroughly suppressed—thus it is said.

Evaṃbhūtotiādīsu [V 2.0212] evaṃ kāmavitakkādīnaṃ anadhivāsena suvisuddhāsayo samāno tāya ca āsayasampattiyā tannimittāya ca payogasampattiyā [M 2.0233] parisuddhasīlo indriyesu guttadvāro bhojane mattaññū satisampajaññena samannāgato jāgariyaṃ anuyutto tadaṅgādivasena kilesānaṃ ātāpanalakkhaṇena vīriyena samannāgatattā ātāpī. Sabbaso pāputrāsena samannāgatattā ottāpī satataṃ rattindivaṃ. Samitaṃ nirantaraṃ samathavipassanānuyogavasena catubbidhasammappadhānasiddhiyā āraddhavīriyo pahitatto. Nibbānaṃ pati pesitacittoti vuccati kathīyatīti attho.

In passages like 'one of such nature,' being thus purified in disposition by not consenting to sensual thoughts and the like, and by that excellence of disposition and the excellence of effort directed toward it, he is purified in virtue, guarded in the senses, moderate in eating, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, and devoted to wakefulness. By means of temporary suppression and other aspects, he is endowed with energy characterized by the burning away of defilements—ardent. Being entirely endowed with fear of evil, he is conscientious, constantly day and night. Continuously, without interruption, through the practice of serenity and insight, by way of accomplishing the fourfold right striving, he is resolute in energy, intent. His mind is directed toward Nibbāna—it is said, he is declared, that is the meaning.

Gāthāsu gehanissitanti ettha gehavāsīhi apariccattattā gehavāsisabhāvattā gehadhammattā vā gehaṃ vuccati vatthukāmo. Atha vā gehappaṭibaddhabhāvato, kilesakāmānaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānabhāvato vā gehāti vuccanti, taṃvatthukattā kāmavitakkādi gehanissitaṃ nāma. Kummaggapaṭipannoti yasmā ariyamaggassa uppathabhāvato abhijjhādayo tadekaṭṭhadhammā ca kummaggo, tasmā kāmavitakkādibahulo kummaggapaṭipanno. Mohaneyyesu mucchitoti mohasaṃvattaniyesu rūpādīsu mucchito sammatto ajjhopanno. Sambodhinti ariyamaggañāṇaṃ. Phuṭṭhanti phusituṃ pattuṃ pāpo so tādiso micchāsaṅkappagocaro puggalo abhabbo, na kadāci taṃ pāpuṇātīti attho.

In the verses, 'attached to the household'—here, because of not being abandoned by householders, because of the state of being a householder, or because of the nature of a household, sensual objects are called 'the household.' Or alternatively, because of being bound to the household, or because they are the dwelling place of sensual defilements, they are called 'households'—thus, sensual thoughts and the like, being based on them, are called 'attached to the household.' 'Gone astray on the wrong path'—because greed and the like, and the states associated with them, are the wrong path, being a deviation from the noble path, thus one abundant in sensual thoughts and the like is 'gone astray on the wrong path.' 'Infatuated with deluding things'—infatuated, intoxicated, obsessed with forms and the like that conduce to delusion. 'Awakening'—the knowledge of the noble path. 'Touched'—to touch, to reach—such a person whose resort is wrong thought is incapable, never able to reach it—that is the meaning.

Vitakkaṃ samayitvānāti yathāvuttaṃ micchāvitakkaṃ paṭisaṅkhānabhāvanābalena vūpasametvā. Vitakkūpasame ratoti navannampi mahāvitakkānaṃ accantūpasamabhūte arahatte, nibbāne eva vā ajjhāsayena rato abhirato. Bhabbo soti so yathāvutto sammāpaṭipajjamāno puggalo pubbabhāge samathavipassanābalena sabbavitakke yathārahaṃ tadaṅgādivasena vūpasametvā ṭhito vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā arahattamaggañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānasaṅkhātañca anuttaraṃ sambodhiṃ phuṭṭhuṃ adhigantuṃ bhabbo arahā. Evamettha pāḷivaṇṇanā veditabbā.

Having calmed the thought means having pacified wrong thoughts, as described above, by the power of contemplative development. Delighting in the calming of thoughts means being pleased and content with arahantship, the ultimate pacification of the nine great thoughts, or being inclined and delighted in Nibbāna itself. Capable means that person, as described, practicing rightly, having appropriately pacified all thoughts in the preliminary stage through the power of tranquility and insight by means of temporary suppression and so on, standing firm, developing insight, is capable of realizing and attaining the unsurpassed enlightenment, known as the path-knowledge of arahantship and also known as Nibbāna, through the sequence of the path, and is worthy. Thus, the explanation of the Pali here should be understood.

Carasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Cara Sutta is concluded.

2. Sīlasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Sīla Sutta

12. Dutiye sampannasīlāti ettha tividhaṃ sampannaṃ paripuṇṇasamaṅgimadhuravasena. Tattha –

12. In the second sutta, regarding ‘endowed with virtue,’ here ‘endowed’ is threefold: complete, endowed with constituents, and sweet. Herein –

“Sampannaṃ [M 2.0234] sālikedāraṃ, suvā bhuñjanti kosiya;

Paṭivedemi te brahme, na ne vāretumussahe”ti. (jā. 1.14.1) –

“The rice field is well-endowed; parrots and owls feast upon it. I report this to you, brahmin: I am unable to stop them.”

Idaṃ [V 2.0213] paripuṇṇasampannaṃ nāma. “Iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti samupeto upāgato samupāgato upapanno sampanno samannāgato”ti (vibha. 511) idaṃ samaṅgisampannaṃ nāma. “Imissā, bhante, mahāpathaviyā heṭṭhimatalaṃ sampannaṃ, seyyathāpi khuddamadhuṃ anīlakaṃ, evamassāda”nti (pārā. 17) idaṃ madhurasampannaṃ nāma. Idha paripuṇṇasampannavasena atthaṃ dassento “sampannasīlāti paripuṇṇasīlā”ti āha. Samaṅgisampannavasenapi attho yujjatiyeva, tasmā sampannasīlāti paripuṇṇasīlā hutvātipi sīlasamaṅgino hutvātipi evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Tattha sīlassa anavasesasamādānena akhaṇḍādibhāvappattiyā paripuṇṇasīlā, samādānato paṭṭhāya avicchindanato sīlasamaṅgino. Samādānavato hi accantavirodhidhammānuppattiyā sīlasamaṅgitā veditabbā, cetanādīnaṃ pana sīlanalakkhaṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ pavattilakkhaṇena vattabbameva natthi.

This is called ‘complete endowment.’ “Endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha, fully endowed, attained, fully attained, possessed, perfected, fully possessed” (Vibh. 511)—this is called ‘endowment with constituents.’ “Venerable sir, the lower surface of this great earth is endowed, like pure honey without blemish, such is its taste” (Pārā. 17)—this is called ‘sweet endowment.’ Here, showing the meaning in terms of complete endowment, it is said, “‘endowed with virtue’ means complete in virtue.” The meaning also fits in terms of endowment with constituents; therefore, ‘endowed with virtue’ should be understood here as both ‘being complete in virtue’ and ‘being endowed with the constituents of virtue.’ In this context, one is ‘complete in virtue’ by undertaking virtue without omission and by attaining the state of being unbroken, etc. From the moment of undertaking it without interruption, one is ‘endowed with the constituents of virtue.’ For the state of being endowed with the constituents of virtue should be understood as arising from the non-arising of qualities entirely opposed to it, for one who has undertaken it. However, regarding the characteristic of occurrence of phenomena such as volition, which bear the mark of virtue, there is nothing to be said.

Tattha “paripuṇṇasīlā”ti iminā atthena khettadosavigamena khettapāripūrī viya sīladosavigamena sīlapāripūrī vuttā hoti. Yathā hi khettaṃ bījakhaṇḍaṃ, vappakhaṇḍaṃ, udakakhaṇḍaṃ, ūsakhaṇḍanti catudosasamannāgataṃ aparipūraṃ hoti. Tattha bījakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha antarantarā bījāni khaṇḍāni vā pūtīni vā honti, tāni yattha patanti, tattha sassaṃ na uṭṭheti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti, aparipūraṃ hotīti attho. Vappakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha akusalo bījāni vapanto antarantarā nipāteti. Evañhi sabbattha sassaṃ na uṭṭheti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti. Udakakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha katthaci udakaṃ atibahuṃ vā hoti, na vā hoti. Tatrāpi hi sassāni na uṭṭhenti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti. Ūsakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha kassako kismiñci padese naṅgalena bhūmiṃ cattāro pañca vāre kasanto atigambhīraṃ karoti, tato ūsaṃ uppajjati. Tatrāpi hi sassaṃ na uṭṭheti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti, tādisañca khettaṃ na mahapphalaṃ hoti na mahānisaṃsaṃ. Tatrāpi bahumpi vapitvā appaṃ labhati. Imesaṃ pana catunnaṃ dosānaṃ vigamā khettaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, tādisañca khettaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ. Evameva khaṇḍaṃ, chiddaṃ, sabalaṃ, kammāsanti catudosasamannāgataṃ sīlaṃ aparipūraṃ hoti, tādisañca [M 2.0235] sīlaṃ na mahapphalaṃ hoti na mahānisaṃsaṃ. Imesaṃ pana catunnaṃ dosānaṃ vigamā sīlaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, tādisañca sīlaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ.

Here, by the meaning of ‘complete in virtue,’ the perfection of virtue through the absence of faults in virtue is stated, just as the perfection of a field through the absence of faults in the field. For example, a field may be incomplete due to being subject to four faults: seed-deficiency, sowing-deficiency, water-deficiency, and barren-soil deficiency. Seed-deficiency means that where seeds are broken or rotten here and there, crops do not grow wherever they fall, making the field deficient, that is, incomplete. Sowing-deficiency means where an unskilled sower drops seeds with gaps in between. Thus, crops do not grow everywhere, making the field deficient. Water-deficiency means places where water is either too abundant or lacking. There too, crops do not grow, making the field deficient. Barren-soil deficiency means that where a farmer, plowing the soil four or five times in some area, makes the ground too deep with a plow, causing barren soil to arise. There too, crops do not grow, making the field deficient. Such a field is neither highly fruitful nor greatly beneficial. Even if much is sown, little is gained. But when these four faults are absent, the field becomes complete. Such a field is highly fruitful and greatly beneficial. Similarly, virtue that is fragmented, flawed, mottled, or spotty, being endowed with these four faults, is incomplete. Such virtue is neither highly fruitful nor greatly beneficial. However, when these four faults are absent, virtue becomes complete. Such virtue is highly fruitful and greatly beneficial.

“Sīlasamaṅgino”ti iminā panatthena sīlena samaṅgibhūtā samodhānagatā samannāgatā hutvā viharathāti idameva vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha dvīhi kāraṇehi sampannasīlatā hoti sīlavipattiyā ādīnavadassanena, sīlasampattiyā ca ānisaṃsadassanena. Tadubhayampi visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.14) vitthāritaṃ[V 2.0214]. Tattha “sampannasīlāti ettāvatā ca kira bhagavā catupārisuddhisīlaṃ uddisitvā ‘pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā’ti iminā tattha jeṭṭhakasīlaṃ vitthāretvā dassetī”ti divāvihāravāsī sumatthero āha. Antevāsiko panassa tepiṭakacūḷanāgatthero āha – “ubhayatthāpi pātimokkhasaṃvaro bhagavatā vutto, pātimokkhasaṃvaroyeva hi sīlaṃ, itarāni pana tīṇi sīlanti vuttaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthī”ti vatvā taṃ ananujānanto āha – “indriyasaṃvaro nāma chadvārarakkhāmattakameva, ājīvapārisuddhi dhammena samena paccayuppattimattakaṃ, paccayanissitaṃ paṭiladdhapaccaye idamatthanti paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanamattakaṃ. Nippariyāyena pātimokkhasaṃvarova sīlaṃ. Yassa so bhinno, ayaṃ chinnasīso viya puriso hatthapāde, sesāni rakkhissatīti na vattabbo. Yassa pana so arogo, ayaṃ acchinnasīso viya puriso jīvitaṃ, sesāni puna pākatikāni katvā rakkhituṃ sakkoti. Tasmā ‘sampannasīlā’ti iminā pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ uddisitvā ‘sampannapātimokkhā’ti tasseva vevacanaṃ vatvā taṃ vitthāretvā dassento ‘pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā’tiādimāhā”ti.

“Endowed with virtue”—by this phrase, it is simply meant: “Dwell having become endowed with virtue, united with it, and possessed of it.” Herein, the state of being endowed with virtue comes about through two reasons: seeing the danger in the failure of virtue and seeing the benefits in the success of virtue. Both of these are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 1.14). Here, the elder Sumatthera, who dwelled by day, said: “‘Endowed with virtue’—to this extent, the Blessed One, having declared the fourfold purified virtue, elaborates and shows the foremost virtue here with the phrase ‘restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint.’” However, his pupil, the elder Cūḷanāgatthera, who was versed in the three baskets, said: “The Pātimokkha restraint is spoken of by the Blessed One in both contexts, for the Pātimokkha restraint itself is virtue, while the other three are called ‘virtue’ in name only.” Disagreeing with him, he further stated: “Restraint of the senses is merely the guarding of the six sense-doors. Purification of livelihood is simply the proper acquisition of requisites by just and lawful means. The virtue dependent on requisites is merely the use of obtained requisites after reflecting on their purpose. In the strictest sense, only the Pātimokkha restraint is virtue. For one whose Pātimokkha restraint is broken, like a man with a severed head, it cannot be said that he will protect his hands and feet, or the rest of his body. But for one whose Pātimokkha restraint is intact, he is like a man with his head unharmed; he is able to protect his life and can restore the other parts to their natural state and protect them. Therefore, having declared the Pātimokkha restraint with the phrase ‘endowed with virtue,’ and then stating its synonym ‘complete in the Pātimokkha,’ he elaborates and shows it by saying ‘restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint,’ and so forth.”

Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlena saṃvutāti yo naṃ pāti rakkhati, taṃ mokkheti moceti āpāyikādīhi dukkhehīti pātimokkhanti laddhanāmena sikkhāpadasīlena pihitakāyavacīdvārā. Evaṃbhūtā ca tena upetā samannāgatā nāma hontīti āha “upetā hutvā”ti. Ācārena ca gocarena ca sampannāti kāyikavācasikaavītikkamasaṅkhātena ācārena, na-vesiyagocaratādisaṅkhātena gocarena ca sampannā, sampannaācāragocarāti attho. Aṇuppamāṇesūti atiparittakesu anāpattigamanīyesu. Dukkaṭadubbhāsitamattesūti apare. Dosesūti [M 2.0236] gārayhesu akusaladhammesu. Bhayato dassanasīlāti paramāṇumattampi vajjaṃ sineruppamāṇaṃ viya katvā bhāyanasīlā. Sabbasikkhākoṭṭhāsesūti mūlapaññattianupaññattisabbatthapaññattipadesapaññattiādibhedesu. Taṃ taṃ samādātabbaṃ samādāyāti yaṃ kiñci sikkhākoṭṭhāsesu mūlapaññattiādibhedesu sikkhitabbaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ pūritabbaṃ kāyikaṃ vācasikaṃ vā sīlaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ sammā ādāya, sammadeva sakkaccaṃ sabbaso ca ādiyitvāti attho.

“Restrained by the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint” means having the doors of body and speech closed by the virtue of the training rules. This virtue is called Pātimokkha because it frees (mokkheti) and liberates one who protects (pāti) and guards it from sufferings such as those in the lower realms. Being thus, they are said to be ‘endowed’ and ‘possessed’ by it, hence it is said ‘having become endowed.’ “Perfect in conduct and resort” means endowed with conduct, understood as the non-transgression of bodily and verbal actions, and with resort, understood as not frequenting unsuitable resorts like those of courtesans—thus, the meaning is ‘having perfect conduct and resort.’ “In the slightest faults” refers to the extremely minor ones that do not lead to an offense. Others say this refers to mere wrongdoings and wrong speech. “In faults” refers to blameworthy unwholesome qualities. “Seeing danger in the slightest fault” means being one who is fearful of even a fault as small as an atom, regarding it as massive as Mount Sineru. “In all the training precepts” refers to the root precepts, the derived precepts, the precepts for all, the individual precepts, and so on. “Undertaking them, they train” means whatever precepts, bodily or verbal, are to be learned, practiced, and fulfilled among the training precepts—whether root precepts or others—they undertake all that rightly, properly, and completely. This is the meaning.

Udayaṃ passanto pañcavīsati lakkhaṇāni passatīti “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. Taṇhāsamudayā…pe… kammasamudayā…pe… āhārasamudayā rūpasamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. Nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. Rūpakkhandhassa udayaṃ passanto imāni [V 2.0215] pañca lakkhaṇāni passati. Tathā avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. Taṇhāsamudayā…pe… kammasamudayā…pe… phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayoti paccayasamudayaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. Nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passati. Vedanākkhandhassa udayaṃ passanto imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni passatī”tiādinā nayena ekekasmiṃ khandhe pañca pañca katvā vuttāni pañcavīsati udayalakkhaṇāni passati.

Seeing the arising, one sees twenty-five characteristics: “With the arising of ignorance comes the arising of form”—thus one sees the arising of the form aggregate in the sense of causal arising. With the arising of craving… with the arising of kamma… with the arising of nutriment comes the arising of form—thus one sees the arising of the form aggregate in the sense of causal arising. Seeing the characteristic of origination, one also sees the arising of the form aggregate. Seeing the arising of the form aggregate, one sees these five characteristics. Similarly, “With the arising of ignorance comes the arising of feeling”—thus one sees the arising of the feeling aggregate in the sense of causal arising. With the arising of craving… with the arising of kamma… with the arising of contact comes the arising of feeling—thus one sees the arising of the feeling aggregate in the sense of causal arising. Seeing the characteristic of origination, one also sees the arising of the feeling aggregate. Seeing the arising of the feeling aggregate, one sees these five characteristics. In this way, for each aggregate, five characteristics are stated, making twenty-five characteristics of arising that one sees.

Vayaṃ passanto pañcavīsati lakkhaṇāni passatīti “avijjānirodhā rūpanirodhoti paccayanirodhaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Taṇhānirodhā…pe… kammanirodhā…pe… āhāranirodhā rūpanirodhoti paccayanirodhaṭṭhena rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Rūpakkhandhassa vayaṃ passanto imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni passati. Avijjānirodhā…pe… taṇhānirodhā…pe… phassanirodhā vedanānirodhoti paccayanirodhaṭṭhena vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passati. Vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ passantopi vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passatī. Vedanākkhandhassa vayaṃ passanto imāni pañca lakkhaṇāni passati”tiādinā nayena ekekasmiṃ khandhe pañca pañca katvā vuttāni pañcavīsati vayalakkhaṇāni passati. Pesitattoti nibbānaṃ pati pesitacitto. Kathayantīti tathāvidhaṃ bhikkhuṃ buddhādayo ariyā ācikkhanti.

One who sees cessation perceives twenty-five characteristics: “With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of form”—thus, one perceives the cessation of the form aggregate in the sense of the cessation of its condition. With the cessation of craving… With the cessation of kamma… With the cessation of nutriment comes the cessation of form—thus, one perceives the cessation of the form aggregate in the sense of the cessation of its condition. One who also perceives the characteristic of change perceives the cessation of the form aggregate. Perceiving the cessation of the form aggregate, one perceives these five characteristics. “With the cessation of ignorance… With the cessation of craving… With the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling”—thus, one perceives the cessation of the feeling aggregate in the sense of the cessation of its condition. One who also perceives the characteristic of change perceives the cessation of the feeling aggregate. Perceiving the cessation of the feeling aggregate, one perceives these five characteristics.” In this way, by the method beginning with this, one perceives the twenty-five characteristics of cessation, stated as five for each aggregate. ‘Directed’ (pesita) means having the mind directed towards Nibbāna. ‘Speaking’ (kathayanti) means that the noble ones, beginning with the Buddhas, declare such a bhikkhu.

Yataṃ [M 2.0237] careti vāyamamāno careyya, caṅkamanādivasena gamanaṃ kappentopi “anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamatī”tiādinā (vibha. 432) nayena vuttappadhānavīriyaṃ karonto ghaṭento vāyamanto yathā akusaladhammā pahīyanti, kusaladhammā bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchanti, evaṃ gamanaṃ kappeyyāti attho. Esa nayo sesesupi. Yatamenaṃ pasārayeti etaṃ pasāretabbaṃ hatthapādādiṃ yataṃ yatamāno yathāvuttavīriyasamaṅgī hutvā pasāreyya, sabbattha padhānaṃ na jaheyyāti adhippāyo.

‘He should walk restrained’ (yataṃ care) means he should walk striving. Even when arranging his walking by way of pacing back and forth, etc., making, striving, and exerting the aforementioned primary effort as stated in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 432) with the words “he generates desire and strives for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states,” he should arrange his walking so that unwholesome states are abandoned and wholesome states reach full development through cultivation—this is the meaning. This principle applies to the rest as well. ‘He should extend it restrainedly’ (yatamenaṃ pasāraye) means he should extend his hands, feet, etc., which are to be extended, being restrained and endowed with the aforementioned effort; the intention is that he should not abandon primary effort in any situation.

Idāni yathā paṭipajjanto yataṃ yatanto nāma hoti, taṃ paṭipadaṃ dassetuṃ “uddha”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha uddhanti upari. Tiriyanti parito, puratthimadisādivasena samantato disābhāgesūti attho. Apācīnanti heṭṭhā. Yāvatā jagato gatīti yattakā sattasaṅkhārabhedassa lokassa pavatti, tattha sabbatthāti attho. Ettāvatā anavasesatā sammasanañāṇassa visayaṃ saṅgahetvā dasseti. Samavekkhitāti samā hetunā ñāyena avekkhitā, aniccādivasena [V 2.0216] vipassitāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammānanti sattasuññānaṃ. Khandhānanti rūpādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ. Udayabbayanti udayañca vayañca. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – upari tiriyaṃ adhoti tidhā saṅgahite sabbasmiṃ loke atītādibhedabhinnānaṃ pañcupādānakkhandhasaṅkhātānaṃ sabbesaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ aniccādisammasanādhigatena udayabbayañāṇena pañcavīsatiyā ākārehi udayaṃ, pañcavīsatiyā ākārehi vayaṃ samavekkhitā samanupassitā bhaveyyāti.

Now, to show the path by which one practicing becomes known as ‘restrained’ (yata) and ‘striving’ (yatanta), the words ‘above’ (uddhaṃ) and so on are stated. Herein, ‘above’ (uddhaṃ) means upwards. ‘Across’ (tiriyaṃ) means all around, that is, in all the divisions of the directions, such as the eastern quarter. ‘Below’ (apācīnaṃ) means downwards. ‘As far as the world extends’ (yāvatā jagato gati) means as far as the occurrence of the world consisting of the diversity of beings and formations, that is, everywhere therein. By this much, it shows the domain of comprehension-knowledge as being without remainder, having encompassed it. ‘He discerns’ (samavekkhitā) means he discerns with right reason and method; that is to say, he has insight into impermanence and so on. ‘Phenomena’ (dhammānaṃ) refers to things empty of a being. ‘Aggregates’ (khandhānaṃ) refers to the five aggregates beginning with form. ‘Rising and falling’ (udayabbayaṃ) means both arising and ceasing. This is what is meant: in the entire world, encompassed in three ways—above, across, and below—all phenomena of form and formlessness, designated as the five aggregates of clinging, which are divided into distinctions such as past, should be discerned and contemplated with the knowledge of arising and ceasing, attained through comprehension by way of impermanence and so on, in twenty-five modes of arising and twenty-five modes of ceasing.

Cetosamathasāmīcinti cittasaṃkilesānaṃ accantavūpasamanato cetosamathasaṅkhātassa ariyamaggassa anucchavikaṃ paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhiṃ. Sikkhamānanti paṭipajjamānaṃ bhāventaṃ ñāṇaparamparā nibbattentaṃ. Sadāti sabbakālaṃ rattiñceva divā ca. Satanti catusampajaññasamannāgatāya satiyā satokārī. Evampettha gāthāvaṇṇanā daṭṭhabbā. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

‘The proper practice of mental tranquility’ (cetosamathasāmīci) refers to the purification of knowledge and vision of the path, which is appropriate for the Noble Path—designated as ‘mental tranquility’ due to the complete pacification of mental defilements. ‘Practicing’ (sikkhamānaṃ) means undertaking, developing, and producing a succession of knowledges. ‘Always’ (sadā) means at all times, both night and day. ‘Mindful’ (sataṃ) means acting with mindfulness, endowed with the four kinds of thorough understanding. Thus, the explanation of the verse should be understood here. The rest here is quite easy to understand.

Sīlasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sīla Sutta is concluded.

3. Padhānasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Padhāna Sutta

13. Tatiye [M 2.0238] uttamavīriyānīti seṭṭhavīriyāni visiṭṭhassa atthassa sādhanato. Māro dhiyyati etthāti māradheyyaṃ, kilesamārassa pavattiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ, taṃ tebhūmakavaṭṭanti āha “tebhūmakavaṭṭasaṅkhātaṃ māradheyya”nti. Jātimaraṇato jātaṃ bhayaṃ jātimaraṇabhayaṃ, jātimaraṇameva vā bhayahetuto bhayanti jātimaraṇabhayaṃ. Tenāha “jātiñca maraṇañca…pe… bhayassā”ti sesaṃ uttānameva.

13. In the third (sutta), ‘highest efforts’ (uttamavīriyāni) means supreme efforts, because they accomplish an excellent purpose. ‘Māra’s domain’ (māradheyyaṃ) means that in which Māra is established, which is the place of occurrence for the Māra of defilements. That is the round of the three realms; hence it is said, “Māra’s domain, designated as the round of the three realms.” ‘The fear of birth and death’ (jātimaraṇabhayaṃ) means the fear born from birth and death; or birth and death itself, being the cause of fear, is called the fear of birth and death. Therefore, it is said, “birth and death…fear.” The rest is clear.

Padhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Padhāna Sutta is concluded.

4. Saṃvarasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Saṃvara Sutta

14. Catutthe saṃvarādīnaṃ sādhanavasena padahati etehīti padhānāni. Saṃvarantassa uppannavīriyanti yathā abhijjhādayo na uppajjanti, evaṃ satiyā upaṭṭhāne cakkhādīnaṃ pidahane analasassa uppannavīriyaṃ. Pajahantassāti vinodentassa. Uppannavīriyanti tasseva pahānassa sādhanavasena pavattavīriyaṃ. Bhāventassa uppannavīriyanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Samādhinimittanti samādhi eva. Purimuppannasamādhi hi parato uppajjanakasamādhissa kāraṇaṃ hotīti “samādhinimitta”nti vuttaṃ.

14.
