In the fourth (sutta), ‘efforts’ (padhānāni) means that one strives by means of these for the accomplishment of restraint and so forth. ‘The energy that arises in one who is restraining’ (saṃvarantassa uppannavīriyaṃ) means the energy that arises in one who is unwearied in closing off the senses such as the eye, with the establishment of mindfulness, so that covetousness and other defilements do not arise. ‘For one who abandons’ (pajahantassa) means for one who dispels. ‘The energy that arises’ (uppannavīriyaṃ) means the energy that occurs by way of accomplishing that abandonment. ‘For one who develops, energy arises’ (bhāventassa uppannavīriyaṃ)—here too, the same method applies. ‘The condition for concentration’ (samādhinimittaṃ) is concentration itself. For previously arisen concentration is indeed the cause for subsequently arising concentration; thus, it is called the ‘condition for concentration.’

Upadhivivekattāti [V 2.0217] khandhūpadhiādiupadhīhi vivittattā vinissaṭattā. Taṃ āgammāti taṃ nibbānaṃ maggena adhigamahetu. Rāgādayo virajjanti ettha, etenāti virāgo. Evaṃ nirodhopi daṭṭhabbo. Yasmā idha bojjhaṅgamissakavasena icchitā, tasmā “ārammaṇavasena vā adhigantabbavasena vā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha adhigantabbavasenāti tanninnatāvasena. Vossaggapariṇāminti vossaggavasena pariṇāmitaṃ pariccajanavasena ceva pakkhandanavasena ca pariṇāmanasīlaṃ. Tenāha “dve vossaggā”tiādi. Khandhānaṃ pariccajanaṃ nāma tappaṭibaddhakilesappahānavasenāti yenākārena vipassanā kilese pajahati, tenevākārena tannimittakkhandhe ca pajahatīti vattabbataṃ arahatīti āha “vipassanā…pe… pariccajatī”ti. Yasmā vipassanā vuṭṭhānagāminibhāvaṃ pāpuṇantī ninnapoṇapabbhārabhāvena ekaṃsato nibbānaṃ pakkhandatīti vattabbataṃ labhati, maggo ca samucchedavasena kilese [M 2.0239] khandhe ca rāgaṃ pariccajati, tasmā yathākkamaṃ vipassanāmaggānaṃ vasena pakkhandanapariccāgavossaggā veditabbā. Vosaggatthāyāti pariccāgavossaggatthāya ceva pakkhandanavossaggatthāya ca. Pariṇamatīti pariccajati. Taṃ pana pariṇāmanaṃ vuṭṭhānagāminibhāvappattiyā ceva ariyamaggabhāvappattiyā ca icchitanti āha “vipassanābhāvañca maggabhāvañca pāpuṇātī”ti. Sesapadesūti “dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvetī”tiādīsu sesasambojjhaṅgakoṭṭhāsesu.

‘Because of detachment from attachments’ (upadhivivekattā) means being free and separated from attachments such as the aggregates-attachment. ‘On account of that’ (taṃ āgamma) means that Nibbāna is the cause for attainment by the path. ‘Dispassion’ (virāgo) means that lust and other defilements fade away here, by this. Similarly, cessation should also be understood. Since here they are intended by way of being mixed with the enlightenment factors, it is said, “either by way of the object or by way of what should be attained.” In this context, ‘by way of what should be attained’ means by way of inclination toward it. ‘Resulting in relinquishment’ (vossaggapariṇāmi) means transformed by way of relinquishment, having the nature of transforming both by way of abandoning and by way of inclining. Hence it is said, “there are two kinds of relinquishment,” etc. The abandoning of the aggregates means by way of the abandoning of the defilements connected to them. It deserves to be said that in whatever way insight abandons defilements, in that same way it abandons the aggregates that are their condition; therefore, it is said, “Insight… abandons.” Because insight, when it attains the state of leading to emergence, gains the right to be called ‘inclining decisively towards Nibbāna’ by way of its downward, sloping, and leaning nature; and because the path, by way of eradication, abandons the defilements, the aggregates, and lust, therefore, the relinquishments of inclining and abandoning should be understood respectively by way of insight and the path. ‘For the purpose of relinquishment’ (vosaggatthāya) means both for the purpose of the relinquishment of abandoning and for the purpose of the relinquishment of inclining. ‘Transforms’ (pariṇamati) means abandons. This transformation, however, is intended for the attainment of both the state leading to emergence and the state of the Noble Path; hence it is said, “It attains both the state of insight and the state of the path.” ‘In the remaining sections’ (sesapadesu) refers to the remaining sections of the enlightenment factors, such as “develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena,” etc.

Bhaddakanti abhaddakānaṃ nīvaraṇādipāpadhammānaṃ vikkhambhanena rāgavigamanena ekantahitattā dullabhattā ca bhaddakaṃ sundaraṃ. Na hi aññaṃ samādhinimittaṃ evaṃ dullabhaṃ rāgassa ujuvipaccanīkabhūtaṃ atthi. Anurakkhatīti ettha anurakkhanā nāma adhigatasamādhito yathā parihāni na hoti, evaṃ paṭipattisāsana-tappaṭipakkhavigamanenāti āha “samādhī”tiādi. Aṭṭhikasaññādikāti aṭṭhikajjhānādikā. Saññāsīsena hi jhānaṃ vadati. Sesamettha uttānameva.

‘Fortunate’ (bhaddakaṃ) means auspicious and beautiful because it is entirely beneficial and rare, by way of suppressing unfortunate, unwholesome states such as the hindrances, and by the elimination of lust. Indeed, there is no other condition for concentration so rare and directly opposed to lust as this. ‘He guards it’ (anurakkhati)—here, guarding means ensuring that the attained concentration does not decline, by means of the practice and by eliminating its opposites; thus he said, “concentration,” etc. ‘The bone-perception, etc.’ (aṭṭhikasaññādikā) refers to the bone-meditation, etc. For he speaks of absorption by way of perception as the chief. The rest here is straightforward.

Saṃvarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṃvara Sutta is concluded.

5. Paññattisuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Paññatti Sutta

15. Pañcame attabhāvo etesaṃ atthīti attabhāvino, tesaṃ attabhāvīnaṃ. Tenāha “attabhāvavantāna”nti. Yāva chattiṃsāya indānaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ, tāva paṇīte kāme paribhuñjīti mandhāturājā kira ekadivasaṃ attano pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pucchi – “atthi nu kho manussalokato ramaṇīyataraṃ ṭhāna”nti. Kasmā deva evaṃ bhaṇasi, kiṃ na passasi candimasūriyānaṃ ānubhāvaṃ, nanu etesaṃ ṭhānaṃ ito ramaṇīyataranti? Rājā cakkaratanaṃ purakkhatvā tattha agamāsi.

15. In the fifth (sutta), ‘attabhāvo’ means ‘existence’ for these, thus ‘attabhāvino,’ meaning ‘of those who have existence.’ Therefore, it is said, ‘attabhāvavantānaṃ’ (of those possessing existence). It is said that King Mandhātu enjoyed excellent sensual pleasures for as long as the lifespan of thirty-six Indras. One day, he asked his directing jewel, 'Is there any place more delightful than the human world?' The jewel replied, 'Why do you speak thus, O king? Do you not see the splendor of the sun and moon? Is not their realm more delightful than this?' The king, placing the wheel-treasure before him, went there.

Cattāro [V 2.0218] mahārājāno “mandhātumahārājā āgato”ti sutvā “tāvamahiddhiko mahārājā na sakkā yuddhena paṭibāhitu”nti sakarajjaṃ niyyātesuṃ. So taṃ gahetvā puna pucchi – “atthi nu kho ito ramaṇīyataraṃ ṭhāna”nti. Athassa tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ kathayiṃsu. “Tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ, deva, ramaṇīyaṃ, tattha sakkassa devarañño ime cattāro mahārājāno [M 2.0240] pāricārikā dovārikabhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭhanti. Sakko devarājā mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo. Tassimāni upabhogaṭṭhānāni – yojanasahassubbedho vejayantapāsādo, pañcayojanasatubbedhā sudhammadevasabhā, diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko vejayantaratho, tathā erāvaṇo hatthī, dibbarukkhasahassappaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nandanavanaṃ, cittalatāvanaṃ, phārusakavanaṃ, yojanasatubbedho pāricchattako koviḷāro, tassa heṭṭhā saṭṭhiyojanāyāmā paññāsayojanavitthārā pañcadasayojanubbedhā jayasumanapupphavaṇṇā paṇḍukambalasilā, yassā mudutāya sakkassa nisīdato upaḍḍhakāyo anuppavisatī”ti.

The four great kings, hearing, 'King Mandhāta has arrived,' thought, 'A king of such great power cannot be repelled by battle,' and surrendered their kingdoms. He took them and then asked again, 'Is there any place more delightful than this?' Then they described the realm of the Thirty-Three to him: 'The realm of the Thirty-Three, O king, is delightful. There, these four great kings stand as attendants in the position of doorkeepers for Sakka, the king of the gods. Sakka, the king of the gods, is of great power and might. These are his places of enjoyment: the Vejayanta Palace, a thousand yojanas high; the Sudhamma Assembly Hall, five hundred yojanas high; the Vejayanta Chariot, one hundred and fifty yojanas; and likewise the elephant Erāvaṇa; the Nandana Grove adorned with a thousand celestial trees; the Cittalatā Grove; the Phārusaka Grove; the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree, a hundred yojanas high, beneath which lies the Paṇḍukambala stone, the color of Jayasumana flowers, sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas thick, so soft that when Sakka sits upon it, half his body sinks in.'

Taṃ sutvā rājā tattha gantukāmo cakkaratanaṃ abbhukkiri. Taṃ ākāse uṭṭhahi saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya. Atha dvinnaṃ devalokānaṃ vemajjhato cakkaratanaṃ otaritvā pathaviyā āsanne ṭhāne aṭṭhāsi saddhiṃ pariṇāyakaratanappamukhāya caturaṅginiyā senāya. Rājā ekakova attano ānubhāvena tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ agamāsi. Sakko “mandhātā āgato”ti sutvā tassa paccuggamanaṃ katvā “svāgataṃ, mahārāja, sakaṃ, te mahārāja, anusāsa mahārājā”ti vatvā saddhiṃ nāṭakehi rajjaṃ dve bhāge katvā ekaṃ bhāgamadāsi. Rañño tāvatiṃsabhavane patiṭṭhitamattasseva manussagandhasarīranissandādimanussabhāvo vigacchi, devaloke pavattivipākadāyino aparapariyāyavedanīyassa kammassa katokāsattā sabbadā soḷasavassuddesikatāmālāmilāyanādidevabhāvo pāturahosi. Tassa sakkena saddhiṃ paṇḍukambalasilāya nisinnassa akkhinimisanamattena nānattaṃ paññāyati. Taṃ asallakkhentā devā sakkassa ca tassa ca nānatte muyhanti. So tattha dibbasampattiṃ anubhavamāno tadā manussānaṃ asaṅkhyeyyāyukatāya yāva chattiṃsa sakkā upapajjitvā cutā, tāva sakkarajjaṃ kāretvā “kiṃ me iminā upaḍḍharajjenā”ti atitto kāmehi tato cavitvā attano uyyāne patito manussaloke utukakkhaḷatāya vātātapena phusitagatto kālamakāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “devaloke pana yāva chattiṃsāya indānaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ, tāva paṇīte kāme paribhuñjī”ti.

Hearing that, the king, wishing to go there, sprinkled the wheel-treasure. It rose into the sky along with his fourfold army. Then, midway between the two divine worlds, the wheel-treasure descended and stood in a place near the earth, accompanied by the fourfold army headed by the directing-jewel. The king alone, by his own power, went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm. Sakka, hearing, 'Mandhātā has arrived,' went out to welcome him and said, 'Welcome, great king! This is your own, great king. Rule, great king!' Then, along with his retinue of celestial musicians, he divided the kingdom into two parts and gave one part to him. As soon as the king was established in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, his human characteristics, such as human scent and bodily emanations, vanished. Because an opportunity was made for karma to be experienced in a later existence, which gives its fruit of existence in the divine world, the state of a deity—such as appearing to be sixteen years old and having garlands that do not fade—always manifested. While he was sitting with Sakka on the Paṇḍukambala stone, a difference was perceived only by the blinking of his eyes. The gods, not noticing this, were confused about the difference between Sakka and him. Enjoying divine prosperity there—because humans at that time had an immeasurable lifespan—he ruled the kingdom of Sakka for as long as it took for thirty-six Sakkas to arise and pass away. Then, unsatisfied with sensual pleasures, he thought, 'What is this half-kingdom to me?' He fell from there into his own park and, his body being afflicted by wind and heat due to the harshness of the climate in the human world, he passed away. Therefore, it is said: 'In the divine world, he enjoyed refined sensual pleasures for as long as the lifespan of thirty-six Indras.'

Paññattisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Paññatti Sutta is concluded.

6. Sokhummasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Sokhumma Sutta

16. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0241][V 2.0219] sukhumalakkhaṇappaṭivijjhanakānīti aniccādisukhumalakkhaṇānaṃ paṭivijjhanakāni. Sukhumalakkhaṇapariggāhakañāṇenāti sukhumalakkhaṇapariggāhakena ñāṇena. Parato jānitvāti avasavattanena aññato jānitvā. Saṅkhārā hi “mā bhijjiṃsū”ti icchitāpi bhijjanteva, tasmā te avasavattitāya pare nāma. Sā ca nesaṃ paratā aniccadassane pākaṭā hotīti vuttaṃ “iminā hi padena aniccānupassanā kathitā”ti. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

16. In the sixth, 'penetrative understanding of subtle characteristics' means the penetrative understanding of subtle characteristics such as impermanence. 'By knowledge that grasps subtle characteristics' means by knowledge that grasps subtle characteristics. 'Having known as other' means knowing as other due to its not being subject to one's will. For formations, even when it is wished, 'May they not break apart,' still break apart. Therefore, they are called 'other' due to their being not subject to one's will. And their otherness becomes evident in the seeing of impermanence. Thus it is said, 'By this term, the contemplation of impermanence is stated.' The rest is clear.

Sokhummasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sokhumma Sutta is concluded.

7-10. Paṭhamaagatisuttādivaṇṇanā

7-10. The Commentary on the First Sutta on Wrong Courses, etc.

17-20. Sattame chandāgatinti ettha sandhivasena saralopoti dassento āha “chandena agati”nti. Chandāti hetumhi nissakkavacananti āha “chandenā”ti, pemenāti attho. Chandasaddo hettha taṇhāpariyāyo, akusalacchandapariyāyo vā. Sesesūti “dosāgatiṃ gacchatī”tiādīsu.

17-20. In the seventh, regarding 'chandāgati,' showing that there is an elision of a vowel by way of sandhi, he says, 'a wrong course due to chanda.' 'Chanda' is a term denoting the ablative in the sense of cause, and he says 'by chanda,' meaning by affection. Here, the word 'chanda' is a synonym for craving, or a synonym for unwholesome desire. In the remaining cases, as in 'one goes on a wrong course due to hatred,' and so on.

Ettha ca yo “ayaṃ me mittoti vā, sandiṭṭhoti vā, ñātakoti vā, lañcaṃ vā pana me detī”ti chandavasena assāmikaṃ sāmikaṃ karoti, ayaṃ chandena akattabbaṃ karoti nāma. Yo “ayaṃ me verī”ti cirakālānubaddhaveravasena vā, taṅkhaṇuppannakodhavasena vā sāmikaṃ assāmikaṃ karoti, ayaṃ dosena akattabbaṃ karoti nāma. Yo pana mandattā momūhattā yaṃ vā taṃ vā ayuttaṃ akāraṇaṃ vatvā assāmikaṃ sāmikaṃ karoti, ayaṃ mohena akattabbaṃ karoti nāma. Yo pana “ayaṃ rājavallabhoti vā visame corādike visamāni vā kāyaduccaritādīni samādāya vattanena visamanissito vā, anatthampi me kareyyā”ti bhīto assāmikaṃ sāmikaṃ karoti, ayaṃ bhayena akattabbaṃ karoti nāma.

Here, one who, due to desire—thinking, 'This is my friend,' or 'This is my acquaintance,' or 'This is my relative,' or 'He gives me bribes'—makes a non-owner into an owner, such a person is said to do what should not be done due to desire. One who, due to hatred—thinking, 'This is my enemy,' whether due to long-standing enmity or to anger that has arisen at that moment—makes an owner into a non-owner, such a person is said to do what should not be done due to hatred. One who, due to dullness and bewilderment, says something improper or baseless and makes a non-owner into an owner, such a person is said to do what should not be done due to delusion. One who, due to fear—thinking, 'This person is a favorite of the king,' or 'is supported by the unjust, such as thieves and the like, who act having undertaken unjust bodily misconduct and so on,' or 'he might even do me harm'—makes a non-owner into an owner, such a person is said to do what should not be done due to fear.

Yo pana kiñci bhājento “ayaṃ me sandiṭṭho vā sambhatto vā”ti pemavasena atirekaṃ deti, “ayaṃ me verī”ti dosavasena ūnakaṃ deti[M 2.0242], yo muyhanto dinnādinnaṃ ajānamāno kassaci ūnaṃ, kassaci adhikaṃ deti, “ayaṃ imasmiṃ adīyamāne mayhaṃ anatthampi [V 2.0220] kareyyā”ti sīto kassaci atirekaṃ deti, so catubbidhopi yathānukkamena chandāgatiādīni gacchanto akattabbaṃ karoti nāma.

Furthermore, one who, while distributing something, gives an excessive share out of affection, thinking, 'This is my acquaintance or my supporter'; or gives a lesser share out of hatred, thinking, 'This is my enemy'; or who, being deluded and not knowing what has been given and not given, gives less to one and more to another; or who, being frightened, gives an excessive share to someone, thinking, 'If something is not given to this person, he might even do me harm'; such a person, in all four ways, going on the wrong courses of desire and so on, is said to do what should not be done.

Nihīyati tassa yasoti tassa agatigāmino kittiyasopi parivārayasopi nihīyati parihāyati. Yassati tena kittīyatīti hi yaso, kitti thutighoso. Yassati tena purecarānucarabhāvena parivārayatīti yaso, parivāro. Aṭṭhamanavamadasamāni uttānatthāneva.

'His fame diminishes' means that for one who goes on a wrong course, both his fame as renown and his fame as a retinue diminish and decline. For, 'yasa' is so called because one is renowned (kittīyati) by it; it is renown, a sound of praise. 'Yasa' is also so called because it surrounds (parivārayati) one by way of being followers and attendants; it is a retinue. The eighth, ninth, and tenth are clear in meaning.

Caravaggo dutiyo.

The Second Chapter: On Conduct.

3. Uruvelavaggo

3. The Chapter on Uruvelā

1. Paṭhamauruvelasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the First Uruvelā Sutta

21. Tatiyassa paṭhame mahāvelā viya mahāvelā, vipulavālikapuñjatāya mahanto velātaṭo viyāti attho. Tenāha “mahāvālikarāsīti attho”ti. Uru, maru, sikatā, vālukā, vaṇṇu, vālikāti ime saddā samānatthā, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Tenāha “urūti vālikā vuccatī”ti.

21. In the first of the third, 'mahāvelā' is like a great shore, meaning like a great riverbank on account of a vast heap of sand. Therefore, he says, 'the meaning is a great heap of sand.' The words 'uru,' 'maru,' 'sikatā,' 'vālukā,' 'vaṇṇu,' and 'vālikā' have the same meaning; only the expression is different. Therefore, he says, 'by “uru,” sand is meant.'

Najjāti nadati saddāyatīti nadī, tassā najjā, nadiyā ninnagāyāti attho. Nerañjarāyāti “nelañjalāyā”ti vattabbe la-kārassa ra-kāraṃ katvā “nerañjarāyā”ti vuttaṃ, kaddamasevālapaṇakādidosarahitasalilāyāti attho. Keci “nīlaṃ-jalāyāti vattabbe nerañjarāyā”ti vadanti. Nāmameva vā etaṃ tassā nadiyāti veditabbaṃ. Tassā nadiyā tīre yattha bhagavā vihāsi, taṃ dassetuṃ “ajapālanigrodhe”ti vuttaṃ. Kasmā panāyaṃ ajapālanigrodho nāma jātoti āha “tassā”tiādi. Keci pana “yasmā tattha vede sajjhāyituṃ asamatthā mahallakabrāhmaṇā pākāraparikkhepayuttāni nivesanāni katvā sabbe vasiṃsu, tasmāssa ajapālanigrodhoti nāmaṃ jāta”nti vadanti[M 2.0243]. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – na japantīti ajapā, mantānaṃ anajjhāyakāti attho. Ajapālanti ādiyanti nivāsaṃ etthāti ajapāloti. Apare [V 2.0221] pana vadanti “yasmā majjhanhikasamaye antopaviṭṭhe aje attano chāyāya pāleti rakkhati, tasmā ‘ajapālo’tissa nāmaṃ ruḷha”nti. Sabbatthāpi nāmametaṃ tassa rukkhassa.

The river (najjā) is called “nadī” because it makes a sound (nadati), meaning it is a river, a flowing stream. Regarding “Nerañjarā,” it is said “Nerañjarā” by changing the ‘la’ sound to ‘ra’ where “nelañjalā” should be said, meaning it has water free from the faults of mud, moss, water plants, and so on. Some say “Nerañjarā” should be “nīlaṃ-jalā” (blue water). Or it should be understood that this is simply the name of that river. To show the spot on the bank of that river where the Blessed One dwelt, it is said “at the Ajapāla banyan tree.” Why, then, did this come to be called the Ajapāla banyan tree? He says, “Its…” and so on. Some say that because elderly brahmins, unable to recite the Vedas there, built houses surrounded by walls and all lived there, the name “Ajapāla banyan tree” arose for it. Here, the meaning of the word is: `ajapā` means 'not reciting,' that is, they were not reciters of mantras. `Ajapāla` is so called because the `ajapā` take up residence here. Others, however, say that because at midday, it protects and guards the goats that have entered its shade, the name “Ajapāla” became established for it. In any case, this is simply the name of that tree.

Paṭhamābhisambuddhoti paṭhamaṃ abhisambuddho, anunāsikalopenāyaṃ niddeso. Tenevāha “sambuddho hutvā paṭhamamevā”ti. Paṭhamanti ca bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, tasmā abhisambuddho hutvā paṭhamaṃ ajapālanigrodhe viharāmīti evamettha sambandho veditabbo. Ayaṃ vitakkoti ayaṃ “kinnu khvāhaṃ…pe… vihareyya”nti evaṃ pavattavitakko. Hatthī ca vānaro ca tittiro ca hatthivānaratittirā.

“Paṭhamābhisambuddho” means “first fully enlightened”; this is an explanation by elision of the nasal sound. Therefore, he says, “having become fully enlightened, indeed first.” And “paṭhamaṃ” is a neuter designation in the sense of ‘being’ or ‘occurrence’; therefore, the connection here should be understood thus: “Having become fully enlightened, I dwelt first at the Ajapāla banyan tree.” “This thought” refers to the thought that arose thus: “What if I… should dwell…” An elephant, a monkey, and a partridge—these are the elephant-monkey-partridge.

Ye vuddhamapacāyantīti jātivuddho, vayovuddho, guṇavuddhoti tayo vuddhā. Tesu jātisampanno jātivuddho nāma, vaye ṭhito vayovuddho nāma, guṇasampanno guṇavuddho nāma. Tesu guṇasampanno vayovuddho imasmiṃ ṭhāne vuddhoti adhippeto. Apacāyantīti jeṭṭhāpacāyikākammena pūjenti. Dhammassa kovidāti jeṭṭhāpacāyanadhammassa kovidā kusalā. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Pāsaṃsāti pasaṃsārahā. Samparāye ca suggatīti samparetabbe imaṃ lokaṃ hitvā gantabbe paralokepi tesaṃ sugatiyeva. Ayaṃ panettha piṇḍattho – khattiyā vā hontu brāhmaṇā vā vessā vā suddā vā gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā tiracchānagatā vā, ye keci sattā jeṭṭhāpacitikammena sīlādiguṇasampannānaṃ vayovuddhānaṃ apacitiṃ karonti, te imasmiñca attabhāve jeṭṭhāpacitikārakāti pasaṃsaṃ vaṇṇanaṃ thomanaṃ labhanti, kāyassa ca bhedā sagge nibbattantīti.

“Those who honor the elders”: there are three kinds of elders: elders by birth, elders by age, and elders by virtue. Among them, one accomplished in birth is called an elder by birth; one established in age is called an elder by age; one accomplished in virtue is called an elder by virtue. Among these, an elder by age who is accomplished in virtue is intended as the elder in this context. “Honor” means they venerate with the act of honoring elders. “Skilled in the Dhamma” means skilled and capable in the Dhamma of honoring elders. “In this very life” means in this very existence. “Praiseworthy” means worthy of praise. “And in the next life, a happy destiny” means that even in the next world, which is to be gone to after leaving this world, they have a happy destiny. Here, the concise meaning is this: whether they are nobles, brahmins, merchants, workers, householders, renunciants, or even animals, whatever beings, through the act of honoring elders, show respect to elders by age who are accomplished in virtue and other qualities, they receive praise, commendation, and acclaim in this very existence, and after the breakup of the body, they are reborn in heaven.

Aññasminti parasmiṃ. Attā na hotīti añño, paro. So panettha na yo koci adhippeto, atha kho garuṭṭhāniyo. Tenāha “kañci garuṭṭhāne aṭṭhapetvā”ti. Patissati garuno āṇaṃ sampaṭicchatīti patisso, na patisso appatisso, patissayarahito, garupassayarahitoti attho.

“In another” (aññasmiṃ) means in another (parasmiṃ). “Not oneself” (attā na hoti) means another, a different person (añño, paro). Here, it does not refer to just anyone, but specifically to one worthy of respect. Therefore, he says, “having placed someone in a position of respect.” “Patissa” means one who accepts the elder’s command; “na patisso” (not patissa) is “appatisso,” meaning devoid of compliance, devoid of respect for elders.

Sadevaketi [M 2.0244] avayavena viggaho samudāyo samāsattho. Sadevakaggahaṇena pañcakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ pārisesañāyena itaresaṃ padantarehi saṅgahitattā. Samārakaggahaṇena chaṭṭhakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ paccāsattiñāyena. Tattha hi māro jāto tannivāsī ca hoti. Sabrahmakavacanena brahmakāyikādibrahmaggahaṇaṃ paccāsattiñāyeneva. Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāyāti sāsanassa paccatthikasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇaṃ. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ apaccatthikānaṃ asamitābāhitapāpānañca samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ [V 2.0222] teneva vacanena gahitattā. Kāmaṃ “sadevake”tiādivisesanānaṃ vasena sattavisayo lokasaddoti viññāyati tulyayogavisayattā tesaṃ, “salomako sapakkhako”tiādīsu pana atulyayoge ayaṃ samāso labbhatīti byabhicāradassanato pajāgahaṇanti pajāvacanena sattalokaggahaṇaṃ.

“With the devas” (sadevake) is a collective compound, meaning a collection of parts. By the inclusion of “with the devas,” the devas of the five sense-sphere realms are included, while the others are included by implication through other terms. By the inclusion of “with Māra,” the devas of the sixth sense-sphere realm are included by proximity, for Māra is born there and dwells there. By the phrase “with the Brahmās,” the Brahmās of the Brahmā-kāyika realms and so on are included by proximity. “With the generation of ascetics and brahmins” refers to ascetics and brahmins who are opponents of the Teaching. And this is merely an illustration, for even ascetics and brahmins who are not opponents and who have not eradicated evil are included by that same term. Although by means of qualifiers such as “with the devas,” the word “world” is understood to refer to the realm of beings due to their equal application, this type of compound is also found in cases of unequal application, such as “with fur and feathers.” To show there is no such inconsistency here, the word `pajā` (generation) is included. By this word `pajā`, the inclusion of the world of beings is to be understood.

Devabhāvasāmaññena mārabrahmesu gahitesupi itarehi tesaṃ labbhamānavisesadassanatthaṃ visuṃ gahaṇanti dassento “māro nāmā”tiādimāha. Māro brahmānampi vicakkhukammāya pahotīti āha “sabbesa”nti. Uparīti uparibhāge. Brahmāti dasasahassibrahmānaṃ sandhāyāha. Tathā cāha “dasahi aṅgulīhī”tiādi. Idha dīghanikāyādayo viya bāhirakānampi ganthanikāyo labbhatīti āha “ekanikāyādivasenā”ti. Vatthuvijjādīti ādi-saddena vijjāṭṭhānāni saṅgayhanti. Yathāsakaṃ kammakilesehi pajātattā nibbattattā pajā, sattanikāyo, tassā pajāya. Sadevamanussāyāti vā iminā sammutidevaggahaṇaṃ tadavasiṭṭhamanussalokaggahaṇañca daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Showing that even though Māra and Brahmā are included by the common designation of devas, they are mentioned separately to show their distinctive qualities not found in others, he says, “Māra by name,” and so on. Māra is capable of hindering even the Brahmās in the work of insight; therefore, he says, “all.” “Above” (uparī) means in the upper region. “Brahmā” refers to the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world system. Accordingly, he says, “with ten fingers,” and so on. Here, just as the Dīghanikāya and others are considered collections, so too are even the external texts considered a collection; therefore, he says, “as in one Nikāya,” and so on. “Vatthuvijjā, etc.”—by the word “etc.,” the bases of knowledge are included. “Beings” (pajā) are so called because they are begotten or produced by their respective kammas and defilements; “the world of beings” (sattanikāyo) refers to that multitude of beings. Or by “with devas and humans,” the conventional devas are included, and what remains, the human world, should also be understood.

Evaṃ bhāgaso lokaṃ gahetvā yojanaṃ dassetvā idāni abhāgaso lokaṃ gahetvā yojanaṃ dassetuṃ “apicetthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Lokavasena vuttāni “lokīyanti ettha kammaṃ kammaphalānī”ti katvā. Pajāvasena “hetupaccayehi pajātā”ti katvā. Sīlasampannataranti ettha paripuṇṇasampannatā adhippetā “sampannaṃ sālikedāra”ntiādīsu (jā. 1.14.1) viya. Tenāha “adhikataranti attho”ti. Paripuṇṇañhi adhikataranti vattuṃ arahati. Kāraṇanti yuttiṃ. Atthanti aviparītatthaṃ. Vaḍḍhinti ativaḍḍhinimittaṃ.

Having taken the world part by part and explained it, now, to take the world as a whole and explain it, the phrase 'Even here' (apicetthā) and so on was stated. Regarding the term 'world' (loka), it is so called because 'action and the fruits of action are seen (lokīyanti) in it'. Regarding the term 'beings' (pajā), they are so called because they are 'born (pajātā) from causes and conditions'. Here, by 'more accomplished in virtue' (sīlasampannatara), complete accomplishment is intended, as in 'a fully accomplished rice field' (sampannaṃ sālikedāra) and the like. Therefore, he said, 'The meaning is "more abundant" (adhikatara).' For what is complete is indeed fit to be called 'more abundant'. 'Reason' (kāraṇa) means fitness. 'Meaning' (attha) means the unperverted meaning. 'Increase' (vaḍḍhi) means the cause for great increase.

Iminā [M 2.0245] vacanenāti imasmiṃ sutte anantaraṃ vuttavacanena. Na kevalaṃ imināva, suttantarampi ānetvā paṭibāhitabboti dassento “na me ācariyo atthī”tiādimāha. Tattha na me ācariyo atthīti lokuttaradhamme mayhaṃ ācariyo nāma natthi. Kiñcāpi lokiyadhammānampi yādiso lokanāthassa adhigamo, na tādiso adhigamo parūpadeso atthi. Lokuttaradhamme panassa lesopi natthi. Natthi me paṭipuggaloti mayhaṃ sīlādīhi guṇehi paṭinidhibhūto puggalo nāma natthi. Saranti karaṇe etaṃ paccattavacananti āha “sarantenā”ti, saranti vā saraṇahetu cāti attho.

By this statement (iminā vacanena), he means by the words spoken immediately before in this discourse. Showing that it should be refuted not only by this but also by bringing in other discourses, he says, 'I have no teacher' (na me ācariyo atthī), and so on. Here, 'I have no teacher' means that in the supramundane Dhamma, there is no teacher for me. Although even in worldly matters, there is no instruction from another that results in an attainment such as that of the Lord of the World, in the supramundane Dhamma, there is not even a trace of another's instruction for him. 'There is no individual like me' (natthi me paṭipuggalo) means that there is no individual who is a match for me in virtues such as morality, and so on. He says `sarantena` to show that this is a personal term in the instrumental sense, `saranti`. The meaning is either 'they remember' or 'it is a cause for refuge'.

Yatoti bhummatthe tosaddoti āha “yasmiṃ kāle”ti. Rattiyo jānantīti rattaññū, attano pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya bahū rattiyo jānanti, cirapabbajitāti vuttaṃ hoti. Rattaññūnaṃ [V 2.0223] mahantabhāvo rattaññumahantaṃ. Bhāvappadhāno esa niddeso. “Rattaññumahatta”nti vā pāṭho. Esa nayo sesesupi. Theranavamajjhimānaṃ vasena vipulabhāvo vepullamahantaṃ. Sikkhattayasaṅgahitassa sāsanabrahmacariyassa jhānābhiññādivasena vipulabhāvo brahmacariyamahantaṃ. Visiṭṭhassa paccayalābhassa vipulabhāvo lābhaggamahantaṃ. Catubbidhena mahantenāti catubbidhena mahantabhāvena. Mahāpajāpatiyā dussayugadānakāleti bhagavato saṅghe gāravassa pākaṭakāladassanamattaṃ. Na hi bhagavā tato pubbe saṅghe gāravarahito vihāsi.

Regarding `yato`, the particle `-to` is in the locative sense; therefore, he says, 'at which time.' 'Rattiyo jānantīti rattaññū' means one who knows nights, knowing many nights from the day of their own ordination—thus, it is said, 'long-ordained.' The greatness of those who know nights is 'greatness in terms of seniority' (rattaññumahantaṃ). This explanation emphasizes the state (bhāva). Alternatively, the reading may be 'rattaññumahatta.' This same method applies to the rest. The abundance with respect to elders, those of middle standing, and novices is 'greatness in terms of abundance' (vepullamahantaṃ). The abundance of the holy life (brahmacariya) of the Dispensation, comprised of the threefold training and distinguished by jhāna, higher knowledges, and so on, is 'greatness in terms of the holy life' (brahmacariyamahantaṃ). The abundance of superior gain is 'greatness in terms of supreme gain' (lābhaggamahantaṃ). 'By fourfold greatness' (catubbidhena mahantena) means by the fourfold state of greatness. 'At the time of Mahāpajāpati's offering of the pair of cloths' (Mahāpajāpatiyā dussayugadānakāle) refers merely to showing the time when the Blessed One's reverence for the Saṅgha became manifest. For the Blessed One had not dwelt without reverence for the Saṅgha before that.

Paṭhamauruvelasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Uruvela Sutta is finished.

2.Dutiyauruvelasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Uruvela Sutta

22. Dutiye huhuṅkajātikenāti so kira diṭṭhamaṅgaliko mānavasena kodhavasena ca “huhu”nti karonto vicarati, tasmā huhuṅkajātikoti vuccati. “Huhukkajātiko”tipi paṭhanti, tena saddhiṃ āgatāti attho. Jarājiṇṇāti jarāya khaṇḍadantapalitakesādibhāvaṃ āpāditā. Vayovuddhāti aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ vuddhimariyādappattā. Jātimahallakāti upapattiyā mahallakabhāvena samannāgatā. Mahattaṃ lanti gaṇhantīti [M 2.0246] mahallakā, jātiyā mahallakā, na vibhavādināti jātimahallakā. Vayoanuppattāti pacchimavayaṃ sampattā, pacchimavayo nāma vassasatassa pacchimo tatiyo bhāgo. Jiṇṇāti vā porāṇā, cirakālappavattakulanvayāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vuddhāti sīlācārādiguṇavuddhiyuttā. Mahallakāti vibhavamahantatāya samannāgatā. Mahaddhanāti mahābhogā. Addhagatāti maggappaṭipannā brāhmaṇānaṃ vatacariyādimariyādaṃ avītikkamma caramānā. Vayoanuppattāti jātivuddhabhāvaṃ antimavayaṃ anuppattā. Sutaṃ netanti ettha sutaṃ no etanti padacchedo. Noti ca karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ. Tenāha “amhehi suta”nti.

22. In the second sutta, regarding 'one of a huhuṅka nature' (huhuṅkajātika): it is said that he, being a superstitious believer in omens, wanders about making the sound 'huhu' out of pride and anger. Hence, he is called 'one of a huhuṅka nature.' Some also read it as 'Huhukkajātiko,' meaning 'one who has come along with that.' 'Worn out by old age' (Jarājiṇṇa) means having reached the state of broken teeth, gray hair, etc., due to old age. 'Advanced in years' (Vayovuddha) means having reached the limit of growth in limbs major and minor. 'Elderly by birth' (Jātimahallaka) means one who is endowed with the state of being an elder by birth. They take (`lanti`) greatness (`mahattaṃ`), hence 'elders' (mahallakā); elderly by birth, not by wealth or other means, hence 'elderly by birth' (jātimahallakā). 'Having reached the end of their lifespan' (Vayoanuppatta) means having reached the final age; the final age is the last third of a hundred years. Alternatively, 'worn out' (jiṇṇa) means ancient, referring to a long-standing family lineage. 'Advanced' (vuddha) means one endowed with growth in qualities such as good conduct and behavior. 'Elderly' (mahallaka) means one endowed with greatness of wealth. 'Of great wealth' (Mahaddhana) means possessing great riches. 'Having gone the way' (Addhagata) refers to those who have entered upon the path, adhering to the traditional vows and conduct of brahmins without transgression. 'Having reached the end of their lifespan' (Vayoanuppatta) means having reached the final age, the state of being advanced in years by birth. Regarding 'sutaṃ netaṃ,' here the phrase is divided as 'sutaṃ no etaṃ.' The word 'no' is a genitive pronoun in the instrumental sense. Hence, it is explained as 'heard by us' (amhehi suta).

Akāleti ayuttakāle. Asabhāvaṃ vadatīti yaṃ natthi, taṃ vadati. Anatthaṃ vadatīti akāraṇanissitaṃ vadati. Akāraṇanissitanti ca nipphalanti attho. Phalañhi kāraṇanissitaṃ. Akāraṇanissitatā ca tadavinābhāvato akāraṇe nissitaṃ, nipphalaṃ samphanti vuttaṃ hoti. Avinayaṃ vadatīti na saṃvaravinayappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ vadati, attano suṇantassa ca na saṃvaravinayāvahaṃ vadatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Na hadaye nidhetabbayuttakanti ahitasaṃhitattā cittaṃ anuppavesetvā nidhetuṃ ayuttaṃ. Kathetuṃ ayuttakālenāti dhammaṃ kathentena yo attho yasmiṃ kāle [V 2.0224] vattabbo, tato pubbe pacchā ca tassa akālo, tasmiṃ ayuttakāle vattā. Apadesarahitanti suttāpadesarahitaṃ. Sāpadesaṃ sakāraṇaṃ katvā na kathetīti “bhagavatā asuke sutte evaṃ vutta”nti evaṃ sāpadesaṃ kāraṇasahitaṃ katvā na katheti.

'At an improper time' (akāle) means at an unsuitable time. 'He speaks what is not real' (asabhāvaṃ vadati) means he speaks of that which does not exist. 'He speaks what is unbeneficial' (anatthaṃ vadati) means he speaks what is not based on a reason. And 'not based on a reason' (akāraṇanissitaṃ) means fruitless, for fruit is based on a reason. And because being without a basis in reason is inseparable from that, what is based on no reason is said to be fruitless, frivolous talk. 'He speaks what is not discipline' (avinayaṃ vadati) means he does not speak what is connected with restraint and discipline; that is to say, he speaks what does not bring restraint and discipline to himself or to the listener. 'Not fit to be stored in the heart' (na hadaye nidhetabbayuttakaṃ) means, because it is connected with what is harmful, it is not fit to be stored by letting it enter the mind. Regarding 'a speaker at an unsuitable time': for one teaching the Dhamma, there is a time when a certain meaning should be spoken; before or after that is an unsuitable time for it, and he is a speaker at that unsuitable time. 'Without reference' (apadesarahitaṃ) means without reference to the suttas. 'He does not speak making it referential and with reason' means he does not speak with reference and accompanied by reason, such as by saying, 'The Blessed One said thus in such-and-such a sutta.'

Pariyantarahitanti paricchedarahitaṃ, suttaṃ vā jātakaṃ vā nikkhipitvā tassa anuyogaṃ upamaṃ vā vatthuṃ vā āharitvā yaṃ suttaṃ jātakaṃ vā nikkhipitaṃ, tassa sarīrabhūtaṃ kathaṃ anāmasitvā bāhirakathaṃyeva katheti, nikkhittaṃ nikkhittamattameva hoti, “suttaṃ nu kho katheti jātakaṃ nu kho, nāssa antaṃ vā koṭiṃ vā passāmā”ti vattabbataṃ āpajjati. Yathā vaṭarukkhasākhānaṃ gatagataṭṭhāne pārohā otaranti, otiṇṇo-tiṇṇaṭṭhāne viruḷhiṃ āpajjitvā puna vaḍḍhantiyeva, evaṃ aḍḍhayojanampi yojanampi gacchatiyeva. Gacchante gacchante pana mūlarukkho vinassati, anujātapārohamūlāniyeva tiṭṭhanti, evaṃ ayampi nigrodhadhammakathiko nāma hoti. Nikkhittaṃ nikkhittameva katvā passeneva pariharanto gacchati. Yo pana bahumpi [M 2.0247] bhaṇanto “etadatthamidaṃ vutta”nti nikkhittasuttato aññampi anuyogūpamāvatthuvasena tadupayogīnaṃ āharitvā āharitvā jānāpetuṃ sakkoti, tathārūpassa dhammakathikassa bahumpi kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Na lokiyalokuttaraatthanissitanti attano paresañca na lokiyalokuttarahitāvahaṃ.

'Without a conclusion' (pariyantarahitaṃ) means lacking a limit. Having set aside a sutta or a jātaka, and having brought up a connection, a comparison, or a story, one speaks only of external matters without touching upon the discourse that is the very body of the sutta or jātaka that was set aside. What was set aside remains merely set aside, and one becomes liable to be told: 'Is he speaking a sutta or a jātaka? We see neither its end nor its conclusion.' Just as the aerial roots of a banyan tree descend wherever the branches have gone, and having taken root where they have descended, they grow again, extending for half a league or even a full league. But as they continue to go, the original tree perishes, and only the subsequently-born aerial roots remain. In the same way, this one is called a 'banyan-Dhamma-preacher.' Leaving what was set aside just as it was, he proceeds by passing it by. However, one who, even while speaking much, is able to make it known by repeatedly bringing up other things useful for that purpose—by way of connections, comparisons, and stories—in addition to the sutta that was set aside, understanding, 'This was said for this purpose'—for such a Dhamma-preacher, it is proper to speak at length. 'Not based on worldly or supramundane meaning' (na lokiyalokuttaraatthanissitaṃ) means not bringing worldly or supramundane benefit to oneself and others.

Pakaṭṭhānaṃ ukkaṭṭhānaṃ sīlādiatthānaṃ bodhanato sabhāvaniruttivasena ca buddhādīhi bhāsitattā pakaṭṭhānaṃ vacanappabandhānaṃ āḷīti pāḷi, pariyattidhammo. Purimassa atthassa pacchimena atthena anusandhānaṃ anusandhi, atthamukhena pana pāḷippadesānampi anusandhi hotiyeva. Svāyaṃ anusandhi pucchānusandhiajjhāsayānusandhiyathānusandhiādivasena catubbidho, taṃtaṃdesanānaṃ pana pubbāparapāḷivasena anusandhivasena pubbāparavasenāti paccekaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Uggahitanti byañjanaso atthaso ca uddhaṃ uddhaṃ gahitaṃ, pariyāpuṇanavasena ceva paripucchāvasena ca hadayena gahitanti attho. Vaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇatthikehi sotabbato sutaṃ, pariyattidhammo. Taṃ dhāretīti sutadharo. Yo hi sutadharo, sutaṃ tasmiṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ hoti suppatiṭṭhitaṃ arogikaṃ, tasmā vuttaṃ “sutassa ādhārabhūto”ti. Tenāha “yassa hī”tiādi. Ekaṃ padaṃ ekakkharampi avinaṭṭhaṃ hutvā sannicīyatīti sannicayo, sutaṃ sannicayo etasminti sutasannicayo. Ajjhosāyāti anuppavisitvā. Tiṭṭhatīti na sammussati.

Because it makes known the excellent and supreme meanings such as virtue, and because it was spoken by the Buddhas and others through natural expression and language, it is the 'line' (āḷi) of excellent verbal compositions, hence 'Pāḷi,' the teaching to be learned. The connection of the former meaning with the latter meaning is 'connection' (anusandhi); indeed, by way of the meaning, there is also a connection between sections of the Pāḷi text. This 'connection' (anusandhi) is fourfold: by way of question (pucchānusandhi), by way of intention (ajjhāsayānusandhi), by way of sequence (yathānusandhi), and so on. For each respective teaching, however, it should be applied individually by way of the preceding and succeeding Pāḷi, by way of the connection, and by way of the preceding and succeeding context. 'Learned' (uggahitaṃ) means what has been grasped progressively, both in terms of wording and meaning; the meaning is that it is grasped by the heart through study and inquiry. 'Heard' (sutaṃ) refers to what should be listened to by those seeking liberation from the suffering of the cycle of existence—this is the teaching to be learned. 'He retains it' means one who retains what has been heard (sutadharo). For one who retains what has been heard, the teaching becomes established, well-established, and sound in him. Therefore, it is said, 'He is a receptacle for what has been heard' (sutassa ādhārabhūto). Hence it is stated, 'For whom...' (yassa hi) and so on. Because even a single word or syllable, if not lost, is accumulated, this is 'accumulation' (sannicayo). What has been heard is an accumulation in him, hence 'an accumulation of what has been heard' (sutasannicayo). 'Having settled on' (ajjhosāya) means having entered into. 'It stands' (tiṭṭhati) means he does not forget.

Paguṇāti vācuggatā. Niccalikanti aviparivattaṃ. Saṃsanditvāti aññehi saṃsanditvā. Samanuggāhitvāti [V 2.0225] paripucchāvasena atthaṃ ogāhitvā. Pabandhassa vicchedābhāvato gaṅgāsotasadisaṃ. “Bhavaṅgasotasadisa”nti vā pāṭho, akittimaṃ sukhappavattīti attho. Suttekadesassa suttamattassa ca vacasā paricayo idha nādhippeto, vaggādivasena pana adhippetoti āha “suttadasaka…pe… sajjhāyitā”ti, “dasasuttāni gatāni, dasavaggāni gatānī”tiādinā sallakkhetvā vācāya sajjhāyitāti attho. Manasā anu anu pekkhitā bhāgaso nijjhāyitā cintitā manasānupekkhitā. Rūpagataṃ viya paññāyatīti rūpagataṃ viya cakkhussa vibhūtaṃ hutvā paññāyati. Suppaṭividdhāti nijjaṭaṃ niggumbaṃ katvā suṭṭhu yāthāvato paṭividdhā.

"Paguṇāti" means well-practiced in speech. "Niccalikanti" means without alteration. "Saṃsanditvāti" means having connected with others. "Samanuggāhitvāti" means having grasped the meaning by way of questioning. Because there is no interruption in the flow of the discourse, it is like the current of the Ganges. The alternative reading, “Bhavaṅgasotasadisaṃ,” means “natural and flowing smoothly with ease.” Here, familiarity with a portion of the Sutta or merely the words of the Sutta by rote is not intended; rather, familiarity with sections like the vaggas is intended. Thus it is said, “suttadasaka…pe… sajjhāyitā,” meaning “having recited ten suttas, having gone through ten sections,” and so forth, having ascertained or considered them and recited them aloud. "Manasā anu anu pekkhitā" means having repeatedly examined, contemplated in parts, reflected upon, and mentally observed. "Rūpagataṃ viya paññāyatīti" means it becomes clear to the understanding as if it were a visible form. "Suppaṭividdhāti" means thoroughly penetrated, made clear, freed from obscurity, and well-understood as it truly is.

Adhikaṃ [M 2.0248] cetoti abhiceto, upacārajjhānacittaṃ. Tassa pana adhikatā pākatikakāmāvacaracittehi sundaratāya, sā paṭipakkhato suddhiyāti āha “abhikkantaṃ visuddhaṃ citta”nti. Adhicittanti samādhimāha. Sopi upacārasamādhi daṭṭhabbo. Vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ, samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ, apītijaṃ kāyasukhaṃ, satipārisuddhijaṃ ñāṇasukhanti catubbidhampi jhānasukhaṃ paṭipakkhato nikkhantataṃ upādāya nekkhammasukhanti vuccatīti āha “nekkhammasukhaṃ vindatī”ti. Icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjituṃ samatthoti iminā tesu jhānesu samāpajjanavasībhāvamāha. Nikāmalābhīti pana vacanato āvajjanādhiṭṭhānapaccavekkhaṇavasiyopi vuttā evāti veditabbā. Sukheneva paccanīkadhamme vikkhambhetvāti etena tesaṃ jhānānaṃ sukhappaṭipadataṃ khippābhiññatañca dasseti.

"Adhikaṃ ceto" (superior mind) refers to abhiceto, the mind of access concentration. Its superiority, however, lies in its beauty compared to ordinary sense-sphere minds; that is, its purity from the opposing factors. Thus it is said, "exceedingly pure mind." "Adhicitta" (higher mind) refers to concentration. This too should be understood as access concentration. The four kinds of jhanic happiness—the joy and happiness born of seclusion, the joy and happiness born of concentration, the bodily happiness free of joy, and the happiness of knowledge purified by mindfulness—are called the happiness of renunciation because they have emerged from the opposing factors. Thus it is said, "he experiences the happiness of renunciation." By "able to enter at will, at the desired moment," the mastery of entering those jhānas is stated. By the word "nikāmalābhī" (one who obtains at will), the mastery of adverting, resolving, and reviewing is also stated, so it should be understood. By "having suppressed the opposing factors with ease," the easy practice and swift direct knowledge of those jhānas are shown.

Vipulānanti vepullaṃ pāpitānaṃ jhānānaṃ. Vipulatā nāma subhāvitabhāvena ciratarappavattiyā, sā ca paricchedānurūpāva icchitabbāti “vipulāna”nti vatvā “yathāparicchedena vuṭṭhātuṃ samatthoti vuttaṃ hotī”ti āha. Paricchedakālañhi appatvāva vuṭṭhahanto akasiralābhī na hoti yāvadicchitaṃ pavattetuṃ asamatthattā. Idāni yathāvutte samāpajjanādivasībhāve byatirekavasena vibhāvetuṃ “ekacco hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha lābhīyeva hotīti idaṃ paṭiladdhamattassa jhānassa vasena vuttaṃ. Tathāti icchiticchitakkhaṇe. Pāripanthiketi vasībhāvassa paccanīkadhamme. Jhānādhigamassa pana paccanīkadhammā pageva vikkhambhitā, aññathā jhānādhigamo eva na siyā. Kicchena vikkhambhetīti kicchena visodheti. Kāmādīnavapaccavekkhaṇādīhi kāmacchandādīnaṃ viya aññesampi samādhipāripanthikānaṃ dūrasamussāraṇaṃ idha vikkhambhanaṃ visodhanañcāti veditabbaṃ. Nāḷikayantanti kālamānanāḷikayantamāha.

"Vipulānaṃ" refers to the jhānas that have attained greatness. Greatness (vipulatā) is the sustained continuation due to being well cultivated. And since it should be desired only according to the determined limit, having said "vipulānaṃ," he says, "it is said that one is able to arise according to the determined limit." For one who arises without reaching the determined time is not one who obtains easily, because of being unable to sustain the jhāna as long as desired. Now, to distinguish the mastery of entering, etc., as stated above, by way of contrast, "ekacco hi" (for some) etc., is said. There, "he is just a gainer" is said with reference to the jhāna that has only just been attained. "Tathā" (thus) means at the desired moment. "Pāripanthika" means qualities opposed to mastery. However, the qualities opposed to the attainment of jhāna are suppressed beforehand; otherwise, there would be no attainment of jhāna. "He suppresses with difficulty" means he purifies with difficulty. Here, "suppression" and "purification" should be understood as the removal at a distance of other hindrances to concentration as well, like the contemplation of the drawbacks of sensual pleasures etc., in the case of sensual desire etc. "Nāḷikayantam" means a water clock for measuring time.

Aṭṭhapitasaṅkappoti [V 2.0226] na sammāpaṇihitasaṅkappo. Abhiññāpāragūti sabbesaṃ lokiyalokuttaradhammānaṃ abhiññāya pāraṃ gato, sabbadhamme abhivisiṭṭhāya aggamaggapaññāya jānitvā ṭhitoti attho. Pariññāpāragūti pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ pariññāya pāraṃ gato, pañcakkhandhe parijānitvā ṭhitoti attho. Bhāvanāpāragūti catunnaṃ maggānaṃ bhāvanāya pāraṃ gato, cattāro magge bhāvetvā ṭhitoti attho. Pahānapāragūti sabbakilesānaṃ pahānena pāraṃ gato, sabbakilese pajahitvā ṭhitoti attho[M 2.0249]. Sacchikiriyāpāragūti nirodhasacchikiriyāya pāraṃ gato, nirodhaṃ sacchikatvā ṭhitoti attho. Samāpattipāragūti sabbasamāpattīnaṃ samāpajjanena pāraṃ gato, sabbā samāpattiyo samāpajjitvā ṭhitoti attho. Brahmacariyassa kevalīti yaṃ brahmacariyassa kevalaṃ sakalabhāvo, tena samannāgato, sakalacatumaggabrahmacariyavāsoti attho. Tenāha “sakalabrahmacariyo”ti, paripuṇṇamaggabrahmacariyoti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

"Aṭṭhapitasaṅkappo" means not rightly established intention. "Abhiññāpāragū" (one who has gone beyond through direct knowledge) means having reached the far shore through direct knowledge of all worldly and supramundane phenomena, standing firm after knowing all phenomena with the highest wisdom of the path. "Pariññāpāragū" (one who has gone beyond through full understanding) means having reached the far shore through full understanding of the five aggregates, standing firm after fully understanding the five aggregates. "Bhāvanāpāragū" (one who has gone beyond through development) means having reached the far shore through development of the four paths, standing firm after developing the four paths. "Pahānapāragū" (one who has gone beyond through abandonment) means having reached the far shore through abandonment of all defilements, standing firm after abandoning all defilements. "Sacchikiriyāpāragū" (one who has gone beyond through realization) means having reached the far shore through realization of cessation, standing firm after directly realizing cessation. "Samāpattipāragū" (one who has gone beyond through attainment) means having reached the far shore through entering all attainments, standing firm after entering all attainments. "Brahmacariyassa kevalī" (the consummate one in the holy life) means endowed with the entirety of the holy life, dwelling in the complete fourfold-path holy life. Hence, it is said, "sakalabrahmacariyo" (the complete holy life), meaning the fully perfected path of the holy life. The rest is easily understood.

Dutiyauruvelasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Uruvela Sutta is concluded.

3. Lokasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Loka Sutta

23. Tatiye lokoti lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena loko. Atthato purimasmiṃ ariyasaccadvayaṃ, idha pana dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tenāha “lokoti dukkhasacca”nti. Visaṃyuttoti visaṃsaṭṭho na paṭibaddho, sabbesaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ sammadeva samucchinnattā tato vippamuttoti attho. Lokasamudayoti suttantanayena taṇhā, abhidhammanayena pana abhisaṅkhārehi saddhiṃ diyaḍḍhakilesasahassaṃ. Lokanirodhoti nibbānaṃ. Sacchikatoti attapaccakkho kato. Lokanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti sīlādikkhandhattayasaṅgaho ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. So hi lokanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ gacchati adhigacchati, tadatthaṃ ariyehi paṭipajjīyati cāti lokanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti vuccati.

23. In the third sutta, “the world” refers to the world in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating. In meaning, in the former case, the two noble truths are implied; but here, the noble truth of suffering should be understood. Therefore, it is said, “the world is the truth of suffering.” “Disconnected” means detached, not bound, completely liberated because all fetters have been rightly severed; that is, freed from it. “The origin of the world” is craving according to the Sutta method, but according to the Abhidhamma method, it is one and a half thousand defilements together with volitional formations. “The cessation of the world” is Nibbāna. “Realized” means made evident to oneself. “The path leading to the cessation of the world” is the noble eightfold path, included in the threefold aggregate of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. For it goes to, attains, and is practiced by the noble ones for the purpose of Nibbāna, the cessation of the world; therefore, it is called the path leading to the cessation of the world.

Ettāvatā tathāni abhisambuddho yāthāvato gatoti tathāgatoti ayamattho dassito hoti. Cattāri hi ariyasaccāni tathāni nāma. Yathāha –

By this, the meaning of 'Tathāgata' is shown to be one who has fully awakened to the truths and has gone according to reality.

“Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni. Katamāni cattāri? Idaṃ dukkhanti, bhikkhave, tathametaṃ avitathametaṃ anaññathameta”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.1090; paṭi. ma. 2.8) vitthāro.

“Monks, these four are true, unfailing, not otherwise. Which four? ‘This is suffering’—monks, this is true, unfailing, not otherwise.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1090; Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.8) The full text should be consulted.

Apica [V 2.0227] tathāya gatoti tathāgato, gatoti ca avagato atīto patto paṭipannoti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā bhagavā [M 2.0250] sakalalokaṃ tīraṇapariññāya tathāya aviparītāya gato avagato, tasmā loko tathāgatena abhisambuddhoti tathāgato. Lokasamudayaṃ pahānapariññāya tathāya gato atītoti tathāgato. Lokanirodhaṃ sacchikiriyāya tathāya gato pattoti tathāgato. Lokanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ tathaṃ aviparītaṃ gato paṭipannoti tathāgatoti. Evaṃ imissā pāḷiyā tathāgatabhāvadīpanavasena attho veditabbo.

Moreover, he has gone to the truth, thus he is the Tathāgata; and “gone” means comprehended, passed beyond, attained, and practiced—this is the meaning. This is what is said: because the Blessed One has gone to and comprehended the undeviating truth regarding the entire world by means of full understanding through judgment, therefore the world has been fully awakened by the Tathāgata; thus he is the Tathāgata. He has gone to and passed beyond the truth regarding the origin of the world by means of full understanding for abandoning, thus he is the Tathāgata. He has gone to and attained the truth regarding the cessation of the world by means of realization, thus he is the Tathāgata. He has gone upon and practiced the true, undeviating path leading to the cessation of the world, thus he is the Tathāgata. In this way, the meaning should be understood, as this Pāli passage illuminates the state of being of the Tathāgata.

Iti bhagavā catusaccābhisambodhavasena attano tathāgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetvā idāni tattha diṭṭhādiabhisambodhavasenapi taṃ dassetuṃ “yaṃ, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “catūhi saccehi attano buddhabhāvaṃ kathetvā”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ tathāgatasaddabuddhasaddānaṃ atthato ninnānākaraṇataṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā ceva hi pāḷi pavattāti. Diṭṭhanti rūpāyatanaṃ daṭṭhabbato. Tena yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ yaṃ dissati, yaṃ dakkhati, yaṃ samavāye passeyya, taṃ sabbaṃ diṭṭhanteva gahitaṃ kālavisesassa anāmaṭṭhabhāvato yathā “duddha”nti dasseti. Sutantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Sutanti saddāyatanaṃ sotabbato. Mutanti sanissaye indriye nissayaṃ muñcitvā pāpuṇitvā gahetabbaṃ. Tenāha “patvā gahetabbato”ti. Viññātanti vijānitabbaṃ. Taṃ pana diṭṭhādivinimuttaṃ viññeyyanti āha “sukhadukkhādi dhammārammaṇa”nti. Pattanti yathā tathā patvā hatthagataṃ, adhigatanti attho. Tenāha “pariyesitvā vā apariyesitvā vā”ti. Pariyesitanti pattiyā atthaṃ pariyiṭṭhaṃ. Taṃ pana pattaṃ vā siyā appattaṃ vā, ubhayathāpi pariyesitamevāti āha “pattaṃ vā appattaṃ vā”ti. Dvayenapi dvippakārampi pattaṃ dvippakārampi pariyesitaṃ tena tena pakārena tathāgatena abhisambuddhanti dasseti. Cittena anusañcaritanti te pana apāpetvā citteneva anu anu sañcaritaṃ, viparitakkitanti attho.

Thus the Blessed One, having declared his state as a Tathāgata through the full awakening to the four truths, now proceeds to show it also by means of the full awakening to what is seen, heard, etc., beginning with, “Monks, whatever is seen…” In the commentary, it is stated, “Having spoken of his Buddhahood through the four truths.” This is said to show that the terms “Tathāgata” and “Buddha” do not have different meanings in essence. The Pāli text proceeds accordingly. “Seen” refers to the visual sense-sphere, because it is to be seen. Thus, whatever was seen, whatever is seen, whatever will be seen, whatever one might perceive in combination—all that is included under “seen,” as there is no restriction of time, just as in the example of “milked.” The same method applies to “heard,” etc. “Heard” refers to the sound sense-sphere, because it is to be heard. “Sensed” is that which is to be grasped by reaching the sense faculty with its physical basis and relying upon it. Hence, it is said, “because it is to be grasped by having reached it.” “Cognized” refers to what is to be understood. But what is distinct from the seen, heard, etc., is called “the cognizable,” namely, “mental objects such as pleasure and pain.” “Attained” means attained in whatever way, as if taken into hand, i.e., realized. Therefore, it is said, “whether sought or not sought.” “Sought” means sought for with the aim of attainment. Whether attained or not attained, in both cases, it is still “sought.” Hence, it is said, “whether attained or not attained.” He shows that what is attained in two ways and what is sought in two ways, in this way or that, is fully understood by the Tathāgata. “Mentally traversed” means that, without having attained them, they are repeatedly traversed by the mind—that is, speculated about.

Pītakantiādīti ādisaddena lohitaodātādisabbaṃ rūpārammaṇabhāgaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sumanoti rāgavasena lobhavasena saddhādivasena vā sumano. Dummanoti byāpādavitakkavasena vā vihiṃsāvitakkavasena vā dummano. Majjhattoti aññāṇavasena, ñāṇavasena vā majjhatto. Esa nayo sabbattha. Tattha ādisaddena saṅkhasaddo, paṇavasaddo, pattagandho, pupphagandho, puppharaso, phalaraso, upādinnaṃ, anupādinnaṃ, majjhattavedanā [M 2.0251] kusalakammaṃ akusalakammanti evamādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Appattanti ñāṇena asampattaṃ, aviditanti attho. Tenāha “ñāṇena asacchikata”nti. Lokena gatanti lokena ñātaṃ. Tatheva gatattāti tatheva ñātattā abhisambuddhattā[V 2.0228], gatasaddena ekattaṃ buddhiatthanti attho. Gatiattho hi dhātavo buddhiatthā bhavantīti akkharacintakā.

In ‘yellow, etc.,’ the word ‘etc.’ includes all visual objects such as red, white, and so on. ‘Joyful’ refers to being joyful due to lust, greed, faith, or similar states. ‘Displeased’ refers to being displeased due to ill will or harmful thoughts. ‘Neutral’ refers to being neutral due to ignorance or knowledge. This principle applies everywhere. Here, the word ‘etc.’ includes terms like conch sound, tambourine sound, leaf scent, flower scent, flower taste, fruit taste, appropriated, unappropriated, neutral feeling, wholesome kamma, unwholesome kamma, and so on. ‘Unattained’ means not attained by knowledge, that is, not understood. Hence it is said, “not realized by knowledge.” ‘Gone to by the world’ means known by the world. ‘Because of being gone to in that very way’ means because of being known in that very way, because of being fully awakened to it; the word ‘gata’ has the same meaning as understanding. For roots with the meaning of ‘going’ are indeed the meanings of understanding, as the grammarians say.

Yañca, bhikkhave, ratiṃ tathāgato anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhatīti yassañca visākhapuṇṇamāya rattiyaṃ tathāāgatattādiatthena tathāgato bhagavā bodhimaṇḍe aparājitapallaṅke nisinno tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ matthakaṃ madditvā uttaritarābhāvato anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ āsavakkhayañāṇena saddhiṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ adhigacchati. Yañca rattiṃ anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyatīti yassañca visākhapuṇṇamāya rattiyaṃyeva kusinārāyaṃ upavattane mallānaṃ sālavane yamakasālānamantare anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyati. Yaṃ etasmiṃ antareti imāsaṃ dvinnaṃ saupādisesaanupādisesanibbānadhātūnaṃ majjhe pañcacattālīsavassaparimāṇakāle paṭhamabodhiyampi majjhimabodhiyampi pacchimabodhiyampi yaṃ suttageyyādippabhedaṃ dhammaṃ bhāsati nidassanavasena, lapati uddisanavasena, niddisati pariniddisanavasena. Sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva hotīti taṃ etthantare desitaṃ sabbaṃ suttageyyādinavaṅgaṃ buddhavacanaṃ atthato byañjanato ca anūnaṃ anadhikaṃ sabbākāraparipuṇṇaṃ rāgamadanimmadanaṃ dosamadanimmadanaṃ mohamadanimmadanaṃ, natthi tattha vālaggamattampi avakkhalitaṃ, ekamuddikāya lañchitaṃ viya ekāya nāḷiyā mitaṃ viya ekatulāya tulitaṃ viya ca taṃ tatheva hoti yassatthāya bhāsitaṃ, ekanteneva tassa sādhanato, no aññathā, tasmā tathaṃ avitathaṃ anaññathaṃ. Etena tathāvāditāya tathāgatoti dasseti. Gadaattho ayaṃ gatasaddo da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā, tasmā tathaṃ gadatīti tathāgatoti attho. Atha vā āgadanaṃ āgado, vacananti attho. Tato aviparīto āgado assāti da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā tathāgatoti evamettha padasiddhi veditabbā.

And the night, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata fully awakens to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—that is, on the night of the full moon in the month of Visākha, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata (by the meaning of 'thus come' and so on), seated on the unconquered throne at the Bodhi tree, having crushed the heads of the three Māras, attains unsurpassed perfect enlightenment together with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints and omniscient knowledge. And the night he attains final nibbāna without remainder—that is, on the very night of the full moon in the month of Visākha, in the sal grove of the Mallas at Kusinārā, between the twin sal trees, he attains final nibbāna in the nibbāna-element without remainder. What lies between these two—that is, in the interval of forty-five years between these two nibbāna-elements, with remainder and without remainder—whether in the first enlightenment, the middle enlightenment, or the final enlightenment, whatever Dhamma he speaks, whether in the form of suttas, geyyas, and so on, by way of illustration, by way of pointing out, or by way of full explanation—all of it is just so. All that is taught in this interval—the entire ninefold dispensation of the Buddha’s word—is complete in meaning and phrasing, lacking nothing, exceeding nothing, perfect in every way. It crushes the intoxication of lust, the intoxication of hatred, and the intoxication of delusion. There is not even a hair’s breadth of deviation. It is like being stamped with a single seal, measured with a single measure, weighed with a single weight—just as it was spoken, it is entirely for the sake of accomplishing that purpose, not otherwise. Therefore, it is true, unfailing, not otherwise. By this truth-speaking, he is called the Tathāgata. Here, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'gada' (to speak), having changed the 'da' to 'ta'; therefore, the meaning is 'Tathāgata' because he speaks truly. Or alternatively, 'āgadana' is 'āgada', meaning 'speech'. From that, 'one whose speech is not contrary'—having changed the 'da' to 'ta', thus 'Tathāgata.' In this way, the formation of the word should be understood here.

Yathāvādīti ye dhamme bhagavā “ime dhammā akusalā sāvajjā viññugarahitā samattā samādinnā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattantī”ti paresaṃ dhammaṃ desento vadati, te dhamme ekanteneva sayaṃ pahāsi. Ye pana [M 2.0252] dhamme bhagavā – “ime dhammā kusalā anavajjā viññuppasatthā samattā samādinnā hitāya sukhāya saṃvattantī”ti vadati, te dhamme ekanteneva sayaṃ upasampajja viharati, tasmā yathāvādī bhagavā tathākārīti veditabbo. Tathā sammadeva sīlādiparipūraṇavasena sammāpaṭipadāyaṃ yathākārī bhagavā, tatheva dhammadesanāya paresaṃ tattha patiṭṭhāpanavasena tathāvādī. Bhagavato hi vācāya kāyo anulometi, kāyassapi vācā, tasmā [V 2.0229] yathāvādī tathākārī, yathākārī tathāvādī ca hoti. Evaṃbhūtassa ca yathā vācā, kāyopi tathā gato pavatto. Yathā ca kāyo, vācāpi tathā gatā pavattāti attho.

As he speaks, so he acts: Those qualities that the Blessed One declares, saying to others, “These qualities are unskillful, blameworthy, censured by the wise, and when undertaken and adhered to, lead to harm and suffering”—those very qualities he has entirely abandoned himself. And those qualities that the Blessed One declares, saying, “These qualities are skillful, blameless, praised by the wise, and when undertaken and adhered to, lead to welfare and happiness”—those very qualities he has fully attained and lives by. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One is one who speaks as he acts. Just as the Blessed One acts rightly in the right practice through the perfect fulfillment of virtue and so on, so too he speaks rightly in teaching the Dhamma to others, establishing them in it. For the Blessed One, his body conforms to his speech, and his speech conforms to his body. Thus, he is one who speaks as he acts and acts as he speaks. For one of such nature, as his speech is, so his body behaves and proceeds. And as his body behaves, so his speech proceeds—this is the meaning.

Abhibhū anabhibhūtoti upari bhavaggaṃ, heṭṭhā avīcinirayaṃ pariyantaṃ katvā tiriyaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu bhagavā sabbasatte abhibhavati sīlenapi samādhināpi paññāyapi vimuttiyāpi, na tassa tulā vā pamāṇaṃ vā atthi. Asamo asamasamo appaṭimo appaṭibhāgo appaṭipuggalo atulo appameyyo anuttaro dhammarājā devadevo sakkānaṃ atisakko brahmānaṃ atibrahmā, tato eva ayaṃ na kenaci abhibhūto. Dakkhatīti sabbaṃ passati. Visesavacanicchāyapi abhāvato anavasesavisayo dasasaddo. Tena yaṃ kiñci neyyaṃ nāma, sabbaṃ taṃ hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya passatīti dīpeti. Aviparītaṃ āsayādiavabodhena hitūpasaṃhārādinā ca satte, bhāvaññatthattūpanayavasena saṅkhāre, sabbākārena suciṇṇavasitāya samāpattiyo, cittañca vase vattetīti vasavattīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

The Conqueror, the Unconquered: having made the highest existence the limit above and the Avīci hell the limit below, the Blessed One overcomes all beings across immeasurable world-systems through virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation. There is no equal or measure for Him. Incomparable, matchless, unequaled, without counterpart, without peer, beyond compare, immeasurable, unsurpassed, the King of Dhamma, the God of gods, surpassing Sakka, surpassing Brahmā—thus, He is unconquered by anyone. He sees: He perceives all. The word for seeing has an all-encompassing scope, even in the absence of a desire for specific expressions. Thus, it is shown that whatever is to be known, He sees it all as clearly as an āmalaka fruit in the palm of His hand. Without error, through understanding the inclinations of beings and guiding them to their welfare, He comprehends formations by way of their nature, meaning, and application. Having fully mastered all meditative attainments in every aspect with well-practiced mastery, and having brought the mind under his power, He is the Master of Power—this is how the meaning should be understood here.

Visaṃyuttoti catūhi yogehi visaṃyutto. Tenāha “catunnaṃ yogānaṃ pahānena visaṃyutto”ti. Taṇhādiṭṭhiupayehi virahitoti sabbasmimpi loke taṇhādiṭṭhisaṅkhātehi upayehi virahito.

Unattached: unattached to the four yokes. Therefore, it is said, 'Unattached through the abandonment of the four yokes.' Devoid of craving, views, and attachments: He is devoid of those attachments in the entire world that are characterized as craving and views.

Abhibhavitvā ṭhitoti tabbisayakilesappahānena abhibhuyya atikkamitvā ṭhito. Cattāropi ganthe mocetvā ṭhitoti sabbe abhijjhākāyaganthādike sakasantānato mocetvā ṭhito. Veneyyasantāne vā attano desanāvilāsena tesaṃ pamocanoti sabbaganthappamocano. Phuṭṭhassa paramā santīti assa anena khīṇāsavena buddhena [M 2.0253] paramā santi ñāṇaphusanena phuṭṭhāti evamettha sambandho veditabbo. Tenāha “phuṭṭhassā”tiādi. Nibbāne kutoci bhayaṃ natthīti kutoci bhayakāraṇato nibbāne bhayaṃ natthi asaṅkhatabhāvena sabbaso khemattā. Tenāha bhagavā – “khemañca vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi khemagāminiñca paṭipada”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 4.379-408). Nibbānappattassa vā kutoci bhayaṃ natthīti nibbānaṃ akutobhayanti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo, na kutoci bhayaṃ ettha etasmiṃ adhigateti akutobhayaṃ, nibbānanti evamettha nibbacanañca daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Having overcome, he stands' means he stands having overcome and transcended by abandoning the defilements related to their respective objects. 'Having been freed from the four knots' means he stands having been freed from all the knots of the body, such as covetousness, within his own continuum. Or, through the grace of his teaching, he frees those in the continuum of trainable beings—thus, he is the one who frees from all knots. 'For him who is touched, there is supreme peace' means that for this one whose cankers are destroyed, this Buddha, supreme peace is touched by the contact of knowledge; the connection here should be understood thus. Therefore, it is said, 'For him who is touched,' etc. 'In Nibbāna, there is no fear from anywhere' means that in Nibbāna, there is no fear from any cause of fear, because it is unconditioned and entirely secure. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma that is secure and the path leading to security,' etc. (Saṃ. Ni. 4.379-408). Or, 'For one who has attained Nibbāna, there is no fear from anywhere'—thus Nibbāna is 'fearless from any quarter' (akutobhaya). Here, the meaning should be seen thus. 'No fear from any quarter arises here, in this attainment,' hence it is called akutobhaya, Nibbāna; the derivation should also be seen in this way.

Anīgho niddukkho. Sabbakammakkhayaṃ pattoti sabbesaṃ kammānaṃ khayaṃ pariyosānaṃ accantabhāvaṃ patto. Upadhī sammadeva khīyanti etthāti upadhisaṅkhayo, nibbānanti āha “upadhisaṅkhayasaṅkhāte nibbāne”ti. Cakkanti dhammacakkaṃ. Pavattayīti teparivaṭṭaṃ dvādasākāraṃ pavattesi[V 2.0230]. Mahantehi sīlādiguṇehi samannāgatattā mahantaṃ. Vītasāradanti catuvesārajjayogena vītasāradaṃ. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

`Anīgho` means without anguish; `niddukkho`, without suffering. 'Having reached the destruction of all kamma' means he has reached the destruction, the end, the absolute non-existence of all kammas. `Upadhisaṅkhayo` (the exhaustion of the substrates) is so called because 'herein the substrates are altogether exhausted'; this refers to Nibbāna. Therefore, it is said, 'in Nibbāna, known as the exhaustion of the substrates.' 'The wheel' is the Dhamma-wheel. 'He set it rolling' means he set rolling the threefold revolution with its twelve aspects. 'Great' because he is endowed with great qualities such as virtue. 'Free from fear' (`vītasārada`) means free from fear due to the possession of the four kinds of intrepidity. The rest is clear.

Lokasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Lokasutta is concluded.

4. Kāḷakārāmasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Kāḷakārāma Sutta

24. Catutthe bāḷhaṃ kho ne pasaṃsasīti ne samaṇe bāḷhaṃ katvā pasaṃsasi vaṇṇayasi. Kīdisaṃ sīlaṃ etesanti kiṃsīlā. Ko samācāro etesanti kiṃsamācārā. Guṇamaggasaṇṭhitāti guṇaggasaṇṭhitā. Ma-kāro padasandhikaro, aggaguṇe patiṭṭhitāti vuttaṃ hoti. Santindriyā santamānasā, “santaṃ tesaṃ gataṃ ṭhita”ntipi paṭhanti. Ekakiyāti ekakā, catūsu iriyāpathesu ekakā hutvā viharantīti adhippāyo. Tenevāha “adutiyā”ti. Tādisā samaṇā mamātīti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho. Tena –

24. In the fourth, 'You praise them highly' means you praise and extol them, the ascetics, highly. 'Of what virtue are they?' means `kiṃsīlā`. 'What is their conduct?' means `kiṃsamācārā`. 'Established in the path of virtues' means established in the highest virtues. The letter 'm' is a euphonic consonant; it means 'established in the highest virtues.' 'With senses calmed, minds calmed'; some also read, 'their going and standing are calm.' 'Solitary' means alone; the meaning is that they dwell alone in the four postures. Therefore it is said, 'without a second.' 'Such ascetics are mine'—here, the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so on.' Therefore:

“Kāyakammaṃ suci nesaṃ, vācākammaṃ anāvilaṃ;

Manokammaṃ suvisuddhaṃ, tādisā samaṇā mama.

'Their bodily action is pure, their verbal action is unstained; their mental action is thoroughly pure—such ascetics are mine.'

“Vimalā [M 2.0254] saṅkhamuttābhā, suddhā antarabāhirā;

Puṇṇā suddhehi dhammehi, tādisā samaṇā mama.

'Spotless, like the lustre of a conch shell, pure within and without; filled with pure qualities—such are my ascetics.'

“Lābhena unnato loko, alābhena ca onato;

Lābhālābhena ekaṭṭhā, tādisā samaṇā mama.

'The world is elated by gain, and dejected by loss; but those who are steadfast in gain and loss—such are my ascetics.'

“Yasena unnato loko, ayasena ca onato;

Yasāyasena ekaṭṭhā, tādisā samaṇā mama.

'The world is uplifted by fame, and cast down by lack of fame; those who stand firm in both fame and lack of fame—such are my ascetics.'

“Pasaṃsāyunnato loko, nindāyapi ca onato;

Samā nindāpasaṃsāsu, tādisā samaṇā mama.

'The world is uplifted by praise and cast down by blame; those who are impartial in blame and praise—such are my ascetics.'

“Sukhena [V 2.0231] unnato loko, dukkhenapi ca onato;

Akampā sukhadukkhesu, tādisā samaṇā mamā”ti. (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.303 cūḷasubhaddāvatthu) –

'The world is elated by pleasure, and dejected by pain; unshaken in pleasure and pain—such are my ascetics.'

Evamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

Thus, it includes these and similar verses.

“Dūre santo”tiādigāthāya ayamattho. Santoti rāgādīnaṃ santatāya buddhādayo santo nāma, idha pana pubbabuddhesu katādhikārā ussannakusalamūlā bhāvitabhāvanā sattā santoti adhippetā. Pakāsantīti dūre ṭhitāpi buddhānaṃ ñāṇapathaṃ āgacchantā pākaṭā honti. Himavantovāti yathā tiyojanasahassavitthato pañcayojanasatubbedho caturāsītiyā kūṭasahassehi paṭimaṇḍito himavantapabbato dūre ṭhitānampi abhimukhe ṭhito viya pakāsati, evaṃ pakāsantīti attho. Asantettha na dissantīti lābhagarukā, vitthiṇṇaparalokā, āmisacakkhukā, jīvikatthāya pabbajitā, bālapuggalā asanto nāma. Te ettha buddhānaṃ dakkhiṇassa jāṇumaṇḍalassa santike nisinnāpi na dissanti na paññāyanti. Rattiṃ khittā yathā sarāti rattiṃ caturaṅgasamannāgate andhakāre khittā sarā viya tathārūpassa upanissayabhūtassa pubbahetuno abhāvena na paññāyantīti attho.

The meaning of the verse beginning 'The good, though far...' is as follows: 'The good' (`santo`) refers to the Buddhas and others who are so called because of the calming of lust and so on. Here, however, 'the good' is intended to mean beings who have made aspirations under past Buddhas, whose wholesome roots are abundant, and who have cultivated what is to be cultivated. 'They shine' (`pakāsanti`) means that even from afar, they become manifest by entering the range of the Buddhas' knowledge. 'Like the Himālaya mountain' means that just as the Himālaya mountain—three thousand leagues in breadth and five hundred leagues in height, adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks—appears as if right in front even to those standing far away, so too do they shine. 'The bad are not seen here' refers to those who are not good (`asanto`): those who are intent on gain, who are lost in the vastness of the next world, who have an eye for material things, who have gone forth for the sake of a livelihood—such foolish people are called 'the bad.' Even if they sit near the Buddha's right kneecap, they are not seen or discerned. 'Like arrows shot at night' means that just as arrows shot in the deep darkness of night are not discerned, so too, due to the absence of a prior cause that would be their supporting condition, they are not discerned.

Brahmadeyyanti seṭṭhadeyyaṃ, yathā dinnaṃ na puna gahetabbaṃ hoti nissaṭṭhaṃ pariccattaṃ, evaṃ dinnanti attho.

'A noble gift' (`brahmadeyya`) means the best gift; the meaning is that it is given in such a way that it is not to be taken back, being given up and relinquished.

Diṭṭhaṃ na maññatīti ettha diṭṭhanti maṃsacakkhunāpi diṭṭhaṃ, dibbacakkhunāpi diṭṭhaṃ, rūpāyatanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yañhi cakkhudvayena katadassanakiriyāsamāpanaṃ, yaṃ [M 2.0255] cakkhudvayaṃ passati apassi passissati, samavāye passeyya, taṃ sabbaṃ kālavisesavacanicchāya abhāvato “diṭṭha”nteva vuttaṃ yathā “duddha”nti. Tenevāha “diṭṭhaṃ rūpāyatana”nti. Evarūpāni hi vacanānīti “daṭṭhabbaṃ sotabba”ntiādīni.

In 'He does not conceive the seen,' here 'the seen' (`diṭṭha`) means what is seen, whether with the physical eye or the divine eye; this is a designation for the visible sense sphere. For whatever completion of the act of seeing is done by the two eyes—whatever the two eyes see, saw, or will see, or might see in conjunction with other factors—all of that, due to the absence of a desire for specific temporal expressions, is simply called 'seen,' just as 'milked' (`duddha`) is used to refer to milk. Therefore, it is said, 'The seen is the visible sense sphere.' Indeed, such are these expressions, like 'what should be seen, what should be heard,' and so on.

Lābhepi tādī, alābhepi tādīti yathā alābhakāle lābhassa laddhakālepi tathevāti tādiso. Yasepīti yase satipi mahāparivārakālepi. Sesamettha uttānameva.

'Such in gain, and such in loss' means that just as he is at a time of loss, so he is also at a time when gain is received; thus he is 'such' (`tādī`). 'Even in fame' means even when there is fame, that is, even at a time of a great retinue. The rest here is clear.

Kāḷakārāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kāḷakārāma Sutta is concluded.

5. Brahmacariyasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Brahmacariya Sutta

25. Pañcame [V 2.0232] nayidanti ettha na-iti paṭisedhe nipāto, tassa “vussatī”ti iminā sambandho “na vussatī”ti, ya-kāro padasandhikaro. Idaṃ-saddo “ekamidāhaṃ, bhikkhave, samayaṃ ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharāmi subhagavane sālarājamūle”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.91; ma. ni. 1.501) nipātamattaṃ, “idaṃ kho taṃ, bhikkhave, appamattakaṃ sīlamattaka”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.27) yathāvutte āsannapaccakkhe āgato.

25. In the fifth instance, in “nayidanti” the particle “na” is a negative, and it connects with “vussati” to form “na vussati,” the “ya” being a euphonic link. The word “idaṃ” is merely a particle in phrases such as, “At one time, monks, I was dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhagavana at the foot of the Sāla king tree,” etc. (DN 2.91; MN 1.501); while in contexts such as, “This, monks, is a minor, trifling virtue” (DN 1.27), it refers to something near, immediate, and previously mentioned.

“Idañhi taṃ jetavanaṃ, isisaṅghanisevitaṃ;

Āvutthaṃ dhammarājena, pītisañjananaṃ mamā”ti. (ma. ni. 3.387-388; saṃ. ni. 1.48, 101) –

“This, indeed, is that Jetavana, frequented by the community of sages; inhabited by the King of the Dhamma, a generator of joy for me.”

Ādīsu vakkhamāne āsannapaccakkhe. Idhāpi vakkhamāneyeva āsannapaccakkhe daṭṭhabbo.

In the following examples, it refers to what is near and directly perceived. Here too, it should be understood as referring to what is near and directly perceived in the passage that follows.

Brahmacariya-saddo –

The term “brahmacariya”–

“Kiṃ te vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ,

Kissa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Iddhī jutī balavīriyūpapatti,

Idañca te nāga mahāvimānaṃ.

“What is your vow? What, indeed, your holy life? Of what well-practiced deed is this the fruit? Psychic power, radiance, strength, and the arising of energy, and this great mansion of yours, O Nāga?”

“Ahañca bhariyā ca manussaloke,

Saddhā ubho dānapatī ahumhā;

Opānabhūtaṃ me gharaṃ tadāsi,

Santappitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca.

“I and my wife, in the human world, were both devout donors; my home was then a watering place, and ascetics and brahmins were satisfied.”

“Taṃ [M 2.0256] me vataṃ taṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ,

Tassa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Iddhī jutī balavīriyūpapatti,

Idañca me vīra mahāvimāna”nti. –

“That was my vow, that was my holy life, of that well-practiced deed this is the fruit; psychic power, radiance, strength, and the arising of energy, and this great celestial mansion of mine, O hero!”

Imasmiṃ [V 2.0233] puṇṇakajātake (jā. 2.22.1595) dāne āgato.

In this Puṇṇaka Jātaka (Jā 2.22.1595), it refers to generosity.

“Kena pāṇi kāmadado, kena pāṇi madhussavo;
