Kena te brahmacariyena, puññaṃ pāṇimhi ijjhatī”ti. –

“By what is your hand a giver of wishes? By what is your hand a shower of honey? By what holy life of yours is merit accomplished in your hand?”

Imasmiṃ aṅkurapetavatthusmiṃ (pe. va. 275, 277) veyyāvacce.

In this Aṅkura Petavatthu (Pv 275, 277), it refers to service.

“Evaṃ kho taṃ, bhikkhave, tittiriyaṃ nāma brahmacariyaṃ ahosī”ti imasmiṃ tittirajātake (cūḷava. 311) pañcasikkhāpadasīle.

“Thus, monks, that was the holy life called ‘Partridge-like.’” In this Tittira Jātaka (Cv 311), it refers to the morality of the five training rules.

“Taṃ kho pana me, pañcasikha, brahmacariyaṃ neva nibbidāya na virāgāya…pe… yāvadeva brahmalokūpapattiyā”ti imasmiṃ mahāgovindasutte (dī. ni. 2.329) brahmavihāre.

“But, Pañcasikha, that holy life of mine was not for disenchantment, nor for dispassion… but only for rebirth in the Brahma-world.” In this Mahāgovinda Sutta (DN 2.329), it refers to the divine abodes.

“Pare abrahmacārī bhavissanti, mayamettha brahmacārī bhavissāmā”ti imasmiṃ sallekhasutte (ma. ni. 1.83) methunaviratiyaṃ.

“Others will be unchaste, but here we will be celibate.” In this Sallekha Sutta (MN 1.83), it refers to abstinence from sexual intercourse.

“Mayañca bhariyā nātikkamāma,

Amhe ca bhariyā nātikkamanti;

Aññatra tāhi brahmacariyaṃ carāma,

Tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare”ti. –

“We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us; apart from them, we live the holy life, thus, our young ones do not die.”

Imasmiṃ mahādhammapālajātake (jā. 1.10.97) sadārasantose.

In this Mahādhammapāla Jātaka (Jā 1.10.97), it refers to contentment with one’s own wife.

“Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ caritā, tapassī sudaṃ homī”ti lomahaṃsasutte (ma. ni. 1.155) vīriye.

“I recall, Sāriputta, having lived the holy life possessed of four factors; I was truly an ascetic.” In the Lomahaṃsa Sutta (MN 1.155), it refers to energy.

“Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati;

Majjhimena ca devattaṃ, uttamena visujjhatī”ti. –

“By an inferior holy life, one is reborn as a noble; by a middling one, as a god; by the highest, one is purified.”

Nimijātake (jā. 2.22.429) attadamanavasena kate aṭṭhaṅgike uposathe.

In the Nimi Jātaka (Jā 2.22.429), it refers to the eight-factored Uposatha practiced by way of self-control.

“Idaṃ [M 2.0257][V 2.0234] kho pana me, pañcasikha, brahmacariyaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya…pe… ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti mahāgovindasutteyeva (dī. ni. 2.329) ariyamagge.

“Now, Pañcasikha, this holy life of mine is solely for complete disenchantment, for dispassion… this very Noble Eightfold Path.” In the Mahāgovinda Sutta (DN 2.329) itself, it refers to the Noble Path.

“Tayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsita”nti pāsādikasutte (dī. ni. 3.174) sikkhattayasaṅgahite sakalasmiṃ sāsane. Idhāpi ariyamagge sāsane ca vattati.

“This holy life is successful, flourishing, widespread, known to many, extensive, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans.” In the Pāsādika Sutta (DN 3.174), it refers to the entire Dispensation which is included in the threefold training. Here too, it applies to the Noble Path and the Dispensation.

Vussatīti vusīyati, carīyatīti attho. Janakuhanatthanti “aho ayyo sīlavā vattasampanno appiccho santuṭṭho mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo”tiādinā janassa sattalokassa vimhāpanatthaṃ. Keci pana “kuhanatthanti pāpicchassa icchāpakatassa sato sāmantajappanairiyāpathanissitapaccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātena tividhena kuhanavatthunā kuhakabhāvena janassa vimhāpanattha”nti vadanti. Idhāpi ayamevattho dassito. Tenevāha “tīhi kuhanavatthūhi janassa kuhanatthāyā”ti, janassa vimhāpanatthāyāti attho. Janalāpanatthanti “evarūpassa nāma ayyassa dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ bhavissatī”ti pasannacittehi “kenattho, kiṃ āharīyatū”ti vadāpanatthaṃ. “Janalapanattha”ntipi paṭhanti, tassa pāpicchassa sato paccayatthaṃ parikathobhāsādivasena lapanabhāvena upalāpakabhāvena janassa lapanatthanti attho. Tenevāha “na janalapanatthanti na janassa upalāpanattha”nti.

“Vussati” means it is lived, it is practiced. “The purpose of deceiving people” is to astonish the people, the world of beings, with such thoughts as, “Oh, this venerable one is virtuous, accomplished in conduct, of few desires, content, of great power and great might,” and so on. Some, however, say that “the purpose of deception” is to astonish people through the deceitful behavior of one with evil desires and concealed wishes, which consists of the threefold ground of deception: hinting, affected deportment, and the use of requisites dependent thereon. Here too, this very meaning is shown. Therefore, it is said, “for the purpose of deceiving people by the three grounds of deception,” meaning for the purpose of astonishing people. “The purpose of ingratiating oneself with people” is to make those with faithful hearts say, “What is given to such a venerable one will be of great fruit,” and to prompt them to ask, “What is needed? What should be brought?” Some also read it as “the purpose of wheedling people,” meaning the purpose of wheedling people through the act of coaxing, such as by roundabout talk or allusions, on the part of one with evil desires for the sake of requisites. Therefore, it is said, “not for the purpose of wheedling people,” meaning not for the purpose of coaxing people.

Na itivādappamokkhānisaṃsatthanti ettha “na lābhasakkārasilokānisaṃsattha”ntipi paṭhanti. Tattha yvāyaṃ “ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ‘lābhī assaṃ cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna’nti, sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī”ti (ma. ni. 1.65) sīlānisaṃsabhāvena vutto catupaccayalābho ca. Catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ sakkaccadānasaṅkhāto ādarabahumānagarukaraṇasaṅkhāto ca sakkāro, yo ca “sīlasampanno bahussuto sutadharo āraddhavīriyo”tiādinā nayena uggacchanakathutighosasaṅkhāto siloko brahmacariyaṃ vasantānaṃ diṭṭhadhammiko ānisaṃso, tadatthanti attho. Keci pana “lābhasakkārasilokānisaṃsatthanti pāpicchasseva sato lābhādigarutāya lābhasakkārasilokasaṅkhātassa ānisaṃsassa udayassa nipphādanattha”nti evamatthaṃ vadanti.

Here, in the phrase “not for the benefit of release through such-and-such a doctrine,” some also read it as “not for the sake of the benefits of gain, honor, and fame.” In that context, there is the gain of the four requisites—robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites—which is mentioned as a benefit of virtue, as stated: “If a monk, monks, should wish, ‘May I be one who obtains robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites,’ let him be a perfect fulfiller of virtue.” And there is honor, which consists of respectfully giving the four requisites, and of showing respect, deference, and reverence. And there is fame, which consists of the rising sound of praise and renown in such a way as, “virtuous, learned, a retainer of the teachings, energetic,” etc., which is a benefit in this very life for those living the holy life. This is the meaning of “for that purpose.” However, some explain the meaning thus: “for the sake of the benefits of gain, honor, and fame” refers to the production of the benefit called gain, honor, and fame by one with evil desires, due to their valuing of gain and so on.

Na [M 2.0258] iti maṃ jano jānātūti evaṃ brahmacariyavāse sati “sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo”tiādinā [V 2.0235] maṃ loko jānātu sambhāvetūti attano santaguṇavasena sambhāvanatthampi na idaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vussatīti sambandho. Keci pana “pāpicchassa sato asantaguṇasambhāvanādhippāyena ‘iti evaṃguṇoti maṃ loko jānātū’ti na idaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”ti evamettha atthaṃ vadanti. Sabbatthāpi panettha purimo purimoyeva atthavikappo sundarataro.

Regarding 'Not for the purpose of “Let people know me thus”': The connection is that this holy life is not lived even for the purpose of being esteemed for one's own existing good qualities, with the thought, 'While I am living the holy life, let the world know and esteem me as virtuous, of good character,' and so on. Some, however, explain the meaning here thus: For one with evil desires, with the intention of being esteemed for non-existent good qualities, this holy life is not lived with the thought, 'Let the world know me as having such qualities.' In all these cases, however, the very first explanation of the meaning is more beautiful.

Atha khoti ettha athāti aññatthe nipāto, khoti avadhāraṇe. Tena kuhanādito aññadatthaṃyeva idaṃ, bhikkhave, brahmacariyaṃ vussatīti dasseti. Idāni taṃ payojanaṃ dassento “saṃvaratthaṃ pahānattha”nti āha. Tattha pañcavidho saṃvaro – pātimokkhasaṃvaro, satisaṃvaro, ñāṇasaṃvaro, khantisaṃvaro, vīriyasaṃvaroti. “Iti iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti samupeto”tiādinā (vibha. 511) nayena āgato ayaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvaro, sīlasaṃvarotipi vuccati. “Rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.295; saṃ. ni. 4.239; a. ni. 3.16) āgato ayaṃ satisaṃvaro.

Herein, ‘atha’ is a particle indicating another meaning, and ‘kho’ is for emphasis. Thus, it shows that this holy life, O bhikkhus, is lived for a purpose other than deception and the like. Now, to show its purpose, it is said: “For the purpose of restraint, for the purpose of abandoning.” Therein, restraint is fivefold: restraint by the monastic code, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy. This restraint by the monastic code, which comes by way of the passage beginning, “Thus, endowed and fully endowed with this restraint by the monastic code,” and so forth (Vibh. 511), is also called restraint of virtue. This restraint by mindfulness comes from the passage, “He guards the eye faculty, he undertakes restraint over the eye faculty” (MN 1.295; SN 4.239; AN 3.16).

“Yāni sotāni lokasmiṃ, sati tesaṃ nivāraṇaṃ;

Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi, paññāyete pidhīyare”ti. (su. ni. 1041; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddeso 4; netti. 4.11, 45) –

“Whatever currents there are in the world, mindfulness is their prevention. I declare the restraint of the currents; by wisdom they are closed off.”

Āgato ayaṃ ñāṇasaṃvaro. “Khamo hoti sītassa uṇhassā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.24; a. ni. 4.114; 6.58) nayena āgato ayaṃ khantisaṃvaro.

This restraint by knowledge is derived from the preceding. This restraint by patience comes by way of the passage beginning, “He is patient with cold and heat,” and so forth (MN 1.24; AN 4.114; 6.58).

“Uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 4.114; 6.58) nayena āgato ayaṃ vīriyasaṃvaro.

This restraint by energy comes by way of the passage beginning, “He does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire,” and so forth (MN 1.26; AN 4.114; 6.58).

Atthato pana pāṇātipātādīnaṃ pajahanavasena vattappaṭivattānaṃ pūraṇavasena ca pavattā cetanā ceva virati ca. Saṅkhepato sabbo kāyavacīsaṃyamo, vitthārato sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ avītikkamo sīlasaṃvaro. Sati eva satisaṃvaro, satippadhānā vā kusalā khandhā. Ñāṇameva ñāṇasaṃvaro. Adhivāsanavasena adoso, adosappadhānā vā [M 2.0259] tathāpavattā kusalā khandhā khantisaṃvaro, paññāti eke. Kāmavitakkādīnaṃ abhibhavanavasena pavattaṃ vīriyameva vīriyasaṃvaro. Tesu paṭhamo kāyaduccaritādīsu dussīlassa saṃvaraṇato saṃvaro, dutiyo muṭṭhassaccassa[V 2.0236], tatiyo aññāṇassa, catuttho akkhantiyā, pañcamo kosajjassa saṃvaraṇato pidahanato saṃvaroti veditabbo. Evametassa saṃvarassa atthāya saṃvaratthaṃ saṃvaranipphādanatthanti attho.

In terms of meaning, however, it is both the volition and the abstinence that proceed by way of abandoning the killing of living beings and so forth, and by way of fulfilling duties and observances. In brief, it is all restraint of body and speech; in detail, the non-transgression of the seven classes of offenses is restraint of virtue. Mindfulness itself is restraint by mindfulness, or it is the wholesome aggregates of which mindfulness is the chief. Knowledge itself is restraint by knowledge. Non-aversion by way of endurance, or the wholesome aggregates that proceed in such a way with non-aversion as their chief, is restraint by patience; some say it is wisdom. Energy itself, which proceeds by way of overcoming thoughts of sensual desire and the like, is restraint by energy. Among these, the first is restraint because it restrains an immoral person from bodily misconduct and so forth; the second, because it restrains forgetfulness; the third, ignorance; the fourth, impatience; the fifth is to be understood as restraint because it restrains and closes off laziness. Thus, ‘for the purpose of restraint’ means for the sake of this restraint, that is, for the purpose of accomplishing restraint.

Tīhi pahānehīti tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedasaṅkhātehi tīhi pahānehi. Pañcavidhappahānampi idha vattuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Pañcavidhañhi pahānaṃ tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedappaṭippassaddhinissaraṇavasena. Tattha yaṃ dīpālokeneva tamassa paṭipakkhabhāvato alobhādīhi lobhādikassa nāmarūpaparicchedādivipassanāñāṇehi tassa tassa anatthassa pahānaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – pariccāgena lobhādimalassa, sīlena pāṇātipātādidussīlyassa, saddhādīhi assaddhiyādikassa, nāmarūpavavatthānena sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā, paccayapariggahena ahetuvisamahetudiṭṭhīnaṃ, tasseva aparabhāgena kaṅkhāvitaraṇena kathaṃkathībhāvassa, kalāpasammasanena ahaṃmamāti gāhassa, maggāmaggavavatthānena amagge maggasaññāya, udayadassanena ucchedadiṭṭhiyā, vayadassanena sassatadiṭṭhiyā, bhayadassanena sabhaye abhayasaññāya, ādīnavadassanena assādasaññāya, nibbidānupassanena abhiratisaññāya, muccitukamyatāñāṇena amuccitukamyatāya, upekkhāñāṇena anupekkhāya, anulomena dhammaṭṭhitiyaṃ nibbāne ca paṭilomabhāvassa, gotrabhunā saṅkhāranimittaggāhassa pahānaṃ, etaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ nāma.

By three kinds of abandoning—namely, the three abandonings known as abandoning by substitution of opposites, by suppression, and by eradication. The fivefold abandoning is also appropriate to mention here. For the fivefold abandoning is by way of substitution of opposites, suppression, eradication, tranquillization, and escape. Herein, the abandoning of this or that harmful thing that occurs through insight-knowledges such as the determination of name-and-form, by means of non-greed and so forth, which are opposed to greed and so forth, just as darkness is opposed by the light of a lamp—for example: the abandoning of the defilement of greed and so forth by generosity; of the immorality of killing living beings and so forth by virtue; of lack of faith and so forth by faith and so forth; of identity view by the determination of name-and-form; of views of causelessness and distorted causes by the comprehension of conditions; of the state of doubt by the overcoming of doubt in the subsequent part of that same knowledge; of the grasping of 'I' and 'mine' by the comprehension of groups; of the perception of a path in what is not the path by the determination of path and not-path; of the annihilation view by the seeing of arising; of the eternalist view by the seeing of passing away; of the perception of safety in what is fearful by the seeing of fear; of the perception of gratification by the seeing of danger; of the perception of delight by the contemplation of disenchantment; of the unwillingness to be freed by the knowledge of the desire for deliverance; of non-equanimity by the knowledge of equanimity; of opposition to the stability of phenomena and to Nibbāna by conformity; and of the grasping of the signs of formations by change-of-lineage—this is called abandoning by substitution of opposites.

Yaṃ pana upacārappanābhedena samādhinā pavattibhāvanivāraṇato ghaṭappahāreneva udakapiṭṭhe sevālassa, tesaṃ tesaṃ nīvaraṇādidhammānaṃ pahānaṃ, etaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ nāma. Yaṃ catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ bhāvitattā taṃtaṃmaggavato attano santāne “diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāyā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 277; vibha. 628) nayena vuttassa samudayapakkhiyassa kilesagahaṇassa accantaṃ appavattibhāvena samucchindanaṃ, etaṃ samucchedappahānaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana phalakkhaṇe paṭippassaddhatthaṃ kilesānaṃ, etaṃ paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ nāma. Yaṃ sabbasaṅkhatanissaṭattā pahīnasabbasaṅkhataṃ nibbānaṃ, etaṃ nissaraṇappahānaṃ nāma[M 2.0260]. Tassa pañcavidhassapi tathā tathā rāgādikilesānaṃ paṭinissajjanaṭṭhena samatikkamanaṭṭhena vā pahānassa atthāya, pahānasādhanatthanti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Moreover, the abandoning of those various hindrances and other states by preventing their arising through concentration—of the kinds access and absorption—like the parting of moss on the surface of water by a blow with a pot, is called abandoning by suppression. The complete eradication of the grasping of defilements belonging to the side of origination—spoken of in the way of 'for the abandoning of wrong views' and so forth (Dhs. 277; Vibh. 628)—in the mental continuum of one who possesses this or that path, due to the development of the four noble paths, by means of their utter non-arising, is called abandoning by eradication. The tranquillizing of defilements at the moment of fruition is called abandoning by tranquillization. Nibbāna, which has escaped from all conditioned things and in which all conditioned things are abandoned, is called abandoning by escape. Thus, the meaning here should be understood as: for the purpose of abandoning, that is, for the accomplishment of abandoning, for the sake of abandoning defilements such as lust in this way or that by way of relinquishing or by way of transcending, even of these five kinds.

Tattha saṃvarena kilesānaṃ cittasantāne pavesanivāraṇaṃ pahānena ca pavesanivāraṇameva samugghāto cāti vadanti. Ubhayenapi pana yathārahaṃ ubhayaṃ sampajjatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sīlādidhammā eva hi saṃvaraṇato saṃvaraṃ, pajahanato pahānanti.

Therein, they say that by restraint there is the prevention of the entry of defilements into the mental continuum, and by abandoning there is both the prevention of entry and uprooting. But it should be understood that by both, both are accomplished as is fitting. For, it is states such as virtue that are restraint because they restrain, and abandoning because they abandon.

Anītihanti [V 2.0237] ītiyo vuccanti upaddavā diṭṭhadhammikā samparāyikā ca. Ītiyo hantīti ītihaṃ, anu ītihanti anītihaṃ, sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ maggabrahmacariyañca. Atha vā ītīhi anatthehi saddhiṃ hananti gacchanti pavattantīti ītihā, taṇhādiupakkilesā. Natthi ettha ītihāti anītihaṃ. Ītihā vā yathāvuttenatthena titthiyasamayā, tappaṭipakkhato idaṃ anītihaṃ. “Anitiha”ntipi pāṭho. Tassattho – “itihāya”nti dhammesu anekaṃsaggāhabhāvato vicikicchā itihaṃ nāma, sammāsambuddhappaveditattā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjantānaṃ nikkaṅkhabhāvasādhanato ca natthi ettha itihanti anitihaṃ, aparapattiyanti attho. Vuttañhetaṃ “paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī”ti, “atakkāvacaro”ti (dī. ni. 2.67; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7-8) ca. Gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ pana “anītiha”nti dīghaṃ katvā paṭhanti. Pacchimaṃ panettha atthavikappaṃ dassetuṃ “itihaparivajjita”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

Anītihaṃ. ‘Ītiyo’ are called calamities, both in this life and the next. That which destroys calamities (ītiyo hanti) is ‘ītihaṃ’. That which is without ‘ītihaṃ’ is ‘anītihaṃ’, referring to the holy life of the Dispensation and the holy life of the Path. Alternatively, ‘ītihā’ are the defilements such as craving that strike, go, or proceed together with calamities and harmful things. There is no ‘ītihā’ here, hence ‘anītihaṃ’. Or, ‘ītihā’ are the doctrines of heretical sects in the sense mentioned; this teaching is ‘anītihaṃ’ because it is opposed to them. The reading ‘anitihaṃ’ is also found. Its meaning is: doubt (vicikicchā), from the state of grasping at uncertainty regarding the teachings, is called ‘itihaṃ’. Because it is proclaimed by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, and because it establishes a state of freedom from doubt for those who practice as instructed, there is no ‘itihaṃ’ here, hence ‘anitihaṃ’, meaning it is not reliant on another. For it has been said: ‘To be understood individually by the wise’ and ‘beyond the scope of reasoning’ (DN 2.67; MN 1.281; 2.337; SN 1.172; Mahāva. 7-8). However, for the sake of metrical ease in the verse, they recite ‘anītihaṃ’ by lengthening the vowel. To explain this last alternative meaning, ‘devoid of tradition’ and so forth has been stated.

Nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ ogadhaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ pāraṃ gacchatīti nibbānogadhagāmī, vimuttirasattā ekanteneva nibbānasampāpakoti attho, taṃ nibbānogadhagāminaṃ brahmacariyaṃ. Nibbānogadhoti vā ariyamaggo vuccati tena vinā nibbānāvagāhaṇassa asambhavato tassa ca nibbānaṃ anālambitvā appavattanato, tañcetaṃ ekantasampādanena gacchatīti nibbānogadhagāmī. Atha vā nibbānogadhagāminanti nibbānassa antogāminaṃ. Maggabrahmacariyañhi nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karitvā tassa anto eva pavattatīti. Imameva ca atthavikappaṃ dassetuṃ “nibbānassa antogāmina”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Soti yo so samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbakilese bhañjitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, so bhagavā adesayi desesi[M 2.0261]. Mahantehīti mahāātumehi uḷārajjhāsayehi. Mahantaṃ nibbānaṃ, mahante vā sīlakkhandhādike esanti gavesantīti mahesino, buddhādayo ariyā. Tehi anuyāto paṭipanno.

The holy life that goes to the immersion, the support, the far shore called Nibbāna, is 'nibbānogadhagāmī'; the meaning is that it is the one and only means of attaining Nibbāna, due to its taste of liberation. That is the holy life that leads to Nibbāna. Or, the Noble Path is called 'nibbānogadha' because without it, immersion in Nibbāna is impossible, and because it does not proceed without taking Nibbāna as its object; and that path goes to the complete accomplishment of Nibbāna, hence 'nibbānogadhagāmī'. Alternatively, 'nibbānogadhagāmī' means 'entering into Nibbāna'. For the holy life of the Path takes Nibbāna as its object and proceeds only within it. And to explain this very alternative meaning, 'entering into Nibbāna' and so forth has been stated. He—that is, the Blessed One—having fulfilled the thirty perfections, having shattered all defilements, and having attained unsurpassed perfect Self-Enlightenment, taught and proclaimed. By the great ones—that is, by those of great self, of lofty aspiration. They are great sages (mahesino) because they seek and search for the great Nibbāna, or for the great aggregates such as the aggregate of virtue; these are the Noble Ones such as the Buddhas. Followed and practiced by them.

Yathā buddhena desitanti yathā abhiññeyyādibhāvena sammāsambuddhena mayā desitaṃ, evaṃ ye etaṃ maggabrahmacariyaṃ tadatthaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyañca paṭipajjanti. Te diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ anusāsantassa satthu mayhaṃ sāsanakārino ovādappaṭikarā sakalassa vaṭṭadukkhassa antaṃ pariyantaṃ appavattiṃ karissanti, dukkhassa vā antaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikarissantīti.

As taught by the Buddha—that is, as taught by me, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, by way of what is to be directly known and so forth—thus, those who practice this holy life of the Path, and for that purpose, the holy life of the Dispensation, being followers of my Dispensation and receptive to the advice of me, the Teacher, who instructs them appropriately regarding the ultimate goals in this life and the next, will make an end, a cessation, a non-occurrence, of all the suffering of the round of rebirths, or they will realize Nibbāna, the end of suffering.

Brahmacariyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Brahmacariya Sutta is concluded.

6. Kuhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Kuhasutta

26. Chaṭṭhe [V 2.0238] kuhakāti sāmantajappanādinā kuhanavatthunā kuhakā, asantaguṇasambhāvanicchāya kohaññaṃ katvā paresaṃ viddhaṃsakāti attho. Thaddhāti “kodhano hoti upāyāsabahulo, appampi vutto samāno abhisajjati kuppati byāpajjati patitthīyatī”ti (a. ni. 3.25, 27) evaṃ vuttena kodhena ca, “dubbaco hoti dovacassakaraṇehi dhammehi samannāgato akkhamo appadakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsani”nti (ma. ni. 1.181; pārā. 426). Evaṃ vuttena dovacassena ca, “jātimado, gottamado, lābhamado, ārogyamado, yobbanamado, jīvitamado”ti (vibha. 832) evaṃ vuttajātimadādibhedena mānena ca garukātabbesu garūsupi nipaccakāraṃ akatvā ayosalākaṃ gilitvā ṭhitā viya anonatā hutvā vicaraṇakā. Tenāha “kodhena cā”tiādi.

26. Sixth, 'deceptive' (kuhakā) means those who are deceptive by means of grounds for deception such as flattery and so on. The meaning is that they are destroyers of others by practicing deception with the desire to be regarded as possessing virtues they do not have. 'Stubborn' (thaddhā) means those who wander about unbending, as if they had swallowed an iron spike, even towards superiors who ought to be respected, without performing acts of humility, due to anger as stated thus: "prone to anger, with many causes for vexation, even when spoken to a little he abuses, is angry, hostile, resists" (AN 3.25, 27); and due to being difficult to speak to as stated thus: "difficult to speak to, possessing qualities causing difficulty to speak to, impatient, unskilful at grasping, resistant to instruction" (MN 1.181; Pārā. 426); and due to pride, distinguished by intoxication with birth and so on, as stated thus: "intoxicated with birth, intoxicated with lineage, intoxicated with gain, intoxicated with health, intoxicated with youth, intoxicated with life" (Vibh 832). Therefore, it is said, 'with anger' and so on.

Upalāpakāti micchājīvavasena kulasaṅgaṇhakā. Lapāti paccayatthaṃ payuttavācāvasena nippesikatāvasena lapakāti attho. Siṅganti siṅgāraṃ. Tañhi kusalassa vijjhanato suṭṭhu āsevitatāya sīse parikkhittaṃ sunibbattaṃ visāṇaṃ viya thirattā ca siṅgaṃ viyāti siṅgaṃ, nāgarikabhāvasaṅkhātassa kilesasiṅgassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Siṅgārabhāvo siṅgāratā, siṅgārakaraṇakaākāro vā. Cāturabhāvo cāturatā. Tathā [M 2.0262] cāturiyaṃ. Parikkhatabhāvo parikkhatatā, parikhaṇitvā ṭhapitasseva daḷhasiṅgārassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Evaṃ sabbehi vārehi kilesasiṅgāratāva kathitā.

'Upalāpakā' means those who gather families by way of wrong livelihood. 'Lapā' means 'cajoler' (lapaka) by way of speech employed for the sake of requisites, by way of tale-bearing. 'Siṅga' means charm (siṅgāra). For indeed, because it pierces the wholesome and is well cultivated, and because of its stability, like a well-formed horn fixed on the head, it is like a horn (siṅga), hence 'siṅga'; this is a name for the horn of defilements, which is known as urbanity. The state of being charming is siṅgāratā, or the manner of acting charmingly. The state of being clever is cāturatā. Likewise, cāturiya (cleverness). The state of being entrenched (parikkhatabhāva) is parikkhatatā; this is a name for a strong horn that is as if dug around and set firmly. The other is a synonym for that same thing. Thus, in all instances, only the charming quality of defilements has been spoken of.

Uggatanaḷāti naḷasadisaṃ tucchamānaṃ ukkhipitvā vicaraṇakā. Tenāha “tucchamānaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitā”ti. Yasmā te kuhanādiyogato na sammāpaṭipannā, tasmā “mama santakā na hontī”ti vuttaṃ. Apagatāti yadipi te mama sāsane pabbajitā, yathānusiṭṭhaṃ pana appaṭipajjanato apagatā eva imasmā dhammavinayā, ito te suvidūre ṭhitāti dasseti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'Uggatanaḷā' (those with an uplifted reed) means those who wander about raising up empty conceit, like a reed. Therefore, it is said, 'They stand having lifted up empty conceit.' Because they are not rightly practicing due to their engagement in deception and so on, it is said, 'They are not mine.' 'Gone away' (apagatā) means that although they have gone forth in my dispensation, because they do not practice as instructed, they have indeed gone away from this Dhamma-Vinaya. This shows that they stand very far away from it. For this has been said:

“Nabhañca dūre pathavī ca dūre,

Pāraṃ samuddassa tadāhu dūre;

Tato have dūrataraṃ vadanti,

Satañca dhammo asatañca rājā”ti. (jā. 2.21.414);

"The sky is far, the earth is far, The ocean's shore is said to be far; But still farther, they say, are these: The Dhamma of the good and the king of the unrighteous." (Ja 2.21.414);

Sabbattha [V 2.0239] patthaṭatāya vepullaṃ pāpuṇantīti sabbattha patthaṭabhāvena sīlādidhammakkhandhapāripūriyā vepullaṃ pāpuṇanti.

'By spreading everywhere, they attain greatness' means that through being spread everywhere, they attain greatness through the complete fulfillment of the aggregates of the Dhamma, such as virtue and so on.

Kuhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kuhasutta is concluded.

7. Santuṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Santuṭṭhi Sutta

27. Sattame niddosānīti avajjarahitāni āgamanasuddhito kāyamaṇḍanādikilesavatthubhāvābhāvato ca. Tattha sulabhatāya pariyesanadukkhassa abhāvo dassito, appatāya pariharaṇadukkhassapi abhāvo dassito, anavajjatāya agarahitabbatāya bhikkhusāruppabhāvo dassito hoti. Appatāya vā parittāsassa avatthutā, sulabhatāya gedhādīnaṃ avatthutā, anavajjatāya ādīnavadassananissaraṇapaññānaṃ atthitā dassitā hoti. Appatāya vā lābhena na somanassaṃ janayanti, alābhena na domanassaṃ janayanti, anavajjatāya vippaṭisāranimittaṃ aññāṇupekkhaṃ na janayanti avippaṭisāravatthubhāvato.

27. Seventh, 'free from faults' (niddosāni) means they are free from blame, both due to purity of acquisition and due to the absence of grounds for defilement such as bodily adornment and so on. Here, their easy availability shows the absence of the suffering of searching; their fewness shows the absence of the suffering of guarding; and their blamelessness shows their suitability for a monk, being beyond reproach. Or, their fewness indicates the non-existence of anxiety about them; their easy availability indicates the non-existence of greed and so on; and their blamelessness shows the existence of wisdom that discerns dangers and provides escape. Or, due to their fewness, they do not produce joy when obtained nor sorrow when not obtained; and due to their blamelessness, they do not produce ignorant indifference which is a cause for regret, because they are a basis for non-remorse.

Paṃsukūlanti [M 2.0263] saṅkārakūṭādīsu yattha katthaci paṃsūnaṃ upari ṭhitattā abbhuggataṭṭhena paṃsukūlaṃ viyāti paṃsukūlaṃ, paṃsu viya kucchitabhāvaṃ ulati gacchatīti paṃsukūlanti evaṃ laddhanāmaṃ rathikādīsu patitanantakāni uccinitvā katacīvaraṃ. Rukkhamūlanti vivekānurūpaṃ yaṃ kiñci rukkhasamīpaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci muttanti yaṃ kiñci gomuttaṃ. Keci panettha “gomuttaparibhāvitaharītakakhaṇḍaṃ pūtimutta”nti vadanti. “Pūtibhāvena āpaṇādito vissaṭṭhaṃ chaḍḍitaṃ apariggahitaṃ yaṃ kiñci bhesajjaṃ pūtimuttanti adhippeta”nti apare.

'Paṃsukūla' (rag-robe) is so called because it stands above dust in places like garbage heaps and so on, being prominent due to its elevated position, thus it is like a 'dust-heap' (paṃsukūla). It is also called 'paṃsukūla' because it goes to (ulati) a despicable state like dust, thus it has obtained this name. Such a robe is made by collecting discarded cloths fallen in streets and so on. 'The root of a tree' means any place near a tree suitable for seclusion. 'Whatever urine' refers to any cow urine. Some here say, 'A piece of harītaki treated with cow urine is 'putrid urine.'' Others explain, 'Whatever medicine discarded from a shop and so on due to its putrid condition, abandoned and unowned, is what is meant by 'putrid urine.''

Yato khoti paccatte nissakkavacanaṃ, yaṃ khoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tena tuṭṭho hotīti vuttakiriyaṃ parāmasati. Tuṭṭhoti santuṭṭho. Idamassāhanti yvāyaṃ catubbidhena yathāvuttena paccayena appena sulabhena santoso, idaṃ imassa bhikkhuno sīlasaṃvarādīsu aññataraṃ ekaṃ sāmaññaṅgaṃ samaṇabhāvakāraṇanti ahaṃ vadāmi. Santuṭṭhassa hi catupārisuddhisīlaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, samathavipassanā ca bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gacchanti. Atha vā sāmaññaṃ nāma ariyamaggo, tassa saṅkhepato dve aṅgā bāhiraṃ ajjhattikanti. Tattha bāhiraṃ sappurisūpanissayo saddhammassavanañca. Ajjhattikaṃ pana yonisomanasikāro dhammānudhammappaṭipatti ca. Tesu yasmā yathārahaṃ dhammānudhammappaṭipattibhūtā tassa mūlabhūtā cete dhammā, yadidaṃ appicchatā santuṭṭhitā pavivittatā asaṃsaṭṭhatā [V 2.0240] āraddhavīriyatāti evamādayo, tasmā vuttaṃ “idamassāhaṃ aññataraṃ sāmaññaṅganti vadāmī”ti.

'Yato kho' is a particle specifying an individual, meaning 'whatever is said.' It refers to the action stated, 'He is pleased.' 'Pleased' (tuṭṭho) means content (santuṭṭho). 'This is his, I say' (idamassāhaṃ) means: 'Whatever contentment arises for him from the four kinds of requisites, as stated, which are few and easily obtained—this, I say, is one aspect of the ascetic life of this monk, a cause for the state of being an ascetic, among virtue-restraint and so on.' For one who is content, the virtue of fourfold purity is fulfilled, and both serenity and insight meditation reach full development. Alternatively, the ascetic life (sāmañña) is the Noble Path. Briefly, it has two aspects: external and internal. The external includes reliance on good people and listening to the true Dhamma. The internal consists of wise attention and practice in accordance with the Dhamma. Among these, because these qualities—namely, fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, non-entanglement, energetic effort, and so on—are practice in accordance with the Dhamma as is proper, and are fundamental to it, therefore it is said, 'This, I say, is one of the aspects of the ascetic life.'

Senāsanamārabbhāti vihārādiṃ mañcapīṭhādiñca senāsanaṃ nissāya. Cīvaraṃ pānabhojananti nivāsanādicīvaraṃ ambapānakādipānaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyādibhuñjitabbavatthuñca ārabbhāti sambandho. Vighātoti vighātabhāvo, cittassa dukkhaṃ na hotīti yojanā. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – “amukasmiṃ nāma āvāse paccayā sulabhā”ti labhitabbaṭṭhānagamanena vā “mayhaṃ pāpuṇāti, na tuyha”nti vivādāpajjanena vā navakammakaraṇādivasena vā senāsanādīni pariyesantānaṃ asantuṭṭhānaṃ icchitālābhādinā yo vighāto cittassa hoti, so tattha santuṭṭhassa na hoti. Disā nappaṭihaññatīti santuṭṭhiyā cātuddisabhāvena disā na paṭihanati. Vuttañhetaṃ “cātuddiso appaṭigho ca hoti, santussamāno itarītarenā”ti (su. ni. 42).

'Concerning the lodging' (senāsanamārabbha) means relying on lodging such as a monastery, and on beds, chairs, and so on. The connection is with 'concerning' (ārabbha) 'robes, drinks, and food,' which refers to robes such as the under-robe, drinks such as mango juice, and foods to be consumed, such as hard and soft foods. 'Disturbance' (vighāto) means the state of being disturbed; the application is that suffering of the mind does not occur. Here, the brief meaning is this: For those who are discontented and seeking lodgings and so on, whether by going to a place thinking, 'In such-and-such a dwelling, requisites are easily obtained,' or by entering into disputes, saying, 'It is for me, not for you,' or on account of new construction work—whatever disturbance of mind arises from not obtaining what they desire, that disturbance does not arise for one who is content. 'One is not obstructed in any direction' (disā nappaṭihaññati) means that due to contentment, one is unobstructed in the four directions. For it has been said: 'One is open in all directions, unhindered, and content with whatever comes.' (Snp 1.42)

Samaṇadhammassa [M 2.0264] anulomāti samaṇadhammassa samathavipassanābhāvanāya, ariyamaggasseva vā anucchavikā appicchatādayo. Tuṭṭhacittassa bhikkhunoti tuṭṭhacittena bhikkhunā. Adhiggahitā hontīti paṭipakkhadhamme abhibhavitvā gahitā honti. Antogatāti abbhantaragatā. Na paribāhirāti na bāhirā katā.

'In accordance with the ascetic's practice' (samaṇadhammassa anulomā) means qualities such as having few wants, which are suitable for the ascetic's practice—that is, for the development of serenity and insight, or for the Noble Path itself. 'For a monk with a contented mind' (tuṭṭhacittassa bhikkhuno) means 'by a monk with a contented mind.' 'They are mastered' (adhiggahitā honti) means they are grasped, having overcome opposing states. 'Internalized' (antogatā) means they have gone within. 'Not externalized' (na paribāhirā) means they are not made external.

Santuṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Santuṭṭhi Sutta is completed.

8. Ariyavaṃsasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Discourse on the Noble Lineages

28. Aṭṭhame vaṃsa-saddo “piṭṭhivaṃsaṃ atikkamitvā nisīdatī”tiādīsu dvinnaṃ gopānasīnaṃ sandhānaṭṭhāne ṭhapetabbadaṇḍake āgato.

28. In the eighth [sutta], the word 'vaṃsa' appears. It is found [meaning] a rod to be placed at the joint of two rafters; and in such phrases as, 'having passed beyond the backbone, he sits down'.

“Vaṃso visālo ca yathā visatto,

Puttesu dāresu ca yā apekkhā;

Vaṃsakkaḷīrova asajjamāno,

Eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti. –

Just as a spreading bamboo is entangled, so is the longing for children and spouses. Like a bamboo shoot, not clinging, let one wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.

Ādīsu kaṭṭhake. “Bherisaddo mudiṅgasaddo vaṃsatālasaddo”tiādīsu tūriyavisese, veṇūtipi vuccati[V 2.0241]. “Bhinnena piṭṭhivaṃsena mato hatthī”tiādīsu hatthiādīnaṃ piṭṭhivemajjhe padese. “Kulavaṃsaṃ ṭhapessāmī”tiādīsu kulanvaye. “Vaṃsānurakkhako paveṇīpālako”tiādīsu guṇānupubbiyaṃ guṇānaṃ pabandhappavattiyaṃ. Idha pana catupaccayasantosabhāvanārāmatāsaṅkhātaguṇānaṃ pabandhe daṭṭhabbo. Tassa pana vaṃsassa kulanvayaṃ guṇanvayañca nidassanavasena dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha khattiyavaṃsoti khattiyakulavaṃso. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Samaṇavaṃso pana samaṇatanti samaṇapaveṇī. Mūlagandhādīnanti ādi-saddena yathā sāragandhādīnaṃ saṅgaho, evamettha gorasādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo, dutiyena pana ādi-sadena kāsikavatthasappimaṇḍādīnaṃ.

In [the verse] beginning ['Vaṃso...'], it means wood. In phrases such as 'the sound of the drum, the sound of the mudiṅga, the sound of the flute,' it refers to a particular musical instrument; it is also called 'veṇū'. In phrases such as 'an elephant killed by a broken backbone,' it refers to the middle part of the backbone of elephants and such. In phrases such as 'I will establish the family lineage,' it refers to the family line. In phrases such as 'a protector of the lineage, a guardian of the tradition,' it refers to the succession of qualities, the continuous progression of qualities. Here, however, it should be understood as the continuous progression of qualities designated as contentment with the four requisites and delight in cultivation. To illustrate both the family line and the succession of qualities of that lineage by way of example, the phrase 'just as' and so on is used. Therein, 'khattiyavaṃso' means the family line of the khattiya. This is the method for the remaining terms as well. The 'samaṇavaṃso,' however, is the ascetic's lineage, the ascetic's tradition. By way of analogy, just as in the phrase 'roots, scents, and so on,' the word 'and so on' includes things like heartwood-scent, so too here the inclusion of things like milk-products should be understood; and by a second 'and so on,' things like Kāsi cloth, the cream of ghee, and so on.

Ariya-saddo amilakkhesupi manussesu pavattati, yesaṃ nivasanaṭṭhānaṃ ariyaṃ āyatananti vuccati. Yathāha “yāvatā, ānanda, ariyaṃ āyatana”nti [M 2.0265] (dī. ni. 2.152; udā. 76). Lokiyasādhujanesupi “ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhakāyasamācārā, tesaṃ ahaṃ aññataro”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.35). Idha pana ye “ārakā kilesehī”tiādinā laddhanibbacanā paṭividdhaariyasaccā, te eva adhippetāti dassetuṃ “ke pana te ariyā”ti pucchaṃ katvā “ariyā vuccantī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ye mahāpaṇidhānakappato paṭṭhāya yāvāyaṃ kappo, etthantare uppannā sammāsambuddhā. Te tāva sarūpato dassetvā tadaññepi sammāsambuddhe paccekabuddhe buddhasāvake ca saṅgahetvā anavasesato ariye dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yāva sāsanaṃ antaradhāyati, tāva satthā dharati eva nāmāti imameva bhagavantaṃ. Ye cetarahi buddhasāvakā, te ca sandhāya paccuppannaggahaṇaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle te te paccuppannāti ce, atītānāgataggahaṇaṃ na kattabbaṃ siyā.

The term 'ariya' is used even for non-barbarian people, whose dwelling place is called a 'noble sphere.' As it is said: 'So far, Ānanda, as the noble sphere extends' (Dī. Ni. 2.152; Udā. 76). It is also used for worldly virtuous people, as in: 'For those of you who are noble, of pure bodily conduct, I am one among them' (Ma. Ni. 1.35), and so forth. Here, however, to show that those intended are precisely the ones who have obtained the etymological definition 'far from defilements' and so on, and who have penetrated the noble truths, the question is asked, 'But who are those noble ones?' and the answer is given, 'They are called noble,' and so forth. Among them, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas who have arisen in the interval from the eon of the great resolution until this very eon are first shown in their own nature. Then, to include all the noble ones without omission—other Fully Enlightened Buddhas, Private Buddhas, and disciples of the Buddha—the phrase 'and moreover' is used. Herein, 'as long as the Dispensation does not disappear, the Teacher still endures by name' refers precisely to this Blessed One. The reference to 'the present' is in regard to those who are at present disciples of the Buddha. If in each and every period, they were considered 'the present ones,' then reference to past and future would not be made.

Idāni yathā bhagavā “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāsessāmi, yadidaṃ cha chakkānī”ti chachakkadesanāya (ma. ni. 3.420) aṭṭhahi padehi vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi. Evaṃ mahāariyavaṃsadesanāya ariyānaṃ vaṃsaṃ “cattārome, bhikkhave, ariyavaṃsā aggaññā rattaññā vaṃsaññā porāṇā, asaṃkiṇṇā asaṃkiṇṇapubbā na saṃkīyanti na saṃkīyissanti, appaṭikuṭṭhā samaṇehi brāhmaṇehi viññūhī”ti yehi navahi padehi vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi, tāni tāva ānetvā thomanāvaseneva vaṇṇento “te kho panete”tiādimāha. Aggāti jānitabbā sabbavaṃsehi seṭṭhabhāvato seṭṭhabhāvasādhanato ca.

Now, just as the Blessed One, in the discourse on the six sets of six (MN 148), spoke its praise with eight terms, saying: 'Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing; I will proclaim the holy life that is utterly complete and pure, that is, the six sets of six.' Similarly, in the great discourse on the noble lineages, he spoke praise of the lineage of the noble ones with these nine terms: 'Monks, these four noble lineages are foremost, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, unadulterated in the past, not being adulterated now, nor will they be adulterated in the future; they are unreproached by wise ascetics and brahmins.' Having first brought these terms forward, explaining them by way of praise, he said, 'And indeed, these...' and so on. 'Foremost' (aggaññā) should be understood as such because it is the best of all lineages and because it establishes that state of being the best.

Rattaññā cirarattāti jānitabbā rattaññūhi buddhādīhi tehi ca tathā anuṭṭhitattā. Vaṃsāti jānitabbāti [V 2.0242] buddhādīnaṃ ariyānaṃ vaṃsāti jānitabbā. Porāṇāti purātanā. Na adhunappattikāti na adhunātanā. Avikiṇṇāti na khittā na chaḍḍitā. Tenāha “anapanītā”ti. Na apanītapubbāti na chaḍḍitapubbā, tissannampi sikkhānaṃ paripūraṇūpāyabhāvato na pariccattapubbā. Tato eva idānipi na apanīyanti, anāgatepi na apanīyissantiyeva. Dhammasabhāvassa vijānanena viññū. Samitapāpā samaṇā ceva [M 2.0266] bāhitapāpā brāhmaṇā ca. Tehi appaṭikuṭṭhā appaṭikkhittā. Ye hi na paṭikkositabbā, te aninditabbā. Agarahitabbā apariccajitabbatāya appaṭikkhipitabbā hontīti.

'Long-known' (rattaññā) should be understood as 'long-enduring' (cirarattā), because it has been practiced accordingly by the long-known ones, such as the Buddhas. 'Lineage' (vaṃsā) should be understood as the lineage of the noble ones, such as the Buddhas. 'Ancient' (porāṇā) means old, not newly attained, not modern. 'Unmixed' (avikiṇṇā) means not scattered, not discarded. Therefore, it is said, 'not removed' (anapanītā). 'Never removed' (na apanītapubbā) means never discarded before, never abandoned before, because it is the means to fully perfect the three trainings. For that very reason, even now it is not removed, and in the future, it will never be removed. 'The wise' (viññū) are those who understand the nature of the Dhamma. Those who have pacified evil are ascetics (samaṇā), and those who have warded off evil are brahmins (brāhmaṇā). By them, it is unreviled (appaṭikuṭṭhā), unrejected (appaṭikkhittā). Indeed, those who are not to be reviled are not to be blamed. They are not to be reproached; because they are not to be abandoned, they are not to be rejected.

Santuṭṭhoti ettha yathādhippetasantosameva dassentena paccayasantosavasena santuṭṭhoti vuttaṃ, jhānavipassanādivasenapi idha bhikkhuno santuṭṭhatā hotīti. Itarītarenāti itarena itarena. Itarasaddo aniyamavacano dvikkhattuṃ vuccamāno yaṃ-kiñcisaddehi samānattho hotīti vuttaṃ “yena kenacī”ti. Svāyaṃ aniyamavācitāya eva yathā thūlādīnaṃ aññataravacano, evaṃ yathāladdhādīnampi aññataravacanoti. Tattha dutiyapakkhasseva idha icchitabhāvaṃ dassento “atha kho”tiādimāha. Nanu ca yathāladdhādayopi thūlādayo eva? Saccametaṃ, tathāpi atthi viseso. Yo hi yathāladdhesu thūlādīsu santoso, so yathālābhasantosova, na itaro. Na hi so paccayamattasannissayo icchito, atha kho attano kāyabalasāruppabhāvasannissayopi. Thūladukādayo tayopi cīvare labbhanti, majjhimo catupaccayasādhāraṇo, pacchimo pana cīvare senāsane ca labbhatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ime tayo santoseti idaṃ sabbasaṅgāhikanayena vuttaṃ. Ye hi parato gilānapaccayaṃ piṇḍapāte eva pakkhipitvā cīvare vīsati, piṇḍapāte pannarasa, senāsane pannarasāti samapaññāsa santosā vuccanti, te sabbepi yathārahaṃ imesu eva tīsu santosesu saṅgahaṃ samosaraṇaṃ gacchantīti.

'Contentment' (santuṭṭhi) here is said to be contentment based on requisites, showing precisely the contentment intended, for a bhikkhu's contentment here also occurs by way of jhāna, insight, and so on. 'By one or the other' (itarītarena) means by one thing and by another. The word 'itara' is an indefinite term; when spoken twice, it has the same meaning as words like 'whatever,' as in 'by whatever.' This, by its very indefiniteness, just as it refers to any one of 'coarse' and so on, so too it refers to any one of 'what is obtained' and so on. Here, showing the desired nature of the second alternative, he said, 'but rather,' and so on. Now, are not 'what is obtained' and so on the same as 'coarse' and so on? Indeed, it is so, yet there is a distinction. For the contentment with 'coarse' and so on among 'what is obtained' is contentment with what is gained, not the other. For it is not mere reliance on requisites that is desired, but rather reliance on what is suitable to one's bodily strength and constitution. The three—coarse, etc.—are obtainable in robes; the middle one is common to all four requisites, while the last is obtainable in robes and lodgings—this should be understood. These three kinds of contentment are stated here by way of an all-inclusive method. For the fifty contentments that are spoken of—twenty regarding robes, fifteen regarding almsfood, and fifteen regarding lodgings—all of them, as is appropriate, are included within these very three kinds of contentment.

Cīvaraṃ jānitabbanti “idaṃ nāma cīvaraṃ kappiya”nti jātito cīvaraṃ jānitabbaṃ. Cīvarakhettanti cīvarassa uppattikkhettaṃ. Paṃsukūlanti paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ, paṃsukūlalakkhaṇappattaṃ cīvaraṃ jānitabbanti attho. Cīvarasantosoti cīvare labbhamāno sabbo santoso jānitabbo. Cīvarappaṭisaṃyuttāni dhutaṅgāni jānitabbāni, yāni gopento cīvarasantosena sammadeva santuṭṭho hotīti. Khomakappāsikakoseyyakambalasāṇabhaṅgāni khomādīni. Tattha khomaṃ nāma khomasuttehi vāyitaṃ khomapaṭṭacīvaraṃ. Tathā sesānipi. Sāṇanti sāṇavākasuttehi katacīvaraṃ. Bhaṅganti pana khomasuttādīni sabbāni, ekaccāni vā missetvā katacīvaraṃ. Bhaṅgampi vākamayamevāti keci. Chāti gaṇanaparicchedo. Yadi evaṃ ito aññā [M 2.0267] vatthajāti natthīti? No natthi. Sā pana [V 2.0243] etesaṃ anulomāti dassetuṃ “dukūlādīnī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddena pattuṇṇaṃ, somārapaṭṭaṃ, cīnapaṭṭaṃ, iddhijaṃ, devadinnanti tesaṃ saṅgaho. Tattha dukūlaṃ sāṇassa anulomaṃ vākamayattā. Pattuṇṇadese sañjātavatthaṃ pattuṇṇaṃ. “Koseyyaviseso”ti hi abhidhānakose vuttaṃ. Somāradese cīnadese ca jātavatthāni somāracīnapaṭṭāni. Pattuṇṇādīni tīṇi koseyyassa anulomāni pāṇakehi katasuttamayattā. Iddhijaṃ ehibhikkhūnaṃ puññiddhiyā nibbattacīvaraṃ, taṃ khomādīnaṃ aññataraṃ hotīti tesaṃ eva anulomaṃ. Devatāhi dinnacīvaraṃ devadinnaṃ, taṃ kapparukkhe nibbattaṃ jāliniyā devakaññāya anuruddhattherassa dinnavatthasadisaṃ, tampi khomādīnaṃyeva anulomaṃ hoti tesu aññatarabhāvato.

'The robe should be known' (cīvaraṃ jānitabbaṃ) means the robe should be known by its kind, as in 'this kind of robe is allowable.' 'Robe-field' (cīvarakhetta) means the field of the robe's arising. 'Rag-robe' (paṃsukūla) means a rag-robe, meaning a robe that has attained the characteristics of a rag-robe should be known. 'Contentment with robes' (cīvarasantosa) means all contentment obtained regarding robes should be known. The ascetic practices associated with robes should be known—those which, when maintained, lead to proper contentment with robes. Linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and mixed fabrics—these are khoma and so on. Among them, linen (khoma) refers to a linen-cloth robe woven from linen threads. The same applies to the rest. Hemp (sāṇa) means a robe made from sāṇa-fiber threads. Mixed fabric (bhaṅga), however, refers to a robe made by mixing all or some of the threads like linen, etc. Some say mixed fabric is made entirely of bark fiber. 'Six' (cha) is a numerical limitation. If so, are there no other types of fabric besides these? It is not that there are none. But to indicate that other types are in line with these, it is said: "Dukūla, etc." The term "etc." includes pattuṇṇa, somāra-cloth, Chinese cloth, miraculously-produced cloth, and deva-given cloth. Among these, dukūla is akin to hemp because it is made of bark fiber. Pattuṇṇa is cloth produced in the pattuṇṇa region. Indeed, it is said in the dictionary that it is 'a special type of silk.' Somāra-cloth and Chinese cloth are fabrics produced in the Somāra and Chinese regions. Pattuṇṇa and the other two are akin to silk because they are made from threads spun by living beings. Miraculously-produced cloth (iddhija) is a robe produced through the merit-power of 'Come, Bhikkhu!' monks; it is one of the types like linen, etc., thus akin to them. Deva-given cloth (devadinna) is a robe given by deities. It is produced on the wishing-tree, like the cloth given by the nymph Jālinī to the Elder Anuruddha. It, too, is akin to linen, etc., being one of them.

Imānīti antogadhāvadhāraṇavacanaṃ, imāni evāti attho. Buddhādīnaṃ paribhogayoggatāya kappiyacīvarāni. Idāni avadhāraṇena nivattitāni ekadesena dassetuṃ “kusacīra”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha kusatiṇehi aññehi vā tādisehi tiṇehi katacīvaraṃ kusacīraṃ. Akkavākādīhi vākehi katacīvaraṃ vākacīraṃ. Catukkoṇehi tikoṇehi vā phalakehi katacīvaraṃ phalakacīraṃ. Manussānaṃ kesehi katakambalaṃ kesakambalaṃ. Cāmarivālaassavālādīhi kataṃ vālakambalaṃ. Makacitantūhi vāyito potthako. Cammanti migacammādi yaṃ kiñci cammaṃ. Ulūkapakkhehi ganthitvā katacīvaraṃ ulūkapakkhaṃ. Bhujapattatacādimayaṃ rukkhadussaṃ. Tirīṭakanti attho. Sukhumatarāhi latāhi latāvākehi vā vāyitaṃ latādussaṃ. Erakavākehi kataṃ erakadussaṃ. Tathā kadalidussaṃ. Sukhumehi veḷuvilīvehi kataṃ veḷudussaṃ. Ādi-saddena vakkalādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Akappiyacīvarāni titthiyaddhajabhāvato.

The word 'these' (imāni) is a term of inclusion and specification; the meaning is 'these very things.' Robes suitable for the use of the Buddha and others are permissible robes. Now, to show a portion of those excluded by this specification, terms like 'grass-cloth' and so on are mentioned. Here, a robe made from kusa grass or other similar grasses is a 'grass-cloth' (kusacīra). A robe made from akka bark or other barks is a 'bark-cloth' (vākacīra). A robe made from square or triangular wooden boards is a 'board-cloth' (phalakacīra). A blanket made from human hair is a 'hair-blanket' (kesakambala). A blanket made from the tails of cāmarī yaks, horse tails, or similar animal tails is a 'tail-blanket' (vālakambala). A 'spider-silk cloth' (potthako) is woven from spider threads. 'Hide' (camma) refers to any hide, such as deer hide. A robe made by intertwining owl feathers is an 'owl-feather cloth' (ulūkapakkha). A 'tree-cloth' (rukkhadussa) is made from bhujapatta bark or other tree bark; the meaning is 'tirīṭaka.' A 'vine-cloth' (latādussa) is woven from very fine vines or vine-bark. An 'eraka-cloth' (erakadussa) is made from eraka fibers. Similarly, a 'plantain-cloth' (kadalidussa). A 'bamboo-cloth' (veḷudussa) is made from fine bamboo strips. The word 'etcetera' (ādi-saddena) includes vakkala and other similar materials. These are impermissible robes because they are the sectarian banners of non-Buddhist ascetics.

Aṭṭhannaṃ mātikānaṃ vasenāti “sīmāya deti, katikāya detī”tiādinā (mahāva. 379) āgatānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ cīvaruppattimātikānaṃ vasena. Cīvarānaṃ paṭilābhakkhettadassanatthañhi bhagavatā “aṭṭhimā, bhikkhave, mātikā”tiādinā mātikā ṭhapitā. Mātikāti hi mātaro cīvaruppattijanikāti.

By means of the eight matrices (aṭṭhannaṃ mātikānaṃ vasena) means by means of the eight matrices of robe-origination, such as 'He gives within the boundary, he gives by agreement,' as stated in the Mahāvagga (379). Indeed, for the purpose of showing the fields for obtaining robes, the Blessed One established the matrices, saying, 'Monks, there are these eight matrices,' and so on. For 'matrices' (mātikā) are indeed the mothers, the generators of robe-origination.

Sosānikanti [M 2.0268] susāne patitaṃ. Pāpaṇikanti āpaṇadvāre patitaṃ. Rathiyanti puññatthikehi vātapānantarena rathikāya chaḍḍitacoḷakaṃ. Saṅkārakūṭakanti saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍitacoḷakaṃ. Sinānanti nahānacoḷakaṃ, yaṃ bhūtavejjehi sasīsaṃ nahāyitvā kālakaṇṇicoḷanti chaḍḍetvā gacchanti. Titthanti titthacoḷaṃ, sinānatitthe chaḍḍitapilotikā. Aggidaḍḍhanti agginā daḍḍhappadesaṃ. Tañhi manussā chaḍḍenti. Gokhāyitādīni pākaṭāneva. Tānipi hi manussā chaḍḍenti. Dhajaṃ ussāpetvāti [V 2.0244] nāvaṃ ārohantehi vā yuddhaṃ pavisantehi vā dhajayaṭṭhiṃ ussāpetvā, tattha baddhaṃ vātena ānītaṃ tehi chaḍḍitanti adhippāyo.

'Corpse-cloth' (sosānika) is that which has fallen in a cemetery. 'Shop-cloth' (pāpaṇika) is that which has fallen at a shop's entrance. 'Street-cloth' (rathiye) is a discarded rag thrown into the street through a window by people desiring merit. 'Refuse-heap-cloth' (saṅkārakūṭaka) is a discarded rag at a garbage dump. 'Bathing-cloth' (sināna) is a bathing garment which spirit-doctors discard as a 'bad-luck cloth' after bathing someone's head and then depart. 'Ford-cloth' (tittha) is a ford-rag, a discarded piece of cloth at a bathing ford. 'Fire-burnt-cloth' (aggidaḍḍha) is a portion burned by fire, which people indeed discard. The 'cow-chewed' (gokhāyita) and similar cloths are obvious; these too people indeed discard. 'Having hoisted a flag' (dhajaṃ ussāpetvā) means that when people are boarding a ship or entering battle, they hoist a flagpole, and the cloth tied there, having been carried away by the wind, is considered discarded by them—this is the intended meaning.

Sādakabhikkhunāti gahapaticīvarassa sādiyanabhikkhunā. Ekamāsamattanti cīvaramāsasaññitaṃ ekamāsamattaṃ vitakketuṃ vaṭṭati, na tato paranti adhippāyo. Sabbassapi hi taṇhāniggahatthā sāsane paṭipattīti. Paṃsukūliko addhamāseneva karoti aparappaṭibaddhattā paṭilābhassa, itarassa pana parappaṭibaddhattā māsamattaṃ anuññātaṃ. Idaṃ māsaḍḍhamāsamattaṃ…pe… vitakkasantoso vitakkentassa parimitakālikattā. Mahātheraṃ tattha attano sahāyaṃ icchantopi garugāravena “gāmadvāraṃ, bhante, gamissāmi”iccevāha. Theropi tassa ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā “ahampāvuso, gamissāmī”ti āha. “Imassa bhikkhuno vitakkassa avasaro mā hotū”ti pañhaṃ pucchamāno gāmaṃ pāvisi. Uccārapalibuddhoti uccārena pīḷito. Tadā bhagavato dukkarakiriyānussaraṇamukhena tathāgate uppannassa pītisomanassavegassa balavabhāvena kilesānaṃ vikkhambhitattā tasmiṃyeva…pe… tīṇi phalāni patto.

'A monk who accepts' (sādakabhikkhunā) means a monk who approves of a householder's robe. 'One month at most' (ekamāsamattaṃ) means it is permissible to reflect on it for a period of one month, designated as a 'robe-month,' but not beyond that—this is the meaning. For indeed, all practice in the Dispensation is for the sake of restraining craving. A rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūliko) may do so in just half a month because the acquisition is not dependent on others; but for others, since it depends on others, a month at most is permitted. This period of a month or half a month... is contentment with reflection, due to its limited duration for one who reflects. Even though he wished for the Great Elder to be his companion there, out of deep reverence he said only, 'Venerable sir, I will go to the village gate.' The Elder, knowing his inclination, replied, 'Friend, I too will go.' Thinking, 'May there be no opportunity for this monk's reflection,' he entered the village asking a question. 'Obstructed by the need to relieve himself' (uccārapalibuddho) means oppressed by the need to defecate. Then, through recalling the Blessed One's difficult deeds, the surge of joy and gladness that arose in him toward the Tathāgata was so powerful that his defilements were suppressed. Right there... he attained the three fruits.

Kattha labhissāmīti cintanāpi lābhāsāpubbikāti tathā “acintetvā”ti vuttaṃ. “Sundaraṃ labhissāmi, manāpaṃ labhissāmī”tievamādicintanāya kā nāma kathā, kathaṃ pana gantabbanti āha “kammaṭṭhānasīseneva gamana”nti. Tena cīvaraṃ paṭicca kiñcipi na cintetabbamevāti dasseti. Apesalo appatirūpāyapi pariyesanāya paccayo bhaveyyāti “pesalaṃ bhikkhuṃ gahetvā”ti vuttaṃ. Āhariyamānanti susānādīsu patitaṃ vatthaṃ “ime bhikkhū paṃsukūlapariyesanaṃ carantī”ti ñatvā kenaci purisena tato ānīyamānaṃ. Evaṃ laddhaṃ gaṇhantassapīti evaṃ paṭilābhasantosaṃ akopetvā laddhaṃ gaṇhantassapi. Attano pahonakamattenevāti [M 2.0269] yathāladdhānaṃ paṃsukūlānaṃ ekapaṭṭadupaṭṭānaṃ atthāya attano pahonakappamāṇeneva. Avadhāraṇena upari paccāsaṃ nivatteti. Gāme bhikkhāya āhiṇḍantena sapadānacārinā viya dvārappaṭipāṭiyā caraṇaṃ loluppavivajjanaṃ nāma loluppassa dūrasamussāritattā.

Even the thought 'Where shall I find it?' (kattha labhissāmi) is a precursor to the desire for gain; therefore, it is said, 'without thinking' (acintetvā). What need is there to even speak of such thoughts as 'I shall find something beautiful, I shall find something delightful'? Instead, how should one proceed? It is said, 'one should go simply with the meditation topic in mind' (kammaṭṭhānasīseneva gamana). Thus, it is shown that one should not think of anything at all regarding the robe. An unvirtuous monk might become a cause for an unsuitable search; hence, it is said, 'taking a virtuous monk along' (pesalaṃ bhikkhuṃ gahetvā). 'Being brought' (āhariyamānaṃ) refers to a cloth fallen in a charnel ground or such, which, knowing that 'these monks are searching for discarded rags,' is brought by someone from there. 'Even when receiving what is obtained in this way' (evaṃ laddhaṃ gaṇhantassapi) means even when receiving what is obtained without disturbing contentment with the gain. 'Only as much as one can manage' (attano pahonakamatteneva) means only to the extent sufficient for oneself, for the purpose of making a single-layer or double-layer robe from the discarded rags that have been obtained. By this determination, one prevents anticipation beyond that. While wandering for alms in the village, walking in regular order from door to door, like one practicing a continuous alms-round (sapadānacārinā), is called 'avoiding greed' (loluppavivajjanaṃ) because greed is cast far away.

Yāpetunti attabhāvaṃ pavattetuṃ. Dhovanupagenāti dhovanayoggena. Paṇṇānīti ambajambādipaṇṇāni. Akopetvāti santosaṃ akopetvā. Pahonakanīhārenevāti antaravāsakādīsu yaṃ kātukāmo, tassa pahonakaniyāmeneva yathāladdhaṃ thūlasukhumādiṃ gahetvā karaṇaṃ. Timaṇḍalappaṭicchādanamattassevāti nivāsanaṃ ce nābhimaṇḍalaṃ, jāṇumaṇḍalaṃ, itarañce galavāṭamaṇḍalaṃ[V 2.0245], jāṇumaṇḍalanti timaṇḍalappaṭicchādanamattasseva karaṇaṃ. Taṃ pana atthato tiṇṇaṃ cīvarānaṃ heṭṭhimantena vuttaparimāṇaṃyeva hoti. Avicāretvā na vicāretvā.

'To maintain life' (yāpetuṃ) means to sustain one's existence. 'With things suitable for washing' (dhovanupagena) means with means suitable for washing. 'Leaves' (paṇṇāni) refers to leaves such as mango and rose apple. 'Without destroying' (akopetvā) means without disturbing contentment. 'Just with sufficient resources' (pahonakanīhāreneva) means that whatever one wishes to make among the undergarments and so on, should be done just with the appropriate standard of resources, taking whatever coarse or fine material is obtained. 'Merely covering the three circles' (timaṇḍalappaṭicchādanamattasseva) means that if the lower robe (nivāsana) covers the navel circle and the knee circle, and the other (upper robe) covers the neck circle and the knee circle, then it should be made merely covering these three circles. But that, in essence, is just the stated measure which is the lowest limit for the three robes. 'Without examining' (avicāretvā) means not examining.

Kusibandhanakāleti maṇḍalāni yojetvā sibbanakāle. Satta vāreti satta sibbanavāre. Kappabinduapadesena kassaci vikārassa akaraṇaṃ kappasantoso.

'At the time of sewing the seams' (kusibandhanakāle) means at the time of joining and sewing the patches. 'Seven rounds' (satta vāre) means seven sewing rounds. Not making any alteration on the pretext of applying the dye-mark (kappabindu) is contentment with what is allowable (kappasantoso).

Sītappaṭighātanādi atthāpattito sijjhatīti mukhyameva cīvaraparibhoge payojanaṃ dassetuṃ “hirikopīnappaṭicchādanamattavasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā “yāvadeva hirikopīnappaṭicchādanattha”nti (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58; mahāni. 206). Vaṭṭati, na tāvatā santoso kuppati sambhārānaṃ dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ alābhato. Sāraṇīyadhamme ṭhatvāti sīlavantehi bhikkhūhi sādhāraṇabhogibhāve ṭhatvā. Itītiādinā paṭhamasseva ariyavaṃsassa paṃsukūlikaṅgatecīvarikaṅgānaṃ tesañcassa paccayataṃ dassento “iti ime dhammā aññamaññassa samuṭṭhāpakā upatthambhakā cā”ti dīpeti. Esa nayo ito paresu.

Since warding off cold and so on is accomplished as a consequence, to show that the primary purpose in using a robe is 'merely for covering the private parts out of a sense of shame' (hirikopīnappaṭicchādanamattavasena), it was said thus. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'just for the purpose of covering the private parts out of a sense of shame' (MN 1.23; AN 6.58; Mahāni. 206). It is fitting, and contentment does not become disturbed by not obtaining requisites from donors. 'By abiding in the qualities that endear' (sāraṇīyadhamme ṭhatvā) means by virtuous monks abiding in a state of sharing resources. By 'and so on' (iti), it is shown that the first noble lineage is the condition for the rag-robe practice (paṃsukūlikaṅga) and the three-robe practice (tecīvarikaṅga), demonstrating that 'these qualities mutually give rise to and support one another.' The same method applies to the rest.

Santuṭṭho hoti vaṇṇavādīti ettha catukkoṭikaṃ sambhavati. Tattha catutthoyeva pakkho vaṇṇitathomitoti tathā desanā katā. Eko santuṭṭho hoti, santosassa vaṇṇaṃ na katheti seyyathāpi thero nāḷako. Eko na santuṭṭho hoti, santosassa vaṇṇaṃ katheti seyyathāpi upanando sakyaputto. Eko neva santuṭṭho hoti, na santosassa vaṇṇaṃ katheti seyyathāpi thero lāḷudāyi[M 2.0270]. Eko santuṭṭho ceva hoti, santosassa ca vaṇṇaṃ katheti seyyathāpi thero mahākassapo.

Here, a fourfold distinction is possible regarding 'He is content and speaks in praise' (santuṭṭho hoti vaṇṇavādī). In this regard, only the fourth position is praised and extolled, and thus the teaching was given. One is content, but does not speak in praise of contentment, like the Elder Nālaka. One is not content, but speaks in praise of contentment, like Upananda the Sakyan. One is neither content nor speaks in praise of contentment, like the Elder Lāludāyi. One is both content and speaks in praise of contentment, like the Elder Mahākassapa.

Anesananti ayuttaṃ esanaṃ. Tenāha “appatirūpa”nti, sāsane ṭhitānaṃ appatirūpaṃ ayoggaṃ. Kohaññaṃ karontoti cīvaruppādananimittaṃ paresaṃ kuhanaṃ vimhāpanaṃ karonto. Uttasatīti taṇhāsantāsena uparūpari tasati. Paritassatīti parito tassati. Yathā sabbe kāyavacippayogā tadatthā eva jāyanti, evaṃ sabbabhāgehi tasati. Gadhitaṃ vuccati giddho, so cettha abhijjhālakkhaṇo adhippeto. Gadhitaṃ etassa natthīti agadhitoti āha “vigatalobhagiddho”ti. Mucchanti taṇhāvasena muyhanaṃ. Tassa samussayassa adhigataṃ anāpanno anupagato. Anotthato anajjhotthato. Apariyonaddhoti taṇhacchadanena acchādito. Ādīnavaṃ passamānoti diṭṭhadhammikaṃ samparāyikañca dosaṃ passanto. Gadhitaparibhogato nissarati etenāti nissaraṇaṃ[V 2.0246], idamaṭṭhikatā. Taṃ pajānātīti nissaraṇapañño. Tenāha “yāvadeva…pe… jānanto”ti.

'Seeking that is improper' (anesana) is called unseemly seeking. Therefore, it is said, 'unfitting' (appatirūpa)—unsuitable, inappropriate for those established in the Dispensation. 'Deceiving others' (kohaññaṃ karonto) means one who, for the sake of obtaining robes, engages in deception or astonishing others. 'He trembles' (uttasati) means he trembles repeatedly due to the agitation of craving. 'He is anxious' (paritassati) means he trembles all around. Just as all bodily and verbal actions arise for that purpose, so he trembles in every way. 'Grasping' (gadhita) is called greed; here, it refers to the characteristic of covetousness (abhijjhā). 'He is not grasping' (agadhita) means he is free from greed, thus it is said, 'devoid of greed and greediness' (vigatalobhagiddho). '(They) are bewildered' (mucchanti) means becoming confused due to craving. He has not attained, not fallen into, not approached that accumulation. 'Not submerged, not overwhelmed' (anotthato anajjhotthato). 'Not entangled' (apariyonaddho) means not covered by the covering of craving. 'Seeing the danger' (ādīnavaṃ passamāno) means perceiving the faults both in this life and in the next. 'Escape' (nissaraṇa) is that by which one escapes from greedy enjoyment; this is the meaning. 'He understands it' (taṃ pajānāti) means he has the wisdom of escape (nissaraṇapañño). Therefore, it is said, 'knowing only... as far as...'

Nevattānukkaṃsetīti attānaṃ neva ukkaṃseti na ukkhipati na ukkaṭṭhato dahati. Ahantiādi ukkaṃsanākāradassanaṃ. Na vambheti na hīḷeti na nihīnato dahati. Tasmiṃ cīvarasantoseti tasmiṃ yathāvutte vīsatividhe cīvarasantose. Kāmañcettha vuttappakārasantosaggahaṇeneva cīvarahetu anesanāpajjanādipi gahitameva tasmiṃ sati tassa bhāvato, asati ca abhāvato. Vaṇṇavāditāattukkaṃsanaparavambhanāni pana gahitāni na hontīti “vaṇṇavādādīsu vā”ti vikappo vutto. Ettha ca dakkhotiādi yesaṃ dhammānaṃ vasenassa yathāvuttasantosādī ijjhanti, taṃdassanaṃ. Tattha dakkhoti iminā tesaṃ samuṭṭhāpanapaññaṃ dasseti. Analasoti iminā paggaṇhanavīriyaṃ, sampajānoti iminā pārihāriyapaññaṃ, paṭissatoti iminā tattha asammosavuttiṃ dasseti.

"He does not exalt himself" means he neither exalts himself, nor uplifts himself, nor considers himself superior. "I am," and so forth, is a showing of the manner of self-exaltation. "He does not disparage others" means he does not scorn them, does not belittle them, nor does he consider them inferior. 'In that contentment with the robe' (tasmiṃ cīvarasantose) means in the twenty kinds of contentment with robes as stated. Moreover, here, by the very inclusion of contentment of the kind stated, the faults of improper seeking of robes, etc., are also included, since when contentment is present, those faults are absent, and when it is absent, they are present. However, praise, self-exaltation, and disparagement of others are not included. Hence, the alternative phrasing, "or in praise, etc.," is stated. And here, "skillful," and so forth, is a showing of those qualities by the power of which his aforementioned contentment, etc., are successful. There, by "skillful," he shows the wisdom that gives rise to those qualities. By "not lazy," he shows the effort of exertion; by "comprehending," he shows protective wisdom; by "recollected," he shows undistracted conduct in that matter.

Piṇḍapāto jānitabboti pabhedato piṇḍapāto jānitabbo. Piṇḍapātakkhettanti piṇḍapātassa uppattiṭṭhānaṃ. Piṇḍapātasantoso jānitabboti [M 2.0271] piṇḍapātasantosappabhedo jānitabbo. Idha bhesajjampi piṇḍapātagatikameva. Āharitabbato hi sappiādīnampi gahaṇaṃ kataṃ.

"Alms-food should be understood" means alms-food should be understood according to its distinctions. "The field of alms-food" means the place of origin of alms-food. "Contentment with alms-food should be understood" means the distinctions of contentment with alms-food should be understood. Here, medicine too is included in the category of alms-food, for even ghee and so forth are included on account of being things to be obtained.

Piṇḍapātakkhettaṃ piṇḍapātassa uppattiṭṭhānaṃ khettaṃ viya khettaṃ. Uppajjati ettha, etenāti ca uppattiṭṭhānaṃ. Saṅghato vā hi bhikkhuno piṇḍapāto uppajjati uddissavasena vā. Tattha sakalassa saṅghassa dātabbabhattaṃ saṅghabhattaṃ. Katipaye bhikkhū uddisitvā uddesena dātabbabhattaṃ uddesabhattaṃ. Nimantetvā dātabbabhattaṃ nimantanaṃ. Salākāya dātabbabhattaṃ salākabhattaṃ. Ekasmiṃ pakkhe ekadivasaṃ dātabbabhattaṃ pakkhikaṃ. Uposathe uposathe dātabbabhattaṃ uposathikaṃ. Pāṭipadadivase dātabbabhattaṃ pāṭipadikaṃ. Āgantukānaṃ dātabbabhattaṃ āgantukabhattaṃ. Dhuragehe eva ṭhapetvā dātabbabhattaṃ dhurabhattaṃ. Kuṭiṃ uddissa dātabbabhattaṃ kuṭibhattaṃ. Gāmavāsiādīhi vārena dātabbabhattaṃ vārabhattaṃ. Vihāraṃ uddissa dātabbabhattaṃ vihārabhattaṃ. Sesāni pākaṭāneva.

The field of alms-food is the place of origin of alms-food, just as a field is a field. It arises here, and by this; thus it is the place of origin. For alms-food arises for a bhikkhu from the Saṅgha, or by way of designation. Therein, a meal to be given to the entire Saṅgha is a Saṅgha meal. A meal to be given by designating a few bhikkhus is a designated meal. A meal to be given after inviting is an invitation meal. A meal to be given by lottery ticket is a lottery meal. A meal to be given for one day in a fortnight is a fortnightly meal. A meal to be given on each observance day is an observance-day meal. A meal to be given on the first day of the fortnight is a first-day meal. A meal to be given to newly arrived bhikkhus is a newcomer meal. A meal to be given by keeping it specifically at the main building is a duty meal. A meal to be given for a hut is a hut meal. A meal to be given by village residents and others in turns is a turn meal. A meal to be given for the monastery is a monastery meal. The remaining ones are indeed well-known.

Vitakketi “kattha nu kho ahaṃ ajja piṇḍāya carissāmī”ti. “Sve kattha piṇḍāya carissāmā”ti therena vutte “asukagāme, bhante”ti kāmametaṃ paṭivacanadānaṃ, yena pana cittena cintetvā taṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ sandhāyāha “ettakaṃ cintetvā”ti. Tato paṭṭhāyāti vitakkamāḷake ṭhatvā [V 2.0247] vitakkitakālato paṭṭhāya. Tato paraṃ vitakkento ariyavaṃsā cuto hotīti idaṃ tiṇṇampi ariyavaṃsikānaṃ vasena gahetabbaṃ, na ekacārikasseva. Sabbopi hi ariyavaṃsiko ekavārameva vitakketuṃ labhati, na tato paraṃ. Paribāhiroti ariyavaṃsikabhāvato bahibhūto. Svāyaṃ vitakkasantoso kammaṭṭhānamanasikārena na kuppati visujjhati ca. Ito paresupi eseva nayo. Tenevāha “kammaṭṭhānasīsena gantabba”nti. Gahetabbamevāti aṭṭhānappayutto eva-saddo. Yāpanamattameva gahetabbanti yojetabbaṃ.

He reflects, "Where indeed shall I go for alms today?" When the elder says, "Tomorrow, where shall we go for alms?" and one replies, "In such-and-such village, venerable sir," this is merely giving a response. But what is meant by "having reflected so much" refers to the intention with which he thought and then spoke. "From that point onward" means from the time of reflection, while standing in the area of reflection. Then, if he reflects further, he falls away from the noble lineage. This should be understood in the case of all three who belong to the noble lineage, not just one who goes alone. For all who belong to the noble lineage are allowed to reflect only once, not beyond that. "An outsider" means one who is outside of the state of being of the noble lineage. This contentment with reflection does not become disturbed by attention to the meditation subject, and it becomes purified. The same principle applies to what follows. Therefore, it is said, "One should proceed with the meditation subject as the foremost." Regarding "Only what should be taken," the word "eva" (only) is used inappropriately. It should be construed to mean "only what is sufficient for sustaining life should be taken."

Etthāti etasmiṃ piṇḍapātappaṭiggahaṇe. Appanti attano yāpanappamāṇatopi appaṃ gahetabbaṃ dāyakassa cittārādhanatthaṃ. Pamāṇenevāti attano pamāṇeneva appaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Pamāṇena gahetabbanti ettha kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “paṭiggahaṇasmiñhī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Makkhetīti viddhaṃseti apaneti. Vinipāteti vināseti aṭṭhānaviniyogena. Sāsananti satthusāsanaṃ anusiṭṭhiṃ na karoti na paṭipajjati. Sapadānacārinā viya [M 2.0272] dvārapaṭipāṭiyā caraṇaṃ loluppavivajjanasantosoti āha “dvārapaṭipāṭiyā gantabba”nti.

"Here" means in this instance of receiving alms-food. "A little" means even less than the amount needed for one's own sustenance should be taken, for the sake of pleasing the donor's mind. "Only by measure" means a small amount should be taken according to one's own measure. To show the reason for stating that "one should take in moderation," the phrase "For in receiving..." and so on, is stated. "Makkheti" means he destroys, he removes. "Vinipāteti" means he ruins, he destroys by improper application. "The Dispensation" means he does not do, does not practice the Teacher's instruction or advice. Walking in sequence from door to door, like one who practices a continuous alms-round, is the contentment of avoiding greed; therefore it is said, "One should go by the sequence of houses."

Harāpetvāti adhikaṃ apanetvā. Āhāragedhato nissarati etenāti nissaraṇaṃ. Jighacchāya paṭivinodanatthaṃ katā, kāyassa ṭhitiādipayojanaṃ pana atthāpattito āgatamevāti āha “jighacchāya…pe… santoso nāmā”ti. Nidahitvā na paribhuñjitabbaṃ tadahupīti adhippāyo. Itarattha pana sikkhāpadeneva vāritaṃ. Sāraṇīyadhamme ṭhitenāti sīlavantehi bhikkhūhi sādhāraṇabhogibhāve ṭhitena.

"Harāpetvā" means having removed the excess. It is called "nissaraṇaṃ" because by it one issues forth (nissarati) from craving for food. It is made for the relief of hunger, but the purpose of maintaining the body and so forth comes by implication; hence it is said, "for the relief of hunger... contentment indeed." The intention is that it should not be stored and consumed, even on the same day. In other cases, it is prohibited by the training rule itself. "Established in the memorable principles" means dwelling in a state of shared use with virtuous bhikkhus.

Senāsanenāti sayanena āsanena ca. Yattha yattha hi mañcādike vihārādike ca seti, taṃ senaṃ. Yattha yattha pīṭhādike āsati, taṃ āsanaṃ. Tadubhayaṃ ekato katvā “senāsana”nti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “mañco”tiādi. Tattha mañco masārakādi. Tathā pīṭhaṃ. Mañcabhisi, pīṭhabhisīti duvidho bhisi. Vihāro pākāraparicchinno sakalo āvāso, “dīghamukhapāsādo”ti keci. Aḍḍhayogo dīghapāsādo, “ekapassacchādanakasenāsana”nti keci. Pāsādoti caturassapāsādo, “āyatacaturassapāsādo”ti keci. Hammiyanti muṇḍacchadanapāsādo. Guhāti kevalā pabbataguhā. Leṇaṃ dvārabandhaṃ. Aṭṭo bahalabhittikagehaṃ, yassa gopānasiyo aggahetvā iṭṭhakāhi eva chadanaṃ hoti, “aṭṭalākārena karīyatī”tipi vadanti. Māḷo ekakūṭasaṅgahito anekakoṇo paṭissayaviseso, “vaṭṭākārena katasenāsana”nti keci.

"Senāsana" means both a place for lying down and a seat. Wherever one lies down, such as on a couch or in a dwelling, that is a sena. Wherever one sits, such as on a stool, that is an āsana. Combining both, it is called "senāsana." Hence, it is said, "a couch," and so on. Here, "couch" includes couches with frames and the like. Similarly, a "stool" (pīṭha). A "bhisi" (cushion) is of two kinds: a cushion for a couch and a cushion for a stool. A "vihāra" (dwelling) refers to an entire residence enclosed by walls; some call it a "long-faced mansion." An "aḍḍhayoga" is a long mansion; some describe it as "a resting place with a roof on one side." A "pāsāda" is a four-sided mansion; some call it an "elongated four-sided mansion." A "hammiya" is a mansion with a flat roof. A "guhā" (cave) refers solely to a mountain cave. A "leṇa" (shelter) has a doorframe. An "aṭṭa" is a house with thick walls, where the roof is made of bricks without wooden rafters; some also say it is "constructed in the shape of a tower." A "māḷa" is a pavilion with a single peak and multiple corners, a special kind of lodging; some describe it as "a resting place built in a circular shape."

Piṇḍapāte [V 2.0248] vuttanayenevāti “sādako bhikkhu ‘ahaṃ kattha vasissāmī’ti vitakketī”tiādinā yathārahaṃ piṇḍapāte vuttanayeneva veditabbā. “Tato paraṃ vitakkento ariyavaṃsā cuto hoti paribāhiro, senāsanaṃ kuhiṃ labhissāmīti acintetvā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva gantabba”nti ca evamādi sabbaṃ purimanayeneva.

"In the same way as stated regarding alms-food" means it should be understood as appropriate in the same way as stated regarding alms-food, beginning with 'a bhikkhu who is a practitioner considers: "Where shall I dwell?"' and so on. And 'if he reflects further, he falls away from the noble lineage and becomes an outsider. Without thinking "Where shall I obtain lodging?" he should proceed with the meditation subject as foremost'—all such things are to be understood in the same way as before.

Kasmā panettha paccayasantosaṃ dassentena bhagavatā gilānapaccayasantoso na gahitoti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbanti dassento “gilānapaccayo pana piṇḍapāte eva paviṭṭho”ti āha, āharitabbatāsāmaññenāti adhippāyo. Yadi evaṃ tatthāpi piṇḍapāte viya vitakkasantosādayopi [M 2.0273] pannarasa santosā icchitabbāti? Noti dassento āha “tatthā”tiādi. Nanu cettha dvādaseva dhutaṅgāni viniyogaṃ gatāni, ekaṃ pana nesajjikaṅgaṃ na katthaci viniyuttanti āha “nesajjikaṅgaṃ bhāvanārāmaariyavaṃsaṃ bhajatī”ti. Ayañca attho aṭṭhakathāruḷho evāti dassento “vuttampi ceta”ntiādimāha.

Why then, when the Blessed One showed contentment with requisites here, was contentment with the requisites for the sick not included? Showing that this should not be seen in that way, he said, "But the requisite for the sick is included in alms-food," the intention being that this is due to the commonality of being something to be brought. If so, should not the fifteen kinds of contentment, such as contentment with reflection, also be desired there, just as with alms-food? Showing that this is not so, he said, "there," etc. Now, in this regard, are there not only twelve ascetic practices that are applied, while one, the practice of not lying down, is not applied anywhere? He said, "The practice of not lying down serves the noble lineage of one who delights in cultivation." And showing that this meaning is indeed established in the commentary, he said, "Moreover, it is said," etc.

Pathaviṃ pattharamāno viyātiādi ariyavaṃsadesanāya sudukkarabhāvadassanaṃ mahāvisayattā tassā desanāya. Yasmā nayasahassapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ hoti, ariyamaggādhigamāya vitthārato pavattiyamānā desanā cittuppādakaṇḍe ayañca bhāvanārāmaariyavaṃsakathā ariyamaggādhigamāya vitthārato pavattiyamānā eva hotīti vuttaṃ “sahassanayapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ…pe… desanaṃ ārabhī”ti.

"As if spreading out the earth," and so forth—this shows the extreme difficulty of the teaching of the noble lineage due to the vast scope of that teaching.
