Because it is adorned with a thousand methods, and because this discourse on the noble lineage of one who delights in cultivation is indeed a detailed exposition leading to the attainment of the noble path, just as the teaching in the chapter on the arising of consciousness is a detailed exposition leading to the attainment of the noble path, it is therefore said: "Adorned with a thousand methods... he began the teaching."

Paṭipakkhavidhamanato abhimukhabhāvena ramaṇaṃ āramaṇaṃ ārāmoti āha “abhiratīti attho”ti. Byadhikaraṇānampi padānaṃ vasena bhavati bāhiratthasamāso yathā “urasilomo kaṇṭhekāḷo”ti āha “bhāvanāya ārāmo assāti bhāvanārāmo”ti. Abhiramitabbaṭṭhena vā ārāmo, bhāvanā ārāmo assāti bhāvanārāmoti evampettha samāsayojanā veditabbā. Bhāvento ramatīti etena bhāvanārāmasaddānaṃ kattusādhanataṃ kammadhārayasamāsatañca dasseti. “Pajahanto ramatī”ti vuttattā pahānārāmoti etthāpi eseva nayo.

"Because of destroying what is opposed, and because of facing towards, `ramaṇaṃ` is `āramaṇaṃ`, and hence `ārāma`"—thus it is said, meaning "delight." Even in the case of words with differing case relations, a compound referring to an external attribute occurs, as in "hairy-chested, black-throated." Thus it is said, "Development is a delight to him; therefore, delight-in-development (bhāvanārāma)." Or, `ārāma` is so called because it is something to be delighted in; or "development is a delight to him"—thus should the compounding be understood here. By "one who develops delights," he shows that the word `bhāvanārāma` is an agent-formative and a karmadhāraya compound. Because it was said, "one who abandons delights," the same method applies here as well to "delight in abandoning (pahānārāma)."

Kāmaṃ “nesajjikaṅgaṃ bhāvanārāmaariyavaṃsaṃ bhajatī”ti vuttaṃ bhāvanānuyogassa anucchavikattā, nesajjikaṅgavasena pana nesajjikassa bhikkhuno ekaccāhi āpattīhi anāpattibhāvoti tampi saṅgaṇhanto “terasannaṃ dhutaṅgāna”nti vatvā vinayaṃ patvā garuke ṭhātabbanti icchitattā sallekhassa apariccajanavasena paṭipatti nāma vinaye ṭhitassevāti āha [V 2.0249] “terasannaṃ…pe… kathitaṃ hotī”ti. Kāmaṃ suttābhidhammapiṭakesupi tattha tattha sīlakathā āhaṭāyeva, yehi pana guṇehi sīlassa vodānaṃ hoti, tesu kathitesu yathā sīlakathābāhullaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ kathitaṃ hoti, evaṃ bhāvanākathābāhullaṃ suttapiṭakaṃ abhidhammapiṭakañca catutthena ariyavaṃsena kathitena kathitameva hotīti vuttaṃ “bhāvanārāmena avasesaṃ piṭakadvayaṃ kathita”nti. “So nekkhammaṃ bhāvento [M 2.0274] ramatī”ti nekkhammapadaṃ ādiṃ katvā tattha desanāya pavattattā sabbesampi vā samathavipassanāmaggadhammānaṃ yathāsakaṃ paṭipakkhato nikkhamanena nekkhammasaññitānaṃ tattha āgatattā so pāṭho nekkhammapāḷīti vuccatīti āha “nekkhamapāḷiyā kathetabbo”ti. Tenāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sabbepi kusalā dhamā, nekkhammanti pavuccare”ti. Dasuttarasuttantapariyāyenāti dasuttarasuttantadhammena (dī. ni. 3.350 ādayo) dasuttarasuttante āgatanayenāti vā attho. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo.

Indeed, it is said, "He resorts to the noble lineage of delighting in development, the sitter's practice," because it is suitable for one devoted to development. However, by also including the fact that for a monk who undertakes the sitter's practice there is a state of no offense regarding certain offenses, and having said 'of the thirteen ascetic practices,' and because it is desired that, having reached the Vinaya, one should stand firm in grave matters, and that practice, by way of not abandoning austerity, belongs only to one established in the Vinaya, he says, 'of the thirteen... it is spoken.' Indeed, in the Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas too, discourses on virtue are brought up here and there. But when those qualities by which virtue is purified are discussed, just as the Vinaya Piṭaka is spoken of as being extensive in discourses on virtue, so too the Sutta Piṭaka and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka are spoken of as being extensive in discourses on development, which is spoken of by the fourth noble lineage. Thus, it is said, "By delight in development, the remaining two Piṭakas are spoken of." Because the teaching there proceeds by taking the word 'renunciation' as the starting point in 'He delights, developing renunciation,' and because all states of serenity, insight, and path are designated as 'renunciation' due to their emerging from their respective opposites and are included there, that passage is called the 'Pāḷi of Renunciation.' Thus he says, 'it should be spoken of by the Pāḷi of Renunciation.' Therefore it is said in the commentary: "All wholesome states are called renunciation." 'By the method of the Dasuttara Suttanta' means by the Dhamma of the Dasuttara Suttanta (Dī. Ni. 3.350 ff.) or by the method presented in the Dasuttara Suttanta. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well.

Soti jāgariyaṃ anuyutto bhikkhu. Nekkhammanti kāmehi nikkhantabhāvato nekkhammasaññitaṃ paṭhamajjhānūpacāraṃ, so “abhijjhaṃ loke pahāyā”tiādinā (vibha. 508) āgato. Paṭhamajjhānassa pubbabhāgabhāvanā hi idhādhippetā, tasmā “abyāpāda”ntiādīsupi evameva attho veditabbo. Saupāyānañhi aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ aṭṭhārasannaṃ mahāvipassanānaṃ catunnaṃ ariyamaggānañca vasenettha desanā pavattāti. Tattha abyāpādanti mettā. Ālokasaññanti vibhūtaṃ katvā manasikaraṇena upaṭṭhitaālokasañjānanaṃ. Avikkhepanti samādhiṃ. Dhammavavatthānanti kusalādidhammānaṃ yāthāvanicchayaṃ, “sapaccayanāmavavatthāna”ntipi vadanti. Evaṃ kāmacchandādinīvaraṇappahānena “abhijjhaṃ loke pahāyā”tiādinā vuttassa paṭhamajjhānassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya bhāvanārāmataṃ pahānārāmatañca dassetvā idāni saha upāyena aṭṭhasamāpattīhi aṭṭhārasahi ca mahāvipassanāhi taṃ dassetuṃ “ñāṇa”ntiādimāha. Nāmarūpapariggahaṇakaṅkhāvitaraṇānañhi vibandhabhūtassa mohassa dūrīkaraṇena ñātapariññāya ṭhitassa aniccasaññādayo sijjhanti. Tathā jhānasamāpattīsu anabhiratinimittena pāmojjena tattha anabhiratiyā vinoditāya jhānādīnaṃ samadhigamoti samāpattivipassanaṃ arativinodanaavijjāpadālanaupāyo. Uppaṭipāṭiniddeso pana nīvaraṇasabhāvāya avijjāya heṭṭhānīvaraṇesu saṅgahadassanatthanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kiñcāpi paṭhamajjhānūpacāreyeva dukkhaṃ, catutthajjhānūpacāreyeva sukhaṃ pahīyati, atisayappahānaṃ pana sandhāyāha “catutthajjhānaṃ sukhadukkhe”ti.

He is a bhikkhu devoted to wakefulness. 'Renunciation' means the access to the first jhāna, which is called 'renunciation' because it is a state of having gone forth from sensual pleasures. This is what is meant by the phrase 'having abandoned covetousness in the world,' etc. (Vibh. 508). Indeed, the preliminary development of the first jhāna is intended here; therefore, the meaning should be understood similarly in phrases like 'without ill will,' etc. For here, the teaching proceeds by way of the eight attainments with their means, the eighteen great insights, and the four noble paths. In this context, 'without ill will' means loving-kindness. 'Perception of light' means the perception of light that has arisen through making it distinct and attending to it mentally. 'Non-distraction' means concentration. 'Discrimination of phenomena' means the accurate determination of wholesome and other states; some also call it 'discrimination of name-and-form with its conditions.' Thus, having shown the delight in development and the delight in abandoning in the preliminary practice of the first jhāna, which is mentioned in 'having abandoned covetousness in the world,' etc., through the abandonment of hindrances such as sensual desire, he now says 'knowledge,' etc., to demonstrate it along with the means—through the eight attainments and the eighteen great insights. For the perceptions of impermanence, etc., succeed in one who is established in the knowledge of discernment by dispelling the delusion that obstructs the comprehension of name-and-form and the overcoming of doubt. Similarly, in the jhāna attainments, through gladness which is a sign of non-delight, when that non-delight is dispelled, there is the attainment of jhāna and so forth; thus, insight through attainments is a means for removing discontent and splitting asunder ignorance. The reverse order of explanation, however, should be seen as for the purpose of showing the inclusion of the lower hindrances within ignorance, which is of the nature of a hindrance. Although suffering is abandoned just in the access to the first jhāna, and pleasure just in the access to the fourth jhāna, the phrase 'the fourth jhāna regarding pleasure and pain' is stated with reference to a surpassing abandonment.

Aniccassa[M 2.0275], aniccanti ca anupassanā aniccānupassanā, tebhūmakadhammānaṃ aniccataṃ gahetvā [V 2.0250] pavattāya anupassanāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Niccasaññanti saṅkhatadhammesu niccā sassatāti pavattaṃ micchāsaññaṃ. Saññāsīsena diṭṭhicittānampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Nibbidānupassananti saṅkhāresu nibbindanākārena pavattaṃ anupassanaṃ. Nandinti sappītikataṇhaṃ. Virāgānupassananti virajjanākārena pavattaṃ anupassanaṃ. Nirodhānupassananti saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhassa anupassanaṃ. “Te saṅkhārā nirujjhantiyeva, āyatiṃ samudayavasena na uppajjantī”ti evaṃ vā anupassanā nirodhānupassanā. Tenevāha “nirodhānupassanāya nirodheti no samudetī”ti. Muccitukāmatā hi ayaṃ balappattāti. Paṭinissajjanākārena pavattā anupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā. Paṭisaṅkhā santiṭṭhanā hi ayaṃ. Ādānanti niccādivasena gahaṇaṃ. Santatisamūhakiccārammaṇānaṃ vasena ekattaggahaṇaṃ ghanasaññā. Āyūhanaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ. Avatthāvisesāpatti vipariṇāmo. Dhuvasaññanti thirabhāvaggahaṇaṃ.

The contemplation of the impermanent, and as 'impermanent,' is the contemplation of impermanence; this name is given to the contemplation that proceeds by grasping the impermanence of phenomena of the three planes. 'Perception of permanence' is the wrong perception that arises regarding conditioned phenomena, thinking them permanent and eternal. It should be understood that by way of perception, the grasping of views and thoughts is also included. The same method applies to what follows as well. 'Contemplation of disenchantment' is the contemplation that proceeds in the manner of being disenchanted with formations. 'Delight' means craving accompanied by pleasure. 'Contemplation of fading away' is the contemplation that proceeds in the manner of fading away. 'Contemplation of cessation' is the contemplation of the cessation of formations. Or, the contemplation thus: 'those formations are indeed ceasing; in the future they do not arise by way of origination' is the contemplation of cessation. Therefore he says, "Through the contemplation of cessation, one causes it to cease; it does not arise." Indeed, this is the desire to be liberated, having attained strength. The contemplation that proceeds in the manner of relinquishing is the contemplation of relinquishment. Indeed, this is a settling down through reflection. 'Grasping' is taking hold by way of permanence, etc. 'Perception of compactness' is the grasping of oneness in terms of continuity, collection, function, and object. 'Accumulation' is formation. 'Transformation' is the attainment of a different state. 'Perception of stability' is the grasping of a stable nature.

Nimittanti samūhaghanavasena, sakiccaparicchedatāya ca saṅkhārānaṃ saviggahataṃ. Paṇidhinti rāgādipaṇidhiṃ. Sā panatthato taṇhāvasena saṅkhāresu ninnatā. Abhinivesanti attānudiṭṭhi. Aniccadukkhādivasena sabbadhammatīraṇaṃ adhipaññādhammavipassanā. Sārādānābhinivesanti asāre sāranti gahaṇavipallāsaṃ. “Issarakuttādivasena loko samuppanno”ti abhiniveso sammohābhiniveso. Keci pana “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhānantiādinā (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) pavattasaṃsayāpatti sammohābhiniveso”ti vadanti. Saṅkhāresu tāṇaleṇabhāvaggahaṇaṃ ālayābhiniveso. “Ālayaratā ālayasammuditā”ti (dī. ni. 2.64, 67; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7, 8) ca vacanato ālayo taṇhā, sāyeva cakkhādīsu rūpādīsu ca abhinivesavasena pavattiyā ālayābhinivesoti keci. Evaṃ ṭhitā te saṅkhārā paṭinissajjīyantīti pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanā. Vaṭṭato vigatattā vivaṭṭaṃ nibbānaṃ, tattha ārammaṇasaṅkhātena anupassanena pavattiyā vivaṭṭānupassanā gotrabhu. Saṃyogābhinivesanti saṃyujjanavasena saṅkhāresu nivesanaṃ. Diṭṭhekaṭṭheti diṭṭhiyā sahajātekaṭṭhe pahānekaṭṭhe ca. Oḷāriketi uparimaggavajjhe kilese [M 2.0276] apekkhitvā vuttaṃ, aññathā dassanappahātabbāpi dutiyamaggavajjhehipi oḷārikāti. Aṇusahagateti aṇubhūte. Idaṃ heṭṭhimamaggavajjhe apekkhitvā vuttaṃ. Sabbakileseti avasiṭṭhasabbakilese. Na hi paṭhamādimaggehipi pahīnā kilesā puna pahīyantīti.

'Sign' means the state of formations being a compact mass and being distinct through the delimitation of their respective functions. 'Aspiration' means aspiration based on lust and so on. In essence, it is the inclination toward formations driven by craving. 'Adherence' means the view of self. The thorough examination of all phenomena by way of impermanence, suffering, and so on, is the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. 'Adherence to grasping the essence' is the perversion of perception, taking what is essenceless as essence. The adherence that 'the world arose through the act of a creator, etc.' is adherence born of delusion. Some, however, say that the arising of doubt, such as 'Did I exist in the past?' and so on (M I 28; S II 20), is adherence born of delusion. Grasping formations as a shelter and refuge is adherence as clinging. And because of the statement, 'delighting in clinging, rejoicing in clinging' (D II 58, 61; M I 136; M II 266; S I 136; Vin I 5, 6), clinging is craving itself. Some say that this very craving, by its proceeding as adherence in relation to the eye, forms, and so on, is adherence as clinging. The knowledge that proceeds thus, 'These formations thus existing are to be relinquished,' is the contemplation of reflection. Nibbāna is the turning away because it is free from the round of existence. The contemplation of turning away, which proceeds with Nibbāna as its object, is the change-of-lineage. 'Adherence to fetters' is fixation on formations by way of binding. 'Of one function with view' refers to having one function in co-arising with the view and one function in abandonment. 'Coarse' is said with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths; otherwise, even those to be abandoned by seeing and those to be abandoned by the second path would be coarse. 'Subtly accompanied' means subtle. This is said with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the lower paths. 'All defilements' means all remaining defilements. For defilements abandoned by the first path and so on are not abandoned again.

Evanti paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.41, 95) nekkhammapāḷiyā yojanaṃ nigametvā dīghanikāyetiādinā dasuttarapariyāyena (dī. ni. 3.350 ādayo) yojanaṃ dasseti[V 2.0251]. Ekaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvento ramati, ekaṃ dhammaṃ pajahanto ramatīti ca nayidaṃ dasuttarasutte (dī. ni. 3.350 ādayo) āgataniyāmena vuttaṃ, tattha pana “eko dhammo bhāvetabbo, eko dhammo pahātabbo”ti desanā āgatā. Evaṃ santepi yasmā atthato bhedo natthi, tasmā paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 1.41, 95) nekkhammapāḷiyaṃ āgatanīhāreneva “ekaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvento ramati, ekaṃ dhammaṃ pajahanto ramatī”ti vuttaṃ. Esa nayo sesavāresupi.

Thus, having concluded the application to the section on renunciation in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭis I 41, 95), he shows the application by way of the Dasuttara Sutta method, beginning with 'in the Dīgha Nikāya' (D III 272ff.). The statement, 'One delights in developing one thing, one delights in abandoning one thing,' is not stated in the Dasuttara Sutta (D III 272ff.) according to the transmitted method; rather, the teaching transmitted there is: 'One thing is to be developed, one thing is to be abandoned.' Even so, since there is no difference in meaning, it is therefore stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭis I 41, 95), in the section on renunciation, in accordance with the transmitted method: 'One delights in developing one thing, one delights in abandoning one thing.' This same method applies to the remaining sections as well.

Evantiādinā dasuttarapariyāyena (dī. ni. 3.350 ādayo) yojanaṃ nigametvā idāni satipaṭṭhānasuttantapariyāyena (ma. ni. 1.105 ādayo) yojanaṃ dassetuṃ “majjhimanikāye”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Kāmañcettha kāyānupassanāvaseneva saṃkhipitvā yojanā katā, ekavīsatiyā pana ṭhānānaṃ vasenapi yojanā kātabbā. Idāni abhidhammaniddesapariyāyena dassetuṃ “abhidhamme niddesapariyāyenā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Aniccatotiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāsu (visuddhi. 2.698; visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.698) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

Thus, having concluded the application by the method of the Dasuttara Sutta (D III 272ff.), the section beginning 'in the Majjhima Nikāya' is now commenced to show the application by the method of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta (M I 55ff.). Although here the application has been made concisely, only by way of the contemplation of the body, the application should also be made by way of the twenty-one bases. Now, to show the application by way of the Abhidhamma exposition, the section beginning 'in the Abhidhamma by way of the exposition' is commenced. As for what should be said regarding 'impermanence' and so forth, that should be understood in accordance with the method stated in the commentaries on the Visuddhimagga (Vism 698; Vism-mhṭ 698).

Ukkaṇṭhitanti adhikusalesu dhammesu pantasenāsanesu ca ukkaṇṭhādiñca, ananuyogoti attho. Ariyavaṃsapūrako dhīro sīlavā bhikkhu ariyavaṃsaparipūraṇassa bhedaṃ anicchanto samāhito vipassako ca paccayaghātena aratiyā ratiyā ca sahitā abhibhavitā hotīti vuttaṃ “aratiratisaho, bhikkhave, dhīro”ti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

'Discontented' means discontent with regard to higher wholesome states and secluded dwellings; the meaning is non-application. The wise, virtuous monk who fulfills the noble lineage, not wishing for a breach in the fulfillment of the noble lineage, being concentrated and an insight meditator, overcomes both discontent and delight by destroying their conditions. Thus it is said: 'The wise one, bhikkhus, endures discontent and delight.' The remainder is easily understood.

Ariyavaṃsasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta is concluded.

9. Dhammapadasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Dhammapada Sutta

29. Navame [M 2.0277] jhānādibhedo dhammo pajjati etenāti dhammapadaṃ, anabhijjhāva dhammapadaṃ anabhijjhādhammapadaṃ, anabhijjhāpadhāno vā dhammakoṭṭhāso anabhijjhādhammapadaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Atthato pana anabhijjhādhammapadaṃ nāma alobho vā alobhasīsena adhigatajjhānavipassanāmaggaphalanibbānāni vā. Abyāpādo dhammapadaṃ nāma mettā vā mettāsīsena adhigatajjhānādīni vā. Sammāsatidhammapadaṃ nāma sūpaṭṭhitassati vā satisīsena adhigatajjhānādīni vā. Sammāsamādhidhammapadaṃ nāma aṭṭhasamāpatti vā aṭṭhasamāpattisīsena adhigatajjhānavipassanāmaggaphalanibbānāni vā. Dasaasubhavasena vā adhigatajjhānādīni anabhijjā dhammapadaṃ. Catubrahmavihāravasena [V 2.0252] adhigatāni abyāpādo dhammapadaṃ. Dasānussati āhārepaṭikūlasaññāvasena adhigatāni sammāsatidhammapadaṃ. Dasakasiṇaānāpānavasena adhigatāni sammāsamādhidhammapadaṃ. Anabhijjhālūti anabhijjhāyanasīlo. Abhipubbo jhesaddo abhijjhāyanaṭṭho. Tenevāha “nittaṇho hutvā”ti. Pakatibhāvaṃ avijahantenāti parisuddhabhāvaṃ sabhāvasaṅkhātaanavajjasaṅkhātaṃ pakatibhāvaṃ avijahantena. Sāvajjadhammasamuppattiyā hi cittassa anavajjabhāvo jahito hotīti.

29. In the ninth section: the Dhamma, distinguished as jhāna and so on, is attained by this; hence, it is a 'dhammapada' (path of Dhamma). The dhammapada of non-covetousness is the 'anabhijjhādhammapada'; or, the portion of Dhamma with non-covetousness as its principal element is the 'anabhijjhādhammapada.' So too in the remaining cases. In terms of meaning, the 'anabhijjhādhammapada' is either non-greed or the jhānas, insight, paths, fruitions, and Nibbāna attained with non-greed as their head. The 'abyāpādodhammapada' is either loving-kindness or the jhānas and so on attained with loving-kindness as their head. The 'sammāsatidhammapada' is either well-established mindfulness or the jhānas and so on attained with mindfulness as their head. The 'sammāsamādhidhammapada' is either the eight attainments or the jhānas, insight, paths, fruitions, and Nibbāna attained with the eight attainments as their head. Alternatively, the jhānas and so on attained by way of the ten kinds of foulness are the 'anabhijjhādhammapada.' Those attained by way of the four divine abidings are the 'abyāpādodhammapada.' Those attained by way of the ten recollections and the perception of revulsion toward food are the 'sammāsatidhammapada.' Those attained by way of the ten kasiṇas and mindfulness of breathing are the 'sammāsamādhidhammapada.' 'Not covetous' means one whose nature is not to covet. The root 'jhā' with the prefix 'abhi' has the meaning of coveting. Therefore, it is said, 'having become free from craving.' 'By not abandoning the natural state' means by not abandoning the pure state, the natural state which is designated as 'own-nature' and designated as 'blameless.' For with the arising of blameworthy states, the blameless state of the mind is abandoned.

Dhammapadasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Dhammapada Sutta is concluded.

10. Paribbājakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Paribbājaka Sutta

30. Dasame abhiññātāti ediso ca ediso cāti abhilakkhaṇavasena ñātā. Tenāha “ñātā pākaṭā”ti. Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti ettha paṭisallānanti tehi tehi saddhivihārikaantevāsikaupāsakādisattehi ceva rūpārammaṇādisaṅkhārehi ca paṭinivattitvā apasakkitvā sallīnaṃ nilīyanaṃ, ekībhāvo pavivekoti vuttaṃ hoti. Yo tato vuṭṭhito, so paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito nāma hoti. Bhagavā pana yasmā paṭisallānā uttamato phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhāsi, tasmā vuttaṃ “paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti phalasamāpattito vuṭṭhito”ti. Vatthukāmesūti rūpādīsu kilesakāmassa vatthubhūtesu kāmesu. Bahalarāganti thiramūladummocanīyatāhi ajjhosānena bahalabhūtaṃ kilesakāmaṃ[M 2.0278]. Sakāraṇāti yehi kāraṇehi paresaṃ vāde dosaṃ dassenti, tehi kāraṇehi sakāraṇā. Na hi lakkhaṇayuttena hetunā vinā paravādesu dosaṃ dassetuṃ sakkā.

30. In the tenth section: 'Well-known' means known by way of distinguishing marks, such as 'of such a kind and such a kind.' Therefore it is said: 'known, manifest.' Regarding 'arisen from seclusion': here 'seclusion' means having turned back and retreated from various beings—such as co-residents, pupils, and lay followers—and from formations such as visible objects. It is said to be a state of merging, concealment, solitude, and isolation. One who has arisen from that is called 'arisen from seclusion.' And since the Blessed One arose from the supreme seclusion, that is, the attainment of fruition, it is therefore said: ''arisen from seclusion' means arisen from the attainment of fruition.' 'In the objects of sensual pleasure' means in the sensual pleasures, such as forms, that are the basis for the defilement of sensual desire. 'Abundant passion' means the defilement of sensual desire that has become abundant through attachment, having firm roots and being difficult to release. 'With reason' means with those reasons by which they point out a fault in the doctrines of others. For it is not possible to point out a fault in the doctrines of others without a reason endowed with characteristics.

Evamādīti ettha ādisaddena “natthi hetu natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāyā”ti (dī. ni. 1.168) evamādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti, tasmā evamādivādino evaṃ hetuppaṭikkhepavādinoti attho. Ettha ca natthikadiṭṭhi vipākaṃ paṭibāhati, akiriyadiṭṭhi kammaṃ paṭibāhati, ahetukadiṭṭhi ubhayaṃ paṭibāhati. Tattha kammaṃ paṭibāhantena vipāko paṭibāhito hoti, vipākaṃ paṭibāhantenapi kammaṃ paṭibāhitaṃ. Iti sabbepete atthato ubhayapaṭibāhakā ahetuvādā ceva akiriyavādā ca natthikavādā ca honti.

Here, by the word 'etc.' (evamādi) is included the statement beginning 'There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings' (Dīgha Nikāya 1.168). Therefore, those who speak thus are deniers of causes—this is the meaning. Here, the nihilistic view rejects result, the inaction view rejects kamma, and the no-cause view rejects both. By rejecting kamma, the result is rejected; and by rejecting the result, kamma is also rejected. Thus, all these are, in terms of meaning, rejecters of both: no-cause views, inaction views, and nihilistic views.

Okkantaniyamāti ogāḷhamicchattaniyamā. Sajjhāyatīti taṃ diṭṭhidīpakaṃ ganthaṃ uggahetvā paṭhati. Vīmaṃsatīti tassa atthaṃ vicāreti. Tassātiādi vīmaṃsanākāradassanaṃ. Tasmiṃ [V 2.0253] ārammaṇeti yathāparikappitahetupaccayābhāvādike natthi hetūtiādinayappavattāya laddhiyā ārammaṇe. Micchāsati santiṭṭhatīti “natthi hetū”tiādivasena anussavūpaladdhe atthe tadākāraparivitakkanehi saviggahe viya sarūpato cittassa paccupaṭṭhite cirakālaparicayena evametanti nijjhānakkhamabhāvūpagamanena nijjhānakkhantiyā tathāgahite punappunaṃ tatheva āsevantassa bahulīkarontassa micchāvitakkena samānīyamānā micchāvāyāmopatthambhitā ataṃsabhāvaṃ taṃsabhāvanti gaṇhantī micchāsatīti laddhanāmā taṃladdhisahagatā taṇhā santiṭṭhati. Cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hotīti yathāvuttavitakkādipaccayalābhena tasmiṃ ārammaṇe avaṭṭhitatāya anekaggataṃ pahāya cittaṃ ekaggaṃ appitaṃ viya hoti micchāsamādhinā. Sopi hi paccayavisesena laddhabhāvanābalo kadāci samādhānapaṭirūpakiccakaro hotiyeva paharaṇavijjhanādīsu viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

By 'the determination of entry' (okkaṇṭaniyama) is meant the fixed state of wrongness into which one has plunged. By 'recites' (sajjhāyati) is meant having learned that text which illuminates views and reciting it. By 'examines' (vīmaṃsati) is meant pondering its meaning. The phrase 'thus' and so on shows the manner of examination. By 'in that object' (tasmiṃ ārammaṇe) is meant in the object of the conviction that proceeds by way of the statement beginning 'there is no cause,' etc., regarding the absence of causes and conditions as one has wrongly conceived. By 'wrong mindfulness becomes established' (micchāsati santiṭṭhati) is meant that when the meaning apprehended by hearsay, such as 'there is no cause,' etc., is present to the mind in its own form, as if with a body, through thoughts of that nature, and through long familiarity, by reaching a state of being fit for contemplation and by acceptance through contemplation, it is grasped as 'this is so,' then for one who repeatedly engages in it and cultivates it in just that way, craving becomes established. This craving is accompanied by that conviction and has received the name 'wrong mindfulness' because, being brought about by wrong thought and supported by wrong effort, it takes what is not its nature as its nature. By 'the mind becomes one-pointed' (cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti) is meant that by abandoning distraction and becoming settled on that object through the attainment of conditions such as the aforementioned wrong thoughts, the mind becomes one-pointed, as if fixed, through wrong concentration. For even that, when strengthened by the power of development through specific conditions, can at times perform functions resembling concentration, as seen in striking, piercing, etc.—this should be understood.

Javanāni javantīti anekakkhattuṃ tenākārena pubbabhāgiyesu javanavāresu pavattesu sabbapacchime javanavāre satta javanāni javanti. Paṭhamajavane satekiccho hoti, tathā dutiyādīsūti dhammasabhāvadassanametaṃ, na pana tasmiṃ khaṇe tesaṃ satekicchabhāvāpādanaṃ kenaci [M 2.0279] sakkā kātuṃ. Tatthāti tesu tīsu micchādassanesu. Koci ekaṃ dassanaṃ okkamatīti yassa ekasmiṃyeva abhiniveso āsevanā pavattā, so ekaṃyeva dassanaṃ okkamati. Yassa dvīsu tīsupi vā abhiniveso āsevanā pavattā, so dve tīṇi okkamati. Etena yā pubbe ubhayapaṭibāhikatāmukhena pavattā atthasiddhā sabbadiṭṭhikā, sā pubbabhāgiyā, micchāniyāmokkantiyā pana yathāsakaṃ paccayasamudāgamadiṭṭhito bhinnārammaṇānaṃ viya visesādhigamānaṃ ekajjhaṃ anuppattiyā abhikiṇṇā evāti dasseti. Ekasmiṃ okkantepi dvīsu tīsu okkantesupi niyatamicchādiṭṭhikova hotīti iminā tissannampi diṭṭhīnaṃ samānaphalataṃ samānabalañca dasseti. Tasmā tissopi cetanā ekassa uppannā aññamaññaṃ anubalappadāyikā honti.

By 'the javanās run' is meant that when they have occurred repeatedly in that manner in the preliminary javana-courses, seven javanās run in the very last javana-course. In the first javana, one is with effort, and similarly in the second and so forth—this is a showing of the nature of phenomena, but at that moment no one can cause them to be with effort. By 'therein' (tattha) is meant in those three wrong views. By 'someone enters one view' (koci ekaṃ dassanaṃ okkamati) is meant that one whose inclination and practice have occurred in only one view enters only one view. One whose inclination and practice have occurred in two or even three enters two or three. By this it is shown that all those views which previously occurred and accomplished their purpose by way of refuting both are preliminary. However, upon entering the fixed state of wrongness, it is shown that they are confounded by the non-attainment of distinct achievements together, unlike things with different objects which arise from their respective conditions. Even if one enters one, or enters two or three, one is indeed of fixed wrong view. By this it is shown that all three views have equal results and equal strength. Therefore, the three volitions, having arisen in one person, are mutually supportive.

Kiṃ panesa etasmiññeva attabhāve niyato, udāhu aññasmimpīti? Etasmiññeva niyato. Akusalañhi nāmetaṃ abalaṃ, na kusalaṃ viya mahābalaṃ. Aññathā sammattaniyāmo viya accantiko siyā, āsevanavasena pana bhavantarepi taṃ taṃ diṭṭhiṃ rocetiyeva. Tenevāha “vaṭṭakhāṇuko nāmesa satto”ti. Tasmā “sakiṃ nimuggo nimuggo eva bālo”ti viya vaṭṭakhāṇujotanā, yādisehi pana paccayehi ayaṃ taṃ dassanaṃ okkanto puna kadāci micchattaniyāmo tappaṭikkhepapaccaye paṭicca tato sīsukkhepanamassa na hotīti na vattabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “yebhuyyenā”ti. Edisāti “buddhānampi atekicchā”tiādinā vuttasadisā.

Is this fixed only in this very existence, or also in another? It is fixed only in this very existence. For the unwholesome is indeed weak, not mighty like the wholesome. Otherwise, it would be absolute like the fixed state of rightness; but by way of repeated practice, in a future existence too, one delights in that very view. Therefore it is said: 'This being is indeed like a tethering post.' Therefore, the illustration of the tethering post is like 'once a fool is submerged, he remains submerged.' However, it should not be said that because this person has entered that view due to certain conditions, a lifting up of his head from it might not occur at some point in the future, dependent on counter-conditions for the rejection of that wrong fixedness. Therefore it is said: 'for the most part.' By 'such types' (edisā) is meant those similar to what is stated in the phrase beginning 'even the Buddhas find them incurable,' etc.

Attano [V 2.0254] nindābhayenāti “sammā diṭṭhiñca nāma te garahantī”tiādinā attano upari parehi vattabbanindābhayena. Ghaṭṭanabhayenāti tathā paresaṃ apasādanabhayena. Sahadhammena parena attano upari kātabbaniggaho upārambho, tato parittāso upārambhabhayaṃ. Taṃ pana atthato upavādabhayaṃ hotīti āha “upavādabhayenā”ti. Paṭippassaddhivasena abhijjhā vinayati etenāti abhijjhāvinayo, arahattaphalaṃ. Tenāha “abhijjhāvinayo vuccati arahatta”nti.

Out of fear of being reproached: meaning, out of fear of the blame others might direct at oneself, such as, 'They even disparage right view,' and so on. Out of fear of friction: meaning, out of fear of the disparagement of others. The censure or rebuke that another might inflict on oneself in accordance with the Dhamma is called 'upārambha'; the fear arising from that is 'upārambhabhaya.' This, in essence, is fear of reproach, hence it is said, 'out of fear of reproach.' 'The removal of covetousness' (abhijjhāvinayo) is so called because by this, through pacification, one removes covetousness; it is the fruit of arahantship. Therefore, it is said, 'the removal of covetousness is called arahantship.'

Paribbājakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Paribbājaka Sutta is concluded.

Uruvelavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Uruvela Vagga is concluded.

4. Cakkavaggo

4. The Chapter on the Wheel

1. Cakkasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Cakka Sutta

31. Catutthassa [M 2.0280] paṭhame cattāri cakkānīti ettha cakkaṃ nāma dārucakkaṃ, ratanacakkaṃ, dhammacakkaṃ, iriyāpathacakkaṃ, sampatticakkanti pañcavidhaṃ. Tattha “yaṃ panidaṃ, samma, rathakāracakkaṃ chahi māsehi niṭṭhitaṃ chārattūnehī”ti (a. ni. 3.15) idaṃ dārucakkaṃ. “Pitarā pavattitaṃ cakkaṃ anuvattetī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.215) idaṃ ratanacakkaṃ. “Mayā pavattitaṃ cakka”nti (su. ni. 562; bu. vaṃ. 27.17; jā. 1.1.104; 1.5.100, 103) idaṃ dhammacakkaṃ. “Catucakkaṃ navadvāra”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.29, 109) idaṃ iriyāpathacakkaṃ. “Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, cakkāni yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussānaṃ catucakkaṃ pavattatī”ti (a. ni. 4.31) idaṃ sampatticakkaṃ. Idhāpi etadeva adhippetanti āha “cattāri sampatticakkāni vattantī”ti. Anucchavike deseti puññakiriyāya sammāpaṭipattiyā anurūpadese. Sevanaṃ kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamanaṃ. Bhajanaṃ bhattivasena payirupāsanaṃ. Attano sammā ṭhapananti attano cittasantānassa yoniso ṭhapanaṃ. Saddhādīsu nivesananti āha “sace”tiādi. Idameva cettha pamāṇanti idameva pubbekatapuññatāsaṅkhātaṃ sampatticakkaṃ eva etesu sampatticakkesu pamāṇabhūtaṃ itaresaṃ kāraṇabhāvato[V 2.0255]. Tenāha “yena hī”tiādi. So eva ca katapuñño puggalo attānaṃ sammā ṭhapeti akatapuññassa tadabhāvato.

31. In the first sutta of the fourth vagga, regarding the four wheels: here, the term 'wheel' refers to five types—the wooden wheel, the jeweled wheel, the Dhamma wheel, the wheel of deportment, and the wheel of success. Among these, 'the wheel made by the chariot-maker, completed in six months, lacking six spokes' (AN 3.15) refers to the wooden wheel. 'He keeps rolling the wheel set in motion by his father' (SN 1.215) refers to the jeweled wheel. 'The wheel I have set in motion' (Snp 562; Bv 27.17; J 1.1.104; 1.5.100, 103) refers to the Dhamma wheel. 'Four-wheeled, nine-gated' (SN 1.29, 109) refers to the wheel of deportment. 'These four wheels, bhikkhus, endowed with which the four-wheeled vehicle of gods and humans rolls on' (AN 4.31) refers to the wheel of success. Here too, this is what is intended, as stated: 'the four wheels of success are turning.' 'Living in a suitable place' means in a place appropriate for meritorious deeds and right practice. 'Associating' means approaching from time to time. 'Serving' means attending with devotion. 'Establishing oneself rightly' means wisely establishing one’s own mental continuum. 'Establishing in faith, etc.' is as stated: 'if,' etc. This alone is the measure here—this very wheel of success, designated as past merit, is indeed the standard among these wheels of success, because it is the cause of the others. Hence it is said: 'for by which,' etc. And indeed, that meritorious person rightly establishes themselves, because one without merit lacks that.

Cakkasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cakka Sutta is concluded.

2. Saṅgahasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Saṅgaha Sutta

32. Dutiye tassa dānameva dātabbanti pabbajitassa pabbajitaparikkhāraṃ pattacīvarādi, gihino gihiparikkhāraṃ vatthāvudhayānasayanādi dātabbaṃ. Sabbanti sabbaṃ upakāraṃ. Makkhetvā nāseti makkhibhāve ṭhatvā. Telena viya makkhetīti satadhotatelena makkheti viya. Atthavaḍḍhanakathāti hitāvahakathā. Kathāgahaṇañcettha nidassanamattaṃ, paresaṃ hitāvaho kāyappayogopi [M 2.0281] atthacariyā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vacippayogavaseneva atthacariyā vuttā. Samānattatāti sadisabhāvo, samānaṭṭhāne ṭhapanaṃ, taṃ panassa samānaṭṭhapanaṃ attasadisatākaraṇamukhena ekasambhogatā. Attano sukhuppattiyaṃ tassa ca dukkhuppattiyaṃ tena dukkhena attanā ekasambhogatāti āha “samānasukhadukkhabhāvo”ti. Sā ca samānasukhadukkhatā ekato nisajjādinā pākaṭā hotīti dassento “ekāsane”tiādimāha.

32. In the second, 'what should be given is indeed giving to him' means: to the renunciant, a renunciant's requisites such as bowl and robes; to the householder, a householder's requisites such as clothes, weapons, vehicles, and beds. 'All' means every helpful thing. 'He destroys by smearing' means he does so while remaining in a state of hypocrisy. 'As if one smears with oil' means as if one smears with oil purified a hundred times. 'Benefit-increasing speech' means speech that brings welfare. Here, the mention of speech is merely an illustration; even bodily action that benefits others is beneficial conduct. In the commentary, however, beneficial conduct is explained only in terms of verbal action. 'Equality of self' means a similar nature, placing oneself in the same position; and that placing in the same position, by means of making oneself similar, is a shared experience. When happiness arises for oneself and suffering for that person, one has a shared experience with that suffering as one's own; thus it is said, 'a state of shared happiness and suffering.' And showing that this state of shared happiness and suffering becomes evident through sitting together and the like, he says, 'on one seat,' etc.

Tattha jātiyā hīno bhogena adhiko dussaṅgaho hoti. Na hi sakkā tena saddhiṃ ekaparibhogo kātuṃ jātiyā hīnattā. Tassa tathā akariyamāne ca so kujjhati bhogena adhikattā, tasmā so dussaṅgaho. Bhogena hīno jātiyā adhikopi dussaṅgaho hoti. So hi “ahaṃ jātimā”ti bhogasampannena saddhi ekaparibhogaṃ icchati, tasmiṃ akariyamāne kujjhati. Ubhohipi hīno susaṅgaho hoti. Na hi so itarena saddhiṃ ekaparibhogaṃ icchati jātiyā hīnabhāvato, na akariyamāno kujjhati bhogena hīnabhāvato. Ubhohi sadisopi susaṅgahoyeva. Sadisabhāveneva itarena saha ekaparibhogassa paccāsīsāya, akaraṇe ca tassa kujjhanassa abhāvato. Bhikkhu dussīlo dussaṅgaho hoti. Na hi sakkā tena saddhiṃ ekaparibhogaṃ kātuṃ, akariyamāne ca kujjhati. Sīlavā pana susaṅgaho hoti. Sīlavā hi adīyamānepi kismiñci āmise akariyamānepi saṅgahe na kujjhati, aññaṃ attanā saddhiṃ paribhogaṃ akarontampi na pāpakena cittena passati pesalabhāvato. Tato eva paribhogopi anena saddhiṃ sukaro hoti, tasmā gihi ce, ubhohi sadiso. Pabbajito ce, sīlavā puggalo[V 2.0256]. Evaṃ samānattatāya saṅgahetabbo. Tenevāha “so sace gahaṭṭhassa jātiyā pabbajitassa sīlena sadiso hoti, tassāyaṃ samānattatā kātabbā”ti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

In this context, one who is inferior in birth but superior in wealth is difficult to associate with. Indeed, it is not possible to have equal sharing with such a person due to their inferior birth. And when this is not done, they become angry because of their superior wealth; therefore, they are difficult to associate with. One who is inferior in wealth but superior in birth is also difficult to associate with. Thinking, 'I am of high birth,' they desire equal sharing with the wealthy one, and when this is not done, they become angry. One who is inferior in both respects is easy to associate with. They do not desire equal sharing with the other due to their inferiority in birth, nor do they become angry when it is not done, due to their inferiority in wealth. One who is equal in both respects is also easy to associate with, because, due to their similar nature, they expect equal sharing with the other, and there is no anger on their part when it is not done. An immoral bhikkhu is difficult to associate with. It is not possible to have equal sharing with them, and when it is not done, they become angry. A virtuous person, however, is easy to associate with. A virtuous person does not become angry even when not given any material things or when not shown support. Even if another does not share with them, they do not view that person with an evil mind, due to their amiable nature. Therefore, sharing with them is also easy. Thus, if it is a householder, one who is equal in both respects is to be associated with; if it is a renunciant, a virtuous person. In this way, they should be associated with through equality of self. Therefore it is said: 'If one is equal to a householder in birth, and to a renunciant in virtue, this equality of self should be practiced.' The rest is easily understood.

Saṅgahasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṅgaha Sutta is concluded.

3. Sīhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Sīha Sutta

33. Tatiye [M 2.0282] sīhoti parissayasahanato paṭipakkhahananato ca “sīho”ti laddhanāmo migādhipati. Cattāroti samānepi sīhajātibhāve vaṇṇavisesādisiddhena visesena cattāro sīhā. Te idāni nāmato vaṇṇato āhārato dassetvā idhādhippetasīhaṃ nānappakārato vibhāvetuṃ “tiṇasīho”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tiṇabhakkho sīho tiṇasīho purimapade uttarapadalopena yathā “sākapatthivo”ti (pāṇini 2.1.60). Kāḷavaṇṇatāya kāḷasīho. Tathā paṇḍusīho. Tenāha “kāḷagāvisadiso, paṇḍupalāsavaṇṇagāvisadiso”ti ca. Rattakambalassa viya kesaro kesarakalomo etassa atthīti kesarī. Lākhāparikammakatehi viya pādapariyantehīti ca yojanā.

33. In the third, 'lion' refers to the lord of beasts who has obtained the name 'lion' from enduring dangers and destroying adversaries. 'Four' means that although they are of the same lion species, there are four lions distinguished by specific differences established by color and so on. Now, having shown them by name, color, and food, in order to analyze the lion intended here in various ways, the section beginning 'grass-lion' is commenced. A lion that eats grass is a 'grass-lion,' with the elision of the latter part of the compound from the former part, as in 'sākapatthivo.' Due to its black color, it is a 'black-lion.' Similarly, a 'pale-lion.' Therefore, he said, 'resembling a black cow' and 'resembling a cow the color of a pale palāsa leaf.' 'Maned' (kesarī) means one who has a mane, a tuft of hair, like a red blanket. And the connection is to be made with 'the edges of its feet as if treated with lacquer'.

Kammānubhāvasiddhaadhipaccamahesakkhatāhi sabbamigagaṇassa rājā. Suvaṇṇaguhato vātiādi “sīhassa vihāro kiriyā evaṃ hotī”ti katvā vuttaṃ.

He is king of the entire herd of beasts, with sovereignty and great might established by the power of his kamma. The passage beginning 'from the golden cave' was said taking it that 'the lion's dwelling and activity is thus'.

Samaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvāti sabbabhāgehi samameva bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā. Ākaḍḍhitvāti purato ākaḍḍhitvā. Abhiharitvāti abhimukhaṃ haritvā. Saṅghātanti vināsaṃ. Vīsatiyaṭṭhikaṃ ṭhānaṃ usabhaṃ.

'Having placed it evenly' means having placed it evenly on the ground with all its parts. 'Having dragged it' means having dragged it forward. 'Having brought it' means having brought it toward. 'Saṅghāta' means destruction. A distance of twenty yaṭṭhis is an usabha.

Samasīhoti samajātiko samappabhāvo ca sīho. Samānosmīti desanāmattaṃ, samappabhāvatāya eva na bhāyati. Sakkāyadiṭṭhibalavatāyāti “ke aññe amhehi uttaritarā, atha kho mayameva mahābalā”ti evaṃ balātimānanimittāya ahaṃkārahetubhūtāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā balavabhāvena. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā pahīnattāti nirahaṃkārattā attasinehassa suṭṭhu samugghātattā na bhāyati.

'A sama-lion' means a lion of equal birth and equal power. 'I am equal' is merely a declaration; he does not fear precisely because of his equal power. 'Because of the strength of identity view' means by the powerful nature of identity view—which is the cause of egoism and the basis for conceit about strength—expressed as: 'Who else is superior to us? Indeed, we ourselves are very strong!' 'Because identity view is abandoned' means he does not fear due to the absence of egoism and the thorough eradication of self-affection.

Tathā [V 2.0257] tathāti sīhasadisatādinā tena tena pakārena attānaṃ kathesīti vatvā tamatthaṃ vivaritvā dassetuṃ “sīhoti kho”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Having said that 'thus, thus' means he described himself in this and that manner, by way of being like a lion and so on, the section beginning 'Indeed, a lion...' was stated in order to explain and show that meaning.

Katamahābhinīhārassa lokanāthassa bodhiyā niyatabhāvappattiyā ekantabhāvī buddhabhāvoti katvā “tīsu pāsādesu nivāsakālo[M 2.0283], magadharañño paṭiññādānakālo, pāyāsassa paribhuttakālo”tiādinā abhisambodhito purimāvatthāpi sīhasadisā katvā dassitā. Bhāvini bhūtūpacāropi hi lokavohāro. Vijjābhāvasāmaññato dvivijjaṃ itaravijjampi ekajjhaṃ gahetvā paṭiccasamuppādasammasanato taṃ puretarasiddhaṃ viya katvā āha “tisso vijjā sodhetvā”ti. Anulomapaṭilomato pavattañāṇassa vasena “yamakañāṇamanthanenā”ti vuttaṃ.

Considering that the Buddhahood of the World-Protector, who had made the great aspiration, was inevitable due to his having reached the state of certainty regarding enlightenment, even the states prior to his full awakening—such as 'the time spent dwelling in the three palaces, the time of giving the promise to the king of Magadha, the time of consuming the milk-rice'—were shown as being like a lion's. For it is a worldly convention to refer to a future event as if it were past. Due to the commonality of the state of knowledge, taking the two knowledges and the other knowledge together as one, and through thoroughly considering dependent origination, he spoke as if it were already accomplished, saying, 'having purified the three knowledges.' By means of the knowledge that proceeds forwards and backwards, it was said, 'by churning with the twin knowledge'.

Tattha viharantassāti ajapālanigrodhamūle viharantassa. Ekādasame divaseti sattasattāhato paraṃ ekādasame divase. Acalapallaṅketi isipatane dhammacakkappavattanatthaṃ nisinnapallaṅke. Tampi hi kenaci appaṭivattiyaṃ dhammacakkappavattanatthaṃ nisajjāti katvā vajirāsanaṃ viya acalapallaṅkaṃ vuccati. Imasmiñca pana padeti “dveme, bhikkhave, antā”tiādinayappavatte ca imasmiṃ saddhammakoṭṭhāse. Dhammaghoso…pe… dasasahassilokadhātuṃ paṭicchādesi “sabbattha ṭhitā suṇantū”ti adhiṭṭhānena. Soḷasahākārehīti dukkhapariññā, samudayappahānaṃ, nirodhasacchikiriyā, maggabhāvanāti ekekasmiṃ magge cattāri cattāri katvā soḷasahi ākārehi.

'Dwelling there' means dwelling at the root of the Ajapāla banyan tree. 'On the eleventh day' means on the eleventh day after seven weeks. 'The immovable seat' means the seat at Isipatana where he sat for the purpose of turning the Wheel of Dhamma. Indeed, that too is called the 'immovable seat,' like the Diamond Throne, because it was a sitting for the purpose of turning the Wheel of Dhamma, which could not be turned back by anyone. 'And in this passage' means in this section of the True Dhamma which proceeds in the manner beginning, 'These two extremes, O monks...' The sound of the Dhamma... covered the ten-thousandfold world-system with the determination, 'May those standing everywhere hear!' 'By sixteen aspects' means by sixteen aspects, making four for each of the four truths: the full understanding of suffering, the abandoning of its origin, the realization of cessation, and the development of the path.

Paṭhamena nayena abhisambodhito purimatarāvatthāpi avassaṃbhāvitāya gahetvā sīhasadisataṃ dassetvā idāni abhisambuddhāvatthāsu eva sīhasadisataṃ dassetuṃ “aparo nayo”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Aṭṭhahi kāraṇehīti “tathā āgatoti tathāgato, tathā gatoti tathāgato, tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato, tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato, tathadassitāya tathāgato, tathavāditāya tathāgato, tathākāritāya tathāgato, abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgato”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.12; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.78; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.170; udā. aṭṭha. 18; itivu. aṭṭha. 38; theragā. aṭṭha. 1.3; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 1.2 nidānakathā; mahāni. aṭṭha. 14; paṭi. ma. 1.37) evaṃ vuttehi aṭṭhahi tathāgatasādhakehi kāraṇehi. Yadipi bhagavā bodhipallaṅke nisinnamatteva abhisambuddho na jāto, tathāpi tāya nisajjāya nisinnova panujja sabbaṃ parissayaṃ abhisambuddho jāto. Tathā hi taṃ [V 2.0258] “aparājitapallaṅka”nti vuccati, tasmā “yāva bodhipallaṅkā vā”ti vatvā tena aparitussanto “yāva arahattamaggañāṇā vā”ti āha.

By the first method, having taken even the states prior to full enlightenment as inevitable and having shown their lion-like quality, now, to show the lion-like quality in the states of full enlightenment itself, the section beginning with 'another method' is commenced. By eight reasons: 'Because he has come thus, he is the Tathāgata; because he has gone thus, he is the Tathāgata; because he has come to the true characteristic, he is the Tathāgata; because he has fully awakened to the true dhammas as they are, he is the Tathāgata; because of seeing thus, he is the Tathāgata; because of speaking thus, he is the Tathāgata; because of acting thus, he is the Tathāgata; because of overcoming, he is the Tathāgata'—thus, by these eight reasons that establish the Tathāgata. Although the Blessed One did not become fully enlightened merely by sitting on the seat of awakening, nevertheless, by that very sitting, having dispelled all obstacles, he became fully enlightened. For that reason, it is called the 'unconquered seat.' Therefore, having said 'up to the seat of awakening,' and not being satisfied with that, he said 'up to the knowledge of the path of arahantship.'

Iti [M 2.0284] sakkāyoti ettha itisaddo nidassanattho. Tena sakkāyo sarūpato parimāṇato paricchedato ca dassitoti āha “ayaṃ sakkāyo”tiādi. “Ayaṃ sakkāyo”ti iminā pañcupādānakkhandhā sarūpato dassitā. “Ettako sakkāyo”ti iminā te parimāṇato dassitā. Tassa ca parimāṇassa ekantikabhāvaṃ dassentena “na ito bhiyyo sakkāyo atthī”ti vuttaṃ. Sabhāvatoti salakkhaṇato. Sarasatoti sakiccato. Pariyantatoti parimāṇapariyantato. Paricchedatoti yattake ṭhāne tassa pavattitassa paricchindanato. Parivaṭumatoti pariyosānappavattito. Sabbepi pañcupādānakkhandhā dassitā honti yathāvuttena vibhāgena. Ayaṃ sakkāyassa samudayo nāmāti ayaṃ āhārādisakkāyassa samudayo nāma. Tenāha “ettāvatā”tiādi. Atthaṅgamoti nirodho. “Āhārasamudayā āhāranirodhā”ti ca asādhāraṇameva taṃ gahetvā sesesu ādi-saddena saṅgaṇhāti.

Here, in 'iti sakkāyo' (thus, personal identity), the word 'iti' has the meaning of illustration. Therefore, to show personal identity in terms of its own nature, its measure, and its delimitation, he said, 'This is personal identity,' and so on. By 'This is personal identity,' the five aggregates subject to clinging are shown in terms of their own nature. By 'Such is the extent of personal identity,' they are shown in terms of their measure. And by indicating the definitive nature of that measure, it was said, 'There is no personal identity greater than this.' 'By its own nature' means by its specific characteristic. 'By its own function' means by its task. 'By its limit' means by the limit of its measure. 'By its delimitation' means by delimiting the sphere in which it occurs. 'By its final occurrence' means by its occurrence up to the end. All five aggregates subject to clinging are shown in this way, through the stated analysis. 'This is the origin of personal identity'—this is called the origin of personal identity through nutriment and so on. Hence he said, 'To this extent,' and so on. 'Passing away' means cessation. And taking that as specific, 'with the arising of nutriment, with the cessation of nutriment,' he includes the rest with the word 'ādi' (and so on).

Paṇṇāsalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitanti paṇṇāsaudayavayalakkhaṇavibhūsitaṃ samudayatthaṅgamaggahaṇato. Khīṇāsavattāti anavasesaṃ sāvasesañca āsavānaṃ parikkhīṇattā. Anāgāmīnampi hi bhayaṃ cittutrāsañca na hotīti. Ñāṇasaṃvego bhayatupaṭṭhānapaññā. Itarāsaṃ pana devatānanti akhīṇāsavadeve sandhāya vadati. Bhoti dhammālapanamattanti sabhāvakathanamattaṃ.

'Adorned with the fifty characteristics' means adorned with the fifty characteristics of arising and passing away, due to the comprehension of their origin and cessation. 'One whose taints are destroyed' means because the taints are completely exhausted, both those with and without remainder. For indeed, even for non-returners, there is no fear or mental terror. The spiritual urgency born of knowledge is the wisdom of the appearance of terror. As for 'the other deities,' he speaks with reference to deities whose taints are not destroyed. 'Bhoti' is merely a term of address, merely a statement of nature.

Cakkanti satthu āṇācakkaṃ. Taṃ pana dhammato āgatanti dhammacakkaṃ. Tattha ariyasāvakānaṃ paṭivedhadhammato āgatanti dhammacakkaṃ. Itaresaṃ desanādhammato āgatanti dhammacakkaṃ. Duvidhepi ñāṇaṃ padhānanti ñāṇasīsena vuttaṃ “paṭivedhañāṇampi desanāñāṇampī”ti. Idāni taṃ ñāṇaṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ “paṭivedhañāṇaṃ nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Yasmā tassa ñāṇassa paṭividdhattā bhagavā tāni saṭṭhi nayasahassāni veneyyānaṃ dassetuṃ samattho ahosi, tasmā tāni saṭṭhi nayasahassāni tena ñāṇena saddhiṃyeva siddhānīti katvā dassento “saṭṭhiyā ca nayasahassehi paṭivijjhī”ti āha. Tiparivaṭṭanti “idaṃ dukkha”nti ca “pariññeyya”nti ca “pariññāta”nti ca evaṃ tiparivaṭṭaṃ, taṃyeva dvādasākāraṃ. Tanti desanāñāṇaṃ. Esa bhagavā. Appaṭipuggaloti paṭinidhibhūtapuggalarahito. Ekasadisassāti nibbikārassa.

'The wheel' is the wheel of the Teacher’s command. That, however, is called the Wheel of the Dhamma because it comes from the Dhamma. Therein, for the noble disciples, it is called the Wheel of the Dhamma because it comes from the Dhamma as penetrated. For others, it is called the Wheel of the Dhamma because it comes from the Dhamma as taught. In both cases, knowledge is primary; thus, it is said under the heading of knowledge: 'both the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching.' Now, to show that knowledge according to its own nature, the section beginning 'The knowledge of penetration is...' was stated. Because the Blessed One, through having penetrated that knowledge, was able to show those sixty thousand methods to those who could be trained, therefore, showing that those sixty thousand methods were accomplished together with that knowledge, he said, 'He penetrated with sixty thousand methods.' 'The three turnings' are: 'This is suffering,' 'It is to be fully understood,' and 'It has been fully understood'—thus the three turnings, which are the same as the twelve aspects. That is the knowledge of teaching. This is the Blessed One. 'Without an equal person' means devoid of a counterpart. 'Of one who is unique' means of one who is unchangeable.

Sīhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sīha Sutta is concluded.

4. Aggapasādasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Aggappasāda Sutta

34. Catutthe [M 2.0285][V 2.0259] aggesu pasādāti seṭṭhesu pasādā. Aggā vā pasādāti seṭṭhabhūtā pasādā. Seṭṭhavacano hettha aggasaddo. Purimasmiṃ atthavikappe aggasaddena buddhādiratanattayaṃ vuccati. Tesu bhagavā tāva asadisaṭṭhena, guṇavisiṭṭhaṭṭhena, asamasamaṭṭhena ca aggo. So hi mahābhinīhāraṃ dasannaṃ pāramīnaṃ pavicayañca ādiṃ katvā bodhisambhāraguṇehi ceva buddhaguṇehi ca payojanehi ca sesajanehi asadisoti asadisaṭṭhenapi aggo. Ye cassa te guṇā mahākaruṇādayo, tehi sesasattānaṃ guṇehi visiṭṭhaṭṭhenapi sabbasattuttamatāya aggo. Ye pana purimakā sammāsambuddhā sabbasattehi asamā, tehi saddhiṃ ayameva rūpakāyaguṇehi ceva dhammakāyaguṇehi ca samoti asamasamaṭṭhenapi aggo. Tathā dullabhapātubhāvato acchariyamanussabhāvato bahujanahitasukhāvahato adutiyaasahāyādibhāvato ca bhagavā loke aggoti vuccati. Yathāha –

34. In the fourth sutta, 'confidence in the foremost' means confidence in the supreme. Or, 'confidence that is foremost' means confidence that has become supreme. Here, the word 'agga' has the meaning of 'foremost.' In the former interpretation, the word 'agga' refers to the Triple Gem, beginning with the Buddha. Among these, the Blessed One is foremost by being incomparable, by being distinguished in qualities, and by being equal to the unequaled. For he, having made the great aspiration and the investigation of the ten perfections his starting point, is incomparable to other people by reason of the qualities that are the requisites for enlightenment, the qualities of a Buddha, and his purposes; thus he is foremost by being incomparable. And those qualities of his, such as great compassion, are superior to the qualities of other beings; thus he is foremost by being the highest of all beings. And those past Perfectly Enlightened Ones were unequaled by all beings; yet this very one is equal to them in the qualities of his physical body and the qualities of his Dhamma-body; thus he is foremost by being equal to the unequaled. Similarly, the Blessed One is called the foremost in the world due to his rare appearance, his marvelous human nature, his bringing of welfare and happiness to many people, and his being without a second, without a companion, and so forth. As it is said:

“Ekapuggalassa, bhikkhave, pātubhāvo dullabho lokasmiṃ. Katamassa ekapuggalassa? Tathāgatassa arahato sammāsammuddhassa. Ekapuggalo, bhikkhave, loke uppajjamāno uppajjati acchariyamanusso. Ekapuggalo, bhikkhave, loke uppajjamāno uppajjati bahujana…pe… sammāsambuddho. Ekapuggalo, bhikkhave, loke uppajjamāno uppajjati adutiyo asahāyo appaṭimo appaṭibhāgo appaṭipuggalo asamo asamasamo dvipadānaṃ aggo. Katamo ekapuggalo? Tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti (a. ni. 1.171-173).

“Bhikkhus, the appearance of one individual is rare in the world. Of which one individual? Of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Bhikkhus, one individual, arising in the world, arises as a marvelous human being. Bhikkhus, one individual, arising in the world, arises for the welfare of many people… the Perfectly Enlightened One. Bhikkhus, one individual, arising in the world, arises as second to none, without a companion, without a match, without a peer, without a counterpart, unequaled, equal to the unequaled, the foremost of bipeds. Which one individual? The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”

Dhammasaṅghā aññadhammasaṅghehi asadisaṭṭhena visiṭṭhaguṇatāya dullabhapātubhāvādinā ca aggā. Tathā hi tesaṃ svākkhātatādisuppaṭipannatādiguṇavisesehi aññe dhammasaṅghasadisā appataraṃ nihīnā vā natthi, kuto seṭṭhā. Sayameva tehi visiṭṭhaguṇatāya seṭṭhā. Tathā dullabhuppādaacchariyabhāvabahujanahitasukhāvahaadutiyāsahāyādisabhāvā ca te. Yadaggena hi bhagavā dullabhapātubhāvo, tadaggena [M 2.0286] dhammasaṅghāpīti. Acchariyādīsupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ aggesu seṭṭhesu uttamesu pavaresu guṇavisiṭṭhesu pasādāti aggappasadā.

The Dhamma and the Sangha are foremost in comparison to other Dhammas and Sanghas by being incomparable, by their distinguished qualities, and by their rare appearance, and so forth. Indeed, in such distinguished qualities as being well-proclaimed and well-practiced, there are no other Dhammas and Sanghas similar to them, or even slightly inferior, let alone superior. They themselves are supreme by reason of their distinguished qualities. Similarly, they are of the nature of rare arising, marvelous, bringing welfare and happiness to many, without a second, without a companion, and so forth. For in the same respect that the Blessed One is of rare appearance, so too are the Dhamma and the Sangha. The same method applies to their marvelous nature and so forth. Thus, confidence in the foremost—the supreme, the highest, the excellent, those distinguished in qualities—is 'supreme confidence.'

Dutiyasmiṃ panatthe yathāvuttesu aggesu buddhādīsu uppattiyā aggabhūtā pasādā aggappasādā. Ye pana ariyamaggena āgatā aveccappasādā, te ekanteneva aggabhūtā pasādāti aggappasādā. Yathāha – “idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako buddhe aveccappasādena samannāgato [V 2.0260] hotī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.1037-1038). Aggavipākattāpi cete aggappasādā. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “agge kho pana pasannānaṃ aggo vipāko”ti (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90).

In the second meaning, however, the confidence that arises in the aforementioned foremost ones, such as the Buddha, is foremost, hence it is “supreme confidence.” And those unwavering instances of confidence that have come about through the noble path are, without doubt, confidence that has become foremost, hence “supreme confidence.” As it is said: “Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha,” and so on (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1037-1038). And these are also “supreme confidence” because they have supreme results. And it has been said: “For those who are confident in the foremost, the result is foremost” (A. Ni. 4.34; Itivu. 90).

Apadā vātiādīsu vā-saddo samuccayattho, na vikappattho. Yathā “anuppanno vā kāmāsavo uppajjati, uppanno vā kāmāsavo pavaḍḍhatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.17) ettha anuppanno ca uppanno cāti attho. Yathā ca “bhūtānaṃ vā sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā sambhavesīnaṃ vā anuggahāyā”ti ettha bhūtānañca sambhavesīnañcāti attho. Yathā ca “aggito vā udakato vā mithubhedato vā”ti (dī. ni. 2.152) ettha aggito ca udakato ca mithubhedato cāti attho, evaṃ “apadā vā…pe… aggamakkhāyatī”ti (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) etthāpi apadā ca dvipadā cāti sampiṇḍanavasena attho daṭṭhabbo. Tena vuttaṃ “vā-saddo samuccayattho, na vikappattho”ti.

In “apadā vā” and so forth, the word “vā” has the meaning of conjunction, not disjunction. For example, in “the unarisen canker of sensual desire arises, and the arisen canker of sensual desire increases” (Ma. Ni. 1.17), the meaning is “both the unarisen and the arisen.” And just as in “for the maintenance of beings that have come into existence, and for the support of those who are coming into existence,” the meaning is “both for beings that have come into existence and for those who are coming into existence.” And just as in “from fire, and from water, and from the breaking of alliances” (Dī. Ni. 2.152), the meaning is “from fire, and from water, and from the breaking of alliances.” Likewise, in “apadā vā… and so forth… is declared the foremost” (A. Ni. 4.34; Itivu. 90), the meaning should be understood in the sense of combining “footless” and “two-footed.” Therefore it is said: “The word ‘vā’ has the meaning of conjunction, not disjunction.”

Rūpinoti rūpavanto. Na rūpinoti arūpino. Saññinoti saññavanto. Na saññinoti asaññino. “Apadā vā”tiādisabbapadehi kāmabhavo, rūpabhavo, arūpabhavo, ekavokārabhavo, catuvokārabhavo, pañcavokārabhavo, saññibhavo, asaññibhavo, nevasaññināsaññibhavoti navavidhepi bhave sattepi anavasesato pariyādiyitvā dasseti. Ettha hi rūpiggahaṇena kāmabhavo, rūpabhavo, pañcavokārabhavo, ekavokārabhavo ca dassito, arūpiggahaṇena arūpabhavo, catuvokārabhavo ca dassito, saññibhavādayo pana sarūpeneva dassitā. Apadādiggahaṇena kāmabhavapañcavokārabhavasaññibhavānaṃ ekadesova dassito.

“Rūpī” means possessing form. “Na rūpī” means formless. “Saññī” means possessing perception. “Na saññī” means without perception. By all the terms beginning with “apadā vā,” it shows beings completely and without remainder in all nine kinds of existence: sensual existence, form existence, formless existence, existence with one constituent, existence with four constituents, existence with five constituents, existence with perception, existence without perception, and existence with neither perception nor non-perception. Here, by the inclusion of “rūpī,” sensual existence, form existence, existence with five constituents, and existence with one constituent are shown; by the inclusion of “arūpī,” formless existence and existence with four constituents are shown; but existence with perception and the others are shown by their own forms. By the inclusion of “apadā” and so forth, only a part of sensual existence, existence with five constituents, and existence with perception is shown.

Kasmā [M 2.0287] panettha yathā adutiyasutte “dvipadānaṃ aggo”ti dvipadā eva gahitā, evaṃ dvipadaggahaṇameva akatvā apadādiggahaṇaṃ katanti? Vuccate – adutiyasutte tāva seṭṭhataravasena dvipadaggahaṇameva kataṃ. Imasmiñhi loke seṭṭho nāma uppajjamāno apadacatuppadabahupadesu na uppajjati, dvipadesuyeva uppajjati. Kataresu dvipadesu? Manussesu ceva devesu ca. Manussesu uppajjamāno sakalalokaṃ vase vattetuṃ samattho buddho hutvā uppajjati, devesu uppajjamāno dasasahassilokadhātuṃ vase vattanako mahābrahmā hutvā uppajjati, so tassa kappiyakārako vā ārāmiko vā sampajjati. Iti tatopi seṭṭhataravasenesa dvipadānaṃ aggoti tattha vuttaṃ. Idha pana anavasesapariyādānavasena evaṃ vuttaṃ “yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā…pe… nevasaññināsaññino vā, tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti[V 2.0261]. Niddhāraṇe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Ma-kāro padasandhikaro, aggo akkhāyatīti padavibhāgo. Tenevāha “guṇehi aggo”tiādi.

Why here, unlike in the Adutiyasutta where only bipeds are taken, as in 'the foremost of bipeds,' is the inclusion of 'footless' and so forth made, instead of just the inclusion of bipeds? It is said: In the Adutiyasutta, the inclusion of bipeds was made precisely in terms of greater excellence. For in this world, the foremost being, when arising, does not arise among footless, four-footed, or many-footed creatures, but only among bipeds. Among which bipeds? Humans and devas. When arising among humans, he arises as a Buddha, capable of bringing the entire world under his sway; when arising among devas, he arises as a Great Brahmā, capable of bringing the ten-thousandfold world-system under his sway, and that Great Brahmā becomes his (the Buddha's) proper attendant or monastery attendant. Thus, it is said there, 'the foremost of bipeds,' in terms of greater excellence. Here, however, it is stated in terms of exhaustive comprehensiveness: 'Bhikkhus, as far as beings—whether footless… or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared their foremost.' And this is a genitive case of determination. The syllable 'ma' is a word-connector, and the word division is 'foremost is declared.' Therefore it is said, 'foremost in qualities,' and so forth.

Aggo vipāko hotīti agge sammāsambuddhe pasannānaṃ yo pasādo aggo seṭṭho uttamakoṭibhūto vā, tasmā tassa vipākopi aggo seṭṭho uttamakoṭibhūto uḷāratamo paṇītatamo hoti. So pana pasādo duvidho lokiyalokuttarabhedato. Tesu lokiyassa tāva –

“The foremost result occurs” means that for those who have confidence in the foremost, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the confidence that is foremost, supreme, or of the highest kind, therefore its result is also foremost, supreme, of the highest kind, most excellent, and most sublime. And that confidence is twofold, by way of worldly and supramundane. Among these, the worldly is as follows:

“Ye keci buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse,

Na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ;

Pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ,

Devakāyaṃ paripūressanti. (dī. ni. 2.332; itivu. aṭṭha. 90; saṃ. ni. 1.37);

“Those who have gone to the Buddha for refuge will not go to the states of woe. Having abandoned the human body, they will fill the ranks of the devas.” (Dī. Ni. 2.332; Itivu. Aṭṭha. 90; Saṃ. Ni. 1.37)

“Buddhoti kittayantassa, kāye bhavati yā pīti;

Varameva hi sā pīti, kasiṇenapi jambudīpassa. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.6; itivu. aṭṭha. 90);

“The joy that arises in the body of one who extols ‘Buddha’—that joy is indeed supreme, better than sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa.” (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.6; Itivu. Aṭṭha. 90)

“Sataṃ hatthī sataṃ assā, sataṃ assatarīrathā;

Sataṃ kaññāsahassāni, āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalā;

Ekassa padavītihārassa, kalaṃ nāgghanti soḷasiṃ”. (cūḷava. 305);

“A hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred mule-drawn chariots, a hundred thousand maidens adorned with jeweled earrings, are not worth a sixteenth part of a single footstep.” (Cūḷava. 305)

“Sādhu [M 2.0288] kho, devānaminda, buddhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ hoti, buddhaṃ saraṇagamanahetu kho, devānaminda, evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjanti. Te aññe deve dasahi ṭhānehi adhiggaṇhanti dibbena āyunā, dibbena vaṇṇena, dibbena sukhena, dibbena yasena, dibbena ādhipateyyena, dibbehi rūpehi, dibbehi saddehi, dibbehi gandhehi, dibbehi rasehi, dibbehi phoṭṭhabbehī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.341) –

“Good indeed, O Sakka, lord of devas, is going to the Buddha for refuge. Because of going to the Buddha for refuge, some beings here, after the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, the heavenly world. They excel other devas in ten respects: divine lifespan, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, divine sovereignty, divine forms, divine sounds, divine scents, divine tastes, and divine tactile objects.” (Saṃ. Ni. 4.341)

Evamādīnaṃ suttapadānaṃ vasena pasādaphalavisesayogo veditabbo, tasmā so apāyadukkhavinivattanena saddhiṃ sampattibhavesu sukhavisesadāyakova daṭṭhabbo.

By means of such sutta passages, the specific connection of the fruit of confidence should be understood. Therefore, it should be seen as a giver of specific happiness in fortunate existences, together with the removal of suffering in the states of woe.

Lokuttaro [V 2.0262] pana sāmaññaphalavipākadāyako vaṭṭadukkhavinivattako. Sabbopi cāyaṃ pasādo paramparāya vaṭṭadukkhaṃ vinivattetiyeva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

But the supramundane confidence gives the result of the fruits of recluseship and averts the suffering of the round. And all this confidence, in succession, averts the suffering of the round. For it has been said:

“Yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako attano saddhaṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosapariyuṭṭhitaṃ…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti, ujugatacittassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

“Monks, at the time when a noble disciple recollects their own confidence, their mind is not overcome by lust, not overcome by hate… not overcome by delusion. At that time, their mind is indeed straight. With a straight mind, gladness arises; for one who is gladdened, rapture arises… and they understand: ‘There is nothing further for this state of being.’”

Dhammāti sabhāvadhammā. Saṅkhatāti samecca sambhūya paccayehi katāti saṅkhatā, sapaccayā dhammā. Hetūhi paccayehi ca na kehici katā saṅkhatāti asaṅkhatā, apaccayo nibbānaṃ. Saṅkhatānaṃ pariyositabhāvena “asaṅkhatā”ti puthuvacanaṃ. Virāgo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatīti tesaṃ saṅkhatāsaṅkhatadhammānaṃ yo virāgasaṅkhāto asaṅkhatadhammo, so sabhāveneva saṇhasukhumabhāvato santatarapaṇītatarabhāvato gambhīrādibhāvato madanimmadanādibhāvato aggaṃ seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ pavaranti vuccati. Yadidanti nipāto, yo ayanti attho. Madanimmadanotiādīni sabbāni nibbānavevacanāni. Tenevāha “virāgotiādīni nibbānasseva nāmānī”ti. Rāgamadādayoti ādi-saddena mānamadapurisamadādike saṅgaṇhāti[M 2.0289]. Sabbā pipāsāti kāmapipāsādikā sabbā pipāsā. Sabbe ālayā samugghātaṃ gacchantīti kāmālayādikā sabbepi ālayā samugghātaṃ yanti. Vaṭṭānīti kammavaṭṭavipākavaṭṭāni. Taṇhāti aṭṭhasatappabhedā sabbāpi taṇhā.

Phenomena means states in their own nature. Conditioned means made by causes, having come together and arisen together; thus, conditioned states are those with causes. Unconditioned means not made by any causes or conditions; the unconditioned is Nibbāna, which is without cause. The plural term 'unconditioned' is used because of the cessation of conditioned things. Dispassion is declared the highest among them: that unconditioned state called dispassion, among both conditioned and unconditioned states, is said to be the highest, the best, the supreme, the most excellent, by its very nature, due to its subtle and refined quality, its more peaceful and sublime quality, its profundity, and its power to dispel intoxication and the like. 'Yadidaṃ' is a particle meaning 'that which is this.' All terms like 'dispeller of intoxication' and so forth are synonyms for Nibbāna. Hence it is said: 'Dispassion and the like are solely names for Nibbāna.' In 'intoxications such as lust,' by the word 'etc.' intoxications like conceit and intoxication concerning persons are included. 'All thirsts' means all thirsts, such as thirst for sensual pleasures. 'All attachments are uprooted' means all attachments, such as attachment to sensual pleasures, are uprooted. 'The cycles' means the cycles of kamma and the cycles of its results. 'Craving' means all craving, with its one hundred and eight divisions.

Aggo vipāko hotīti etthāpi –

Here too, the highest result occurs:

“Ye keci dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse…pe…”. (dī. ni. 2.332; saṃ ni. 1.37);

“Whatever beings have gone to the Dhamma for refuge…” (Dī. Ni. 2.332; Saṃ. Ni. 1.37);

“Dhammoti kittayantassa, kāye bhavati yā pīti…pe…”. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.6; itivu. aṭṭha. 90);

“For one proclaiming ‘Dhamma,’ the joy that arises in the body…” (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.6; Itivu. Aṭṭha. 90);

“Sādhu kho, devānaminda, dhammaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ hoti, dhammaṃ saraṇagamanahetu kho, devānaminda, evamidhekacce…pe… dibbehi phoṭṭhabbehī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.341) –

“Good indeed, O lord of devas, is going for refuge to the Dhamma. Because of going for refuge to the Dhamma, O lord of devas, some here… with divine tactile objects.” (Saṃ. Ni. 4.341)

Evamādīnaṃ [V 2.0263] suttapadānaṃ vasena dhamme pasādassa phalavisesayogo veditabbo.

By means of such sutta passages, the connection to the special fruit of faith in the Dhamma should be understood.

Saṅghā vā gaṇā vāti janasamūhasaṅkhātā yāvatā loke saṅghā vā gaṇā vā. Tathāgatasāvakasaṅghoti aṭṭhaariyapuggalasamūhasaṅkhāto diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhato tathāgatassa sāvakasaṅgho. Aggamakkhāyatīti attano sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttiādiguṇavisesena tesaṃ saṅghānaṃ aggo seṭṭho uttamo pavaroti vuccati. Yadidanti yāni imāni. Cattāri purisayugāni yugaḷavasena, paṭhamamaggaṭṭho paṭhamaphalaṭṭhoti idamekaṃ yugaḷaṃ, yāva catutthamaggaṭṭho catutthaphalaṭṭhoti idamekaṃ yugaḷanti evaṃ cattāri purisayugāni. Aṭṭha purisapuggalāti purisapuggalavasena eko paṭhamamaggaṭṭho, eko paṭhamaphalaṭṭhoti iminā nayena aṭṭha purisapuggalā. Ettha ca purisoti vā puggaloti vā ekatthāni etāni padāni, veneyyavasena panevaṃ vuttaṃ. Esa bhagavato sāvakasaṅghoti yānimāni yugaḷavasena cattāri yugāni pāṭiyekkato aṭṭha purisapuggalā, esa bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho. Āhuneyyotiādīni vuttatthāneva. Idhāpi –

“Saṅghas or gaṇas” refers to whatever groups or assemblies of people are known in the world as a ‘saṅgha’ or a ‘gaṇa’. “The Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's disciples” means the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's disciples, which is the assembly of the eight noble individuals, united by a commonality of view and virtue. “It is declared supreme” means that, due to its own distinction in qualities such as virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation, this Saṅgha is called the highest, the best, the supreme, the excellent of those saṅghas. “Yadidaṃ” means “these which are.” “The four pairs of persons” means in terms of pairs: the one established in the first path and the one established in the first fruition—this is one pair; up to the one established in the fourth path and the one established in the fourth fruition—this is one pair. Thus there are four pairs of persons. “The eight individual persons” refers to the eight persons counted individually: one established in the first path, one established in the first fruition, and so on; in this manner, there are eight individual persons. Here, the terms “purisa” (person) and “puggala” (individual) have the same meaning; it is said thus for the sake of those to be trained. “This is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples” means these four pairs of persons, or individually the eight individual persons, constitute the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples. The terms “āhuneyya” (worthy of offerings), etc., have the same meaning as was stated. Here too:

“Ye keci saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse…pe…”. (dī. ni. 2.332; saṃ. ni. 1.37);

“Whatever beings have gone to the Sangha for refuge…” (Dī. Ni. 2.332; Saṃ. Ni. 1.37);

“Saṅghoti kittayantassa, kāye bhavati yā pīti…pe…”. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.6; itivu. aṭṭha. 90);

“For one proclaiming ‘Sangha,’ the joy that arises in the body…” (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.6; Itivu. Aṭṭha. 90);

“Sādhu [M 2.0290] kho, devānaminda, saṅghaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ hoti, saṅghaṃ saraṇagamanahetu kho, devānaminda…pe… dibbehi phoṭṭhabbehī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.341) –

“Good indeed, O lord of devas, is going for refuge to the Sangha. Because of going for refuge to the Sangha, O lord of devas… with divine tactile sensations.” (Saṃ. Ni. 4.341)

Ādīnaṃ suttapadānaṃ vasena saṅghe pasādassa phalavisesayogo tassa aggavipākatā ca veditabbā. Tathā anuttariyapaṭilābho sattamabhavādito paṭṭhāya vaṭṭadukkhasamucchedo anuttarasukhādhigamoti evamādiuḷāraphalanipphādanavasena aggavipākatā veditabbā.

By means of such sutta passages, the connection to the special fruit of faith in the Sangha and its supreme result should be understood. Likewise, its supreme result should be understood by way of producing such abundant results as the attainment of the unsurpassed, the cutting off of the suffering of the round of existence beginning from the seventh existence, and the attainment of unsurpassed happiness.

Gāthāsu aggatoti agge ratanattaye, aggabhāvato vā pasannānaṃ. Aggaṃ dhammanti aggasabhāvaṃ buddhasubodhiṃ dhammasudhammataṃ saṅghasuppaṭipattiṃ, ratanattayassa anaññasādhāraṇaṃ uttamasabhāvaṃ, dasabalādisvākkhātatādisuppaṭipannatādiguṇasabhāvaṃ vā. Vijānatanti vijānantānaṃ. Evaṃ sādhāraṇato aggappasādavatthuṃ dassetvā idāni asādhāraṇato taṃ vibhāgena dassetuṃ [V 2.0264] “agge buddhe”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha pasannānanti aveccappasādena ca itarappasādena ca pasannānaṃ adhimuttānaṃ. Virāgūpasameti virāge upasame ca, sabbassa rāgassa sabbesaṃ kilesānaṃ accantavirāgahetubhūte accantaupasamahetubhūte cāti attho. Sukheti vaṭṭadukkhakkhayabhāvena saṅkhārūpasamasukhabhāvena sukhe.

In the verses, 'aggato' means in the supreme Triple Gem, or because of the supreme state of those who are faithful. 'Aggaṃ dhammaṃ' refers to the supreme nature—the Buddha’s perfect awakening, the Dhamma’s perfect state, and the Sangha’s perfect practice; the unparalleled, supreme nature of the Triple Gem; or the nature of their qualities, such as the ten powers and so on, being well-proclaimed and so on, and being of good practice and so on. 'Vijānataṃ' means for those who understand. Thus, having shown the object of supreme faith in a general sense, now to explain it distinctly by way of its specific aspects, it is said: 'in the supreme Buddha' and so on. Here, 'pasannānaṃ' refers to those who are faithful with unwavering faith and with other faith, those who are resolved. 'Virāgūpasame' means in dispassion and pacification—that is, being the cause for the utter dispassion from all lust and the utter pacification of all defilements. 'Sukhe' means in happiness, due to the destruction of the suffering of the round of existence and due to the happiness that is the pacification of formations.

Aggasmiṃ dānaṃ dadatanti agge ratanattaye dānaṃ dadantānaṃ deyyadhammaṃ pariccajantānaṃ. Tattha dharamānaṃ bhagavantaṃ catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahantā pūjentā sakkarontā, parinibbutaṃ bhagavantaṃ uddissa dhātucetiyādike upaṭṭhahantā pūjentā sakkarontā buddhe dānaṃ dadanti nāma. “Dhammaṃ pūjessāmā”ti dhammadhare puggale catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahantā pūjentā sakkarontā dhammañca ciraṭṭhitikaṃ karontā dhamme dānaṃ dadanti nāma. Tathā ariyasaṅghaṃ catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahantā pūjentā sakkarontā taṃ uddissa itarasmimpi tathā paṭipajjantā saṅghe dānaṃ dadanti nāma. Aggaṃ puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti evaṃ ratanattaye pasannena cetasā uḷāraṃ pariccāgaṃ uḷārañca pūjāsakkāraṃ pavattentānaṃ divase divase aggaṃ uḷāraṃ kusalaṃ upacīyati. Idāni tassa puññassa aggavipākatāya aggabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “aggaṃ āyū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha āyūti dibbaṃ vā mānusaṃ vā aggaṃ uḷāraṃ paramaṃ āyu pavaḍḍhati uparūpari [M 2.0291] brūhati. Vaṇṇoti rūpasampadā. Yasoti parivārasampadā. Kittīti thutighoso. Sukhanti kāyikaṃ cetasikañca sukhaṃ. Balanti kāyabalañceva ñāṇabalañca.

“Giving a gift to the supreme” means giving a gift to the supreme Triple Gem, relinquishing an offering. Here, those who serve, revere, and honor the Blessed One with the four requisites while he is living, or who serve, revere, and honor relic-shrines and so on dedicated to the Blessed One after he has attained parinibbāna, are said to give a gift to the Buddha. Those who think, “We will revere the Dhamma,” and serve, revere, and honor individuals who uphold the Dhamma with the four requisites, and who make the Dhamma long-lasting, are said to give a gift to the Dhamma.
