Similarly, those who serve, revere, and honor the noble Sangha with the four requisites, and who, on their account, practice similarly towards others as well, are said to give a gift to the Sangha. “Supreme merit increases” means that for those who, with a faithful mind in the Triple Gem, engage in great relinquishment and great reverence and honor, supreme, abundant wholesome merit accumulates day by day. Now, to show the supreme state of that merit by way of its supreme result, it is said: “supreme lifespan” and so on. Here, “lifespan” means that a divine or human supreme, abundant, ultimate lifespan increases and grows ever more. “Vaṇṇa” means perfection of form. “Yasa” means perfection of retinue. “Kitti” means the sound of praise. “Sukha” means physical and mental happiness. “Bala” means both bodily strength and the strength of wisdom.

Aggassa ratanattayassa dānaṃ dātā. Atha vā aggassa deyyadhammassa dānaṃ uḷāraṃ katvā tattha puññaṃ pavattetā. Aggadhammasamāhitoti aggena pasādadhammena dānādidhammena ca saṃhito samannāgato acalappasādayutto, tassa vā vipākabhūtehi bahujanassa piyamanāpatādidhammehi yutto. Aggappatto pamodatīti yattha yattha sattanikāye uppanno, tattha tattha aggabhāvaṃ seṭṭhabhāvaṃ adhigato, aggabhāvaṃ vā lokuttaramaggaphalaṃ adhigato pamodati abhiramati paritussatīti.

A giver of a gift to the supreme Triple Gem. Or, having made an abundant gift of a supreme offering, one who generates merit therein. “Composed in the supreme Dhamma” means endowed and possessed with the supreme quality of faith and the quality of giving and so on, possessed of unshakable faith; or, possessed of the qualities that are its results, such as being dear and pleasant to many people. “Having attained the supreme, one rejoices” means that wherever one is born in a class of beings, there one attains the supreme state, the most excellent state; or, having attained the supreme state of the supramundane path and fruition, one rejoices, delights, and is greatly pleased.

Aggapasādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Aggapasādasutta is completed.

5. Vassakārasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Vassakārasutta

35. Pañcame [V 2.0265] ariye ñāyeti saṃkilesato ārakattā ariye niddose parisuddhe niyyānikadhammabhāvato ñāye kāraṇeti attho. Ñāyati nicchayena kamati nibbānaṃ, taṃ vā ñāyati paṭivijjhīyati etenātī ñāyo, ariyamaggo. So eva ca sampāpakahetubhāvato kāraṇanti vuccati. Idha pana saha vipassanāya ariyamaggo adhippetoti āha “sahavipassanake magge”ti. Gāthāsu “ñāyaṃ dhamma”nti etthāpi eseva nayo.

35. In the fifth, regarding 'in the noble path': it is noble because it is far from defilements; the meaning is 'in the path, in the cause' because it is faultless, pure, and has the nature of a liberating dhamma. One decisively goes towards Nibbāna, or Nibbāna is known and penetrated by it—hence, it is the path, the Noble Path. And it is also called 'cause' because it is the condition for attainment. Here, however, the Noble Path along with insight is intended, as stated: 'in the path together with insight.' In the verses, regarding 'the Dhamma as the path,' here too, this is the method.

Vassakārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta is finished.

6. Doṇasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Doṇa Sutta

36. Chaṭṭhe ukkāhi dhāriyamānāhīti dīpikāhi dhāriyamānāhi, daṇḍadīpikāsu jāletvā dhāriyamānāsu māpitattāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tañhi nagaraṃ “maṅgaladivase sukhaṇe sunakkhattaṃ mā atikkamī”ti rattimpi ukkāsu dhāriyamānāsu māpitaṃ. Ukkāsu ṭhāti ukkaṭṭhā, ukkāsu vijjotayantīsu [M 2.0292] ṭhitā patiṭṭhitāti mūlavibhūjādipakkhepena (pāṇini 3.2.5) saddasiddhi veditabbā. Niruttinayena vā ukkāsu ṭhitāsu ṭhitā āsīti ukkaṭṭhā. Apare pana bhaṇanti “bhūmibhāgasampattiyā manussasampattiyā upakaraṇasampattiyā ca sā nagarī ukkaṭṭhaguṇayogato ukkaṭṭhāti nāmaṃ labhatī”ti. Setabyanti tassa nagarassa nāmaṃ. Taṃ pana kassapadasabalassa jātanagaranti āha “atīte kassapasammāsambuddhassa jātanagara”nti.

36. In the sixth, 'being held by torches' means being held by lamps; that is, it is said to have been laid out while torches were lit and held on poles. For that city was laid out even at night with torches held aloft, with the thought, 'On the auspicious day, at an auspicious moment, may the auspicious constellation not pass by.' 'Ukkaṭṭhā' means 'standing amidst torches'; when torches are blazing, it stands established—this derivation of the word should be understood through the root mūlavibhūjādi with the pakkhepa suffix (Pāṇini 3.2.5). Alternatively, according to etymological analysis, 'ukkaṭṭhā' means 'it stood when torches were standing.' Others, however, say: 'Due to the excellence of its location, the excellence of its people, and the excellence of its resources, that city acquired the name "Ukkaṭṭhā" because of its connection with superior qualities.' 'Setabya' is the name of that city. It is said to be the birthplace of Kassapa Dasabala, thus it is said: 'In the past, it was the birthplace of the Fully Enlightened Buddha Kassapa.'

Vijjantarikāyāti vijjuniccharaṇakkhaṇe. Antaratoti hadaye. Antarāti ārambhanibbattīnaṃ vemajjhe. Antarikāyāti antarāḷe. Ettha ca “tadantaraṃ ko jāneyya (a. ni. 6.44; 10.75), etesaṃ antarā kappā gaṇanato asaṅkhyeyyā (bu. vaṃ. 28.3), antarantarā kathaṃ opapātetī”ti (ma. ni. 2.426) ca ādīsu viya kāraṇavemajjhesu vattamānā antarāsaddā eva udāharitabbā siyuṃ, na pana cittakkhaṇavivaresu vattamānā antaraantarikasaddā. Antarāsaddassa hi ayamatthuddhāroti.

'Vijjantarikāya' means at the moment of lightning's discharge. 'Antarato' means in the heart. 'Antarā' means in the middle of arising and production. 'Antarikāya' means in the interval. And here, as in examples like: 'Who could know that interval?' (A.N. 6.44; 10.75), 'Between these, aeons are countless in calculation' (Bu.Va. 28.3), 'How could one be reborn in the intervening existences?' (M.N. 2.426)—the word 'antarā' should be cited as referring to causal intervals, not the words 'antara' and 'antarika' as referring to intervals between moments of consciousness. This is, indeed, the explanation of the meaning of the word 'antarā.'

Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo siyā – yesu antarāsaddo vattati, tesu antarasaddopi vattatīti samānatthattā antarāsaddatthe vattamāno antarasaddo udāhaṭo. Antarāsaddo eva vā “yassantarato”ti [V 2.0266] ettha gāthāsukhatthaṃ rassaṃ katvā vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Antarāsaddo eva pana ikasaddena padaṃ vaḍḍhetvā “antarikā”ti vuttoti evamettha udāharaṇodāharitabbānaṃ virodhābhāvo daṭṭhabbo. Ayojiyamāne upayogavacanaṃ na pāpuṇāti sāmivacanassa pasaṅge antarāsaddayogena upayogavacanassa icchitattā. Tenevāha “antarāsaddena pana yuttattā upayogavacanaṃ kata”nti.

Here this might be the intended meaning: where the word 'antarā' applies, there the word 'antara' also applies due to having the same meaning. Thus, the word 'antara' is cited as occurring in the meaning of the word 'antarā'. Alternatively, it should be understood that the word 'antarā' itself, in the phrase 'yassantarato,' has been spoken with a short vowel for the sake of metrical ease in the verse. Moreover, the word 'antarā' itself, when the word is expanded with the suffix 'ika,' becomes 'antarikā.' Therefore, in this context, no contradiction should be seen between the examples given and those to be cited. If it is not connected, the accusative case cannot be obtained, because in the context of the genitive case, the accusative case is desired due to its connection with the word 'antarā'. Therefore, it is said, 'But due to its connection with the word "antarā," the accusative case is used.'

Sakalajambudīpe uppannaṃ mahākalahaṃ vūpasametvāti parinibbute bhagavati dhātūnaṃ atthāya kusināranagaraṃ parivāretvā ṭhitehi sesarājūhi “amhākaṃ dhātuyo vā dentu yuddhaṃ vā”tiādinā kosinārakehi mallehi saddhiṃ kataṃ vivādaṃ vūpasametvā. So kira brāhmaṇo tesaṃ vivādaṃ sutvā “ete rājāno bhagavato parinibbutaṭṭhāne vivādaṃ karonti, na kho panetaṃ patirūpaṃ, alaṃ iminā kalahena, vūpasamessāmi na”nti gantvā unnate padese ṭhatvā dvebhāṇavāraparimāṇaṃ doṇagajjitaṃ nāma [M 2.0293] avoca. Tattha paṭhamabhāṇavāre tāva ekapadampi te na jāniṃsu. Dutiyabhāṇavārapariyosāne ca “ācariyassa viya bho saddo, ācariyassa viya bho saddo”ti sabbe niravā ahesuṃ. Jambudīpatale kira kulaghare jāto yebhuyyena tassa na-antevāsiko nāma natthi, atha kho so attano vacanaṃ sutvā nirave tuṇhībhūte viditvā puna –

'Having pacified the great conflict that arose in the entire Jambudīpa' means having pacified the dispute that the remaining kings, who had surrounded the city of Kusinārā for the sake of the relics, had made with the Mallas of Kusinārā, saying, 'Either give us the relics or give us battle,' and so on, after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna. It is said that when the Brahmin heard their dispute, he thought: 'These kings are quarreling at the place where the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna. This is not proper. Enough with this conflict—I will pacify it.' So he went and, standing on an elevated spot, uttered what is called the Doṇagajjita, lasting the span of two recitations. During the first recitation, they did not understand even a single word. But at the end of the second recitation, they all became silent, saying, 'This voice is like our teacher’s! This voice is like our teacher’s!' It is said that on the surface of Jambudīpa, there was generally no one born in a good family who was not his pupil. Then, hearing his own words and realizing they had all become silent, he spoke again—

“Suṇantu bhonto mama ekavācaṃ,

Amhāka buddho ahu khantivādo;

Na hi sādhuyaṃ uttamapuggalassa,

Sarīrabhāge siyā sampahāro.

'Listen, sirs, to my single word, Our Buddha was a teacher of forbearance; It is not good that there should be conflict over the bodily share of the supreme person.

“Sabbeva bhonto sahitā samaggā,

Sammodamānā karomaṭṭhabhāge;

Vitthārikā hontu disāsu thūpā,

Bahū janā cakkhumato pasannā”ti. (dī. ni. 2.237) –

'Sirs, let us all, united, harmonious, and rejoicing together, make eight shares. May the stūpas be widespread in all directions, for many people are devoted to the One with Vision.' (D.N. 2.237)

Imaṃ gāthādvayaṃ vatvā taṃ kalahaṃ vūpasametvā dhātuyo aṭṭhadhā bhājetvā adāsi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “sakalajambudīpe uppannaṃ mahākalahaṃ vūpasametvā dhātuyo bhājessatī”ti. Lakkhaṇacakkānīti dvīsu pādatalesu dve lakkhaṇacakkāni.

Having spoken these two verses and resolved the conflict, he divided the relics into eight portions and gave them away. With reference to that, this was said: 'Having quelled the great conflict that arose in the whole of Jambudīpa, he will divide the relics.' 'Marks of the wheels' means two characteristic wheel-marks on the two soles of the feet.

Āsavenāti [V 2.0267] kammakilesakāraṇena āsavena. Ettha hi tebhūmakañca kammaṃ, avasesā ca akusalā dhammā “āsavā”ti vuttā. Devūpapattīti devesu uppatti nibbatti. Ettha ca yakkhagandhabbatāya vinimuttā sabbe devā devaggahaṇena gahitā. Gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo ākāsacārī. Ahanti vibhattivipariṇāmena yojetabbaṃ.

'By an influx' means by an influx that is the cause of kamma and defilements. Here, kamma pertaining to the three planes of existence and the remaining unwholesome states are called 'influxes.' 'Rebirth among devas' means arising and being born among the devas. And here, all the devas apart from yakkhas and gandhabbas are included by the term 'deva.' A gandhabba is a bird, a sky-goer. 'Ahaṃ' should be connected by way of transformation of grammatical case.

Doṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Doṇa Sutta is finished.

7. Aparihāniyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Aparihāniya Sutta

37. Sattame nibbānasantikeyeva caratīti kilesanibbānassa anupādāparinibbānassa ca santikeyeva carati “na cirasseva adhigamissatī”ti katvā[M 2.0294]. Gāthāya appamādaratoti samathavipassanāya appamajjane rato abhirato, appamādeneva rattindivaṃ vītināmentoti attho. Pamādaṃ bhayato passantoti nirayūpapattiādibhayahetuto pamādaṃ bhayato passanto. Abhabbo parihānāyāti so evarūpo samathavipassanādhammehi maggaphalehi vā parihānāya abhabbo. Samathavipassanāto hi sampattato na parihāyati, itarāni ca appattāni pāpuṇātīti.

37. In the seventh, 'he dwells ever close to Nibbāna' means he dwells close to the Nibbāna of defilements and the Nibbāna without residue of clinging, thinking, 'He will attain it before long.' In the verse, 'delighting in heedfulness' means he delights and rejoices in being heedful in serenity and insight; the meaning is that he spends his days and nights in heedfulness. 'Seeing heedlessness as fearful' means seeing heedlessness as fearful because it is the cause of dangers such as rebirth in hell. 'He is incapable of decline' means such a one is incapable of declining from the qualities of serenity and insight or from the path and fruition. For one does not decline from the attainment of serenity and insight; and what has not yet been attained, one attains.

Aparihāniyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Aparihāniya Sutta is finished.

8. Patilīnasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Paṭilīna Sutta

38. Aṭṭhame antavā lokoti ekapassena vaḍḍhitaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ “loko”ti gāhena vā takkena vā uppannadiṭṭhi. Lābhī hi jhānacakkhunā passitvā gaṇhāti, itaro takkamattena. Anantavāti samantato vaḍḍhitaṃ appamāṇaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ “loko”ti gāhena vā takkena vā uppannadiṭṭhi. Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti jīvo sarīrañca ekameva vatthūti uppannadiṭṭhi. Vissaṭṭhānīti sakapariccajanavasena nissaṭṭhāni. Vantānīti idaṃ puna anādiyanabhāvadassanavasena vuttaṃ. Cattampi hi keci gaṇhanti, nayidamevanti dassanatthaṃ “vantānī”ti vuttaṃ. Na hi yaṃ yena vantaṃ, na so taṃ puna ādīyati. Vantampi kiñci sasantatilaggaṃ siyā, nayidamevanti dassanatthaṃ “muttānī”ti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “chinnabandhanāni katānī”ti, santatito vinimocanavasena chinnabandhanāni katānīti attho. Muttampi kiñci muttabandhanaṃ viya phalaṃ kuhiñci tiṭṭhati, na evamidanti dassanatthaṃ “pahīnānī”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā kiñci dunnissaṭṭhaṃ puna [V 2.0268] ādāya sammadeva nissaṭṭhaṃ “paṭinissaṭṭha”nti vuccati, evaṃ vipassanāya nissaṭṭhāni ādinnasadisāni maggena pahīnāni paṭinissaṭṭhāni nāma hontīti dassanatthaṃ “paṭinissaṭṭhānī”ti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “yathā na puna cittaṃ ārohanti, evaṃ paṭinissajjitānī”ti.

38. In the eighth, 'the world is finite' is a view that has arisen from grasping or reasoning that the kasiṇa-sign, expanded on one side, is 'the world.' For one who has attained it, one sees and grasps it with the jhāna-eye, while another does so by mere reasoning. 'The world is infinite' is a view that has arisen from grasping or reasoning that the immeasurable kasiṇa-sign, expanded on all sides, is 'the world.' 'The soul is the same as the body' is a view that has arisen that the soul and the body are one and the same thing. 'Relinquished' means given up by way of self-renunciation. 'Vomited' is said to show the state of not taking them up again. For some grasp even what has been discarded, but to show this is not the case here, it is said 'vomited.' For what is vomited by someone is not taken up again by them. Even something vomited might have a trace of sesame clinging to it, but to show this is not the case here, it is said 'released.' Therefore, it is said, 'the bonds have been cut.' The meaning is that the bonds have been cut by way of liberation from the continuity of existence. Even something released might remain somewhere, like a fruit released from its stalk, but to show this is not the case here, it is said 'abandoned.' Just as something poorly given up is taken up again, but when properly given up, it is called 'relinquished,' so too, what is given up by insight is like something taken up; when abandoned by the path, it is called 'relinquished.' To show this, it is said 'relinquished.' Therefore, it is said, 'they are relinquished in such a way that they do not arise in the mind again.'

Kāmesanāti kāmānaṃ esanā, kāmasaṅkhātā vā esanā kāmesanā. Vuttañhetaṃ “tattha katamā kāmesanā? Yo kāmesu kāmacchando kāmarāgo kāmanandī kāmapipāsā kāmamucchā kāmajjhosānaṃ, ayaṃ [M 2.0295] vuccati kāmesanā”ti, tasmā kāmarāgo “kāmesanā”ti veditabbo. Tenevāha “kāmesanā…pe… anāgāmimaggena pahīnā”ti. Bhavānaṃ esanā bhavesanā. Vuttampi cetaṃ “tattha katamā bhavesanā? Yo bhavesu bhavacchando…pe… bhavajjhosānaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati bhavesanā”ti, tasmā bhavesanarāgo rūpārūpabhavapatthanāti veditabbo. Tenevāha “bhavesanā pana arahattamaggena pahīyatī”ti.

'Search for sensual pleasures' (kāmesanā) is the search for sensual pleasures, or the search designated as 'sensual pleasure.' For it was said: "Therein, what is the search for sensual pleasures? Whatever desire for sensual pleasures, lust for sensual pleasures, delight in sensual pleasures, thirst for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, obsession with sensual pleasures—this is called the search for sensual pleasures." Therefore, lust for sensual pleasures should be understood as 'search for sensual pleasures.' Therefore, it is said, "the search for sensual pleasures... is abandoned by the path of the non-returner." The search for states of existence is 'bhavesanā.' And it was also said: "Therein, what is the search for existence? Whatever desire for existence... obsession with existence—this is called the search for existence." Therefore, lust for existence should be understood as the desire for existence in the realms of form and formlessness. Therefore, it is said, "but the search for existence is abandoned by the path of arahantship."

Brahmacariyassa esanā brahmacariyesanā. Sā ca maggabrahmacariyassa, diṭṭhigatikasammatabrahmacariyassa ca gavesanavasena dvippakārāti āha “brahmacariyaṃ esissāmī”tiādi. Diṭṭhigatikasammatassa brahmacariyassa esanāpi hi brahmacariyesanāti vuccati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

The search for the holy life is 'brahmacariyesanā.' It is twofold, by way of seeking the holy life of the path and the holy life deemed proper according to views and observances. Thus it is said: "I will seek the holy life," and so on. For the search for the holy life deemed proper according to views and observances is also called 'the search for the holy life.' And this has also been said—

“Tattha katamā brahmacariyesanā? Sassato lokoti vā, asassato lokoti vā, antavā lokoti vā, anantavā lokoti vā, taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīranti vā, aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīranti vā, hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā, na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā, hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā, neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti vā, yā evarūpā diṭṭhi diṭṭhigataṃ diṭṭhigahanaṃ diṭṭhikantāraṃ diṭṭhivisūkāyikaṃ diṭṭhivipphanditaṃ diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ gāho patiṭṭhāho abhiniveso parāmāso kummaggo micchāpatho micchattaṃ titthāyatanaṃ vipariyesaggāho, ayaṃ vuccati brahmacariyesanā”ti (vibha. 919).

"Therein, what is the search for the holy life? The view that 'the world is eternal,' or 'the world is not eternal,' or 'the world is finite,' or 'the world is infinite,' or 'the soul and the body are the same,' or 'the soul and the body are different,' or 'the Tathāgata exists after death,' or 'the Tathāgata does not exist after death,' or 'the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' or 'the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'—any such view, a tenet of views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, an agitation of views, a fetter of views, a grasping, a firm adherence, an insistence, a clinging, a wrong road, a false path, wrongness, a sectarian basis, a perverted grasping—this is called the search for the holy life."

Tasmā diṭṭhigatikasammatassa brahmacariyassa esanā diṭṭhabrahmacariyesanāti veditabbā. Tenevāha “diṭṭhibrahmacariyesanā pana sotāpattimaggeneva paṭippassambhatī”ti. Ettāvatā ca rāgadiṭṭhiyo esanāti [V 2.0269] dassitaṃ hoti. Na kevalañca rāgadiṭṭhiyo eva esanā, tadekaṭṭhaṃ kammampi. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Therefore, the search for the holy life deemed proper according to views and observances should be understood as the 'search for the holy life of views.' Hence it is said, "But the search for the holy life of views is allayed only by the path of stream-entry." By this much, it has been shown that lust and views are 'searches.' And not only are lust and views 'searches,' but also the kamma connected with them. And this has also been said:

“Tattha katamā kāmesanā? Kāmarāgo tadekaṭṭhaṃ akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati kāmesanā. Tattha katamā bhavesanā? Bhavarāgo tadekaṭṭhaṃ akusalaṃ [M 2.0296] kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati bhavesanā. Tattha katamā brahmacariyesanā? Antaggāhikā diṭṭhi tadekaṭṭhaṃ akusalaṃ kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati brahmacariyesanā”ti (vibha. 919).

"Therein, what is the search for sensual pleasures? Sensual lust and the unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental kamma connected with it—this is called the search for sensual pleasures. Therein, what is the search for existence? Lust for existence and the unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental kamma connected with it—this is called the search for existence. Therein, what is the search for the holy life? A view grasping at extremes and the unwholesome bodily, verbal, and mental kamma connected with it—this is called the search for the holy life."

Navavidhamānoti “seyyassa seyyohamasmī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 4.108; dha. sa. 1121; vibha. 866; mahāni. 21) āgato navavidhamāno.

'Ninefold conceit' means the ninefold conceit that comes in the texts (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.108; Dhammasaṅgaṇī 1121; Vibhaṅga 866; Mahāniddesa 21) beginning with 'With respect to a superior person, I am superior,' and so on.

“Kāmesanā”tiādigāthāya pana brahmacariyesanā sahāti brahmacariyesanāya saddhiṃ. Vibhattilopena hi ayaṃ niddeso. Karaṇatthe vā etaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “brahmacariyesanāya saddhiṃ kāmesanā bhavesanāti tisso esanā”ti. Tāsu brahmacariyesanaṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ “itisaccaparāmāso, diṭṭhiṭṭhānā samussayā”ti vuttaṃ. Tassattho – iti evaṃ saccanti parāmāso itisaccaparāmāso. Idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti diṭṭhiyā pavattiākāraṃ dasseti. Diṭṭhiyo eva sabbānatthahetubhāvato diṭṭhiṭṭhānā. Vuttañhetaṃ – “micchādiṭṭhiparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, vajjaṃ vadāmī”ti (a. ni. 1.310). Tā eva ca uparūpari vuddhiyā mānalobhādikilesasamussayanena vaṭṭadukkhasamussayanena ca samussayā, “idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti micchābhinivisamānā sabbānatthahetukā kilesadukkhūpacayato hetubhūtā ca diṭṭhiyo brahmacariyesanāti vuttaṃ hoti. Etena pavattiākārato nibbattito ca brahmacariyesanā dassitāti veditabbā.

In the verse beginning with 'Kāmesanā,' 'brahmacariyesanā sahā' means 'together with the search for the holy life.' This expression is by way of elision of the case ending, or it is a singular term in the instrumental sense. This is what is meant: 'The three searches are the search for sensual pleasures and the search for existence, together with the search for the holy life.' Among these, to show the search for the holy life in its own nature, it is said: 'Clinging to this as truth, the bases of views, accumulations.' Its meaning is: 'clinging to this as truth' is clinging to something as 'thus true.' It shows the manner in which a view occurs: 'This alone is true, all else is futile.' Because views are the cause of all ruin, they are 'the bases of views.' As it is said: 'Monks, I declare wrong view to be the foremost fault' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.310). And those very views are 'accumulations' because they grow ever more and more, by accumulating defilements such as conceit and greed, and by accumulating the suffering of the round. The meaning is that the search for the holy life is said to be those views which, through wrong adherence to 'this alone is true, all else is futile,' are the cause of all ruin and the source for the accumulation of defilements and suffering. By this, it should be understood that the search for the holy life has been shown in terms of its mode of occurrence and its origin.

Sabbarāgavirattassāti sabbehi kāmabhavarāgehi virattassa. Tato eva taṇhākkhayasaṅkhāte nibbāne vimuttattā taṇhākkhayavimuttino arahato. Esanā paṭinissaṭṭhāti kāmesanā, bhavesanā sabbaso nissaṭṭhā pahīnā. Diṭṭhiṭṭhānā samūhatāti brahmacariyesanāsaṅkhātā diṭṭhiṭṭhānā ca paṭhamamaggeneva samugghātitā. Evampi imissā gāthāya atthavaṇṇanā veditabbā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

'For one detached from all lust' means for one detached from all lust for sensual pleasures and for existence. Precisely because of that, for the Arahant, who is liberated by the destruction of craving, being liberated in Nibbāna, which is designated as the destruction of craving. 'The searches are relinquished' means the search for sensual pleasures and the search for existence are entirely given up, abandoned. 'The bases of views are uprooted' means that the bases of views, designated as the search for the holy life, are eradicated by the very first path. In this way also the explanation of the meaning of this verse should be understood. The rest is easily understood.

Patilīnasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Paṭilīna Sutta is finished.

9. Ujjayasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Ujjaya Sutta

39. Navame [M 2.0297][V 2.0270] anukulayaññanti anukulaṃ kulānukkamaṃ upādāya dātabbadānaṃ. Tenāha “amhākaṃ…pe… kulānukulavasena yajitabba”nti. Vaṃsaparamparāya pacchā duggatapurisehi padātabbadānaṃ. Evarūpaṃ kulaṃ sīlavante uddissa nibaddhadānaṃ, tasmiṃ kule daliddānipi na upacchindanti. Tatridaṃ vatthu – anāthapiṇḍikassa ghare pañca salākabhattasatāni dīyiṃsu. Dantamayasalākānaṃ pañcasatāni ahesuṃ. Atha taṃ kulaṃ anukkamena dāliddiyena abhibhūtaṃ. Ekā tasmiṃ kule dārikā ekasalākato uddhaṃ dātuṃ nāsakkhi. Sāpi pacchā sātavāhanaṃ raṭṭhaṃ gantvā khalaṃ sodhetvā laddhadhaññena taṃ salākaṃ adāsi. Eko thero rañño ārocesi. Rājā taṃ ānetvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sā tato paṭṭhāya puna pañcapi salākasatāni pavattesi.

39. In the ninth [sutta], 'anukulayañña' means a gift that should be given in accordance with the family lineage. Therefore it is said: 'For us... an offering should be made according to family tradition.' This means a gift to be given by poor persons later in the family lineage. In such a family that has a perpetual offering dedicated to the virtuous, even the poor do not cease to give. Here is a story: In Anāthapiṇḍika’s household, five hundred meal offerings with tokens were given. There were five hundred tokens made of ivory. Then that family was gradually overcome by poverty. One girl in that family was not able to give more than a single token. Later, she went to the Sātavāhana kingdom, cleaned a threshing floor, and with the grain she received, gave that token. A certain elder informed the king. The king had her brought and established her in the position of chief queen. From then on, she again provided the five hundred tokens for the offerings.

Assamedhantiādīsu porāṇakarājakāle kira sassamedhaṃ, purisamedhaṃ, sammāpāsaṃ, vācāpeyyanti cattāri saṅgahavatthūni ahesuṃ, yehi rājāno lokaṃ saṅgaṇhiṃsu. Tattha nipphannasassato dasamabhāgaggahaṇaṃ sassamedhaṃ nāma, sassasampādane medhāvitāti attho. Mahāyodhānaṃ chamāsikabhattavetanānuppadānaṃ purisamedhaṃ nāma, purisasaṅgaṇhane medhāvitāti attho. Daliddamanussānaṃ hatthe lekhaṃ gahetvā tīṇi vassāni vinā vaḍḍhiyā sahassadvisahassamattadhanānuppadānaṃ sammāpāsaṃ nāma. Tañhi sammā manusse pāseti hadaye bandhitvā viya ṭhapeti, tasmā sammāpāsanti vuccati. “Tāta, mātulā”tiādinā pana saṇhavācābhaṇanaṃ vācāpeyyaṃ nāma, peyyavajjaṃ piyavacanatāti attho. Evaṃ catūhi vatthūhi saṅgahitaṃ raṭṭhaṃ iddhañceva hoti phītañca pahūtaannapānaṃ khemaṃ nirabbudaṃ, manussā mudā modanā ure putte naccentā apārutagharadvārā viharanti. Idaṃ gharadvāresu aggaḷānaṃ abhāvato niraggaḷanti vuccati. Ayaṃ porāṇikā paveṇī. Aparabhāge pana okkākarājakāle brāhmaṇā imāni cattāri saṅgahavatthūni imañca raṭṭhasampattiṃ parivattentā ummūlaṃ katvā assamedhaṃ purisamedhantiādike pañca yaññe nāma akaṃsu. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā brāhmaṇadhammiyasutte –

Regarding 'assamedha' and so forth: It is said that in ancient royal times, there were four means of unification—namely, the grain offering (sassamedha), the human offering (purisamedha), the righteous bond (sammāpāsa), and gentle speech (vācāpeyya)—by which kings united the world. Among these, taking a tenth portion from the produced grain was called 'sassamedha,' meaning 'wise in ensuring grain prosperity.' Providing six-monthly food and wages to great warriors was called 'purisamedha,' meaning 'wise in uniting people.' Taking a written pledge from poor people and providing wealth of one or two thousand [coins] without interest for three years was called 'sammāpāsa.' For it rightly binds people, holding them as if in the heart; therefore, it is called 'sammāpāsa.' Speaking gentle words like 'Father, uncle,' and so forth, was called 'vācāpeyya,' meaning 'sweet and endearing speech.' A kingdom united by these four means became prosperous and abundant, with plentiful food and drink, secure, and free from calamity, with people living joyfully, dancing with their children on their chests, their house doors unbarred. This was called 'niraggaḷa' (without bolts) due to the absence of bolts on house doors. This was the ancient custom. Later, however, in the time of King Okkāka, brahmins, distorting these four means of unification and this prosperity of the kingdom, uprooted them and instituted the five sacrifices, such as the horse sacrifice and the human sacrifice. This was spoken by the Blessed One in the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta:

“Tesaṃ [M 2.0298] āsi vipallāso, disvāna aṇuto aṇuṃ…pe…;

Te tattha mante ganthetvā, okkākaṃ tadupāgamu”nti. (su. ni. 301-304);

"A perversion arose in them, seeing one subtle thing after another... Having composed mantras there, they approached Okkāka." (Su. Ni. 301–304)

Idāni [V 2.0271] tehi parivattetvā ṭhapitamatthaṃ dassento “assamedha”ntiādimāha. Tattha medhantīti vadhenti. Dvīhi pariyaññehīti mahāyaññassa pubbabhāge pacchā ca pavattetabbehi dvīhi parivārayaññehi. Sattanavutipañcapasusataghātabhiṃsanassāti sattanavutādhikānaṃ pañcannaṃ pasusatānaṃ māraṇena bheravassa pāpabhīrukānaṃ bhayāvahassa. Tathā hi vadanti –

Now, showing the meaning that was distorted and established by them, he says 'assamedha' and so forth. There, 'medhanti' means 'they kill.' 'With two surrounding sacrifices' means with two subsidiary sacrifices that should be performed before and after the great sacrifice. 'Of the terror from the slaughter of five hundred and ninety-seven animals' means terrifying due to the killing of five hundred and ninety-seven animals, dreadful and fear-inducing for those who are afraid of evil. For thus they say:

“Chasatāni niyujjanti, pasūnaṃ majjhime hani;

Assamedhassa yaññassa, ūnāni pasūhi tīhī”ti. (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.120);

"Six hundred animals are employed on the middle day; for the horse sacrifice, it is short by three animals." (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.120)

Sammanti yugacchidde pakkhipitabbadaṇḍakaṃ. Pāsantīti khipanti. Saṃhārimehīti sakaṭehi vahitabbehi. Pubbe kira eko rājā sammāpāsaṃ yajanto sarassatinaditīre pathaviyā vivare dinne nimuggoyeva ahosi, andhabālabrāhmaṇā gatānugatigatā “ayaṃ tassa saggagamanamaggo”ti saññāya tattha sammāpāsayaññaṃ paṭṭhapenti. Tena vuttaṃ “nimuggokāsato pabhutī”ti. Ayūpo appakadivaso yāgo, sayūpo bahudivasaṃ neyyo satrayāgoti. Mantapadābhisaṅkhatānaṃ sappimadhūnaṃ vājamiti samaññā. Hiraññasuvaṇṇagomahiṃsādi sattarasakadakkhiṇassa. Sāragabbhakoṭṭhāgārādīsu natthi ettha aggaḷanti niraggaḷo. Tattha kira yaññe attano sāpateyyaṃ anavasesato anigūhitvā niyyātīyati.

'Sammā' refers to the pin that should be placed in the yoke-hole. 'Pāsanti' means 'they throw.' 'Saṃhārimehi' means 'by carts that are to be drawn.' In the past, it is said, a certain king, while performing the Sammāpāsa sacrifice on the banks of the Sarasvatī River, sank into a fissure in the earth and disappeared. Blind, foolish brahmins, following the trodden path, declared, 'This is the path to his heavenly journey,' and established the Sammāpāsa sacrifice there. Hence it is said, 'from the place of sinking onwards.' 'Ayūpa' is a sacrifice of few days; 'sayūpa' is a satrayāga that should be conducted for many days. 'Vāja' is a designation for clarified butter and honey consecrated with mantra verses. Of the seventeenfold gift, including gold, silver, cows, buffaloes, and so forth. 'Niraggaḷa' means there is no bolt in treasure-chambers, storehouses with valuable cores, and so forth. There, it is said, in the sacrifice, one gives away one's own property completely, without hiding anything.

Mahārambhāti bahupasughātakammā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “vividhā yattha haññare”ti vakkhamānattā “mahākiccā mahākaraṇīyā”ti paṭhamo atthavikappo vutto. Dutiyo pana atthavikappo “mahārambhāti papañcavasena ajeḷakā”tiādi vuttanti adhippāyena “apicā”tiādinā āraddho. Nirārambhāti etthāpi vuttanayena attho veditabbo. Nanu ca pāṇātipātādiakusalakammassa appamattakampi phalaṃ nupalabbhati, tasmā tassa nipphalabhāvaṃ avatvā “na te honti mahapphalā”ti kasmā vuttanti āha “niravasesatthe”tiādi. Anugataṃ kulanti anukulaṃ, kulānugatanti attho. Ye niccabhattādiṃ pubbapurisehi paṭṭhapitaṃ aparāparaṃ anupacchindantā manussā [M 2.0299] dadanti, te anukulaṃ yajanti nāma. Tenevāha “ye aññe anukulaṃ yajantī”tiādi.

'Mahārambhā' means actions involving the killing of many animals. In the commentary, however, because it will be stated 'where various [beings] are slain,' the first alternative interpretation given is 'great tasks, great undertakings.' The second alternative interpretation, however, beginning with 'moreover,' and so forth, is introduced with the intention that 'mahārambhā' means 'goats, etc., by way of proliferation,' as has been stated. 'Nirārambhā'—here too, the meaning should be understood in the same way as stated. But surely, an unwholesome act like killing living beings has a result; therefore, instead of stating its fruitlessness, why is it said, 'they do not have great fruit'? He says, 'in the sense of completeness,' and so forth. 'Anugataṃ kulaṃ' is 'anukulaṃ,' meaning 'following the family tradition.' Those people who give without interrupting the continuous practice established by their ancestors—such as providing regular meals—are said to perform sacrifices in accordance with their family. Hence it is said, 'those others who perform sacrifices in accordance with their family,' and so forth.

Ujjayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Ujjaya Sutta is concluded.

10. Udāyisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Udāyi Sutta

40. Dasame [V 2.0272] pāṇasamārambharahitanti pāṇaghātarahitaṃ. Abyābajjhaṃ sukhaṃ lokaṃ, paṇḍito upapajjatīti kāmacchandādibyāpādavirahitattā abyābajjhaṃ niddukkhaṃ. Parapīḷābhāve pana vattabbaṃ natthi. Jhānasamāpattivasena sukhabahulattā sukhaṃ ekantasukhaṃ brahmalokaṃ jhānapuññena, itarapuññena pana tadaññasampattibhavasaṅkhātaṃ sukhaṃ lokaṃ paṇḍito sappañño upeti. Sesaṃ uttānameva.

40. In the tenth [discourse], 'free from undertaking against beings' means free from killing beings. 'A happy world, free from affliction, the wise one attains'—because it is free from the affliction of sensual desire and so forth, it is free from affliction and suffering. As for the absence of harming others, there is nothing further to say. Due to the abundance of happiness through jhāna attainment, the Brahma world is an entirely happy world, attained by the wise one through the merit of jhāna. Through other merits, however, the wise one, being discerning, attains a happy world, which is a state of fortunate existence different from that. The rest is self-evident.

Udāyisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Udāyi Sutta is concluded.

Cakkavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Cakkavagga is concluded.

5. Rohitassavaggo

5. The Rohitassa Chapter

1. Samādhibhāvanāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Samādhibhāvanā Sutta

41. Pañcamassa paṭhame diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāyāti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve sukhavihāratthāya, nikkilesatāya nirāmisena sukhena viharaṇatthāyāti attho. Iminā cattāri phalasamāpattijjhānāni khīṇāsavassa āsavakkhayādhigamato aparabhāge adhigatarūpārūpajjhānāni ca kathitāni. Dibbacakkhuñāṇadassanappaṭilābhāyāti dibbacakkhuñāṇappaṭilābhatthāya. Dibbacakkhuñāṇañhi rūpagatassa dibbassa itarassa ca dassanaṭṭhena idha “ñāṇadassana”nti adhippetaṃ. Ālokasaññaṃ manasi karotīti divā vā rattiṃ vā sūriyadīpacandamaṇiukkāvijjulatādīnaṃ āloko divā rattiñca upaladdho, yathāladdhavaseneva ālokaṃ manasi karoti citte ṭhapeti, tathā ca naṃ manasi karoti, yathāssa subhāvitālokakasiṇassa viya kasiṇāloko yathicchakaṃ yāvadicchakañca so āloko rattiyaṃ upatiṭṭhati[M 2.0300], yena tattha divāsaññaṃ ṭhapeti, divā viya vigatathinamiddho hoti. Tenāha “yathā divā tathā ratti”nti.

41. In the first discourse of the fifth chapter, 'for the sake of dwelling happily in this very life' means for the purpose of dwelling happily in this very existence, for the sake of dwelling with the unworldly happiness that comes from being free from defilements. By this are explained the four jhānas of fruition attainment of one whose taints are destroyed, as well as the form and formless jhānas attained after the realization of the destruction of the taints. 'For the attainment of the divine eye, knowledge, and vision' means for the purpose of attaining the divine eye-knowledge. For the divine eye-knowledge is here intended by 'knowledge and vision' in the sense of seeing forms, both divine and ordinary. 'He attends to the perception of light' means that whether by day or night, the light of the sun, lamps, the moon, gems, torches, lightning, and so forth, is perceived. According to how it has been perceived, he attends to the light and establishes it in his mind. He attends to it in such a way that, like one whose light-kasiṇa is well-developed, that kasiṇa-light appears to him at night as he wishes and for as long as he wishes. By this, he establishes the perception of day at night, and he is free from sloth and torpor by night, just as by day. Hence it is said, 'as by day, so by night.'

Yathā divā ālokasaññā manasi katā, tatheva naṃ rattimpi manasi karotīti yathā divā diṭṭho āloko, tatheva taṃ rattiṃ manasi karoti. Dutiyapadeti “yathā rattiṃ tathā divā”ti imasmiṃ [V 2.0273] vākye. Esa nayoti iminā yathā rattiyaṃ candālokādi āloko diṭṭho, evameva rattiṃ diṭṭhākāreneva divā taṃ ālokaṃ manasi karoti citte ṭhapetīti imamatthaṃ atidisati. Iti vivaṭena cetasāti evaṃ apihitena cittena, thinamiddhāpidhānena apihitacittenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Apariyonaddhenāti samantato anaddhena asañchāditena. Kiñcāpītiādinā attanā vuttamevatthaṃ samattheti. Ālokasadisaṃ kataṃ “yathā divā tathā ratti”ntiādinā.

'Just as the perception of light is attended to by day, so too he attends to it by night' means that just as the light is seen by day, so he attends to it at night. Regarding the second phrase, 'as by night, so by day,' this method indicates the meaning that just as light such as moonlight is seen at night, so too during the day he attends to that light with the same appearance as seen at night, establishing it in his mind. 'Thus, with an open mind' means with a mind thus uncovered; that is to say, with a mind not covered by the covering of sloth and torpor. 'Unenclosed' means not covered or concealed on all sides. By 'although...' and so forth, he confirms the meaning stated by himself. It is made similar to light by 'as by day, so by night,' and so forth.

Sattaṭṭhānikassāti “abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hotī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.214; 2.376; ma. ni. 1.109) vuttassa sattaṭṭhānikassa satisampajaññassa atthāya. Pariggahitavatthārammaṇatāyāti vatthuno ārammaṇassa ca yāthāvato viditabhāvena. Yathā hi sappaṃ pariyesantena tassa āsaye vidite sopi vidito gahito eva ca hoti mantāgadabalena tassa gahaṇassa sukarattā, evaṃ vedanāya āsayabhūte vatthumhi ārammaṇe ca vidite ādikammikassapi vedanā viditā gahitā eva hoti salakkhaṇato sāmaññalakkhaṇato ca tassā gahaṇassa sukarattā. Pageva pariññātavatthukassa khīṇāsavassa. Tassa hi uppādakkhaṇepi ṭhitikkhaṇepi bhaṅgakkhaṇepi vedanā viditā pākaṭā honti “tā vedanā evaṃ uppajjitvā”tiādinā. Na kevalañca vedanā eva, idha vuttā saññādayopi avuttā cetanādayopi viditāva uppajjanti ceva tiṭṭhanti ca nirujjhanti ca. Nidassanamattañhetaṃ, yadidaṃ pāḷiyaṃ vedanāsaññāvitakkaggahaṇaṃ. Tena anavasesato sabbadhammānampi uppādādito viditabhāvaṃ dasseti.

'Of the sevenfold' means for the purpose of the sevenfold mindfulness and clear comprehension, as stated in 'one acts with clear comprehension in going forward and backward' (Dī. Ni. 1.214; 2.376; Ma. Ni. 1.109). 'By the thorough comprehension of the basis and object' means by having truly understood the basis and the object. For just as one searching for a snake, upon recognizing its lair, thereby knows and has as good as grasped the snake itself—because capturing it becomes easy with the power of charms and antidotes—so too, for a beginner, when the basis and the object that are the abode of feeling are understood, the feeling itself is known and as good as grasped, because its comprehension through its specific and general characteristics becomes easy. How much more so for an arahant with destroyed taints, who has fully understood the basis! For such a one, at the moment of arising, the moment of presence, and the moment of cessation, feelings are known and evident: 'These feelings arise thus...' and so forth. Not only feelings, but the mentioned perceptions and so forth, and the unmentioned volitions and so forth, are also known as they arise, persist, and cease. This is merely an illustration, namely, the mentioning of feelings, perceptions, and thoughts in the Pāli text. Thus, it indicates that all phenomena are known without remainder from their arising onward.

Apica vedanāya uppādo vidito hoti, upaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti, atthaṅgamo vidito hoti. Kathaṃ vedanāya uppādo vidito hoti[M 2.0301]? Avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayo, taṇhāsamudayā kammasamudayo, phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayoti nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ passantopi vedanākkhandhassa samudayaṃ passati. Evaṃ vedanāya uppādo vidito hoti. Kathaṃ vedanāya upaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti? Aniccato manasikaroto khayatupaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti, dukkhato manasikaroto bhayatupaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti, anattato manasikaroto suññatupaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti. Evaṃ vedanāya upaṭṭhānaṃ viditaṃ hoti. Iti khayato bhayato suññato jānāti. Kathaṃ vedanāya atthaṅgamo vidito hoti? Avijjānirodhā vedanānirodho…pe… evaṃ vedanāya atthaṅgamo vidito hoti. Imināpi nayenettha attho veditabbo.

Furthermore, the arising of feeling is known, its presence is known, its passing away is known. How is the arising of feeling known? 'With the arising of ignorance comes the arising of feeling; with the arising of craving comes the arising of kamma; with the arising of contact comes the arising of feeling.' By seeing the characteristic of origination in this way, one sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling. Thus, the arising of feeling is known. How is the presence of feeling known? By attending to it as impermanent, its presence as dissolution is known; by attending to it as suffering, its presence as fear is known; by attending to it as non-self, its presence as emptiness is known. Thus, the presence of feeling is known. In this way, one knows it as dissolution, as fear, and as emptiness. How is the passing away of feeling known? 'With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of feeling…' and so forth. Thus, the passing away of feeling is known. By this method, the meaning here should be understood.

Iti rūpanti ettha itisaddo anavasesato rūpassa sarūpanidassanatthoti tassa idaṃ rūpanti [V 2.0274] etena sādhāraṇato sarūpanidassanamāha, ettakaṃ rūpanti etena anavasesato, na ito paraṃ rūpaṃ atthīti tabbinimuttassa aññassa abhāvaṃ. Iti vedanātiādīsupi ayaṃ vedanā, ettakā vedanā, ito paraṃ vedanā natthi. Ayaṃ saññā…pe… ime saṅkhārā…pe… idaṃ viññāṇaṃ, ettakaṃ viññāṇaṃ, ito paraṃ viññāṇaṃ natthīti evamattho daṭṭhabboti āha “vedanādīsupi eseva nayo”ti.

In 'Thus, form,' the word 'thus' serves to indicate the nature of form completely. By 'this is form,' it states the general nature of form. By 'this much is form,' it indicates its totality, meaning there is no other form apart from this, showing the absence of anything else separate from it. Similarly, regarding 'Thus, feeling' and so forth, the meaning should be understood as: 'This is feeling, this much is feeling, there is no feeling beyond this. This is perception… and so forth… These are formations… and so forth… This is consciousness, this much is consciousness, there is no consciousness beyond this.' Therefore, it is said, 'The same method applies to feeling and so forth.'

Ñāṇena jānitvā paroparāni. Paroparānīti parāni ca oparāni ca. Uttamādhamānīti parattabhāvasakattabhāvādīni uttamādhamāni. Calitanti taṇhādiṭṭhivipphanditaṃ. Anīghoti rāgādiīgharahito. Atāri soti so evarūpo arahā jātijaraṃ atari.

Having known with knowledge the higher and lower. 'Higher and lower' means both the higher and the lower. 'Superior and inferior' means superior and inferior states such as others' existence and one's own existence. 'Agitated' means agitated by craving and views. 'Free from distress' means devoid of the distress of lust and so forth. 'He has crossed over' means such an arahant has crossed over birth and aging.

Samādhibhāvanāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Samādhibhāvanā Sutta is concluded.

2-4. Pañhabyākaraṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

2-4. Commentary on the Pañhabyākaraṇa Sutta and so forth

42-44. Dutiye etesaṃ pañhānanti ekaṃsabyākaraṇādīnaṃ catunnaṃ pañhānaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne byākaraṇaṃ jānātīti “cakkhuṃ anicca”nti puṭṭhe “anicca”nti ekaṃseneva byākātabbaṃ. “Aniccā nāma cakkhu”nti puṭṭhe pana “na kevalaṃ cakkhumeva, sotampi anicca”nti evaṃ vibhajitvā byākātabbaṃ. “Yathā [M 2.0302] cakkhuṃ tathā sotaṃ, yathā sotaṃ tathā cakkhu”nti puṭṭhe “kenaṭṭhena pucchasī”ti paṭipucchitvā “dassanaṭṭhena pucchāmī”ti vutte “na hī”ti byākātabbaṃ. “Aniccaṭṭhena pucchāmī”ti vutte “āmā”ti byākātabbaṃ. “Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”ntiādīni puṭṭhena pana “abyākatametaṃ bhagavatā”ti ṭhapetabbo, esa pañho na byākātabboti evaṃ jānātīti attho. Atthasamāgamenāti atthassa paṭilābhena laddhabbena. Samiti saṅgati samodhānanti samayo, paṭilābho. Samayo eva abhisamayo, abhimukhabhāvena vā samayo abhisamayoti evamettha padattho veditabbo. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Tatiyacatutthāni uttānatthāneva.

42-44. In the second, 'of these questions' refers to the four types of questions beginning with those requiring a categorical answer. One knows the answer in each particular situation. For example, when asked, 'Is the eye impermanent?' one should answer categorically, 'It is impermanent.' But when asked, 'Is the eye what is called impermanent?' one should answer analytically, 'Not only the eye, but the ear too is impermanent.' When asked, 'Is the eye as the ear, is the ear as the eye?' one should first counter-question, 'In what sense are you asking?' If the reply is, 'In the sense of seeing,' one should answer, 'No.' If the reply is, 'In the sense of impermanence,' one should answer, 'Yes.' But when asked questions such as 'Is the life-principle the same as the body?' the question should be set aside with, 'This has not been declared by the Blessed One.' The meaning is that one knows that such a question should not be answered. 'By the attainment of meaning' means by the gain of the meaning that is to be obtained. 'Meeting, coming together, union' are synonyms for 'concurrence' and 'attainment.' Concurrence itself is realization; or, concurrence is realization in the sense of facing directly. Thus the meaning of the word should be understood here. The rest is easily understood. The third and fourth have a straightforward meaning.

Pañhabyākaraṇasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pañhabyākaraṇa Sutta and so forth is concluded.

5-6. Rohitassasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-6. Commentary on the Rohitassa Sutta and so forth

45-46. Pañcame [V 2.0275] (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.107) ekokāseti cakkavāḷassa pariyantasaññite ekasmiṃ okāse. Bhummanti “yatthā”ti idaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Sāmaññato vuttampi “so lokassa anto”ti vacanato visiṭṭhavisayameva hoti. “Na jāyati, na mīyatī”ti vatvā puna “na cavati, na upapajjatī”ti kasmā vuttanti āha “idaṃ aparāparaṃ…pe… gahita”nti. Padagamanenāti padasā gamanena. Satthā saṅkhāralokassa antaṃ sandhāya vadati upari sabbāni pakāsetukāmo. Saṅkhāralokassa hi anto nibbānaṃ.

45-46. In the fifth (Saṃyutta Nikāya, Ṭīkā 1.1.107), 'ekokāse' means in one space, designated as the boundary of the world-sphere. 'Bhummanti'—this word 'yatthā' (where) is in the locative case. Although stated generally, from the statement 'that is the end of the world', it has a specific object. Having stated, 'is not born, does not die,' why is it then said, 'does not pass away, is not reborn'? He says, 'This is successively... grasped.' 'Padagamanena' means by proceeding word by word. The Teacher speaks with reference to the end of the conditioned world, wishing to reveal all these things further on. For the end of the conditioned world is Nibbāna.

Daḷhaṃ thiraṃ dhanu etassāti daḷhadhanvā, so eva “daḷhadhammā”ti vutto. Tenāha “daḷhadhanū”ti. Uttamappamāṇaṃ nāma sahassathāmadhanu. Dhanuggaṇhanasippacittakatāya dhanuggaho, na dhanuggahaṇamattenāti āha “dhanuggahoti dhanuācariyo”ti. “Dhanuggaho”ti vatvā “sikkhito”ti vutte dhanusikkhāya sikkhitoti viññāyati. Sikkhā ca ettakena kālena sikkhantassa ukkaṃsagatā hotīti āha “dvādasa vassāni dhanusippaṃ sikkhito”ti. Usabhappamāṇeti vīsati yaṭṭhiyo usabhaṃ, tasmiṃ usabhappamāṇe padese. Vālagganti vālakoṭiṃ. Katahatthoti paricitahattho. Katasarakkhepoti thiralakkhe ca calalakkhe ca paresaṃ dassanavasena [M 2.0303] sarakkhepassa katāpī. Tenāha “dassitasippo”ti, “katayoggo”ti keci. Asanti etenāti asanaṃ, kaṇḍo. Tālacchādinti tālacchāyaṃ. Sā pana ratanamattā vidatthicaturaṅgulā.

'Daḷhaṃ thiraṃ dhanu etassāti': 'daḷhadhanvā' means one whose bow is strong and firm. He is also called 'daḷhadhammā'. Therefore, he said 'daḷhadhanū'. The highest standard is called a bow with the strength of a thousand. 'Dhanuggaho' is due to the art of handling a bow being perfected, not merely from holding a bow; thus he said, ''dhanuggaho' is a bow-master'. Having said 'dhanuggaho,' when 'sikkhito' is said, it is understood as 'trained in the skill of the bow'. And the training of one who trains for such a time reaches its peak; thus he said, 'trained in the art of the bow for twelve years'. 'Usabhappamāṇeti': twenty yaṭṭhis are an usabha; in a place of that usabha-measure. 'Vālagganti' means the tip of a hair. 'Katahatthoti' means one with a practiced hand. 'Katasarakkhepoti' means one who has accomplished the shooting of arrows at both still and moving targets for the purpose of demonstrating to others. Therefore, he said 'dassitasippo' (one who has demonstrated skill); some say 'katayoggo' (one who has practiced). 'Asanti etenāti': 'asanaṃ' is that by which one shoots, an arrow, a shaft. 'Tālacchādinti' means in the shade of a palm tree. That, however, is a ratana in measure, or a span and four fingers.

Puratthimā samuddāti ekasmiṃ cakkavāḷe puratthimā samuddā. Samuddasīsena puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiṃ vadati. Pacchimasamuddoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Nippapañcatanti adantakāritaṃ. Sampatteti tādisena javena gacchantena sampatte. Anotatteti etthāpi “sampatte”ti padaṃ ānetvā sambandho, tathā “nāgalatādantakaṭṭha”nti etthāpi. Tadāti yadā so lokantagavesako ahosi, tadā. Dīghāyukakāloti anekavassasahassāyukakālo. Cakkavāḷalokassāti sāmaññavasena ekavacanaṃ, cakkavāḷalokānanti attho. Imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷe nibbattipubbaparicayasiddhāya nikantiyā.

'Puratthimā samuddā' means the eastern oceans in one world-sphere. By 'samuddasīsena' he speaks of the rim of the mouth of the eastern world-sphere. 'Pacchimasamuddo'—here too, the same method applies. 'Nippapañcatanti' means not made by a tooth-stick. 'Sampatte' means having reached, having gone with such speed. 'Anotatte'—here too, the word 'sampatte' is brought in to make the connection; likewise with 'nāgalatādantakaṭṭha'. 'Tadā' means: when he was a seeker of the end of the world, then. 'Dīghāyukakālo' means a time of long life, a life-span of many thousands of years. 'Cakkavāḷalokassa' is a singular form used in a general sense; the meaning is 'of the world-spheres'. In this very world-sphere, due to the craving established by familiarity with previous births.

Sasaññimhi samanaketi na rūpadhammamattake, atha kho pañcakkhandhasamudāyeti dasseti. Samitapāpoti samucchinnasaṃkilesadhammo. Chaṭṭhaṃ uttānameva.

'Sasaññimhi samanake' means not merely in material phenomena, but rather it shows the collection of the five aggregates. 'Samitapāpo' means one whose defiling states are extirpated. The sixth is straightforward.

Rohitassasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Rohitassa Sutta and so forth is concluded.

7. Suvidūrasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Suvidūra Sutta

47. Sattame [V 2.0276] suvidūravidūra-saddānaṃ samānatthānaṃyeva ekattha gahaṇaṃ idha niddeso dūrāsannabhāvassa apekkhāsiddhattā idhādhippetassa dūrabhāvassa kenaci pariyāyena anāsannabhāvadassanatthaṃ katanti āha “kenaci pariyāyena anāsannāni hutvā”tiādi. Sesamettha uttānameva.

47. In the seventh (sutta), regarding the taking together of the words 'suvidūra' and 'vidūra', which have the same meaning, the explanation here is made to show, by some means, the state of not-being-near of the farness intended here, since the state of being far or near is established by reference. Thus, he says: 'having become unproximate by some means,' etc. The rest here is clear.

Suvidūrasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Suvidūra Sutta is concluded.

8. Visākhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Visākha Sutta

48. Aṭṭhame vākkaraṇacāturiyato vacanaguṇahetūnaṃ pūriyā porī, poriyaṃ bhavāti porī, tāya poriyā. Tenāha “paripuṇṇavācāyā”ti, akkharapadaparipuṇṇāya vācāyāti attho. Apalibuddhāyāti pittādīhi [M 2.0304] na vibaddhāya ananubundhitāya. Anelagalāyāti anelāya agalāya niddosāya agaḷitapadabyañjanāya ca. Therassa hi kathayato padaṃ vā byañjanaṃ vā na parihāyati. Tenāha “anelagalāyāti niddosāya ceva agaḷitāya cā”tiādi. Tattha niddosāyāti atthato ca byañjanato ca vigatadosāya. Apatitapadabyañjanāyāti avirahitapadabyañjanāya. Atha vā anelagalāyāti na elaṃ dosaṃ galatīti anelagalā. Avicchinnavācāya anelagalāya yathā dandhamanussā mukhena kheḷaṃ gaḷantena vācaṃ bhāsanti, na evarūpāya. Atha kho niddosāya visadavācāyāti attho. Vivaṭṭappakāsinī vācā na kadāci vivaṭṭamuttāti katvā āha “vivaṭṭapariyāpannāyā”ti, vivaṭṭaṃ amuñcitvā pavattāyāti attho. Vivaṭṭappakāsinī hi vācā vivaṭṭaṃ paricchijja āpādentī pavattati. Navalokuttaradhammo sabbadhammehi samussitaṭṭhena abbhuggataṭṭhena ca dhajo nāmāti āha “abbhuggataṭṭhenā”tiādi. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

48. In the eighth (sutta), 'porī' is from 'pūriyā' (fulfillment) of the causes of the qualities of speech, from skill in expression. 'Poriyaṃ bhavati' (it becomes full) is 'porī'. By that 'porī'. Therefore, he said 'paripuṇṇavācāya' (with complete speech), meaning speech complete in syllables and words. 'Apalibuddhāya' means not bound by bile, etc., not tied down. 'Anelagalāya' means without fault, without defect, faultless, and with unslurred syllables and words. For when the Elder speaks, neither a word nor a syllable is lost. Therefore, he said: ''Anelagalāya' means faultless and unslurred,' etc. Therein, 'faultless' means free from faults both in meaning and in letter. 'Apatitapadabyañjanāya' means with words and syllables not omitted. Alternatively, 'anelagalā' is 'na elaṃ dosaṃ galati' (does not let a fault flow). With uninterrupted speech, 'anelagalā' means not of the kind that slow people speak, letting saliva drip from the mouth, but rather the meaning is faultless, clear speech. Because speech that illuminates the turning away (from saṃsāra) is never released from the turning away, he said 'vivaṭṭapariyāpannāya' (included in the turning away); the meaning is 'proceeding without abandoning the turning away'. For speech that illuminates the turning away proceeds by defining and bringing about the turning away. The nine supramundane Dhammas are called a banner because they are exalted and lofty above all other dhammas; thus he said 'by the meaning of being lofty,' etc. The rest here is easy to understand.

Visākhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Visākha Sutta is concluded.

9. Vipallāsasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Vipallāsa Sutta

49. Navame aniccādīni vatthūni niccantiādinā viparītato asantīti vipallāsā[V 2.0277], saññāya vipallāso saññāvipallāso. Itaresupi tīsu eseva nayo. Evamete catunnaṃ vatthūnaṃ vasena cattāro, tesu vatthūsu saññādīnaṃ vasena dvādasa honti. Tesu aṭṭha sotāpattimaggena pahīyanti. Asubhe subhanti saññācittavipallāsā sakadāgāmimaggena tanukā honti, anāgāmimaggena pahīyanti. Dukkhe sukhanti saññācittavipallāsā arahattamaggena pahīyantīti veditabbā. Sesamettha uttānameva.

49. In the ninth (sutta), because things such as the impermanent are perceived contrarily as permanent, etc., they are 'vipallāsas' (distortions), as they are non-existent in that way. The distortion of perception is 'saññāvipallāso'. The same method applies to the other three. Thus, there are four by way of the four objects, and in relation to those objects, there are twelve by way of perception, etc. Among them, eight are abandoned by the path of stream-entry. The distortions of perception and mind that perceive the foul as beautiful become attenuated by the path of the once-returner and are abandoned by the path of the non-returner. The distortions of perception and mind that perceive suffering as pleasure are abandoned by the path of arahantship—this should be understood. The rest here is clear.

Vipallāsasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vipallāsa Sutta is concluded.

10. Upakkilesasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Upakkilesa Sutta

50. Dasame [M 2.0305] upakkiliṭṭhabhāvakaraṇenāti malīnabhāvakaraṇena. Pañcavidhāya surāya catubbidhassa ca merayassāti ettha pūvasurā, piṭṭhasurā, odanasurā, kiṇṇapakkhittā, sambhārasaṃyuttāti pañca surā. Pupphāsavo, phalāsavo, madhvāsavo, guḷāsavoti cattāro āsavā, catubbidhaṃ merayaṃ nāma. Tattha pūve bhājane pakkhipitvā tajjaṃ udakaṃ datvā madditvā katā pūvasurā. Evaṃ sesasurāpi. Kiṇṇāti pana tassā surāya bījaṃ vuccati. Ye surā “modakā”tipi vuccanti, te pakkhipitvā katā kiṇṇapakkhittā. Dhātakiāsavādinānāsambhārehi saṃyojitā sambhārasaṃyuttā.Madhukatālanāḷikerādipuppharaso ciraparivāsito pupphāsavo. Panasādiphalaraso phalāsavo. Muddikāraso madhvāsavo. Ucchuraso guḷāsavo.

50. In the tenth (sutta), 'by making a defiled state' means by making an impure state. Regarding 'five kinds of surā and four kinds of meraya,' here the five kinds of surā are: pūva-surā (cake-liquor), piṭṭha-surā (flour-liquor), odana-surā (rice-liquor), kiṇṇa-pakkhittā (liquor with ferment added), and sambhāra-saṃyuttā (liquor combined with ingredients). The four kinds of āsava are: flower-liquor, fruit-liquor, honey-liquor, and molasses-liquor—these are called the four kinds of meraya. Among these, pūva-surā is made by placing cakes in a vessel, adding suitable water, and mashing it. The other kinds of surā are made similarly. 'Kiṇṇa' (ferment) is said to be the 'seed' of that surā. Those surā also called 'modakā' are made by adding them; this is 'kiṇṇa-pakkhittā'. 'Sambhāra-saṃyuttā' is prepared by combining it with various ingredients such as dhātakī flowers. Flower-liquor is the long-fermented juice of flowers such as madhuka, tāla, and nāḷikera. Fruit-liquor is the juice of fruits such as panasa. Honey-liquor is the juice of grapes (muddikā). Molasses-liquor is the juice of sugarcane.

Upakkilesasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Upakkilesa Sutta is concluded.

Rohitassavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Rohitassa Vagga is concluded.

Paṭhamapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The First Fifty (Paṇṇāsaka) is concluded.

2. Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

2. The Second Fifty

(6) 1. Puññābhisandavaggo

(6) 1. The Chapter on the Streams of Merit

1. Paṭhamapuññābhisandasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Streams of Merit

51. Dutiyassa [M 2.0306][V 2.0278] paṭhame puññābhisandāti vā puññanadiyo. Avicchedena niccaṃ pavattiyamānāni hi puññāni abhisandanaṭṭhena “puññābhisandā”ti vuttā. Aparimitanti āḷhakagaṇanāya aparimitaṃ, yojanavasena panassa parimāṇaṃ atthi. Tathā hi heṭṭhā mahāpathaviyā upari ākāsena parato cakkavāḷapabbatena majjhe tattha tattha ṭhitehi dīpapabbatapariyantehi paricchinnattā yojanato sakkā pamāṇaṃ kātuṃ. Bheravārammaṇehīti saviññāṇakāviññāṇakehi bheravārammaṇehi. Tathā hi taṃ mahāsarīramacchakumbhīlayakkharakkhasamahānāgadānavādīnaṃ saviññāṇakānaṃ vaḷavāmukhapātālādīnaṃ aviññāṇakānañca bheravārammaṇānaṃ vasena “bahubherava”nti vuccati. Sesamettha uttānameva.

51. In the first sutta of the second chapter, ‘streams of merit’ or ‘rivers of merit.’ Because merits flow continuously without interruption, they are called ‘streams of merit’ in the sense of flowing abundantly. ‘Immeasurable’ means it is immeasurable by the count of āḷhakas, but in terms of leagues, it has a measure. For it is bounded below by the great earth, above by the sky, beyond by the Cakkavāḷa mountain, and in between by the island-mountains situated here and there; thus it is possible to estimate its measure in leagues. ‘With terrifying objects’ means with terrifying objects, both animate and inanimate. For that great body of water is called ‘very terrifying’ because it contains terrifying objects, both animate, such as great fish, crocodiles, yakkhas, rakkhasas, great nāgas, and dānavas, and inanimate, such as the Vaḷavāmukha abyss and the underworld Pātāla. The rest here is clear.

Paṭhamapuññābhisandasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on Streams of Merit is concluded.

2. Dutiyapuññābhisandasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Streams of Merit

52. Dutiye sotāpannassa saddhā adhippetāti sotāpannassa maggenāgatā saddhā adhippetā.

52. In the second sutta, “the faith of a stream-enterer is intended” means the faith attained through the path of a stream-enterer is intended.

Dutiyapuññābhisandasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Discourse on Streams of Merit is concluded.

3-4. Paṭhamasaṃvāsasuttādivaṇṇanā

3–4. Commentary on the First Discourse on Co-residence and others

53-54. Tatiye yathākammaṃ tā tā gatiyo aranti upagacchantīti ariyā, sattā. Ime pana kucchitā ariyāti kadariyā. Thaddhamaccharino, thaddhena maccharena samannāgatāti attho. Thaddhamacchariyasadisañhi [V 2.0279] kucchitaṃ [M 2.0307] sabbadā nihīnaṃ natthi sabbaguṇānaṃ ādibhūtassa bhogasampattiādisabbasampattīnaṃ mūlabhūtassa dānassa nisedhanato. Tenāha “kadariyāti thaddhamaccharino”ti. Ekacco hi attano vasanaṭṭhāne bhikkhū hatthaṃ pasāretvāpi na vandati. Aññattha gato vihāraṃ pavisitvā sakkaccaṃ vanditvā madhurappaṭisanthāraṃ karoti “kiṃ, bhante, amhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ nāgacchatha, sampanno padeso, paṭibalāhaṃ ayyānaṃ yāgubhattādīhi upaṭṭhānaṃ kātu”nti. Bhikkhu “saddho ayaṃ upāsako”ti yāgubhattādīhi saṅgaṇhāti.

53–54. In the third sutta, beings who go to (aranti) or reach (upagacchanti) their various destinations according to their kamma are called ariyā. But these wretched ariyā are called kadariyā (misers). They are ‘stiff and miserly,’ meaning they are endowed with stiff miserliness. For there is nothing so wretched and always base as stiff miserliness, because it obstructs giving, which is the origin of all virtues and the root of all attainments, such as the attainment of wealth. Therefore, it is said: “‘Misers’ means those who are stiff and miserly.” For instance, a certain person does not even salute monks by extending his hand while in his own dwelling place. But when he goes elsewhere and enters a monastery, he respectfully salutes them and makes pleasant conversation, saying: “Venerable sirs, why do you not come to our dwelling place? The region is prosperous, and I am able to attend to the venerable ones with rice-gruel, meals, and so on.” A monk, thinking, “This lay follower is faithful,” accepts his offerings of rice-gruel, meals, and so on.

Atheko thero tassa gāmaṃ gantvā piṇḍāya carati. So taṃ disvā aññena vā gacchati, gharaṃ vā pavisati. Sacepi sammukhībhāvaṃ āgacchati, hatthena vanditvā “ayyassa bhikkhaṃ detha, ahaṃ ekena kammena gacchāmī”ti pakkamati. Thero sakalagāmaṃ caritvā tucchapattova nikkhamati. Idaṃ tāva mudumacchariyaṃ nāma. Yena adāyakopi dāyako viya paññāyati. Idha pana thaddhamacchariyaṃ adhippetaṃ. Yena samannāgato bhikkhūsu piṇḍāya paviṭṭhesu “therā ṭhitā”ti vutte “kiṃ mayhaṃ pādā rujjantī”tiādīni vatvā silāthambho viya khāṇuko viya ca thaddho hutvā tiṭṭhati, sāmīcimpi na karoti, kuto dānaṃ. Ayamidha adhippeto. Tena vuttaṃ “thaddhamaccharinoti thaddhena maccharena samannāgatāti attho”ti. Maccharaṃ maccheraṃ macchariyanti atthato ekaṃ.

Then a certain elder goes to that person’s village and walks for alms. Seeing the elder, that person either goes another way or enters a house. If he happens to come face to face with him, he salutes him with his hand and says, “Give alms to the venerable sir; I am going on some business,” and then departs. The elder, having walked through the entire village, leaves with an empty bowl. This is called ‘soft miserliness,’ by which even a non-giver appears to be a giver. But here ‘stiff miserliness’ is intended. One endowed with this, when monks have entered for alms and it is said, “The elders are standing here,” replies, “Are my feet hurting?” and so on, and stands there stiff like a stone pillar or a tree stump. He does not even perform a proper greeting, let alone give a gift. This is what is intended here. Therefore, it was said: “‘Stiff and miserly’ means endowed with stiff miserliness.” ‘Miserliness’ (maccharaṃ), ‘miserliness’ (maccheraṃ), and ‘miserliness’ (macchariyaṃ) are one in meaning.

Paribhāsakāti bhikkhū gharadvāre ṭhite disvā “kiṃ tumhe kasitvā āgatā vapitvā lāyitvā, mayaṃ attanopi na labhāma, kuto tumhākaṃ, sīghaṃ nikkhamathā”tiādīhi santajjakā. Yācakānaṃ vacanassa atthaṃ jānantīti ettha kiñcāpi bhikkhū gharadvāre ṭhitā tuṇhī honti, atthato pana “bhikkhaṃ dethā”ti vadanti nāma ariyāya yācanāya. Vuttañhetaṃ “uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhanti, esā ariyāna yācanā”ti (mi. pa. 4.5.9). Tatra ye “mayaṃ pacāma, ime na pacanti, pacamāne patvā alabhantā kuhiṃ labhissatī”ti deyyadhammaṃ saṃvibhajanti, te vadaññū yācakānaṃ vacanassa atthaṃ jānanti nāma ñatvā kattabbakaraṇato. Catutthaṃ uttānameva.

‘Revilers’ are those who, seeing monks standing at their door, threaten them with words like: “What, did you come here after plowing, sowing, and reaping? We ourselves do not get enough, so how could we give to you? Get out quickly!” Here, regarding ‘knowing the meaning of the words of supplicants’: although the monks stand silently at the door, in reality they are saying, “Give alms,” through the noble way of asking. As it is said: “The noble ones stand with a purpose; this is the asking of the noble ones.” Among them, those who think, “We cook, but these monks do not cook; if they do not receive anything from those who are cooking, where will they get it?” and share their alms-gifts, they are called ‘generous’ (vadaññū), as they are said to know the meaning of the supplicants’ words because they know what ought to be done. The fourth is clear.

Paṭhamasaṃvāsasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on Co-residence and others is concluded.

5-6. Samajīvīsuttādivaṇṇanā

5–6. Commentary on the Discourse on Living in Harmony and others

55-56. Pañcame [V 2.0280][M 2.0308] anuggaṇhanatthanti nakulamātā nakulapitāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ saṅgahatthāya. Nakulassa dārakassa pitā nakulapitā. Nakulamātāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sesamettha uttānameva. Chaṭṭhe natthi vattabbaṃ.

55–56. In the fifth sutta, ‘for the purpose of favoring’ means for the sake of helping these two, Nakulamātā and Nakulapitā. Nakulapitā is the father of the child Nakula. The same method applies to Nakulamātā. The rest here is clear. In the sixth, there is nothing to be said.

Samajīvīsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on Living in Harmony and others is concluded.

7-10. Suppavāsāsuttādivaṇṇanā

7–10. Commentary on the Discourse to Suppavāsā and others

57-60. Sattame āyubhāgapaṭilābhinī hotīti āyukoṭṭhāsassa paṭilābhinī hoti. Tividhalokanti sattasaṅkhārabhājanasaṅkhātaṃ tividhaṃ lokaṃ. Viditaṃ katvāti vibhūtaṃ katvā. Lokavidūnanti karaṇatthe sāmivacananti āha “buddhehi pasatthā”ti. Aṭṭhamanavamadasamāni uttānatthāneva.

57–60. In the seventh sutta, “she becomes a recipient of a share of life” means she becomes a recipient of a portion of the lifespan. “The threefold world” refers to the threefold world designated as the world of beings, the world of formations, and the world of space. “Having made it known” means having made it manifest. Regarding ‘of the knowers of the world’ (lokavidūnaṃ), the genitive case is used here in the sense of the instrumental; therefore it means ‘praised by the Buddhas’. The eighth, ninth, and tenth are clear in meaning.

Suppavāsāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse to Suppavāsā and others is concluded.

Puññābhisandavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Streams of Merit is concluded.

(7) 2. Pattakammavaggo

(7) 2. The Chapter on Suitable Action

1-4. Pattakammasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–4. Commentary on the Discourse on Suitable Action and others

61-64. Dutiyassa paṭhame ye aniṭṭhā na honti, te iṭṭhāti adhippetāti āha “aniṭṭhapaṭikkhepena iṭṭhā”ti. Iṭṭhāti ca pariyiṭṭhā vā hotu mā vā, iṭṭhārammaṇabhūtāti attho. Gavesitampi hi iṭṭhanti vuccati, taṃ idha nādhippetaṃ. Maneti manasmiṃ. Kantāti vā kamanīyā, kāmetabbāti attho. Manaṃ appāyantīti iṭṭhabhāvena manaṃ vaḍḍhenti. Kammasādhano idha bhoga-saddoti āha “bhogāti bhuñjitabbā”tiādi. Dhammūpaghātaṃ katvā kusaladhammaṃ vinodetvā. Upanijjhāyīyantīti [V 2.0281] upajjhāyāti [M 2.0309] āha “sukhadukkhesu upanijjhāyitabbattā”ti, sukhadukkhesu uppannesu anussaritabbattāti attho. Sandiṭṭhasambhattehīti ettha tattha tattha saṅgamma diṭṭhamattā nātidaḷhamittā sandiṭṭhā, suṭṭhu bhattā sinehavanto daḷhamittā sambhattā.

61–64. In the first point of the second sutta, that which is not undesirable is intended to be desirable; hence it is said, “desirable by the exclusion of the undesirable.” And “desirable” means being a desirable object, whether it is sought after or not. For even what is sought after is called “desirable,” but that is not intended here. The word mane means “in the mind.” Kantā (“pleasing”) means lovely, to be desired. “Delighting the mind” means they increase the mind through their desirability. Here, the word bhoga (“wealth”) is derived in the objective sense, hence it is said, “bhogā means that which is to be enjoyed,” and so on. “Having harmed the Dhamma” means having eliminated wholesome qualities. The term upajjhāya (“preceptor”) is explained via upanijjhāyanti (“they contemplate”), hence it is said, “because they are to be contemplated in happiness and suffering,” meaning they are to be remembered when happiness and suffering arise. Regarding “acquaintances and close friends” (sandiṭṭhasambhattehi): here, “acquaintances” (sandiṭṭhā) are those met and merely seen here and there, who are not very firm friends; “close friends” (sambhattā) are those who are well-devoted, affectionate, and firm friends.

Visamalobhanti balavalobhaṃ. Sukhitanti sañjātasukhaṃ. Pīṇitanti dhātaṃ suhitaṃ. Tathābhūto pana yasmā balasampanno hoti, tasmā “balasampannaṃ karotī”ti vuttaṃ.

“Wrong greed” means strong greed. “Happy” means with happiness arisen. “Nourished” means satisfied and satiated. Because such a person is endowed with strength, it is said, “it makes one endowed with strength.”

Sobhane kāyikavācasikakamme ratoti sūrato ukārassa dīghaṃ katvā, tassa bhāvo soraccaṃ, kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo. So pana atthato susīlabhāvoti āha “khantisoracce niviṭṭhāti adhivāsanakkhantiyañca susīlatāya ca niviṭṭhā”ti. Ekamattānanti ekaṃ cittanti attho. Rāgādīnañhi pubbabhāgiyaṃ damanādi paccekaṃ icchitabbaṃ, na maggakkhaṇe viya ekajjhaṃ paṭisaṅkhānamukhena pajahanato. Ekamattānanti vā vivekavasena ekaṃ ekākinaṃ attānaṃ. Tenevāha “ekaṃ attanova attabhāva”ntiādi. Uparūparibhūmīsūti chakāmasaggasaṅkhātāsu uparūparikāmabhūmīsu. Kammassa phalaṃ aggaṃ nāma. Taṃ panettha uccagāmīti āha “uddhamaggamassā”ti. Suvagge niyuttā, suvaggappayojanāti vā sovaggikā. Dasannaṃ visesānanti dibbaāyuvaṇṇayasasukhaādhipateyyānañceva iṭṭharūpādīnañca phalavisesānaṃ. Vaṇṇaggahaṇena cettha sako attabhāvavaṇṇo gahito, rūpaggahaṇena bahiddhā rūpārammaṇaṃ. Dutiyatatiyacatutthāni uttānatthāneva.

'One who delights in beautiful bodily and verbal conduct' is a sūrata. By elongating the vowel 'u', its state becomes soracca, gentleness, which is non-transgression in bodily and verbal conduct. This, in meaning, is the state of good conduct, as it is said, 'established in patience and gentleness,' meaning established in the patience of forbearance and in good conduct. 'One with a single self' means with one mind. For of lust and so on, the preliminary subduing and the like should be desired for each individually, not as at the moment of the path where they are abandoned all at once by way of reflective understanding. Alternatively, 'one with a single self' means a solitary self, alone through seclusion. Hence it is said, 'one's own single being,' and so on. 'In higher and higher planes' refers to the higher sensual planes, known as the six sensual heavens. The foremost result of kamma is called supreme. Here, it is said to be 'upward-bound,' meaning 'for one on the upward path.' 'Leading to a good destination' means destined for a good destination or having a good destination as its purpose. 'Of the ten distinctions' refers to the special fruits of divine lifespan, beauty, fame, happiness, lordship, and desirable forms, and so on. Here, by the term 'beauty,' one's own bodily beauty is meant; by the term 'form,' an external form-object is meant. The second, third, and fourth are of obvious meaning.

Pattakammasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sutta on Meritorious Deeds, etc., is concluded.

5. Rūpasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Rūpa Sutta.

65. Pañcame paminoti uḷāratādivisesaṃ etenāti pamāṇaṃ, rupakāyo pamāṇaṃ etassāti rūpappamāṇo. Tato eva rūpe pasannoti rūpappasanno. Ghosoti cettha thutighoso. Lūkhanti paccayalūkhatā. Dhammāti sīlādayo guṇadhammā adhippetā. Imesaṃ pana catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ pāḷiyaṃyeva āgataṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

65. In the fifth, 'one measures distinctions such as excellence by means of this,' thus it is a measure; 'the physical body is a measure for this one,' thus 'one who measures by form.' 'From that very form one is pleased,' thus 'one pleased by form.' Here, 'sound' (ghosa) means the sound of praise. 'Coarse' (lūkha) means coarseness of requisites. 'Qualities' (dhammā) are intended to mean virtuous qualities such as morality. Now, the distinctions among these four types of individuals are given in the Pāli text itself. For it has been said:

“Katamo [M 2.0310] ca puggalo rūpappamāṇo rūpappasanno? Idhekacco puggalo ārohaṃ vā passitvā [V 2.0282] pariṇāhaṃ vā passitvā saṇṭhānaṃ vā passitvā pāripūriṃ vā passitvā tattha pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasādaṃ janeti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo rūpappamāṇo rūpappasanno.

“And what sort of person is one who measures by form and is pleased by form? Here, a certain person, having seen height or girth or shape or completeness, takes that as a measure and generates faith. This is called a person who measures by form and is pleased by form.”

“Katamo ca puggalo ghosappamāṇo ghosappasanno? Idhekacco puggalo paravaṇṇanāya parathomanāya parapasaṃsanāya paravaṇṇahārikāya tattha pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasādaṃ janeti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo ghosappamāṇo ghosappasanno.

“And what sort of person is one who measures by sound and is pleased by sound? Here, a certain person, by the praise of others, by the extolling of others, by the commendation of others, or by the spreading of others' fame, takes that as a measure and generates faith. This is called a person who measures by sound and is pleased by sound.”

“Katamo ca puggalo lūkhappamāṇo lūkhappasanno? Idhekacco puggalo cīvaralūkhaṃ vā passitvā pattalūkhaṃ vā passitvā senāsanalūkhaṃ vā passitvā vividhaṃ vā dukkarakārikaṃ passitvā tattha pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasādaṃ janeti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo lūkhappamāṇo lūkhappasanno.

“And what sort of person is one who measures by roughness and is pleased by roughness? Here, a certain person, having seen rough robes or a rough bowl or a rough dwelling, or various difficult practices, takes that as a measure and generates faith. This is called a person who measures by roughness and is pleased by roughness.”

“Katamo ca puggalo dhammappamāṇo dhammappasanno? Idhekacco puggalo sīlaṃ vā passitvā samādhiṃ vā passitvā paññaṃ vā passitvā tattha pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasādaṃ janeti. Ayaṃ vuccati puggalo dhammappamāṇo dhammappasanno”ti (pu. pa. 171-172).

“And what sort of person is one who measures by the Dhamma and is pleased by the Dhamma? Here, a certain person, having seen virtue or concentration or wisdom, takes that as a measure and generates faith. This is called a person who measures by the Dhamma and is pleased by the Dhamma.” (Pug. 171–172)

Tattha ārohanti uccataṃ. Sā ca kho tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle pamāṇayuttā daṭṭhabbā. Pariṇāhanti nātikisathūlatāvasena pīṇataṃ. Saṇṭhānanti tesaṃ tesaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ susaṇṭhitataṃ dīgharassavaṭṭādiyuttaṭṭhānesu tathābhāvaṃ. Pāripūrinti sabbesaṃ sarīrāvayavānaṃ paripuṇṇataṃ avikalataṃ. Tattha pamāṇaṃ gahetvāti tasmiṃ rūpe rūpasampattiyaṃ pamāṇabhāvaṃ upādāya. Pasādaṃ janetīti adhimokkhaṃ janeti uppādeti.

Here, 'height' means tallness. This should be seen as appropriate in each particular case. 'Girth' means plumpness, in the sense of not being too thin nor too stout. 'Shape' means the well-formed state of the various major and minor limbs, their being as they should be in places appropriate to length, shortness, roundness, and so on. 'Completeness' means the perfect state of all bodily parts, their being without defect. 'Taking that as a measure' means taking the perfection of form in that form as a measure. 'Generates faith' means generates and produces conviction.

Paravaṇṇanāyāti “asuko ediso ca ediso cā”ti parassa guṇavacanena. Parathomanāyāti parammukhā parassa silāghuppādakena abhitthavanena parena thutivasena, gāthādiupanibandhanena vuttāya thomanāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Parapasaṃsanāyāti parammukhā parassa guṇasaṃkittanena. Paravaṇṇahārikāyāti [M 2.0311] paramparavaṇṇahārikāya paramparāya parassa kittanasaddassa upasaṃhārena. Tatthāti tasmiṃ thutighose.

'By the praise of others' means by speaking of another's qualities, saying, 'So-and-so is such and such.' 'By the extolling of others' means by extolling another in their presence with praise that produces applause, by way of praise spoken by another; that is to say, by praise spoken through the composition of verses and so on. 'By the commendation of others' means by recounting another's virtues in their presence. 'By the spreading of others' fame' means by bringing up the word of praise for another that has been passed down through a succession of people. 'Therein' refers to that sound of praise.

Cīvaralūkhanti thūlajiṇṇabahutunnakatādicīvarassa lūkhabhāvaṃ. Pattalūkhanti anekaganthikāhaṭatādipattassa [V 2.0283] lūkhabhāvaṃ. Vividhaṃ vā dukkarakārikanti dhutaṅgādivasena pavattanānāvidhaṃ dukkaracariyaṃ. Sīlaṃ vā passitvāti sīlapāripūrivasena visuddhaṃ kāyavacīsucaritaṃ ñāṇacakkhunā passitvā, jhānādiadhigamasuddhisamādhiṃ vā vipassanābhiññāsaṅkhātaṃ paññaṃ vā passitvāti attho.

'Coarseness of robes' means the coarse nature of robes that are thick, old, much-mended, and so on. 'Coarseness of a bowl' refers to the coarse nature of a bowl that is put together with many joints or patches, and so on. 'Various difficult practices' means the diverse difficult conduct practiced by way of the ascetic practices and the like.
