'Having seen virtue' means having seen, with the eye of wisdom, the pure good conduct of body and speech perfected by way of the complete fulfillment of virtue; or having seen the purity of concentration attained through jhāna and so on; or having seen wisdom consisting of insight and higher knowledge. This is the meaning.

Evametasmiṃ catuppamāṇe lokasannivāse buddhesu appasannā mandā, pasannā bahukā. Rūpappamāṇassa hi buddharūpato uttari pasādāvahaṃ rūpaṃ nāma natthi. Ghosappamāṇassa buddhānaṃ kittighosato uttari pasādāvaho ghoso nāma natthi. Lūkhappamāṇassa kāsikāni vatthāni mahārahāni kañcanabhājanāni tiṇṇaṃ utūnaṃ anucchavike sabbasampattiyutte pāsādavare pahāya paṃsukūlacīvaraselamayapattarukkhamūlādisenāsanasevino buddhassa bhagavato lūkhato uttari pasādāvahaṃ aññaṃ lūkhaṃ nāma natthi. Dhammappamāṇassa sadevake loke asādhāraṇasīlādiguṇassa tathāgatassa sīlādiguṇato uttari pasādāvaho añño sīlādiguṇo nāma natthi. Iti bhagavā imaṃ catuppamāṇikaṃ lokasannivāsaṃ muṭṭhinā gahetvā viya ṭhitoti.

Thus, in this world-assembly of four measures, those not pleased with the Buddhas are few, while those pleased are many. For one who measures by form, there is no form more inspiring of faith than the Buddha's form. For one who measures by sound, there is no sound more inspiring of faith than the fame of the Buddhas. For one who measures by roughness, there is no roughness more inspiring of faith than that of the Blessed One, the Buddha, who, having abandoned fine Kāsī garments, priceless golden vessels, and excellent palaces equipped with all comforts suitable for the three seasons, resorts to rag-robes, a stone bowl, and lodgings at the root of a tree and the like. For one who measures by the Dhamma, there is no virtue or quality more inspiring of faith than the unparalleled virtues, such as morality, of the Tathāgata in the world with its devas. Thus, the Blessed One stands as if holding this world-assembly of four measures in his fist.

Pamāṇiṃsūti pamāṇaṃ aggahesuṃ. Niyakajjhatte tassa guṇaṃ na jānātīti tassa abbhantare pavattamānaṃ sīlādiguṇaṃ na jānāti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

'They measured' means 'they took a measure.' 'He does not know the quality in his own self' means he does not know the virtues such as morality occurring within him. The rest is quite easily understood.

Rūpasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Rūpa Sutta is concluded.

7. Ahirājasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Ahirāja Sutta

67. Sattame daṭṭhavisānevāti avadhāraṇena diṭṭhavisādayo nivatteti. Kaṭṭhamukhādayo hi cattāro āsīvisā daṭṭhaviso, diṭṭhaviso, phuṭṭhaviso, vātavisoti paccekaṃ catubbidhā hontīti visavegavikāravasena [M 2.0312] soḷasa vuttā. Tesu daṭṭhavisānaṃyeva idha gahaṇaṃ, na itaresanti dasseti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

67. In the seventh sutta, by the specification 'only poison from biting,' it excludes poison from sight and so on. For the four kinds of venomous snakes, such as Kaṭṭhamukha, are each fourfold: those with poison from biting, those with poison from sight, those with poison from touch, and those with wind poison. Thus, sixteen are mentioned based on the variations in the force of their poison. Among these, it is shown that only those with poison from biting are taken here, not the others. The rest is easily understood.

Ahirājasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ahirāja Sutta is concluded.

8. Devadattasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Devadatta Sutta

68. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0284] kāle sampatteti gabbhassa paripākagatattā vijāyanakāle sampatte. Potakanti assatariyā puttaṃ. “Phalaṃ ve kadaliṃ hantī”tiādigāthāya kukkujakeneva pattavaṭṭipasavassa ucchinnattā phaluppatti kadaliyā parābhavāya hotīti āha “phalaṃ ve kadaliṃ hantī”ti. Kukkujakaṃ nāma kadaliyā pupphanāḷaṃ. Tathā phalapākapariyosānattā osadhīnaṃ “phalaṃ veḷuṃ naḷa”nti vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha piṇḍattho – yathā attano phalaṃ kadaliveḷunaḷe vināseti, gabbho ca assatariṃ, evaṃ attano kammabhūto sakkāro asappurisaṃ vināsetīti.

68. In the eighth [sutta], 'kāle sampatte' (when the time has arrived) means when the time for birth has arrived due to the maturity of the womb. 'Potaka' means the offspring of a mule. By the verse beginning 'The fruit indeed destroys the banana,' it is said 'the fruit indeed destroys the banana' because the arising of the fruit leads to the banana's ruin, since the production of its leaf-sheaths is cut off by the flower stalk itself. 'Kukkujaka' is the name for the banana's flower stalk. Similarly, because medicinal plants perish with the ripening of their fruit, it is said, 'the fruit destroys the bamboo and reed.' Here, the condensed meaning is this: just as its own fruit destroys the banana, bamboo, and reed, and the embryo destroys the mule, so too does the honor that has arisen from one's actions destroy an unworthy person.

Devadattasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Devadatta Sutta is concluded.

9. Padhānasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Padhāna Sutta

69. Navame padahati etehīti padhānāni. Uttamavīriyāni seṭṭhavīriyāni visiṭṭhassa atthassa sādhanato. Kilesānaṃ saṃvaratthāyāti yathā abhijjhādayo na uppajjanti, evaṃ satiyā upaṭṭhānena kilesānaṃ saṃvaraṇatthāya. Pajahanatthāyāti kāmavitakkādīnaṃ vinodanatthāya. Padhānanti tasseva pajahanassa sādhanavasena pavattavīriyaṃ. Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ brūhanatthāyāti bojjhaṅgasaṅkhātānaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ vaḍḍhanatthāya. Padhānanti tasseva vaḍḍhanassa sādhanavasena pavattavīriyaṃ.

69. In the ninth [sutta], 'padhānāni' (exertions) means 'they strive with these.' They are supreme efforts, excellent efforts, because they accomplish a distinguished goal. 'For the sake of restraint of defilements' means for the purpose of restraining defilements by the establishment of mindfulness, so that defilements such as covetousness and so on do not arise. 'For the sake of abandoning' means for the purpose of removing thoughts of sensuality and the like. 'Exertion' means the effort that occurs as a means of accomplishing that very abandoning. 'For the sake of the cultivation of wholesome qualities' means for the purpose of increasing wholesome qualities reckoned as the enlightenment factors. 'Exertion' means the effort that occurs as a means of accomplishing that very cultivation.

Padhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Padhāna Sutta is concluded.

10. Adhammikasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Adhammika Sutta

70. Dasame visamanti bhāvanapuṃsakametaṃ. Tenāha “visamā hutvā”ti. Asamayenāti akāle. Bhummatthe hetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Pakaṭṭhaṃ [M 2.0313] padhānaṃ añjasaṃ etesanti pañjasā, añjasaṃ pagatā paṭipannāti vā pañjasā, pakatimaggagāmino. Na pañjasā apañjasā, amaggappaṭipannā. Te pana yasmā maggato apagatā nāma honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “maggato apagatā”tiādi.

70. In the tenth [sutta], 'visamaṃ' (uneven) is a neuter noun indicating a state. Therefore it is said, 'having become uneven.' 'Asamayena' (at the wrong time) means at an inopportune time. This instrumental case has the sense of the locative. 'Pañjasā' are those for whom the straight path is pre-eminent and primary; or, they are those who have gone forth and are practicing on the straight path; they are those who go on the natural path. Not 'pañjasā' are 'apañjasā', those who are practicing on the non-path. But because they are indeed said to have departed from the path, therefore it is stated, 'they have departed from the path,' and so on.

Gāthāsu pana evamettha sambandho veditabbo. Gunnaṃ ce taramānānanti gāvīsu mahoghaṃ tarantīsu. Jimhaṃ gacchati puṅgavoti yadi yūthapati usabho kuṭilaṃ gacchati. Sabbā tā jimhaṃ gacchantīti [V 2.0285] sabbā tā gāviyo kuṭilameva gacchanti. Kasmā? Nette jimhaṃ gate sati tassa kuṭilagatattā. So hi tāsaṃ paccayiko upaddavaharo ca. Evamevanti yathā cetaṃ, evameva yo manussesu padhānasammato, yadi so adhammacārī siyā, ye tassa anujīvino, sabbepi adhammikā honti. Sāmisampadā hi pakatisampadaṃ sampādeti. Yasmā etadevaṃ, tasmā sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ dukkhaṃ seti, rājā ce hoti adhammiko.

In the verses, however, the connection here should be understood as follows: 'When the cattle are crossing' (Gunnaṃ ce taramānānaṃ) means when the cows are crossing a great flood. 'The leader goes crookedly' (Jimhaṃ gacchati puṅgavo) means if the herd leader, the bull, goes crookedly. 'All go crookedly' (Sabbā tā jimhaṃ gacchanti) means all those cows go crookedly indeed. Why? Because the leader has gone crooked, due to his crooked movement. For he is their authority and remover of dangers. 'Just so' (Evameva) means just as this is, so too among humans, if one who is considered a leader were to be unrighteous, all those who live in dependence on him would also be unrighteous. For the excellence of the master brings about the excellence of the retinue. Since this is so, therefore, the whole realm lies in misery if the king is unrighteous.

Adhammikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Adhammika Sutta is concluded.

Pattakammavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Due Performance is concluded.

(8) 3. Apaṇṇakavaggo

(8) 3. The Apaṇṇaka Chapter

1-2. Padhānasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Padhāna Sutta and others

71-72. Tatiyavaggassa paṭhame yavati tena phalaṃ missitaṃ viya hotīti yoni, ekantikaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Assāti yathāvuttassa bhikkhuno. Paripuṇṇanti avikalaṃ anavasesaṃ. Āsave khepetīti āsavakkhayo, aggamaggo. Idha pana arahattaphalaṃ adhippetanti āha “arahattatthāyā”ti. Dutiyaṃ uttānameva.

71-72. In the first [sutta] of the third chapter, 'yoni' (origin) means that by which the fruit is as if mixed; it is the exclusive cause. 'Assa' (his) refers to the bhikkhu as previously described. 'Paripuṇṇaṃ' (complete) means without defect, without remainder. 'Āsave khepeti' (he destroys the taints) means the destruction of the taints, the supreme path. Here, however, the fruit of arahantship is intended; therefore it is said, 'for the sake of arahantship' (arahattatthāya). The second [sutta] is self-explanatory.

Padhānasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Padhāna Sutta and others is concluded.

3-5. Sappurisasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-5. Commentary on the Sappurisa Sutta and others

73-75. Tatiye [M 2.0314] pañhatthāya abhinītoti pañhakaraṇatthāya abhimukhaṃ nīto. Alambitaṃ katvāti alambaṃ katvā, ayameva vā pāṭho, vipalambaṃ akatvāti attho. Avajānātīti avaññaṃ karoti, nindatīti attho. Catutthapañcame natthi vattabbaṃ.

73-75. In the third [sutta], 'pañhatthāya abhinīto' (led forward for the sake of a question) means led forward for the purpose of questioning. 'Alambitaṃ katvā' means having made a support; or alternatively, this is the reading: 'vipalambaṃ akatvā,' meaning not having made a delay. 'Avajānāti' (he despises) means he shows contempt; the meaning is he censures. In the fourth and fifth [suttas], there is nothing to be said.

Sappurisasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sappurisa Sutta and others is concluded.

6. Kusinārasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Kusināra Sutta

76. Chaṭṭhe [V 2.0286] nagaraṃ pavisitukāmā uyyānato upecca vattanti gacchanti etenāti upavattanaṃ. Yatheva hi kalambanaditīrato rājamātuvihāradvārena thūpārāmaṃ gantabbaṃ hoti, evaṃ hiraññavatikāya pārimatīrato sālavanaṃ uyyānaṃ, yathā anurādhapurassa thūpārāmo dakkhiṇapacchimadisāya, evaṃ taṃ uyyānaṃ kusinārāya dakkhiṇapacchimadisāya hoti. Yathā thūpārāmato dakkhiṇadvārena nagaraṃ pavisanamaggo pācīnamukho gantvā uttarena nivattati, evaṃ uyyānato sālapanti pācīnamukhā gantvā uttarena nivattā, tasmā taṃ “upavattana”nti vuccati. Antareti dvinnaṃ sālarukkhānaṃ vemajjhe. Tattha hi paññāpiyamānassa mañcassa ekā sālapanti sīsabhāge hoti, ekā pādabhāge. Tatrapi eko taruṇasālo sīsabhāgassa āsanno hoti, eko pādabhāgassa. Apica yamakasālā nāma mūlakhandhaviṭapapattehi aññamaññaṃ saṃsibbitvā ṭhitasālātipi vadanti.

76. In the sixth [sutta], 'Upavattana' is so called because, wishing to enter the city, one approaches from the park and proceeds along this way. Just as from the bank of the Kalamba River, one must go to the Thūpārāma through the gate of the Queen Mother’s monastery, so from the far bank of the Hiraññavatī River, one reaches the Sāla Grove park. Just as the Thūpārāma of Anurādhapura is in the southwest direction, so that park is in the southwest direction of Kusinārā. Just as from the Thūpārāma, the path to enter the city through the southern gate goes eastward and then turns north, so from the park, the row of Sāla trees goes eastward and then turns north; therefore, it is called 'Upavattana.' 'Between' means in the middle of the two Sāla trees. There, for the couch being prepared, one row of Sāla trees was at the head end, and another at the foot end. Also, one young Sāla tree was near the head end, and another near the foot end. Furthermore, they also say that the 'twin Sāla trees' (yamakasālā) are Sāla trees standing intertwined with each other by their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves.

Dveḷhakanti dvidhāgāho, anekaṃsaggāhoti attho. Vimatīti saṃsayāpattīti āha “vinicchituṃ asamatthatā”ti. Taṃ vo vadāmīti taṃ saṃsayavantaṃ bhikkhuṃ sandhāya vo tumhe vadāmīti. Nikkaṅkhabhāvapaccakkhakaraṇanti buddhādīsu tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ nikkaṅkhabhāvassa paccakkhakāriyā yāthāvato tamatthaṃ paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇameva. Etthāti etasmiṃ atthe.

'Dveḷhaka' means a two-fold grasp; the meaning is an inconclusive grasp. 'Doubt' (vimati) means falling into uncertainty; it is said, 'the inability to decide.' 'I say this to you' means, referring to that monk who has doubt, 'I say this to you all.' 'Making apparent the state of being without doubt' is the omniscient knowledge itself, which, having penetrated that meaning as it actually is and being established therein, makes apparent the state of being without doubt of those monks regarding the Buddha and others. 'Here' (ettha) means in this meaning.

Kusinārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kusināra Sutta is concluded.

7. Acinteyyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Acinteyya Sutta

77. Sattame [M 2.0315] lokacintāti lokasannivesappaṭisaṃyuttā vīmaṃsā. Tenāha “kena nu kho candimasūriyā”tiādi. Nāḷikerādayoti ādi-saddena avuttānaṃ osadhitiṇavanappatiādīnaṃ saṅgaho. Evarūpā lokacintāti edisā vuttasadisā aññāpi sā lokacintā.

77. In the seventh [sutta], 'worldly speculation' is investigation connected with the constitution of the world. Hence it is said, 'By what means are the sun and moon,' and so on. 'Coconut trees, etc.': by the word 'etc.' there is the inclusion of the unmentioned medicinal herbs, grasses, great trees, and so on. 'Such worldly speculation' means this kind of worldly speculation, similar to what has been mentioned, as well as other kinds.

Acinteyyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Acinteyya Sutta is concluded.

8. Dakkhiṇasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Dakkhiṇā Sutta

78. Aṭṭhame [V 2.0287] dānasaṅkhātāya dakkhiṇāyāti deyyadhammasaṅkhātāya dakkhiṇāya. Visuddhi nāma mahājutikatā. Sā pana mahapphalatāya veditabbāti āha “mahapphalabhāvenā”ti. Visujjhatīti na kilissati, amalinā mahājutikā mahāvipphārā hotīti attho. Sucidhammoti rāgādiasucividhamanena sucisabhāvo. Lāmakadhammoti hīnasabhāvo pāpakiriyāya. Akusaladhammā hi ekantanihīnā. Jūjako sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo na hoti, tassa mahābodhisattassa attano puttadānaṃ dānapāramiyā matthakaṃ gaṇhantaṃ mahāpathavikampanasamatthaṃ jātaṃ. Svāyaṃ dāyakaguṇoti āha “vessantaramahārājā kathetabbo”tiādi. Uddharatīti bahulaṃ pāpakammavasena laddhabbavinipātato uddharati, tasmā natthi mayhaṃ kiñci cittassa aññatthattanti adhippāyo.

78. In the eighth [sutta], 'by the offering reckoned as giving' means by the offering reckoned as a gift-object. Purity means great radiance. But that should be understood by its great fruitfulness, hence it is said, 'by way of great fruitfulness.' 'It becomes pure' means it is not defiled; the meaning is that, being stainless, it becomes greatly radiant and greatly pervasive. 'Of pure dhamma' means having a pure nature through the dispelling of impurities such as lust. 'Of base dhamma' means having a low nature through evil action. For unwholesome dhammas are utterly base. Jūjaka was not virtuous nor of good qualities; but the giving of his own children by that Great Bodhisatta, which attained the summit of the perfection of giving, was capable of causing the great earth to tremble. This is the quality of the donor, hence it is said, 'King Vessantara should be spoken of,' and so on. 'He lifts up' means he lifts one up from the woeful state to be obtained through abundant evil deeds; therefore, the intention is, 'there is for me no other state of mind whatsoever.'

Petadakkhiṇanti pete uddissa dātabbadakkhiṇaṃ. Pāpitakāleyevāti “idaṃ dānaṃ asukassa petassa hotū”ti taṃuddisanavasena pattiyā pāpitakāleyeva. Assāti petassa. Pāpuṇīti phalasampattilabhāpanavasena pāpuṇi. Ayañhi pete uddissa dāne dhammatā. Tadā kosalarañño pariccāgavasena ativiya dānajjhāsayataṃ buddhappamukhassa ca saṅghassa ukkaṃsagataguṇavisiṭṭhataṃ sandhāyāha “asadisadānaṃ kathetabba”nti.

'An offering to the departed' means an offering to be given having designated the departed. 'At the very moment it is conveyed' means that at the very moment it is conveyed by way of dedication with the thought, 'May this gift be for such-and-such a departed one.' 'To him' means to the departed one. 'He attains' means he attains by way of receiving the fruition. For this is the natural law in giving for the sake of the departed. At that time, referring to King Kosala's generosity, his exceedingly charitable disposition, and the supreme distinction of the qualities of the Sangha headed by the Buddha, it was said: 'An incomparable gift should be spoken of.'

Dakkhiṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dakkhiṇā Sutta is concluded.

9-10. Vaṇijjasuttādivaṇṇanā

9-10. Commentary on the Vaṇijja Sutta and so on.

79-80. Navame [M 2.0316] taṃsadisāti yādisā vaṇijjā payuttā ayathādhippāyā aññā vā sampajjati, tādisāvāti attho. Chedaṃ gacchatīti vināsaṃ pāpuṇāti. Adhippāyato parā visiṭṭhāti parādhippāyo. Tenevāha “ajjhāsayato adhikataraphalā hotī”ti. Cīvarādinā paccayena vadeyyāsīti cīvarādipaccayahetu maṃ vadeyyāsi pattheyyāsi. Atha vā yadā cīvarādinā paccayena attho hoti, tadā maṃ yāceyyāsīti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva. Dasamaṃ uttānameva.

79-80. In the ninth, 'like that' means: whatever trade is undertaken, whether it turns out not according to intention or otherwise, it is like that—this is the meaning. 'Goes to destruction' means it reaches ruin. 'Exceeding the intention' means superior to the intention. Therefore, it is said, 'It bears greater fruit due to one's disposition.' 'You would speak to me for the sake of robes and other requisites' means you would address me, you would request me, on account of robes and other requisites. Or else, when there is a need for robes and other requisites, then you should ask of me—this is the meaning. The rest is easily understood. The tenth is clear.

Vaṇijjasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vaṇijja Sutta and so on is concluded.

Apaṇṇakavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Vagga is concluded.

(9) 4. Macalavaggo

(9) 4. The Macala Chapter

1-6. Pāṇātipātasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-6. Commentary on the Pāṇātipāta Sutta and so on.

81-86. Catutthassa [V 2.0288] paṭhamādīni uttānatthāneva. Pañcame (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.132) “nīce kule paccājāto”tiādikena appakāsabhāvena tamatīti tamo, tena tamena yuttoti tamo puggalo vuccati. Tathā hi taṃyogato puggalassa tabbohāro yathā “maccherayogato maccharo”ti, tasmā tamoti appakāsabhāvena tamo tamabhūto andhakāraṃ viya jāto, andhakārattaṃ vā pattoti attho. Vuttalakkhaṇaṃ tamameva paramparato ayanaṃ gati niṭṭhā etassāti tamaparāyaṇo. Ubhayenapi tamaggahaṇena khandhatamo kathito, na andhakāratamo. Khandhatamoti ca sampattirahitā khandhapavattiyeva daṭṭhabbā. “Ucce kule paccājāto”tiādikena pakāsabhāvena jotetīti joti, tena jotināyuttotiādi sabbaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Itare dveti jotitamaparāyaṇo, jotijotiparāyaṇoti itare dve puggale.

81-86. The first and following of the fourth are clear in meaning. In the fifth, regarding the phrase beginning 'born in a low family,' due to an inconspicuous nature one is obscured (tamatīti), hence this is 'darkness' (tamo). One who is connected with that darkness is called a 'dark person' (tamo puggalo). For the designation of a person is from their association, as 'a stingy person' (maccharo) is from association with stinginess (maccherayogato). Therefore, 'darkness' means being inconspicuous; one has become darkness, is like darkness, or has attained the state of darkness—this is the meaning. He is 'one bound for darkness' (tamaparāyaṇo) for whom that very darkness with the aforementioned characteristic is the subsequent course, destination, and final state. By both uses of 'darkness,' the darkness of the aggregates is meant, not literal darkness. And 'darkness of the aggregates' should be understood as simply the continuation of the aggregates, devoid of attainment. Regarding the phrase beginning 'born in a high family,' due to a conspicuous nature one illuminates (jotetīti), hence this is 'light' (joti). One who is connected with that light (jotināyutto), and so on—all this should be understood in the way that has been explained. 'The other two' refers to the other two persons: the one going from light to darkness (jotitamaparāyaṇo) and the one going from light to light (jotijotiparāyaṇo).

Veṇuvettādivilīvehi peḷabhājanādikārakā vilīvakārakā. Migamacchādīnaṃ nisādanato nesādā, māgavikamacchabandhādayo. Rathesu cammena [M 2.0317] nahaṇakaraṇato rathakārā, cammakārā. Puiti karīsassa nāmaṃ, taṃ kusenti apanentīti pukkusā, pupphachaḍḍakā. Dubbaṇṇoti virūpo. Okoṭimakoti ārohābhāvena heṭṭhimako, rassakāyoti attho. Tenāha “lakuṇḍako”ti. Laku viya ghaṭikā viya ḍeti pavattatīti lakuṇḍako, rasso. Kaṇati nimīlatīti kāṇo. Taṃ panassa nimīlanaṃ ekena akkhinā dvīhipi vāti āha “ekacchikāṇo vā ubhayacchikāṇo vā”ti. Kuṇanaṃ kuṇo, hatthavekallaṃ, so etassa atthīti kuṇī. Khañjo vuccati pādavikalo. Heṭṭhimakāyasaṅkhāto sarīrassa pakkho padeso hato assāti pakkhahato. Tenāha “pīṭhasappī”ti. Padīpe padīpane etabbaṃ netabbanti padīpeyyaṃ, telakapālādiupakaraṇaṃ. Vuttanti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Those who make items such as baskets and containers from split bamboo, cane, and so on, are basket-weavers (vilīvakārakā). Because they kill deer, fish, and so on, they are hunters (nesādā), such as trappers and fishermen. Because they make bindings with leather on chariots, they are chariot-makers (rathakārā), that is, leather-workers (cammakārā). 'Pūti' is a name for dung. Because they remove (kusenti) it, they are 'pukkusā'; they are flower-sweepers. 'Dubbaṇṇa' means deformed. 'Okoṭimaka' means one who is low due to a lack of stature; the meaning is short-bodied. Hence it is said, 'lakuṇḍaka' (a dwarf). One who moves (ḍeti) like a club (laku) or a small pot (ghaṭikā) is a 'lakuṇḍaka'; a short person. One who squints (kaṇati), that is, blinks, is 'one-eyed' (kāṇo). That blinking of his may be with one eye or with both, hence it is said, 'one-eyed in one eye or one-eyed in both eyes.' A crippled state (kuṇanaṃ) is a 'kuṇa,' a defect of the hand; he who has this is 'one with a crippled hand' (kuṇī). A 'lame person' (khañjo) is said to be one with a defective foot. He is 'paralyzed on one side' (pakkhahato) for whom a side-region of the body, that is, the lower body, is afflicted. Hence it is said, 'one who moves on his buttocks' (pīṭhasappī). That which should be brought for a lamp, for lighting it, is 'lamp-requisites' (padīpeyyaṃ); equipment such as an oil-bowl. 'It is said' means it is said in the commentary.

Āgamanavipattīti āgamanaṭṭhānavasena vipatti “āgamo etthā”ti katvā. Pubbuppannapaccayavipattīti paṭhamuppannapaccayavasena viparāvatti. Caṇḍālādisabhāvā hissa mātāpitaro paṭhamuppannapaccayo. Pavattapaccayavipattīti pavatte sukhapaccayavipatti. Tādise nihīnakule uppannopi koci vibhavasampanno siyā, ayaṃ pana duggato durūpo. Ājīvupāyavipattīti [V 2.0289] ājīvanupāyavasena vipatti. Sukhena hi jīvikaṃ pavattetuṃ upāyabhūtā hatthisippādayo imassa natthi, pupphachaḍḍanasilākoṭṭanādikammaṃ pana katvā jīvikaṃ pavatteti. Tenāha “kasiravuttike”ti. Attabhāvavipattīti upadhivipatti. Dukkhakāraṇasamāyogoti kāyikacetasikadukkhuppattiyā paccayasamodhānaṃ. Sukhakāraṇavipattīti sukhapaccayaparihāni. Upabhogavipattīti upabhogasukhassa vināso anupaladdhi. Joti ceva jotiparāyaṇabhāvo ca sukkapakkho. Chaṭṭhaṃ uttānameva.

'Failure of arrival' means failure with respect to the place of arrival. 'Failure of previously arisen conditions' means an adverse turn due to the first-arisen conditions. For him, parents who are outcastes and the like are the first-arisen conditions. 'Failure of ongoing conditions' means the failure of conditions for happiness during the course of existence. For though someone born in such a low family might become wealthy, this one is unfortunate and deformed. 'Failure in the means of livelihood' means failure with respect to the means of livelihood. For he has no means for living comfortably, such as the art of handling elephants; instead, he makes a living by doing work like sweeping up flowers and breaking stones. Hence it is said, 'one with a difficult livelihood.' 'Failure of individual existence' means failure of the substratum of existence. 'Association with the cause of suffering' means the convergence of conditions for the arising of physical and mental suffering. 'Failure of the cause of happiness' means the loss of conditions for happiness. 'Failure of enjoyment' means the destruction or non-attainment of the happiness of enjoyment. Both light and being bound for light belong to the bright side. The sixth is clear in meaning.

Pāṇātipātasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pāṇātipāta Sutta and so on is concluded.

7. Puttasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Putta Sutta

87. Sattame ma-kāro padasandhikaro “aññamañña”ntiādīsu viya. Niccalasamaṇoti thirasamaṇo. Abhisiñcitabboti abhisekoti kammasādhano [M 2.0318] abhisekasaddo. Tenāha “abhisekaṃ kātuṃ yutto”ti.

87. In the seventh, the letter 'ma' is a euphonic consonant connecting words, as in 'aññamañña' and so on. 'A steadfast ascetic' (niccalasamaṇo) means a firm ascetic (thirasamaṇo). 'To be consecrated' (abhisiñcitabbo) means consecration (abhiseko); the word 'abhiseka' is derived in the sense of the action. Hence it is said, 'fit to perform the consecration.'

Bākulatthero viyāti thero hi mahāyasassī, tassa puttadhītaro nattupanattakā sukhumasāṭakehi cīvarāni kāretvā rajāpetvā samugge pakkhipitvā pahiṇanti. Therassa nahānakāle nahānakoṭṭhake ṭhapenti. Thero tāni nivāseti ceva pārupati ca. Tenevetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Like the Elder Bākula—for the Elder was of great repute—his sons and daughters, grandsons, and great-grandsons had robes made from fine cloth, had them dyed, placed them in a casket, and sent them. At the time of the Elder’s bath, they placed them in the bathing chamber. The Elder would wear them as an under-robe and an outer-robe. For this reason it was said.

Khadiravanamagge sīvalitthero viyāti satthari kira taṃ maggaṃ paṭipanne devatā “amhākaṃ ayyassa sīvalittherassa sakkāraṃ karissāmā”ti cintetvā ekekayojane vihāraṃ kāretvā ekayojanato uddhaṃ gantuṃ adatvā pātova uṭṭhāya dibbāni yāguādīni gahetvā “amhākaṃ ayyo sīvalitthero kahaṃ nisinno”ti vicaranti. Thero attano abhihaṭaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dāpesi. Evaṃ satthā saparivāro tiṃsayojanikaṃ kantāraṃ sīvalittherassa puññaphalaṃ anubhavamānova agamāsi. Tenevetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Like the Elder Sīvali on the Khadiravana road—when the Teacher was traveling that road, deities thought, "We will honor our master, the Elder Sīvali," and had a monastery made every yojana, not allowing him to go beyond one yojana. In the morning, they rose, took divine gruel and other offerings, and wandered about asking, "Where is our master, the Elder Sīvali, seated?" The Elder had what was brought to him given to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Thus, the Teacher and his retinue traversed the thirty-yojana wilderness while experiencing the fruit of the Elder Sīvali’s merit. For this reason it was said.

Aṭṭhakanāgarasutte ānandatthero viyāti aṭṭhakanāgarako kira gahapati therassa dhammadesanāya pasīditvā pañcasatagghanakaṃ vihāraṃ kāretvā adāsi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

Like the Elder Ānanda in the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta—it is said the householder of Aṭṭhakanagara, pleased with the Elder’s teaching of the Dhamma, had a monastery worth five hundred built and gave it. This was said in reference to that.

Pilindavacchatthero viyāti therassa kira iddhānubhāvena pasannā manussā sappiādīni bahūni [V 2.0290] bhesajjāni abhihariṃsu. Pakatiyāpi ca āyasmā pilindavaccho lābhī hoti pañcannaṃ bhesajjānaṃ, laddhaṃ laddhaṃ parisāya vissajjeti. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ “gilānapaccayaṃ pilindavacchatthero viyā”ti.

Like the Elder Pilindavaccha—it is said that people, inspired with confidence by the Elder's psychic power, brought many medicines such as ghee and so forth. Moreover, by nature, the Venerable Pilindavaccha was a recipient of the five kinds of medicines, and whatever he received, he distributed to the assembly. Therefore, it is said: "Like the Elder Pilindavaccha with regard to requisites for the sick."

Tiṇṇampi sannipātena nibbattānīti pittādīnaṃ tiṇṇampi visamānaṃ sannipātena jātāni. Atisītādibhāvena utūnaṃ pariṇāmoti āha “atisītaatiuṇhaututo jātānī”ti. Purimaututo visadiso utu utupariṇāmo, tato jātāni utupariṇāmajāni, visabhāgaututo jātānīti attho. Jaṅgaladesavāsīnañhi anūpadese vasantānaṃ visabhāgova utu uppajjati, anūpadesavāsīnañca jaṅgaladeseti. Evaṃ malayasamuddatīrādivasenapi utuvisabhāgatā uppajjatiyeva. Tato jātāni utupariṇāmajāni nāma.

'Born from the conjunction of the three' means born from the conjunction of the three imbalanced humors: bile, and so forth. The transformation of seasons through excessive cold and so on is stated as: 'born from excessive cold, excessive heat, and the seasons.' A season dissimilar to the previous season is a seasonal transformation; born from that are those 'born from seasonal transformation,' meaning born from an unsuitable season. For those living in jungle regions, when dwelling in watery regions, an unsuitable season arises; and for those living in watery regions, when in a jungle region. In this way, due to residing near the Malaya mountains or the seashore, an unsuitability of season certainly arises. Those born from that are called 'born from seasonal transformation.'

Attano [M 2.0319] pakaticariyānaṃ visamaṃ kāyassa pariharaṇavasena visamaparihārajāni. Tāni pana accāsanaatiṭṭhānādinā veditabbānīti āha “accāsanaatiṭṭhānādikā”ti. Ādi-saddena mahābhāravahaṇasudhākoṭṭanaadesakālacaraṇādīni saṅgaṇhāti. Parassa upakkamato nibbattāni opakkamikāni, ayaṃ coroti vā pāradārikoti vā gahetvā jaṇṇukakapparamuggarādīhi nippothanaupakkamaṃ paccayaṃ katvā uppannānīti attho. Tenāha “vadhabandhanādiupakkamena nibbattānī”ti. Kevalanti bāhiraṃ paccayaṃ anapekkhitvā kevalaṃ, tena vināti attho. Tenāha “pubbekatakammavipākavaseneva jātānī”ti.

'Born from improper care' are those arising from care of the body that is improper, contrary to one's natural disposition. These are to be understood through excessive sitting, excessive standing, and so forth, as it is said: 'from excessive sitting, excessive standing, and so forth.' The word 'and so forth' includes carrying heavy loads, pounding plaster, and conduct in unsuitable places and at unsuitable times. 'Arising from assault' are those that arise from the assault of another. This means they arise by making an assault a condition, for instance, after seizing someone as a thief or an adulterer, beating them with knees, potsherds, mallets, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: 'born from assaults such as killing, imprisonment, etc.' 'Solely' means without depending on an external condition; that is, without that. Therefore, it is said: 'born solely by the power of the ripening of past kamma.'

Puttasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Puttasutta is finished.

8-10. Saṃyojanasuttādivaṇṇanā

8–10. Commentary on the Saṃyojana Sutta and so forth.

88-90. Aṭṭhame sotāpanno catūhi vātehi indakhīlo viya parappavādehi akampiyo acalasaddhāya samannāgatattā sāsane laddhappatiṭṭho samaṇamacalo nāmāti āha “sāsane laddhappatiṭṭhattā”tiādi. Thaddhabhāvakarānaṃ kilesānaṃ sabbaso samucchinnattāti cittassa thaddhabhāvakarānaṃ uddhambhāgiyakilesānaṃ sabbaso abhāvā samaṇasukhumālo nāma sukhumālabhāvappattito. Navamadasamāni suviññeyyāneva.

88–90. In the eighth, a stream-enterer, like an Indakhīla pillar unshaken by the four winds, is unshaken by the doctrines of others. Due to being endowed with unwavering faith and having gained a footing in the Dispensation, he is called an 'unshakable ascetic' (samaṇamacala); thus it is said, 'because of having gained a footing in the Dispensation,' and so forth. Because the defilements that cause rigidity have been completely cut off—that is, due to the complete absence of the higher fetters that cause rigidity of mind—one is called a 'delicate ascetic' (samaṇasukhumāla), from having attained a state of delicacy. The ninth and tenth are easily understood.

Saṃyojanasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Saṃyojana Sutta and so forth is finished.

Macalavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Macala Chapter is finished.

(10) 5. Asuravaggo

(10) 5. The Asura Chapter.

1-2. Asurasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–2. Commentary on the Asura Sutta and so forth.

91-92. Pañcamassa [V 2.0291] paṭhamadutiyāni uttānatthāneva.

91–92. The first and second of the fifth chapter are of obvious meaning.

Asurasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Asura Sutta and so forth is finished.

3. Dutiyasamādhisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Second Samādhi Sutta.

93. Tatiye [M 2.0320] appaṭivānīti bhāvappadhāno niddesoti āha “anivattanatā”ti. “Appaṭivānitā”ti vattabbe “appaṭivānī”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi vīriyappavāhe vattamāne antarā eva paṭigamanaṃ nivattanaṃ paṭivānaṃ, taṃ assa atthīti paṭivānī, na paṭivānī appaṭivānī, tassa bhāvo appaṭivānitā, anivattanāti attho. Appaṭivānīti vā itthiliṅgavasenevāyaṃ niddeso. Antarāyeva paṭigamanaṃ nivattanaṃ paṭivānī, na paṭivānī appaṭivānī, anivattanāti attho.

93. In the third, regarding 'appaṭivānī,' it is an explanation where the state is primary; thus it is said, 'non-returning.' When 'appaṭivānitā' should be said, 'appaṭivānī' is said. For, while the flow of energy is proceeding, turning back midway is a return, a retreat (paṭivāna). One who does this is a 'retreater' (paṭivānī); one who does not is a 'non-retreater' (appaṭivānī). The state of being so is non-retreat (appaṭivānitā), meaning non-returning. Alternatively, this explanation 'appaṭivānī' is simply in the feminine gender. Turning back midway is a retreat (paṭivānī); not retreating is non-retreat (appaṭivānī), meaning non-returning.

Dutiyasamādhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Samādhi Sutta is finished.

4. Tatiyasamādhisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Third Samādhi Sutta.

94. Catutthe saṇṭhapetabbanti sammadeva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Yathā pana ṭhapitaṃ saṇṭhapitaṃ hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “sannisādetabba”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sannisādetabbanti samādhippaṭipakkhe kilese sannisīdāpentena cittaṃ gocarajjhatte sannisīdāpetabbanti. Ekodi kātabbanti abyaggabhāvāpādanena ekaggaṃ kātabbaṃ. Samādahitabbanti yathā ārammaṇe suṭṭhu appitaṃ hoti, evaṃ sammā sammadeva ādahitabbaṃ, suṭṭhu āropetabbaṃ samāhitaṃ kātabbanti attho.

94. In the fourth, 'should be steadied' (saṇṭhapetabbaṃ) means it should be properly established. To show how what is established becomes steadied, 'should be calmed' (sannisādetabbaṃ), and so forth, is said. Therein, 'should be calmed' means the mind should be made to settle down within its domain by causing the defilements opposed to concentration to subside. 'Should be unified' (ekodi kātabbaṃ) means it should be made one-pointed by bringing it to a state of non-distraction. 'Should be concentrated' (samādahitabbaṃ) means that it should be rightly and properly placed so that it is well-applied to its object; it should be made concentrated. This is the meaning.

Tatiyasamādhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Third Samādhi Sutta is finished.

5-6. Chavālātasuttādivaṇṇanā

5–6. Commentary on the Firebrand Sutta and so forth.

95-96. Pañcame [V 2.0292] chavālātanti chavānaṃ daḍḍhaṭṭhāne alātaṃ. Tenevāha “susāne alāta”nti. Majjhaṭṭhāne gūthamakkhitanti pamāṇena aṭṭhaṅgulamattaṃ dvīsu ṭhānesu ādittaṃ majjhe gūthamakkhitaṃ. Kaṭṭhatthanti kaṭṭhena kātabbakiccaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva. Chaṭṭhaṃ uttānameva.

95–96. In the fifth, 'chavālāta' is a firebrand in a place where corpses are burned. Therefore it is said, 'a firebrand in the charnel ground.' 'Smeared with dung in the middle' means a firebrand of about eight finger-breadths in measure, lit at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle. 'For the sake of wood' (kaṭṭhatthaṃ) means for the purpose served by wood. The rest here is of obvious meaning. The sixth is also of obvious meaning.

Chavālātasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Firebrand Sutta and so forth is finished.

7-10. Khippanisantisuttādivaṇṇanā

7–10. Commentary on the Khippanisanti Sutta and so forth.

97-100. Sattame [M 2.0321] khippanisantīti khippapañño. Tenāha “khippanisāmano”tiādi. Anurūpadhammanti lokuttarādhigamassa anucchavikasabhāvaṃ. Kalyāṇā sundarā parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanā vācā assāti kalyāṇavāco. Tenāha “sundaravacano”ti. Kalyāṇaṃ madhuraṃ vākkaraṇaṃ udāhāraghoso assāti kalyāṇavākkaraṇo. Guṇaparipuṇṇabhāvena pūre puṇṇabhāve bhavāti porī, tāya poriyā. Tenāha “guṇaparipuṇṇāyā”ti. Pure bhavattā poriyā nāgarikitthiyā sukhumālattanena sadisāti porī, tāya poriyā. “Sukhumālattanenā”ti iminā tassā vācāya mudusaṇhabhāvo vutto. Apalibuddhāyāti pittasemhādīhi na paliveṭhitāya. Adosāyāti sandiddhavilambitādidosarahitāya agaḷitapadabyañjanāyāti apatitapadabyañjanāya avirahitapadabyañjanāya. Ubhayametaṃ anelagalāyāti imasseva atthavacanaṃ. Anelagalāyāti hi anelāya ceva agalāya cāti attho. Atthaṃ viññāpetuṃ samatthāyāti ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā bhāsitatthassa viññāpanasatthāya. Aṭṭhamanavamadasamāni uttānatthāneva.

97–100. In the seventh, 'khippanisanti' means one with swift wisdom. Therefore it is said, 'one who understands quickly,' and so forth. 'A suitable teaching' (anurūpadhammaṃ) means the state suitable for the attainment of the supramundane. 'One with fine speech' (kalyāṇavāco) is one whose speech is lovely, beautiful, with well-rounded words and syllables. Therefore it is said, 'one with beautiful speech.' 'One with fine articulation' (kalyāṇavākkaraṇo) is one whose articulation and utterance is fine and sweet. 'Polished' (porī): because it exists in a full, complete state due to the perfection of its qualities, it is called 'polished.' Therefore it is said, 'due to its perfection of qualities.' Or, because it exists in a pure state, it is 'polished' (porī); it is like a refined city woman in its delicacy. By this 'delicacy,' the soft and smooth nature of that speech is stated. 'Unobstructed' (apalibuddhāya) means not impeded by bile, phlegm, or the like. 'Faultless' (adosāya) means free from faults such as being indistinct or slow. 'With non-slurred words and syllables' means with words and syllables that are not dropped or missing. Both of these are the meaning of 'fluent' (anelagalāya). For 'fluent' means both 'not mumbling' (anelāya) and 'not halting' (agalāya). 'Capable of conveying the meaning' means capable of making known the meaning that is spoken by making the beginning, middle, and end clear. The eighth, ninth, and tenth are of obvious meaning.

Khippanisantisuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Khippanisanti Sutta and so forth is finished.

Asuravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Asura Chapter is finished.

Dutiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Second Fifty is finished.

3. Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ

3. The Third Fifty.

(11) 1. Valāhakavaggo

(11) 1. The Cloud Chapter

1-2. Valāhakasuttadvayavaṇṇanā

1-2. Commentary on the Two Valāhaka Suttas

101-2. Tatiyapaṇṇāsakassa [V 2.0293][M 2.0322] paṭhame gajjitāti thanitā. Tattha gajjitvā novassanabhāvo nāma pāpako. Manussā hi yadā devo gajjati, tadā “suvuṭṭhitā bhavissatī”ti bījāni nīharitvā vapanti. Atha deve avassante khette bījāni khetteyeva nassanti, gehe bījāni geheyeva nassantīti dubbhikkhaṃ hoti. Nogajjitvā vassanabhāvopi pāpako. Manussā hi imasmiṃ kāle “dubbuṭṭhikā bhavissatī”ti ninnaṭṭhānesuyeva vappaṃ karonti. Atha devo vassitvā sabbabījāni mahāsamuddaṃ pāpeti, dubbhikkhameva hoti. Gajjitvā vassanabhāvo pana bhaddako. Tadā hi subhikkhaṃ hoti. Nogajjitvā novassanabhāvo ekantapāpakova. Bhāsitā hoti no kattāti “idāni ganthadhuraṃ pūressāmi, vāsadhuraṃ pūressāmī”ti kathetiyeva, na uddesaṃ gaṇhāti, na kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāveti.

101-102. In the first of the third fifty, 'roaring' means thundering. Here, thundering without raining is bad. For when the sky-god thunders, people think, 'There will be good rain,' and they bring out seeds to sow. But if the god does not rain, the seeds in the fields perish right there, and the seeds in the houses perish right there—thus a famine occurs. Not thundering but raining is also bad. At such times, people think, 'There will be a poor rainfall,' and they sow only in low-lying areas. But when the god rains, all the seeds are washed into the great ocean, and a famine still occurs. Thundering and raining, however, is good, for then there is abundance. Not thundering and not raining is entirely bad. 'One who speaks but does not act' is one who only says, 'Now I will fulfill the burden of study, now I will fulfill the burden of practice,' but does not take up a text for recitation or develop a meditation subject.

Kattā hoti no bhāsitāti “ganthadhuraṃ pūressāmi, vāsadhuraṃ vā”ti na bhāsati, sampatte pana kāle samattaṃ sampādeti. Iminā nayena itarepi veditabbā. Atha vā sabbaṃ panetaṃ paccayadāyakeheva kathitaṃ. Eko hi “asukadivase nāma dānaṃ dassāmī”ti saṅghaṃ nimanteti, sampatte kāle no karoti. Ayaṃ puggalo puññena parihāyati, bhikkhusaṅgho pana lābhena parihāyati. Aparo saṅghaṃ animantetvā sakkāraṃ katvā “bhikkhū ānessāmī”ti na labhi, sabbe aññattha nimantitā honti. Ayampi puññena parihāyati, saṅghopi lābhena parihāyati. Aparo paṭhamaṃ saṅghaṃ nimantetvā pacchā sakkāraṃ katvā dānaṃ deti, ayaṃ kiccakārī hoti. Aparo neva saṅghaṃ nimanteti, na dānaṃ deti, ayaṃ pāpapuggaloti veditabbo. Dutiyaṃ uttānameva.

One is a doer, not a speaker—one does not say, 'I will fulfill the burden of study or the burden of dwelling,' but when the time comes, one completes it fully. The others should be understood in the same way. Alternatively, all this has been said regarding the providers of requisites. For one person invites the Sangha, saying, 'I will give a gift on such-and-such a day,' but when the time comes, they do not do it. This person declines in merit, and the monastic Sangha declines in gain. Another, without inviting the Sangha, having prepared an offering, is unable to get monks, thinking, 'I will bring the monks,' for all have been invited elsewhere. This one also declines in merit, and the Sangha also declines in gain. Another first invites the Sangha and afterward, having prepared the offering, gives the gift. This one is one who does what needs to be done. Another neither invites the Sangha nor gives a gift. This one should be understood as a wicked person. The second is self-evident.

Valāhakasuttadvayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the two Valāhaka Suttas is finished.

3. Kumbhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Kumbha Sutta

103. Tatiye [M 2.0323][V 2.0294] rittakoti anto ritto. Pihitamukhoti pidahitvā ṭhapito. Apārutamukhoti vivaritvā ṭhapito, upamitapuggalesu panettha antoguṇasāravirahito ca tuccho, bāhirasobhanatāya pihito puggaloti veditabbo. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

103. In the third, 'empty' means empty inside. 'With a closed mouth' means placed with it closed. 'With an open mouth' means placed with it open. Among the persons used in the simile, here a person should be understood as empty—that is, devoid of the essence of inner virtue and hollow—and covered by external beauty. This same method applies to the remaining cases.

Kumbhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kumbha Sutta is finished.

4. Udakarahadasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Udakarahada Sutta

104. Catutthe udakarahado jaṇṇukamattepi udake sati paṇṇarasasambhinnavaṇṇattā vā bahalattā vā udakassa apaññāyamānatalo uttāno gambhīrobhāso nāma hotīti āha “purāṇapaṇṇarasa…pe… gambhīrobhāso nāmā”ti. Tiporisacatuporise pana udake sati acchattā udakassa paññāyamānatalo gambhīro uttānobhāso nāma hotīti āha “acchavippasannamaṇivaṇṇaudako uttānobhāso nāmā”ti. Ubhayakāraṇasambhavato pana itare dve veditabbā. Puggalepi kilesussadabhāvato guṇagambhīratāya ca abhāvato guṇagambhīrānaṃ sadisehi abhikkamanādīhi yutto uttāno gambhīrobhāso nāma. Iminā nayena sesā veditabbā.

104. In the fourth, regarding a pool of water: even when the water is only knee-deep, because its color is like a mixture of old leaves or because of its density, its bottom is not discernible; it is shallow but has the appearance of being deep. Thus it is said: 'like old leaves... it has the appearance of being deep.' But when the water is three or four persons deep, because of the water's clarity, its bottom is discernible; it is deep but has the appearance of being shallow. Thus it is said: 'with water the color of a clear, bright gem... it has the appearance of being shallow.' The other two should be understood as arising from a combination of both causes. With a person, too, one is called 'shallow with the appearance of being deep' due to an abundance of defilements and an absence of depth in virtue, while being endowed with deportment and so on that is similar to those who are deep in virtue. The rest should be understood in this way.

Udakarahadasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Udakarahada Sutta is finished.

5-6. Ambasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-6. Commentary on the Amba Sutta and others

105-6. Pañcame āmakaṃ hutvāti anto āmaṃ hutvā. Pakkaṃ āmavaṇṇīti anto pakkaṃ bahi āmasadisaṃ. Tattha yathā ambe apakkabhāvo āmatā hoti, evaṃ puggalepi puthujjanatā. Yathā ca tattha pakkasadisatā pakkavaṇṇitā, evaṃ puggalepi ariyānaṃ abhikkamanādisadisatā pakkavaṇṇitāti iminā nayena sesā veditabbā. Chaṭṭhaṃ uttānameva.

105-6. In the fifth, 'being raw' means being raw inside. 'Ripe with a raw appearance' means ripe inside but resembling raw on the outside. Therein, just as in a mango the state of being unripe is rawness, so too in a person is the state of being a worldling. And just as therein the similarity to ripeness is the appearance of ripeness, so too in a person the similarity to the noble ones' deportment and so on is the appearance of ripeness. The rest should be understood in this way. The sixth is self-evident.

Ambasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Amba Sutta and others is finished.

7. Mūsikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Mūsika Sutta

107. Sattame [M 2.0324][V 2.0295] āvāṭaṃ khanatīti attano āsayaṃ bilakūpaṃ khanati. Na ca tattha vasatīti tattha avasitvā kismiñcideva ṭhāne vasati, evaṃ biḷārādiamittavasaṃ gacchati. Vasitā no gādhaṃ kattāti sayaṃ na khanati, parena kate bile vasati, evaṃ jīvitaṃ rakkhati. Tatiyā dvepi karontī jīvitaṃ rakkhati. Catutthī dvepi akarontī amittavasaṃ gacchati. Imāya pana upamāya upamitesu puggalesu paṭhamo yathā sā mūsikā gādhaṃ khanati, evaṃ navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ uggaṇhāti. Yathā pana sā tattha na vasati, kismiñcideva ṭhāne vasantī amittavasaṃ gacchati, tathā ayampi pariyattivasena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā catusaccadhammaṃ na paṭivijjhati, lokāmisaṭṭhānesu vicaranto maccumārakilesamāradevaputtamārasaṅkhātānaṃ vasaṃ gacchati. Dutiyo yathā mūsikā gādhaṃ na khanati, evaṃ navaṅgaṃ satthusāsanaṃ na uggaṇhāti. Yathā pana parena khanite bile vasantī jīvitaṃ rakkhati, evaṃ parassa kathaṃ sutvā catusaccadhammaṃ paṭivijjhitvā tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ vasaṃ atikkamati. Iminā nayena tatiyacatutthesupi opammasaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

107. In the seventh, 'digs a hole' means it digs its own dwelling, a pit-like burrow. 'But it does not dwell there' means: not dwelling there, it lives in some other place, thus falling under the power of enemies like cats. 'One who dwells but does not make a safe place' means: it does not dig itself but lives in a hole made by another, thus it protects its life. The third does both and protects its life. The fourth does neither and falls under the power of enemies. By this simile, among the persons compared: the first is like the mouse that digs a safe place—thus, this person learns the ninefold teaching of the Teacher. But just as that mouse does not dwell there, living in some other place and falling under the power of enemies, so too does this person, having applied knowledge by way of scriptural learning, not penetrate the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths; wandering in places of worldly bait, they fall under the power of those called Māra as death, Māra as defilements, and Māra as a son of the devas. The second is like the mouse that does not dig a safe place—thus, this person does not learn the ninefold teaching of the Teacher. But just as the mouse protects its life by dwelling in a hole dug by another, so too this person, having heard the talk of another, penetrates the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths and transcends the power of the three Māras. In this way, the application of the simile should be understood for the third and fourth as well.

Mūsikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mūsika Sutta is finished.

8. Balībaddasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Balībadda Sutta

108. Aṭṭhame balībaddo tāva yo attano gogaṇaṃ ghaṭṭeti ubbejeti, paragoṇe pana sūrato sukhasīlo hoti, ayaṃ sagavacaṇḍo no paragavacaṇḍo nāma. Puggalopi attano parisaṃ ghaṭṭento vijjhanto pharuse samudācaranto, paraparisāya pana soraccaṃ nivātavuttitaṃ āpajjanto sagavacaṇḍo nāmāti iminā nayena sesāpi veditabbā.

108. In the eighth, an ox that strikes and harasses its own herd of cattle, but is gentle and well-behaved among other cattle, is called 'fierce with its own herd, not fierce with others.' Similarly, a person who harasses, vexes, and speaks harshly toward their own assembly, but displays gentleness and humble conduct in other assemblies, is called 'fierce with their own.' The rest should be understood in this way.

Balībaddasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Balībadda Sutta is finished.

9. Rukkhasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Rukkha Sutta

109. Navame rukkho tāva pheggu sāraparivāroti vanajeṭṭhakarukkho sayaṃ pheggu hoti, parivārarukkhā [V 2.0296] panassa sārā honti. Iminā nayena [M 2.0325] sesā veditabbā. Puggalesu pana sīlasāravirahitato pheggutā, sīlācārasamannāgamena ca sāratā veditabbā.

109. In the ninth, a tree that is 'worthless wood surrounded by heartwood' means that the chief tree of the forest is itself worthless wood, but its surrounding trees are heartwood. The rest should be understood in this way. Among persons, however, worthlessness is to be understood as the lack of the essence of virtue, while substance is to be understood as the possession of virtuous conduct.

Rukkhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Rukkha Sutta is finished.

10. Āsīvisasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Āsīvisa Sutta

110. Dasame yassa visaṃ pajjalitatiṇukkāya aggi viya sīghaṃ abhiruhitvā akkhīni gahetvā khandhaṃ gahetvā sīsaṃ gahetvā ṭhitanti vattabbataṃ āpajjati maṇisappādīnaṃ visaṃ viya, mantaṃ pana parivattetvā kaṇṇavātaṃ datvā daṇḍakena pahaṭamatte otaritvā daṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ āgataviso na ghoraviso nāma. Yassa pana visaṃ saṇikaṃ abhiruhati, āruḷhāruḷhaṭṭhāne pana āsittaudakaṃ viya hoti udakasappādīnaṃ viya, dvādasavassaccayenapi kaṇṇaviddhakhandhapiṭṭhikādīsu paññāyati, mantaparivattanādīsu ca kariyamānesu sīghaṃ na otarati, ayaṃ ghoraviso na āgataviso nāma. Yassa pana visaṃ sīghaṃ abhiruhati, na sīghaṃ otarati aneḷakasappādīnaṃ visaṃ viya, ayaṃ āgataviso ca ghoraviso ca. Aneḷakasappo nāma mahāāsīviso. Yassa visaṃ mandaṃ hoti, ohāriyamānampi sukheneva otarati nīlasappadhamanisappādīnaṃ visaṃ viya, ayaṃ neva āgataviso na ghoraviso. Nīlasappo nāma sākhavaṇṇo rukkhaggādīsu vicaraṇasappo.

110. In the tenth, there is a venom that spreads quickly like fire on a blazing grass torch, and having seized the eyes, the shoulders, and the head, it reaches a state where it is said to have settled there, like the venom of a jeweled serpent and so on. But when a mantra is recited, air is blown into the ear, and it is struck with a stick, it subsides and remains only at the site of the bite. This is called 'fast-acting venom,' not 'fierce venom.' Then there is a venom that spreads slowly, and at each place it has spread to, it is like sprinkled water, like the venom of water serpents and so on. Even after the passing of twelve years, it is apparent in pierced ears, shoulders, back, and so on. And when mantras are recited and so on, it does not subside quickly. This is called 'fierce venom,' not 'fast-acting venom.' The venom that spreads quickly but does not subside quickly, like the venom of the aneḷaka serpent and so on, is both 'fast-acting venom' and 'fierce venom.' The aneḷaka serpent is a great venomous snake. The venom that is mild and subsides easily when treated, like the venom of the blue serpent or the dhamani serpent, is neither 'fast-acting venom' nor 'fierce venom.' The blue serpent is a snake the color of a branch that moves about on treetops and so on.

Āsīvisasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Āsīvisa Sutta is finished.

Valāhakavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Valāhaka Chapter is finished.

(12) 2. Kesivaggo

(12) 2. The Kesi Chapter

1-7. Kesisuttādivaṇṇanā

1–7. Commentary on the Kesi Sutta and so forth

111-117. Dutiyassa [V 2.0297] paṭhame assadammeti dammanayogge asse. Sāretīti sikkhāpeti pavatteti. Sesamettha uttānameva. Dutiyādīni uttānatthāneva.

111–117. In the first of the second, 'horses to be tamed' means horses suitable for taming. 'He trains' means he instructs, he makes them proceed. The rest here is self-evident. The second and so forth are also of self-evident meaning.

Kesisuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Kesi Sutta and so forth is finished.

8-10. Saṃvejanīyasuttādivaṇṇanā

8–10. Commentary on the Saṃvejanīya Sutta and so forth

118-120. Aṭṭhame [M 2.0326] saddhassāti buddhādīsu pasannacittassa vattasampannassa, yassa pāto vuṭṭhāya cetiyaṅgaṇavattādīni sabbavattāni katāneva paññāyanti. Dassanīyānīti dassanārahāni. Saṃvego nāma sahottappaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Abhijātiṭṭhānādīnipi tassa uppattihetūni bhavantīti sikkhāpento āha “saṃvegajanakānī”ti. Ṭhānānīti kāraṇāni, padesaṭṭhānāni vā. Navamadasamāni suviññeyyāni.

118–120. In the eighth case, 'for one of faith' means for one whose mind is serene towards the Buddha and so forth, who is accomplished in duties, for whom, on rising at dawn, all duties like sweeping the courtyard of the shrine and so forth are seen to be already done. 'Worthy of seeing' means deserving to be seen. 'Urgency' is knowledge accompanied by moral dread. Instructing that places of noble birth and so forth are causes of its arising, he says, 'productive of urgency.' 'Places' means reasons, or locations. The ninth and tenth are easily understood.

Saṃvejanīyasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Saṃvejanīya Sutta and so forth is concluded.

Kesivaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Kesi Chapter is concluded.

(13) 3. Bhayavaggo

(13) 3. The Bhaya Chapter

1. Attānuvādasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Attānuvāda Sutta

121. Tatiyassa paṭhame attānaṃ anuvadantassa uppajjanakabhayanti attānaṃ anuvadantassa pāpakammino uppajjanakabhayaṃ. Dvattiṃsakammakāraṇe paṭicca uppajjanakabhayanti agārikānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ[V 2.0298], anagārikānaṃ pana vinayadaṇḍaṃ paṭicca uppajjanakabhayampi daṇḍabhayanteva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

121. In the first of the third, 'the fear that arises for one who reproaches oneself' means the fear that arises for an evildoer who reproaches oneself. 'The fear that arises with reference to the thirty-two grounds for action' is stated with reference to householders; but for the homeless, the fear that arises due to disciplinary punishment is also counted as the fear of punishment. The rest is easily understood.

Attānuvādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Attānuvāda Sutta is concluded.

2. Ūmibhayasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Ūmibhaya Sutta

122. Dutiye kodhūpāyāsassetaṃ adhivacananti ettha kujjhanaṭṭhena kodho, sveva cittassa kāyassa ca atippamaddanamathanuppādanehi daḷhaāyāsaṭṭhena upāyāso. Anekavāraṃ pavattitvā attanā samavetaṃ sattaṃ ajjhottharitvā sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ adatvā ūmisadisatā daṭṭhabbā. Yathā hi bāhiraṃ udakaṃ otiṇṇo ūmīsu osīditvā marati, evaṃ [M 2.0327] imasmiṃ sāsane kodhūpāyāse osīditvā vibbhamati, tasmā kodhūpāyāso “ūmibhaya”nti vutto. Odarikattassetaṃ adhivacananti yathā hi bāhiraṃ udakaṃ otiṇṇo kumbhīlena khādito marati, evaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane odarikattena odarikabhāvena āmisagedhena micchājīvena jīvikakappanena nāsitasīlādiguṇatāya khāditadhammasarīro vibbhamati, tasmā odarikattaṃ “kumbhīlabhaya”nti vuttaṃ.

122. In the second case, 'anger and distress' is a designation for this: anger in the sense of being provoked; and distress in the sense of intense affliction due to the crushing and tormenting of mind and body. One should see it as like being overwhelmed by a wave—after repeatedly surging, it overwhelms the being, not allowing them to raise their head. Just as someone who has fallen into external water sinks and dies in the waves, so too in this Dispensation, one sinks into anger and distress and falls away. Therefore, anger and distress are called 'the danger of waves.' 'Gluttony' is a designation for this: just as someone who has fallen into external water is devoured by a crocodile and dies, so too in this Dispensation, one whose virtues and good qualities are destroyed by gluttony—by greed for material gains, wrong livelihood, and seeking a livelihood by dishonest means—falls away, having had the body of Dhamma eaten away. Therefore, gluttony is called 'the danger of crocodiles.'

Anupaṭṭhitāya satiyāti kāyagataṃ satiṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā. Asaṃvutehīti apihitehi. Pañcannetaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ adhivacananti yathā hi bāhiraṃ udakaṃ otiṇṇo āvaṭṭe nimujjitvā marati, evaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajito pañcakāmaguṇāvaṭṭe nimujjitvā vibbhamati. Kāmarāgābhibhūto hi satto ito ca etto, etto ca itoti evaṃ manāpiyarūpādivisayasaṅkhāte āvaṭṭe attānaṃ saṃsāretvā yathā tato bahibhūte nekkhamme cittampi na uppādeti, evaṃ āvaṭṭetvā byasanāpādanena kāmaguṇānaṃ āvaṭṭasadisatā daṭṭhabbā.

'For one whose mindfulness is not present' means not establishing mindfulness of the body. 'Unguarded' means unrestrained. This is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure: just as one who has fallen into a whirlpool in external water sinks and dies, so too does one who has gone forth in this Dispensation sink into the whirlpool of the five strands of sensual pleasure and becomes bewildered. For a being overcome by sensual desire, they revolve themselves in the whirlpool consisting of agreeable forms and so forth, going from here to there and from there to here, so that they do not even generate the mind toward renunciation, which is external to it. Thus, the whirlpool-like nature of the strands of sensual pleasure should be seen as leading to disaster through entangling.

Anuddhaṃsetīti kilameti vilolati. Rāgānuddhaṃsitenāti rāgena anuddhaṃsitena. Mātugāmassetaṃ adhivacananti. Yathā hi bāhiraṃ udakaṃ otiṇṇo caṇḍamacchaṃ āgamma laddhappahāro marati, evaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane mātugāmaṃ ārabbha uppannakāmarāgo vibbhamati, tasmā mātugāmo “susukābhaya”nti vutto. Mātugāmo hi yonisomanasikārarahitaṃ adhīrapurisaṃ itthikuttabhūtehi attano hāsabhāvavilāsehi abhibhuyya gahetvā dhīrajātikampi attano [V 2.0299] rūpādīhi sampalobhanavasena anavasesaṃ attano upakāradhamme sīlādike sampādetuṃ asamatthaṃ karonto anayabyasanaṃ pāpeti.

'He agitates' means he tires and shakes. 'Not agitated by lust' means not agitated by lust. This is a designation for woman. Just as one who has fallen into external water meets their death when attacked by a fierce fish, so too in this Dispensation, sensual desire arising in relation to woman causes one to go astray. Therefore, woman is called 'the danger of the susukā fish.' For woman overpowers an irresolute man who is devoid of wise reflection with her womanly wiles, laughter, and charms; and by captivating even a wise person with her beauty and so forth, she renders him completely incapable of accomplishing for himself beneficial qualities such as morality, leading him to misfortune and ruin.

Imāni pana cattāri bhayāni bhāyitvā yathā udakaṃ anorohantassa udakaṃ nissāya udakapipāsāvinayanaṃ sarīrasuddhipariḷāhūpasamo kāyautuggāhāpananti, evamādi ānisaṃso natthi, evamevaṃ imāni cattāri bhayāni bhāyitvā sāsane apabbajantassapi imaṃ sāsanaṃ nissāya saṅkhepato vaṭṭadukkhūpasamo, vitthārato pana sīlānisaṃsādivasena anekavidho ānisaṃso natthi. Yathā pana imāni cattāri bhayāni abhāyitvā [M 2.0328] udakaṃ orohantassa vuttappakāro ānisaṃso hoti, evaṃ imāni abhāyitvā sāsane pabbajantassapi vuttappakāro ānisaṃso hoti. Mahādhammarakkhitatthero panāha “cattāri bhayāni bhāyitvā udakaṃ anotaranto sotaṃ chinditvā paratīraṃ pāpuṇituṃ na sakkoti, abhāyitvā otaranto sakkoti, evamevaṃ bhāyitvā sāsane apabbajantopi taṇhāsotaṃ chinditvā nibbānapāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ na sakkoti, abhāyitvā pabbajanto sakkotī”ti.

However, having feared these four dangers, just as for one who does not enter the water, there is no benefit such as relying on water to quench thirst, to cleanse the body, to relieve bodily heat, or to refresh the body, and so forth; in the same way, having feared these four dangers, for one who does not go forth in this Dispensation there is no benefit such as, briefly, the cessation of the suffering of the cycle, or, in detail, various benefits like the advantages of morality and so forth. Just as for one who enters the water without fear, the aforementioned benefits arise, so too for one who goes forth in this Dispensation without fear, the aforementioned benefits arise. The Elder Mahādhammarakkhita said: 'One who does not enter the water out of fear cannot cut the stream and reach the other shore, but one who enters without fear can. Similarly, one who does not go forth in the Dispensation out of fear cannot cut the stream of craving and see the far shore of Nibbāna, but one who goes forth without fear can.'

Ūmibhayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Ūmibhaya Sutta is concluded.

3. Paṭhamanānākaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary to the First Nānākaraṇa Sutta.

123. Tatiye brahmakāyikānaṃ devānanti ettha brahmānaṃ kāyo samūhoti brahmakāyo, tappariyāpannatāya tattha gatāti brahmakāyikā. Etāya ca sabbassapi brahmakāyassa samaññāya bhavitabbaṃ. Ābhassarānaṃ devānantiādinā pana dutiyajjhānabhūmikādīnaṃ upari gahitattā gobalībaddaññāyena tadavasiṭṭhānaṃ ayaṃ samaññā, tasmā “brahmakāyikānaṃ devāna”nti paṭhamajjhānabhūmikānaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Saha byayati gacchatīti sahabyo, sahavattanako. Tassa bhāvo sahabyatā, sahapavattīti āha “sahabhāvaṃ upagacchatī”ti. Kappo āyuppamāṇanti ettha yadipi brahmapārisajjādīnaṃ āyuno antaraṃ atthi, ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena panetaṃ vuttanti dassento “paṭhamajjhānaṃ atthi hīna”ntiādimāha.

123. In the third, regarding "the devas of Brahmā's retinue (brahmakāyikānaṃ devānaṃ)": here, the body (kāya) of Brahmā is a collection (samūha), hence 'Brahmā-body' (brahmakāya); and those who are included in that or have gone there are called 'of Brahmā's retinue' (brahmakāyikā). And this designation should apply to the entire Brahmā-group. But since "the radiant devas (ābhassarānaṃ devānaṃ)" and so on, are taken as pertaining to the second jhāna plane and above, this designation is for the remaining ones by the analogy of the cow and the ox. Therefore, it should be understood that "the devas of Brahmā's retinue" refers only to those of the first jhāna plane. "Accompanied" (sahabyo) means going together (saha byayati), associated (sahavattanako). Its state is companionship (sahabyatā), co-existence (sahapavattīti). Thus, it is said, "they attain companionship" (sahabhāvaṃ upagacchati). Regarding "an eon is the measure of their lifespan (kappo āyuppamāṇanti)": here, although there is a difference in lifespan among Brahmā's attendants (brahmapārisajjā) and others, this is stated with reference to the highest limit (ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena). To show this, it is said, "the first jhāna has a lower [limit]" and so on.

Dve kappā āyuppamāṇanti ettha pana hīnajjhānena nibbattānaṃ vasena ayaṃ paricchedo katoti dassetuṃ “dutiyajjhānaṃ vuttanayeneva tividhaṃ hotī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Cattāro kappāti ettha pana ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena catusaṭṭhi kappā vattabbāti dassento “yaṃ heṭṭhā vuttaṃ ‘kappo dve kappā’ti[V 2.0300], kampi āharitvā attho veditabbo”ti āha. Kathaṃ panettha ayamattho labbhatīti āha “kappoti ca guṇassapi nāma”nti. Tattha paṭhamaṃ vutto kappo, tato ekena guṇena, ekasmiṃ vāre gaṇanāyāti attho. Dve kappā hontīti ekavāragaṇanāya kappassa dviguṇitattā dve mahākappā hontīti attho. Dutiyenāti dutiyavāragaṇanāya. Cattāroti dutiyavāragaṇanāya dvīsu kappesu dviguṇitesu [M 2.0329] cattāro mahākappā hontīti attho. Puna te cattāro kappāti vuttanayena dve vāre guṇetvā ye cattāro kappā dassitā, puna te cattāro kappā catugguṇā hontīti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – dve vāre guṇetvā ye cattāro kappā dassitā, tesu catukkhattuṃ guṇitesu catusaṭṭhi kappā sampajjantīti. Tathā hi cattāro ekasmiṃ vāre guṇitā aṭṭha honti, puna te aṭṭha dutiyavāre guṇitā soḷasa honti, puna te soḷasa tatiyavāre guṇitā dvattiṃsa honti, puna te dvattiṃsa catutthavāre guṇitā catusaṭṭhi honti. Tenevāha “imehi catūhi guṇehi guṇitā ekena guṇena aṭṭha hontī”tiādi. Ettha ca heṭṭhā uposathasutte (a. ni. 3.71) –

Regarding "two aeons are the measure of their lifespan": here, to show that this limit is made with reference to those born from inferior jhāna, it is begun with: "The second jhāna is threefold as previously explained," and so on. Regarding "four aeons": here, to show that sixty-four aeons should be stated by the highest reckoning, it is said: "What was stated earlier as 'one aeon, two aeons,' the meaning should be understood by taking 'kappa' as a factor." How then is this meaning obtained here? It is said: "The word 'kappa' is also a name for a factor." Here, first, the aeon is mentioned. Then, by one multiplication, that is, by counting once, is the meaning. "Two aeons exist" means that by counting once, since the aeon is doubled, two great aeons are meant. "By the second [factor]" means by counting a second time. "Four" means that by counting a second time, when two aeons are doubled, four great aeons are meant. Again, "those four aeons" means that the four aeons shown by multiplying twice in the manner stated, again those four aeons, become quadrupled. This is what is said: the four aeons shown by multiplying twice, when multiplied four times, result in sixty-four aeons. For example, four, when multiplied once, become eight; again those eight, when multiplied a second time, become sixteen; again those sixteen, when multiplied a third time, become thirty-two; again those thirty-two, when multiplied a fourth time, become sixty-four. Therefore, it is said: "When these are multiplied by these four factors, by one multiplication they become eight," and so on. Here, in the earlier Uposatha Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.71)—

“Yāni mānusakāni paññāsa vassāni, cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ eso eko rattindivo”ti –

"Fifty human years are but a single day and night for the devas of the Realm of the Four Great Kings."

Ādinā kāmāvacaradevānameva āyuppamāṇaṃ dassitaṃ. Heṭṭhāyeva –

In this way, the lifespan of the devas of the sense sphere was shown. Even lower—

“Tayome, bhikkhave, puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ. Katame tayo? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā…pe… ākāsānañcāyatanūpagānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjati. Ākāsānañcāyatanūpagānaṃ, bhikkhave, devānaṃ vīsati kappasahassāni āyuppamāṇa”nti (a. ni. 3.117) –

"These three kinds of persons, bhikkhus, are found existing in the world. Which three? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person, having entirely transcended perceptions of form…reappears in the company of the devas who have attained the base of infinite space. The lifespan of the devas who have attained the base of infinite space, bhikkhus, is twenty thousand aeons."

Ādinā arūpāvacarānaṃyeva āyuppamāṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Idha pana rūpāvacarānameva āyuppamāṇaṃ dassitaṃ. Vibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ (vibha. 1022) pana “manussānaṃ kittakaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ, vassasataṃ appaṃ vā bhiyyo”tiādinā devamanussānañceva rūpārūpāvacarasattānañca āyuppamāṇaṃ dassitaṃ.

In this way, the lifespan of only the formless-sphere beings was mentioned. Here, however, only the lifespan of the form-sphere beings is shown. In the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 1022), however, it is stated: "What is the lifespan of humans? A hundred years or a little more," and so on, showing the lifespan of gods and humans, as well as beings in the form and formless spheres.

Tattha sammāsambuddhena manussānaṃ devānañca āyuṃ paricchindamānena catūsu apāyesu bhummadevesu [V 2.0301] ca āyu na paricchinnaṃ. Taṃ kasmāti? Niraye tāva kammameva pamāṇaṃ. Yāva kammaṃ na khīyati, tāva paccanti. Tathā sesaapāyesu. Bhummadevānampi kammameva pamāṇaṃ. Tattha nibbattā hi keci sattāhamattaṃ tiṭṭhanti, keci aḍḍhamāsaṃ, kappaṃ tiṭṭhamānāpi atthiyeva. Tattha manussesu gihibhāve ṭhitāyeva sotāpannāpi honti, sakadāgāmiphalaṃ anāgāmiphalaṃ arahattampi pāpuṇanti, tesu sotāpannādayo yāvajīvaṃ [M 2.0330] tiṭṭhanti, khīṇāsavā pana parinibbāyanti vā pabbajanti vā. Kasmā? Arahattaṃ nāma seṭṭhaguṇaṃ, gihiliṅgaṃ hīnaṃ, taṃ hīnatāya uttamaṃ guṇaṃ dhāretuṃ na sakkoti, tasmā te parinibbātukāmā vā honti pabbajitukāmā vā. Bhummadevā pana arahattaṃ pattāpi yāvajīvaṃ tiṭṭhanti, chasu kāmāvacaresu devesu sotāpannasakadāgāmino yāvajīvaṃ tiṭṭhanti, anāgāminā rūpabhavaṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭati khīṇāsavena parinibbātuṃ. Kasmā? Nilīyanokāsassa abhāvā. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacaresu sabbepi yāvajīvaṃ tiṭṭhanti, tattha rūpāvacare nibbattā sotāpannasakadāgāmino na puna idhāgacchanti, tattheva parinibbāyanti. Ete hi jhānaanāgāmino nāma.

There, when the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One defined the lifespan for humans and gods, he did not define the lifespan for beings in the four lower realms and for the terrestrial deities. Why is that? In hell, karma alone is the measure. As long as the karma is not exhausted, so long do they suffer. The same applies to the other lower realms. For terrestrial deities as well, karma alone is the measure. Among them, some beings remain for only a week, some for half a month, and some even exist for an aeon. Among humans, even while living as householders, some attain the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or even arahantship. Among them, stream-enterers and others remain for their entire lifespan, but those whose taints are destroyed either attain final Nibbāna or go forth into homelessness. Why? Arahantship is a supreme quality, whereas the householder’s state is inferior. Because of its inferiority, it cannot sustain the supreme quality. Therefore, they either wish to attain final Nibbāna or to go forth. However, terrestrial deities who attain arahantship remain for their entire lifespan. Among the six sense-sphere heavens, stream-enterers and once-returners remain for their entire lifespan. It is fitting for a non-returner to go to the form realm, and for one whose taints are destroyed to attain final Nibbāna. Why? Because there is no opportunity for seclusion. In the realms of form and the formless realms, all beings remain for their entire lifespan. There, stream-enterers and once-returners who are reborn in the form realm do not return here; they attain final Nibbāna there itself. These are called jhāna-non-returners.

Aṭṭhasamāpattilābhīnaṃ pana kiṃ niyameti? Paguṇajjhānaṃ. Yadevassa paguṇaṃ hoti, tena upapajjati. Sabbesu paguṇesu kiṃ niyameti? Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpatti. Ekaṃseneva hi so nevasaññānāsaññāyatane upapajjati. Navasu brahmalokesu nibbattaariyasāvakānaṃ tatrūpapattipi uparūpapattipi, na heṭṭhūpapatti. Puthujjanānaṃ pana tatrūpapattipi hoti, uparūpapattipi, heṭṭhūpapattipi. Pañcasu suddhāvāsesu catūsu ca arūpesu ariyasāvakānaṃ tatrūpapattipi hoti uparūpapattipi. Paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ nibbatto anāgāmī nava brahmaloke sodhetvā matthake ṭhito parinibbāti. Vehapphalaṃ, akaniṭṭhaṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti ime tayo devalokā seṭṭhabhavā nāma. Imesu tīsu ṭhānesu nibbattaanāgāmino neva uddhaṃ gacchanti, na adho, tattha tattheva parinibbāyantīti idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ.

For those who attain the eight meditative attainments, what determines it? Mastery of jhāna. One is reborn according to whichever jhāna is mastered. Among all the mastered jhānas, what determines it? The attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Assuredly, one is reborn in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Among the nine Brahmā worlds, for noble disciples reborn there, their rebirth is either in the same world or a higher one, but not in a lower one. However, for ordinary beings, their rebirth may be in the same world, a higher one, or a lower one. In the five Pure Abodes and the four formless realms, for noble disciples, their rebirth is either in the same world or a higher one. An anāgāmī reborn in the first jhāna plane, having purified the nine Brahmā worlds, standing at the summit, attains final nibbāna. The realms of Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these three deva-worlds are called the supreme existences. Anāgāmins reborn in these three places neither go upwards nor downwards; they attain final nibbāna right there. This miscellaneous section should be understood.

Paṭhamanānākaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Nānākaraṇa Sutta is concluded.

4-6. Dutiyanānākaraṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

4-6. Commentary on the Second Nānākaraṇa Sutta, etc.

124-6. Catutthe te dhammeti te “rūpagata”ntiādinā nayena vutte rūpādayo dhamme. Aniccatoti iminā niccappaṭikkhepato tesaṃ aniccatamāha, tato eva ca udayavayavantato vipariṇāmato tāvakālikato ca te aniccāti jotitaṃ hoti. Yañhi nibbattaṃ hoti, taṃ udayavayaparicchinnaṃ[V 2.0302]. Jarāya maraṇena ca tadeva viparītaṃ, ittarakkhaṇameva ca hotīti. Dukkhatoti iminā sukhappaṭikkhepato tesaṃ [M 2.0331] dukkhatamāha. Tato eva ca abhiṇhappaṭipīḷanato dukkhavatthuto ca te dukkhāti jotitaṃ hoti. Udayavayavantatāya hi te abhiṇhappaṭipīḷanato nirantaradukkhatāya dukkhasseva ca adhiṭṭhānabhūtā. Paccayayāpanīyatāya rogamūlatāya ca rogato. Dukkhatāsūlayogato kilesāsucipaggharaṇato uppādajarābhaṅgehi uddhumātaparipakkapabhinnato ca gaṇḍato. Pīḷājananato, antotudanato, dunnīharaṇato ca sallato. Avaḍḍhiāvahanato aghavatthuto ca aghato. Aseribhāvajananato ābādhapadaṭṭhānatāya ca ābādhato. Avasavattanato avidheyyatāya ca parato. Byādhijarāmaraṇehi palujjanīyatāya palokato. Sāminivāsikārakavedakaadhiṭṭhāyakavirahato suññato. Attappaṭikkhepaṭṭhena anattato. Rūpādidhammā hi na ettha attā atthīti anattā. Evaṃ sayampi attā na hontīti anattā. Tena abyāpārato nirīhato tucchato anattāti dīpitaṃ hoti. Lakkhaṇattayameva sukhāvabodhanatthaṃ ekādasahi padehi vibhajitvā gahitanti dassetuṃ “tatthā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pañcamachaṭṭhāni uttānatthāneva.

124-6. In the fourth section, when it is said, 'these phenomena,' the phenomena referred to are form and so forth, as explained by the method beginning with 'related to form.' By 'impermanent,' their impermanence is declared through the denial of permanence. From this very denial, their impermanence is illuminated by their nature of arising and ceasing, changing, and being momentary. For whatever is produced is bounded by arising and ceasing. It is overturned by aging and death, and it exists only for a brief moment. By 'suffering,' their suffering-nature is declared through the denial of happiness. From this very denial, their suffering is illuminated by their constant oppression and being a basis for suffering. Due to their nature of arising and ceasing, they are constantly oppressive, marked by uninterrupted suffering, and serve as the foundation for suffering itself. Because they are sustained by conditions and rooted in disease, they are like a disease. Because they are yoked to the thorn of suffering, due to the oozing of the impurity of defilements, and from being swollen, ripened, and burst by arising, aging, and dissolution, they are like a boil. They are like a thorn, causing torment, piercing inwardly, and being difficult to remove. They bring decline and are a basis for misery, thus being like misery. They generate a state of non-independence and are a ground for affliction, thus being like an affliction. They are uncontrollable and ungovernable, thus being as other. They are liable to be destroyed by sickness, aging, and death, thus being perishable. They are empty because they lack an owner, dweller, doer, feeler, or controller. They are non-self in the sense of rejecting a self. The phenomena of form and so forth are non-self because 'there is no self here.' In this way, they themselves are not a self; thus, they are non-self. Therefore, being without activity, without initiative, and void, their non-self nature is illuminated. To show that the three characteristics have been divided and taken up in eleven phrases for the sake of easy understanding, 'there' and so forth was said. The fifth and sixth sections are clear in meaning.

Dutiyanānākaraṇasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Discourse on Diverse Elements and so forth is complete.

7. Paṭhamatathāgataacchariyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Marvels of the Tathāgata

127. Sattame vattamānasamīpe vattamāne viya voharitabbanti “okkamatī”ti āha “okkanto hotīti attho”ti. Dasasahassacakkavāḷapattharaṇo samujjalabhāvena uḷāro. Devānubhāvanti devānaṃ pabhānubhāvaṃ. Devānañhi pabhaṃ so obhāso adhibhavati, na deve. Tenāha “devāna”ntiādi. Rukkhagacchādinā kenaci na haññatīti aghā, asambādhā. Tenāha “niccavivarā”ti. Asaṃvutāti heṭṭhā upari kenaci apihitā. Tenāha “heṭṭhāpi appatiṭṭhā”ti. Tattha pi-saddena yathā heṭṭhā udakassa pidhāyikā sandhārikā pathavī natthi asaṃvutā lokantarikā, evaṃ uparipi cakkavāḷesu devavimānānaṃ abhāvato asaṃvutā appatiṭṭhāti dasseti. Andhakāro ettha atthīti andhakārā. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ na jāyati ālokassa abhāvato, na cakkhuno. Tathā hi “tenobhāsena [M 2.0332] aññamaññaṃ sañjānantī”ti vuttaṃ. Jambudīpe ṭhitamajjhanhikavelāya pubbavidehavāsīnaṃ atthaṅgamavasena upaḍḍhaṃ sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ paññāyati, aparagoyānavāsīnaṃ uggamanavasena. Evaṃ sesadīpesupīti āha “ekappahāreneva tīsu dīpesu paññāyantī”ti. Ito aññathā dvīsu eva dīpesu paññāyanti. Ekekāya disāya navanavayojanasatasahassāni andhakāravidhamanampi imināva nayena daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pabhāya nappahontīti [V 2.0303] attano pabhāya obhāsituṃ nābhisambhuṇanti. Yugandharapabbatamatthakasamappamāṇe ākāse vicaraṇato “cakkavāḷapabbatassa vemajjhena carantī”ti vuttaṃ.

127. In the seventh, the present tense is used for the near present; thus, it says 'he descends,' which means 'he has descended.' The radiance spreading over the ten-thousandfold world-sphere is magnificent due to its brilliance. 'The power of the gods' means the splendor of the gods' light. For that radiance surpasses the light of the gods, not the gods themselves. Hence it is said, 'of the gods,' and so forth. 'Unharmed' means not harmed by anything, such as trees or bushes; unobstructed. Hence it is said, 'always open.' 'Uncovered' means not covered by anything above or below. Hence it is said, 'below, too, unsupported.'
