There, the particle 'pi' indicates that just as below there is no supporting or holding earth to contain the water—thus the world-interstice is uncovered—so too above, due to the absence of celestial mansions in the world-spheres, it is uncovered and unsupported. 'Darkness' means darkness exists here. Eye-consciousness does not arise due to the absence of light, not of the eye. For it is said, 'By that radiance, they recognize one another.' In Jambudīpa, at midday, half of the sun's disk is visible to the inhabitants of the eastern continent as it sets, and to those of the western continent as it rises. Similarly in the other continents—hence it is said, 'visible in three continents at once.' Otherwise, it would be visible in only two continents. The dispelling of darkness for nine hundred thousand yojanas in each direction should be understood in the same way. 'They are not able' means they are unable to illuminate with their own radiance. Because they move in the sky at a height equal to the summit of Mount Yugandhara, it is said, 'they travel through the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountain range.'

Byāvaṭāti khādanatthaṃ gaṇhituṃ upakkamantā. Viparivattitvāti vivaṭṭitvā. Chijjitvāti mucchāpavattiyā ṭhitaṭṭhānato muccitvā, aṅgapaccaṅgachedanavasena vā chijjitvā. Accantakhāreti ātapasantapābhāvena atisītabhāvaṃ sandhāya accantakhāratā vuttā siyā. Na hi taṃ kappasaṇṭhānaudakaṃ sampattikaramahāmeghavuṭṭhaṃ pathavisandhārakaṃ kappavināsakaudakaṃ viya khāraṃ bhavitumarahati, tathā sati pathavīpi vilīyeyya, tesaṃ vā pāpakammaphalena petānaṃ pakatiudakassa pubbakheḷabhāvāpatti viya tassa udakassa khārabhāvāpatti hotīti vuttaṃ “accantakhāre udake”ti.

'They are busy' means they are endeavoring to take it for the purpose of eating. 'Having turned it over' means having opened it. 'Having been cut' means having been freed from the place where one was due to fainting, or having been cut by way of severing limbs and parts of limbs. 'Extremely salty': the extreme saltiness might be spoken of in reference to the state of extreme coldness due to the absence of heat and warmth. For that water could not be salty like the world-establishing water, the rain from great prosperity-bringing clouds, the earth-supporting water, or the world-destroying water. If it were so, even the earth would dissolve. Or, due to the result of their evil kamma, for those petas, just as their natural water becomes like stale spittle, so too does that water become salty—thus it is said, 'in the extremely salty water.'

Paṭhamatathāgataacchariyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Discourse on the Marvels of the Tathāgata is complete.

8. Dutiyatathāgataacchariyasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Marvels of the Tathāgata

128. Aṭṭhame ālīyanti āramitabbaṭṭhena sevīyantīti ālayā, pañca kāmaguṇā. Āramantīti ratiṃ vindanti kīḷanti laḷanti. Ālīyanti vā allīyantā abhiramaṇavasena sevantīti ālayā, taṇhāvicaritāni. Tehi ālayehi ramantīti ālayārāmā. Yatheva hi susajjitaṃ pupphaphalabharitarukkhādisampannauyyānaṃ paviṭṭho rājā tāya sampattiyā ramati, sammudito āmoditappamodito hoti, na ukkaṇṭheti, sāyampi nikkhamituṃ na icchati, evamimehi kāmālayataṇhālayehi sattā ramanti, saṃsāravaṭṭe pamuditā anukkaṇṭhitā vasanti. Tena tesaṃ bhagavā duvidhampi ālayaṃ uyyānabhūmiṃ viya dassento “ālayārāmā”tiādimāha. Sesamettha uttānameva.

128. In the eighth discourse, the five strands of sensual pleasure are called “ālayā” because they are clung to and resorted to in the sense of being delighted in. They delight, find enjoyment, play, and revel. Alternatively, they are called “ālayā” because beings cling to them, become attached, and resort to them by way of delighting in them; these are the wanderings of craving. Those who delight in these attachments are called “ālayārāmā.” Just as a king, entering a well-adorned park filled with flowering and fruit-laden trees, delights in its splendor, becomes joyful, happy, and elated, and does not feel discontent, nor does he wish to leave even in the evening, so too do beings delight in these sensual attachments and craving-attachments, dwelling happily and without discontent in the cycle of existence. Therefore, the Blessed One, illustrating these two kinds of attachment as being like a pleasure grove, declares them as “ālayārāmā,” and so forth. The rest here is clear.

Dutiyatathāgataacchariyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Marvels of the Tathāgata is concluded.

9-10. Ānandaacchariyasuttādivaṇṇanā

9-10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Marvels of Ānanda and so forth

129-130. Navame [M 2.0333] paṭisanthāradhammanti pakaticārittavasena vuttaṃ, upagatānaṃ pana bhikkhūnaṃ [V 2.0304] bhikkhunīnañca pucchāvissajjanavasena ceva cittarucivasena ca yathākālaṃ dhammaṃ desetiyeva, upāsakaupāsikānaṃ pana upanisinnakakathāvasena. Dasamaṃ uttānameva.

129-130. In the ninth, 'the practice of hospitality' is spoken of in terms of habitual conduct. However, for monks and nuns who have come, he teaches the Dhamma to them at the appropriate time, both by way of questions and answers and according to their inclinations. For laymen and laywomen, however, he teaches by way of conversation while seated nearby. The tenth is clear.

Ānandaacchariyasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse on the Marvels of Ānanda and so forth is concluded.

Bhayavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Fear is concluded.

(14) 4. Puggalavaggo

(14) 4. The Chapter on Individuals

1. Saṃyojanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Fetters

131. Catutthassa paṭhame upapattippaṭilābhaṃ saṃvattanikānīti upapattipaṭilābhiyāni. Bhavapaṭilābhiyānīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Yehīti yehi saṃyojanehi hetubhūtehi, karaṇabhūtehi vā. Nanu ca sotāpannassapi orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni appahīnāni, kasmā pana sakadāgāmīyeva idha gahitoti āha “sakadāgāmissāti idaṃ appahīnasaṃyojanesu ariyesu uttamakoṭiyā gahita”nti. Tattha appahīnasaṃyojanesūti appahīnaorambhāgiyasaṃyojanesu. Uttamakoṭiyā gahitanti ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena gahitaṃ. Sakadāgāmito parañhi appahīnaorambhāgiyasaṃyojano ariyo nāma natthi. Nanu ca sakadāgāmissa pahīnānipi orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni atthi diṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsasaṃyojanānaṃ pahīnattā, tasmā “orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni appahīnānī”ti kasmā vuttanti āha “orambhāgiyesu ca appahīnaṃ upādāyā”tiādi. Yasmā kāmarāgabyāpādasaṃyojanāni sakadāgāmissa appahīnāni, tasmā tāni appahīnāni upādāya “orambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni appahīnānī”ti vuttaṃ, na sabbesaṃ appahīnattāti adhippāyo.

131. In the first discourse of the fourth chapter, 'conducive to the attainment of rebirth' means 'pertaining to the attainment of rebirth.' For 'pertaining to the attainment of existence,' the same method applies. 'By which' means by those fetters that are the cause or the instrument. But are not the lower fetters unabandoned even for a stream-enterer? Why then is only the once-returner mentioned here? It is said: 'The once-returner is mentioned here as the highest instance among noble ones with unabandoned fetters.' Here, 'with unabandoned fetters' means with unabandoned lower fetters. 'As the highest instance' means taken as the supreme limit. For beyond the once-returner, there is no noble one with unabandoned lower fetters. But does the once-returner not also have abandoned lower fetters, since the fetters of views, doubt, and attachment to rites and rituals are abandoned? Why then is it said, 'the lower fetters are unabandoned'? It is said: 'With reference to what is unabandoned among the lower fetters,' and so forth. Since the fetters of sensual desire and ill will are unabandoned for the once-returner, it is with reference to these unabandoned fetters that it is said, 'the lower fetters are unabandoned'—not because all of them are unabandoned. This is the intended meaning.

Saṃyojanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṃyojana Sutta is concluded.

2. Paṭibhānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Paṭibhāna Sutta

132. Dutiye [M 2.0334][V 2.0305] paṭibhānaṃ vuccati ñāṇampi ñāṇassa upaṭṭhitavacanampi, taṃ idha adhippetaṃ, atthayuttaṃ kāraṇayuttañca paṭibhānamassāti yuttappaṭibhāno. Pucchānantarameva sīghaṃ byākātuṃ asamatthatāya nomuttappaṭibhānamassāti nomuttappaṭibhāno. Iminā nayena sesā veditabbā. Ettha pana paṭhamo kañci kālaṃ vīmaṃsitvā yuttameva pekkhati tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero viya. So pana pañhaṃ puṭṭho pariggahetvā yuttappattakāraṇameva katheti. Dutiyo pucchānantarameva yena vā tena vā vacanena paṭibāhati, vīmaṃsitvāpi ca yuttaṃ na pakkheti catunikāyikapiṇḍatissatthero viya. So pana pañhaṃ puṭṭho pañhapariyosānampi nāgameti, yaṃ vā taṃ vā kathetiyeva, vacanatthaṃ panassa vīmaṃsiyamānaṃ katthaci na lagati. Tatiyo pucchāsamakālameva yuttaṃ pekkhati, taṃkhaṇaṃyeva ca naṃ byākaroti tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero viya. So pana pañhaṃ puṭṭho sīghameva katheti, yuttappattakāraṇo ca hoti. Catuttho puṭṭho samāno neva yuttaṃ pekkhati, na yena vā tena vā paṭibāhituṃ sakkoti, tibbandhakāranimuggo viya hoti lāḷudāyitthero viya.

132. In the second discourse, paṭibhāna is said to be both knowledge and the ready word of knowledge. Here, what is intended is that one's paṭibhāna is endowed with meaning and reason—thus, one has fitting paṭibhāna. Due to the inability to answer quickly immediately after being questioned, one's paṭibhāna is not ready—thus, one is not quick in response. The rest should be understood in this way. Here, the first person, after considering for some time, discerns what is fitting, like the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga. When questioned, he grasps the question and speaks only what is fitting and reasoned. The second, immediately after being questioned, deflects it with some words or other, and even after reflection, does not arrive at what is fitting, like the Elder Catunikāyika Piṇḍatissa. When questioned, he does not even wait for the question to end but says whatever comes to mind, and when the meaning of his words is examined, it does not hold up anywhere. The third discerns what is fitting at the very moment of being questioned and answers it at that instant, like the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya. When questioned, he speaks quickly, and his speech is fitting and reasoned. The fourth, when questioned, neither discerns what is fitting nor is able to deflect the question in any way; he is like one submerged in intense darkness, like the Elder Lāḷudāyi.

Paṭibhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Paṭibhāna Sutta is concluded.

3-4. Ugghaṭitaññūsuttādivaṇṇanā

3–4. Commentary on the Ugghaṭitaññū Sutta and so forth

133-4. Tatiye ugghaṭitaññūti ettha ugghaṭanaṃ nāma ñāṇugghaṭanaṃ, ñāṇena ugghaṭitamatteyeva jānātīti attho. Saha udāhaṭavelāyāti udāhāre udāhaṭamatteyeva. Dhammābhisamayo hotīti catusaccadhammassa ñāṇena saddhiṃ abhisamayo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā (vibha. 355) nayena saṃkhittena mātikāya ṭhapiyamānāya desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhituṃ samattho puggalo “ugghaṭitaññū”ti vuccati. Vipañcitaṃ vitthāritameva atthaṃ jānātīti vipañcitaññū. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ saṃkhittena mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā vitthārena atthe bhājiyamāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ samattho puggalo “vipañcitaññū”ti vuccati[M 2.0335]. Uddesādīhi netabboti neyyo. Anupubbena dhammābhisamayoti anukkamena arahattappatti. Byañjanapadameva paramaṃ assāti padaparamo. Na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hotīti tena attabhāvena jhānaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā nibbattetuṃ na sakkotīti attho. Catutthaṃ uttānameva.

133–4. In the third sutta, regarding 'one of quick understanding' (ugghaṭitaññū): here, 'quick understanding' (ugghaṭana) means the opening up of knowledge. The meaning is that one understands at the very moment knowledge is opened up. 'At the time of utterance' means at the very moment of utterance. 'There is penetration of the Dhamma' means the penetration of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths together with knowledge. 'This one is called': this person, who is capable of attaining arahantship by directing their knowledge according to the teaching when a summary is laid down in brief, such as 'the four establishments of mindfulness,' is called 'one of quick understanding.' 'One who understands through elaboration' (vipañcitaññū) means one who understands the meaning only when it is explained in detail. 'This one is called': this person, who is capable of attaining arahantship when the meaning is analyzed in detail after a summary has been laid down in brief, is called 'one who understands through elaboration.' 'One who is to be guided' (neyyo) means one who must be led by exposition and so forth. 'Gradual penetration of the Dhamma' means the gradual attainment of arahantship. 'One for whom the letter is the highest' (padaparamo) means one for whom the mere letter and word is supreme. 'There is no penetration of the Dhamma in that life' means that in that existence one is incapable of producing jhāna, insight, path, or fruition. The fourth is self-evident.

Ugghaṭitaññūsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ugghaṭitaññū Sutta and so forth is concluded.

5-8. Sāvajjasuttādivaṇṇanā

5–8. Commentary on the Sāvajja Sutta and so forth

135-8. Pañcame [V 2.0306] sāvajjoti sadoso. Sāvajjena kāyakammenāti sadosena pāṇātipātādinā kāyakammena. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ puggalo tīhi dvārehi āyūhanakammassa sadosattā gūthakuṇapādibharito padeso viya “sāvajjo”ti vuccati. Sāvajjena bahulanti yassa sāvajjameva kāyakammaṃ bahulaṃ hoti, appaṃ anavajjaṃ. So “sāvajjena bahulaṃ kāyakammena samannāgato appaṃ anavajjenā”ti vuccati. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Ko pana evarūpo hotīti? Yo gāmadhammatāya vā nigamadhammatāya vā kadāci karahaci uposathaṃ samādiyati, sīlāni pūreti. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ puggalo tīhi dvārehi āyūhanakammesu sāvajjasseva bahulatāya anavajjassa appatāya “vajjabahulo”ti vuccati. Yathā hi ekasmiṃ padese dubbaṇṇāni duggandhāni pupphāni rāsikatānassu, tesaṃ upari tahaṃ tahaṃ adhimuttakavassikapāṭalāni patitāni bhaveyyuṃ, evarūpo ayaṃ puggalo veditabbo. Yathā pana ekasmiṃ padese adhimuttakavassikapāṭalāni rāsikatānassu, tesaṃ upari tahaṃ tahaṃ duggandhāni badarapupphādīni patitāni bhaveyyuṃ. Evarūpo tatiyo puggalo veditabbo. Catuttho pana tīhi dvārehi āyūhanakammassa niddosattā ca catumadhurabharitasuvaṇṇavāti viya daṭṭhabbo. Chaṭṭhādīni uttānatthāneva.

135–8. In the fifth sutta, ‘blameworthy’ (sāvajja) means with fault. ‘With blameworthy bodily action’ means with faulty bodily action such as killing living beings and so forth. The same method applies to the others as well. ‘This one is called’: this person is called ‘blameworthy’ because their accumulative kamma through the three doors is faulty, like a place filled with dung, corpses, and so forth. ‘Predominantly with the blameworthy’ means one whose bodily kamma is mostly blameworthy, with little that is blameless. Such a person is said to be ‘endowed with predominantly blameworthy bodily kamma and little that is blameless.’ The same method applies to the others as well. Who, then, is such a person? It is one who, due to village custom or town custom, occasionally observes the Uposatha and fulfills the precepts. ‘This one is called’: this person is called ‘abounding in faults’ (vajjabahulo) because of the predominance of the blameworthy and the scarcity of the blameless among their accumulative kammas through the three doors. Just as in one place there might be a heap of discolored, foul-smelling flowers, with adhimuttaka, vassika, and pāṭalā flowers scattered here and there on top, so is this person to be understood. And just as in another place there might be a heap of adhimuttaka, vassika, and pāṭalā flowers, with foul-smelling jujube flowers and so forth scattered here and there on top, so is the third person to be understood. The fourth person, however, on account of the faultlessness of their accumulative kamma through the three doors, should be seen as like a golden bowl filled with the four sweets. The sixth and following suttas are plain in meaning.

Sāvajjasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sāvajja Sutta and so forth is concluded.

9-10. Dhammakathikasuttādivaṇṇanā

9–10. Commentary on the Dhammakathika Sutta and so forth

139-140. Navame [M 2.0336] appañca bhāsatīti sampattaparisāya thokameva katheti. Asahitañcāti kathento ca pana na atthayuttaṃ kālayuttaṃ katheti. Parisā cassa na kusalā hotīti sotuṃ nisinnaparisā cassa yuttāyuttaṃ kāraṇākāraṇaṃ siliṭṭhāsiliṭṭhaṃ na jānātīti attho. Evarūpoti ayaṃ evaṃjātiko bāladhammakathiko evaṃjātikāya bālaparisāya dhammakathikotveva nāmaṃ labhati. Iminā nayena sabbattha attho veditabbo. Ettha ca dveyeva janā sabhāvadhammakathikā, na itare. Itare pana dhammakathikānaṃ anto paviṭṭhattā evaṃ vuttā. Dasamaṃ uttānameva.

139–140. In the ninth sutta, ‘he speaks little’ means he speaks only a little to the assembled company. ‘And incoherently’ means that when he speaks, he does not speak what is connected to the meaning or what is timely. ‘And his assembly is not skilled’ means that the assembly seated to listen does not know what is fitting and unfitting, what is a reason and not a reason, what is polished and unpolished. ‘Such a one’: this kind of foolish Dhamma speaker gains the name of ‘Dhamma speaker’ only in relation to such a foolish assembly. The meaning should be understood in this way in all cases. And here, only two persons are Dhamma speakers by nature; the others are not. The others, however, are spoken of thus because they are included among Dhamma speakers. The tenth sutta is self-evident.

Dhammakathikasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Dhammakathika Sutta and so forth is concluded.

Puggalavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Individuals is concluded.

(15) 5. Ābhāvaggo

(15) 5. The Chapter on Radiance

1-6. Ābhāsuttādivaṇṇanā

1–6. Commentary on the Ābhā Sutta and so forth

141-146. Pañcamassa [V 2.0307] paṭhamādīni uttānatthāneva.

141–146. The first sutta and so forth of the fifth chapter are plain in meaning.

Ābhāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ābhā Sutta and so forth is concluded.

7-10. Dutiyakālasuttādivaṇṇanā

7–10. Commentary on the Second Kālasutta and so forth

147-150. Sattame paramatthato avijjamānasabhāvassa kālassa bhāvanādiyogo na sambhavatīti āha “kālāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle dhammassavanādivasena pavattānaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ etaṃ adhivacana”nti. Kālasahacaritā hi kusalā dhammā idha kāla-saddena gahitā aparassa asambhavato. Aṭṭhamādīni uttānatthāneva.

147–150. In the seventh sutta, it is said that, in the ultimate sense, since time has no inherent existence, the application of cultivation and so forth to it is not possible. He says: ‘Time’ (kāla) is a designation for wholesome states that arise at various times by way of hearing the Dhamma and so forth. For here, wholesome states concurrent with time are taken by the word ‘time’ because the other meaning is not possible. The eighth and following suttas are plain in meaning.

Dutiyakālasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Suttas Beginning with the Second Kālasutta is concluded.

Ābhāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Ābhāvagga is concluded.

Tatiyapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Third Fifty is concluded.

4. Catutthapaṇṇāsakaṃ

4. The Fourth Fifty

(16) 1. Indriyavaggo

(16) 1. The Chapter on the Faculties

1-5. Indriyasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-5. Commentary on the Suttas Beginning with the Indriya Sutta

151-155. Catutthassa [V 2.0308][M 2.0337] paṭhamādīni uttānāneva.

151-155. The first and subsequent suttas of the fourth fifty are straightforward in meaning.

Indriyasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Suttas Beginning with the Indriya Sutta is concluded.

6-8. Kappasuttādivaṇṇanā

6-8. Commentary on the Suttas Beginning with the Kappa Sutta

156-158. Chaṭṭhe saṃvaṭṭanaṃ vinassanaṃ saṃvaṭṭo, saṃvaṭṭato uddhaṃ tathā ṭhāyī saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī. Vivaṭṭanaṃ nibbattanaṃ, vaḍḍhanaṃ vā vivaṭṭo. “Tejosaṃvaṭṭo, āposaṃvaṭṭo, vāyosaṃvaṭṭoti evaṃ saṃvaṭṭasīmānukkamena saṃvaṭṭesu vattabbesu tathā avatvā āposaṃvaṭṭo, tejosaṃvaṭṭo, vāyosaṃvaṭṭoti vacanaṃ saṃvaṭṭamahābhūtadesanānupubbiyā”ti keci. “Bhāvīsaṃvaṭṭānupubbiyā”ti apare. Āpena saṃvaṭṭo āposaṃvaṭṭo. Saṃvaṭṭasīmāti saṃvaṭṭanamariyādā. Saṃvaṭṭatīti vinassati. Sadāti sabbakālaṃ, tīsupi saṃvaṭṭakālesūti attho. Ekaṃ buddhakkhettaṃ vinassatīti ettha buddhakkhettaṃ nāma tividhaṃ hoti jātikkhettaṃ, āṇākkhettaṃ, visayakkhettañca.

156-158. In the sixth sutta, dissolution (saṃvaṭṭo) is destruction (saṃvaṭṭanaṃ), perishing (vinassanaṃ). Saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī means remaining as such after dissolution. Evolution (vivaṭṭo) is arising (vivaṭṭanaṃ), generation (nibbantanaṃ), or expansion (vaḍḍhanaṃ). Some say that when describing the dissolutions in the sequence of the limits of dissolution, instead of saying ‘dissolution by fire, dissolution by water, dissolution by wind,’ the statement ‘dissolution by water, dissolution by fire, dissolution by wind’ is made in accordance with the sequence of the teaching on the great elements of dissolution. Others say it is in accordance with the sequence of future dissolutions. Āposaṃvaṭṭo means dissolution by water. Saṃvaṭṭasīmā means the boundary of dissolution. Saṃvaṭṭati means it perishes. Sadā means always, that is, in all three periods of dissolution. Here, when it is said that one Buddha-field perishes, a Buddha-field is of three kinds: the field of birth, the field of authority, and the field of domain.

Tattha jātikkhettaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷapariyantaṃ hoti, tathāgatassa paṭisandhiggahaṇādīsu kampati. Āṇākkhettaṃ koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷapariyantaṃ, yattha ratanasuttaṃ (khu. pā. 6.1 ādayo; su. ni. 224 ādayo) khandhaparittaṃ (a. ni. 4.67; cūḷava. 251) dhajaggaparittaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.249) āṭānāṭiyaparittaṃ (dī. ni. 3.277-278) moraparittanti (jā. 1.2.17-18) imesaṃ parittānaṃ ānubhāvo vattati. Visayakkhettaṃ anantāparimāṇaṃ, yaṃ “yāvatā vā panākaṅkheyyā”ti (a. ni. 3.81) vuttaṃ. Tattha yaṃ yaṃ tathāgato ākaṅkhati, taṃ taṃ jānāti. Evametesu tīsu buddhakkhettesu ekaṃ āṇākkhettaṃ vinassati[V 2.0309], tasmiṃ pana vinassante jātikkhettaṃ vinaṭṭhameva hoti, vinassantañca ekatova vinassati, saṇṭhahantañca [M 2.0338] ekatova saṇṭhahati. Sesamettha visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāsu (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.404) vuttanayeneva gahetabbaṃ. Sattamaṭṭhamāni uttānatthāneva.

There, the field of birth extends to the limit of ten thousand world-systems, which trembles at the Tathāgata's conception and other events. The field of authority extends to the limit of a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems, where the power of these protective chants operates: the Ratana Sutta, the Khandha Paritta, the Dhajagga Paritta, the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, and the Mora Paritta. The field of domain is infinite and immeasurable, as stated: "As far as one might wish." There, whatever the Tathāgata wishes, he knows it. Thus, among these three Buddha-fields, when one field of authority perishes, the field of birth perishes as well; and when they perish, they perish together, and when they are established, they are established together. The rest here should be understood according to the method stated in the commentaries on the Path of Purification. The seventh and eighth suttas are straightforward in meaning.

Kappasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Suttas Beginning with the Kappa Sutta is concluded.

9. Bhikkhunīsuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Sutta

159. Navame evaṃ pavattaṃ paccuppannataṇhaṃ nissāyāti “kudāssu nāmāhampi āsavānaṃ khayā”tiādinā nayena anuttare vimokkhe pihaṃ uppādentassa uppannataṇhaṃ nissāya. Kathaṃ pana lokuttaradhamme ārabbha āsā uppajjatīti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na ārammaṇakaraṇavasena tattha pihā pavattati avisayattā puggalassa ca anadhigatabhāvato. Anussavūpaladdhe pana anuttaravimokkhe uddissa pihaṃ uppādento tattha pihaṃ uppādeti nāma. Nākaḍḍhatīti kammapathabhāvaṃ appattatāya paṭisandhiṃ na deti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

159. In the ninth sutta, ‘dependent on the present craving that has arisen thus’ means: dependent on the craving that has arisen in one who generates longing for the unsurpassed liberation, in the manner beginning with ‘When indeed shall I too attain the destruction of the taints?’ But how does desire arise concerning supramundane states? This should not be viewed in that way, for longing does not occur there by way of taking it as an object, since it is beyond the person's sphere and because of its unattained nature. However, one who generates longing directed towards the unsurpassed liberation, which is apprehended through oral tradition, is said to generate longing for it. ‘It does not draw along’ (nākaḍḍhati) means it does not give rise to rebirth because it has not attained the state of a path of action. The rest is easily understood.

Bhikkhunīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Sutta is concluded.

10. Sugatavinayasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Sugatavinaya Sutta

160. Dasame vaḷañjentīti sajjhāyanti ceva vācuggataṃ karontā dhārenti ca. Avigatataṇhatāya taṃ taṃ parikkhārajātaṃ bahumpi ādiyantīti bahulā, te eva bāhulikā yathā “venayiko”ti (ma. ni. 1.246; a. ni. 8.11; pārā. 8). Te pana yasmā paccayabahulabhāvā yuttappayuttā nāma honti, tasmā āha “paccayabāhullāya paṭipannā”ti. Sithilaṃ gaṇhantīti sāthalikā, sikkhāya ādaragāravābhāvena sithilaṃ adaḷhaṃ gaṇhantīti attho. Sithilanti ca bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, sithila-saddena vā samānatthassa sāthalasaddassa vasena sāthalikāti padasiddhi veditabbā. Avagamanatoti adhogamanato, orambhāgiyabhāvatoti attho. Nibbīriyāti ujjhitussāhā tadadhigamāya ārambhampi akurumānā.

160. In the tenth sutta, ‘they make use of’ (vaḷañjenti) means they recite and also retain it by making it vocal. Due to their unabandoned craving, they take up many kinds of requisites; hence, they are called ‘abundant’ (bahulā), and they are indeed ‘given to abundance’ (bāhulikā), like ‘a Vinaya expert’ (venayiko). Since they are engaged in this way because of an abundance of requisites, they are called ‘devoted and dedicated,’ therefore it is said, ‘they are devoted to an abundance of requisites.’ ‘They grasp loosely’ (sithilaṃ gaṇhanti) means they are ‘lax’ (sāthalikā); that is, they grasp the training loosely, not firmly, due to a lack of respect and reverence. Sithilaṃ is a neuter noun indicating a state. Or, the derivation of the word sāthalikā should be understood by means of the word sāthala, which has the same meaning as sithila. ‘From decline’ (avagamanato) means from going downward, that is, from being of the nature of the lower fetters. ‘Without energy’ (nibbīriyā) means having abandoned enthusiasm, not even making an effort to attain it.

Sugatavinayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sugatavinaya Sutta is concluded.

Indriyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Faculties is concluded.

(17) 2. Paṭipadāvaggo

(17) 2. The Chapter on the Practices

1. Saṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Saṃkhitta Sutta

161. Dutiyassa paṭhame [M 2.0339][V 2.0310] dukkhāpaṭipadā dandhābhiññātiādīsu pāḷiyā āgatanayena attho veditabbo. Tathā hi –

161. In the first sutta of the second chapter, the meaning of ‘painful practice with slow direct knowledge’ and so on should be understood according to the method found in the Pāli text. Thus:

“Tattha katamā dukkhapaṭipadā dandhābhiññā paññā? Kicchena kasirena samādhiṃ uppādentassa dandhaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ abhijānantassa yā uppajjati paññā pajānanā…pe… amoho dhammavicayo sammādiṭṭhi, ayaṃ vuccati dukkhapaṭipadā dandhābhiññā paññā. Tattha katamā dukkhapaṭipadā khippābhiññā paññā? Kicchena kasirena samādhiṃ uppādentassa khippaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ abhijānantassa yā uppajjati paññā pajānanā…pe… sammādiṭṭhi, ayaṃ vuccati dukkhapaṭipadā khippābhiññā paññā. Tattha katamā sukhapaṭipadā dandhābhiññā paññā? Akicchena akasirena samādhiṃ uppādentassa dandhaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ abhijānantassa yā uppajjati paññā pajānanā…pe… sammādiṭṭhi, ayaṃ vuccati sukhapaṭipadā dandhābhiññā paññā. Tattha katamā sukhapaṭipadā khippābhiññā paññā? Akicchena akasirena samādhiṃ uppādentassa khippaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ abhijānantassa yā uppajjati paññā pajānanā…pe… sammādiṭṭhi, ayaṃ vuccati sukhapaṭipadā khippābhiññā paññā”ti (vibha. 801) – ayamettha pāḷi.

“Here, what is the wisdom of painful practice with slow direct knowledge? When one arouses concentration with difficulty and hardship, and slowly directly knows that state, the wisdom that arises—the understanding… non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called the wisdom of painful practice with slow direct knowledge. Here, what is the wisdom of painful practice with quick direct knowledge? When one arouses concentration with difficulty and hardship, and quickly directly knows that state, the wisdom that arises—the understanding… right view—this is called the wisdom of painful practice with quick direct knowledge. Here, what is the wisdom of pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge? When one arouses concentration without difficulty or hardship, and slowly directly knows that state, the wisdom that arises—the understanding… right view—this is called the wisdom of pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge. Here, what is the wisdom of pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge? When one arouses concentration without difficulty or hardship, and quickly directly knows that state, the wisdom that arises—the understanding… right view—this is called the wisdom of pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge.” This is the Pāli text here.

Tattha kicchena kasirena samādhiṃ uppādentassāti pubbabhāge āgamanakāle kicchena kasirena dukkhena sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilese vikkhambhetvā lokuttarasamādhiṃ uppādentassa. Dandhaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ abhijānantassāti vikkhambhitesu kilesesu vipassanāparivāse ciraṃ vasitvā taṃ lokuttarasamādhisaṅkhātaṃ ṭhānaṃ dandhaṃ saṇikaṃ abhijānantassa paṭivijjhantassa, pāpuṇantassāti attho. Ayaṃ vuccatīti yā esā evaṃ uppajjati, ayaṃ kilesavikkhambhanappaṭipadāya dukkhattā, vipassanāparivāsapaññāya ca dandhattā maggakāle ekacittakkhaṇe uppannāpi paññā āgamanavasena “dukkhapaṭipadā [M 2.0340] dandhābhiññā nāmā”ti vuccati. Upari tīsu padesupi iminā nayena attho veditabbo.

Here, ‘when one arouses concentration with difficulty and hardship’ means: in the preliminary stage, at the time of approach, with difficulty, with hardship, with suffering, with exertion, with striving, having suppressed the defilements, one arouses supramundane concentration. ‘And slowly directly knows that state’ means: having dwelt long in the development of insight with the defilements suppressed, slowly, gradually, one directly knows, penetrates, and attains that state known as supramundane concentration—this is the meaning. ‘This is called’ means that this wisdom, which arises thus, even though it arises in a single mind-moment at the moment of the path, is called ‘painful practice with slow direct knowledge’ in terms of its approach, due to the painfulness of the practice of suppressing defilements and the slowness of the wisdom of insight development. The meaning should be understood in the same way in the three remaining cases.

Saṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṃkhitta Sutta is concluded.

2. Vitthārasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Vitthāra Sutta

162. Dutiye [V 2.0311] akatābhinivesoti akatādhikāro. Rūpānaṃ lakkhaṇādīhi paricchinditvā gahaṇaṃ rūpapariggaho. Tīsu addhāsu kilamatīti pubbante aparante pubbantāparanteti evaṃ tīsu padesesu kilamati. Pañcasu ñāṇesūti rūpapariggahādīsu pañcasu ñāṇesu. Navasu vipassanāñāṇesūti udayabbayādinavavipassanāñāṇesu. Sesamettha uttānameva.

162. In the second discourse, 'not committed to the unmade' means having no mastery over it. The comprehension of form by defining it through its characteristics and so on is the delimitation of form. 'He wearies in the three times' means he wearies in the three aspects, namely, the past, the future, and both the past and the future. 'In the five knowledges' means in the five knowledges beginning with the delimitation of form. 'In the nine insight knowledges' means in the nine insight knowledges such as that of arising and passing away. The remainder here is evident.

Vitthārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vitthāra Sutta is concluded.

3. Asubhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Asubha Sutta

163. Tatiye “yathā etaṃ, tathā ida”nti iminā nayenāti etena –

163. In the third discourse, 'as that, so this' means by this method, namely:

“Yathā idaṃ tathā etaṃ, yathā etaṃ tathā idaṃ;

Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca, kāye chandaṃ virājaye”ti. (su. ni. 205); –

“As this, so that; as that, so this; one should dispel desire for the body, both internal and external.” (Snp 205)

Imaṃ desanānayaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tassattho – yathā idaṃ saviññāṇakāsubhaṃ āyuusmāviññāṇānaṃ anapagamā carati tiṭṭhati nisīdati sayati, tathā etaṃ etarahi susāne sayitaṃ aviññāṇakampi pubbe tesaṃ dhammānaṃ anapagamā ahosi. Yathā ca etaṃ etarahi matasarīraṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ apagamā na carati na tiṭṭhati na nisīdati na seyyaṃ kappeti, tathā idaṃ saviññāṇakampi tesaṃ dhammānaṃ apagamā bhavissati. Yathā ca idaṃ saviññāṇakaṃ netarahi susāne mataṃ seti na uddhumātakādibhāvamupagataṃ, tathā etaṃ etarahi matasarīrampi pubbe ahosi. Yathā panetaṃ [M 2.0341] etarahi aviññāṇakāsubhaṃ matakasusāne seti uddhumātakādibhāvañca upagataṃ, tathā idaṃ saviññāṇakampi bhavissatīti. Tattha yathā idaṃ tathā etanti attanā matasarīrassa samānabhāvaṃ karonto bāhire dosaṃ pajahati. Yathā etaṃ tathā idanti matasarīrena attano samānabhāvaṃ karonto ajjhattike rāgaṃ pajahati. Yenākārena ubhayaṃ samaṃ karoti, taṃ sampajānanto ubhayattha mohaṃ pajahati.

This method of teaching is embraced. Its meaning is: Just as this conscious foul body moves, stands, sits, and lies down due to the non-departure of life, heat, and consciousness, so too this now lifeless body lying in the charnel ground was also like that previously, when those states had not departed. And just as this now dead body, with the departure of those states, does not move, stand, sit, or adopt a lying posture, so too this conscious body will be when those states have departed. And just as this conscious body does not now lie dead in the charnel ground, not having reached the state of being bloated and so forth, so too this now dead body was previously. And just as this now lifeless foul body lies in the charnel ground, having reached the state of being bloated and so forth, so too this conscious body will become. Herein, by making oneself equal to the dead body, one abandons aversion toward the external. By making the dead body equal to oneself, one abandons internal lust. By clearly comprehending the way in which both are the same, one abandons delusion in both cases.

Bahiddhā diṭṭhānanti bahiddhā susānādīsu diṭṭhānaṃ uddhumātakādidasannaṃ asubhānaṃ. “Navannaṃ pāṭikulyānaṃ vasenā”ti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu antimajīvikābhāvato piṇḍapātassa alābhalābhesu paritassanagedhādisamuppattito [V 2.0312] bhattassa sammadajananato kimikulasaṃvaddhanatoti evamādīhipi ākārehi āhārepaṭikūlatā paccavekkhitabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ – “antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikānaṃ yadidaṃ piṇḍolyaṃ atipāpoyaṃ lokasmiṃ yadidaṃ piṇḍolyo vicarati pattapāṇīti (saṃ. ni. 3.80; itivu. 91). Aladdhā ca piṇḍapātaṃ paritassati, laddhā ca piṇḍapātaṃ gadhito mucchito ajjhopanno anādīnavadassāvī anissaraṇapañño paribhuñjatīti (a. ni. 3.124). Bhutto ca āhāro kassaci kadāci maraṇaṃ vā maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ āvahatī”ti.

‘Of things seen externally’ means of the ten foul objects, such as the bloated corpse, seen in external places like charnel grounds. ‘Why is it said, “By way of the nine kinds of repulsiveness”?’ Surely, the repulsiveness of food should be reflected upon in these and other ways: because it is the last resort for livelihood; because of the arising of anxiety, greed, and so on, in the gain or loss of almsfood; because of the intoxication produced by food; and because it fosters families of worms. For it is said: ‘This, monks, is the lowest of livelihoods—this alms-gathering. It is a curse in the world to go about as an alms-gatherer, bowl in hand.’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.80; Itivuttaka 91) ‘Not having received almsfood, one frets; having received almsfood, one consumes it greedily, infatuated, attached, not seeing the danger, and without the wisdom of escape.’ (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.124) ‘And the food eaten sometimes brings death or death-like suffering.’

Kaṭukīṭakādayo dvattiṃsakulappabhedā kimiyo naṃ upanissāya jīvantīti? Vuccate – antimajīvikābhāvo tāva cittasaṃkilesavisodhanatthaṃ kammaṭṭhānābhinivesanato pageva manasi kātabbo “māhaṃ chavālātasadiso bhaveyya”nti. Tathā piṇḍapātassa alābhalābhesu paritassanagedhādisamuppattinivāraṇaṃ pageva anuṭṭhātabbaṃ suparisuddhasīlassa paṭisaṅkhānavato tadabhāvato. Bhattasammado anekantiko paribhoge antogadhovāti veditabbo. Kimikulasaṃvaddhanaṃ pana saṅgahetabbaṃ, saṅgahitameva vā “navannaṃ pāṭikulyānaṃ vasenā”ti ettha niyamassa akatattā. Iminā vā nayena itaresampettha saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo yathāsambhavamettha paṭikūlatāpaccavekkhaṇassa adhippetattā.

Regarding the thirty-two kinds of creatures, such as worms and insects, that live dependent on this body, it is said: Firstly, the state of being the last resort for livelihood should be considered beforehand in one's mind for the purpose of purifying mental defilements by applying oneself to a meditation subject, thinking, 'May I not become like a firebrand from a pyre.' Likewise, for one of perfectly pure virtue who reflects wisely, the prevention of the arising of anxiety, greed, and so on, in the gain or loss of almsfood should be undertaken beforehand, due to the absence of those things in such a person. The intoxication from food is not invariable and should be understood as being included in its consumption. The fostering of families of worms, however, should be included, or is already included, because no fixed rule is made here regarding 'the nine kinds of repulsiveness.' Or, in this way, the inclusion of other things here should be seen, insofar as possible, since the contemplation of repulsiveness is intended here.

Evañca [M 2.0342] katvā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.294-295) dasahi ākārehi paṭikūlatā veditabbā. Seyyathidaṃ – gamanato, pariyesanato, paribhogato, āsayato, nidhānato, aparipakkato, paripakkato, phalato, nissandato, sammakkhanatoti. Evaṃ dasannaṃ vasena pāṭikulyavacanenapi idha “navanna”nti vacanaṃ na virujjhati, sammakkhanassa paribhogādīsu labbhamānabhāvā visuṃ taṃ aggahetvā na vadanti. Visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.304) pana sammakkhanaṃ paribhogādīsu labbhamānampi nissandavasena visesato paṭikūlanti dassetuṃ sabbapacchā ṭhapitā.

Therefore, in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. I, 294–95), repulsiveness should be understood in ten aspects. Namely: by way of going, by way of seeking, by way of consuming, by way of its receptacle, by way of its deposit, by way of being undigested, by way of being digested, by way of its result, by way of its outflow, and by way of smearing. Thus, even though repulsiveness is spoken of in terms of ten aspects, the statement here ‘nine’ is not contradicted, because smearing is obtainable within consuming and so forth, and they do not mention it separately. However, in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. I, 304), although smearing is obtainable within consuming and so forth, it is placed last to specifically show its repulsiveness by way of outflow.

Ukkaṇṭhitasaññāya samannāgatoti tīsu bhavesu aruccanavasena pavattāya vipassanāpaññāya samannāgato. Nibbidānupassanā hesā saññāsīsena vuttā. Sesamettha uttānameva.

Endowed with the perception of weariness—this means being endowed with insight-wisdom that occurs by way of displeasure with the three planes of existence. This is the contemplation of disenchantment, stated under the heading of ‘perception.’ The remainder here is evident.

Asubhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Asubha Sutta is concluded.

4-6. Paṭhamakhamasuttādivaṇṇanā

4–6. Commentary on the First Discourse on Forbearance and Others

164-166. Catutthe [V 2.0313] padhānakaraṇakāle sītādīni nakkhamati na sahatīti akkhamā. Khamati sahati abhibhavatīti khamā. Indriyadamanaṃ damā. “Uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 4.14; 6.58) nayena vitakkasamanaṃ samāti āha “akusalavitakkānaṃ vūpasamanapaṭipadā”ti. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ, sabbesampi kilesānaṃ samanavasena pavattā paṭipadā samā. Pañcamachaṭṭhāni uttānatthāneva.

164–166. In the fourth discourse: when making an effort, one does not endure or bear cold and the like—thus it is ‘intolerance.’ One endures, bears, and overcomes—thus it is ‘forbearance.’ The taming of the senses is ‘restraint.’ By the method beginning, “He does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought” (Majjhima Nikāya 1.26; Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.14; 6.58), the calming of thoughts is ‘serenity,’ as stated: “the practice for the stilling of unwholesome thoughts.” This is merely an illustration, for the practice that proceeds by way of calming all defilements is ‘serenity.’ The fifth and sixth are clear in meaning.

Paṭhamakhamasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Discourse on Forbearance and Others is concluded.

7-8. Mahāmoggallānasuttādivaṇṇanā

7–8. Commentary on the Mahāmoggallāna Sutta and Others

167-168. Sattamaṭṭhamesu mahāmoggallānattherassātiādinā moggallānattherassa heṭṭhā tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ sukhapaṭipadadandhābhiññabhāvo, arahattamaggassa dukkhapaṭipadakhippābhiññabhāvo vutto, sāriputtattherassa pana heṭṭhimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ sukhapaṭipadadandhābhiññabhāvo, arahattamaggassa ca sukhapaṭipadakhippābhiññabhāvo dassito. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.801) “buddhānaṃ [M 2.0343] pana cattāropi maggā sukhapaṭipadakhippābhiññāva ahesuṃ, tathā dhammasenāpatissa. Mahāmoggallānattherassa pana paṭhamamaggo sukhapaṭipadakhippābhiñño ahosi, upari tayo dukkhapaṭipadadandhābhiññā”ti. Yañca vuttaṃ aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1476) “tathāgatassa hi sāriputtattherassa ca cattāropi maggā sukhapaṭipadakhippābhiññāva ahesuṃ, mahāmoggallānattherassa pana paṭhamamaggo sukhapaṭipadakhippābhiñño upari tayo dukkhapaṭipadakhippābhiññā”ti, taṃ sabbaṃ aññamaññaṃ nānulometi. Imāya pāḷiyā imāya ca aṭṭhakathāya na sameti, tasmā vīmaṃsitabbametaṃ. Taṃtaṃbhāṇakānaṃ vā matena tattha tattha tathā tathā vuttanti gahetabbaṃ.

167–168. In the seventh and eighth sections, by the passage beginning 'regarding the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna,' it is stated that for the Venerable Moggallāna, the three lower paths were of pleasant practice with slow realization, while the path of arahantship was of painful practice with quick realization. For the Venerable Sāriputta, however, it is shown that the three lower paths were of pleasant practice with slow realization, and the path of arahantship was of pleasant practice with quick realization. But in the Visuddhimagga (Vism. 2.801) it is said: “For the Buddhas, all four paths were of pleasant practice with quick realization, and likewise for the General of the Dhamma. For the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, however, the first path was of pleasant practice with quick realization, while the upper three were of painful practice with slow realization.” And in the Aṭṭhasālinī (DhsA. 1476) it is stated: “For the Tathāgata and the Venerable Sāriputta, all four paths were of pleasant practice with quick realization, but for the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the first path was of pleasant practice with quick realization, while the upper three were of painful practice with quick realization.” All these statements do not accord with one another. They do not agree with this Pāli text and this commentary; therefore, this matter should be carefully examined. Or it should be understood that it was stated thus and thus in various places according to the opinions of the respective reciters.

Mahāmoggallānasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahāmoggallāna Sutta and others is concluded.

9. Sasaṅkhārasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sasaṅkhāra Sutta

169. Navame sasaṅkhārena dukkhena kasirena adhimattapayogaṃ katvāva kilesaparinibbānadhammoti sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Asaṅkhārena appayogena adhimattapayogaṃ akatvāva kilesaparinibbānadhammoti [V 2.0314] asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī. Dhammānusārī puggalo hi āgamanamhi kilese vikkhambhento appadukkhena akasirena akilamantova vikkhambhetuṃ sakkoti. Saddhānusārī puggalo pana dukkhena kasirena kilamanto hutvā vikkhambhetuṃ, tasmā dhammānusārissa pubbabhāgamaggakkhaṇe kilesacchedakaṃ ñāṇaṃ adandhaṃ tikhiṇaṃ sūraṃ hutvā vahati. Yathā nāma tikhiṇena asinā kadaliṃ chindantassa chinnaṭṭhānaṃ maṭṭhaṃ hoti, atisīghaṃ vahati, saddo na suyyati, balavavāyāmakiccaṃ na hoti, evarūpā dhammānusārino pubbabhāgabhāvanā hoti. Saddhānusārino pana pubbabhāgakkhaṇe kilesacchedakaṃ ñāṇaṃ dandhaṃ atikhiṇaṃ asūraṃ hutvā vahati. Yathā nāma kuṇṭhena asinā kadaliṃ chindantassa chinnaṭṭhānaṃ na maṭṭhaṃ hoti, atisīghaṃ na vahati, saddo suyyati, balavavāyāmakiccaṃ icchitabbaṃ hoti, evarūpā saddhānusārino pubbabhāgabhāvanā hoti. Evaṃ santepi nesaṃ kilesakkhaye nānattaṃ natthi, anavasesāva kilesā khīyanti.

169. In the ninth discourse, one who attains the final quenching of defilements with exertion—that is, through suffering and hardship, having made an intense effort—is called 'one who attains final quenching with exertion.' One who attains the final quenching of defilements without exertion—that is, with little effort, without having made an intense effort—is called 'one who attains final quenching without exertion.' A Dhamma-follower, when suppressing defilements on the path, is able to suppress them with little suffering, without hardship, and without fatigue. A faith-follower, however, suppresses them with suffering, hardship, and fatigue. Therefore, for the Dhamma-follower, at the moment of the preliminary path, the knowledge that cuts off defilements functions as not slow, sharp, and bold. Just as when one cuts a plantain stalk with a sharp blade, the cut is smooth, the blade passes through very quickly, no sound is heard, and no strong effort is needed—such is the preliminary development of the Dhamma-follower. For the faith-follower, however, at the moment of the preliminary path, the knowledge that cuts off defilements functions as slow, not sharp, and not bold. Just as when one cuts a plantain stalk with a blunt blade, the cut is not smooth, the blade does not pass through very quickly, a sound is heard, and strong effort is needed—such is the preliminary development of the faith-follower. Even so, there is no difference in their destruction of defilements; the defilements are destroyed without remainder.

Sasaṅkhārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sasaṅkhāra Sutta is concluded.

10. Yuganaddhasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Yuganaddha Sutta

170. Dasame [M 2.0344] samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāvetīti idaṃ samathayānikassa vasena vuttaṃ. So hi paṭhamaṃ upacārasamādhiṃ vā appanāsamādhiṃ vā uppādeti, ayaṃ samatho. So tañca taṃsampayutte ca dhamme aniccādīhi vipassati, ayaṃ vipassanā, iti paṭhamaṃ samatho, pacchā vipassanā. Tena vuccati “samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāvetī”ti. Vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāvetīti idaṃ pana vipassanāyānikassa vasena vuttaṃ. So taṃ vuttappakāraṃ samathaṃ asampādetvā pañcupādānakkhandhe aniccādīhi vipassati. Paṭhamo lokuttaramaggo nibbattatīti sotāpattimaggaṃ sandhāya vadati, lokiyamaggavaseneva vā imissā pāḷiyā attho veditabbo. Kathaṃ? Maggo sañjāyati, pubbabhāgiyo lokiyamaggo uppajjati. Āsevati nibbidānupassanāvasena. Bhāveti muccitukamyatāvasena. Bahulīkaroti paṭisaṅkhānupassanāvasena. Āsevati vā bhayatupaṭṭhānādiñāṇavasena. Bhāveti muccitukamyatādiñāṇavasena. Bahulīkaroti vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanāvasena. Saṃyojanāni pahīyanti. Anusayā byantī hontīti maggappaṭipāṭiyā pahīyanti byantī honti.

170. In the tenth discourse, “One develops insight preceded by serenity”—this is said with reference to one who follows the path of serenity. For such a person first arouses either access concentration or absorption concentration; this is serenity. Then one discerns that serenity and the states associated with it as impermanent, and so forth; this is insight. Thus, serenity comes first, followed by insight. Therefore, it is said, “One develops insight preceded by serenity.” “One develops serenity preceded by insight”—this is said with reference to one who follows the path of insight. Without achieving serenity in the manner described, such a person discerns the five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent, and so forth. “The first supramundane path arises”—this is said with reference to the stream-entry path, or the meaning of this Pāli passage should be understood in terms of the mundane path. How? The path is generated; the preliminary mundane path arises. One cultivates it by means of the contemplation of disenchantment. One develops it by means of the desire for liberation. One makes it abundant by means of the contemplation of reflection. Alternatively, one cultivates it by means of knowledge such as the appearance of danger. One develops it by means of knowledge such as the desire for liberation. One makes it abundant by means of insight leading to emergence. The fetters are abandoned. “The underlying tendencies are brought to an end” means they are abandoned and brought to an end in the sequence of the paths.

Dhammuddhaccaviggahitamānasanti obhāsādīsu ariyadhammoti pavattaṃ uddhaccaṃ vikkhepo dhammuddhaccaṃ[V 2.0315], tena dhammuddhaccena vipassanāvīthito uggamanena virūpaṃ gahitaṃ pavattiyamānaṃ dhammuddhaccaviggahitamānasaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'A mind seized by restlessness concerning phenomena': Restlessness—that is, distraction—that arises regarding phenomena such as light with the thought, 'This is the noble Dhamma,' is 'restlessness concerning phenomena.' A mind that, due to that restlessness concerning phenomena, is improperly seized and proceeds by deviating from the path of insight is a 'mind seized by restlessness concerning phenomena.' As it is said:

“Dhammuddhaccaviggahitamānasaṃ hoti, aniccato manasi karoti, obhāso uppajjati, obhāso dhammoti obhāsaṃ āvajjati, tato vikkhepo uddhaccaṃ, tena uddhaccena viggahitamānaso aniccato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Dukkhato…pe… anattato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Tathā aniccato manasikaroto ñāṇaṃ uppajjati…pe… pīti passaddhi sukhaṃ adhimokkho paggaho upaṭṭhānaṃ upekkhā nikanti uppajjati, nikanti dhammoti nikantiṃ āvajjati, tato vikkhepo uddhaccaṃ, tena uddhaccena viggahitamānaso aniccato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ [M 2.0345] nappajānāti. Dukkhato…pe… anattato upaṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātī”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.6). Sesamettha uttānameva.

“One’s mind becomes seized by restlessness concerning phenomena. One attends to impermanence, and a light arises. One adverts to the light, thinking, 'The light is the Dhamma,' and from that, distraction and restlessness arise. With a mind seized by that restlessness, one does not understand the manifestation of impermanence as it really is. One does not understand the manifestation of suffering… or of non-self as it really is. Likewise, when one attends to impermanence, knowledge arises… joy, tranquility, happiness, conviction, exertion, establishment, equanimity, and liking arise. One adverts to the liking, thinking, 'The liking is the Dhamma,' and from that, distraction and restlessness arise. With a mind seized by that restlessness, one does not understand the manifestation of impermanence as it really is. One does not understand the manifestation of suffering… or of non-self as it really is.” (Paṭis II 6). The remainder here is self-evident.

Yuganaddhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Yuganaddha Sutta is concluded.

Paṭipadāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Path is concluded.

(18) 3. Sañcetaniyavaggo

(18) 3. The Chapter on Volitional Action

1. Cetanāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Cetanā Sutta

171. Tatiyassa paṭhame kāyasañcetanāhetūti kāyakammanimittaṃ, kāyikassa kammassa kaṭattā upacitattāti attho. Esa nayo sesasañcetanādvayepi. Uddhaccasahagatacetanā pavattivipākaṃ detiyevāti “vīsatividhā”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā vacīsañcetanā manosañcetanāti ettha kāmāvacarakusalākusalavasena vīsati cetanā labbhanti. Idaṃ tathā-saddena upasaṃharati. Apicettha nava mahaggatacetanāpi labbhantīti iminā navahi rūpārūpakusalacetanāhi saddhiṃ manodvāre ekūnatiṃsāti tīsu dvāresu ekūnasattati cetanā hontīti dasseti. Avijjāpaccayāvāti idaṃ tāpi cetanā avijjāpaccayāva hontīti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathāvuttā hi ekūnasattati [V 2.0316] cetanā kusalāpi avijjāpaccayā honti, pageva itarā appahīnāvijjasseva uppajjanato pahīnāvijjassa anuppajjanato.

171. In the first sutta of the third chapter, 'on account of bodily volition' means the sign of bodily kamma; the meaning is that bodily kamma has been performed and accumulated. This same method applies to the other two volitions. Because volition accompanied by restlessness produces a result in the course of existence, the classification 'twentyfold' is stated. Similarly, regarding verbal volition and mental volition, twenty volitions are obtained by way of wholesome and unwholesome sense-sphere states. This is summarized by the word 'similarly.' Moreover, here nine sublime volitions are also obtained; thus, it is shown that together with these nine wholesome volitions pertaining to the form and formless realms, there are twenty-nine volitions at the mind-door, and across the three doors, there are sixty-nine volitions. 'Conditioned by ignorance'—this is said to show that these volitions are also conditioned by ignorance. For the aforementioned sixty-nine volitions, even the wholesome ones, are conditioned by ignorance—how much more so the others!—since they arise only for one whose ignorance is not abandoned, and do not arise for one whose ignorance is abandoned.

Yasmā yaṃ taṃ yathāvuttaṃ cetanābhedaṃ kāyasaṅkhārañceva vacīsaṅkhārañca manosaṅkhārañca parehi anussāhito sāmampi asaṅkhārikacittena karoti, parehi kāriyamāno sasaṅkhārikacittenapi karoti, “idaṃ nāma kammaṃ karontopi tassa evarūpo nāma vipāko bhavissatī”ti evaṃ kammaṃ vipākañca jānantopi karoti, mātāpitūsu cetiyavandanādīni karontesu anukaronto dārako viya kevalaṃ kammaññeva vijjānanto “imassa pana kammassa ayaṃ vipāko”ti vipākaṃ ajānantopi karoti[M 2.0346], tasmā taṃ dassetuṃ “sāmaṃ vā ta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Parehi anāṇattoti saraseneva vattamāno. Jānantoti anussavādivasena jānanto.

Because one performs that aforesaid division of volition—bodily volitional formation, verbal volitional formation, and mental volitional formation—either oneself with an unprompted mind, unurged by others; or when caused to do so by others, with a prompted mind; or one does it knowing both the kamma and its result, thinking, 'By doing this kamma, such and such a result will come about'; or one does it like a child imitating his parents paying homage to a shrine, knowing only the kamma but not its result—therefore, to show this, it is said, 'whether by oneself…' and so on. 'Not instructed by others' means acting of one's own accord. 'Knowing' means knowing through oral tradition or the like.

Nanu ca khīṇāsavo cetiyaṃ vandati, dhammaṃ bhaṇati, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karoti, kathamassa kāyakammādayo na hontīti? Avipākattā. Khīṇāsavena hi katakammaṃ neva kusalaṃ hoti nākusalaṃ, avipākaṃ hutvā kiriyāmatte tiṭṭhati. Tenassa te kāyādayo na honti. Tenevāha “khīṇāsavassa kāyena karaṇakammaṃ paññāyatī”tiādi. Tanti kusalākusalaṃ.

But does not the one whose taints are destroyed pay homage to a shrine, teach the Dhamma, and attend to a meditation subject? How then are his bodily kamma and so forth not his? Because they are without result. For the kamma done by one whose taints are destroyed is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; being without result, it remains merely functional. Therefore, that bodily kamma and so forth is not his. Hence it is said: 'For one whose taints are destroyed, an action done with the body is discerned,' and so on. 'That' refers to wholesome and unwholesome.

Khiḍḍāya padussantīti khiḍḍāpadosino, khiḍḍāpadosino eva khiḍḍāpadosikā. Khiḍḍāpadoso vā etesaṃ atthīti khiḍḍāpadosikā. Te kira puññavisesādhigatena mahantena attano sirivibhavena nakkhattaṃ kīḷantā tāya sampattiyā mahantatāya “āhāraṃ paribhuñjimhā na paribhuñjimhā”tipi na jānanti. Atha ekāhārātikkamato paṭṭhāya nirantaraṃ khādantāpi pivantāpi cavantiyeva na tiṭṭhanti. Kasmā? Kammajatejassa balavatāya karajakāyassa mandatāya. Manussānañhi kammajatejo mando, karajakāyo balavā. Tesaṃ tejassa mandatāya kāyassa balavatāya sattāhampi atikkamitvā uṇhodakaacchayāguādīhi sakkā karajakāyaṃ upatthambhetuṃ. Devānaṃ pana tejo balavā hoti uḷārapuññanibbattattā uḷāragarusiniddhasudhāhārajīraṇato ca. Karajaṃ mandaṃ mudusukhumālabhāvato. Te ekaṃ āhāravelaṃ akkamitvāva saṇṭhāpetuṃ na sakkonti. Yathā nāma gimhānaṃ majjhanhike tattapāsāṇe ṭhapitaṃ padumaṃ vā uppalaṃ vā sāyanhasamaye ghaṭasatenapi siñciyamānaṃ pākatikaṃ na hoti vinassatiyeva, evameva pacchā nirantaraṃ khādantāpi pivantāpi cavantiyeva na tiṭṭhanti. Katame pana te devāti? “Ime nāmā”ti aṭṭhakathāya vicāraṇā natthi, “āhārūpacchedena ātape khittamālā viyā”ti vuttattā ye keci kabaḷīkārāhārūpajīvino devā evaṃ karonti, te evaṃ cavantīti [V 2.0317] veditabbā. Abhayagirivāsino panāhu “nimmānaratiparanimmitavasavattino te devā, khiḍḍāya padussanamatteneva hete khiḍḍāpadosikāti vuttā”ti. Ko panettha devānaṃ āhāro, kā āhāravelāti? “Sabbesampi kāmāvacaradevānaṃ sudhā āhāro, sā heṭṭhimehi heṭṭhimehi [M 2.0347] uparimānaṃ uparimānaṃ paṇītatamā hoti. Taṃ yathāsakaṃ divasavaseneva divase divase bhuñjanti. Keci pana badarappamāṇaṃ sudhāhāraṃ paribhuñjanti. So jivhāyaṃ ṭhapitamattoyeva yāva kesagganakhaggā kāyaṃ pharati, tesaṃyeva divasavasena sattadivasaṃ yāpanasamatthova hotī”ti vadanti.

Those who are corrupted by play are the 'khiḍḍāpadosins'; the 'khiḍḍāpadosins' are indeed the 'khiḍḍāpadosikas.' Or, because the corruption of play exists in them, they are 'khiḍḍāpadosikas.' It is said that these devas, having attained great prosperity through exceptional merit, play at a festival with their own magnificent glory and splendor, and due to the greatness of their attainment, they do not even know whether they have eaten or not. Then, from the time they miss a single meal, even if they continuously eat and drink, they still pass away and do not endure. Why? Because of the strength of their kamma-born heat-element and the weakness of their physical body. For humans, the kamma-born heat-element is weak, but the physical body is strong. Due to the weakness of their heat-element and the strength of their body, even after seven days have passed, it is possible to sustain the physical body with things like warm water and clear rice-gruel. But for the devas, their heat-element is strong because it is produced by sublime merit and from the digestion of sublime, rich, and luscious ambrosial food. Their physical body is weak, because it is soft, delicate, and tender. They are unable to endure after missing even a single mealtime. Just as a lotus or water lily placed on a scorching stone at midday in summer does not recover its natural state even if watered with a hundred pots in the evening, but withers away, so too do these devas pass away without enduring, even if they later eat and drink continuously. Now, which devas are these? The commentary does not specify them by name, but since it is said, 'Like a garland thrown into the heat when deprived of its food-source,' it should be understood that any devas who live on edible material food act in this way and thus pass away. The residents of Abhayagiri, however, say: 'These are the devas of the Nimmānaratī and Paranimmitavasavattī realms, who are called 'khiḍḍāpadosikas' merely because they are corrupted by play.' But what is the food of these devas, and what is their mealtime? 'For all sense-sphere devas, ambrosia is their food, and for each higher realm it is more refined than for the realm below it. They consume it daily according to their own day. Some, however, consume a jujube-sized portion of ambrosial food. Merely placing it on the tongue suffices to pervade their bodies from the tips of their hair to the tips of their nails, and according to their own day, it is capable of sustaining them for seven days,' so they say.

Issāpakatattā paduṭṭhena manasā padussantīti manopadosikā. Usūyavasena vā manaso padoso manopadoso, so etesaṃ atthi vināsahetubhūtoti manopadosikā. Akkuddho rakkhatīti kuddhassa so kodho itarasmiṃ akkujjhante anupādāno ekavārameva uppattiyā anāsevano cāvetuṃ na sakkoti, udakantaṃ patvā aggi viya nibbāyati, tasmā akkuddho taṃ cavanato rakkhati. Ubhosu pana kuddhesu bhiyyo bhiyyo aññamaññamhi parivaḍḍhanavasena tikhiṇasamudācāro nissayadahanaraso kodho uppajjamāno hadayavatthuṃ nidahanto accantasukhumālaṃ karajakāyaṃ vināseti, tato sakalopi attabhāvo antaradhāyati. Tenāha “ubhosu panā”tiādi. Tathā cāha bhagavā “aññamaññamhi paduṭṭhacittā kilantakāya…pe… cavantī”ti (dī. ni. 1.47).

Because they are corrupted by a mind that is corrupt on account of envy, they are the 'manopadosikas' (mind-corrupted ones). Or, the corruption of the mind (manopadoso) is due to jealousy; since this exists for them as a cause of destruction, they are 'manopadosikas.' 'The one who is not angry protects': when the other person is not angry, the anger of the angry person, being without fuel and not being cultivated since it arises only once, is unable to cause them to fall; like a fire that has reached water, it is extinguished. Therefore, the one who is not angry protects the other from passing away. But when both are angry, anger arises with a sharp and harsh demeanor through ever-increasing mutual escalation. With its characteristic of burning its support, it burns up the heart-base and destroys the extremely delicate physical body. Then the entire individual existence vanishes. Hence it is said: 'But when both…' and so on. And so the Blessed One has said: 'With minds mutually corrupted, their bodies exhausted… they pass away' (DN 1.47).

Katame tena devā daṭṭhabbāti ettha tenāti paccatte karaṇavacananti āha “katame nāma te devā daṭṭhabbā”ti. Karaṇattheyeva vā etaṃ karaṇavacananti dassento āha “tena vā attabhāvenā”ti. Sesamettha uttānameva.

Regarding 'By what are those devas to be seen?': here, 'by that' is the instrumental case in the sense of the agent, as he says, 'Which devas, indeed, are to be seen?' Or, showing that this is the instrumental case purely in the sense of the instrument, he says, 'or by that individual existence.' The rest here is clear in meaning.

Cetanāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Cetanā Sutta is finished.

2. Vibhattisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Vibhatti Sutta

172. Dutiye atthappabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ atthe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā. Atthoti cettha saṅkhepato hetuphalaṃ. Tañhi hetuvasena araṇīyaṃ gantabbaṃ pattabbaṃ, tasmā “attho”ti vuccati. Pabhedato pana yaṃ kiñci paccayasamuppannaṃ, nibbānaṃ, bhāsitattho, vipāko, kiriyāti ime pañca dhammā “attho”ti veditabbā[M 2.0348], taṃ atthaṃ paccavekkhantassa [V 2.0318] tasmiṃ atthe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā. Tenāha “pañcasu atthesu pabhedagataṃ ñāṇa”nti. Ācikkhāmītiādīsu ādito kathento ācikkhati nāma, uddisatīti attho. Tameva uddesaṃ pariyosāpento deseti. Yathāuddiṭṭhamatthaṃ uddisanavasena pakārehi ñāpento ñāpeti. Pakārehi eva tamatthaṃ patiṭṭhāpento paṭṭhapeti. Yathāuddiṭṭhaṃ paṭiniddisanavasena vivarati. Vivaṭaṃ vibhajati. Vibhattaatthaṃ hetūdāharaṇadassanehi pākaṭaṃ karonto uttāniṃ karoti.

172. In the second case, the knowledge capable of discerning, distinguishing, and establishing the characteristics of distinctions in meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning. Here, 'meaning' briefly refers to cause and effect. For it is to be approached, to be gone to, to be attained by way of cause; therefore, it is called 'meaning.' In detail, however, whatever is conditionally arisen, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, result, and action—these five things are to be understood as 'meaning.' The analytical knowledge of meaning is the knowledge that discerns distinctions in that meaning as one reflects upon that meaning. Therefore, it is said, 'the knowledge that discerns distinctions in the five meanings.' In phrases like 'I will explain,' one who speaks from the beginning is called 'explaining'; it means to point out. Having completed that pointing out, he teaches. Making known the meaning as pointed out by way of explaining it in various ways, he makes it known. By means of various aspects, he establishes that meaning. He reveals it by way of re-pointing out what was announced. He divides what has been revealed. Making the divided meaning evident by showing causes and examples, he makes it plain.

Tisso paṭisambhidāti dhammaniruttipaṭibhānapaṭisambhidā. Tattha dhammapaṭisambhidā nāma dhammappabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Dhammoti ca saṅkhepato paccayo. So hi yasmā taṃ taṃ vidahati pavatteti ceva pāpeti ca, tasmā “dhammo”ti vuccati. Pabhedato pana yo koci phalanibbattako hetu, ariyamaggo, bhāsitaṃ, kusalaṃ, akusalanti ime pañca dhammā “dhammo”ti veditabbā, taṃ dhammaṃ paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ dhamme pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Niruttippabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ niruttābhilāpe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidāti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – atthe ca dhamme ca yā sabhāvanirutti, taṃ sabhāvaniruttiṃ saddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ sabhāvaniruttābhilāpe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidāti.

There are three kinds of analytical knowledge: analytical knowledge of phenomena, analytical knowledge of language, and analytical knowledge of perspicuity. Herein, analytical knowledge of phenomena is the knowledge capable of noting, distinguishing, and determining the classification of phenomena. Briefly, 'phenomenon' refers to a condition. For it is called 'phenomenon' because it arranges, produces, and brings about various states. In detail, any cause that produces a result, the Noble Path, what is spoken, the wholesome, and the unwholesome—these five are to be understood as 'phenomenon.' The knowledge concerning the classification within that phenomenon for one who reviews it is analytical knowledge of phenomena. Analytical knowledge of language is the knowledge concerning the classification within linguistic expression, capable of noting, distinguishing, and determining the classification of language. This is what is meant: for meaning and for phenomena there is a natural expression. When one takes that natural expression, sound, as an object and reviews it, the knowledge that arises concerning the classification within that natural linguistic expression is the analytical knowledge of language.

Evamayaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā saddārammaṇā nāma jātā, na paññattiārammaṇā. Kasmā? Yasmā saddaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ sabhāvaniruttī”ti jānanti. Paṭisambhidāppatto hi “phasso”ti vutte “ayaṃ sabhāvaniruttī”ti jānāti, “phassā”ti vā “phassa”nti vā vutte pana “ayaṃ asabhāvaniruttī”ti jānāti. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Aññaṃ panesa nāmākhyātaupasaggabyañjanasaddaṃ jānāti na jānātīti? Yadaggena saddaṃ jānitvā “ayaṃ sabhāvanirutti, ayaṃ asabhāvaniruttī”ti jānāti, tadaggena tampi jānissatīti. Taṃ pana “nayidaṃ paṭisambhidākicca”nti paṭikkhipitvā idaṃ vatthu kathitaṃ –

Thus this analytical knowledge of language arises with sound as its object, not with concept as its object. Why? Because upon hearing a sound, they know, 'This is natural expression.' One who has attained analytical knowledge, when 'contact' is said, knows, 'This is natural expression.' But when 'contacts' or 'contact' is said in other forms, they know, 'This is unnatural expression.' The same method applies to feeling and so forth. But does this person recognize other sounds like nouns, verbs, prefixes, and consonants? To the extent that one recognizes a sound and knows, 'This is natural expression, this is unnatural expression,' to that extent, one will also recognize those. However, rejecting the notion that 'this is not the function of analytical knowledge,' this subject matter has been explained.

Tissadattatthero kira bodhimaṇḍe suvaṇṇasalākaṃ gahetvā “aṭṭhārasasu bhāsāsu katarabhāsāya kathemī”ti pavāresi. Taṃ pana tena attano uggahe ṭhatvā pavāritaṃ, na paṭisambhidāya ṭhitena. So hi mahāpaññatāya [M 2.0349] taṃ taṃ bhāsaṃ kathāpetvā uggahetvā evaṃ pavāresi. “Bhāsaṃ nāma sattā uggaṇhantī”ti vatvā panettha idaṃ kathitaṃ. Mātāpitaro hi daharakāle kumārake mañce vā pīṭhe vā nipajjāpetvā taṃ taṃ kathayamānā tāni tāni kiccāni karonti. Dārakā tesaṃ taṃ taṃ bhāsaṃ vavatthāpenti “iminā idaṃ vutta”nti. Gacchante [V 2.0319] gacchante kāle sabbampi bhāsaṃ jānanti. Mātā damiḷī, pitā andhako. Tesaṃ jāto dārako sace mātukathaṃ paṭhamaṃ suṇāti, damiḷabhāsaṃ bhāsissati. Sace pitukathaṃ paṭhamaṃ suṇāti, andhakabhāsaṃ bhāsissati. Ubhinnampi pana kathaṃ assuṇanto māgadhabhāsaṃ bhāsissati. Yopi agāmake mahāaraññe nibbatto, tattha añño kathento nāma natthi. Sopi attano dhammatāya vacanaṃ samuṭṭhāpento, māgadhabhāsameva bhāsissati. Niraye, tiracchānayoniyaṃ, pettivisaye, manussaloke, devaloketi sabbattha māgadhabhāsāva ussannā, sesā oṭṭakirātaandhakayonakadamiḷabhāsādikā aṭṭhārasa bhāsā parivattanti, kālantarena aññathā honti ca nassanti ca.

It is said that the Elder Tissadatta, holding a golden stylus at the Bodhi-terrace, made an offer, saying, 'In which of the eighteen languages shall I speak?' However, he made that offer based on his own learning, not from the standpoint of analytical knowledge. Due to his great wisdom, he had learned those various languages and thus made such an offer. Here, it is said, 'Beings learn languages.' For instance, parents, when their children are young, lay them on a bed or a seat and, while speaking to them, perform their tasks. The children discern their speech, thinking, 'This was said by this person.' As time goes on, they come to know the entire language. If the mother is a Tamil and the father an Andhaka, the child born to them will speak the Tamil language if they first hear their mother’s speech, or the Andhaka language if they first hear their father’s speech. But if they hear the speech of neither, they will speak the Māgadhī language. Even one born in a great forest without villages, where there is no one else speaking, will, by their own nature, produce speech and speak the Māgadhī language. In hell, the animal realm, the sphere of ghosts, the human world, and the heavenly world—everywhere—the Māgadhī language is prevalent. The other eighteen languages, such as Oṭṭa, Kirāta, Andhaka, Yonaka, and Tamil, change, become different over time, and eventually perish.

Ayamevekā yathābhuccabrahmavohāraariyavohārasaṅkhātā māgadhabhāsā na parivattati. Sā hi katthaci kadāci parivattantīpi na sabbattha sabbadā sabbathāva parivattati, kappavināsepi tiṭṭhatiyeva. Sammāsambuddhopi hi tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ tantiṃ āropento māgadhabhāsāya eva āropesi. Kasmā? Evañhi āharituṃ sukhaṃ hoti. Māgadhabhāsāya hi tantiṃ āruḷhassa buddhavacanassa paṭisambhidāppattānaṃ sotapathāgamanameva papañco. Tena saṅghaṭitamatteneva nayasatena nayasahassena attho upaṭṭhāti. Aññāya bhāsāya tantiṃ āruḷhakaṃ sodhetvā uggahetabbaṃ hoti, bahumpi uggahetvā pana puthujjanassa paṭisambhidāppatti nāma natthi, ariyasāvako nopaṭisambhidāppatto nāma natthi.

This one Māgadhī language alone, known as the true speech, the speech of Brahmā, and the speech of the nobles, does not change. For though it may change somewhere at some time, it does not change everywhere, always, and in every way; it endures even at the destruction of the aeon. The Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha, too, when establishing the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, as the canon, established it in the Māgadhī language itself. Why? Because in this way it is easy to transmit. For those who have attained analytical knowledge, the Buddha's word established in the Māgadhī canon is a proliferation of meaning merely by its coming to the path of the ear. By that mere connection, the meaning presents itself through hundreds and thousands of methods. But that which is established in the canon in another language must be corrected and then learned. And even after learning much, there is no attainment of analytical knowledge for an ordinary person; and there is no noble disciple who has not attained analytical knowledge.

Paṭibhānappabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ paṭibhāne pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā. Atthadhammādivisayesu hi tīsu ñāṇesu “imāni ñāṇāni idamatthajotakānī”ti (vibha. 725-731) evaṃ pavattañāṇassetaṃ [M 2.0350] adhivacanaṃ. Imā pana catasso paṭisambhidā dvīsu ṭhānesu pabhedaṃ gacchanti, pañcahi kāraṇehi visadā hontīti veditabbā. Katamesu dvīsu? Sekkhabhūmiyañca asekkhabhūmiyañca, tattha sāriputtattherassa mahāmoggallānattherassa mahākassapattherassa mahākaccāyanattherassa mahākoṭṭhikattherassāti asītiyāpi mahātherānaṃ paṭisambhidā asekkhabhūmiyaṃ pabhedagatā. Ānandattherassa, cittassa gahapatino, dhammikassa upāsakassa, upālissa gahapatino, khujjuttarāya upāsikāyāti evamādīnaṃ paṭisambhidā sekkhabhūmiyaṃ pabhedagatāti imāsu dvīsu bhūmīsu pabhedaṃ gacchanti. Pabhedo nāma maggehi adhigatānaṃ paṭisambhidānaṃ pabhedagamanaṃ.

The knowledge concerning the divisions of perspicuity, capable of noting, distinguishing, and determining those divisions, is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity. For this is the designation for the knowledge that proceeds regarding the three preceding knowledges—concerning meaning, phenomena, and language—in this way: 'These knowledges illuminate this meaning.' Now, it should be understood that these four analytical knowledges are differentiated on two grounds and become clear through five causes. On which two grounds? On the ground of the trainees and the ground of the non-trainees. Therein, the analytical knowledge of the eighty great elders—such as the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita—is differentiated on the ground of the non-trainees. The analytical knowledge of the Venerable Ānanda, the householder Citta, the layman Dhammika, the householder Upāli, the laywoman Khujjuttarā, and others like them is differentiated on the ground of the trainees. Thus, they are differentiated on these two grounds. Differentiation here means the arising of differentiation in the analytical knowledges attained through the paths.

Katamehi pañcahi kāraṇehi paṭisambhidā visadā hontīti? Adhigamena, pariyattiyā, savanena[V 2.0320], paripucchāya, pubbayogena. Tattha adhigamo nāma arahattaṃ. Tañhi pattassa paṭisambhidā visadā honti. Savanaṃ nāma dhammassavanaṃ. Sakkaccaṃ suṇantassa hi paṭisambhidā visadā honti. Paripucchā nāma aṭṭhakathā. Uggahitapāḷiyā atthaṃ kathentassa hi paṭisambhidā visadā honti. Pubbayogo nāma pubbayogāvacaratā haraṇapaccāharaṇanayena parihaṭakammaṭṭhānatā. Pubbayogāvacarassa hi paṭisambhidā visadā honti.

By which five causes do the analytical knowledges become clear? By attainment, by learning, by listening, by inquiry, and by previous practice. Herein, 'attainment' means Arahantship; for one who has attained it, the analytical knowledges become clear. 'Listening' means listening to the Dhamma; for one who listens respectfully, the analytical knowledges become clear. 'Inquiry' means commentary; for one who explains the meaning of the Pāli they have learned, the analytical knowledges become clear. 'Previous practice' means being conversant with previous practice, which is the state of having practiced a meditation subject by the method of carrying forward and bringing back; for one who is conversant with previous practice, the analytical knowledges become clear.

Etesu pana pariyatti, savanaṃ, paripucchāti imāni tīṇi pabhedasseva balavakāraṇāni, pubbayogo adhigamassa balavapaccayo. Pabhedassa hoti na hotīti? Hoti, na pana yathā adhigamassa balavapaccayo hoti, tathā pabhedassa. Pariyattisavanaparipucchā hi pubbe hontu vā mā vā, pubbayogena pana pubbe ceva etarahi ca saṅkhārasammasanaṃ vinā paṭisambhidādhigamo nāma natthi. Ime pana dvepi ekato hutvā paṭisambhidā upatthambhetvā visadā hontīti.

Among these, learning, listening, and inquiry are the three strong causes for the differentiation. Previous practice is a strong condition for the attainment. Is previous practice a condition for the differentiation or not? It is, but it is not a strong condition for the differentiation in the same way that it is for the attainment. For whether learning, listening, and inquiry have occurred previously or not, without previous practice—that is, the contemplation of formations both in the past and now—there is no attainment of analytical knowledge. But these two groups of factors together support the analytical knowledges and make them clear.

Vibhattisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vibhatti Sutta is concluded.

3-4. Mahākoṭṭhikasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-4. Commentary on the Mahākoṭṭhika Sutta and Others

173-4. Tatiye [M 2.0351] phassāyatanānanti ettha ākaraṭṭho āyatanasaddoti āha “phassākarāna”ntiādi. “Suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ, rajatāyatana”ntiādīsu ākaropi “āyatana”nti vutto, sañjātisamosaraṇādivasenapi āyatanaṭṭho labbhatiyeva. Mā-iti paṭisedhe nipāto. Svāyaṃ channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ asesaṃ virāganirodhā atthaññaṃ vacanaṃ kiñcīti sandhāyāhāti āha “mā bhaṇīti attho”ti. Pañcaphassāyatanāni niruddhānīti cakkhādīnañca tattha abhāvaṃ sandhāya vadati. Chaṭṭhassāti manāyatanassa. Catutthe natthi vattabbaṃ.

173-4. In the third (section), regarding 'the sense-bases of contact,' the meaning of the word 'āyatana' as a source is stated, as in 'sources of contact' (phassākarānaṃ). In phrases like 'gold mine' (suvaṇṇāyatanaṃ) and 'silver mine' (rajatāyatanaṃ), even a mine is called 'āyatana,' and the meaning of 'āyatana' as a place of arising, coming together, etc., is indeed obtained. 'Mā' is a prohibitive particle. This statement, implying that there is nothing further to be said beyond the complete fading away and cessation of the six sense-bases of contact, is spoken with the intention, 'the meaning is "do not say".' When it is said, 'the five sense-bases of contact have ceased,' this refers to the absence of the eye and the others. The sixth refers to the mind-base. In the fourth (section), there is nothing to be said.

Mahākoṭṭhikasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mahākoṭṭhika Sutta and Others is concluded.

5-6. Upavāṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-6. Commentary on the Upavāṇa Sutta and Others.

175-6. Pañcame vijjāyāti dibbacakkhupubbenivāsānussatiāsavakkhayañāṇasaṅkhātāya tividhāya vijjāya, aṭṭhavidhāya vā. Aṭṭhavidhāpi hi vijjā vipassanāñāṇena manomayiddhiyā ca saha abhiññā pariggahetvā vuttā. Pannarasadhammabhedena caraṇena samannāgatoti sīlasaṃvaro, indriyesu [V 2.0321] guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, jāgariyānuyogo, saddhā, hirī, ottappaṃ, bāhusaccaṃ, vīriyaṃ, sati, paññā, cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānānīti evaṃ pannarasabhedena caraṇadhammena samannāgato. Imeyeva hi pannarasa dhammā yasmā etehi carati ariyasāvako gacchati amataṃ disaṃ, tasmā “caraṇa”nti vuttā. Chaṭṭhe natthi vattabbaṃ.

175-6. In the fifth (section), 'through knowledge' refers to the threefold knowledge—the divine eye, recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints—or the eightfold knowledge. For even the eightfold knowledge is stated as having been comprehended with the higher knowledges, including insight knowledge and the power of the mind-made body. 'Endowed with the fifteenfold conduct' means endowed with the fifteen kinds of conduct, namely: restraint in virtue, guarding the sense doors, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, faith, moral shame, moral dread, learning, energy, mindfulness, wisdom, and the four jhānas of the form realm. These fifteen qualities are called 'conduct' because the noble disciple, by means of them, fares on and goes to the deathless realm; therefore they are called 'conduct'. In the sixth (section), there is nothing to be said.

Upavāṇasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
