The commentary on the Upavāṇa Sutta and Others is concluded.

7. Rāhulasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Rāhula Sutta.

177. Sattame pathavīdhāturevesāti duvidhāpesā thaddhaṭṭhena, kakkhaḷaṭṭhena, pharusaṭṭhena ekalakkhaṇā pathavīdhātu evāti ajjhattikaṃ bāhirāya saddhiṃ yojetvā dasseti. Kasmā? Bāhirāya pathavīdhātuyā acetanābhāvo pākaṭo, na ajjhattikāya, tasmā bāhirāya saddhiṃ [M 2.0352] ekasadisā acetanāyevāti gaṇhantassa sukhapariggāhā hoti, yathā kiṃ? Dantena goṇena saddhiṃ yojito adanto katipāhameva visukāyati vipphandati, atha na cirasseva damathaṃ upeti, evaṃ ajjhattikaṃ bāhirāya saddhiṃ ekasadisāti gaṇhantassa katipāhameva acetanabhāvena upaṭṭhāti, atha na cirenevassā acetanabhāvo pākaṭo hoti dhātumattatāya dassanato. Netaṃ mama…pe… daṭṭhabbanti taṃ ubhayampi “na etaṃ mama, na esohamasmi, na eso me attā”ti evaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathābhūtanti yathāsabhāvaṃ. Tañhi aniccādisabhāvaṃ, tasmā aniccaṃ dukkhamanattāti evaṃ daṭṭhabbanti attho. Yasmā “netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā”ti passanto neva katthaci attānaṃ passati, na taṃ parassa kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ passati, na parassa attānaṃ attano kiñcanabhāve upanetabbaṃ passati, tasmā vuttaṃ “catukoṭikasuññatā nāma kathitā”ti.

177. In the seventh (section), 'the earth element itself' (pathavīdhāturevesāti) means that this earth element, though twofold, is of one characteristic by way of stiffness, hardness, and roughness. Thus, it is shown by combining the internal with the external. Why? Because the non-sentient nature of the external earth element is evident, but not that of the internal. Therefore, for one who grasps it as equally non-sentient like the external, comprehension becomes easy. For example, an untamed ox yoked with a tamed one struggles and resists for a few days, but soon submits to taming. Similarly, for one who considers the internal and external as alike, the non-sentient nature becomes apparent within a few days. Before long, its non-sentient nature becomes clear due to seeing it as merely an element. Regarding 'This is not mine... to be seen' (netaṃ mama... daṭṭhabbaṃ), both should be seen with right wisdom as they truly are: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' 'As they truly are' means according to their own nature. For indeed, their nature is impermanence and so forth; therefore, the meaning is that they should be seen as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Since one who sees thus—'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self'—does not see a self anywhere, nor does he see that (element) as belonging to another, nor does he see another's self as belonging to himself, therefore it is said: 'The fourfold emptiness is thus explained.'

Rāhulasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Rāhula Sutta is concluded.

8. Jambālīsuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Jambālī Sutta.

178. Aṭṭhame santanti aṅgasantatāya ceva ārammaṇasantatāya ca kamanīyaṃ manoharaṃ. Cetovimuttinti rūpārūpāvacaraṃ cittavimuttiṃ. Tenevāha “aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ aññataraṃ samāpatti”nti. Lepamakkhitenāti lākhāmakkhitena. Pāripanthike asodhetvāti kāmacchandādipāripanthike [V 2.0322] asodhetvā. Yo hi kāmādīnavapaccavekkhaṇādīhi kāmacchandaṃ na suṭṭhu vikkhambhetvā kāyappassaddhivasena duṭṭhullaṃ suppaṭippassaddhaṃ akatvā ārambhadhātumanasikārādivasena thinamiddhaṃ na suṭṭhu paṭivinodetvā samathanimittamanasikārādivasena uddhaccakukkuccaṃ na samūhataṃ katvā aññepi samādhiparipanthe dhamme na suṭṭhu sodhetvā jhānaṃ samāpajjati. So asodhitaṃ āsayaṃ paviṭṭhabhamaro viya asuddhaṃ uyyānaṃ paviṭṭharājā viya ca khippameva nikkhamati. Yo pana samādhiparipanthe dhamme suṭṭhu visodhetvā jhānaṃ samāpajjati, so suvisodhitaṃ āsayaṃ paviṭṭhabhamaro viya suparisuddhaṃ uyyānaṃ paviṭṭharājā viya ca sakalampi divasabhāgaṃ antosamāpattiyaṃyeva hoti.

178. In the eighth (section), 'pleasing' (santaṃ) means lovely and delightful by way of the continuity of the constituents (of jhāna) and the continuity of the object. 'Liberation of mind' (cetovimuttiṃ) refers to the liberation of mind pertaining to the form and formless realms. Therefore, it is said, 'one of the eight attainments.' 'Dyed with lac' (lepamakkhitena) means smeared with lac. 'Without purifying the obstacles' (pāripanthike asodhetvā) means without purifying the obstacles such as sensual desire and so forth. For one who, by reflecting on the drawbacks of sensual pleasures and so forth, does not thoroughly suppress sensual desire; who, by means of bodily tranquility, does not thoroughly pacify coarseness; who, by means of attention to the element of exertion and so forth, does not thoroughly dispel sloth and torpor; and who, by means of attention to the sign of serenity and so forth, does not eradicate restlessness and remorse—such a one, without thoroughly purifying other qualities that are obstacles to concentration, attains jhāna and quickly emerges from it, like a bee entering an unpurified hive or a king entering an impure garden. But one who thoroughly purifies the qualities that are obstacles to concentration before attaining jhāna remains in that attainment for the entire day, like a bee entering a well-purified hive or a king entering a perfectly clean garden.

Āyamukhānīti [M 2.0353] naditaḷākakandarapadarādito āgamanamaggā. Te ca kandarāyevāti āha “catasso pavisanakandarā”ti. Apāyamukhānīti apagamanamaggā. Apenti apagacchanti etehīti hi apāyā, te eva mukhānīti apāyamukhāni. Tāni ca udakanikkhamanacchiddānīti āha “apavāhanacchiddānī”ti, apāyasaṅkhātāni udakanikkhamanacchiddānīti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

'Entrances' (āyamukhāni) are the paths of arrival, such as from rivers, lakes, caves, and mountain clefts. And those are indeed the caves, as it is said, 'four entrance caves.' 'Exits' (apāyamukhāni) are the paths of departure. For they lead away, they depart by these—hence, 'apāyā'; these very openings are the 'apāyamukhāni.' And those are the holes for water drainage, as it is said, 'drainage holes' (apavāhanacchiddāni), meaning the holes for water drainage designated as 'apāyā.' The rest is easily understood.

Jambālīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Jambālī Sutta is concluded.

9. Nibbānasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Nibbāna Sutta.

179. Navame abhidhamme vuttanayenāti –

179. In the ninth (section), according to the method stated in the Abhidhamma—

“Katamā hānabhāginī paññā? Paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhiṃ kāmasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti hānabhāginī paññā, tadanudhammatā sati santiṭṭhati ṭhitibhāginī paññā. Avitakkasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti visesabhāginī paññā. Nibbidāsahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti virāgūpasañhitā nibbedhabhāginī paññā”ti (vibha. 799) –

"What wisdom is liable to decline? For one who has attained the first jhāna, perceptions and attention connected with sensual things arise—this is wisdom liable to decline. Mindfulness in accordance with that abides, stands firm—this is wisdom conducive to stability. Perceptions and attention connected with the absence of initial thought arise—this is wisdom conducive to distinction. Perceptions and attention connected with disenchantment arise—this is wisdom conducive to penetration, imbued with dispassion." (Vibhaṅga 799)

Ādinā vibhaṅge vuttanayena evamattho veditabbo.

The meaning should be understood thus, by the method stated in the Vibhaṅga, as cited.

Tattha paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhinti yvāyaṃ appaguṇassa paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī, taṃ. Kāmasahagatā [V 2.0323] saññāmanasikārā samudācarantīti tato vuṭṭhitaṃ ārammaṇavasena kāmasahagatā hutvā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti tudanti codenti. Tassa kāmānupakkhandānaṃ saññāmanasikārānaṃ vasena sā paṭhamajjhānapaññā hāyati parihāyati, tasmā “hānabhāginī paññā”ti vuttā. Tadanudhammatāti tadanurūpasabhāvā. Sati santiṭṭhatīti idaṃ micchāsatiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na sammāsatiṃ. Yassa hi paṭhamajjhānānurūpasabhāvā paṭhamajjhānaṃ santato paṇītato disvā assādayamānā abhinandamānā nikanti uppajjati, tassa nikantivasena paṭhamajjhānapaññā neva hāyati na vaḍḍhati, ṭhitikoṭṭhāsikā hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “ṭhitibhāginī paññā”ti. Avitakkasahagatāti avitakkaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ [M 2.0354] santato paṇītato manasikaroto ārammaṇavasena avitakkasahagatā saññāmanasikārā. Samudācarantīti paguṇato paṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhitaṃ dutiyajjhānādhigamatthāya tudanti codenti, tassa upari dutiyajjhānānupakkhandānaṃ saññāmanasikārānaṃ vasena sā paṭhamajjhānapaññā visesabhūtassa dutiyajjhānassa uppattipadaṭṭhānatāya “visesabhāginī”ti vuttā.

Herein, regarding 'one who attains the first jhāna': this refers to one who is a gainer of the first jhāna of lesser quality. 'Perceptions and attention connected with sensuality arise' means that, having emerged from that jhāna, perceptions and attention connected with sensuality arise by way of the object, prodding and urging one. By means of these perceptions and attention that incline toward sensuality, that wisdom of the first jhāna declines and deteriorates; therefore, it is called 'wisdom partaking of decline.' 'Conforming to that' means having a nature in accordance with that. 'Mindfulness is established' refers to wrong mindfulness, not right mindfulness. For one in whom, having a nature in accordance with the first jhāna, seeing the first jhāna as peaceful and sublime, delighting in it, and rejoicing in it, craving arises—for such a one, by means of that craving, the wisdom of the first jhāna neither declines nor increases but becomes stagnant. Therefore, it is called 'wisdom partaking of stagnation.' 'Accompanied by what is without thought' means that for one who attends to the second jhāna, which is without thought, as peaceful and sublime, perceptions and attention accompanied by what is without thought arise by way of the object. 'They arise' means that, having emerged from the proficient first jhāna, they prod and urge one for the attainment of the second jhāna. By means of these perceptions and attention that incline toward the higher second jhāna, that wisdom of the first jhāna, being the basis for the arising of the superior second jhāna, is called 'wisdom partaking of distinction.'

Nibbidāsahagatāti taṃyeva paṭhamajjhānalābhiṃ jhānato vuṭṭhitaṃ nibbidāsaṅkhātena vipassanāñāṇena sahagatā. Vipassanāñāṇañhi jhānaṅgabhede vattante nibbindati ukkaṇṭhati, tasmā “nibbidā”ti vuccati. Samudācarantīti nibbānasacchikiriyatthāya tudanti codenti. Virāgūpasañhitāti virāgasaṅkhātena nibbānena upasaṃhitā. Vipassanāñāṇañhi sakkā iminā maggena virāgaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikātunti pavattito “virāgūpasaṃhita”nti vuccati. Taṃsampayuttasaññāmanasikārāpi virāgūpasaṃhitā eva nāma. Tassa tesaṃ saññāmanasikārānaṃ vasena sā paṭhamajjhānapaññā ariyamaggappaṭivedhassa padaṭṭhānatāya “nibbedhabhāginī”ti vuttāti.

'Accompanied by disenchantment': For that very same attainer of the first jhāna, having emerged from that jhāna, perceptions and attention arise accompanied by insight-knowledge, which is known as disenchantment. For insight-knowledge, while occurring with the analysis of the jhāna factors, becomes disenchanted and averse; therefore, it is called 'disenchantment.' 'They arise' means they prod and urge one for the sake of realizing Nibbāna. 'Connected with dispassion': They are connected with Nibbāna, which is known as dispassion. For insight-knowledge, because it proceeds with the thought, 'It is possible by this path to realize dispassion, Nibbāna,' it is called 'connected with dispassion.' The perceptions and attention associated with it are also indeed named 'connected with dispassion.' By means of those perceptions and attention, that wisdom of the first jhāna, being the basis for the penetration of the noble path, is called 'wisdom partaking of penetration.'

Nibbānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nibbāna Sutta is concluded.

10. Mahāpadesasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Mahāpadesa Sutta.

180. Dasame mahāokāseti mahante okāse mahantāni dhammassa patiṭṭhāpanaṭṭhānāni. Yesu patiṭṭhāpito dhammo nicchīyati asandehato. Kāni pana tāni? Āgamanavisiṭṭhāni suttotaraṇādīni. Dutiyavikappe apadisīyantīti apadesā, mahantā apadesā etesanti mahāpadesā. “Sammukhā metaṃ, āvuso, bhagavato suta”ntiādinā kenaci ābhatassa dhammoti vinicchayane kāraṇaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti? Tassa yathābhatassa suttotaraṇādi eva. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ [V 2.0324] cattāroti? Yasmā dhammassa dve sampadāyo satthā sāvako ca. Tesu sāvakā saṅghagaṇapuggalavasena tividhā. Evamimamhā mayāyaṃ dhammo paṭiggahitoti apadisitabbānaṃ bhedena cattāro. Tenāha [M 2.0355] “sammukhā metaṃ, āvuso, bhagavato suta”ntiādi. Tathā ca vuttaṃ nettiyaṃ (netti. 4.18) “cattāro mahāpadesā buddhāpadeso, saṅghāpadeso, gaṇāpadeso, puggalāpadeso. Ime cattāro mahāpadesā”ti. Buddho apadeso etassāti buddhāpadeso. Esa nayo sesesupi. Tenāha “buddhādayo…pe… mahākāraṇānī”ti.

180. In the tenth, 'in a great instance' (`mahāokāse`) means in a great place, great grounds for the establishment of the Dhamma. When the Dhamma is established upon these, it is determined without doubt. What are they? They are the eminent traditions of checking against the Sutta and so on. In the second alternative, because they are referred to, they are 'references' (`apadesā`); great are their references, thus they are 'great references' (`mahāpadesā`). The phrase 'Friend, I have heard this from the Blessed One's own lips,' and so on, is the reason for determining the Dhamma that has been brought forward by someone. But what is that reason? It is precisely the checking against the Sutta and so on of what was brought forward. If so, how are there four? Because there are two lines of transmission for the Dhamma: the Teacher and the disciple. Among them, the disciples are threefold: the Saṅgha, a group, and an individual. Thus, by the distinction of those who are to be cited with 'This Dhamma was received by me from so-and-so,' there are four. Therefore, he said, 'Friend, I have heard this from the Blessed One's own lips,' and so on. And so it is said in the Netti: 'There are four great references: the Buddha-reference, the Saṅgha-reference, the group-reference, and the individual-reference. These are the four great references.' 'The Buddha is the reference for this,' thus it is a 'Buddha-reference.' This is the method for the rest as well. Therefore, he said, 'The Buddha and others... and so on... are the great reasons.'

Neva abhinanditabbanti na sampaṭicchitabbaṃ, ganthassa sampaṭicchanaṃ nāma savananti āha “na sotabba”nti. Padabyañjanānīti padāni ca byañjanāni ca, atthapadāni byañjanapadāni cāti attho. Pajjati attho etehīti padāni, akkharādīni byañjanapadāni. Pajjitabbato padāni, saṅkāsanādīni atthapadāni. “Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ padasaṅkhātāni byañjanānīti byañjanapadāneva vuttānī”ti keci. Atthaṃ byañjentīti byañjanāni, byañjanapadāni. Tehi byañjitabbato byañjanāni, atthapadānīti ubhayasaṅgahato. Imasmiṃ ṭhāneti tenābhatasuttassa imasmiṃ padese. Pāḷi vuttāti kevalo pāḷidhammo vutto. Attho vuttoti pāḷiyā attho vutto niddiṭṭho. Anusandhi kathitoti yathāraddhadesanāya uparidesanāya ca anusandhānaṃ kathitaṃ, sambandho kathito. Pubbāparaṃ kathitanti pubbena paraṃ avirujjhanañceva visesaṭṭhānañca kathitaṃ pakāsitaṃ. Evaṃ pāḷidhammādīni sammadeva sallakkhetvā gahaṇaṃ sādhukaṃ uggahaṇanti āha “suṭṭhu gahetvā”ti. Sutte otāretabbānīti ñāṇena sutte ogāhetvā tāretabbāni. Taṃ pana ogāhetvā taraṇaṃ tattha otaraṇaṃ anuppavesanaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ “otaritabbānī”ti. Saṃsandetvā dassanaṃ sandassananti āha “vinaye saṃsandetabbānī”ti.

'Should not be delighted in' means should not be accepted. Since accepting a text is called listening, he said, 'should not be listened to.' 'Words and phrasing' means words and phrasing; the meaning is words of meaning and words of phrasing. 'Meaning is attained through them,' thus they are 'words' (`padāni`); letters and so on are words of phrasing. 'Because they are to be attained,' they are 'words'; elucidations and so on are words of meaning. Some say, 'In the commentary, what are counted as words are the phrasing, thus only words of phrasing are meant.' 'They make the meaning clear,' thus they are 'phrasing' (`byañjanāni`), i.e., words of phrasing. 'Because it is to be made clear by them,' it is 'phrasing,' i.e., words of meaning—thus both are included. 'In this place' means in this part of the Sutta brought by him. 'The Pāḷi is stated' means the mere Pāḷi text is stated. 'The meaning is stated' means the meaning of the Pāḷi is stated, pointed out. 'The connection is told' means the connection with the preceding and subsequent teaching is told; the relation is told. 'The sequence is told' means that the latter does not contradict the former, and also the special points, are told and made clear. 'Thus, having correctly noted the Pāḷi text and so on, the grasping is a good grasping,' thus he said, 'having grasped it well.' 'Should be checked against the Sutta' means they should be immersed in the Sutta by means of knowledge and verified. That immersing and verifying is an entering into, a penetration; thus it is said, 'should be checked against.' 'Showing by comparing is comparison,' thus he said, 'should be compared with the Vinaya.'

“Kiṃ pana taṃ suttaṃ, ko vā vinayo”ti vicāraṇāyaṃ ācariyānaṃ matibhedamukhena tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “ettha cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Vinayoti vibhaṅgapāṭhamāha. So hi mātikāsaññitassa suttassa atthe sūcanato “sutta”nti vattabbataṃ arahati. Vividhanayattā visiṭṭhanayattā ca vinayo, khandhakapāṭho. Evanti evaṃ suttavinayesu pariggayhamānesu vinayapiṭakampi na pariyādiyati parivārapāḷiyā asaṅgahitattā. Suttantābhidhammapiṭakāni vā suttaṃ atthasūcanādiatthasambhavato. Evampīti suttantābhidhammapiṭakāni suttaṃ, vinayapiṭakaṃ vinayoti evaṃ suttavinayavibhāge vuccamānepi. Na tāva pariyādiyantīti na tāva anavasesato pariggayhanti[M 2.0356]. Kasmāti ceti āha “asuttanāmakañhī”tiādi. Yasmā suttanti imaṃ nāmaṃ anāropetvā saṅgītaṃ jātakādibuddhavacanaṃ atthi, tasmā vuttanayena tīṇi piṭakāni [V 2.0325] na pariyādiyantīti. Suttanipātaudānaitivuttakāni dīghanikāyādayo viya suttanti nāmaṃ āropetvā asaṅgītānīti adhippāyenettha jātakādīhi saddhiṃ tānipi gahitāni. Buddhavaṃsacariyāpiṭakānaṃ panettha aggahaṇe kāraṇaṃ maggitabbaṃ, kiṃ vā etena magganena. Sabbopāyaṃ vaṇṇanānayo theravādadassanamukhena paṭikkhitto evāti.

'What then is that Sutta, or what is the Vinaya?' In this inquiry, to show the meaning of that through the various opinions of the teachers, 'And here...' and so on was said. By 'Vinaya,' he means the text of the Vibhaṅga. For it, by indicating the meaning of the Sutta designated as the Mātikā, deserves to be called 'Sutta.' Because of its various and specific methods, the Vinaya is the text of the Khandhakas. In this way, when the Sutta and Vinaya are being defined, the Vinaya Piṭaka is not completely included, because the Parivāra text is not included. Or, the Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are the 'Sutta,' because of the possibility of meanings such as the indication of meaning. Even so—even when the division of Sutta and Vinaya is stated thus, that the Suttanta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas are 'Sutta' and the Vinaya Piṭaka is 'Vinaya'—they are still not completely included. Why is that? He says, 'For there is that which is not named Sutta,' and so on. Because there is the word of the Buddha, such as the Jātakas, that was recited without being given the name 'Sutta,' therefore, in the way stated, the three Piṭakas are not completely included. With the intention that the Suttanipāta, Udāna, and Itivuttaka were not recited having been given the name 'Sutta' in the same way as the Dīgha Nikāya and so on, they too are included here along with the Jātakas and so on. The reason for the non-inclusion here of the Buddhavaṃsa and Cariyāpiṭaka should be sought. But what is the use of this seeking? Every method of explanation is indeed rejected from the viewpoint of the Theravāda.

Kiṃ atthīti asuttanāmakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ natthiyevāti dasseti. Taṃ sabbaṃ paṭikkhipitvāti “suttanti vinayo”tiādinā vuttasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ “nāyamattho idhādhippeto”ti paṭisedhetvā. Vineti etena kileseti vinayo, kilesavinayanūpāyo, so eva kāraṇanti āha “vinayo pana kāraṇa”nti.

What is this? It indicates that there is no such thing as a Buddha's word called 'asutta' at all. Having rejected all that: having refuted in the commentary on the statement beginning 'sutta means Vinaya' with the words, 'This meaning is not intended here.' It tames defilements by this, thus it is Vinaya; it is a means for subduing defilements, and that very fact is the reason. Thus he said, 'but Vinaya is the cause.'

Dhammeti pariyattidhamme. Sarāgāyāti sarāgabhāvāya kāmarāgabhavarāgaparibrūhanāya. Saṃyogāyāti bhavasaṃyojanāya. Saupādānāyāti caturūpādānūpasaṃhitatāya. Mahicchatāyāti mahicchabhāvāya. Asantuṭṭhiyāti asantuṭṭhabhāvāya. Kosajjāyāti kusītabhāvāya. Saṅgaṇikāyāti kilesasaṅgaṇikavihārāya. Ācayāyāti tividhavaṭṭācayāya. Virāgāyāti sakalavaṭṭato virajjanatthāya. Visaṃyogāyāti kāmarāgādīhi visaṃyujjanatthāya. Anupādānāyāti sabbassapi kammabhavassa aggahaṇāya. Appicchatāyāti paccayappicchatādivasena sabbaso icchāya apagamāya. Santuṭṭhiyāti dvādasavidhasantuṭṭhabhāvāya. Vīriyārambhāyāti kāyikassa ceva cetasikassa ca vīriyassa paggaṇhanatthāya. Vivekāyāti pavivittabhāvāya kāmavivekāditadaṅgavivekādivivekasiddhiyā. Apacayāyāti sabbassapi vaṭṭassa apacayanāya, nibbānāyāti attho. Evaṃ yo pariyattidhammo uggahaṇadhāraṇaparipucchāmanasikāravasena yoniso paṭipajjantassa sarāgādibhāvaparivajjanassa kāraṇaṃ hutvā virāgādibhāvāya saṃvattati, ekaṃsato eso dhammo, eso vinayo sammadeva apāyādīsu apatanavasena dhāraṇato kilesānaṃ vinayanato ca. Satthu sammāsambuddhassa ovādānurūpappavattibhāvato etaṃ satthusāsananti ca jāneyyāsīti attho.

'Dhamma' means the Dhamma of learning. 'For passion' means for the state of passion, for the increase of sensual passion and passion for becoming. 'For bondage' means for the fetter of becoming. 'For grasping' means for being associated with the four clingings. 'For great desire' means for the state of great desire. 'For discontent' means for the state of discontent. 'For laziness' means for the state of laziness. 'For socializing' means for dwelling in the company of defilements. 'For accumulation' means for the threefold accumulation of the round of existence. 'For dispassion' means for the purpose of detachment from the entire round of existence. 'For release' means for the purpose of being freed from sensual passion and so on. 'For non-grasping' means for not clinging to any kamma-becoming. 'For fewness of wishes' means for the complete abandonment of desire, by way of fewness of wishes regarding requisites and so on. 'For contentment' means for the state of twelvefold contentment. 'For exertion' means for the purpose of arousing bodily and mental energy. 'For seclusion' means for the state of solitude, for the achievement of seclusion by way of seclusion from sensual pleasures, temporary suppression, and so on. 'For reduction' means for the reduction of the entire round of existence, which means Nibbāna. Thus, the Dhamma of learning, when properly practiced by one who engages in learning, retaining, questioning, and wise attention, becomes a cause for avoiding states like passion and leads to states like dispassion. Unquestionably, this is the Dhamma, this is the Discipline, rightly so, because it upholds by preventing one from falling into states of misery, and because it subdues defilements. Since it accords with the guidance of the Teacher, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, one should understand this as the teaching of the Teacher—this is the meaning.

Catusaccatthasūcanaṃ [M 2.0357] suttanti āha “sutteti tepiṭake buddhavacane”ti. Tepiṭakañhi buddhavacanaṃ saccavinimuttaṃ natthi. Rāgādivinayakāraṇaṃ yathā tena suttapadena pakāsitanti āha “vinayeti etasmiṃ rāgādivinayakāraṇe”ti. Sutte otaraṇañcettha tepiṭakabuddhavacanapariyāpannatāvaseneva veditabbaṃ, na aññathāti āha “suttappaṭipāṭiyā katthaci anāgantvā”ti. Challiṃ uṭṭhapetvāti arogassa mahato rukkhassa tiṭṭhato upakkamena challikāya sakalikāya papaṭikāya vā uṭṭhāpanaṃ viya arogassa sāsanadhammassa tiṭṭhato byañjanamattena tappariyāpannaṃ [V 2.0326] viya hutvā challisadisaṃ pubbāparaviruddhatādidosaṃ uṭṭhapetvā paridīpetvā. Tādisāni pana ekaṃsato guḷhavessantarādipariyāpannāni hontīti āha “guḷhavessantara…pe… paññāyantīti attho”ti. Rāgādivinayeti rāgādivinayanatthena atadākāratāya apaññāyamānāni chaḍḍetabbāni cajitabbāni na gahetabbāni. Sabbatthāti sabbavāresu.

The sutta is an indicator of the meaning of the Four Truths, thus it is said, 'Sutta means the Buddha’s word in the Tipiṭaka.' Indeed, the Buddha’s word in the Tipiṭaka is not devoid of the truths. The cause for subduing lust and so on is revealed by that sutta passage, thus it is said, 'Vinaya means this cause for subduing lust and so on.' Here, inclusion in the sutta should be understood only by way of being comprised within the Buddha’s word in the Tipiṭaka, not otherwise. Thus, it is said, 'without appearing anywhere in the sequence of the sutta.' 'Having raised up a splinter' is like raising up a splinter, a chip, or a piece of bark from a large, healthy, standing tree by effort. Similarly, while the teaching of the Dhamma stands unharmed, by a mere expression, becoming as if comprised within it, one raises up and illuminates faults similar to splinters—such as contradictions between earlier and later parts. But such things are entirely comprised under categories like the 'Guḷha Vessantara,' etc. Thus, it is said, 'The Guḷha Vessantara… are understood'—this is the meaning. Regarding 'subduing lust and so on': those things which, by the meaning of subduing lust and so on, are not understood as having that nature, should be discarded, abandoned, and not taken up. 'Everywhere' means in all cases.

Mahāpadesasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mahāpadesa Sutta is concluded.

Sañcetaniyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sañcetaniya Vagga is concluded.

(19) 4. Brāhmaṇavaggo

(19) 4. The Brahmin Chapter

1-3. Yodhājīvasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-3. Commentary on the Yodhājīva Sutta and others.

181-183. Catutthassa paṭhamādīni uttānatthāneva.

181-183. The first suttas of the fourth chapter have a plain meaning.

4. Abhayasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Abhaya Sutta

184. Catutthe socatīti citte uppannabalavasokena socati, cittasantāpena anto nijjhāyatīti attho. Kilamatīti tasseva sokassa vasena kāye ca uppannadukkhena kilamati. Paridevatīti sokuddehakavasena taṃ taṃ vippalapanto vācāya paridevati. Urattāḷinti urattāḷaṃ, uraṃ tāḷetvāti attho. Tenāha “uraṃ tāḷetvā”ti. Kaṅkhāvicikicchāti ettha “ekamevidaṃ pañcamaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ. Kiṃ nu kho ida”nti [M 2.0358] ārammaṇaṃ kaṅkhanato kaṅkhā, “idameva vara”nti nicchetuṃ asamatthabhāvato “vicikicchā”ti vuccati – “dhammasabhāvaṃ vicinanto kicchati, vigatā cikicchā”ti vā katvā.

184. In the fourth, 'he grieves' (socati) means he grieves due to the powerful sorrow arising in the mind, inwardly tormented by mental agitation—this is the meaning. 'He is wearied' (kilamati) means he is wearied by the suffering that arises in the body due to that grief. 'He laments' (paridevati) means he wails with words, rambling on about this and that by way of expressing sorrow. 'He beats his breast' (urattāḷi) means breast-beating, that is, striking the breast—this is the meaning. Therefore it is said, 'having struck the breast.' Regarding 'doubt and uncertainty' (kaṅkhāvicikicchā): here, doubt (kaṅkhā) is from doubting the object, thinking, 'Is this just the fifth hindrance? What is this?' Uncertainty (vicikicchā) is so called because of the inability to decisively conclude, 'This alone is the best.' Alternatively, it is said, 'one struggles (kicchati) while investigating the nature of phenomena,' or 'it is the absence of a remedy (vigatā cikicchā).'

Abhayasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Abhaya Sutta is concluded.

5. Brāhmaṇasaccasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Brāhmaṇasacca Sutta

185. Pañcame [V 2.0327] etthāti etasmiṃ suññatānupassanādhikāre. Kvacīti katthaci ṭhāne, kāle, dhamme vā. Atha vā kvacīti ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā vā. Attano attānanti sakattānaṃ “ayaṃ kho, bho brahmā, mahābrahmā…pe… vasī pitā bhūtabhabyāna”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 1.42) parehi parikappitaṃ attānañca kassaci kiñcanabhūtaṃ na passatīti dassento “kassacī”tiādimāha. Tattha parassāti parajāti paro purisoti vā evaṃ gahitassa. Na ca mama kvacanīti ettha mama-saddo aṭṭhānappayuttoti āha “mama-saddaṃ tāva ṭhapetvā”ti. Parassa cāti attano aññassa. Paro puriso nāma atthi mamatthāya ṭhito. Tassa vasena mayhaṃ sabbaṃ ijjhatīti ekaccadiṭṭhigatikaparikappitavasena paraṃ attānaṃ tañca attano kiñcanabhūtaṃ na passatīti dassento “na ca kvacanī”tiādimāha. Ettha ca nāhaṃ kvacanīti sakaattano sabbhāvaṃ na passati. Na kassaci kiñcanatasminti sakaattano eva kassaci attaniyataṃ na passati. Na ca mamāti etaṃ dvayaṃ yathārahaṃ sambandhitabbaṃ, atthi-padaṃ paccekaṃ. Na ca kvacani parassa attā atthīti parassa attano abhāvaṃ passati. Tassa parassa attano mama kiñcanatā natthīti parassa attano anattaniyataṃ passati. Evaṃ ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā khandhānaṃ attattaniyasuññatā-suddhasaṅkhārapuñjatā-catukoṭikasuññatāpariggaṇhanena niṭṭhā hoti. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

185. In the fifth, 'here' refers to this section on the contemplation of emptiness. 'Somewhere' means in some place, time, or phenomenon. Alternatively, 'somewhere' means internally or externally. 'One’s own self' means one’s own self. Showing that one does not see one’s own self, nor the self conceived by others (as in, 'This, venerable sir, is Brahmā, the Great Brahmā… sovereign, father of beings past and future,' etc. (Dī. Ni. 1.42)), nor anything belonging to anyone, he says 'of anyone' and so on. Here, 'another’s' means of one thus grasped as belonging to another species or another person. Regarding 'nor is mine anywhere,' the word 'mine' is used in an inappropriate place, as stated: 'First, set aside the word ‘mine.’' 'And another’s' means of someone other than oneself. Showing that one does not see another self, nor anything belonging to oneself, by way of the conception of some speculative thinkers who think, 'There is another person who stands for my sake. Through his agency, everything succeeds for me,' he says 'nor anywhere' and so on. Here, 'I am not anywhere' means not seeing the inherent existence of one’s own self. 'I am not a something of anyone' means not seeing one’s own self as belonging to anyone. And 'nor mine'—these two phrases should be connected appropriately, with the word 'is' understood separately for each. 'Nor is there anywhere a self of another' means seeing the non-existence of another’s self. 'That other’s self is not a something of mine' means seeing that another's self does not belong to oneself. Thus, internally and externally, the culmination is reached by comprehending the emptiness of the aggregates regarding self and what belongs to self, their nature as a mere heap of formations, and the four-aspected emptiness. The rest here is easily understood.

Brāhmaṇasaccasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Brāhmaṇasacca Sutta is concluded.

6. Ummaggasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Ummagga Sutta

186. Chaṭṭhe [M 2.0359] ākaḍḍhīyatīti cittavasiko loko tattha tattha upakaḍḍhīyati. Tesaṃyevettha gahaṇaṃ veditabbanti ye apariññātavatthukā cittassa vasaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ. Na hi pariññātakkhandhā pahīnakilesā cittassa vasaṃ gacchanti, cittaṃ pana attano vase vattenti. Saha sīlenāti cārittavārittasīlena saddhiṃ. Pubbabhāgapaṭipadanti dhutaṅgamādiṃ katvā yāva gotrabhuñāṇaṃ, tāva pavattetabbaṃ samathavipassanāsaṅkhātaṃ sammāpaṭipadaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

186. In the sixth, 'is dragged along' means the world, being under the sway of the mind, is pulled here and there. Here, it is the inclusion of those that is to be understood, namely, those whose subject matter is not fully understood and who come under the mind's control. For those who have fully understood the aggregates and abandoned defilements do not come under the mind's control; rather, they bring the mind under their own control. 'Together with virtue' means along with the virtue of conduct and restraint. 'The preliminary practice' refers to the right practice, consisting of serenity and insight, to be developed from the ascetic practices and so forth up to the knowledge of change-of-lineage. The rest is easily understood.

Ummaggasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ummagga Sutta is concluded.

7. Vassakārasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta

187. Sattame [V 2.0328] vassakāro brāhmaṇo magadhamahāmattoti ettha vassakāroti tassa brāhmaṇassa nāmaṃ. Mahatiyā issariyamattāya samannāgato mahāmatto. Issariyamattāyāti ca issariyappamāṇenāti attho, issariyena ceva vittūpakaraṇena cāti evaṃ vā ettha attho daṭṭhabbo, upabhogūpakaraṇānipi hi loke “mattā”ti vuccanti. Magadharañño, magadharaṭṭhe vā mahāmattoti magadhamahāmatto. Tudisaññito gāmo nivāso etassāti todeyyo. Tenevāha “tudigāmavāsikassā”ti. Tudigāmavāsitā cassa tattha adhipatibhāvenāti daṭṭhabbā. So hi taṃ gāmaṃ soṇadaṇḍo viya, campaṃ kūṭadanto viya, khāṇumataṃ adhipatibhāvena ajjhāvasati. Mahaddhano hoti pañcacattālīsakoṭivibhavo. Parisatīti parisāyaṃ, janasamūheti attho. Tenāha “sannipatitāya parisāyā”ti. Abhippasannoti ettha abhikkamanattho abhi-saddoti āha “atikkamma pasanno”ti, pasādanīyaṃ ṭhānaṃ atikkamitvā appasādanīyaṭṭhāne pasannoti adhippāyo. Taṃ taṃ kiccaṃ atthaṃ passatīti atthadasā, alaṃ samatthā paṭibalā atthadasā alamatthadasā, alamatthadase atisayantīti alamatthadasatarā. Tenāha “atthe passituṃ samatthā”tiādi. Neva sappurisaṃ na asappurisaṃ jānāti sappurisadhammānaṃ asappurisadhammānañca [M 2.0360] yāthāvato ajānanato. Sesamettha uttānameva.

187. In the seventh section, regarding 'Vassakāra, the Brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha': here, 'Vassakāra' is the name of that Brahmin. He is a chief minister, one endowed with a great measure of power. 'With a great measure of power' means 'by the measure of power'; or, alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as 'with both power and the instruments of wealth,' for in the world, the instruments of enjoyment are also called 'measure.' He is the chief minister of the king of Magadha, or the chief minister in the kingdom of Magadha, hence 'chief minister of Magadha.' 'Todeyya' means one whose dwelling is the village named Tudi. Therefore, it is said, 'of the resident of Tudi village.' And his residence in Tudi village should be understood as being due to his lordship there. For he dwells in that village, exercising lordship, just as Soṇadaṇḍa did over Campā, and Kūṭadanta over Khāṇumata. He is very wealthy, possessing a fortune of forty-five crores. 'In the assembly' (parisati) means in a gathering of people. Therefore, it is said, 'in the assembled gathering.' In 'highly pleased' (abhippasanno), the prefix 'abhi-' has the meaning of 'exceeding'; thus, it is said, 'exceedingly pleased.' The intention is that he is pleased even in a situation not conducive to pleasure, having gone beyond a situation that is conducive to pleasure. 'Atthadasā' are those who see the purpose in this or that matter. 'Alamatthadasā' are those who are adequate, competent, and capable of seeing the purpose. 'Alamatthadasatarā' are those who surpass the alamatthadasā. Therefore, it is said, 'capable of seeing the purpose,' and so forth. He does not know a virtuous person or an unvirtuous person, due to not knowing in accordance with reality the qualities of virtuous people and the qualities of unvirtuous people. The rest here is self-evident.

Vassakārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vassakāra Sutta is concluded.

8. Upakasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Upaka Sutta

188. Aṭṭhame nibbattivasena nirayaṃ arahati, nirayasaṃvattaniyena vā kammunā niraye niyuttoti nerayiko. Avīcimhi uppajjitvā tattha āyukappasaññitaṃ antarakappaṃ tiṭṭhatīti kappaṭṭho. Nirayūpapattiṃ pariharaṇavasena tikicchituṃ asakkuṇeyyoti atekiccho. Apariyādinnāvāti aparikkhīṇāyeva. Sace hi eko bhikkhu kāyānupassanaṃ pucchati, añño vedanānupassanaṃ…pe… cittānupassanaṃ. “Iminā puṭṭhe ahaṃ pucchāmī”ti eko ekaṃ na oloketi, evaṃ santepi tesaṃ vāro paññāyati eva, buddhānaṃ pana vāro na paññāyati. Vidatthicaturaṅgulaṃ chāyaṃ atikkamanato puretaraṃyeva bhagavā cuddasavidhena kāyānupassanaṃ, navavidhena vedanānupassanaṃ, soḷasavidhena cittānupassanaṃ, pañcavidhena dhammānupassanaṃ katheti. Tiṭṭhantu vā evaṃ cattāro. Sace hi aññe cattāro sammappadhānesu, aññe iddhipādesu, aññe pañcindriyesu[V 2.0329], aññe pañcabalesu, aññe sattabojjhaṅgesu, aññe aṭṭhamaggaṅgesu pañhe puccheyyuṃ, tampi bhagavā katheyya. Tiṭṭhantu vā ete aṭṭha. Sace aññe sattatiṃsa janā bodhipakkhiyesu pañhe puccheyyuṃ, tampi bhagavā tāvadeva katheyya. Kasmā? Yāvatā hi lokiyamahājane ekaṃ padaṃ kathente tāva ānandatthero aṭṭha padāni katheti. Ānandatthere pana ekaṃ padaṃ kathenteyeva bhagavā soḷasa padāni katheti. Kasmā? Bhagavato hi jivhā mudu, dantāvaraṇaṃ suphusitaṃ, vacanaṃ agaḷitaṃ, bhavaṅgaparivāso lahuko. Tena vuttaṃ – “apariyādinnāvassa tathāgatassa dhammadesanā, apariyādinnaṃ dhammapadabyañjana”nti.

188. In the eighth section, one is called a 'hell-dweller' (nerayiko) because they deserve hell by way of being reborn there, or because they are bound to hell by kamma that leads to hell. One is called 'lasting for an aeon' (kappaṭṭho) because, having arisen in Avīci, they remain there for an intermediate aeon, which is designated as a life-aeon. One is called 'incurable' (atekiccho) because they are unable to be treated in such a way as to avoid rebirth in hell. 'Not taken to the end' (apariyādinnāva) means not yet exhausted. For if one monk asks about the contemplation of the body, another about the contemplation of feelings, and so on, up to the contemplation of the mind, one does not look at another thinking, 'Since I was asked by this one, I will ask.' Even so, their turn is discernible, but for the Buddhas, a turn is not discernible. Before the shadow has moved more than a span and four fingerbreadths, the Blessed One explains the contemplation of the body in fourteen ways, the contemplation of feelings in nine ways, the contemplation of the mind in sixteen ways, and the contemplation of phenomena in five ways. Or let these four stand. If four others were to ask questions on the four right strivings, others on the bases of power, others on the five faculties, others on the five powers, others on the seven factors of enlightenment, and others on the eight path factors, the Blessed One would explain that too. Or let these eight stand. If another thirty-seven people were to ask questions on the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment, the Blessed One would explain that as well in that same moment. Why? Because in the time a great person of the world speaks one phrase, the Elder Ānanda speaks eight phrases. But in the time the Elder Ānanda speaks one phrase, the Blessed One speaks sixteen phrases. Why? Because the Blessed One’s tongue is soft, his teeth are well-fitted, his speech is unhindered, and the turning of his life-continuum is swift. Thus it is said: 'The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma has not been taken to its end; the phrases and syllables of the Dhamma have not been taken to their end.'

Tattha dhammadesanāti tantiṭṭhapanā. Dhammapadabyañjananti ettha dhammoti pāḷi. Pajjati attho etenāti padaṃ. Vākyañca padeneva saṅgahitaṃ. Atthaṃ byañjetīti byañjanaṃ, akkharaṃ. Tañhi padavākyaṃ paricchijjamānaṃ taṃ taṃ atthaṃ byañjeti pakāseti. Etena aparāparehi padabyañjanehi sucirampi kālaṃ kathentassa [M 2.0361] tathāgatassa na kadāci tesaṃ pariyādānaṃ atthīti dasseti. Guṇadhaṃsīti guṇadhaṃsanasīlo. Pagabboti vācāpāgabbiyena samannāgato.

Here, 'teaching of the Dhamma' (dhammadesanā) means the establishing of the teaching. In 'phrases and syllables of the Dhamma' (dhammapadabyañjana), 'Dhamma' means the Pāli text. 'Pada' (phrase) is that by which the meaning is understood. And a sentence (vākya) is included in 'pada' itself. 'Byañjana' (syllable) means a letter, for it is that which makes the meaning clear. For when a phrase or sentence is analyzed, it clarifies and reveals this or that meaning. This shows that even when the Tathāgata speaks for a very long time with successive phrases and syllables, there is never any exhaustion of them. 'Guṇadhaṃsī' means one whose nature is to destroy virtues. 'Pagabbha' means endowed with boldness of speech.

Upakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Upaka Sutta is concluded.

9. Sacchikaraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Sacchikaraṇīya Sutta

189. Navame nāmakāyenāti sahajātanāmakāyena. Sesamettha uttānameva.

189. In the ninth sutta, 'by the mental body' (nāmakāyena) means by the co-arisen mental body. The rest here is self-evident.

Sacchikaraṇīyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sacchikaraṇīya Sutta is concluded.

10. Uposathasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Uposatha Sutta

190. Dasame tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtanti āmeḍitavacanaṃ byāpanicchāvasena vuttanti āha “yato yato anuviloketī”ti. Anuviloketvāti ettha anu-saddopi byāpanicchāvacanamevāti anu anu viloketvāti attho, pañcapasādappaṭimaṇḍitāni akkhīni ummīletvā tato tato viloketvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Alanti yuttaṃ, opāyikanti attho “alameva nibbinditu”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.272; saṃ. ni. 2.124-126) viya. Puṭabandhanena pariharitvā asitabbaṃ [V 2.0330] puṭosaṃ sambalaṃ a-kārassa o-kāraṃ katvā. Tenāha “pātheyya”nti. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

190. In the tenth sutta, the phrase 'utterly silent, utterly silent' (tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ) is a reduplicated expression, spoken with a sense of pervasiveness. Thus it is said, 'from wherever he looked around.' Here, in 'having looked around' (anuviloketvā), the prefix 'anu-' is also an expression of pervasiveness, meaning 'looking again and again'; that is to say, opening his eyes, which were adorned with the five sensitivities, he gazed here and there. 'Enough' (alaṃ) means 'it is fit' (yuttaṃ), 'it is suitable' (opāyika), as in 'it is indeed enough to become disenchanted' and so on. Provisions (puṭosaṃ sambalaṃ) are what is to be eaten after being carried in a packet (puṭabandhanena), the word being formed by changing the letter 'a' to 'o'. Therefore, it is said 'provisions for a journey' (pātheyya). The rest here is easy to understand.

Uposathasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Uposatha Sutta is concluded.

Brāhmaṇavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Vagga is concluded.

(20) 5. Mahāvaggo

(20) 5. The Great Chapter

1. Sotānugatasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Sotānugata Sutta

191. Pañcamassa paṭhame sotānugatānanti pasādasotaṃ anugantvā gatānaṃ, paguṇānaṃ vācuggatānanti attho. Evaṃbhūtā ca pasādasotaṃ odahitvā [M 2.0362] ñāṇasotena suṭṭhu vavatthapitā nāma hontīti āha “pasādasota”ntiādi. Ekaccassa hi uggahitapubbavacanaṃ taṃ taṃ paguṇaṃ niccharitaṃ suṭṭhu vavatthapitaṃ na hoti. “Asukaṃ suttaṃ vā jātakaṃ vā kathehī”ti vutte “sajjhāyitvā saṃsanditvā samanuggāhitvā jānissāmī”ti vadanti. Ekaccassa taṃ taṃ paguṇaṃ bhavaṅgasotasadisaṃ hoti “asukaṃ suttaṃ vā jātakaṃ vā kathehī”ti vutte uddharitvā tameva katheti. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “ñāṇasotena vavatthapitāna”nti. Itthiliṅgādīni tīṇi liṅgāni. Nāmādīni cattāri padāni. Paṭhamādayo satta vibhattiyo.

191. In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, 'heard' (sotānugatāni) means those that have followed the stream of faith, or those that are fluent and learned by heart; this is the meaning. Such things, having been attended to through the stream of faith, are indeed well established by the stream of knowledge; thus it is said, 'the stream of faith,' and so on. For some, a teaching previously learned is not fluent, does not come forth, and is not well established. When asked, 'Recite such-and-such a sutta or jātaka,' they say, 'I will know it after reciting, comparing, and thoroughly reviewing it.' For others, a certain teaching is fluent, like the stream of the life-continuum. When asked, 'Recite such-and-such a sutta or jātaka,' they bring it to mind and recite it. It is with reference to this that it is said, 'established by the stream of knowledge.' There are three genders: feminine, and so on. There are four parts of speech: nouns, and so on. There are seven cases: the nominative, and so on.

Vaḷañjetīti pāḷiṃ anusandhiṃ pubbāparavasena vācuggataṃ karonto dhāreti. Vacasā paricitāti suttadasakavaggadasakapaṇṇāsadasakavasena vācāya sajjhāyitā, “dasasuttāni gatāni, dasavaggāni gatānī”tiādinā sallakkhetvā vācāya sajjhāyitāti attho. Vaggādivasena hi idha vacasā paricayo adhippeto, na pana suttekadesassa suttamattassa vacasā paricayo. Manasā anu anu pekkhitā bhāgaso nijjhāyitā viditā manusānupekkhitā. Yassa vācāya sajjhāyitaṃ buddhavacanaṃ manasā cintentassa tattha tattha pākaṭaṃ hoti, mahādīpaṃ jāletvā ṭhitassa rūpagataṃ viya vibhūtaṃ hutvā paññāyati. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Suppaṭividdhāti nijjaṭaṃ niggumbaṃ katvā suṭṭhu yāthāvato paṭividdhā. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

One who recites is one who maintains the Pāḷi text by vocalizing it in sequence, connecting the preceding and the following. 'Familiar with speech' means having recited by speech in the manner of tens of suttas, tens of sections, and fifties of sections, reflecting thus: 'Ten suttas have been covered, ten sections have been covered,' and so on—this is the meaning. Here, familiarity by speech is intended in terms of sections and the like, not, however, familiarity by speech with a portion of a sutta or with a single sutta. 'Examined again and again with the mind' means having contemplated in parts, having discerned, having mentally reflected upon. For one who recites the Buddha’s words by speech and reflects on them with the mind, it becomes clear here and there, appearing vividly like forms seen by one standing with a great lamp lit. This was said in reference to that. 'Thoroughly penetrated' means having made it free from entanglements and thickets, having penetrated it well and exactly as it is. The rest here is easily understood.

Sotānugatasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sotānugata Sutta is concluded.

2. Ṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Ṭhāna Sutta

192. Dutiye [V 2.0331] saṃvāsenāti sahavāsena. Sīlaṃ veditabbanti “ayaṃ susīlo vā dussīlo vā”ti saha vasantena upasaṅkamantena jānitabbo. Tañca kho dīghena addhunā, na ittaranti tañca sīlaṃ dīghena kālena veditabbaṃ, na ittarena. Dvīhatīhañhi saṃyatākāro ca saṃvutindriyākāro ca na sakkā dassetuṃ. Manasi karotāti tampi “sīlamassa pariggahessāmī”ti manasikarontena paccavekkhanteneva sakkā jānituṃ, na itarena. Paññavatāti tampi sappaññeneva paṇḍitena. Bālo hi manasikarontopi jānituṃ na sakkoti.

192. In the second sutta, 'by living together' means by cohabiting. 'Virtue is to be known' means that whether a person is virtuous or unvirtuous is to be known by one who lives with them or approaches them. And that virtue is to be known over a long period, not a short one. For in two or three days, an appearance of restraint and of controlled senses cannot be shown. 'By paying attention' means that it can be known only by one who pays attention and reflects, 'I will examine their virtue,' and not otherwise. 'By one who is wise' means only by a wise and learned person. For a fool, even if they pay attention, is unable to know.

Saṃvohārenāti [M 2.0363] aparāparaṃ kathanena.

'By conversation' means by repeated talk.

“Yo hi koci manussesu, vohāraṃ upajīvati;

Evaṃ vāseṭṭha jānāhi, vāṇijo so na brāhmaṇo”ti. (ma. ni. 2.457; su. ni. 619) –

‘Whoever among humans earns a living by trade, know this, Vāseṭṭha: he is a merchant, not a brahmin.’ (MN 98; Snp 3.9)

Ettha hi byavahāro nāma. “Cattāro ariyavohārā, cattāro anariyavohārā”ti (dī. ni. 3.313) ettha cetanā. “Saṅkhā samaññā paññatti vohāro”ti (dha. sa. 1313-1315; mahāni. 73) ettha paññatti. “Vohāramattena so vohareyyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.25) ettha kathāvohāro. Idhāpi esova adhippeto. Ekaccassa hi sammukhākathā parammukhākathāya na sameti parammukhākathā sammukhākathāya. Tathā purimakathā pacchimakathāya, pacchimakathā ca purimakathāya. So kathaneneva sakkā jānituṃ “asuci eso puggalo”ti. Sucisīlassa pana purimaṃ pacchimena, pacchimañca purimena sameti. Sammukhākathitaṃ parammukhākathitena sameti, parammukhākathitañca sammukhākathitena, tasmā kathanena sakkā sucibhāvo jānitunti pakāsento evamāha.

Here, this is indeed the meaning of 'vohāra'. In the passage, ‘Four noble modes of expression, four ignoble modes of expression’ (DN 3.232), it means intention. In, ‘Nomenclature, designation, concept, expression’ (Dhs §1306), it means concept. In, ‘He would speak only by way of convention’ (SN 1.25), it refers to conversational expression. Here too, this is the intended meaning. For some, face-to-face talk does not agree with behind-the-back talk, nor does behind-the-back talk agree with face-to-face talk. Similarly, former talk does not agree with later talk, nor does later talk agree with former talk. Just by their talk, it is possible to know, 'This person is impure.' But for one of pure conduct, the former talk agrees with the latter, and the latter with the former. Talk to their face agrees with talk behind their back, and talk behind their back agrees with talk to their face. Therefore, revealing that it is possible to know a person's purity just by their talk, he says thus.

Thāmoti ñāṇathāmo. Yassa hi ñāṇathāmo natthi, so uppannesu upaddavesu gahetabbaṃ gahaṇaṃ kattabbaṃ kiccaṃ apassanto advārakagharaṃ paviṭṭho viya carati. Tenāha “āpadāsu, bhikkhave, thāmo veditabbo”ti.

'Strength' means the strength of wisdom. For one who lacks the strength of wisdom, when troubles arise, they fail to see what should be grasped, what should be done, and what must be accomplished, and wander about like one who has entered a house without doors. Therefore, it is said, 'In times of adversity, monks, strength is to be known.'

Sākacchāyāti saṃkathāya. Duppaññassa hi kathā udake geṇḍu viya uppilavati. Paññavato [V 2.0332] kathentassa paṭibhānaṃ anantaṃ hoti. Udakavipphanditeneva hi maccho khuddako vā mahanto vāti ñāyati.

'By discussion' means by conversation. For the unwise, their talk floats like a ball on water. For the wise, as they speak, their eloquence is endless. Just as a fish, whether small or large, is known by how it thrashes in the water.

Ñātivināsoti corarogabhayādīhi ñātīnaṃ vināso. Bhogānaṃ byasanaṃ bhogabyasanaṃ, rājacorādivasena bhogavināsoti attho. Tenāha “dutiyapadepi eseva nayo”ti. Pañhummaggoti pañhagavesanaṃ, ñātuṃ icchitassa atthassa vīmaṃsananti attho. Atappakanti atittikaraṭṭhena atappakaṃ sādurasabhojanaṃ viya. Saṇhanti sukhumasabhāvaṃ.

'The destruction of relatives' means the loss of kin due to thieves, disease, fear, and the like. 'The ruin of wealth' or 'the ruin of possessions' means the loss of wealth due to kings, thieves, and so forth. Therefore, it is said, 'The same principle applies to the second term.' 'Inquiry' means seeking an answer, that is, investigating the meaning of a thing one wishes to know. 'Unsatisfying' means that in the sense that it does not bring satisfaction, it is like delicious food. 'Subtle' means of a subtle nature.

Ṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ṭhāna Sutta is concluded.

3. Bhaddiyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Bhaddiya Sutta

193. Tatiye [M 2.0364] karaṇassa uttaraṃ kiriyaṃ karaṇuttariyaṃ, taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇo. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

193. In the third sutta, `karaṇuttariya` means the subsequent action of the cause is superior; that is its characteristic, hence it is called `karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇa`. The rest is easily understood.

Bhaddiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Bhaddiya Sutta is concluded.

4. Sāmugiyasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Sāmugiya Sutta

194. Catutthe puggalassa pārisuddhiyā padhānabhūtāni vā aṅgāni pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgāni. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

194. In the fourth sutta, the `pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgāni` are the factors that are primary for a person's purity. The rest here is easily understood.

Sāmugiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sāmugiya Sutta is concluded.

5. Vappasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Vappa Sutta

195. Pañcame pihitattāti akusalassa pavesanadvāraṃ pidahitvā ṭhitattā. Kāyena saṃvaritabbañhi apihitena dvārena pavattanakaṃ pāpadhammaṃ saṃvaritvā ṭhito kāyena saṃvuto nāma. Khayavirāgenāti accantakhayasaṅkhātena virajjanena, anuppādanirodhenāti attho. Kiṃ vijjā pubbe uppannāti? Ubhayametaṃ na vattabbaṃ. Pahānābhisamayabhāvanābhisamayānaṃ abhinnakālattā padīpujjalanena [V 2.0333] andhakāraṃ viya vijjuppādena avijjā niruddhāva hoti, vattabbaṃ vā hetuphalattamupacāravasena. Yathā hi padīpujjalanahetuko andhakāravigamo, evaṃ vijjuppādahetuko avijjānirodho. Hetuphaladhammā ca samānakālāpi pubbāparakālā viya voharīyanti yathā “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”nti (ma. ni. 1.400; 3.421, 425, 426; saṃ. ni. 2.43-44; 2.4.60; kathā. 465, 467) paccayādānuppajjanakiriyā. Cittassa kāyassa ca vihananato vighāto, dukkhaṃ. Paridahanato pariḷāho.

195. In the fifth sutta, 'because it is closed' means because it stands having shut the door through which the unwholesome enters. For one must restrain with the body. One who stands having restrained the evil qualities that arise through an unclosed door is called 'restrained in body'. 'Through destruction and fading away' means through dispassion, which is defined as utter destruction; that is, cessation through non-arising. 'Was knowledge arisen before?' Neither of these should be said. Because the realization of abandonment and the realization of development occur simultaneously, just as darkness is dispelled by the lighting of a lamp, so ignorance ceases with the arising of knowledge. Or it may be said metaphorically in terms of cause and effect. For just as the disappearance of darkness is caused by the lighting of a lamp, so the cessation of ignorance is caused by the arising of knowledge. Though cause and effect are simultaneous, they are spoken of as if having earlier and later times, as in: 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises.' This is the action of arising by taking up conditions. Affliction is from the injuring of mind and body; it is suffering. Distress is from burning.

Niccavihārāti sabbadā pavattanakavihārā. Ṭhapetvā hi samāpattivelaṃ bhavaṅgavelañca khīṇāsavā iminā chaḷaṅgupekkhāvihārena sabbakālaṃ viharanti. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ disvā. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti [M 2.0365] hi nissayavohārena vuttaṃ. Sasambhārakathā hesā yathā “dhanunā vijjhatī”ti, tasmā nissayasīsena nissitassa gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Rāgavasena na somanassajāto hotīti gehasitapemavasenapi javanakkhaṇe somanassajāto na hoti maggena samucchinnattā, na domanassajāto pasādaññathattavasenapi. Upekkhako majjhatto hutvā viharatīti asamapekkhanena mohaṃ anuppādento ñāṇupekkhāvaseneva upekkhako viharati majjhatto. Khīṇāsavo hi iṭṭhepi aniṭṭhepi majjhattepi ārammaṇe yo asamapekkhanena samasamā ayonisogahaṇe akhīṇāsavānaṃ moho uppajjati, taṃ anuppādento maggeneva tassa samugghātitattā ñāṇupekkhāvaseneva upekkhako viharati, ayañcassa paṭipatti sativepullapattiyā paññāvepullapattiyā cāti vuttaṃ “satisampajaññapariggahitāyā”ti.

'Constant dwelling' means a dwelling that proceeds at all times. For, except for the times of attainment and the life-continuum, the destroyers of the cankers dwell at all times with this six-factored equanimity. 'Having seen a form with the eye' means having seen a form with eye-consciousness. The phrase 'having seen a form with the eye' is spoken in terms of the convention of dependence. This is talk that includes the instrument, just as it is said, 'He shoots with a bow.' Therefore, the dependent thing should be understood in terms of its support. 'Pleasure does not arise due to lust' means that even due to household-based affection, pleasure does not arise in the impulsion moment because it has been cut off by the path; nor does displeasure arise due to the alteration of the sensitive faculty. 'He dwells equanimous, being neutral' means that by not looking on wrongly, he does not give rise to delusion, and he dwells equanimous and neutral solely through the equanimity of wisdom. For a destroyer of the cankers, whether the object is pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral, does not give rise to the delusion that arises in those whose cankers are not destroyed through wrong looking on and improper grasping. Since it has been uprooted by the path, he dwells equanimous solely through the equanimity of wisdom. And this practice of his is due to the attainment of an abundance of mindfulness and the attainment of an abundance of wisdom, as it is said, 'guarded by mindfulness and clear comprehension.'

Ettha ca “chasu dvāresu upekkhako viharatī”ti iminā chaḷaṅgupekkhā kathitā. “Sampajāno”ti vacanato pana cattāri ñāṇasampayuttacittāni labbhanti tehi vinā sampajānatāya asambhavato. “Satatavihārā”ti vacanato aṭṭhapi mahākiriyacittāni labbhanti ñāṇuppattipaccayarahitakālepi pavattijotanato. “Arajjanto adussanto”ti vacanato hasituppādavoṭṭhabbanehi saddhiṃ dasa cittāni labbhanti. Arajjanādussanavasena pavatti hi tesampi sādhāraṇāti. Nanu cettha “upekkhako viharatī”ti chaḷaṅgupekkhāvasena imesaṃ satatavihārānaṃ āgatattā somanassaṃ kathaṃ labbhatīti? Āsevanatoti. Kiñcāpi hi khīṇāsavo iṭṭhāniṭṭhepi ārammaṇe majjhatte viya bahulaṃ upekkhako viharati attano parisuddhappakatibhāvāvijahanato, kadāci pana tathā cetobhisaṅkhārabhāve yaṃ taṃ sabhāvato iṭṭhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ[V 2.0334], tassa yāthāvato sabhāvaggahaṇavasenapi arahato cittaṃ somanassasahagataṃ hutvā pavattateva, tañca kho pubbāsevanavasena.

Here, the phrase 'remains equanimous at the six sense-doors' refers to the six-factored equanimity. The statement 'fully aware' indicates the four consciousnesses associated with knowledge, for without them, full awareness is impossible. The phrase 'constantly dwells' indicates the eight great functional consciousnesses, as they manifest activity even when there is no condition for the arising of knowledge. The words 'without delighting or resenting' imply ten consciousnesses, including the smile-producing and determining consciousnesses, because occurrence by way of non-delighting and non-resenting is common to them as well. Now, one might ask: Since these constant dwellings are included here under 'remains equanimous' by way of six-factored equanimity, how can joy be obtained? It is due to prior cultivation. Although one whose cankers are destroyed often remains equanimous toward pleasant and unpleasant objects, as if they were neutral, not abandoning their naturally purified state, occasionally, when there is such a mental formation toward an object that is naturally agreeable, the arahant's consciousness does arise accompanied by joy, even through grasping the true nature of that object—and that, too, is due to prior cultivation.

Kāyoti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.2.51) pañcadvārakāyo, so anto avasānaṃ etissāti kāyantikā, taṃ kāyantikaṃ. Tenāha – “yāva pañcadvārakāyo pavattati, tāva pavatta”nti. Jīvitantikanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Pacchā uppajjitvāti etasmiṃ attabhāve manodvārikavedanāto pacchā uppajjitvā tato paṭhamaṃ [M 2.0366] nirujjhati, tato eva atthasiddhamatthaṃ sarūpeneva dassetuṃ “manodvārikavedanā paṭhamaṃ uppajjitvā pacchā nirujjhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni tameva saṅkhepena vuttaṃ vivarituṃ “sā hī”tiādimāha. Yāva tettiṃsavassāni paṭhamavayo. Paññāsavassakāleti paṭhamavayato yāva paññāsavassakālā, tāva. Ṭhitā hotīti vaḍḍhihāniyo anupagantvā samarūpeneva ṭhitā hoti. Mandāti mudukā atikhiṇā. Tadāti asītinavutivassakāle vadantepi tathāciraparicitepīti adhippāyo. Bhaggāti tejobhaggena bhaggā dubbaṇṇā. Hadayakoṭiṃyevāti cakkhādivatthūsu appavattitvā tesaṃ ādiantakoṭibhūtaṃ hadayavatthuṃyeva. Tāvāti yāva vedanā vattati, tāva.

'Kāya' (body) (as in Saṃyutta Nikāya, Ṭīkā 2.2.51) refers to the five-door body. That which has this as its end (anta), its termination, is 'body-ending' (kāyantika). Hence it is said: 'As long as the five-door body continues, so long does it continue.' The same method applies to 'life-ending' (jīvitantika). 'Having arisen later' means that in this existence, having arisen after the mind-door feeling, it ceases before it. Therefore, to show the established meaning in its own form, it is said: 'The mind-door feeling, having arisen first, ceases later.' Now, to elaborate on what was briefly stated, the text says, 'For it is...' and so on. Up to thirty-three years is the first age. 'At the time of fifty years' means from the first age up to the time of fifty years. 'Remains steady' means it remains in the same state without undergoing increase or decrease. 'Diminished' means soft, very weak. 'At that time' refers to the age of eighty or ninety years; the intention is 'even when speaking to someone so long familiar.' 'Broken' means broken due to the loss of radiance, discolored. 'Only the heart-base' means that, not operating in the eye and other bases, it is only the heart-base, which is the initial and final point of those bases. 'So long' means as long as the feeling lasts.

Vāpiyāti mahātaḷākena. Pañcaudakamaggasampannanti pañcahi udakassa pavisananikkhamanamaggehi yuttaṃ. Tato tato vissandamānaṃ sabbaso puṇṇattā. Paṭhamaṃ deve vassantetiādi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Imaṃ vedanaṃ sandhāyāti imaṃ yathāvuttaṃ pariyosānappattaṃ manodvārikavedanaṃ sandhāya.

'By a lake' means by a large reservoir. 'Endowed with five watercourses' means furnished with five channels for the entry and exit of water. Flowing out from here and there because it is completely full. 'When the deva rains first...' and so on is the application of the simile. 'Referring to this feeling' means referring to this aforesaid mind-door feeling which has reached its conclusion.

Kāyassa bhedāti attabhāvassa vināsanato. Parato agantvāti paralokavasena agantvā. Vedanānaṃ sītibhāvo nāma saṅkhāradarathapariḷāhābhāvo. So panāyaṃ sabbaso appavattivasenevāti āha “appavattanadhammāni bhavissantī”ti.

'Upon the breaking up of the body' means from the destruction of individual existence. 'Not going beyond' means not going by way of a future world. The cooling of feelings is the absence of the distress and fever of formations. But this is entirely due to non-occurrence; thus it is said: 'They will become of a non-arising nature.'

Attabhāvaṃ nāsetukāmassa daḷhaṃ uppannaṃ saṃvegañāṇaṃ sandhāyāha “kudālo viya paññā”ti. Tato nibbattitajjhānasamādhiṃ sandhāya “piṭakaṃ viya samādhī”ti. Tannissāya pavattetabbavipassanārambhañāṇaṃ sandhāya “khanitti viya vipassanā”ti ca vuttaṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva.

Referring to the firmly arisen knowledge of spiritual urgency in one who wishes to destroy individual existence, it is said, 'wisdom is like a spade.' Then, referring to the concentration of absorption produced from that, it is said, 'concentration is like a basket.' And referring to the initial knowledge for insight to be developed in dependence on that, it is said, 'insight is like a pickaxe.' The rest here is self-evident.

Vappasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vappa Sutta is concluded.

6. Sāḷhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Sāḷha Sutta.

196. Chaṭṭhe [V 2.0335] kāyadaḷhibahulataṃ tapatīti tapo, attakilamathānuyogavasena pavattaṃ vīriyaṃ. Tena kāyadaḷhibahulatānimittassa pāpassa jigucchanaṃ virajjanaṃ tapojigucchāti āha “dukkarakārikasaṅkhātenā”tiādi. Tapojigucchavādātiādīsu tapojigucchaṃ vadanti, manasāpi tameva sārato [M 2.0367] gahetvā vicaranti, kāyenapi tameva allīnā nānappakāraṃ attakilamathānuyogamanuyuttā viharantīti attho. Aparisuddhakāyasamācārāti aparisuddhena pāṇātipātādinā kāyasamācārena samannāgatā. Aparisuddhavacīsamācārāti aparisuddhena musāvādādinā vacīsamācārena samannāgatā. Aparisuddhamanosamācārāti aparisuddhena abhijjhādinā manosamācārena samannāgatā. Kāmaṃ akusalakāyasamācāravacīsamācārappavattikālepi abhijjhādayo pavattantiyeva, tadā pana te cetanāpakkhikā vā abbohārikā vāti, manosamācāravāre eva abhijjhādivasena yojanā katā. Atha vā dvārantare pavattānaṃ pāṇātipātādīnaṃ vacīsamācārādibhāvābhāvo viya dvārantare pavattānampi abhijjhādīnaṃ kāyasamācārādibhāvo asiddho, manosamācārabhāvo eva pana siddhoti katvā manosamācāravāre eva abhijjhādayo uddhaṭā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

196. In the sixth sutta, austerity (tapo) is exertion that proceeds by way of the practice of self-mortification, so called because it ‘burns’ (tapati) the body’s firmness and bulk. By that, disgust for and dispassion towards evil, which is caused by the body’s firmness and bulk, is called ‘austerity-disgust.’ Hence it is said, ‘through what is called the practice of arduous asceticism,’ and so on. In phrases such as ‘those who profess austerity-disgust,’ it means that they speak of austerity-disgust; mentally, they grasp it as the essence and go about; and bodily, clinging to it, they dwell engaged in various forms of self-mortification. ‘Impure bodily conduct’ means endowed with impure bodily conduct such as killing living beings. ‘Impure verbal conduct’ means endowed with impure verbal conduct such as lying. ‘Impure mental conduct’ means endowed with impure mental conduct such as covetousness. Indeed, covetousness and the like also arise at the time of the occurrence of unwholesome bodily and verbal conduct, but since at that time they are either secondary to volition or are not designated as such, the explanation in terms of covetousness and so on is made only in the section on mental conduct. Alternatively, just as the status of killing and so on, occurring through another door, as verbal conduct and so on is not established, so too, the status of covetousness and so on, occurring through another door, as bodily conduct and so on is not established. However, their status as mental conduct is indeed established. Therefore, covetousness and so on are mentioned only in the section on mental conduct. For thus it is said—

“Dvāre caranti kammāni, na dvārā dvāracārino;

Tasmā dvārehi kammāni, aññamaññaṃ vavatthitā”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 kāmāvacarakusaladvārakathā);

“Actions occur at the doors; the doors are not the agents. Therefore, actions are distinguished from one another by the doors.”

Aparisuddhājīvāti aparisuddhena vejjakammadūtakammavaḍḍhiyogādinā ekavīsatianesanābhedena ājīvena samannāgatā. Idañca sāsane pabbajitānaṃyeva vasena vuttaṃ, “yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā”ti pana vacanato bāhirakavasena gahaṭṭhavasena ca yojanā veditabbā. Gahaṭṭhānampi hi jātidhammakuladhammadesadhammavilomanavasena aññathāpi micchājīvo labbhateva.

'Impure livelihood' means endowed with an impure livelihood divided into twenty-one kinds of improper seeking, such as the practice of medicine, acting as a messenger, practicing usury, and so on. This is said specifically with regard to those who have gone forth in the Dispensation, but from the phrase 'those ascetics and brahmins,' the application should be understood to apply to outsiders and householders as well. For wrong livelihood is indeed found for householders also, by way of acting contrary to the customs of caste, family, and country, or otherwise.

Ñāṇadassanāyāti ettha ñāṇadassananti maggañāṇampi vuccati phalañāṇampi sabbaññutaññāṇampi paccavekkhaṇañāṇampi vipassanāñāṇampi. “Kiṃ nu kho, āvuso, ñāṇadassanavisuddhatthaṃ bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.257) hi ettha maggañāṇaṃ “ñāṇadassana”nti vuttaṃ. “Ayamañño uttarimanussadhammo alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso adhigato phāsuvihāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.328) ettha phalañāṇaṃ. “Bhagavatopi kho ñāṇaṃ [V 2.0336] udapādi sattāhakālakato āḷāro kālāmo”ti (mahāva. 10) ettha sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. “Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi, akuppā me vimutti, ayamantimā jātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; mahāva. 16; paṭi. ma. 2.30) ettha paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. “Ñāṇadassanāya cittaṃ abhinīharatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.234-235) ettha vipassanāñāṇaṃ. Idha pana ñāṇadassanāyāti [M 2.0368] maggañāṇaṃ “ñāṇadassana”nti vuttaṃ. Tenāha “maggañāṇasaṅkhātāya dassanāyā”ti. Avirādhitaṃ vijjhatīti avirādhitaṃ katvā vijjhati. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

Here, 'knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassana) is said to be path knowledge, fruition knowledge, omniscient knowledge, reviewing knowledge, and insight knowledge. For instance, in 'Friend, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One for the sake of purification of knowledge and vision?' (MN 1.257), path knowledge is called 'knowledge and vision.' In 'This is another superhuman quality, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, attained for a pleasant abiding' (MN 1.328), it refers to fruition knowledge. In 'Knowledge arose in the Blessed One: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago’' (Mhv. 10), it refers to omniscient knowledge. In 'Knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘Unshakable is my liberation; this is my last birth’' (SN 5.1081; Mhv. 16; Patis. 2.30), it refers to reviewing knowledge. In 'He directs his mind towards knowledge and vision' (DN 1.234-235), it refers to insight knowledge. Here, however, 'for knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassanāya) refers to path knowledge, which is called 'knowledge and vision.' Hence it is said, 'for the sake of vision, reckoned as path knowledge.' 'He pierces without failing' (avirādhitaṃ vijjhati) means he pierces having made it unfailing. The rest here is easily understood.

Sāḷhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sāḷha Sutta is concluded.

7. Mallikādevīsuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Mallikādevī Sutta

197. Sattame appesakkhāti appānubhāvā. Sā pana appesakkhatā ādhipateyyasampattiyā parivārasampattiyā ca abhāvena pākaṭā hoti. Tattha parivārasampattiyā abhāvaṃ dassento “appaparivārā”ti āha. Issarāti ādhipateyyasaṃvattanakammabalena īsanasīlā. Sā panassā issaratā vibhavasampattipaccayā pākaṭā jātāti aḍḍhatāpariyāyabhāvena vadanto “aḍḍhāti issarā”ti āha. Mahantaṃ dhanametissā bhūmigatañceva vaḷañjanakañcāti mahaddhanā. Idha pana vaḷañjanakeneva dhanena mahaddhanataṃ dassento “vaḷañjanakadhanena mahaddhanā”ti āha. Īsatīti īsā, abhibhūti attho. Mahatī īsā mahesā, suppatiṭṭhitamahesatāya pana parehi mahesoti akkhātabbatāya mahesakkhā. Yasmā pana so mahesakkhābhāvo ādhipateyyaparivārasampattiyā viññāyati, tasmā “mahāparivārā”ti vuttaṃ.

197. In the seventh sutta, 'of little influence' (appesakkhā) means of little power. This lack of influence is evident due to the absence of both the attainment of sovereignty and the attainment of a retinue. To show the absence of the attainment of a retinue, it is said, 'with a small retinue' (appaparivārā). 'She is a ruler' (issarā) means she is of a ruling nature through the power of kamma that leads to sovereignty. Her rulership becomes evident on account of her attainment of prosperity; therefore, speaking by way of a synonym for richness, it is said, 'rich, thus a ruler' (aḍḍhā ti issarā). She has great wealth, both that which is in the ground and that which is in use, hence she is 'greatly wealthy' (mahaddhanā). Here, however, to show her great wealth by means of wealth in use, it is said, 'greatly wealthy through wealth in use' (vaḷañjanakadhanena mahaddhanā). 'She overpowers' (īsati) is 'power' (īsā), which has the meaning of 'dominance.' Great power is 'great power' (mahesā). Because her state of great power is well-established, she is to be called 'of great power' by others, hence she is 'one of great influence' (mahesakkhā). Since that state of being of great influence is known through the attainment of sovereignty and a retinue, it is therefore said, 'with a great retinue' (mahāparivārā).

Saṇṭhānapāripūriyā adhikaṃ rūpamassāti abhirūpā. Saṇṭhānapāripūriyāti ca hatthapādādisarīrāvayavānaṃ susaṇṭhitatāyāti attho. Avayavapāripūriyā hi samudāyapāripūrisiddhi. Rūpanti ca sarīraṃ “rūpavanteva saṅkhyaṃ gacchatī”tiādīsu viya. Dassanayuttāti surūpabhāvena passitabbayuttā, dissamānā cakkhūni piyāyatīti aññakiccavikkhepaṃ hitvāpi daṭṭhabbāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dissamānāva somanassavasena cittaṃ pasādetīti pāsādikā. Tenāha “dassanena pāsādikā”ti. Pokkharatāti vuccati sundarabhāvo, vaṇṇassa pokkharatā vaṇṇapokkharatā, tāya vaṇṇasampattiyāti attho. Porāṇā pana pokkharanti sarīraṃ vadanti[V 2.0337], vaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇameva. Tesaṃ matena vaṇṇañca pokkharañca vaṇṇapokkharāni, tesaṃ bhāvo vaṇṇapokkharatā[M 2.0369]. Iti paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāyāti uttamaparisuddhena vaṇṇena ceva sarīrasaṇṭhānasampattiyā cāti attho daṭṭhabbo. Tenevāha “vaṇṇena ceva sarīrasaṇṭhānena cā”ti. Tattha vaṇṇenāti vaṇṇadhātuyā. Sarīraṃ nāma sannivesavisiṭṭho karacaraṇagīvāsīsādiavayavasamudāyo, so ca saṇṭhānamukhena gayhatīti āha “sarīrasaṇṭhānenā”ti.

'Beautiful' (abhirūpā) means that her form is excellent due to the perfection of her proportions. 'Perfection of proportions' means the excellent proportion of bodily parts such as hands, feet, and so on. For the perfection of the whole is accomplished through the perfection of the parts. And 'form' (rūpa) means the body, as in such phrases as 'one endowed with form is counted as such.' 'Worthy of being seen' (dassanayuttā) means worthy of being seen due to her beautiful appearance; because she delights the eyes when seen, it is said that she should be looked at even while setting aside the distraction of other duties. Simply by being seen she gladdens the mind by way of joy, hence she is 'pleasing' (pāsādikā). Therefore, it is said, 'pleasing by sight.' 'Lotus-like beauty' (pokkharatā) is said to be a state of beauty; 'lotus-like beauty of complexion' (vaṇṇapokkharatā) means the attainment of a beautiful complexion. But the ancients say 'pokkhara' means the body, and 'vaṇṇa' means just complexion. According to their view, 'complexion and body' are 'vaṇṇapokkharāni,' and their state is 'vaṇṇapokkharatā.' Thus, 'by supreme lotus-like beauty' means by a supremely pure complexion and by the attainment of perfect bodily proportions—this meaning should be understood. Therefore, it is said, 'by complexion and by bodily proportions.' Therein, 'by complexion' means by the element of color. The body is the assemblage of parts such as hands, feet, neck, and head, distinguished by its arrangement, and it is grasped by way of its proportions—hence, it is said, 'by bodily proportions.'

Abhisajjatīti kujjhanavaseneva kuṭilakaṇṭako viya tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samuṭṭhāne makaradanto viya lagati. Yañhi kodhassa uppattiṭṭhānabhūte ārammaṇe upanāhassa paccayabhūtaṃ kujjhanavasena abhisajjanaṃ, taṃ idhādhippetaṃ, na lubbhanavasena. Kuppatītiādīsu pubbuppatti kopo, tato balavataro byāpādo laddhāsevanatāya cittassa byāpajjanato. Sātisayaṃ laddhāsevanatāya tato byāpādatopi balavatarā paccatthikabhāvena thāmappatti patitthiyanā. Annaṃ pānantiādīsu adīyato annaṃ, khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyañca. Pātabyato pānaṃ, yaṃkiñci pānaṃ. Vasitabbato acchādetabbato vatthaṃ, nivāsanapāvuraṇaṃ. Yanti tenāti yānaṃ, chattupāhanavayhasivikādi yaṃkiñci gamanapaccayaṃ. Chattampi hi vassātapadukkhanivāraṇena maggagamanasādhananti katvā “yāna”nti vuccati. Mālanti yaṃkiñci sumanamālādipupphaṃ. Gandhanti yaṃkiñci candanādivilepanaṃ.

'He is attached' (abhisajjati) means it sticks, like a crooked thorn or a sea-monster's tooth, in each respective instance, only by way of anger. For what is intended here is the attachment by way of anger, which is a condition for resentment towards an object that is the basis for the arising of anger, not attachment by way of greed. In such phrases as 'he is angered' (kuppati), the initial arising is 'anger' (kopo); stronger than that is 'ill will' (byāpādo), due to the mind becoming malevolent through repeated practice. Stronger even than ill will, through excessive practice, is 'hostility' (paṭiṭṭhiyanā), which is the attainment of firmness in the state of an enemy. In such phrases as 'food and drink,' 'food' (annaṃ) is what is to be eaten—edibles and meals. 'Drink' (pānaṃ) is what is to be drunk, any kind of drink. 'Cloth' (vatthaṃ) is what is to be worn or what is to be covered with—an undergarment and an outer robe. 'A vehicle' (yānaṃ) is that by which one goes—any means of travel, such as an umbrella, sandals, a litter, a palanquin, and so on. For even an umbrella is called a 'vehicle' because it is a means for going on a path by warding off the suffering from rain and sun. 'A garland' (mālaṃ) is any flower, such as a jasmine garland. 'Perfume' (gandhaṃ) refers to any scented unguent, such as sandalwood.

Mallikādevīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mallikādevī Sutta is concluded.

8. Attantapasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Attantapa Sutta

198. Aṭṭhame āhito ahaṃmāno etthāti attā, attabhāvo. Idha pana yo paro na hoti, so attā, taṃ attānaṃ. Paranti attato aññaṃ. Diṭṭheti paccakkhabhūte. Dhammeti upādānakkhandhadhamme. Tattha hi attā bhavati, attasaññādiṭṭhi bhavatīti attabhāvasamaññā. Tenāha “diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve”ti. Chātaṃ vuccati taṇhā jighacchāhetutāya. Anto tāpanakilesānanti attano santāne darathapariḷāhajananena santāpanakilesānaṃ.

198. In the eighth sutta, the conceit 'I am' is placed in this, hence 'self' (attā), or individual existence. Here, however, that which is not other is the self; that is, that self. 'Other' means different from the self. 'In the seen' means in what has become directly perceptible. 'Dhamma' means the phenomena of the aggregates subject to clinging. For there the self exists, the perception and view of self exist—hence, the designation 'individual existence.' Therefore it is said: 'in the seen Dhamma' means in this very individual existence. 'Hunger' (chātaṃ) is said to be craving (taṇhā), because it is the cause of the state of hunger (jighacchā). 'The defilements that torment within' means the defilements that torment by generating anguish and burning in one's own mental continuum.

Paresaṃ [M 2.0370] hananaghātanādinā rodāpanato luddo. Tathā vighātakabhāvena kāyacittānaṃ vidālanato dāruṇo. Thaddhahadayo kakkhaḷo. Bandhanāgāre niyutto bandhanāgāriko.

He is cruel (luddo) because he makes others cry by killing and slaying them. Likewise, he is harsh (dāruṇo) because he tears apart bodies and minds by way of destructiveness. He is hard-hearted (thaddhahadayo), unyielding (kakkhaḷo). Appointed in a prison (bandhanāgāre), he is a prison guard (bandhanāgāriko).

Khattiyābhisekenāti [V 2.0338] khattiyānaṃ kātabbaabhisekena. Santhāgāranti santhāravasena kataṃ agāraṃ yaññāgāraṃ. Sappitelenāti sappimissena telena. Yamakasnehena hi esā tadā kāyaṃ abbhañjati. Vacchabhāvaṃ taritvā ṭhito vacchataro. Parikkhepakaraṇatthāyāti navamālāhi saddhiṃ dabbhehi vediyā parikkhipanatthāya. Yaññabhūmiyanti avasesayaññaṭṭhāne.

'By the anointing of a khattiya' means by the anointing that is to be performed for khattiyas. 'Assembly hall' (santhāgāra) means a house made by way of strewing, a sacrificial hall. 'With ghee and oil' means with oil mixed with ghee. For at that time, she anoints his body with a twofold unguent. Having passed beyond the calf stage, he is a young bull (vacchataro). 'For the purpose of encircling' means for the purpose of encircling the altar with fresh garlands and ladles. 'On the sacrificial ground' means at the remaining site of the sacrifice.

Dūrasamussāritamānasseva sāsane sammāpaṭipatti sambhavati, na mānajātikassāti āha “nihatamānattā”ti. Ussannattāti bahubhāvato. Bhogārogyādivatthukā madā suppahiyā honti nimittassa avaṭṭhānato, na tathā kulavijjāmadāti khattiyabrāhmaṇakulānaṃ pabbajitānampi jātivijjā nissāya mānajappanaṃ duppajahanti āha “yebhuyyena hi…pe… mānaṃ karontī”ti. Vijātitāyāti nihīnajātitāya. Patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkontīti suvisuddhaṃ katvā sīlaṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkonti. Sīlavasena hi sāsane patiṭṭhahanti. Patiṭṭhātunti vā saccappaṭivedhena lokuttarāya patiṭṭhāya patiṭṭhātuṃ. Yebhuyyena hi upanissayasampannā sujātāyeva honti, na dujjātā.

‘Right practice in the Teaching arises only for one whose pride is far removed, not for one born of pride,’ thus he said, ‘because pride is destroyed.’ ‘Because it is excessive’ means due to its abundance. Pride based on wealth, health, and similar things is easily abandoned because its basis is not firmly established, but not so the pride of lineage and knowledge. Even those gone forth from khattiya and brahmin families find it hard to give up their prideful boasting, clinging to birth and knowledge.
