Thus he said, ‘For the most part...they act with pride.’ ‘Because of low birth’ means due to inferior birth. ‘They cannot establish themselves’ means they are unable to perfectly purify and maintain virtue. For in the Teaching, one establishes oneself through virtue. ‘To establish themselves’ can also mean to establish themselves with the supramundane establishment through the penetration of truth. For the most part, those endowed with the necessary conditions are of good birth, not of bad birth.

Parisuddhanti rāgādīnaṃ accantameva pahānadīpanato nirupakkilesatāya sabbaso visuddhaṃ. Saddhaṃ paṭilabhatīti pothujjanikasaddhāvasena saddahati. Viññujātikānañhi dhammasampattiggahaṇapubbikā saddhāsiddhi dhammappamāṇadhammappasannabhāvato. Jāyampatikāti gharaṇipatikā. Kāmaṃ “jāyampatikā”ti vutte gharasāmikagharasāminivasena dvinnaṃyeva gahaṇaṃ viññāyati, yassa pana purisassa anekā pajāpatiyo honti, tattha kiṃ vattabbanti ekāyapi saṃvāso sambādhoti dassanatthaṃ “dve”ti vuttaṃ. Rāgādinā sakiñcanaṭṭhena, khettavatthuādinā sapalibodhaṭṭhena rāgarajādīnaṃ āgamanapathatāpi uppajjanaṭṭhānatā evāti dvepi vaṇṇanā ekatthā, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Alagganaṭṭhenāti asajjanaṭṭhena appaṭibaddhabhāvena. Evaṃ akusalakusalappavattīnaṃ ṭhānabhāvena gharāvāsapabbajjānaṃ sambādhabbhokāsataṃ dassetvā idāni [M 2.0371] kusalappavattiyāyeva aṭṭhānaṭṭhānabhāvena tesaṃ taṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

‘Purified’ means completely pure due to being without impurities, as this indicates the utter abandoning of lust and so on. ‘He acquires faith’—he believes with the faith of an ordinary person. For those of discerning nature, the attainment of faith arises from first grasping the excellence of the Dhamma, due to being convinced by the Dhamma as the standard. ‘Jāyampatikā’ means husband and wife. Though ‘jāyampatikā’ is stated, it is understood to refer to two, the master and mistress of the house. But if a man has multiple wives, what should be said? To show that even with one, cohabitation is crowded, ‘two’ is said. Due to lust and so on, it is ‘with impediments’; due to fields, property, and so on, it is ‘with obstacles.’ It is also the path of arrival and the place of arising for lust, defilements, and so on. Thus, both explanations have the same meaning; only the wording differs. ‘Not clinging’ means not sticking, not being bound. Having thus shown the crowded and open nature of household life and monastic life as the basis for unwholesome and wholesome activities, now, to show their suitability or unsuitability for wholesome activities, ‘furthermore’ is said, etc.

Saṅkhepakathāti visuṃ visuṃ paduddhāraṃ akatvā saṅkhepato atthavaṇṇanā. Ekampi divasanti ekadivasamattampi. Akhaṇḍaṃ katvāti dukkaṭamattassapi anāpajjanena akhaṇḍitaṃ katvā. Kilesamalena amalinanti taṇhāsaṃkilesādivasena asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ katvā. Paridahitvāti nivāsetvā ceva pārupitvā ca. Agāravāso agāraṃ uttarapadalopena, tassa vaḍḍhiāvahaṃ agārassa hitaṃ.

‘A brief explanation’ means explaining the meaning concisely without separately extracting each word. ‘Even a single day’ means just one day. ‘Making it unbroken’ means making it unbroken by not incurring even a minor offense. ‘Unstained by the defilements’ means making it unstained by the defilements of craving, etc. ‘Wearing’ means both clothing oneself and covering oneself. ‘Household life’ (agāravāsa) is ‘home’ (agāra) by elision of the final word; it brings growth to the household and is for its benefit.

Bhogakkhandhoti [V 2.0339] bhogarāsi bhogasamudāyo. Ābandhanaṭṭhenāti putto nattātiādinā pemavasena saparicchedavasena bandhanaṭṭhena. Amhākameteti ñāyantīti ñātī, pitāmahapituputtādivasena parivattanaṭṭhena parivaṭṭo. Sāmaññavācīpi sikkhā-saddo ājīvasaddasannidhānato uparivuccamānavisesāpekkhāya ca visesaniviṭṭhova hotīti vuttaṃ “yā bhikkhūnaṃ adhisīlasaṅkhātā sikkhā”ti. Sikkhitabbaṭṭhena sikkhā, saha ājīvanti etthāti sājīvo. Sikkhanabhāvenāti sikkhāya sājīve ca sikkhanabhāvena. Sikkhaṃ paripūrentoti sīlasaṃvaraṃ paripūrento. Sājīvañca avītikkamantoti “nāmakāyo, padakāyo, niruttikāyo, byañjanakāyo”ti (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.39) vuttaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ bhagavato ca vacanaṃ avītikkamanto hutvāti attho. Idameva ca “sikkhana”nti vuttaṃ, tattha sājīvānaṃ avītikkamo sikkhāpāripūriyā paccayo. Tato hi yāva maggā sikkhāpāripūrī hotīti.

‘Wealth’ (bhogakkhandha) is a mass of riches, a heap of wealth. ‘By way of bondage’ means by way of binding through affection for sons, grandsons, and the like, with a sense of confinement. ‘They are known as ours’—thus they are called relatives (ñātī); by the sense of revolving through generations like grandfathers, fathers, and sons, hence ‘revolving’ (parivaṭṭo). Even though it is a general term, the word ‘training’ (sikkhā), due to its association with the word ‘livelihood’ (ājīva), and with reference to the specific qualities to be mentioned later, is indeed established as a specific term—as stated: ‘The training known as the higher virtue of the monks.’ ‘Training’ (sikkhā) is in the sense of what should be trained; and ‘with livelihood’ (sājīva) is so called because one lives together with it. ‘By way of training’ means by way of training in both training (sikkhā) and livelihood (sājīva). ‘Fulfilling the training’ means fulfilling the restraint of virtue. ‘And not transgressing livelihood’ means not transgressing the training rule and the words of the Blessed One, as stated: ‘the body of names, the body of words, the body of expressions, the body of syllables’ (Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 1.39). This itself is called ‘training,’ wherein non-transgression of livelihood is a condition for the perfection of training. From this, the perfection of training occurs up to the path.

Anuppadātāti anubalappadātā, anuvattanavasena vā padātā. Kassa pana anuvattanaṃ padānañcāti? “Sahitāna”nti vuttattā sandhānassāti viññāyati. Tenāha “sandhānānuppadātā”ti. Yasmā pana anuvattanavasena sandhānassa padānaṃ ādhānaṃ ārakkhanaṃ vā daḷhakaraṇaṃ hoti, tena vuttaṃ “dve jane samagge disvā”tiādi. Āramanti etthāti ārāmo, ramitabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Yasmā pana ā-kārena vināpi ayamattho labbhati, tasmā vuttaṃ “samaggarāmotipi pāḷi, ayamevattho”ti.

‘Anuppadātā’ means giving support, or giving in the sense of following. But whose following and giving is it? Since it is said ‘for those who are united,’ it is understood as giving to unity. Therefore, it is said, ‘sandhānānuppadātā’ (giving support to unity). Moreover, because giving in the sense of following provides foundation, protection, or strengthening of unity, it is said, ‘seeing two people in harmony,’ etc. ‘Ārāmo’ means a place where one delights, a place to be enjoyed. Since this meaning can also be obtained without the ā prefix, it is said, ‘samaggarāmo is also a reading; this is the meaning.’

Etthāti [M 2.0372] –

Here:

“Nelaṅgo setapacchādo, ekāro vattatī ratho;

Anīghaṃ passa āyantaṃ, chinnasotaṃ abandhana”nti. (saṃ. ni. 4.347; udā. 65; peṭako. 25) –

‘The chariot without a pole, with a white canopy, with one wheel, rolls on. Behold it coming, untroubled, with the stream cut off, without bonds.’

Imissā gāthāya. Sīlañhettha nelaṅganti vuttaṃ. Tenevāha – “citto gahapati, nelaṅganti kho, bhante, sīlānametaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.347). Sukumārāti appharusatāya mudukā. Purassa esāti ettha pura-saddo tannivāsivācako daṭṭhabbo – “gāmo āgato”tiādīsu viya. Tenevāha “nagaravāsīna”nti. Manaṃ appāyati vaḍḍhetīti manāpo. Tena vuttaṃ “cittavuḍḍhikarā”ti.

In this verse. Herein, virtue is called ‘nelaṅga.’ Therefore, it is said: ‘Householder Citta, “nelaṅga,” venerable sir, is a designation for virtues’ (Saṃ. Ni. 4.347). ‘Sukumārā’ means soft due to a lack of harshness. ‘Purassa esa’—here, the word ‘pura’ should be understood as referring to its inhabitants—just as in phrases like ‘the village has come.’ Therefore, it is said, ‘for town-dwellers.’ ‘It pleases and increases the mind’—thus ‘manāpo’ (delightful). Hence, it is said, ‘mind-enhancing.’

Kālavādītiādi [V 2.0340] samphappalāpā paṭiviratassa paṭipattidassanaṃ. Atthasaṃhitāpi hi vācā ayuttakālappayogena atthāvahā na siyāti anatthaviññāpanavācaṃ anulometi, tasmā samphappalāpaṃ pajahantena akālavāditā pariharitabbāti vuttaṃ “kālavādī”ti. Kālena vadantenapi ubhayānatthasādhanato abhūtaṃ parivajjetabbanti āha “bhūtavādī”ti. Bhūtañca vadantena yaṃ idhalokaparalokahitasampādakaṃ, tadeva vattabbanti dassetuṃ “atthavādī”ti vuttaṃ. Atthaṃ vadantenapi lokiyadhammasannissitameva avatvā lokuttaradhammasannissitaṃ katvā vattabbanti dassanatthaṃ “dhammavādī”ti vuttaṃ. Yathā ca attho lokuttaradhammasannissito hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “vinayavādī”ti vuttaṃ. Pañcannañhi saṃvaravinayānaṃ pañcannañca pahānavinayānaṃ vasena vuccamāno attho nibbānādhigamanahetubhāvato lokuttaradhammasannissito hotīti. Evaṃ guṇavisesayuttova attho vuccamāno desanākosalle sati sobhati, kiccakaro ca hoti, na aññathāti dassetuṃ “nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni taṃ desanākosallaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “kālenā”tiādimāha. Pucchādivasena hi otiṇṇavācāvatthusmiṃ ekaṃsādibyākaraṇavibhāgaṃ sallakkhetvā ṭhapanāhetūdāharaṇasandassanādiṃ taṃtaṃkālānurūpaṃ vibhāventiyā parimitaparicchinnarūpāya vipulataragambhīrodāraparamatthavitthārasaṅgāhikāya kathāya ñāṇabalānurūpaṃ pare yāthāvato dhamme patiṭṭhāpento “desanākusalo”ti vuccatīti evamettha atthayojanā veditabbā.

‘He speaks at the right time,’ etc.—this shows the practice of one who abstains from idle chatter. For even speech connected with benefit, if spoken at an improper time, would not bring benefit; thus, it is akin to speech conveying what is not beneficial. Therefore, one abandoning idle chatter should avoid speaking at an improper time—hence, ‘he speaks at the right time.’ Even when speaking at the right time, one should avoid falsehood, as it accomplishes what is not beneficial for both parties—hence, ‘he speaks truthfully.’ And when speaking truthfully, one should speak only what leads to welfare in this life and the next—to show this, ‘he speaks what is beneficial’ is said. Though speaking what is beneficial, one should not speak merely of worldly matters but should base one’s speech on the supramundane Dhamma—to show this, ‘he speaks the Dhamma’ is said. And to show how the meaning is connected with the supramundane Dhamma, ‘he speaks in accordance with the discipline’ is said. For the meaning, when explained through the aspects of the fivefold discipline of restraint and the fivefold discipline of abandoning, is connected with the supramundane Dhamma because it serves as a cause for attaining Nibbāna. Thus, when meaning is conveyed and endowed with such special qualities, it shines when skill in teaching is present and accomplishes its purpose—not otherwise. To show this, ‘he speaks words worth treasuring’ is said. Now, to elaborate on that skill in teaching, he said, ‘at the right time,’ etc. For when one is questioned on a subject, one discerns the distinctions of categorical answers, etc., regarding the subject matter and presents them appropriately—whether through reasoning, examples, demonstrations, or other means—suited to the occasion. With a talk that is limited and defined in form, yet encompasses a very wide, deep, lofty, and extensive highest meaning, one establishes others in the Dhamma as it truly is, in accordance with their own knowledge and strength. Such a one is called ‘skilled in teaching.’ This is how the meaning should be understood here.

Evaṃ [M 2.0373] paṭipāṭiyā satta mūlasikkhāpadāni vibhajitvā abhijjhādippahānaṃ indriyasaṃvarajāgariyānuyogehi vibhāvetuṃ tampi nīharitvā ācārasīlasseva vibhajanavasena pāḷi pavattāti tadatthaṃ vivarituṃ “bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha bījānaṃ gāmo samūho bījagāmo. Bhūtānaṃ jātānaṃ nibbattānaṃ rukkhagacchalatādīnaṃ samūho bhūtagāmo. Nanu ca rukkhādayo cittarahitatāya na jīvā, cittarahitatā ca paripphandābhāvato chinne viruhanato visadisajātibhāvato catuyoniapariyāpannato ca veditabbā, vuddhi pana pavāḷasilālavaṇānampi vijjatīti na tesaṃ jīvabhāve kāraṇaṃ, visayaggahaṇañca nesaṃ parikappanāmattaṃ supanaṃ viya ciñcādīnaṃ, tathā dohaḷādayo, atha kasmā bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambhā paṭivirati icchitāti? Samaṇasāruppato tannivāsisattānurakkhaṇato ca. Tenevāha – “jīvasaññino hi moghapurisa manussā rukkhasmi”ntiādi (pāci. 89).

Thus, having classified the seven root training rules in order, and having explained the abandoning of covetousness and so forth through restraint of the senses and the practice of wakefulness, and having extracted that, the Pāli proceeds by way of classifying the code of conduct. To clarify its meaning, it is said: “The destruction of seed-plants and plant-life,” and so on. Here, a collection of seeds is called “seed-plants.” A collection of born, produced trees, shrubs, and creepers is called “plant-life.” Now, trees and the like are not living beings because they lack consciousness, and their lack of consciousness is to be understood from the absence of movement, from their regrowing when severed, from their dissimilar nature, and from their not being included in the four kinds of generation. Moreover, growth is also found in things like coral, rocks, and salt, so that is no reason for them to be living beings. Their perception of objects is merely a supposition, like a dream, as in the case of the tamarind and others, and likewise for longings and the like. Why then is refraining from the destruction of seed-plants and plant-life desired? Because it is fitting for an ascetic and because it protects the living beings that dwell therein. Therefore, it is said: “For, foolish man, people are percipient of life in a tree,” and so on (Pāc. 89).

Mūlameva bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ, mūlaṃ bījaṃ etassātipi mūlabījaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Phaḷubījanti pabbabījaṃ. Paccayantarasamavāye sadisaphaluppattiyā visesakāraṇabhāvato viruhanasamatthe [V 2.0341] sāraphale niruḷho bīja-saddo tadatthasaṃsiddhiyā mūlādīsupi kesuci pavattatīti mūlādito nivattanatthaṃ ekena bīja-saddena visesetvā vuttaṃ “bījabīja”nti “rūparūpaṃ, dukkhadukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.327) ca yathā. Kasmā panettha bījagāmabhūtagāmaṃ uddharitvā bījagāmo eva niddiṭṭhoti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, nanu avocumhā “mūlameva bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ, mūlaṃ bījaṃ etassātipi mūlabīja”nti. Tattha purimena bījagāmo niddiṭṭho, dutiyena bhūtagāmo. Duvidhopesa mūlabījañca mūlabījañca mūlabījanti sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesanayena vā uddiṭṭhoti veditabbo. Tenevāha “pañcavidhassā”tiādi. Nīlatiṇarukkhādikassāti allatiṇassa ceva allarukkhādikassa ca. Ādi-saddena osadhigacchalatādīnaṃ saṅgaho.

The root itself is the seed, hence 'root-seed'; or that which has the root as its seed is also a 'root-seed'. The same principle applies to the rest. 'Phaḷubīja' means joint-seed. Because of the concurrence of various conditions, the production of similar fruit, and its special function of being a cause, the term ‘seed’ is established in the sense of essential fruit capable of sprouting. To establish that meaning, the term is also used by some for roots and so forth. To distinguish it from roots and the like, it is specified with the single term ‘seed-proper,’ just as it is said ‘form-proper’ and ‘suffering-proper’ (Saṃ. Ni. 4.327). But why here, having mentioned seed-plants and plant-life, are only seed-plants specified? This should not be seen in that way. Did we not say, ‘The root itself is the seed, hence root-seed; or that which has the root as its seed is also a root-seed’? There, seed-plants are specified by the first definition, and plant-life by the second. This twofold kind should be understood as indicated by the general designation 'root-seed', or by the principle of the single remainder. Therefore, it is said, ‘of five kinds,’ etc. The phrase 'of green grass, trees, etc.' means of both fresh grass and fresh trees, etc. The term ‘etc.’ includes medicinal herbs, shrubs, and vines.

Ekaṃ bhattaṃ ekabhattaṃ, taṃ assa atthīti ekabhattiko. So pana rattibhojanenapi siyāti tannivattanatthaṃ āha “rattūparato”ti. Evampi aparaṇhabhojīpi siyā ekabhattikoti tannivattanatthaṃ “virato vikālabhojanā”ti [M 2.0374] vuttaṃ. Aruṇuggamanato paṭṭhāya yāva majjhanhikā ayaṃ buddhādīnaṃ ariyānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo bhojanassa kālo nāma, tadañño vikālo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana dutiyapadena rattibhojanassa paṭikkhittattā “atikkante majjhanhike yāva sūriyatthaṅgamanā bhojanaṃ vikālabhojanaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ.

One meal is a single meal (ekabhatta); one who has that is a one-meal practitioner (ekabhattiko). But he might also partake of food at night; to prevent that, it is said, “abstaining from night-eating.” Even so, a one-meal practitioner might eat in the afternoon; to prevent that, it is said, “refraining from untimely eating.” From the rising of the dawn until midday is the time for eating that is habitually observed by the noble ones such as the Buddha; any other time is untimely. In the commentary, however, because eating at night is prohibited by the second phrase, it is said, “Eating after midday has passed until sunset is called untimely eating.”

Dārumāsakoti ye vohāraṃ gacchantīti iti-saddena evaṃpakāre dasseti. Aññehi gāhāpane upanikkhittasādiyane ca paṭiggahaṇattho labbhatīti “neva taṃ uggaṇhāti, na uggahāpeti, na upanikkhittaṃ sādiyatī”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā tividhaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ kāyena, vācāya, manasāti. Tattha kāyena paṭiggahaṇaṃ uggaṇhanaṃ, vācāya paṭiggahaṇaṃ uggahāpanaṃ, manasā paṭiggahaṇaṃ sādiyananti tividhampi paṭiggahaṇaṃ ekajjhaṃ gahetvā paṭiggahaṇāti vuttanti āha “neva taṃ uggaṇhātī”tiādi. Esa nayo āmakadhaññapaṭiggahaṇātiādīsupi. Nīvārādiupadhaññassa sāliādimūladhaññantogadhattā vuttaṃ “sattavidhassā”ti. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañca vasāni bhesajjāni acchavasaṃ, macchavasaṃ, susukāvasaṃ, sūkaravasaṃ, gadrabhavasa”nti (mahāva. 262) vuttattā idaṃ odissa anuññātaṃ nāma. Tassa pana “kāle paṭiggahita”nti (mahāva. 262) vuttattā paṭiggahaṇaṃ vaṭṭati sati paccayeti āha “aññatra odissa anuññātā”ti.

In 'dārumāsakoti', the word 'iti' indicates such kinds of things that are in common usage. Since the meaning of 'receiving' also applies to causing others to take something and to consenting to what has been deposited, it is said, “He neither takes it himself, nor causes it to be taken, nor consents to what is deposited.” Alternatively, there are three kinds of receiving: by body, by speech, and by mind. Therein, receiving by body is taking, receiving by speech is causing it to be taken, and receiving by mind is consenting. Thus, all three kinds of receiving, taken together, are called “receiving,” as stated in “He neither takes it himself,” etc. The same principle applies to receiving raw grain, etc. Because secondary grains like wild rice are included within primary grains like cultivated rice, it is said, “of seven kinds.” Because it is said, “I allow, monks, five kinds of medicinal fats: bear fat, fish fat, alligator fat, pig fat, and donkey fat” (Mahāvagga 262), this is called specifically permitted. However, because it is said, “received at the proper time” (Mahāvagga 262), receiving is allowed when there is a reason; therefore it is said, “except what is specifically permitted.”

Sāruppena vañcanaṃ rūpakūṭaṃ, patirūpena vañcanāti attho. Aṅgena attano sarīrāvayavena vañcanaṃ [V 2.0342] aṅgakūṭaṃ. Gaṇhanavasena vañcanaṃ gahaṇakūṭaṃ. Paṭicchannaṃ katvā vañcanaṃ paṭicchannakūṭaṃ. Akkamatīti nippīḷeti, pubbabhāge akkamatīti sambandho. Hadayanti nāḷiādimānabhājanānaṃ abbhantaraṃ. Telādīnaṃ nāḷiādīhi minanakāle ussāpitā sikhāyeva sikhābhedo, tassā hāpanaṃ. Kecīti sārasamāsācariyā uttaravihāravāsino ca.

Deception by means of what is similar is “deception by appearance,” meaning deception by what is counterfeit. Deception by means of a limb, one’s own bodily part, is “deception by limb.” Deception by way of grasping is “deception by grasping.” Deception by making something hidden is “hidden deception.” “Tramples” means oppresses; the connection is “he tramples on the front part.” “Heart” refers to the interior of measuring vessels such as tubes. When measuring oil and so forth with tubes and so forth, “peak-breaking” is the lowering of the raised peak. “Some” refers to the teachers of the Sārasamāsa and the residents of the Uttaravihāra.

Vadhoti muṭṭhippahārakasātāḷanādīhi hiṃsanaṃ, viheṭhananti attho. Viheṭhanatthopi hi vadha-saddo dissati “attānaṃ vadhitvā vadhitvā rodatī”tiādīsu. Yathā hi apaṭiggahabhāvasāmaññe satipi pabbajitehi appaṭiggahitabbavatthuvisesabhāvasandassanatthaṃ itthikumāridāsidāsādayo vibhāgena vuttā, evaṃ parassaharaṇabhāvato adinnādānabhāvasāmaññe satipi [M 2.0375] tulākūṭādayo adinnādānavisesabhāvadassanatthaṃ vibhāgena vuttā. Na evaṃ pāṇātipātapariyāyassa vadhassa puna gahaṇe payojanaṃ atthi, tattha sayaṃkāro, idha paraṃkāroti ca na sakkā vattuṃ “kāyavacippayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā chappayogā”ti (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.10) vacanato, tasmā yathāvutto evamettha attho yutto. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “vadhoti māraṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Tampi pothanameva sandhāyāti ca sakkā viññātuṃ māraṇasaddassa vihiṃsanepi dissanato.

'Vadha' is harming with fist-blows, slaps, and the like; the meaning is torment. The term 'vadha' is also seen in the sense of torment, as in phrases like “having tormented himself again and again, he weeps.” Just as, despite the general principle of non-acceptance, specific items that should not be accepted by the ordained, like women, girls, male and female slaves, etc., are separately mentioned to show the specific nature of prohibited objects—so too, despite the general principle of taking what is not given, specific forms like using false weights, etc., are separately mentioned to show particular instances of taking what is not given. In the same way, there is no purpose in taking up 'vadha' again as a synonym for 'pāṇātipāta' (destroying life). And it cannot be said that the former refers to an action done by oneself and the latter to an action done by another, because of the statement, “Volition that originates bodily and verbal action has six applications” (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.10). Therefore, the meaning here is fitting as stated above. In the commentary, however, it is said, “'Vadha' is killing.” That too can be understood as referring to striking, since the term ‘killing’ is also seen in the sense of harming.

Cīvarapiṇḍapātānaṃ yathākkamaṃ kāyakucchipariharaṇamattajotanāyaṃ avisesato aṭṭhannaṃ parikkhārānaṃ tappayojanatā sambhavatīti dassento “te sabbepī”tiādimāha. Etepīti navaparikkhārikādayopi appicchā ca santuṭṭhā ca. Na hi tattakena mahicchatā asantuṭṭhitā hotīti.

He said, 'All of them too,' etc., to show that the purposefulness of all eight requisites is possible without distinction, for the mere maintenance of the body and belly, just as it is for robes and almsfood respectively. 'These too' means that those with nine requisites and so on are also of few wishes and are contented. For with just that much, one is not of great wishes or discontented.

Catūsu disāsu sukhaṃ viharati, tato eva sukhavihāraṭṭhānabhūtā catasso disā assa santīti cātuddiso. Tattha cāyaṃ satte vā saṅkhāre vā bhayena nappaṭihaññatīti appaṭigho. Dvādasavidhassa santosassa vasena santussanato santussamāno. Itarītarenāti uccāvacena parissayānaṃ bāhirānaṃ sīhabyagghādīnaṃ, abbhantarānañca kāmacchandādīnaṃ kāyacittūpaddavānaṃ abhibhavanato parissayānaṃ sahitā. Bandhanabhāvakarabhayābhāvena acchambhi. Eko asahāyo. Tato eva khaggamigasiṅgasadisatāya khaggavisāṇakappo careyyāti attho.

In the four directions, one dwells happily; for that reason, the four directions are the grounds for his happy dwelling—hence, ‘one of the four directions.’ Therein, this being is not repelled by fear on account of beings or conditioned phenomena—thus, ‘unobstructed.’ Being contented through the twelve kinds of satisfaction, he is contented. He endures dangers by overcoming, by one means or another, various external dangers such as lions and tigers, and internal bodily and mental afflictions such as sensual desire. Unperturbed because there is no fear that causes bondage. Solitary, without a companion. Thus, like a rhinoceros horn, one should wander—this is the meaning.

Chinnapakkho, asañjātapakkho vā sakuṇo gantuṃ na sakkotīti pakkhi-saddena visesetvā sakuṇo pāḷiyaṃ vuttoti āha “pakkhayutto sakuṇo”ti. Yassa sannidhikāraparibhogo kiñci ṭhapetabbaṃ sāpekkhāṭhapanañca natthi, tādiso ayaṃ bhikkhūti dassento “ayamettha [V 2.0343] saṅkhepattho”tiādimāha. Ariyanti apenti tato dosā, tehi vā ārakāti ariyoti āha “ariyenāti niddosenā”ti. Ajjhattanti attani. Niddosasukhanti nirāmisasukhaṃ kilesavajjarahitattā.

A bird with clipped wings or undeveloped wings cannot go; therefore, in the Pāli, the word 'bird' is specified by the word 'winged,' thus he says, 'a bird endowed with wings.' Showing that this monk is one for whom there is no consumption by storing up, nor any storing up with expectation, he says, 'This here is the brief meaning,' and so on. 'Noble' is so-called because faults depart from him, or because he is far from them; thus it is said: 'by the noble, that is, by the faultless.' 'Internal' means in oneself. 'Faultless happiness' is non-carnal happiness, because it is devoid of the fault of the defilements.

Yathāvutte sīlasaṃvare patiṭṭhitasseva indriyasaṃvaro icchitabbo tadadhiṭṭhānato tassa ca paripālakabhāvatoti vuttaṃ “so iminā ariyena [M 2.0376] sīlakkhandhena samannāgato bhikkhū”ti. Sesapadesūti “na nimittaggāhī hotī”tiādipadesu. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – na nimittaggāhīti itthipurisanimittaṃ vā subhanimittādikaṃ vā kilesavatthubhūtaṃ nimittaṃ na gaṇhāti, diṭṭhamatteyeva saṇṭhāti. Nānubyañjanaggāhīti kilesānaṃ anu anu byañjanato pākaṭabhāvakaraṇato anubyañjanantiladdhavohāraṃ hatthapādasitahasitakathitavilokitādibhedaṃ ākāraṃ na gaṇhāti. Yaṃ tattha bhūtaṃ, tadeva gaṇhāti. Yatvādhikaraṇamenantiādimhi yaṃkāraṇā yassa cakkhundriyāsaṃvarassa hetu etaṃ puggalaṃ satikavāṭena cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ apihitacakkhudvāraṃ hutvā viharantaṃ ete abhijjhādayo dhammā anvassaveyyuṃ anuppabandheyyuṃ. Tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjatīti tassa cakkhundriyassa satikavāṭena pidahanatthāya paṭipajjati. Evaṃ paṭipajjantoyeva ca “rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti vuccati. Sotena saddaṃ sutvātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Evamidaṃ saṅkhepato rūpādīsu kilesānubandhanimittādiggāhaparivajjanalakkhaṇaṃ indriyasaṃvaraṃ sīlaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāsu (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 1.13) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Kilesehi anavasittasukhantiādīsu rūpādīsu nimittādiggāhaparivajjanalakkhaṇattā indriyasaṃvarassa kilesehi anavasittasukhatā avikiṇṇasukhatā cassa vuttā.

For one established in the aforementioned restraint of virtue, restraint of the sense faculties should be desired, for it is its foundation and its protector. Thus it is said, "A bhikkhu endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue." The remaining passages refer to such phrases as "he is not one who grasps at signs." Here is the condensed meaning: "Not grasping at signs" means he does not grasp at signs that are grounds for defilements, such as signs of women or men, or beautiful marks and the like; he merely stands firm in what is seen. "Not grasping at secondary features" means he does not grasp at modes of behavior—such as gestures of hands and feet, smiles, laughter, speech, or glances—that are conventionally termed "secondary features" because they repeatedly make defilements evident. He grasps only what is actual there. In the passage beginning with "for whatever reason," the meaning is this: Due to that reason, because of the unrestraint of the eye faculty, these states of covetousness and so on would flow in and cling to this person who dwells with the eye faculty unguarded by the door of mindfulness, with the eye-door unclosed. "He practices for its restraint" means he practices for the purpose of closing off that eye faculty with the door of mindfulness. And by practicing thus, it is said, "he guards the eye faculty, he enters upon restraint of the eye faculty." The same method applies to passages beginning with "having heard a sound with the ear," and so on. Thus, in brief, this restraint of the sense faculties, which is a virtue characterized by avoiding the grasping of signs and secondary features connected with defilements regarding forms and so on, should be understood. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the commentaries on the Visuddhimagga (Vism. Mahāṭī. 1.13). In passages such as "happiness unassailed by defilements," because restraint of the sense faculties is characterized by avoiding the grasping of signs and the like regarding forms and so on, its happiness unassailed by defilements and unscattered happiness are stated.

Abhikkamanaṃ abhikkanto, purato gamanaṃ. Paṭikkamanaṃ paṭikkanto, paccāgamanaṃ. Tadubhayampi catūsu iriyāpathesu labbhati. Gamane tāva purato kāyaṃ abhiharanto abhikkamati nāma, paṭinivattento paṭikkamati nāma. Ṭhānepi ṭhitakova kāyaṃ purato oṇamanto abhikkamati nāma, pacchato apanāmento paṭikkamati nāma. Nisajjāyapi nisinnakova āsanassa purimaaṅgābhimukho saṃsaranto abhikkamati nāma, pacchimaṃ aṅgappadesaṃ paccāsaṃsaranto paṭikkamati nāma. Nipajjāyapi eseva nayo.

Going forward is 'abhikkamana,' which means advancing. Going backward is 'paṭikkamana,' which means returning. Both of these are found in the four postures. In walking, when one moves the body forward, it is called 'abhikkamati'; when one turns back, it is called 'paṭikkamati.' Even while standing, if one bends the body forward, it is called 'abhikkamati'; if one draws the body backward, it is called 'paṭikkamati.' Even while sitting, if one shifts towards the front part of the seat, it is called 'abhikkamati'; if one shifts back towards the back part of the seat, it is called 'paṭikkamati.' The same method applies to lying down.

Sātthakasampajaññantiādīsu samantato pakārehi, pakaṭṭhaṃ vā savisesaṃ jānātīti sampajāno, sampajānassa bhāvo sampajaññaṃ, tathāpavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Dhammato vaḍḍhisaṅkhātena saha atthena [V 2.0344] vattatīti sātthakaṃ, abhikkantādisātthakassa sampajaññaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Sappāyassa attano upakārāvahassa sampajaññaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Abhikkamādīsu [M 2.0377] bhikkhācāragocare, aññatthāpi pavattesu avijahitakammaṭṭhānasaṅkhāte gocare sampajaññaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ. Abhikkamādīsu asammuyhanameva sampajaññaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ. Tattha (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.214; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.109) abhikkamanacitte uppanne cittavaseneva agantvā “kinnu me ettha gatena attho atthi natthī”ti atthānatthaṃ pariggahetvā atthapariggahaṇaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Tattha ca atthoti cetiyadassanabodhidassanasaṅghadassanatheradassanaasubhadassanādivasena dhammato vaḍḍhi. Cetiyaṃ vā bodhiṃ vā disvāpi hi buddhārammaṇaṃ, saṅghadassanena saṅghārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ uppādetvā tadeva khayavayato sammasanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. There disvā tesaṃ ovāde patiṭṭhāya asubhaṃ disvā tattha paṭhamajjhānaṃ uppādetvā tadeva khayavayato sammasanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmā etesaṃ dassanaṃ “sātthaka”nti vuttaṃ. Keci pana “āmisatopi vaḍḍhi atthoyeva taṃ nissāya brahmacariyānuggahāya paṭipannattā”ti vadanti.

In the terms such as 'clear comprehension with a purpose' (sātthakasampajañña), etc., 'clearly comprehending' (sampajāno) means knowing in all aspects, or knowing excellently and specifically. The state of being clearly comprehending is clear comprehension (sampajañña), which is knowledge that proceeds accordingly. 'With a purpose' (sātthaka) refers to what proceeds with meaning, which is designated as growth in the Dhamma. Clear comprehension of what has a purpose, such as going forward, etc., is 'clear comprehension with a purpose' (sātthakasampajañña). Clear comprehension of what is suitable, bringing benefit to oneself, is 'clear comprehension of suitability' (sappāyasampajañña). Clear comprehension of the domain—in the sphere of a bhikkhu’s alms-round conduct, such as going forward, etc., or in other situations where the meditation subject is not abandoned—is 'clear comprehension of the domain' (gocarasampajañña). Clear comprehension as non-delusion in activities like going forward, etc., is 'clear comprehension of non-delusion' (asammohasampajañña). Here (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.214; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.109), when a thought of going forward arises, one should not proceed merely due to the thought itself, but rather consider: 'What benefit or non-benefit is there for me in going there?' The grasping of the benefit is 'clear comprehension with a purpose.' In this context, 'benefit' refers to growth in the Dhamma in connection with seeing shrines, the Bodhi tree, the Saṅgha, elders, or foul objects, and so on. For instance, upon seeing a shrine or the Bodhi tree, one can generate joy with the Buddha as the object, and by contemplating just that in terms of decay and vanishing, one attains arahantship. Having seen elders and established oneself in their advice, or having seen a foul object and generated the first jhāna based on it, one attains arahantship by contemplating just that in terms of decay and vanishing. Therefore, such seeing is called 'with a purpose.' Some, however, say that even growth from material things is a purpose, since relying on it, one undertakes the practice for the support of the holy life.

Tasmiṃ pana gamane sappāyāsappāyaṃ pariggahetvā sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ – cetiyadassanaṃ tāva sātthaṃ. Sace pana cetiyassa mahāpūjāya dasadvādasayojanantare parisā sannipatanti, attano vibhavānurūpaṃ itthiyopi purisāpi alaṅkatapaṭiyattā cittakammarūpakāni viya sañcaranti. Tatra cassa iṭṭhe ārammaṇe lobho, aniṭṭhe paṭigho, asamapekkhane moho uppajjati, kāyasaṃsaggāpattiṃ vā āpajjati, jīvitabrahmacariyānaṃ vā antarāyo hoti. Evaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ asappāyaṃ hoti, vuttappakāraantarāyābhāve sappāyaṃ. Bodhidassanepi eseva nayo. Saṅghadassanampi sātthaṃ. Sace pana antogāme mahāmaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā sabbarattiṃ dhammassavanaṃ karontesu manussesu vuttappakāreneva janasannipāto ceva antarāyo ca hoti. Evaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ asappāyaṃ, antarāyābhāve sappāyaṃ. Mahāparisāparivārānaṃ therānaṃ dassanepi eseva nayo. Asubhadassanampi sātthaṃ maggaphalādhigamahetubhāvato. Dantakaṭṭhatthāya sāmaṇeraṃ gahetvā gatadaharabhikkhuno vatthupettha kathetabbaṃ. Evaṃ sātthampi panetaṃ purisassa mātugāmāsubhaṃ asappāyaṃ, mātugāmassa ca purisāsubhaṃ. Sabhāgameva sappāyanti evaṃ sappāyapariggaṇhanaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ nāma.

In that journey, discerning what is suitable and unsuitable and then taking up what is suitable is 'awareness of suitability' (sappāyasampajañña). For example, seeing a shrine is beneficial. However, if for a great festival at the shrine, crowds gather within a distance of ten or twelve yojanas, and men and women, adorned according to their wealth, move about like painted figures, then desire may arise toward pleasant objects, aversion toward unpleasant ones, and delusion toward those not properly attended to. One may commit an offense involving bodily contact or face obstacles to one's life and the holy life. Thus, such a place is unsuitable; if such obstacles as mentioned are absent, it is suitable. The same method applies to seeing the Bodhi tree. Seeing the Saṅgha is also beneficial. But if a great pavilion is built within a village and people listen to the Dhamma all night, the same issues of crowds and obstacles as mentioned arise. Thus, such a place is unsuitable; if obstacles are absent, it is suitable. The same method applies to seeing elders surrounded by large assemblies. Seeing the unattractive is beneficial, as it is a cause for attaining the path and fruition. Here, the story of the young bhikkhu who went with a novice to get a tooth-stick should be told. Though this practice is beneficial, for a man, the contemplation of the unattractive aspects of a woman is unsuitable, and for a woman, the contemplation of the unattractive aspects of a man is unsuitable. Only what is of a similar kind is suitable. Thus, discerning what is suitable is called awareness of suitability.

Evaṃ [M 2.0378] pariggahitasātthakasappāyassa pana aṭṭhatiṃsāya kammaṭṭhānesu attano cittaruciyaṃ kammaṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ gocaraṃ uggahetvā bhikkhācāragocare taṃ gahetvāva gamanaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ nāma.

For one who has thus discerned what is beneficial and suitable, taking up a meditation subject—a 'field'—from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects according to one's own mental inclination, and then going into the alms-round domain while holding to it, is called 'awareness of the field' (gocarasampajañña).

Abhikkamādīsu [V 2.0345] pana asammuyhanaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ. Taṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ – idha bhikkhu abhikkamanto vā paṭikkamanto vā yathā andhaputhujjanā abhikkamādīsu “attā abhikkamati, attanā abhikkamo nibbattito”ti vā, “ahaṃ abhikkamāmi, mayā abhikkamo nibbattito”ti vā sammuyhanti, tathā asammuyhanto “abhikkamāmī”ti citte uppajjamāne teneva cittena saddhiṃ cittasamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati, iti cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravasena ayaṃ kāyasammato aṭṭhisaṅghāṭo abhikkamati, tassevaṃ abhikkamato ekekapaduddharaṇe pathavīdhātu, āpodhātūti dve dhātuyo omattā honti mandā, itarā dve adhimattā honti balavatiyo. Tathā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesu. Vossajjane tejodhātu, vāyodhātūti dve dhātuyo omattā honti mandā, itarā dve adhimattā balavatiyo. Tathā sannikkhepanasannirumbhanesu. Tattha uddharaṇe pavattā rūpārūpadhammā atiharaṇaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tathā atiharaṇe pavattā vītiharaṇaṃ, vītiharaṇe pavattā vossajjanaṃ, vossajjane pavattā sannikkhepanaṃ, sannikkhepane pavattā sannirumbhanaṃ na pāpuṇanti. Tattha tattheva pabbapabbaṃ sannisandhi odhiodhi hutvā tattakapāle pakkhittatilaṃ viya paṭapaṭāyantā bhijjanti. Tattha ko eko abhikkamati, kassa vā ekassa abhikkamanaṃ? Paramatthato hi dhātūnaṃyeva gamanaṃ, dhātūnaṃ ṭhānaṃ, dhātūnaṃ nisajjanaṃ, dhātūnaṃ sayanaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiñhi koṭṭhāse saddhiṃ rūpena –

Regarding going forward and other activities, non-confusion is 'awareness free from delusion' (asammohasampajañña). This should be understood thus: here, when a bhikkhu goes forward or backward, he is not confused like blind ordinary people who, in going forward and other activities, become confused, thinking, 'The self goes forward, going forward is produced by the self,' or 'I go forward, going forward is produced by me.' Being unconfused, when the thought 'I am going forward' arises in the mind, together with that thought, the mind-born wind element arises, generating bodily intimation. Thus, this collection of bones called a 'body' goes forward by means of the activity of the mind and the diffusion of the wind element. As it goes forward thus, with each lifting of a foot, the earth element and water element become diminished and weak, while the other two become excessive and strong. The same applies to carrying forward and moving past. In putting down the foot, the fire element and wind element become diminished and weak, while the other two become excessive and strong. The same applies to placing down and pressing firm. Therein, the material and immaterial phenomena that occur during lifting do not reach the carrying forward; similarly, those that occur during carrying forward do not reach the moving past; those that occur during moving past do not reach the putting down; those that occur during putting down do not reach the placing down; and those that occur during placing down do not reach the pressing firm. There, at each and every point, they break up, joint by joint, connection by connection, part by part, sputtering like sesame seeds thrown onto a hot pan. Therein, what single being goes forward, or whose is this going forward? In the ultimate sense, it is merely the elements that go, the elements that stand, the elements that sit, the elements that lie down. In each and every part, together with form—

“Aññaṃ uppajjate cittaṃ, aññaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhati;

Avīcimanusambandho, nadīsotova vattatī”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.214; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.109; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.368);

One mind arises, another mind ceases; as an uninterrupted continuity, it flows on like the current of a river.

Evaṃ abhikkamādīsu asammuyhanaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ nāmāti. Paccayasampattinti paccayapāripūriṃ. Ime cattāroti sīlasaṃvaro, santoso, indriyasaṃvaro, satisampajaññanti ime cattāro araññavāsassa sambhārā[M 2.0379]. Vattabbataṃ āpajjatīti “asukassa bhikkhuno araññe tiracchānagatānaṃ viya vanacarakānaṃ viya ca nivāsamattameva, na araññavāsānucchavikā kāci sammāpaṭipattī”ti apavādavasena vattabbataṃ, āraññakehi vā tiracchānagatehi vanacarakavisabhāgajanehi vippaṭipattivasena vatthabbataṃ āpajjati. Bheravasaddaṃ sāventi, tāvatā apalāyantānaṃ hatthehi sīsaṃ…pe… karonti. Kāḷakasadisattā kāḷakaṃ, vītikkamasaṅkhātaṃ thullavajjaṃ. Tilakasadisattā tilakaṃ, micchāvitakkasaṅkhātaṃ aṇumattavajjaṃ. Tanti pītiṃ. Vibhūtabhāvena upaṭṭhānato khayato sammasanto.

Thus, non-confusion in regard to going forward and so on is called 'awareness free from delusion.' 'Fulfillment of conditions' means the complete fulfillment of requisites. 'These four' means: restraint through virtue, contentment, restraint of the sense faculties, and mindfulness with clear comprehension—these four are the provisions for dwelling in the forest. 'He becomes subject to criticism' means he becomes subject to reproach in this way: 'For such and such a bhikkhu, dwelling in the forest is merely a residence, like that of beasts or forest-folk; there is no right practice befitting a forest-dweller.' Or, he becomes subject to criticism due to wrong practice, being dissimilar to true forest-dwellers, beasts, and other forest-folk. They make a terrifying sound, and for those who do not flee from it, they... with their hands on their heads... 'Kāḷakaṃ' (a black mark), so called because of its resemblance to something black, is a gross offense, reckoned as a transgression. 'Tilakaṃ' (a sesame seed mark), so called because of its resemblance to a sesame seed, is a minute offense, reckoned as a wrong thought. 'Tanti' (a thread) means rapture. Contemplating from the standpoint of destruction, due to its manifest appearance.

Vivittanti [V 2.0346] janavivittaṃ. Tenāha “suñña”nti. Taṃ pana janasaddanigghosābhāvena veditabbaṃ saddakaṇṭakattā jhānassāti āha “appasaddaṃ appanigghosanti attho”ti. Etadevāti nissaddataṃyeva. Vihāro pākāraparicchinno sakalo āvāso. Aḍḍhayogo dīghapāsādo, “garuḷasaṇṭhānapāsādo”tipi vadanti. Pāsādo caturassapāsādo. Hammiyaṃ muṇḍacchadanapāsādo. Aṭṭo paṭirājūnaṃ paṭibāhanayoggo catuppañcabhūmako patissayaviseso. Māḷo ekakūṭasaṅgahito anekakoṇavanto patissayaviseso. Aparo nayo – vihāro nāma dīghamukhapāsādo. Aḍḍhayogo ekapassacchadanakasenāsanaṃ. Tassa kira ekapasse bhitti uccatarā hoti, itarapasse nīcā. Etena taṃ ekapassacchadanakaṃ hoti. Pāsādo nāma āyatacaturassapāsādo. Hammiyaṃ muṇḍacchadanaṃ candikaṅgaṇayuttaṃ. Guhā nāma kevalā pabbataguhā. Leṇaṃ dvārabaddhaṃ pabbhāraṃ. Maṇḍapoti sākhāmaṇḍapo. Āvasathabhūtaṃ senāsanaṃ viharitabbaṭṭhena vihārasenāsanaṃ. Masārakādi mañcapīṭhaṃ tattha attharitabbabhisi upadhānañca mañcapīṭhasambandhato mañcapīṭhasenāsanaṃ. Cimilikādi bhūmiyaṃ santharitabbatāya santhatasenāsanaṃ. Abhisaṅkhatābhāvato kevalaṃ sayanassa nisajjāya ca okāsabhūtaṃ rukkhamūlādi paṭikkamitabbaṭṭhānaṃ okāsasenāsanaṃ. Senāsanaggahaṇena gahitamevāti “vivittaṃ senāsana”nti iminā senāsanaggahaṇena gahitameva sāmaññajotanābhāvato.

'Secluded' means secluded from people. Therefore, he said 'empty' (suñña). This should be understood as the absence of the sound and clamor of people, for he said, 'sound is a thorn to jhāna'; the meaning is 'with little sound, with little noise.' This very thing is silence. A 'vihāra' is an entire residence enclosed by a wall. An 'aḍḍhayoga' is a long mansion; some also call it a 'garuḷa-shaped mansion.' A 'pāsāda' is a square mansion. A 'hammiya' is a mansion with a flat roof. An 'aṭṭa' is a particular type of lodging, a four or five-storied watchtower suitable for repelling enemy kings. A 'māḷa' is a particular type of lodging with a single pinnacle and many corners. Another method: a 'vihāra' is a mansion with a long facade. An 'aḍḍhayoga' is a lodging with a lean-to roof; it is said that on one side the wall is higher, and on the other side lower, thus it has a lean-to roof. A 'pāsāda' is a rectangular mansion. A 'hammiya' is a flat-roofed building with a moonlit terrace. A 'guhā' is simply a mountain cave. A 'leṇa' is a hillside shelter fitted with a door. A 'maṇḍapa' is a pavilion of branches. A lodging that is a residence is a 'dwelling-lodging' (vihārasenāsana) because it is a place to dwell. A bed or bench such as a masāraka, and the mattress and pillow to be spread on it, is a 'bed-and-bench lodging' (mañcapīṭhasenāsana) due to its connection with a bed and bench. A ground-covering such as a cimilikā is a 'spread-lodging' (santhatasenāsana) because it is to be spread on the ground. A place to resort to, such as the root of a tree, which is merely a space for lying down and sitting and is not constructed, is an 'open-space lodging' (okāsasenāsana). It is already included by the term 'lodging.' Thus, by the use of the term 'lodging' in the phrase 'a secluded lodging,' it is already included, because this does not denote a mere generality.

Yadi evaṃ kasmā “arañña”nti vuttanti āha “imassa panā”tiādi. Bhikkhunīnaṃ vasena āgatanti idaṃ vinaye tathā āgataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ[M 2.0380], abhidhammepi (vibha. 529) pana “araññanti nikkhamitvā bahi indakhilā sabbametaṃ arañña”nti āgatameva. Tattha hi yaṃ na gāmappadesantogadhaṃ, taṃ araññanti nippariyāyavasena tathā vuttaṃ. Dhutaṅganiddese (visuddhi. 1.31) yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ, tasmā tattha vuttanayena gahetabbanti adhippāyo. Rukkhamūlanti rukkhasamīpaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “yāvatā majjhanhike kāle samantā chāyā pharati, nivāte paṇṇāni patanti, ettāvatā rukkhamūla”nti. Sela-saddo avisesato pabbatapariyāyoti katvā vuttaṃ “pabbatanti sela”nti, na silāmayameva. Paṃsumayādiko hi tividhopi pabbato evāti. Vivaranti dvinnaṃ pabbatānaṃ mitho āsannatare ṭhitānaṃ ovarakādisadisaṃ vivaraṃ. Ekasmiṃyeva vā pabbate. Umaṅgasadisanti suduṅgāsadisaṃ. Manussānaṃ anupacāraṭṭhānanti pakatisañcāravasena manussehi na sañcaritabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Ādi-saddena “vanapatthanti vanasaṇḍānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vanapatthanti bhiṃsanakānametaṃ. Vanapatthanti salomahaṃsānametaṃ. Vanapatthanti pariyantānametaṃ. Vanapatthanti na manussūpacārānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacana”nti (vibha. 531) imaṃ pāḷippadesaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Acchannanti kenaci chadanena antamaso rukkhasākhāyapi na chāditaṃ. Nikkaḍḍhitvāti nīharitvā. Pabbhāraleṇasadiseti pabbhārasadise, leṇasadise vā.

If so, why is it called 'forest'? He says, 'But in this case,' and so on. This is spoken with reference to what has come down in the Vinaya concerning bhikkhunīs. In the Abhidhamma, too (Vibhaṅga 529), it is said: 'Forest means having gone out beyond the boundary post; all this is forest.' There, indeed, whatever is not included within the vicinity of a village is called 'forest' in an unqualified sense. What is said in the Dhutaṅga-niddesa (Visuddhimagga 1.31) is appropriate; therefore, the intention is that it should be understood according to the method stated there. 'The foot of a tree' means near a tree. For it is said: 'As far as the shadow extends at midday all around, and as far as leaves fall in a windless place—that is the foot of a tree.' The word 'sela' is used here without distinction as a synonym for 'mountain,' hence it is said 'mountain means sela,' not exclusively a rocky mountain. For a mountain is indeed of three kinds, such as one made of earth. 'A cleft' means a hollow space resembling a recess, etc., between two closely situated mountains, or even within a single mountain. 'Like a tunnel' means similar to a deep tunnel. 'A place not frequented by people' means a place where people do not ordinarily travel. The word 'etc.' includes this Pāli passage: 'Wilderness' is a term for these remote forest dwellings. 'Wilderness' is a term for these frightening places. 'Wilderness' is a term for these places that make the hair stand on end. 'Wilderness' is a term for these boundary places. 'Wilderness' is a term for these dwellings not frequented by people (Vibhaṅga 531). 'Uncovered' means not covered by any covering, not even by a tree branch. 'Having removed' means having taken out. 'Like a mountain slope or a cave' means similar to a mountain slope, or similar to a cave.

Piṇḍapātapariyesanaṃ [V 2.0347] piṇḍapāto uttarapadalopenāti āha “piṇḍapātapariyesanato paṭikkanto”ti. Pallaṅkanti ettha pari-saddo samantatoti etasmiṃ atthe, tasmā vāmoruṃ dakkhiṇoruñca samaṃ ṭhapetvā ubho pāde aññamaññaṃ sambandhe katvā nisajjā pallaṅkanti āha “samantato ūrubaddhāsana”nti. Ūrūnaṃ bandhanavasena nisajjā pallaṅkaṃ. Ābhujitvāti ca yathā pallaṅkavasena nisajjā hoti, evaṃ ubho pāde ābhujite samiñjite katvā. Taṃ pana ubhinnaṃ pādānaṃ tathāsambandhatākaraṇanti āha “bandhitvā”ti. Heṭṭhimakāyassa anujukaṃ ṭhapanaṃ nisajjāvacaneneva bodhitanti ujuṃ kāyanti ettha kāya-saddo uparimakāyavisayoti āha “uparimasarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā”ti. Taṃ pana ujukaṃ ṭhapanaṃ sarūpato payojanato ca dassetuṃ “aṭṭhārasā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Na paṇamantīti na oṇamanti. Na paripatatīti na vigacchati vīthiṃ na laṅgheti, tato [M 2.0381] eva pubbenāparaṃ visesasampattiyā kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuddhiṃ phātiṃ gacchati. Parimukhanti ettha pari-saddo abhi-saddena samānatthoti āha “kammaṭṭhānābhimukha”nti, bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇato nivāretvā kammaṭṭhānaṃyeva purakkhatvāti attho. Samīpattho vā pari-saddoti dassento “mukhasamīpe vā katvā”ti āha. Ettha ca yathā “vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajatī”tiādinā bhāvanānurūpaṃ senāsanaṃ dassitaṃ, evaṃ nisīdatīti iminā alīnānuddhaccapakkhiyo santo iriyāpatho dassito. “Pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā”ti iminā nisajjāya daḷhabhāvo. “Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti iminā ārammaṇapariggahūpāyo.

`Piṇḍapātapariyesanaṃ` (seeking almsfood) is `piṇḍapāto` (almsfood) by way of elision of the latter word; hence he says, 'returned from seeking almsfood.' Regarding 'cross-legged': here the prefix 'pari-' means 'all around,' hence sitting with the left thigh and right thigh placed evenly, and with both feet connected to each other, is called 'cross-legged.' He says, 'seated with the thighs bound all around.' The sitting posture with the thighs bound is the cross-legged posture. 'Having bent': just as one sits cross-legged, so too, having bent and drawn in both feet. This act of connecting both feet in such a way is what is meant by 'having bound.' The straight placement of the lower body is understood by the very word 'sitting'; hence regarding 'a straight body,' the word 'body' here refers to the upper body. Thus he says, 'having placed the upper body straight.' To explain this straight placement both in its nature and its purpose, the phrase 'eighteen,' and so on, is stated. 'Not leaning' means not bending downwards. 'Not swaying' means not moving away, not transgressing the path; for that very reason, the meditation subject grows and flourishes due to the attainment of special qualities one after another. Regarding 'in front': here the prefix 'pari-' has the same meaning as 'abhi-,' hence he says, 'facing the meditation subject.' The meaning is that, having prevented various external objects, one places only the meditation subject in front. Or, showing that the prefix 'pari-' has the meaning of proximity, he says, 'or having placed it near the face.' Here, just as a dwelling suitable for cultivation is indicated by phrases like 'resorting to a secluded dwelling,' so too, by 'sits down,' a calm posture on the side of non-sloth and non-restlessness is indicated. By 'having bent his legs cross-wise,' the firmness of the sitting posture is shown. By 'having established mindfulness in front,' the method for grasping the object is shown.

Parīti pariggahaṭṭho “pariṇāyikā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 16, 20) viya. Mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho “suññatavimokkhamukha”ntiādīsu viya. Paṭipakkhato niggamanaṭṭho hi niyyānaṭṭho, tasmā pariggahitaniyyānaṃ satinti sabbathā gahitāsammosaṃ pariccattasammosaṃ satiṃ katvā, paramasatinepakkaṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti attho.

'Pari-' has the meaning of 'grasping,' as in passages such as 'pariṇāyikā' (guide) (Dhs. 16, 20). 'Mukha' has the meaning of 'egress,' as in passages such as 'the door to liberation through emptiness.' For the meaning of egress is emerging from what is contrary. Therefore, 'mindfulness as a grasped egress' means having made mindfulness thoroughly grasped and unconfused, with confusion abandoned, one establishes supreme mindfulness and clear comprehension. This is the meaning.

Abhijjhāyati gijjhati abhikaṅkhati etāyāti abhijjhā, lobho. Lujjanaṭṭhenāti bhijjanaṭṭhena, khaṇe khaṇe bhijjanaṭṭhenāti attho. Vikkhambhanavasenāti ettha vikkhambhanaṃ anuppādanaṃ appavattanaṃ paṭipakkhena suppahīnattā. Pahīnattāti ca pahīnasadisataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ jhānassa anadhigatattā. Tathāpi nayidaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ viya sabhāvato vigatābhijjhaṃ, atha kho bhāvanāvasena. Tenāha “na cakkhuviññāṇasadisenā”ti. Eseva nayoti yathā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ sabhāvena vigatābhijjhaṃ abyāpannañca na bhāvanāya vikkhambhitattā, na evamidaṃ. Idaṃ pana cittaṃ bhāvanāya parisodhitattā abyāpannaṃ vigatathinamiddhaṃ anuddhataṃ nibbicikicchañcāti attho. Purimapakatinti parisuddhapaṇḍarasabhāvaṃ. “Yā tasmiṃ samaye cittassa [V 2.0348] akalyatā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1162; vibha. 546) thinassa, “yā tasmiṃ samaye kāyassa akalyatā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1163; vibha. 546) ca middhassa abhidhamme niddiṭṭhattā vuttaṃ “thinaṃ cittagelaññaṃ, middhaṃ cetasikagelañña”nti. Satipi hi aññamaññaṃ avippayoge cittakāyalahutādīnaṃ viya cittacetasikānaṃ yathākkamaṃ taṃtaṃvisesassa yā tesaṃ akalyatādīnaṃ visesapaccayatā, ayametesaṃ sabhāvoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ālokasaññīti ettha atisayattavisiṭṭhaatthiatthāvabodhakoyamīkāroti dassento āha “rattimpi…pe… samannāgato”ti. Idaṃ ubhayanti satisampajaññamāha.

One covets, desires, and longs for by means of it, thus it is 'covetousness' (`abhijjhā`), which is greed (`lobho`). In the sense of perishing means in the sense of breaking; the meaning is, in the sense of breaking moment by moment. By way of suppression: here, suppression means non-arising, non-occurrence, due to being well abandoned by the opposing factor. And 'abandoned' is said with reference to the similarity to abandonment, because jhāna has not been attained. Still, this is not like eye-consciousness, which is by nature free from covetousness; rather, it is so due to cultivation. Therefore, he said, 'not like eye-consciousness.' This is the method: just as eye-consciousness is by nature free from covetousness and ill will, not because of being suppressed by cultivation, so this is not. But this mind, being purified by cultivation, is free from ill will, free from sloth and torpor, unagitated, and free from doubt—this is the meaning. 'Original nature' means a state of pure and bright nature. Because in the Abhidhamma sloth is defined by 'Whatever unwieldiness of mind there is at that time,' etc. (Dhs. 1162; Vibh. 546), and torpor by 'Whatever unwieldiness of body there is at that time,' etc. (Dhs. 1163; Vibh. 546), it is said: 'Sloth is sickness of the mind, torpor is sickness of mental factors.' For even though they are mutually unassociated, like lightness of mind and body, etc., it should be understood that this is their nature: the specific condition for their respective unwieldiness, etc., is, in due order, the mind and mental factors. Regarding 'perceiving light': here, to show that this long 'ī' sound indicates the meaning of possessing a distinguished quality of excellence, he said, 'even at night... endowed.' This pair refers to mindfulness and clear comprehension.

Atikkamitvāti [M 2.0382] vikkhambhanavasena pajahitvā. Kathamidaṃ kathamidanti pavattiyā kathaṃkathā, vicikicchā, sā etassa atthīti kathaṃkathī, na kathaṃkathīti akathaṃkathī, nibbicikiccho. Lakkhaṇādibhedatoti ettha ādi-saddena paccayaparihānappahāyakādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tepi hi pabhedato daṭṭhabbāti. Ucchinditvā pātentīti ettha ucchindanaṃ pātanañca tāsaṃ paññānaṃ anuppannānaṃ uppajjituṃ appadānameva. Iti mahaggatānuttarapaññānaṃ ekaccāya ca parittapaññāya anuppattihetubhūtā nīvaraṇadhammā itarāya ca samatthataṃ vihanantiyevāti “paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā”ti vuttā. Appentoti nigamento.

'Having overcome' means having abandoned by way of suppression. 'How is this? How is this?' is perplexity regarding occurrence, which is doubt. One who has this is perplexed. Not being perplexed means being unperplexed, free from doubt. Regarding 'by the distinction of characteristic, etc.': here, by the word 'etc.', the inclusion of conditions, decline, the abandoner, etc., should also be understood. For these too should be seen by way of their distinctions. 'Cutting off and casting down' here means simply not giving an opportunity to arise for those wisdoms that have not yet arisen. Thus, the hindering states are causes for the non-arising of exalted and unsurpassed wisdoms and of some limited wisdom, and they indeed obstruct the capability of other limited wisdom; hence, they are called 'weakening of wisdom.' 'Applying' means concluding.

Attantapasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Attantapa Sutta is concluded.

9-10. Taṇhāsuttādivaṇṇanā

9-10. Commentary on the Taṇhā Sutta and others.

199-200. Navame tayo bhave ajjhottharitvā ṭhitaṃ “ajjhattikassa upādāya aṭṭhārasa taṇhāvicaritānī”tiādinā vuttaṃ taṃ taṃ attano koṭṭhāsabhūtaṃ jālametissā atthīti jālinī. Tenāha “tayo vā bhave”tiādi. Tattha tatthāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave, ārammaṇe vā. Apicātiādinā niddesanayena visattikāpadassa atthaṃ dassento niddesapāḷiyā ekadesaṃ dasseti “visamūlā”tiādinā. Ayañhettha niddesapāḷi (mahāni. 3; cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddeso 22, khaggavisāṇasuttaniddeso 124) –

199-200. In the ninth section, having encompassed the three existences, it stands as 'the eighteen craving-activities pertaining to the internal basis of clinging,' and so forth—this is called 'ensnaring' (jālinī) because it has that particular net as its own portion. Hence it is said, 'the three existences,' and so on. Herein, 'therein' means in that particular existence or in the object. By means of 'moreover,' and so on, while showing the meaning of the term visattikā according to the method of the Niddesa, he presents a part of the Niddesa Pāḷi: 'rooted in poison,' and so on. For here is the Niddesa Pāḷi (Mahāni. 3; Cūḷani. Mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddeso 22, Khaggavisāṇasuttaniddeso 124) —

“Visattikāti kenaṭṭhena visattikā? Visatāti visattikā, visaṭāti visattikā, visālāti visattikā, visakkatīti visattikā, visaṃharatīti visattikā, visaṃvādikāti visattikā, visamūlāti visattikā, visaphalāti visattikā[V 2.0349]. Visaparibhogāti visattikā. Visālā vā pana sā taṇhā rūpe sadde gandhe rase phoṭṭhabbe kule gaṇe āvāse lābhe yase pasaṃsāya sukhe cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāre kāmadhātuyā rūpadhātuyā arūpadhātuyā kāmabhave rūpabhave arūpabhave saññibhave asaññibhave nevasaññināsaññibhave [M 2.0383] ekavokārabhave catuvokārabhave pañcavokārabhave atīte anāgate paccuppanne diṭṭhasutamutaviññātabbesu visaṭā vitthatāti visattikā”ti.

'By what meaning is 'visattikā' (clinging) so called? It is called 'visattikā' because it clings ('visatā'). It is called 'visattikā' because it spreads ('visaṭā'). It is called 'visattikā' because it is extensive ('visālā'). It is called 'visattikā' because it entangles ('visakkatī'). It is called 'visattikā' because it carries away ('visaṃharatī'). It is called 'visattikā' because it is deceptive ('visaṃvādikā'). It is called 'visattikā' because its root is poisonous ('visamūlā'). It is called 'visattikā' because its fruit is poisonous ('visaphalā'). It is called 'visattikā' because its consumption is poisonous ('visaparibhogā'). Moreover, that craving is extensive ('visālā'), spread out ('visaṭā'), and extended ('vitthatā') in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects, families, groups, dwelling places, gains, fame, praise, happiness, robes, almsfood, lodgings, medicines and provisions for the sick, requisites; in the sense-sphere, the form-sphere, the formless-sphere; in sense-sphere existence, form-sphere existence, formless-sphere existence; in existence with perception, existence without perception, existence with neither perception nor non-perception; in one-constituent existence, four-constituent existence, five-constituent existence; in the past, the future, and the present; and in things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. Thus, it is called 'visattikā'.

Tattha (mahāni. aṭṭha. 3; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.1 oghataraṇasuttavaṇṇanā) visatāti vitthatā rūpādīsu tebhūmakadhammabyāpanavasena. Visaṭāti purimavacanameva ta-kārassa ṭa-kāraṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Visālāti vipulā. Visakkatīti parisahati. Ratto hi rāgavatthunā parena tāḷiyamānopi sahati, vipphandanaṃ vā “visakkana”nti vadanti. Visaṃharatīti tathā tathā kāmesu ānisaṃsaṃ dassentī vividhehi ākārehi nekkhammābhimukhappavattito cittaṃ saṃharati saṃkhipati. Visaṃ vā dukkhaṃ, taṃ harati upanetīti attho. Aniccādiṃ niccādito gaṇhantī visaṃvādikā hoti. Dukkhanibbattakassa kammassa hetubhāvato visamūlā, visaṃ vā dukkhadukkhādibhūtā vedanā mūlaṃ etissāti visamūlā. Dukkhasamudayattā visaṃ phalaṃ etissāti visaphalā. Taṇhāya rūpādikassa dukkhassa paribhogo hoti, na amatassāti sā visaparibhogā vuttā. Sabbattha niruttivasena padasiddhi veditabbā. Yo panettha padhāno attho, taṃ dassetuṃ puna “visaṭā vā panā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Here (Mahāni. Aṭṭha. 3; Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1.1 Oghataraṇasuttavaṇṇanā), 'visatā' means extensive, by way of pervading phenomena of the three realms, such as form. 'Visaṭā' is the same as the previous term, with the 'ta' sound changed to 'ṭa.' 'Visālā' means vast. 'Visakkatī' means to endure. A passionate person, even when struck by another because of an object of passion, endures; or else, struggling is called 'visakkana.' 'Visaṃharatī' means that, by showing the advantages of sensual pleasures in various ways, it withdraws and contracts the mind from its inclination towards renunciation. Alternatively, 'visaṃ' means suffering, and it brings that; this is the meaning. It is deceptive (visaṃvādikā) by taking the impermanent, etc., as permanent, etc. It is rooted in poison (visamūlā) because it is the cause of kamma that produces suffering, or because poison—that is, feeling in the form of suffering-as-pain and so on—is its root. It bears the fruit of poison (visaphalā) because it is the origin of suffering. Through craving, there is consumption of the suffering of form, etc., not of the deathless—hence it is called 'visaparibhogā.' Everywhere, the establishment of the words should be understood through etymology. To show the principal meaning here, the text beginning 'visaṭā vā pana' is stated again.

Tantaṃ vuccati (dī. ni. ṭī. 2.95 apasādanāvaṇṇanā; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 2.2.60) vatthavinanatthaṃ tantavāyehi daṇḍake āsañcitvā pasāritasuttavaṭṭi “tanīyatī”ti katvā, taṃ pana suttaṃ santānākulatāya nidassanabhāvena ākulameva gahitanti āha “tantaṃ viya ākulajāto”ti. Saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ “yathā nāmā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Samānetunti pubbenāparaṃ samaṃ katvā ānetuṃ, avisamaṃ ujuṃ kātunti attho. Tantameva vā ākulaṃ tantākulaṃ, tantākulaṃ viya jāto bhūtoti tantākulakajāto. Vinanato gulāti itthiliṅgavasena laddhanāmassa tantavāyassa guṇṭhikaṃ nāma ākulabhāvena aggato vā mūlato vā duviññeyyameva khalibaddhatantasuttanti āha “gulāguṇṭhikaṃ vuccati pesakārakañjiyasutta”nti.

The term 'tantaṃ' (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 2.95 Apasādanāvaṇṇanā; Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 2.2.60) refers to a roll of thread stretched out by weavers for weaving cloth, having wound it on a rod, because it is 'stretched' (tanīyatī). But that thread, due to its continuous entanglement, is taken as an example of confusion—hence the phrase 'tantaṃ viya ākulajāto' (born confused like a tangled thread). To explain the meaning given briefly, the text beginning 'yathā nāmā' is stated. 'Samānetuṃ' means to bring the latter part even with the former; that is, to make it straight and not uneven. Alternatively, the tangled thread itself is 'tantākulaṃ,' and one born like a tangled thread is 'tantākulakajāto.' Because of weaving, 'gulā' is the name given in the feminine gender to the weaver's ball of thread (guṇṭhikaṃ), which is the thread fastened to the shuttle, so tangled at its beginning or end that it is difficult to discern. Hence it is said: 'A tangled ball (gulāguṇṭhikaṃ) is said of the weaver's shuttle-thread (pesakārakañjiyasuttaṃ).'

Sakuṇikāti paṭapadasakuṇikā. Sā hi rukkhasākhāsu olambanakuṭavā hoti. Tañhi [M 2.0384][V 2.0350] sā kuṭavaṃ tato tato tiṇahīrādike ānetvā tathā vinati, yathā te pesakārakañjiyasuttaṃ viya aggena vā aggaṃ, mūlena vā mūlaṃ samānetuṃ vivecetuṃ vā na sakkā. Tenāha “yathā”tiādi. Tadubhayampi “gulāguṇṭhika”nti vuttaṃ kañjiyasuttaṃ kulāvakañca. Purimanayenevāti “evameva sattā”tiādinā vuttanayeneva. Kāmaṃ muñjapabbajatiṇāni yathājātānipi dīghabhāvena patitvā araññaṭṭhāne aññamaññaṃ vinandhitvā ākulabyākulāni hutvā tiṭṭhanti, tāni pana na tathā dubbiveciyāni yathā rajjubhūtānīti dassetuṃ “yathā tānī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sesamettha heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

The bird is a weaver bird, specifically, the paṭapada weaver bird. It builds a hanging nest on tree branches. It weaves that nest by bringing grass, fibers, and other materials from here and there, so intricately that the ends and roots cannot be brought together, distinguished, or separated, just like the weaver's shuttle-thread. Therefore, it is said: 'Just as...' Both—the shuttle-thread and the nest—are called 'a tangled ball.' 'By the previous method' means by the method stated beginning with 'In the same way, beings...'. Indeed, muñja, pabbaja, and other grasses, even as they have grown, fall down due to their length and lie in the wilderness entangled and disordered with one another; but they are not as difficult to disentangle as when they have become ropes. To show this, it is said: 'Just as those...' The rest here follows the method explained below.

Apāyāti avaḍḍhikā, sukhena, sukhahetunā vā virahitāti attho. Dukkhassa gatibhāvatoti āpāyikassa dukkhassa pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato. Sukhasamussayatoti abbhudayato. Vinipatitattāti virūpaṃ nipātattā, yathā tenattabhāvena sukhasamussayo na hoti, evaṃ nipatitattā. Itaroti saṃsāro. Nanu “apāya”ntiādinā vuttopi saṃsāro evāti? Saccametaṃ, nirayādīnaṃ pana adhimattadukkhabhāvadassanatthaṃ apāyādiggahaṇaṃ. Gobalībaddañāyenāyamattho veditabbo.

A state of loss is a decline; the meaning is that it is devoid of happiness or the cause of happiness. 'A destination of suffering' means it is the place where suffering pertaining to the woeful states occurs. 'From the accumulation of happiness' means from prosperity. 'Due to being utterly ruined' means because of falling in a bad way, falling in such a way that by that very nature there is no accumulation of happiness. 'The other' refers to saṃsāra. But is not saṃsāra itself also what is spoken of by 'state of loss,' and so forth? This is true. However, the terms 'state of loss' and the like are used to highlight the exceedingly painful nature of realms like hell. This meaning should be understood by the maxim of the ox and the bull.

Khandhānañca paṭipāṭīti pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ hetuphalabhāvena aparāparappavatti. Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānāti avicchedena vattamānā. Taṃ sabbampīti taṃ “apāya”ntiādinā vuttaṃ sabbaṃ apāyadukkhañca vaṭṭadukkhañca. Mahāsamudde vātakkhittā nāvā viyāti idaṃ paribbhamanaṭṭhānassa mahantadassanatthañceva paribbhamanassa anavaṭṭhitatādassanatthañca upamā. Yante yuttagoṇo viyāti idaṃ pana avasībhāvadassanatthañceva duppamokkhabhāvadassanatthañcāti veditabbaṃ.

“And the sequence of aggregates” (khandhānañca paṭipāṭī) means the successive occurrence of the five aggregates by way of cause and effect. “Uninterrupted and ongoing” (abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā) means occurring without cessation. “All of that” (taṃ sabbampi) refers to all that was spoken of by “state of loss” and so forth, namely the suffering of the state of loss and the suffering of the round of existence. “Like a ship tossed by winds in the great ocean” (mahāsamudde vātakkhittā nāvā viya) – this simile is for showing both the vastness of the place of wandering and the instability of the wandering. “And like an ox yoked to a mill” (yante yuttagoṇo viya) – this, however, should be understood as illustrating both the state of powerlessness and the difficulty of liberation.

“Samūhaggāhoti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīnaṃ sādhāraṇaggāho”ti vadanti, “itthaṃ evaṃ aññathā”ti pana visesaṃ akatvā gahaṇaṃ samūhaggāhoti daṭṭhabbo. Visesaṃ akatvāti ca anupanidhānaṃ samato asamato ca upanidhānanti imaṃ vibhāgaṃ akatvāti attho. Itthanti hi anupanidhānaṃ kathitaṃ. Evaṃ aññathāti pana samato asamato ca upanidhānaṃ. Aññaṃ ākāranti parasantānagataṃ ākāraṃ.

They say that ‘collective grasping’ (samūhaggāho) is the common grasping of craving, conceit, and views. But collective grasping should be understood as grasping without making distinctions such as ‘this way, thus, or otherwise.’ And ‘without making distinctions’ (visesaṃ akatvā) means not making this classification of non-comparison and comparison, whether similar or dissimilar. ‘This way’ (itthaṃ) indeed refers to non-comparison. ‘Thus or otherwise’ (evaṃ aññathā), however, refers to comparison, whether similar or dissimilar. ‘Another aspect’ (aññaṃ ākāraṃ) refers to an aspect belonging to another’s mental continuum.

Atthīti [M 2.0385] sadā saṃvijjatīti attho. Sīdatīti nassati. Saṃsayaparivitakkavasenāti “kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ siyaṃ, na siya”nti evaṃ parivitakkavasena. Patthanākappanavasenāti “api nāma sādhu panāhaṃ siya”nti evaṃ patthanāya kappanavasena. Suddhasīsāti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīnaṃ [V 2.0351] sādhāraṇā sīsā. “Itthaṃ evaṃ aññathā”ti vuttassa visesassa anissitattā “suddhasīsā”ti vuttā. Tattha diṭṭhisīsehi diṭṭhiyā gahitāya tadavinābhāvinī taṇhā dassitā, catūhi sīsehi dvādasahi ca sīsamūlakehi mānadiṭṭhīhi ayameva taṇhā dassitāti āha “evamete…pe… taṇhāvicaritadhammā veditabbā”ti. Nanu ca mānadiṭṭhiggāhopi idhādhippeto, yato “taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena samūhaggāho”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā kathaṃ taṇhāvicaritānīti idaṃ vacanaṃ? Vuccate – diṭṭhimānesupi taṇhāvicaritānīti vacanaṃ aññamaññaṃ vippayogīnaṃ diṭṭhimānānaṃ taṇhāya avippayogānaṃ taṃmūlakattā tappadhānatāya katanti veditabbaṃ. Dasamaṃ uttānameva.

“It exists” (atthīti) means it is always present. “It perishes” (sīdatīti) means it is destroyed. “Through doubt and speculation” (saṃsayaparivitakkavasena) means through speculating thus: “Could I be, or could I not be?” “Through longing and supposition” (patthanākappanavasena) means through supposing with longing thus: “Oh, if only I could be well!” “Pure-headed” (suddhasīsā) refers to the heads common to craving, conceit, and views. Because it does not rely on the distinction stated as “this way, thus, or otherwise,” it is called “pure-headed.” Here, craving, which is inseparable from views when views are grasped, is shown by the heads of views. And by the four heads and the twelve root-heads of conceit and views, this very craving is shown. Thus it is said: “In this way… these states are to be understood as pervaded by craving.” But is not the grasping of conceit and views also intended here, since the commentary states, “Collective grasping is through craving, conceit, and views”? Therefore, how can this statement be “pervaded by craving”? It is said: Even in the case of views and conceit, the statement “pervaded by craving” should be understood as made because views and conceit, though mutually distinct, are inseparable from craving, being rooted in it and having it as their primary factor. The tenth is self-explanatory.

Taṇhāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Taṇhā Sutta and others is completed.

Mahāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Great Chapter is completed.

Catutthapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Fourth Fifty is completed.

5. Pañcamapaṇṇāsakaṃ

5. The Fifth Fifty

(21) 1. Sappurisavaggo

(21) 1. The Chapter on Good Persons

1-10. Sikkhāpadasuttādivaṇṇanā

1-10. The commentary on the Sikkhāpada Sutta and others.

201-210. Pañcamassa [M 2.0386][V 2.0352] paṭhame asappurisoti lāmakapuriso. Pāṇaṃ atipātetīti pāṇātipātī. Adinnaṃ ādiyatīti adinnādāyī. Kāmesu micchā caratīti kāmesumicchācārī. Musā vadatīti musāvādī. Surāmerayamajjapamāde tiṭṭhatīti surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāyī. Pāṇātipāte samādapetīti yathā pāṇaṃ atipāteti, tathā naṃ tattha gahaṇaṃ gaṇhāpeti. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ vuccatīti ayaṃ evarūpo puggalo yasmā sayaṃkatena ca dussīlyena samannāgato, yañca samādapitena kataṃ, tato upaḍḍhassa dāyādo, tasmā “asappurisena asappurisataro”ti vuccati. Sappurisoti uttamapuriso. Sappurisena sappurisataroti attanā ca katena susīlyena samannāgatattā yañca samādapito karoti, tato upaḍḍhassa dāyādattā uttamapurisena uttamapurisataro. Ettha ca parena kataṃ dussīlyaṃ susīlyaṃ vā āṇattiyā attanā ca vacippayogena katanti āṇāpanavasena pasutapāpassa puññassa vā dāyādo “tato upaḍḍhassa dāyādo”ti vutto. Dutiyādīni uttānatthāneva.

201-210. In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, “an ignoble person” (asappuriso) means a base individual. “One who destroys life” (pāṇaṃ atipāteti) means a killer of living beings. “One who takes what is not given” (adinnaṃ ādiyati) means one who takes what is not given. “One who engages in misconduct in regard to sensual pleasures” (kāmesu micchā carati) means one who engages in misconduct in regard to sensual pleasures. “One who speaks falsely” (musā vadati) means one who speaks falsely. “One who abides in intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness” (surāmerayamajjapamāde tiṭṭhati) means one who is addicted to intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. “One who encourages killing” (pāṇātipāte samādapeti) means that just as one destroys life, so too does one cause another to undertake it. The same method applies to the rest. “This is called” (ayaṃ vuccati): this kind of person, because they are endowed with the unwholesome conduct done by themselves, and also with that done by one instigated by them, is therefore an heir to half of that, and thus is called “more ignoble than an ignoble person.” “A good person” (sappuriso) means an excellent individual. “A better person than a good person” (sappurisena sappurisataro) means that because they are endowed with the wholesome conduct done by themselves, and also with that which one instigated by them does, they are therefore an heir to half of that, and thus are called “more excellent than an excellent person.” Here, regarding the unwholesome or wholesome conduct done by another through one's instruction, it is considered as done by oneself through verbal effort. Thus, through the act of instructing, one becomes an heir to the demerit or merit produced, and is therefore called “heir to half of that.” The second and following suttas are indeed straightforward in meaning.

Sikkhāpadasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sikkhāpada Sutta and others is completed.

Sappurisavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Good Persons is completed.

211-220. Dutiyo parisāvaggo uttānatthoyeva.

211-220. The second Chapter on Assemblies is indeed straightforward in meaning.

(23) 3. Duccaritavaggavaṇṇanā

(23) 3. The commentary on the Chapter on Misconduct

221-231. Tatiyassa [V 2.0353] paṭhamādīni uttānatthāneva. Cintākavītiādīsu vatthuanusandhiubhayameva cirena cintetvā karaṇavasena cintākavi veditabbo. Kiñci sutvā sutena assutaṃ anusandhetvā karaṇavasena sutakavi, kiñci atthaṃ upadhāretvā tassa saṅkhipanavitthāraṇādivasena atthakavi [M 2.0387] yaṃkiñci parena kataṃ kabbaṃ nāṭakaṃ vā disvā taṃsadisameva aññaṃ attano ṭhānuppattikappaṭibhānena karaṇavasena paṭibhānakavi veditabbo.

221-231. The first and following suttas of the third chapter are indeed straightforward in meaning. Regarding “the reflective poet” and so forth: A reflective poet should be understood as one who composes by reflecting for a long time on both the subject matter and its connection. A learned poet (sutakavi) is one who composes by connecting the unheard with the heard, having heard something. A meaning-poet (atthakavi) is one who composes by summarizing, elaborating, and so forth, on a meaning, having grasped that meaning. A poet of inspiration (paṭibhānakavi) should be understood as one who composes by creating something similar to any poem or play done by another, having seen it, through their own spontaneous ingenuity arising on the occasion.

Duccaritavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Misconduct is completed.

(24) 4. Kammavaggo

(24) 4. The Chapter on Action

1. Saṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Concise Discourse

232. Catutthassa paṭhame kāḷakanti malīnaṃ, cittassa appabhassarabhāvakaranti attho. Taṃ panettha kammapathappattameva adhippetanti āha “dasaakusalakammapatha”nti. Kaṇhābhijātihetuto vā kaṇhaṃ. Tenāha “kaṇhavipāka”nti. Apāyūpapatti manussesu ca dobhaggiyaṃ kaṇhavipāko, yaṃ tassa tamabhāvo vutto. Nibbattanatoti nibbattāpanato. Paṇḍarakanti odātaṃ, cittassa pabhassarabhāvakaranti attho. Sukkābhijātihetuto vā sukkaṃ. Tenāha “sukkavipāka”nti. Saggūpapatti manussasobhaggiyañca sukkavipāko, yaṃ tassa jotibhāvo vutto. Ukkaṭṭhaniddesena pana “sagge nibbattanato”ti vuttaṃ, nibbattāpanatoti attho. Missakakammanti kālena kaṇhaṃ kālena sukkanti evaṃ missakavasena katakammaṃ. Sukhadukkhavipākanti vatvā tattha sukhadukkhānaṃ pavattiākāraṃ dassetuṃ “missakakammaṃ hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kammassa kaṇhasukkasamaññā kaṇhasukkābhijātihetutāyāti apacayagāmitāya tadubhayaviddhaṃsakassa kammakkhayakarakammassa idha sukkapariyāyopi icchitoti āha “ubhaya…pe… ayamettha attho”ti. Tattha ubhayavipākassāti [V 2.0354] yathādhigatassa ubhayavipākassa. Sampattibhavapariyāpanno hi vipāko idha sukkaṃ sukkavipākoti adhippeto, na accantaparisuddho ariyaphalavipāko.

232. In the first discourse of the fourth chapter, ‘dark’ (kāḷaka) means stained (malīna), signifying that which makes the mind lack radiance. Here, however, it is intended to refer specifically to that which constitutes a course of action; thus it is said: 'the ten unwholesome courses of action'. Alternatively, it is ‘dark’ (kaṇha) because it is a cause for a dark destiny (kaṇhābhijāti). Hence, it is said to be ‘dark in result’ (kaṇhavipāka). Rebirth in the lower realms and misfortune among humans is the dark result, which is said to be its dark nature. ‘Leading to rebirth’ (nibbattanato) means causing rebirth (nibbattāpanato). ‘Bright’ (paṇḍaraka) means white (odāta), signifying that which makes the mind radiant. Alternatively, it is ‘bright’ (sukka) because it is a cause for a bright destiny (sukkābhijāti). Hence, it is said to be ‘bright in result’ (sukkavipāka). Rebirth in the heavens and good fortune among humans is the bright result, which is said to be its luminous nature. However, by way of an emphatic designation, ‘leading to rebirth in heaven’ (sagge nibbattanato) is stated, meaning causing rebirth (nibbattāpanato). ‘Mixed action’ (missakakamma) refers to action performed in a mixed manner, sometimes dark, sometimes bright. Having stated that the result is pleasure and pain, in order to show the manner in which pleasure and pain occur there, the passage beginning with 'For mixed action...' is stated. The designations ‘dark’ and ‘bright’ for action are due to their being causes for dark and bright destinies. And because it leads to decline (apacayagāmitāya), even the action that destroys both of those—the action that leads to the cessation of action (kammakkhayakarakamma)—is intended here as a synonym for ‘bright’ (sukka). Hence, it is said: ‘both… this is the meaning here.’ There, ‘of both results’ (ubhayavipākassa) refers to the experienced result of both. For the result included in the realm of fortunate existence is here intended by ‘bright’ and ‘bright result,’ not the perfectly pure result of noble fruition.

Saṃkhittasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Concise Discourse is finished.

2. Vitthārasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Detailed Discourse

233. Dutiye [M 2.0388] sabyābajjhanti vā sadukkhaṃ, attanā uppādetabbena dukkhena sadukkhanti attho, dukkhasaṃvattanikanti vuttaṃ hoti.
