Kāyasaṅkhārādīsu kāyadvāre gahaṇādivasena copanappattā dvādasa akusalacetanā abyābajjhakāyasaṅkhāro nāma. Vacīdvāre hanusaṃcopanavasena vacībhedappavattikā tāyeva dvādasa vacīsaṅkhāro nāma. Ubhayacopanaṃ appatvā raho cintentassa manodvāre pavattā manosaṅkhāro nāma. Iti tīsupi dvāresu kāyaduccaritādibhedā akusalā cetanāva saṅkhārāti veditabbā. Abhisaṅkharotīti āyūhati, taṃ pana āyūhanaṃ paccayasamavāyasiddhito saṅkaḍḍhitvā piṇḍanaṃ viya hoti. Sadukkhaṃ lokanti apāyalokamāha. Vipākaphassāti phassasīsena tattha vipākappavattamāha. Vemānikapetāti idaṃ bāhullato vuttaṃ, itaresampi vinipātikānaṃ kālena sukhaṃ, kālena dukkhaṃ hoti. Tassa pahānāyāti tassa yathāvuttassa kammassa anuppattidhammatāpādanāya. Yā cetanāti yā apacayagāminicetanā. Tenevāha “vivaṭṭagāminī maggacetanā veditabbā”ti.

233. In the second discourse, ‘afflictive’ (sabyābajjha) or ‘painful’ (sadukkha) means with suffering, that is, with suffering to be produced by oneself; it is said to be conducive to suffering (dukkhasaṃvattanika). Among bodily formations and so forth, the twelve unwholesome volitions that have reached a state of movement by way of grasping, etc., at the body door are called the afflictive bodily formation. At the speech door, those same twelve volitions that occur as breaking into speech by way of moving the jaw are called the verbal formation. Those that occur at the mind door when one is thinking in solitude, without having reached the movement of both body and speech, are called the mental formation. Thus, it should be understood that in all three doors, the unwholesome volitions, differentiated as bodily misconduct and so forth, are the formations. ‘They construct’ (abhisaṅkharoti) means they strive (āyūhati); and that striving, from the accomplishment of the conjunction of conditions, is like drawing things together and making a bundle. ‘The painful world’ (sadukkhaṃ lokaṃ) refers to the world of the lower realms (apāyaloka). ‘Resultant contact’ (vipākaphassa) refers to the occurrence of the result there, with contact as its head. ‘Vemānika petas’ is mentioned here as a general case; for other beings in the lower realms (vinipātika) too, there is sometimes pleasure and sometimes pain. ‘For abandoning that’ (tassa pahānāya) means for bringing about the state of non-arising of that aforementioned action. ‘That volition’ (yā cetanā) refers to the volition leading to decline (apacayagāminī cetanā). Therefore it is said, ‘The path volition leading to the rolling back of saṃsāra (vivaṭṭagāminī maggacetanā) should be understood.’

Vitthārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Detailed Discourse is finished.

3-9. Soṇakāyanasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-9. Commentary on the Soṇakāyana Discourse and others

234-240. Tatiye purimāni, bhante, divasāni purimatarānīti ettha hiyyo divasaṃ purimaṃ nāma, tato paraṃ purimataranti āha “atītānantaradivasato paṭṭhāyā”tiādi. Iti imesu dvīsu pavattito yathākkamaṃ purimapurimatarabhāvo dassito. Evaṃ santepi yadettha “purimatara”nti vuttaṃ, tato pabhuti yaṃ yaṃ oraṃ, taṃ taṃ purimaṃ. Yaṃ yaṃ paraṃ, taṃ taṃ purimataraṃ orapārabhāvassa viya purimatarabhāvassa ca apekkhāsiddhattā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Catutthādīni uttānatthāneva.

234-240. In the third discourse, regarding the phrase ‘former days, venerable sir, even earlier days,’ it is said that yesterday is called ‘former,’ and what is before that is called ‘even earlier’—starting from the immediately preceding day, and so on. Thus, in these two instances, the progressive state of ‘former’ and ‘even earlier’ is shown respectively. Even so, when ‘even earlier’ is mentioned here, from that point onwards, whatever is nearer is ‘former,’ and whatever is further is ‘even earlier’—just as the relationship of near and far depends on perspective, so too does the state of being ‘even earlier.’ The rest is as previously stated. The fourth and following discourses are clear in meaning.

Soṇakāyanasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Soṇakāyana Sutta and Others is finished.

10-11. Samaṇasuttādivaṇṇanā

10-11. Explanation of the Samaṇa Sutta and Others

241-2. Dasame [V 2.0355][M 2.0389] sesapadesupīti “idha dutiyo samaṇo”tiādīsu sesapadesupi. Yathā hi “vivicceva kāmehī”ti (dī. ni. 1.226; ma. ni. 1.271, 287, 297; saṃ. ni. 2.152; a. ni. 4.123) ettha kato niyamo “vivicca akusalehī”ti etthāpi katoyeva hoti sāvadhāraṇaatthassa icchitabbattā, evamidhāpīti. Tenāha “dutiyādayopi hī”tiādi. Sāmaññaphalādhigamavasena nippariyāyato samaṇabhāvoti tesaṃ vasenettha cattāro samaṇā desitā. Imasmiñhi ṭhāne cattāro phalaṭṭhakasamaṇāva adhippetā samitapāpasamaṇaggahaṇato. Kasmā panettha mahāparinibbāne viya maggaṭṭhā tadatthāya paṭipannāpi na gahitāti? Veneyyajjhāsayato. Tattha hi maggādhigamatthāya vipassanāpi ito bahiddhā natthi, kuto maggaphalānīti dassentena bhagavatā “ñāyassa dhammassa padesavattī, ito bahiddhā samaṇopi natthī”ti (dī. ni. 2.214) vuttaṃ. Idha pana niṭṭhānappattameva taṃtaṃsamaṇabhāvaṃ gaṇhantena phalaṭṭhakasamaṇāva gahitā, maggaṭṭhato phalaṭṭho savisesaṃ dakkhiṇeyyoti. Svāyamattho dvīsu suttesu desanābhedeneva viññāyatīti. Rittāti vivittā. Tucchāti nissārā paṭipannakasārābhāvato.

241-2. In the tenth discourse, ‘even in the remaining phrases’ refers to remaining phrases like ‘here, the second ascetic.’ Just as the restriction made in ‘secluded from sensual pleasures’ also applies to ‘secluded from unwholesome things’ because a precise understanding of the meaning is desired, so too is it in this case. Hence, it is said, ‘the second and others too,’ and so on. The state of being an ascetic is unreservedly explained through the attainment of the fruits of asceticism; by way of these, four ascetics are taught here. In this context, only the four ascetics who have attained the fruits are intended, as indicated by the phrase ‘ascetics who have pacified evil.’ But why are those on the path towards that goal not included here, as they are in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta? Because of the disposition of those to be taught. For there, the Blessed One, showing that insight for attaining the path does not exist outside of this teaching—so how could the path and its fruits?—said: ‘a follower of a portion of the true Dhamma; outside of this there is no ascetic.’ Here, however, only those who have reached the culmination and attained the respective ascetic state are included—for the fruit-attainer is especially more worthy of offerings than the path-attainer. This very meaning is understood in the two suttas by the difference in teaching. ‘Empty’ means secluded. ‘Hollow’ means without substance, because of the absence of the essence of a practitioner.

Pavadanti etehīti pavādā. Diṭṭhigatikānaṃ nānādiṭṭhidīpakasamayāti āha “cattāro sassatavādā”tiādi. Tattha cattāro sassatavādāti lābhivasena tayo, takkivasena ekoti evaṃ cattāro sassatavādā. Pubbenivāsañāṇalābhī titthiyo mandapañño anekajātisatasahassamattaṃ anussarati, majjhapañño dasa saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappāni, tikkhapañño cattālīsa saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappāni, na tato paraṃ. So evaṃ anussaranto “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti abhivadati, takkī pana takkapariyāhataṃ vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti abhivadati. Tena vuttaṃ “lābhivasena tayo, takkivasena ekoti evaṃ cattāro sassatavādā”ti.

They proclaim through these, therefore they are ‘proclamations’ (pavādā). For those following particular views, these are various doctrines illuminating their views. Hence, it is said, ‘four eternalism doctrines,’ and so on. Here, ‘four eternalism doctrines’ means three based on attainment and one based on reasoning; thus, four eternalism doctrines. A heretic who has attained the knowledge of previous existences—one of dull wisdom recalls approximately a hundred thousand existences, one of middling wisdom recalls ten cycles of contraction and expansion, one of sharp wisdom recalls forty cycles of contraction and expansion, and no further than that. Thus recollecting, he declares, ‘The self and the world are eternal.’ However, a reasoner, based on what is hammered out by reasoning, pursued by investigation, and his own insight, declares, ‘The self and the world are eternal.’ Therefore it was said, ‘three based on attainment and one based on reasoning; thus, four eternalism doctrines.’

Sattesu [M 2.0390] saṅkhāresu ca ekaccaṃ sassatanti pavatto vādo ekaccasassatavādo. So pana brahmakāyikakhiḍḍāpadosikamanopadosikattabhāvato cavitvā idhāgatānaṃ takkino ca uppajjanavasena catubbidhoti āha “cattāro ekaccasassatavādā”ti.

The doctrine that some among beings and conditioned things are eternal is partial eternalism (ekaccasassatavāda). It is fourfold, arising for a reasoner, and for those who, having passed away from the state of being in the Brahma realms—specifically, the realms of Brahma’s retinue, those corrupted by play, or those corrupted in mind—have been reborn here. Thus, it is said: ‘There are four kinds of partial eternalism.’

Cattāro antānantikāti ettha amati gacchati ettha vosānanti anto, mariyādā. Tappaṭisedhena [V 2.0356] ananto. Anto ca ananto ca antānanto sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesena vā “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.126; udā. 1) viya. Antānantasahacarito vādo antānanto yathā “kuntā carantī”ti. Antānantasannissayo vā yathā “mañcā ghosantī”ti. So etesaṃ atthīti antānantikā. “Antavā attā ca loko ca, anantavā attā ca loko ca, antavā ca anantavā ca attā ca loko ca, nevantavā nānantavā”ti evaṃ pavattavādā cattāro. Avaḍḍhitakasiṇassa taṃ kasiṇaṃ attāti ca lokoti ca gaṇhantassa vasena paṭhamo vutto, dutiyo vaḍḍhitakasiṇassa vasena vutto, tatiyo tiriyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā uddhamadho avaḍḍhitakasiṇassa, catuttho takkivasena vutto. Ettha ca yuttaṃ tāva purimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vādānaṃ antañca anantañca antānantañca ārabbha pavattavādattā antānantikattaṃ, pacchimassa pana tadubhayanisedhanavasena pavattavādattā kathamantānantikattanti? Tadubhayappaṭisedhanavasena pavattavādattā eva. Antānantikappaṭisedhavādopi hi antānantavisayo eva taṃ ārabbha pavattattā.

Regarding ‘four views concerning finitude and infinitude’ (cattāro antānantikā), here ‘finitude’ (anto) means limit (mariyādā), where one stops and reaches an end. By its negation, it is ‘infinitude’ (ananto). The combination of finitude and infinitude is ‘both finite and infinite’ (antānanto), through a general designation or through the one-remaining figure of speech, as in ‘with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases,’ and so on. Alternatively, ‘finite and infinite’ may refer to a doctrine associated with both, as in ‘spears move.’ Or it may denote a dependency, as in ‘beds creak.’ One who holds such views possesses them, thus, is called one who is concerned with finitude and infinitude (antānantika). The four views that arise are as follows: ‘The self and the world are finite’; ‘The self and the world are infinite’; ‘The self and the world are both finite and infinite’; ‘The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.’ The first is stated as arising from one taking an unexpanded kasiṇa as the self and the world; the second is stated as arising from an expanded kasiṇa; the third from a kasiṇa unexpanded up and down but expanded horizontally; the fourth is stated through reasoning. Here, it is indeed fitting that the first three views are called ‘concerning finitude and infinitude’ because they are views that arise concerning finitude, infinitude, or both. But how is the last, which arises through denying both, called ‘concerning finitude and infinitude’? It is precisely because it is a view that arises through denying both. For even a view denying finitude and infinitude is still on the subject of finitude and infinitude, since it arises in relation to that.

Na maratīti amarā. Kā sā? “Evantipi me no”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.62) nayena pariyantarahitā diṭṭhigatikassa diṭṭhi ceva vācā ca. Vividho khepoti vikkhepo, amarāya diṭṭhiyā, vācāya vā vikkhepoti amarāvikkhepo, so etassa atthīti amarāvikkhepiko. Atha vā amarā nāma macchajāti, sā ummujjanādivasena udake sandhāvamānā gāhaṃ na gacchati, evamevaṃ ayampi vādo ito cito ca sandhāvati, gāhaṃ na upagacchatīti amarāvikkhepoti vuccati, so etesaṃ atthīti amarāvikkhepikā. Svāyaṃ vādo musāvādānuyogachandarāgabhayamohabhāvahetukatāya catudhā pavattoti āha “cattāro amarāvikkhepikā”ti.

It does not die, thus it is deathless (amarā). What is that? By the method beginning with the phrase, “I do not hold it so,” it is the boundless view and speech of one who holds to a view. Diverse distraction is 'vikkhepo'; the distraction due to the deathless view or speech is 'amarāvikkhepo.' One who has this is an 'amarāvikkhepika.' Alternatively, 'amarā' is a kind of fish that, because of rising and diving while moving about in the water, is not caught. Just so, this doctrine runs here and there and is not grasped; therefore it is called 'amarāvikkhepo.' Those who hold this are called 'amarāvikkhepikā.' This doctrine arises in four ways, because it is caused by addiction to false speech, desire and lust, fear, and delusion. Therefore, it is said, “There are four evasive wrigglers.”

Adhicca [M 2.0391] yathicchakaṃ yaṃ kiñci kāraṇaṃ kassaci buddhipubbaṃ vā vinā samuppannoti attalokasaññitānaṃ khandhānaṃ adhicca pavattiākārārammaṇaṃ dassanaṃ tadākārasannissayena pavattito tadākārasahacaritatāya ca “adhiccasamuppanna”nti vuccati yathā “mañcā ghosanti”, “kuntā carantī”ti ca. Taṃ etesaṃ atthīti adhiccasamuppannikā. Lābhivasena takkivasena ca “dve adhiccasamuppannikā”ti vuttaṃ.

The view whose object is the mode of the chance occurrence of the aggregates conceived as self and world—the view that they have arisen by chance (adhicca), that is, spontaneously, without any cause or anyone's prior intention—is called ‘adhiccasamuppanna’ because it proceeds in dependence on and is associated with that mode, just as in ‘couches creak’ or ‘spears move.’ Those who hold this are called adhiccasamuppannikā. It is said that there are ‘two kinds of adhiccasamuppannikā’ based on attainment and on reasoning.

Saññīti pavatto vādo saññivādo, so etesaṃ atthīti saññivādā. Rūpicatukkaṃ ekantasukhacatukkanti imesaṃ catunnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena soḷasa saññivādā. Imesuyeva purimānaṃ dvinnaṃ [V 2.0357] catukkānaṃ vasena aṭṭha saññivādā, aṭṭha nevasaññināsaññivādā veditabbā. Kevalañhi tattha “saññī attā”ti gaṇhantānaṃ tā diṭṭhiyo, idha asaññīti ca nevasaññīnāsaññīti ca.

The doctrine that proceeds as ‘percipient’ is the percipient-doctrine (saññivādo); those who hold this are called saññivādā. By way of four tetrads—such as the tetrad concerning materiality and the tetrad concerning absolute happiness—there are sixteen percipient-doctrines. Based on the first two tetrads among these, eight are percipient-doctrines, and eight should be understood as neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient doctrines. For, in that context, those views belong to those who grasp ‘the self is percipient’; here, it is also about ‘non-percipient’ and ‘neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient’.

Satta ucchedavādāti manussattabhāve kāmāvacaradevattabhāve rūpāvacarattabhāve catubbidhārūpattabhāve ca ṭhatvā sattassa ucchedapaññāpanavasena satta ucchedavādā.

Seven annihilationist doctrines: by taking a stand in human existence, in the existence of sense-sphere deities, in form-sphere existence, and in the fourfold formless existence, they proclaim the annihilation of a being; hence, there are seven annihilationist doctrines.

Pañca diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādāti pañcakāmaguṇaupabhogavasena catubbidharūpajjhānasukhaparibhogavasena ca diṭṭhadhamme nibbūtipaññāpanavādā. Diṭṭhadhammoti paccakkhadhammo vuccati, tattha tattha paṭiladdhattabhāvassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Diṭṭhadhamme nibbānaṃ diṭṭhadhammanibbānaṃ, imasmiṃyeva attabhāve dukkhavūpasamanti attho. Taṃ vadantīti diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā.

Five doctrines of Nibbāna in the present life—they are doctrines that proclaim quenching in this very life through the enjoyment of the five strands of sensual pleasures and through the enjoyment of the bliss of the fourfold form jhānas. 'The present life' refers to the directly experienced state; this is a term for the state attained in each instance. Nibbāna in the present life means the calming of suffering in this very existence. Those who speak thus are called 'diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādā' (those who proclaim Nibbāna in the present life).

Ñāyati kamati paṭivijjhatīti ñāyo, so eva nibbānasampāpakahetutāya dhammoti āha “ñāyassa dhammassā”ti. Ito bahiddhā samaṇopi natthītiādīsu kasmā panete aññattha natthīti? Akkhettatāya. Yathā hi na āragge sāsapo tiṭṭhati, na udakapiṭṭhe aggi jalati, na piṭṭhipāsāṇe bījāni viruhanti, evamevaṃ bāhiresu titthāyatanesu na ime samaṇā uppajjanti, imasmiṃyeva sāsane uppajjanti. Kasmā? Sukkhettatāya. Sā pana nesaṃ akkhettatā sukkhettatā ca ariyamaggassa abhāvato bhāvato ca veditabbā. Tenāha bhagavā –

‘It is known, it proceeds, it penetrates’—this is the method. Because it is the cause leading to Nibbāna, it is the Dhamma; thus it is said, ‘of the Dhamma of the method.’ In the phrase, ‘Outside of this, there are no ascetics,’ and so on, why then do these not exist elsewhere? Because of being unfertile ground. Just as a mustard seed does not stay on the tip of an awl, fire does not burn on the surface of water, and seeds do not sprout on a stone slab, so too these ascetics do not arise in external sectarian abodes—they arise only in this dispensation. Why? Because of being fertile ground. Their being unfertile ground and fertile ground should be understood as due to the absence and presence of the Noble Path. Thus the Blessed One said—

“Yasmiṃ kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo na upalabbhati, samaṇopi tattha na upalabbhati, dutiyopi tattha [M 2.0392] samaṇo na upalabbhati, tatiyopi tattha samaṇo na upalabbhati, catutthopi tattha samaṇo na upalabbhati. Yasmiñca kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo upalabbhati, samaṇopi tattha upalabbhati, dutiyopi tattha… tatiyopi tattha… catutthopi tattha samaṇo upalabbhati. Imasmiṃ kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo upalabbhati. Idheva, subhadda, samaṇo, idha dutiyo samaṇo, idha tatiyo samaṇo, idha catuttho samaṇo, suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (dī. ni. 2.214).

“In whatever teaching and discipline, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is not found, an ascetic is not found there, nor a second, nor a third, nor a fourth ascetic. But in whatever teaching and discipline, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found, an ascetic is found there, and also a second, a third, and a fourth ascetic. In this teaching and discipline, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found. Here, Subhadda, is the ascetic, here the second ascetic, here the third ascetic, here the fourth ascetic. Other doctrines are empty of ascetics.”

Ariyamaggassa ca abhāvo bhāvo ca suparisuddhassa sīlassa suparisuddhāya samathavipassanābhāvanāya abhāvato bhāvato ca veditabbo. Tadubhayañca durakkhātasvākkhātabhāvahetukaṃ[V 2.0358]. So ca asammāsambuddhappaveditattā. Yasmā titthāyatanaṃ akkhettaṃ, sāsanaṃ khettaṃ, tasmā yathā surattahatthapādo bhāsurakesarabhāro sīho migarājā na susāne vā saṅkārakūṭe vā paṭivasati, tiyojanasahassavitthataṃ pana himavantaṃ ajjhogāhetvā maṇiguhāyameva vasati, yathā ca chaddanto nāgarājā na gocariyahatthikulādīsu navasu kulesu uppajjati, yathā ca valāhako assarājā na gadrabhakule vā ghoṭakakule vā uppajjati, sindhutīre pana sindhavakuleyeva uppajjati, yathā ca sabbakāmadadaṃ manoharaṃ maṇiratanaṃ na saṅkārakūṭe vā paṃsupabbatādīsu vā uppajjati, vipulapabbatabbhantareyeva uppajjati, yathā ca timirapiṅgalo maccharājā na khuddakapokkharaṇīsu uppajjati, caturāsītiyojanasahassagambhīre mahāsamuddeyeva uppajjati, yathā ca diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko supaṇṇarājā na gāmadvāre eraṇḍavanādīsu paṭivasati, mahāsamuddaṃ pana ajjhogāhetvā simbalidahavaneyeva paṭivasati, yathā ca dhataraṭṭho suvaṇṇahaṃso na gāmadvāre āvāṭakādīsu paṭivasati, navutihaṃsasahassaparivāro pana hutvā cittakūṭeyeva paṭivasati, yathā ca catuddīpissaro cakkavattirājā na nīcakule uppajjati, asambhinnajātiyakhattiyakuleyeva pana uppajjati, evamevaṃ imesu samaṇesu ekasamaṇopi na aññattha titthāyatane uppajjati, ariyamaggaparikkhate pana buddhasāsaneyeva [M 2.0393] uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā – “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (ma. ni. 1.139-140; a. ni. 4.241). Ekādasame natthi vattabbaṃ.

The absence and presence of the Noble Path should be understood by the absence and presence of perfectly purified virtue and the perfectly purified development of serenity and insight. And both of these are caused by whether the teaching is poorly explained or well-explained. And that, in turn, is due to its being proclaimed by one who is not a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Since the sectarian abodes are an unfertile field, but the Dispensation is a fertile field, therefore, just as a lion, the king of beasts, with very red paws and a splendid mane, does not dwell in a charnel ground or on a rubbish heap, but having entered the Himalayas that stretch for three thousand leagues, dwells only in a jeweled cave; and just as the royal elephant Chaddanta is not born among the nine classes of elephants, such as the domestic elephants; and just as the royal horse Valāhaka is not born in the lineage of donkeys or ordinary horses, but is born only in the lineage of Sindh horses on the banks of the Sindhu river; and just as the wish-fulfilling, delightful jewel does not arise on a rubbish heap or on a dusty mountain, but arises only within a vast mountain; and just as the fish king Timirapiṅgala is not born in small ponds, but is born only in the great ocean, eighty-four thousand leagues deep; and just as the garuḍa king Supaṇṇa, one hundred and fifty leagues in size, does not dwell at village gates or in castor-oil groves, but having entered the great ocean, dwells only in the silk-cotton tree grove; and just as the golden goose Dhataraṭṭha does not dwell at village gates or in pits, but, surrounded by ninety thousand geese, dwells only on Mount Cittakūṭa; and just as a universal monarch ruling the four continents is not born in a lowly family, but is born only in an unmixed lineage of noble warrior families—in the same way, not even a single one of these ascetics arises elsewhere in a sectarian abode, but arises only within the Buddha's Dispensation, which is defined by the Noble Path. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Here alone, monks, is the ascetic… empty are the doctrines of others of other ascetics.” (MN 1.139-140; AN 4.241). In the eleventh, there is nothing to be said.

Samaṇasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Samaṇa Sutta and others is concluded.

Kammavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kamma Vagga is concluded.

(25) 5. Āpattibhayavaggo

(25) 5. The Chapter on the Fear of an Offense

1. Saṅghabhedakasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Saṅghabhedaka Sutta

243. Pañcamassa paṭhame vivādādhikaraṇādīsūti vivādādhikaraṇaṃ anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ āpattādhikaraṇaṃ kiccādhikaraṇanti imesu catūsu. Tattha dhammoti vā adhammoti vā aṭṭhārasahi vatthūhi vivadantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yo vivādo, idaṃ vivādādhikaraṇaṃ nāma. Sīlavipattiyā vā ācāradiṭṭhiājīvavipattiyā [V 2.0359] vā anuvadantānaṃ yo anuvādo upavadanā ceva codanā ca, idaṃ anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ nāma. Mātikāya āgatā pañca, vibhaṅge dveti sattapi āpattikkhandhā, idaṃ āpattādhikaraṇaṃ nāma. Saṅghassa apalokanādīnaṃ catunnaṃ kammānaṃ karaṇaṃ, idaṃ kiccādhikaraṇaṃ nāma. Sesamettha uttānameva.

243. In the first of the fifth, regarding ‘in legal questions such as disputes,’ this refers to these four: the legal question of a dispute, the legal question of an accusation, the legal question of an offense, and the legal question of a duty. Among these, the dispute among bhikkhus who argue based on eighteen grounds about what is Dhamma or not Dhamma is called the legal question of a dispute. The accusation—which is both a reproof and a charge—of those who accuse others regarding a failure in morality, conduct, view, or livelihood is called the legal question of an accusation. The five categories of offenses that appear in the Mātikā and the two in the Vibhaṅga, totaling seven categories of offenses, are called the legal question of an offense. The performance of the four formal acts of the Saṅgha, beginning with seeking consent, is called the legal question of a duty. The rest here is self-evident.

Saṅghabhedakasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Saṅghabhedaka Sutta is concluded.

2-3. Āpattibhayasuttādivaṇṇanā

2–3. Commentary on the Āpattibhaya Sutta and others

244-5. Dutiye bhassati niratthakabhāvena khipīyatīti bhasmaṃ, chārikā. Tassa puṭaṃ bhaṇḍikā bhasmapuṭaṃ. Tenāha “bhasmapuṭanti chārikābhaṇḍika”nti. Tatiyaṃ uttānatthameva.

244–5. In the second sutta, ‘ashes’ (bhasma) is so called because it is scattered (bhassati) due to its uselessness; it is cinders. A container (puṭa) for that, a bundle (bhaṇḍikā), is a ‘bundle of ashes’ (bhasmapuṭa). Therefore it is said: ‘“A bundle of ashes” means a bundle of cinders.’ The third has a self-evident meaning.

Āpattibhayasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Āpattibhaya Sutta and others is concluded.

4-7. Seyyāsuttādivaṇṇanā

4–7. Commentary on the Seyyā Sutta and others

246-9. Catutthe [M 2.0394] petāti peccabhāvaṃ gatā. Te pana yasmā idha katakālakiriyā kālena katajīvitucchedā honti, tasmā vuttaṃ “kālakatā vuccantī”ti, matāti attho. Atha vā peccabhavaṃ gatā, petūpapattivasena nibbattiṃ upagatāti attho. Tenāha “atha vā petavisaye nibbattā petā nāmā”ti. Ekena passena sayituṃ na sakkonti dukkhuppattito.

246–9. In the fourth sutta, ‘departed beings’ (petā) means those who have gone to the state after death. Because they have died here, their lives cut off by time, they are called ‘deceased,’ meaning ‘dead.’ Or, having gone to the state after death, the meaning is they have attained rebirth by way of birth as a departed being. Therefore it is said: ‘Or, they are called “departed beings” because they are born in the realm of departed beings.’ They cannot lie on one side due to the arising of suffering.

Tejussadattāti iminā sīhassa abhīrukabhāvaṃ dasseti. Bhīrukā sesamigā attano āsayaṃ pavisitvā santāsapubbakaṃ yathā tathā sayanti, sīho pana abhīruko sabhāvato satokārī bhikkhu viya satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāva sayati. Tenāha “dve purimapāde”tiādi. Dakkhiṇe purimapāde vāmassa purimapādassa ṭhapanavasena dve purimapāde ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapetvā. Pacchimapāde vuttanayeneva idhāpi ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapanaṃ veditabbaṃ, ṭhitokāsasallakkhaṇaṃ abhīrukavaseneva. Sīsaṃ pana ukkhipitvātiādinā vuttasīhakiriyā anutrastappabujjhanā viya abhīrubhāvasiddhadhammatāvasenevāti veditabbā. Sīhavijambhanaṃ ativelaṃ ekākāre ṭhapitānaṃ sarīrāvayavānaṃ gamanādikiriyāsu yogyabhāvāpādanatthaṃ. Tikkhattuṃ sīhanādanadanaṃ appesakkhamigarājehi parittāsapariharaṇatthaṃ.

By `tejussadattā` is shown the lion's fearlessness. Other timid animals enter their lairs and sleep anxiously, but the lion, naturally fearless, like a mindful bhikkhu, sleeps only after having established mindfulness. Therefore it is said: 'the two forefeet,' and so forth. He places the two forefeet in one place by placing the right forefoot upon the left forefoot. Similarly, the hind feet should also be understood as being placed in one place in the manner stated; the marking of its position is due to its fearless nature. The lion's actions described as 'lifting its head,' and so forth, should be understood as being due to its nature established from fearlessness, like awakening without being startled. The lion's stretching is for the purpose of making the body's limbs, which have been kept in one posture for a very long time, fit for activities like moving. The lion's triple roar is for the purpose of warding off the lesser, timid animal kings through terror.

Ayaṃ [V 2.0360] vuccati, bhikkhave, tathāgataseyyāti iminā catutthajjhānaseyyā tathāgataseyyā nāmāti dasseti. Seti abyāvaṭabhāvena pavattati etthāti seyyā, catutthajjhānameva seyyā catutthajjhānaseyyā. Kiṃ pana taṃ catutthajjhānanti? Ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ. Tattha hi ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā bhagavā anukkamena aggamaggaṃ adhigantvā tathāgato jātoti. Tayidaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ nāma na seyyā, tathāpi yasmā “catutthajjhānasamanantarā bhagavā parinibbāyī”ti mahāparinibbāne (dī. ni. 2.219) āgataṃ, tasmā lokiyacatutthajjhānasamāpatti eva tathāgataseyyāti keci. Evaṃ sati parinibbānakālikāva tathāgataseyyā āpajjati, na ca bhagavā lokiyacatutthajjhānasamāpajjanabahulo vihāsi. Aggaphalavasena pavattaṃ [M 2.0395] panettha catutthajjhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha yathā sattānaṃ niddūpagamalakkhaṇā seyyā bhavaṅgacittavasena hoti, sā pana nesaṃ paṭhamajātisamanvayā yebhuyyavuttikā, evaṃ bhagavato ariyajātisamanvayaṃ yebhuyyavuttikaṃ aggaphalabhūtaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ tathāgataseyyāti veditabbaṃ. Pañcamādīni uttānatthāni.

'This is called, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata's repose'—by this statement it is shown that the repose of the fourth jhāna is called the Tathāgata's repose. It is called a repose (`seyyā`) because one reposes (`seti`) in it, abiding without distraction. The fourth jhāna itself is the repose, the repose of the fourth jhāna. But what is that fourth jhāna? It is the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing. For, having established himself in that and developed insight, the Blessed One gradually attained the highest path and became a Tathāgata. That foundation is not called a repose. Nevertheless, since it is stated in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16), 'The Blessed One attained final Nibbāna immediately after the fourth jhāna,' some say that the mundane attainment of the fourth jhāna is indeed the Tathāgata's repose. If this is so, the Tathāgata's repose would occur only at the time of final Nibbāna, but the Blessed One did not frequently abide in the mundane attainment of the fourth jhāna. Here, the fourth jhāna should be understood as that which occurs by way of the highest fruit. Just as the repose of beings, characterized by falling asleep, occurs by way of the life-continuum consciousness, and that is mostly connected with their first birth, so too the Blessed One's fourth jhāna, which is mostly connected with the noble birth and constitutes the highest fruit, should be understood as the Tathāgata's repose. The fifth and so forth are clear in meaning.

Seyyāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Seyyā Sutta and others is concluded.

8. Paṭhamavohārasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the First Sutta on Expressions

250-253. Aṭṭhame anariyānanti asādhūnaṃ nihīnānaṃ. Vohārāti saṃvohārā abhilāpā vā, “diṭṭhaṃ mayā”ti evaṃvāditā. Ettha ca taṃtaṃsamuṭṭhāpakacetanāvasena attho veditabbo. Navamādīsu natthi vattabbaṃ.

250-253. In the eighth sutta, 'of the ignoble' means of the bad and inferior. 'Expressions' means communications or utterances, such as the assertion, 'I have seen.' And here, the meaning should be understood according to the volition that gives rise to each. Regarding the ninth and following suttas, there is nothing to be said.

Paṭhamavohārasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the First Sutta on Expressions is concluded.

Āpattibhayavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on the Fear of Offenses is concluded.

Pañcamapaṇṇāsakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Fifth Fifty is concluded.

(26) 6. Abhiññāvaggo

(26) 6. The Chapter on Direct Knowledges

1-3. Abhiññāsuttādivaṇṇanā

1-3. Commentary on the Sutta on Direct Knowledges and others

254-256. Chaṭṭhassa [V 2.0361] paṭhame paccanīkasamanato samatho, samādhīti āha “cittekaggatā”ti. Aniccādinā vividhenākārena dassanato vipassanā, saṅkhārapariggāhakañāṇaṃ. Tenāha “saṅkhārapariggahavipassanāñāṇa”nti.

254-256. In the first sutta of the sixth chapter, serenity (samatha) is so called because it calms down adversaries. As for concentration (samādhi), it is said to be 'one-pointedness of mind.' Insight (vipassanā) is seeing in various ways, such as through impermanence; it is the knowledge that comprehends formations. Therefore, it is said to be 'the knowledge of insight that comprehends formations.'

Dutiye anariyehi pariyesitabbattā anariyānaṃ pariyesanāti anariyapariyesanā. Sayaṃ lāmakatāya anariyānaṃ pariyesanāti vā anariyapariyesanā. Jarāsabhāvanti jīraṇapakatikaṃ. Tatiyaṃ uttānameva.

In the second sutta, an 'ignoble search' is the search of the ignoble because what is sought is ignoble. Or, an 'ignoble search' is the search of the ignoble due to its own baseness. 'Subject to old age' means having the nature of decay. The third sutta is self-explanatory.

Abhiññāsuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sutta on Direct Knowledges and others is concluded.

4-10. Mālukyaputtasuttādivaṇṇanā

4-10. Commentary on the Mālukyaputta Sutta and others

257-263. Catutthe [M 2.0396] apasādetīti niggaṇhāti. Ussādetīti paggaṇhāti. Apasādanākāraṃ ussādanākārañca vibhāvetuṃ “katha”ntiādi āraddhaṃ. Pañcamādīni uttānāneva. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

257-263. In the fourth sutta, `apasādeti` means to censure. `Ussādeti` means to praise. To clarify the manner of censuring and the manner of praising, the passage beginning with 'how' is introduced. The fifth and following suttas are straightforward. The rest is easily understood.

Mālukyaputtasuttādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mālukyaputta Sutta and others is concluded.

Abhiññāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Direct Knowledges is concluded.

Iti manorathapūraṇiyā aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus in the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya,

Catukkanipātavaṇṇanāya anuttānatthadīpanā samattā.

the explanation of non-obvious meanings in the commentary on the Book of the Fours is complete.

Dutiyo bhāgo niṭṭhito.

The second volume is concluded.
